name: Aarskog syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare genetic condition, also called Aarskog–Scott syndrome, that mainly affects boys and can alter the development of the face, hands, feet, genitals, and skeleton. Short stature and developmental differences may also occur. It is usually caused by a change in the FGD1 gene on the X chromosome. Most girls and women with one altered copy have no symptoms, though some have mild features.

name: abacavir
clinical_significance: An antiretroviral medicine in the nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor class, used with other medicines to treat HIV. The HLA-B*57:01 gene variant greatly increases the risk of a serious hypersensitivity reaction, so testing is done before treatment; people with this variant should not receive abacavir. It must never be restarted after a suspected hypersensitivity reaction.

name: abandoned lead
clinical_significance: A pacemaker or defibrillator lead that remains in the body but is no longer connected to the device. It may be functional or nonfunctional and may be left in place when it is no longer needed or has been replaced. Keeping it avoids the immediate risks of removal, but it can make later device procedures or extraction more complex and may be associated with infection or blocked veins.

name: abarelix
clinical_significance: An injectable medicine that blocks receptors for gonadotropin-releasing hormone, reducing testosterone production. It was used as hormone treatment for selected men with advanced symptomatic prostate cancer when GnRH agonists were unsuitable and they declined surgery. Serious immediate allergic reactions and effects of low testosterone, such as hot flashes, can occur.
subclassification: gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonist; antineoplastic hormonal therapy

name: abatacept
clinical_significance: A biologic medicine that reduces activation of immune cells called T cells by blocking a signal they need for full activation. It is used to treat rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and with other medicines to help prevent acute graft-versus-host disease after certain stem-cell transplants. It can increase the risk of infection.

name: abdomen
clinical_significance: The part of the trunk between the chest and pelvis, extending from the diaphragm to the pelvic brim. It contains most digestive organs, as well as the kidneys, spleen, and major blood vessels.

name: abdominal abscess
clinical_significance: A walled-off pocket of pus within the abdomen, usually caused by infection. It may develop after surgery or as a complication of inflammation or infection, such as appendicitis or diverticulitis. Common features include fever and abdominal pain.

name: abdominal aorta
clinical_significance: The large artery that carries blood through the back of the abdomen. It continues from the chest aorta below the diaphragm and divides into the right and left common iliac arteries, which carry blood toward the pelvis and legs. Its branches also supply abdominal organs, kidneys, and the abdominal wall. An aneurysm, tear, or blockage can interrupt blood flow and be life-threatening.

name: abdominal bruit
clinical_significance: A blowing or whooshing sound heard with a stethoscope over an abdominal blood vessel. It is produced by turbulent blood flow and can occur with a narrowed artery or an aortic aneurysm; its presence alone does not establish a diagnosis.

name: abdominal cavity
clinical_significance: The space inside the abdomen, below the diaphragm and above the pelvic cavity. It contains most digestive organs, including the stomach, intestines, liver, gallbladder, and pancreas, as well as the spleen.

name: abdominal colic
clinical_significance: Cramping abdominal pain that comes in waves, usually as a hollow organ contracts against a blockage. It can arise from the intestines, bile ducts, or urinary tract.

name: abdominal distention
clinical_significance: A visible increase in abdominal size or a feeling of fullness, pressure, or swelling. Common causes include gas and constipation; other causes include slowed or blocked bowel movement, fluid buildup, pregnancy, enlarged organs, or a mass. Sudden swelling with pain, vomiting, fever, or inability to pass stool or gas may signal a serious cause.

name: abdominal fluid
clinical_significance: Fluid in the abdominal cavity. A small amount can be normal, but excess fluid in the space around the abdominal organs is called ascites. Ascites may result from liver, heart, or kidney disease, cancer, infection, inflammation, or bleeding; its significance depends on the amount and cause.

name: abdominal mass
clinical_significance: A lump or localized swelling in the abdomen, felt during an examination or seen on imaging. It may be caused by an enlarged organ, cyst, hernia, pregnancy, or tumor; the cause may be benign or cancerous.

name: abdominal muscle
clinical_significance: Abdominal wall muscles support and move the trunk, stabilize the spine, and compress abdominal contents. Their contraction raises abdominal pressure during coughing, forced expiration, and other expulsive actions.
subclassification: skeletal muscle of the abdominal wall

name: abdominal neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth of tissue in an abdominal organ or structure (a tumor). It may be benign (noncancerous) or malignant (cancerous), and may start in the abdomen or spread there from another site. It can cause no symptoms or symptoms that depend on its location and size.

name: abdominal pain
clinical_significance: Pain or discomfort felt in the abdomen, between the chest and pelvis. It may arise from abdominal organs or the abdominal wall, or be referred from another area. Sudden or severe pain, a rigid or tender abdomen, fainting, persistent vomiting, fever, or blood in the stool can signal a serious condition. In pregnancy, abdominal pain is common, but severe or persistent pain or pain with bleeding needs prompt assessment.

name: abdominal pregnancy
clinical_significance: This rare form of ectopic pregnancy implants in the abdominal cavity rather than the uterus. It carries a high risk of severe internal bleeding and other serious maternal complications; fetal complications are also common.

name: abdominal radiography
clinical_significance: A plain abdominal X-ray can show bowel gas patterns, signs of bowel obstruction or perforation (such as free air), swallowed objects visible on X-ray, and some calcified stones. It may miss important causes of abdominal symptoms, so a normal image does not rule them out.

name: abdominal wall
clinical_significance: The abdominal wall contains and protects abdominal organs, supports the trunk, and helps generate pressure for coughing, forced expiration, and straining. Weakness can permit a hernia, while injury may cause pain or bleeding into the wall. Its layers are important landmarks during abdominal surgery.
subclassification: muscular and fascial abdominal wall structure

name: abdominoperineal resection
clinical_significance: The anus and rectum, often with part of the sigmoid colon, are removed, leaving a permanent colostomy. It is used mainly for low rectal cancer when the anal sphincter cannot be preserved, and sometimes for anal cancer that persists or returns after chemoradiation.

name: abducens nerve
clinical_significance: The sixth cranial nerve, which supplies the lateral rectus muscle that moves the eye outward. Damage can limit outward movement of the affected eye and cause horizontal double vision.

name: abetalipoproteinemia
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which the body makes almost no apolipoprotein B–containing particles, which carry fats and fat-soluble vitamins from the intestine into the blood. This impairs fat absorption and can cause vitamin deficiencies, abnormally shaped red blood cells, and progressive nerve and retinal damage, especially from vitamin E deficiency.

name: abexinostat
clinical_significance: An investigational histone deacetylase inhibitor studied in clinical trials for cancers, including lymphoma. By changing gene regulation in tumor cells, it may slow their growth; its safety and clinical benefit remain under study.
subclassification: histone deacetylase inhibitor; investigational anticancer drug

name: abiotrophia
clinical_significance: A genus of Gram-positive bacteria, including Abiotrophia defectiva, which may require special nutrients to grow in culture. These bacteria can cause bloodstream infection and infective endocarditis, sometimes with serious heart-valve damage.

name: abiotrophia defectiva
clinical_significance: A Gram-positive bacterium found in the oral, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts. It is a rare but important cause of bloodstream infection and infective endocarditis, and may be missed in routine cultures because it requires special growth conditions.

name: abiraterone acetate
clinical_significance: A prodrug that inhibits CYP17, an enzyme needed to produce androgens such as testosterone. Given with prednisone, it is used for metastatic castration-resistant or high-risk metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer; lowering androgen levels can slow tumor growth.

name: ablation
clinical_significance: Ablation destroys or removes targeted tissue or interrupts its function using methods such as heat, cold, electricity, chemicals, or surgery. It is used, for example, to destroy tumors or interrupt abnormal electrical pathways in the heart.

name: ablepharon
clinical_significance: A rare congenital absence or severe underdevelopment of the eyelids, sometimes occurring as part of ablepharon–macrostomia syndrome. Incomplete eyelid coverage exposes the eye surface to drying and injury and can threaten vision; reconstructive surgery may be needed.

name: abnormal
clinical_significance: Different from the usual healthy structure, function, or appearance. An abnormal finding may be harmless or may indicate a disease, depending on its type and context.

name: abnormal color
clinical_significance: A change in the usual color of skin, moist tissues, body fluids, or another structure. Its meaning depends on the color, location, duration, and associated symptoms.

name: abnormal fissure
clinical_significance: An unusually positioned long, narrow groove or cleft that divides tissue into distinct areas. Its clinical significance depends on the affected structure and any associated abnormalities.

name: abnormal virilization
clinical_significance: Excess androgen exposure can cause typically masculinizing features, such as increased facial or body hair, a deeper voice, or clitoral enlargement. Causes include endocrine disorders, hormone-producing tumors, and androgen medicines.

name: abnormality
clinical_significance: A difference from the usual structure, function, development, or test result. An abnormality may be harmless, temporary, or a sign of disease; its importance depends on the finding, symptoms, and clinical evaluation.

name: abomasum
clinical_significance: The fourth, glandular compartment of the stomach in ruminants, where acid and enzymes digest feed and microbes after fermentation in the first three compartments.

name: abrasion
clinical_significance: A superficial injury in which the skin is scraped or rubbed away, usually by friction. In dentistry, abrasion means mechanical wearing away of tooth structure by an external force.

name: abrin
clinical_significance: A highly toxic plant protein found in rosary pea seeds that blocks protein synthesis and kills cells. Ingestion can cause severe gastrointestinal illness and organ failure, while inhalation can cause breathing problems and lung injury. There is no specific antidote; treatment is supportive.

name: abruptio placentae
clinical_significance: Premature separation of the placenta from the uterus before delivery, usually after 20 weeks of pregnancy. It can cause vaginal bleeding, abdominal or back pain, and reduced oxygen to the fetus; severe cases can cause major maternal blood loss.

name: abscess
clinical_significance: A pocket of pus that forms in tissue, an organ, or a body cavity, usually because of an infection. It may cause pain, swelling, warmth, or fever. Depending on its site and cause, treatment may include drainage, antibiotics, or both.

name: absence epilepsy
clinical_significance: A generalized epilepsy with brief seizures that cause a sudden pause in activity and impaired awareness, often with staring or small repetitive movements. Awareness usually returns quickly without confusion; the seizures may occur many times a day.

name: absence seizure
clinical_significance: A brief seizure causing sudden staring and reduced awareness, usually lasting only seconds with rapid recovery. The person may stop speaking or responding and may make small repetitive movements; an EEG helps confirm the diagnosis.

name: absent reflex
clinical_significance: Failure of an expected reflex to occur after appropriate stimulation, such as a tendon tap. It can indicate disruption of the reflex pathway, commonly from peripheral nerve disease, but an absent reflex may occur normally and must be interpreted with other examination findings.

name: absenteeism
clinical_significance: Chronic absence from work or other duties. As a health or public-health measure, work absences can reflect illness or injury, but absenteeism can also have nonmedical causes.

name: absidia
clinical_significance: A genus of environmental filamentous fungi in the order Mucorales. Older literature uses the name Absidia corymbifera for Lichtheimia corymbifera, an occasional cause of invasive mucormycosis.

name: abstract idea
clinical_significance: A general information-classification concept with no direct clinical significance.

name: abulia
clinical_significance: Marked reduction in motivation, initiative, and spontaneous activity, usually caused by dysfunction of frontal-subcortical brain circuits or related neurologic disease.

name: abutment
clinical_significance: A natural tooth, dental implant, or component that supports a dental prosthesis. Abutments may hold a bridge, denture, or implant crown in position and transfer chewing forces to the supporting tooth, implant, or bone.

name: acalculous cholecystitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the gallbladder without gallstones. It usually occurs suddenly in people who are critically ill, injured, recovering from surgery, unable to eat, or in shock. Reduced bile flow and poor blood supply can contribute, and severe cases may cause tissue death or a hole in the gallbladder. Fever and pain in the upper-right abdomen may occur; ultrasound is commonly used for evaluation.

name: acamprosate
clinical_significance: A medicine used with psychosocial support to help maintain abstinence from alcohol after withdrawal, once a person has stopped drinking. It does not treat acute alcohol withdrawal.

name: acanthamoeba
clinical_significance: A free-living amoeba found in soil and water that can cause corneal infection, skin or sinus infection, or rarely granulomatous amoebic encephalitis. Contact-lens exposure to contaminated water increases keratitis risk, while invasive disease is more likely with impaired immunity.

name: acanthamoeba astronyxis
clinical_significance: A free-living amoeba species (genotype T7) rarely associated with human infection, including keratitis and granulomatous amoebic encephalitis. Its clinical importance appears lower than that of more commonly implicated Acanthamoeba species.

name: acanthamoeba castellanii
clinical_significance: A free-living amoeba found in soil and water. It can infect people, especially through contaminated contact-lens water or damaged tissue, and may cause a serious corneal infection called amoebic keratitis or a rare brain infection called granulomatous amoebic encephalitis.

name: acanthamoeba culbertsoni
clinical_significance: A free-living amoeba species that can cause granulomatous amoebic encephalitis and amoebic keratitis. Encephalitis is rare and usually affects people with weakened immune systems; keratitis can occur in contact-lens wearers or after corneal injury.

name: acanthamoeba griffini
clinical_significance: A free-living amoeba species linked to human Acanthamoeba keratitis, a corneal infection. Acanthamoeba species can also cause rare granulomatous amoebic encephalitis, usually in people with impaired immunity.

name: acanthamoeba hatchetti
clinical_significance: A free-living amoeba species implicated in human Acanthamoeba keratitis, a corneal infection often associated with contact-lens exposure. Acanthamoeba species can also cause rare brain and disseminated infections, usually in people with impaired immunity; A. hatchetti has also been reported in equine placentitis.

name: acanthamoeba keratitis
clinical_significance: A rare, potentially sight-threatening corneal infection caused by Acanthamoeba. It is most often linked to contact-lens use with contaminated water or poor lens hygiene, but can also follow corneal injury; severe infection may cause scarring and permanent vision loss.

name: acanthamoeba lugdunensis
clinical_significance: A free-living amoeba species associated with Acanthamoeba keratitis, a sight-threatening corneal infection. It belongs to genotype T4, the genotype most often identified in human Acanthamoeba infections; the genus can also cause rare brain and disseminated infections.

name: acanthamoeba palestinensis
clinical_significance: A free-living amoeba species of genotype T2 that has been associated with rare granulomatous amoebic encephalitis. Invasive Acanthamoeba infections mainly affect people with impaired immunity; the genus also causes corneal infection, especially in contact-lens wearers.

name: acanthamoeba polyphaga
clinical_significance: A free-living amoeba species that can cause Acanthamoeba keratitis, a sight-threatening corneal infection, and has also been associated with granulomatous amoebic encephalitis. Keratitis is often linked to contact-lens use; invasive infection is rare.

name: acanthamoeba quina
clinical_significance: A free-living amoeba species associated with Acanthamoeba keratitis, a sight-threatening corneal infection; it belongs to genotype T4, which is common in human infections. Acanthamoeba species can also cause rare granulomatous amoebic encephalitis, usually in people with impaired immunity.

name: acanthamoeba rhysodes
clinical_significance: A free-living amoeba species associated with Acanthamoeba keratitis, a sight-threatening corneal infection; it belongs to genotype T4, which is common in human infections. Acanthamoeba species can also cause rare granulomatous amoebic encephalitis, usually in people with impaired immunity.

name: acanthocephala
clinical_significance: A phylum of parasitic thorny-headed worms, also called acanthocephalans. Human infection is uncommon and may occur through ingestion of infected intermediate hosts, potentially causing intestinal disease.

name: acanthocyte
clinical_significance: An abnormal red blood cell with a few irregular, unevenly spaced projections of different sizes, visible on a blood smear. Acanthocytes occur in advanced liver disease (spur-cell anemia), abetalipoproteinemia, neuroacanthocytosis, and other disorders affecting red-cell membrane lipids.

name: acantholysis
clinical_significance: Loss of adhesion between keratinocytes, the main cells of the epidermis (outer skin layer). The cells separate, sometimes forming blisters or surface erosions. Acantholysis is a microscopic finding seen in disorders such as pemphigus and some inherited or infectious skin diseases; it is not a disease by itself.

name: acanthoma
clinical_significance: A usually benign skin growth made of thickened squamous epidermal cells. Its appearance can resemble other lesions, so a changing or uncertain lesion may need examination or biopsy.

name: acanthosis nigricans
clinical_significance: Dark, thickened, velvety skin, usually in folds such as the neck, armpits, or groin. It is often associated with insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, hormonal disorders, or medicines; rarely, sudden extensive disease can signal an underlying cancer. Treating the cause may improve the skin changes.

name: acarbose
clinical_significance: An oral medicine used with meals to improve blood-glucose control in type 2 diabetes. It slows the digestion of carbohydrates in the intestine, reducing the rise in blood glucose after meals.

name: acatalasia
clinical_significance: A rare inherited deficiency of catalase, an enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide. Many people have no symptoms, but some develop mouth ulcers and tissue damage (Takahara disease); good oral health may reduce these complications.

name: accelerated growth
clinical_significance: An increase in a child's growth velocity above the expected rate for age and developmental stage, determined from serial height or length measurements. It may occur during normal puberty or catch-up growth; abnormal acceleration, especially with early pubertal signs or advanced bone age, may suggest precocious puberty or another endocrine disorder.

name: accelerometry
clinical_significance: Measurement of movement or acceleration using a sensor. It can assess physical activity, walking, tremor, falls, sleep, or rehabilitation progress, depending on the device and the recording method.

name: accessory nerve
clinical_significance: The eleventh cranial nerve (CN XI), a primarily motor nerve whose spinal component supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. It enables head rotation and shoulder elevation; injury may cause weak head rotation, impaired shoulder shrug, and shoulder droop.

name: accident
clinical_significance: An unintentional event that causes injury or other harm. In clinical and public-health settings, the resulting injury is usually described by its cause and intent, such as an unintentional fall or burn.

name: accident proneness
clinical_significance: A historical term for a supposed tendency to experience repeated accidents. A stable personality trait causing accidents is not an established clinical diagnosis; repeated injuries are better assessed in relation to a person’s health, behavior, surroundings, and exposure to hazards.

name: accidental death
clinical_significance: Death caused by an unintentional injury or event rather than disease, suicide, or homicide. The cause is determined through medical, scene, and sometimes legal investigation.

name: accidental fall
clinical_significance: An unintentional movement to the ground or a lower level. Falls can cause bruises, fractures, head injury, or internal bleeding, especially in older adults; loss of consciousness, severe pain, or confusion requires urgent care.

name: acclimatization
clinical_significance: Physiological adjustment to a new environment, such as high altitude or heat. Gradual acclimatization can improve tolerance and reduce the risk of altitude illness or heat-related illness.

name: accreditation
clinical_significance: Formal recognition that a healthcare organization, laboratory, or training program meets defined quality and safety standards. Accreditation can support quality improvement, though it does not guarantee that every aspect of care is error-free.

name: ACE inhibitor
clinical_significance: A group of medicines that lower blood pressure by reducing formation of angiotensin II. They are used for hypertension and other cardiovascular or kidney conditions; kidney function and blood potassium are monitored because treatment can raise potassium or affect kidney function.

name: acebutolol
clinical_significance: Acebutolol is a beta-adrenergic blocker with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity used in some settings for hypertension and cardiac rhythm disorders; it can slow heart rate and conduction.

name: acenocoumarol
clinical_significance: An oral vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant used to prevent or treat blood clots. It reduces production of several clotting factors, so the dose is adjusted using blood clotting tests (INR); excessive anticoagulation can cause serious bleeding.

name: acephalostomia
clinical_significance: An extremely rare and severe birth defect involving absence or major failure of development of the head and mouth. It is usually incompatible with survival and is identified during prenatal or newborn examination.

name: acepromazine
clinical_significance: A phenothiazine sedative used mainly in veterinary medicine, for example to calm animals before procedures. It can lower blood pressure and cause prolonged sedation; it is not a routine human medicine.

name: acetaldehyde
clinical_significance: A chemical produced when the body metabolizes alcohol. Accumulation may contribute to flushing, nausea, and vomiting.

name: acetaminophen
clinical_significance: A widely used medication that relieves mild-to-moderate pain and reduces fever, but lacks significant anti-inflammatory effects. While safe at recommended therapeutic doses, excessive amounts can cause severe, life-threatening liver injury, especially when taken with alcohol or other products containing acetaminophen.

name: acetate
clinical_significance: A form of acetic acid and a small molecule used by cells in energy and building processes. The body can convert acetate into acetyl-CoA, which helps make or break down fats and other substances.

name: acetazolamide
clinical_significance: A medicine that changes salt and fluid handling in the kidneys. It is used for glaucoma, prevention or treatment of altitude illness, and selected fluid, metabolic, or neurologic conditions.

name: acetic acid
clinical_significance: A weak acid found in vinegar and used in some topical preparations. Dilute acetic acid ear drops may be used for selected cases of outer-ear infection, but suitability depends on the ear condition and eardrum status.

name: acetoacetate
clinical_significance: A ketone body made by the liver during fasting or increased fat breakdown and used as fuel by tissues. Elevated acetoacetate can occur in ketosis and ketoacidosis; it is also measured in urine ketone tests, which do not measure beta-hydroxybutyrate.

name: acetobacteraceae
clinical_significance: A family of bacteria that includes acetic acid bacteria, which convert alcohol to acetic acid and are used in vinegar production. Members are not common causes of human infection.

name: acetohexamide
clinical_significance: An older sulfonylurea medicine for type 2 diabetes that stimulates insulin release from the pancreas. It can cause low blood sugar and weight gain; newer diabetes medicines are more commonly used in many settings.

name: acetone
clinical_significance: A volatile ketone body produced during increased fat metabolism. It may contribute to the characteristic breath odor of ketosis and ketoacidosis.

name: acetylation
clinical_significance: A chemical change that adds a small acetyl group to a protein, medicine, or DNA-related molecule. This can alter how the molecule works, how long it lasts, how it is moved, or how strongly a gene is active.

name: acetylcarnitine
clinical_significance: A form of carnitine involved in cellular energy metabolism and the transfer of acetyl groups. Acetyl-L-carnitine supplements have been studied for neurologic and other conditions, but their benefits vary by condition and they are not established treatment for most disorders.

name: acetylcholine
clinical_significance: A major neurotransmitter synthesized from choline and acetyl-CoA by choline acetyltransferase. Operating throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems, it mediates neuromuscular transmission at motor endplates, autonomic ganglionic neurotransmission, parasympathetic postganglionic signaling, and central cognitive/memory processing.

name: acetylcysteine
clinical_significance: A medicine that loosens thick mucus so it is easier to clear. It is also the main antidote for acetaminophen overdose because it restores glutathione, a substance the liver uses to neutralize the overdose’s toxic breakdown product.

name: acetylgalactosamine
clinical_significance: N-acetylgalactosamine is a sugar used to build cell-surface and secreted glycans. It forms part of the A blood-group antigen and is common in O-linked protein sugars, so changes in its attachment can affect blood-group recognition and other cell interactions.

name: acetylglucosamine
clinical_significance: N-acetylglucosamine is a sugar building block in many human glycans and in the precursor structure for ABO blood-group antigens. It also occurs in bacterial cell walls, which can make it a target in antimicrobial research.

name: Achilles tendon
clinical_significance: The Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel and helps push the foot down during walking, running, and jumping. Tendinopathy can cause pain and stiffness; a tear or rupture can impair walking and standing on tiptoe.

name: achlorhydria
clinical_significance: A condition in which the stomach produces no hydrochloric acid; reduced but not absent acid is called hypochlorhydria. It can occur with autoimmune gastritis or loss of acid-producing stomach cells and may impair absorption of iron or vitamin B12. Acid-suppressing medicines usually reduce acid rather than cause complete achlorhydria.

name: achondrogenesis
clinical_significance: A group of severe inherited disorders in which cartilage and bone development is profoundly impaired. Affected fetuses have very short limbs and poorly formed bones, and most cases are fatal before or shortly after birth.

name: achondroplasia
clinical_significance: An autosomal dominant bone-growth disorder caused by a disease-causing change in the \textit{FGFR3} gene. It causes short arms and legs, short stature, a larger head, and a prominent forehead. One altered gene copy usually causes the condition; two copies cause a severe, often fatal form.

name: achromatopsia
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder causing absent or greatly reduced color vision, often with light sensitivity and poor visual acuity.

name: achromobacter
clinical_significance: A genus of environmental Gram-negative bacteria that can act as opportunistic pathogens, particularly in people with cystic fibrosis or weakened immunity. Achromobacter may cause respiratory, bloodstream, or other healthcare-associated infections, and accurate species identification can be difficult.

name: achromobacter piechaudii
clinical_significance: A soil- and water-associated Achromobacter species that only rarely causes human infection. Reported infections include ear infection and bloodstream infection, sometimes in people with serious underlying illness or an intravascular catheter.

name: achromobacter ruhlandii
clinical_significance: An Achromobacter species found in the environment and reported in respiratory samples from people with cystic fibrosis. Achromobacter infections can be difficult to identify to species and may matter in chronic airway infection, though the clinical impact of individual species is not fully established.

name: acid
clinical_significance: A substance that increases acidity by releasing hydrogen ions or accepting electrons. Strong acids can damage tissue, while acids also take part in normal digestion, metabolism, and body-fluid regulation.

name: acid phosphatase
clinical_significance: An enzyme found in several tissues. Prostatic acid phosphatase was once used as a blood marker for advanced prostate cancer, but prostate-specific antigen largely replaced it; acid phosphatase measurement is not a routine general screening test.

name: acid reflux
clinical_significance: Backward flow of acidic stomach contents into the esophagus, causing heartburn, sour regurgitation, cough, or throat irritation. Frequent reflux may be gastroesophageal reflux disease and can injure the esophagus.

name: acidaminococcus
clinical_significance: A genus of anaerobic bacteria found in the intestinal tract of humans and other animals. Its presence in gut-microbiome studies does not by itself indicate infection or establish a cause of disease.

name: acidaminococcus intestini
clinical_significance: An anaerobic intestinal bacterium first characterized from human clinical samples. It can be found in the gut microbiome; detecting it does not by itself show that it is causing infection, and reported disease associations do not establish causation.

name: acidosis
clinical_significance: A process that raises acid or removes base in the body, tending to lower blood pH. Acidemia means the measured blood pH is actually low; compensation or mixed disorders can affect the final pH. Causes include breathing problems, kidney disease, severe infection, diabetes, and poisoning.

name: acidovorax
clinical_significance: A genus of mostly environmental Gram-negative bacteria, many associated with plants or water. Human infections are rare; related organisms have occasionally caused opportunistic infections, so clinical isolates may require careful identification.

name: acidovorax delafieldii
clinical_significance: An environmental Acidovorax species that is rarely reported in human clinical specimens. Its clinical significance is uncertain, and identification alone does not establish that it caused disease.

name: acidovorax facilis
clinical_significance: An environmental Acidovorax species with no established common role in human disease. If recovered from a clinical sample, its significance depends on the specimen, symptoms, and whether it is repeatedly isolated.

name: acidovorax temperans
clinical_significance: An environmental Acidovorax species not established as a common human pathogen. Recovery from a clinical specimen should be interpreted with the patient's symptoms and other microbiology findings.

name: acinar cell
clinical_significance: A cell in a small cluster that makes and releases a fluid or substance. In the pancreas, acinar cells release digestive enzymes into small ducts.

name: acinetobacter
clinical_significance: Acinetobacter are environmental Gram-negative bacteria that can cause healthcare-associated pneumonia, bloodstream, urinary-tract, and wound infections, especially in seriously ill patients. Some strains resist many antibiotics; colonization does not always mean infection.

name: acinetobacter calcoaceticus
clinical_significance: Acinetobacter calcoaceticus is an environmental species included in the A. calcoaceticus–A. baumannii complex, whose members can cause healthcare-associated infections. Because species in this complex can be hard to distinguish, a laboratory result may not identify A. calcoaceticus specifically.

name: acinetobacter johnsonii
clinical_significance: Acinetobacter johnsonii commonly occurs on human skin and can occasionally cause opportunistic healthcare-associated infection, including bloodstream infection, particularly in people with serious illness or invasive devices.

name: acinetobacter junii
clinical_significance: Acinetobacter junii is an uncommon opportunistic pathogen reported in healthcare-associated bloodstream, eye, and other infections, including occasional outbreaks in newborn units. A positive culture must be interpreted in context because Acinetobacter can also colonize people or contaminate specimens.

name: acinetobacter lwoffii
clinical_significance: Acinetobacter lwoffii commonly lives on human skin but can rarely cause opportunistic infection, including bloodstream infection, pneumonia, or meningitis, especially in hospitalized or immunocompromised people.

name: acinetobacter parvus
clinical_significance: Acinetobacter parvus is an uncommon species recovered from human blood and other clinical specimens. It has been associated with opportunistic healthcare-related infection, but its role should be judged from the specimen and the patient's clinical findings.

name: acinetobacter ursingii
clinical_significance: Acinetobacter ursingii is a rare opportunistic cause of healthcare-associated infection, especially bloodstream infection linked to intravascular catheters in people with serious underlying illness. Accurate identification can be difficult.

name: acitretin
clinical_significance: An oral retinoid used for severe psoriasis. It can cause serious fetal harm: people who can become pregnant must avoid pregnancy during treatment and for at least 3 years after stopping it. Treatment also requires monitoring for other adverse effects, including changes in blood lipids and liver tests.

name: acivicin
clinical_significance: An experimental anticancer compound that inhibits enzymes involved in making DNA building blocks. It has been studied in cancer research, but it is not an established routine cancer treatment.

name: aclarubicin
clinical_significance: An anthracycline anticancer medicine used in some countries to treat leukemia. Like other anthracyclines, it can suppress bone marrow and requires specialist monitoring during chemotherapy.

name: acne
clinical_significance: A common inflammatory disorder of hair follicles and oil glands. Blocked follicles form blackheads or whiteheads, while inflammation can cause papules, pustules, nodules, scarring, and dark marks, especially on the face, chest, and back.

name: acne keloid
clinical_significance: A chronic inflammatory disorder of hair follicles at the back of the scalp or neck, often called acne keloidalis nuchae. It can cause firm bumps, scarring, and permanent hair loss; friction and close shaving may aggravate it.

name: acne vulgaris
clinical_significance: A common disorder of hair follicles involving follicular plugging, increased oil production, and inflammation in which Cutibacterium acnes may contribute. It causes blackheads or whiteheads and may also cause inflamed papules, pustules, or deep nodules on the face, chest, back, and upper arms; deeper disease can scar.

name: acolbifene hydrochloride
clinical_significance: An investigational selective estrogen-receptor modulator studied for possible breast-cancer prevention and treatment. Its clinical benefit and safety have not been established for routine use.

name: aconitate hydratase
clinical_significance: An enzyme in the citric acid cycle that converts citrate to isocitrate. Inherited defects in mitochondrial aconitase (ACO2) can cause a rare neurologic disorder with features such as poor muscle tone, unsteady movement, seizures, and vision loss.

name: acoustic nerve
clinical_significance: The acoustic nerve, properly called the vestibulocochlear nerve, carries signals for hearing and balance from the inner ear to the brain. It is the eighth cranial nerve.

name: acoustic neuroma
clinical_significance: A benign, slow-growing neoplasm arising from Schwann cells of the vestibular division of the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII) within the internal auditory canal or cerebellopontine angle. It classically presents with insidious, progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, asymmetric high-pitched tinnitus, and dysequilibrium.

name: acoustic trauma
clinical_significance: Inner-ear injury from a very loud sound, such as an explosion or gunshot. It can cause sudden hearing loss, ringing in the ears, or dizziness; damage to the sensory cells may be permanent.

name: acquired feminization
clinical_significance: Development of breast tissue or other feminizing changes in a male due to hormonal or medication-related causes. Possible causes include reduced androgen action, liver disease, or a hormone-producing tumor; assessment depends on the pattern, timing, and associated symptoms.

name: acquisition duration
clinical_significance: The time required to collect a measurement, image, or body signal. Longer acquisition may improve detail or accuracy but can increase motion problems, discomfort, radiation exposure, or equipment time.

name: acremonium
clinical_significance: A genus of environmental molds that only occasionally cause human infection. Reported infections include nail, eye, skin, and deeper tissue disease; disseminated infection is most concerning in people with severely weakened immunity, and a culture may sometimes represent contamination.

name: acridine
clinical_significance: A chemical ring structure found in several compounds. Some acridine derivatives bind to DNA and have been studied or used as dyes, antimicrobial agents, or anticancer drugs, but their effects and clinical uses differ by compound.

name: acridine orange
clinical_significance: A fluorescent dye that binds to DNA and RNA and helps visualize cells or microorganisms in laboratory samples. It is used in microscopy and some specialized specimen-screening methods, not as a treatment.

name: acridines
clinical_significance: A family of compounds built around an acridine ring. Some derivatives have been used as dyes or studied for antimicrobial and anticancer effects; clinical use and toxicity depend on the specific compound.

name: Acrocallosal syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare congenital genetic syndrome involving abnormal development of the corpus callosum, extra fingers or toes, and distinctive facial features. Developmental delay or intellectual disability is common; some affected people also have seizures or other brain abnormalities.

name: acrocephalosyndactylia
clinical_significance: rocephalosyndactylia: (acrocephalosyndactyly) A genetic disorder characterized by craniosynostosis and fusion of the fingers and toes. NCI U.S. National Cancer Institute, 2021 (acrocephalosyndactyly) A rare group of inherited congenital malformation disorders characterized by craniosynostosis and fusion or webbing of the fingers or toes, often with other associated manifestations. OrphaNet INSERM, 2021 Congenital craniostenosis with syndactyly. NLM Medical Subject Headings U.S. National Library of Medicine, 2025

name: acrocyanosis
clinical_significance: Persistent bluish or purplish discoloration and coolness of the hands, feet, nose, or ears, usually without pain, caused by narrowing of small skin blood vessels. It is often worse in cold conditions and may be primary or due to another disorder.

name: acrodermatitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation affecting skin on the hands, feet, or other body extremities. Causes vary and include infections, nutritional deficiency, inherited disorders, medicines, and immune reactions; appearance and treatment depend on cause.

name: acrolein
clinical_significance: A highly irritating chemical found in smoke and produced during combustion. Inhalation can irritate the eyes and airways; acrolein is also a toxic breakdown product of cyclophosphamide and can injure the bladder lining.

name: acromegaly
clinical_significance: A disorder caused by excess growth hormone after height growth has ended, usually from a noncancerous pituitary adenoma. It enlarges the hands, feet, jaw, and soft tissues and may cause headaches, joint problems, diabetes, or vision changes.

name: acromion
clinical_significance: A bony projection from the shoulder blade that forms the highest point of the shoulder. It joins the collarbone and forms a roof over the shoulder joint, with a tendon and lubricating sac passing beneath it.

name: acronine
clinical_significance: A plant-derived alkaloid studied for anticancer activity in laboratory and early research. It is not an established cancer treatment in routine clinical care.

name: acro-osteolysis
clinical_significance: Resorption or destruction of the terminal bones of the fingers or toes. It can occur with inherited disorders, autoimmune disease, severe vascular disease, trauma, or repeated occupational exposure and may cause shortened, painful, or deformed digits.

name: acrosin
clinical_significance: An enzyme released from the cap-like structure at a sperm’s tip. It helps sperm pass through the egg’s surrounding layers during fertilization, although successful fertilization requires many additional steps.

name: acrosome
clinical_significance: A cap-like structure on the head of a sperm cell containing enzymes that help it attach to and enter the egg during fertilization.

name: acrosome reaction
clinical_significance: The release of enzymes from the cap at the front of a sperm cell after it contacts an egg. These enzymes help the sperm pass through the egg’s outer coating; other steps are also needed for fertilization.

name: acrylamide
clinical_significance: A chemical used to make polymers that can injure peripheral nerves after substantial occupational exposure. Acrylamide also forms in some starchy foods cooked at high temperatures; its potential cancer risk is under study, and food exposure is not equivalent to high-dose workplace exposure.

name: acrylonitrile
clinical_significance: An industrial chemical used to make plastics and synthetic fibers. High exposure can irritate the eyes and airways and affect the nervous system; long-term occupational exposure is associated with cancer risk.

name: actigraphy
clinical_significance: Recording movement over days or weeks with a small wearable sensor, usually worn on the wrist. The pattern of movement helps estimate when a person is asleep or awake and how active they are, but it does not measure sleep directly and cannot by itself diagnose every sleep problem.

name: actin
clinical_significance: A protein that helps cells keep their shape and move. In muscle, actin works with myosin to produce contraction; in other cells, it supports movement, internal transport, and changes in cell structure.

name: actin myofilament
clinical_significance: A thin muscle fiber made mainly of actin that interacts with myosin, allowing muscle cells to shorten and produce force during contraction and movement.

name: actin-binding protein
clinical_significance: A protein that attaches to actin filaments and helps build, organize, move, or anchor the cell's internal framework. Examples include myosin, gelsolin, and alpha-actinin.

name: acting out
clinical_significance: Expressing emotional conflict or distress through behavior rather than words.

name: actinic keratosis
clinical_significance: A rough, scaly, sandpaper-like lesion caused by cumulative ultraviolet damage, usually on sun-exposed skin such as the face, scalp, ears, neck, forearms, or hands. It is a keratinocytic precancer and may progress to cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma, so changing, thick, tender, or bleeding lesions need assessment and treatment.

name: actinium
clinical_significance: Actinium is a radioactive element with no routine use as the element itself. The isotope actinium-225 is being studied in targeted alpha-radiation treatments for cancers, including prostate cancer.

name: actinobacillus
clinical_significance: A genus of Gram-negative bacteria that includes animal pathogens and occasional human opportunistic pathogens. Some species cause actinobacillosis in livestock; Actinobacillus ureae and related species can rarely cause respiratory or invasive infections in people.

name: actinobacillus equuli
clinical_significance: A bacterium carried by horses and pigs that can cause serious infection in foals and other animals. Human infection is rare but has been reported, usually after animal exposure or injury.

name: actinobacillus suis
clinical_significance: A bacterial pathogen mainly affecting pigs, in which it can cause septicemia, reproductive disease, and lesions in multiple organs. It is an uncommon cause of disease in other animals and people.

name: actinobacillus ureae
clinical_significance: A bacterium found in the human upper respiratory tract that can occasionally cause opportunistic infection, including meningitis, pneumonia, or bloodstream infection. Its role depends on whether it is recovered from a normally sterile site and fits the clinical picture.

name: actinomadura
clinical_significance: A genus of soil-associated bacteria that includes major causes of actinomycetoma, a chronic infection usually entering through the skin after injury. The infection can produce swelling, nodules, draining sinus tracts, and tissue damage.

name: actinomadura madurae
clinical_significance: A soil-associated bacterium and an important cause of actinomycetoma, a chronic infection of skin and underlying tissue that can extend into bone. It often causes swelling with draining sinus tracts and visible grains in the discharge.

name: actinomadura pelletieri
clinical_significance: A soil-associated bacterium that causes actinomycetoma, a chronic skin and soft-tissue infection that may extend to bone. It is associated with red grains in draining lesions and occurs mainly in tropical and subtropical regions.

name: actinomyces
clinical_significance: A genus of bacteria that normally live in the mouth, digestive tract, and genital tract. If they enter deeper tissue through a break in a mucosal surface, they can rarely cause chronic actinomycosis, with abscesses and sinus tracts that may cross tissue planes.

name: actinomyces bovis
clinical_significance: A bacterium that causes lumpy jaw in cattle, a chronic infection with inflammation and abnormal bone growth in the jaw, often after injury to the mouth. It is primarily a veterinary pathogen.

name: actinomyces europaeus
clinical_significance: An Actinomyces species that can act as an opportunistic pathogen, particularly in skin and soft-tissue or genitourinary infections. Because Actinomyces may also be normal flora or appear in mixed cultures, a positive result needs clinical interpretation.

name: actinomyces meyerii
clinical_significance: An uncommon Actinomyces species that can cause pulmonary actinomycosis and has a tendency to spread through the bloodstream to sites such as bone and skin. Infection is rare but can be serious without prolonged treatment.

name: actinomyces naeslundii
clinical_significance: A common inhabitant of the mouth that contributes to dental plaque. It has been associated with tooth decay and gum disease as part of the broader oral bacterial community, rather than acting as a sole cause.

name: actinomyces neuii
clinical_significance: An uncommon Actinomyces species that can cause abscesses, infected skin structures, eye infections, urinary infections, and occasionally bloodstream infection or endocarditis. It usually causes localized disease and may be mistaken for a harmless skin bacterium.

name: actinomyces odontolyticus
clinical_significance: A bacterium normally found in the mouth that can rarely cause invasive infection, including lung or soft-tissue infection and bloodstream infection, particularly when tissue barriers are disrupted or the person is medically vulnerable.

name: actinomyces viscosus
clinical_significance: An Actinomyces species found in the mouth and dental plaque. It may contribute to tooth decay or gum disease as part of a mixed oral bacterial community and can rarely cause invasive infection.

name: actinomycetaceae
clinical_significance: A bacterial family that includes Actinomyces, organisms normally found in the mouth, digestive tract, or genital tract. Some members can cause actinomycosis or other opportunistic infections when they enter deeper tissues.

name: actinomycetales
clinical_significance: A traditional taxonomic order of bacteria that includes medically important groups such as Actinomyces and Nocardia. Species in the order range from harmless environmental or normal-flora organisms to causes of serious infection.

name: actinomycetales infection
clinical_significance: An infection caused by a bacterium classified in the order Actinomycetales. The clinical picture depends on the organism; examples include chronic actinomycosis and nocardiosis, which require different diagnosis and treatment.

name: actinomycin
clinical_significance: Actinomycin D, also called dactinomycin, is an anticancer medicine used with other chemotherapy drugs for cancers such as Wilms tumor, rhabdomyosarcoma, and Ewing sarcoma. It can severely suppress bone marrow and damage tissue if it leaks outside a vein.

name: actinomycosis
clinical_significance: A chronic infection caused by Actinomyces bacteria that normally live in the mouth, digestive tract, and genital tract. After a break in a mucosal surface, it can form firm masses and abscesses that cross tissue planes and drain through sinus tracts, often containing yellow sulfur granules. It most often affects the face and neck, chest, or abdomen and pelvis.

name: actinotignum schaalii
clinical_significance: A bacterium that normally inhabits the urinary tract and can cause urinary infections, especially in older adults and people with urinary-tract abnormalities. It grows slowly and may be missed by routine urine culture; it can occasionally cause bloodstream or other invasive infection.

name: action potential
clinical_significance: A brief electrical signal that travels along a nerve or muscle cell. It begins when the cell’s electrical charge changes enough to trigger the signal and allows nerves to communicate and muscles to contract.

name: activated lymphocyte
clinical_significance: A lymphocyte that has received signals to respond to an antigen or other immune stimulus. Activated lymphocytes multiply and carry out immune functions; their activation markers are measured in immune testing and research.

name: activation action
clinical_significance: A general term for a process that initiates or increases a biological response. Its clinical meaning depends on what is being activated, such as an immune cell, receptor, or signaling pathway.

name: activation analysis
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that identifies and measures elements in a sample by detecting characteristic radiation emitted after neutron exposure. It is used mainly in research and specialized materials analysis, rather than routine patient testing.

name: active control
clinical_significance: A comparison treatment used in a clinical trial that is already known to have an effect, such as standard therapy. It helps researchers assess whether a new treatment works as well as or better than current care.

name: active ingredient
clinical_significance: The component of a medicine or product responsible for its intended effect. Its identity and amount determine the main therapeutic action, while other ingredients may help with delivery, stability, or formulation.

name: activin
clinical_significance: A signaling protein in the transforming growth factor beta family that helps regulate reproductive hormones, cell growth, and tissue development. It is important in research and some laboratory investigations, but activin itself is not a routine medicine.

name: acupressure
clinical_significance: A complementary treatment in which firm pressure is applied to selected points on the body, often with the fingers. It may provide short-term relief of symptoms such as nausea or pain, but evidence of benefit varies by condition.

name: acupuncture point
clinical_significance: A location on the body used as a target in acupuncture or acupressure. Point maps guide these practices, but a point is not generally a distinct anatomical structure identifiable in every person.

name: acustimulation therapy
clinical_significance: A noninvasive technique that applies electrical stimulation through the skin at sites selected as acupuncture points. It has been studied for pain and nausea, but evidence and benefit vary by condition.

name: acute
clinical_significance: Describing symptoms or a condition that begins or worsens quickly and usually lasts a limited time. It is commonly contrasted with chronic, which develops or continues over a longer period.

name: acute bronchitis
clinical_significance: Short-term inflammation of the large airways in the lungs, usually caused by a virus such as a cold or flu. It causes a cough that may bring up clear, yellow, or green mucus and may cause chest soreness, mild fever, tiredness, or wheezing. The cough often lasts 1 to 3 weeks. Because viruses cause more than 90% of cases, antibiotics usually do not help; care focuses on rest, fluids, and symptom relief.

name: acute cholecystitis
clinical_significance: Acute inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by a gallstone blocking the cystic duct. It typically causes persistent pain in the upper right abdomen, often with nausea, vomiting, or fever, and needs prompt medical assessment because complications can include infection, tissue death, or perforation. Treatment often includes gallbladder removal.

name: acute disease
clinical_significance: An illness that begins suddenly or develops over a short period. It often lasts a limited time, although it can be mild, severe, or life-threatening and may sometimes lead to a longer-term condition.

name: acute hepatitis
clinical_significance: Sudden inflammation and injury of the liver, developing over days to months. It may cause tiredness, nausea, pain under the right ribs, dark urine, jaundice, or no symptoms. Causes include viruses, alcohol, medicines, toxins, and autoimmune disease.

name: acute kidney failure
clinical_significance: A rapid loss of kidney function, now usually called acute kidney injury. It develops over hours or days and can cause waste products, fluid, acids, or electrolytes to build up; urgent assessment is needed to identify and treat the cause.

name: acute leukemia
clinical_significance: A fast-growing blood cancer in which immature abnormal blood cells crowd the bone marrow and interfere with normal blood-cell production. It can cause anemia, infections, and bleeding and needs urgent treatment.

name: acute lymphocytic leukemia
clinical_significance: A fast-growing cancer of immature lymphoid cells in the bone marrow and blood, usually called acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). It can cause anemia, infections, and bleeding and requires prompt treatment; outcomes vary with age, disease features, and response to therapy.

name: acute onset pain
clinical_significance: Pain that begins suddenly, often over seconds, minutes, or hours.

name: acute pancreatitis
clinical_significance: Sudden inflammation of the pancreas, most often caused by gallstones or alcohol. It usually causes severe upper-abdominal pain that may reach the back, with nausea or vomiting; complications can include fluid loss, infection, organ failure, or pancreatic collections.

name: acute promyelocytic leukemia
clinical_significance: A subtype of acute myeloid leukemia that can quickly cause severe bleeding or abnormal clotting. It is linked to a specific chromosome change and needs immediate specialist treatment.

name: acute sinusitis
clinical_significance: Short-term inflammation of the nasal passages and sinuses, usually caused by a virus after a cold. It can cause a blocked or runny nose, facial pressure or pain, and reduced smell. Most cases improve without antibiotics; persistent symptoms, severe fever with facial pain, or worsening after initial improvement may suggest bacterial infection or a complication.

name: acyclovir
clinical_significance: An antiviral drug that inhibits herpesvirus DNA polymerase and is used for infections caused by herpes simplex virus and varicella-zoster virus.

name: acylation
clinical_significance: A biochemical reaction that adds an acyl group to a molecule. Acylation can change how a protein, medicine, or other molecule behaves, and is involved in processes such as lipid metabolism and drug processing.

name: acyltransferase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that transfers an acyl group from one molecule to another. Acyltransferases help build and modify fats and other molecules; inherited defects in some of these enzymes can cause metabolic disease.

name: adalimumab
clinical_significance: A biologic medicine that blocks tumor necrosis factor (TNF), an immune signaling protein. It treats several inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, and psoriasis; it increases the risk of serious infections, so screening for tuberculosis and monitoring during treatment are important.

name: adapalene
clinical_significance: A topical retinoid used to treat acne. It helps keep pores from becoming blocked and reduces inflammation; skin dryness, redness, peeling, or irritation can occur, especially when treatment starts.

name: adaptive design
clinical_significance: A clinical-study design allowing planned changes based on accumulating data while preserving scientific validity. Changes may involve sample size, treatment groups, or enrollment and must follow a prespecified plan.

name: adaptive immunity
clinical_significance: The part of the immune system that learns to recognize specific germs or abnormal cells. B cells make targeted antibodies, T cells coordinate or destroy affected cells, and memory cells help produce a faster response to a later exposure.

name: addictive behavior
clinical_significance: A pattern of repeated substance use or behavior that continues despite harm or loss of control. It may signal a substance-use disorder or another treatable health problem; assessment should consider the person's circumstances and avoid blame.

name: Addisonian crisis
clinical_significance: A life-threatening emergency caused by too little cortisol, usually in someone with adrenal insufficiency. Infection, injury, surgery, or missed steroid medicine can trigger it; symptoms may include vomiting, abdominal pain, severe weakness, confusion, and dangerously low blood pressure. It needs immediate emergency treatment with steroid medicine and fluids.

name: Addison's disease
clinical_significance: A chronic condition in which the adrenal glands do not make enough cortisol and often do not make enough aldosterone, usually because of autoimmune damage. Lifelong hormone replacement is needed; illness, injury, or missed medicine can trigger a life-threatening adrenal crisis.

name: adefovir
clinical_significance: An antiviral medicine used to suppress chronic hepatitis B. It can slow liver injury but does not cure the infection, and it may damage the kidneys, so kidney function is monitored during treatment.

name: adenine
clinical_significance: A purine nitrogenous nucleobase that forms complementary base pairs with thymine in DNA (via two hydrogen bonds) and with uracil in RNA. It also forms essential components of adenosine, cellular energy carriers (ATP, ADP, AMP), second messengers (cAMP), and key metabolic cofactors (NAD+, FAD).

name: adenocarcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer that begins in cells lining or forming glands. It can arise in organs such as the colon, breast, lung, pancreas, prostate, stomach, or uterus and may invade or spread.

name: adenoidectomy
clinical_significance: Surgical removal of the adenoids (pharyngeal tonsil) from the back of the nasal passage. It is commonly performed in children to treat chronic nasal obstruction, pediatric obstructive sleep apnea, recurrent ear infections, or persistent rhinosinusitis that does not improve with medical therapy.

name: adenoids
clinical_significance: A collection of lymphatic tissue located in the upper airway at the back of the nasopharynx, forming part of Waldeyer's ring. In infants and young children, they help sample and trap inhaled germs to build immunity, but typically shrink in size during late childhood and adolescence.

name: adenolipoma
clinical_significance: A benign tumor composed of glandular cells and mature fat cells. It may occur in the skin, breast, thyroid, parathyroid, or salivary glands.

name: adenolymphoma
clinical_significance: A benign salivary-gland tumor, also called Warthin tumor, composed of oncocytic epithelium and lymphoid stroma and occurring most often in the parotid gland.

name: adenoma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous gland-forming tumor arising from epithelial tissue. Some adenomas produce hormones or other secretions, and some—especially certain colon and rectal adenomas—contain precancerous changes and may later become cancerous.

name: adenomatoid tumor
clinical_significance: A usually benign tumor of mesothelial cells, most often found near the epididymis or in the uterus or fallopian tube. It may resemble a more serious mass on imaging or examination, but it generally does not spread.

name: adenomatous polyp
clinical_significance: A precancerous type of colon polyp that can develop into colorectal cancer over time. Removing it lowers cancer risk; follow-up colonoscopy timing depends on the number, size, and microscopic features of the polyps.

name: adenomyoepithelioma
clinical_significance: A rare breast tumor made of both glandular and myoepithelial cells. It may be benign, atypical, or malignant, so tissue examination is needed to assess its behavior and guide removal and follow-up.

name: adenomyoma
clinical_significance: A benign uterine lesion composed of endometrial glands and stroma within a proliferation of smooth muscle; it may cause abnormal uterine bleeding or mimic other uterine tumors.

name: adenosarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare malignant tumor containing both gland-like and sarcoma-like tissue, most often arising in the uterus. It can recur or spread, so specialist assessment and long-term follow-up are important.

name: adenosine
clinical_significance: A purine nucleoside made of adenine linked to ribose that participates in energy transfer and cell signaling. Given rapidly by injection, it can briefly slow conduction through the atrioventricular node and is used for selected supraventricular tachycardias.

name: adenosine deaminase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that breaks down adenosine and deoxyadenosine. Inherited deficiency can cause severe combined immunodeficiency; measurement of adenosine deaminase in pleural fluid can also help assess for tuberculosis, but results must be interpreted with other findings.

name: adenosine diphosphate
clinical_significance: A nucleotide formed when ATP loses one phosphate group. ADP can be converted back to ATP to support cellular energy use, and released ADP also activates nearby platelets and promotes platelet aggregation during clot formation.

name: adenosine monophosphate
clinical_significance: A small molecule made of adenine, ribose, and one phosphate group. It is formed when cells break down or recycle energy-carrying molecules and helps regulate energy use and cell signaling.

name: adenosine triphosphatases
clinical_significance: A group of enzymes that split ATP to release energy for cellular work. They power processes such as muscle contraction and movement of ions across cell membranes; defects in particular ATPases can cause neurologic, muscle, or metabolic disorders.

name: adenosine triphosphate
clinical_significance: The main short-term energy source inside cells. Cells make it from nutrients and use it to power muscle contraction, movement of substances across cell membranes, chemical reactions, and many other essential processes; it is commonly called ATP.

name: adenosis
clinical_significance: An increase in the number or size of glands or gland-like tissue. It is often noncancerous, but its meaning depends on the organ involved, such as the breast or lung, and the specific pattern.

name: adenosquamous carcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer containing both malignant gland-forming cells and malignant squamous cells. It can arise in organs such as the cervix, lung, or pancreas; behavior and treatment depend on the site and stage.

name: adenovirus
clinical_significance: A group of DNA viruses that commonly cause respiratory illness, such as cold-like symptoms, sore throat, bronchitis, or pneumonia. Some types cause conjunctivitis, diarrhea, or bladder infection. Most infections are mild, but severe disease is more likely in people with weakened immunity or heart or lung disease.

name: adenovirus infection
clinical_significance: An illness caused by adenovirus, commonly involving the respiratory tract, eyes, or digestive system. Most cases are mild and need only supportive care, but infants, people with heart or lung disease, and people with weakened immunity are at higher risk of severe illness.

name: adenovirus vaccine
clinical_significance: A live oral vaccine against adenovirus types 4 and 7, which can cause outbreaks of respiratory illness in military recruits. In the United States it is approved for military personnel at higher risk and is not available to the general public.

name: adherens junction
clinical_significance: A connection that helps neighboring cells stick together. It links proteins on one cell to the internal support fibers of another, helping tissues keep their shape, strength, and protective barrier.

name: adhesive
clinical_significance: A material used in healthcare to close low-tension wounds, secure dressings or devices, or attach medical products to skin. Some adhesives can cause allergic or irritant dermatitis or skin injury when removed.

name: Adie syndrome
clinical_significance: A neurologic syndrome that usually causes one enlarged pupil that reacts poorly to light but constricts slowly when focusing close up. Reduced or absent tendon reflexes may also occur; the pupil finding is often benign, but a new unequal pupil needs assessment to exclude urgent causes.

name: adipocyte
clinical_significance: A fat cell that stores energy and releases hormones and other signals affecting appetite, blood sugar, inflammation, and metabolism. White fat mainly stores energy, while brown and beige fat can produce heat; enlarged or excessive fat cells can contribute to insulin resistance.

name: adipogenesis
clinical_significance: The process by which immature cells develop into fat cells. It helps form and maintain body-fat tissue, which stores energy and produces hormones; abnormal increases in the number or size of fat cells can contribute to obesity and metabolic disease.

name: adipokine
clinical_significance: A chemical messenger released by body fat. Adipokines help control appetite, blood sugar, fat use, inflammation, blood pressure, and immune activity; abnormal levels may contribute to obesity, diabetes, and heart or blood-vessel disease.

name: adiponectin
clinical_significance: A hormone produced mainly by fat cells that helps regulate fatty-acid use, glucose metabolism, insulin sensitivity, and inflammation. Levels are often lower with obesity and insulin resistance, but a blood level is not diagnostic by itself.

name: adipose tissue
clinical_significance: Tissue made mainly of fat cells that stores energy, cushions organs, helps regulate body temperature, and releases hormones and immune signals. Excess or abnormally distributed adipose tissue can contribute to insulin resistance and other metabolic disease.

name: adiposis dolorosa
clinical_significance: Adiposis dolorosa, or Dercum disease, is a rare disorder characterized by painful fatty deposits, often with obesity, fatigue, and other systemic symptoms.

name: adjustment disorders
clinical_significance: A mental-health condition in which emotional or behavioral symptoms develop after a stressful life event and cause significant distress or interfere with daily functioning. Symptoms may include anxiety, low mood, or behavior changes; assessment distinguishes it from other conditions and normal grief.

name: adjuvant therapy
clinical_significance: Additional treatment given after the main treatment to reduce the chance of disease returning. Examples include chemotherapy, radiation, hormone treatment, or immune treatment after surgery for selected cancers.

name: ADME
clinical_significance: The four processes that describe what the body does to a medicine: absorption into the bloodstream, distribution through tissues, chemical breakdown, and excretion from the body. These processes influence a medicine’s dose, timing, and effects.

name: administration procedure
clinical_significance: A method used to give a medicine, fluid, vaccine, nutrition, or other treatment, such as by mouth, injection, inhalation, skin application, or infusion. The method affects speed, dose, and risks.

name: adnexal dysplasia
clinical_significance: A nonspecific term for abnormal development of an adnexal structure. Because “adnexa” can refer to structures around different organs, the affected site and pathology findings are needed to determine whether the change is benign, precancerous, or clinically significant.

name: adnexal mass
clinical_significance: A mass involving an ovary, fallopian tube, or nearby tissue. Many are benign, but evaluation considers symptoms, age, imaging, and family history to assess cancer risk; sudden severe pain can indicate torsion or rupture and needs urgent assessment.

name: adnexitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of one or more uterine adnexa, usually the fallopian tubes and sometimes the ovaries. It commonly occurs as part of pelvic inflammatory disease and may cause lower abdominal pain, fever, abnormal discharge, or pain during sex; untreated infection can lead to an abscess, infertility, or ectopic pregnancy.

name: adolescence
clinical_significance: The developmental period between childhood and adulthood, involving physical maturation, puberty, and major psychological and social changes.

name: adopted child
clinical_significance: Adoption is relevant to a child's social and medical history, not a diagnosis. When available, birth-family health information can help assess inherited risks; clinicians may also review previous medical records and developmental history.

name: adoption
clinical_significance: Adoption can affect access to a person's early medical records and birth-family health history, which may be useful when assessing inherited conditions. Adoption itself is not a disease or health disorder.

name: adoptive immunotherapy
clinical_significance: Treatment in which immune cells are collected, activated or genetically modified, and returned to the patient to attack disease, especially cancer. Fever, inflammation, and other immune reactions may occur.

name: ADP-ribosylation
clinical_significance: A chemical change in which a small molecule is attached to a protein or other cell molecule. This can switch the molecule’s activity on or off and is used by normal cell processes and by some bacterial toxins.

name: adrenal cancer
clinical_significance: A malignant tumor arising in an adrenal gland, most often an adrenocortical carcinoma. Some tumors produce excess hormones; others cause symptoms as they grow or spread. Most adrenal masses are benign, so imaging and hormone testing help determine whether a mass is cancerous.

name: adrenal cortex
clinical_significance: The outer part of each adrenal gland that produces steroid hormones, including cortisol, aldosterone, and adrenal androgens. These hormones help regulate stress responses, blood pressure, salt balance, and metabolism.

name: adrenal gland
clinical_significance: One of two hormone-producing glands above the kidneys. The outer cortex makes aldosterone, cortisol, and adrenal androgens; the inner medulla makes adrenaline and noradrenaline. Adrenal hormones help regulate blood pressure, metabolism, stress responses, and salt balance.

name: adrenal hyperplasia
clinical_significance: Enlargement or overgrowth of adrenal tissue. The cause and hormone effects vary: congenital adrenal hyperplasia can alter cortisol, aldosterone, or androgen production, while other forms may be driven by hormonal signals or a tumor.

name: adrenal medulla
clinical_significance: The inner part of each adrenal gland, which sits above a kidney. It releases adrenaline and noradrenaline during stress, helping increase heart rate, blood pressure, alertness, and blood flow to muscles.

name: adrenalectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove one or both adrenal glands, usually for a tumor or severe hormone overproduction. Removing one gland may leave enough hormone production; removing both requires lifelong hormone replacement and an emergency steroid plan.

name: adrenergic agent
clinical_significance: A medicine or substance that stimulates or blocks receptors responding to adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine). These agents can change heart rate, blood pressure, airway size, and pupil size.

name: adrenergic agonist
clinical_significance: A medicine or substance that copies the effects of adrenaline or noradrenaline by activating specific cell receptors. Depending on the receptor, it may raise blood pressure, speed the heart, open the airways, or improve heart pumping.

name: adrenergic antagonists
clinical_significance: Medicines or other substances that block adrenaline-like signaling at alpha or beta adrenergic receptors. They can lower blood pressure, slow the heart, reduce cardiac workload, or relax smooth muscle; effects and risks depend on the receptor targeted and the medicine used.

name: adrenergic beta-antagonists
clinical_significance: Medicines that block beta-adrenergic receptors, reducing some effects of adrenaline and noradrenaline. They are used for conditions such as certain heart-rhythm disorders, angina, and heart failure; they can slow the heart and may cause low blood pressure or worsen some breathing problems.

name: adrenergic receptor
clinical_significance: A cell-surface receptor activated by adrenaline (epinephrine), noradrenaline (norepinephrine), or related medicines. Alpha and beta receptors help control heart rate, blood pressure, airway size, pupil size, and other body responses.

name: adrenocortical carcinoma
clinical_significance: A rare cancer arising in the outer layer of an adrenal gland. Some tumors produce excess hormones, causing features such as weight gain, high blood pressure, muscle weakness, or changes in sexual characteristics; others cause abdominal or back pain as they grow. It can spread to other organs and needs specialist evaluation.

name: Adrenogenital syndrome
clinical_significance: A group of disorders, usually caused by congenital adrenal hyperplasia, in which excess adrenal androgens cause atypical genital development or early puberty.

name: adrenoleukodystrophy
clinical_significance: A group of inherited disorders, most often X-linked, in which very-long-chain fatty acids accumulate and damage myelin, the adrenal glands, or both. Childhood cerebral disease can cause behavior and learning changes, seizures, and loss of neurologic function; adrenal insufficiency may also occur.

name: adrenomedullin
clinical_significance: A hormone-like substance made by many tissues that widens blood vessels and helps regulate blood pressure, circulation, fluid balance, kidney activity, and responses to injury.

name: adsorption
clinical_significance: The sticking of molecules to the outside surface of a solid or liquid rather than entering its substance. Activated charcoal works partly by adsorbing some poisons in the digestive tract.

name: adult
clinical_significance: A life-stage category used in healthcare because disease risks, normal test ranges, preventive screening, and medicine doses can differ between adults and children. The exact age used to define adulthood depends on the clinical or legal context.

name: adult rickets
clinical_significance: Impaired bone mineralization in an adult, usually called osteomalacia. It can cause bone pain, muscle weakness, and fractures, often because of vitamin D, calcium, or phosphate deficiency or an underlying disorder.

name: advance directive
clinical_significance: A legal document stating a person's wishes about future medical care and, in some cases, naming a health-care proxy to make decisions if the person cannot decide or communicate. It may address resuscitation, life support, artificial nutrition, and other treatments and is reviewed as circumstances change.

name: advanced cancer
