clinical_significance: Cancer that has grown into nearby tissues or spread to lymph nodes or distant parts of the body. The term does not always mean incurable: some advanced cancers can be controlled for years, and treatment may aim to shrink or slow the cancer, relieve symptoms, or prolong life.

name: adventitia
clinical_significance: The outer layer of connective tissue around a blood vessel or hollow organ. It supports and anchors the structure and contains small nerves and blood vessels that nourish the wall.

name: adverse event
clinical_significance: Any new or worsening health problem that happens during or after a medicine, procedure, or other treatment, whether or not the treatment caused it. Clinicians record its timing, severity, and likely cause separately.

name: adverse reaction
clinical_significance: An unintended and harmful response to a medicine, treatment, or other exposure. It may be predictable from the medicine's effects, such as bleeding with an anticoagulant, or unpredictable, such as an allergic reaction. Severity ranges from mild nausea or rash to serious organ injury, breathing difficulty, or shock; suspected severe reactions need urgent medical attention.

name: aerobic
clinical_significance: Requiring or using oxygen. In microbiology, an aerobic organism grows with oxygen; in the body, aerobic energy production uses oxygen to release energy from nutrients for muscles and other cells.

name: aerobic exercise
clinical_significance: Physical activity using large muscles continuously while the body produces energy with oxygen. Walking, cycling, swimming, and dancing can improve heart, lung, blood-vessel, muscle, mood, and endurance health.

name: aerobiosis
clinical_significance: Life or biological activity that occurs when oxygen is available. Many human cells use oxygen to release energy from food, and some microorganisms need oxygen to grow.

name: aerococcaceae
clinical_significance: A family of bacteria that includes Aerococcus species. Some members are part of the genitourinary microbiota, while others can cause urinary infections or, rarely, invasive disease such as bloodstream infection or endocarditis.

name: aerococcus
clinical_significance: A genus of Gram-positive bacteria that can cause urinary tract infections and, less often, bloodstream infection or endocarditis. Aerococcus infections are often reported in older adults with urinary-tract disease, and these bacteria can be mistaken for other cocci in laboratory cultures.

name: aerococcus sanguinicola
clinical_significance: An Aerococcus species associated with urinary tract infection and occasional bloodstream infection or endocarditis. It may be missed or misidentified in routine laboratory testing, so results should be interpreted with the symptoms and specimen findings.

name: aerococcus urinae
clinical_significance: A bacterium that can cause urinary tract infection, particularly in older men with urinary-tract abnormalities, and can occasionally cause bloodstream infection or endocarditis. Accurate identification matters because it may be mistaken for other bacteria in culture.

name: aeromonadaceae
clinical_significance: A family of water-associated bacteria that includes Aeromonas. Some species cause food- or water-associated diarrhea and wound infections after contact with contaminated water; invasive infection is less common but can be severe.

name: aeromonas
clinical_significance: A genus of bacteria commonly found in fresh and brackish water. Some species cause diarrhea after contaminated food or water and wound infections after water-exposed injuries; bloodstream or deep-tissue infection is uncommon but can be severe, especially in medically vulnerable people.

name: aeromonas hydrophila
clinical_significance: A water-associated bacterium that can cause gastroenteritis and wound or soft-tissue infection, especially after an injury exposed to fresh water. Infection may progress rapidly and occasionally spread to blood or deeper tissues.

name: aeromonas jandaei
clinical_significance: An Aeromonas species found in water and human clinical samples. It is an uncommon cause of human disease but has been linked to diarrhea and occasional wound, bloodstream, or other invasive infections.

name: aeromonas salmonicida
clinical_significance: A bacterium that mainly causes disease in fish, especially salmonids. Human infection is very rare, but isolated bloodstream and other infections have been reported; its usual clinical importance is in fish health and aquaculture.

name: aeromonas schubertii
clinical_significance: An uncommon Aeromonas species isolated from human clinical specimens, including skin abscesses. It can act as an opportunistic pathogen, but documented human infections are rare.

name: aeromonas sobria
clinical_significance: Aeromonas sobria sensu stricto is mainly associated with fish and is rarely reported as a human pathogen. Older clinical reports using this name may instead refer to Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria, which can cause diarrhea and invasive infections.

name: aeromonas veronii
clinical_significance: A water-associated bacterium that can cause diarrhea, wound or soft-tissue infection, and occasionally bloodstream or other invasive infection. It is one of the Aeromonas species found in human clinical samples.

name: aerophagy
clinical_significance: Repeated swallowing of too much air, which can cause frequent belching, abdominal fullness, bloating, or discomfort. It may occur with rapid eating, chewing gum, anxiety, or difficulty swallowing.

name: aerosol
clinical_significance: Very small solid particles or liquid drops floating in a gas such as air. Aerosols can carry inhaled medicines, pollutants, or infectious particles and may remain in the air or settle on surfaces.

name: afatinib
clinical_significance: An oral targeted cancer medicine that blocks the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). It is used for certain metastatic non-small cell lung cancers with specific EGFR mutations; common adverse effects include diarrhea, rash, and mouth sores, and serious lung inflammation can occur.

name: afferent neuron
clinical_significance: A sensory nerve cell carrying signals from receptors in the body toward the spinal cord and brain, where information is processed and appropriate responses begin.

name: afferent pathway
clinical_significance: A sensory nerve route carrying information from the skin, muscles, organs, or other tissues toward the spinal cord or brain, where the signals are processed and responses can begin.

name: affinity chromatography
clinical_significance: A laboratory method for separating and purifying a substance by allowing it to stick to a partner designed to recognize it. Other substances are washed away, and the desired substance is then released.

name: afibrinogenemia
clinical_significance: A rare congenital or severe acquired coagulation disorder characterized by the complete or near-complete absence of circulating fibrinogen (factor I, <0.1 g/L). Inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern (mutations in \textit{FGA}, \textit{FGB}, or \textit{FGG}), it manifests with umbilical cord bleeding in neonates, spontaneous mucosal and intracranial hemorrhages, hemarthroses, and prolonged bleeding times.

name: afimoxifene
clinical_significance: An investigational topical form of 4-hydroxytamoxifen, an estrogen-receptor blocker. It has been studied for cyclical breast pain and localized breast treatment, but is not an established routine medicine.

name: aflatoxin
clinical_significance: A toxin made by certain molds that can contaminate foods such as grains, nuts, and spices. Long-term exposure can damage the liver and increase the risk of liver cancer.

name: african trypanosomiasis
clinical_significance: An infection caused by \textit{Trypanosoma} parasites and spread by infected tsetse flies in sub-Saharan Africa. It may cause fever and swollen lymph nodes, followed by sleep changes and nervous-system problems; untreated disease can be fatal.

name: after breakfast
clinical_significance: A medication-timing instruction meaning that a dose should be taken after breakfast. Whether food changes absorption or stomach irritation depends on the specific medicine, so follow the medicine's directions.

name: agammaglobulinemia
clinical_significance: A serious immune deficiency in which the blood contains very few or no antibodies. It often results from abnormal B-cell development and causes repeated bacterial infections of the ears, sinuses, lungs, or bloodstream.

name: agaricales
clinical_significance: An order of mushrooms that includes both edible species and poisonous species. Ingestion of a toxic mushroom can cause severe illness, and poisoning risk depends on accurate identification of the species.

name: agatolimod sodium
clinical_significance: An investigational immune-stimulating compound that activates Toll-like receptor 9. It has been studied as a vaccine adjuvant and in cancer treatment, but it is not an established routine therapy.

name: age
clinical_significance: A factor that affects normal test ranges, disease risk, prevention, and treatment choices. Age-related differences in development, organ function, and drug handling can change how a finding or dose is interpreted.

name: agent orange
clinical_significance: A herbicide mixture used during the Vietnam War that was contaminated with dioxin (TCDD). Exposure has been associated with several cancers and other chronic illnesses, including type 2 diabetes, ischemic heart disease, Parkinson's disease, and some blood disorders; the health risk depends on exposure history.

name: ageusia
clinical_significance: Complete loss of the ability to taste. It may result from infections, mouth or nose problems, medicines, chemotherapy, head injury, nerve damage, nutritional deficiency, or neurological disease. Loss of smell can also make food seem tasteless.

name: agglutination test
clinical_significance: A laboratory test that mixes a patient sample with a known antibody or antigen. Visible clumping suggests that the matching substance is present and may help identify blood groups or infections.

name: agglutinin
clinical_significance: An antibody or other substance that causes cells or particles to stick together in visible clumps. Agglutinins are used in laboratory tests, including blood-group testing and some infection tests.

name: aggregatibacter
clinical_significance: A genus of bacteria that normally inhabit the mouth or upper airway. Some species are linked to gum disease, and several belong to the HACEK group, which can rarely cause infective endocarditis.

name: aggregatibacter aphrophilus
clinical_significance: A bacterium normally found in the mouth and throat and part of the HACEK group. It can rarely cause infective endocarditis and has also been associated with brain abscess and other invasive infections.

name: aggregatibacter segnis
clinical_significance: A bacterium found in the upper respiratory tract and included in the HACEK group. It is a rare cause of infective endocarditis and may be difficult to identify in routine cultures.

name: aggresome
clinical_significance: A temporary cellular compartment where misfolded or damaged proteins are gathered for processing or disposal. Aggresome formation is studied in relation to the cell's protein-clearance systems and neurodegenerative diseases, but is not itself a clinical diagnosis.

name: aggression
clinical_significance: Words or actions intended to threaten, harm, or intimidate another person or damage property. Aggression may result from emotional distress, pain, mental illness, brain disorders, medicines, or substance use.

name: aging
clinical_significance: The gradual biological changes that occur over time. Aging changes immune function, muscle and bone strength, senses, and how the body handles medicines; it also increases the risk of many chronic diseases, but it is not itself a disease.

name: agitation
clinical_significance: An uncomfortable state of inner tension, restlessness, or increased activity. It may cause pacing, irritability, or inability to remain calm and can result from medical illness, pain, medicines, substance use, or mental health conditions.

name: agnosia
clinical_significance: An inability to recognize familiar objects, people, sounds, or other sensations even though the related sense works normally. It usually results from damage to areas of the brain that interpret sensory information.

name: agonist
clinical_significance: A drug or other ligand that binds to a receptor and activates it, producing a biological response. A full agonist can produce the maximum response in a given system, whereas a partial agonist produces a submaximal response even when occupying receptors.

name: agoraphobia
clinical_significance: An anxiety disorder involving persistent, intense fear of places or situations where escape may be difficult, help may be unavailable, or panic-like symptoms may feel embarrassing. People may avoid crowds, public transportation, shops, or leaving home alone; the fear and avoidance cause significant distress or interfere with daily functioning.

name: agranulocytosis
clinical_significance: A serious condition in which the blood has an extremely low number of granulocytes, especially neutrophils, white blood cells that fight infection. It may be caused by medicines, chemotherapy, infection, autoimmune disease, or bone-marrow problems and can cause fever, sore throat, and severe infections.

name: agraphia
clinical_significance: Loss of a previously learned ability to write because of brain damage or disease. It may follow a stroke, head injury, brain tumour, or neurodegenerative disease and may occur with problems speaking or reading.

name: agriculture
clinical_significance: The cultivation of crops and raising of animals provide food and livelihoods. Agricultural work can also involve health risks from machinery, heat, pesticides, dust, and animal-borne infections; the specific risk depends on the task and exposure.

name: agrin
clinical_significance: A protein that helps organize and maintain the neuromuscular junction, where a motor nerve communicates with a muscle. Pathogenic changes in the AGRN gene can disrupt nerve-to-muscle signaling and cause congenital myasthenic syndrome with muscle weakness.

name: agrobacterium
clinical_significance: A genus of soil bacteria best known for causing plant diseases. Human infection is rare, but some species can act as opportunistic pathogens, particularly in people with weakened immunity or indwelling medical devices.

name: agrobacterium tumefaciens
clinical_significance: A soil-associated plant pathogen that has rarely caused opportunistic human infection, including bloodstream infection linked to a central venous catheter. Reported cases mainly involve people with serious illness or implanted devices.

name: AH amyloidosis
clinical_significance: A rare form of systemic amyloidosis in which abnormal immunoglobulin heavy chains form deposits, often in the kidneys. It can cause protein in the urine, nephrotic syndrome, and loss of kidney function; diagnosis requires tissue and blood or urine evaluation.

name: Aicardi's syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare neurodevelopmental disorder, occurring almost exclusively in girls, involving an absent or underdeveloped corpus callosum, retinal abnormalities, and seizures that often begin as infantile spasms. Developmental and vision problems are common, and seizure control may be difficult.

name: AIDS
clinical_significance: The most advanced stage of HIV infection, when the immune system is severely weakened. AIDS is diagnosed when the CD4 count is below 200 cells/mm$^3$ or certain serious infections or cancers develop.

name: AIDS vaccine
clinical_significance: A vaccine intended to prevent or treat HIV infection. No HIV vaccine is currently approved or available; candidates are being studied in clinical trials.

name: AIDS-associated nephropathy
clinical_significance: Kidney disease caused by HIV, usually in untreated or poorly controlled infection. It often causes large amounts of protein in the urine and may rapidly worsen kidney function, leading to kidney failure.

name: ainhum
clinical_significance: A rare disorder in which a painful fibrous band slowly tightens around a toe, usually the little toe. The band can damage bone and blood supply and may eventually cause loss of the affected part.

name: air
clinical_significance: Air supplies oxygen for breathing and can carry inhaled medicines. Pollutants or infectious particles in air can harm health, especially by worsening respiratory or cardiovascular disease.

name: air embolism
clinical_significance: A blockage of blood flow caused by air or another gas bubble entering a blood vessel. It can occur during medical procedures, injury, or rapid pressure changes and may cause sudden breathing, heart, or brain problems.

name: air pollution
clinical_significance: Air contaminated with harmful gases, particles, smoke, chemicals, or germs. Breathing polluted air can irritate the eyes and lungs and increase the risk of asthma attacks, infections, heart disease, stroke, and other health problems.

name: air sac
clinical_significance: A small, thin-walled space that contains air. In the human lung, an air sac is called an alveolus and is where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it; birds also have larger air sacs that help breathing.

name: air trapping
clinical_significance: A condition in which extra air remains in the lungs after breathing out because narrowed or damaged airways prevent complete exhalation. It commonly occurs in asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and bronchiolitis.

name: airway management
clinical_significance: The methods and equipment used to keep a person’s airway open and support breathing when airflow is threatened. They may include positioning, suction, airway devices, or a breathing tube connected to a ventilator.

name: airway obstruction
clinical_significance: Partial or complete blockage of airflow through the breathing passages. Causes include an inhaled object, mucus, swelling, injury, tumour, or relaxed airway muscles. It may cause noisy breathing, wheezing, low oxygen, severe breathing difficulty, or respiratory arrest.

name: airway resistance
clinical_significance: The difficulty air encounters while moving through the breathing tubes. Narrowing from muscle tightening, swelling, mucus, or loss of support increases resistance and makes the breathing muscles work harder.

name: ajellomyces capsulatus
clinical_significance: The sexual-stage name formerly used for Histoplasma capsulatum, the fungus that causes histoplasmosis. Inhaling spores can cause lung infection; severe or disseminated disease is more likely in people with weakened immunity.

name: akathisia
clinical_significance: A movement disorder causing an uncomfortable inner restlessness and a strong urge to move, often with pacing, rocking, or repeated shifting of the legs. It is commonly a side effect of antipsychotic or other medicines.

name: akinesia
clinical_significance: An inability to initiate or perform voluntary movement, or a marked lack of spontaneous movement. It may occur in Parkinson disease and related disorders, severe depression, or other conditions affecting the brain’s movement-control systems.

name: akinetic mutism
clinical_significance: A state in which a person is awake but makes little or no voluntary movement or speech. It usually results from severe damage or dysfunction in brain areas that control motivation, attention, and movement.

name: Alagille syndrome
clinical_significance: A genetic disorder in which too few or abnormal bile ducts can cause liver disease and jaundice. It may also affect the heart, kidneys, eyes, blood vessels, bones, and facial features. Most cases involve changes in the JAG1 gene.

name: alanine
clinical_significance: An amino acid, or protein-building molecule, made by the body and obtained from food. Cells use it to make proteins and to help move nitrogen and produce glucose for energy.

name: alanosine
clinical_significance: An experimental anticancer compound that interferes with purine synthesis and can reduce tumor-cell growth. It has been studied in clinical trials but is not an established routine cancer treatment.

name: alarmin
clinical_significance: A signal released by injured or severely stressed cells that alerts the immune system. It helps start inflammation and attract protective cells to damaged tissue, even before the body identifies whether infection is present.

name: albendazole
clinical_significance: An antiparasitic medicine that damages the internal structures parasites need to absorb nutrients and survive. It treats several worm infections, including some intestinal and tissue infections, when prescribed for the appropriate parasite.

name: albinism
clinical_significance: A group of inherited conditions in which reduced melanin affects the skin, hair, and/or eyes. Eye involvement can cause reduced vision, light sensitivity, and involuntary eye movements; low skin pigment increases sunburn and skin-cancer risk, so eye care and sun protection are important.

name: albumin
clinical_significance: The main protein in blood plasma, made by the liver. It helps keep fluid inside blood vessels and carries substances such as hormones, fatty acids, and some medicines through the bloodstream.

name: albumin clearance
clinical_significance: A measure of how quickly the blood protein albumin leaves the bloodstream or another body space. It is used mainly in specialized kidney, liver, or research tests to study leakage, transport, or removal of the protein.

name: albuminuria
clinical_significance: An abnormally high amount of albumin in the urine, showing that the kidneys are allowing this blood protein to pass through. It may be temporary or persistent; ongoing albuminuria can indicate kidney damage and increased cardiovascular risk.

name: albuterol
clinical_significance: A short-acting inhaled bronchodilator used for quick relief or prevention of bronchospasm in asthma and other reversible airway disease. It relaxes airway muscle; tremor, nervousness, and a fast heartbeat can occur. Increasing need for it can indicate worsening airway control.

name: alcaligenaceae
clinical_significance: Members of this bacterial family are found widely in the environment; a few can cause uncommon opportunistic infections, especially in people with serious underlying illness or indwelling medical devices. Their significance depends on the species and whether the culture fits the clinical picture.

name: alcaligenes
clinical_significance: This genus includes environmental Gram-negative bacteria that only rarely cause human infection. Alcaligenes recovered from a normally sterile site or a compatible clinical specimen may represent an opportunistic infection, particularly in a medically vulnerable patient; susceptibility testing can matter because resistance occurs.

name: alcaligenes faecalis
clinical_significance: An environmental Gram-negative bacterium that can rarely cause opportunistic infections, including urinary, wound, respiratory, or bloodstream infection, especially in people with underlying illness or healthcare devices. Some strains resist multiple antibiotics, so treatment is guided by culture and susceptibility results.

name: alcian blue
clinical_significance: A histology stain that highlights acidic mucins and related substances in tissue. It helps pathologists characterize mucus-producing cells and tissue changes, but the stain result is interpreted with the tissue pattern and other tests.

name: alcohol abuse
clinical_significance: A dated, stigmatizing label often used for alcohol use disorder (AUD), a treatable condition involving impaired control over drinking and continued use despite harm. AUD can damage the liver, brain, heart, and other organs and increases risks of injury and some cancers.

name: alcohol dehydrogenase
clinical_significance: An enzyme found mainly in the liver that begins breaking down alcohol. It changes alcohol into acetaldehyde, a harmful intermediate that is then processed into less toxic substances.

name: alcohol deterrents
clinical_significance: A term for medicines intended to support abstinence from alcohol. Disulfiram is one example: drinking while taking it can trigger flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, and other potentially serious effects. Medication choice requires clinical assessment; other AUD medicines work differently.

name: alcohol intolerance
clinical_significance: An unpleasant reaction after drinking alcohol, often caused by inherited difficulty breaking down alcohol or sensitivity to an ingredient in the drink. Symptoms may include flushing, headache, nausea, rapid heartbeat, or worsening asthma.

name: alcoholic hepatitis
clinical_significance: An acute inflammation and injury of the liver caused by heavy alcohol use. It commonly causes jaundice, fatigue, fever, nausea, and abdominal pain and can become severe enough to cause liver failure.

name: alcoholic intoxication
clinical_significance: Acute impairment from drinking more alcohol than the body can process, causing poor coordination, confusion, vomiting, or reduced consciousness. Severe poisoning can slow or stop breathing and cause choking, coma, or death; a person who is hard to wake or breathing slowly needs emergency care.

name: alcoholic neuropathy
clinical_significance: Nerve damage associated with long-term heavy alcohol use and related nutritional deficiency. It commonly causes burning pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness, especially in the feet and lower legs.

name: alcoholism
clinical_significance: An older term for alcohol use disorder (AUD), a treatable pattern of impaired control over drinking and continued use despite harm. AUD can cause serious medical, psychological, and social consequences; non-stigmatizing language is preferred.

name: alcohols
clinical_significance: A class of organic chemicals that includes ethanol, the intoxicating alcohol in beverages, as well as toxic substances such as methanol and isopropanol. Effects vary by compound and dose; some exposures can cause life-threatening poisoning.

name: aldehyde
clinical_significance: A reactive chemical group present in many substances, including acetaldehyde produced when the body breaks down alcohol. Health effects depend on the specific aldehyde and exposure; some are toxic or irritating to the eyes, skin, or airways.

name: aldehyde reductase
clinical_significance: An enzyme name used for proteins that reduce aldehydes and other carbonyl compounds during metabolism. These reactions help process reactive chemicals; clinical effects depend on the particular enzyme and substrate.

name: aldehyde-lyases
clinical_significance: A group of enzymes that cleave carbon–carbon bonds in aldehyde-containing molecules during specialized metabolic pathways. Their significance is mainly biochemical, rather than as a routine clinical test or diagnosis.

name: aldesleukin
clinical_significance: A recombinant form of interleukin-2 used in selected adults with metastatic renal-cell cancer or melanoma. It can cause life-threatening capillary leak, neurologic toxicity, and serious infection, so it is given in a hospital with intensive monitoring.

name: aldicarb
clinical_significance: A highly toxic carbamate pesticide that inhibits cholinesterase. Exposure can cause excessive secretions, sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, breathing difficulty, muscle weakness, seizures, or collapse and requires urgent poison-control or emergency assessment.

name: aldosterone
clinical_significance: A hormone made by the adrenal glands that helps the kidneys retain sodium and water and remove potassium. It helps control blood volume and blood pressure.

name: alefacept
clinical_significance: A biologic immune-modifying medicine formerly used for chronic plaque psoriasis. It reduces T-cell activity and can increase infection risk; it is no longer routinely used, as safer or more effective psoriasis treatments are available.

name: alemtuzumab
clinical_significance: A monoclonal antibody used for selected adults with relapsing multiple sclerosis after other treatments have not worked well enough. It can cause serious autoimmune disease, infusion reactions, infections, and malignancies, requiring restricted distribution and prolonged monitoring.

name: alendronate
clinical_significance: A bisphosphonate used to prevent or treat osteoporosis and to treat Paget disease of bone. It reduces fracture risk, but can irritate the oesophagus and rarely cause jaw or atypical femur problems; it must be taken with water while remaining upright.

name: alendronate sodium
clinical_significance: The sodium salt form of alendronate, a bisphosphonate used to prevent or treat osteoporosis and to treat Paget disease of bone. It reduces fracture risk; correct dosing helps limit oesophageal irritation, and long-term treatment is periodically reassessed.

name: alethine
clinical_significance: An investigational immune-modulating compound studied for possible cancer treatment. It is not an established routine therapy, and its clinical benefit and safety remain under study.

name: Alexander disease
clinical_significance: A rare genetic disorder in which abnormal GFAP protein damages the brain’s supporting cells and white matter. It may begin in infancy, childhood, or adulthood and can cause enlarged head size, developmental problems, movement difficulty, seizures, or progressive weakness.

name: alexia
clinical_significance: Loss of the ability to understand written words despite adequate eyesight, usually because of brain damage from a stroke, injury, tumour, or degenerative disease. It may occur with other language or reading problems.

name: alexithymia
clinical_significance: Difficulty recognizing, understanding, or describing one’s own emotions. It is a trait or symptom rather than a diagnosis and may occur with autism, depression, trauma, stress, or other conditions.

name: alfentanil
clinical_significance: A potent, short-acting opioid used by anaesthesia professionals for analgesia during procedures. It can suppress breathing, especially with other sedatives, and requires close respiratory monitoring and access to resuscitation.

name: algae
clinical_significance: A broad group of photosynthetic organisms. Some algal blooms produce toxins that can contaminate seafood or water and cause neurologic, gastrointestinal, or liver illness; risks depend on the organism and exposure.

name: aliquot
clinical_significance: A measured portion of a specimen or solution taken for testing or processing. Accurate aliquoting helps ensure reliable laboratory results, especially when samples are small or analytes are unevenly distributed.

name: alistipes
clinical_significance: A genus of anaerobic bacteria commonly found in the human gut. Its abundance has been linked to health and disease in microbiome studies, but these associations are inconsistent and do not establish it as a cause or diagnostic marker.

name: alistipes putredinis
clinical_significance: A species of anaerobic gut bacterium commonly detected in human stool. Research links its abundance with different health states, but findings are not consistent enough for it to serve as a clinical diagnosis or treatment target.

name: alistipes shahii
clinical_significance: A species of anaerobic bacterium found in the human gut. Its clinical significance is not established; microbiome associations alone do not show that it causes disease or require treatment.

name: alitretinoin
clinical_significance: A retinoid medicine used as a skin gel to treat cutaneous lesions of AIDS-related Kaposi sarcoma. It can irritate treated skin and does not cure the cancer; treatment is selected and monitored by a clinician.

name: alkaline phosphatase
clinical_significance: An enzyme found mainly in the liver, bile ducts, bones, intestine, and placenta. A high blood level may reflect liver or bile-duct disease, increased bone activity, pregnancy, or another condition and must be interpreted with other tests.

name: alkalinization
clinical_significance: The process of making a body fluid or tissue more alkaline. In clinical care, alkalinization may be used in selected settings, such as to increase urinary removal of certain toxins or to reduce the harmful effects of some chemotherapy drugs; the method and monitoring depend on the indication.

name: alkaloid
clinical_significance: A naturally occurring chemical containing nitrogen, often made by plants, that can strongly affect the body. Examples include morphine, quinine, nicotine, and atropine.

name: alkalosis
clinical_significance: A condition in which the blood becomes too alkaline. It may result from repeated vomiting, certain medicines, hormone disorders, or breathing too rapidly, and can cause muscle cramps, tingling, confusion, or abnormal heart rhythms.

name: alkane
clinical_significance: A family of hydrocarbons found in fuels and solvents. Exposure to some alkanes can irritate or depress the nervous system, and swallowing them creates a serious risk of aspiration into the lungs; toxicity varies by compound and route.

name: alkanesulfonates
clinical_significance: A chemical class that includes alkylating compounds such as busulfan, a cancer medicine that damages DNA in dividing cells. These drugs can also injure normal bone marrow and other tissues, so their use requires specialist monitoring.

name: alkaptonuria
clinical_significance: A rare inherited metabolic disorder caused by reduced activity of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, usually because of disease-causing variants in the \textit{HGD} gene. Homogentisic acid accumulates, darkens urine, and can deposit in cartilage, tendons, skin, and other tissues in a process called ochronosis. Over time it may cause arthritis and stiffness of the spine and large joints, urinary stones, or changes involving heart valves.

name: alkenes
clinical_significance: Alkenes are hydrocarbons used in chemical manufacturing. They have no single medical effect; toxicity depends on the specific compound and exposure, and some vapours can irritate or depress the nervous system.

name: alkylating agent
clinical_significance: An anticancer drug that damages DNA in dividing cells. Alkylating agents treat several cancers but can also suppress bone marrow, damage organs, and increase the risk of later cancers; effects vary by drug and dose.

name: alkylation
clinical_significance: The addition of an alkyl group to a molecule. In medicine, DNA alkylation is one way chemotherapy damages cancer cells, but alkylation of normal-cell DNA can also cause mutations and tissue injury.

name: alkynes
clinical_significance: A class of hydrocarbons containing a carbon–carbon triple bond, used mainly as industrial chemicals. Health effects depend on the compound and exposure; some vapours are flammable, irritating, or harmful to the nervous system.

name: allantoic cyst
clinical_significance: A fluid-filled structure related to the fetal allantois and urachus, usually detected near the umbilical cord before birth. It may be associated with a persistent connection between the bladder and umbilicus, so prenatal and postnatal assessment helps clarify urinary tract anatomy.

name: allele
clinical_significance: One of two or more versions of a gene. A person usually inherits one allele from each parent; different alleles can influence traits or the risk of inherited disease.

name: allelic imbalance
clinical_significance: An imbalance in the relative amounts of maternal and paternal gene copies or alleles in a cell sample. It can be a clue to chromosomal changes in a tumour and may help characterize cancer, but it is interpreted with other molecular findings.

name: allergen
clinical_significance: A usually harmless substance that triggers an allergic immune response in a sensitive person. Common allergens include foods, pollen, medicines, animal proteins, insect venom, and natural rubber.

name: allergic
clinical_significance: Describes a response involving allergy, such as allergic inflammation or symptoms. The term alone does not identify the trigger or severity; breathing difficulty, throat swelling, or faintness can signal anaphylaxis and require emergency care.

name: allergic conjunctivitis
clinical_significance: Allergic conjunctivitis causes itchy, watery red eyes and often accompanies nasal allergies; pain, light sensitivity, or reduced vision suggests another eye problem and needs prompt assessment.

name: allergic reaction
clinical_significance: An immune response to a usually harmless substance. It may cause sneezing, itching, hives, swelling, vomiting, or breathing difficulty and can sometimes become life-threatening anaphylaxis.

name: allodynia
clinical_significance: Pain caused by something that normally should not hurt, such as light touch, clothing, or gentle pressure. It can occur with nerve injury, migraine, shingles, fibromyalgia, or other pain conditions.

name: alloimmunisation
clinical_significance: An immune response against red-cell or other tissue antigens from another person, often after pregnancy, transfusion, or transplantation. Red-cell alloimmunisation can complicate future transfusions or pregnancy by causing haemolytic disease of the fetus or newborn.

name: alloprevotella tannerae
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterium identified in the human oral cavity. Its role in health or disease is not established well enough to guide diagnosis or treatment; detection in microbiome studies alone does not prove infection.

name: allopurinol
clinical_significance: A medicine that lowers uric acid to prevent gout attacks and can also prevent or treat high uric acid from rapid tumour breakdown. It does not relieve an acute gout attack and can rarely cause a severe hypersensitivity reaction, including a dangerous rash.

name: alloxan
clinical_significance: A chemical that damages insulin-producing pancreatic cells and is used to create experimental diabetes in laboratory animals. It is not a treatment for diabetes; human exposure can be toxic.

name: alloy
clinical_significance: A mixture of metals used in devices such as dental restorations and orthopaedic implants. Clinical effects depend on composition and placement; corrosion, wear, or metal sensitivity can occasionally cause local inflammation or device problems.

name: all-trans-retinol
clinical_significance: The alcohol form of vitamin A, important for vision, immunity, growth, and tissue maintenance. Deficiency can impair night vision and damage the eye surface, while excessive preformed vitamin A can harm the liver and a developing fetus.

name: allyl compounds
clinical_significance: A broad chemical group found in plants and industrial products. Some compounds are irritants or toxic after exposure, but clinical effects differ widely by substance and route.

name: almitrine
clinical_significance: A respiratory stimulant formerly used orally for chronic breathing problems. Oral almitrine was withdrawn in the European Union after review found risks of potentially lasting peripheral neuropathy and weight loss without an established role in current routine treatment.

name: alopecia
clinical_significance: Hair loss from the scalp or another part of the body. It may be nonscarring, in which the hair follicles remain and hair may regrow, or scarring, in which inflammation or injury destroys the follicles and can cause permanent hair loss. Causes include inherited pattern hair loss, autoimmune disease, hormonal changes, illness, medicines, nutritional problems, infection, repeated pulling, or other injury. The amount, pattern, and speed of hair loss vary with the cause.

name: alopecia areata
clinical_significance: An autoimmune, usually nonscarring hair-loss disorder in which immune cells attack anagen hair follicles. It often causes sharply demarcated smooth patches with exclamation-mark hairs and may involve the scalp, beard, eyebrows, or nails; regrowth is possible but relapses and extensive forms can occur.

name: alopecia totalis
clinical_significance: Complete loss of hair from the scalp, usually caused by alopecia areata. Hair may regrow, remain absent, or fall out again, and other autoimmune conditions may occur.

name: alopecia universalis
clinical_significance: Complete or near-complete loss of hair from the scalp and body, usually caused by extensive alopecia areata. Hair may regrow or recur unpredictably.

name: alpha radiation
clinical_significance: High-energy particles emitted during radioactive decay. They travel only a short distance outside the body, but inhaled or swallowed alpha-emitting material can deliver damaging radiation to nearby tissues and increase cancer risk.

name: alpha-amylases
clinical_significance: An enzyme that breaks down starch and is produced mainly by the pancreas and salivary glands. Blood or urine levels may help evaluate pancreatitis or salivary-gland disease, but abnormal results are not specific and are interpreted with symptoms and other tests.

name: alphacoronavirus
clinical_significance: A subfamily of coronaviruses that includes human viruses such as 229E and NL63, which commonly cause respiratory infections. Most cause mild illness, though infection can be more serious in infants or people with weakened immunity.

name: alpha-fetoprotein
clinical_significance: A protein made mainly by a developing fetus. Measuring it in maternal blood can help screen for some fetal conditions, while measuring it in adults can help assess selected liver or germ-cell tumours. An abnormal result does not establish a diagnosis.

name: alpha-globulin
clinical_significance: One of several groups of proteins in the liquid part of blood. These proteins carry substances and help with inflammation, clotting, and immune defence; their levels may change with liver disease, inflammation, or other conditions.

name: alpha-glucosidase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that breaks down complex sugars. Reduced activity of specific alpha-glucosidases causes rare disorders such as Pompe disease; medicines that inhibit intestinal alpha-glucosidase can slow carbohydrate absorption in diabetes.

name: alphaherpesvirinae
clinical_significance: A subfamily of herpesviruses that includes herpes simplex viruses and varicella-zoster virus. These infections can remain latent and reactivate; severe disease can include encephalitis, neonatal infection, or shingles-related complications.

name: alpha-lactalbumin
clinical_significance: A whey protein in human and other mammalian milk that supports infant nutrition. It is also a food allergen in some people, particularly as part of cow’s-milk protein allergy.

name: alpha-linolenic acid
clinical_significance: An essential plant-derived omega-3 fatty acid that the body can convert in limited amounts to longer-chain omega-3 fats. It contributes to dietary fat intake, but it is not a substitute for prescribed treatment of cardiovascular or inflammatory disease.

name: alpha-mannosidosis
clinical_significance: A rare inherited lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient alpha-mannosidase. It can affect the brain, bones, hearing, immunity, and other organs; enzyme replacement is available in some regions for selected symptoms.

name: alpharetrovirus
clinical_significance: A group of retroviruses best known for infecting birds and causing tumours in poultry. Alpharetroviruses are not recognized as a usual cause of human disease.

name: alpha-synuclein
clinical_significance: A protein found mainly in nerve cells that helps regulate nerve-cell functions. Abnormal forms can collect into clumps in Parkinson disease, Lewy-body dementia, and related disorders, although the clumps are not the only cause of these diseases.

name: alpha-thalassemia
clinical_significance: An inherited blood disorder, usually autosomal recessive, in which the body makes too little alpha-globin, a part of hemoglobin that carries oxygen. The condition may cause no symptoms, mild anemia, or severe anemia before or shortly after birth, depending on the number of affected alpha-globin genes.

name: alpha-tocopherol
clinical_significance: The main biologically active form of vitamin E in the body, an antioxidant obtained from food. Deficiency is uncommon but can cause nerve and muscle problems, especially with fat malabsorption or inherited transport disorders; excessive supplements can increase bleeding risk.

name: alphavirus
clinical_significance: A group of mosquito-borne viruses that includes chikungunya and several causes of encephalitis. Illness may cause fever, rash, and severe joint pain or, for some species, neurologic disease; geography and travel help guide testing.

name: Alport syndrome
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder of collagen that can cause progressive kidney disease, hearing loss, and changes in the eyes. It may be caused by changes in the \textit{COL4A3}, \textit{COL4A4}, or \textit{COL4A5} genes and may follow X-linked, autosomal dominant, or autosomal recessive inheritance.

name: alprazolam
clinical_significance: A benzodiazepine medicine used for anxiety and panic disorder. It calms brain activity but can cause sleepiness, impaired coordination, dependence, and dangerous slowing of breathing, especially with opioids or alcohol.

name: alprostadil
clinical_significance: A prostaglandin medicine used as an injection for erectile dysfunction and in newborns with certain heart defects to keep the ductus arteriosus open before surgery. Injection for erectile dysfunction can cause prolonged erection or priapism.

name: Alstrom syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder caused by changes in the ALMS1 gene. It may cause progressive vision and hearing loss, obesity, diabetes or insulin resistance, heart disease, and kidney or liver problems.

name: alteplase
clinical_significance: A clot-dissolving medicine used in selected emergencies, including acute ischaemic stroke, massive pulmonary embolism, and some heart attacks. It can cause severe or fatal bleeding, so clinicians assess eligibility and monitor closely.

name: altered consistency
clinical_significance: Describes a change in the texture or firmness of a substance, such as stool, sputum, or a tissue specimen. Its clinical meaning depends on what has changed and the accompanying symptoms or test findings.

name: alternaria
clinical_significance: A common outdoor and indoor mould whose spores can trigger allergic rhinitis or asthma. It can rarely cause invasive infection, mainly in people with severe immune suppression or damaged lungs.

name: alternative splicing
clinical_significance: Alternative splicing allows one gene to produce different RNA and protein forms; errors can cause inherited disease or alter cancer behavior and may affect molecular test interpretation.

name: altitude
clinical_significance: Exposure to high elevation can cause acute mountain sickness, with headache, nausea, dizziness, and fatigue. Rapid ascent can rarely lead to life-threatening brain or lung swelling; gradual ascent and prompt descent for severe symptoms reduce risk.

name: altretamine
clinical_significance: An anticancer medicine used for selected persistent or recurrent ovarian cancer. It can suppress blood-cell production and cause nausea or nerve effects, so treatment requires specialist oversight and blood-count monitoring.

name: alu element
clinical_significance: A repetitive DNA sequence that makes up a substantial part of the human genome and can copy itself into new locations. Rare insertions can disrupt genes and cause disease; Alu variation is also studied in human ancestry and genetic research.

name: aluminum
clinical_significance: A metal found in medicines, food, water, and some medical products. People with healthy kidneys usually remove small absorbed amounts, but aluminium can accumulate in advanced kidney disease and affect bone or the nervous system.

name: aluminum hydroxide
clinical_significance: A medicine used as an antacid and, in selected people with kidney disease, to bind phosphate in the gut. It can cause constipation and reduce absorption of other medicines; prolonged use may allow aluminium to build up, especially when kidney function is poor.

name: aluminum oxide
clinical_significance: A hard ceramic material used in dental restorations and some joint implants. Its clinical importance is mainly as a durable biomaterial; rarely, wear, fracture, or local tissue reaction can affect an implant.

name: alveolar adenoma
clinical_significance: A very rare, usually benign lung tumour often found as an incidental nodule on imaging. It can resemble other lung tumours, so the diagnosis depends on pathology and may affect whether surgery or imaging follow-up is appropriate.

name: alveolar air
clinical_significance: The mixture of gases inside the lung air sacs, where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it. Changes in alveolar gas exchange occur in conditions such as pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, or acute respiratory distress.

name: alveolar macrophage
clinical_significance: An immune cell that lives in the lung air sacs and removes inhaled dust, microbes, and damaged cells. It also helps regulate inflammation in the lungs.

name: alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma
clinical_significance: A cancer of immature muscle-forming cells, usually affecting children or adolescents. It may arise in the limbs, trunk, head, or neck and can spread early to lymph nodes, lungs, bones, or other tissues.

name: alveolar ridge
clinical_significance: The bony and soft-tissue ridge that supports the teeth and remains after teeth are lost. Its shape and bone loss can affect denture fit, chewing, and planning for dental implants.

name: alveoloplasty
clinical_significance: A dental operation that reshapes or smooths the jaw ridge, often after tooth removal or before dentures. It can improve the fit of a prosthesis, but as with other oral surgery it carries risks such as pain, bleeding, infection, or delayed healing.

name: alveolus
clinical_significance: One of the microscopic air sacs at the ends of the lung airways. Oxygen passes from an alveolus into the blood and carbon dioxide passes from the blood into it.

name: Alzheimer's
clinical_significance: A common possessive form of Alzheimer disease, a progressive neurodegenerative disorder causing worsening memory, thinking, behavior, and ability to perform daily activities.

name: amacrine cell
clinical_significance: A retinal nerve cell that helps process visual signals before they leave the eye. Amacrine-cell dysfunction or loss can contribute to impaired retinal signalling in some eye diseases, but it is not usually assessed as a standalone clinical test.

name: amantadine
clinical_significance: A medicine used to improve movement symptoms in Parkinson disease and to reduce some medication-related involuntary movements. It can cause confusion, hallucinations, dizziness, or swelling; it is no longer recommended for routine influenza treatment because circulating influenza A strains are resistant.

name: amantadine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: The hydrochloride salt form of amantadine, used for Parkinson disease symptoms and some related movement problems. It may cause confusion or hallucinations, particularly in older adults or people with kidney impairment.

name: amatuximab
clinical_significance: An investigational antibody targeting mesothelin, studied mainly for cancers such as mesothelioma. It is not an established standard treatment; benefit and safety depend on ongoing clinical research.

name: amaurosis fugax
clinical_significance: Sudden, temporary loss of vision in one eye, often described as a curtain or shade, caused by briefly reduced blood flow to the retina or optic nerve. It can warn of vascular disease or stroke risk.

name: ambenonium chloride
clinical_significance: An acetylcholinesterase-inhibiting medicine used to relieve muscle weakness in myasthenia gravis. Excess effect can cause abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, sweating, excess saliva, or worsening weakness, so dosing requires clinical supervision.

name: ambiguous genitalia
clinical_significance: External genital anatomy that does not have typical male or female features. It usually reflects a difference in sex development, which may involve chromosomes, hormones, or the formation of reproductive organs.

name: amblyopia
clinical_significance: Reduced vision in one eye (rarely both) resulting from abnormal brain visual processing during early childhood, occurring despite a structurally normal eye. When the brain receives conflicting, blurry, or misaligned visual signals, it suppresses input from the weaker eye and favors the dominant eye. Common causes include crossed or misaligned eyes (strabismic amblyopia), unequal refractive focusing power between the eyes (anisometropic amblyopia), or physical blockage of the visual axis (depriva

name: ambulance
clinical_significance: An emergency vehicle and service that provides care and transport before arrival at a hospital. Promptly calling emergency services for stroke, severe breathing problems, major injury, or loss of consciousness can shorten time to lifesaving treatment.

name: amdinocillin
clinical_significance: An older name for mecillinam, a penicillin-family antibiotic active against selected Gram-negative bacteria. It is used mainly for urinary infections, and the choice of treatment depends on the likely organism and susceptibility.

name: amdinocillin pivoxil
clinical_significance: An oral prodrug of mecillinam, a penicillin-family antibiotic used for selected uncomplicated urinary tract infections. In the United States it is approved for adult women with infection caused by susceptible bacteria; unnecessary use contributes to antibiotic resistance.

name: amebiasis
clinical_significance: An infection caused by the parasite Entamoeba histolytica, usually spread by swallowing contaminated food, water, or material from contaminated hands. It may cause no symptoms, diarrhea, abdominal pain, or bloody diarrhea. In some cases, the infection can spread from the intestine to the liver.

name: amebic colitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the large intestine caused by Entamoeba histolytica. It may cause abdominal pain, diarrhoea, bloody stools, or fever.

name: amelanotic melanoma
clinical_significance: A melanoma that produces little or no dark pigment and may appear pink, red, or skin-coloured instead of black or brown. Its appearance can delay recognition; diagnosis requires examination of a tissue sample.

name: amelia
clinical_significance: A rare birth condition in which one or more arms or legs are completely absent. It may occur alone or with other developmental differences.

name: ameloblast
clinical_significance: A cell that forms tooth enamel during development. Damage or genetic disruption of ameloblasts can result in thin, weak, or absent enamel, and related cells can give rise to rare jaw tumours.

name: ameloblastic carcinoma
clinical_significance: A rare malignant tumour arising from enamel-forming tissue, usually in the jaw. Unlike the more common benign ameloblastoma, it can invade nearby structures or spread, so it requires specialist treatment and follow-up.

name: ameloblastoma
clinical_significance: A usually slow-growing tumour that begins in cells involved in tooth development, most often in the lower jaw. It can grow into nearby bone, deform the jaw, and return after treatment.

name: amelogenesis
clinical_significance: The process by which developing teeth form and harden enamel, the tough outer covering of each tooth. Problems with this process can make enamel thin, weak, discoloured, or easily damaged.

name: amelogenesis imperfecta
clinical_significance: A group of inherited conditions in which tooth enamel does not form normally. The enamel may be thin, soft, rough, discoloured, or easily worn on most or all teeth.

name: amelogenin
clinical_significance: A protein produced by developing tooth-forming cells and involved in enamel formation. Changes in the AMELX gene can cause inherited enamel defects; amelogenin testing also has specialized applications in forensic biology.

name: amenorrhea
clinical_significance: Absence of menstrual periods. Primary amenorrhea means menstruation has not started by the expected age; secondary amenorrhea means periods stop after they have begun. It may be normal during pregnancy, breastfeeding, or menopause, or may result from hormonal, reproductive, medical, nutritional, or exercise-related conditions.

name: americium
clinical_significance: A radioactive metal whose isotope americium-241 is used in some smoke detectors and industrial devices. The sealed source presents very little risk during normal use, but inhaling or swallowing americium dust can expose tissue to damaging alpha radiation.

name: amide
clinical_significance: A common chemical linkage found in proteins and many medicines. The term alone has no specific clinical meaning; the effects depend on the particular amide-containing substance.

name: amidines
clinical_significance: A chemical group found in some medicines and biologically active compounds. Clinical effects depend on the specific drug or substance rather than on amidines as a group.

name: amifampridine
clinical_significance: A medicine that improves nerve-to-muscle signalling in Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome and can reduce muscle weakness. It can increase seizure risk and requires careful dosing and monitoring.

name: amifostine
clinical_significance: A medicine that can reduce kidney injury from cisplatin and reduce dry mouth in selected patients receiving head-and-neck radiotherapy. It can cause severe low blood pressure, nausea, and low calcium, and is given with clinical monitoring.

name: amikacin
clinical_significance: An aminoglycoside antibiotic used for serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria, including some resistant Gram-negative infections. It can cause kidney injury and sometimes permanent hearing or balance damage, so dosing and organ function are monitored.

name: amiloride
clinical_significance: A potassium-sparing diuretic used for high blood pressure, heart failure, or fluid retention, sometimes with other diuretics. It can cause dangerously high blood potassium, especially in kidney disease or when combined with other potassium-raising medicines.

name: aminacrine
clinical_significance: An older acridine dye used as a topical antiseptic. It has largely been superseded by other antiseptics and is not a routine modern treatment for infection.

name: amine
clinical_significance: A broad class of nitrogen-containing chemicals that includes neurotransmitters, amino acids, and many medicines. Health effects depend on the specific amine; the chemical class alone does not indicate a disorder.

name: amino acid
clinical_significance: A small molecule used to build proteins. Amino acids also support energy production and other chemical processes in the body.

name: amino acid biosynthesis
clinical_significance: The set of biochemical pathways by which cells make amino acids. Inherited defects in particular pathways can cause metabolic disease, while some medicines exploit amino-acid synthesis differences between microbes, cancer cells, and human cells.

name: amino alcohols
clinical_significance: A broad chemical group that includes some medicines and naturally occurring signalling molecules. Clinical effects differ by compound, so the class name alone does not identify a treatment or health risk.

name: amino sugar
clinical_significance: A sugar molecule containing nitrogen that is part of larger structures such as cartilage components and bacterial cell walls. Amino sugars are relevant to tissue biology and to some antimicrobial drug targets, but the term itself is not a diagnosis.

name: aminocarb
clinical_significance: A carbamate pesticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Significant exposure can cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, diarrhoea, pinpoint pupils, muscle twitching, seizures, or breathing failure and requires urgent toxicology assessment.

name: aminoglutethimide
clinical_significance: A medicine that suppresses production of adrenal and sex hormones, formerly used for selected breast cancers and adrenal disorders. It is now rarely used because of toxicity and the availability of newer treatments; it can cause adrenal insufficiency and other serious adverse effects.

name: aminolevulinic acid
clinical_significance: A precursor used in photodynamic treatment of actinic keratoses and in specialised fluorescence-guided procedures. Light activates a product formed from aminolevulinic acid, so treated areas become temporarily light-sensitive and require precautions.

name: aminophylline
clinical_significance: A medicine that opens the airways, used less often now for asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease because safer treatments are available. Its dose is difficult to predict, and high blood levels can cause dangerous vomiting, abnormal heart rhythms, or seizures.

name: aminopropionitrile
clinical_significance: A toxic chemical that blocks enzymes involved in collagen cross-linking and is used experimentally to study connective-tissue disease. Exposure can damage connective tissue and blood vessels; it is not a human medicine.

name: aminopterin
clinical_significance: A folate-blocking drug studied and formerly used as chemotherapy. It can severely disrupt fetal development and cause pregnancy loss, so exposure during pregnancy is highly dangerous.

name: aminopyridines
clinical_significance: A group of potassium-channel-blocking medicines that improve nerve signalling. Amifampridine treats Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome, while dalfampridine can improve walking in some people with multiple sclerosis; these medicines can increase seizure risk.

name: aminosalicylic acid
clinical_significance: Usually refers to para-aminosalicylic acid, an antibiotic used in combination regimens for drug-resistant tuberculosis. It can cause gastrointestinal effects and requires specialist supervision; it is different from mesalamine, an anti-inflammatory bowel medicine.

name: amiodarone
clinical_significance: An antiarrhythmic medicine used to treat selected abnormal heart rhythms, including atrial fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia. It can affect the lungs, liver, thyroid, eyes, skin, nerves, and heart rhythm.

name: amiodarone hydrochloride
clinical_significance: The hydrochloride salt form of amiodarone, a potent antiarrhythmic used for selected serious heart rhythm disorders. Long-term treatment can injure the lungs, liver, thyroid, eyes, skin, or nerves and requires monitoring.

name: amitriptyline
clinical_significance: A tricyclic antidepressant that changes serotonin and noradrenaline signalling in the brain. It is also used for some nerve pain and migraine prevention; common effects include sleepiness, dry mouth, and constipation.

name: amitrole
clinical_significance: A herbicide that can interfere with thyroid hormone production. Its clinical importance is mainly toxicologic and occupational; exposure risk depends on dose and route.

name: amlodipine
clinical_significance: A calcium-channel blocker used to treat high blood pressure and angina. Common effects include ankle swelling, flushing, and dizziness; excessive blood-pressure lowering can cause faintness.

name: ammonia
clinical_significance: A nitrogen-containing waste product made when the body processes proteins. The liver normally changes it into urea for removal; high blood levels can affect brain function, especially in severe liver disease.

name: ammonium chloride
clinical_significance: A medicine that can acidify the blood or urine in selected situations, though safer alternatives are often preferred. Excess can cause serious metabolic acidosis, so use requires careful monitoring.

name: ammonium compounds
clinical_significance: A broad class of ammonium-containing chemicals, including disinfectants and industrial compounds. Some are corrosive or toxic if swallowed, inhaled, or applied to skin; clinical effects depend on the specific compound and exposure.

name: amnesia
clinical_significance: Loss or impairment of memory beyond ordinary forgetfulness. It may prevent a person from forming new memories, recalling past events, or doing both, and may result from brain injury, illness, medicines, or emotional trauma.

name: amniocentesis
clinical_significance: A procedure in which a thin needle removes a small sample of fluid from around the developing baby. The sample can be tested for genetic, chromosomal, or infection-related conditions.

name: amnioinfusion
clinical_significance: A procedure that adds sterile fluid to the sac around the developing baby, usually during labour, to reduce pressure on the umbilical cord or dilute thick meconium.

name: amnion
clinical_significance: The thin inner membrane forming the fluid-filled sac around the developing baby. It holds the amniotic fluid and helps protect the fetus during pregnancy.

name: amnioscope
clinical_significance: An instrument formerly inserted through the cervix to examine the amniotic fluid and membranes. It is rarely used now because ultrasound is safer and more practical.

name: amniotic band
clinical_significance: A strand of amniotic membrane that can wrap around a developing body part, restricting growth or blood flow and causing a deformity or loss of tissue.

name: amniotic fluid
clinical_significance: The liquid surrounding the developing baby inside the amniotic sac. It cushions the baby, allows movement and growth, and helps maintain a stable environment during pregnancy. It is continually produced, swallowed, and replaced.

name: amodiaquine
clinical_significance: An antimalarial drug used in some combination treatments, usually with artesunate, for uncomplicated malaria. It can rarely cause serious blood or liver problems, so use is guided by local resistance patterns and medical supervision.

name: amoeba
clinical_significance: A broad group of single-celled organisms, some harmless and others capable of infection. Entamoeba histolytica causes intestinal amoebiasis and can spread to the liver; other amoebae can cause rare, severe brain or eye infections.

name: amoebozoa
clinical_significance: A major group of amoeboid microorganisms that includes Acanthamoeba and Balamuthia, which can rarely cause severe brain infection, and Acanthamoeba, which can cause painful corneal infection. These illnesses are uncommon but may be difficult to treat.

name: amonafide
clinical_significance: An investigational anticancer compound studied for effects on DNA and topoisomerase II. It is not a standard cancer treatment, and its clinical role depends on research findings.

name: amoxapine
clinical_significance: An antidepressant also used for some nerve pain. It can cause sleepiness, dry mouth, constipation, and low blood pressure; overdose may cause seizures, abnormal heart rhythms, or coma.

name: amoxicillin
clinical_significance: A penicillin antibiotic used for susceptible bacterial infections, including some ear, throat, chest, dental, and urinary infections. It does not treat viral illnesses and can cause allergic reactions or antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.

name: ampa receptor
clinical_significance: A receptor for glutamate, the main excitatory chemical messenger in the brain. Changes in AMPA-receptor signalling are studied in epilepsy and other neurologic disorders, and antibodies against the receptor can rarely cause autoimmune encephalitis.

name: ampere
clinical_significance: The SI unit of electric current. In clinical contexts it may appear in descriptions of medical-device output, but the unit itself is not a diagnosis or treatment.

name: amphetamine
clinical_significance: A stimulant medicine that increases certain chemical signals in the brain. It is used for selected attention, activity, or sleep disorders; misuse can cause dependence, high blood pressure, abnormal heart rhythms, or psychosis.

name: amphibians
clinical_significance: A diverse group of animals that can carry microbes such as Salmonella, which may spread to people through handling or contaminated surfaces. Some species also produce skin toxins that can cause illness after contact or ingestion.

name: amphotericin B
clinical_significance: A potent antifungal medicine used for life-threatening or severe fungal infections. It can cause infusion reactions and kidney injury, so clinicians monitor kidney function and blood salts during treatment.

name: ampicillin
clinical_significance: A penicillin antibiotic used for selected bacterial infections, including some infections of the blood, brain coverings, respiratory tract, and urinary tract. It is ineffective against viruses and may cause allergy or antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.

name: amprenavir
clinical_significance: An older HIV protease-inhibitor medicine that was used in combination antiretroviral therapy. It is no longer a commonly used treatment; HIV care now relies on more effective regimens with fewer interactions and adverse effects.

name: ampule
clinical_significance: A small sealed container, usually holding a single dose of medicine or solution. Correct handling and single-use practice help prevent contamination, medication errors, and accidental cuts from glass.

name: ampullary gland
clinical_significance: A gland near the male reproductive tract that contributes fluid to semen. Its secretions are part of normal reproductive physiology; the gland is not a common site of a distinct clinical disorder.

name: amputation
clinical_significance: Surgical removal of all or part of a limb, finger, toe, or other body part, often because of severe injury, infection, poor blood flow, or cancer. Traumatic amputation is tissue loss caused by an injury. The level removed depends on healthy tissue, blood supply, healing, and expected function.

name: amputation stump
clinical_significance: The part of a limb left after amputation. It may develop wound problems, infection, poor circulation, nerve pain, phantom-limb pain, or skin irritation from a prosthesis.

name: amrubicin
clinical_significance: An anticancer medicine used in some countries for selected cancers, including lung cancer. It can markedly suppress bone marrow and may affect the heart, so treatment requires specialist oversight and blood-count monitoring.

name: amsacrine
clinical_significance: An anticancer medicine that interferes with topoisomerase II and DNA function, used mainly in selected leukaemias. It can severely suppress bone marrow and may affect heart rhythm, requiring specialist monitoring.

name: amsilarotene
clinical_significance: An investigational synthetic retinoid studied for effects on cell growth and differentiation. It is not an established routine treatment, and clinical benefits and risks remain under evaluation.

name: amuvatinib
clinical_significance: An investigational kinase inhibitor studied in early trials for selected cancers. It is not an established standard treatment; its benefit and safety depend on clinical research.

name: amygdalin
clinical_significance: A plant compound also called laetrile when used in alternative cancer products. It has no proven cancer benefit and can release cyanide, causing potentially fatal poisoning, especially when taken by mouth.

name: amygdaloid
clinical_significance: A term for the amygdala, a group of brain structures involved in processing emotion, memory, and threat signals. It is relevant to some neurologic and psychiatric research but is not a diagnosis by itself.

name: amylase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that begins breaking down starch. It is made mainly by the salivary glands and pancreas and can be measured in blood or urine when pancreatic or salivary-gland disease is suspected.

name: amylin
clinical_significance: A hormone released with insulin from pancreatic beta cells that helps regulate after-meal blood sugar. An amylin analogue, pramlintide, is used with insulin for selected people with diabetes; amylin deposits are also found in the pancreas in type 2 diabetes.

name: amyloid
clinical_significance: An abnormal protein material that forms insoluble deposits in tissues. These deposits can interfere with the function of organs such as the kidneys, heart, nerves, liver, or brain.

name: amyloid neuropathy
clinical_significance: Nerve damage caused by amyloid deposits in or around peripheral nerves. It may cause numbness, tingling, burning pain, weakness, or problems with automatic body functions such as blood-pressure control.

name: amyloid protein
clinical_significance: A protein that can misfold and aggregate into amyloid deposits. The specific protein determines the type of amyloidosis and which organs are affected; identifying it is essential to diagnosis and treatment.

name: amyloidosis
clinical_significance: A group of diseases in which proteins fold abnormally, clump together, and form deposits called amyloid in tissues or organs. Amyloidosis may be localized to one site or systemic, affecting several organs such as the kidneys, heart, liver, nerves, or digestive tract. Major forms include light-chain (AL), serum amyloid A (AA), and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis; effects vary with the amyloid protein and organs involved.

name: amylopectin
clinical_significance: A branched form of starch that stores glucose in plants and is digested to provide dietary carbohydrate. Its medical relevance is mainly nutritional and metabolic rather than as a disease marker.

name: amyloplast
clinical_significance: A plant-cell structure that stores starch. Its relevance to human health is indirect, through the starch content of foods and their contribution to dietary carbohydrate.

name: amylose
clinical_significance: A form of starch that is broken down into glucose during digestion. It contributes to dietary carbohydrate and can affect post-meal blood glucose, especially in people with diabetes.

name: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
clinical_significance: A progressive disease in which the nerve cells controlling voluntary muscles gradually die. It causes worsening muscle weakness, stiffness, cramps, twitching, and wasting, often beginning in an arm, leg, or the muscles used for speaking and swallowing. It may lead to difficulty walking, speaking, swallowing, or breathing. Sensation is usually preserved, but some people develop changes in thinking or behavior. Most cases are not inherited and have no known cause. Also called ALS or Lou Gehrig dis

name: anabasine
clinical_significance: A toxic alkaloid found in tobacco and some related plants. It can contribute to nicotine-like poisoning and may be measured as a marker of tobacco exposure, including exposure to some nicotine-replacement products.

name: anabolism
clinical_significance: The set of body processes that use energy to build larger molecules from smaller ones, such as making proteins from amino acids or storing glucose as glycogen.

name: anaerobic
clinical_significance: Able to live, grow, or function without oxygen. Anaerobic bacteria can cause infections in deep wounds, abscesses, the mouth, abdomen, or pelvis.

name: anaerobic bacteria
clinical_significance: Bacteria that can grow without oxygen. Obligate anaerobes cannot use oxygen and may be harmed by it, while facultative anaerobes can grow with or without oxygen. Anaerobic bacteria normally live in places such as the mouth, intestine, and vagina. They can cause infections in deep wounds, abscesses, the abdomen, pelvis, or other tissues with low oxygen.

name: anaerobic coccus
clinical_significance: A group of round-shaped bacteria that grow without oxygen. Some species normally live on body surfaces but can contribute to deep abscesses, pelvic or abdominal infections, and wound infections when they enter normally sterile tissue.

name: anaerobiosis
clinical_significance: A condition or process in which oxygen is absent. It occurs in normal environments such as parts of the gut, but prolonged oxygen deprivation in human tissue can cause cell injury and organ damage.

name: anaerococcus
clinical_significance: A genus of anaerobic Gram-positive bacteria that can live on mucosal surfaces and sometimes cause opportunistic infections. Recovery from blood, abscesses, or another normally sterile site must be interpreted with the clinical findings.

name: anaerococcus hydrogenalis
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterium found among human-associated microbial communities. Its disease-causing role is not well established; detection alone, especially in a mixed sample, does not prove infection.

name: anaerococcus prevotii
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterium that has been recovered from vaginal, abscess, wound, and blood specimens. It can be an opportunistic cause of infection, but its significance depends on the sample site and accompanying clinical evidence.

name: anaerococcus tetradius
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterium reported in genital-tract and abscess specimens. It may contribute to polymicrobial infection, but isolation from a nonsterile site alone does not establish disease.

name: anaerococcus vaginalis
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterium reported in vaginal and wound specimens and occasionally in blood. It may act as an opportunistic pathogen when found in a compatible infection, but cultures must be interpreted in context.

name: anagrelide
clinical_significance: A medicine used to lower very high platelet counts in essential thrombocythaemia. It can cause palpitations, fluid retention, heart failure, bleeding, or pulmonary hypertension, so blood counts and cardiovascular symptoms are monitored.

name: anakinra
clinical_significance: An interleukin-1 blocker used for rheumatoid arthritis and certain rare autoinflammatory disorders. It can increase the risk of serious infection and lower white-cell counts; treatment is avoided during active serious infection.

name: anal canal
clinical_significance: The final part of the digestive tract, extending from the rectum to the anus. It contains muscles that control the passage of stool and has different nerve and blood supplies along its length.

name: anal carcinoma
clinical_significance: Cancer arising in the anal canal or anal margin, most often squamous-cell cancer associated with persistent high-risk human papillomavirus infection. It may cause bleeding, pain, itching, or a lump.

name: anal fissure
clinical_significance: A small tear in the lining of the anus, usually caused by hard stools, constipation, or repeated diarrhea. It can cause sharp pain during bowel movements and bright-red blood on the toilet paper.

name: anal mucositis
clinical_significance: Inflammation and open sores of the anal lining, often caused by radiation or chemotherapy. It can cause pain, burning, bleeding, discharge, and difficulty passing stool.

name: anal necrosis
clinical_significance: Death of tissue around the anus, anal canal, or nearby skin. It may result from severe infection, poor blood flow, injury, or radiation and can cause severe pain, skin discolouration, blisters, fever, or rapid worsening.

name: anal pain
clinical_significance: Pain around the anus or nearby skin. Common causes include a fissure, abscess, thrombosed haemorrhoid, muscle spasm, infection, or inflammation.

name: anal sac
