clinical_significance: A small gland and duct beside the anal opening, best known as a structure in dogs and other animals. Blockage or infection can cause painful swelling or an abscess; veterinary examination is needed for animal anal-sac disease.

name: analgesia
clinical_significance: Relief or absence of pain without necessarily causing unconsciousness. It may result from medicines, a nerve block, or another treatment; touch, pressure, or movement may still be felt.

name: analgesic
clinical_significance: A medicine or other treatment that relieves pain. Choice depends on the cause and severity; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can injure the stomach or kidneys, while opioids can cause sedation, dependence, and slowed breathing.

name: analog
clinical_significance: A substance, structure, or process that resembles another and has a similar function but is not identical in chemical makeup or structure.

name: analysis
clinical_significance: A careful examination of information, samples, measurements, symptoms, or clinical problems to identify patterns, understand causes, or support a medical decision.

name: analyte
clinical_significance: A substance measured in a laboratory test, such as glucose, a hormone, or a drug. Accurate identification and measurement of the analyte are essential for interpreting results and making clinical decisions.

name: analytic chemistry
clinical_significance: The branch of chemistry that identifies and measures substances in samples. It underlies clinical laboratory tests used to detect disease, monitor treatment, and assess organ function.

name: analytical balance
clinical_significance: A precision scale used to measure small masses in laboratory work. Calibration and correct weighing help ensure reliable test reagents, medicines, and research results.

name: anaphase
clinical_significance: A stage of cell division when duplicated chromosomes separate. Errors during this process can produce abnormal chromosome numbers, a feature of some cancers and developmental disorders.

name: anaphylaxis
clinical_significance: A sudden, potentially life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction that can involve the skin, airways, lungs, circulation, or gastrointestinal tract. It may cause hives or swelling, breathing difficulty, vomiting, dizziness, dangerously low blood pressure, or collapse; skin findings may be absent. Immediate intramuscular epinephrine and emergency medical care are required.

name: anaplasia
clinical_significance: Loss of the normal mature features and specialized function of cells. Anaplastic cells may vary greatly in size and shape, have abnormal nuclei, and divide rapidly or unusually. Anaplasia is most often seen in high-grade cancers and usually suggests more aggressive behavior. It is different from metaplasia, in which one mature cell type changes into another cell type.

name: anaplastic astrocytoma
clinical_significance: An older term for a high-grade tumour arising from star-shaped supporting cells in the brain. Modern classification relies on its genetic features as well as its appearance; symptoms depend on its location.

name: anaplastic ependymoma
clinical_significance: A high-grade tumour arising from cells lining the brain’s fluid-filled spaces or the spinal canal. It can grow quickly and may obstruct the flow of cerebrospinal fluid.

name: anasarca
clinical_significance: Severe, widespread swelling caused by excess fluid under the skin and sometimes around organs. It can occur with serious heart, kidney, or liver disease or very low blood protein and may cause rapid weight gain or breathing difficulty.

name: anastasis
clinical_significance: A process in which some cells recover after activating parts of the programmed cell-death pathway. It is an emerging research topic because surviving cancer cells may contribute to treatment resistance or recurrence; it is not currently a routine clinical diagnosis.

name: anastrozole
clinical_significance: A medicine that lowers the body’s production of oestrogen. It is used mainly for hormone-sensitive breast cancer, especially after menopause.

name: anatomical conduit
clinical_significance: A natural or surgically created passage that carries air, fluid, tissue, or another structure between body regions, such as an airway, blood vessel, or surgical channel.

name: anatomical orifice
clinical_significance: A natural opening into or out of the body or through a body structure, such as the mouth, nostril, anus, urethra, or an opening of a blood vessel.

name: anatomist
clinical_significance: A scientist or health professional who studies the structure of the human or animal body, including its organs, tissues, blood vessels, nerves, and their relationships.

name: anatomy
clinical_significance: The study of body structure and how its parts relate to one another. It includes visible structures, tissues and cells seen with magnification, and how the body develops.

name: ancestim
clinical_significance: A recombinant stem-cell factor formerly used with a growth factor to mobilize blood-forming stem cells before collection for transplantation. Use is limited by allergic and mast-cell reactions, and availability varies by country.

name: ancillary study
clinical_significance: A supplemental research project that uses data, samples, or participants from a larger study to investigate an additional question. It can extend scientific findings but does not usually provide direct clinical care to an individual participant.

name: ancitabine
clinical_significance: An anticancer prodrug that is converted in the body to cytarabine, a medicine that blocks DNA replication. It has been studied for leukaemia and other cancers but is not a routine current treatment.

name: ancrod
clinical_significance: A defibrinogenating enzyme derived from snake venom that was investigated as a way to reduce blood clotting, including in stroke. It is not a standard approved treatment; clinical use would carry serious bleeding risk.

name: ancylostoma
clinical_significance: A genus of hookworms that includes species infecting humans and animals. Human intestinal infection can cause blood loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, abdominal symptoms, and poor growth, especially with heavy infection.

name: ancylostoma caninum
clinical_significance: A hookworm of dogs and cats that can infect people. Larvae most often cause intensely itchy, winding skin tracks called cutaneous larva migrans; rarely, deeper migration causes intestinal inflammation.

name: ancylostomatoidea
clinical_significance: A superfamily of hookworms that includes parasites of humans and animals. Human infection by intestinal species can cause chronic blood loss and iron-deficiency anaemia, while animal species more often cause skin larva migrans.

name: ancylostomiasis
clinical_significance: A parasitic nematode infection caused by species of the genus \textit{Ancylostoma} (such as \textit{Ancylostoma duodenale}), acquired through transcutaneous penetration of infective larvae from contaminated soil, characteristically leading to chronic intestinal blood loss, iron deficiency anemia, and hypoproteinemia.

name: Andersen syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder, usually caused by changes in the KCNJ2 gene, that can combine episodes of muscle weakness with abnormal heart rhythms. Because arrhythmias may be serious, evaluation includes cardiac monitoring as well as assessment of periodic paralysis.

name: androgen
clinical_significance: A hormone such as testosterone that helps regulate sexual development, fertility, muscle, bone, and hair growth in people of all sexes.

name: androgen excess
clinical_significance: Abnormally high levels or effects of androgen hormones. It may cause acne, increased facial or body hair, scalp hair loss, irregular periods, infertility, or a deeper voice, especially in females.

name: androgen insufficiency
clinical_significance: A level or effect of androgen hormones that is too low for normal body function. Symptoms may include reduced sexual desire, erectile difficulty, infertility, low energy, reduced muscle mass, or weaker bones.

name: androgen receptor
clinical_significance: A protein in cells that binds testosterone and related hormones. This allows the hormones to influence sexual development, reproduction, muscle, bones, hair, and some cancers.

name: androgen suppression
clinical_significance: Lowering the production of androgen hormones or blocking their action in the body. It is used mainly for some hormone-sensitive cancers, especially prostate cancer, and can cause hot flushes, sexual problems, bone loss, weight change, and metabolic effects.

name: androstane
clinical_significance: A chemical family of steroid compounds related to testosterone. Androstanes include hormones and their metabolites; specific compounds may be measured when evaluating steroid production or hormone-related disorders.

name: androstenediol
clinical_significance: A steroid hormone and intermediate in the production of testosterone and oestrogens. Its levels may be assessed in specialised endocrine testing, but interpretation depends on age, sex, symptoms, and other hormone measurements.

name: androstenedione
clinical_significance: A steroid hormone precursor made mainly by the adrenal glands and gonads. Blood levels may help evaluate excess androgen production, including polycystic ovary syndrome or adrenal disorders, but do not establish a diagnosis alone.

name: androsterone
clinical_significance: A metabolite of testosterone and other androgens found in urine. Measurements can help assess steroid metabolism in specialised endocrine or anti-doping investigations, but are interpreted with other hormone tests.

name: anemia
clinical_significance: A lower-than-normal amount of haemoglobin in the blood, often with too few red blood cells. Because haemoglobin carries oxygen, anemia can reduce the oxygen delivered to body tissues. It may cause tiredness, weakness, shortness of breath, or dizziness, though mild anemia may cause no symptoms. Causes include blood loss, reduced red-cell production, or increased red-cell breakdown. Evaluation usually starts with a complete blood count, and treatment depends on the cause.

name: anencephaly
clinical_significance: A serious neural tube birth defect in which the upper part of the neural tube fails to close during the first weeks of pregnancy. As a result, much of the brain, especially the forebrain, and parts of the skull and scalp do not develop. It is usually detected before birth and is fatal; most affected babies are stillborn or die shortly after birth. There is no treatment that can correct the defect.

name: anesthesia
clinical_significance: A medically controlled loss of feeling caused by medicines during a procedure. Anesthetic medicines mainly block nerve signals, especially pain signals, from reaching the brain. Local anesthesia numbs a small area while the person remains awake. Regional anesthesia blocks nerves supplying a larger part of the body and may be used while the person remains awake. General anesthesia also changes brain activity to cause controlled unconsciousness. Before modern anesthesia, surgery was extremely pain

name: anesthesiologist
clinical_significance: A doctor trained to provide anesthesia and manage pain, breathing, blood pressure, and other vital functions during procedures. Anesthesiologists also assess patients before surgery and may treat critical illness or severe pain.

name: anesthesiology
clinical_significance: The medical specialty covering anesthesia, monitoring and support of vital functions during procedures, care before and after surgery, critical care, and treatment of acute or chronic pain.

name: anesthetic
clinical_significance: A medicine that reduces pain or awareness during a procedure. Local, regional, and general anaesthetics have different effects; all require appropriate dosing and monitoring for complications such as low blood pressure, breathing problems, or allergic reactions.

name: anethole trithione
clinical_significance: A medicine used in some countries to stimulate saliva and relieve dry mouth (xerostomia), including in selected people with reduced salivary function. Its availability and evidence base vary, and the cause of dry mouth should also be assessed.

name: aneuploidy
clinical_significance: An abnormal number of whole chromosomes in a cell, caused by an error during cell division. A cell may have an extra or missing chromosome, as in trisomy 21, and this can affect development or pregnancy.

name: aneurysm
clinical_significance: An abnormal bulge or widening in an artery caused by weakness in its wall. Many aneurysms cause no symptoms. Depending on their location and size, they may enlarge, press on nearby structures, or rupture and cause serious bleeding.

name: Angelman syndrome
clinical_significance: A genetic disorder affecting brain development and function, usually because the maternal copy of the \textit{UBE3A} gene is missing or inactive. It causes severe developmental delay, very limited speech, movement and balance problems, seizures, and a characteristic happy or excitable manner.

name: anger
clinical_significance: An emotional response to frustration, unfairness, danger, or a perceived threat. It may range from irritation to intense rage; persistent or uncontrollable anger can affect relationships, safety, and health.

name: angina pectoris
clinical_significance: Chest discomfort caused by temporarily reduced blood flow to the heart muscle, usually from coronary artery disease. New, worsening, or persistent chest pain can signal a heart attack and needs urgent assessment.

name: angiocardiography
clinical_significance: Imaging of the heart and major blood vessels, usually after contrast material is given. X-ray, CT, or MRI can show the heart chambers, valves, narrowed vessels, leaks, abnormal connections, or other structural problems.

name: angioedema
clinical_significance: Sudden, localized swelling of deeper skin or mucosal tissues, often affecting the lips, eyelids, tongue, throat, hands, feet, or bowel wall. Histamine-mediated episodes may occur with hives and itching, whereas bradykinin-mediated forms usually lack hives; tongue or throat swelling, voice change, or breathing difficulty is an emergency.

name: angiofibroma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous growth made of blood vessels and fibrous tissue. It commonly appears as a small facial papule in adolescents or, in a different form, as a vascular tumour in the back of the nose that may cause blockage or nosebleeds.

name: angiogenesis inhibition
clinical_significance: Preventing or slowing the growth of new blood vessels. This can limit a tumor’s blood supply or reduce harmful vessel growth in some eye diseases. Treatment may increase the risk of high blood pressure, bleeding, or delayed wound healing.

name: angiogenesis inhibitor
clinical_significance: A therapeutic agent that inhibits the formation of new blood vessels, predominantly by antagonizing vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) or its receptors, used in oncology to restrict tumor blood supply and in ophthalmology to treat neovascular macular degeneration.

name: angiography
clinical_significance: Imaging of blood vessels to show their shape and blood flow. It may use X-rays with injected contrast material, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or a catheter placed inside a blood vessel. Angiography can show narrowing, blockage, aneurysms, abnormal connections, bleeding, or other vascular abnormalities; catheter angiography may also allow treatment during the same procedure.

name: angioid streak
clinical_significance: Irregular dark lines caused by breaks in a tough layer beneath the retina. They may bleed or allow abnormal blood vessels to grow, reducing vision, and can be associated with some inherited disorders.

name: angiokeratoma
clinical_significance: Angiokeratomas are usually benign vascular skin papules that may bleed after friction; widespread lesions can be associated with Fabry disease or other systemic disorders and may warrant evaluation.

name: angiolipoma
clinical_significance: A usually benign fatty lump containing many small blood vessels, often found beneath the skin of an arm or trunk. It may be tender or painful; pathology may be needed to distinguish it from other soft-tissue tumours.

name: angiomatosis
clinical_significance: An abnormal proliferation of blood vessels in multiple sites or tissues. Some forms occur with genetic syndromes, while bacillary angiomatosis is a treatable infection seen especially in people with severe immune suppression.

name: angiomyolipoma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous kidney tumour made of blood vessels, muscle, and fat. It may occur alone or with tuberous sclerosis and can bleed, especially when large.

name: angiomyoma
clinical_significance: A usually benign tumour made of smooth muscle cells around blood vessels, often arising in the skin. It may be painful, especially with cold or pressure, and can be mistaken for other small skin nodules.

name: angioplasty
clinical_significance: A catheter procedure used to widen a narrowed or blocked blood vessel, most often an artery. A catheter with a small, deflated balloon is guided to the narrowed area, usually with imaging. The balloon is inflated to widen the vessel, then deflated and removed. A stent may be placed to help keep the vessel open. Angioplasty is used in coronary and other arteries and, in some cases, veins.

name: angiopoietins
clinical_significance: A family of proteins that helps regulate blood-vessel development and stability. Angiopoietin signalling is important in conditions involving abnormal vessels and is studied as a target in cancer and vascular disease.

name: angioscopes
clinical_significance: An instrument used to view the inside of a blood vessel during a procedure. Direct vascular imaging can assist selected interventions, but angioscopy is uncommon because other imaging methods are generally more practical.

name: angiostatin
clinical_significance: A naturally occurring protein fragment that can inhibit the formation of new blood vessels. It has been studied as an anticancer strategy, but it is not an established routine treatment.

name: angiostrongylus
clinical_significance: A genus of parasitic worms that includes rat lungworm and species that cause abdominal angiostrongyliasis. Human infection can follow ingestion of contaminated raw produce or intermediate hosts and may cause severe neurologic or abdominal illness.

name: angiostrongylus cantonensis
clinical_significance: A parasitic worm, often called rat lungworm, that can cause eosinophilic meningitis in people after contaminated food exposure. Severe headache, neck stiffness, tingling, or neurologic symptoms after exposure require urgent medical assessment.

name: angiotensin
clinical_significance: A group of hormones that help regulate blood pressure and the body’s salt and water balance. Angiotensin II narrows blood vessels and signals the kidneys and adrenal glands to retain salt and water.

name: angiotensin i
clinical_significance: A mostly inactive hormone made from angiotensinogen. Angiotensin-converting enzyme changes it into angiotensin II, which narrows blood vessels and promotes salt and water retention.

name: angiotensin receptor
clinical_significance: A cell-surface protein that binds angiotensin II. Medicines called angiotensin-receptor blockers inhibit this pathway to treat high blood pressure, heart failure, and some kidney conditions.

name: angiotensinogen
clinical_significance: A liver-produced protein that is the starting material for angiotensin, a hormone system controlling blood pressure and fluid balance. Its concentration or genetic variants may relate to cardiovascular risk, but it is not usually measured as a stand-alone diagnostic test.

name: angle closure glaucoma
clinical_significance: A type of glaucoma in which the outer edge of the iris blocks the eye’s drainage angle. Fluid then builds up, causing eye pressure to rise and potentially damaging the optic nerve and vision. It may develop suddenly with severe eye pain, blurred vision, halos, headache, nausea, or vomiting, or develop slowly without symptoms.

name: angular cheilitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation, soreness, and cracking at one or both corners of the mouth. Moisture and saliva, yeast or bacterial infection, dentures, irritation, or iron and vitamin deficiencies can contribute.

name: anhedonia
clinical_significance: Reduced or absent ability to feel pleasure or interest in activities that were previously enjoyable. It can occur with depression, schizophrenia, substance use, and other conditions.

name: anhidrosis
clinical_significance: Absent or greatly reduced sweating. It may result from nerve damage, skin disease, dehydration, medicines, or an inherited condition. Without enough sweat, the body may overheat dangerously, especially during exercise or hot weather.

name: anhydrovinblastine
clinical_significance: A chemical related to the vinca alkaloid family and used as an intermediate in developing or producing anticancer medicines. It is not generally used as a stand-alone treatment.

name: anidulafungin
clinical_significance: An echinocandin antifungal medicine used for serious Candida infections, including bloodstream infection and some forms of oesophageal candidiasis. It is given intravenously and can rarely cause liver-test abnormalities or infusion reactions.

name: aniline
clinical_significance: An industrial chemical used to make dyes, rubber, and other products. It can be absorbed through the skin or lungs and may cause methemoglobinaemia, which reduces oxygen delivery; chronic exposure is linked to bladder cancer.

name: aniline mustard
clinical_significance: An alkylating mustard compound investigated as an anticancer drug. It damages DNA and is not a routine modern therapy; exposure to mustard compounds can also injure skin, eyes, and airways.

name: animal model
clinical_significance: A nonhuman system used to study disease or test a treatment before human trials. Animal models can reveal mechanisms and safety concerns, but their results do not always predict effects in people.

name: animal oviduct
clinical_significance: The egg-carrying tube of a female animal. It is relevant to veterinary reproduction and fertility; the human equivalent is the uterine (fallopian) tube.

name: anion
clinical_significance: A particle with a negative electrical charge. Important anions in body fluids include chloride, bicarbonate, and phosphate, which help maintain fluid balance, electrical activity, and the blood’s acid level.

name: aniridia
clinical_significance: A congenital, bilateral, complete or partial absence of the iris, typically caused by mutations in the PAX6 gene. It is accompanied by photophobia, nystagmus, reduced visual acuity, foveal hypoplasia, and an increased risk of early-onset glaucoma and cataracts, and may occur as part of the WAGR syndrome.

name: anisakiasis
clinical_significance: A parasitic infection acquired from raw or undercooked marine fish or squid. It can cause sudden abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or bowel inflammation and may also trigger allergy, rarely including anaphylaxis.

name: anisakis
clinical_significance: A genus of parasitic worms found in marine fish and squid. Eating larvae in raw or undercooked seafood can cause anisakiasis, with gastrointestinal symptoms or an allergic reaction.

name: anisakis simplex
clinical_significance: A marine parasite found in fish and squid that can infect people who eat raw or undercooked seafood. It may cause acute stomach or intestinal pain and can trigger allergic reactions even after the parasite has been killed.

name: anisocoria
clinical_significance: An unequal size of the pupils, the black centers of the eyes. In about 20\% of healthy people, a slight difference is natural and harmless. When abnormal, it is caused by eye injury, certain eye drops, or nerve disorders that prevent a pupil from widening or shrinking normally. Doctors test how the pupils react in bright light and darkness to identify the underlying cause.

name: anisocytosis
clinical_significance: Greater-than-usual variation in the size of red blood cells. It is a laboratory finding rather than a disease and may occur with iron deficiency, vitamin deficiency, or other types of anemia.

name: anisometropia
clinical_significance: A difference in the focusing power of the two eyes. It can cause unequal image size, blurred vision, eyestrain, or reduced development of vision in one eye during childhood.

name: anisopoikilocytosis
clinical_significance: Marked variation in both red-cell size and shape on a blood smear. It is a finding rather than a diagnosis and may occur in iron or vitamin deficiency, mixed anaemias, or other disorders affecting red-cell production.

name: ankle
clinical_significance: The joint connecting the lower leg and foot. It is formed mainly by the tibia, fibula, and talus and allows the foot to move up and down while ligaments provide stability.

name: ankle fracture
clinical_significance: A break in one or more bones forming the ankle, usually the tibia, fibula, or talus. It may cause pain, swelling, bruising, and inability to bear weight; displaced or unstable fractures need prompt assessment.

name: ankle joint
clinical_significance: The hinge-like joint between the lower ends of the tibia and fibula and the talus. It mainly moves the foot upward and downward and is supported by surrounding ligaments.

name: ankyloglossia
clinical_significance: Ankyloglossia can restrict tongue movement and interfere with infant latch or speech; treatment is based on functional problems, not appearance alone.

name: ankylosing spondylitis
clinical_significance: A long-term inflammatory arthritis that mainly affects the joints between the spine and pelvis (sacroiliac joints) and the spine itself. It usually causes lower-back or hip pain and stiffness that is worse after rest or inactivity and may improve with movement. Inflammation can reduce spinal movement and, in severe cases, cause vertebrae to fuse. The hips, ribs, knees, or feet may also be affected. Some people develop eye inflammation (uveitis), psoriasis, or inflammatory bowel disease. HLA-B27

name: ankylosis
clinical_significance: Abnormal reduction or complete loss of movement in a joint. It may result from fibrous scar tissue, bone fusion, injury, infection, chronic inflammation, or surgery. Fibrous ankylosis involves scar tissue, while bony ankylosis involves fusion of neighboring bones. In dentistry, ankylosis may describe fusion of a tooth root to the surrounding jawbone.

name: ankyrin
clinical_significance: A protein that connects selected cell-surface proteins to the cell’s internal support framework. It helps red blood cells keep their shape; inherited changes can make the cells fragile and cause anemia.

name: ankyrin repeat
clinical_significance: A repeated protein sequence structure found in many proteins, including ankyrin. Changes in genes containing ankyrin repeats can disrupt protein function, but the motif itself is not a clinical diagnosis.

name: annelida
clinical_significance: A group of segmented worms that includes earthworms and leeches. Leeches used in some surgical settings can relieve venous congestion, but uncontrolled leech attachment may cause prolonged bleeding or infection.

name: annexin
clinical_significance: A family of proteins involved in cell-membrane organization, inflammation, and blood clotting. Some annexins are studied as disease markers or treatment targets, but clinical significance depends on the specific protein and setting.

name: annul
clinical_significance: To formally cancel or invalidate an action, agreement, or finding. The word has no specific clinical meaning by itself.

name: annular pancreas
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which pancreatic tissue forms a ring around part of the duodenum, the first section of the small intestine. The ring may narrow the intestine and cause vomiting, abdominal swelling, or feeding problems.

name: anoikis
clinical_significance: A form of programmed cell death triggered when a cell loses attachment to its surrounding support. It helps prevent misplaced cells from surviving; cancer cells that evade anoikis may be better able to spread and form metastases.

name: anomia
clinical_significance: Difficulty finding or saying a familiar word, especially the name of an object or person, even though its meaning is known. It can occur after a stroke or with other brain or language disorders.

name: anopheles genus
clinical_significance: A genus of mosquitoes; females of some Anopheles species transmit malaria parasites to people. The species present and local conditions determine malaria transmission risk.

name: Anophthalmos
clinical_significance: Congenital absence of one or both eyes, often with a very small eye socket. It can cause profound visual impairment and may occur with other developmental or genetic conditions, so assessment includes eye and broader health evaluation.

name: anoplura
clinical_significance: A group of lice that includes human body lice. Body lice can cause itchy bites and spread epidemic typhus, trench fever, and louse-borne relapsing fever, particularly in crowded settings with limited access to clean clothing.

name: anorectal fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal tunnel between the anus or rectum and nearby skin or another organ. It often develops after an abscess or infection and may cause persistent drainage, pain, or repeated abscesses.

name: anorectal infection
clinical_significance: Infection of the anus, rectum, or nearby tissues. It may cause pain, swelling, discharge, fever, or difficulty passing stool and can lead to an abscess that requires drainage.

name: anorectal malformation
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the anus or rectum does not form normally or does not connect correctly to the skin. The opening may be absent, misplaced, or abnormally connected to another organ.

name: anorexia
clinical_significance: Loss or reduction of appetite. It can result from illness, pain, medicines, emotional distress, or other causes and is different from anorexia nervosa, an eating disorder.

name: anorexia nervosa
clinical_significance: A serious eating disorder involving persistent restriction of food, intense fear of gaining weight, and a distorted view of body size or shape. It can cause severe weight loss, malnutrition, slow heart rate, low blood pressure, and organ damage.

name: anorgasmia
clinical_significance: Persistent or repeated difficulty reaching orgasm or inability to reach orgasm despite adequate sexual stimulation. It may result from medicines, illness, hormonal changes, pain, stress, trauma, or relationship factors.

name: anosmia
clinical_significance: Complete loss of the sense of smell. It may follow a viral infection, blocked or inflamed nasal passages, head injury, medicines, toxic exposure, or a neurological or inherited disorder.

name: anosognosia
clinical_significance: Lack of awareness of, or inability to recognize, one’s own illness or neurological impairment. It can occur after certain brain injuries or strokes and is not simply deliberate denial.

name: anovulation
clinical_significance: Failure to release an egg from an ovary during a menstrual cycle. It can cause irregular or absent periods, abnormal bleeding, or infertility and may result from hormonal disorders, low body weight, stress, excessive exercise, or polycystic ovary syndrome.

name: anoxia
clinical_significance: Complete lack of oxygen reaching body tissues. It can quickly damage or kill cells, especially in the brain, heart, and kidneys, and may result from blocked blood flow, breathing failure, or severe poisoning.

name: ansamycins
clinical_significance: A family of antibiotics that includes rifampin, rifabutin, and rifapentine. These medicines are important in tuberculosis and selected other bacterial infections, but drug interactions and antimicrobial resistance require careful prescribing.

name: anserine
clinical_significance: A naturally occurring dipeptide found in skeletal muscle and some animal foods. Its clinical role in humans is not established, and it is not a routine diagnostic marker or treatment.

name: antacid
clinical_significance: A medicine that neutralizes stomach acid to relieve heartburn or indigestion. Antacids can interfere with absorption of other medicines, and aluminium- or magnesium-containing products may be unsuitable in significant kidney disease.

name: antazoline
clinical_significance: An antihistamine used in some topical eye preparations for allergic conjunctivitis and occasionally in other formulations. It can cause local irritation or sleepiness depending on route and should be used according to the product instructions.

name: ante cibus
clinical_significance: A medication instruction meaning before food or before a meal. Timing can affect how well a medicine is absorbed or tolerated; follow the specific prescription directions.

name: antepartum hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from the vagina during the second half of pregnancy and before birth. Causes include placenta previa, placental abruption, and problems with the cervix or vagina; any significant bleeding needs urgent assessment.

name: antepartum stillbirth
clinical_significance: Fetal death before delivery after a pregnancy has reached the locally defined gestational threshold for stillbirth. Evaluation may identify placental, maternal, fetal, or genetic causes and can guide care and counselling in future pregnancies.

name: anterior
clinical_significance: Relating to the front of the body or positioned nearer the front than another structure. The term is used to describe body parts, scan findings, injuries, and disease locations.

name: anterior chamber
clinical_significance: The fluid-filled space between the cornea and iris at the front of the eye. It contains aqueous fluid, which nourishes the cornea and lens and helps maintain eye pressure; impaired drainage can contribute to glaucoma.

name: anterior mediastinotomy
clinical_significance: A surgical opening through the front of the chest to reach the anterior mediastinum, often to obtain a tissue sample from a mass or lymph node. It can help diagnose or stage disease, including lung cancer, and carries risks such as bleeding, infection, or injury to nearby structures.

name: anterior mediastinum
clinical_significance: The front part of the lower mediastinum, located behind the sternum and in front of the heart sac. It contains fat, connective tissue, lymph nodes, and part of the thymus.

name: anterior uveitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation in the front part of the eye, usually involving the iris and sometimes nearby tissue. It can cause eye pain, redness, light sensitivity, blurred vision, and floating spots.

name: anthelmintic
clinical_significance: A medicine that kills or removes parasitic worms, used for infections such as intestinal worms or some tissue parasites. The appropriate drug depends on the parasite, and treatment may require evaluation for complications or reinfection.

name: anthocyanidins
clinical_significance: Plant pigments related to anthocyanins that contribute to red, purple, and blue colours in foods. Their biological effects are studied, but they are not established medicines or substitutes for treatment.

name: anthocyanin
clinical_significance: Plant pigments that give many foods red, purple, or blue colours. They are studied for antioxidant effects, but eating anthocyanin-rich foods has not been shown to treat disease; their value is mainly as part of a varied diet.

name: Anthozoa
clinical_significance: A class of marine animals that includes corals and sea anemones. Contact with some species can cause painful stings or skin irritation, and coral injuries can become infected.

name: anthracene
clinical_significance: An industrial chemical used to make dyes and other products. Exposure can irritate skin and airways; some forms or exposure routes may pose long-term cancer risks.

name: anthracosilicosis
clinical_significance: A lung disease caused by inhaling coal and silica dust, typically in mining or related work. It can cause lung scarring, chronic cough, and breathlessness, and may coexist with other occupational lung diseases.

name: anthracosis
clinical_significance: A benign, non-fibrotic form of pneumoconiosis characterized by the asymptomatic accumulation of inhaled carbon and soot pigment in the lung parenchyma, alveolar macrophages, and draining hilar lymph nodes, commonly seen in urban dwellers and cigarette smokers.

name: anthralin
clinical_significance: A topical medicine formerly used for psoriasis. It can slow skin-cell growth but often causes irritation and stains skin or clothing; newer therapies are more commonly used.

name: anthramycin
clinical_significance: An experimental antitumour antibiotic that binds DNA and can inhibit cell growth. It is not a routine clinical treatment.

name: anthraquinone
clinical_significance: A broad chemical group that includes compounds used in some stimulant laxatives and some anticancer medicines. Effects and risks vary; stimulant laxative misuse can cause diarrhoea and electrolyte disturbance.

name: anthrax
clinical_significance: A potentially life-threatening infection caused by Bacillus anthracis. Skin, inhaled, or intestinal exposure can cause rapidly progressive illness; prompt recognition and antibiotics are important, and exposed people may need preventive treatment.

name: anthrax disease
clinical_significance: A potentially fatal infection caused by Bacillus anthracis, acquired through spores entering the skin, lungs, or digestive tract. Treatment and post-exposure prevention are time-sensitive and should be directed by public-health and medical teams.

name: anthrax vaccine
clinical_significance: A vaccine used for adults with certain occupational or other high-risk exposures and, with antibiotics, in some post-exposure situations. It is not routinely recommended for the general population; eligibility depends on exposure risk and current public-health guidance.

name: anthropology
clinical_significance: The study of human cultures and social life, including how beliefs, resources, and institutions shape health and medical care. It can help clinicians and health systems understand barriers to care and differences in treatment practices.

name: anthropometry
clinical_significance: The measurement of body size and proportions, such as height, weight, waist size, limb length, and skinfold thickness. These measurements help assess growth, nutrition, and body composition.

name: antiandrogen therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that lowers androgen production or blocks androgen action, used especially for prostate cancer and some other hormone-sensitive conditions. Possible effects include sexual dysfunction, hot flushes, bone loss, fatigue, and metabolic changes.

name: antiangiogenesis therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that blocks the formation or growth of new blood vessels. It is used in some cancers and eye diseases; adverse effects can include high blood pressure, bleeding, blood clots, and delayed wound healing.

name: anti-anxiety agents
clinical_significance: Medicines used to reduce excessive anxiety or panic. Different medicines work in different ways and may cause sleepiness, dependence, or other side effects; the choice depends on the person and the condition.

name: anti-bacterial agent
clinical_significance: A substance or medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing. It does not treat viral infections, and unnecessary use can cause side effects and select for antibiotic resistance.

name: antibiotic
clinical_significance: A medicine that kills bacteria or inhibits their growth. The correct antibiotic depends on the infection and organism; unnecessary or incomplete use can cause adverse effects and promote resistance.

name: antibiotic prophylaxis
clinical_significance: Antibiotic use before or around a procedure, or in selected high-risk situations, to reduce the chance of infection. The drug and timing are chosen for the expected bacteria and patient risk; unnecessary prophylaxis can cause allergy, diarrhoea, or resistance.

name: antibiotic resistance
clinical_significance: The ability of bacteria to survive medicines that would normally kill them or stop their growth. Resistance can make infections harder to treat and is promoted by inappropriate or excessive antibiotic use.

name: antibody
clinical_significance: A protein made by the immune system that attaches specifically to a foreign substance, germ, toxin, or abnormal cell and may block it or mark it for removal.

name: antibody formation
clinical_significance: The immune system’s production of antibodies after encountering an antigen, infection, or vaccine. Antibodies can protect against future infection, but they can also target self-tissues or complicate transfusion, pregnancy, or transplantation.

name: antibody specificity
clinical_significance: The ability of an antibody to recognize its intended target rather than similar molecules. Specificity affects how well antibody-based tests and treatments work and whether cross-reactions produce misleading results or adverse effects.

name: antibody therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment using specially prepared antibodies to block, activate, or target a particular molecule or cell. It can be used for cancer, autoimmune disease, infection, inflammation, and other conditions.

name: anticachexia agent
clinical_significance: A medicine intended to reduce severe weight and muscle loss associated with chronic disease or cancer. Benefits vary by cause and drug; assessment of the underlying illness, nutrition, symptoms, and treatment goals remains central.

name: anticholesteremic agents
clinical_significance: Medicines that lower cholesterol or other blood lipids, especially to reduce cardiovascular risk. Statins are common examples; treatment choice depends on a person’s overall risk and may require monitoring for muscle symptoms or liver effects.

name: anticholinergic agent
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors. It may be used for conditions such as overactive bladder, motion sickness, or airway disease, but can cause dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, and confusion, especially in older adults.

name: anticoagulant
clinical_significance: A medicine that reduces blood clot formation, used to prevent or treat conditions such as atrial-fibrillation-related stroke or venous clots. The main risk is bleeding, and the need for monitoring depends on the drug.

name: anticonvulsant
clinical_significance: A medicine used to prevent or control seizures; some are also used for nerve pain, migraine, or mood disorders. Adverse effects vary and may include sedation, mood changes, severe rash, or pregnancy-related risks.

name: antidepressant
clinical_significance: A medicine used to treat depression and some other conditions, including anxiety, pain, or sleep problems. Benefits may take time; effects and safety risks differ by drug, and treatment should be reviewed if symptoms worsen or severe side effects occur.

name: antidiarrheal
clinical_significance: A medicine that reduces diarrhoea or its symptoms. It may be unsafe in bloody diarrhoea, high fever, or suspected invasive infection, and it does not replace fluid and electrolyte replacement.

name: antidote
clinical_significance: A substance that counteracts or limits the harmful effects of a poison. The correct antidote depends on the substance involved; some antidotes block the poison, remove it, or restore a chemical process disrupted by it.

name: antiemetic
clinical_significance: A medicine that prevents or relieves nausea and vomiting. Selection depends on the cause; some antiemetics can cause sleepiness, movement problems, or abnormal heart rhythms.

name: antifibrinolytic agent
clinical_significance: A medicine that slows the breakdown of blood clots, used to control bleeding in selected settings such as heavy menstrual bleeding or surgery. It can increase clotting risk in some patients and should be used for an appropriate indication.

name: antifungal agent
clinical_significance: A medicine that treats fungal infection by killing fungi or limiting their growth. Choice depends on the fungus and infection site; some drugs can injure the liver or kidneys or interact with other medicines.

name: antigen
clinical_significance: A substance or part of a substance that the immune system can recognize. It may come from a germ, toxin, transplanted tissue, or abnormal cell and can trigger antibodies or other immune responses.

name: antigen binding
clinical_significance: The attachment of an antibody or receptor to a particular antigen. Binding strength and selectivity affect immune responses, laboratory tests, and antibody-based treatments.

name: antigen presentation
clinical_significance: The process by which an immune or other cell displays small pieces of proteins on its surface for T cells to inspect. This helps the immune system recognize infections, abnormal cells, transplanted tissue, and sometimes the body’s own tissues.

name: antigen receptor
clinical_significance: A protein on an immune cell that recognizes a particular substance or protein fragment. B-cell receptors can bind whole substances, while T-cell receptors recognize fragments displayed by other cells.

name: antigenic variation
clinical_significance: Changes in a germ’s surface markers that help it avoid recognition by the immune system. Variation may happen gradually through mutations or suddenly when genetic material is exchanged between different strains.

name: antigen-presenting cell
clinical_significance: An immune cell that breaks proteins into small pieces and displays them on its surface so T cells can recognize them. Important antigen-presenting cells include dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells.

name: antihypertensive agent
clinical_significance: A medicine that lowers high blood pressure, reducing long-term risk of stroke, heart disease, and kidney damage. Different classes have different side effects and may be combined based on a person’s conditions and response.

name: anti-idiotype antibody
clinical_significance: An antibody that recognizes the antigen-binding region of another antibody. Anti-idiotype antibodies are used in research and vaccine development and may help investigate immune responses; they are not a general treatment class.

name: anti-infective agent
clinical_significance: A medicine or substance used against infection, including antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal, or antiparasitic agents. Effective treatment depends on the pathogen, infection site, and susceptibility, and unnecessary use can cause harm or resistance.

name: antileukemic agent
clinical_significance: A treatment that acts against leukaemia, including chemotherapy, targeted drugs, or immunotherapy. Effects depend on the leukaemia subtype and may include infection risk, low blood counts, infertility, or organ toxicity.

name: antilymphocyte serum
clinical_significance: A preparation of antibodies that suppresses lymphocytes, formerly used in some transplant settings. It can prevent rejection but carries risks of severe infection, infusion reactions, and serum sickness; modern products and protocols are more specific.

name: antimalarial
clinical_significance: A medicine used to prevent or treat malaria. The correct drug depends on the Plasmodium species, where the infection was acquired, pregnancy status, and drug resistance; malaria needs prompt diagnosis and treatment.

name: antimetabolite
clinical_significance: A substance that resembles a chemical needed by cells and interferes with the cell’s normal chemical reactions or DNA production. Some are used to treat cancer or suppress an overactive immune system.

name: antimitotic
clinical_significance: A medicine that stops cells from dividing by disrupting structures needed to separate chromosomes. Antimitotic drugs are used in cancer treatment but can also damage normal dividing cells, causing low blood counts, nerve symptoms, or hair loss.

name: antimony
clinical_significance: A metallic chemical element whose compounds can be poisonous. Some antimony compounds have been used to treat leishmaniasis; exposure can affect the heart, liver, kidneys, or nervous system.

name: antineoplastic
clinical_significance: Antineoplastic drugs treat cancer by killing or slowing malignant cells; many also injure normal tissues, so selection, monitoring, and supportive care depend on the specific medicine and tumor.

name: antineoplastic antibiotic
clinical_significance: An antibiotic that also damages cancer cells by interfering with DNA or other cell processes, such as doxorubicin or bleomycin. These drugs can cause serious organ-specific toxicity and are used with specialist monitoring.

name: antineoplaston agent
clinical_significance: An experimental cancer treatment promoted as a way to alter tumour-cell growth. The U.S. National Cancer Institute reports that antineoplastons are not FDA-approved, have no published randomized controlled trials showing benefit, and can cause serious side effects.

name: antinuclear autoantibody
clinical_significance: An antibody that reacts with components of a cell nucleus. It can occur in autoimmune diseases such as lupus, but also in healthy people; a positive result must be interpreted with symptoms and more specific tests.

name: antioxidant
clinical_significance: A substance that helps neutralize or limit damage from reactive molecules, including free radicals and some reactive oxygen or nitrogen species. The body makes antioxidant enzymes and obtains other antioxidants from food; high-dose supplements are not automatically beneficial and may be harmful or interact with treatment.

name: antiparasitic agent
clinical_significance: A medicine used to treat parasites, including worms, protozoa, or other organisms. Drug selection depends on the parasite and infection site, and some infections require treatment of close contacts or follow-up testing.

name: antiparkinson agent
clinical_significance: A medicine used to relieve movement symptoms in Parkinson disease or related conditions. Benefits and risks vary by drug; treatment may cause low blood pressure, sleepiness, hallucinations, or involuntary movements.

name: Antiphospholipid syndrome
clinical_significance: An autoimmune condition in which persistent antiphospholipid antibodies occur together with blood clots or certain pregnancy complications. Assessment uses the person’s medical history and blood tests; antibody positivity alone does not establish the syndrome, and positive tests generally need confirmation at least 12 weeks later.

name: antiplatelet agent
clinical_significance: A medicine that reduces platelet clumping to prevent arterial clots, such as heart attack or some strokes. It can increase bleeding and is selected according to a person’s cardiovascular risk and bleeding history.

name: antiporter activity
clinical_significance: The activity of a membrane protein that moves one substance across a cell membrane while moving another in the opposite direction. Antiporter defects can contribute to inherited or acquired disease, depending on the transporter and tissue.

name: antiprotozoal agent
clinical_significance: A medicine used to treat infections caused by protozoa, such as malaria or giardiasis. Drug choice depends on the organism and location of infection; resistance and pregnancy can affect treatment selection.

name: antipsychotic agent
clinical_significance: A medicine used for psychosis, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and sometimes severe agitation or other symptoms. Possible harms include sedation, weight and blood-sugar changes, movement disorders, and heart-rhythm effects; benefits and risks require review.

name: antipyretic
clinical_significance: A medicine that lowers fever and may ease related discomfort. Acetaminophen and ibuprofen are common examples. Aspirin is generally avoided in children and teenagers with viral illnesses because of the risk of Reye syndrome.

name: antipyrine
clinical_significance: An older pain- and fever-relieving medicine, also called phenazone. It is not widely used in many countries; safety concerns and approved uses depend on the formulation and location.

name: antiretroviral therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment of HIV infection with a combination of medicines that block several steps in HIV reproduction. It lowers the amount of virus, protects immune function, reduces illness, and greatly lowers the chance of sexual transmission when the virus remains undetectable.

name: antirheumatic agents
clinical_significance: Medicines used to reduce joint inflammation, pain, and long-term damage in rheumatic disease. Some modify the immune system and can raise infection or organ-toxicity risks, so monitoring depends on the drug.

name: antisense oligonucleotide
clinical_significance: A short synthetic strand of nucleic acid designed to bind a specific RNA and alter its processing or expression. Antisense medicines can treat selected genetic or neuromuscular diseases, but may require repeated injections and laboratory monitoring.

name: antisense RNA
clinical_significance: An RNA sequence that pairs with another RNA molecule and can reduce or change its activity. This mechanism is used in molecular research and underlies some gene-targeted therapies.

name: antisense therapy
clinical_significance: A treatment that uses a designed nucleic-acid sequence to bind a target RNA and change how a gene’s message is processed or translated. It is used for selected uncommon diseases; effects and risks depend on the medicine and delivery route.

name: antisepsis
clinical_significance: Use of a chemical product on living skin or tissue to reduce harmful microorganisms and lower infection risk. It does not make tissue completely sterile and must be used in a way that avoids injury.

name: antiserum
clinical_significance: Blood serum containing antibodies against a specific germ, toxin, or other substance. It can provide temporary immune protection or help neutralize a toxin.

name: antisocial behavior
clinical_significance: Behaviour that violates social expectations or rules. It is a descriptive term rather than a psychiatric diagnosis; persistent harmful behaviour should be assessed in its developmental, social, and mental-health context.

name: antisocial personality
clinical_significance: A long-term pattern of disregarding other people’s rights, safety, rules, and responsibilities, often including deceit, impulsive behaviour, aggression, or lack of remorse.

name: antispasmodic
clinical_significance: A medicine that reduces involuntary muscle or intestinal spasms. Some act on the nervous system and can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, or drowsiness.

name: antispermatogenic agents
clinical_significance: A medicine or chemical that reduces sperm production. It may be used in research or occur as a harmful effect of chemotherapy, hormones, or toxic exposures; fertility effects may persist after exposure.

name: antithrombin
clinical_significance: A natural blood protein that slows clotting by blocking thrombin and other clotting proteins, especially factor Xa. Too little antithrombin, whether inherited or acquired, increases the risk of clots in veins.

name: antithrombin iii
clinical_significance: An older name for antithrombin, a protein that limits blood clotting. Inherited or acquired deficiency raises the risk of venous clots; antithrombin concentrate may be used in selected high-risk situations.

name: antitoxin
clinical_significance: An antibody or antibody preparation that binds to and neutralizes a toxin. It can provide temporary protection or treatment for selected poisonings and infections that produce toxins.

name: antitrichomonal agents
clinical_significance: Medicines used to treat trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection caused by Trichomonas vaginalis. Sexual partners should be treated at the same time to reduce reinfection, and testing for other sexually transmitted infections may be advised.

name: antitubercular agent
clinical_significance: A medicine used as part of combination treatment for tuberculosis. Multiple drugs are needed to cure infection and prevent resistance; several can cause liver, nerve, or vision problems that require monitoring.

name: antitussive agent
clinical_significance: A medicine that suppresses coughing. It may relieve a troublesome dry cough, but it does not treat the cause; some products cause drowsiness or interact with other medicines.

name: antiulcer agent
clinical_significance: A medicine used to prevent or treat ulcers and related acid disorders, including reflux. The type depends on the cause; long-term acid suppression should be reviewed when risks or ongoing need change.

name: antivenin
clinical_significance: An antibody preparation that neutralizes venom from a specific animal, used for clinically significant bites or stings. It can be lifesaving but may cause allergic reactions and must be selected and given by clinicians.

name: antiviral agent
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks viral replication or entry into cells. Antivirals treat selected viral infections; early treatment may matter, and incorrect or incomplete use can lead to resistance.

name: antiviral response
clinical_significance: The immune and cellular response that limits viral replication and clears infected cells. An impaired or excessive response can worsen illness, and response patterns help guide research and some diagnostic tests.

name: Anura
clinical_significance: A group of amphibians that includes frogs and toads. Contact with some species or their skin secretions can cause poisoning, and amphibians can carry Salmonella that may spread through handling.

name: anuria
clinical_significance: Almost complete absence of urine production, often defined in an adult as less than about 100 millilitres in 24 hours. It can signal severe kidney failure, blockage, shock, or another emergency.

name: anus
clinical_significance: The opening at the end of the digestive tract through which stool leaves the body. Two ring-shaped muscles help control when stool and gas are released.

name: anus disease
clinical_significance: A general term for conditions affecting the anus, including haemorrhoids, fissures, abscesses, tumours, and skin disease. Bleeding, persistent pain, discharge, or a new lump may need clinical assessment.

name: anxiety
clinical_significance: A feeling of worry, fear, or unease that can be a normal response to danger or stress. It becomes a disorder when it is excessive, persistent, difficult to control, or interferes with daily life.

name: anxiety disorder
clinical_significance: An anxiety disorder can cause persistent fear, avoidance, physical symptoms, and impaired daily function; assessment also considers medical causes, substance use, and risk of self-harm.

name: aorta
clinical_significance: The body’s largest artery, carrying oxygen-rich blood from the left side of the heart to the rest of the body. It passes through the chest and abdomen and divides into the arteries supplying the pelvis and legs.

name: aortic aneurysm
clinical_significance: An abnormal bulge or widening in the aorta, the large artery that carries blood from the heart to the body, caused by weakness in its wall. It may occur in the chest or abdomen and often causes no symptoms. If it enlarges, it may rupture or the aortic wall may tear (dissect); either can be life-threatening.

name: aortic arch
clinical_significance: The curved part of the aorta between its upward and downward sections. Three major arteries branch from it to supply the head, neck, and arms; disease here can affect blood flow or press on nearby structures.

name: aortic body
clinical_significance: A small group of sensory cells near the aortic arch that detects changes in blood oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acidity. It sends signals to the brain to help adjust breathing and circulation.

name: aortic coarctation
clinical_significance: A narrowing of the aorta present from birth, usually just beyond the branches that supply the head and arms. It can cause higher blood pressure in the arms than in the legs, weak leg pulses, poor growth, or heart strain. Some people have no symptoms until later in life.

name: aortic disease
clinical_significance: Any disorder affecting the aorta, the body’s main artery, including aneurysm, dissection, narrowing, inflammation, or fatty deposits. Some cases cause no symptoms; sudden severe chest, back, or abdominal pain is an emergency.

name: aortic dissection
clinical_significance: A tear in the inner lining of the aorta that allows blood to split the layers of its wall. It can suddenly cause severe chest or back pain, stroke, organ damage, or death and needs emergency assessment.

name: aortic injury
clinical_significance: Damage to the aorta, often caused by severe chest trauma or a medical procedure. A tear can cause internal bleeding, reduced blood flow, shock, and a life-threatening emergency.

name: aortic rupture
clinical_significance: A life-threatening break through the wall of the aorta, often following an aneurysm or dissection. It can cause sudden severe chest, back, or abdominal pain, internal bleeding, collapse, and shock.

name: aortic valve
clinical_significance: A valve between the heart’s left pumping chamber and the aorta. It opens to let blood leave the heart and closes to stop blood flowing backward.

name: aortic valve insufficiency
clinical_significance: Leakage of the aortic valve that allows blood to flow backward into the left pumping chamber between heartbeats. The extra workload can enlarge or weaken the heart over time.

name: aortic valve stenosis
clinical_significance: Aortic valve stenosis obstructs blood leaving the heart and can cause exertional breathlessness, chest pain, fainting, or heart failure; severe symptomatic disease may require valve replacement.

name: aortitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the aorta, the body’s largest artery. It may result from an autoimmune disease or infection and can weaken the artery or cause narrowing, aneurysm, dissection, or leakage of the aortic valve.

name: aortopulmonary window
clinical_significance: A rare birth defect in which an opening connects the aorta and pulmonary artery. Too much blood may flow to the lungs, causing breathing problems, poor growth, or heart failure in infancy.

name: apathy
clinical_significance: Reduced motivation, interest, or emotional response. It can occur with depression, dementia, Parkinson disease, brain injury, other neurological illness, or medicines and is different from ordinary tiredness or sadness.

name: apatite
clinical_significance: A calcium-phosphate mineral that forms much of bone and tooth enamel. Similar crystals can accumulate abnormally in tissues or contribute to some kidney stones; synthetic apatite is also used in bone-repair materials.

name: APC gene
clinical_significance: A tumour-suppressor gene that helps control cell growth. Inherited harmful variants can cause familial adenomatous polyposis, with many colon polyps and a very high risk of colorectal cancer unless managed with regular surveillance and preventive care.

name: apelin
clinical_significance: A signalling peptide involved in blood-vessel function, fluid balance, and energy metabolism. Apelin is studied in cardiovascular and metabolic disease, but it is not a routine diagnostic test or established treatment target.

name: Apert syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited condition in which some skull bones join too early. It causes an unusually shaped head and face and often joined fingers or toes; breathing, vision, hearing, or development may also be affected.

name: apgar score
clinical_significance: A quick assessment of a newborn’s colour, heart rate, reflex response, muscle tone, and breathing, usually recorded one and five minutes after birth. It describes immediate adaptation and helps guide care but does not predict long-term health by itself.

name: aphakia
clinical_significance: Absence of the eye’s natural lens, usually after cataract surgery, injury, or a birth difference. It causes major focusing problems and is usually corrected with an intraocular lens, contact lens, or strong glasses.

name: aphasia
clinical_significance: A brain-related disorder that impairs speaking, understanding, reading, or writing language. It most often follows a stroke but can also result from head injury, brain tumour, infection, or degeneration.

name: apheresis
clinical_significance: A procedure in which blood passes through a machine that removes a selected component, such as plasma, platelets, red cells, or abnormal cells, and returns the remaining blood to the person.

name: aphidicolin
clinical_significance: A laboratory compound that blocks DNA polymerase and stops cells from copying DNA. It is used to study cell division and cancer biology, not as a standard human medicine.

name: aphonia
clinical_significance: Complete loss of the ability to produce a normal voice, although whispering may remain possible. Causes include inflammation, vocal-cord paralysis, injury, growths, nerve disease, or psychological factors.

name: aphthous stomatitis
clinical_significance: Repeated painful ulcers on the moist lining of the mouth, commonly called canker sores. They are usually shallow, heal without scarring, and are not contagious.

name: aphthovirus
clinical_significance: A genus of viruses that causes foot-and-mouth disease in cloven-hoofed animals. Human infection is exceptionally rare; the major clinical and economic impact is disease in livestock.

name: apical
clinical_significance: Relating to or located at the tip of a body structure, such as the tip of a lung, heart, or tooth.

name: apicoectomy
clinical_significance: Dental surgery that removes the tip of a tooth root and nearby infected tissue, usually when infection persists after root-canal treatment. The end of the root is then sealed.

name: apicomplexa
clinical_significance: A large group of parasites that includes the organisms causing malaria, toxoplasmosis, and cryptosporidiosis. These infections range from mild to life-threatening, particularly in pregnancy or in people with weakened immunity.

name: apicoplast
clinical_significance: An organelle found in many apicomplexan parasites, including malaria parasites, that contains bacterial-like machinery. It is an important research target for developing medicines that can harm the parasite while sparing human cells.

name: apigenin
clinical_significance: A plant flavonoid found in some fruits and vegetables and studied for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. It is not proven to prevent or treat disease, and supplements may interact with medicines.

name: aplastic anemia
clinical_significance: A rare, serious bone-marrow failure disorder in which the marrow cannot make enough blood cells, usually because blood-forming stem cells are damaged. It lowers red cells, white cells, and platelets—not just red cells—so it can cause tiredness, infections, and easy bruising or bleeding. Causes include immune attack, some medicines, toxic chemicals, radiation, infections, and inherited conditions; sometimes no cause is found.

name: aplysia
clinical_significance: A marine sea slug used as a model organism in neuroscience because its large nerve cells make learning and memory easier to study. Findings support basic research but do not directly diagnose or treat human disease.

name: apnea
clinical_significance: A temporary pause in breathing. Prolonged or repeated episodes can lower oxygen, raise carbon dioxide, slow the heartbeat, cause loss of consciousness, or lead to death.

name: apobec deaminases
clinical_significance: A family of enzymes that edits DNA or RNA by converting cytosine into another base. APOBEC enzymes help defend against some viruses, but abnormal activity can also create mutations in cancer; they are active research targets.

name: apocrine adenoma
clinical_significance: A rare, usually benign tumour arising from apocrine sweat glands. It most often appears as a skin nodule; examination or biopsy may be needed to distinguish it from other skin tumours.

name: apocrine cystadenoma
clinical_significance: A rare cystic tumour arising from apocrine sweat glands, usually in the skin. It is generally benign, but a growing or changing lesion may need clinical examination and sometimes removal for diagnosis.

name: apoenzyme
clinical_significance: The protein part of an enzyme before its required helper substance has attached. It is usually inactive or less active until the helper, called a cofactor, binds to it.

name: apolipoprotein
clinical_significance: A protein that helps carry fats and cholesterol in the blood. Different apolipoproteins identify lipoprotein particles and can be measured to assess inherited or acquired lipid disorders and cardiovascular risk.

name: apolipoprotein E
clinical_significance: A protein involved in carrying cholesterol and a gene with variants associated with late-onset Alzheimer disease and lipid disorders. APOE ε4 raises risk but does not by itself determine who will develop Alzheimer disease; genotype can also inform risk of brain swelling or bleeding with some anti-amyloid medicines.

name: apolipoproteins A
clinical_significance: A group of proteins found mainly on HDL particles that help transport cholesterol. Levels can be associated with cardiovascular risk, but they are interpreted with the full lipid profile and other risk factors.

name: apolipoproteins B
clinical_significance: A protein present on LDL and other atherogenic lipoprotein particles. Blood apolipoprotein B can help estimate cardiovascular risk and guide lipid treatment in selected people, particularly those with diabetes or high triglycerides.

name: apolizumab
clinical_significance: An investigational monoclonal antibody directed at HLA-DR, studied for certain blood cancers. It is not an established standard treatment, and its benefits and risks remain dependent on clinical research.

name: apomine
clinical_significance: An investigational oral bisphosphonate studied for possible anticancer effects. It is not an established cancer treatment; clinical benefit and safety have not been confirmed in routine care.

name: apomorphine
clinical_significance: A dopamine-activating medicine used for sudden “off” episodes in advanced Parkinson disease. It can cause nausea, sleepiness, low blood pressure, hallucinations, or falls and requires careful dose titration.

name: aponeurosis
clinical_significance: A broad, flat sheet of tough connective tissue that attaches a muscle to bone, another muscle, or other tissues and helps transmit the muscle’s force.

name: apophysomyces elegans
clinical_significance: A mould that can cause mucormycosis, a rare but rapidly destructive fungal infection. Infection may follow skin trauma or surgery and can occur even without severe immune suppression; urgent antifungal treatment and often surgery are needed.

name: apoptosis
clinical_significance: A controlled process of cell death in which a cell dismantles itself and is removed with little inflammation. It helps shape developing organs and remove old, damaged, or abnormal cells; failure of this process can contribute to cancer.

name: apoptosome
clinical_significance: A protein complex that activates enzymes involved in programmed cell death. Its function is studied in cancer and degenerative disease, but it is not a routine clinical test.

name: apoptotic body
clinical_significance: A small membrane-bound piece of a cell that has begun controlled cell death. Immune or neighbouring cells can recognize and remove these pieces without causing much inflammation.

name: appearance
clinical_significance: A general observation of how a person or body part looks. Changes in appearance can be clinically useful signs, but they must be interpreted with the history, examination, and relevant tests.

name: appendectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove the appendix, usually to treat appendicitis. It may be performed laparoscopically through small incisions using a camera or through a larger open incision; the approach depends on the condition and clinical needs.

name: appendiceal neoplasm
clinical_significance: A tumour arising in the appendix, including neuroendocrine and mucin-producing tumours. Some are found incidentally during appendicitis surgery, while others can spread within the abdomen or cause pseudomyxoma peritonei; management depends on tumour type and stage.

name: appendicitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the appendix, often after its opening becomes blocked by hardened stool, mucus, or swollen tissue. It commonly causes pain that moves to the lower right abdomen, nausea, loss of appetite, and fever and can lead to rupture.

name: appendicular skeleton
clinical_significance: The bones of the arms and legs and the shoulder and pelvic girdles that attach them to the central skeleton.

name: appendix
clinical_significance: A small, finger-shaped pouch attached to the beginning of the large intestine. It contains immune tissue and may help support healthy gut bacteria, although its exact function is not fully understood and it is not essential for digestion. Inflammation of the appendix is called appendicitis.

name: appetite
clinical_significance: The psychological desire to eat food, distinct from physiological hunger, modulated by central nervous system pathways, neuroendocrine signaling, sensory stimuli, emotional states, and metabolic demands.

name: appetite regulation
clinical_significance: The control of hunger and fullness by the brain, digestive tract, hormones, emotions, habits, sleep, and surroundings. Signals such as ghrelin promote hunger, while leptin and other signals help promote fullness.

name: apraxia
clinical_significance: Difficulty performing a learned, purposeful movement even though strength, sensation, coordination, and understanding are sufficient. It results from a problem in the brain’s planning of movement rather than simple weakness.

name: aprepitant
clinical_significance: A medicine used with other drugs to prevent nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy or surgery. It can interact with many medicines, including warfarin and hormonal contraceptives, so medication review is important.

name: aprinocarsen
clinical_significance: An investigational antisense medicine studied for certain cancers. It is not an established standard treatment, and evidence of clinical benefit is limited.

name: aprotinin
clinical_significance: A medicine that slows breakdown of blood clots and can reduce bleeding during selected adult heart-bypass operations. Because it can increase serious complications, including kidney injury and clotting, its use is restricted to carefully selected patients and settings.

name: apud cell
clinical_significance: A neuroendocrine cell that takes up and processes chemical precursors to make signalling substances. Tumours arising from these cells can release hormones and cause symptoms such as flushing, diarrhoea, or abnormal blood pressure.

name: apudoma
clinical_significance: An older term for a tumour arising from cells of the diffuse neuroendocrine system. Modern classification uses the specific neuroendocrine tumour type and site, which guide diagnosis and treatment.

name: aqueous humor
clinical_significance: The clear fluid in the front part of the eye. It nourishes the cornea and lens, removes waste, and helps maintain pressure and the shape of the eye.

name: arabinose
clinical_significance: A simple five-carbon sugar found in some plants and microbes. It has no routine role as a human diagnostic marker or treatment; its importance is mainly biochemical and nutritional.

name: arachidic acid
clinical_significance: A long-chain saturated fatty acid found in foods such as peanut oil. It contributes to dietary fat intake but has no specific diagnostic or therapeutic role on its own.

name: arachidonic acid
clinical_significance: A fatty acid used by cells to make signalling molecules involved in inflammation, blood clotting, and smooth-muscle activity. Medicines such as aspirin and other anti-inflammatory drugs can alter pathways that use arachidonic acid.

name: arachnodactyly
clinical_significance: Abnormally long, thin fingers or toes. It may occur alone or as a feature of inherited connective-tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome.

name: arachnoid cyst
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous, fluid-filled sac between layers of the membrane covering the brain or spinal cord. Many cause no symptoms, but a large cyst may cause headache, seizures, weakness, or pressure on nearby tissue.

name: arachnoiditis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the arachnoid, one of the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord, most often in the spine. Inflammation may cause thickening, scarring, and bands that make nerve roots stick together or interfere with the normal flow of cerebrospinal fluid. Possible causes include infection, bleeding around the spinal cord, spinal injury, chronic nerve compression, surgery or another spinal procedure, and chemical irritation. Symptoms may include severe or burning back and limb pain, numbne

name: arbitrary unit
clinical_significance: A relative measurement unit used when a laboratory method does not report an absolute concentration. Arbitrary-unit results are assay-dependent and usually cannot be directly compared across different laboratories or methods.

name: arbovirus
clinical_significance: A virus spread by a biting insect or tick, such as a mosquito, tick, or sandfly. Arboviruses can cause fever, rash, joint pain, bleeding, or inflammation of the brain, depending on the virus.

name: arbovirus encephalitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the brain caused by a virus spread by mosquitoes, ticks, or other biting arthropods. It can cause confusion, seizures, weakness, or coma and may be life-threatening; travel and exposure history help guide testing.

name: arbovirus infection
clinical_significance: Infection with a virus transmitted by mosquitoes, ticks, or other biting arthropods. Illness ranges from no symptoms or fever to severe joint disease, bleeding, or brain inflammation, depending on the virus.

name: arcanobacterium
clinical_significance: A bacterium that can cause pharyngitis, often in adolescents, sometimes with a rash resembling scarlet fever. It can also cause skin infection and, rarely, invasive disease.

name: archaea
clinical_significance: A domain of microorganisms distinct from bacteria and eukaryotes. Archaea are common in the environment and human gut, but their role in most human disease is uncertain and they are not usually treated as pathogens.

name: arcobacter
clinical_significance: A genus of bacteria found in water, animals, and food; some species can cause gastrointestinal illness in people and rarely bloodstream infection. Recovery from a clinical sample must be interpreted with the symptoms and specimen source.

name: arcobacter butzleri
