clinical_significance: A bacterium associated with diarrhoeal illness after contaminated food or water exposure. It can occasionally be found in blood, particularly in people with serious underlying illness; susceptibility testing may guide treatment in severe cases.

name: arcobacter cryaerophilus
clinical_significance: A bacterium reported in gastrointestinal and bloodstream infections and in some animal-associated specimens. Human disease is uncommon, and whether a positive culture represents infection depends on the sample and clinical findings.

name: arcus senilis
clinical_significance: A greyish-white, circular lipid deposition ring appearing in the peripheral corneal stroma, commonly seen in elderly individuals as a benign finding, or in younger patients (arcus juvenilis) associated with familial hyperlipidemia.

name: area striata
clinical_significance: The primary visual area of the brain’s occipital lobe. Injury or disease here can cause loss of part of the visual field or difficulty recognizing visual information despite healthy eyes.

name: arecoline
clinical_significance: A stimulant alkaloid in areca nut that affects the nervous system and saliva production. Arecoline is possibly carcinogenic, and areca-nut or betel-quid use is established as a cause of oral cancer and precancerous oral disease.

name: arenaviridae
clinical_significance: A family of viruses that includes Lassa virus and lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus. Some cause severe haemorrhagic fever or brain infection, while others are usually mild; risk depends on the virus and exposure.

name: arenavirus
clinical_significance: A genus of viruses that includes Lassa virus and lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus. Infection ranges from mild illness to severe haemorrhagic fever or meningitis, depending on the species.

name: areola
clinical_significance: The darker circular area surrounding the nipple. It contains small glands that help lubricate and protect the skin, especially during breastfeeding.

name: argentaffin cell
clinical_significance: A neuroendocrine cell that takes up silver stains and can release serotonin and other signalling substances. Tumours arising from related cells can cause hormone-related symptoms and may be found in the gut or lungs.

name: arginine
clinical_significance: An amino acid used to make proteins, nitric oxide, and other molecules in the body. It is converted into urea in the liver; severe enzyme defects can cause arginine or ammonia accumulation, while supplements may interact with blood-pressure medicines.

name: arginine butyrate
clinical_significance: An experimental compound studied for increasing fetal haemoglobin in sickle-cell disease and beta-thalassaemia. It is not a routine approved treatment, and its clinical benefit and safety remain under study.

name: argininosuccinic acid
clinical_significance: A compound produced in the urea cycle that helps the body remove nitrogen from protein breakdown. Elevated blood levels can indicate argininosuccinate lyase deficiency, a rare inherited disorder that may cause dangerous hyperammonaemia.

name: argininosuccinic aciduria
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which the body cannot safely remove waste nitrogen produced when protein is broken down. Ammonia and argininosuccinic acid build up and may cause vomiting, sleepiness, seizures, liver problems, or developmental impairment.

name: argipressin
clinical_significance: A synthetic form of vasopressin used in some settings to raise blood pressure, control bleeding, or treat diabetes insipidus. It can reduce blood flow to the heart, gut, or limbs and requires careful fluid and electrolyte monitoring.

name: argon
clinical_significance: An inert gas used in industrial and medical settings. It can displace oxygen in enclosed spaces and cause rapid asphyxiation without warning because it has no colour or smell.

name: argonaute proteins
clinical_significance: A family of proteins that helps regulate gene expression by binding small RNA molecules. Argonaute proteins are central to gene-silencing pathways and are studied in cancer and other diseases, but are not routine clinical tests.

name: aripiprazole
clinical_significance: A second-generation antipsychotic used for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and as an add-on treatment for depression. It can cause restlessness, sleepiness, weight changes, and rarely new compulsive urges such as gambling.

name: armodafinil
clinical_significance: A wake-promoting medicine used for excessive sleepiness from narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnoea, or shift-work disorder. It does not replace treatment of airway obstruction and can cause insomnia, headache, or serious rash.

name: arnold-chiari malformation
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which part of the lower brain extends through the opening at the base of the skull into the spinal canal. It may block the normal flow of brain fluid and cause headache, neck pain, balance problems, swallowing difficulty, or weakness.

name: aromatase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that changes androgen hormones into oestrogen. It is found in tissues including the ovaries, fat, and breast and helps regulate hormone levels.

name: aromatase inhibitor
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks oestrogen production, used mainly for hormone-sensitive breast cancer after menopause or with ovarian suppression before menopause. It can cause joint pain and accelerate bone loss, so bone health may need monitoring.

name: aromatherapy
clinical_significance: Use of plant-derived scents or oils to promote comfort or well-being. Evidence for treating disease is limited; oils can cause skin or airway irritation, allergy, or poisoning if swallowed.

name: arousal
clinical_significance: A state of alertness or responsiveness in the brain; in sexual health, the term can also refer to a bodily response to sexual stimulation. Reduced or excessive arousal may be a symptom, but its cause depends on the clinical context.

name: arrestin
clinical_significance: A protein that regulates signalling by many cell-surface receptors. Arrestin proteins are studied in heart, brain, and cancer biology, but their measurement is not a routine clinical test.

name: arrhythmia
clinical_significance: An abnormal heart rate or rhythm. The heartbeat may be too fast, too slow, irregular, or start from the wrong place; some arrhythmias are harmless, while others reduce blood flow or cause cardiac arrest.

name: arsanilic acid
clinical_significance: An organic arsenic compound formerly used in some veterinary products. It has no routine human medical use; exposure to arsenic compounds can be toxic, and risk depends on the form, dose, and route.

name: arsenic
clinical_significance: A naturally occurring element that is poisonous in many forms. Exposure can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, nerve problems, heart problems, skin changes, and increased cancer risk; some compounds have limited medical uses.

name: arsenic trioxide
clinical_significance: A medicine used with tretinoin to treat selected cases of acute promyelocytic leukaemia. It can cause life-threatening heart-rhythm changes, liver problems, and differentiation syndrome, so treatment requires specialist monitoring.

name: arsenical
clinical_significance: A compound containing arsenic. Some arsenicals have limited medical or research uses, but many are toxic; exposure can damage the digestive, nervous, cardiovascular, and skin systems and increase cancer risk.

name: art therapy
clinical_significance: A structured use of art-making with a trained therapist to support emotional expression and coping. It may help with distress or quality of life but is not a substitute for treatment of the underlying medical or mental-health condition.

name: arterial embolization
clinical_significance: A procedure that deliberately blocks a selected artery, usually to stop bleeding, reduce blood supply to a tumour, or treat an abnormal blood-vessel connection.

name: arterial injury
clinical_significance: Damage to an artery that may cause severe bleeding, a clot, narrowing, reduced blood flow, tissue loss, or life-threatening complications. It can result from trauma, surgery, or a medical procedure.

name: arterial stenosis
clinical_significance: Narrowing of an artery that reduces blood flow to the tissues beyond it. Common causes include fatty plaque, inflammation, injury, or an inherited abnormality of the artery wall.

name: arterial thrombosis
clinical_significance: Formation of a blood clot inside an artery, often where a fatty plaque has damaged the vessel lining. The clot can block blood flow to the heart, brain, limb, intestine, or another organ.

name: arteriography
clinical_significance: An imaging study in which contrast material is injected into an artery and X-ray images show the arterial lumen and blood flow.

name: arteriole
clinical_significance: A small branch of an artery that delivers blood to a network of tiny vessels called capillaries. Its muscular wall can narrow or widen to control blood flow and blood pressure.

name: arteriolosclerosis
clinical_significance: A form of vascular disease affecting small arteries and arterioles, characterized by mural thickening, luminal narrowing, and loss of elasticity, classically manifesting as hyaline arteriolosclerosis (associated with aging and diabetes) or hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis (associated with severe hypertension).

name: arteriosclerosis
clinical_significance: Thickening, hardening, and loss of elasticity in artery walls. It includes several processes, including age-related stiffening and plaque buildup, and can reduce blood flow to the heart, brain, legs, or other organs.

name: arteriovenous fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal connection between an artery and a vein that bypasses the normal capillary network. It may be present from birth, follow injury or a procedure, or be created to provide access for haemodialysis.

name: arteriovenous malformation
clinical_significance: An abnormal tangle of arteries and veins joined without the usual capillaries between them. It can bleed, cause seizures or other neurological symptoms, or put extra strain on the heart.

name: arteritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of an artery wall. The inflammation can narrow, weaken, or block the artery, reducing blood flow and causing pain or organ damage in the affected area.

name: artery
clinical_significance: A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Most arteries carry oxygen-rich blood, except the pulmonary arteries, which carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. Their elastic, muscular walls withstand and regulate pressure.

name: artery occlusion
clinical_significance: A blockage inside an artery, often caused by a clot, fatty plaque, or material that travelled from elsewhere. It can cut off blood flow; sudden pain, paleness, coldness, numbness, weakness, or absent pulse is an emergency.

name: arthrinium phaeospermum
clinical_significance: A fungus found in soil and plant material that has rarely been recovered from human infections. Its clinical significance is uncertain unless it is isolated from a compatible infected site and supported by clinical findings.

name: arthritis
clinical_significance: A group of conditions that affect joints and the tissues around them; it is not one single disease. Depending on the type, arthritis may involve inflammation, gradual breakdown of joint tissues, infection, or crystal deposits. It can cause joint pain, swelling, warmth, stiffness, and reduced movement. Some types can also affect the skin, eyes, heart, lungs, or other organs. Examples include osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, and ankylosing spondylitis.

name: arthrobacter
clinical_significance: A genus of bacteria commonly found in soil and water. Human infection is uncommon, but some species have been recovered in opportunistic infections; a culture result must be interpreted according to specimen quality and symptoms.

name: arthrocentesis
clinical_significance: A procedure in which a needle removes fluid from a joint. The fluid can be tested for infection, blood, or crystals and may be removed to reduce pain and pressure.

name: arthroderma obtusum
clinical_significance: A rare dermatophyte fungus related to species that infect keratinized skin, hair, or nails. It can cause superficial ringworm-like disease, but human infections are uncommon.

name: arthroderma otae
clinical_significance: A dermatophyte fungus historically associated with Microsporum canis, which can cause ringworm of the skin or scalp, often after contact with infected cats or dogs.

name: arthroderma persicolor
clinical_significance: A dermatophyte fungus that can cause superficial skin infection in people after contact with animals or contaminated soil. The infection is generally limited to the skin but may be mistaken for other rashes.

name: arthrodesis
clinical_significance: Surgery that permanently joins the bones of a damaged joint so they heal as one solid unit. It can relieve severe pain and improve stability, but the fused joint no longer moves.

name: arthrographis
clinical_significance: A genus of environmental fungi that rarely causes human infection, including eye, skin, joint, or invasive disease. Identification matters in compatible cases because treatment is specialist-led and antifungal susceptibility can vary.

name: arthrogryposis
clinical_significance: A group of conditions present from birth in which two or more joints are permanently stiff or limited in movement. It usually results from reduced movement before birth and may involve muscles, nerves, or connective tissue.

name: arthropathy
clinical_significance: Any disease or abnormal condition affecting a joint. It may result from inflammation, wear, injury, infection, bleeding, nerve damage, or crystals such as those that cause gout.

name: arthroplasty
clinical_significance: Surgery to repair, reshape, or replace a damaged joint to reduce pain and improve movement or alignment. It may replace part or all of the joint and is used for severe arthritis, fractures, or other joint damage.

name: arthropod vector
clinical_significance: An insect, tick, or related animal that carries and transmits an infectious organism between hosts. Examples include mosquitoes spreading malaria or ticks spreading Lyme disease.

name: arthropod venom
clinical_significance: A toxic substance injected or released by some spiders, scorpions, and other arthropods. Effects range from local pain and swelling to muscle, neurologic, or allergic reactions; severe symptoms require urgent assessment.

name: arthropoda
clinical_significance: A large group of animals that includes insects, ticks, spiders, and crustaceans. Some transmit infections, inject venom, cause allergic reactions, or infest skin, making identification and exposure history clinically useful.

name: arthroscope
clinical_significance: A thin instrument with a light and camera used to look inside a joint through a small cut. It can help diagnose damage and guide keyhole surgery to repair or remove abnormal tissue.

name: arthroscopy
clinical_significance: Keyhole surgery in which a camera and small instruments are inserted through small cuts to examine or treat a joint. It may be used to repair cartilage or ligaments, remove loose tissue, or treat an inflamed joint lining.

name: arthus reaction
clinical_significance: A local immune reaction that causes redness, swelling, pain, and sometimes tissue damage several hours after exposure to a substance. It occurs when antibodies and the substance form deposits that activate inflammation in the affected tissue.

name: articular cartilage
clinical_significance: Smooth, tough tissue covering the ends of bones inside a joint. It allows bones to move with little friction and helps spread forces across the joint.

name: articular ligament
clinical_significance: A strong band of connective tissue joining bones around a joint. It stabilizes the joint and limits excessive bending, sliding, or twisting.

name: artificial heart
clinical_significance: A mechanical device that supports or replaces the heart’s pumping action. It may support one or both lower chambers temporarily or long term and requires management of power, infection, bleeding, and blood clots.

name: artificial immunosuppression
clinical_significance: Deliberate reduction of immune activity to prevent transplant rejection or treat autoimmune disease, inflammation, or cancer. It can increase the risk of serious infection and some cancers, and may require blood tests or infection prevention.

name: artificial insemination
clinical_significance: A fertility procedure in which prepared sperm is placed into the cervix or uterus to increase the chance of pregnancy. The sperm may come from a partner or a donor.

name: artificial intelligence
clinical_significance: Computer systems that learn from data to recognize patterns, make predictions, or support healthcare decisions. Medical AI can assist diagnosis, treatment, and research, but it must be tested, monitored for bias, and supervised by qualified professionals.

name: artificial saliva
clinical_significance: A product that moistens the mouth and temporarily relieves discomfort from dry mouth. It may improve speaking, swallowing, and comfort but does not replace fluids, dental care, or treatment of the cause.

name: artificial skin
clinical_significance: A biological or manufactured covering placed over a wound to protect it and support growth of new skin. It may reduce fluid loss and contamination, but some wounds later need a permanent skin graft.

name: aryldialkylphosphatase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that can break down some organophosphate chemicals. Related enzyme activity is studied in pesticide detoxification and toxicology, but it is not a standard clinical test for diagnosing poisoning.

name: arytenoid cartilage
clinical_significance: One of a pair of small cartilages at the back of the voice box. They anchor the vocal cords and help the laryngeal muscles open, close, and adjust the cords for breathing and speech.

name: asbestos
clinical_significance: A group of naturally occurring minerals that can release hazardous fibres when disturbed. Inhaling fibres can cause asbestosis, lung cancer, and mesothelioma, often decades after exposure.

name: asbestosis
clinical_significance: Permanent scarring of the lungs caused by long-term inhalation of asbestos fibres. It can gradually cause breathlessness, dry cough, and reduced lung function and increases the risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma.

name: ascariasis
clinical_significance: Infection with a roundworm acquired by swallowing eggs from contaminated soil, food, or water. It may cause no symptoms, abdominal pain, poor nutrition, intestinal blockage, or cough while larvae pass through the lungs.

name: ascaridida
clinical_significance: An order of parasitic roundworms that includes Ascaris and related worms. Human infections may cause intestinal symptoms, nutritional problems, or, with heavy worm burden, bowel or bile-duct obstruction.

name: ascaris
clinical_significance: A genus of parasitic roundworms that infects people and animals. Ascaris lumbricoides infection can cause abdominal symptoms, poor nutrition, and occasionally intestinal blockage or migration into the bile ducts.

name: ascaris lumbricoides
clinical_significance: A large parasitic roundworm that infects the human intestine after eggs are swallowed from contaminated soil, food, or water. Heavy infection can impair nutrition and rarely cause bowel blockage or migrate into the bile or pancreatic ducts.

name: ascending colon
clinical_significance: The first part of the large intestine, running upward on the right side of the abdomen from the appendix region to the bend beneath the liver. It absorbs water and helps form stool.

name: ascites
clinical_significance: Abnormal buildup of fluid inside the abdomen. It commonly results from advanced liver disease but may also be caused by cancer, heart failure, kidney disease, infection, or pancreatitis and can cause swelling, discomfort, or breathlessness.

name: ascitic fluid
clinical_significance: Fluid collected from the abdomen in a person with ascites. Laboratory testing can help identify liver disease, infection, cancer, pancreatitis, or other causes of the fluid buildup.

name: ascorbic acid
clinical_significance: Vitamin C, a water-soluble vitamin needed to make collagen, heal wounds, absorb iron, protect cells, and support normal immune and connective-tissue function.

name: aseptic meningitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord without the usual evidence of bacterial meningitis. Viruses are common causes, but medicines, autoimmune disease, and other infections can also be responsible.

name: Asherman syndrome
clinical_significance: Scar tissue inside the uterus that partly or completely joins the uterine walls. It most often follows a procedure inside the uterus or complications of pregnancy and may cause light or absent periods, infertility, or repeated miscarriage.

name: asparaginase
clinical_significance: An enzyme medicine used as part of chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and some related cancers. It deprives cancer cells of asparagine but can cause severe allergy, pancreatitis, liver injury, blood clots, or bleeding.

name: asparagine
clinical_significance: An amino acid used to build proteins and support cell function. Some leukaemia cells depend heavily on external asparagine, which is why asparaginase is used in selected cancer treatments.

name: aspartic acid
clinical_significance: An amino acid that the body can make and uses to build proteins and carry out cell reactions. It is one of the components of aspartame but is not the same substance as the sweetener.

name: aspartylglucosaminuria
clinical_significance: A rare inherited lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient aspartylglucosaminidase. It can lead to progressive developmental, cognitive, and motor impairment and may be managed with supportive multidisciplinary care.

name: Asperger syndrome
clinical_significance: A former diagnostic classification for a neurodevelopmental profile within the autism spectrum characterized by qualitative differences in social communication and social reciprocity, accompanied by restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior and intense focal interests, without significant delays in general language acquisition or cognitive development.

name: aspergillosis
clinical_significance: A group of infections and allergic conditions caused by Aspergillus molds. It may affect the airways, sinuses, or lungs and can include allergic disease, a fungal growth in an existing lung cavity, or invasive infection.

name: aspergillus
clinical_significance: A genus of saprophytic molds whose airborne conidia are ubiquitous in the environment, capable of causing allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, aspergilloma formation in pre-existing cavitary lung lesions, or severe invasive tissue infections in immunocompromised hosts.

name: aspergillus flavus
clinical_significance: A mould that can cause allergic or invasive aspergillosis, especially in people with weakened immunity or underlying lung disease. It can also contaminate crops and produce aflatoxins, which increase liver-cancer risk when present in food.

name: aspergillus fumigatus
clinical_significance: A common environmental mould and a major cause of invasive aspergillosis, especially in people with severe immune suppression or lung disease. Some strains resist azole antifungal medicines, which can complicate treatment.

name: aspergillus glaucus
clinical_significance: A mould found in the environment and on stored foods. Human infection is very rare but can occur opportunistically; a positive result is clinically meaningful mainly when supported by compatible tissue or infection findings.

name: aspergillus niger
clinical_significance: A mould found in soil, food, and indoor environments. It rarely causes human infection, but can cause ear or invasive fungal disease in susceptible people and some strains can produce food-contaminating mycotoxins.

name: aspergillus ochraceus
clinical_significance: A mould that can contaminate stored food and produce ochratoxin A, a toxin that damages kidneys in animals. The significance of typical dietary exposure for human disease remains uncertain; the organism is also a rare cause of infection.

name: aspergillus versicolor
clinical_significance: A mould found indoors and in stored materials that can produce sterigmatocystin, a toxin related to aflatoxin. Human infection is uncommon, but exposure to damp or contaminated materials can worsen allergy or asthma in susceptible people.

name: asphyxia
clinical_significance: A life-threatening lack of oxygen caused by inability to breathe or by blocked blood oxygen delivery, such as from choking, drowning, strangulation, or severe airway blockage. It can quickly cause unconsciousness, brain injury, or death.

name: asphyxia neonatorum
clinical_significance: Failure of a newborn to start or maintain effective breathing at or soon after birth. It can reduce oxygen to the brain and other organs and requires immediate assessment and breathing support.

name: aspirate (substance)
clinical_significance: Material drawn or inhaled into the airway or lungs, such as food, liquid, or vomit. It can obstruct breathing or cause chemical lung injury and aspiration pneumonia, particularly when swallowing or consciousness is impaired.

name: aspiration
clinical_significance: Breathing food, liquid, saliva, vomit, blood, or another substance into the voice box or lungs instead of swallowing it into the oesophagus. It can cause choking, airway blockage, inflammation, or pneumonia.

name: aspiration pneumonia
clinical_significance: A lung infection that develops after inhaling saliva, food, liquid, or stomach contents. It is more likely with swallowing difficulty, reduced consciousness, stroke, or tube feeding and may cause cough, fever, breathlessness, or chest pain.

name: aspirin
clinical_significance: A medicine that can relieve pain, lower fever, reduce inflammation, and make platelets less likely to form blood clots. Low-dose aspirin is often used after a heart attack, stroke, or some heart procedures, but it is not suitable for everyone because it can cause serious bleeding. It should not be taken daily for prevention without medical advice.

name: assay
clinical_significance: A laboratory method used to detect or measure a substance, biological activity, genetic feature, or response in a sample.

name: assessed
clinical_significance: Assessed indicates that a finding or risk has been evaluated; documenting the method and result supports follow-up and avoids treating an unverified concern as confirmed.

name: assisted circulation
clinical_significance: Mechanical or procedural support that maintains blood flow when the heart cannot pump enough on its own. It may use a pump, oxygenator, or other device for a short time or longer-term support.

name: association cortex
clinical_significance: Areas of the brain’s outer layer that combine information from different senses. They support memory, language, planning, judgment, learning, and other complex behavior rather than controlling one simple movement or sensation.

name: association learning
clinical_significance: Learning that occurs by connecting events or stimuli, such as associating a sound with a reward or an unpleasant experience. It is studied in behavioural science and can inform approaches to habits, fear, and rehabilitation.

name: astacoidea
clinical_significance: A superfamily of freshwater crayfish. Some freshwater crustaceans can carry lung-fluke larvae in endemic regions, so eating them raw or undercooked can transmit paragonimiasis.

name: astaxanthin
clinical_significance: A red-orange pigment found in algae, seafood, and some supplements. It is studied for antioxidant effects, but evidence is insufficient to use it to prevent or treat disease, and supplements can interact with medicines.

name: astemizole
clinical_significance: An older antihistamine withdrawn from many markets after reports of dangerous heart-rhythm disturbances, especially with high drug levels or interacting medicines. It is not a current routine allergy treatment.

name: asterixis
clinical_significance: Brief, repeated lapses in holding a posture that cause a flapping movement, often when the arms are stretched out and the wrists are bent back. It can occur with liver or kidney failure, breathing disorders, or some medicines.

name: asthenia
clinical_significance: Abnormal lack of physical strength or energy. It is a symptom rather than a disease and may occur with infection, chronic illness, malnutrition, depression, or medicine effects.

name: asthenopia
clinical_significance: Eye strain or visual fatigue that may cause aching, burning, blurred vision, headache, or difficulty focusing. Refractive errors, dry eyes, poor lighting, and prolonged screen use can contribute.

name: asthenozoospermia
clinical_significance: Abnormally reduced movement of sperm, which can make fertilization more difficult. It is assessed by semen analysis and may result from infection, a varicocele, toxins, illness, or an unknown cause.

name: asthma
clinical_significance: A long-term inflammatory disease of the airways in the lungs. The airways are overly sensitive and can narrow when triggered because their lining swells, the surrounding muscles tighten, and extra mucus forms. This variable narrowing makes it harder for air to move, especially when breathing out. Symptoms may include wheezing, cough, chest tightness, and shortness of breath; they can come and go and may be triggered by allergens, infections, smoke, air pollution, exercise, certain medicines, or

name: astigmatism
clinical_significance: A focusing problem caused by an unevenly curved cornea or lens. Light is not focused at one clear point on the retina, causing blurred or distorted vision at near or far distances.

name: astringent
clinical_significance: A substance that makes surface tissues contract and may reduce minor secretions or bleeding. It is used in some skin, mouth, or wound products but can irritate tissue and does not replace assessment of persistent bleeding or serious injury.

name: astroblastoma
clinical_significance: A rare circumscribed brain tumour, now classified more specifically as astroblastoma, MN1-altered. It often affects children or young adults and may recur locally; diagnosis depends on pathology and molecular testing.

name: astrocyte
clinical_significance: A star-shaped support cell in the brain and spinal cord. It helps nourish nerve cells, maintain the blood–brain barrier, regulate the chemical environment, and respond to injury.

name: astrocytoma
clinical_significance: A tumour arising from astrocytes, the star-shaped support cells of the brain or spinal cord. Astrocytomas vary from slow-growing to aggressive, and symptoms depend on their location and size.

name: astroviridae
clinical_significance: A family of viruses that includes human astroviruses, a cause of gastroenteritis, especially in children, older adults, and immunocompromised people. Rarely, astroviruses can spread beyond the gut and cause neurologic disease.

name: asymptomatic
clinical_significance: Having a disease, infection, or abnormal finding without noticeable symptoms. A person may still have detectable disease, develop complications, or transmit an infection; this differs from presymptomatic illness, in which symptoms appear later.

name: asymptomatic infections
clinical_significance: Infections in which the person has no noticeable symptoms. The organism may still be detectable, cause later complications, or spread to others; this differs from presymptomatic infection, in which symptoms develop later.

name: atamestane
clinical_significance: An investigational aromatase inhibitor studied for hormone-sensitive breast cancer. It is not an established routine treatment, and clinical benefit and safety depend on research evidence.

name: ataxia
clinical_significance: Loss of smooth control and coordination of movement. It is a sign rather than one specific disease and may cause an unsteady walk, poor balance, clumsy movements, slurred speech, shaking, or abnormal eye movements. It can result from a problem in the cerebellum, spinal cord, sensory nerves, or balance organs and is different from muscle weakness alone. Causes include inherited disorders, stroke, multiple sclerosis, infection, vitamin deficiency, medicines, alcohol, or other toxins. The onset may

name: ataxia telangiectasia
clinical_significance: A rare autosomal-recessive DNA-repair disorder causing progressive cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasias of the eyes or skin, immune deficiency, radiosensitivity, and increased risk of leukemia, lymphoma, or other cancers. Respiratory infections and elevated alpha-fetoprotein may occur.

name: atazanavir sulfate
clinical_significance: An HIV protease-inhibitor medicine used with other antiretroviral drugs to suppress HIV. It can cause jaundice from raised bilirubin, kidney stones, and important drug interactions; the complete regimen and resistance history guide use.

name: atelectasis
clinical_significance: Partial or complete collapse of a region of lung, reducing the amount of air it contains. It may result from blocked airways, pressure from outside the lung, shallow breathing, or scarring and can reduce oxygen exchange.

name: atenolol
clinical_significance: A beta-blocker used for high blood pressure, angina, and after some heart attacks. It slows heart rate and can cause fatigue or dizziness; it may be unsuitable in some people with asthma, a very slow pulse, or certain heart blocks.

name: atherectomy
clinical_significance: A minimally invasive endovascular catheter technique utilizing directional, rotational, orbital, or laser devices to physically excise, shave, vaporize, or pulverize calcified or atheromatous plaque from the intraluminal wall of diseased arteries.

name: atherosclerosis
clinical_significance: A disease in which fatty, cholesterol-rich plaques build up inside artery walls. Plaques can narrow arteries or rupture and form clots, reducing blood flow to the heart, brain, legs, or other organs.

name: atherosclerotic plaque
clinical_significance: A buildup of cholesterol, fat, inflammatory cells, and scar-like tissue inside an artery wall. It can gradually narrow the artery or rupture and cause a blood clot.

name: athetosis
clinical_significance: Slow, involuntary, writhing movements that may affect the hands, fingers, feet, face, neck, or trunk. They result from abnormal function in brain areas that help control movement and may occur with inherited or acquired brain injury.

name: atomoxetine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: A nonstimulant medicine used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). It can raise blood pressure or heart rate, reduce appetite, and rarely cause serious liver problems or suicidal thoughts, especially early in treatment.

name: atopic dermatitis
clinical_significance: A chronic, relapsing, intensely itchy inflammatory skin disease involving epidermal-barrier dysfunction and immune dysregulation. It causes dry, inflamed, scaly, or lichenified lesions whose distribution varies with age; scratching can produce infection, excoriations, and sleep disturbance.

name: atopic rhinitis
clinical_significance: Allergy-related inflammation inside the nose. Exposure to pollen, dust mites, mould, animals, or other triggers can cause sneezing, itching, a blocked or runny nose, and reduced smell.

name: atopobium minutum
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterium found in the mouth and gut. It has been reported in dental and periodontal microbiome studies, but its role as a cause of disease is not established and detection alone does not require treatment.

name: atopobium parvulum
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterium found in the mouth and associated with dental plaque and periodontal or endodontic samples. It may contribute to mixed oral infections, but a positive sample must be interpreted in context.

name: atopobium rimae
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterium occasionally detected in dental plaque and oral infection samples. Its independent role in disease is uncertain because it may be part of a mixed microbial community.

name: atopobium vaginae
clinical_significance: A former name for Fannyhessea vaginae, an anaerobic bacterium associated with bacterial vaginosis. Its detection can support a BV-associated microbiome pattern, but alone does not define symptoms or determine treatment.

name: atopy
clinical_significance: A genetic tendency to develop allergic conditions such as eczema, allergic rhinitis, asthma, or food allergy after exposure to common triggers.

name: atorvastatin
clinical_significance: A medicine that lowers low-density lipoprotein cholesterol by reducing cholesterol production in the liver. It lowers the risk of heart attack and stroke in appropriate people; muscle symptoms and liver problems are uncommon but important side effects.

name: atorvastatin calcium
clinical_significance: The calcium salt form of atorvastatin, a statin used to lower LDL cholesterol and reduce heart attack and stroke risk in appropriate patients. Unexplained muscle pain or weakness should be reported because serious muscle injury is rare but possible.

name: atovaquone
clinical_significance: An antiparasitic medicine used with proguanil to prevent or treat malaria and, in other regimens, to prevent or treat Pneumocystis pneumonia. It can cause gastrointestinal symptoms and is not suitable for everyone with severe kidney impairment.

name: atrasentan
clinical_significance: An endothelin-receptor blocker approved in the United States to reduce protein in the urine in adults with primary IgA nephropathy at risk of rapid progression. Approval is accelerated and long-term benefit on kidney function is still being confirmed; swelling, anaemia, or liver effects may occur.

name: atrial ablation
clinical_significance: A procedure that uses heat, cold, or another form of energy to create small scars in heart tissue responsible for an abnormal atrial rhythm. The scars block unwanted electrical signals.

name: atrial arrhythmia
clinical_significance: An abnormal heart rhythm that begins in one of the heart’s upper chambers. It may cause palpitations, breathlessness, dizziness, chest discomfort, or fainting; examples include atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter.

name: atrial fibrillation
clinical_significance: An abnormal heart rhythm in which the heart's upper chambers (atria) beat chaotically instead of contracting in an organized way. The heartbeat is often irregular and may be fast, but some people have no symptoms. Blood may pool in the atria and form clots, increasing the risk of stroke.

name: atrial flutter
clinical_significance: A supraventricular arrhythmia characterized by a rapid, organized, macro-reentrant electrical circuit within the atria, typically circulating around the cavotricuspid isthmus of the right atrium. Manifested on ECG as rapid, regular sawtooth flutter waves (typically 250–350 bpm) with variable AV nodal conduction block (often 2:1), it presents with palpitations, fatigue, and elevated thromboembolic risk.

name: atrial septal defect
clinical_significance: A hole present from birth in the wall between the heart’s upper chambers. A small defect may cause no problems. A larger one can increase blood flow to the lungs and enlarge or strain the right side of the heart; it may also cause abnormal rhythms or, rarely, allow a clot to pass into an artery and cause a stroke.

name: atrial standstill
clinical_significance: Failure of the heart’s upper chambers to produce normal electrical signals or contractions. It can cause a very slow heartbeat, dizziness, fainting, poor circulation, or heart failure.

name: atrial thrombosis
clinical_significance: Formation of a blood clot inside one of the heart’s upper chambers, especially during atrial fibrillation. The clot can break loose and block blood flow to the brain or another organ.

name: atrioventricular block
clinical_significance: Delayed or interrupted electrical signals between the heart’s upper and lower chambers. It may cause a slow heartbeat, tiredness, dizziness, fainting, or no symptoms; severe block can require urgent treatment and pacing.

name: atrioventricular bundle
clinical_significance: A bundle of specialized electrical fibers that carries signals from the heart’s central relay point into the lower chambers. Its branches help both pumping chambers contract in a coordinated way.

name: atrioventricular node
clinical_significance: A small area of specialized tissue near the junction of the heart’s upper and lower chambers that receives electrical signals and briefly delays them before passing them to the lower chambers. This delay allows the upper chambers to empty first.

name: atrium
clinical_significance: One of the heart’s two upper chambers, which receive returning blood and pass it to the lower pumping chambers. The right atrium receives blood from the body; the left receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.

name: atrophoderma maculatum
clinical_significance: A rare skin condition causing flat, slightly sunken patches in which the skin becomes thinner and changes colour. The patches usually have no open sore or active infection.

name: atrophy
clinical_significance: Shrinkage and loss of function of a tissue, organ, or muscle because its cells become smaller or fewer. Causes include disuse, nerve damage, poor blood supply, malnutrition, hormone deficiency, chronic disease, and ageing; it may be partly reversible.

name: atropine
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks acetylcholine signals at certain nerve endings. It can increase heart rate, reduce secretions, widen the pupils, and counteract selected poisonings or dangerously slow heartbeats.

name: atropine sulfate
clinical_significance: The sulfate salt form of atropine, used for selected slow heart rhythms, organophosphate poisoning, and to reduce secretions or dilate the pupil. It can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, rapid heartbeat, or confusion.

name: attention
clinical_significance: The ability to select information, focus on it, and maintain that focus while limiting distraction. Attention can be affected by sleep loss, stress, illness, medicines, or brain disorders.

name: attenuated vaccine
clinical_significance: A vaccine made from a weakened form of a pathogen that can still stimulate immunity. It often produces strong protection, but may be unsafe for some people with severe immune suppression or during pregnancy; eligibility depends on the specific vaccine.

name: attitude
clinical_significance: A person’s way of thinking or feeling about a situation, condition, or treatment. In healthcare it may affect communication or adherence, but it is not by itself a diagnosis or a measure of a person’s character.

name: attogram
clinical_significance: A unit of mass equal to 10⁻¹⁸ grams. It is used mainly in scientific measurements of very small quantities and has no routine clinical interpretation by itself.

name: attribution
clinical_significance: The act of assigning a cause or meaning to an observation or outcome. In clinical research, mistaken attribution can confuse association with causation and lead to incorrect conclusions about diagnosis or treatment.

name: atypia morphology
clinical_significance: An unusual appearance or arrangement of cells or tissue under a microscope. It may result from irritation or inflammation, or represent a precancerous or cancerous change; its meaning depends on the whole sample and clinical setting.

name: atypical lymphocyte
clinical_significance: An activated-looking lymphocyte often seen during infections such as Epstein–Barr virus or cytomegalovirus. It is a nonspecific blood-smear finding and must be interpreted with symptoms and other test results.

name: audiologist
clinical_significance: A health professional who assesses hearing and fits hearing aids.

name: audiology
clinical_significance: The healthcare field concerned with hearing, balance, and related communication problems. Audiologists test hearing and balance, provide hearing aids and other devices, offer training and support, and identify when medical or surgical care may be needed.

name: audiometry
clinical_significance: Measurement of hearing sensitivity at different sound frequencies and intensities, usually using headphones or insert earphones.

name: auditory area
clinical_significance: A region of the cerebral cortex that processes sound information.

name: auditory fatigue
clinical_significance: Temporary listening fatigue after prolonged sound exposure or effort. It usually improves with rest, but persistent hearing changes or tinnitus after loud noise can indicate lasting auditory injury.

name: auditory ossicle
clinical_significance: One of three small middle-ear bones—the malleus, incus, and stapes—that transmit and amplify vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear. Disease, injury, or fixation of these bones can cause conductive hearing loss.

name: auditory pathway
clinical_significance: A chain of nerve structures carrying sound signals from the inner ear through the brainstem to the auditory cortex for recognition and interpretation.

name: auditory threshold
clinical_significance: The quietest sound a person can hear at a particular pitch or frequency. It is measured during a hearing test and helps describe the degree and type of hearing loss in each ear.

name: augmentation mammoplasty
clinical_significance: An operation to increase breast size or change breast shape, usually with implants or transferred fat. Possible risks include infection, bleeding, changes in sensation, scarring, and the need for further surgery.

name: aura
clinical_significance: A temporary sensory, visual, or other warning symptom that can precede a migraine headache or, in some people, a seizure. New sudden weakness, speech difficulty, or vision loss can also signal stroke and needs urgent assessment.

name: auranofin
clinical_significance: An oral gold-containing medicine used for selected cases of rheumatoid arthritis. It may reduce joint inflammation but can cause diarrhoea, rash, mouth sores, low blood counts, or kidney injury, so blood and urine tests are required.

name: aureobasidium
clinical_significance: A genus of dark-pigmented fungi commonly found on plants, soil, and indoor surfaces. Some species can rarely cause skin, eye, catheter, or bloodstream infections, particularly after injury or in people with weakened immunity.

name: aureobasidium pullulans
clinical_significance: An environmental, dark-pigmented fungus that rarely causes human infection, including skin or eye disease and, in vulnerable patients, catheter-associated or disseminated infection. Recovery from a nonsterile sample may represent contamination.

name: auricular artery
clinical_significance: An artery supplying the outer ear and nearby scalp. Injury can cause bleeding or threaten blood flow to the ear; its branches may be relevant in ear surgery and vascular procedures.

name: auricular vein
clinical_significance: A vein draining the outer ear and nearby scalp into larger neck veins. It is relevant to venous access, surgery, and evaluation of uncommon clots or malformations in the region.

name: aurothioglucose
clinical_significance: An injectable gold compound formerly used to treat rheumatoid arthritis. Gold therapy can cause serious skin, mouth, blood, kidney, or lung reactions and has largely been replaced by more effective disease-modifying medicines.

name: auscultation
clinical_significance: Listening to sounds produced inside the body, usually with a stethoscope. Clinicians use it to assess the heart, lungs, abdomen, and blood vessels for findings such as murmurs, wheezing, crackles, or abnormal blood-flow sounds.

name: autism
clinical_significance: Autism affects social communication and may involve restricted or repetitive behaviors; early support, communication accommodations, and assessment for coexisting conditions can improve participation and well-being.

name: autism spectrum disorder
clinical_significance: A lifelong neurodevelopmental condition involving persistent differences in social communication and interaction, along with restricted or repetitive behaviors, interests, or sensory patterns. Features begin during the developmental period, vary widely among individuals, and may affect communication, learning, relationships, daily activities, or the type and amount of support needed.

name: autoantibody
clinical_significance: An immune protein that mistakenly recognizes and binds a substance from the person's own body. It may damage tissues or interfere with their function, or it may be present only as a laboratory sign without causing disease.

name: autoantigen
clinical_significance: A substance normally found in the body that is mistakenly recognized as foreign by the immune system. This mistaken response can lead to inflammation or damage to the person's own cells or tissues.

name: autocrine communication
clinical_significance: A signalling process in which a cell releases a chemical messenger that acts on receptors on the same cell. It helps regulate immune responses, growth, and tissue repair; abnormal signalling can contribute to cancer and inflammation.

name: autocrine systems
clinical_significance: Networks in which cells release signals that act back on themselves to regulate their own behaviour. Autocrine signalling is important in immune and tissue biology and can help sustain growth in some cancers.

name: autogenic training
clinical_significance: A relaxation method using repeated exercises in heaviness, warmth, breathing, and heartbeat awareness. It may help some people manage stress or anxiety but does not replace medical or psychological treatment when needed.

name: autograft material
clinical_significance: A graft made from a person’s own tissue, such as skin, bone, or tendon. It avoids rejection from another person’s tissue but still carries surgical risks and may require a second site of tissue removal.

name: autoimmune
clinical_significance: Describing an immune response that mistakenly targets the body's own cells, tissues, or proteins. It can cause inflammation, tissue damage, or impaired organ function.

name: autoimmune disorder
clinical_significance: A condition in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own cells, tissues, or organs. It may be limited to one organ or affect many organs, causing inflammation and impaired function.

name: autoimmune enteropathy
clinical_significance: A rare disease in which the immune system damages the lining of the small intestine, causing ongoing diarrhoea, poor nutrient absorption, weight loss, or growth problems. It may occur with other immune disorders.

name: autoimmune hemolytic anemia
clinical_significance: Anaemia caused when immune proteins attach to and destroy red blood cells faster than the body can replace them. It may cause tiredness, pale or yellow skin, dark urine, rapid heartbeat, or shortness of breath.

name: autoimmune hypophysitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the pituitary gland caused by autoimmunity or, increasingly, immune-checkpoint cancer therapy. It can reduce pituitary hormones and cause headache, fatigue, low blood pressure, or adrenal and thyroid deficiencies.

name: autoimmune thyroiditis
clinical_significance: Immune-mediated inflammation and damage of the thyroid gland. See \textit{Hashimoto Thyroiditis}.

name: autolysis
clinical_significance: The breakdown of cells or tissues by their own enzymes, usually after the cells die. This natural process contributes to tissue decomposition and can affect specimens examined after death.

name: autolysosome
clinical_significance: A cell compartment formed when an autophagosome fuses with a lysosome to break down and recycle cell material. Its function is studied in neurodegenerative disease, infection, and cancer, but it is not a routine clinical test.

name: autonomic agents
clinical_significance: Medicines that alter the activity of the autonomic nervous system, which controls functions such as heart rate, blood pressure, pupil size, and digestion. Effects and risks depend on whether the drug stimulates or blocks specific nerve signals.

name: autonomic disorder
clinical_significance: A problem affecting nerves that control automatic body functions such as blood pressure, heart rate, digestion, sweating, bladder emptying, sexual function, and pupil size. Causes include diabetes, nerve disease, infection, immune disease, and medicines; symptoms depend on the affected functions.

name: autonomic ganglion
clinical_significance: A small group of nerve-cell bodies outside the brain and spinal cord that passes signals between the autonomic nervous system and organs such as the heart, intestines, glands, and bladder.

name: autonomic nervous system
clinical_significance: The part of the nervous system that controls body functions that usually happen without conscious effort, including heart rate, blood pressure, digestion, sweating, pupil size, bladder activity, and sexual responses.

name: autonomic neuropathy
clinical_significance: Damage to nerves that control automatic functions such as blood pressure, heart rate, digestion, sweating, bladder emptying, and sexual function. Diabetes is common, but other diseases, toxins, and medicines can also cause it.

name: autophagosome
clinical_significance: A membrane-bound cell structure that encloses material targeted for autophagy and later fuses with a lysosome for recycling. Autophagosomes are studied in cell stress, infection, and cancer biology.

name: autophagy
clinical_significance: A normal process in which cells break down and recycle worn-out proteins and cell parts. It helps cells survive stress and remove damaged material, but abnormal autophagy may contribute to some cancers and other diseases.

name: autopsy
clinical_significance: A medical examination of a body after death. It may include external examination, examination of internal organs, tissue testing, and sometimes toxicology to help determine the cause of death or study disease.

name: autoradiography
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that uses a radioactive label and a photographic or digital detector to show where a substance is located in a tissue, cell, or biological sample.

name: autosome
clinical_significance: Any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome. Humans usually have 22 pairs of autosomes. Genes on these chromosomes can cause inherited conditions in people of any sex.

name: average
clinical_significance: A statistical measure representing the sum of values divided by the number of observations. Clinical averages can summarize groups but may hide outliers or differences between patients, so they should not be treated as an individual result.

name: avian crop
clinical_significance: A pouch in a bird’s oesophagus where food can be stored and softened before digestion. It is important in avian veterinary medicine but has no direct human clinical counterpart.

name: avian influenza
clinical_significance: An infection caused by avian-adapted influenza A virus strains (such as H5N1, H5N6, or H7N9) transmitted to humans primarily via direct contact with infected poultry or contaminated environments. Clinical manifestations range from conjunctivitis and upper respiratory symptoms to fulminant viral pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), multi-organ failure, and death.

name: avidin
clinical_significance: A protein that binds the vitamin biotin. Avidin is used in laboratory tests and purification methods; eating large amounts of raw egg white over time can interfere with biotin absorption, while cooking reduces this effect.

name: avoidance
clinical_significance: A way of coping that involves staying away from feared thoughts, places, or situations. It can maintain anxiety or trauma-related symptoms when it limits daily activities, although temporary avoidance can be protective during real danger.

name: avoidance behavior
clinical_significance: Actions taken to stay away from a feared or distressing situation, thought, place, person, or activity. Avoidance may briefly reduce anxiety but can keep the fear going and interfere with treatment, work, relationships, or daily life.

name: avulavirus
clinical_significance: A genus of avian paramyxoviruses, including Newcastle disease virus, that mainly infect birds. Human infection is uncommon and usually causes mild conjunctivitis after close contact with infected poultry.

name: avulsion fracture
clinical_significance: A break in which a tendon or ligament pulls off a small piece of attached bone, usually during a sudden movement or injury. Treatment depends on the bone, fragment position, joint involvement, age, and associated damage.

name: awareness
clinical_significance: Conscious recognition of oneself, surroundings, thoughts, or sensations. Clinicians assess it along with alertness, attention, memory, and orientation when examining brain function.

name: axial
clinical_significance: Axial describes structures or symptoms along the central body axis, including the head, neck, and trunk; axial pain or imaging findings can help localize spinal or systemic disease.

name: axial skeleton
clinical_significance: The bones forming the central framework of the body: the skull, spine, ribs, breastbone, and associated small bones of the neck. It supports the body and protects the brain, spinal cord, heart, and lungs.

name: axilla
clinical_significance: The hollow area beneath the shoulder, commonly called the armpit. It contains major blood vessels, nerves, lymph nodes, and tissues connecting the chest and neck with the arm.

name: axillary lymphadenectomy
clinical_significance: An operation to remove lymph nodes from the armpit, usually to assess or treat breast cancer or melanoma. Possible complications include pain, numbness, shoulder stiffness, a fluid collection, nerve injury, and arm swelling.

name: axis
clinical_significance: The second bone in the neck. Its tooth-like projection acts as a pivot for the first neck bone, allowing the head and upper neck to rotate.

name: axis vertebra
clinical_significance: The second neck vertebra, whose tooth-like projection allows the first vertebra and head to rotate while protecting the spinal cord.

name: axitinib
clinical_significance: A targeted cancer medicine used alone or with other drugs for advanced renal-cell carcinoma. It blocks tumour blood-vessel growth and can cause high blood pressure, diarrhoea, fatigue, bleeding, or impaired wound healing.

name: axolemma
clinical_significance: The thin outer membrane surrounding a nerve cell's axon. It maintains the electrical difference needed for nerve impulses and contains channels that allow those impulses to travel along the axon.

name: axon
clinical_significance: The long extension of a nerve cell that carries electrical signals away from the cell body toward another nerve cell, muscle, or gland.

name: axon fasciculation
clinical_significance: The process during development in which growing nerve fibres group together to form organized nerve pathways. Chemical guidance signals and cell connections help them reach their correct targets.

name: axon guidance
clinical_significance: The process by which growing nerve fibres find and connect with their correct targets during development. Chemical signals and surrounding cells help direct their path.

name: axon hillock
clinical_significance: The cone-shaped part where a nerve cell's main body joins its axon, the long fiber that carries signals away. It combines incoming electrical signals and usually starts the nerve impulse when those signals are strong enough.

name: axonal transport
clinical_significance: The movement of proteins, cell parts, and other materials along a nerve cell's axon between the cell body and the axon terminal. It supports nerve-cell maintenance and communication.

name: axoneme
clinical_significance: The internal framework of tiny tubes inside a cilium or sperm tail. Together with motor proteins, it produces the bending movements that help move fluid over cells or propel sperm.

name: azacitidine
clinical_significance: Azacitidine is a hypomethylating chemotherapy used for selected myelodysplastic syndromes and related marrow cancers; it commonly suppresses blood counts, increasing infection and bleeding risk, so blood monitoring is essential.

name: azacosterol
clinical_significance: Azacosterol is an experimental cholesterol-lowering compound that inhibits sterol synthesis; it is not a routine clinical medicine and is mainly of historical or research interest.

name: azaguanine
clinical_significance: Azaguanine is an antimetabolite research compound that interferes with purine metabolism and cell growth; it is not a routine human treatment.

name: azamethiphos
clinical_significance: Azamethiphos is an organophosphate insecticide used mainly in veterinary and public-health pest control; exposure can inhibit acetylcholinesterase and cause cholinergic poisoning.

name: azaserine
clinical_significance: Azaserine is an antimetabolite that inhibits glutamine-dependent enzymes and has been used mainly in research; it is not an established clinical therapy and can be toxic to rapidly dividing cells.

name: azaspirane
clinical_significance: Azaspirane compounds have been studied for immune-modulating effects; they are not established routine therapies, and clinical significance depends on the specific molecule and trial evidence.

name: azathioprine
clinical_significance: Azathioprine suppresses immune activity and is used in transplantation and selected autoimmune diseases; it can cause serious infection, marrow suppression, liver injury, and rare pregnancy-related cholestasis, so blood and liver monitoring are important.

name: azathioprine sodium
clinical_significance: Azathioprine sodium is an injectable salt form of the immunosuppressant azathioprine; risks include infection, low blood counts, liver toxicity, and rare intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, requiring specialist monitoring.

name: azauridine
clinical_significance: Azauridine is an older antimetabolite studied and used for selected cancers; it can suppress bone marrow and damage rapidly dividing tissues, limiting its current clinical use.

name: azepines
clinical_significance: Azepines are a chemical class found in medicines and biologically active compounds; therapeutic effects and toxicity depend on the specific drug, not the shared ring structure alone.

name: azide
clinical_significance: Azide compounds can be highly toxic and may release hydrazoic acid; exposure can cause low blood pressure, seizures, and cardiovascular collapse and requires urgent toxicology management.

name: azinphos ethyl
clinical_significance: Azinphos-ethyl is an organophosphate pesticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase; exposure can cause sweating, secretions, muscle weakness, seizures, and respiratory failure.

name: azinphosmethyl
clinical_significance: Azinphos-methyl is a highly toxic organophosphate pesticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase; poisoning is a medical emergency requiring decontamination and specialist treatment.

name: aziridine
clinical_significance: Aziridine is a reactive chemical used in industry and research; it can cause severe irritation and is a potential carcinogen, so exposure control is important.

name: aziridines
clinical_significance: Aziridines are reactive chemical compounds used in some medicines and industrial products; toxicity varies, and some are alkylating agents that can damage DNA and tissue.

name: azithromycin
clinical_significance: Azithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic used for selected bacterial infections; QT prolongation, liver injury, gastrointestinal effects, and antimicrobial resistance are important considerations.

name: azlocillin
clinical_significance: Azlocillin is an antipseudomonal penicillin used for susceptible serious bacterial infections; allergy, kidney function, and culture susceptibility influence treatment.

name: azo compounds
clinical_significance: Azo compounds are dyes and chemicals; some can be metabolized to harmful aromatic amines, while clinical risk depends on the compound, exposure, and route.

name: azole
clinical_significance: Azole medicines inhibit fungal sterol synthesis and treat many fungal infections; liver toxicity, QT effects, and major drug interactions vary by agent.

name: azoospermia
clinical_significance: The absence of sperm in semen on laboratory examination. It may result from a blockage that prevents sperm from leaving the reproductive tract or from reduced or absent sperm production in the testes.

name: azotemia
clinical_significance: A build-up of nitrogen-containing waste products in the blood, usually because the kidneys are filtering less effectively. It may occur with dehydration, reduced kidney blood flow, or kidney disease.

name: azotobacter
clinical_significance: Azotobacter are soil bacteria that fix nitrogen and are mainly relevant to environmental and agricultural biology; they are not usual human pathogens.

name: azotobacter vinelandii
clinical_significance: Azotobacter vinelandii is a nitrogen-fixing soil bacterium used in microbiology and biotechnology research; it is not a common cause of human disease.

name: azoxymethane
clinical_significance: Azoxymethane is a laboratory chemical used to induce colon tumors in animal research; it is a carcinogen and not a human diagnostic or therapeutic agent.

name: azurin
clinical_significance: Azurin is a bacterial copper-containing protein studied for electron transfer and possible anticancer activity; it is experimental and not an established clinical treatment.

name: babesia
clinical_significance: A group of parasites transmitted mainly by certain ticks. They infect red blood cells and can cause fever, tiredness, anaemia, low platelets, jaundice, or dark urine; severe illness is more likely without a spleen or with weak immunity.

name: babesia divergens
clinical_significance: A species of parasite that infects red blood cells and can cause babesiosis, especially in Europe. It may cause severe destruction of red cells, particularly in people without a spleen or with a weakened immune system.

name: babesia microti
clinical_significance: A parasite and the most common cause of babesiosis in North America. It is spread by black-legged ticks, infects red blood cells, and may cause no symptoms or severe anaemia, jaundice, and organ failure.

name: babesiosis
clinical_significance: An infection caused by Babesia parasites, usually spread by ticks. The parasites enter red blood cells and may cause fever, tiredness, anaemia, low platelets, jaundice, or dark urine; severe disease can affect several organs.

name: babinski reflex
clinical_significance: A reflex tested by stroking the sole of the foot. In babies, the big toe normally moves upward and the other toes spread; in older children and adults, the toes usually curl downward. An upward response later in life may indicate a brain or spinal-cord problem.

name: bacillaceae
clinical_significance: A family of rod-shaped bacteria that includes species able to form resistant spores. Some members are harmless or useful, while others can cause infections such as anthrax or food poisoning.

name: bacillary angiomatosis
clinical_significance: A vascular infection caused mainly by \textit{Bartonella henselae} or \textit{Bartonella quintana}, usually in people with weakened immunity. It produces friable red-to-purple papules or nodules and may involve lymph nodes, liver, spleen, bone, or other organs; biopsy and special stains or molecular testing may help distinguish it from Kaposi sarcoma. Antibiotic treatment is usually effective.

name: bacillus
clinical_significance: A rod-shaped bacterium. The word can describe bacterial shape or members of the Bacillus genus, many of which form resistant spores; some are harmless, while others cause disease.

name: bacillus anthracis
clinical_significance: A spore-forming bacterium that causes anthrax in people and animals. Infection may affect the skin, digestive tract, or lungs and can rapidly become life-threatening, requiring urgent specialist treatment and public-health action.

name: bacillus cereus
clinical_significance: A spore-forming bacterium that can cause food poisoning after contaminated food is eaten. It may cause sudden vomiting or watery diarrhoea and, rarely, serious infections in people with weakened immunity.

name: bacillus lentus
clinical_significance: Bacillus lentus is an environmental and industrial species rarely implicated in human infection; a clinical isolate should be assessed for contamination versus true disease.

name: bacillus licheniformis
clinical_significance: Bacillus licheniformis is common in soil and food and can rarely cause opportunistic infection or food poisoning; specimen source and symptoms determine whether an isolate is clinically significant.

name: bacillus megaterium
clinical_significance: Bacillus megaterium is an environmental bacterium that rarely causes opportunistic human infection; it is often a contaminant, but recovery from a sterile site may warrant evaluation.

name: bacillus mycoides
clinical_significance: Bacillus mycoides is a soil-associated bacterium that is rarely pathogenic in humans; clinical culture results require correlation with specimen quality and patient findings.

name: bacillus pumilus
clinical_significance: Bacillus pumilus is an environmental spore-forming bacterium that can rarely cause wound or bloodstream infection; persistent recovery from a sterile site is more concerning than a single contaminated sample.

name: bacillus subtilis
clinical_significance: Bacillus subtilis is common in soil and can contaminate food or laboratory specimens; it rarely causes opportunistic infection, particularly in people with devices or impaired immunity.

name: bacitracin
clinical_significance: An antibiotic applied to the skin that prevents susceptible bacteria from building their protective cell wall. It is used for selected superficial infections, but it can cause skin irritation or allergic reactions.

name: back
clinical_significance: Back pain is common and often musculoskeletal, but neurologic deficits, fever, trauma, cancer history, or bladder and bowel changes can indicate serious disease requiring prompt assessment.

name: back injury
clinical_significance: Damage to the muscles, ligaments, joints, discs, bones, or nerves of the back after trauma, lifting, or repeated strain. Pain and stiffness are common; weakness, numbness, loss of bladder or bowel control, or major-trauma pain requires urgent assessment.

name: backache
clinical_significance: Pain or discomfort in the back, from the neck to the buttocks. It is a symptom rather than a disease and may result from muscles, joints, discs, nerves, or pain referred from an internal organ.

name: baclofen
clinical_significance: A medicine that reduces muscle spasm by lowering nerve signals in the spinal cord. It can cause sleepiness, weakness, dizziness, or confusion; stopping it suddenly after regular use can cause dangerous withdrawal symptoms.

name: bacteremia
clinical_significance: The presence of living bacteria in the bloodstream. It may be temporary, intermittent, or continuous. Some cases cause no illness, while others produce fever and can progress to sepsis or infection of distant organs.

name: bacteria
clinical_significance: Microscopic single-celled organisms. Many live harmlessly or help the body, while others cause infections; bacteria can live alone or in communities and may develop resistance to antibiotics.

name: bacteria present
clinical_significance: A urinalysis finding indicating bacteria were seen or detected in the urine. It may reflect a urinary infection, harmless bacteria without symptoms, or contamination during collection; symptoms, culture results, pregnancy, and planned procedures guide its significance.

name: bacterial capsule
clinical_significance: A protective outer coating around some bacteria, often made of sugars. It can help bacteria avoid being swallowed by immune cells, survive in the body, and cause disease.

name: bacterial conjunctivitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by bacteria. It can cause redness, irritation, and thick or pus-like discharge that may stick the eyelids together; it is often contagious. Eye pain, light sensitivity, reduced vision, or contact-lens use needs prompt assessment.

name: bacterial endocarditis
clinical_significance: A serious infection of the heart’s inner lining or valves. It may cause fever, chills, tiredness, a new or changing murmur, or weight loss. Bacteria can damage valves or break off and block blood vessels; diagnosis usually requires blood cultures and heart imaging.

name: Bacterial Infections
clinical_significance: Infections caused by bacteria. They range from localized illnesses to infections involving the blood or multiple organs; the likely organism, infection site, and resistance pattern guide testing and antibiotic treatment.

name: bacterial meningitis
clinical_significance: A serious infection of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord. It can cause fever, severe headache, stiff neck, vomiting, confusion, seizures, or a rash and requires immediate hospital treatment.

name: bacterial pneumonia
clinical_significance: A bacterial infection of the lungs that causes inflammation and may fill air spaces with fluid or pus. It can cause fever, cough, phlegm, chest pain, shortness of breath, and low oxygen levels.

name: bacterial protein
clinical_significance: A protein produced by a bacterium that may form part of its structure, support its metabolism, help it attach to host cells, or contribute to disease.

name: bacterial toxemia
clinical_significance: The presence or effects of harmful bacterial substances in the bloodstream. It can occur during severe infection and may cause widespread inflammation, low blood pressure, shock, or organ injury.

name: bacterial toxin
clinical_significance: A harmful substance made or released by bacteria. It may kill or injure cells, interfere with body functions, or trigger severe inflammation; toxins may be secreted or released when bacteria break apart.

name: bacterial tracheitis
clinical_significance: A bacterial infection and swelling of the windpipe. It can cause fever, a harsh cough, noisy or difficult breathing, and rapid narrowing of the airway, making urgent treatment necessary.

name: bacterial typing
clinical_significance: Methods used to distinguish bacterial strains, often by their genetic or antigen patterns. Typing can help trace outbreaks, identify transmission, and support infection-control decisions, but it does not by itself establish that a strain causes disease.

name: bacterial vaccine
clinical_significance: A vaccine made from whole bacteria or selected bacterial components to train the immune system to recognize a bacterial infection. Protection and safety depend on the specific vaccine and the person receiving it.

name: bacterial vaginosis
clinical_significance: A common change in the vaginal bacteria in which protective lactobacilli decrease and other bacteria increase. It may cause a thin, grey or white discharge and a fish-like smell, but many people have no symptoms.

name: bacteriocin
clinical_significance: A protein-like substance made by some bacteria that inhibits or kills other susceptible bacteria nearby. It gives the producing bacterium a competitive advantage, but its medical importance depends on the organism and setting.

name: bacteriology
clinical_significance: The study of bacteria, including their structure, genes, growth, spread, effects on health, and role in disease. It includes laboratory methods used to identify bacteria and test antibiotic sensitivity.

name: bacteriophage lambda
clinical_significance: A virus that infects the bacterium Escherichia coli. It may multiply and burst the bacterial cell or insert its genetic material into the cell’s DNA and remain inactive until later.

name: bacteriophage t4
clinical_significance: A virus that infects Escherichia coli, makes many copies inside the bacterium, and usually breaks the cell open to release them.

name: Bacteriophages
clinical_significance: Viruses that infect bacteria and use them to make more viruses. They may destroy the bacterial cell or insert their genetic material into it and remain inactive for a time.

name: bacteriorhodopsin
clinical_significance: A light-sensitive protein in some microorganisms. It uses light energy to move charged particles across the cell membrane, helping the organism produce energy.

name: bacteriuria
clinical_significance: The presence of bacteria in urine detected by testing. It may occur with urinary symptoms as part of an infection or without symptoms; the result must be interpreted with the sample quality, amount of bacteria, pregnancy, and other medical factors.

name: bacteroidaceae
clinical_significance: A family of bacteria that commonly live in the intestine and grow without oxygen. They are usually harmless in the gut but can cause abscesses or other infections if they enter wounds or body areas that should be free of bacteria.

name: bacteroides
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria that normally live in the intestine and grow without oxygen. They are usually harmless there but can cause abscesses or bloodstream infection if bowel contents enter wounds or other sterile areas.

name: bacteroides caccae
clinical_significance: A bacterium that normally lives in the intestine without oxygen. It is usually harmless there but may be found in mixed abdominal or bloodstream infections when intestinal bacteria escape into other tissues.

name: bacteroides dorei
clinical_significance: A bacterium that normally lives in the human intestine and grows without oxygen. It is generally considered a harmless member of the gut microbiota.

name: bacteroides eggerthii
clinical_significance: A species of anaerobic bacteria found in the human intestinal microbiota. It is not a common cause of human disease, but like related gut bacteria it may contribute to opportunistic infection if it enters normally sterile tissue.

name: bacteroides faecis
clinical_significance: A species of anaerobic bacteria associated with the intestinal microbiota. Its clinical significance is limited; detection in a specimen should be interpreted according to the sample site and whether there is evidence of infection.

name: bacteroides fragilis
clinical_significance: A bacterium that normally lives in the intestine without oxygen. If bowel contents leak into the abdomen, it is an important cause of abscesses, abdominal infection, bloodstream infection, and sepsis.

name: bacteroides gingivalis
clinical_significance: An older name for Porphyromonas gingivalis, a bacterium that grows without oxygen in dental plaque. It is associated with inflammation and destruction of the tissues supporting the teeth.

name: bacteroides heparinolyticus
