clinical_significance: A species of anaerobic bacteria reported in human mucosal and clinical samples. Its presence may be associated with infection in some settings, but the finding must be interpreted with symptoms and specimen source.

name: bacteroides intestinalis
clinical_significance: A species of anaerobic bacteria found in the intestinal tract. It may be relevant in mixed infections when gut organisms reach normally sterile sites; isolation from stool alone does not indicate disease.

name: bacteroides nordii
clinical_significance: A species of anaerobic bacteria associated with the human gut. It is an uncommon clinical isolate, and its significance depends on whether it is recovered from a normally sterile site and matches the patient’s illness.

name: bacteroides ovatus
clinical_significance: An anaerobic Gram-negative bacterium that is part of the intestinal microbiota and can contribute to opportunistic infection if it enters damaged or normally sterile tissue.

name: bacteroides pyogenes
clinical_significance: A species name historically used for anaerobic bacteria associated with animal or human infections. Because taxonomy and clinical reports vary, identification should be interpreted by a microbiology laboratory in the context of the specimen and symptoms.

name: bacteroides salyersiae
clinical_significance: A species of anaerobic bacteria reported in the human intestinal microbiota and clinical specimens. Its role in disease is not well established; recovery from a nonsterile sample may represent colonization.

name: bacteroides stercoris
clinical_significance: A species of anaerobic bacteria associated with the intestinal microbiota. It is not a frequent human pathogen but may be relevant in opportunistic or mixed infection outside the bowel.

name: bacteroides thetaiotaomicron
clinical_significance: An anaerobic Gram-negative bacterium that is an important member of the human gut microbiota and helps break down complex dietary carbohydrates; it can cause opportunistic infection outside the intestine.

name: bacteroides uniformis
clinical_significance: A species of anaerobic bacteria commonly found in the intestine. It is generally a commensal organism but may contribute to opportunistic infection if it enters normally sterile tissue.

name: bacteroides ureolyticus
clinical_significance: A bacterial name historically applied to an anaerobic, urease-producing organism now generally classified as Campylobacter ureolyticus, which can be associated with wound or bloodstream infection.

name: bacteroides vulgatus
clinical_significance: An anaerobic Gram-negative bacterium commonly found in the human intestine that can contribute to infection when the intestinal barrier is disrupted.

name: bacteroides xylanisolvens
clinical_significance: A species of anaerobic bacteria in the human intestinal microbiota that can break down xylan, a plant fibre. It is generally considered a commensal; detection in stool alone does not indicate infection.

name: bacteroidete
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria formerly called Bacteroidetes and now commonly named Bacteroidota. Many are normal members of the gut microbiota, while some can cause opportunistic infections outside their usual body sites.

name: baculoviridae
clinical_significance: A family of viruses that infect insects and other invertebrates, not people. Related viruses are used in biological research and as tools for delivering genes in some experimental or veterinary applications.

name: bad protein
clinical_significance: A name used for abnormal prion protein associated with transmissible spongiform encephalopathies. Prion proteins can accumulate in the brain and cause progressive, fatal neurodegeneration; this is a specialized research term rather than a routine clinical result.

name: bagassosis
clinical_significance: An allergic lung inflammation caused by breathing dust from mouldy bagasse, the fibrous waste left after sugarcane juice is extracted. It may cause cough, fever, breathlessness, and fatigue after workplace exposure.

name: bak protein
clinical_significance: A protein on the outer membrane of mitochondria, the cell’s energy-producing structures, that can help start controlled cell death. When activated, it makes openings that release cell-death signals; abnormal control may contribute to cancer.

name: balamuthia
clinical_significance: A genus of free-living amoebas found in soil and water. Some species can rarely infect people, usually causing slowly progressive inflammation of the brain and sometimes skin disease.

name: balamuthia mandrillaris
clinical_significance: A free-living amoeba found in soil and water that can rarely infect humans. It may enter through broken skin or the nose and cause severe, gradually worsening infection of the brain or skin.

name: balanced study
clinical_significance: A clinical study design in which participant characteristics are evenly distributed between comparison groups at baseline, either by design or by randomization, to reduce confounding and allow fair comparison of interventions.

name: balanitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the glans penis, sometimes involving the foreskin as well. It can cause redness, tenderness, swelling, or discharge and may result from irritation, infection, or a skin condition; recurrent episodes may warrant evaluation for diabetes or another underlying cause.

name: balantidiasis
clinical_significance: Balantidiasis is intestinal infection caused by the protozoan Balantidium coli, producing diarrhea, abdominal pain, or colitis, especially after fecal exposure.

name: balantidium
clinical_significance: A genus of large, single-celled parasites that can infect the large intestine. Infection may cause diarrhoea, abdominal pain, or inflammation of the colon, although many infected people have no symptoms.

name: balantidium coli
clinical_significance: A single-celled parasite that can infect the large intestine, usually after contact with food or water contaminated by animal or human stool. It may cause diarrhoea, abdominal pain, or colitis.

name: balbiani body
clinical_significance: A temporary cluster of cell parts and genetic messages near the nucleus of a developing egg cell. It helps organize materials that the early embryo needs after fertilization.

name: balloon angioplasty
clinical_significance: A minimally invasive procedure that widens a narrowed or blocked artery by inflating a small balloon on a catheter. It can restore blood flow, but the vessel may narrow again and complications can include bleeding, vessel injury, or clot formation.

name: balloon brachytherapy
clinical_significance: A form of internal radiation treatment in which a balloon catheter is placed in a body space, often the cavity left after breast-cancer surgery, and radioactive material is temporarily put inside it to treat nearby tissue.

name: balloon dilatation
clinical_significance: A procedure that widens a narrowed passage or opening by inflating a balloon catheter within it. It is used in selected blood vessels and other organs; risks depend on the site and include bleeding, tearing, or re-narrowing.

name: bandage
clinical_significance: A material or device placed over an injury or wound to protect it, absorb fluid, apply pressure, or support healing. The type and frequency of change depend on the wound and its risk of infection or skin damage.

name: Barakat syndrome
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder that can cause low parathyroid hormone, hearing loss, and kidney abnormalities. These problems may occur together because of genetic changes affecting the development of several organs.

name: barbiturates
clinical_significance: Medicines that reduce activity in the brain and spinal cord. They may be used for anaesthesia or selected seizure disorders, but their risk of breathing suppression, dependence, and overdose means safer alternatives are often preferred.

name: Bardet-Biedl syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder that may cause retinal degeneration, obesity, extra fingers or toes, kidney disease, and developmental or reproductive problems.

name: bariatric surgery
clinical_significance: Operations that reduce stomach capacity or change digestion to support substantial weight loss and improve obesity-related disease. They require long-term changes in eating, supplements, follow-up, and monitoring for complications.

name: barium
clinical_significance: A metallic element used medically mainly as barium sulfate, a substance that outlines the digestive tract during certain X-ray examinations. Soluble barium compounds are poisonous and are different from barium sulfate.

name: barium enema
clinical_significance: An X-ray examination of the large intestine after barium is put into the rectum. Sometimes air is added to show the bowel lining more clearly. It may be used to examine blockage, diverticula, or changes after surgery; other tests are now preferred for routine colon-cancer screening.

name: barium sulfate
clinical_significance: A liquid or paste swallowed or placed in the rectum to outline the digestive tract during X-ray examinations. It is not absorbed normally, but breathing it into the lungs or leakage through a bowel hole can cause serious complications.

name: Barlow test
clinical_significance: A physical examination maneuver for detecting hip instability in infants. With the hip flexed, gentle pressure is applied to see whether the femoral head can be displaced out of the socket, suggesting developmental dysplasia of the hip.

name: baroreflex
clinical_significance: A rapid reflex that helps regulate blood pressure by adjusting heart rate and blood-vessel tone in response to changes in arterial pressure.

name: barrett esophagus
clinical_significance: A change in the lower lining of the swallowing tube caused by long-term acid reflux. The changed lining can increase the risk of precancerous changes and cancer.

name: bartholin gland
clinical_significance: One of two small glands beside the vaginal opening that release lubricating fluid. A blocked duct can cause a cyst, and infection can cause a painful abscess with swelling and difficulty sitting or walking.

name: bartonella
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria usually spread by fleas, lice, ticks, or contact with animals. Different species can cause cat-scratch disease, trench fever, skin lesions, heart-valve infection, or bloodstream infection.

name: bartonella elizabethae
clinical_significance: A species of Bartonella bacteria that has rarely been linked to bloodstream infection and inflammation of the heart valves, especially in people with underlying health problems.

name: bartonella henselae
clinical_significance: The bacterium that most commonly causes cat-scratch disease. It is usually spread by a kitten scratch or bite and may cause a small skin bump, swollen nearby lymph nodes, fever, or, rarely, disease of other organs.

name: bartonella infections
clinical_significance: Infections caused by Bartonella bacteria. They may produce swollen lymph nodes, fever, skin lesions, anaemia, heart-valve infection, or inflammation of organs; symptoms and severity depend on the species and immune status.

name: bartonella quintana
clinical_significance: A Bartonella species spread mainly by body lice. It causes trench fever, with recurring fever, headache, bone pain, and weakness, and can sometimes cause bloodstream or heart-valve infection.

name: bartonellaceae
clinical_significance: A family of bacteria that includes Bartonella species. Members can cause cat-scratch disease, trench fever, skin and blood-vessel lesions, bloodstream infection, or infection of the heart valves.

name: bart's hemoglobinopathy
clinical_significance: A severe inherited blood disorder caused when all four genes needed to make alpha-globin are missing or inactive. The fetus cannot make enough normal haemoglobin, causing severe anaemia, swelling, and often death before or soon after birth.

name: Bartter disease
clinical_significance: Bartter syndrome causes renal salt wasting with low potassium and metabolic alkalosis; it can impair growth and cause dehydration, weakness, and kidney complications.

name: basal
clinical_significance: Relating to the base of a structure or to a person's resting level of activity, such as resting metabolism or temperature measured after sleep.

name: basal body
clinical_significance: A small structure at the base of a cilium or flagellum, such as a cell hair or sperm tail. It anchors the structure to the cell and helps organize the parts that produce movement.

name: basal cell
clinical_significance: A cell in the deepest layer of an epithelial tissue, where it can divide and produce new cells. In the epidermis, basal cells help renew the skin and contain keratinocyte stem and progenitor cells.

name: basal cell carcinoma
clinical_significance: The most common skin cancer, arising from basal keratinocytes and associated mainly with cumulative ultraviolet exposure. It may appear as a pearly or translucent papule, a sore that repeatedly bleeds or does not heal, or a scar-like patch; local invasion can destroy nearby tissue, although distant spread is uncommon. Diagnosis requires biopsy, and treatment commonly involves excision, Mohs surgery, or selected nonsurgical or targeted therapies.

name: basal ganglia
clinical_significance: Deep brain structures that help control movement, habits, learning, and emotions. Problems in these structures can cause tremor, stiffness, slowed movement, or unwanted movements.

name: basal lamina
clinical_significance: A thin layer beneath many lining cells that anchors them to supporting tissue. It also helps control movement of substances between the lining and the tissue below.

name: basal tear
clinical_significance: A tear that is continuously present on the eye's surface. It keeps the cornea moist, smooth, and protected and helps wash away dust and microorganisms.

name: base
clinical_significance: A substance that can accept hydrogen ions or reduce acidity. In water, a base usually has a pH above 7; strong bases can burn tissue, while weaker bases are important in body fluids and chemical reactions.

name: base pair
clinical_significance: Two matching building blocks joined inside DNA or RNA. In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine pairs with guanine; in RNA, adenine usually pairs with uracil.

name: base pairing
clinical_significance: The matching of complementary DNA or RNA building blocks. This matching helps copy genetic information accurately and allows RNA molecules to fold into useful shapes or attach to other molecules.

name: base sequence
clinical_significance: The exact order of DNA or RNA building blocks in a molecule. It carries genetic information and can be examined to identify inherited changes, mutations, or infectious organisms.

name: baseline
clinical_significance: A starting measurement or description of a person's health before treatment, illness, or observation. Later findings are compared with it to identify improvement, worsening, or change.

name: basement membrane
clinical_significance: A thin supporting layer beneath many cells that line organs and body surfaces. It anchors the cells, helps control exchange with underlying tissue, and can act as a barrier to tumour spread.

name: basic fuchsin
clinical_significance: A magenta dye used in microscopy and laboratory staining, including methods for visualizing bacteria. It is a laboratory reagent rather than a treatment; handling requires appropriate precautions because some formulations may be hazardous.

name: basic research
clinical_significance: Research that builds fundamental knowledge about biology and disease mechanisms without aiming at an immediate clinical application. It can inform later diagnostic methods or treatments but does not itself establish that an intervention benefits patients.

name: basidiomycota
clinical_significance: A major fungal group that reproduces by forming spores on club-shaped structures called basidia. It includes mushrooms, rusts, smuts, and some fungi that can cause human disease.

name: basilar membrane
clinical_significance: A flexible membrane in the cochlea that supports the organ of Corti and vibrates in response to sound. Different parts respond best to different sound frequencies.

name: basiliximab
clinical_significance: A monoclonal antibody that blocks the interleukin-2 receptor alpha chain on activated T cells. It is used as induction immunosuppression, especially in kidney transplantation, and increases susceptibility to infection.

name: basis pontis
clinical_significance: The basis pontis is the front portion of the pons containing descending motor fibers and pontine nuclei that relay signals to the cerebellum.

name: basophil
clinical_significance: A rare type of white blood cell involved in allergic and inflammatory reactions. It releases substances such as histamine and can increase in number with some allergies, infections, and blood disorders.

name: basophil adenoma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous tumour of hormone-producing cells in the pituitary gland. It may release too much hormone or press on nearby structures, causing headache, vision problems, or other hormone-related symptoms.

name: basophilic focus
clinical_significance: An area in a tissue sample that stains blue or purple with a laboratory dye. The finding describes appearance under the microscope and must be interpreted with the surrounding tissue and other tests.

name: basosquamous carcinoma
clinical_significance: A skin cancer with features of both basal-cell and squamous-cell carcinoma. It usually develops on sun-damaged skin and may behave more aggressively than ordinary basal-cell cancer, so complete treatment and follow-up are important.

name: batabulin
clinical_significance: An experimental anticancer compound studied for disrupting microtubules, structures cells use during division. It has been investigated in clinical research, but it is not an established routine treatment.

name: batimastat
clinical_significance: An experimental matrix metalloproteinase inhibitor studied as a potential anticancer drug. Clinical benefit was not established, and it is not a routine treatment.

name: batrachotoxin
clinical_significance: A very powerful poison found in some frogs and birds. It keeps nerve and heart sodium channels open, causing abnormal nerve activity, dangerous heart rhythms, paralysis, and potentially death.

name: batracylin
clinical_significance: An experimental anticancer compound studied for effects on DNA and tumour-cell growth. It is not a standard treatment in current clinical practice.

name: batroxobin
clinical_significance: An enzyme derived from snake venom that changes fibrinogen, a blood protein, into fibrin, the material that strengthens a blood clot. It has been studied or used in selected bleeding and clotting settings and can alter bleeding risk.

name: battey bacillus
clinical_significance: An older name for the group of nontuberculous mycobacteria now called Mycobacterium avium complex. These organisms can cause lung disease, swollen lymph nodes, or widespread infection, especially when immunity is severely weakened.

name: bax protein
clinical_significance: A protein that helps start programmed cell death when a cell is damaged or no longer needed. Excessive or insufficient Bax activity can affect cell survival and has been studied in cancer and other diseases.

name: B-cell activation
clinical_significance: The process in which a B cell receives signals after recognizing a foreign substance, then multiplies and develops into antibody-producing cells or long-lasting memory cells.

name: B-cell lymphoma
clinical_significance: A group of cancers that begin in B lymphocytes. Different types grow at different speeds and may affect lymph nodes or organs; diagnosis and treatment depend on the exact type, extent, and person's health.

name: bcgosis
clinical_significance: An infection caused by the weakened mycobacteria used in BCG treatment or vaccination. It may remain local or spread to organs, especially in people with weakened immunity, and can cause fever, cough, or inflammation.

name: beacopp regimen
clinical_significance: A combination chemotherapy regimen used mainly to treat Hodgkin lymphoma; it includes bleomycin, etoposide, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, procarbazine, and prednisone, with dosing and supportive care determined by the oncology team.

name: beat number
clinical_significance: The number assigned to a particular heartbeat or rhythmic event when beats are counted or analysed. It can help describe timing, rate, or changes in a recorded heart rhythm.

name: Beau's lines
clinical_significance: Transverse grooves or depressions across a fingernail or toenail caused by temporary interruption of nail growth. They may follow severe illness, injury, or some treatments; multiple nails can show lines after a systemic event.

name: becaplermin
clinical_significance: Becaplermin is a recombinant platelet-derived growth factor gel used in selected diabetic foot ulcers with appropriate wound care.

name: becatecarin
clinical_significance: An investigational anticancer compound studied for activity against tumour cells. It is not an established routine treatment, and its clinical role remains limited to research.

name: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
clinical_significance: An overgrowth condition present from birth that may cause a large body or tongue, abdominal-wall defects, enlarged organs, low blood sugar in newborns, and increased risk of certain childhood cancers. Regular specialist monitoring is needed.

name: beclomethasone
clinical_significance: Beclomethasone is a corticosteroid used by inhalation, nasal spray, or topical routes to reduce inflammation in asthma, rhinitis, or skin disease.

name: becquerel
clinical_significance: The International System (SI) derived unit of radionuclide activity, defined as one nuclear decay or disintegration per second ($1\text{ Bq} = 1\text{ s}^{-1}$). Clinical diagnostic and therapeutic radioisotope doses are typically quantified in megabecquerels (MBq) or gigabecquerels (GBq).

name: bed rest
clinical_significance: Staying in bed or remaining mostly reclined to limit activity. It is used only for selected medical reasons because prolonged inactivity can cause muscle loss, blood clots, constipation, pressure injuries, and reduced independence.

name: bedwetting
clinical_significance: Bedwetting may reflect normal development, constipation, sleep or bladder problems, diabetes, or stress; new onset or associated symptoms warrant assessment without blame or punishment.

name: behavior
clinical_significance: The observable actions, responses, and activities of an organism, influenced by genetic, neurobiological, psychological, and environmental factors. In medicine, behavioral assessment helps diagnose psychiatric, developmental, and neurological conditions.

name: behavior disorder
clinical_significance: A persistent pattern of actions or emotional responses that causes significant distress, interferes with daily life, or harms relationships. Causes may be developmental, psychological, medical, or environmental.

name: behavior test
clinical_significance: A structured assessment of behavior, mood, attention, thinking, or social functioning. It may use observation, interviews, questionnaires, or standardized tasks to help identify developmental, psychiatric, or neurologic concerns.

name: behavior therapy
clinical_significance: A form of psychotherapy based on learning principles that uses reinforcement, extinction, and other behavioral techniques to modify maladaptive behaviors. It is effective for anxiety disorders, phobias, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and habit disorders.

name: behavioral abnormality
clinical_significance: A deviation from typical patterns of behavior that may indicate a psychiatric, neurodevelopmental, or neurologic condition. It is assessed by history, observation, standardized measures, and developmental norms to determine clinical significance.

name: behavioral genetics
clinical_significance: The study of how genes and environmental factors influence behavior and mental traits. Most behaviors reflect many genes interacting with life experiences, not one gene alone.

name: behavioral medicine
clinical_significance: An interdisciplinary field applying behavioural and biomedical knowledge to prevent illness, support health, and improve the management of disease. It includes approaches such as smoking cessation, stress management, and adherence support.

name: Behcet syndrome
clinical_significance: Another name for Behcet disease, an inflammatory illness that causes repeated mouth and genital sores and may affect the eyes, skin, joints, blood vessels, brain, or digestive tract.

name: behenic acid
clinical_significance: A saturated fatty acid found in small amounts in foods and body lipids and used in some personal-care and industrial products. It has no established role as a medicine or diagnostic marker.

name: Behr syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited neurological disorder causing progressive optic-nerve damage, poor vision, muscle stiffness, unsteady movement, and sometimes weakness or bladder problems.

name: belinostat
clinical_significance: A cancer medicine that blocks enzymes involved in turning genes on and off. It is used for some peripheral T-cell lymphomas that have returned or resisted earlier treatment.

name: Bell palsy
clinical_significance: Sudden weakness or paralysis of one side of the face caused by dysfunction of the facial nerve. The eyelid may not close fully, and taste or hearing may change. Most cases improve, but urgent assessment is needed to distinguish it from stroke and to protect the eye.

name: belotecan hydrochloride
clinical_significance: An investigational topoisomerase-inhibiting anticancer medicine studied for selected cancers. It can suppress bone marrow and cause low blood counts, but it is not a routinely used treatment.

name: benchmarking
clinical_significance: Comparing healthcare results, safety, costs, or processes with a standard or similar service. The comparison can identify areas for improvement but does not by itself prove that one service causes better outcomes.

name: bendamustine
clinical_significance: A cancer medicine that damages tumour-cell DNA and is used for selected blood cancers. It can also damage healthy bone-marrow cells, causing low blood counts, infection, tiredness, nausea, or other side effects.

name: bendamustine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: The hydrochloride form of bendamustine, a chemotherapy medicine used for selected blood cancers. It damages DNA and may cause low blood counts, infection, infusion reactions, nausea, tiredness, or other side effects.

name: bendiocarb
clinical_significance: A carbamate insecticide that can overstimulate nerves after significant exposure. Poisoning may cause sweating, salivation, vomiting, diarrhoea, small pupils, muscle twitching, breathing difficulty, or weakness and requires urgent medical treatment.

name: bendroflumethiazide
clinical_significance: A diuretic medicine that helps the kidneys remove salt and water. It is used for high blood pressure or fluid retention and may lower potassium or sodium and increase uric acid or blood sugar.

name: benfuracarb
clinical_significance: A carbamate insecticide that can overstimulate nerves after significant exposure. It may cause sweating, salivation, vomiting, diarrhoea, small pupils, muscle twitching, breathing difficulty, or weakness and requires urgent medical treatment.

name: benign
clinical_significance: Not cancerous. A benign growth does not invade nearby tissues or spread to other parts of the body, but it can still cause problems because of its size, location, or hormone production.

name: benign ameloblastoma
clinical_significance: A usually slow-growing tumour arising from cells involved in tooth development, most often in the jaw. It is not cancer but can expand, damage bone, and displace teeth, so treatment usually requires specialist surgery.

name: benign epithelioma
clinical_significance: A noncancerous growth arising from cells that line the skin or an organ. It does not invade or spread, but removal or testing may be needed if it bleeds, grows, causes symptoms, or is difficult to distinguish from cancer.

name: benign hemangiopericytoma
clinical_significance: A tumor previously called benign hemangiopericytoma may recur or metastasize despite bland appearance; expert pathology and long-term follow-up guide risk assessment.

name: benign meningioma
clinical_significance: A usually slow-growing, noncancerous tumour arising from the membranes around the brain or spinal cord. It may cause seizures, headache, weakness, or vision problems by pressing on nearby structures.

name: benign mesenchymoma
clinical_significance: A rare noncancerous tumour containing more than one type of tissue such as fat, cartilage, or bone. Its symptoms depend on the site and size, and diagnosis requires examination of tissue.

name: benign myoepithelioma
clinical_significance: A noncancerous tumour of myoepithelial cells, often arising in a salivary gland or other glandular tissue. It usually grows slowly and may cause a painless lump; diagnosis depends on tissue examination.

name: benign neoplasm
clinical_significance: A noncancerous growth of cells that remains at its original site and does not spread to distant organs. It may still cause harm by pressing on nearby structures, blocking a passage, bleeding, or producing hormones.

name: benign paraganglioma
clinical_significance: A usually slow-growing tumour of specialized nerve-related cells. It may release adrenaline-like hormones or press on nearby nerves and blood vessels; symptoms and treatment depend on its site and activity.

name: benign prostate hyperplasia
clinical_significance: A noncancerous enlargement of the prostate that can narrow the urethra and make urination difficult or frequent, especially at night. Severe obstruction can cause urinary retention, bladder stones, infection, or kidney problems; symptoms should be assessed because other conditions can cause them too.

name: benzaldehyde
clinical_significance: A chemical with an almond-like smell used in flavourings, fragrances, and manufacturing. Concentrated exposure can irritate the eyes, skin, or lungs; it is not a routine medical treatment.

name: benzazepines
clinical_significance: A family of chemical structures made from joined benzene and seven-membered nitrogen-containing rings. Individual compounds may have different biological or medicinal effects, so the family name alone does not identify a treatment.

name: benzene
clinical_significance: An industrial chemical and solvent found in some fuels and smoke. High short-term exposure can affect the brain and heart; repeated exposure can damage bone marrow and increase the risk of leukaemia.

name: benzoates
clinical_significance: Salts or chemical forms of benzoic acid used mainly as food preservatives or ingredients in some products. Their effects and safety depend on the specific compound and amount; some people develop irritation or sensitivity.

name: benzocaine
clinical_significance: A local anaesthetic applied to skin or moist body surfaces to reduce sensation. Rarely, especially after excessive use, it can cause methemoglobinaemia, a condition in which blood cannot carry oxygen normally.

name: benzodiazepines
clinical_significance: A group of medicines that slow activity in the brain and are used for conditions such as anxiety, seizures, muscle spasms, or insomnia. They can cause sedation and impaired coordination; regular use can lead to dependence, and abrupt stopping may cause dangerous withdrawal.

name: benzopyran
clinical_significance: A chemical ring structure formed by joining benzene and pyran rings. It occurs in some natural substances and medicines; the term describes chemistry rather than one specific disease or treatment.

name: benzopyrene
clinical_significance: A group of chemicals produced by incomplete burning and found in tobacco smoke, vehicle exhaust, and heavily charred food. Some forms can damage DNA and increase cancer risk after the body changes them chemically.

name: benzopyrenes
clinical_significance: Chemicals with a benzopyrene structure that form during incomplete combustion. Several occur in smoke and pollution, can damage DNA, and are linked with increased cancer risk.

name: benzoyl peroxide
clinical_significance: A topical medicine that kills acne-causing bacteria and helps remove blocked skin cells. It can cause dryness, peeling, irritation, or bleaching of hair and fabrics.

name: benzoylphenylurea
clinical_significance: A class of insecticides that disrupts chitin formation in insects and is used mainly in agriculture or pest control. It is not a human medicine; poisoning or exposure risk depends on the particular compound and route.

name: benzphetamine
clinical_significance: A sympathomimetic amine and stimulant formerly used in some countries as a short-term adjunct for weight reduction; it can cause dependence, cardiovascular effects, and insomnia and is restricted or unavailable in many jurisdictions.

name: benztropine
clinical_significance: An anticholinergic medicine used mainly for movement problems caused by some medicines and for acute muscle spasms called dystonia. It can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, confusion, or worsen glaucoma.

name: benzydamine
clinical_significance: A topical anti-inflammatory pain-relieving medicine used for painful inflammation in the mouth, throat, or skin. It may cause temporary numbness, irritation, or an allergic reaction.

name: benzylamines
clinical_significance: Chemical compounds containing a benzyl group joined to an amino group. Some are used to make medicines or other chemicals, while their effects depend on the individual compound.

name: BEP regimen
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy combination of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin, commonly used for some germ-cell cancers. It can cause low blood counts, infection, kidney damage, hearing changes, nerve symptoms, or lung injury and requires monitoring.

name: berberine
clinical_significance: A plant compound sold in some supplements and studied for blood-sugar, cholesterol, and antimicrobial effects. Evidence varies, and it can cause stomach symptoms, low blood sugar, drug interactions, or harm during pregnancy.

name: bereavement
clinical_significance: The emotional response to the death of someone important. Grief may include sadness, yearning, anger, numbness, sleep or appetite changes, and waves of distress; it varies widely and can sometimes lead to prolonged grief or depression.

name: bergeyella
clinical_significance: A genus of aerobic bacteria found in animals and occasionally isolated from human clinical specimens. Human infection is rare; significance depends on the species, specimen source, and evidence of infection rather than colonization or contamination.

name: bergeyella zoohelcum
clinical_significance: A bacterium commonly found in the mouths and upper airways of dogs, cats, and other mammals. Human infections are rare but have included wound infection, abscess, and bloodstream infection, sometimes after animal contact or a bite.

name: beriberi
clinical_significance: Illness caused by severe vitamin B1 deficiency. It may damage nerves and cause weakness, numbness, or difficulty walking, or affect the heart and cause swelling, fast heartbeat, and heart failure; urgent vitamin replacement is needed.

name: berylliosis
clinical_significance: A long-term lung disease caused by sensitivity to inhaled beryllium dust or fumes. It can cause cough, breathlessness, fatigue, and scarring or inflammation that resembles sarcoidosis.

name: beryllium
clinical_significance: A light metal used in some industrial products. Breathing its dust or fumes can cause allergic lung inflammation, long-term lung disease, and increased cancer risk, especially after repeated workplace exposure.

name: best practice
clinical_significance: A method or guideline judged to be appropriate based on available evidence, expertise, and the clinical context. In healthcare, best practice can improve consistency and safety but should be adapted to the individual patient and updated as evidence changes.

name: beta 2-microglobulin
clinical_significance: A small protein released by most cells. Blood or urine levels may rise with inflammation, some blood cancers, or reduced kidney removal; the result is interpreted with symptoms and other tests.

name: beta carotene
clinical_significance: A plant pigment that the body can convert into vitamin A. It occurs in foods such as carrots and leafy greens; high-dose supplements may increase lung-cancer risk in smokers and are not a substitute for a balanced diet.

name: beta globulin
clinical_significance: A group of blood proteins identified together during a protein blood test. They include proteins that carry iron or fats and support immunity; abnormal levels can occur with inflammation, liver disease, or immune disorders.

name: beta particle
clinical_significance: A fast-moving electron or positively charged equivalent released by some radioactive atoms. It can damage nearby tissue and is therefore used carefully in selected radiation treatments and laboratory applications.

name: beta radiation
clinical_significance: Radiation made of fast electrons or their positively charged counterparts released by unstable atoms. It can injure living tissue but can also be directed at selected tissues for treatment or used in medical testing.

name: beta thalassemia
clinical_significance: An autosomal recessive disorder in which the body makes too little or no beta-globin, a part of haemoglobin. Severity ranges from mild carrier status to severe anaemia requiring regular transfusions and monitoring for iron overload.

name: beta tocopherol
clinical_significance: One naturally occurring form of vitamin E. It acts as a fat-soluble antioxidant, but the body generally uses alpha-tocopherol more effectively; its specific clinical importance is still being studied.

name: beta-chemokines
clinical_significance: Small immune signals that attract white blood cells to areas of infection or inflammation. They help coordinate defense, but excessive activity can contribute to long-lasting inflammation and tissue damage.

name: betacoronavirus
clinical_significance: A group of coronaviruses that includes viruses causing respiratory illnesses in people and animals. Individual viruses differ in spread and severity; some cause mild colds, while others can cause severe pneumonia.

name: beta-endorphin
clinical_significance: A natural pain-relieving substance made in the brain and pituitary gland. It acts on opioid receptors and also influences stress responses, mood, and some hormone functions.

name: beta-glucans
clinical_significance: Complex carbohydrates found in foods such as oats, barley, mushrooms, and yeast. Their effects vary by source; some provide fibre and may modestly affect cholesterol, blood glucose, or immune activity.

name: betaherpesvirinae
clinical_significance: A subgroup of herpes viruses that includes cytomegalovirus and human herpesviruses 6 and 7. They remain in the body after infection and can reactivate, especially when immunity is weakened.

name: betaine
clinical_significance: A natural substance involved in processing homocysteine and helping cells maintain their water balance. It is also sold as a supplement, but high doses can cause side effects or interact with medicines.

name: beta-lactamase
clinical_significance: An enzyme made by some bacteria that breaks down certain penicillin-like antibiotics and makes them ineffective. Laboratory testing can identify this resistance, and some medicines block selected beta-lactamases.

name: beta-mannosidosis
clinical_significance: A rare autosomal recessive disorder in which cells cannot break down certain complex sugars. The stored material can cause developmental delay, hearing loss, repeated infections, seizures, or skeletal and skin problems.

name: betamethasone
clinical_significance: A strong corticosteroid medicine that reduces inflammation and immune activity. It may be applied to skin or given in other forms; prolonged or extensive use can thin the skin, worsen infections, or suppress the body's steroid production.

name: betamethasone valerate
clinical_significance: A corticosteroid applied to the skin to reduce inflammation and itching in conditions such as eczema or psoriasis. Excessive, prolonged, or covered application can thin the skin and increase absorption into the body.

name: betaretrovirus
clinical_significance: A group of animal retroviruses related to, but distinct from, the human retroviruses. They are studied in veterinary and comparative medicine; the term does not refer to a single human disease.

name: beta-sheet
clinical_significance: A common folded shape in proteins in which extended strands lie beside one another and are held by chemical bonds. Excessive beta-sheet folding can contribute to abnormal protein deposits in some diseases.

name: betaxolol
clinical_significance: A relatively beta-1-selective blocker used orally for some cardiovascular conditions and topically to lower intraocular pressure in glaucoma. It may cause bradycardia, hypotension, or bronchospasm.

name: betazole
clinical_significance: A histamine-like medicine formerly used in some settings to stimulate stomach acid secretion and assess gastric function. It is now rarely used and has largely been superseded by safer, more direct diagnostic tests.

name: bevacizumab
clinical_significance: A monoclonal antibody that blocks vascular endothelial growth factor and inhibits new blood-vessel formation. It is used for selected cancers and some eye diseases; important risks include hypertension, bleeding, thrombosis, proteinuria, impaired wound healing, and gastrointestinal perforation.

name: bexarotene
clinical_significance: An oral retinoid X-receptor agonist used mainly for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma; it commonly causes hypertriglyceridaemia, hypothyroidism, and liver abnormalities and is teratogenic.

name: bezafibrate
clinical_significance: Bezafibrate is a fibrate lipid-lowering drug that activates PPAR-alpha and lowers triglycerides; muscle and liver effects require monitoring.

name: bibliotherapy
clinical_significance: The use of reading materials as a therapeutic intervention to support mental health, educate patients about conditions, or promote behavioral change. It may be used alone or alongside other treatments for depression, anxiety, or chronic disease self-management.

name: bicalutamide
clinical_significance: A non-steroidal androgen-receptor antagonist used in prostate cancer, usually with androgen-deprivation therapy; adverse effects include hot flushes, breast enlargement, sexual dysfunction, and possible liver injury.

name: bicarbonate
clinical_significance: A substance in the blood that helps keep the body’s acid level balanced. The lungs and kidneys regulate it, and a blood bicarbonate result can help identify acid–base or metabolic problems.

name: bicuculline
clinical_significance: A laboratory compound that blocks GABA-A receptors, reducing an important inhibitory signal in the nervous system. It can provoke seizure-like activity and is used mainly in neuroscience research, not as a treatment.

name: bicuspid
clinical_significance: Having two points or flaps. The term describes some teeth, which have two main points, and some heart valves, which have two flaps instead of the usual three.

name: bid protein
clinical_significance: A protein that helps connect signals from outside a cell with programmed cell death inside it. When activated, it can help mitochondria release signals that lead to destruction of a damaged or unwanted cell.

name: bifidobacterium
clinical_significance: A genus of bacteria commonly found in the human intestine and in some fermented foods. Some strains are used in probiotic products, but benefits are strain-specific and evidence for many health claims is limited; people who are severely ill or immunocompromised may face greater risks from live-microbe products.

name: bifidobacterium adolescentis
clinical_significance: A species of Bifidobacterium found in the human intestine and sometimes in fermented foods. It is studied as part of the gut microbiota and in probiotic products, but a health benefit cannot be assumed from the species name alone.

name: bifidobacterium animalis
clinical_significance: A species of Bifidobacterium found in the intestines of humans and other animals. Some strains are used in fermented foods or studied as probiotics, but effects depend on the strain and evidence for a specific clinical benefit.

name: bifidobacterium bifidum
clinical_significance: A species of Bifidobacterium that commonly inhabits the human intestine and is also found in the mouth. Its role depends on the body site: intestinal strains may be studied as probiotics, while oral detection can occur in dental plaque; neither finding alone diagnoses disease.

name: bifidobacterium breve
clinical_significance: A species of Bifidobacterium commonly found in the human intestine, especially early in life. It is studied in gut microbiome research and probiotic products, but effects are strain-specific and are not a substitute for proven treatment.

name: bifidobacterium dentium
clinical_significance: A species of Bifidobacterium found in the mouth and digestive tract. In the mouth it has been associated with dental caries, while intestinal detection may reflect normal microbiota; significance depends on the body site and clinical context.

name: bifidobacterium longum
clinical_significance: A group of Bifidobacterium strains found in the human intestine and used in some fermented foods and probiotic products. Proposed benefits vary by strain and condition, and strong evidence does not support assuming a general treatment effect.

name: biglycan
clinical_significance: A protein-and-sugar component of the tissue framework around cells. It helps organize collagen and may influence inflammation, wound healing, and blood-vessel changes.

name: biguanides
clinical_significance: A group of medicines that lower blood glucose mainly by reducing glucose production in the liver and improving insulin sensitivity. They are used chiefly in type 2 diabetes.

name: bilateral
clinical_significance: Affecting both sides of the body or both members of a paired structure, such as both eyes, ears, knees, lungs, or kidneys.

name: bilateral microphthalmos
clinical_significance: A birth condition in which both eyes are unusually small. Vision may be reduced, and other eye or developmental differences may occur; assessment by an eye specialist is needed.

name: bilateral oophorectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove both ovaries, sometimes performed for cancer, severe endometriosis, or high inherited cancer risk. Before natural menopause it causes immediate loss of ovarian hormones and infertility, so long-term effects need discussion.

name: bile
clinical_significance: A fluid made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder that helps digest fats. It carries bile salts, cholesterol, pigments, and waste products into the intestine.

name: bile duct
clinical_significance: A tube that carries bile from the liver and gallbladder into the first part of the small intestine. Blockage or inflammation can prevent bile flow and cause pain, jaundice, infection, or pancreatitis.

name: bile pigment
clinical_significance: A coloured substance, mainly bilirubin, made when haemoglobin from old red blood cells is broken down. The liver processes it and excretes it in bile; build-up causes yellowing of the skin and eyes.

name: biliary
clinical_significance: Relating to bile, the gallbladder, or the tubes that carry bile from the liver to the intestine.

name: biliary atresia
clinical_significance: A serious disease in newborns in which the bile ducts outside the liver are absent, scarred, or blocked. Bile cannot drain normally, causing persistent jaundice, pale stools, dark urine, liver injury, and progressive cirrhosis without prompt treatment.

name: biliary calculi
clinical_significance: Stones formed from hardened bile in the gallbladder or bile ducts. They may cause no symptoms or block bile flow, producing pain, jaundice, infection, or inflammation of the gallbladder or pancreas.

name: biliary cirrhosis
clinical_significance: Permanent liver scarring caused by long-term injury or blockage of the bile ducts. The term has also been used for primary biliary cholangitis, an immune disease affecting small bile ducts.

name: biliary colic
clinical_significance: Steady pain in the upper right abdomen or upper middle abdomen caused by a gallstone temporarily blocking the gallbladder outlet. It often follows a meal and lasts minutes to hours; fever or persistent pain suggests a complication.

name: biliary dyskinesia
clinical_significance: Gallbladder pain without gallstones or another obvious structural problem, often associated with abnormal emptying. Diagnosis requires typical symptoms and exclusion of other causes; a scan may help but is not decisive alone.

name: biliary fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal passage allowing bile to leak from the gallbladder or bile ducts into another organ, the abdominal cavity, or the skin. It may cause pain, infection, bile drainage, or skin irritation.

name: biliary tract
clinical_significance: The network of ducts carrying bile from the liver and gallbladder to the small intestine. Blockage or inflammation can cause upper-abdominal pain, jaundice, infection, or pancreatitis.

name: bilirubin
clinical_significance: A yellow substance made mainly when old red blood cells are broken down. The liver changes it and sends it into bile; too much bilirubin in the blood causes yellowing of the skin and eyes.

name: bilophila
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria that can live without oxygen in the human intestine. Most are harmless there, but Bilophila wadsworthia has been found in some appendicitis, abdominal, wound, and bloodstream infections.

name: bilophila wadsworthia
clinical_significance: A bacterium that tolerates bile and normally occurs in small numbers in the colon. If intestinal bacteria enter damaged or normally sterile tissue, it may contribute to appendicitis, abdominal infection, or wound infection.

name: bimatoprost
clinical_significance: Bimatoprost is a prostaglandin analogue used as eye drops to lower intraocular pressure and, in some formulations, promote eyelash growth.

name: binder excipient
clinical_significance: An inactive ingredient added during tablet manufacture to help powder particles stick together. It has no intended treatment effect but affects the tablet's strength and breakdown.

name: binding protein
clinical_significance: A protein that attaches specifically to another molecule, such as a hormone, medicine, nutrient, DNA segment, or cell-surface signal. Binding can transport, store, activate, or block the other molecule.

name: binding site
clinical_significance: The particular area of a molecule where another molecule attaches. The interaction can change activity, transmit a signal, allow transport, or enable a laboratory test to detect the target.

name: binge drinking
clinical_significance: A pattern of consuming enough alcohol over a short period to produce a high blood alcohol concentration and increased risk of injury or acute toxicity.

name: binocular vision
clinical_significance: The use of both eyes together to produce one image and judge depth. Misalignment or poor coordination between the eyes can cause double vision, eyestrain, or reduced depth perception.

name: binomial distribution
clinical_significance: A probability model for the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials when each trial has the same chance of success. It is used in clinical research to estimate event counts and calculate probabilities, not as a diagnostic test by itself.

name: Binswanger disease
clinical_significance: A form of small-vessel disease in the brain that damages deep white matter. It can cause gradually worsening thinking, walking difficulty, mood changes, and urinary problems.

name: bioaccumulation
clinical_significance: The gradual build-up of a substance in an organism when absorption is faster than removal. Pollutants, medicines, and metals can accumulate in tissues and may cause harm when levels become high.

name: bioassay
clinical_significance: A test that measures the effect or activity of a substance by observing its action on living cells, tissues, organisms, or a biological system. It can be used to estimate potency, toxicity, or biologic activity.

name: biochanin A
clinical_significance: A naturally occurring isoflavone found mainly in legumes and other plants. It is studied for biologic effects but is not established as a treatment for disease.

name: biochemical reaction
clinical_significance: A chemical change occurring in a living cell or body, usually controlled by enzymes. It may build or break down molecules and supports energy production, growth, repair, and normal organ function.

name: biochemistry
clinical_significance: The study of the chemical substances and reactions occurring in living organisms. Clinical biochemistry uses laboratory measurements to assess health and disease.

name: bioengineering
clinical_significance: The application of engineering principles to biology and medicine, including the design of medical devices, biomaterials, tissue-engineering systems, prostheses, and diagnostic technologies.

name: bioethics
clinical_significance: The study of moral questions in medicine, biology, research, and healthcare technology. It considers consent, privacy, fairness, benefit, harm, quality of life, and respect for patients and communities.

name: biofeedback
clinical_significance: A technique that shows information about a body function, such as muscle tension, heart rate, or breathing, so a person can learn to control it. It may support treatment of selected pain, stress, or movement problems.

name: bio-informatics
clinical_significance: The use of computers and statistics to store, compare, and interpret biological information such as DNA sequences, genes, proteins, and medical data.

name: biological
clinical_significance: Relating to living organisms, their parts, functions, processes, or products. In medicine, a biological product is made from or resembles a substance from a living source.

name: biological availability
clinical_significance: The amount and speed at which a medicine or other substance becomes available to produce an effect in the body. It depends on the route, absorption, breakdown, and removal of the substance.

name: biological clock
clinical_significance: The body's internal timing system that helps coordinate daily sleep, alertness, hormone release, body temperature, and other repeating functions in response to light and other environmental signals.

name: biological model
clinical_significance: A cell, tissue, organism, computational system, or other representation used to study biological mechanisms, disease, or treatment responses.

name: biological process
clinical_significance: A coordinated series of molecular, cellular, or physiological events in a living organism, such as metabolism, cell division, inflammation, or tissue repair.

name: biological relative
clinical_significance: A person who shares genetic ancestry with someone. Family medical history uses biological relatives to assess inherited risks, while relatives by marriage or legal relationship do not share that genetic information.

name: biological therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment using biological substances, cells, vaccines, antibodies, or similar products to change immune activity or target a specific disease pathway. It is used in selected cancers, immune disorders, and other conditions.

name: biological transport
clinical_significance: The movement of substances such as water, salts, nutrients, medicines, or cells within the body or across cell membranes. It may occur by diffusion, channels, pumps, filtration, or transport vesicles.

name: biology
clinical_significance: The study of living organisms and how they function, develop, interact, and cause or resist disease. Medical biology provides the foundation for understanding physiology, genetics, infection, and disease mechanisms.

name: bioluminescence
clinical_significance: Light produced by a living organism through a chemical reaction. It is used by some organisms for communication or defense and is used in laboratories to detect biological activity.

name: biomarker
clinical_significance: A measurable feature that gives information about a normal body process, disease, likely outcome, or response to treatment. It may be measured in blood, tissue, genes, images, or other samples.

name: biomaterial
clinical_significance: A natural or manufactured material designed to contact or interact with the body. Examples include implant surfaces, artificial joints, wound dressings, prostheses, and materials that release medicines.

name: biomechanical compliance
clinical_significance: How easily a body structure changes size or shape when pressure or force is applied. Lung and blood-vessel compliance affect breathing and circulation, while joint compliance affects movement and stability.

name: biomechanics
clinical_significance: The study of how forces and movement affect the body. It examines walking, posture, joints, muscles, and loads to understand injury, improve rehabilitation, or design supportive devices.

name: biomedical cement
clinical_significance: A medical material used to fill gaps, stabilize broken bone, anchor an implant, or repair tissue. Its use and strength depend on the procedure and the tissue being treated.

name: biomedical research
clinical_significance: Research that investigates health, disease, and healthcare using laboratory, clinical, population, or computational methods. It can lead to better diagnostics and treatments, but findings need appropriate evaluation before changing patient care.

name: biomedical tape
clinical_significance: Adhesive tape designed for medical use, such as securing dressings, tubes, sensors, or small devices. Different types vary in strength, flexibility, water resistance, and risk of skin irritation.

name: biomedicine
clinical_significance: Medicine grounded in the biological sciences, including the study of disease mechanisms, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment through laboratory and clinical research.

name: biometry
clinical_significance: Measurement of body structures or functions. In eye care, optical biometry measures the eye to help calculate the strength of an artificial lens before cataract surgery.

name: biomimetics
clinical_significance: The design of materials, devices, or processes inspired by structures and functions found in living organisms. In medicine it can inform implants, tissue engineering, drug delivery, and diagnostic tools.

name: biomphalaria
clinical_significance: A group of freshwater snails that can carry the parasite Schistosoma mansoni. The parasite develops in the snails and can later infect people who contact contaminated freshwater.

name: biophysics
clinical_significance: The application of physics to living systems, including the forces, energy, electrical signals, and molecular interactions involved in biological function. It supports research and technologies such as medical imaging and physiological measurement.

name: biopolymer
clinical_significance: A large molecule made of repeating biological building blocks, such as proteins, DNA, or some carbohydrates. Biopolymers form cell structures and can be used in medical materials, drug delivery, or tissue engineering.

name: biopsy
clinical_significance: Removal of a small sample of cells or tissue so it can be examined under a microscope to diagnose disease, including cancer. Types include fine-needle aspiration (cells or fluid), core-needle (a tissue cylinder), incisional (part of an area), excisional (the whole area), punch (a circular piece of skin), and endoscopic biopsy (through a viewing tube). Possible complications include pain, bleeding, and infection; risks vary with the body site and procedure.

name: biopsy lung
clinical_significance: Removal of a small lung-tissue sample using a needle, bronchoscope, or operation. Examination can investigate infection, inflammation, scarring, or cancer; the method depends on the lesion and procedural risks.

name: biopsy site
clinical_significance: The body location from which cells or tissue are removed for testing. It is chosen to sample the abnormal area while limiting injury to nearby organs, nerves, and blood vessels.

name: biopsy specimen
clinical_significance: Cells or tissue removed from the body for laboratory examination. Microscopy, special stains, immune tests, or genetic tests may be used to identify cancer, infection, inflammation, or another condition.

name: bioreactor
clinical_significance: A controlled vessel or system in which living cells or microorganisms grow under managed conditions. Bioreactors are used to make products such as vaccines, antibodies, and other biological medicines.

name: biospecimen
clinical_significance: A sample of human tissue, cells, blood, urine, or another body fluid collected for testing or research. Correct collection, labelling, storage, and handling help keep the sample reliable.

name: biotechnology
clinical_significance: The use of living cells, organisms, or biological molecules to develop products and processes such as vaccines, biological medicines, genetic tests, and gene therapies.

name: biotin
clinical_significance: A water-soluble B vitamin needed for enzymes involved in processing fats, sugars, and amino acids. Deficiency is uncommon but can cause a skin rash, hair loss, weakness, or neurological symptoms.

name: biotinidase deficiency
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which the body cannot recycle biotin efficiently. Without treatment it can cause seizures, developmental problems, hearing or vision loss, skin rash, and weakness; lifelong biotin usually prevents symptoms.

name: biotinylation
clinical_significance: The attachment of biotin to another molecule, usually a protein, so it can be found or separated in a laboratory test. The biotin acts as a tag that binds to special substances, making the target easier to detect or collect. Biotinylation can occur naturally or be done artificially.

name: bipartite ossification
clinical_significance: Formation or persistence of two separate ossification centers in a bone. If they do not fuse, a bipartite bone, such as a bipartite patella, may result. This is usually an incidental developmental variant but can become painful after injury or repetitive stress.

name: biphenyl compounds
clinical_significance: Chemicals made of two linked benzene rings. Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are long-lasting industrial pollutants; exposure can harm the liver, immune system, and hormone system and may increase cancer risk.

name: bipolar disorder
clinical_significance: A mental health condition involving episodes of mania, hypomania, and/or major depression. Bipolar I is defined by at least one manic episode; depressive episodes are common but not required. Bipolar II includes at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, without a history of mania. Episodes can affect mood, sleep, energy, judgment, and daily functioning.

name: bipolar neuron
clinical_significance: A bipolar neuron has one dendrite and one axon extending from opposite sides of its cell body, as found in the retina and sensory pathways.

name: bipolaris
clinical_significance: A genus of fungi found mainly in soil and plants. Some species can rarely cause eye, sinus, skin, or invasive infections, particularly in people with reduced immunity. Identification requires laboratory culture or molecular testing because treatment depends on the species and site of infection.

name: birth
clinical_significance: The process by which a baby leaves the uterus, including labour, delivery of the baby, and delivery of the placenta.

name: birth injury
clinical_significance: Physical harm to a newborn during labour or delivery. It may affect the skin, bones, nerves, muscles, or brain and can result from difficult delivery, the baby's position, or medical complications.

name: birth order
clinical_significance: The sequence in which siblings are born within a family. While birth order has been studied for psychological effects, its direct medical significance is limited to obstetric considerations such as risks associated with grand multiparity.

name: birth rate
clinical_significance: The number of live births in a population during a specified period, usually expressed per 1,000 people per year.

name: birth weight
clinical_significance: The first weight recorded after birth; for a liveborn infant, it is preferably measured within the first hour, before significant postnatal weight loss. Low birth weight is less than 2,500 g regardless of gestational age; very low birth weight is less than 1,500 g, and extremely low birth weight is less than 1,000 g. These are overlapping categories, and lower birth weight is associated with greater risk of neonatal complications.

name: bisacodyl
clinical_significance: A stimulant laxative that increases bowel movement and helps empty the bowel. It is used short term for constipation or before some procedures; cramps, diarrhoea, and dehydration can occur.

name: bisbenzimidazole
clinical_significance: A group of laboratory dyes that bind to DNA and are used to stain chromosomes or cells for microscopy. Some compounds in this chemical family can damage genetic material, so laboratory handling and exposure precautions matter.

name: bisexuality
clinical_significance: Bisexuality is a sexual orientation involving attraction to more than one gender; it is not a disease or disorder.

name: bismuth
clinical_significance: A metal used in some medicines and industrial products. Certain bismuth compounds can soothe diarrhoea or stomach symptoms, but excessive or prolonged exposure can cause nervous-system or kidney toxicity.

name: bisoprolol
clinical_significance: A beta-1-selective blocker used to treat hypertension, angina, and selected patients with heart failure. It lowers heart rate and blood pressure and may cause bradycardia, hypotension, or fatigue.

name: bizelesin
clinical_significance: An experimental anticancer compound designed to bind and cross-link DNA, thereby blocking tumour-cell growth. It was studied in clinical trials but is not an established routine cancer treatment.

name: BK virus
clinical_significance: A common virus that usually remains inactive after childhood infection. It can reactivate when immunity is suppressed, especially after organ transplantation, and damage the transplanted kidney or urinary tract.

name: blackwater fever
clinical_significance: A severe complication of malaria in which red blood cells break down inside blood vessels. It can cause dark urine, severe anaemia, jaundice, kidney failure, and shock and requires emergency treatment.

name: bladder carcinoma
clinical_significance: Cancer that begins in the lining of the urinary bladder, most often in cells called urothelial cells. Blood in the urine is common; smoking and some workplace chemical exposures increase risk.

name: bladder exstrophy
clinical_significance: Bladder Exstrophy is a rare birth defect in which the bladder is open and exposed outside the body through a defect in the lower abdominal wall. It is part of the exstrophy–epispadias complex and may also affect the urethra, pelvic bones, pelvic floor, abdominal muscles, and genitals. It can cause difficulty storing urine, urinary leakage, urine-control problems, and risks to the kidneys.

name: bladder fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal passage between the bladder and another organ or the skin, often the vagina, bowel, or uterus. It may cause constant urine leakage, repeated infection, gas or stool in urine, or unusual vaginal wetness.

name: bladder neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth arising in the bladder. It may be noncancerous or cancerous; diagnosis requires examination, imaging, cystoscopy, and often a tissue sample to determine its type and extent.

name: bladder pain
clinical_significance: Pain or pressure felt in the lower abdomen or pelvis that may relate to infection, stones, inflammation, bladder pain syndrome, injury, or cancer. Blood in urine, fever, severe pain, or inability to urinate needs prompt assessment.

name: bladder perforation
clinical_significance: A tear or hole in the bladder wall caused by trauma, pelvic surgery, catheterization, or another procedure. Urine may leak into surrounding tissues or the abdomen, causing pain, bleeding, infection, or impaired healing; prompt assessment and treatment are needed.

name: bladder spasm
clinical_significance: An involuntary contraction of the bladder muscle that can cause sudden urgency, cramping, frequent urination, or leakage. It may occur with a urinary infection, bladder irritation, neurologic disease, or after catheterization or surgery.

name: blast cell
clinical_significance: An immature precursor cell, especially one in the bone marrow that will normally develop into a blood cell. Too many blasts can indicate acute leukaemia or another marrow disorder.

name: blast injury
clinical_significance: Harm caused by an explosion. The pressure wave can injure lungs, ears, or organs; flying objects can cause wounds; being thrown can cause fractures; burns, smoke, toxins, and crushing can add further injuries.

name: blast phase
clinical_significance: An advanced phase of some blood cancers in which many immature blast cells appear in the blood or marrow. The disease becomes more aggressive and may resemble acute leukaemia.

name: blastocyst
clinical_significance: An early embryo formed about five to six days after fertilization. It is a hollow group of cells with an inner group that can become the fetus and an outer layer that helps form the placenta.

name: blastocystis
clinical_significance: A common microscopic organism that may be found in the digestive tract after contaminated food or water is swallowed. Many people have no symptoms, and it is not always clear whether it causes illness. Diarrhoea, stomach cramps, bloating, or nausea may occur. Stool testing can detect it, but a positive result does not prove that it caused the symptoms; treatment is considered only in selected persistent cases.

name: blastocystis hominis
clinical_significance: Blastocystis detection in stool is common and does not always explain gastrointestinal symptoms; evaluate other causes before attributing illness or treating.

name: blastoma
clinical_significance: A cancer that develops from immature or embryonic cells. The specific name identifies the organ and tumour type, such as a kidney, nerve, liver, or eye blastoma.

name: blastomyces dermatitidis
clinical_significance: A fungus found in soil and damp organic material that can cause blastomycosis when its spores are inhaled. Infection usually affects the lungs but can spread to skin, bones, joints, or other organs.

name: blastomycosis
clinical_significance: A fungal infection acquired by inhaling Blastomyces spores, usually from soil. It commonly causes pneumonia and may spread to the skin, bones, joints, or other organs; symptoms can develop gradually.

name: Blautia producta
clinical_significance: A bacterium that normally lives in the human intestine and grows without oxygen. It is usually harmless but has occasionally been found in infections, especially in people with serious illness.

name: bleeding tendency
clinical_significance: An increased susceptibility to bleeding, which may result from platelet disorders, coagulation factor deficiencies, vascular abnormalities, or anticoagulant medications. Evaluation includes personal and family history, complete blood count, and coagulation studies.

name: bleeding time
clinical_significance: An older test measuring how long a small skin puncture takes to stop bleeding. It mainly reflected platelet function and small blood vessels and has largely been replaced by more reliable laboratory tests.

name: bleomycin
clinical_significance: A cancer medicine that damages tumour-cell DNA and is used for selected cancers. Its most important serious risk is lung injury; fever, skin changes, low blood counts, and allergic reactions can also occur.

name: bleomycin sulfate
clinical_significance: The sulphate form of bleomycin, a cancer medicine that damages DNA. It can cause potentially permanent lung injury, so breathing symptoms and lung function may need monitoring during treatment.

name: blepharitis
clinical_significance: A common, usually chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins that can cause itchy or burning eyelids, redness, tearing, dry-eye symptoms, and crusting at the base of the eyelashes. Anterior blepharitis affects the skin, lash follicles, and lash bases; posterior blepharitis affects the meibomian oil glands and often accompanies rosacea or dry eye. Lid hygiene and warm compresses may help, but pain, marked swelling, light sensitivity, or vision change needs prompt eye assessment.

name: blepharophimosis
clinical_significance: Abnormally short horizontal openings between the eyelids. It may occur with drooping eyelids and other facial or developmental features and can interfere with vision.

name: blepharoptosis
clinical_significance: Drooping of the upper eyelid because of a weak muscle, damaged nerve, stretched tendon, birth difference, ageing, or a heavy eyelid. It can obstruct vision and may signal a neurological emergency if sudden.

name: blepharospasm
clinical_significance: Involuntary tightening of the muscles around the eyes, causing repeated blinking or forceful eyelid closure. It may occur alone or with eye irritation, medicines, or a movement disorder.

name: blinded
clinical_significance: In a research study, describing a participant, clinician, assessor, or analyst who does not know the assigned treatment or relevant result. This helps reduce expectations from influencing care or measurements.

name: blindness
clinical_significance: Severe or complete loss of vision in one or both eyes caused by disease, injury, or a developmental condition affecting the eye, optic nerve, or brain. Sudden vision loss is an emergency.

name: bloating
clinical_significance: A feeling of abdominal fullness, tightness, or visible swelling. Gas, constipation, food intolerance, or digestive disorders are common causes; persistent bloating with weight loss, vomiting, pain, or early fullness needs assessment.

name: blocking antibody
clinical_significance: An immune protein that prevents another molecule from attaching to its target or interferes with a biological interaction. It may be used as treatment, protect against disease, or contribute to an autoimmune disorder.

name: blood
clinical_significance: A body fluid made of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. It carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and waste and helps fight infection, stop bleeding, and regulate temperature.

name: blood bank
clinical_significance: A specialized medical facility and laboratory service that collects, tests, separates, and safely stores donated blood and its components (such as red blood cells, platelets, and plasma). It performs vital compatibility testing, blood typing, and antibody screening (crossmatching) before transfusions to prevent severe transfusion reactions and ensure patient safety.

name: blood cell
clinical_significance: A cellular part of blood, including red blood cells that carry oxygen, white blood cells that help fight infection, and platelets that help stop bleeding. Most are made in the bone marrow.

name: blood circulation
clinical_significance: The continuous movement of blood from the heart through the lungs and body and back again. It delivers oxygen and nutrients and carries away carbon dioxide and other waste.

name: blood clot
clinical_significance: A mass of thickened blood formed during clotting. It is protective when it seals an injury, but a clot inside a blood vessel can block flow or travel to the lungs, brain, heart, or another organ.

name: blood coagulation
clinical_significance: The linked process that changes blood from a liquid to a firm clot after injury. Too little clotting causes bleeding, while excessive or misplaced clotting can cause dangerous vessel blockage.

name: blood coagulation disorder
clinical_significance: A condition in which blood clots too little, too much, or at the wrong time. Bleeding disorders result from inadequate clot formation, whereas thrombophilic disorders cause excessive or misplaced clotting. Causes include genetic variants, medicines, liver disease, immune conditions, cancer, and other illness. Examples include hemophilia, von Willebrand disease, thrombocytopenia, thrombophilia, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

name: blood donor
clinical_significance: A person who gives blood or blood components for transfusion or medical use. Screening protects the donor and helps ensure that donated blood is safe for the recipient.

name: blood glucose
clinical_significance: The amount of sugar called glucose in the blood. The body regulates it using food absorption, liver production, insulin, and other hormones; levels that are too low or high can cause illness.

name: blood group
clinical_significance: A classification of blood based on specific inherited markers (antigens) on the surface of red blood cells. The two most vital systems are the ABO system (types A, B, AB, and O) and the Rhesus (Rh) system (positive or negative based on the RhD marker). Accurate blood grouping and crossmatching are essential before transfusions to prevent life-threatening immune reactions and during pregnancy to prevent Rh disease (hemolytic disease of the newborn).

name: blood preservation
clinical_significance: The controlled collection, processing, cooling, freezing, and storage of donated blood or its components so they remain safe and effective until transfusion.

name: blood pressure
clinical_significance: The force of circulating blood against artery walls, recorded as two numbers in millimetres of mercury. The systolic number is the pressure when the heart contracts; the diastolic number is the pressure between beats.

name: blood product
clinical_significance: A component made from donated blood for medical treatment, such as red blood cells, platelets, plasma, or cryoprecipitate. The product is selected according to the person's bleeding, anaemia, or clotting problem.

name: blood protein
clinical_significance: A protein dissolved in blood plasma. These proteins help transport substances, maintain fluid balance, support immunity, and control clotting; abnormal amounts can occur with inflammation, liver or kidney disease, immune disorders, or some cancers.

name: blood sedimentation
clinical_significance: The settling of red blood cells in a tube of treated blood. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate is a nonspecific sign that may rise with inflammation, infection, anaemia, pregnancy, or other conditions.

name: blood smear
