clinical_significance: A thin layer of blood spread on a glass slide, stained, and examined under a microscope. It shows the size, shape, and appearance of blood cells and can reveal abnormal cells, parasites, or cell fragments.

name: blood substitutes
clinical_significance: Fluids or artificial products intended to replace some functions of blood. Most restore circulating volume; some are designed to carry oxygen. They do not replace every function of blood and are used only in selected situations.

name: blood transfusion
clinical_significance: The administration of donated blood or a blood component, such as red cells, platelets, or plasma, through a vein. It can treat severe anaemia or bleeding, but requires compatibility checks and monitoring for reactions, fluid overload, or infection.

name: blood treatment
clinical_significance: A treatment involving blood or a blood component, such as transfusion, collection, filtration, or removal of a harmful substance. The term is broad; the exact procedure and reason determine its benefits and risks.

name: blood vessel
clinical_significance: A tube that carries blood through the body. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins return it, and tiny capillaries allow oxygen, nutrients, and waste products to pass between blood and tissues.

name: blood viscosity
clinical_significance: How thick blood is and how much it resists flowing. It is influenced mainly by the number of red blood cells, but also by blood proteins and temperature. Excessively thick blood can slow circulation and increase clot risk.

name: blood volume
clinical_significance: The total amount of blood circulating in the body, including plasma and blood cells. Too little can cause low blood pressure and shock; too much can strain the heart and lungs.

name: blood-brain barrier
clinical_significance: A protective filter formed by specialized cells lining brain blood vessels and their supporting tissues. It controls which medicines, chemicals, germs, and immune cells can move from the blood into brain tissue.

name: Bloom syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare autosomal-recessive disorder caused by pathogenic changes in both copies of the \textit{BLM} gene, which encodes a DNA helicase. It causes marked short stature, a sun-sensitive telangiectatic facial rash, recurrent infections, and a greatly increased risk of multiple cancers, often at unusually young ages; specialist surveillance and strong sun protection are important.

name: blue nevus
clinical_significance: A usually harmless blue-gray or blue-black mole caused by pigment-producing cells located deeper than those in most moles. A new, changing, bleeding, or painful lesion requires examination.

name: blunted affect
clinical_significance: Reduced outward expression of emotion. A person may show less facial movement, voice variation, or body language than expected, although their internal feelings may be stronger. It can occur in mental or neurologic disorders.

name: blurred vision
clinical_significance: Vision that appears out of focus, hazy, or unclear. Causes include an incorrect glasses prescription, dry eye, eye disease, medicines, migraine, or neurologic illness. Sudden blurring, pain, weakness, or vision loss needs urgent assessment.

name: B-lymphocyte
clinical_significance: B lymphocytes produce antibodies and support immune memory; abnormal B-cell numbers or function can underlie immunodeficiency, autoimmune disease, or lymphoma.

name: bocavirus
clinical_significance: A group of small viruses that can infect humans and animals. Human bocavirus most often affects the airways of young children, although infection may cause illness in other tissues or people with weakened immunity.

name: bodily secretion
clinical_significance: A substance made and released by cells or glands, such as sweat, saliva, mucus, tears, digestive juices, or hormones. Secretions protect tissues, aid digestion, regulate body functions, or help remove waste.

name: body cavity
clinical_significance: An enclosed space inside the body that contains and protects organs. Major cavities include the skull, spinal canal, chest, abdomen, and pelvis; their linings may produce small amounts of lubricating fluid.

name: body composition
clinical_significance: The relative amounts of fat, muscle and other lean tissue, bone mineral, and water in the body. It provides more information about health and nutrition than body weight alone, although estimates vary by method.

name: body fluid
clinical_significance: Water and dissolved substances, including electrolytes, nutrients, proteins, and gases, distributed inside and outside cells. These fluids support circulation, temperature regulation, chemical balance, and organ function; abnormal volume or composition can cause serious illness.

name: body height
clinical_significance: The vertical distance from the soles of the feet to the top of the head, measured while standing when possible. It helps assess growth and nutrition and is used in medication, kidney-function, and other calculations.

name: body image
clinical_significance: A person's thoughts, feelings, and beliefs about their body and appearance. Distress or inaccurate beliefs about appearance can occur in body dysmorphic disorder, eating disorders, depression, or other mental-health conditions.

name: body odor
clinical_significance: Smell produced when skin secretions, especially sweat, are broken down by skin microorganisms. A sudden or unusual change may be related to diet, medicines, infection, or a metabolic disorder.

name: body piercing
clinical_significance: Creation of an opening through skin or a mucous membrane to insert jewellery. Possible complications include pain, bleeding, infection, scarring, allergic reaction, and damage to teeth, nerves, or cartilage.

name: body position
clinical_significance: The arrangement of the body or a body part, such as standing, lying on the back, lying face down, or lying on the side. Position can affect breathing, circulation, examination results, and medical procedures.

name: body region
clinical_significance: A named area of the body used to describe the location of an organ, symptom, injury, or examination finding, such as the chest, abdomen, pelvis, or arm.

name: body space
clinical_significance: A normal or potential compartment inside the body, such as the space around the lungs or abdominal organs. Air, blood, fluid, or infection can collect there and interfere with organ function.

name: body substance
clinical_significance: Material produced by or found in the body, including blood, saliva, urine, faeces, mucus, tissue, and other secretions. Some substances can carry infection and require appropriate handling precautions.

name: body surface
clinical_significance: The outside of the body, mainly the skin and accessible mucous membranes. Clinicians may estimate its area when assessing burns, calculating some medicine doses, or making physiological measurements.

name: body temperature
clinical_significance: The degree of heat in the body, determined by the balance between heat production and heat loss. It varies with age, activity, time of day, illness, and measurement site; fever and hypothermia require clinical interpretation.

name: body wall
clinical_significance: The layers of skin, connective tissue, muscle, and sometimes bone that surround and protect a body compartment, such as the chest or abdomen. They also help movement, breathing, and support.

name: body weight
clinical_significance: The measured mass of a person, including fat, muscle, bone, water, and organs. It helps assess growth, nutrition, and fluid changes and is used with other information for some medical calculations.

name: Bohring syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare genetic disorder associated with severe developmental delay, poor growth before birth, distinctive facial features, reduced movement, and frequent feeding or breathing difficulties.

name: bolt device
clinical_significance: A bolt is a threaded fastener used to hold parts together. In medicine, the term may describe a device component or a specific product name, so its meaning depends on the clinical context.

name: bolus infusion
clinical_significance: Delivery of a measured amount of fluid or medicine into a vein over a short period. The dose and speed depend on the medicine, the person's condition, and the intended effect; errors can cause serious harm.

name: bombesin
clinical_significance: A peptide first identified in amphibian skin that resembles mammalian gastrin-releasing peptide. It is used mainly in research on gut, hormone, and nervous-system signalling; the term does not refer to a routine human treatment.

name: bombesin receptor
clinical_significance: A protein on or inside a cell that binds bombesin-like signalling substances and changes cell activity. These receptors help regulate processes such as hormone release, digestion, and cell growth and are studied in some cancers.

name: bone
clinical_significance: A strong living tissue that forms the skeleton, supports the body, protects organs, enables movement with muscles, stores minerals, and contains marrow that makes blood cells. Bone is continually broken down and rebuilt.

name: bone callus
clinical_significance: New tissue that forms around a broken bone during healing. It first consists of a soft blood clot and connective tissue, then cartilage and immature bone, which are gradually reshaped into stronger bone.

name: bone cement
clinical_significance: A self-curing acrylic biomaterial composed of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) utilized in orthopedic and spine surgery to anchor prosthetic joint components, fill osseous voids, and stabilize vertebral compression fractures during vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty.

name: bone cyst
clinical_significance: A fluid-filled or blood-filled space within bone. Many bone cysts are benign, but they can weaken the bone and cause pain, swelling, or fracture. Common types include simple bone cysts and aneurysmal bone cysts.

name: bone density
clinical_significance: The amount of mineral packed into a measured area of bone. It is usually estimated with a DXA scan; lower density is associated with greater fracture risk, but results must be interpreted with age and other risk factors.

name: bone development
clinical_significance: The formation, growth, and shaping of bones from before birth through adulthood. Bones lengthen and widen as new tissue is made and old tissue is removed; hormones, nutrition, activity, and injury influence this process.

name: bone disease
clinical_significance: Any condition that weakens, deforms, inflames, infects, or otherwise damages bone. Examples include osteoporosis, fractures, infections, tumours, inherited skeletal disorders, and diseases caused by abnormal mineral or hormone levels.

name: bone fracture
clinical_significance: A partial or complete break in a bone caused by injury, repeated stress, or weakened bone. Pain, swelling, bruising, deformity, and loss of function may occur. An open fracture or loss of sensation or circulation needs emergency care.

name: bone infection
clinical_significance: Infection of bone, usually caused by bacteria. It may reach bone through the bloodstream, spread from nearby tissue, or enter through surgery or an open injury, causing pain, swelling, fever, or poor healing.

name: bone marrow
clinical_significance: Soft tissue inside many bones. Red marrow makes red cells, white cells, and platelets; yellow marrow stores fat and can produce more blood cells when the body needs them.

name: bone marrow disorder
clinical_significance: Any disease that affects the marrow's production of red cells, white cells, or platelets. It may cause anaemia, frequent infections, bleeding, abnormal blood counts, or symptoms from abnormal marrow cells.

name: bone marrow transplantation
clinical_significance: A treatment that replaces damaged or diseased blood-forming marrow with healthy stem cells from the patient or a donor. It is used for selected blood cancers, marrow failure, and some inherited disorders.

name: bone matrix
clinical_significance: The material surrounding bone cells that gives bone its shape and strength. It contains a flexible framework, mainly type I collagen, reinforced with mineral crystals made largely from calcium and phosphate.

name: bone necrosis
clinical_significance: Death of bone tissue, usually because its blood supply is reduced or because of severe injury, infection, radiation, or prolonged corticosteroid use. It can cause pain, bone collapse, joint damage, and fracture.

name: bone neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth of cells arising in bone. It may be noncancerous or cancerous; imaging and often a biopsy determine its type, behaviour, extent, and appropriate treatment.

name: bone pain
clinical_significance: Aching or other discomfort arising from bone. Causes include injury, fracture, infection, reduced blood supply, metabolic disease, overuse, or cancer. Persistent, severe, or unexplained pain requires medical assessment.

name: bone plate
clinical_significance: A metal or other body-compatible plate fixed to bone with screws. It holds broken pieces in position, supports healing, or helps correct a deformity during orthopaedic surgery.

name: bone regeneration
clinical_significance: Formation of new bone to repair or replace bone that is damaged, missing, or diseased. It occurs naturally during fracture healing and may be supported by grafts, implants, or other treatments.

name: bone remodeling
clinical_significance: The lifelong replacement of old bone with new bone. Cells remove worn bone and other cells build replacement bone, helping maintain strength, shape, and the body's calcium balance.

name: bone resorption
clinical_significance: The removal and breakdown of bone tissue, which releases minerals into the blood. It is normal during bone renewal, but excessive resorption can weaken bones and contribute to osteoporosis.

name: bone screws
clinical_significance: Screws used during orthopaedic surgery to hold broken bone pieces together or attach plates, joint components, or other implants. Their size, material, and placement depend on the bone and the operation.

name: bone transplantation
clinical_significance: Transfer of bone tissue or a bone substitute to repair a defect, support fracture healing, or assist reconstruction of the spine, jaw, or a joint. The graft may come from the person, a donor, or a manufactured material.

name: bony labyrinth
clinical_significance: A system of channels inside the dense part of the skull bone that houses the inner ear. It contains the cochlea for hearing and the vestibule and semicircular canals for balance.

name: boranes
clinical_significance: A family of chemical compounds containing boron and hydrogen. Some are used in chemical research or industry; exposure to certain boranes can be highly toxic and may damage the lungs, nervous system, or other tissues.

name: border definition
clinical_significance: The sharpness and shape of the edge of a skin lesion or abnormal growth. A poorly defined or irregular edge can be concerning, but the border alone cannot distinguish harmless from cancerous disease.

name: borderline
clinical_significance: Describes a result or condition near the boundary between normal and abnormal or between diagnostic categories. It usually requires interpretation with symptoms, repeat testing, or other findings; the meaning depends on the clinical context.

name: bordetella
clinical_significance: A group of small bacteria that can infect the airways of humans or animals. Bordetella pertussis causes whooping cough; other species usually affect animals but can rarely cause opportunistic human infection.

name: bordetella avium
clinical_significance: A bacterium that mainly causes respiratory disease in turkeys and other birds. Human infection is very rare and is usually reported in people with weakened immunity or serious underlying illness.

name: bordetella bronchiseptica
clinical_significance: A bacterium that commonly causes respiratory infection in dogs and other animals. It rarely infects humans, but may cause pneumonia or bloodstream infection, especially in people with weakened immunity.

name: bordetella hinzii
clinical_significance: A bacterium found mainly in poultry. It rarely causes respiratory or bloodstream infection in humans, usually in people with weakened immunity or significant underlying disease.

name: bordetella parapertussis
clinical_significance: A bacterium that can cause a whooping-cough-like respiratory infection. Illness is often milder than infection with Bordetella pertussis, but prolonged coughing can still occur and the infection can spread to others.

name: bordetella pertussis
clinical_significance: The bacterium that causes whooping cough, a highly contagious respiratory infection. It attaches to airway lining, produces toxins that disrupt airway function, and can cause repeated coughing, vomiting, breathing pauses, and serious illness in infants.

name: bordetella petrii
clinical_significance: An environmental bacterium that rarely causes human disease. When it is found in a specimen, clinicians decide whether it represents true infection by considering the body site, symptoms, and other test results.

name: boric acid
clinical_significance: A chemical used in some industrial products, insecticides, and limited topical preparations. Swallowing it or absorbing a large amount can poison the body; significant exposure requires prompt medical assessment.

name: boron
clinical_significance: A chemical element found naturally in food, water, soil, and industrial materials. Small dietary amounts are generally tolerated, but excessive exposure can cause digestive symptoms, skin problems, reproductive effects, or developmental toxicity.

name: borrelia
clinical_significance: A group of spiral-shaped bacteria spread mainly by ticks or lice. Different species cause Lyme disease, relapsing fever, or other infections, with symptoms and treatment depending on the species and exposure.

name: borrelia burgdorferi
clinical_significance: A spiral-shaped bacterium spread by infected blacklegged ticks and the main cause of Lyme disease in North America and parts of Europe. Infection may affect the skin, joints, nervous system, or heart.

name: borrelia infection
clinical_significance: Infection with a Borrelia bacterium. Depending on the species, it may cause Lyme disease or relapsing fever, with symptoms such as fever, headache, fatigue, rash, muscle pain, or joint and nerve problems.

name: borrelia miyamotoi
clinical_significance: A bacterium spread by some hard-bodied ticks that causes hard-tick relapsing fever. Illness commonly includes repeated episodes of fever, headache, fatigue, chills, and muscle or joint aches.

name: bortezomib
clinical_significance: A cancer medicine that blocks proteasomes, cell structures that remove unwanted proteins. This can kill susceptible cancer cells and is used mainly for multiple myeloma and some lymphomas; nerve damage, low blood counts, digestive symptoms, and infections can occur.

name: bosentan
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks endothelin, a substance that narrows blood vessels. It is used for pulmonary arterial hypertension, but can injure the liver and harm a developing fetus, so liver tests and pregnancy prevention are important.

name: botany
clinical_significance: The scientific study of plants, including their structure, growth, reproduction, classification, and interactions with the environment. Plant biology is relevant to medicine through food, medicines, allergens, and plant-derived toxins.

name: bottle feeding
clinical_significance: Feeding an infant expressed breast milk or infant formula from a bottle. Safe preparation, clean equipment, correct formula mixing, and responsive feeding help prevent infection, choking, overfeeding, and poor nutrition.

name: botulinum toxin
clinical_significance: A substance made by Clostridium botulinum that temporarily blocks nerve signals to muscles and some glands. Carefully measured injections treat selected muscle spasms, movement disorders, migraine, sweating, and cosmetic concerns; too much can cause weakness or breathing failure.

name: botulism
clinical_significance: A rare, life-threatening illness caused by botulinum toxin, which blocks nerve signals. It causes blurred or double vision, drooping eyelids, difficulty swallowing, progressive weakness, and sometimes breathing failure; urgent antitoxin and intensive care may be needed.

name: Bouchard's node
clinical_significance: A hard enlargement of one middle finger joint, usually caused by osteoarthritis. It results from changes in the joint and surrounding bone and may cause pain, stiffness, or reduced movement.

name: Bouin's solution
clinical_significance: A laboratory liquid containing picric acid, formaldehyde, and acetic acid that preserves tissue for microscopic examination. It is hazardous to handle and can interfere with some later genetic tests.

name: bovine anaplasmosis
clinical_significance: A tick- or blood-spread infection of cattle caused by Anaplasma marginale. The bacterium infects red blood cells and destroys them, causing anaemia, weakness, fever, reduced milk production, or death.

name: bovine papillomavirus
clinical_significance: A group of papillomaviruses that infect cattle and can cause skin warts or other growths. Different strains vary in their effects; human disease is not the usual concern.

name: bowel burn
clinical_significance: Injury to the bowel lining caused by heat, chemicals, radiation, reduced blood flow, or another damaging exposure. It can cause pain, bleeding, perforation, infection, or narrowing and requires assessment according to the cause.

name: bowel urgency
clinical_significance: A sudden, hard-to-delay need to pass stool. It can occur with diarrhoea, infection, irritable bowel syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, or disorders of the rectum and may lead to accidents.

name: Bowen's disease
clinical_significance: Squamous cell carcinoma in situ, a cancer limited to the epidermis. It usually appears as a persistent scaly or crusted red patch and can progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma if untreated.

name: bowman membrane
clinical_significance: A thin, strong layer near the front of the cornea that supports and protects the eye's clear surface. Significant injury can scar it because it does not normally grow back.

name: brachial artery
clinical_significance: The main artery of the upper arm. It carries blood from the armpit toward the elbow, where it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries, and it is commonly used to measure a pulse or blood pressure.

name: brachial plexus
clinical_significance: A network of nerves from the lower neck and upper chest that supplies movement and sensation to the shoulder, arm, forearm, and hand. Its branches include the musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, and ulnar nerves.

name: brachial plexus neuropathies
clinical_significance: Disorders affecting the nerve network that supplies the shoulder, arm, and hand. They can cause pain, weakness, numbness, or loss of movement because of injury, pressure, inflammation, tumours, or radiation.

name: brachiocephalic trunk
clinical_significance: The first large branch of the aorta in the chest. It carries blood toward the right side of the head, neck, and arm and divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.

name: brachycephaly
clinical_significance: A broad, short skull shape. It may develop from pressure on an infant's head or from early joining of skull bones; assessment determines whether brain growth or treatment is affected.

name: brachydactyly
clinical_significance: A birth condition in which one or more fingers or toes are shorter than usual because of altered development of their bones or surrounding tissues. It may occur alone or as part of an inherited syndrome.

name: brachytherapy
clinical_significance: Internal radiation treatment in which a radioactive source is placed inside or close to a tumour. It delivers a concentrated dose to a limited area and may use a temporary applicator or a source left in place permanently.

name: bradycardia
clinical_significance: A slower-than-usual heart rate, often below 60 beats per minute in adults. It can be normal during sleep or in trained athletes, but may result from heart-conduction disease or medicines and cause dizziness, fainting, tiredness, or breathlessness.

name: bradykinesia
clinical_significance: Slowness and reduced size of voluntary movements. It can make starting or repeating actions difficult and may occur with stiffness, tremor, reduced arm swing, a less expressive face, or a shuffling walk in Parkinson disease and related disorders.

name: bradykinin
clinical_significance: A natural chemical messenger that widens some blood vessels and allows more fluid to leave them. It contributes to inflammation, swelling, pain, and rare reactions to certain blood-pressure medicines.

name: brain
clinical_significance: The main organ of the nervous system, protected inside the skull. It processes senses, controls movement and body functions, and supports thinking, memory, emotions, language, and consciousness.

name: brain abscess
clinical_significance: A pocket of pus and infection inside the brain. It can develop when infection spreads from the blood, nearby ear or sinus disease, surgery, or an injury and may cause headache, fever, seizures, or weakness.

name: brain concussion
clinical_significance: A concussion is a mild traumatic brain injury that can temporarily affect memory, balance, mood, and concentration; worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, or weakness requires urgent evaluation.

name: brain death
clinical_significance: Permanent loss of all brain and brainstem function, including consciousness, reflexes, and the ability to breathe independently. When formally confirmed according to law and medical standards, it means the person has died.

name: brain disorder
clinical_significance: Any illness or abnormality affecting the brain's structure or function, including stroke, infection, tumour, epilepsy, injury, degenerative disease, or a condition present from birth.

name: brain edema
clinical_significance: Swelling caused by extra fluid in brain tissue. It can increase pressure inside the skull after injury, stroke, infection, bleeding, tumour, or severe illness and may cause headache, vomiting, seizures, confusion, or reduced consciousness.

name: brain fornix
clinical_significance: A curved bundle of nerve fibres deep in the brain that helps connect the hippocampus with other areas involved in memory. Damage may cause difficulty learning or remembering information.

name: brain injury
clinical_significance: Damage or impaired function of the brain caused by trauma, lack of oxygen, stroke, infection, toxins, or another disease. Effects vary with the location and severity and may affect movement, sensation, thinking, behaviour, or consciousness.

name: brain mapping
clinical_significance: Methods used to identify where brain functions and structures are located. Imaging, electrical recordings, or direct stimulation may guide research or help surgeons avoid important areas during selected operations.

name: brain neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth of cells in the brain or its coverings. It may be noncancerous or cancerous; imaging and sometimes biopsy determine its type, behaviour, extent, and treatment options.

name: brain stem
clinical_significance: The lower part of the brain connecting the cerebrum with the spinal cord and controlling essential functions such as breathing and consciousness.

name: brain stem glioma
clinical_significance: A tumor arising from glial cells in the brainstem, the part of the brain controlling important functions such as breathing, swallowing, eye movement, and balance. Symptoms and treatment depend on its exact location and behavior.

name: brain wave
clinical_significance: A pattern of electrical activity made by groups of nerve cells and recorded with an electroencephalogram. Patterns change with sleep, alertness, seizures, and some disorders of brain function.

name: branchioma
clinical_significance: A rare cyst or growth arising from tissue related to early head-and-neck development. It often presents as a lump in the neck and requires examination and imaging to establish its nature.

name: Branchio-Oto-Renal syndrome
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder that can cause neck cysts or openings, hearing loss, and kidney abnormalities. The combination and severity vary, and some affected people have only one or two of these features.

name: brassicasterol
clinical_significance: A plant sterol found especially in rapeseed and related oils. It is mainly used to identify the composition of plant oils and has no routine role as a medical treatment.

name: brassidic acid
clinical_significance: A long-chain fatty acid found in some plant oils. It is mainly a chemistry term and is not an established medicine or routine clinical test.

name: breakthrough pain
clinical_significance: A short flare of pain that occurs despite otherwise controlled persistent pain. It may happen unexpectedly or after activity; treatment depends on the cause, pattern, regular pain medicines, and safety risks.

name: breast
clinical_significance: One of the two organs on the front of the chest, made of milk-producing tissue, ducts, fat, connective tissue, blood vessels, nerves, and skin. It can be affected by benign conditions and cancer.

name: breast carcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer that begins in breast tissue, usually in the ducts or milk-producing lobules. Its treatment depends on the cell type, hormone and other markers, tumour size, lymph nodes, and spread.

name: breast cyst
clinical_significance: A fluid-filled sac in breast tissue. Simple breast cysts are benign and do not increase breast cancer risk; cysts with internal debris or solid components are distinct findings and may have different significance.

name: breast density
clinical_significance: The relative amount of milk-gland and connective tissue compared with fat on a mammogram. Dense breast tissue can hide small cancers and is linked with higher breast-cancer risk; screening plans depend on individual risk and local guidance.

name: breast duct
clinical_significance: A channel that carries milk from milk-producing areas toward the nipple. Blockage, inflammation, or abnormal cells in a duct can cause a lump, pain, or nipple discharge.

name: breast feed
clinical_significance: To feed an infant directly from the breast with human milk. Human milk provides nutrients and immune protection, but feeding may need support when the parent or infant has illness, difficulty latching, or medicine-related concerns.

name: breast finding
clinical_significance: Any noticeable breast change, such as a lump, pain, skin change, nipple inversion, or discharge. Its significance depends on the examination and imaging and sometimes requires a biopsy.

name: breast lobe
clinical_significance: One of the larger sections of a breast's milk-producing gland. It contains smaller lobules and ducts that carry milk toward the nipple.

name: breast lobule
clinical_significance: A small milk-producing unit within the breast, made of tiny milk glands and ducts. Lobules enlarge and become more active during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

name: breast neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth of cells in breast tissue. It may be noncancerous or cancerous; imaging and often a biopsy determine its type, behaviour, extent, and treatment.

name: breast self-examination
clinical_significance: Looking at and feeling one's own breasts to notice a new lump, skin or nipple change, or discharge. It may improve familiarity with normal changes but does not replace recommended screening or clinical assessment.

name: breath test
clinical_significance: Analysis of exhaled air to detect a substance made by the body or by microorganisms. Examples include tests for Helicobacter pylori and tests measuring hydrogen or methane after a sugar drink to assess digestion and absorption.

name: breech presentation
clinical_significance: A fetal position in which the buttocks or feet point toward the birth canal. Types include frank, complete, and footling breech; risks include cord prolapse, difficulty delivering the head, and birth injury, so delivery needs careful planning.

name: brefeldin A
clinical_significance: A fungal metabolite used in laboratory research to disrupt protein transport within cells. It has helped scientists study the Golgi apparatus and secretion pathways but is not a human treatment.

name: brenner tumor
clinical_significance: A rare ovarian growth made of cells resembling those lining the urinary tract. Most are small, one-sided, noncancerous, and found incidentally, but uncommon borderline or cancerous forms also occur.

name: bretylium tosylate
clinical_significance: An older medicine that can suppress certain dangerous abnormal heart rhythms, especially ventricular fibrillation. It is now rarely used because of limited availability, side effects, and newer treatments.

name: brevibacillus
clinical_significance: A group of spore-forming bacteria found in soil, water, and food. Human infection is uncommon but can occur opportunistically, especially in people with weakened immunity or medical devices.

name: brevibacterium
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria found on skin, in soil, and in food. They commonly contribute to body or cheese odour; rare species can cause opportunistic infection, particularly in people with serious illness or devices.

name: brevibacterium casei
clinical_significance: A species of Brevibacterium found in the environment and occasionally on people. It rarely causes bloodstream or device-related infection, usually in a person with major underlying illness or an indwelling device.

name: brevundimonas
clinical_significance: A group of environmental water-associated bacteria that rarely cause human disease. Opportunistic infections, including bloodstream or wound infection, are more likely in people with weakened immunity or medical devices.

name: brevundimonas diminuta
clinical_significance: An environmental water-associated bacterium that rarely causes opportunistic human infection. Reported illnesses include bloodstream, wound, or device-related infection, mainly in people with serious underlying disease.

name: brevundimonas vesicularis
clinical_significance: An environmental bacterium that rarely causes human infection. When it is isolated from a clinical sample, symptoms, specimen quality, and other results determine whether it represents true disease or contamination.

name: brimonidine tartrate
clinical_significance: A medicine that reduces certain nerve signals and blood-vessel activity. Eye drops lower pressure inside the eye, and skin preparations can reduce some facial redness; side effects and interactions may require medical attention.

name: brivanib
clinical_significance: An investigational cancer medicine that inhibits vascular endothelial and fibroblast growth-factor receptors, pathways that can support tumour growth and blood-vessel formation. It is not an established routine treatment.

name: brivanib alaninate
clinical_significance: An orally absorbed prodrug form of brivanib, an investigational inhibitor of vascular endothelial and fibroblast growth-factor receptors. It has been studied in cancer trials but is not an established routine treatment.

name: brivudine
clinical_significance: An antiviral medicine used in some countries for shingles. It is not used with fluoropyrimidine cancer medicines or certain related treatments because the interaction can be fatal.

name: broad ligament
clinical_significance: A sheet of tissue extending from the sides of the uterus to the pelvic walls. It helps support the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries and contains blood vessels, nerves, and connective tissue.

name: bromelain
clinical_significance: A mixture of enzymes from pineapple. It is sold as a supplement and studied for pain and inflammation, but evidence and product strength vary; it can cause allergy, stomach upset, or interactions with medicines.

name: bromhexine
clinical_significance: A medicine that thins sticky mucus in the airways so it may be coughed up more easily. It can cause stomach upset or rash and rarely causes a serious skin reaction.

name: bromine
clinical_significance: A reactive chemical used in industry and some flame-resistant materials. Bromine and many bromine compounds can irritate or burn tissue, while substantial exposure can cause poisoning affecting several organs.

name: bromobenzenes
clinical_significance: Industrial chemicals made by attaching one or more bromine atoms to benzene. Exposure can irritate the eyes, skin, and airways or cause other toxic effects, depending on the specific compound and amount.

name: bromocriptine
clinical_significance: A medicine that stimulates dopamine receptors and reduces prolactin release. It is used for high prolactin and selected movement or hormone disorders; nausea, dizziness, low blood pressure, hallucinations, and other effects may occur.

name: bromodeoxyuridine
clinical_significance: A thymidine-like laboratory marker that becomes incorporated into newly made DNA, allowing researchers to identify cells that are dividing. It is used in cell-growth studies and is not a routine clinical test or treatment.

name: bromophos
clinical_significance: An organophosphate insecticide. Exposure can overstimulate nerves and cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, breathing difficulty, weakness, seizures, or collapse and requires urgent poison or emergency care.

name: bromouracil
clinical_significance: A chemical base analogue of uracil that can be incorporated into DNA in laboratory research and may cause mutations by mispairing. It is used to study DNA replication and mutation, not as a routine medicine.

name: bromovirus
clinical_significance: A genus of RNA viruses that infect plants, often causing mosaic or other crop diseases. These viruses do not ordinarily infect people.

name: bromthymol blue
clinical_significance: A chemical indicator that changes colour according to acidity and alkalinity. It is used in laboratories and is not a medicine or treatment.

name: bronchial
clinical_significance: Relating to the bronchi, the large airways branching from the windpipe. Bronchial disease may cause cough, wheezing, mucus production, narrowing, or reduced airflow.

name: bronchial fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal passage between an airway and another structure, such as the space around the lung, food pipe, or skin. It can cause persistent air leakage, coughing, infection, or breathing failure.

name: bronchial hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from airway blood vessels, usually seen as coughing up blood. Heavy bleeding can block the airway or cause breathing failure and requires emergency treatment.

name: bronchial obstruction
clinical_significance: Partial or complete blockage of an airway by mucus, an inhaled object, a tumour, swelling, or pressure from outside. It can reduce airflow and lead to lung collapse, repeated infection, wheezing, or breathlessness.

name: bronchial stricture
clinical_significance: Abnormal narrowing of an airway caused by scarring, inflammation, infection, a tumour, or previous instrumentation. It may produce localised wheezing, cough, repeated infection, or collapse of the lung beyond the narrowing.

name: bronchiectasis
clinical_significance: A long-term condition in which parts of the airways become permanently widened and damaged. The airways may not clear mucus well, so mucus builds up and can lead to a persistent cough, repeated chest infections, and breathlessness. Causes include severe or repeated infections, other lung or immune conditions, and airway blockage; sometimes the cause is unknown. Some people also cough up blood.

name: bronchiole
clinical_significance: A small airway without cartilage that branches from a bronchus and carries air toward the lung's air sacs. Its smooth muscle can narrow or widen the passage and regulate airflow.

name: bronchiolitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation and blockage of the smallest airways, usually from a viral infection in infants and young children. It can cause cough, wheezing, fast breathing, chest retractions, poor feeding, and low oxygen.

name: bronchiolitis obliterans
clinical_significance: A rare disease in which inflammation and scarring permanently narrow or close the smallest airways. It can follow severe infection, inhaled injury, autoimmune disease, or transplantation and causes persistent cough and breathlessness.

name: bronchitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the larger airways. Acute bronchitis is usually caused by a virus and causes cough, with or without mucus, while chronic bronchitis means mucus-producing cough for at least three months in two successive years.

name: bronchoconstriction
clinical_significance: Narrowing of the airways because their muscle tightens, the lining swells, or mucus builds up. It increases resistance to airflow and commonly occurs in asthma, allergic reactions, or irritant exposure.

name: bronchoconstrictor agents
clinical_significance: Substances that narrow the airways by tightening airway muscle or causing inflammation. Examples include histamine, leukotrienes, irritant gases, and some medicines.

name: bronchodilator
clinical_significance: A medicine that relaxes muscles around the airways, widening them and making breathing easier. It can relieve or prevent wheezing and breathlessness in asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and other conditions with narrowed airways.

name: bronchogenic carcinoma
clinical_significance: Bronchogenic carcinoma is lung cancer arising from bronchial or related lung tissue; smoking is a major risk factor, and early diagnosis and staging guide treatment.

name: bronchomalacia
clinical_significance: Weakness of an airway wall that allows it to collapse too much, especially during breathing out. It may cause noisy breathing, cough, breathlessness, repeated infections, or difficulty clearing mucus.

name: bronchopleural fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal connection between an airway and the space around the lung, often after lung surgery or severe infection. It can cause a persistent air leak, breathlessness, infection, or air under the skin.

name: bronchopneumonia
clinical_significance: Infection causing scattered areas of inflammation and consolidation around the small airways in one or more lung lobes. It may cause fever, cough, mucus, chest pain, fast breathing, and low oxygen.

name: bronchopulmonary dysplasia
clinical_significance: A chronic lung disease in some premature infants whose developing lungs have been affected by immaturity, inflammation, oxygen, or breathing support. It may cause ongoing oxygen need, fast breathing, or wheezing.

name: bronchoscope
clinical_significance: A thin tube with a light and camera used to examine the windpipe and airways. Instruments passed through it can remove an object or collect tissue, fluid, or mucus for testing.

name: bronchoscopy
clinical_significance: Examination of the windpipe and airways with a flexible or rigid camera tube. It can investigate persistent cough, infection, bleeding, or a lung mass and can remove foreign material or collect samples; sedation or anaesthesia is used.

name: bronchospasm
clinical_significance: Sudden tightening of airway muscles that narrows the breathing passages. It can cause wheezing, cough, chest tightness, and difficulty breathing and may be triggered by asthma, allergy, infection, irritants, or airway procedures.

name: bronchus
clinical_significance: One of the two main branches of the windpipe that carries air into a lung. Each divides into smaller branches; the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical, making it a more common site for inhaled objects to lodge.

name: bronchus disease
clinical_significance: Any condition affecting one or more bronchi, the air passages leading into the lungs. Infection, asthma, chronic inflammation, blockage, scarring, or a tumour may reduce airflow and cause cough, wheezing, or repeated infection.

name: bronchus neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth arising in a bronchus. It may be noncancerous or cancerous; imaging, bronchoscopy, and tissue testing help determine its type, extent, and treatment.

name: brown fat
clinical_significance: A type of body fat containing many energy-producing structures that generate heat. It is especially important for keeping newborns warm and can also be activated by cold in adults.

name: brucella
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria that usually infect animals but can infect people through unpasteurised dairy products, inhalation, or contact with infected animals or tissues. Human infection causes brucellosis.

name: brucella abortus
clinical_significance: A Brucella species mainly associated with cattle. It can infect people exposed to infected animals, tissues, or unpasteurised dairy products and cause prolonged fever and other brucellosis symptoms.

name: brucella canis
clinical_significance: A Brucella species associated with dogs. It rarely infects people after contact with infected dogs or reproductive material and may cause prolonged fever or other brucellosis symptoms.

name: brucella melitensis
clinical_significance: A Brucella species mainly associated with goats and sheep and a frequent cause of severe human brucellosis, usually acquired through unpasteurised dairy products or infected animals.

name: brucella suis
clinical_significance: A Brucella species associated with pigs and some wildlife. It can infect people through animal contact or contaminated food and may cause prolonged illness or infection in bones and organs.

name: brucellaceae
clinical_significance: A family of bacteria that includes Brucella and related animal-associated species. Some members cause brucellosis, an infection that can pass from animals to people.

name: brucellosis
clinical_significance: An infection caused by Brucella bacteria, usually acquired from infected animals, animal tissues, or unpasteurised dairy products. It may cause prolonged fever, sweats, tiredness, headache, and muscle or joint pain.

name: brunner gland
clinical_significance: A gland in the first part of the small intestine that releases mucus and alkaline fluid. These secretions protect the intestinal lining and help neutralise acid arriving from the stomach.

name: brush
clinical_significance: A tool with bristles or a soft tip used to collect or spread a sample, clean a surface, or apply a substance. In medicine, brushes may collect cells from the cervix or an organ lining for laboratory examination.

name: bruxism
clinical_significance: Repeated clenching or grinding of the teeth, often during sleep. It can wear or fracture teeth and cause jaw, face, ear, or headache pain; dental review can assess damage and possible sleep, stress, or medicine-related causes.

name: bryostatin
clinical_significance: A natural compound that alters protein kinase C signalling and has been investigated as an experimental medicine, including in cancer and neurologic research. It is not an established routine treatment.

name: buccal mucosa
clinical_significance: The non-keratinized stratified squamous mucous membrane lining the inside of the cheeks, bounded by the labial commissures anteriorly, the retromolar trigone posteriorly, and the alveolar sulci superiorly and inferiorly. It contains the opening of the parotid duct (Stensen duct) opposite the maxillary second molar and serves as a site for clinical examination of exanthems (such as Koplik spots in measles), oral lichen planus (Wickham striae), aphthous stomatitis, leukoplakia, and drug absorption

name: buccalmucosa
clinical_significance: A spelling variant of buccal mucosa, the moist lining on the inside of the cheeks.

name: budesonide
clinical_significance: A corticosteroid that reduces inflammation. It is used in selected inhaled, nasal, digestive, or rectal treatments for conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive lung disease, allergic symptoms, and inflammatory bowel disease; side effects depend on the route and dose.

name: budvicia
clinical_significance: A group of water-associated bacteria related to Yersinia. They rarely cause human disease, but some isolates have been associated with urinary or other opportunistic infections.

name: budvicia aquatica
clinical_significance: A water-associated bacterium that has rarely been isolated from human urinary infections, including infections in people with urinary catheters. Its significance depends on symptoms and specimen quality.

name: buffer
clinical_significance: A chemical solution that resists a change in acidity when small amounts of acid or base are added. Buffers help maintain stable conditions in blood, cells, medicines, and laboratory tests.

name: bufonidae
clinical_significance: The family of amphibians commonly called true toads. Some species produce bufotoxins in their skin glands; swallowing or absorbing these toxins can affect the heart and nervous system.

name: buformin
clinical_significance: An older biguanide medicine for diabetes that has been withdrawn or restricted in many countries because it can cause dangerous lactic-acid buildup, especially when kidney function is poor.

name: bulbar conjunctiva
clinical_significance: The part of the eye's clear moist covering that lies over the white of the eye. It joins the inner surface of the eyelids around the front of the eye and can become inflamed or injured.

name: bulbourethral glands
clinical_significance: Two small male reproductive glands, also called Cowper glands, that release mucus-like fluid into the urethra during sexual arousal. The fluid lubricates the urethra and may reduce acidity.

name: bulimia
clinical_significance: Bulimia nervosa can cause electrolyte abnormalities, dental erosion, gastrointestinal injury, and cardiac arrhythmias; confidential assessment and coordinated medical and mental-health care are important.

name: bulimia nervosa
clinical_significance: An eating disorder involving recurrent binge-eating episodes, a sense of loss of control, and recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, laxative misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise. Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape or weight, and the pattern causes clinically significant distress or impairment.

name: bulla
clinical_significance: A large fluid-filled blister on the skin or mucous membrane, or a large air-filled space in an organ such as the lung. The cause and treatment depend on its location.

name: bullous pemphigoid
clinical_significance: An autoimmune skin disease, usually in older adults, that often begins with an itchy, hive-like rash followed by firm, fluid-filled blisters. The blisters are less fragile than those of pemphigus, and mouth involvement is less common. Diagnosis may involve a skin biopsy and blood tests for related antibodies.

name: bully
clinical_significance: A person who repeatedly harms, threatens, or intimidates someone with less power. Bullying can cause injury, anxiety, depression, sleep problems, school avoidance, and other health effects.

name: bumetanide
clinical_significance: A diuretic that makes the kidneys remove extra salt and water in urine. It is used for swelling related to heart, liver, or kidney disease; excessive fluid loss can cause dehydration and abnormal blood salts.

name: bundle-branch block
clinical_significance: Delayed or interrupted electrical signalling through one of the heart's lower-chamber conduction branches. It can change the ECG and heartbeat pattern and may be harmless or related to underlying heart disease.

name: bungarotoxins
clinical_significance: Poisons in the venom of krait snakes that disrupt nerve signals to muscles. A bite can cause drooping eyelids, weakness, progressive paralysis, and breathing failure and requires emergency treatment.

name: bunion
clinical_significance: A change in the joint at the base of the big toe that pushes the toe toward the others and creates a bump on the inner foot. It may cause pain, redness, swelling, stiffness, and difficulty wearing shoes.

name: bunyaviridae
clinical_significance: An older virus-family grouping that included several viruses spread by insects, ticks, or rodents. Modern classification has changed; individual viruses differ in the illnesses they cause.

name: buphthalmos
clinical_significance: Enlargement of an infant's or young child's eye caused by high pressure inside the eye while its outer coat is still flexible. It is usually associated with congenital or infantile glaucoma and needs urgent eye care.

name: bupivacaine
clinical_significance: A long-acting local anaesthetic that temporarily blocks nerve signals to prevent pain during local, nerve-block, or epidural procedures. Too much in the bloodstream can cause seizures, dangerous heart effects, or cardiac arrest.

name: bupivacaine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: The hydrochloride form of bupivacaine, a long-acting local anaesthetic used to block pain signals. Accidental injection into a blood vessel can cause severe neurologic or heart toxicity.

name: buprenorphine
clinical_significance: A medicine that partly activates opioid receptors and is used to treat opioid-use disorder and some pain. It can cause dependence and overdose, especially with other sedatives, although respiratory suppression is limited compared with full opioid agonists.

name: bupropion
clinical_significance: A medicine used for depression and, in some settings, to help stop smoking. It changes norepinephrine and dopamine signalling and may cause insomnia, dry mouth, or anxiety; it increases seizure risk and is unsuitable for some seizure or eating disorders.

name: burkholderia
clinical_significance: A group of environmental bacteria found in soil and water. Some species cause melioidosis or glanders, while others cause difficult-to-treat lung, bloodstream, or wound infections, especially in people with chronic lung disease or weakened immunity.

name: burkholderia cenocepacia
clinical_significance: A bacterium in the Burkholderia cepacia complex that can cause severe, persistent lung infection, especially in people with cystic fibrosis or other chronic lung disease.

name: burkholderia cepacia
clinical_significance: An environmental bacterium in the Burkholderia cepacia complex. It can cause opportunistic lung, bloodstream, wound, or device-related infection, particularly in people with cystic fibrosis or weakened immunity.

name: burkholderia gladioli
clinical_significance: An environmental bacterium that can rarely cause lung, bloodstream, or wound infection, especially in people with cystic fibrosis or weakened immunity.

name: burkholderia mallei
clinical_significance: The bacterium that causes glanders, an infection mainly affecting horses and related animals. People can become infected through contact with infected animals or tissues.

name: burkholderia pseudomallei
clinical_significance: The bacterium that causes melioidosis. Infection follows contact with contaminated soil or water and may cause pneumonia, abscesses, bloodstream infection, or long-term illness.

name: burkholderiaceae
clinical_significance: A family of mainly environmental bacteria that includes Burkholderia. Some members cause serious infections in people or animals, while others are harmless or used in environmental research.

name: Burkitt's lymphoma
clinical_significance: A very fast-growing cancer of B lymphocytes. It may affect the abdomen, jaw, bone marrow, or brain and spinal cord and needs prompt intensive treatment with careful supportive care.

name: burn
clinical_significance: An injury to the skin or deeper tissue caused by heat, chemicals, electricity, radiation, friction, or extreme cold. Severity depends on depth, size, location, and associated injury; extensive or deep burns need urgent medical care.

name: Burning Mouth syndrome
clinical_significance: A chronic oral pain disorder causing daily burning, scalding, or tingling discomfort in the mouth, often involving the tongue, lips, or palate, usually with a normal-appearing mucosa. Altered taste or dry mouth may occur. It may be primary, with no identifiable cause, or secondary to conditions or exposures such as nutritional deficiency, oral infection, medication effects, allergy, diabetes, or hormonal change; evaluation excludes treatable causes.

name: bursa of fabricius
clinical_significance: An organ in the bursa of Fabricius, a pouch near the cloaca of young birds. It is the site where B lymphocytes mature in birds and is important in poultry immunology; humans do not have this organ.

name: bursitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of a bursa, the small fluid-filled sac that cushions movement between tendons, muscles, bones, and skin. It causes localized pain, tenderness, swelling, or reduced movement and may result from pressure, injury, infection, or arthritis.

name: buruli ulcer
clinical_significance: A chronic skin infection caused by \textit{Mycobacterium ulcerans}, usually affecting an arm or leg. Its toxin, mycolactone, causes a painless nodule, plaque, or swelling that can progress to an undermined ulcer with extensive tissue destruction and little early inflammation; antibiotic treatment, wound care, and selected surgery can prevent disability.

name: buserelin
clinical_significance: A synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogue. Continuous treatment first briefly increases and then suppresses pituitary reproductive hormones, lowering ovarian or testicular hormone production in selected fertility and hormone-sensitive conditions.

name: buspirone
clinical_significance: A nonbenzodiazepine medicine used mainly for generalized anxiety disorder. It acts on serotonin signaling and usually takes days to weeks to help; it does not provide immediate relief from an acute panic attack.

name: busulfan
clinical_significance: An alkylating chemotherapy medicine used mainly to prepare the body for blood-forming stem-cell transplantation and sometimes to treat chronic myeloid leukemia. It can suppress bone marrow and may cause seizures, infertility, lung injury, or liver damage.

name: butanol
clinical_significance: A flammable industrial alcohol used as a solvent. Swallowing it or substantial exposure to its vapor can irritate the eyes, skin, and airways and may cause dizziness, vomiting, drowsiness, or other nervous-system effects.

name: buthionine sulfoximine
clinical_significance: A laboratory compound that inhibits glutamine-dependent synthesis of glutathione, an antioxidant made by cells. It is used to study oxidative stress and has been investigated experimentally with cancer treatments, but is not a routine medicine.

name: butocarboxim
clinical_significance: A carbamate insecticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Significant exposure can cause cholinergic poisoning, with sweating, salivation, vomiting, diarrhea, wheezing, muscle weakness, seizures, or respiratory failure.

name: buttiauxella
clinical_significance: A genus of environmental gram-negative bacteria in the Enterobacterales; human infection is uncommon and usually opportunistic.

name: buttiauxella agrestis
clinical_significance: A species of environmental Gram-negative bacteria found in water, soil, and other natural settings. It is rarely reported from human clinical samples; when detected, the specimen source and the patient’s symptoms determine whether it represents infection or harmless contamination.

name: buttiauxella ferragutiae
clinical_significance: A species of environmental Gram-negative bacteria. It is uncommon in human disease, and a laboratory finding requires interpretation with the specimen source, repeat cultures, symptoms, and other evidence before deciding whether treatment is needed.

name: buttiauxella gaviniae
clinical_significance: A species of Buttiauxella bacteria found mainly in environmental samples. Human infection is uncommon; identification from a clinical specimen should be reviewed with the microbiology laboratory and interpreted according to the patient’s condition.

name: buttiauxella noackiae
clinical_significance: A species of environmental Gram-negative bacteria that is rarely associated with human infection. Its significance depends on where it was found, whether it was recovered repeatedly, and whether the patient has compatible symptoms or signs of infection.

name: buttocks
clinical_significance: The paired fleshy regions overlying the gluteal muscles at the back of the pelvis, formed mainly by muscle and subcutaneous fat.

name: butylated hydroxyanisole
clinical_significance: A synthetic antioxidant used to slow rancidity in some foods, cosmetics, and other products. Exposure at permitted food-use levels is generally regulated; high or occupational exposures raise different toxicology concerns.

name: butylated hydroxytoluene
clinical_significance: A synthetic antioxidant used in some foods, cosmetics, and materials to slow oxidation. Its safety depends on dose and route of exposure; it is not a treatment or diagnostic test.

name: butylhydroxybutylnitrosamine
clinical_significance: A laboratory chemical in the nitrosamine family used mainly in toxicology and carcinogenesis research. Nitrosamines can damage DNA, and exposure should be controlled; this compound is not a medicine.

name: butylscopolamine bromide
clinical_significance: An anticholinergic antispasmodic used in some countries to relieve cramping pain from smooth-muscle spasm, including intestinal or urinary-tract colic. It can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, fast heartbeat, or urinary retention and may be unsuitable in some conditions.

name: butyrate
clinical_significance: A short-chain fatty acid produced by gut bacteria when they ferment dietary fibre. It is an energy source for cells lining the colon and is studied for effects on the gut barrier and inflammation; supplements are not established treatments for most conditions.

name: butyric acid
clinical_significance: Butyric acid is a short-chain fatty acid produced by gut bacteria during fiber fermentation and used by colon cells as an energy source; concentrated exposure irritates tissue.

name: butyrophenone
clinical_significance: A class of medicines that includes some antipsychotics and anti-nausea drugs. Depending on the drug, they may cause movement-related side effects, sedation, or heart-rhythm changes; the specific medicine and dose determine risk.

name: bypass
clinical_significance: Creation of an alternative route around a blocked or narrowed passage. A bypass can restore blood flow or redirect body contents, using a natural pathway, tube, vein, or artificial graft depending on the organ involved.

name: byssinosis
clinical_significance: An occupational lung disease caused by repeated inhalation of dust from cotton, flax, hemp, or other textile fibers. It can cause chest tightness, cough, and breathing difficulty that worsen during or after work exposure.

name: byssochlamy
clinical_significance: A genus of fungi found in soil and on plants and foods. Some species tolerate heat and can spoil canned or processed foods; they are not common human pathogens.

name: byssochlamys spectabilis
clinical_significance: A fungus found in soil and plant material and known for heat-resistant spores that can spoil processed foods. Human disease is not a usual concern; its main practical significance is food spoilage.

name: c fiber
clinical_significance: A thin nerve fiber that carries slow, aching pain, warmth, and itch from the skin and other tissues to the spinal cord and brain.

name: cabazitaxel
clinical_significance: A taxane chemotherapy medicine used with prednisone for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after docetaxel. It can cause low white-cell counts, infection, diarrhea, and serious allergic reactions.

name: cabergoline
clinical_significance: A dopamine D2-receptor agonist used to suppress prolactin secretion and treat hyperprolactinemia; it is also used in selected Parkinson disease settings and requires monitoring for adverse effects.

name: cachexia
clinical_significance: A wasting syndrome caused by serious long-term illness, marked by ongoing unintentional loss of weight, muscle, and body fat. It may cause poor appetite, weakness, and inflammation and cannot be corrected by nutrition alone.

name: CADASIL syndrome
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder of small brain blood vessels caused by changes in the NOTCH3 gene. It may cause migraine with aura, repeated strokes, mood changes, and gradually worsening memory or thinking problems.

name: cadaver
clinical_significance: A human body after death, examined in medical education, forensic investigation, or an autopsy. Postmortem findings can help establish the cause of death or improve understanding of disease, with handling governed by consent, law, and respectful practice.

name: cadherin
clinical_significance: A cell-surface protein that helps neighboring cells attach to one another and keeps tissues organized. Loss or alteration of cadherins can allow some cancer cells to invade nearby tissue and spread.

name: cadmium
clinical_significance: A toxic metal found in tobacco smoke, some batteries and pigments, workplace dust, and contaminated food or soil. Long-term exposure can damage the kidneys, lungs, and bones and increases the risk of some cancers.

name: cadmium chloride
clinical_significance: A toxic cadmium salt used in some industrial and laboratory processes. Exposure can damage the lungs and kidneys and, with prolonged exposure, contribute to bone injury and cancer risk; it requires strict handling controls.

name: cadusafos
clinical_significance: An organophosphate pesticide that blocks acetylcholinesterase, causing excess nerve signaling after exposure. Poisoning may produce sweating, salivation, vomiting, diarrhea, small pupils, muscle weakness, breathing difficulty, or seizures.

name: caenorhabditis elegans
clinical_significance: A microscopic roundworm used as a model organism in genetics, development, and neuroscience research. It is not a human parasite, but studies of its conserved cell processes can inform basic biomedical research.

name: cafe-au-lait spot
clinical_significance: Multiple café-au-lait macules can be a clue to neurofibromatosis type 1 or other genetic syndromes; number, size, age, and associated findings guide evaluation.

name: caffeic acid
clinical_significance: A plant-derived phenolic compound found in coffee, fruits, and vegetables. It is studied for antioxidant and other biological effects, but it is not an established treatment or routine clinical marker.

name: caffeine
clinical_significance: A stimulant found in coffee, tea, chocolate, soft drinks, and energy drinks. It increases alertness and can raise heart rate, cause shakiness, or disturb sleep.

name: calbindin
clinical_significance: A protein that binds calcium inside cells and helps control calcium levels and cell signaling, especially in nerve and intestinal cells. Laboratories may also use it as a marker to identify certain tissues.

name: calcifediol
clinical_significance: The main circulating storage form of vitamin D, also called 25-hydroxyvitamin D. A blood test for calcifediol is used to assess vitamin-D status before the body converts it to the active hormone calcitriol.

name: calcification
clinical_significance: Deposition of calcium salts in body tissue. It may be a normal part of bone formation, a response to injury or aging, or a sign of abnormal calcium or phosphate balance; its importance depends on the site and pattern.

name: calcineurin
clinical_significance: A protein that helps activate T cells, which are immune cells, after they receive signals. Medicines that block it reduce immune activity and are used to prevent transplant rejection and treat selected immune diseases.

name: calcinosis
clinical_significance: Abnormal deposition of insoluble calcium salts in the skin or deeper soft tissues, often associated with autoimmune connective-tissue disease, kidney disease, trauma, or an abnormal calcium-phosphate balance. Firm white or yellow nodules or plaques may be painful, restrict movement, ulcerate, or release chalky material.

name: calciphylaxis
clinical_significance: A life-threatening vascular calcification syndrome predominantly affecting patients with end-stage renal disease on dialysis or secondary hyperparathyroidism. Progressive medial calcification and intimal fibroplasia of small dermal and subcutaneous arterioles lead to luminal thrombosis, severe tissue ischemia, intensely painful violaceous plaques with livedoid patterns, and rapidly progressive non-healing ischemic skin necrosis with black eschar formation.

name: calcitonin
clinical_significance: A hormone made by specialized cells in the thyroid gland. It helps lower blood calcium by reducing calcium release from bone and increasing calcium loss through the kidneys, although it has a smaller role than parathyroid hormone in adults.

name: calcitriol
clinical_significance: The active hormone made from vitamin D, mainly by the kidneys. It increases intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate and helps regulate parathyroid hormone, bone formation, and blood-mineral levels.

name: calcium
clinical_significance: A mineral needed for strong bones and teeth, muscle movement, nerve signals, blood clotting, and normal cell function. Blood calcium exists in an active free form and forms attached to proteins or other substances.

name: calcium carbonate
clinical_significance: A calcium supplement and antacid that neutralizes stomach acid. Excessive use can cause constipation, high blood calcium, or kidney problems and may interfere with medicine absorption.

name: calcium channel
clinical_significance: A protein in the cell membrane that controls calcium entry into cells. Calcium channels help regulate muscle contraction, the release of substances, nerve signals, and heart rhythm.

name: calcium chloride
clinical_significance: A calcium salt given by injection for severe low blood calcium, dangerously high potassium, or certain toxic exposures. It can cause serious tissue injury if it leaks outside the vein and therefore requires careful administration.

name: calcium citrate
clinical_significance: A calcium supplement that is absorbed even when stomach acid is low. It may prevent or treat calcium deficiency but can cause constipation and, in some people, contribute to kidney stones.

name: calcium gluconate
clinical_significance: A calcium salt taken by mouth or given by injection to treat calcium deficiency and some emergencies, including dangerously high potassium or magnesium. Intravenous treatment requires medical monitoring because it can affect the heart and veins.

name: calcium phosphate
clinical_significance: A mineral that forms much of the hard structure of bones and teeth. Excess calcium phosphate can also deposit in soft tissues, especially after tissue damage or when blood calcium or phosphate levels are abnormal.

name: calcium signaling
clinical_significance: A way cells communicate using changes in calcium concentration. These signals help control muscle contraction, secretion of substances, energy use, movement, and activity of genes.

name: calculation
clinical_significance: A mathematical operation or result obtained by combining numbers according to specified rules. In healthcare, calculations support tasks such as medicine doses, body-surface area, and risk estimates, so inputs and units must be checked carefully.

name: calculi
clinical_significance: Hardened mineral concretions, such as gallstones, kidney stones, or salivary stones, formed when dissolved substances precipitate and aggregate within a body organ or duct.

name: calibration
clinical_significance: Checking and, when necessary, adjusting a medical or laboratory instrument against a known standard so its measurements are accurate and reliable. Regular calibration supports correct diagnosis, treatment, and patient safety.

name: caliciviridae
clinical_significance: A family of viruses that includes norovirus and sapovirus, which commonly cause vomiting and diarrhea. Other members infect animals; illness depends on the particular virus, the person or animal infected, and the route of exposure.

name: calmodulin
clinical_significance: A protein inside cells that senses calcium and passes its signals to other proteins. It helps control muscle contraction, movement of substances through cell membranes, chemical reactions, and activity of genes.

name: calnexin
clinical_significance: A protein inside cells that helps newly made proteins fold into the correct shape. It checks proteins before they are sent to other parts of the cell or broken down.

name: calories
clinical_significance: A unit used to express energy in food and bodily metabolism. Nutrition labels commonly report kilocalories as “Calories”; energy needs vary with age, body size, activity, and health.

name: calorimetry
clinical_significance: Measurement of heat production or gas exchange to estimate how much energy the body uses. Indirect calorimetry uses oxygen consumption and carbon-dioxide production to help assess metabolism and nutritional needs.

name: calpain
clinical_significance: A group of enzymes activated by calcium that cut selected proteins inside cells. They help regulate cell movement, signaling, programmed cell death, and platelet activity; abnormal calpain activity contributes to some muscle and nervous-system diseases.

name: calponin
clinical_significance: A protein that binds to actin, a component of the cell's internal framework, and helps regulate contraction in smooth muscle. Laboratory staining for calponin can help identify muscle-related cells in tissue samples.

name: calreticulin
clinical_significance: A protein inside cells that helps newly made proteins fold correctly and helps regulate calcium storage and immune signaling. Harmful changes in its gene are found in some blood cancers involving excessive production of blood cells.

name: calretinin
clinical_significance: A calcium-binding protein found in certain nerve cells and cells lining body cavities. Pathologists may use calretinin staining to help distinguish mesothelioma from some other cancers in a tissue sample.

name: calvarium
clinical_significance: The dome-like portion of the skull formed mainly by the frontal, parietal, and occipital bones. It encloses and protects the upper parts of the brain.

name: campesterol
clinical_significance: A plant sterol found in many vegetable oils and nuts and used in research and food analysis. It can help assess plant-oil composition; it is not a routine medical test or treatment.

name: camphor
clinical_significance: A strong-smelling substance used in some topical products and traditional remedies. Swallowing even a relatively small amount can cause nausea, agitation, drowsiness, or rapidly developing seizures and may be life-threatening.

name: campomelic dysplasia
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder caused by changes affecting the SOX9 gene. It causes bowed long bones, poorly developed shoulder blades, characteristic facial features, and often serious problems with breathing or other organs.

name: camptothecin
clinical_significance: A natural compound that blocks topoisomerase I, an enzyme needed for DNA replication, and can kill rapidly dividing cells. It provided a basis for anticancer medicines such as irinotecan and topotecan, but the parent compound itself is not a routine treatment.

name: camptothecin analogue
clinical_significance: A family of medicines derived from camptothecin that inhibit topoisomerase I and interfere with cancer-cell DNA replication. Some members, including irinotecan and topotecan, are established cancer treatments; risks include low blood counts and, depending on the drug, severe diarrhoea.

name: campylobacter
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria that commonly cause foodborne intestinal infection. Illness may include fever, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, or bloody stools; some species can invade the bloodstream or cause later nerve or joint problems.

name: campylobacter coli
clinical_significance: A Campylobacter species that can cause foodborne intestinal infection, usually after contaminated meat, water, or other food. Symptoms include fever, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, and sometimes bloody stools.

name: campylobacter concisus
clinical_significance: A Campylobacter species commonly found in the human mouth and sometimes detected in stool or intestinal samples. It has been associated with diarrhoea and inflammatory bowel disease, but its role is not always clear; detection alone does not prove it caused symptoms.

name: campylobacter curvus
clinical_significance: A species of Campylobacter associated with the mouth and occasionally isolated from clinical specimens. Human infection is uncommon, and a positive culture should be interpreted with the specimen site, symptoms, and other results.

name: campylobacter fetus
clinical_significance: A Campylobacter species that can cause bloodstream infection and infections of blood vessels, joints, the brain, or other tissues. Serious disease is more likely in older adults and people with weakened immunity.

name: campylobacter gracilis
clinical_significance: A species of Campylobacter associated with the human oral cavity and reported from clinical infections, including occasional bloodstream infection. Its disease-causing role is uncommon; significance depends on isolation site and the patient’s clinical findings.

name: campylobacter infection
clinical_significance: A bacterial infection, usually caused by C. jejuni or C. coli, acquired from contaminated poultry, food, water, or unpasteurized milk. It causes fever, cramps, and diarrhea that may be bloody; rare complications include bloodstream infection, arthritis, or Guillain--Barré syndrome.

name: campylobacter jejuni
clinical_significance: A major cause of foodborne intestinal infection, usually acquired from undercooked poultry, contaminated water, or unpasteurized milk. It commonly causes fever, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea that may contain blood.

name: campylobacter lari
clinical_significance: A Campylobacter species that can cause foodborne intestinal infection. It is less common than C. jejuni and C. coli, but can produce fever, abdominal cramps, and diarrhoea; laboratory identification may guide public-health investigation.

name: campylobacter rectus
clinical_significance: A Campylobacter species commonly found in the mouth and associated with periodontal disease. It has also been recovered from other clinical samples, but its role as a cause of illness is not established in every setting.

name: campylobacter upsaliensis
clinical_significance: A Campylobacter species found in dogs and cats that can cause human diarrhoeal illness, especially in young children or people with weakened immunity. Infection can be foodborne or associated with animal contact.

name: campylobacteraceae
clinical_significance: A family of bacteria that includes Campylobacter, organisms that can cause foodborne intestinal illness and, less commonly, infections of blood or other tissues. Clinical significance depends on the species and specimen source.
