name: canagliflozin
clinical_significance: A medicine that lowers blood glucose by causing the kidneys to remove more glucose in urine. It may also reduce some heart-failure and kidney risks, but can cause genital infections, dehydration, low blood pressure, or ketoacidosis.

name: canarypox virus
clinical_significance: A poxvirus of birds used as a vector in some experimental or veterinary vaccines. It does not ordinarily cause disease in humans, and its clinical relevance is mainly as a vaccine-delivery platform.

name: Canavan disease
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which deficiency of the ASPA enzyme damages the brain's white matter. It usually begins in infancy with poor muscle tone, delayed development, increasing head size, feeding problems, and later severe movement and communication impairment.

name: cancell
clinical_significance: This is not a complete standalone medical term. If it is intended to refer to cancellous bone, it describes the porous inner structure of bone; clinical relevance depends on the surrounding anatomical or imaging context.

name: cancellous bone
clinical_significance: Porous bone made of thin supporting plates or struts. It is found inside many bones, especially near joints and in the vertebrae, and contains marrow while helping distribute forces.

name: cancer cluster
clinical_significance: A group or area with more cancer cases than expected during a specified time. Investigation compares the number and types of cancers with reliable background rates and examines possible shared exposures while considering chance variation.

name: cancer immunotherapy
clinical_significance: Cancer treatment that helps the immune system recognize or attack cancer cells. Methods include checkpoint inhibitors, engineered immune cells, immune-stimulating proteins, and some vaccines; use and side effects depend on the cancer and treatment.

name: cancer pain
clinical_significance: Pain caused by a tumor, its spread, or its treatment. It may be constant or intermittent and can arise from bone, nerves, organs, surgery, radiation, or medicines; treatment combines control of the cause with suitable pain relief and supportive care.

name: cancer prevention
clinical_significance: Actions that lower the chance of developing cancer or find precancerous changes early. They include avoiding tobacco, limiting alcohol, vaccination against cancer-causing infections, protecting skin from ultraviolet light, reducing harmful exposures, and recommended screening.

name: cancer risk
clinical_significance: The likelihood that a person will develop cancer. It is influenced by age, inherited variants, family history, tobacco, alcohol, certain infections, radiation, environmental exposures, body weight, and chance; having a risk factor does not guarantee cancer.

name: cancer screening
clinical_significance: Testing people who have no symptoms to find selected cancers or precancerous changes early, when treatment may work better. Each test has specific age, risk, interval, benefits, and possible harms.

name: cancer vaccine
clinical_significance: A vaccine intended either to prevent cancers caused by infections, such as HPV-related cancers, or to treat an existing cancer by helping the immune system recognize tumour cells. These are distinct uses; only selected vaccines are established treatments, while many therapeutic cancer vaccines remain under study.

name: candela
clinical_significance: The international unit used to measure the brightness of a light source in a specified direction. It is a physical unit, not a measure of a medicine's light dose or the amount of light reaching tissue.

name: candida
clinical_significance: A group of yeasts that may normally live on the skin, in the mouth, or in the digestive and genital tracts. Overgrowth can cause mouth, genital, skin, or, in vulnerable people, bloodstream and organ infections.

name: candida albicans
clinical_significance: The Candida species most often causing human infection. It can cause oral thrush, vaginal yeast infection, moist skin-fold rash, or serious bloodstream and organ infection in people with weakened defenses.

name: candida boidinii
clinical_significance: A yeast species used in biotechnology and enzyme production that is not a common cause of human disease. Rare clinical isolates should be interpreted with the specimen source and evidence of infection.

name: candida dubliniensis
clinical_significance: A yeast related to Candida albicans that can live in the mouth and cause oral thrush or, rarely, invasive infection. It is more likely to cause disease when immune defenses are impaired.

name: candida esophagitis
clinical_significance: Yeast infection of the esophagus, usually caused by Candida. It commonly causes painful or difficult swallowing and chest discomfort, especially in people with weakened immunity or after certain medicines.

name: candida famata
clinical_significance: A yeast species now often classified as Debaryomyces hansenii. It is commonly found in food and the environment and rarely causes opportunistic human infection, mainly in medically vulnerable patients.

name: candida glabrata
clinical_significance: A Candida species that can cause genital, urinary, bloodstream, or other invasive infection. It may resist some commonly used antifungal medicines, so laboratory susceptibility testing can help guide treatment.

name: candida inconspicua
clinical_significance: A yeast species that can rarely cause bloodstream or other opportunistic infection, often in people with serious underlying illness. Some isolates may be difficult to identify or treat, so laboratory species identification and susceptibility results matter.

name: candida intermedia
clinical_significance: A yeast species found in the environment and occasionally isolated from human specimens. It is an uncommon opportunistic pathogen; a positive result should be interpreted according to the site, symptoms, and other evidence.

name: candida orthopsilosis
clinical_significance: A member of the Candida parapsilosis species complex that can cause bloodstream or device-related infection, especially in hospitalized or immunocompromised patients. Species identification can matter because antifungal susceptibility may differ.

name: candida parapsilosis
clinical_significance: A Candida species that can cause bloodstream and catheter-related infection, especially in newborns, hospitalized people, and those receiving intravenous treatment. It may spread between patients through hands or contaminated equipment.

name: candida sake
clinical_significance: A yeast species associated with fermented foods and the environment. Human infection is rare; isolation from a clinical sample needs interpretation in light of the specimen and the patient’s condition.

name: candida tropicalis
clinical_significance: A Candida species that can cause mouth or genital infection and may invade the bloodstream or organs. Serious infection is more likely in people with neutropenia, cancer, or other immune impairment.

name: candida zeylanoides
clinical_significance: A yeast found in the environment and occasionally recovered from human specimens. It is an uncommon cause of opportunistic infection, and culture results should be assessed alongside symptoms and sample quality.

name: candidiasis
clinical_significance: Candidiasis ranges from localized thrush or genital infection to invasive disease in severely ill or immunocompromised patients; unnecessary antifungal treatment can obscure the cause of symptoms.

name: cane
clinical_significance: A walking stick used to improve balance, reduce load on a painful leg, or support mobility. The correct height and use can reduce falls and strain; the need and type of aid depend on strength, balance, and walking ability.

name: canertinib dihydrochloride
clinical_significance: An investigational oral cancer medicine that irreversibly blocks several epidermal growth-factor receptor family proteins. It was studied in clinical trials but is not an established routine treatment.

name: canfosfamide hcl
clinical_significance: An investigational chemotherapy medicine studied for several solid tumours. It is activated in cancer cells to damage DNA, but it has not become an established routine treatment.

name: cannabidiol
clinical_significance: A cannabinoid from the cannabis plant that usually does not produce the “high” caused by THC. A purified form treats selected severe seizure disorders; other products vary in strength, purity, side effects, and medicine interactions.

name: cannabinoid
clinical_significance: A substance that acts on cannabinoid receptors or related signaling systems. Cannabinoids may come from plants, the body, or laboratories; effects can include pain relief, appetite changes, sedation, impaired memory, or intoxication.

name: cannabinoid receptor
clinical_significance: A cell-surface protein, mainly CB1 or CB2, that responds to cannabinoids made by the body or found in cannabis and medicines. It helps regulate pain, appetite, mood, memory, immune activity, and inflammation.

name: cannabinol
clinical_significance: A cannabinoid formed as THC breaks down with age or exposure to air. It may have mild psychoactive effects, but its medical benefits and safety are less well established than those of some other cannabinoids.

name: cannula
clinical_significance: A thin hollow tube placed in a blood vessel, body cavity, or tissue to deliver medicines or fluids, remove material, measure pressure, provide oxygen, or allow access for another device.

name: cannula hub
clinical_significance: The connector at the outer end of a cannula that attaches it to tubing, a syringe, or another device. It may include a port or valve for giving fluids, taking samples, or flushing the cannula.

name: canola oil
clinical_significance: A vegetable oil relatively low in saturated fat and containing mostly monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats. Replacing solid fats with canola oil can support a heart-healthy eating pattern when total calories remain appropriate.

name: canrenone
clinical_significance: A metabolite related to spironolactone that blocks aldosterone's action. It promotes loss of sodium and water while reducing potassium loss and has been used in some countries for conditions involving fluid retention or excess aldosterone.

name: canthaxanthin
clinical_significance: A red-orange pigment used as a food colour and found in some supplements. High-dose tanning products have been associated with crystals in the retina and visual changes; such tanning use is not approved in the United States.

name: cantuzumab ravtansine
clinical_significance: An investigational antibody-drug conjugate designed to deliver a cell-killing drug to cancers expressing a tumour-associated antigen. It has been studied in cancer trials but is not an established routine treatment.

name: capecitabine
clinical_significance: An oral chemotherapy medicine that the body converts to fluorouracil, which interferes with cancer-cell DNA production. It is used for selected cancers and can cause diarrhea, mouth sores, hand-foot syndrome, low blood counts, or heart problems.

name: Capgras syndrome
clinical_significance: A fixed false belief that someone familiar has been replaced by an identical impostor. It may occur with psychotic illness, dementia, brain injury, seizures, or other neurologic disorders and needs clinical assessment.

name: capillaria
clinical_significance: A group of parasitic roundworms. Different species can cause intestinal infection, liver disease, or infection of other tissues; symptoms and treatment depend on the species and affected organ.

name: capillaria philippinensis
clinical_significance: A parasitic roundworm acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish. It infects the intestine and can cause persistent watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, poor absorption of nutrients, and loss of blood proteins.

name: capillary
clinical_significance: The smallest type of blood vessel, forming networks that connect arterioles with venules. Its thin wall allows exchange of oxygen, nutrients, fluid, and waste between blood and tissues.

name: capillary electrophoresis
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that separates charged molecules in a very thin tube using an electric field. It can analyze proteins, medicines, DNA, or other substances in a sample, depending on the test.

name: capillary leak syndrome
clinical_significance: A condition in which fluid and proteins escape from small blood vessels into surrounding tissues. It can cause sudden swelling, low blood pressure, thickened blood, shock, and organ failure; severe infection, medicines, immune disease, or rare unexplained episodes may trigger it.

name: capillary plasma
clinical_significance: The liquid component of blood obtained from small vessels in skin or tissue, containing water, electrolytes, proteins, hormones, nutrients, and waste products.

name: capillary vessel
clinical_significance: A microscopic vessel with a thin endothelial wall where blood exchanges oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, fluid, and waste with surrounding tissue.

name: capnocytophaga
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria found mainly in the mouths of dogs, cats, and people. Some species can cause serious human infection after animal bites or scratches, especially in people without a functioning spleen or with weakened immunity.

name: capnocytophaga gingivalis
clinical_significance: A bacterium commonly found in the human mouth and dental plaque. It has been associated with gum disease, but it is not a common cause of invasive infection.

name: capnocytophaga ochracea
clinical_significance: A bacterium found mainly in the human mouth and associated with dental plaque and gum disease. Infection outside the mouth is uncommon but can occur when immune defenses are severely weakened.

name: capnocytophaga sputigena
clinical_significance: A species of Capnocytophaga found in the mouth and dental plaque. It may be associated with periodontal disease; serious infection outside the mouth is uncommon.

name: capreomycin
clinical_significance: An injectable antibiotic formerly used for some drug-resistant tuberculosis infections. It can damage the kidneys and hearing or balance nerves, so use requires specialist oversight and toxicity monitoring; newer regimens have reduced its role.

name: capromab pendetide
clinical_significance: A radiolabelled antibody formerly used in selected imaging studies of prostate cancer. It is no longer routinely used; current imaging choices and availability differ by setting.

name: capsaicin
clinical_significance: The substance that makes chili peppers feel hot. Applied in controlled amounts to the skin, it can reduce some nerve and joint pains by temporarily lowering pain signaling; it commonly causes initial burning or redness.

name: capsid
clinical_significance: The protein shell surrounding a virus's genetic material. It protects the genome and helps the virus attach to and enter host cells; its structure influences which cells can be infected and how the immune system responds.

name: capsid proteins
clinical_significance: Proteins that assemble around a virus's genetic material to form its protective shell. Some also help the virus attach to and enter cells and are recognized by the immune system.

name: capsule
clinical_significance: A protective covering around an organ, joint, or other structure, or an oral medicine enclosed in a dissolvable shell. The exact meaning depends on whether the term is used in anatomy or pharmacology.

name: capsule endoscope
clinical_significance: A swallowable capsule containing a tiny camera and transmitter. As it travels through the digestive tract, it sends images, especially of the small intestine, where conventional endoscopes may not reach easily.

name: captopril
clinical_significance: An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor used for high blood pressure, heart failure, and some kidney problems. It can cause cough, high potassium, low blood pressure, or swelling.

name: carbachol
clinical_significance: A medicine that mimics acetylcholine and stimulates muscarinic receptors. In selected eye procedures, it constricts the pupil and can lower pressure inside the eye; effects may include sweating, slow heartbeat, or breathing problems.

name: carbadox
clinical_significance: An antimicrobial veterinary drug used in swine feed to control certain intestinal infections and support growth. FDA has raised concerns about carcinogenic residues and has proposed withdrawal of approvals; it remains available in the United States unless those approvals are withdrawn.

name: carbamate
clinical_significance: A chemical group found in some medicines and pesticides. Carbamate insecticides can temporarily block acetylcholinesterase, causing excess nerve activity with sweating, salivation, vomiting, weakness, wheezing, or seizures.

name: carbamazepine
clinical_significance: A medicine used for focal seizures, trigeminal neuralgia, and selected bipolar disorder. Important risks include severe skin reactions, low blood counts, liver injury, low sodium, dizziness, and interactions with many other medicines.

name: carbapenem
clinical_significance: A group of powerful beta-lactam antibiotics that kill bacteria by blocking construction of their cell wall. They are reserved mainly for serious infections because resistance and important side effects can limit treatment choices.

name: carbaryl
clinical_significance: A carbamate insecticide that temporarily blocks acetylcholinesterase. Substantial exposure can cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, diarrhea, small pupils, muscle weakness, wheezing, seizures, or breathing failure.

name: carbazilquinone
clinical_significance: An experimental quinone-related anticancer compound studied for its ability to damage tumour-cell DNA. It is not an established routine treatment.

name: carbenicillin
clinical_significance: A penicillin-family antibiotic formerly used for serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria, including some Pseudomonas infections. It is now rarely used because of resistance, availability, and the use of newer alternatives.

name: carbidopa
clinical_significance: A medicine given with levodopa for Parkinson disease. It blocks conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the brain, allowing more levodopa to reach the brain and reducing nausea, vomiting, and low blood pressure.

name: carbofuran
clinical_significance: A highly toxic carbamate pesticide that blocks acetylcholinesterase. Ingestion, inhalation, or skin exposure can rapidly cause sweating, vomiting, muscle weakness, seizures, breathing failure, and death.

name: carbogen
clinical_significance: A mixture of oxygen and carbon dioxide used in some respiratory tests and research, including studies of blood flow or oxygen response. It must be administered with appropriate monitoring because carbon dioxide can alter breathing and blood acidity.

name: carbohydrate
clinical_significance: One of the three main macronutrients, found in sugars, starches, fruits, grains, vegetables, legumes, and milk. Sugars and most starches are digested into simple sugars, mainly glucose, for energy; dietary fiber is a carbohydrate that is not fully digested.

name: carbohydrate metabolism
clinical_significance: The processes cells use to break down, store, and make sugars. These processes provide energy and help keep blood glucose stable; problems can occur in diabetes and inherited disorders of sugar storage.

name: carbon
clinical_significance: A chemical element forming the backbone of organic molecules such as carbohydrates, fats, proteins, and nucleic acids.

name: carbon dioxide
clinical_significance: A gas produced when cells use energy and removed mainly by the lungs during exhalation. The body controls its blood level through breathing; excess can cause headache, confusion, drowsiness, or respiratory failure.

name: carbon monoxide
clinical_significance: A colorless, odorless gas that binds hemoglobin and prevents blood from delivering enough oxygen. Poisoning may cause headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, collapse, or death and requires immediate fresh air and emergency care.

name: carbon tetrachloride
clinical_significance: A toxic industrial solvent that can damage the liver and kidneys when swallowed or inhaled. Suspected exposure requires urgent contact with poison-control or emergency services.

name: carbonate
clinical_significance: A chemical form of carbon dioxide found in minerals and body fluids. Carbonate salts are used in some antacids and supplements; their effects, absorption, and risks depend on the particular salt.

name: carbophenothion
clinical_significance: An organophosphate insecticide that blocks acetylcholinesterase. Significant exposure can cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, muscle weakness, confusion, seizures, breathing failure, and death.

name: carboplatin
clinical_significance: A platinum chemotherapy medicine that damages cancer-cell DNA and prevents it from being copied. It can lower blood counts, especially platelets, and may cause nausea, anemia, kidney effects, nerve symptoms, or allergic reactions.

name: carboprost
clinical_significance: A prostaglandin medicine that strongly contracts the uterus. It is used in selected cases of severe bleeding after childbirth and for some pregnancy-related procedures; it can cause diarrhea, vomiting, fever, and dangerous airway tightening in people with asthma.

name: carbosulfan
clinical_significance: A carbamate insecticide that blocks acetylcholinesterase and overstimulates nerves. Exposure can cause sweating, salivation, vomiting, diarrhea, small pupils, muscle weakness, wheezing, seizures, or breathing failure.

name: carboxyhemoglobin
clinical_significance: A compound formed when carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin. It prevents hemoglobin from carrying and releasing oxygen normally, causing headache, dizziness, confusion, collapse, or death in severe poisoning.

name: carboxyl group
clinical_significance: A chemical group containing carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen that gives many molecules acidic properties. It is found in amino acids, fatty acids, and numerous medicines and metabolic compounds.

name: carboxylesterase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that breaks ester bonds in medicines, toxins, and natural fats. Differences in its activity can change how quickly some substances are broken down and can affect their effects, interactions, or toxicity.

name: carboxylic acid
clinical_significance: An organic compound containing a carboxyl group, which gives it acidic properties. Many important fatty acids, amino-acid products, and substances involved in metabolism are carboxylic acids.

name: carboxy-lyases
clinical_significance: Enzymes that break a carbon-carbon bond and release carbon dioxide. They participate in many biochemical reactions, including processes that make or break down amino acids and other molecules.

name: carboxypeptidase h
clinical_significance: An enzyme inside cells that helps turn newly made precursor proteins into active hormones and nerve-signalling substances by trimming amino acids from one end.

name: carbuncle
clinical_significance: A group of connected boils, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus, forming a painful swollen area with several pus-draining openings. Fever may occur, and risk is increased by diabetes or a weakened immune system.

name: carbutamide
clinical_significance: An early sulfonylurea medicine once used to lower blood glucose in type 2 diabetes. It was largely abandoned because of serious blood disorders and has been replaced by safer diabetes medicines.

name: carcinoembryonal antigen
clinical_significance: Another name for carcinoembryonic antigen, or CEA, a blood marker that may rise in colorectal and other cancers. It can also increase for noncancerous reasons and is not suitable for general cancer screening.

name: carcinogen
clinical_significance: A substance, form of radiation, or infection that can cause cancer by damaging cells or changing how they grow. Risk depends on the type and amount of exposure.

name: carcinogen testing
clinical_significance: Laboratory or population methods used to determine whether a substance or exposure can cause cancer. Results support hazard and risk assessment, but the actual risk depends on the exposure amount, duration, route, and individual factors.

name: carcinogenesis
clinical_significance: The multistep process by which normal cells acquire changes that allow uncontrolled growth and become cancer. Changes may arise from inherited traits, random errors, infections, tobacco, radiation, chemicals, or other exposures and often accumulate over time.

name: carcinoid tumor
clinical_significance: A usually well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor arising in hormone-producing cells, commonly in the appendix, small intestine, rectum, or lungs. Its behavior ranges from slow-growing to capable of spreading and causing hormone-related symptoms.

name: carcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer that begins in epithelial cells, which cover body surfaces and line organs and glands. Common types include adenocarcinoma, squamous-cell carcinoma, basal-cell carcinoma, and urothelial carcinoma; behavior depends on site and cell features.

name: carcinoma in situ
clinical_significance: Abnormal cancer-like cells occupying the full thickness of an epithelial lining but not yet invading through its supporting boundary. It is an early, noninvasive stage that may progress if untreated.

name: carcinomatosis
clinical_significance: Widespread spread of carcinoma to multiple surfaces or organs, often along the lining of the abdomen, chest, or other body cavities. It usually indicates advanced cancer and may cause fluid buildup, pain, bowel problems, or breathing difficulty.

name: carcinosarcoma
clinical_significance: An uncommon cancer containing both gland- or surface-lining cancer cells and connective-tissue cancer cells. It most often begins in the uterus, tends to grow aggressively, and is diagnosed by examining a tissue sample.

name: cardia
clinical_significance: The upper part of the stomach surrounding the opening where the esophagus enters. It helps receive swallowed food and can be affected by reflux, inflammation, hiatal hernia, or stomach cancer.

name: cardiac ablation
clinical_significance: A procedure that uses heat, cold, or another form of energy to create a small scar in heart tissue causing an abnormal rhythm. The scar blocks faulty electrical signals and may restore a regular rhythm.

name: cardiac arrest
clinical_significance: Sudden stopping of effective heart pumping, causing collapse, unresponsiveness, and absent or abnormal breathing. Immediate emergency action includes calling for help, starting chest compressions, and using an automated defibrillator if available.

name: cardiac care
clinical_significance: Medical care for people with heart disease, including assessment, monitoring, medicines, procedures, rehabilitation, and emergency treatment. The appropriate care depends on the specific heart condition and the person’s symptoms and risks.

name: cardiac catheter
clinical_significance: A thin flexible tube inserted through a blood vessel and guided to the heart. It can measure pressures, take blood samples, inject contrast for imaging, or deliver treatment.

name: cardiac fibroma
clinical_significance: A rare noncancerous tumor made of fibrous tissue in the heart, usually in a ventricle or septum. It may obstruct blood flow, interfere with electrical signals, or cause rhythm problems and heart failure.

name: cardiac glycoside
clinical_significance: A medicine or plant substance that can strengthen heart contraction and slow electrical conduction through the heart. Digoxin is the main clinical example; the safe dose is narrow and toxicity can cause dangerous rhythms.

name: cardiac hemangioma
clinical_significance: A rare noncancerous tumor made of blood-vessel tissue in or around the heart. Many cause no symptoms, but a large or strategically located tumor may obstruct flow, disturb rhythm, or cause fluid around the heart.

name: cardiac index
clinical_significance: The amount of blood the heart pumps each minute adjusted for body size. It helps assess pumping function, especially in seriously ill people, but a single value must be interpreted with blood pressure, symptoms, organ function, and the overall clinical situation.

name: cardiac myocyte
clinical_significance: A specialized heart-muscle cell that contracts to pump blood. Electrical signals and movement of calcium inside the cell coordinate its contraction and relaxation.

name: cardiac output
clinical_significance: The volume of blood pumped by the heart each minute. It depends mainly on heart rate and stroke volume, the amount ejected with each beat, and helps indicate whether circulation is adequate.

name: cardiac perforation
clinical_significance: A hole or tear through the heart wall, sometimes caused by injury or a medical procedure. It can cause bleeding around the heart, cardiac tamponade, shock, and death and requires immediate treatment.

name: cardiac rehabilitation
clinical_significance: A medically supervised program after conditions such as heart attack, coronary procedures, bypass surgery, or heart failure. It combines gradual exercise, education, risk-factor reduction, medicine support, nutrition, and emotional care to improve recovery and reduce future risk.

name: cardiac rhabdomyoma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous tumor of heart muscle, most often found in children and associated with tuberous sclerosis. It may shrink on its own but can obstruct blood flow or disturb rhythm and pumping if large.

name: cardiac sarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare cancer arising from supporting or connective tissue of the heart. It may obstruct blood flow, disturb heart rhythm, impair pumping, or release clots that travel to other parts of the body.

name: cardiac ventriculography
clinical_significance: Imaging of the heart's lower chambers to assess their size, wall movement, and ability to pump blood. It may use x-rays with contrast or another imaging method and is now often replaced by echocardiography or MRI.

name: cardiac volume
clinical_significance: The amount of blood in a heart chamber at a particular time. The amount before contraction and after contraction helps assess chamber size, filling, and pumping function.

name: cardiac wall
clinical_significance: The three-layered wall of the heart: the inner endocardium, muscular myocardium, and outer epicardium. It supports the heart's structure, electrical activity, contraction, and interaction with surrounding tissues.

name: cardinal body part
clinical_significance: A major body region or structure used in anatomical description or clinical examination, such as the head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, limbs, or an important internal organ.

name: cardinal cell part
clinical_significance: A main component of a cell, such as its membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, or an organelle. Each part has a role in maintaining the cell, processing information, or performing specialized functions.

name: cardiobacteriaceae
clinical_significance: A family of bacteria that includes Cardiobacterium. Some members can enter the bloodstream and infect heart valves, causing infective endocarditis.

name: cardiobacterium
clinical_significance: A slow-growing bacterium in the HACEK group that can enter the bloodstream and infect heart valves. It may cause prolonged fever, fatigue, weight loss, a new murmur, or embolic complications.

name: cardiobacterium hominis
clinical_significance: The Cardiobacterium species most often associated with human infection. It can cause slowly developing infective endocarditis with fever, fatigue, weight loss, a new heart murmur, valve damage, or clots traveling to other organs.

name: cardiogenic shock
clinical_significance: A life-threatening state in which a severely weakened heart cannot supply enough blood to the body. It may cause low blood pressure, confusion, cold skin, little urine, breathing difficulty, and failure of important organs.

name: cardiolipin
clinical_significance: A fat-like molecule found mainly in the inner membrane of mitochondria, the cell's energy-producing structures. Antibodies against cardiolipin can be associated with antiphospholipid syndrome and abnormal blood clotting.

name: cardiologist
clinical_significance: A doctor trained to diagnose and treat diseases of the heart and blood vessels, including coronary disease, rhythm disorders, valve disease, heart failure, and high blood pressure.

name: cardiomegaly
clinical_significance: Enlargement of the heart seen on examination or imaging. It may result from enlarged chambers, thickened heart muscle, fluid around the heart, or a combination; causes include high blood pressure, valve disease, cardiomyopathy, and congenital disease.

name: cardiomyopathy
clinical_significance: A disease of the heart muscle that can make it enlarged, thickened, stiff, or weak. These changes can make it harder for the heart to pump or fill with blood and may cause heart failure or abnormal heart rhythms. Major types include dilated, hypertrophic, and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

name: cardiopulmonary
clinical_significance: Relating to the heart and lungs or to their combined function. For example, cardiopulmonary exercise testing assesses how the heart, lungs, blood, and muscles respond during physical activity.

name: cardiopulmonary resuscitation
clinical_significance: An emergency procedure for a person in cardiac arrest, combining chest compressions with rescue breaths when appropriate to maintain blood flow and oxygen delivery until an automated defibrillator or emergency team can restore circulation. Immediate CPR improves the chance of survival.

name: cardiospasm
clinical_significance: Achalasia impairs passage of food from the esophagus into the stomach, causing swallowing difficulty, regurgitation, and weight loss; evaluation also excludes obstructing cancer.

name: cardiotocography
clinical_significance: Continuous recording of a fetus's heart rate and the mother's uterine contractions during pregnancy or labor. The pattern helps assess fetal well-being, but results must be interpreted with the stage of labor and the overall clinical situation.

name: cardiotonic agent
clinical_significance: A medicine or substance that increases the force of heart contraction or otherwise supports cardiac pumping. Such agents are used only for selected conditions because they can also cause abnormal heart rhythms, increased oxygen demand, or other serious effects.

name: cardiotoxicity
clinical_significance: Injury or impaired function of the heart caused by a medicine, toxin, radiation, or disease. It may produce rhythm problems, reduced heart-muscle strength, chest pain from poor blood flow, or heart failure.

name: cardiotoxin
clinical_significance: A substance that directly injures heart muscle or disrupts the heart's electrical activity or blood supply. It may cause abnormal rhythms, reduced pumping, heart failure, or heart-muscle injury.

name: cardiovascular
clinical_significance: Relating to the heart and blood vessels, including circulation, blood pressure, and diseases affecting the heart or vascular system.

name: cardiovascular agents
clinical_significance: Medicines that act on the heart or blood vessels. They include treatments for high blood pressure, abnormal rhythms, angina, heart failure, blood clots, and abnormal cholesterol levels.

name: cardiovascular disease
clinical_significance: Disease of the heart or blood vessels, including coronary artery disease, heart failure, abnormal rhythms, valve disease, stroke-related vascular disease, and disorders of arteries or veins.

name: cardiovascular infection
clinical_significance: An infection involving the bloodstream, heart, heart valves, or blood vessels. Examples include infective endocarditis, myocarditis, infected vascular grafts, and infected pacemakers or other devices.

name: cardiovascular injury
clinical_significance: Damage to the heart or blood vessels caused by trauma, reduced blood flow, inflammation, toxins, surgery, or another disease. Effects may include bleeding, impaired circulation, heart-muscle injury, or abnormal rhythms.

name: cardiovascular neoplasm
clinical_significance: A noncancerous or cancerous tumor arising in the heart, blood vessels, or related tissues. Its symptoms and treatment depend on the tissue type, location, size, effect on circulation, and whether it has spread.

name: cardiovascular pharmacology
clinical_significance: The study of how medicines affect the heart, blood vessels, blood pressure, rhythm, blood clotting, and cholesterol or lipid metabolism, including their uses, interactions, benefits, and risks.

name: cardiovascular surgery
clinical_significance: Operations on the heart or major blood vessels, including bypass surgery, valve repair or replacement, aortic surgery, and heart transplantation. Many open procedures require a heart-lung machine and specialized care before and after surgery.

name: cardiovascular system
clinical_significance: The heart, blood, and network of arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, and veins that circulate blood through the pulmonary and systemic circuits. It delivers oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and immune cells, carries carbon dioxide and other waste for removal, and helps regulate temperature and blood pressure.

name: cardiovirus
clinical_significance: A group of viruses in the picornavirus family. Some infect people or animals and may cause fever, muscle inflammation, heart inflammation, or other illness; effects depend on the species and the person's defenses.

name: caregiver
clinical_significance: A family member, friend, or paid worker who helps another person with health care, personal activities, daily tasks, transportation, medicines, or emotional support.

name: carina
clinical_significance: The ridge at the bottom of the windpipe where it divides into the right and left main bronchi. It is a landmark during bronchoscopy and breathing-tube placement; inhaled objects more often enter the wider, more vertical right bronchus.

name: carisoprodol
clinical_significance: A prescription muscle relaxant used short term for acute painful muscle conditions. It can cause drowsiness, dizziness, impaired coordination, misuse, dependence, and dangerous breathing suppression, especially with alcohol or sedatives.

name: carmine
clinical_significance: A red coloring made from cochineal insects and used in some foods, cosmetics, and medicines. Rarely, it causes allergy, wheezing, hives, or anaphylaxis in sensitive people.

name: carmustine
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy medicine that damages DNA and is used for selected brain tumors, blood cancers, and other cancers. It can lower blood counts and cause nausea, infertility, liver problems, or delayed lung injury.

name: carney complex
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder, usually caused by a PRKAR1A gene change, that can produce multiple noncancerous skin, heart, and endocrine tumors. It may also cause excess hormones and requires lifelong, organ-specific monitoring.

name: carney triad
clinical_significance: A rare condition involving combinations of a stomach gastrointestinal stromal tumor, a benign cartilage tumor in the lung, and a paraganglioma outside the adrenal gland. It usually occurs sporadically and more often affects young women.

name: carnitine
clinical_significance: A substance that transports long-chain fats into mitochondria, the cell structures that make energy, so the fats can be used as fuel. The body usually makes enough; severe deficiency can cause weakness, low blood sugar, or heart and muscle disease.

name: carnobacteriaceae
clinical_significance: A family of lactic-acid bacteria found mainly in food and the environment. Some species are used in food fermentation; they are not common human pathogens.

name: carnosine
clinical_significance: A small molecule made from beta-alanine and histidine, found mainly in muscle and nervous tissue. It helps buffer acidity; claims that supplements prevent disease or improve performance remain uncertain.

name: carnosinemia
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which deficient carnosinase causes excess carnosine in blood and urine. Children may have developmental delay, low muscle tone, seizures, or other neurologic problems of varying severity.

name: Caroli disease
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which the larger bile ducts inside the liver are widened in segments. It can cause repeated bile-duct infections, stones, abdominal pain, jaundice, and, in some people, liver scarring or kidney disease.

name: carotene
clinical_significance: An orange-yellow plant pigment found in foods such as carrots and leafy vegetables. Some forms, especially beta-carotene, can be converted to vitamin A; excess intake may harmlessly turn the skin yellow-orange.

name: carotenoid
clinical_significance: A family of fat-soluble yellow, orange, or red pigments found mainly in plants and some microorganisms. Some, such as beta-carotene, can form vitamin A; others, such as lutein, support eye tissues.

name: carotid artery
clinical_significance: One of the major arteries supplying the head and neck. Each common carotid divides into an internal branch that supplies the brain and an external branch that supplies much of the face, scalp, and neck.

name: carotid artery stenosis
clinical_significance: Narrowing of an artery in the neck that supplies the brain, usually from fatty plaque. It may reduce blood flow or release a clot and increase the risk of a transient ischemic attack or stroke.

name: carotid body
clinical_significance: A small group of sensing cells near the division of the common carotid artery. It detects changes in blood oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acidity and sends signals that help adjust breathing.

name: carotid endarterectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to open a carotid artery and remove fatty plaque from its inner wall. It can reduce stroke risk in selected people with significant narrowing, especially after symptoms, but carries risks such as stroke, heart attack, and nerve injury.

name: carpal bones
clinical_significance: The eight small bones forming the wrist: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate. They connect the forearm to the hand and work together to allow wrist movement and transmit force.

name: carpal joints
clinical_significance: The joints between the wrist bones and between the wrist, forearm, and hand bones. Together they allow the wrist to bend, straighten, move side to side, and rotate with the forearm.

name: carpal tunnel syndrome
clinical_significance: Pressure on the median nerve as it passes through the narrow wrist tunnel. It commonly causes numbness, tingling, burning, or pain in the thumb, index, middle, and part of the ring finger, sometimes with thumb weakness.

name: carpometacarpal joint
clinical_significance: A joint between a wrist bone and the base of a hand bone. The thumb joint is a mobile saddle-shaped joint that allows opposition and is commonly affected by osteoarthritis.

name: carrageenan
clinical_significance: A substance extracted from red seaweed and used to thicken or stabilize some foods and medicines. Different forms have different properties; evidence about effects on human inflammation depends on the type and amount consumed.

name: carrier excipient
clinical_significance: An inactive ingredient that supports an active medicine in a formulation. It may help control the medicine's dose, stability, absorption, appearance, or delivery and can occasionally cause allergy or intolerance.

name: carry-over effect
clinical_significance: Persistence of an earlier treatment's effect into a later measurement or treatment period. It can distort results in crossover studies or make a person's current clinical state difficult to interpret.

name: carteolol
clinical_significance: A nonselective beta-blocker used mainly as eye drops to lower pressure inside the eye in open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension. It can sometimes slow the heartbeat, lower blood pressure, or worsen breathing problems.

name: cartilage
clinical_significance: A tough, flexible tissue found in joints, the ear, nose, rib cage, and spinal discs. It cushions joints, supports body structures, and resists pressure, but it has limited blood supply and heals slowly after injury.

name: cartilage disease
clinical_significance: A disorder that damages cartilage in joints or supporting structures. It can cause pain, stiffness, swelling, deformity, impaired growth, or loss of smooth movement and may result from injury, aging, inflammation, or inherited disease.

name: carubicin
clinical_significance: An experimental anthracycline-related anticancer medicine studied for its ability to damage tumour-cell DNA. It is not a standard treatment in current practice.

name: carvedilol
clinical_significance: A beta-blocker that also relaxes blood vessels. It slows the heart and reduces its workload and is used for selected cases of high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack; it can lower blood pressure and heart rate.

name: carvedilol phosphate
clinical_significance: An extended-release oral formulation of carvedilol, a beta-blocker that also relaxes blood vessels. It is used for selected heart and blood-pressure conditions; dose changes and monitoring are important because it can lower heart rate and blood pressure.

name: carzelesin
clinical_significance: An investigational anticancer compound designed to damage DNA and block tumour-cell replication. It has been studied in research but is not an established routine treatment.

name: casanthranol
clinical_significance: A stimulant laxative that increases bowel movement and secretion of water into the intestine. Prolonged or excessive use can cause diarrhea, dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, and reliance on laxatives.

name: case management
clinical_significance: Coordinated planning, referral, and follow-up of health and social services to help a person receive appropriate care, avoid gaps or duplication, and meet clinical, functional, and personal goals.

name: case study
clinical_significance: A detailed account of one patient, event, or clinical setting used to describe an unusual presentation or generate research questions. A case study can illustrate possibilities but cannot establish how common an outcome is or prove that a treatment caused it.

name: case-control studies
clinical_significance: An observational study comparing people with a condition (cases) with people without it (controls) to look for prior exposures or characteristics. It is useful for rare diseases but can be affected by selection and recall bias and cannot by itself prove causation.

name: casein
clinical_significance: The main family of proteins in cow's milk and other mammalian milk. It supplies amino acids and minerals and forms curds during digestion and cheese-making; it can trigger reactions in people with cow's-milk protein allergy.

name: casein kinase
clinical_significance: A family of enzymes that attach phosphate groups to proteins and thereby change their activity. Casein kinases help regulate cell signaling, growth, DNA repair, development, and the body's internal clock.

name: caspase
clinical_significance: A group of enzymes that cut specific proteins inside cells. Some initiate orderly programmed cell death, while others activate inflammation and immune defense against infection.

name: caspase activation
clinical_significance: Conversion of inactive caspase enzymes into their active form inside a cell. Depending on the caspase and triggering signal, this can start programmed cell death or activate inflammation and immune defense.

name: caspase inhibitor
clinical_significance: A substance that blocks one or more caspase enzymes, which regulate programmed cell death and inflammation. Caspase inhibitors are mainly experimental tools or research candidates and are not routine treatments.

name: caspofungin
clinical_significance: An intravenous antifungal medicine that blocks construction of an important fungal cell-wall component. It is used for serious Candida infections and selected Aspergillus infections and may cause liver-test abnormalities, infusion reactions, or low potassium.

name: caspofungin acetate
clinical_significance: The acetate salt form of caspofungin, an intravenous antifungal medicine that blocks fungal cell-wall construction. It is used for selected serious Candida and Aspergillus infections under medical supervision.

name: castor oil
clinical_significance: A vegetable oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis. Taken by mouth, it acts as a stimulant laxative; excessive use can cause cramping, diarrhea, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances.

name: castration
clinical_significance: Removal or functional suppression of the testes or ovaries, reducing production of sex hormones. It may be surgical or achieved with medicines and can affect fertility, sexual function, mood, and bone health.

name: catabolism
clinical_significance: The set of chemical processes that break down complex molecules such as carbohydrates, fats, and proteins into simpler substances, releasing energy that cells can use. Examples include digestion-related breakdown, glycolysis, and fat oxidation.

name: catalase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. It protects cells from oxidative damage and helps some bacteria survive inside immune cells.

name: catalepsy
clinical_significance: A state of greatly reduced movement and responsiveness in which a person may remain rigid or hold an imposed posture. It can occur with catatonia, narcolepsy, neurologic disease, or some psychiatric conditions.

name: catalog
clinical_significance: A structured list of medical or scientific resources, products, or concepts. A catalog can help locate a test, specimen, medicine, or research item, but a catalog entry is administrative information rather than a clinical finding.

name: catalog number
clinical_significance: An identifying number assigned to an item in a catalog, such as a specimen, medicine, device, or research record. It supports tracking and retrieval but has no clinical meaning by itself.

name: catalyst
clinical_significance: A substance that speeds a chemical reaction without being used up. It works by providing an easier reaction pathway; enzymes are biological catalysts, and catalysts change reaction speed without changing the final balance of products and reactants.

name: cataplexy
clinical_significance: A sudden, brief loss of muscle strength triggered by strong emotion such as laughter, surprise, or anger. Awareness usually remains clear; it is strongly associated with narcolepsy and may cause the head, jaw, knees, or whole body to buckle.

name: cataract
clinical_significance: Clouding of the eye's natural lens, which reduces the passage of light to the retina. It can cause blurred or faded vision, glare, poor contrast, and difficulty seeing at night.

name: cataract surgery
clinical_significance: Removal of a clouded eye lens and replacement with an artificial lens to improve vision. Possible complications include infection, bleeding, retinal problems, increased eye pressure, or a need for later treatment, though serious complications are uncommon.

name: catechin
clinical_significance: A group of plant compounds found in tea, cocoa, some fruits, and other foods. They show antioxidant effects in laboratory studies, but catechin supplements are not proven treatments and may cause side effects or interact with medicines.

name: catechol
clinical_significance: A chemical compound with two neighboring hydroxyl groups, used in industry and involved in making some biologically active substances. Contact or inhalation can irritate tissues and substantial exposure may be toxic.

name: catecholamine
clinical_significance: A group of hormones and nerve-signaling chemicals that includes epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine. They help control the body's stress response, heart rate, blood pressure, alertness, and metabolism.

name: catenin
clinical_significance: A family of proteins that helps neighboring cells attach and communicate. Beta-catenin also carries growth signals inside cells; abnormal activity can allow some cancers to grow or spread.

name: cathartic
clinical_significance: A substance that promotes bowel emptying, usually by increasing stool water, intestinal movement, or both. Excessive or prolonged use can cause diarrhea, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, or dependence on laxatives.

name: cathepsin
clinical_significance: A family of enzymes that break down proteins inside cells, especially in lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments. They help with immune activity, tissue remodeling, and bone turnover; abnormal activity may contribute to inflammation, bone loss, or cancer.

name: cathepsin d
clinical_significance: An enzyme in lysosomes that breaks down proteins in an acidic environment. It also participates in cell death and immune processes; abnormal activity has been studied in cancer and nervous-system disease.

name: cathepsin h
clinical_significance: An enzyme in lysosomes that breaks down proteins and helps activate some biologically active peptides. It contributes to normal cell maintenance and may be altered in certain diseases.

name: cathepsin k
clinical_significance: An enzyme made by osteoclasts, the cells that remove old bone. It breaks down the protein framework of bone; excessive activity can contribute to bone loss and osteoporosis.

name: cathepsin l
clinical_significance: An enzyme in lysosomes that breaks down proteins and helps process antigens for immune recognition. It also participates in tissue remodeling and can assist entry or spread of some infectious agents.

name: cathepsin z
clinical_significance: An enzyme found mainly in lysosomes that cuts proteins into smaller pieces. It helps cells process materials and may contribute to immune responses and inflammation.

name: cathepsins b
clinical_significance: A group of protein-cutting enzymes, including cathepsin B, that help recycle proteins inside cells. Abnormal activity can contribute to inflammation, tissue remodeling, invasion of nearby tissue by tumors, and spread of cancer.

name: catheter
clinical_significance: A thin flexible tube placed in a blood vessel, body cavity, or duct to deliver medicines or fluids, drain urine or other material, measure pressure, collect samples, or guide a procedure.

name: catheterization
clinical_significance: Placement of a catheter into a blood vessel, body cavity, duct, or other passage to drain, infuse, measure, collect samples, or perform a procedure. Risks include pain, bleeding, infection, blockage, and injury to nearby tissue.

name: catheter-related infections
clinical_significance: Infections caused by microorganisms entering along or contaminating an indwelling catheter. They may cause local redness, pain, drainage, fever, or bloodstream infection; treatment may require antibiotics and catheter removal or replacement.

name: cathexis
clinical_significance: The investment of emotional or psychological energy in a person, idea, object, or activity, a term used mainly in psychology and psychoanalytic theory.

name: cation
clinical_significance: An atom or molecule with a positive electrical charge, such as sodium, potassium, calcium, or hydrogen. These charged particles help control fluid balance, nerve signals, muscle contraction, and blood acidity.

name: cat-scratch disease
clinical_significance: An infection caused by Bartonella henselae, usually after a scratch or bite from an infected cat. It commonly causes a small skin bump, nearby swollen lymph nodes, fever, and fatigue; rarely it affects the eye, liver, spleen, brain, or heart.

name: Caucasian
clinical_significance: An older racial label historically used in medical records and research. It is imprecise and should not be treated as a biological diagnosis or a substitute for a person’s ancestry, lived experience, or specific risk factors.

name: cauda equina
clinical_significance: The bundle of lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal nerve roots that continues below the end of the spinal cord. These nerves control sensation and movement in the legs and help control the bladder, bowel, and sexual organs.

name: caudal
clinical_significance: Positioned toward the tail or lower part of the body; in human anatomy, usually toward the feet or away from the head.

name: caudal dysplasia
clinical_significance: A group of birth defects in which the lower spine and nearby structures do not develop fully. It may cause abnormalities of the legs, pelvis, bowel, bladder, or genital organs and is more common with maternal diabetes.

name: caudal vein
clinical_significance: A vein in the tail region of some animals, used in veterinary anatomy and laboratory research for blood sampling or injections. It is not a major clinical vein in humans.

name: caudate nucleus
clinical_significance: A curved group of nerve cells deep in the brain that helps control movement, learning, memory, motivation, and behavior. Disease affecting it may contribute to movement or cognitive problems.

name: caulobacter
clinical_significance: A genus of bacteria commonly found in freshwater and soil. It is not a typical human pathogen; clinical detection is uncommon and should be interpreted with the specimen source and evidence of infection.

name: caulobacteraceae
clinical_significance: A family of bacteria that includes Caulobacter, organisms commonly found in water and soil. They have little routine clinical relevance and are not usual causes of human disease.

name: causalgia
clinical_significance: Severe persistent burning pain, sensitivity, and other sensory changes after injury to a peripheral nerve. It is now usually considered complex regional pain syndrome type II and may include swelling, color or temperature changes, and movement difficulty.

name: cautery device
clinical_significance: A medical instrument that uses heat, electricity, or another energy source to seal bleeding vessels or destroy unwanted tissue. Use can cause burns or damage surrounding structures if poorly controlled.

name: caveola
clinical_significance: A small pocket-like fold in a cell membrane that helps organize signals, move materials into or out of the cell, and respond to stretching or mechanical stress.

name: caveolins
clinical_significance: Proteins that form or regulate caveolae, small pockets in cell membranes. They help organize cell signals, handle fats, move materials across membranes, and respond to mechanical stress.

name: cavernous hemangioma
clinical_significance: A cluster of enlarged, thin-walled blood vessels that may occur in the skin, brain, spinal cord, or other tissues. Symptoms depend on location and may result from bleeding, pressure, pain, or altered function.

name: cd antigens
clinical_significance: Proteins or other markers on the surface of cells that help identify cell types, especially immune cells. Laboratory antibodies against these markers can classify cells, diagnose blood disorders, and guide selected treatments.

name: CEA assay
clinical_significance: A laboratory test measuring carcinoembryonic antigen in a specimen, usually blood. It is mainly used to monitor selected known cancers and cannot diagnose or exclude cancer by itself.

name: cebocephaly
clinical_significance: A rare facial malformation, usually associated with holoprosencephaly, characterized by closely spaced eyes and a nose with a single nostril. It can accompany severe brain and airway abnormalities and requires specialist neonatal assessment.

name: cecal hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from the caecum, the first part of the large intestine. Causes include inflammation, infection, reduced blood flow, polyps, diverticular disease, or cancer and may produce blood in the stool or anemia.

name: cecal infection
clinical_significance: Infection or inflammation of the caecum caused by microorganisms, reduced blood flow, inflammatory bowel disease, or nearby disease. It may cause right-sided abdominal pain, fever, diarrhea, or tenderness.

name: cecal neoplasm
clinical_significance: A noncancerous or cancerous growth arising in the caecum. It may cause bleeding, anemia, abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, or blockage and is usually evaluated with colonoscopy and tissue sampling.

name: cecostomy
clinical_significance: A surgically created opening from the caecum to the abdominal wall to release pressure, drain bowel contents, or divert stool. It may be temporary or permanent depending on the underlying problem.

name: cecum
clinical_significance: The first pouch-like part of the large intestine, in the lower right abdomen where the small intestine joins the colon. The appendix arises from it; disease can include inflammation, tumors, bleeding, or twisting that blocks the bowel.

name: cedecea
clinical_significance: A genus of environmental Gram-negative bacteria that rarely causes human infection. Reported illnesses include bloodstream, respiratory, urinary, and soft-tissue infections, often in people with major underlying disease; treatment should be guided by susceptibility testing.

name: cedecea davisae
clinical_significance: A rare species of Cedecea that has occasionally caused opportunistic human infection, including bloodstream or wound infection. Its significance depends on specimen source and compatible illness; antibiotic susceptibility testing is important because resistance can vary.

name: cedecea lapagei
clinical_significance: A species of Cedecea that has rarely caused human infections, including bloodstream, respiratory, urinary, or wound infection. It is an opportunistic pathogen, and treatment should be guided by laboratory susceptibility results.

name: cedecea neteri
clinical_significance: A species of Cedecea rarely reported in human infection. When isolated from a clinical specimen, clinicians assess whether it is causing disease and use susceptibility testing to guide antimicrobial treatment.

name: cediranib maleate
clinical_significance: An investigational oral medicine that blocks vascular endothelial growth-factor receptors and may slow tumour blood-vessel formation. It has been studied in clinical trials but is not an established routine treatment.

name: cefaclor
clinical_significance: A second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used for selected susceptible bacterial infections. It can cause allergic reactions, nausea, diarrhea, or antibiotic-associated colitis and should be used only when appropriate.

name: cefadroxil
clinical_significance: An oral first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used for selected susceptible skin, throat, urinary, and other infections. Possible effects include allergy, nausea, diarrhea, and antibiotic-associated colitis.

name: cefamandole
clinical_significance: A second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used in some settings for susceptible bacterial infections. It can cause allergy or diarrhea and may increase bleeding risk, especially in people with poor nutrition or liver disease.

name: cefatrizine
clinical_significance: An older oral cephalosporin antibiotic used in some countries for susceptible bacterial infections. Its usefulness depends on local availability, bacterial resistance, allergy risk, and current treatment guidance.

name: cefazolin
clinical_significance: An injectable first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used for selected susceptible infections and commonly given before surgery to prevent infection. Allergy, diarrhea, and dose adjustment in kidney disease may be important.

name: cefdinir
clinical_significance: An oral third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used for selected susceptible respiratory, skin, and other infections. It may cause diarrhea, nausea, allergic reactions, or antibiotic-associated colitis and can interact with iron-containing products.

name: cefepime
clinical_significance: An injectable fourth-generation cephalosporin used for serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria, including some hospital-acquired infections. Kidney-dose adjustment is important because accumulation can cause confusion, seizures, or other neurologic toxicity.

name: cefixime
clinical_significance: An oral third-generation cephalosporin used for selected susceptible urinary, respiratory, ear, and other bacterial infections. It can cause diarrhea or allergy, and unnecessary use promotes antibiotic resistance.

name: cefmenoxime
clinical_significance: An injectable third-generation cephalosporin used in some countries for susceptible bacterial infections. Possible effects include allergic reactions, diarrhea, and antibiotic-associated colitis.

name: cefmetazole
clinical_significance: An injectable cephamycin antibiotic used in some countries for selected abdominal, pelvic, and other infections caused by susceptible bacteria. Allergy, diarrhea, and antibiotic-associated colitis are possible.

name: cefonicid
clinical_significance: A long-acting second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used for selected susceptible infections. Its use is limited in many places; dose selection depends on kidney function, local resistance, and the infection site.

name: cefoperazone
clinical_significance: A third-generation cephalosporin active against many gram-negative bacteria and sometimes combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor. It can cause allergy, diarrhea, bleeding, or impaired bile flow and requires appropriate monitoring.

name: cefotaxime
clinical_significance: An injectable third-generation cephalosporin used for serious susceptible infections, including meningitis, pneumonia, bloodstream infection, and sepsis. Allergy, diarrhea, and antibiotic-associated colitis are possible.

name: cefotetan
clinical_significance: An injectable cephamycin antibiotic used for selected serious infections and surgical prevention. It covers some anaerobic bacteria but can cause allergy, diarrhea, bleeding, or a reaction if alcohol is consumed around treatment.

name: cefotiam
clinical_significance: A second-generation cephalosporin used in some countries for susceptible respiratory, urinary, skin, and other bacterial infections. Allergy, gastrointestinal effects, and antibiotic-associated colitis are possible.

name: cefoxitin
clinical_significance: An injectable cephamycin antibiotic used for selected abdominal, pelvic, skin, and other infections, including some involving anaerobic bacteria. Allergy, diarrhea, and antibiotic-associated colitis can occur.

name: cefsulodin
clinical_significance: An older injectable cephalosporin antibiotic with activity mainly against susceptible Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It is rarely used today; organism susceptibility and locally available alternatives guide treatment.

name: ceftazidime
clinical_significance: An injectable third-generation cephalosporin with activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and other susceptible gram-negative bacteria. It is used for selected serious infections and can cause allergy, diarrhea, or neurologic effects when it accumulates in kidney disease.

name: ceftibuten
clinical_significance: An oral cephalosporin antibiotic used for selected susceptible respiratory, urinary, and other bacterial infections. It may cause diarrhea or allergy, and inappropriate use promotes resistance and antibiotic-associated colitis.

name: ceftizoxime
clinical_significance: An injectable third-generation cephalosporin used for selected serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria, including some abdominal, pelvic, urinary, and anaerobic infections. Allergy, diarrhea, and antibiotic-associated colitis are possible.

name: ceftriaxone
clinical_significance: An injectable third-generation cephalosporin used for many serious susceptible bacterial infections, including meningitis, pneumonia, bloodstream infection, and gonorrhea. Allergy, diarrhea, biliary problems, and antibiotic-associated colitis are possible.

name: cefuroxime
clinical_significance: A second-generation cephalosporin available by mouth or injection for selected respiratory, ear, urinary, skin, and other bacterial infections. It can cause allergy, nausea, diarrhea, or antibiotic-associated colitis.

name: celecoxib
clinical_significance: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicine used to relieve pain and inflammation in osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and some other conditions. It may cause stomach bleeding or ulcers and increases the risk of serious cardiovascular events, particularly with higher doses or longer use.

name: celiac artery
clinical_significance: A major branch of the abdominal aorta that supplies the upper digestive organs, including the stomach, liver, gallbladder, spleen, pancreas, and first part of the small intestine. It divides into the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries.

name: celiac disease
clinical_significance: An autoimmune disease in which eating gluten, a protein in wheat, barley, and rye, triggers damage to the small-intestinal lining and reduces nutrient absorption. Symptoms may include diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal pain, bloating, weight loss, fatigue, or anaemia; some people have few or no digestive symptoms. Diagnosis usually requires blood tests and, in many cases, intestinal biopsy while the person is still eating gluten. Lifelong avoidance of gluten is the main treatment.

name: celiac plexus
clinical_significance: A network of nerves in the upper abdomen that carries signals to and from the stomach, liver, pancreas, intestines, and other organs. It can be targeted with an injection for selected severe abdominal pain.

name: cell
clinical_significance: The smallest living unit that can perform life processes. Human cells usually contain DNA in a nucleus and specialized internal structures that produce energy, make proteins, communicate, and maintain the body's tissues.

name: cell adhesion
clinical_significance: The attachment of cells to one another or to the supporting material around them. It helps maintain tissue structure, transmit signals, guide movement, and organize healing and development.

name: cell aggregation
clinical_significance: Clumping of cells through interactions between their surfaces or surrounding proteins. It is important in development, immune responses, wound healing, and formation of blood clots.

name: cell body
clinical_significance: The main part of a cell containing the nucleus and most internal structures. In a nerve cell, it excludes long extensions such as the axon and dendrites.

name: cell count
clinical_significance: The number of cells in a sample of blood, body fluid, tissue, or laboratory culture. It helps assess blood-cell levels, inflammation, infection, immune function, or abnormal cell growth.

name: cell culture
clinical_significance: Growth of cells outside the body in a controlled nutrient environment. It is used for research, medicine testing, diagnosis, production of biological products, and study of how cells respond to disease or treatment.

name: cell cycle
clinical_significance: The series of stages through which a cell grows, copies its DNA, checks for damage, and divides into two cells. Disruption of cycle control can contribute to developmental disorders and cancer.

name: cell death
clinical_significance: The loss of a cell's ability to remain alive. It may be a controlled process that removes old or damaged cells, or an uncontrolled result of injury, infection, toxins, lack of oxygen, or severe disease.

name: cell dedifferentiation
clinical_significance: Loss of some specialized features by a mature cell, making it more like an immature cell. It can occur during repair or development and may contribute to abnormal growth in some cancers.

name: cell density
clinical_significance: The number of cells in a given area or volume of tissue or fluid. It can change with growth, inflammation, healing, infection, or cancer and is measured in laboratory samples and tissue studies.

name: cell differentiation
clinical_significance: The process by which an unspecialized cell develops the structure and function of a specialized cell type, such as a nerve, muscle, blood, or skin cell.

name: cell division
clinical_significance: The process by which one cell produces new cells. Mitosis makes most body cells for growth and repair, while meiosis makes reproductive cells with half the usual number of chromosomes.

name: cell fusion
clinical_significance: Joining of two cells or their outer membranes to form one larger cell, sometimes with several nuclei. It occurs in normal development and repair and can also occur during infection or disease.

name: cell growth
clinical_significance: Increase in a cell's size and contents through production of proteins, membranes, energy stores, and other components. Abnormal growth signals can contribute to tissue overgrowth or cancer.

name: cell maturation
clinical_significance: Development of an immature cell into a mature cell with a specialized structure and function. It is essential for producing healthy blood, nerve, muscle, immune, and other body cells.

name: cell migration
clinical_significance: Movement of cells through tissue or across a surface in response to chemical, mechanical, or environmental signals. It is important in development, immune defense, wound healing, and cancer spread.

name: cell motility
clinical_significance: The ability of cells to move through or across a surface using their internal framework, attachment structures, or specialized projections such as cilia and flagella. It supports development, immunity, wound healing, and cancer spread.

name: cell movement
clinical_significance: Directed or random movement of a cell through tissue or across a surface. It is important in development, immune responses, wound repair, inflammation, and the spread of cancer.

name: cell nucleus
clinical_significance: The membrane-covered compartment containing most of a cell's DNA. It helps control gene activity, growth, division, repair, and production of proteins needed for normal cell function.

name: cell pellet
clinical_significance: The concentrated layer of cells collected at the bottom of a tube after spinning a sample in a centrifuge. It may be removed for microscopic, genetic, chemical, or other laboratory testing.

name: cell physiology
clinical_significance: The study of how cells obtain energy, transport substances, communicate, respond to signals, repair themselves, and perform specialized functions.

name: cell polarity
clinical_significance: The unequal arrangement of structures and activities within a cell, giving it distinct sides or directions. It enables organized transport, signaling, movement, development, and tissue structure.

name: cell proliferation
clinical_significance: Increase in cell number through repeated division. Normal proliferation supports growth and repair, while excessive or uncontrolled proliferation can cause tissue overgrowth, benign tumors, or cancer.

name: cell secretion
clinical_significance: Release of substances made by cells, such as hormones, enzymes, nerve chemicals, mucus, or immune signals. Secretion supports communication, digestion, protection, movement, and regulation of body processes.

name: cell senescence
clinical_significance: A state in which a cell remains active but permanently stops dividing, often because of aging, stress, or DNA damage. Senescent cells can help prevent cancer but may contribute to inflammation when they accumulate.

name: cell sorting
clinical_significance: Separation of cells into groups according to features such as size, density, surface markers, or fluorescence. It is used in research, diagnosis, blood-cell analysis, and preparation of selected cells for treatment.

name: cell structure
clinical_significance: The arrangement of a cell's membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, and internal structures. These parts work together to produce energy, make proteins, communicate, divide, and carry out specialized functions.

name: cell surface
clinical_significance: The outer membrane of a cell and the molecules attached to it. It controls movement of substances, attachment, recognition, communication, and interactions with immune cells and surrounding tissue.

name: cell survival
clinical_significance: The ability of a cell to remain alive and functional despite injury, lack of nutrients, toxins, infection, or other stress. It depends on the cell type, the severity and duration of the stress, and the cell's repair systems.

name: cell therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that uses living cells to replace damaged cells, restore a function, or change an immune response. Uses range from established blood-forming stem-cell transplantation to experimental treatments; benefits and risks depend on the cells and disease.

name: cell transplantation
clinical_significance: Transfer of living cells into a person to replace missing cells, restore tissue function, or modify immunity. Blood-forming stem-cell transplantation is established for selected diseases; rejection, infection, graft-versus-host disease, and other risks may occur.

name: cell wall
clinical_significance: A rigid outer layer surrounding plant, fungal, and bacterial cells. It provides shape and protection; human and animal cells have a flexible membrane but no cell wall.

name: cell-cell junction
clinical_significance: A specialized connection between neighboring cells that provides attachment, communication, or controlled passage of substances. Examples include tight junctions, desmosomes, and gap junctions.

name: cell-cell signaling
clinical_significance: The ways cells send and receive messages through direct contact, electrical activity, or chemicals such as hormones and neurotransmitters. Signaling coordinates growth, movement, immune responses, repair, and other body functions.

name: cell-free system
clinical_significance: A laboratory setup containing cell components but no intact living cells, such as enzymes, ribosomes, or cell extracts. It is used to study gene expression and biochemical reactions without the complexity of a whole cell.

name: cell-matrix junction
clinical_significance: A specialized connection anchoring a cell to the supporting material around it. It also transmits signals that influence cell shape, movement, survival, and tissue organization.

name: cellular
clinical_significance: Relating to cells or to processes occurring within or between cells.

name: cellular immunity
clinical_significance: Immune defense carried out mainly by T cells, natural killer cells, macrophages, and other cells rather than antibodies alone. It helps destroy infected or abnormal cells and control inflammation.

name: cellular metabolic process
clinical_significance: A chemical reaction or linked pathway in a cell that produces energy, builds cell components, or breaks down nutrients and waste.

name: cellular respiration
clinical_significance: The process cells use to release energy from food. Most cells use oxygen to convert nutrients into ATP, the cell's usable energy, while limited energy can be made without oxygen.

name: cellular vesicle
clinical_significance: A small membrane-bound compartment that transports, stores, or releases substances inside or outside a cell. Vesicles help move proteins, fats, hormones, and waste.
