name: cellulitis
clinical_significance: A bacterial infection of the deeper skin and tissue beneath it, causing spreading redness, warmth, swelling, tenderness, and sometimes fever or chills. It commonly follows a break in the skin and can spread rapidly or enter the bloodstream.

name: cellulomonas
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria found mainly in soil, plants, and other environmental materials. They break down cellulose; human infection is rare and usually occurs opportunistically in people with severe illness or weakened immunity.

name: cellulomonas hominis
clinical_significance: A rare environmental bacterium that has occasionally caused human infection, usually in people with weakened immunity or serious underlying illness. Its significance depends on symptoms, the body site, and laboratory identification.

name: cellulose
clinical_significance: A complex carbohydrate forming the structure of plant cell walls. Humans cannot digest it, but it is dietary fiber that adds bulk to stool and can support regular bowel movements when enough fluid is consumed.

name: cellulosimicrobium
clinical_significance: A group of environmental bacteria found mainly in soil. Human infection is rare but may affect people with serious illness, implanted devices, or weakened immune defenses and can involve the blood, heart, or other tissues.

name: cellulosome
clinical_significance: A group of enzymes joined together by some microorganisms to break down cellulose in plant cell walls. It helps the organism digest plant material and is studied for biotechnology and biofuel production.

name: celosomy
clinical_significance: A rare birth defect involving incomplete closure of the body wall, allowing abdominal or chest organs to protrude outside the body. The term is used for severe omphalocele-like malformations and requires specialist newborn care.

name: cementoma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous jaw lesion containing cementum-like mineralized tissue. Its behavior and treatment depend on the specific subtype, location, size, symptoms, and relationship to nearby teeth.

name: cementum
clinical_significance: A thin mineralized layer covering a tooth root. Fibers of the periodontal ligament attach to it and help anchor the tooth in its socket; it can be lost with gum disease.

name: centigram
clinical_significance: A metric unit of mass equal to one hundredth of a gram, or 10 milligrams, used for small quantities of medicines or specimens.

name: centimeter
clinical_significance: A metric unit of length equal to one hundredth of a meter, commonly used in clinical measurements such as wound size, tumor dimensions, and anatomical distances.

name: centipoise
clinical_significance: A unit of dynamic viscosity equal to one millipascal-second, used to describe the flow resistance of blood, fluids, medicines, and other materials.

name: central
clinical_significance: Located near the middle of the body or an organ, rather than near its edge. The word may describe a body structure, nervous-system area, blood line, symptom, or pattern of disease.

name: central apnea
clinical_significance: A pause in breathing caused by absent or reduced respiratory effort from impaired brainstem signaling, rather than upper-airway obstruction.

name: central diabetes insipidus
clinical_significance: Excessive urination and intense thirst caused by too little antidiuretic hormone from the brain. The kidneys cannot conserve enough water, so dehydration and high blood sodium may develop.

name: central hypothyroidism
clinical_significance: A condition with too little thyroid hormone because the brain's pituitary gland or hypothalamus does not provide enough stimulation to the thyroid.

name: central nervous system
clinical_significance: The brain and spinal cord. It receives and interprets information, controls movement and many automatic body functions, and supports thought, memory, emotion, and regulation of hormones.

name: central sleep apnea
clinical_significance: Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep because the brain temporarily stops sending signals to breathe, without physical airway blockage. It may occur with heart failure, high altitude, or opioid use.

name: centrifugation
clinical_significance: Spinning a specimen at high speed to separate components by density, such as cells from plasma or precipitated material from a liquid.

name: centriole
clinical_significance: A cylindrical microtubule structure in the centrosome that helps organize the mitotic spindle and, in some cells, forms the basal body of a cilium or flagellum.

name: centromere
clinical_significance: The constricted chromosome region where sister chromatids remain attached and the kinetochore forms for accurate chromosome segregation during cell division.

name: centrosome
clinical_significance: The main microtubule-organizing center of an animal cell, containing a pair of centrioles and coordinating the spindle during mitosis.

name: cephacetrile
clinical_significance: An older first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis; it is not commonly used in current practice.

name: cephalexin
clinical_significance: An oral first-generation cephalosporin that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis and treats selected skin, respiratory, urinary, and other susceptible infections.

name: cephaloglycin
clinical_significance: An older cephalosporin antibiotic that blocks bacterial cell-wall construction. It is not commonly used in current practice; the exact role depends on local availability and bacterial susceptibility.

name: cephalometry
clinical_significance: Measurement of the skull and facial structures, usually on standardized radiographs, used in orthodontic planning and assessment of craniofacial growth.

name: cephaloridine
clinical_significance: An older injectable first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic whose use declined because of nephrotoxicity and the availability of safer alternatives.

name: cephalosporin
clinical_significance: A beta-lactam antibiotic that kills susceptible bacteria by blocking construction of their protective cell wall. Different generations act against different bacteria; allergy, diarrhea, and resistance are possible.

name: cephalothin
clinical_significance: An older injectable first-generation cephalosporin that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis and was used for susceptible serious infections.

name: cephapirin
clinical_significance: A first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic formerly used for susceptible bacterial infections; current availability and indications vary by country.

name: cephradine
clinical_significance: A first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic related to cephalexin that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis and treats selected susceptible infections.

name: ceramide
clinical_significance: A type of fat that forms part of cell membranes and helps the outer skin retain water and block irritants. Ceramides also participate in signals controlling cell growth and survival.

name: cerebellar ataxia
clinical_significance: Poor coordination caused by disease or injury affecting the cerebellum or its connections. It may cause an unsteady walk, clumsy movements, slurred speech, tremor, or abnormal eye movements.

name: cerebellar cortex
clinical_significance: The folded outer layer of the cerebellum containing Purkinje and granular neurons that coordinates balance, posture, timing, and precision of movement.

name: cerebellar disease
clinical_significance: A disorder of the cerebellum causing impaired coordination, gait ataxia, dysmetria, tremor, abnormal eye movements, or speech changes.

name: cerebellar dysmetria
clinical_significance: Inaccurate control of the distance or force of a movement because of cerebellar dysfunction. A person may reach past a target, stop short, or have difficulty judging movement size.

name: cerebellar hemangioblastoma
clinical_significance: A usually benign, highly vascular tumor of the cerebellum that may cause headache, imbalance, vomiting, or hydrocephalus and can occur with von Hippel-Lindau disease.

name: cerebellar hypoplasia
clinical_significance: Incomplete development of the cerebellum, usually beginning before birth. It may cause poor coordination, abnormal eye movements, seizures, delayed development, or problems with balance and movement.

name: cerebellar neoplasm
clinical_significance: A benign or malignant tumor involving the cerebellum; symptoms may include poor coordination, imbalance, abnormal eye movements, headache, vomiting, or hydrocephalus.

name: cerebellar nuclei
clinical_significance: Deep clusters of cerebellar neurons that receive processed signals from the cerebellar cortex and send coordinated motor output to the brainstem and thalamus.

name: cerebellar vermis
clinical_significance: The midline portion of the cerebellum that helps control trunk posture, gait, balance, and coordination of eye and head movements.

name: cerebellum
clinical_significance: A region at the back of the brain, behind the brainstem, that coordinates balance, posture, eye movements, and accurate voluntary movement. Injury or disease can cause unsteady walking, clumsy movements, tremor, or slurred speech.

name: cerebral aneurysm
clinical_significance: An abnormal bulge in a brain artery wall that may remain silent or rupture and cause bleeding around the brain. Rupture can produce a sudden, severe headache, loss of consciousness, or neurologic deficits and is a medical emergency; management depends on size, site, and risk.

name: cerebral aqueduct
clinical_significance: A narrow channel through the midbrain connecting the third and fourth brain ventricles. It allows cerebrospinal fluid to flow, and blockage can enlarge the ventricles and increase pressure.

name: cerebral artery
clinical_significance: An artery that carries blood to part of the brain. A blockage can cause an ischemic stroke, while a break in the vessel can cause bleeding in or around the brain; the effects depend on which artery is involved.

name: cerebral atrophy
clinical_significance: Loss or shrinkage of brain tissue caused by aging, neurodegenerative disease, injury, infection, stroke, or another condition. Effects vary from none to memory loss, weakness, seizures, or impaired thinking.

name: cerebral calcification
clinical_significance: Abnormal calcium deposition in brain tissue, with causes including inherited, metabolic, infectious, vascular, and age-related disorders.

name: cerebral cortex
clinical_significance: The folded outer layer of the cerebrum containing nerve cells that support thinking, sensation, movement, language, memory, and awareness. Its folds increase the amount of working brain tissue within the skull.

name: cerebral crus
clinical_significance: A bundle of nerve fibers in the midbrain that carries movement signals from the brain’s outer layer toward the brainstem and spinal cord. Damage can cause weakness or poor control on the opposite side.

name: cerebral edema
clinical_significance: Swelling caused by excess fluid in or around brain tissue. It can raise pressure inside the skull, reduce blood flow, and cause headache, vomiting, confusion, seizures, coma, or life-threatening brain displacement.

name: cerebral hemisphere
clinical_significance: One of the two large halves of the cerebrum, each containing specialized but interconnected cortical regions.

name: cerebral hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding into brain tissue, usually from a damaged blood vessel. It can injure nearby brain cells, cause swelling and pressure, and produce sudden weakness, speech trouble, headache, reduced alertness, or death.

name: cerebral infarction
clinical_significance: Permanent brain injury caused by blocked blood flow in a brain artery. The blockage may result from a clot formed in a narrowed artery or a clot traveling from the heart or another vessel.

name: cerebral ischemia
clinical_significance: Reduced blood flow and oxygen reaching brain tissue. It may cause temporary symptoms, such as a transient ischemic attack, or permanent injury if the interruption lasts long enough.

name: cerebral malaria
clinical_significance: A life-threatening form of malaria in which parasites cause brain dysfunction, often with confusion, seizures, abnormal behavior, or coma. It is usually caused by Plasmodium falciparum and requires urgent treatment.

name: cerebral palsy
clinical_significance: A group of lifelong disorders, abbreviated CP, caused by abnormal development or damage to the developing brain. It affects movement, muscle control, balance, coordination, and posture. The brain problem usually does not worsen, but a person’s symptoms and abilities may change with age. Some people also have seizures or problems with learning, speech, swallowing, vision, hearing, or joint movement. Common types include spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic, and mixed cerebral palsy.

name: cerebral peduncle
clinical_significance: One of two bundles of nerve fibers in the midbrain that carry movement signals from the cerebrum to the brainstem and spinal cord. Damage can cause weakness or loss of coordinated movement on the opposite side.

name: cerebral ventricle
clinical_significance: One of four connected spaces inside the brain that contain cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid cushions the brain and spinal cord, carries nutrients and waste, and flows through the ventricles before being absorbed around the brain.

name: cerebral ventriculography
clinical_significance: Imaging of the brain’s fluid-filled ventricles to assess their size, shape, connections, or blockage. Modern scans usually use computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging rather than older invasive methods.

name: cerebral ventriculomegaly
clinical_significance: Enlargement of one or more fluid-filled spaces inside the brain. It may result from blocked fluid drainage, loss of brain tissue, or developmental variation; its importance depends on the cause and severity.

name: cerebrosides
clinical_significance: Fat-containing substances found especially in the membranes and protective coverings of nerve cells. They help maintain nerve structure and are broken down abnormally in some inherited storage diseases.

name: cerebrospinal fluid
clinical_significance: A clear fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord and filling spaces inside the brain. It cushions the nervous system, helps carry nutrients and waste, and is continuously produced and reabsorbed by the body.

name: cerebrovascular
clinical_significance: Relating to the brain's blood vessels and blood flow. Cerebrovascular problems can reduce oxygen delivery and cause strokes, brief warning episodes, bleeding, or lasting problems with movement, speech, vision, or thinking.

name: cerebrovascular disorder
clinical_significance: A disorder of brain blood vessels or cerebral blood flow, including ischemia, hemorrhage, aneurysm, malformation, and venous thrombosis.

name: cerebrum
clinical_significance: The largest part of the brain, made of two connected halves. It supports conscious movement, sensation, language, memory, thinking, emotions, and vision; different areas specialize in different functions.

name: cerium
clinical_significance: A rare-earth metal used mainly in industry and research. Cerium has no routine diagnostic or treatment role in human medicine; exposure to some cerium compounds may irritate or injure tissues.

name: certification
clinical_significance: A formal process confirming that a person, service, laboratory, or facility meets specified training, quality, safety, or professional standards.

name: certolizumab pegol
clinical_significance: A biologic medicine that blocks tumor necrosis factor and treats selected inflammatory diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn disease. It can increase the risk of serious infections.

name: ceruloplasmin
clinical_significance: The main protein that carries copper in the blood. It is made mostly by the liver; unusually low or high levels can occur in Wilson disease, inflammation, liver disease, or other conditions.

name: cerumen
clinical_significance: Earwax, a waxy substance made in the ear canal. It traps dust and helps protect and moisturize the canal; too much can block hearing or cause discomfort.

name: ceruminous adenocarcinoma
clinical_significance: A malignant tumor of the ceruminous glands in the external ear canal that may cause pain, discharge, hearing loss, or a persistent ear-canal mass.

name: cervical
clinical_significance: Relating to the neck or to the cervix, the lower opening of the uterus. The meaning depends on context, such as cervical spine, cervical pain, or cervical cancer.

name: cervical arthritis
clinical_significance: Degenerative or inflammatory disease of the neck joints that can cause neck pain, stiffness, reduced motion, and sometimes nerve or spinal-cord compression.

name: cervical atlas
clinical_significance: The first bone of the neck, called C1. It is a ring-shaped vertebra that supports the skull and moves around the second neck vertebra when the head turns.

name: cervical cancer
clinical_significance: Cancer arising in the cervix, most often after persistent infection with a high-risk human papillomavirus type. Early disease may cause no symptoms; later signs include unusual bleeding, discharge, or pelvic pain.

name: cervical cerclage
clinical_significance: A procedure that places a strong stitch around the cervix during pregnancy to help keep it closed when early opening raises the risk of pregnancy loss or premature birth. It may be placed through the vagina or abdomen.

name: cervical change
clinical_significance: A change in the uterine cervix or cervical spine, depending on context; clinical significance is determined by the specific structural, inflammatory, or pregnancy-related finding.

name: cervical dislocation
clinical_significance: Abnormal displacement of one cervical vertebra relative to another, usually from trauma, that can destabilize the neck and injure the spinal cord.

name: cervical endometriosis
clinical_significance: Endometrial-like tissue in or on the cervix that may cause bleeding after sex, pelvic pain, or an abnormal cervical lesion.

name: cervical ganglion
clinical_significance: A cluster of nerve-cell bodies in the sympathetic chain of the neck that relays autonomic signals to the head, neck, and upper chest.

name: cervical insufficiency
clinical_significance: Painless shortening or opening of the cervix during pregnancy before term, increasing risk of second-trimester loss or spontaneous preterm birth.

name: cervical lymphadenopathy
clinical_significance: Enlarged lymph nodes in the neck, commonly caused by infection but sometimes reflecting malignancy, autoimmune disease, or other systemic illness.

name: cervical rib
clinical_significance: An extra rib growing from a neck vertebra, usually the lowest one. It often causes no symptoms but can narrow the space for nerves or blood vessels and produce arm pain, numbness, or swelling.

name: cervical spine
clinical_significance: The seven bones in the neck, numbered C1 through C7. They support the head, protect the upper spinal cord, allow neck movement, and contain openings for important blood vessels.

name: cervical vertebrae
clinical_significance: The seven bones of the neck, numbered C1 through C7. They support the head, protect the upper spinal cord, and allow neck movement; openings in several of them carry the vertebral arteries.

name: cervicitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the cervix, commonly caused by a sexually transmitted infection, changes in normal vaginal bacteria, chemical irritation, or allergy. It may cause discharge, bleeding after sex, or pelvic discomfort, but can be symptomless.

name: cervix
clinical_significance: The lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina. It lets menstrual blood leave the uterus, allows sperm to enter, produces cervical mucus, and widens during childbirth.

name: cervix carcinoma
clinical_significance: Cancer arising from the cervix, most often related to persistent high-risk human papillomavirus infection; screening and HPV vaccination reduce risk, and treatment depends on stage.

name: cervix disease
clinical_significance: Any disorder affecting the lower part of the uterus, including infection, polyps, precancer, cancer, scarring, or pregnancy-related changes. Symptoms and treatment depend on the specific condition.

name: cervix neoplasm
clinical_significance: A benign, precancerous, or malignant growth of the cervix; evaluation may include pelvic examination, HPV testing, cytology, colposcopy, and biopsy.

name: cesarean section
clinical_significance: A surgical delivery of a baby through incisions in the abdomen and uterus. It may be planned or performed urgently when vaginal birth poses greater risk; complications can include infection, bleeding, blood clots, injury to nearby organs, and risks in future pregnancies.

name: cesium
clinical_significance: A chemical element whose radioactive isotope cesium-137 can cause serious external or internal radiation injury after contamination or exposure.

name: cestoda
clinical_significance: The tapeworm class of flatworms; human infection follows ingestion of eggs or larval tissue and can cause intestinal disease or tissue cysts.

name: cetirizine
clinical_significance: A second-generation H1 antihistamine used for allergic rhinitis and urticaria; it is less sedating than older antihistamines but can still cause drowsiness.

name: cetoleic acid
clinical_significance: A long-chain monounsaturated fatty acid found in some fish oils and other natural fats. It is mainly of nutritional and biochemical interest and is not a routine clinical marker or treatment.

name: cetrorelix
clinical_significance: A hormone-blocking medicine used during assisted reproduction to prevent premature ovulation. It temporarily blocks gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptors; injection-site reactions, headache, nausea, or allergy may occur.

name: cetuximab
clinical_significance: A monoclonal antibody that blocks the epidermal growth factor receptor. It is used for selected colorectal, head-and-neck, and other cancers and commonly causes acne-like rash.

name: cevimeline
clinical_significance: A muscarinic receptor agonist used to stimulate salivary secretion and relieve dry mouth, especially in selected patients with Sjögren syndrome.

name: cevimeline hydrochloride
clinical_significance: A medicine that stimulates muscarinic receptors to increase saliva. It is used mainly for dry mouth in Sjögren syndrome and can cause sweating, nausea, or blurred vision.

name: chaetomium
clinical_significance: A genus of fungi commonly found in soil, plants, and damp indoor materials. Human infections are rare but can include skin, sinus, lung, or brain disease, especially in people with weakened immunity.

name: Chagas cardiomyopathy
clinical_significance: A chronic heart complication of Trypanosoma cruzi infection that can develop years after Chagas disease. It may cause conduction abnormalities, dangerous arrhythmias, heart enlargement, heart failure, apical aneurysm, or blood clots and requires cardiac follow-up.

name: Chagas disease
clinical_significance: An infection caused by the parasite \textit{Trypanosoma cruzi}, usually spread by infected kissing bugs. It can also pass from mother to baby or through contaminated blood, organs, or food. Early illness may be mild or absent; years later, some people develop heart disease or enlargement of the oesophagus or colon.

name: chalazion
clinical_significance: A usually painless, firm eyelid lump caused by blockage and inflammation of a meibomian oil gland; persistent or atypical lesions require ophthalmic assessment.

name: challenge agent
clinical_significance: A substance, organism, allergen, or physiologic stimulus deliberately administered in a controlled test to provoke and measure a response.

name: chamomile extract
clinical_significance: An extract of chamomile flowers used in traditional and complementary products; allergic reactions and medicine interactions are possible, while evidence varies by indication.

name: chaplain
clinical_significance: A trained spiritual-care professional who supports patients and families with religious, existential, emotional, or ethical concerns in healthcare settings.

name: charcoal
clinical_significance: A black carbon-rich material made by heating organic matter with little oxygen. In medicine, specially prepared charcoal may be given in selected poisonings to reduce absorption of some substances, but it is not useful for every poisoning.

name: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
clinical_significance: A group of inherited peripheral-nerve disorders that damage nerves supplying the feet, legs, hands, and arms. Symptoms usually include gradually worsening weakness, muscle wasting, numbness, foot deformity, and difficulty walking. It is genetically heterogeneous and may follow autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked inheritance.

name: CHARGE syndrome
clinical_significance: A genetic condition, usually involving a new change in the CHD7 gene, that can affect the eyes, ears, heart, breathing passages, growth, development, and reproductive system. Features vary widely.

name: Chediak-Higashi syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited immune disorder caused by changes in both copies of the LYST gene. It can cause unusually light or silvery hair, repeated infections, easy bruising, nerve problems, and a severe inflammatory crisis.

name: cheek
clinical_significance: The facial region forming the side wall of the mouth, containing skin, muscle, fat, salivary structures, nerves, and blood vessels.

name: cheek pouch
clinical_significance: A pouch in the cheek of some animals, especially hamsters and monkeys, used to carry food. It has no human anatomical counterpart but is used in research to study oral tissues and tumours.

name: cheilitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of one or both lips causing dryness, scaling, cracks, swelling, pain, or sores. Causes include irritation, allergy, infection, nutritional deficiency, sun exposure, and skin disease; persistent or unusual changes need assessment.

name: cheilodynia
clinical_significance: Pain of the lips, which may result from inflammation, infection, trauma, allergy, dryness, nerve pain, or another oral or dermatologic disorder.

name: cheilognathopalatoschisis
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the upper lip, the gum-bearing part of the jaw, and the roof of the mouth do not join completely before birth. It can interfere with feeding, speech, hearing, and tooth development.

name: cheilognathoschisis
clinical_significance: A congenital cleft of the lip and alveolar part of the upper jaw, with or without associated palatal involvement.

name: cheiromegaly
clinical_significance: Abnormal enlargement of one or both hands, classically associated with excess growth hormone but also possible with local overgrowth or other disorders.

name: chelating agent
clinical_significance: A compound that binds a metal ion through multiple chemical sites, allowing the metal to be measured, mobilized, or removed in selected toxic exposures.

name: chelation therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment using a medicine that binds a specific harmful or excess metal so the body can remove it in urine or stool. It is used only for selected poisonings or disorders because it can harm the kidneys or alter essential minerals.

name: chemexfoliation
clinical_significance: Application of a chemical solution to remove controlled layers of skin, improving selected scars, pigmentation, wrinkles, or superficial lesions.

name: chemical
clinical_significance: A substance defined by its molecular composition and properties; medical effects depend on dose, route, exposure duration, metabolism, and biological target.

name: chemical ablation
clinical_significance: Destruction of unwanted tissue by injecting or applying a chemical irritant or sclerosant, used in selected lesions, vessels, cysts, or other conditions.

name: chemical burn
clinical_significance: Damage to skin, eyes, or internal tissues caused by a corrosive chemical. Injury may worsen while the chemical remains present; contaminated clothing should be removed and the area flushed promptly with plenty of water.

name: chemical carcinogenesis
clinical_significance: Development of cancer after exposure to chemicals that cause DNA damage, abnormal cell signaling, chronic tissue injury, or altered gene regulation.

name: chemical cleavage
clinical_significance: Breaking a chemical bond with a reagent, used in laboratory analysis, molecular biology, synthesis, or controlled degradation of a larger molecule.

name: chemical cofactor
clinical_significance: A nonprotein chemical helper required for an enzyme or biologic reaction, such as a metal ion, vitamin-derived coenzyme, or other small molecule.

name: chemical fractionation
clinical_significance: Separation of a mixture into fractions according to chemical or physical properties such as solubility, charge, size, or binding affinity.

name: chemical impurity
clinical_significance: An unintended chemical present in a medicine, specimen, or material, potentially affecting safety, stability, measurement accuracy, or biologic activity.

name: chemistry
clinical_significance: The study of substances, their composition, properties, reactions, and transformations, forming the basis of biochemistry, pharmacology, toxicology, and laboratory medicine.

name: chemoembolization
clinical_significance: A treatment that delivers cancer medicine through an artery feeding a tumour and then blocks that artery. It is used mainly for selected liver cancers to concentrate treatment and reduce the tumour's blood supply.

name: chemokine
clinical_significance: A small signaling protein that directs immune cells to sites of infection, inflammation, or tissue repair. Different chemokines attract different cell types by binding to matching receptors.

name: chemokine receptor
clinical_significance: A cell-surface receptor that binds chemokines and directs immune-cell movement; some also serve as entry cofactors for viruses such as HIV.

name: chemoprevention
clinical_significance: The use of a medicine or other chemical substance to lower the chance of cancer developing or returning. It may be considered for selected high-risk people, but benefits, side effects, and evidence differ by cancer and medicine.

name: chemoradiotherapy
clinical_significance: Cancer treatment that combines chemotherapy with radiation treatment. The medicines may make cancer cells more sensitive to radiation or treat cells elsewhere, but combined treatment can increase tiredness, nausea, skin changes, and other side effects.

name: chemoreceptor cell
clinical_significance: A sensory cell that detects chemical changes such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, pH, taste molecules, or odorants and converts them into neural or physiologic signals.

name: chemosensitivity
clinical_significance: How strongly cells or a tumor respond to a chemical treatment. A sensitive tumor may shrink or stop growing, but laboratory sensitivity tests do not always predict a person's treatment response.

name: chemosensitivity assay
clinical_significance: A laboratory test that exposes cells or microorganisms to a medicine or chemical and measures the response. It can support research or treatment selection, but results do not always predict how a person will respond.

name: chemosensitization
clinical_significance: Making cancer cells or microorganisms more vulnerable to treatment by adding an agent that improves delivery, blocks resistance, or increases treatment-related damage.

name: chemosis
clinical_significance: Swelling of the clear membrane covering the white part of the eye. It may result from allergy, infection, irritation, injury, surgery, or fluid retention and can make the eye look blistered.

name: chemotactic factors
clinical_significance: Chemical signals that attract or repel cells by forming a concentration gradient. During infection or tissue injury, they help direct immune cells to the affected area.

name: chemotaxis
clinical_significance: Directed movement of a cell or organism toward or away from a chemical signal. It helps guide immune cells to infection or injury and is studied in inflammation, development, and cancer spread.

name: chemotherapy
clinical_significance: Treatment using medicines to kill cancer cells or slow their growth, often by disrupting cell division or damaging DNA. It may be used alone or with surgery or radiation. Healthy fast-growing cells can also be affected, causing nausea, hair loss, anemia, or reduced immunity.

name: chemotherapy regimen
clinical_significance: A specific combination of anticancer drugs, dosing schedule, and treatment cycles designed for a particular cancer type and stage. Regimens are standardized by evidence-based protocols and may be modified based on response, toxicity, and patient factors.

name: cherubism
clinical_significance: A rare inherited condition in which both sides of the jaw enlarge because of overgrowth of bone-removing tissue. It usually begins in childhood and often improves after puberty, but it can affect teeth, chewing, speech, or appearance.

name: chest pain
clinical_significance: Pain, pressure, burning, or discomfort in the chest. Causes include heart, lung, digestive, muscle, bone, or anxiety-related problems. New severe pain, breathlessness, sweating, faintness, or spreading pain requires emergency care.

name: chest tightness
clinical_significance: A sensation of pressure, constriction, or heaviness in the chest that may arise from heart, lung, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, or anxiety-related causes.

name: chest tube
clinical_significance: A flexible tube inserted into the pleural space to remove air, blood, or fluid and help the lung re-expand.

name: chest wall
clinical_significance: The layers of skin, muscle, ribs, breastbone, spine, and supporting tissues that surround the chest. They protect the heart and lungs and move with the breathing muscles to help expand and contract the chest.

name: cheyne-stokes respiration
clinical_significance: A repeating pattern in which breathing gradually becomes deeper and faster, then shallower, followed by a pause. It may occur during sleep with heart failure, stroke, brain disease, or at high altitude.

name: chick embryo
clinical_significance: A developing chicken embryo used in biological research, including studies of development, infectious agents, and vaccine production. It is a research model, not a human clinical finding.

name: chickenpox
clinical_significance: An acute, highly contagious primary infection with varicella-zoster virus. An itchy generalized rash appears in successive crops as spots, blisters, and crusts, often with fever and malaise; adults, pregnant people, newborns, and immunocompromised people have higher risk of pneumonia or other severe complications.

name: chikungunya fever
clinical_significance: An acute arboviral febrile illness caused by the Chikungunya virus (genus \textit{Alphavirus}) transmitted by \textit{Aedes} mosquitoes, characterized by high fever, maculopapular rash, and severe, often incapacitating bilateral polyarthralgia and polyarthritis that may persist chronically.

name: chikungunya virus
clinical_significance: An alphavirus transmitted primarily by infected female Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Infection can cause abrupt fever, severe polyarthralgia, joint swelling, rash, and prolonged inflammatory joint symptoms.

name: chilblain
clinical_significance: An inflammatory skin lesion caused by an abnormal response to cold and damp conditions.

name: child abuse
clinical_significance: Physical, sexual, or emotional harm, or serious neglect, inflicted on a child by a caregiver or another person. Warning signs may include unexplained injuries, changing accounts, fear, developmental changes, or unmet basic needs; suspected abuse requires safeguarding action under local law.

name: child behavior
clinical_significance: The observable actions, responses, and conduct of children, influenced by developmental stage, temperament, environment, and neurobiological factors. Behavioral assessment helps identify developmental disorders, emotional difficulties, and parenting needs.

name: child care
clinical_significance: Care and supervision provided to children outside or in addition to parental care. In health settings, quality and safety can affect injury risk, infection exposure, nutrition, development, and access to routine care.

name: child development
clinical_significance: Progressive physical, cognitive, language, emotional, and social changes from infancy through adolescence, assessed against developmental milestones and individual variation.

name: child psychiatry
clinical_significance: The medical specialty concerned with assessment and treatment of emotional, behavioral, developmental, and psychiatric disorders in children and adolescents.

name: child psychology
clinical_significance: The study of children’s cognitive, emotional, social, and behavioral development and the effects of relationships, learning, biology, and environment.

name: child welfare
clinical_significance: Services and legal processes intended to protect children from abuse, neglect, exploitation, or unsafe living conditions and to support their health and development. Suspected immediate danger requires prompt safeguarding action.

name: childhood angiosarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare malignant tumor arising from blood-vessel or lymphatic-endothelial cells in a child; diagnosis and treatment require specialist pediatric oncology care.

name: childhood ependymoma
clinical_significance: A tumor arising from ependymal cells lining the brain ventricles or spinal canal in children; symptoms depend on location and obstruction of cerebrospinal-fluid flow.

name: childhood fibrosarcoma
clinical_significance: A malignant tumor of fibroblastic connective tissue in children, usually presenting as a growing mass; treatment depends on location, extent, and tumor biology.

name: childhood ganglioglioma
clinical_significance: A usually slow-growing mixed neuronal and glial brain tumor in children or young adults, often presenting with long-standing focal seizures.

name: childhood leiomyosarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare malignant tumor of smooth muscle in a child; it may arise in soft tissue or an organ and requires biopsy, staging, and specialist treatment.

name: childhood leukemia
clinical_significance: Cancer of blood-forming cells in a child, most often acute lymphoblastic or acute myeloid leukemia; symptoms may include pallor, bruising, fever, bone pain, or recurrent infection.

name: childhood liposarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare malignant tumor derived from fat-forming tissue in a child; diagnosis requires imaging and biopsy, and treatment is individualized by a sarcoma team.

name: childhood osteosarcoma
clinical_significance: A malignant bone tumor that commonly develops near the ends of long bones during adolescence; pain, swelling, or a fracture may occur and treatment combines chemotherapy and surgery.

name: childhood rhabdomyosarcoma
clinical_significance: A malignant tumor showing skeletal-muscle differentiation, occurring mainly in children and adolescents; it may arise in the head and neck, urinary or reproductive tract, or limbs.

name: children
clinical_significance: Humans in the developmental period between infancy and adolescence; medical assessment must account for age-specific anatomy, physiology, growth, communication, and consent.

name: chills
clinical_significance: A sensation of cold with involuntary shivering, commonly accompanying fever or infection; chills without measured fever may also occur with anxiety, hypoglycaemia, or environmental cold.

name: chilomastix mesnili
clinical_significance: A usually harmless single-celled organism that may be found in stool. Its presence generally does not cause illness or require treatment, but it can indicate exposure to contaminated food or water.

name: chimera
clinical_significance: An organism or tissue containing genetically distinct cell populations derived from different zygotes or embryos, or a laboratory construct combining genetic material from different sources.

name: chin
clinical_significance: The lower facial prominence formed mainly by the mandible and overlying soft tissue, contributing to facial contour, speech, chewing, and airway anatomy.

name: chironomidae
clinical_significance: A family of non-biting midges whose larvae live in water. Their larvae are used as fish food and environmental indicators; airborne adult or larval material can trigger allergy or asthma in some exposed people.

name: chiropractic
clinical_significance: A healthcare practice that mainly uses hands-on treatment for muscle, joint, and spine problems, especially spinal manipulation. Benefits and risks vary by the condition, technique, and practitioner's training.

name: chitin
clinical_significance: A strong natural substance forming the cell walls of fungi and the outer coverings of insects, spiders, and shellfish. Humans do not digest it, but exposure to chitin-containing material can contribute to allergic or airway irritation in some people.

name: chitosan
clinical_significance: A chitin-derived material used in some wound dressings, surgical materials, and experimental drug-delivery systems. It can absorb fluid and support clotting or tissue repair, but clinical effects depend on the product and application.

name: chlamydia trachomatis
clinical_significance: A bacterium that commonly causes sexually transmitted infection of the urogenital tract and can also cause conjunctivitis or pneumonia.

name: chlamydiaceae
clinical_significance: A family of bacteria that includes Chlamydia species. Some cause sexually transmitted infections, eye disease, or respiratory infection; diagnosis depends on the species, specimen, symptoms, and laboratory testing.

name: chlamydial disease
clinical_significance: Infection caused by Chlamydia bacteria, including sexually transmitted urogenital infection and infections of the eyes or respiratory tract. It may cause no symptoms, but untreated genital infection can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, or pregnancy complications.

name: chlamydomona
clinical_significance: A genus of single-celled green algae found in freshwater and soil. It is not a typical human pathogen and is used mainly in biological and environmental research.

name: chlamydophila
clinical_significance: An older name for the genus now classified within Chlamydia. The former Chlamydophila group includes species that cause respiratory infection and psittacosis; current laboratory reports generally use Chlamydia names.

name: chlamydophila pneumoniae
clinical_significance: An older name for Chlamydia pneumoniae, a bacterium that spreads through respiratory secretions and can cause bronchitis or pneumonia. Infection may be mild or asymptomatic, but can be more serious in older adults or people with underlying illness.

name: chlamydophila psittaci
clinical_significance: An older name for Chlamydia psittaci, a bacterium carried by birds that can infect people after inhaling contaminated dust or secretions. Psittacosis commonly causes fever, headache, muscle aches, and cough, sometimes with pneumonia.

name: chloasma
clinical_significance: Patchy brown or gray-brown darkening of the skin, usually on the face. It is often related to pregnancy, hormones, and sunlight and is commonly called melasma.

name: chloral hydrate
clinical_significance: A sedative-hypnotic compound with limited modern use because of toxicity, dependence, respiratory depression, and cardiac or gastrointestinal adverse effects.

name: chlorambucil
clinical_significance: An oral chemotherapy medicine that damages DNA and is used mainly for some chronic leukemias and lymphomas. It can lower blood counts and increase infection risk.

name: chloramphenicol
clinical_significance: An antibiotic that stops bacteria from making essential proteins. It is reserved for selected serious infections when safer or more suitable medicines are unavailable because it can rarely cause dangerous bone-marrow suppression and other severe effects.

name: chlordane
clinical_significance: A persistent organochlorine insecticide formerly used for termite control; exposure can affect the nervous system and liver and has environmental persistence.

name: chlordecone
clinical_significance: A persistent organochlorine pesticide that can cause neurologic, reproductive, and liver effects after significant exposure and remains in the environment for long periods.

name: chlordiazepoxide
clinical_significance: A benzodiazepine medicine that slows brain activity and may be used short term for alcohol-withdrawal symptoms or severe anxiety. It can cause drowsiness, dependence, impaired coordination, and dangerous breathing suppression with alcohol or opioids.

name: chlorethoxyfos
clinical_significance: An organophosphate insecticide that can block a nerve enzyme, causing sweating, vomiting, weakness, breathing problems, seizures, or other poisoning symptoms after exposure.

name: chlorfenvinphos
clinical_significance: An organophosphate insecticide that can cause cholinergic toxicity by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase; use is restricted or prohibited in many places.

name: chlorhexidine
clinical_significance: A broad-spectrum antiseptic used for skin, mucosal, and oral preparation; it can cause irritation, allergy, or rare severe anaphylaxis.

name: chloride channel
clinical_significance: A protein forming a passage for chloride ions across a cell membrane. Chloride channels help control electrical signals, fluid movement, and muscle or nerve function.

name: chloride ion
clinical_significance: The negatively charged form of chlorine and a major extracellular electrolyte that helps maintain fluid balance, osmotic pressure, acid--base status, and electrical neutrality.

name: chlorine
clinical_significance: A reactive halogen element and disinfectant; inhalation of chlorine gas can injure the eyes and airways and cause chemical pneumonitis or pulmonary edema.

name: chlormadinone acetate
clinical_significance: A synthetic progestogen used in some hormonal medicines; effects and risks include changes in bleeding, mood, metabolism, and thrombotic risk depending on the formulation.

name: chlormerodrin
clinical_significance: A mercury-containing medicine formerly used as a diuretic and in radioactive form for kidney or brain imaging. It is obsolete; mercury toxicity and safer alternatives eliminated its routine clinical role.

name: chlorodeoxyadenosine
clinical_significance: Another name for cladribine, a purine-analog medicine used for selected blood cancers and multiple sclerosis; prolonged lymphocyte suppression and infection risk are important considerations.

name: chloroform
clinical_significance: A volatile solvent and environmental contaminant that can irritate the lungs and nervous system and damage the liver or kidneys after significant exposure.

name: chlorogenic acid
clinical_significance: A natural plant compound found in coffee, fruits, and vegetables. It has antioxidant effects in laboratory studies, but evidence is insufficient to use supplements to prevent or treat disease.

name: chlorophyll
clinical_significance: The green pigment that enables plants and algae to capture light for photosynthesis. It is important in nutrition and biology, but chlorophyll products are not established treatments for disease.

name: Chlorophyta
clinical_significance: A broad group of green algae found in freshwater, marine, and terrestrial environments. They are studied in biology and biotechnology and are not usual human pathogens.

name: chloropicrin
clinical_significance: A pungent soil fumigant and irritant that can injure the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract after exposure.

name: chloroplast
clinical_significance: The compartment in plant and algal cells where photosynthesis occurs. It contains chlorophyll and other machinery that converts light energy into chemical energy; it has no direct human clinical role.

name: chloroplast DNA
clinical_significance: Genetic material inside chloroplasts, the photosynthetic compartments of plants and algae. It is used in plant biology, evolution, and biotechnology research and has no routine role in human diagnosis.

name: chloroprene
clinical_significance: An industrial chemical used to make chloroprene rubber; repeated or high exposure can irritate tissues and has carcinogenic concern.

name: chloroquine
clinical_significance: An antimalarial medicine used for susceptible Plasmodium species and selected autoimmune conditions; retinal toxicity, cardiotoxicity, and drug interactions require attention.

name: chlorothiazide
clinical_significance: A thiazide diuretic used to treat high blood pressure and fluid retention. It increases urine production and may cause low sodium, low potassium, dehydration, or high blood sugar.

name: chlorotoxin
clinical_significance: A small peptide found in scorpion venom that is being studied as a target for brain-tumour imaging and experimental treatment. It is not an established therapy.

name: chlorotrianisene
clinical_significance: An older synthetic estrogen that was used in some countries for menopausal symptoms and other hormone-related conditions. It is rarely used today; estrogen-related risks include blood clots and effects on hormone-sensitive tissues.

name: chlorpheniramine
clinical_significance: A first-generation antihistamine used for allergy symptoms; drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, and other anticholinergic effects may occur.

name: chlorphentermine
clinical_significance: An older stimulant appetite suppressant related to amphetamines; it is not routinely used because of cardiovascular, psychiatric, and dependence risks.

name: chlorpromazine
clinical_significance: A first-generation antipsychotic and phenothiazine used for schizophrenia, severe nausea, and selected other conditions; adverse effects include sedation, hypotension, movement disorders, and QT prolongation.

name: chlorpropamide
clinical_significance: A first-generation sulfonylurea that lowers blood glucose by stimulating pancreatic insulin release; prolonged hypoglycemia and hyponatremia are important risks.

name: chlorpyrifos
clinical_significance: An organophosphate insecticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase; significant exposure can cause cholinergic toxicity with secretions, bronchospasm, bradycardia, weakness, or seizures.

name: chlorthalidone
clinical_significance: A long-acting thiazide-like diuretic used for hypertension and edema; it can cause hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hyperuricemia, and kidney-related electrolyte changes.

name: chlorzoxazone
clinical_significance: A centrally acting muscle relaxant used for painful muscle spasm in some countries; drowsiness and rare serious liver injury are important risks.

name: CHO cell
clinical_significance: A Chinese hamster ovary cell line widely used to produce recombinant proteins, antibodies, vaccines, and other biologic medicines.

name: choanal atresia
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which tissue blocks one or both passages from the nose to the throat. Both sides can cause severe breathing difficulty in a newborn, especially during feeding, and require urgent treatment.

name: choice behavior
clinical_significance: The process of selecting among alternatives, studied in psychology and neuroscience to understand decision-making, impulsivity, and reward processing. Abnormal choice behavior may be relevant to addiction, eating disorders, and psychiatric conditions.

name: choke
clinical_significance: Airway blockage by food or another object that prevents normal airflow and can rapidly cause inability to speak, cyanosis, loss of consciousness, or death.

name: cholangiocarcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer arising in the bile ducts inside or outside the liver. It may cause jaundice, itching, dark urine, pale stools, abdominal discomfort, or weight loss, but early disease can be silent; treatment depends on its site and stage.

name: cholangiography
clinical_significance: Imaging of the bile ducts after contrast material makes them visible. It can show gallstones, narrowing, leaks, or blockage and may be performed during surgery, through the skin, or during endoscopy.

name: cholangitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of the tubes that carry bile from the liver and gallbladder to the intestine. A blockage from a gallstone or narrowing can cause fever, pain, jaundice, and rapidly worsening bloodstream infection.

name: cholate
clinical_significance: The ionized form of cholic acid, a primary bile acid that helps emulsify dietary fat and is conjugated and secreted by the liver.

name: cholecalciferol
clinical_significance: Vitamin D3, produced in skin by ultraviolet light and obtained from food or supplements, then converted to active metabolites that regulate calcium and phosphate.

name: cholecystectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove the gallbladder, a small organ under the liver that stores bile. It may be needed for painful gallstones, gallbladder inflammation, gallstone-related pancreatitis, or selected polyps. It is often done through small cuts using a camera, but open surgery may be needed when this is not safe. Bile still flows from the liver into the intestine after surgery.

name: cholecystitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the gallbladder, most often caused by a gallstone blocking the cystic duct. It commonly causes persistent right-upper abdominal pain, tenderness, nausea, vomiting, or fever; diagnosis uses examination, blood tests, and imaging, and treatment may include hospital care and gallbladder removal.

name: cholecystokinin
clinical_significance: A hormone released by the small intestine after food, especially fat and protein, enters it. It makes the gallbladder release bile, stimulates digestive enzymes, and helps create a feeling of fullness.

name: cholecystolithiasis
clinical_significance: Stones in the gallbladder, sometimes used specifically for stones in the gallbladder lumen. They may cause no symptoms or block bile flow, leading to biliary pain, gallbladder inflammation, jaundice, or pancreatitis.

name: choledochal cyst
clinical_significance: An abnormal widening of one or more bile ducts, usually present from birth. It may cause abdominal pain, jaundice, pancreatitis, or infection and can increase later cancer risk, so specialist evaluation is needed.

name: cholelithiasis
clinical_significance: The presence of stones in the gallbladder or biliary tract. Stones may contain cholesterol, pigment, or mixed material and may cause no symptoms or lead to biliary pain and complications.

name: cholera
clinical_significance: An acute intestinal infection caused by toxigenic \textit{Vibrio cholerae}, usually acquired through contaminated water or food. It can produce sudden profuse watery diarrhoea, vomiting, severe dehydration, shock, and death within hours if untreated; prompt oral or intravenous rehydration is central treatment. Safe water, sanitation, food hygiene, and vaccination in selected settings help prevent spread.

name: cholera toxin
clinical_significance: A toxin released by some strains of Vibrio cholerae that makes intestinal cells secrete large amounts of water and salts. It causes the profuse watery diarrhoea of cholera and can lead rapidly to severe dehydration and shock.

name: cholera vaccine
clinical_significance: An oral vaccine that reduces the risk of cholera in selected people, such as travellers to areas with active transmission or populations affected by outbreaks. It does not replace safe water, sanitation, food hygiene, or prompt rehydration if illness occurs.

name: choleretic
clinical_significance: A substance that encourages the liver to make or release bile. Bile helps digest fats and remove some waste products; a choleretic should be used carefully when gallstones or blocked bile ducts may be present.

name: cholestane
clinical_significance: A steroid-like chemical framework found in cholesterol and related molecules. It is used mainly in biochemistry and chemical classification and has no independent clinical significance as a patient finding.

name: cholestasis
clinical_significance: Reduced production or flow of bile. It may cause itching, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, and abnormal liver tests; a blockage and liver-cell causes must be distinguished.

name: cholesteatoma
clinical_significance: A keratin-filled sac of abnormal squamous epithelium in the middle ear or mastoid that can erode bone and cause chronic discharge, hearing loss, or intracranial complications.

name: cholesterol
clinical_significance: A lipid required for cell membranes and synthesis of steroid hormones and bile acids. Excess atherogenic cholesterol can contribute to arterial plaque.

name: cholesterol cleft
clinical_significance: Empty, needle-shaped spaces seen in tissue after cholesterol crystals dissolve during specimen processing. They may be found in atherosclerotic plaques, xanthomas, or other cholesterol deposits and are interpreted with the surrounding tissue.

name: cholesterol ester
clinical_significance: A form in which cholesterol is linked to a fatty acid for storage or transport. The balance of free and esterified cholesterol is measured in lipid research and can be relevant to disorders of lipid metabolism.

name: cholesterol homeostasis
clinical_significance: The processes that keep cholesterol levels and distribution within cells and tissues balanced. Disruption can contribute to atherosclerosis, fatty liver, or inherited lipid-storage disorders.

name: cholestyramine
clinical_significance: Cholestyramine is a bile-acid sequestrant used to lower LDL cholesterol and sometimes to treat bile-acid diarrhea or itching from cholestasis.

name: choline
clinical_significance: Choline is an essential nutrient used to make cell membranes and acetylcholine and to support liver and nervous-system function.

name: choline deficiency
clinical_significance: A rare deficiency that may occur with inadequate intake or certain medical conditions and can contribute to fatty liver or muscle injury. Most people obtain sufficient choline from food, and routine supplementation is not needed for everyone.

name: cholinergic agent
clinical_significance: A substance that activates or otherwise influences acetylcholine receptors or cholinergic nerve signaling. Medicines in this broad group affect functions such as heart rate, secretions, bowel movement, bladder emptying, and pupil size.

name: cholinergic agonist
clinical_significance: A substance that activates acetylcholine receptors and mimics part of the parasympathetic nervous system. Depending on the drug and receptor, it may increase secretions or bowel and bladder activity and can cause slow heart rate or other cholinergic effects.

name: cholinergic neuron
clinical_significance: A nerve cell that releases acetylcholine as its principal neurotransmitter.

name: cholinergic receptor
clinical_significance: A receptor that responds to acetylcholine, either as a muscarinic or nicotinic receptor. These receptors help control muscle contraction, nerve transmission, heart rate, secretions, memory, and other functions and are targets for many medicines.

name: cholinesterase inhibitor
clinical_significance: A medicine that slows the breakdown of acetylcholine by cholinesterase enzymes, increasing cholinergic signaling. It is used for selected conditions such as myasthenia gravis, dementia, or glaucoma; excess effect can cause sweating, diarrhoea, slow heart rate, or muscle weakness.

name: chondroblastoma
clinical_significance: A chondroblastoma is an uncommon usually benign cartilage-forming bone tumor, often arising near the end of a long bone in adolescents or young adults.

name: chondrocranium
clinical_significance: The cartilage framework that forms much of the developing skull before it is replaced by bone. Abnormal development can contribute to congenital skull-base or facial differences.

name: chondrocyte
clinical_significance: A mature cell that makes and maintains cartilage, the firm flexible tissue found in joints, airways, and other places. Chondrocytes help keep cartilage smooth and strong, but cartilage usually heals slowly because it has little direct blood supply.

name: chondrodysplasia punctata
clinical_significance: A group of uncommon skeletal disorders marked by punctate calcifications in developing cartilage, often with shortened fingers or toes and other bone or eye findings. Causes and severity vary by subtype.

name: chondrodystrophy
clinical_significance: An older broad term for disorders involving abnormal cartilage or bone growth. The specific diagnosis is needed because the conditions grouped under this label differ in cause, complications, and treatment.

name: chondrogenesis
clinical_significance: The formation of cartilage from precursor cells during development or tissue repair. Abnormal chondrogenesis can contribute to skeletal growth disorders, while cartilage repair after injury is often limited.

name: chondrogenic neoplasm
clinical_significance: A cartilage-forming tumour, which may be benign, intermediate, or malignant. Imaging and tissue diagnosis help distinguish lesions such as enchondroma from chondrosarcoma and guide treatment.

name: chondroitin
clinical_significance: A natural component of cartilage and other connective tissue, also sold in supplements for osteoarthritis. Evidence for symptom benefit varies, and it does not rebuild cartilage or replace established care.

name: chondroitin sulfate
clinical_significance: A sulfated glycosaminoglycan found in cartilage and other connective tissues; it is also marketed in supplements for osteoarthritis, with variable evidence of benefit.

name: chondroma
clinical_significance: A usually harmless tumour made of mature cartilage. It most often forms inside a bone, especially in the hands and feet, or on the bone surface. Many cause no symptoms, but pain, growth, or fracture needs assessment.

name: chondromalacia
clinical_significance: Softening or breakdown of cartilage, especially the cartilage under the kneecap. It may cause pain at the front of the knee, grinding, or discomfort with stairs, squatting, or prolonged sitting.

name: chondromatosis
clinical_significance: A condition involving multiple cartilage nodules, often arising in the lining of a joint and sometimes detaching as loose bodies. It can cause pain, swelling, locking, and reduced movement; persistent or recurrent disease may require surgery.

name: chondrosarcoma
clinical_significance: A cancer that forms cartilage, usually within a bone. It is more common in adults and often grows slowly, though some types can grow faster or spread. Rarely, it begins in soft tissue rather than bone.

name: CHOP regimen
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy combination of cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone used for selected non-Hodgkin lymphomas. It can cause low blood counts, infection, nausea, nerve symptoms, and heart toxicity; cancer specialists monitor treatment closely.

name: chordoma
clinical_significance: A rare cancer arising from leftover cells of early spinal development. It usually begins near the tailbone, base of the skull, or spine and can cause pain, weakness, or nerve problems as it grows.

name: chorea
clinical_significance: Uncontrolled, brief, irregular movements that flow unpredictably from one body part to another. It may result from inherited disease, autoimmune illness, medicines, infection, or damage to movement-control areas of the brain.

name: choreoathetosis
clinical_significance: A movement disorder combining brief, unpredictable jerks with slower twisting movements. It can result from injury or disease affecting movement-control areas deep in the brain, inherited conditions, or certain medicines.

name: chorioallantoic membrane
clinical_significance: A membrane in a developing bird embryo used in research on blood-vessel growth, infection, and tumour biology. It is a laboratory model, not a human anatomical structure.

name: chorioamnionitis
clinical_significance: Infection or inflammation of the membranes, amniotic fluid, placenta, or nearby tissues during pregnancy or labour, often associated with fever and maternal or fetal infection. It can increase risks of preterm birth, newborn infection, and serious maternal illness and needs prompt obstetric assessment.

name: chorioangioma
clinical_significance: A usually benign blood-vessel tumour of the placenta. Small lesions often cause no problems, but a large tumour can affect fetal circulation and lead to fetal anaemia, excess amniotic fluid, growth problems, or heart strain, so monitoring may be needed.

name: choriocarcinoma
clinical_significance: A fast-growing cancer arising from cells that normally help form the placenta. It usually develops after a pregnancy or molar pregnancy and produces high levels of the pregnancy hormone hCG; it can spread but often responds well to chemotherapy.

name: chorion
clinical_significance: The outer membrane surrounding an early embryo. Its finger-like projections help form the fetal part of the placenta, where oxygen, nutrients, and waste are exchanged between fetal and maternal blood supplies.

name: chorionic gonadotropin
clinical_significance: A hormone produced mainly by the placenta during pregnancy. Urine and blood tests detect it to assess pregnancy; abnormal levels can also occur in some placental disorders and hormone-producing tumours.

name: chorionic villi
clinical_significance: Tiny finger-like placental structures containing fetal blood vessels that exchange oxygen, nutrients, and waste with maternal blood. Sampling them during chorionic-villus testing can diagnose some fetal genetic or chromosomal conditions.

name: chorioretinitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the choroid and retina, often caused by infection such as toxoplasmosis or by immune disease. It can cause floaters, blurred vision, light sensitivity, or vision loss and requires prompt eye-specialist assessment.

name: choroid
clinical_significance: The blood-vessel-rich layer between the retina and the white outer coat of the eye. It supplies oxygen and nutrients to the outer retina and helps absorb stray light inside the eye.

name: choroid disease
clinical_significance: A disorder affecting the choroid, the blood-vessel layer between the retina and the outer eye wall. It may impair retinal function or vision; the cause and treatment depend on the specific condition.

name: choroid hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from blood vessels in the choroid layer of the eye. It can occur after eye surgery, trauma, or with severe vascular disease and may threaten vision, requiring urgent ophthalmic assessment.

name: choroid neoplasm
clinical_significance: A benign or malignant growth arising in the choroid, the blood-vessel layer of the eye. It may distort or damage the retina and cause blurred vision, visual-field loss, or retinal detachment; imaging and ophthalmic assessment guide care.

name: choroid plexus
clinical_significance: A network of tissue inside the brain’s ventricles that produces most of the cerebrospinal fluid.

name: choroid plexus papilloma
clinical_significance: A usually slow-growing tumour arising from the tissue that produces cerebrospinal fluid in the brain ventricles. It is often benign but can block fluid flow and cause hydrocephalus, especially in infants and young children.

name: choroidal hemangioma
clinical_significance: A benign blood-vessel tumour in the choroid layer of the eye. It may cause no symptoms, but a larger lesion can leak fluid, detach the retina, or reduce vision.

name: choroideremia
clinical_significance: Choroideremia is an X-linked inherited retinal degeneration causing progressive night blindness and loss of peripheral then central vision, mainly in males.

name: choroiditis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the choroid, the blood-vessel-rich layer between the retina and the outer wall of the eye. It is a form of posterior uveitis and may occur with inflammation of the retina; symptoms can include floaters, blurred vision, or blind spots.

name: chrac
clinical_significance: An abbreviation for the chromatin accessibility complex, a protein complex studied for its role in moving or repositioning nucleosomes. It has no routine role as a clinical test or treatment.

name: chromaffin cell
clinical_significance: A catecholamine-producing cell, found mainly in the adrenal medulla and certain nerve-associated tissues. Abnormal growth of these cells can cause pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma, which may release excess adrenaline-like hormones.

name: chromaffin granule
clinical_significance: A small storage vesicle in chromaffin cells that contains catecholamines and related proteins. Its contents are released during the body’s stress response and are studied in adrenal and neuroendocrine biology.

name: chromatid
clinical_significance: One of the two identical DNA-containing copies of a replicated chromosome before cell division. Correct separation of sister chromatids is needed to prevent abnormal chromosome numbers in daughter cells.

name: chromatin
clinical_significance: The combination of DNA and proteins that packages genetic material inside the cell nucleus. Its arrangement controls which genes are available for use and helps regulate DNA copying and repair.

name: chromatin immunoprecipitation
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that isolates DNA-protein complexes using a specific antibody, then identifies the associated DNA. It is used to study gene regulation and chromatin and is mainly a research technique.

name: chromatin remodeling
clinical_significance: Changes in how DNA is packaged with proteins, making genes more or less accessible for use. Abnormal chromatin remodeling can disrupt development and contribute to cancer or inherited disorders.

name: chromatography
clinical_significance: A laboratory separation method in which substances partition between a stationary phase and a moving phase, allowing identification or measurement of components in a mixture.

name: chromatolysis
clinical_significance: Breakdown or dispersal of protein-making material in a nerve cell body, often after axon injury. It is a microscopic sign of neuronal stress or damage and must be interpreted with other tissue findings.

name: chromatophore
clinical_significance: A pigment-containing cell or structure, especially in animals, that changes or reflects coloration. In clinical use the term may describe pigment cells in the eye or skin; its significance depends on the tissue and lesion.

name: chromium
clinical_significance: Chromium is a metallic element; trivalent chromium is a trace nutrient, while hexavalent compounds can be toxic, corrosive, mutagenic, and carcinogenic.

name: chromobacterium
clinical_significance: A genus of bacteria found in soil and water. Chromobacterium violaceum can rarely cause rapidly progressive wound infection, bloodstream infection, and abscesses in multiple organs, so a compatible isolate warrants urgent clinical attention.

name: chromogranin
clinical_significance: A family of proteins stored in secretory granules of hormone-producing and nerve cells. Blood chromogranin A is used as one marker for some neuroendocrine tumours, but elevations are nonspecific and require interpretation with other findings.

name: chromogranin b
clinical_significance: A secretory protein found in granules of some neuroendocrine cells. Chromogranin B is mainly a research or tissue marker and is not a standalone routine diagnostic test.

name: chromogranin c
clinical_significance: A member of the chromogranin protein family found in secretory cells. Its clinical use is limited; it may be studied as a neuroendocrine tissue marker but is not a standalone diagnostic test.

name: chromomycins
clinical_significance: A group of antibiotic substances that interfere with DNA-dependent RNA production and have been studied or used as anticancer agents. Toxic effects limit their use, and they are not routine first-line treatments.

name: chromoplast
clinical_significance: A pigment-containing structure in plant cells that stores or produces coloured pigments. It is relevant to plant biology and has no direct clinical role in humans.

name: chromosomal duplication
clinical_significance: An extra copy of part or all of a chromosome segment. Its clinical effect depends on the genes involved and copy number; some duplications cause developmental or congenital conditions, while others may be benign.

name: chromosomal instability
clinical_significance: A tendency for chromosomes to gain, lose, or rearrange genetic material. It can cause inherited chromosome-instability syndromes and is common in many cancers, where it may affect tumour behaviour and treatment response.

name: chromosomal structure
clinical_significance: The organization of DNA and proteins into chromosomes, including their shape, packaging, and regions of active or inactive genes. Structural changes can affect gene function and cause inherited disorders or cancer.

name: chromosome
clinical_significance: A thread-like structure made of DNA and proteins that carries genetic information. Most human body cells normally contain 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs.

name: chromosome aberration
clinical_significance: An abnormal change in chromosome number or structure, such as a deletion, duplication, inversion, or translocation. Some changes cause genetic conditions or cancer; others are harmless variants, so clinical effect depends on the specific finding.

name: chromosome band
clinical_significance: A visible region of a chromosome with a characteristic staining pattern. Band locations provide a reference for describing chromosome structure and locating large genetic changes.

name: chromosome banding
clinical_significance: A staining method that creates recognizable light and dark chromosome bands for microscopic analysis. It can detect large deletions, duplications, translocations, and other chromosome changes.

name: chromosome breakage
clinical_significance: A break in chromosome DNA that may be repaired accurately or lead to deletion, rearrangement, or cell death. Excessive chromosome breakage can signal DNA-repair disorders or exposure to damaging agents.

name: chromosome condensation
clinical_significance: The compacting of chromosomes before cell division so they can be moved and separated accurately. Abnormal condensation can disrupt cell division and contribute to chromosome instability.

name: chromosome deletion
clinical_significance: Loss of a chromosome segment, which removes one or more genes. The effect depends on the location and size of the deletion and may cause a genetic syndrome or contribute to cancer.

name: chromosome disorder
clinical_significance: A condition caused by an abnormal chromosome number or structure. Effects range from no apparent symptoms to developmental, reproductive, growth, or organ problems, depending on which chromosomes and genes are affected.

name: chromosome inversion
clinical_significance: A chromosome change in which a segment breaks, reverses direction, and rejoins. Many inversions cause no symptoms, but some disrupt a gene or increase the chance of unbalanced chromosomes in eggs or sperm.

name: chromosome mapping
clinical_significance: Determining the locations of genes or other markers along chromosomes. It supports genetic research and can help characterize inherited conditions, tumour changes, or regions of interest for testing.

name: chromosome painting
clinical_significance: A fluorescence in situ hybridization method that uses differently coloured DNA probes to label whole chromosomes or chromosome segments. It can reveal rearrangements, translocations, or the origin of chromosome material in tumour or genetic testing.

name: chromosome pairing
clinical_significance: The alignment of matching maternal and paternal chromosomes during meiosis, the cell division that produces eggs and sperm. Errors can impair fertility or produce reproductive cells with abnormal chromosome numbers.

name: chromosome positioning
clinical_significance: The location and arrangement of chromosomes within a cell nucleus. Research on chromosome positioning helps explain gene activity and cell function but is not usually measured in routine clinical care.

name: chromosome segregation
clinical_significance: The separation of duplicated chromosomes into two daughter cells during cell division. Errors can create cells with extra or missing chromosomes and contribute to infertility, miscarriage, developmental conditions, or cancer.

name: chromosome translocation
clinical_significance: A chromosome rearrangement in which pieces from two chromosomes exchange places. It may be balanced and cause no symptoms, affect fertility or pregnancy, or create a fusion gene involved in cancer.

name: chromosome walking
clinical_significance: A molecular biology method for locating a gene or DNA segment by using overlapping cloned DNA fragments. It is mainly a research technique and has largely been superseded by modern sequencing methods.

name: chromothripsis
clinical_significance: A catastrophic genetic event in which one or a few chromosomes undergo extensive breakage and are reassembled in a disordered pattern. It can contribute to cancer by disrupting tumour-suppressor genes or activating growth-promoting genes.

name: chronic
clinical_significance: Persisting or recurring over a long period, in contrast to acute; the appropriate duration depends on the disease or clinical context.

name: chronic atrophic gastritis
clinical_significance: Long-term inflammation that destroys glands in the stomach lining. It may reduce stomach acid and intrinsic factor, impair iron or vitamin B12 absorption, and increase the risk of anemia or stomach tumors.

name: chronic bronchitis
clinical_significance: A cough producing mucus on most days for at least three months in each of two consecutive years, after other causes are excluded. It reflects long-term airway irritation and commonly occurs with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

name: chronic disease
clinical_significance: A disease or condition that persists for a prolonged period, often months or years, and may require continuing monitoring or management.

name: chronic fatigue syndrome
clinical_significance: A long-term illness involving substantial reduced ability to function, worsening after physical or mental activity, unrefreshing sleep, and often difficulty thinking or standing. Symptoms are not explained by another condition and need careful evaluation.

name: chronic gastritis
clinical_significance: Chronic, progressive inflammation of the gastric mucosa leading over time to mucosal atrophy, loss of specialized parietal and chief cells, and intestinal metaplasia. Major causes include persistent \textit{Helicobacter pylori} infection and autoimmune gastritis targeting parietal cells and intrinsic factor.

name: chronic kidney disease
clinical_significance: Kidney damage, a kidney-structure problem, or reduced kidney function that lasts at least three months.
