clinical_significance: The part of each heartbeat when the heart muscle relaxes and its chambers fill with blood. The lower blood-pressure number is the pressure in the arteries during this phase.

name: diastolic murmurs
clinical_significance: Extra heart sounds heard during the relaxation phase between beats. They commonly result from abnormal flow through a heart valve or major blood vessel and require clinical assessment.

name: diathermy
clinical_significance: Use of high-frequency electrical or electromagnetic energy to produce heat in tissue. It may be used during surgery to cut tissue or stop bleeding, or in selected treatments to warm deeper tissues.

name: diatomaceous earth
clinical_significance: A powder made from the fossilized remains of microscopic algae. Inhalation of fine particles can irritate the lungs, and some forms containing crystalline silica can cause serious lung disease with repeated exposure.

name: diatrizoate meglumine
clinical_significance: An iodinated contrast substance used for selected X-ray or imaging studies. It improves visibility of body structures but may cause allergic-like reactions, kidney injury, aspiration problems, or thyroid effects.

name: diazepam
clinical_significance: A benzodiazepine that calms brain activity and is used for selected anxiety, muscle-spasm, seizure, and alcohol-withdrawal conditions. It can cause drowsiness, falls, dependence, withdrawal, and dangerous breathing depression with opioids or alcohol.

name: diazinon
clinical_significance: An organophosphate insecticide that blocks acetylcholinesterase, causing excess nerve signals. Exposure can lead to sweating, salivation, vomiting, diarrhea, breathing difficulty, muscle weakness, seizures, or respiratory failure.

name: diaziquone
clinical_significance: Diaziquone is an investigational anticancer compound studied for tumors involving the central nervous system because it can cross the blood-brain barrier. It is not a standard approved treatment.

name: diazonium compounds
clinical_significance: Chemicals containing a diazonium group, used in dyes, synthesis, and laboratory reactions. Some are unstable or toxic and may irritate tissues or release hazardous products.

name: diazooxonorleucine
clinical_significance: Diazooxonorleucine is an experimental glutamine antagonist studied for anticancer effects. It has no established routine clinical use.

name: diazoxide
clinical_significance: A medicine that opens potassium channels and can reduce insulin release or relax blood vessels. It is used in selected cases of low blood sugar from excess insulin and severe high blood pressure; fluid retention and high glucose may occur.

name: dibekacin
clinical_significance: An aminoglycoside antibiotic used in some regions for serious bacterial infections. It blocks bacterial protein production but can damage the kidneys, hearing, or balance, especially with prolonged or high-dose treatment.

name: dibucaine
clinical_significance: A long-acting local anesthetic applied to skin or mucous membranes to reduce pain or itching. Excessive use or absorption can cause numbness beyond the treatment area, seizures, heart problems, or other toxicity.

name: dicarboxylic acid
clinical_significance: An organic molecule containing two acid groups. These molecules take part in metabolism and may accumulate in some inherited or acquired metabolic disorders.

name: dichlorophen
clinical_significance: A chemical formerly used in some disinfectants and medicines. Exposure can irritate the skin, eyes, or digestive tract; serious effects depend on the amount, route, and duration of exposure.

name: dichlorvos
clinical_significance: An organophosphate insecticide that can block acetylcholinesterase. Poisoning may cause sweating, salivation, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle weakness, breathing difficulty, seizures, or respiratory failure.

name: dickeya dadantii
clinical_significance: Dickeya dadantii is a plant-pathogenic bacterium that causes soft rot in crops and is not known as a usual human pathogen. Its significance is mainly agricultural and in microbiology research.

name: diclofenac
clinical_significance: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicine used for pain and inflammation. It can cause stomach irritation or bleeding, kidney or liver injury, fluid retention, and increased cardiovascular risk.

name: diclofenac sodium
clinical_significance: A salt form of diclofenac used for pain and inflammation. It can irritate or bleed the stomach and may affect the kidneys, blood pressure, liver, or heart.

name: dicloxacillin
clinical_significance: A penicillin-type antibiotic that blocks bacterial cell-wall production. It is used for susceptible infections, especially some staphylococcal infections; allergy, diarrhea, and liver injury can occur.

name: dicrotophos
clinical_significance: An organophosphate insecticide that can inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Poisoning may cause sweating, salivation, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle weakness, breathing difficulty, seizures, or respiratory failure.

name: dictyostelium
clinical_significance: Dictyostelium is a soil-dwelling amoeba used as a model organism to study cell movement, signaling, and development. It is not a human pathogen.

name: dicumarol
clinical_significance: Dicumarol is an older vitamin K antagonist that reduces blood clotting and has largely been replaced by newer anticoagulants. Its principal hazard is serious bleeding.

name: dicyclomine
clinical_significance: An anticholinergic medicine that relaxes intestinal muscle and may reduce cramping in selected bowel disorders. It can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, fast heartbeat, confusion, or difficulty urinating.

name: didanosine
clinical_significance: Didanosine is an older HIV medicine that is no longer commonly used because safer options are available. It can cause serious pancreatitis, liver injury, lactic acidosis, and persistent nerve damage.

name: diencephalon
clinical_significance: A central part of the brain containing the thalamus and hypothalamus. It helps process sensory information and regulate hormones, temperature, appetite, sleep, movement, and other automatic functions.

name: dientamoeba
clinical_significance: Dientamoeba is a genus of intestinal parasites; Dientamoeba fragilis can be found in people with or without gastrointestinal symptoms. A positive stool result needs clinical interpretation.

name: dientamoeba fragilis
clinical_significance: Dientamoeba fragilis is an intestinal parasite that may be present without symptoms or may be associated with diarrhea and abdominal pain. Diagnosis requires stool testing, and treatment is generally considered when symptoms fit and other causes are excluded.

name: diestrus
clinical_significance: A phase of the reproductive cycle in many mammals between periods of sexual receptivity. It is characterized by activity and later regression of the corpus luteum.

name: diet
clinical_significance: Diet affects energy, nutrient intake, blood glucose, cardiovascular risk, and bowel health. Dietary advice should account for medical conditions, nutritional needs, culture, access, and personal goals.

name: diet therapy
clinical_significance: Use of an individualized eating plan to prevent, manage, or treat a health problem. It may address diabetes, kidney disease, food allergy, malnutrition, digestive disorders, or other needs and is tailored to the person's health and goals.

name: dietary calcium
clinical_significance: Calcium obtained from food or drinks, needed for bones, teeth, muscles, nerves, and blood clotting. Requirements vary with age and health; excess supplements may cause kidney stones or other problems.

name: dietary carbohydrate
clinical_significance: Carbohydrate in foods and drinks, including sugars, starches, and fiber. Digestible carbohydrate provides energy and affects blood glucose; fiber is only partly or not digested and supports bowel function.

name: dietary fats
clinical_significance: Fats obtained from food, including saturated, monounsaturated, polyunsaturated, and trans fats. They provide energy and support cell membranes and vitamin absorption; replacing saturated or trans fats with unsaturated fats is generally healthier.

name: dietary fiber
clinical_significance: Plant material that is not fully digested. It helps form stool, supports regular bowel movements, may improve cholesterol and glucose control, and can increase fullness.

name: dietary iron
clinical_significance: Iron from food or supplements, needed to make hemoglobin, muscle proteins, and enzymes. Too little can cause iron-deficiency anemia; too much can be toxic, especially in children or people with iron-storage disorders.

name: dietary phospholipid
clinical_significance: A food-derived fat containing phosphate that helps form cell membranes and transports fats in the blood. Its digestion and handling depend on food intake, absorption, and liver function.

name: dietary phosphorus
clinical_significance: Phosphorus from food, needed for bones, teeth, cell membranes, and energy use. People with reduced kidney function may need to limit highly absorbable sources to prevent high blood phosphorus.

name: dietary protein
clinical_significance: Protein from food that is digested into amino acids and small peptides. These support muscle and tissue repair, enzymes, hormones, immunity, and energy when needed.

name: dietary steroid
clinical_significance: Dietary steroids are naturally occurring steroid-like compounds in foods, including plant sterols and animal-derived cholesterol. Their absorption and health effects depend on the specific molecule and the overall diet.

name: dietary sterol
clinical_significance: A cholesterol-like substance found in foods, including cholesterol and plant sterols. Absorption and metabolism affect blood cholesterol; plant sterols can reduce intestinal cholesterol absorption in some people.

name: dietary supplement
clinical_significance: A product taken by mouth to provide vitamins, minerals, herbs, amino acids, or other dietary ingredients. Supplements may be useful for a documented need but can interact with medicines or cause toxicity.

name: dietary supplementation
clinical_significance: Deliberate addition of nutrients or other substances to the diet to correct a deficiency, meet increased needs, or support a health goal. The dose and need should be assessed because excess can be harmful.

name: dietetics
clinical_significance: The science and professional practice of using food and nutrition to promote health, prevent disease, and manage medical conditions through individualized dietary advice.

name: diethylhexylphthalate
clinical_significance: Another name for DEHP, a chemical added to some plastics to make them flexible. Repeated or high exposure may affect reproduction, development, or hormone function.

name: diethylnitrosamine
clinical_significance: Diethylnitrosamine is a potent chemical carcinogen used mainly in laboratory research to study liver cancer. Accidental exposure is hazardous and should be managed as a toxic chemical exposure.

name: diethylpropion
clinical_significance: A stimulant appetite suppressant used short term in selected weight-management plans. It can cause insomnia, anxiety, fast heartbeat, high blood pressure, misuse, and dependence; medical supervision is required.

name: diethylstilbestrol
clinical_significance: A synthetic estrogen formerly given to some pregnant people. Exposure before birth can increase the risk of reproductive-tract abnormalities, fertility problems, and certain rare cancers later in life.

name: dietitian
clinical_significance: A nutrition professional who assesses food and nutrient needs and provides individualized advice for health, disease prevention, and medical conditions. Professional titles and licensing rules vary by region.

name: differentiation antigens
clinical_significance: Molecules on a cell’s surface that indicate its tissue type or stage of development. Laboratory tests for them help identify blood-cell disorders, classify cancers, and guide selected treatments.

name: difficulty walking
clinical_significance: Trouble walking safely or normally because of pain, weakness, poor balance, numbness, joint disease, neurologic illness, or heart or lung limitations. Sudden onset requires urgent assessment.

name: diffuse
clinical_significance: Spread broadly or throughout an area rather than limited to one small, clearly defined focus. The term may describe a disease, pain, swelling, imaging finding, or other process.

name: diffuse astrocytoma
clinical_significance: An older name for an infiltrating brain tumor made of astrocyte-like cells. Modern classification depends on molecular findings, including IDH status, which help determine diagnosis, outlook, and treatment.

name: diffuse scleroderma
clinical_significance: A form of systemic sclerosis in which skin thickening extends beyond the hands and face onto the trunk or limbs. It carries a higher risk of lung, kidney, heart, blood-vessel, and digestive complications.

name: diffusion
clinical_significance: Movement of molecules from an area where they are more concentrated to an area where they are less concentrated, caused by their random motion. It helps exchange gases and substances in the body.

name: diffusion anisotropy
clinical_significance: A difference in the direction water moves through tissue, especially along nerve fibers in the brain. MRI can use this pattern to study nerve-fiber structure and injury.

name: diflunisal
clinical_significance: A salicylate nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicine used for pain and inflammation. It can cause stomach irritation or bleeding, kidney injury, fluid retention, allergic reactions, or cardiovascular problems.

name: digastric muscle
clinical_significance: A two-part muscle beneath the jaw that helps open the mouth, lower the jaw, and raise the hyoid bone during swallowing and speech.

name: DiGeorge syndrome
clinical_significance: A genetic disorder usually caused by loss of a small part of chromosome 22. It can affect the heart, immune system, calcium regulation, palate, hearing, learning, and development.

name: digestion
clinical_significance: The process of breaking food into smaller substances that the body can absorb and use. It begins in the mouth and continues through the stomach and intestines with movement, acid, bile, and digestive enzymes.

name: digestive disorder
clinical_significance: A disease affecting the digestive tract or the process of digestion. It may cause abdominal pain, nausea, reflux, diarrhea, constipation, bleeding, vomiting, or poor nutrient absorption.

name: digit
clinical_significance: A finger or toe. Most fingers and toes contain three small bones, while the thumb and great toe usually contain two; muscles, tendons, nerves, and blood vessels allow movement and sensation.

name: digital mammography
clinical_significance: Breast imaging that records X-ray pictures electronically. It helps detect masses, distortions, and calcium deposits and allows images to be enlarged, adjusted, stored, and compared.

name: digitalis preparation
clinical_significance: A preparation containing a cardiac glycoside such as digoxin or digitoxin. It can strengthen heart contraction and slow electrical conduction, but the dose range is narrow and toxicity can cause digestive, visual, or rhythm problems.

name: digitonin
clinical_significance: Digitonin is a plant-derived chemical used in laboratories to selectively disrupt cell membranes. It is toxic if swallowed or absorbed and is not a human medicine.

name: digitoxin
clinical_significance: A cardiac glycoside that can strengthen heart contraction and slow electrical conduction. Its safe and toxic doses are close together, so abnormal rhythms, digestive symptoms, visual changes, and drug interactions are important concerns.

name: digoxin
clinical_significance: A cardiac medicine used in selected people with heart failure or atrial fibrillation. It can strengthen contraction and slow the heart rate, but kidney function, electrolytes, other medicines, and blood levels affect toxicity risk.

name: dihydrotestosterone
clinical_significance: A potent androgen made from testosterone. It contributes to development of male external genitalia, facial and body hair, prostate growth, and other androgen effects.

name: dihydroxyacetone
clinical_significance: A three-carbon sugar involved in metabolism. Its phosphate form is an intermediate used when cells break down glucose or make glucose.

name: dilatation
clinical_significance: Widening or expansion of a hollow organ, blood vessel, duct, opening, or other body structure. It may be normal, caused by disease, or deliberately produced during a procedure.

name: dilated cardiomyopathy
clinical_significance: A heart-muscle disease in which one or more chambers enlarge and pump weakly. Causes include inherited disease, infection, toxins, medicines, pregnancy, blocked arteries, and inflammation; it can lead to heart failure or abnormal rhythms.

name: dilation
clinical_significance: Widening or expansion of a hollow organ, blood vessel, duct, pupil, opening, or other body structure. It may be normal, caused by disease, or deliberately produced during a procedure.

name: dilator
clinical_significance: An instrument or device used to widen a body opening or passage gradually or temporarily. It may be used during examinations, surgery, childbirth care, dental treatment, or treatment of a narrowing.

name: diltiazem
clinical_significance: A calcium-channel blocker used for high blood pressure, angina, and heart-rate control in some abnormal rhythms. It can slow the heart, lower blood pressure, cause constipation, or worsen heart failure in susceptible people.

name: dimenhydrinate
clinical_significance: An antihistamine used to prevent or treat motion sickness and nausea. It can cause drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, confusion, or difficulty urinating.

name: dimercaprol
clinical_significance: An injected medicine that binds certain toxic metals, including arsenic, mercury, and gold, so the body can remove them. It can cause high blood pressure, fast heartbeat, nausea, pain, and other adverse effects.

name: dimesna
clinical_significance: A sulfur-containing compound studied as a protective or detoxifying medicine, including in some chemotherapy-related settings. Its clinical role depends on the specific treatment and available evidence.

name: dimethoate
clinical_significance: An organophosphate insecticide that blocks acetylcholinesterase. Poisoning can cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, diarrhea, small pupils, muscle weakness, breathing problems, seizures, or coma.

name: dimethoxon
clinical_significance: A poisonous breakdown product of some organophosphate pesticides. It can cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, diarrhea, small pupils, muscle twitching, weakness, breathing difficulty, or seizures and requires urgent poisoning advice.

name: dimethyl fumarate
clinical_significance: An oral medicine used for multiple sclerosis and selected skin conditions. It can cause flushing, digestive symptoms, low white-cell counts, liver injury, allergic reactions, or rare serious infections.

name: dimethyl sulfoxide
clinical_significance: An organic solvent used in laboratories and some specialized medical or investigational applications. Contact or ingestion can irritate tissues, and it may carry other substances through the skin.

name: dimethylbenzanthracene
clinical_significance: Dimethylbenzanthracene is a potent experimental carcinogen used to induce tumors in laboratory research. It is hazardous and has no therapeutic use.

name: dimethylhydrazines
clinical_significance: A group of highly toxic chemicals formerly used mainly in rocket fuel. Exposure can irritate or burn tissues and damage the nervous system, liver, blood, or other organs.

name: dimethylnitrosamine
clinical_significance: Dimethylnitrosamine, also called NDMA, is a toxic nitrosamine and potent carcinogen that can injure the liver. It is monitored as an unwanted contaminant in some products and water.

name: dimetilan
clinical_significance: A poisonous carbamate insecticide that disrupts nerve signals by blocking acetylcholinesterase. Exposure can cause sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, small pupils, weakness, breathing difficulty, seizures, or coma and needs urgent help.

name: dinaciclib
clinical_significance: Dinaciclib is an investigational inhibitor of several cyclin-dependent kinases studied for cancer treatment. It can suppress bone marrow and cause other serious adverse effects; it is not an approved standard therapy.

name: dinitrochlorobenzene
clinical_significance: Dinitrochlorobenzene is a strong skin sensitizer used in allergy testing and investigational topical immune treatments. It can cause severe allergic contact dermatitis and is not suitable for unsupervised use.

name: dinitrofluorobenzene
clinical_significance: Dinitrofluorobenzene is a reactive chemical used in laboratory protein analysis and experimental contact-sensitization models. It can cause severe skin and eye irritation or sensitization and requires strict exposure control.

name: dinophyceae
clinical_significance: A group of aquatic microorganisms, including dinoflagellates. Some produce toxins during harmful algal blooms that can contaminate seafood or water and cause neurologic, digestive, or liver illness.

name: dinoprost
clinical_significance: A prostaglandin medicine that stimulates uterine contraction and other smooth-muscle effects. It is used mainly in veterinary medicine and selected reproductive-health settings; pain, diarrhea, breathing difficulty, and blood-pressure changes may occur.

name: dinoprostone
clinical_significance: A prostaglandin medicine used to soften the cervix and help start labor or manage selected pregnancy-related conditions. It requires obstetric monitoring because it can cause contractions that are too frequent, pain, fever, nausea, or fetal heart-rate changes.

name: dinucleoside phosphates
clinical_significance: Molecules containing two nucleosides joined by phosphate groups. They occur in nucleotide metabolism and may take part in cellular signaling, energy transfer, or DNA and RNA-related reactions.

name: dinutuximab
clinical_significance: An antibody-based cancer medicine that attaches to a marker found on many neuroblastoma cells and helps the immune system destroy them. It can cause severe nerve pain, allergic reactions, fever, and fluid leakage from blood vessels.

name: dioxin
clinical_significance: A group of long-lasting environmental chemicals produced by some industrial processes and burning. They can build up in body fat; long-term exposure may affect development, reproduction, immunity, hormones, and cancer risk.

name: dipeptide
clinical_significance: A molecule made of two amino acids joined together. Dipeptides are produced during protein digestion and metabolism and can be absorbed or used in further chemical reactions.

name: dipetalonema
clinical_significance: Dipetalonema is an older genus name for several filarial worms now classified in other genera, including Mansonella. Some species infect humans and can cause mansonellosis, transmitted by biting midges or blackflies.

name: dipetalonema infection
clinical_significance: Infection with a Dipetalonema parasitic worm, usually acquired through an arthropod bite. It may affect skin or tissue beneath the skin; diagnosis and treatment depend on the species and clinical findings.

name: diphenoxylate
clinical_significance: An opioid-related medicine that slows intestinal movement to reduce diarrhea, usually combined with atropine. Excessive use can cause drowsiness, constipation, dependence, breathing depression, or poisoning.

name: diphenylhydramine
clinical_significance: Diphenylhydramine is an alternate spelling of diphenhydramine, a sedating antihistamine used for allergy symptoms, motion sickness, and short-term sleep aid in some settings. It can cause drowsiness, confusion, falls, urinary retention, and dangerous effects in overdose.

name: diphosphate
clinical_significance: A chemical group containing two linked phosphate units. Diphosphate is involved in energy use, nucleotide formation, and other chemical reactions in cells.

name: diphosphonate
clinical_significance: A chemical group found in compounds that can bind strongly to bone mineral. Some related medicines are used or studied for disorders of bone breakdown and calcium balance.

name: diphtheria
clinical_significance: A serious infection caused by toxin-producing Corynebacterium bacteria. It can form a thick coating in the throat and cause airway blockage, heart inflammation, nerve damage, or death; vaccination prevents most cases.

name: diphtheria toxin
clinical_significance: A poisonous protein made by some Corynebacterium bacteria. It blocks protein production inside cells, causing local tissue injury and potentially severe heart, nerve, and airway complications.

name: diphyllobothriasis
clinical_significance: An intestinal infection caused by a fish tapeworm acquired from raw or undercooked freshwater fish. It may cause abdominal symptoms and, rarely, vitamin B12 deficiency and anemia.

name: diphyllobothrium latum
clinical_significance: A fish tapeworm acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish. It lives in the intestine and may cause abdominal symptoms or compete for vitamin B12, occasionally leading to anemia.

name: diploid cell
clinical_significance: A cell containing two complete sets of chromosomes, one inherited from each parent. Most human body cells are diploid; eggs and sperm normally contain only one set.

name: diploidy
clinical_significance: Having two complete sets of chromosomes, usually one from each parent. This is the normal chromosome state of most human body cells.

name: diplopia
clinical_significance: Seeing two images of one object. It may occur with one eye or only when both eyes are open; causes include dry eye, cataract, eye misalignment, nerve disease, muscle disease, or brain disease.

name: dipstick device
clinical_significance: A strip or small device containing chemical pads that change color when placed in a specimen, commonly urine. It provides a rapid screen for substances such as blood, protein, glucose, or infection markers.

name: diptera
clinical_significance: The insect order containing flies and mosquitoes. Some species spread infections through bites or contamination, while others can cause infestations such as myiasis.

name: diptheroid bacillus
clinical_significance: Diphtheroid bacilli are Corynebacterium-like bacteria often present on skin and mucous membranes. They may contaminate specimens, but can cause real device-associated or bloodstream infection in vulnerable patients; interpretation depends on specimen and clinical context.

name: dipylidium caninum
clinical_significance: A tapeworm of dogs and cats that can occasionally infect people, especially children, after an infected flea is swallowed. Infection may cause mild digestive symptoms or visible worm segments in stool.

name: dipyridamole
clinical_significance: A medicine that reduces platelet clumping and widens blood vessels. It is used in selected stroke-prevention plans and heart stress testing; headache, dizziness, low blood pressure, and bleeding may occur.

name: dirty necrosis
clinical_significance: Dead tumor tissue mixed with broken cell material and many white blood cells. It is often seen in rapidly growing cancers and is interpreted by a pathologist with the rest of the tissue sample.

name: disability
clinical_significance: A difficulty with body function, activity, or participation caused by a health condition and influenced by the person’s environment. Disability may be temporary or lifelong and varies in severity and support needs.

name: disaccharide
clinical_significance: A carbohydrate made of two linked simple sugars, such as lactose, sucrose, or maltose. It must be split by digestive enzymes before the intestine can absorb its component sugars.

name: discitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of a spinal disc, often involving the nearby vertebral bones. It may cause severe localized back or neck pain, stiffness, fever, or reduced movement and usually requires imaging and medical evaluation.

name: disclosure
clinical_significance: Disclosure in healthcare may involve sharing a diagnosis, risk, error, or personal information. Clear and timely disclosure supports informed decisions and trust, while privacy rules govern release of identifiable health information.

name: discriminant analysis
clinical_significance: Discriminant analysis is a statistical method used to classify observations into groups based on measured features. It may support clinical prediction or diagnosis research, but its accuracy must be validated in the intended population.

name: discrimination learning
clinical_significance: Discrimination learning is the ability to distinguish between stimuli or situations and respond differently to them. In clinical care it may be used to assess learning, cognition, or behavior, including in developmental and neurologic evaluations.

name: disease
clinical_significance: An abnormal condition that affects the body or mind and changes normal structure or function. Diseases may be infectious, inflammatory, inherited, degenerative, metabolic, immune-related, or cancerous.

name: disease progression
clinical_significance: Change in a disease over time, often meaning worsening. It is assessed through symptoms, examination, laboratory results, imaging, function, complications, and response to treatment.

name: disease reservoir
clinical_significance: A person, animal, environment, or material in which an infectious organism normally lives and from which it can spread to a susceptible host.

name: disease response
clinical_significance: The body’s biological or clinical reaction to a disease or its treatment. It is assessed using symptoms, signs, laboratory results, imaging, physical function, or survival.

name: disease susceptibility
clinical_significance: Increased likelihood of developing a disease because of genes, age, immune status, exposures, behavior, other illnesses, or environmental factors. Susceptibility raises risk but does not mean disease is certain.

name: disease vector
clinical_significance: A living carrier, commonly a mosquito, tick, flea, or other arthropod, that transfers an infectious organism between hosts. The vector may transmit infection without becoming ill itself.

name: disfigurement
clinical_significance: A visible change that substantially alters appearance, caused by injury, disease, surgery, a birth difference, or scarring. Its physical, emotional, and social effects vary between people.

name: disinfectant
clinical_significance: A chemical or physical agent used on nonliving surfaces to destroy or inactivate many microorganisms. Disinfectants are not necessarily safe for skin, wounds, food, or internal use.

name: disk
clinical_significance: A flat, round structure. In the spine, an intervertebral disk lies between neighboring vertebrae, absorbs shock, and helps the back move.

name: diskectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove part or all of a damaged spinal disk pressing on a nerve or the spinal cord. It may relieve pain or weakness caused by disk herniation; risks include infection, bleeding, nerve injury, and recurrence.

name: dislocation
clinical_significance: Complete loss of normal contact between the surfaces of a joint, usually from injury or disease. It can cause severe pain and deformity and may occur with fractures or nerve and blood-vessel injury.

name: disopyramide
clinical_significance: An antiarrhythmic medicine used selectively for certain abnormal heart rhythms. It can slow electrical conduction and weaken heart contraction and may cause dry mouth, urinary retention, low blood pressure, or new arrhythmias.

name: dispensed amount
clinical_significance: The quantity of medicine supplied to a patient. It is determined by the prescribed dose, treatment duration, formulation, refill rules, and applicable safety or legal requirements.

name: disruption
clinical_significance: An interruption or breakdown of normal structure, function, continuity, or process. In medicine, it may describe damaged tissue, a broken barrier, disturbed development, or an interruption in the usual work of an organ or system.

name: dissection
clinical_significance: Separation of tissue layers, either during surgery or because of disease. In an artery, a tear in the inner lining lets blood split the wall layers and can block blood flow or cause the artery to rupture.

name: disseminate
clinical_significance: To spread widely through the body, a tissue, or a population. Infection, cancer, inflammation, or another process may disseminate rather than remain in one limited area.

name: disseminated neuroblastoma
clinical_significance: Neuroblastoma that has spread from its original site to distant organs, bone marrow, bones, liver, or lymph nodes. Treatment and outlook depend on age, spread, tumor biology, and response to specialist care.

name: dissociative disorder
clinical_significance: Dissociative disorders can disrupt memory, identity, perception, or sense of self and cause substantial distress; trauma-informed assessment should distinguish them from neurologic disease, substances, and other psychiatric conditions.

name: dissociative hysteria
clinical_significance: Dissociative hysteria is an outdated term formerly used for dissociative symptoms such as memory loss, altered awareness, or identity disruption. Modern diagnosis uses specific dissociative-disorder criteria and requires assessment for neurologic, substance-related, and other causes.

name: distal
clinical_significance: Farther from the point where a body part attaches or begins, or farther from the center of the body. For example, the hand is distal to the elbow.

name: distal pancreatectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery removing the body or tail of the pancreas, usually while leaving the head. It may be used for selected tumors, cysts, injury, or inflammation; diabetes and leakage from the pancreas are possible risks.

name: distamycins
clinical_significance: A group of antibiotic-like compounds that bind to DNA and have been studied for antimicrobial or anticancer effects. Their clinical use is limited and depends on the specific compound and evidence.

name: distant
clinical_significance: Far from a reference point or original site. In cancer, distant disease means that cancer has spread to remote organs or lymph nodes rather than remaining near the primary tumor.

name: distended
clinical_significance: Abnormally stretched, swollen, or enlarged by gas, fluid, blood, tissue, or pressure. The term may describe the abdomen, bladder, stomach, bowel, veins, or another body structure.

name: distress
clinical_significance: Significant physical or emotional suffering, discomfort, or strain related to illness, injury, treatment, or difficult circumstances. Severe distress may affect sleep, functioning, decisions, or safety and may need support.

name: disulfiram
clinical_significance: Disulfiram is used with counseling and support to help selected people with alcohol use disorder avoid drinking. Alcohol can trigger a severe flushing, vomiting, headache, and blood-pressure reaction during treatment and for up to two weeks after stopping; liver monitoring is important.

name: disulfoton
clinical_significance: A highly toxic organophosphate insecticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Exposure can cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle weakness, breathing failure, seizures, or coma.

name: diterpenes
clinical_significance: Diterpenes are a broad group of plant and microbial compounds with varied biological effects. Some are medicines or drug leads, while others are toxins or irritants; clinical significance depends on the specific compound.

name: ditiocarb
clinical_significance: A term for dithiocarbamate compounds, some of which are used as pesticides or metal-binding chemicals. Toxic effects vary by compound and may involve the nervous system, liver, kidneys, or skin.

name: diuresis
clinical_significance: Increased production of urine. It may result from excess fluid, high blood glucose, diabetes insipidus, medicines called diuretics, or other causes; excessive loss can lead to dehydration and electrolyte problems.

name: diuretic
clinical_significance: A medicine that increases renal excretion of sodium and water, commonly used for hypertension, edema, and heart failure.

name: diutina rugosa
clinical_significance: Diutina rugosa, formerly called Candida rugosa, is a rare opportunistic yeast that can cause bloodstream or other invasive fungal infections, particularly in vulnerable patients. Its antifungal susceptibility may vary, making species identification and testing important.

name: diverticulitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation, and sometimes infection, of one or more diverticula—small pouches that form in the wall of the colon. It commonly causes constant lower-abdominal pain, often on the left side, with localized tenderness, fever, nausea, constipation, or diarrhea; right-sided pain can occur when diverticula affect the right colon. Complicated disease may produce an abscess, perforation with peritonitis, fistula, bowel obstruction, or sepsis.

name: diverticulosis
clinical_significance: Diverticulosis is the presence of small pouches in the colon wall and often causes no symptoms. It can sometimes lead to diverticulitis or painless lower-gastrointestinal bleeding; symptoms or bleeding require evaluation to determine the cause.

name: diverticulum
clinical_significance: A pouch-like projection from the wall of a hollow organ, especially the intestine. It may cause no symptoms or become inflamed, infected, blocked, bleed, or rarely perforate.

name: divorce
clinical_significance: Divorce can be a major psychosocial stressor associated with changes in mental health, housing, finances, and family relationships. It may affect health and care access, especially when safety or support needs are present.

name: dizygotic twin
clinical_significance: One of a pair of fraternal twins formed when two separate eggs are fertilized by two separate sperm. The twins share about half their genetic variation on average, like ordinary siblings.

name: dizziness
clinical_significance: A sensation of spinning, lightheadedness, imbalance, faintness, or being unsteady. Causes include inner-ear, heart, blood-pressure, vision, medicine, blood, metabolic, or neurologic problems.

name: DNA adduct
clinical_significance: A chemical group attached to DNA after exposure to a reactive substance. If not repaired, it can alter DNA copying, cause mutations, and potentially contribute to cancer.

name: DNA alkylation
clinical_significance: Attachment of an alkyl group to DNA. This can change base pairing, block copying or repair, cause mutations, or kill a cell; some anticancer medicines work partly this way.

name: DNA binding
clinical_significance: Attachment of a protein or other molecule to a DNA sequence. This can control gene activity, DNA copying, repair, chromosome organization, or the action of some medicines.

name: DNA damage
clinical_significance: A chemical or structural change in DNA that can interfere with gene function or copying. Cells usually repair such damage, but persistent or incorrectly repaired damage can cause mutations, cell death, or cancer.

name: DNA demethylation
clinical_significance: Removal or loss of small chemical groups called methyl groups from DNA. It can change how accessible a gene is and alter gene activity during development, cell reprogramming, or disease.

name: DNA fingerprinting
clinical_significance: DNA fingerprinting compares selected genetic markers to distinguish individuals or assess biological relationships. It is used in forensics and identity testing, with strict attention to consent, privacy, and sample integrity.

name: DNA footprinting
clinical_significance: DNA footprinting identifies where proteins bind along a DNA sequence by detecting protected regions. It is used to study gene regulation and protein-DNA interactions, not as a routine patient test.

name: DNA fragmentation
clinical_significance: Breaking DNA strands into smaller pieces. It occurs normally during programmed cell death and can also result from injury, radiation, chemicals, disease, or laboratory processing.

name: DNA gyrase
clinical_significance: A bacterial enzyme that twists and untwists DNA so it can be copied and separated. Fluoroquinolone antibiotics block this enzyme, stopping bacterial growth and survival.

name: DNA integration
clinical_significance: Insertion of foreign or copied DNA into a cell’s genome. It occurs in some viral infections, evolution, and gene therapy and can alter nearby gene activity if the insertion affects a control region.

name: DNA ligases
clinical_significance: Enzymes that join breaks in DNA strands during copying, repair, and genetic recombination. They help preserve the continuous structure of chromosomes.

name: DNA ligation
clinical_significance: Joining DNA fragments by forming a chemical bond between them. Cells use it during DNA copying and repair, and laboratories use it in genetic testing and cloning.

name: DNA methylation
clinical_significance: Addition of small chemical groups called methyl groups to DNA, usually at cytosine bases. It can change how strongly a gene is expressed without changing the DNA sequence.

name: DNA packaging
clinical_significance: Arrangement of long DNA molecules around histone proteins and into compact structures called chromosomes. Packaging allows DNA to fit inside the nucleus and helps control access to genes.

name: DNA primase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that makes short RNA starting pieces so other enzymes can begin copying DNA. It is required during cell division and DNA repair.

name: DNA primers
clinical_significance: Short nucleic-acid sequences that provide a starting point for copying DNA. Cells make them during replication, and laboratories use designed primers to amplify selected genetic sequences.

name: DNA probe
clinical_significance: A labeled single-stranded DNA sequence designed to bind a matching target. It can help detect a gene, mutation, chromosome region, or microorganism in a laboratory sample.

name: DNA repair
clinical_significance: Cellular processes that detect and correct damage or copying errors in DNA. Repair pathways address small base changes, bulky chemical damage, mismatched bases, and breaks in one or both DNA strands.

name: DNA replication
clinical_significance: The process by which DNA copies itself before cell division. Each new DNA molecule contains one original strand and one newly made strand, allowing genetic information to pass to daughter cells.

name: DNA virus
clinical_significance: A virus whose genetic material is DNA. DNA viruses vary widely in transmission, tissues affected, and disease; some cause persistent infection, while others cause short-term illness.

name: dobutamine
clinical_significance: An intravenous medicine that increases heart contraction and, sometimes, heart rate. It is used short term for selected cases of severe low-output heart failure or shock and requires close monitoring.

name: docetaxel
clinical_significance: An anticancer medicine that interferes with microtubules, structures needed for cell division. It is used for several cancers and can cause low blood counts, infection, hair loss, nerve problems, or allergic reactions.

name: doconexent
clinical_significance: A pharmaceutical name for docosahexaenoic acid, an omega-3 fatty acid found in oily fish, algae, and cell membranes. Its effects depend on the product, dose, and reason for use.

name: docosadienoic acid
clinical_significance: A 22-carbon fatty acid with two double bonds, present in small amounts in body and dietary lipids. It is studied mainly for possible effects on cell membranes and metabolism.

name: docosahexaenoic acid
clinical_significance: An omega-3 fatty acid that is an important structural part of brain and retinal cell membranes. It comes mainly from oily fish, algae, or supplements and is especially important during brain development.

name: docosapentaenoic acid
clinical_significance: A 22-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid with five double bonds. It occurs as omega-3 and omega-6 forms in foods and tissues; its health effects depend on the form and amount.

name: docosatrienoic acid
clinical_significance: A 22-carbon fatty acid with three double bonds, found in small amounts in body and dietary lipids. It is studied mainly for its possible roles in cell membranes and metabolism.

name: dodecenoic acid
clinical_significance: Dodecenoic acid is an unsaturated 12-carbon fatty acid found in some biological and dietary lipids. Specific forms have antimicrobial effects in laboratory studies, but they are not established treatments.

name: dolasetron
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors and helps prevent nausea and vomiting in selected settings. It can cause headache, constipation, or dangerous heart-rhythm changes.

name: dolasetron mesylate
clinical_significance: A salt form of dolasetron, a medicine that blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors to prevent nausea and vomiting in selected settings. It can cause constipation, headache, or dangerous heart-rhythm changes.

name: dolichol
clinical_significance: A long-chain fatty alcohol used inside cells to assemble sugar chains attached to proteins. This process is important for protein folding, transport, and function.

name: dolosigranulum pigrum
clinical_significance: Dolosigranulum pigrum is a bacterium commonly found in the nose and usually considered part of the normal microbiome. It rarely causes opportunistic infection, so recovery from blood or another sterile site warrants clinical interpretation and confirmation.

name: domestic violence
clinical_significance: A pattern of physical, sexual, emotional, psychological, or financial abuse or coercive control by an intimate partner or household member. It can cause injury, fear, isolation, and serious health effects; confidential support is available.

name: dominant
clinical_significance: Describing a genetic variant whose effect can appear when only one copy is present. An affected parent with an autosomal dominant condition may pass the variant to each child with a one-in-two chance.

name: domperidone
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks dopamine receptors outside the brain and is used in some countries for nausea or slow stomach movement. It can prolong the heart rhythm and cause dangerous arrhythmias.

name: donepezil
clinical_significance: A medicine that increases acetylcholine activity in the brain and may temporarily improve symptoms of Alzheimer disease. It does not cure the disease and can cause nausea, diarrhea, slow heartbeat, fainting, or sleep problems.

name: Donohue syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which the body cannot respond normally to insulin. It causes severe growth and feeding problems, very little body fat, unusual facial features, and serious metabolic complications beginning in infancy.

name: dopa
clinical_significance: A chemical precursor that the body can convert into dopamine. Levodopa, a form that reaches the brain, is used with another medicine to improve movement problems in Parkinson disease.

name: dopamine
clinical_significance: A chemical messenger used by nerve cells and some hormone-producing cells. It helps control movement, motivation, reward, attention, learning, blood-vessel tone, and release of certain hormones.

name: dopamine agonist
clinical_significance: A medicine that stimulates dopamine receptors and mimics some effects of dopamine. It is used for selected movement, hormone, or other disorders and may cause nausea, sleepiness, low blood pressure, hallucinations, or impulse-control problems.

name: dopamine antagonist
clinical_significance: A medicine or compound that blocks dopamine receptors. It is used in selected psychiatric, nausea, or digestive treatments but can cause movement problems, drowsiness, hormone changes, or other adverse effects.

name: dopamine receptor
clinical_significance: A protein on or inside a cell that responds to dopamine. Different receptor types affect movement, mood, hormone release, blood vessels, and other functions and are targets of some medicines.

name: dopamine transporter
clinical_significance: A protein that clears dopamine from the space between nerve cells by moving it back into the releasing nerve cell. Stimulants and some imaging tracers affect or measure its activity.

name: dopaminergic neuron
clinical_significance: A nerve cell that makes and releases dopamine. These cells help control movement, motivation, reward, attention, and hormone regulation; loss of some contributes to Parkinson disease.

name: dorea
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria commonly found in the human intestine and able to grow without oxygen. Finding it usually reflects normal gut organisms unless it comes from a normally sterile site with compatible illness.

name: doripenem
clinical_significance: An intravenous antibiotic that damages bacterial cell walls and is used for selected serious infections. It can cause allergy, diarrhea, seizures, or resistance and should be chosen according to the organism and patient.

name: dorsal
clinical_significance: Relating to the back or upper surface of a body part. In human anatomy it usually means toward the back, although in the hand or foot it refers to the opposite surface from the palm or sole.

name: dorsal funiculus
clinical_significance: A back column of the spinal cord containing nerve fibers that carry vibration, fine touch, and awareness of body position to the brain.

name: dorsolateral
clinical_significance: Describing a position toward the back and side of a body structure. For example, a dorsolateral area is behind and to one side rather than toward the front or middle.

name: dosage
clinical_significance: The amount, frequency, route, and duration of a medicine given to achieve benefit while limiting harm. It may need adjustment for age, weight, kidney or liver function, interactions, and the condition treated.

name: dosage forms
clinical_significance: The physical form in which a medicine is supplied, such as a tablet, capsule, liquid, cream, inhaler, injection, patch, suppository, or implant. The form affects how and how quickly it is given.

name: dose rate
clinical_significance: The amount of a medicine, radiation, or other exposure delivered during a specified time, such as milligrams per hour or grays per minute. It affects both benefit and toxicity.

name: double-blind method
clinical_significance: A research method in which treatment assignments are hidden from participants and relevant study personnel during the blinded phase to reduce expectation and assessment bias.

name: douche
clinical_significance: A stream of water or solution directed into a body cavity, most often the vagina. Vaginal douching is not needed for hygiene and can irritate tissue or disturb normal bacteria and increase infection risk.

name: Down syndrome
clinical_significance: A genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21. It may affect learning, muscle tone, growth, and appearance and is associated with heart, hearing, vision, thyroid, sleep, and digestive problems.

name: doxapram
clinical_significance: A medicine that stimulates breathing and is used rarely in selected situations. It can cause agitation, high blood pressure, fast or abnormal heart rhythms, seizures, or other serious effects.

name: doxazosin
clinical_significance: An alpha-1 blocker that relaxes blood vessels and prostate or bladder-neck muscle. It is used for high blood pressure or urinary symptoms from an enlarged prostate and can cause dizziness or fainting.

name: doxazosin mesylate
clinical_significance: A salt form of doxazosin, an alpha-1 blocker used for high blood pressure and urinary symptoms from an enlarged prostate. It can cause dizziness, low blood pressure, fainting, or falls, especially after the first dose.

name: doxepin
clinical_significance: A tricyclic antidepressant also used in low doses for insomnia or skin itching. It can cause drowsiness, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, abnormal heart rhythms, and dangerous toxicity in overdose.

name: doxercalciferol
clinical_significance: A vitamin D-like medicine used in selected people with chronic kidney disease to reduce excess parathyroid hormone. Calcium and phosphate must be monitored because levels can become too high.

name: doxorubicin
clinical_significance: An anthracycline cancer medicine that damages DNA and blocks cell division. It treats many cancers but can cause low blood counts, infection, nausea, hair loss, tissue injury after leakage, and dose-related heart damage.

name: doxorubicin hydrochloride
clinical_significance: A salt form of doxorubicin, an anthracycline cancer medicine used for many cancers. Important risks include low blood counts, infection, tissue injury after leakage, and dose-related heart damage.

name: doxycycline
clinical_significance: A tetracycline antibiotic that blocks bacterial protein production. It treats many bacterial and tick-borne infections and can cause nausea, sun sensitivity, esophageal irritation, diarrhea, or tooth and bone effects in developing children.

name: doxycycline hyclate
clinical_significance: A salt form of doxycycline, a tetracycline antibiotic that blocks bacterial protein production. It is used for susceptible infections; nausea, sun sensitivity, esophageal irritation, diarrhea, and allergic reactions may occur.

name: doxylamine
clinical_significance: A sedating antihistamine used in some sleep aids and pregnancy-related nausea treatments. It can cause drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, confusion, or impaired driving.

name: dracunculiasis
clinical_significance: Guinea-worm disease caused by a parasite acquired from unsafe drinking water containing infected tiny water fleas. About a year later, a painful blister usually forms on a leg as the adult worm emerges through the skin.

name: dracunculus medinensis
clinical_significance: The parasitic worm that causes Guinea-worm disease. People become infected by drinking water containing tiny infected water fleas; roughly a year later, an adult female worm emerges through the skin.

name: drainage
clinical_significance: Removal of blood, pus, fluid, or air from a body site, wound, or abnormal collection. It may occur naturally or use a needle, catheter, tube, or surgical opening to relieve pressure and aid healing.

name: dream
clinical_significance: A sequence of images, thoughts, sensations, or emotions experienced during sleep. Dreams are often most vivid during rapid-eye-movement sleep and may be influenced by stress, medicines, illness, or sleep disorders.

name: dried specimen
clinical_significance: A biological sample collected and dried on a prepared card or other surface for transport and laboratory testing. Dried blood spots are commonly used for screening, but correct collection and handling are essential.

name: drinking water
clinical_significance: Water safe for human consumption. It should be free of disease-causing organisms and harmful chemicals; boiling, filtration, chlorination, or bottled water may be needed when the supply is contaminated or uncertain.

name: dronabinol
clinical_significance: A medicine related to the active substance in cannabis, used for selected cases of chemotherapy-related nausea or severe appetite loss. It may cause dizziness, sleepiness, confusion, mood changes, or impaired coordination.

name: drool
clinical_significance: Saliva that unintentionally escapes from the mouth. It may result from excess saliva, difficulty swallowing, poor lip closure, dental problems, or a neurologic condition affecting mouth control.

name: droperidol
clinical_significance: A medicine used in selected clinical settings to treat severe nausea or agitation. It can prolong the heart’s electrical recovery time and rarely cause dangerous arrhythmias, so heart-risk factors and monitoring may be important.

name: dropper bottle
clinical_significance: A bottle with a device that releases liquid one drop at a time. The medicine’s concentration, prescribed number of drops, route, and measuring device must be followed because drop size can vary.

name: drosophila proteins
clinical_significance: Drosophila proteins are studied in fruit flies, a model organism used to investigate genes, development, neurologic disease, and drug effects. Findings can guide research but do not by themselves establish human diagnosis or treatment.

name: drosophilidae
clinical_significance: Drosophilidae is the family of fruit flies, including Drosophila melanogaster, a major model organism in genetics and biomedical research. It is not a human pathogen.

name: drowning
clinical_significance: Breathing impairment caused by submersion or immersion in liquid. It may be fatal or nonfatal. Lack of oxygen can injure the brain and other organs; complications include aspiration, lung injury, and respiratory failure.

name: drowsiness
clinical_significance: An increased tendency to fall asleep or reduced alertness. It may result from too little sleep, medicines, alcohol or other substances, metabolic illness, sleep disorders, infection, or neurologic disease; sudden severe drowsiness needs urgent assessment.

name: drug abuse
clinical_significance: Drug abuse refers to harmful or nonmedical use of a medicine or other substance. It can cause injury, overdose, dependence, impaired functioning, and social harms; assessment can connect people with effective treatment and support.

name: drug administration route
clinical_significance: The route of drug administration is how a medicine enters the body, such as by mouth, injection, inhalation, skin, or a body cavity. Route affects absorption, onset, effectiveness, and safety.

name: drug allergy
clinical_significance: A drug allergy is an immune reaction to a medicine that can range from a rash to life-threatening anaphylaxis. Accurate documentation helps prevent re-exposure, while side effects and intolerances should not be mislabeled as allergy.

name: drug dependence
clinical_significance: Drug dependence is a physical or psychological adaptation to repeated substance use. It may cause withdrawal symptoms or compulsive use; safe treatment can include gradual tapering, medication, and behavioral support.

name: drug emulsion
clinical_significance: A drug emulsion is a liquid formulation containing droplets of one liquid dispersed in another. Stability, dose uniformity, and correct storage matter because separation can change the amount delivered.

name: drug eruption
clinical_significance: A drug eruption is a skin reaction caused by a medicine, ranging from a mild rash to a severe, life-threatening reaction. Identifying the likely medicine and recognizing blistering, facial swelling, fever, or organ symptoms can guide urgent care.

name: drug implant
clinical_significance: A solid drug-containing pellet, container, or delivery device placed under the skin or in another tissue to release medicine continuously or slowly over an extended period. It may provide local or whole-body treatment; the product determines whether it biodegrades or requires removal and how it is monitored.

name: drug implants
clinical_significance: Drug implants release medicine from a device or solid formulation placed in tissue. They can provide sustained local or systemic dosing, but insertion-site infection, device problems, dose release, and removal requirements depend on the product.

name: drug interaction
clinical_significance: A drug interaction occurs when another medicine, food, supplement, or health condition changes a drug’s effect or blood level. Interactions can increase toxicity or reduce benefit, so medication review is important when treatment changes.

name: drug metabolism
clinical_significance: Drug metabolism is how the body chemically changes medicines, mainly through liver enzymes, to activate them or prepare them for removal. Age, genes, organ function, and other drugs can alter metabolism and affect dose or toxicity.

name: drug packaging
clinical_significance: Drug packaging protects a medicine from contamination, light, moisture, or damage and provides instructions for safe use. Faulty or confusing packaging can cause loss of potency, contamination, or dosing errors.

name: drug resistance
clinical_significance: Drug resistance occurs when a pathogen, cancer cell, or other target no longer responds to a medicine that previously worked. It can cause treatment failure and may require testing, a different drug, or a combination approach.

name: drug tolerance
clinical_significance: Drug tolerance is reduced response after repeated exposure, so a larger amount may be needed for the same effect. It can develop with some medicines or substances and may increase risk of dependence, overdose, or withdrawal.

name: drug vehicle
clinical_significance: A drug vehicle is the inactive liquid, cream, or other material that carries an active medicine. It affects how the medicine is delivered and absorbed and may itself cause irritation or allergy.

name: drusen
clinical_significance: Yellow-white deposits that form beneath the retina, often with aging. Small deposits may cause no symptoms; many or larger deposits can be associated with age-related macular degeneration and need eye examination.

name: dry cough
clinical_significance: A cough that produces little or no mucus. Common causes include viral infection, asthma, acid reflux, allergies, smoking, certain medicines, and other airway or lung conditions; persistent cough needs assessment.

name: Dry Eye syndrome
clinical_significance: Dry eye can cause burning, grittiness, fluctuating vision, and surface damage; severe pain, redness, or vision loss needs evaluation for corneal or inflammatory disease.

name: dry ice
clinical_significance: Solid carbon dioxide that changes directly into a cold gas. Contact can cause severe cold burns, and gas in an enclosed space can displace oxygen and cause unconsciousness or suffocation; never seal it in a container.

name: dry skin
clinical_significance: Skin that is rough, scaly, tight, or itchy because it has lost moisture or its protective barrier is damaged. Aging, cold or dry air, frequent washing, eczema, medicines, and some illnesses can contribute.

name: Duane retraction syndrome
clinical_significance: A birth-related eye-movement disorder caused by abnormal nerve control of an eye muscle. Turning the eye inward or outward may be limited, and the eyeball may pull backward and the eyelids narrow.

name: Dubowitz syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare developmental condition associated with poor growth, a small head, characteristic facial features, developmental or learning difficulties, and variable immune, skin, or behavioral problems. Features differ among affected people.

name: duct
clinical_significance: A tube or channel that carries fluid within the body, such as bile, pancreatic juice, saliva, tears, or secretions from a gland. Blockage or injury can cause pain, swelling, infection, or impaired organ function.

name: dull pain
clinical_significance: Aching, heavy, or pressure-like pain that is not sharp or stabbing. It can arise from muscles, organs, inflammation, or other tissues, and its significance depends on location, duration, associated symptoms, and examination findings.

name: duloxetine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: The salt form of duloxetine, a medicine used for depression, anxiety, some nerve pain, fibromyalgia, and chronic muscle or bone pain. It may cause nausea, sleep changes, sweating, blood-pressure changes, or withdrawal symptoms.

name: dumbbell ossification
clinical_significance: Bone formation or a bone lesion shaped like a dumbbell, often extending through an opening between the spinal canal and surrounding tissues. Imaging is needed to identify its cause and relationship to nerves or other structures.

name: dumping syndrome
clinical_significance: Symptoms caused by food moving too quickly from the stomach into the small intestine, often after stomach surgery. Early symptoms include cramps, diarrhea, flushing, sweating, dizziness, and a fast heartbeat; later low blood sugar may occur.

name: duocarmycins
clinical_significance: Duocarmycins are potent DNA-damaging compounds studied as anticancer drugs and as payloads for targeted drug conjugates. They are investigational; toxicity and clinical benefit depend on the specific formulation.

name: duodenal adenocarcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer arising from gland-forming cells in the duodenum. It may cause abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, anemia, jaundice, or blockage; diagnosis usually requires imaging, endoscopy, and tissue sampling.

name: duodenal atresia
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the duodenum is completely blocked, preventing food and digestive fluid from passing. Newborns usually develop green vomiting and feeding difficulty; it is often associated with other birth defects and requires surgery.

name: duodenal disease
clinical_significance: Any disorder affecting the duodenum, such as inflammation, ulcer, infection, bleeding, blockage, poor nutrient absorption, or a growth. Symptoms may include upper-abdominal pain, vomiting, anemia, or weight loss.

name: duodenal fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal connection between the duodenum and another organ, bowel segment, or skin. Digestive fluid may leak through it, causing infection, skin damage, dehydration, electrolyte loss, or poor nutrition.

name: duodenal hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from the duodenum, often caused by a peptic ulcer, inflammation, abnormal blood vessel, injury, or cancer. It may cause black stools, vomiting blood, weakness, dizziness, anemia, or shock.

name: duodenal infection
clinical_significance: Infection affecting the duodenum, caused by bacteria, parasites, viruses, or spread from nearby digestive disease. Symptoms can include upper-abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or bleeding.

name: duodenal neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the duodenum that may be benign or cancerous. It can cause pain, bleeding, vomiting, blockage, anemia, or jaundice; evaluation depends on its size, location, appearance, and tissue type.

name: duodenal obstruction
clinical_significance: A partial or complete blockage that prevents food and digestive fluid from passing through the duodenum. It can cause repeated vomiting, abdominal swelling, pain, and dehydration and may need urgent imaging and treatment.

name: duodenal stenosis
clinical_significance: Narrowing of the duodenum that partly blocks passage of food and digestive fluid. It may cause vomiting, abdominal swelling, pain, early fullness, poor feeding, or dehydration; treatment depends on the cause and severity.

name: duodenal ulcer
clinical_significance: An open sore in the duodenal lining, commonly related to Helicobacter pylori infection or anti-inflammatory medicines. It may cause upper-abdominal pain and can bleed, perforate the bowel, or obstruct food passage.

name: duodenitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the duodenal lining, which may result from Helicobacter pylori, excess acid, anti-inflammatory medicines, infection, celiac disease, or inflammatory bowel disease. It can cause upper-abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or bleeding.

name: duodenoscope
clinical_significance: A flexible viewing tube passed through the mouth and stomach to examine the duodenum and reach the openings of the bile and pancreatic ducts. It may be used during procedures to remove stones or place stents.

name: duodenostomy
clinical_significance: A surgically created opening from the duodenum to the skin or another part of the intestine. It may be used in selected cases for feeding, drainage, or bypassing a blockage.

name: duodenum
clinical_significance: The first part of the small intestine, between the stomach and jejunum. It receives bile and pancreatic juice, mixes them with stomach contents, and begins much of the digestion and absorption of nutrients.

name: dupuytren contracture
clinical_significance: Progressive thickening and shortening of tissue in the palm that pulls one or more fingers toward the palm and can limit hand function.

name: dura mater
clinical_significance: The tough outer layer of tissue surrounding and protecting the brain and spinal cord. It helps support blood vessels and contains the fluid-filled coverings around the central nervous system.

name: durapatite
clinical_significance: Another name for hydroxyapatite, the calcium-phosphate mineral that gives bones and teeth much of their hardness. Its amount and arrangement contribute to bone strength and can change in metabolic bone disease.

name: dust
clinical_significance: Small solid particles suspended in air or settled on surfaces. Inhaled dust can irritate the nose and lungs; some types can cause allergy, asthma, infection, poisoning, or long-term lung disease.

name: dutasteride
clinical_significance: A medicine that lowers the hormone dihydrotestosterone and gradually shrinks an enlarged prostate. It improves urinary symptoms and lowers retention risk but may reduce sexual function and lowers the blood-test level used to screen for prostate cancer.

name: dwarfism
clinical_significance: A medical condition causing unusually short adult height, often defined as about 4 feet 10 inches (147 cm) or less. Causes include skeletal disorders, growth-hormone problems, genetic conditions, and chronic disease; features vary by cause.

name: dye
clinical_significance: A colored substance used to stain tissue, identify cells, make structures visible, or provide contrast during a medical test. Some dyes can cause allergic reactions or affect the kidneys, especially when injected.

name: dye lasers
clinical_significance: Lasers that use a liquid organic dye to produce adjustable wavelengths of light. In medicine, selected wavelengths can treat blood-vessel or pigmented skin lesions; eye and skin protection is essential.

name: dynamin gtpase
clinical_significance: A family of GTP-binding proteins that constrict membranes during vesicle budding, endocytosis, and other cell-membrane processes.

name: dynein atpase
clinical_significance: The energy-using activity of dynein, a motor protein that moves materials inside cells along microtubules. Dynein also powers the movement of cilia and flagella, which help move fluid or cells.

name: dynorphin
clinical_significance: A naturally occurring opioid peptide that mainly activates kappa-opioid receptors in the nervous system. It influences pain, stress, mood, movement, and hormone regulation.

name: dyphylline
clinical_significance: A bronchodilator used in some countries to relax airway muscles in asthma or chronic obstructive lung disease. It may cause nausea, tremor, headache, nervousness, or a fast heartbeat.

name: dysarthria
clinical_significance: Slurred, weak, slow, or poorly coordinated speech caused by a problem in the brain, nerves, or muscles used for speaking. Sudden dysarthria can be a sign of stroke.

name: dysautonomia
clinical_significance: A disorder of the automatic nervous system that controls blood pressure, heart rate, sweating, temperature, digestion, bladder function, and sexual function. Causes include nerve disease, diabetes, medicines, and inherited conditions.

name: dysbarism
clinical_significance: Illness caused by a change in surrounding pressure, usually during diving, flying, or hyperbaric treatment. It includes decompression sickness and pressure injury to the ears, sinuses, lungs, or other tissues.

name: dyscalculia
clinical_significance: A persistent difficulty understanding numbers, quantities, or arithmetic that is not explained by inadequate teaching or general intellectual disability. It may begin during development or follow brain injury and can affect school or daily tasks.

name: dysesthesia
clinical_significance: An unpleasant abnormal sensation, such as burning, electric-shock pain, or painful sensitivity to light touch. It may result from injury or disease of nerves in the brain, spinal cord, or limbs.

name: dysfibrinogenemia
clinical_significance: An inherited or acquired condition in which fibrinogen, a blood-clotting protein, has abnormal structure or function. It may cause unusual bleeding, excessive clotting, or no symptoms and is diagnosed with clotting and specialized blood tests.

name: dysgammaglobulinemia
clinical_significance: An abnormal level or pattern of antibodies in the blood, with some antibody types low or absent and others normal or increased. It may cause repeated infections, autoimmune problems, or no symptoms and is identified by blood tests.

name: dysgerminoma
clinical_significance: A cancer of the ovary arising from germ cells, the cells that can develop into eggs. It occurs most often in adolescents and young adults and may cause pelvic pain, swelling, or an abdominal mass.

name: dysgeusia
clinical_significance: An altered sense of taste, including reduced, distorted, or unpleasant taste. Causes include viral infection, mouth or nose disease, nerve injury, nutritional deficiency, dry mouth, medicines, and other illnesses.

name: dysgraphia
clinical_significance: A persistent difficulty with handwriting, spelling, or expressing ideas in writing despite appropriate learning opportunities. It may reflect problems with motor skills, language, attention, or brain function and can occur with other learning disorders.

name: dyskeratosis congenita
clinical_significance: Dyskeratosis congenita is a serious inherited telomere disorder that can cause progressive bone-marrow failure, lung or liver disease, and a markedly increased risk of leukemia and solid cancers. Multispecialty monitoring and family evaluation are important.

name: dyskinesia
clinical_significance: Abnormal movement that is often involuntary, excessive, repetitive, twisting, or irregular. It may result from neurologic disease or medicines, including long-term treatment for movement disorders, and can interfere with walking, speaking, or daily activities.

name: dyslexia
clinical_significance: A learning disorder involving persistent difficulty recognizing words accurately or fluently, decoding them, spelling, or linking letters with speech sounds. It is not caused by low intelligence or poor motivation and may continue into adulthood.

name: dyslipidemias
clinical_significance: Conditions involving abnormal blood fats, including high LDL cholesterol, high triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, or mixed changes. They can increase the risk of artery disease and pancreatitis when triglycerides are very high.

name: dysmenorrhea
clinical_significance: Painful menstrual periods, usually causing cramping in the lower abdomen and sometimes back pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache, or dizziness. Severe, new, or worsening pain may indicate an underlying pelvic disorder.

name: dysostoses
clinical_significance: Inherited or developmental conditions in which one or more bones form or grow abnormally. They may affect the skull, face, spine, ribs, arms, or legs and can alter body shape, movement, growth, hearing, breathing, or other functions.

name: dyspareunia
clinical_significance: Recurrent or persistent genital or pelvic pain before, during, or after sexual activity, especially attempted vaginal penetration. Pain may be at the vaginal opening or deeper in the pelvis and can result from dryness, infection, skin disease, pelvic-floor muscle spasm, endometriosis, inflammation, injury, or emotional factors.

name: dyspepsia
clinical_significance: Persistent indigestion can reflect functional dyspepsia or conditions such as reflux, ulcer disease, or infection with Helicobacter pylori. Ongoing symptoms, bleeding, trouble swallowing, weight loss, or severe pain need medical evaluation.

name: dysphagia
clinical_significance: Swallowing difficulty can cause choking, aspiration pneumonia, dehydration, and malnutrition. Sudden onset may signal stroke; persistent or progressive symptoms need prompt assessment to identify the cause and protect nutrition and airway safety.

name: dysphasia
clinical_significance: Language impairment can follow stroke, brain injury, tumor, infection, or neurodegenerative disease and may affect communication, work, and independent decision-making. Sudden onset is an emergency symptom; speech-language therapy can support recovery.

name: dysphonia
clinical_significance: An abnormal voice, such as hoarseness, breathiness, roughness, strain, weakness, or loss of voice. Causes include infection, vocal-cord swelling or growths, nerve problems, voice overuse, reflux, and cancer; persistent symptoms need evaluation.

name: dysplasia
clinical_significance: Abnormal size, shape, or arrangement of cells in a tissue. It is not cancer, but some forms—especially when severe or persistent—can increase the chance of cancer and may need monitoring or treatment.

name: Dysplastic Nevus
clinical_significance: An atypical mole that may be larger, unevenly colored, or have an irregular border. Most do not become cancer, but having many atypical moles can increase melanoma risk; changing lesions should be examined.

name: dyspnea
clinical_significance: The feeling of difficult, uncomfortable, or insufficient breathing. Causes include asthma, lung or heart disease, anemia, infection, muscle weakness, anxiety, and other conditions.

name: dyssomnias
clinical_significance: Sleep disorders that mainly cause difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, waking at the desired time, or staying awake. Causes include sleep schedules, medical conditions, medicines, mood disorders, and abnormal sleep regulation.

name: dysthymic disorder
clinical_significance: Dysthymic disorder is the former name for persistent depressive disorder, a chronic low mood lasting at least two years. It can impair relationships, work, and daily functioning and may benefit from psychotherapy, medication, or both.

name: dystocia
clinical_significance: Difficult or unusually slow labor caused by ineffective contractions, the baby’s size or position, or the mother’s pelvis or soft tissues. It can increase risks for both parent and baby and may require assisted delivery or cesarean birth.

name: dystonia
clinical_significance: Dystonia can cause painful, disabling postures or movements that interfere with walking, writing, eating, or speaking. It may be inherited, medication-related, or due to brain injury or disease; treatment depends on its cause and affected body regions.

name: dystonia disorder
clinical_significance: A disorder causing repeated or sustained involuntary muscle contractions, which produce twisting movements, tremor, or abnormal postures. Symptoms may be limited to one area or involve the whole body.

name: dystonin
clinical_significance: A protein made from the DST gene that helps attach the internal framework of cells to other cell structures. Harmful gene changes can cause inherited nerve disease, muscle weakness, and fragile or blistering skin.

name: dystrophia unguium
