clinical_significance: Abnormal nail growth, shape, color, or texture. Causes include injury, fungal infection, inflammation, poor nutrition, medicines, reduced blood flow, and inherited disorders; treatment depends on the cause.

name: dystrophin
clinical_significance: A large sub-sarcolemmal cytoskeletal structural protein that anchors the internal actin cytoskeleton of skeletal and cardiac muscle fibers to the extracellular matrix through the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex; mutations in the \textit{DMD} gene lead to Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies.

name: dysuria
clinical_significance: Pain, burning, or discomfort during urination. Common causes include bladder or urethral infection, vaginal or penile inflammation, stones, irritation, and sexually transmitted infections; fever, flank pain, pregnancy, or blood in urine needs medical assessment.

name: ear
clinical_significance: The organ for hearing and balance. The outer ear collects sound, the middle ear transmits vibrations through the eardrum and tiny bones, and the inner ear converts sound and movement into signals sent to the brain.

name: ear canal
clinical_significance: The passage between the outer ear and eardrum. Its skin and earwax protect the middle ear, but infection, injury, foreign objects, or wax buildup can cause pain, discharge, or reduced hearing.

name: ear cartilage
clinical_significance: Flexible connective tissue that forms much of the outer ear and gives it shape. Injury or infection can cause pain, swelling, deformity, or damage that permanently changes the ear.

name: ear disease
clinical_significance: Any disorder of the outer, middle, or inner ear. It may cause pain, discharge, hearing loss, ringing, dizziness, infection, or balance problems; diagnosis requires examination of the ear and sometimes hearing or imaging tests.

name: ear infection
clinical_significance: Infection or inflammation affecting part of the ear, including the outer ear, ear canal, middle ear, or inner ear. It may cause ear pain, fever, discharge, reduced hearing, dizziness, or irritability in children.

name: ear neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the outer, middle, or inner ear that may be benign or cancerous. It can cause a persistent lump, pain, discharge, hearing loss, dizziness, or facial weakness and may require imaging or biopsy.

name: earache
clinical_significance: Pain felt in the ear or nearby area. It may arise inside the ear or be referred from the teeth, jaw, throat, or neck; identifying the source requires an examination when pain persists or is severe.

name: early diagnosis
clinical_significance: Identifying a disease before it has progressed or caused major complications. Earlier diagnosis may provide more treatment choices, but its benefit depends on the disease and the accuracy and usefulness of available tests.

name: early endosome
clinical_significance: A small membrane-bound compartment inside a cell that receives material brought in from the cell surface. It sorts that material for return to the surface, delivery elsewhere in the cell, or breakdown.

name: eat
clinical_significance: Eating behavior affects nutrition, growth, blood glucose, and overall health. Persistent inability to eat, painful eating, or a major change in intake can signal disease or an eating disorder and may lead to malnutrition or dehydration.

name: eating disorder
clinical_significance: A group of mental-health conditions involving harmful eating patterns that cause distress, medical risk, or impaired functioning. Some involve intense concern about food, weight, or body shape, but avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) does not require body-image concerns. Examples include anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge-eating disorder, and ARFID.

name: ebolavirus
clinical_significance: A group of viruses that includes those causing Ebola disease. Infection can produce severe fever, vomiting, diarrhea, bleeding, shock, and organ damage and spreads through contact with infected body fluids.

name: ebstein anomaly
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the tricuspid valve is positioned too low in the right ventricle and does not close normally. It can cause leakage of blood, enlargement of the right heart, blue coloring, heart failure, or abnormal rhythms.

name: eccentrocyte count
clinical_significance: The number or proportion of red blood cells whose hemoglobin is pushed toward one side of the cell. This smear finding may indicate oxidative injury or a hemolytic disorder but must be interpreted with other blood results.

name: ecchymosis
clinical_significance: A flat purple, blue, or brown skin mark caused by blood leaking into tissues, commonly after an injury. Easy or unexplained bruising can also result from medicines, low platelets, clotting disorders, fragile vessels, or illness.

name: eccrine gland
clinical_significance: A small sweat gland found throughout the skin that releases watery sweat onto the surface. It helps cool the body and is especially numerous on the palms, soles, and forehead.

name: eccrine porocarcinoma
clinical_significance: A rare skin cancer arising from cells of sweat-gland ducts. It may appear as a slowly enlarging lump or patch and can recur or spread; biopsy and complete removal are often needed.

name: eccrine poroma
clinical_significance: A usually harmless growth arising from a sweat-gland duct, often appearing as a flesh-colored, pink, or reddish lump on a hand or foot. It may bleed or be tender and can be removed if needed.

name: ecdysone
clinical_significance: Ecdysone is an insect steroid hormone that coordinates molting and metamorphosis. It is mainly relevant to insect biology and research, not human treatment.

name: echinacea
clinical_significance: A group of plants used in some herbal products for colds or claimed immune support. Evidence of benefit is inconsistent; allergic reactions and interactions with medicines can occur, especially in people with plant allergies.

name: echinococcosis
clinical_significance: A parasitic infection caused by larval Echinococcus tapeworms. Cystic disease usually forms cysts in the liver or lungs; alveolar disease grows invasively in the liver and may spread, requiring specialist treatment.

name: echinococcus granulosus
clinical_significance: A tapeworm whose larvae cause cystic echinococcosis. Dogs commonly carry the adult worm, and people become infected by swallowing eggs from contaminated material; cysts most often develop in the liver or lungs.

name: echinococcus multilocularis
clinical_significance: A tapeworm species whose larvae cause alveolar echinococcosis. The infection mainly affects the liver, where it grows slowly and invasively and may spread to other organs.

name: echinococcus vogeli
clinical_significance: A tapeworm species that causes polycystic echinococcosis, a disease producing multiple parasitic cysts mainly in the liver and sometimes other abdominal organs.

name: echinodermata
clinical_significance: Sea urchins, starfish, and related echinoderms are rarely relevant to human disease, but sea urchin spines can cause painful puncture wounds, retained foreign bodies, and persistent inflammation after marine exposure.

name: echinomycin
clinical_significance: An antitumor antibiotic that has been investigated as an experimental cancer treatment. It is not an established routine therapy; its clinical relevance is mainly in oncology research.

name: echocardiography
clinical_significance: Ultrasound imaging of the heart. It shows the chambers, valves, pumping action, and blood flow; the probe usually scans through the chest and may be passed into the esophagus for closer views.

name: echogenic bowel
clinical_significance: An ultrasound finding in which a fetus’s bowel appears unusually bright, sometimes as bright as bone. It may be a normal variation or may be associated with infection, chromosome conditions, cystic fibrosis, bleeding, or other fetal problems.

name: echolalia
clinical_significance: Repeating words or phrases spoken by someone else, either immediately or after a delay. It can occur in autism, developmental conditions, brain disorders, or some psychiatric illnesses and must be interpreted with other symptoms.

name: echolocation
clinical_significance: Echolocation is not a disease. It is a sensory strategy used by some people with severe vision loss, and understanding it can inform rehabilitation and functional assessment.

name: echothiophate iodide
clinical_significance: A long-acting cholinesterase inhibitor formerly used as eye drops to lower intraocular pressure and treat selected cases of accommodative esotropia. It can cause serious cholinergic effects and prolong succinylcholine action during anesthesia, so clinicians need to know about current or recent use.

name: echovirus
clinical_significance: A group of enteroviruses spread mainly by the fecal-oral route and sometimes by respiratory secretions. Infection is often mild or silent but can cause rash, respiratory illness, meningitis, encephalitis, heart inflammation, or severe newborn infection.

name: eclampsia
clinical_significance: A new seizure during pregnancy or after delivery related to preeclampsia or pregnancy-related high blood pressure. It is an emergency requiring protection of breathing, seizure treatment, blood-pressure control, and urgent obstetric care.

name: ecology
clinical_significance: Ecological relationships among organisms and their environments can affect human health by shaping exposure to infectious reservoirs, vectors, allergens, and environmental hazards.

name: econazole
clinical_significance: A topical antifungal that damages the fungal cell membrane and treats ringworm, athlete’s foot, jock itch, and some yeast skin infections. It may cause local irritation, burning, itching, or allergic contact dermatitis.

name: ecotoxicology
clinical_significance: The study of harmful effects of environmental contaminants on organisms. It supports public-health assessment of exposures that may cause poisoning, developmental effects, or other illness in people.

name: ectoderm
clinical_significance: The outer layer of cells in an early embryo. It develops into the skin, hair, nails, nervous system, eyes, ears, and other sense-related structures.

name: ectodermal dysplasia
clinical_significance: A group of inherited disorders affecting tissues such as hair, teeth, nails, skin, and sweat glands. Features may include sparse hair, abnormal teeth, reduced sweating, overheating, dry skin, and repeated infections.

name: ectomesenchymoma
clinical_significance: A rare cancer containing both nerve-related and connective-tissue parts, usually occurring in children. It may appear as a growing mass or cause pain; diagnosis requires tissue examination and specialist cancer treatment.

name: ectopia cordis
clinical_significance: A rare birth defect in which the heart lies partly or completely outside the chest because the chest wall did not form normally. It is usually life-threatening and requires immediate specialist care.

name: ectopia lentis
clinical_significance: Displacement of the eye’s natural lens from its normal position. Injury or inherited connective-tissue disorders may cause it, leading to blurred or double vision, unequal focusing, or increased eye pressure.

name: ectopic pregnancy
clinical_significance: A pregnancy implanted outside the endometrial cavity, most often in a fallopian tube. Less common sites include the cervix, ovary, abdominal cavity, cesarean-scar region, and interstitial portion of the tube. It may cause missed periods, pelvic or abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness, or no early symptoms. Rupture can cause hemoperitoneum, circulatory collapse, and shock.

name: ectopic tissue
clinical_significance: Tissue located in an unusual position, usually because it developed there, failed to move normally during growth, or became implanted elsewhere. Effects depend on the tissue and whether it causes pressure, bleeding, blockage, or abnormal function.

name: ectoplasm
clinical_significance: In cell biology, ectoplasm can refer to the outer, clearer region of cytoplasm, though the term is uncommon in modern clinical use. Spiritualist claims that ectoplasm is a physical substance have no established medical or scientific basis.

name: ectromelia
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which one or more limbs are absent or severely underdeveloped. In laboratory medicine, the same word names a mouse poxvirus infection; these are separate uses and should not be confused.

name: ectropion
clinical_significance: Outward turning of an eyelid, usually the lower lid, so the eye may not close or drain tears normally. It can cause tearing, dryness, irritation, and corneal injury; aging, weakness, scarring, or paralysis may contribute.

name: eculizumab
clinical_significance: An antibody medicine that blocks part of the immune system called complement. It treats selected blood, kidney, and nerve disorders but greatly increases the risk of meningococcal and other serious infections, so vaccination and monitoring are essential.

name: eczema
clinical_significance: A group of skin conditions that cause itchy, dry, inflamed, red, scaly, cracked, or sometimes oozing skin. The skin barrier is weakened, so the skin loses moisture and becomes easier to irritate. Atopic dermatitis is the most common type. Symptoms may worsen because of irritants, dry weather, heat, sweating, stress, or skin infection. Eczema is not contagious.

name: edatrexate
clinical_significance: An experimental antifolate chemotherapy related to methotrexate that was studied in clinical trials for cancer. It is not an established standard treatment; development was limited by toxicity and lack of demonstrated clinical advantage.

name: edema
clinical_significance: Swelling caused by extra fluid in body tissues. It may leave a dent when pressed or feel firm. Common causes include heart, kidney, or liver disease, poor vein drainage, blocked lymph flow, and some medicines.

name: edema trunk
clinical_significance: Abnormal accumulation of fluid in the soft tissues of the chest or abdomen, producing swelling from heart, kidney, liver, lymphatic, venous, inflammatory, or medication-related causes.

name: edetic acid
clinical_significance: Another name for EDTA, a chemical that binds certain metals. It is used in blood-collection tubes, laboratories, and selected treatments for heavy-metal poisoning.

name: edodekin alfa
clinical_significance: A recombinant form of interleukin-12 studied as an experimental immune-stimulating treatment, including in cancer trials. It is not an established routine therapy; clinical-trial use requires monitoring for potentially serious inflammatory and flu-like effects.

name: edotecarin
clinical_significance: An experimental topoisomerase I inhibitor studied in early cancer trials. It is not an approved or standard cancer treatment; reported toxicities included severe neutropenia and other gastrointestinal or infectious complications.

name: edrecolomab
clinical_significance: A monoclonal antibody against EpCAM that was studied for colorectal cancer. A large trial found no survival benefit when it was added to chemotherapy and worse outcomes with antibody alone, so it is not a standard treatment.

name: educational psychology
clinical_significance: Educational psychology can help identify how learning, development, and classroom factors affect a student's functioning. When learning difficulty may reflect a developmental, cognitive, or mental-health condition, educational assessment can support referral and coordinated care but does not itself establish a medical diagnosis.

name: edwardsiella
clinical_significance: Edwardsiella bacteria are associated with fish, reptiles, birds, and water. E. tarda is the species most clearly linked to human illness; E. hoshinae and E. ictaluri have uncertain or exceptionally rare human significance, so species identification matters when interpreting a clinical isolate.

name: edwardsiella hoshinae
clinical_significance: A bacterium found mainly in birds, reptiles, and water. It has occasionally been isolated from human specimens, but its role as a cause of human disease is unproven; detection should be interpreted with the clinical picture and microbiology findings.

name: edwardsiella ictaluri
clinical_significance: A fish pathogen, especially in catfish, that causes severe systemic infection in fish. Human infection is exceptionally uncertain, with only an isolated case report; it is not a recognized common zoonotic cause of illness.

name: edwardsiella tarda
clinical_significance: A bacterium found in fish, reptiles, and water that can rarely infect people. It may cause diarrhea, wound infection, gallbladder or abdominal infection, or bloodstream infection.

name: efalizumab
clinical_significance: A monoclonal antibody formerly used for plaque psoriasis. It was withdrawn after progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and other serious infections were reported; it should not be used as a current psoriasis treatment.

name: efaproxiral
clinical_significance: An experimental hemoglobin modifier studied as a radiosensitizer with whole-brain radiation for brain metastases. Trials did not establish a routine clinical role, and it is not a standard cancer treatment.

name: efavirenz
clinical_significance: An antiretroviral medicine that blocks HIV reverse transcriptase and is used in combination treatment for HIV infection. It can cause vivid dreams, dizziness, mood or nervous-system effects, rash, and important medicine interactions.

name: effectiveness
clinical_significance: How well a treatment, test, or public-health intervention achieves its intended result in usual real-world practice. It differs from efficacy, which describes performance under ideal, controlled study conditions.

name: efferent nerve
clinical_significance: A nerve pathway carrying signals away from the brain or spinal cord to muscles, glands, or organs. Damage can cause weakness, impaired automatic function, or loss of control in the affected area.

name: efferent pathway
clinical_significance: A nerve route carrying signals away from the brain or spinal cord to muscles, glands, or organs. It controls movement and automatic functions such as heart rate, digestion, sweating, and bladder activity.

name: effusion
clinical_significance: Abnormal buildup of fluid in a body space, such as around a joint, lung, or heart. It may cause swelling, pain, stiffness, or breathing difficulty; the cause may be injury, infection, inflammation, heart failure, or cancer.

name: eflornithine
clinical_significance: An inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase used intravenously, with specialist guidance, for selected cases of second-stage West African sleeping sickness; it is ineffective against East African disease. Topical eflornithine cream has also been used to slow unwanted facial-hair growth in women.

name: egg shell
clinical_significance: The hard calcium-containing outer covering of an egg. In medical imaging, “eggshell calcification” describes a thin rim of calcium around a lesion or lymph node.

name: eggerthella
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria that can live in the human intestine without causing disease. Rarely, especially in people with serious illness, they can cause bloodstream infection, abscesses, or other opportunistic infections.

name: eggerthella lenta
clinical_significance: A normal gut anaerobe that can occasionally cause serious bloodstream or deep abdominal infection, often in people with underlying disease or after disruption of the intestinal barrier. Identifying it in blood cultures should prompt assessment for an abdominal source and susceptibility-guided treatment.

name: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
clinical_significance: A group of inherited connective-tissue disorders that can cause unusually flexible joints, stretchy or fragile skin, easy bruising, and poor wound healing. Some types also weaken blood vessels or internal organs and require specialist care.

name: ehrlichia
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria spread mainly by ticks that infect certain white blood cells and cause ehrlichiosis. Infection may produce fever, headache, muscle aches, low blood counts, and serious illness if untreated.

name: ehrlichiosis
clinical_significance: A tick-borne infection caused by Ehrlichia bacteria. It commonly causes fever, headache, muscle aches, weakness, low white-cell or platelet counts, and raised liver enzymes; untreated infection can damage the brain, lungs, or other organs.

name: eicosadienoic acid
clinical_significance: A polyunsaturated fatty acid found in small amounts in human lipids. It is mainly of biochemical interest; measurement is not a routine clinical test and it has no established role as a stand-alone treatment.

name: eicosanoid
clinical_significance: A signaling substance made from certain fats that helps regulate inflammation, blood-vessel width, platelet activity, pain, and muscle contraction. Prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and thromboxanes are examples.

name: eicosanoid degradation
clinical_significance: Breakdown and inactivation of eicosanoids, the body’s short-lived fatty-acid signals. This limits how long and how strongly they affect inflammation, blood vessels, platelets, airways, and other muscles.

name: eicosanoid metabolism
clinical_significance: The body’s production, modification, and breakdown of prostaglandins, leukotrienes, thromboxanes, and related fatty-acid signals that influence inflammation, blood vessels, platelets, pain, and airway function.

name: eicosanoid receptor
clinical_significance: A protein on or inside a cell that responds to prostaglandins, leukotrienes, thromboxanes, or related lipid signals. Activation can change inflammation, blood-vessel tone, platelet activity, pain, or smooth-muscle contraction.

name: eicosapentaenoic acid
clinical_significance: The omega-3 fat EPA, found in oily fish and some supplements. It forms part of cell membranes and can be changed into signaling substances involved in inflammation and blood clotting.

name: eicosatetraenoic acid
clinical_significance: A 20-carbon fatty acid with four double bonds. Arachidonic acid is the best-known form and is used by cells to make prostaglandins, leukotrienes, thromboxanes, and other signaling substances.

name: eicosatrienoic acid
clinical_significance: A family of 20-carbon fatty acids involved in lipid metabolism and, for some forms, production of inflammatory signaling molecules. The specific isomer matters; the term alone does not identify a routine diagnostic marker or treatment.

name: eicosenoic acid
clinical_significance: A family of monounsaturated fatty acids present in dietary and body lipids. It is mainly relevant to biochemical research and nutritional composition, with no routine clinical test or treatment based on this term alone.

name: eikenella
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria found in the mouth. Some species can cause deep wound, bone, joint, or bloodstream infection, especially after human bites or injuries involving a person’s teeth.

name: eikenella corrodens
clinical_significance: A slow-growing bacterium normally found in the mouth that can cause infection after human bites or clenched-fist injuries. It may produce abscesses, bone or joint infection, or rarely bloodstream infection.

name: eisenmenger complex
clinical_significance: Eisenmenger syndrome is advanced pulmonary vascular disease from a longstanding heart shunt, causing cyanosis and high risk during pregnancy, surgery, and anesthesia; specialist care is essential.

name: ejaculation
clinical_significance: The release of semen through the penis, usually during sexual climax. It involves coordinated contractions of reproductive ducts, glands, pelvic muscles, and nerves; pain, blood, or major change in ejaculation needs assessment.

name: elastic cartilage
clinical_significance: Flexible supporting tissue containing many elastic fibers. It helps structures such as the outer ear, epiglottis, and pressure-equalizing ear tube keep their shape while bending.

name: elastic fiber
clinical_significance: A thin connective-tissue fiber that allows skin, lungs, blood vessels, and other structures to stretch and recoil. Damage or loss of elastic fibers can reduce flexibility or weaken tissues.

name: elastic tissue
clinical_significance: Connective tissue containing fibers that let structures stretch and return toward their original shape. It helps arteries pulse, lungs expand, skin recoil, and some ligaments support movement.

name: elasticity
clinical_significance: The ability of a tissue or material to return toward its original shape after stretching or compression. It contributes to the function of skin, lungs, blood vessels, muscles, and ligaments.

name: elastics
clinical_significance: Elastic bands used in medical or dental care, such as orthodontic bands, compression supports, wound devices, or surgical ties. Their purpose and safe use depend on the specific treatment.

name: elastin
clinical_significance: A flexible protein in connective tissue that lets skin, lungs, blood vessels, and other structures stretch and recoil. Aging, inflammation, and chronic sun exposure can damage elastin.

name: elastofibroma
clinical_significance: A harmless, slowly growing mass made of fatty and elastic tissue, most often beneath the lower shoulder blade in older adults. It may cause swelling or movement-related discomfort but often needs no treatment.

name: elastomer
clinical_significance: A flexible rubber-like material that can stretch and return toward its original shape. It is used in some medical tubing, seals, gloves, devices, and implants; biocompatibility depends on the material.

name: elastosis
clinical_significance: Abnormal buildup, breakdown, or alteration of elastic fibers in tissue. It is commonly associated with long-term sun exposure and can occur in some degenerative, inherited, or lung disorders.

name: elbow
clinical_significance: The joint connecting the upper arm and forearm, formed by the humerus, radius, and ulna. It allows bending and straightening and works with nearby joints to rotate the forearm.

name: elbow extensor
clinical_significance: A muscle that straightens the elbow, mainly the triceps and anconeus. These muscles help push, reach, lift, throw, and control lowering of the arm.

name: elbow flexors
clinical_significance: Muscles that bend the elbow, mainly the biceps, brachialis, and brachioradialis. They help lift the forearm and turn the palm upward; injury, pain, nerve problems, or tendon damage can weaken movement.

name: elbow joint
clinical_significance: A joint complex between the humerus, radius, and ulna that allows the arm to bend and straighten and the forearm to rotate. Cartilage, ligaments, muscles, and fluid-filled coverings provide stability and movement.

name: elder abuse
clinical_significance: An intentional act or failure to provide care that harms an older person. It includes physical, emotional, sexual, or financial abuse and neglect; warning signs require sensitive assessment and safeguarding according to local law.

name: elective abortion
clinical_significance: A planned ending of a pregnancy using medicines or a procedure, usually before an immediate medical emergency develops. The method depends on pregnancy duration, health, personal choice, and local clinical and legal requirements.

name: electric impedance
clinical_significance: The opposition a material or tissue offers to alternating electrical current, measured in ohms. Medical devices use impedance changes to assess body composition, monitor signals, or detect contact and function.

name: electric organ
clinical_significance: Electric organs generate electrical discharges in certain fish and are studied as models of excitable tissue and bioelectricity. They are not human organs; contact with some strongly electric species can cause painful shock or injury.

name: electrical alternans
clinical_significance: A beat-to-beat change in the size or direction of ECG complexes. It can occur when the heart moves within a large fluid collection around it and may indicate cardiac tamponade, an emergency.

name: electrical conductance
clinical_significance: The ability of a material or tissue to carry electrical current. It depends on how easily charged particles move and is important in nerve, muscle, heart, and medical-device measurements.

name: electrical injury
clinical_significance: Damage caused by electrical current passing through the body. Severity depends on voltage, current, duration, pathway, and skin resistance; effects may include burns, heart-rhythm problems, muscle breakdown, nerve injury, falls, or breathing failure.

name: electrical synapse
clinical_significance: A direct connection between cells through tiny channels that let charged particles and electrical signals pass rapidly from one cell to another. It helps coordinate some brain, heart, and other tissue activity.

name: electroacupuncture
clinical_significance: A form of acupuncture in which a mild electrical current is passed through inserted needles. It is used as a complementary option for some symptoms, especially pain, but evidence varies by condition; it should not replace indicated care, and clinicians should know about implanted electrical devices or bleeding risks.

name: electrocardiogram lead
clinical_significance: A named viewing direction in an electrocardiogram. Correct lead placement and labeling are essential because errors can distort the tracing and mimic or conceal cardiac abnormalities, including ischemia.

name: electrocardiography
clinical_significance: The process of recording the heart’s electrical activity through skin electrodes, usually as a 12-lead ECG. It assesses rate, rhythm, conduction, chamber strain, reduced blood flow, prior injury, and some medicine or electrolyte effects.

name: electrochemistry
clinical_significance: Principles relating chemical reactions to electrical charge and current. They underpin laboratory sensors such as some glucose and blood-gas analyzers, but the term itself is not a clinical test or diagnosis.

name: electrochemotherapy
clinical_significance: A local cancer treatment that combines a chemotherapy drug with brief electrical pulses to increase drug entry into tumor cells. It is used in selected settings for skin or subcutaneous tumors and metastases; suitability depends on tumor location, drug, and specialist protocols.

name: electrocoagulation
clinical_significance: A surgical technique using electrical energy to heat tissue, seal blood vessels, or destroy selected tissue. It is used to control bleeding and may cause burns, scarring, or unintended injury.

name: electroconvulsive therapy
clinical_significance: A treatment that causes a brief controlled seizure while the person is under general anesthesia. It can rapidly treat severe depression, catatonia, or mania; temporary confusion and memory problems are common risks.

name: electrocorticography
clinical_significance: An invasive recording of electrical activity directly from the brain surface, used in selected epilepsy evaluations and operations to help map seizure-related cortex. Because electrodes are placed inside the skull, it carries procedural risks and is reserved for specialist care.

name: electrode
clinical_significance: A conductive contact that carries electrical signals or current to or from the body, a device, or a laboratory sample. Electrodes are used in tests such as ECG and EEG and in selected treatments.

name: electrodesiccation
clinical_significance: A form of electrosurgery that dries and destroys selected superficial tissue, commonly used for some skin lesions. Choice depends on a secure diagnosis and lesion type; risks include pain, scarring, pigment change, and incomplete removal, and suspicious lesions may need biopsy or excision instead.

name: electroencephalography
clinical_significance: The process of recording brain electrical activity with electrodes on the scalp. It can help identify abnormal patterns associated with seizures, sleep disorders, or diffuse brain dysfunction.

name: electrofocusing
clinical_significance: A laboratory technique that separates proteins according to their isoelectric point using an electric field. It is used in specialized analyses such as protein and hemoglobin characterization, but results need interpretation with other clinical findings.

name: electrolysis
clinical_significance: Hair removal using electrical energy delivered through a fine probe into individual hair follicles. Repeated treatment may permanently reduce hair growth, but pain, irritation, pigment changes, scarring, or infection can occur.

name: electrolyte
clinical_significance: A mineral that carries an electrical charge when dissolved in body fluids, such as sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, chloride, or phosphate. Electrolytes help control nerves, muscles, heart rhythm, fluid balance, and acid-base balance.

name: electromyography
clinical_significance: A test that records the electrical activity of skeletal muscles, often together with nerve-conduction studies, to evaluate peripheral nerve, nerve-root, neuromuscular-junction, and muscle disorders.

name: electron
clinical_significance: Electrons are subatomic particles whose movement underlies electrical signals and many laboratory and imaging technologies. The term itself is not a diagnosis; electron-beam radiation can also be used in selected cancer treatments.

name: electron microscopy
clinical_significance: High-resolution imaging used in specialized diagnostic laboratories to examine tissue ultrastructure, kidney biopsies, cilia, and some infectious agents. It can reveal changes not visible with routine light microscopy, but is not needed for most diagnoses.

name: electron transport
clinical_significance: A series of cellular reactions that transfers electrons to generate energy. Defects in mitochondrial electron transport can cause inherited metabolic disease affecting the brain, muscles, heart, or other organs.

name: electrooculography
clinical_significance: A test that records electrical changes associated with eye movement and retinal-pigment-epithelium function. It may help assess selected retinal disorders, including Best disease, and is interpreted alongside examination and other tests.

name: electro-osmosis
clinical_significance: Movement of fluid through a porous material under an electric field. It is mainly a laboratory and engineering concept, with potential relevance to drug delivery and diagnostic devices rather than a routine clinical test.

name: electrophoresis
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that separates charged molecules by how they move through a gel or liquid in an electric field. It can analyze proteins, hemoglobin, DNA, and other substances.

name: electrophysiology
clinical_significance: The study of electrical activity in living cells and tissues. Clinical electrophysiology includes tests and treatments involving heart rhythm, nerves, muscles, and the connections between them.

name: electroporation
clinical_significance: A brief electrical pulse that temporarily increases cell-membrane permeability, allowing molecules or drugs to enter cells. Medical uses include laboratory gene transfer and selected tumor treatments; risks depend on the tissue, device, and procedure.

name: electroretinography
clinical_significance: A test that records the retina’s electrical response to flashes or patterned light. It helps evaluate inherited or acquired retinal disorders when examination and imaging do not fully explain visual loss.

name: element
clinical_significance: A pure substance made of atoms with the same number of protons. Some elements, such as iron and iodine, are essential nutrients; others can be toxic, and health effects depend on dose and exposure.

name: elephantiasis
clinical_significance: Severe, long-lasting swelling and thickening of skin, usually in a limb or the scrotum, caused by blocked lymph drainage. Lymphatic filariasis is one cause; other causes include repeated infection, surgery, cancer, or injury.

name: elesclomol sodium
clinical_significance: An experimental anticancer compound studied in clinical trials, including combination treatment for melanoma. It has not become an established standard therapy, so its significance is limited to research.

name: eligibility determination
clinical_significance: A decision about whether a person meets stated requirements for a clinical trial, treatment, or service. Eligibility is distinct from clinical suitability; clinicians still weigh expected benefit, risks, alternatives, and the person’s preferences.

name: eligible
clinical_significance: Meeting the requirements for a treatment, clinical trial, screening program, benefit, or healthcare service. Eligibility does not guarantee that an intervention is appropriate or that it will be available.

name: elinafide
clinical_significance: An experimental anticancer agent studied in early clinical research. It has no established routine treatment role and should not be confused with an approved cancer medicine.

name: elixir
clinical_significance: A sweetened liquid preparation, historically sometimes containing alcohol, used to carry a medicine. The exact ingredients and strength determine its medical effects, interactions, and poisoning risk.

name: elizabethkingia
clinical_significance: A group of environmental bacteria that can rarely cause severe infection, especially in newborns, older adults, or people with weakened immunity. Illness may involve the blood, lungs, brain, or other organs.

name: ellagic acid
clinical_significance: A plant-derived polyphenol found in some fruits and nuts and studied for possible antioxidant effects. Evidence does not establish it as a treatment or prevention for disease; concentrated supplements may have uncertain safety and interactions.

name: elliptocyte count
clinical_significance: The number or proportion of oval or elongated red blood cells seen on a blood smear. Increased elliptocytes may occur in an inherited red-cell disorder or some anemias and must be interpreted with other results.

name: elliptocytosis
clinical_significance: A condition in which many red blood cells are oval or elongated rather than round. Inherited forms may cause red cells to break down early and produce anemia, while some people have no symptoms.

name: elongin
clinical_significance: A protein complex that helps RNA polymerase II continue copying genetic information into RNA. It contributes to gene regulation and cell function and is mainly a molecular-biology term.

name: elotuzumab
clinical_significance: An antibody medicine that helps the immune system recognize and attack myeloma cells. It is used with other medicines for selected multiple-myeloma patients and can cause infusion reactions, infection, fatigue, or low blood counts.

name: eltrombopag
clinical_significance: An oral medicine that stimulates the thrombopoietin receptor in bone marrow and increases platelet production. It is used for selected low-platelet conditions and can affect the liver, clotting risk, or blood counts.

name: eltrombopag olamine
clinical_significance: The salt form of eltrombopag, an oral medicine that increases platelet production in selected blood disorders. Liver tests, blood counts, medicine interactions, and clotting risk may require monitoring.

name: emaciation
clinical_significance: Extreme loss of body weight, muscle, and fat caused by severe malnutrition, chronic disease, cancer, infection, or other illness. It can weaken immunity and function and requires assessment of causes and nutritional needs.

name: embolectomy
clinical_significance: Removal of a traveling blood clot or other blockage from a blood vessel with surgery or a catheter procedure to restore blood flow. It may be urgent when a limb or organ is threatened.

name: embolism
clinical_significance: Blockage of a blood vessel by material that traveled through the bloodstream from another site. The material is most often a clot but may be fat, air, infected material, or rarely tumor tissue.

name: embolus
clinical_significance: Material traveling through the bloodstream that may lodge in a smaller vessel and block it. It may be a blood clot, fat, air bubble, infected material, or rarely tumor tissue.

name: embryo
clinical_significance: A developing human from fertilization through the end of the eighth week after fertilization. From the ninth week until birth, the developing human is called a fetus.

name: embryo neoplasm
clinical_significance: A tumor arising from primitive cells resembling developing embryonic tissue, usually in a child. Diagnosis and treatment depend on the tissue of origin, microscopic and molecular features, location, and spread.

name: embryogenesis
clinical_significance: The process by which an embryo develops after fertilization through cell division, movement, specialization, and formation of organs and body structures.

name: embryology
clinical_significance: The study of development from fertilization through the embryonic and fetal stages, including how organs and body structures form, grow, and become specialized.

name: embryonal carcinoma
clinical_significance: An aggressive germ-cell tumor composed of primitive malignant cells, occurring in the testis, ovary, or other sites and often treated with chemotherapy and surgery.

name: embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma
clinical_significance: A malignant skeletal-muscle-lineage tumor that commonly affects young children and may arise in the head and neck, urinary tract, or reproductive tract.

name: embryonic
clinical_significance: Relating to an embryo, the developing human or animal during the early period after fertilization. In humans, the embryonic period ends at about eight weeks after fertilization, followed by the fetal period.

name: embryonic cell
clinical_significance: A cell of an early embryo capable of division and differentiation into specialized tissues; embryonic stem cells have broad developmental potential.

name: embryonic induction
clinical_significance: A developmental process in which one group of embryonic cells signals nearby cells to develop into a particular tissue or structure.

name: embryonic mosaic
clinical_significance: A developing embryo containing two or more groups of cells with different genetic makeups, produced by a change after fertilization. Effects depend on the cells involved and the proportion of each cell group.

name: embryonic stage
clinical_significance: The early developmental period after fertilization during which the basic body plan and major organs begin to form. In human pregnancy it lasts through about eight weeks after fertilization.

name: emergency care
clinical_significance: Immediate assessment and treatment for a serious or time-sensitive illness or injury. Clinicians first protect breathing, circulation, brain function, and control of bleeding, pain, or infection, then arrange continued treatment or transfer.

name: emergency treatment
clinical_significance: Urgent care for an acute illness or injury in which delay could threaten life, limb, or organ function. Priorities include stabilizing breathing and circulation, treating immediately reversible threats, and arranging definitive care.

name: emetic
clinical_significance: A substance or medicine that causes vomiting. Emetics are generally not used for poisoning because vomiting can cause aspiration, worsen burns or injury, and delay safer treatment.

name: emitefur
clinical_significance: An experimental fluoropyrimidine anticancer drug studied in clinical trials. It is not an established routine treatment; potential use and toxicity have been evaluated only in research settings.

name: emodin
clinical_significance: A plant chemical studied for laxative, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer effects. Evidence and safety are not established for routine treatment, and concentrated products may cause diarrhea, dehydration, or medicine interactions.

name: emotion
clinical_significance: A feeling state involving subjective experience, brain and body responses, behavior, and interpretation of events. Emotions are normal, but persistent or extreme changes may occur with mental or physical illness.

name: emotional adjustment
clinical_significance: The process of adapting thoughts, feelings, and behavior to illness, loss, stress, or a major life change. Difficulty adjusting may cause persistent distress or impaired functioning and may benefit from support or treatment.

name: emotional dependency
clinical_significance: Reliance on another person for reassurance, self-worth, or emotional stability to a degree that limits independence or causes distress. It is not a diagnosis by itself and may reflect anxiety, low self-esteem, trauma, or relationship difficulties.

name: empathy
clinical_significance: The ability to understand another person’s feelings and point of view. It supports respectful communication and compassionate care but does not require agreeing with the person or experiencing the same feelings.

name: empedobacter
clinical_significance: A genus of environmental gram-negative bacteria that rarely cause human infection. Some species, especially E. brevis, have been reported in bloodstream, eye, or neonatal infections, so an isolate may matter in a symptomatic or medically vulnerable patient and should be identified and tested for susceptibility.

name: empedobacter brevis
clinical_significance: A rare environmental bacterium that has caused occasional serious human infections, including bloodstream, eye, and neonatal infections. Because cases are uncommon and antimicrobial susceptibility can vary, clinical isolates require careful identification and susceptibility testing.

name: empedobacter falsenii
clinical_significance: A rare environmental bacterium reported in clinical specimens and occasionally associated with opportunistic infection. Its significance depends on the specimen, symptoms, and host risk factors; it should not automatically be treated as a pathogen when found in a nonsterile sample.

name: employee
clinical_significance: A person who works for an employer under an agreement. In occupational health, assessment may consider workplace exposures, safety, physical or mental function, and ability to perform duties safely.

name: employment status
clinical_significance: A social and occupational factor relevant to health assessment. Work status may affect income, insurance or access to care, workplace exposures, functional needs, and eligibility for employment-related support, but it is not itself a medical diagnosis.

name: empyema
clinical_significance: A collection of pus in a normally sterile body space, most often infected fluid around a lung. It can cause fever, chest pain, cough, breathlessness, and sepsis and usually requires antibiotics plus drainage.

name: emtricitabine
clinical_significance: An antiretroviral medicine that blocks HIV reverse transcriptase and is used with other medicines to treat or prevent HIV infection. Kidney function and hepatitis B status are important because stopping it can worsen hepatitis B.

name: emulsion
clinical_significance: A mixture of two liquids that normally do not blend, such as oil and water, with one dispersed in the other. Emulsions are used in some medicines, nutrition products, cosmetics, and laboratory preparations.

name: enalapril
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks formation of angiotensin II, relaxing blood vessels and reducing strain on the heart. It treats high blood pressure and heart failure but can cause cough, high potassium, kidney problems, or rarely facial swelling.

name: enalaprilat
clinical_significance: The active injectable form related to enalapril that blocks angiotensin II formation and lowers blood pressure. It is used in selected settings and can cause low blood pressure, high potassium, kidney problems, or facial swelling.

name: enamel organ
clinical_significance: The developing tissue of a tooth that produces enamel and helps shape the crown. It is present during tooth formation and later contributes to the protective covering around the developing tooth.

name: enanthema
clinical_significance: A rash or lesion on a moist membrane lining the mouth, throat, genitals, or another body surface. Infection, inflammation, medicines, or systemic disease may cause it.

name: encephalitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of brain tissue, often caused by an infection or an abnormal immune reaction. It may cause fever, headache, confusion, seizures, behavior change, weakness, or movement problems and requires urgent medical care.

name: encephalitis virus
clinical_significance: A virus capable of infecting the brain and causing encephalitis. It may spread through mosquitoes, ticks, animals, respiratory secretions, food, or other routes depending on the virus.

name: encephalitozoon
clinical_significance: A group of tiny spore-forming parasites that can infect the intestine, eyes, kidneys, or several organs. Serious disease occurs mainly in people with weakened immunity.

name: encephalocele
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the coverings of the brain and sometimes brain tissue protrude through an opening in the skull. It may cause a visible head swelling and can be associated with seizures, fluid buildup, developmental problems, or other brain abnormalities.

name: encephalomalacia
clinical_significance: Softening or loss of brain tissue after injury, stroke, bleeding, infection, or reduced blood flow. The resulting permanent damage may cause seizures, weakness, movement problems, memory changes, or other neurologic effects.

name: encephalomyelitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation affecting both the brain and spinal cord, caused by infection or an abnormal immune response. It may cause confusion, seizures, weakness, numbness, balance problems, or bladder changes and requires urgent neurologic assessment.

name: encephalopathy
clinical_significance: A disorder that broadly affects brain function, causing confusion, drowsiness, personality change, difficulty thinking, or coma. Causes include infection, toxins, organ failure, medicines, metabolic problems, seizures, and reduced oxygen.

name: enchondroma
clinical_significance: A usually harmless cartilage growth inside a bone, often in the hands or long bones and found by chance. Pain, enlargement, fracture, or unusual imaging features may require evaluation for a more serious tumor.

name: enchondromatosis
clinical_significance: A disorder in which multiple cartilage growths develop inside bones. It can cause uneven growth, limb deformity, pain, or fractures; a small number of lesions may become cancerous and require monitoring.

name: enclomiphene
clinical_significance: An isomer of clomiphene studied for secondary hypogonadism in men, with the aim of stimulating the body’s own testosterone production while preserving sperm production. It is not an FDA-approved treatment; safety concerns in trials included thromboembolic and cardiovascular events, so unregulated use is not appropriate.

name: encopresis
clinical_significance: Repeated passage of stool in inappropriate places by a child at an age or developmental level when bowel control is expected. It is often related to long-term constipation and retained stool but may have other medical, developmental, or emotional contributors.

name: end point
clinical_significance: A predefined outcome or measurement used to judge a clinical study, treatment, diagnostic test, or disease process. It may be a symptom, laboratory result, event, survival measure, or patient-reported outcome.

name: endarterectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery that removes fatty plaque and diseased inner lining from an artery to improve blood flow, most often a carotid artery in the neck. Possible complications include bleeding, stroke, heart attack, or nerve injury.

name: endarteritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the inner lining of an artery that can narrow the vessel and reduce blood flow. Causes include infection, autoimmune disease, injury, and other vascular disorders.

name: endemic diseases
clinical_significance: Diseases that remain present at a predictable level in a particular population or region. Their frequency is shaped by local environment, immunity, behavior, exposures, healthcare access, and prevention measures.

name: endemic goiter
clinical_significance: Thyroid enlargement occurring commonly in a population, traditionally because of insufficient iodine intake. It may occur with normal, low, or high thyroid function depending on the cause.

name: endocannabinoid
clinical_significance: A signaling molecule made naturally by the body that activates cannabinoid receptors. Endocannabinoids help regulate pain, appetite, mood, memory, movement, and immune activity.

name: endocardial fibroelastosis
clinical_significance: Thickening of the inner lining of the heart from excess fibrous and elastic tissue, usually in infants or children. It can stiffen the heart or weaken its pumping and may lead to heart failure.

name: endocarditis
clinical_significance: Infection or inflammation of the heart’s inner lining, usually involving a valve. It can cause fever, fatigue, a new or changed murmur, stroke or other emboli, valve destruction, or heart failure.

name: endocardium
clinical_significance: The thin inner lining of the heart chambers and valves. It provides a smooth surface for blood flow and continues into the inner lining of blood vessels; inflammation or infection can damage it.

name: endocervical
clinical_significance: Relating to the inner canal or lining of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus that connects the uterine cavity with the vagina.

name: endocrine
clinical_significance: Relating to hormones released into the bloodstream by glands or specialized cells. Endocrine organs include the thyroid, pituitary, adrenal glands, pancreas, and reproductive glands.

name: endocrine disease
clinical_significance: A disorder of a hormone-producing gland or hormone action. It may affect growth, metabolism, reproduction, stress responses, blood pressure, or fluid and electrolyte balance.

name: endocrine finding
clinical_significance: A symptom, examination result, imaging result, or laboratory result that may suggest abnormal hormone production, hormone action, or an endocrine-gland disorder.

name: endocrine function
clinical_significance: The production, release, transport, and action of hormones that regulate metabolism, growth, reproduction, stress responses, blood pressure, and fluid or electrolyte balance.

name: endocrine gland
clinical_significance: An organ that releases hormones directly into the bloodstream. Its chemical messages regulate growth, metabolism, reproduction, stress responses, blood pressure, and other body functions.

name: endocrine neoplasm
clinical_significance: A benign or cancerous growth arising in a hormone-producing gland or cell. It may release too much hormone or cause symptoms by pressing on nearby structures; evaluation depends on its location and behavior.

name: endocrine system
clinical_significance: The network of glands and hormone-producing cells and tissues that release chemical messengers into the blood. It includes structures such as the hypothalamus, pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenal glands, pancreatic islets, and gonads; its hormones regulate growth, metabolism, reproduction, stress responses, sleep, blood pressure, fluid balance, and other aspects of homeostasis.

name: endocrinologists
clinical_significance: Physicians specializing in hormone, endocrine-gland, and metabolic disorders, including diabetes, thyroid disease, adrenal disease, osteoporosis, and reproductive hormone problems.

name: endocrinology
clinical_significance: The medical specialty concerned with hormones, endocrine glands, and metabolism. It diagnoses and treats conditions affecting diabetes, thyroid function, growth, reproduction, bones, adrenal glands, and fluid or electrolyte balance.

name: endocytosis
clinical_significance: The process by which a cell folds its outer membrane around material and brings it inside in a small sac. Cells use it to absorb nutrients, remove particles, and control surface signals.

name: endoderm
clinical_significance: The innermost of the three early embryonic cell layers. It develops into the linings of the digestive and respiratory systems and contributes to organs such as the liver, pancreas, thyroid, and bladder.

name: endodontics
clinical_significance: The dental specialty concerned with the soft tissue inside teeth, root canals, and tissues around tooth roots. Endodontists diagnose and treat tooth infection, inflammation, injury, and related pain.

name: endodontist
clinical_significance: A dentist with advanced training in diagnosing and treating disease or injury of the tooth’s inner tissue, root canals, and tissues around tooth roots. They commonly perform complex root-canal treatment.

name: endogenous opiates
clinical_significance: Opioid-like substances naturally made by the body, including endorphins, enkephalins, and dynorphins. They act on opioid receptors and influence pain, stress, mood, reward, movement, and other nervous-system functions.

name: endogenous retrovirus
clinical_significance: A piece of viral DNA inherited in the human genome from an ancient virus that infected a reproductive cell. Most such sequences are inactive, although some can influence gene control or normal development.

name: endolimax
clinical_significance: A group of amoebas that can live in the intestine. They are usually harmless colonizers rather than causes of disease, and a stool finding should be interpreted with symptoms and other test results.

name: endolimax nana
clinical_significance: An amoeba that can live harmlessly in the intestine and appear in stool tests. It usually does not cause illness; its presence may indicate exposure to contaminated food or water and should not alone explain digestive symptoms.

name: endolymph
clinical_significance: Fluid inside the membranous part of the inner ear that helps sensory organs detect sound and head movement. Abnormal pressure or composition can contribute to dizziness, hearing changes, or ringing.

name: endometrial
clinical_significance: Relating to the endometrium, the inner lining of the uterus. This lining changes during the menstrual cycle and can support implantation of a pregnancy; abnormal growth may cause bleeding or affect fertility.

name: endometrial adenocarcinoma
clinical_significance: A gland-forming cancer of the uterine lining. It often causes abnormal bleeding, especially after menopause; treatment depends on the cancer’s type, grade, stage, molecular features, and overall health.

name: endometrial biopsy
clinical_significance: Removal of a small sample of the uterine lining for laboratory examination, often to investigate abnormal bleeding or suspected overgrowth or cancer. Cramping and light bleeding are common; occasionally the sample is insufficient for diagnosis.

name: endometrial carcinoma
clinical_significance: Cancer arising from the uterine lining, often causing abnormal bleeding, particularly after menopause. Diagnosis requires examination of uterine-lining tissue, and treatment depends on type and spread.

name: endometrial disorder
clinical_significance: Any condition affecting the uterine lining, including inflammation, polyps, abnormal overgrowth, endometriosis-related changes, or cancer. It may cause heavy or irregular bleeding, pelvic pain, infertility, or no symptoms.

name: endometrial hyperplasia
clinical_significance: Overgrowth of glands in the uterine lining, often after prolonged estrogen exposure without enough progesterone. It may cause heavy, irregular, or postmenopausal bleeding. It is classified as hyperplasia without atypia or atypical hyperplasia, also called endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia (EIN). Hyperplasia without atypia is not precancer; atypical hyperplasia/EIN is precancerous and can sometimes be found alongside endometrial cancer, so it needs prompt evaluation.

name: endometrial neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth of the uterine lining that may be benign, precancerous, or cancerous. Symptoms, tissue examination, imaging, and—if cancer is present—stage determine treatment.

name: endometrial polyp
clinical_significance: A localized growth of the uterine lining that projects into the uterine cavity. It may cause irregular or heavy bleeding, infertility, or no symptoms; some polyps contain precancerous or cancerous cells.

name: endometrioma
clinical_significance: An ovarian cyst caused by endometriosis in which old blood collects. It may cause pelvic pain, painful periods, pain during sex, or infertility, although some people have no symptoms.

name: endometriosis
clinical_significance: A chronic inflammatory condition in which tissue resembling the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus, most often in the pelvis, ovaries, fallopian tubes, or tissue around the pelvic organs. It can also affect the bowel or bladder. This tissue responds to hormones and can cause repeated inflammation, bleeding, scar tissue, adhesions, or ovarian cysts. Symptoms may include severe period pain, ongoing pelvic pain, heavy or irregular bleeding, pain during sex or bowel movements, painful uri

name: endometritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of the uterine lining, often after childbirth, miscarriage, abortion, or a procedure entering the uterus. It may cause fever, pelvic pain, tenderness, abnormal discharge, or bleeding and needs treatment.

name: endometrium
clinical_significance: The inner lining of the uterus. It thickens each month under hormone control to prepare for pregnancy and sheds during menstruation; abnormal thickening, inflammation, polyps, or cancer can cause bleeding or fertility problems.

name: endomyocardial fibrosis
clinical_significance: Scarring and thickening of the inner heart lining and nearby muscle that makes the heart stiff and reduces filling. It can cause breathlessness, swelling, abnormal rhythms, or heart failure.

name: endopeptidase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that cuts proteins or peptides at internal points rather than removing amino acids only from an end. Digestive enzymes such as pepsin and trypsin are examples.

name: endophthalmitis
clinical_significance: A severe infection or inflammation inside the eye, usually after eye surgery, an injury, or spread through the bloodstream. It can cause severe pain, redness, swelling, and rapid vision loss and requires emergency eye treatment.

name: endoplasmic reticulum
clinical_significance: A network of tiny membrane-lined spaces inside cells. It helps make and transport proteins and fats, stores calcium, and processes substances needed for cell structure and function.

name: endoribonuclease
clinical_significance: An enzyme that cuts RNA at internal chemical bonds. It helps process RNA into usable forms or break down RNA that is damaged, unnecessary, or produced by viruses.

name: endorphin
clinical_significance: A natural chemical made by the body that acts on opioid receptors in the brain and other tissues. It can reduce the feeling of pain and influence stress, mood, and other body responses.

name: endoscope
clinical_significance: A flexible or rigid instrument with a light and camera used to view an internal body passage or cavity. It can sometimes collect tissue, stop bleeding, remove growths, or perform other treatments.

name: endoscopic ultrasound
clinical_significance: A procedure combining an endoscope with ultrasound to view the digestive-tract wall and nearby organs. It can guide needle sampling of lymph nodes, pancreas, or other masses and help assess the depth or spread of disease.

name: endoscopy
clinical_significance: Examination of an internal body passage or cavity with a camera-equipped instrument. Depending on the site, it can directly inspect tissue, collect samples, remove growths, widen narrow areas, or stop bleeding.

name: endosome
clinical_significance: A small membrane-bound compartment inside a cell that receives material taken in from the cell surface and sorts it for recycling, transport, or breakdown.

name: endothelial cell
clinical_significance: A cell lining a blood or lymphatic vessel. It regulates movement between blood and tissues and helps control vessel widening, inflammation, clotting, and formation of new blood vessels.

name: endothelin
clinical_significance: A small protein made mainly by cells lining blood vessels that strongly narrows vessels and affects blood pressure, circulation, inflammation, and tissue growth. Excess signaling contributes to some cases of pulmonary arterial hypertension.

name: endothelium
clinical_significance: The thin layer of specialized cells lining blood and lymphatic vessels. It controls exchange between blood and tissues and helps regulate vessel diameter, inflammation, clotting, and new-vessel growth.

name: endotoxin
clinical_significance: A component of the outer membrane of certain bacteria, especially Gram-negative bacteria. When released into the body, it can trigger fever, inflammation, low blood pressure, organ injury, and life-threatening sepsis.

name: enema
clinical_significance: Introduction of liquid into the rectum through the anus to soften stool, stimulate bowel emptying, deliver selected treatment, or assist a test. Overuse can cause irritation, dehydration, or electrolyte problems.

name: energy increased
clinical_significance: A noticeable rise in energy or activity. It may be normal, but unusually high energy with little need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsive behavior, or irritability can occur with stimulant use, thyroid disease, mania, or hypomania.

name: energy intake
clinical_significance: The amount of energy obtained from food and drink, usually measured in calories. Appropriate intake depends on age, body size, activity, illness, pregnancy, and nutritional goals.

name: energy metabolism
clinical_significance: The chemical processes that convert nutrients into usable energy for cells. They include breaking down carbohydrates, fats, and proteins and storing or using the resulting energy for body functions.

name: enflurane
clinical_significance: An older inhaled general anesthetic that is now rarely used. Like other volatile anesthetics, it can trigger malignant hyperthermia in susceptible people and may cause seizure-like EEG activity; anesthesiologists must account for prior reactions and current availability.

name: enfuvirtide
clinical_significance: An injectable HIV medicine that blocks fusion of HIV with human immune cells. It is used with other antiretroviral medicines for resistant infection; injection-site reactions and allergic reactions can occur.

name: enhanced pause
clinical_significance: An unusually long pause in breathing or another measured body signal. Its significance depends on the test and setting and may require interpretation with symptoms and the complete recording.

name: eniluracil
clinical_significance: An experimental inhibitor of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase studied to alter the action of fluorouracil in cancer treatment. It is not a standard medicine; because it changes fluorouracil metabolism, its use was investigated only in controlled oncology research.

name: enkephalin
clinical_significance: A natural opioid-like peptide made by the body that activates mainly delta and mu opioid receptors. It helps regulate pain, stress, mood, movement, and other nervous-system functions.

name: enophthalmos
clinical_significance: Abnormal backward sinking of an eyeball within the eye socket. It may follow injury, loss of tissue around the eye, dehydration, aging, or a nerve disorder and can cause unequal eye appearance or double vision.

name: enoxaparin
clinical_significance: A low-molecular-weight heparin that reduces clotting by enhancing antithrombin activity, especially against factor Xa. It prevents or treats blood clots but can cause bleeding, low platelets, or injection-site bruising.

name: enrollment
clinical_significance: In clinical research, enrollment is the process of consenting and formally entering eligible participants into a study. Recruitment and enrollment affect whether results represent the people who may later receive the intervention; participation requires voluntary informed consent.

name: entamoeba
clinical_significance: A group of single-celled amoebas that live in the intestine or other tissues. Some species are harmless, while Entamoeba histolytica can cause diarrhea, intestinal ulcers, or liver abscesses.

name: entamoeba coli
clinical_significance: A usually harmless amoeba found in the human intestine and spread by fecal contamination. Its presence in stool indicates exposure to contaminated food or water but usually does not cause illness or require treatment.

name: entamoeba hartmanni
clinical_significance: A small, usually harmless intestinal amoeba spread through fecal contamination. It generally causes no disease; identification in stool mainly indicates possible exposure to contaminated food, water, or hands.

name: entamoeba histolytica
clinical_significance: A parasite spread when contaminated food, water, or hands are swallowed. It can cause diarrhea, abdominal pain, and bloody stools and may invade the intestine or spread to the liver, causing an abscess.

name: entamoeba polecki
clinical_significance: An intestinal amoeba that can infect people after fecal contamination, often through contact with animals or contaminated food and water. It is usually harmless but may occasionally be associated with diarrhea.

name: enteral nutrition
clinical_significance: Delivery of food, fluids, and nutrients through the digestive tract, by mouth or feeding tube. It may be used when swallowing or eating is unsafe or inadequate; aspiration, diarrhea, blockage, and tube displacement are possible complications.

name: enteric bacteria
clinical_significance: Bacteria that live in or affect the intestinal tract. Some are harmless normal residents, while others cause diarrhea or infections outside the intestine, such as urinary, wound, or bloodstream infection.

name: enteritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the small intestine caused by infection, inflammatory disease, radiation, reduced blood flow, medicines, or other injury. It may cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, fever, bleeding, or dehydration.

name: enterobacter
clinical_significance: A group of Gram-negative bacteria that may live in the intestine but can cause healthcare-associated urinary, bloodstream, wound, respiratory, or abdominal infection, especially in vulnerable people.

name: enterobacter aerogenes
clinical_significance: A former name for Klebsiella aerogenes, a Gram-negative bacterium that can cause urinary, lung, wound, abdominal, or bloodstream infection, especially in healthcare settings. It may resist several antibiotics.

name: enterobacter asburiae
clinical_significance: An environmental and intestinal Enterobacter species that is an uncommon cause of human infection. It has been isolated from urine, blood, wounds, and respiratory samples; a positive culture should be assessed in context and treated according to susceptibility results when infection is present.

name: enterobacter cancerogenus
clinical_significance: A rarely encountered Enterobacter species that can cause wound infection or bloodstream infection, particularly after contaminated trauma. Accurate identification and antibiotic susceptibility testing help distinguish true infection from incidental isolation and guide treatment.

name: enterobacter cloacae
clinical_significance: A Gram-negative bacterium that can cause healthcare-associated urinary, bloodstream, lung, wound, or abdominal infection. It may resist several antibiotics, so laboratory susceptibility testing guides treatment.

name: enterobacter hormaechei
clinical_significance: A bacterium in the Enterobacter cloacae group that can cause opportunistic healthcare-associated infection of blood, urine, lungs, wounds, or devices. Testing for antibiotic resistance is often important.

name: enterobacteriaceae
clinical_significance: A family of Gram-negative bacteria that includes Escherichia, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Salmonella, and Shigella. Some normally live in the intestine, while others cause intestinal, urinary, wound, or bloodstream infection.

name: enterobiasis
clinical_significance: Infection with pinworms, small intestinal worms whose eggs spread easily between people. It commonly causes intense itching around the anus at night, disturbed sleep, and sometimes irritation in the genital area.

name: enterobius
clinical_significance: A group of pinworms that live in the intestine. Enterobius vermicularis causes the common pinworm infection, which spreads when eggs are swallowed and often causes nighttime anal itching.

name: enterobius vermicularis
clinical_significance: A small intestinal worm commonly called the pinworm or threadworm. Adult females lay eggs around the anus, usually at night, causing itching and allowing infection to spread through contaminated hands or surfaces.

name: enterococcaceae
clinical_significance: A family of bacteria that includes Enterococcus species. These bacteria may normally live in the intestine but can cause urinary, wound, bloodstream, or heart-valve infections when they enter protected body sites.

name: enterococcus
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria normally found in the intestine that can cause urinary, wound, abdominal, bloodstream, or heart-valve infection. Some strains resist several antibiotics and require laboratory susceptibility testing.

name: enterococcus avium
clinical_significance: A less common intestinal Enterococcus species that can occasionally cause opportunistic infection, including bloodstream or urinary infection. Its significance depends on the specimen and clinical context, and susceptibility testing guides therapy.

name: enterococcus dispar
clinical_significance: A rarely encountered Enterococcus species that may be found in the human intestine and has occasionally been recovered from clinical specimens. Its role as a cause of disease is uncommon and should be judged from symptoms, specimen source, and repeat or confirmatory findings.

name: enterococcus durans
clinical_significance: A bacterium that may live in the bowel but can rarely cause infection in seriously ill or immunocompromised people. It may affect blood, urine, wounds, or other sites, and testing guides antibiotic treatment.

name: enterococcus faecalis
clinical_significance: A common intestinal bacterium that can cause urinary, wound, abdominal, bloodstream, or heart-valve infection. Disease is more likely after surgery, hospitalization, medical-device use, or when immunity is weakened.

name: enterococcus faecium
clinical_significance: An Enterococcus species that can cause healthcare-associated urinary, wound, abdominal, bloodstream, or heart-valve infection. Some strains resist vancomycin and other antibiotics, making laboratory testing essential.

name: enterococcus gallinarum
clinical_significance: An uncommon Enterococcus species that can cause opportunistic infection, including bloodstream or urinary infection. It has intrinsic low-level vancomycin resistance through the VanC mechanism, so correct identification matters when selecting antibiotics.

name: enterococcus hirae
clinical_significance: A less common Enterococcus species associated mainly with animals and the environment that can rarely cause human bloodstream, urinary, or other opportunistic infections. A clinical isolate requires species-level identification and susceptibility testing.

name: enterococcus malodoratus
clinical_significance: A rare Enterococcus species that has occasionally been associated with human infection. As with other uncommon enterococci, a positive culture must be interpreted by site and clinical findings, and antimicrobial susceptibility can vary.

name: enterococcus mundtii
clinical_significance: An uncommon Enterococcus species found in animals and the environment that has occasionally been isolated in human infection, including bloodstream infection. It is a rare opportunistic pathogen; species identification and susceptibility testing are important when a true infection is suspected.

name: enterococcus pseudoavium
clinical_significance: A rare Enterococcus species that may occasionally cause opportunistic human infection. Its clinical importance depends on whether it is recovered from a normally sterile site and whether the patient has compatible symptoms or risk factors.

name: enterococcus raffinosus
clinical_significance: A rare Enterococcus species that has been reported in clinical infections, including bloodstream infection. Correct identification matters because less common enterococci may have different susceptibility patterns from E. faecalis and E. faecium.

name: enterococcus thailandicus
clinical_significance: A rarely encountered Enterococcus species that has been recovered from human clinical specimens, but its disease associations are limited. A positive culture should be interpreted using specimen source, symptoms, and susceptibility testing.

name: enterocolitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the small intestine and colon caused by infection, immune disease, reduced blood flow, toxins, or other injury. It may cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, vomiting, bleeding, dehydration, or severe illness.

name: enterocyte
clinical_significance: A cell lining the small intestine that digests and absorbs nutrients, water, and electrolytes. It also helps form the intestinal barrier and participates in immune defense.

name: enterocytozoon
clinical_significance: A group of tiny spore-forming parasites that can cause persistent diarrhea and intestinal disease, especially in people with weakened immunity. Some species can also affect other organs.

name: enteroendocrine cell
clinical_significance: A specialized cell in the intestinal lining that senses food and releases hormones regulating digestion, appetite, gallbladder and pancreatic activity, and blood-glucose control.

name: enteromonas hominis
clinical_significance: A usually harmless microorganism that may live in the intestine and appear in stool samples. It generally does not cause disease, so its presence should be interpreted with symptoms and other test results.

name: enterostomy procedure
clinical_significance: Surgery that creates an opening from the intestine to the abdominal wall, such as an ileostomy or colostomy. It may divert stool or support feeding; bleeding, infection, blockage, and skin problems can occur.

name: enterotoxin
clinical_significance: A toxin made by some microorganisms that acts on the intestinal lining and can cause vomiting, cramps, watery diarrhea, dehydration, or other intestinal illness.

name: enterovesical fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal connection between the intestine and urinary bladder. It can cause repeated urinary infections, air or stool in the urine, abdominal pain, or urine leaking into the intestine and may result from inflammation, cancer, or surgery.

name: enterovirus
