clinical_significance: A group of viruses spread mainly by respiratory secretions or contact with infected stool. Many infections are mild or cause no symptoms, but some cause hand-foot-and-mouth disease, rash, meningitis, heart inflammation, or severe illness in newborns.

name: enthesitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation where a tendon, ligament, or joint capsule attaches to bone. It can cause localized pain, tenderness, and stiffness and is common in spondyloarthritis, including psoriatic and inflammatory-bowel-disease-related arthritis.

name: entinostat
clinical_significance: An experimental histone deacetylase inhibitor studied in clinical trials for cancer. It is not an established standard treatment; use remains limited to research protocols and combination studies.

name: entorhinal cortex
clinical_significance: A region of the brain that links the hippocampus with other memory and navigation areas. It helps process spatial information and new memories and is affected early in many cases of Alzheimer disease.

name: entropion
clinical_significance: Inward turning of an eyelid, usually the lower lid, so the eyelashes rub against the eye. It can cause irritation, tearing, pain, corneal scratches, infection, and reduced vision.

name: enucleation procedure
clinical_significance: Enucleation removes the entire eye and may be needed for intraocular cancer or a severely damaged painful eye; pathology, prosthetic rehabilitation, and psychosocial support matter.

name: enuresis
clinical_significance: Repeated involuntary urination, usually during sleep in a child expected to remain dry. It may be primary or begin again after dryness; constipation, infection, diabetes, sleep problems, stress, or urinary disorders may contribute.

name: environment
clinical_significance: The physical, chemical, biological, and social surroundings in which a person lives or works. Environmental factors such as air, water, housing, noise, climate, and pollutants can influence health.

name: environmental exposure
clinical_significance: Contact with a chemical, pollutant, organism, physical hazard, or other factor in the surroundings. Health effects depend on the substance, dose, route, duration, timing, and individual susceptibility.

name: environmental health
clinical_significance: The field concerned with how surroundings affect human health. It includes air and water quality, food safety, housing, workplace hazards, climate, radiation, pollution, and prevention of harmful exposures.

name: environmental illness
clinical_significance: Illness caused or worsened by an environmental exposure. Evaluation considers the timing, dose, setting, symptoms, other possible causes, and whether symptoms improve when exposure stops.

name: enzyme
clinical_significance: A protein, or occasionally an RNA molecule, that speeds a specific chemical reaction without being used up. Enzymes are essential for digestion, energy production, DNA processes, and many other cell functions.

name: enzyme activity
clinical_significance: The rate at which an enzyme carries out a chemical reaction under specified conditions. It is affected by temperature, acidity, inhibitors, helper molecules, substrate amount, and enzyme concentration.

name: enzyme deficiency
clinical_significance: Reduced or absent activity of an enzyme, usually inherited or sometimes acquired. It can cause buildup of substances, lack of needed products, and characteristic metabolic or cellular disease.

name: enzyme induction
clinical_significance: Increased production or activity of an enzyme, often after exposure to a medicine or chemical. If liver drug-metabolizing enzymes are induced, some medicines may be broken down faster and become less effective.

name: enzyme inhibitor
clinical_significance: A substance that reduces or blocks an enzyme’s activity. Enzyme inhibitors include many medicines, but effects may be therapeutic or harmful; inhibition can also alter the metabolism of other drugs and cause interactions.

name: enzyme precursors
clinical_significance: Inactive or weakly active proteins that become working enzymes after being cut or chemically changed. This allows the body to activate digestive and other enzymes at the correct place and time.

name: enzyme therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that replaces, supplements, blocks, or uses an enzyme to correct a deficiency or alter a disease process. The purpose, dose, benefits, and risks depend on the specific enzyme and condition.

name: eosine yellowish
clinical_significance: A yellowish form of eosin dye used as a counterstain in hematoxylin-and-eosin tissue slides and in selected laboratory media. It helps pathologists distinguish tissue structures under a microscope; it is not a diagnostic result by itself.

name: eosinophil
clinical_significance: A type of white blood cell involved in allergic inflammation and defense against some parasites. Eosinophils normally make up a small fraction of blood cells; high levels can occur with allergy, infection, medicines, or other disease.

name: eosinophilia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high number of eosinophils in the blood, commonly caused by allergy, parasites, medicines, autoimmune disease, or some blood disorders. Severe or persistent elevation can injure the heart, lungs, skin, nerves, or other organs.

name: eosinophilic esophagitis
clinical_significance: A chronic immune-related disease in which eosinophils inflame the esophagus. It may cause difficulty swallowing, food becoming stuck, chest or upper-abdominal pain, reflux-like symptoms, and narrowing of the esophagus.

name: eosinophilic fasciitis
clinical_significance: A rare inflammatory disease causing painful swelling and hardening of the deeper skin and tissue around muscles, usually in the arms or legs. Blood eosinophils may be high, and joint stiffness or limited movement can develop.

name: eosinophilic granuloma
clinical_significance: A localized form of Langerhans-cell disease in which abnormal immune cells collect, often in bone or skin. Bone lesions can cause pain, swelling, or fractures and may require imaging and tissue examination.

name: ependyma
clinical_significance: A specialized layer of cells lining the brain’s fluid-filled ventricles and the spinal cord’s central canal. It helps separate nervous tissue from cerebrospinal fluid and supports movement of that fluid.

name: ependymal cell
clinical_significance: A supporting cell lining the brain ventricles and spinal cord central canal. It helps maintain the cerebrospinal-fluid boundary and, in some areas, helps move or produce the fluid.

name: ependymal tumor
clinical_significance: A growth arising from cells lining the brain ventricles or spinal canal. It may block cerebrospinal-fluid flow and cause headache, vomiting, balance problems, weakness, or hydrocephalus; treatment depends on its type and extent.

name: ependymoblastoma
clinical_significance: A rare, aggressive brain tumor of childhood made from very immature cells. It may cause headache, vomiting, seizures, or changes in movement or development; tissue and genetic testing guide treatment and outlook.

name: ependymoma
clinical_significance: A tumor arising from cells lining the brain ventricles or spinal canal. It may block fluid flow and cause headache, vomiting, seizures, balance problems, weakness, or hydrocephalus, especially in children.

name: ephedrine
clinical_significance: A stimulant that activates the sympathetic nervous system and can widen airways and raise blood pressure and heart rate. It has limited medical uses and may cause palpitations, insomnia, anxiety, high blood pressure, or misuse.

name: ephrins
clinical_significance: Proteins on the surface of cells that help guide cell position, nerve growth, blood-vessel development, and tissue organization. Abnormal ephrin signaling can contribute to some diseases and cancers.

name: epiblast
clinical_significance: A layer of cells in the early embryo that develops into the three main cell layers of the body and ultimately forms most tissues and organs.

name: epicardium
clinical_significance: The thin outer layer of the heart wall and the inner layer of its surrounding protective sac. It contains connective tissue, fat, blood vessels, and nerves and helps reduce friction as the heart beats.

name: epichlorohydrin
clinical_significance: An industrial chemical used to make resins and other materials. Exposure can irritate or burn the skin, eyes, and airways; swallowing or substantial exposure can cause serious poisoning and requires urgent medical advice.

name: epicondylitis
clinical_significance: Pain and tenderness where a tendon attaches near an epicondyle, usually from repeated strain rather than infection. At the elbow it can weaken gripping and wrist movement and is commonly called tennis or golfer’s elbow.

name: epidemic
clinical_significance: An increase in disease cases above the number normally expected in a population, place, or period. An epidemic may result from infection, environmental exposure, behavior, or another shared cause.

name: epidemiologic method
clinical_significance: A structured way to measure how often a health problem occurs and to study whether exposures, behaviors, or other factors are associated with it in a population. Results guide prevention and policy.

name: epidemiologic studies
clinical_significance: Research that examines the distribution, causes, risk factors, prevention, or outcomes of health events in populations.

name: epidemiologist
clinical_significance: A scientist or public-health professional who studies the distribution, causes, risk factors, and prevention of health conditions in populations.

name: epidemiology
clinical_significance: The study of how often diseases and other health events occur, who is affected, and which factors influence them. It uses population data to identify causes, guide prevention, investigate outbreaks, and evaluate healthcare.

name: epidermal acanthosis
clinical_significance: Thickening of the epidermis caused by increased growth of its cells, seen in conditions such as psoriasis, chronic rubbing, and some inflammatory or genetic skin disorders.

name: epidermal cells
clinical_significance: Cells forming the outer layer of skin, chiefly keratinocytes, which create a protective barrier; melanocytes, immune cells, and touch-associated cells are also present.

name: epidermal growth factor
clinical_significance: A signaling protein that binds the epidermal-growth-factor receptor and promotes cell growth, survival, and tissue repair; abnormal signaling can contribute to cancer.

name: epidermis
clinical_significance: The outer layer of skin that forms a protective barrier against injury, germs, and water loss. It contains cells that make keratin and pigment, as well as immune and touch-sensing cells, and it is replaced continuously.

name: epidermolysis bullosa
clinical_significance: A group of inherited disorders in which fragile skin blisters or tears after minor rubbing or injury because of defects in proteins that join skin layers. Severity varies; some forms heal without scars, while others cause scarring, tight joints, poor nutrition, infection, or increased skin-cancer risk.

name: epidermophyton
clinical_significance: A group of fungi that grow in keratin, a tough protein in skin, hair, and nails. They can cause ringworm infections, including itchy, scaly skin disease and fungal infection of the nails, but do not usually infect living hair shafts.

name: epidermophyton floccosum
clinical_significance: A dermatophyte fungus that commonly causes tinea of the body, groin, and feet and can infect nails.

name: epididymal cyst
clinical_significance: A usually benign, fluid-filled cyst arising in the epididymis. It may be painless and may require treatment only if it causes significant symptoms or complications.

name: epididymal neoplasm
clinical_significance: A benign or malignant growth arising in the epididymis; most palpable epididymal masses are benign, but persistent or enlarging lesions require evaluation.

name: epididymis
clinical_significance: A tightly coiled tube along the back of each testicle where sperm mature, gain the ability to move, and are stored before passing into the vas deferens. It has a head, body, and tail.

name: epididymitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the epididymis, usually caused by infection. It commonly causes gradually developing pain and swelling on one side of the scrotum. Causes include sexually transmitted infections, urinary bacteria, urine-flow problems, and less commonly injury or medicines.

name: epidural anesthesia
clinical_significance: Regional anesthesia produced by injecting numbing medicine, sometimes with an opioid, into the space around the spinal nerves. It blocks pain from part of the body while the person stays awake; low blood pressure, headache, infection, or nerve injury can rarely occur.

name: epidural neoplasm
clinical_significance: A tumor in the space outside the dura surrounding the spinal cord or brain; spinal epidural tumors can compress nerves or the spinal cord and cause pain, weakness, or sensory loss.

name: epigallocatechin gallate
clinical_significance: A major catechin in green tea that is studied for possible biological effects, but it is not an established treatment or cancer-prevention medicine. Concentrated green-tea extracts containing EGCG have been linked to rare liver injury and can interact with some medicines.

name: epigastric
clinical_significance: Relating to the upper middle area of the abdomen between the ribs. Pain there may arise from the stomach, esophagus, pancreas, gallbladder, intestine, or other organs.

name: epigastric artery
clinical_significance: An artery supplying the front abdominal wall. The superior and inferior epigastric arteries provide blood to abdominal muscles and skin and are important landmarks during some procedures.

name: epigastrium
clinical_significance: The upper middle part of the abdomen, below the breastbone and between the ribs. It overlies parts of the stomach, liver, pancreas, and small intestine; pain there has many possible causes.

name: epigenome
clinical_significance: The collection of chemical tags and DNA-packaging features that help control which genes are active in a cell without changing the DNA sequence.

name: epigenomics
clinical_significance: The study of chemical and structural changes that control which genes are active across the genome without changing the DNA sequence. These changes can influence development, disease, and treatment response.

name: epiglottis
clinical_significance: A leaf-shaped flap of flexible tissue at the base of the tongue that helps direct food and liquid into the esophagus during swallowing and away from the airway. Swelling can rapidly obstruct breathing.

name: epiglottitis
clinical_significance: A potentially life-threatening infection or inflammation causing swelling around the epiglottis and upper airway. Fever, severe sore throat, drooling, trouble swallowing, noisy breathing, or sitting forward requires emergency care; the throat should not be examined forcefully.

name: epilepsy
clinical_significance: A chronic brain disorder that causes a lasting tendency to have recurrent unprovoked seizures. A seizure is a brief episode caused by excessive, abnormal electrical activity in the brain and may change movement, sensation, awareness, behavior, or consciousness. Seizures may begin in one area of the brain (focal seizures) or involve both sides from the start (generalized seizures). Causes include genetic conditions, brain injury or malformation, stroke, infection, metabolic or immune disease, or

name: epinephrine
clinical_significance: A hormone and neurotransmitter released during stress that increases heart activity, opens the airways, and narrows many blood vessels. As a medicine, it treats anaphylaxis and selected cardiac or breathing emergencies.

name: epiphysis
clinical_significance: The expanded end of a long bone, usually covered by smooth cartilage where it forms a joint. It contains mostly spongy bone and helps determine the shape and movement of the joint.

name: epipodophyllotoxin
clinical_significance: A group of cancer medicines derived from a plant compound that damage DNA by blocking an enzyme needed for cell division. They treat selected cancers but may cause low blood counts, nausea, hair loss, infection, or rarely a later blood cancer.

name: epiretinal membrane
clinical_significance: A thin layer of cells and connective tissue that forms on the inner surface of the retina, usually over the macula. It may contract, wrinkle the retina, and distort central vision; it is also called macular pucker.

name: epirubicin
clinical_significance: An anthracycline cancer medicine that damages DNA and blocks cell division. Important risks include low blood counts, infection, nausea, hair loss, tissue injury after leakage, and dose-related heart damage.

name: epirubicin hydrochloride
clinical_significance: The salt form of epirubicin, an anthracycline cancer medicine that damages tumor-cell DNA. It is used for selected cancers but can cause low blood counts, tissue injury after leakage, and dose-related heart damage.

name: episcleritis
clinical_significance: Usually short-lived inflammation of the thin tissue over the white of the eye, causing a localized red patch and mild tenderness or discomfort. Severe pain, light sensitivity, or vision loss suggests deeper eye disease.

name: episiotomy
clinical_significance: A cut made in the tissue between the vagina and anus during vaginal birth to enlarge the opening. Routine use is not recommended; selected use may help urgent or assisted delivery but can cause pain, bleeding, infection, or deeper tearing.

name: episodic ataxia
clinical_significance: An inherited condition causing repeated attacks of poor coordination and balance. Episodes may last seconds to hours and can include dizziness, slurred speech, muscle tightening, or abnormal eye movements, with improvement between attacks.

name: epispadias
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the urethral opening is on the upper surface of the penis or in an unusual position in a female. It may affect urine control and is sometimes associated with bladder-exstrophy conditions.

name: epistaxis
clinical_significance: Nosebleeds are usually minor but can cause significant blood loss or airway compromise, especially with anticoagulants, trauma, or recurrent episodes; persistent heavy bleeding needs urgent care.

name: epithalamic
clinical_significance: Relating to the epithalamus, a small region near the center of the brain that includes the pineal gland and structures involved in sleep timing, hormonal rhythms, and responses to reward or stress.

name: epithelial
clinical_significance: Relating to cells that cover the skin, line body passages and organs, or form glands. These cells protect surfaces and may absorb substances, release fluids, or help detect changes.

name: epithelial cells
clinical_significance: Cells that cover the skin, line body passages and organs, and form many glands. They create a protective barrier and may absorb substances, release fluids, move material, or sense changes in their surroundings.

name: epithelial cyst
clinical_significance: A usually benign, enclosed sac lined by surface-type cells and filled with fluid, mucus, or a skin protein called keratin. It may enlarge, become painful, or become infected and sometimes requires removal.

name: epithelioid cell
clinical_significance: A rounded cell that resembles a surface-lining cell. The term often describes an activated immune cell in a granuloma, but it can also describe the appearance of some tumors.

name: epithelioma
clinical_significance: An older or broad term for a tumor arising from epithelial cells; the specific diagnosis should identify whether it is benign, precancerous, or malignant.

name: epithelium
clinical_significance: A layer or sheet of closely packed cells covering the skin, lining body spaces and tubes, or forming glands. It protects surfaces and may absorb substances, release fluids, transport material, or allow exchange.

name: epitope
clinical_significance: The small, specific part of an antigen that is recognized by an antibody or immune-cell receptor. Recognition can trigger an immune response; epitopes are important in infections, vaccines, allergies, and antibody-based treatments.

name: epitope mapping
clinical_significance: The process of identifying an epitope, the small part of an antigen recognized by an antibody or specific immune-cell receptor. It helps researchers understand immune responses and develop vaccines, diagnostic tests, and antibody-based treatments.

name: eplerenone
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks aldosterone, a hormone that promotes salt retention and heart remodeling. It treats high blood pressure and selected heart-failure patients; kidney function and blood potassium require monitoring.

name: epoetin alfa
clinical_significance: A laboratory-made form of erythropoietin that stimulates the bone marrow to produce red blood cells. It treats selected anemias, but can raise blood pressure and the risk of blood clots if hemoglobin rises too high.

name: epoetin beta
clinical_significance: A laboratory-made form of erythropoietin used for selected anemias, including some caused by chronic kidney disease. Treatment is individualized and requires monitoring because it may cause high blood pressure or blood clots.

name: Epoprostenol
clinical_significance: A short-acting medicine that widens blood vessels in the lungs and reduces platelet clumping. Continuous intravenous infusion treats severe pulmonary arterial hypertension; interruption can cause rapid worsening.

name: epothilon
clinical_significance: Epothilones are microtubule-stabilizing compounds studied as anticancer agents because they can disrupt tumor-cell division. The semisynthetic analogue ixabepilone is used for selected advanced breast cancer; most other epothilones remain investigational.

name: epothilone B
clinical_significance: A naturally occurring microtubule-stabilizing compound studied as an anticancer lead. Its semisynthetic analogue ixabepilone is used for selected advanced breast cancer, but epothilone B itself is not a routine medicine.

name: epothilone D
clinical_significance: An experimental microtubule-stabilizing anticancer compound studied in early clinical trials for advanced cancers. It is not an established standard treatment; ixabepilone, a related epothilone analogue, has a limited breast-cancer indication.

name: epoxide hydrolase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that changes reactive chemicals called epoxides into less reactive substances. It helps process some medicines, toxins, and natural fats and can influence their effects and the risk of tissue injury.

name: epoxy compounds
clinical_significance: Chemicals containing a reactive group used in adhesives, coatings, plastics, and other materials. Uncured components can irritate the skin and eyes, cause allergic skin inflammation, or irritate the airways; workplace exposure may cause asthma.

name: epstein-barr virus
clinical_significance: A common virus spread mainly through saliva. It can cause infectious mononucleosis and remains dormant in the body; it is also linked to some lymphomas, other cancers, and immune disorders.

name: eptifibatide
clinical_significance: An injectable antiplatelet medicine used during selected urgent coronary treatments. It prevents platelets from clumping by blocking a platelet-binding receptor, but can cause serious bleeding and requires blood-count and kidney monitoring.

name: equilin
clinical_significance: An estrogen hormone found mainly in pregnant mares and included in some mixtures of conjugated estrogens. Estrogen treatment can increase the risk of blood clots and other adverse effects and requires individualized medical advice.

name: equine morbillivirus
clinical_significance: A virus related to measles that has caused severe respiratory or neurologic disease in horses and can infect other mammals. Suspected cases require veterinary investigation and infection-control measures.

name: equinovarus deformity
clinical_significance: A deformity in which the foot points downward and turns inward. It may be present at birth or develop from muscle, nerve, joint, or bone problems, limiting walking and requiring cause-specific treatment.

name: equipment safety
clinical_significance: Measures that reduce harm from medical devices by using the correct equipment, checking it before use, cleaning it properly, maintaining it, and training users. Faulty equipment should be removed from service.

name: equivalence trial
clinical_significance: A clinical study designed to determine whether a new treatment and an established treatment have effects within a predefined clinically acceptable range of one another. The range must be set before results are analyzed.

name: erbb receptors
clinical_significance: A family of cell-surface proteins that receive growth signals and regulate cell division, survival, and specialization. Abnormal activity in some members can promote cancers and may guide targeted treatment.

name: erbium
clinical_significance: A chemical element used in specialized lasers and materials. Erbium lasers can precisely remove or remodel selected skin and dental tissue; treatment may cause pain, burns, pigment changes, or scarring.

name: ergocalciferol
clinical_significance: Vitamin D2, a form of vitamin D used to prevent or treat deficiency. It helps the body absorb calcium and maintain bones, but excessive doses can cause high blood calcium, nausea, confusion, or kidney injury.

name: ergolines
clinical_significance: A family of compounds related to chemicals made by ergot fungi. Some affect serotonin, dopamine, or adrenaline receptors and are used or studied for migraine, hormone disorders, or neurologic conditions.

name: ergonomics
clinical_significance: Designing work, tools, furniture, and environments to match the body’s abilities and limits. Good ergonomics can reduce strain, awkward posture, repetitive-injury risk, fatigue, and errors.

name: ergosterol
clinical_significance: A fat-like substance that helps maintain fungal cell membranes. Many antifungal medicines damage fungi by binding ergosterol or blocking its production; human cells use cholesterol instead.

name: ergotamine
clinical_significance: A medicine that narrows certain blood vessels and can stop some migraine attacks. It has many interactions and should not be overused because it can cause dangerous loss of blood flow to the limbs or organs.

name: eribulin mesylate
clinical_significance: A cancer medicine that interferes with microtubules, structures needed for cell division. It is used for selected advanced breast cancers and liposarcomas; common risks include low blood counts, nerve damage, fatigue, and nausea.

name: erlotinib hydrochloride
clinical_significance: A cancer medicine that blocks growth signals from the epidermal growth-factor receptor. It treats selected cancers with suitable molecular changes and may cause rash, diarrhea, liver injury, or lung inflammation.

name: erosion lesion
clinical_significance: A shallow area where the surface layer of skin or a moist lining has been lost. It may result from rubbing, inflammation, infection, injury, or chemicals and usually heals when the cause is removed.

name: erratic results
clinical_significance: Test results that change unexpectedly or do not agree with repeated measurements. Possible causes include sample problems, device error, normal biological variation, medicines, or a test that does not fit the clinical question.

name: ertapenem
clinical_significance: A once-daily antibiotic for selected serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria. It does not reliably treat Pseudomonas or enterococcal infections and can cause diarrhea, allergic reactions, seizures, or antibiotic-resistant organisms.

name: erucic acid
clinical_significance: A fatty acid found in some plant oils, including mustard and older varieties of rapeseed oil. Modern edible oils are usually bred to contain little of it; unusually high exposure may harm the heart.

name: erucic acids
clinical_significance: Long-chain fatty acids found mainly in certain plant oils. The amount consumed depends on the oil, and unusually high exposure may be harmful; ordinary low-erucic edible oils provide much less.

name: eructation
clinical_significance: Release of swallowed air or gas from the stomach through the mouth, commonly called belching. Frequent troublesome belching may be related to swallowed air, reflux, food intolerance, or other digestive problems.

name: eryptosis
clinical_significance: A controlled process by which aging or damaged red blood cells shrink and are marked for removal from the bloodstream. It helps maintain blood-cell balance but may increase in some diseases or during oxidative stress.

name: erysipelas
clinical_significance: A sudden bacterial infection of the upper skin and lymph vessels, usually causing a painful, raised, sharply bordered red patch with fever. Prompt antibiotic treatment is important to prevent spread or complications.

name: erysipelothrix
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria found in animals and animal products that can enter broken skin and cause a painful localized infection. Rarely, infection spreads to the bloodstream or heart valves.

name: erythema
clinical_significance: Redness of the skin or a moist body lining caused by increased blood flow near the surface. It may result from inflammation, infection, heat, allergy, or another illness and often fades briefly when pressed.

name: erythema infectiosum
clinical_significance: A usually mild infection caused by parvovirus B19, also called fifth disease. A short flu-like prodrome may be followed by bright-red cheeks and a lacy rash on the trunk and limbs; adults may have joint pain, while infection can cause severe anemia in people with certain blood disorders or immunosuppression and complications in pregnancy.

name: erythema multiforme
clinical_significance: A short-lived immune reaction, often triggered by herpes simplex infection or, less commonly, another infection or medicine. It causes symmetrical target-shaped spots, usually on the hands, feet, arms, or face; mouth involvement may occur.

name: erythema nodosum
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the fat beneath the skin (panniculitis) that causes tender red lumps, usually on both shins. Infections, medicines, inflammatory bowel disease, sarcoidosis, and other conditions may trigger it. The lumps usually fade like bruises without ulcerating or scarring.

name: erythroblast
clinical_significance: An immature red-blood-cell precursor made in the bone marrow. It develops through several stages before becoming a mature red blood cell; abnormal numbers may indicate altered blood-cell production.

name: erythroblastosis fetalis
clinical_significance: A condition in which antibodies from the pregnant person destroy a fetus’s or newborn’s red blood cells. It can cause anemia, jaundice, widespread swelling, heart failure, or death and is often prevented by blood-group screening and preventive treatment.

name: erythrocyte
clinical_significance: A mature red blood cell that carries oxygen from the lungs to tissues and helps return carbon dioxide to the lungs. Its flexible shape allows it to pass through very small blood vessels.

name: erythrocyte membrane
clinical_significance: The flexible outer layer of a red blood cell. It maintains the cell’s shape, allows it to bend through small vessels, and controls movement of water and substances into and out of the cell.

name: erythrodysplasia
clinical_significance: Abnormal development or maturation of red-blood-cell precursors in the bone marrow. It can produce ineffective blood formation and anemia and may occur with a marrow disorder or other illness.

name: erythroid hyperplasia
clinical_significance: An increase in immature red-blood-cell precursors in the bone marrow, usually because the body is responding to anemia, blood loss, red-cell destruction, or low oxygen. The underlying cause needs evaluation.

name: erythroleukoplakia
clinical_significance: A mouth lesion containing both red and white areas. It has a substantial risk of advanced precancerous change or cancer, so a dentist or specialist should examine it and usually perform a biopsy.

name: erythromelalgia
clinical_significance: Repeated attacks of burning pain, warmth, and redness in the feet, hands, or sometimes face, often triggered by heat or exercise and eased by cooling. It may be inherited or linked to blood or nerve disorders.

name: erythromycin
clinical_significance: An antibiotic that blocks bacterial protein production. It treats selected infections and can be used when some other antibiotics are unsuitable; nausea, diarrhea, liver injury, and abnormal heart rhythm are possible.

name: erythromycin estolate
clinical_significance: An oral form of the antibiotic erythromycin. It blocks bacterial protein production and treats selected infections; stomach upset, liver inflammation, allergic reactions, and medicine interactions can occur.

name: erythroplasia
clinical_significance: A sharply bordered red patch on skin or a moist lining. Persistent lesions, especially in the mouth or genital area, may represent a serious precancerous change or cancer and need medical assessment.

name: erythropoiesis
clinical_significance: The process of making mature red blood cells, mainly in the bone marrow. It is stimulated by erythropoietin when oxygen is low and requires healthy marrow plus adequate iron, vitamin B12, and folate.

name: erythropoietin
clinical_significance: A hormone made mainly by the kidneys when body tissues receive too little oxygen. It signals the bone marrow to produce red blood cells; kidney disease can reduce this signal and contribute to anemia.

name: erythropoietin receptor
clinical_significance: A protein on immature red-blood-cell precursors that receives the erythropoietin signal. Activation helps these cells survive, multiply, and mature into red blood cells.

name: erythrosine
clinical_significance: A red dye used in some foods, medicines, and laboratory procedures. Exposure is usually small, but regulations vary and people with a known sensitivity should follow product and medical advice.

name: escape reaction
clinical_significance: A body response that restores an organ’s activity after it has been reduced by a medicine, hormone, nerve signal, or feedback system. The response may lessen the effect of continued treatment or stimulation.

name: escherichia
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria that includes E. coli and related species found in intestines or the environment. Some strains are harmless, while others cause diarrhea, urinary infection, wound infection, or bloodstream infection.

name: escherichia albertii
clinical_significance: An uncommon intestinal bacterium that can cause diarrheal illness. It may be mistaken for certain E. coli strains, so specialized laboratory identification may be needed when infection is suspected.

name: escherichia blattae
clinical_significance: A rarely reported Escherichia species associated mainly with insects and the environment. Its significance in a human sample is uncertain and must be judged from symptoms, the specimen source, and other test results.

name: escherichia coli
clinical_significance: A bacterium that normally lives in the intestine. Some strains are harmless, while others cause urinary, intestinal, wound, or bloodstream infections, including severe bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome.

name: escherichia coli infection
clinical_significance: Infection caused by a harmful strain of E. coli. It may affect the intestine, urinary tract, wounds, or bloodstream; symptoms, contagiousness, and treatment depend on the strain and site.

name: escherichia fergusonii
clinical_significance: An uncommon bacterium that can occasionally cause urinary, wound, intestinal, or bloodstream infection, especially in people with serious illness or weakened immunity. Laboratory identification and susceptibility testing guide treatment.

name: escherichia hermannii
clinical_significance: An uncommon Escherichia species that rarely causes opportunistic infection, including urinary or bloodstream infection. Its importance depends on the patient’s symptoms, immune status, and the specimen in which it is found.

name: escherichia vulneris
clinical_significance: An uncommon bacterium rarely linked to wound, urinary, or bloodstream infection, usually in people with other serious illnesses. A laboratory result requires clinical correlation to distinguish infection from contamination.

name: escitalopram
clinical_significance: An antidepressant that increases available serotonin in the brain. It treats depression and generalized anxiety disorder; nausea, sleep changes, sexual problems, withdrawal symptoms, bleeding risk, and rarely serotonin toxicity may occur.

name: esomeprazole
clinical_significance: A medicine that reduces stomach-acid production by blocking the acid pump in stomach cells. It treats reflux, ulcers, and acid-related disorders; prolonged or inappropriate use may cause infections, low magnesium, or vitamin deficiencies.

name: esomeprazole magnesium
clinical_significance: A magnesium salt of esomeprazole that reduces stomach-acid production by blocking the stomach’s acid pump. It treats reflux and ulcers; long-term use may cause diarrhea, infections, low magnesium, or nutrient deficiencies.

name: esophageal
clinical_significance: Relating to the esophagus, the muscular tube that carries swallowed food and liquid from the throat to the stomach.

name: esophageal atresia
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the esophagus ends in a blind pouch instead of connecting normally to the stomach. A connection to the windpipe may also occur, causing drooling, choking, coughing, and breathing problems during feeds.

name: esophageal bleeding
clinical_significance: Bleeding from the esophagus, which may result from enlarged veins, inflammation, ulcers, tears, injury, or cancer. Vomiting blood, passing black stools, dizziness, or fainting requires emergency medical care.

name: esophageal carcinoma
clinical_significance: Cancer arising in the esophagus, most often squamous-cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma. Progressive difficulty swallowing, weight loss, chest pain, or bleeding may occur; endoscopic biopsy and staging guide treatment.

name: esophageal diverticulum
clinical_significance: A pouch that bulges outward from the wall of the esophagus. It may cause difficulty swallowing, food coming back up, coughing, bad breath, or no symptoms; treatment depends on its size, location, and effects.

name: esophageal duplication
clinical_significance: A rare birth defect consisting of a cyst or extra segment beside the esophagus. It may press on the esophagus or airway, causing swallowing difficulty, breathing problems, infection, or no symptoms.

name: esophageal fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal connection between the esophagus and another organ, often the airway. It can allow food or liquid into the lungs, causing coughing during swallowing, repeated pneumonia, poor nutrition, or severe illness.

name: esophageal infection
clinical_significance: Infection of the esophagus caused by a yeast, virus, or bacterium, usually in people with weakened immunity or damaged lining. It may cause painful swallowing, difficulty swallowing, chest pain, or ulcers.

name: esophageal leukoplakia
clinical_significance: A persistent white patch on the esophageal lining caused by thickened surface cells. It is uncommon but may contain precancerous change, so evaluation and biopsy are often needed to determine its significance.

name: esophageal necrosis
clinical_significance: Death of esophageal lining, sometimes producing a black appearance. It can result from severe low blood flow, shock, acid injury, or caustic substances and may lead to bleeding or perforation.

name: esophageal perforation
clinical_significance: A hole through the full thickness of the esophageal wall, caused by forceful vomiting, an instrument, injury, or disease. It can release contents into the chest, causing severe infection and requiring emergency treatment.

name: esophageal spasm
clinical_significance: A movement disorder in which esophageal muscles contract too strongly or without normal coordination. It can cause intermittent chest pain and difficulty swallowing; pressure testing helps distinguish it from other disorders.

name: esophageal stenosis
clinical_significance: Narrowing of the passage through the esophagus caused by scarring, inflammation, a tumor, radiation, or a birth defect. It commonly causes progressively worsening difficulty swallowing, especially solid foods.

name: esophageal stent
clinical_significance: A tube placed inside a narrowed or leaking esophagus to keep it open and allow swallowing. It is often used for cancer or injury; movement, blockage, bleeding, pain, or perforation can occur.

name: esophageal ulceration
clinical_significance: An open sore in the esophageal lining caused by reflux, infection, medicines, caustic injury, inflammation, or cancer. It may cause painful swallowing, chest pain, or bleeding and often requires endoscopic evaluation.

name: esophageal varices
clinical_significance: Enlarged veins in the esophageal wall, usually caused by high pressure in the portal vein from advanced liver disease. They may rupture without warning and cause life-threatening vomiting of blood.

name: esophageal web
clinical_significance: A thin shelf of tissue projecting into the upper esophagus. It may cause difficulty swallowing solid food and can be associated with iron-deficiency anemia; persistent symptoms may require endoscopy.

name: esophagectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove part or all of the esophagus, usually for cancer or severe irreversible damage. The remaining digestive tract is reconstructed, commonly using the stomach or a segment of intestine.

name: esophagitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or injury of the esophageal lining. Common causes include acid reflux, infection, medicines that irritate the esophagus, eosinophilic or other immune-mediated disease, swallowed irritants, and radiation. Symptoms may include heartburn, painful or difficult swallowing, chest pain, food sticking, or bleeding; persistent inflammation can cause ulcers or narrowing.

name: esophagogastric junction
clinical_significance: The area where the esophagus joins the stomach. Its muscular valve and surrounding structures help food enter the stomach while limiting backward flow of stomach contents.

name: esophagoscope
clinical_significance: A flexible or rigid instrument used to look inside the esophagus. It may allow a clinician to take tissue samples, remove a foreign object, treat bleeding, or perform another procedure.

name: esophagoscopy
clinical_significance: Examination of the esophagus with a camera-equipped instrument. It may investigate swallowing difficulty, bleeding, reflux damage, narrowing, foreign objects, infection, or suspected cancer and may allow treatment or biopsy.

name: esophagram
clinical_significance: An X-ray examination performed while a person swallows contrast liquid. It shows the shape and movement of the esophagus and can reveal narrowing, leaks, pouches, blockage, or abnormal swallowing.

name: esophagus
clinical_significance: A muscular tube that carries food and liquid from the throat to the stomach. Coordinated muscle contractions move swallowed material downward, while valves at each end help limit reflux and air entry.

name: esophagus disease
clinical_significance: A disorder of the esophagus causing swallowing difficulty, pain, reflux, regurgitation, bleeding, obstruction, inflammation, motility disturbance, or cancer.

name: esophagus neoplasm
clinical_significance: A benign, precancerous, or malignant growth in the esophagus; evaluation may require endoscopy, biopsy, imaging, and staging.

name: esotropia
clinical_significance: A type of strabismus in which one or both eyes turn inward toward the nose. It may be constant or intermittent and can occur at any age. Causes include focusing or refractive problems, reduced vision, and disorders affecting eye-movement nerves or brain pathways; evaluation guides treatment.

name: essential hypertension
clinical_significance: Long-term high blood pressure with no single identifiable underlying cause. Many genetic, kidney, blood-vessel, metabolic, and lifestyle factors contribute, and untreated disease raises the risk of stroke, heart disease, kidney damage, and vision problems.

name: essiac
clinical_significance: A herbal mixture promoted as a treatment for cancer and other illnesses. Reliable evidence has not shown that it cures cancer, and its ingredients may interact with medicines or cause liver, kidney, or other harm.

name: estazolam
clinical_significance: A sedative medicine sometimes used short-term for insomnia. It slows brain activity but can cause daytime drowsiness, falls, memory problems, slowed breathing, dependence, and withdrawal; alcohol and opioids increase its dangers.

name: ester
clinical_significance: A chemical formed when an acid combines with an alcohol. Esters occur naturally in fats, medicines, and flavorings; their health effects depend on the specific compound, amount, route of exposure, and duration.

name: esterase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that breaks ester chemical bonds. Esterases help process fats, medicines, and other substances; abnormal activity or inhibition can alter drug effects and may contribute to poisoning.

name: esterification
clinical_significance: A chemical reaction that forms an ester. In medicine and pharmacology, esterification can change a drug’s absorption, distribution, or duration of action, and ester bonds are also broken during metabolism; the clinical effect depends on the particular compound.

name: esthesia
clinical_significance: The ability to sense touch, pain, temperature, movement, or body position. Reduced, increased, or altered sensation may result from nerve injury, brain disease, medicines, or changes in consciousness.

name: esthesiometer
clinical_significance: An instrument used to measure sensitivity to touch, pressure, or other sensations. Eye clinicians may use one to assess corneal sensation when nerve injury or an eye-surface problem is suspected.

name: estivation
clinical_significance: A period of dormancy in some animals during hot or dry conditions, accompanied by reduced activity and metabolism. It is mainly relevant to comparative physiology and veterinary or ecological research, not a human medical diagnosis.

name: estradiol
clinical_significance: The main active estrogen hormone during most reproductive years. It helps regulate ovulation and menstruation and supports the vagina, uterus, bones, brain, and other tissues; levels fall after menopause.

name: estramustine
clinical_significance: A cancer medicine combining an estrogen-like component with a compound that interferes with cell division. It has been used for selected advanced prostate cancers; blood clots, fluid retention, nausea, and heart effects may occur.

name: estriol
clinical_significance: An estrogen produced mainly by the placenta during pregnancy from substances made by the fetus and mother. Maternal blood estriol may be included in prenatal screening, but an abnormal result does not by itself diagnose a problem.

name: estrogen
clinical_significance: A group of hormones involved in reproductive development, menstruation, fertility, bone strength, and many other body functions. The main forms and amounts vary with age, sex, pregnancy, and ovarian function.

name: estrogen inhibitor
clinical_significance: A broad term for medicines or substances that reduce estrogen production or block estrogen’s effects. These treatments are important in hormone-sensitive breast cancer, but can affect bone strength, menopausal symptoms, fertility, and other estrogen-dependent tissues.

name: estrogen receptor
clinical_significance: A cell protein that binds estrogen and changes cell activity. Testing for estrogen receptors helps classify some cancers, especially breast cancer, and can guide hormone-based treatment.

name: estrone
clinical_significance: A naturally occurring estrogen made partly by converting other hormones in body tissues. It is the main estrogen present after menopause, although estradiol is usually more active before menopause.

name: estrous cycle
clinical_significance: The recurring reproductive cycle of many female mammals other than humans. It includes hormonal and physical changes that prepare for ovulation, mating, and possible pregnancy.

name: estrus
clinical_significance: The phase when a nonhuman female mammal is sexually receptive and may ovulate. It is relevant to veterinary reproduction and animal research; humans have a menstrual cycle rather than an estrous cycle.

name: eszopiclone
clinical_significance: A sleep medicine that enhances inhibitory signaling in the brain. It can help insomnia but may cause drowsiness, impaired coordination, memory problems, dependence, unusual sleep behaviors, or a bitter taste.

name: etanercept
clinical_significance: A biologic medicine that blocks tumor-necrosis factor, an inflammation signal. It treats selected arthritis, psoriasis, and other inflammatory diseases but can increase serious infection risk, so tuberculosis and hepatitis screening may be needed.

name: etanidazole
clinical_significance: An experimental nitroimidazole studied as a radiosensitizer to make oxygen-poor tumor cells more sensitive to radiation. Clinical trials did not establish routine benefit, and it is not a standard cancer treatment.

name: etaracizumab
clinical_significance: An investigational monoclonal antibody targeting the αvβ3 integrin, studied for possible effects on tumor growth and blood-vessel formation. It has no established approved treatment role and remains a research agent.

name: ethacrynic acid
clinical_significance: A loop diuretic that increases kidney excretion of salt and water. It can reduce fluid overload but may cause dehydration, low electrolytes, kidney injury, or dose-related hearing damage.

name: ethambutol
clinical_significance: An antibiotic used with other medicines to treat tuberculosis and selected infections caused by related bacteria. It can damage the optic nerve, causing blurred vision or trouble distinguishing colors, so vision testing is important.

name: ethane
clinical_significance: A colorless, highly flammable gas used mainly to make industrial chemicals. It is not usually poisonous through direct action, but high concentrations can displace oxygen and cause suffocation or fire hazards.

name: ethanol
clinical_significance: The alcohol in alcoholic drinks and some disinfectants, medicines, and fuels. Drinking too much can impair judgment, suppress breathing, lower blood sugar, cause dependence, and damage the liver and other organs.

name: ethanol metabolism
clinical_significance: The body’s breakdown of alcohol, mainly in the liver, into acetaldehyde and then acetate. The process affects blood-alcohol levels, drug interactions, intoxication, hangovers, and long-term alcohol-related organ damage.

name: ethanolamine
clinical_significance: A chemical used in some industrial products, medicines, and cosmetic ingredients. Concentrated exposure can irritate or burn the skin, eyes, and airways; health effects depend on the product and amount of exposure.

name: ethchlorvynol
clinical_significance: An older sedative-hypnotic formerly used for insomnia. It can cause marked drowsiness, impaired coordination, dependence, and dangerous respiratory or cardiovascular depression in overdose or when combined with alcohol or other sedatives; it is no longer a routine sleep treatment.

name: ethers
clinical_significance: A group of chemicals containing an oxygen atom between two carbon groups. Some are used as solvents or fuels; exposure can cause irritation, dizziness, unconsciousness, or fire and explosion hazards.

name: ethics
clinical_significance: Principles used to decide what is right, fair, respectful, and responsible in healthcare and research. Medical ethics includes informed choice, privacy, avoiding harm, helping patients, and treating people fairly.

name: ethidium
clinical_significance: A DNA-binding fluorescent dye used in laboratory assays to visualize nucleic acids. Ethidium compounds can be mutagenic, so laboratory handling and waste disposal should follow chemical-safety procedures; they are not medicines or diagnostic results themselves.

name: ethinyl estradiol
clinical_significance: A synthetic estrogen used in many hormonal contraceptives and some other treatments. It can cause nausea or irregular bleeding and increases blood-clot risk, especially with smoking, migraine with aura, or certain medical conditions.

name: ethiodized oil
clinical_significance: An iodine-containing oil used as a contrast material in selected imaging or treatment procedures, including some lymphatic and liver procedures. It can affect thyroid function or rarely enter blood vessels and cause an embolism.

name: ethion
clinical_significance: An organophosphate pesticide that can poison the nervous system by blocking acetylcholinesterase. Exposure may cause sweating, vomiting, pinpoint pupils, muscle twitching, weakness, breathing failure, or death and requires urgent treatment.

name: ethionamide
clinical_significance: An antibiotic used with other medicines for drug-resistant or difficult-to-treat tuberculosis. It interferes with mycobacterial cell-wall production and may cause nausea, liver injury, nerve symptoms, or thyroid problems.

name: ethmocephaly
clinical_significance: A severe birth defect in which the eyes are very close together and the nose is replaced or accompanied by a tube-like structure. It usually occurs with major brain-development abnormalities and is often life-limiting.

name: ethmoid bone
clinical_significance: A light, complex bone between the eye sockets that forms part of the nasal septum, nasal roof, and inner eye socket. It contains air cells and openings for smell nerves, so injury can affect smell or the eye.

name: ethmoid sinus
clinical_significance: One of several small air spaces in the ethmoid bone between the nose and eye sockets. Inflammation or infection can cause nasal blockage, headache, or eye-area pain and may spread to nearby tissues.

name: ethmoid sinusitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of the air spaces between the nose and eyes. It may cause congestion, discharge, fever, headache, or pain around the eyes; eye swelling, vision changes, or severe illness requires urgent care.

name: ethnicity
clinical_significance: A social and cultural identity shaped by shared ancestry, history, language, traditions, or community; it is not a biological diagnosis and should not be used as a substitute for individual risk assessment.

name: ethoglucid
clinical_significance: An older sclerosing substance used historically to treat selected vascular lesions or hemorrhoids; modern use is limited by tissue-injury risks and alternatives.

name: ethosuximide
clinical_significance: An anticonvulsant used mainly for absence seizures; common adverse effects include gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue, and headache, with rare blood or skin reactions.

name: ethoxzolamide
clinical_significance: A carbonic-anhydrase-inhibiting medicine that reduces formation of certain body fluids. It has been used for selected eye and metabolic conditions; possible effects include tingling, nausea, kidney stones, and electrolyte changes.

name: ethyl ether
clinical_significance: A highly flammable liquid formerly used as an anesthetic and still used as a laboratory solvent. Breathing its vapor can cause irritation, dizziness, drowsiness, or loss of consciousness; swallowing it can injure the lungs if it is aspirated. Exposure requires fresh air, fire precautions, and medical assessment when symptoms are severe.

name: ethyl methanesulfonate
clinical_significance: A reactive alkylating chemical used experimentally to induce mutations in cells and organisms. It is reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen based on animal studies, so laboratory exposure requires strict containment and chemical-safety controls.

name: ethylene
clinical_significance: A colorless, flammable gas used in chemical manufacturing and to ripen fruit. High concentrations can displace oxygen and cause headache, dizziness, drowsiness, unconsciousness, or suffocation. Remove a person from exposure only when it is safe and seek emergency help for breathing or consciousness problems.

name: ethylene chlorohydrin
clinical_significance: A toxic industrial chemical used in some manufacturing processes. Exposure can irritate the eyes, skin, and airways and may affect the nervous system, liver, or kidneys. It can be absorbed through skin, so contaminated clothing should be removed safely and urgent poison-control advice obtained.

name: ethylene dibromide
clinical_significance: A toxic chemical formerly used as a soil fumigant and fuel additive. It can irritate the eyes and lungs and may damage the liver, kidneys, or nervous system; long-term exposure is associated with cancer risk. Suspected exposure needs urgent poison-control or occupational-health assessment.

name: ethylene glycol
clinical_significance: A toxic alcohol found in some antifreeze and industrial products. Ingestion can cause severe metabolic acidosis, neurologic impairment, kidney injury, and death.

name: ethylene oxide
clinical_significance: A flammable gas used to sterilize heat-sensitive medical equipment and make other chemicals. It can irritate the skin and airways, cause nerve injury, and with repeated exposure increase cancer risk. Sterilized equipment must be adequately aerated before use, and workplace exposure requires strict controls.

name: ethylenethiourea
clinical_significance: An industrial chemical used in rubber processing and a breakdown product of some fungicides. It can interfere with thyroid function in experimental animals and is a potential occupational hazard; human health effects depend on exposure and are not fully established.

name: ethylnitrosourea
clinical_significance: A potent DNA-alkylating mutagen used mainly in laboratory research to create animal models with defined genetic changes. It causes mutations and tumors in experimental animals and is hazardous to handle; it is not a therapeutic drug.

name: ethynodiol diacetate
clinical_significance: A synthetic progestogen formerly used in some oral contraceptives. It helps prevent pregnancy mainly by suppressing ovulation and changing cervical mucus and the uterine lining.

name: etidronate
clinical_significance: A bisphosphonate medicine used for Paget disease of bone and, in selected circumstances, to prevent or treat abnormal bone formation after hip surgery or spinal-cord injury. Its use requires attention to dosing and risks such as esophageal irritation and impaired bone mineralization.

name: etidronic acid
clinical_significance: A synonym for etidronate, a bisphosphonate used for Paget disease and selected cases of heterotopic bone formation. Prolonged or high-dose treatment can impair normal bone mineralization, so dosing and duration matter.

name: etilefrine
clinical_significance: A medicine that stimulates some of the body’s adrenaline-like receptors and can raise blood pressure. It increases blood-vessel tightening and heart activity, so it may cause fast heartbeat, headache, or other effects and requires medical supervision.

name: etiocholanolone
clinical_significance: A metabolite of adrenal androgens measured in specialized urine or blood steroid profiles. It may help characterize steroid production or metabolism, but an isolated level is not diagnostic and requires interpretation with other hormones and clinical findings.

name: etiology
clinical_significance: The cause or set of causes of a disease or health condition, including genetic, infectious, environmental, immune, traumatic, and behavioural factors.

name: etioplast
clinical_significance: A plant-cell organelle that forms when developing leaves grow without light and can convert into a chloroplast after exposure to light. It is relevant to plant biology and has no direct role as a human clinical finding.

name: etodolac
clinical_significance: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug used for pain and inflammation; gastrointestinal bleeding, kidney injury, cardiovascular events, and hypersensitivity are important risks.

name: etomidate
clinical_significance: A short-acting intravenous anesthetic used for induction, particularly when cardiovascular stability is desired; it can cause myoclonus, nausea, and transient adrenal suppression.

name: etoposide
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy medicine that interferes with DNA repair and cell division. It treats several cancers but can cause low blood counts, infection, hair loss, nausea, mouth sores, or a later risk of leukemia.

name: etoposide phosphate
clinical_significance: A water-soluble form of etoposide that changes into etoposide inside the body. It provides another method of giving the chemotherapy medicine, with similar cancer treatment effects and potential toxicities.

name: etoricoxib
clinical_significance: An anti-inflammatory pain medicine that selectively blocks an enzyme involved in pain and swelling. It may help arthritis or acute pain but can raise blood pressure and increase heart, kidney, fluid-retention, and stomach risks.

name: etretinate
clinical_significance: An older oral retinoid formerly used for severe psoriasis. It is highly teratogenic and persists in body fat for a long time, creating prolonged pregnancy risk; it has been replaced by retinoids with different use and risk profiles and is unavailable in most countries.

name: eubacterium
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria that usually live without oxygen in the mouth and intestine. Most are part of normal microbial communities, but some can rarely cause opportunistic infection in seriously ill people.

name: eubacterium limosum
clinical_significance: A bacterium that lives without oxygen in the intestine and helps break down nutrients. It is rarely associated with human infection, and its importance in a sample depends on symptoms and the collection site.

name: eubacterium rectale
clinical_significance: A common intestinal bacterium that helps ferment dietary fiber and produce short-chain fatty acids. These products support the colon and contribute to normal gut microbial activity.

name: eubacterium ventriosum
clinical_significance: A species of anaerobic bacteria found in the human intestine and studied as part of the gut microbiome. It is not a common pathogen; detection in stool does not by itself indicate disease or require treatment.

name: eucalyptus oil
clinical_significance: A concentrated plant oil containing eucalyptol and other chemicals. Swallowing it can poison the nervous system and cause vomiting, drowsiness, seizures, or breathing problems; it should not be taken internally without medical advice.

name: euchromatin
clinical_significance: A relatively open form of DNA packaging inside the cell nucleus. Its structure makes nearby genes more accessible for reading and activity than DNA in tightly packed regions.

name: euglena
clinical_significance: A genus of single-celled, mostly free-living flagellates found in freshwater and other environments. It is not a recognized common human pathogen; its importance is mainly ecological and research-related.

name: eukaryote
clinical_significance: A cell or organism with a nucleus and membrane-bound compartments. This distinction matters in medicine because human, fungal, and protozoal cells are eukaryotic, while bacteria are not; drug selectivity must account for these similarities and differences.

name: eukaryotic cell
clinical_significance: Human, fungal, and protozoal cells are eukaryotic, which helps explain why treating fungal and parasitic infections can be more difficult than treating bacterial infections: many cellular targets are shared with human cells.

name: euphoria
clinical_significance: An unusually intense feeling of happiness or well-being. It may occur normally, with mania, brain disease, or some medicines and drugs; sudden extreme euphoria with unsafe behavior needs clinical assessment.

name: europium
clinical_significance: A rare-earth element used in specialized fluorescent labels for laboratory immunoassays. Europium itself is not a routine medicine; the clinical value comes from assay reagents that use europium chelates to measure specific substances.

name: eurotium
clinical_significance: A group of molds historically classified as a separate genus; many species are now classified within Aspergillus. These fungi can contaminate foods or indoor environments and may contribute to allergic exposure; human infection is uncommon and species-dependent.

name: eustachian tube
clinical_significance: A passage connecting the middle ear to the back of the nose. It opens during swallowing or yawning to equalize pressure, drain fluid, and help protect the middle ear from throat secretions.

name: euthanasia
clinical_significance: The deliberate ending of a person’s life by another person to relieve suffering. It is ethically and legally distinct from allowing a natural death, stopping unwanted treatment, or providing comfort-focused palliative care.

name: euthyroid goiter
clinical_significance: An enlarged thyroid gland with normal thyroid-hormone production. It may result from iodine imbalance, autoimmune disease, nodules, medicines, or inherited factors and should be assessed if persistent, enlarging, or causing swallowing or breathing problems.

name: Evans syndrome
clinical_significance: An autoimmune disorder characterized by the simultaneous or sequential development of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (positive direct antiglobulin test) and immune thrombocytopenic purpura, occasionally accompanied by autoimmune neutropenia.

name: everolimus
clinical_significance: A medicine that suppresses a cell-growth pathway and immune activity. It is used for selected cancers, transplant care, and some genetic disorders; mouth sores, infection, high blood sugar, lung inflammation, and low blood counts may occur.

name: evoked potential
clinical_significance: An electrical response recorded from the nervous system after a visual, sound, or touch stimulus. The test assesses whether signals travel normally along sensory pathways and may reveal nerve damage or slowed transmission.

name: evolution
clinical_significance: Gradual change in inherited traits of a population across generations. In clinical writing, the term can also describe how a disease, symptom, or treatment response changes over time.

name: ewingella
clinical_significance: A genus of environmental gram-negative bacteria best known for E. americana. It rarely causes human infection, but reported cases include bloodstream, respiratory, and peritoneal infections; culture results should be interpreted with symptoms and specimen source.

name: ewingella americana
clinical_significance: A rare environmental gram-negative bacterium that has caused occasional human bloodstream, respiratory, eye, and peritoneal infections, particularly in people with underlying illness or recent procedures. It may also represent colonization or contamination, so clinical context matters.

name: ewings sarcoma
clinical_significance: An older name for Ewing sarcoma, an aggressive cancer that often begins in bone or nearby soft tissue, especially in children and young adults. Diagnosis requires tumor testing, and treatment usually combines chemotherapy with surgery and/or radiation.

name: exacerbation
clinical_significance: A worsening or flare of a disease or its symptoms after a period of relative stability. Triggers may include infection, allergens, treatment interruption, exertion, or another physical or emotional stress.

name: examination table
clinical_significance: A padded, adjustable surface that supports a person during examination, testing, minor procedures, or treatment. It should be stable, cleanable, accessible, and used with appropriate safety measures.

name: exanthema
clinical_significance: A widespread skin eruption associated with an illness affecting the body. Viral infections are common causes, but medicines, bacteria, and immune disorders may also cause it; blisters, skin pain, mouth sores, or severe illness need prompt assessment.

name: exatecan mesylate
clinical_significance: A topoisomerase I inhibitor studied as an experimental chemotherapy for solid tumors. It is not an established stand-alone cancer treatment; a related exatecan derivative is used as the cytotoxic payload in some antibody-drug conjugates.

name: excessive bruising
clinical_significance: Bruises that occur often, are unusually large, appear without clear injury, or last unusually long. Causes include medicines, fragile skin, low platelets, clotting disorders, liver disease, or other illness.

name: excessive tearing
clinical_significance: Tears overflowing onto the face because the eyes make too many tears or drainage is blocked. Irritation, allergy, infection, dry eye, eyelid problems, or a blocked tear duct may be responsible.

name: excision
clinical_significance: Surgical removal of part or all of a lesion, tissue, or organ. The specimen may be examined to establish a diagnosis, and removal may also treat disease when the affected area can be safely removed.

name: excision biopsy
clinical_significance: An excisional biopsy removes an entire small lesion for diagnosis or treatment; adequate margins and specimen orientation can affect pathology interpretation and further surgery.

name: excitatory synapse
clinical_significance: A junction between nerve cells where chemical signaling makes the receiving cell more likely to produce an electrical impulse. Balanced excitatory and inhibitory signals are needed for normal brain and nerve function.

name: excretion
clinical_significance: Removal of waste, medicines, or other substances from the body, mainly through urine, bile, breath, stool, sweat, or breast milk. Kidney and liver function strongly affect how long many substances remain in the body.

name: executive function
clinical_significance: Mental skills used to plan, focus, remember instructions, control impulses, solve problems, make decisions, and switch between tasks. Problems may follow brain injury, dementia, developmental conditions, or mental illness.

name: exemestane
clinical_significance: A medicine that lowers estrogen production by blocking an enzyme used after menopause. It treats selected hormone-sensitive breast cancers and may cause hot flushes, joint pain, bone loss, fatigue, or abnormal cholesterol.

name: exenatide
clinical_significance: An injectable medicine that imitates a gut hormone, increasing insulin release when glucose is high, reducing glucagon, and slowing stomach emptying. It treats type 2 diabetes but may cause nausea, dehydration, or pancreatitis.

name: exencephaly
clinical_significance: A severe birth defect in which much of the developing brain lies outside the skull because the skull and protective coverings did not form normally. It usually progresses to anencephaly and is not compatible with long-term survival.

name: exenteration
clinical_significance: Extensive surgery removing organs and tissues from a body compartment, such as the pelvis or eye socket. It is reserved for selected advanced cancers or destructive disease and can cause major functional and emotional effects.

name: exercise
clinical_significance: Planned physical activity intended to improve or maintain strength, endurance, flexibility, balance, function, or health. Aerobic, resistance, and balance activities should be chosen and increased according to a person’s abilities and medical risks.

name: exercise intolerance
clinical_significance: An inability to do as much physical activity as expected because of unusual tiredness, breathlessness, chest discomfort, leg pain, weakness, or dizziness. Heart, lung, blood-vessel, muscle, nerve, blood, metabolic, and conditioning problems can cause it.

name: exercise tolerance
clinical_significance: The ability to perform physical activity before symptoms such as breathlessness, fatigue, chest discomfort, or pain limit activity.

name: Exfoliation syndrome
clinical_significance: An age-related eye disorder in which abnormal material collects on the lens and other front-eye structures. It increases the risk of glaucoma and can make cataract surgery more complicated, so regular eye checks are important.

name: exfoliative dermatitis
clinical_significance: Erythroderma is widespread skin redness and scaling that can cause fluid loss, temperature instability, and infection; urgent evaluation is needed to find drug reactions, psoriasis, lymphoma, or other causes.

name: exhibitionism
clinical_significance: Sexual arousal from exposing one’s genitals to an unsuspecting person. Repeated nonconsensual exposure can harm others and becomes a diagnosable disorder when urges or actions cause significant distress, impairment, or risk.

name: exiguobacterium
clinical_significance: A genus of environmental bacteria that has occasionally been isolated from human infections, including bacteremia, respiratory illness, and wound infection. Such infections are rare, and a positive culture needs interpretation based on specimen source and clinical findings.

name: exocervix
clinical_significance: The part of the cervix that projects into the vagina and is covered mainly by flat squamous cells. It is examined during pelvic examination and cervical screening.

name: exocrine gland
clinical_significance: A gland that sends its secretion through a duct to a body surface or internal cavity. Sweat, salivary, tear, and digestive glands are examples; their secretions help protect, lubricate, or digest.

name: exocrine pancreas
clinical_significance: The part of the pancreas that releases digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the small intestine. These secretions help break down fats, proteins, and carbohydrates and neutralize stomach acid.

name: exocytosis
clinical_significance: The process by which a cell releases substances outside itself. Small sacs inside the cell join its outer membrane and release hormones, nerve signals, digestive enzymes, or other proteins.

name: exodeoxyribonuclease
clinical_significance: An enzyme that removes nucleotides from the ends of DNA molecules. DNA exonucleases help replicate and repair genetic material; defects can contribute to genome instability, while laboratory exonuclease activity is used in molecular testing and sequencing.

name: exon
clinical_significance: A segment of a gene that remains in the mature messenger RNA after unused sections are removed. It may contain instructions for making part of a protein or, in some genes, help regulate gene activity.

name: exonuclease
clinical_significance: An enzyme that removes nucleotides one at a time from the end of a DNA or RNA strand. Exonucleases are important in DNA replication, repair, and RNA processing; errors in these pathways can contribute to genetic disease or cancer.

name: exopeptidase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that removes amino acids from the end of a protein. Digestive exopeptidases help break dietary proteins into smaller units that the intestine can absorb.

name: exophiala
clinical_significance: A group of darkly pigmented environmental fungi that can rarely cause skin, lung, eye, or widespread infection. Disease is more likely in people with weakened immunity or implanted medical devices.

name: exophiala dermatitidis
clinical_significance: A darkly pigmented yeast-like fungus that may colonize airways, especially in people with cystic fibrosis, and can cause skin, lung, eye, brain, or disseminated infection. Deep infection is uncommon but may be severe; culture results require specialist interpretation and antifungal testing.

name: exophthalmos
clinical_significance: The abnormal forward protrusion or displacement of one or both eyeballs from the orbit, most frequently caused by Graves disease (thyroid eye disease), orbital tumors, or inflammation.

name: exostosis
clinical_significance: A benign growth of bone. It may be harmless, but location can cause pain, pressure, restricted movement, or blockage; repeated cold-water exposure can produce bony growths in the ear canal.

name: exotropia
clinical_significance: A type of strabismus in which one or both eyes turn outward, away from the nose. It may be intermittent or constant and can occur at any age. It can impair binocular vision or depth perception; in children, persistent misalignment may interfere with visual development. Treatment depends on the cause and may include glasses or surgery.

name: expectorant
clinical_significance: A medicine that helps loosen or thin airway mucus so it can be coughed up more easily. It may ease chest congestion but does not treat the cause of the cough; persistent or severe cough needs assessment, and combination cold products can duplicate ingredients.

name: experience
clinical_significance: A person’s direct knowledge, perception, or emotional response to an event. In healthcare, patient experience includes how care is accessed, communicated, coordinated, and received.

name: expiratory time
clinical_significance: The length of time spent breathing out, measured during respiratory assessment or ventilator monitoring. Too little time to exhale can contribute to air trapping in obstructive lung disease or during mechanical ventilation; interpretation depends on the full breathing pattern.

name: exploratory behavior
clinical_significance: A person’s tendency to investigate unfamiliar surroundings or objects. In children it can inform developmental observation, but changes are nonspecific and must be interpreted with age, environment, and other behavioral or cognitive findings.

name: exposure
clinical_significance: Contact with a physical, chemical, biological, or psychological agent. Health risk depends on what the agent is, how much contact occurred, how it entered the body, and how long exposure lasted.

name: exsanguination
clinical_significance: Life-threatening loss of blood from severe internal or external bleeding. It can rapidly cause shock, organ failure, and death; immediate pressure or bleeding control, emergency care, and blood replacement may be needed.

name: exserohilum
clinical_significance: A group of darkly pigmented molds that can rarely cause sinus, eye, skin, or invasive infection. Serious disease is more likely in people with weakened immunity and requires specialist testing and treatment.

name: extent
clinical_significance: The size, severity, range, or spread of a disease, injury, symptom, or treatment effect. Describing extent helps determine prognosis, further testing, and treatment.

name: external capsule
clinical_significance: A thin bundle of nerve fibers in the brain near the basal ganglia. It carries signals between the cerebral cortex and deeper brain regions involved in movement, attention, and other functions.

name: external ear
