clinical_significance: The visible part of the ear and the ear canal leading to the eardrum. It collects sound, directs it inward, and helps protect the middle and inner ear.

name: external nose
clinical_significance: The visible nose formed by bone, cartilage, skin, and soft tissue. It shapes the nasal passages, helps warm and filter inhaled air, supports smell, and contributes to facial structure.

name: extraamniotic
clinical_significance: Located outside the amniotic sac surrounding a fetus. The term may describe a procedure, device, or fluid placed between the amnion and nearby tissues during pregnancy care.

name: extracellular exosome
clinical_significance: A tiny membrane-covered vesicle released by a cell that can carry proteins, fats, and genetic material to other cells. Exosomes help cells communicate and are being studied as disease markers and treatment vehicles.

name: extracellular matrix
clinical_significance: A network of proteins and other substances outside cells that supports tissues and helps cells attach, communicate, grow, and repair injury. Its composition differs among bone, skin, muscle, and other organs.

name: extracellular region
clinical_significance: The area outside cells. It contains fluid, minerals, proteins, and signals that support tissues and influence how nearby cells grow, move, and function.

name: extracellular space
clinical_significance: The fluid- and matrix-filled area outside cells. Nutrients, waste products, hormones, and signaling molecules move through it, and its composition helps control cell survival, movement, and function.

name: extracellular vesicle
clinical_significance: A membrane-bound particle released by a cell that transfers molecular cargo between cells and is studied in physiology, disease, biomarkers, and drug delivery.

name: extracorporeal circulation
clinical_significance: Movement of a person's blood through equipment outside the body and back again. Heart-lung machines, dialysis, and some life-support systems use it to add oxygen, remove waste, or support circulation; bleeding, clotting, infection, and organ injury are possible.

name: extraction
clinical_significance: Removal of a tooth, tissue, foreign object, or other material from the body using a procedure. The method and risks depend on what is removed, where it is located, and the person’s health.

name: extrahepatic cholestasis
clinical_significance: Reduced or blocked bile flow in the ducts outside the liver. Gallstones, scarring, inflammation, or a tumor may cause yellow skin, dark urine, pale stools, itching, pain, or infection and may need urgent treatment.

name: extranodal
clinical_significance: Located outside the lymph nodes. An extranodal disease or lymphoma affects an organ or other tissue, such as the stomach, skin, lung, bone, or brain.

name: extraocular
clinical_significance: Outside the eyeball or involving the muscles, nerves, and tissues around it. Extraocular structures move the eye, protect it, support vision, and connect it with the brain and face.

name: extraocular muscle
clinical_significance: One of the muscles outside the eyeball that moves the eye in different directions. Weakness or nerve injury can cause double vision, eye misalignment, or difficulty looking in a particular direction.

name: extrapleural pneumonectomy
clinical_significance: An operation that removes an entire lung together with the pleural lining and often part of the diaphragm and pericardium, historically used for selected pleural mesothelioma. It has substantial risks and is reserved for carefully selected patients after multidisciplinary review.

name: extrapyramidal disorder
clinical_significance: A disorder of brain circuits that regulate movement, posture, and muscle tone. It may cause stiffness, slowness, tremor, abnormal movements, or restlessness and can result from disease or medicines.

name: extraskeletal osteosarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare aggressive cancer that produces bone-like material in soft tissue rather than beginning inside bone. It usually affects adults and requires imaging, biopsy, staging, and specialist treatment.

name: extravasation
clinical_significance: Leakage of blood, medicine, urine, or another body fluid from a vessel or duct into nearby tissues. It can cause swelling, pain, inflammation, infection, or tissue death; treatment depends on the substance, location, and severity.

name: extrinsic
clinical_significance: Coming from outside a structure, organ, or person. An extrinsic cause may be an external injury, medicine, infection, toxin, environmental exposure, or other outside influence.

name: exudate
clinical_significance: Protein-rich fluid that leaks from inflamed or injured blood vessels into tissues or a body cavity. Its presence usually indicates inflammation, infection, or tissue injury rather than pressure alone.

name: eye
clinical_significance: The organ that detects light and forms vision. It includes the cornea, lens, iris, retina, optic nerve, and supporting tissues within the eye socket; disease can affect sight, movement, comfort, or appearance.

name: eye development
clinical_significance: Formation and maturation of the eyes, optic nerves, and visual pathways before and after birth. Disruption can cause structural abnormalities, reduced vision, misalignment, or delayed development of visual skills.

name: eye disorder
clinical_significance: A disease or structural problem affecting the eye or visual pathways. It may cause changed vision, pain, redness, discharge, double vision, field loss, or other findings and may require routine or urgent assessment.

name: eye hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding on, inside, or around the eye. A small surface bleed may be painless, while bleeding in the retina, vitreous, or eye socket can impair vision or cause pressure and needs medical assessment.

name: eye infection
clinical_significance: Infection of the eyelid, conjunctiva, cornea, internal eye, or surrounding tissues caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites. Pain, light sensitivity, reduced vision, or swelling around the eye needs prompt care.

name: eye injury
clinical_significance: Damage to the eye or nearby tissues from blunt or penetrating trauma, chemicals, foreign objects, radiation, or heat. Vision change, severe pain, bleeding, or an embedded object requires urgent assessment.

name: eye movement
clinical_significance: Coordinated movement of the eyes that directs gaze and keeps images aligned. It depends on the eye muscles, their nerves, and brain control; abnormal movement may cause double vision or imbalance.

name: eye neoplasm
clinical_significance: A benign or malignant growth arising in the eye or surrounding tissues. Symptoms and treatment depend on the tissue involved, size, location, effect on vision, and whether the growth has spread.

name: eye prosthesis
clinical_significance: An artificial eye or implant used to restore appearance after an eye is lost or severely damaged. It generally does not restore sight; fitting, cleaning, and periodic specialist care are needed.

name: eyebrow
clinical_significance: A strip of hair above the eye socket that helps divert sweat, water, and particles away from the eye and contributes to facial expression.

name: eyeglass
clinical_significance: A lens mounted in a frame to correct focusing problems such as nearsightedness, farsightedness, astigmatism, or presbyopia. The prescription is selected after measuring vision and the eyes.

name: eyelash
clinical_significance: A hair growing from the eyelid edge that helps shield the eye from particles and triggers blinking when touched. Misrouted or infected lashes can irritate the eye surface.

name: eyelid
clinical_significance: A movable fold of skin, muscle, and glands that protects the eye, spreads tears across its surface, and helps regulate light. Swelling, malposition, or weakness can impair protection and vision.

name: eyelid coloboma
clinical_significance: A birth defect causing a notch or missing section of the eyelid. It may leave the eye exposed, impair closure, and occur with other eye or facial abnormalities requiring specialist assessment.

name: eyelid disorder
clinical_significance: A disease or structural problem of the eyelid, such as infection, inflammation, a blocked gland, malposition, weakness, or tumor. It may cause pain, swelling, poor eye protection, irritation, or visual problems.

name: eyelid neoplasm
clinical_significance: A benign, precancerous, or cancerous growth of the eyelid. A persistent, enlarging, changing, bleeding, crusted, or ulcerated lesion needs examination by an eye or skin specialist.

name: ezetimibe
clinical_significance: An oral medicine that reduces absorption of cholesterol from the intestine. It lowers blood cholesterol alone or with another medicine and may cause diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, or rarely liver or muscle problems.

name: fab immunoglobulins
clinical_significance: The target-binding part of an antibody. A laboratory-made Fab fragment can recognize and block a harmful substance or help remove it from the bloodstream in selected treatments.

name: Fabry's disease
clinical_significance: Fabry disease causes progressive glycolipid storage that can damage the kidneys, heart, nerves, and brain; enzyme or genetic diagnosis enables family screening and consideration of disease-specific therapy.

name: face
clinical_significance: The front part of the head, including the eyes, nose, mouth, cheeks, and jaw. Its muscles produce facial expression, its nerves provide movement and sensation, and its structures support breathing, eating, speech, and vision.

name: facelift
clinical_significance: Cosmetic surgery that removes or repositions selected facial and neck skin and deeper tissues to reduce sagging. It does not stop aging and may cause bleeding, infection, nerve injury, scarring, or temporary swelling and numbness.

name: facet joint
clinical_significance: A small joint at the back of the spine connecting neighboring vertebrae and guiding movement. Arthritis, injury, or inflammation can cause localized neck or back pain and stiffness.

name: facial asymmetry
clinical_significance: A difference in the size, position, movement, or shape of the two sides of the face. It may be present from birth or result from injury, nerve weakness, muscle disease, swelling, or a growth.

name: facial cleft
clinical_significance: A birth defect caused by incomplete joining of facial tissues during development. It may affect the lip, nose, mouth, or other facial structures and can interfere with feeding, speech, breathing, hearing, or appearance.

name: facial edema
clinical_significance: Swelling of the face caused by excess fluid in tissues. Allergy, infection, injury, kidney or heart disease, and blocked veins may cause it; sudden lip, tongue, or throat swelling with breathing difficulty is an emergency.

name: facial expression
clinical_significance: The visible movement or position of facial muscles that communicates emotion, pain, intention, or other information. Reduced or unequal expression can indicate facial-nerve or muscle dysfunction.

name: facial muscle
clinical_significance: A muscle that moves the skin of the face for expression and helps with speaking, eating, breathing through the mouth, or closing the eyes. Weakness may result from nerve, muscle, or brain disease.

name: facial neoplasm
clinical_significance: A benign or malignant growth arising in facial skin, soft tissue, bone, salivary glands, nerves, or other structures. Symptoms and treatment depend on its tissue of origin, size, location, and spread.

name: facial nerve
clinical_significance: The seventh cranial nerve, which controls facial expression and carries taste from part of the tongue. It also contributes to tear and saliva production and helps protect the ear from loud sounds.

name: facial nucleus
clinical_significance: A group of nerve cells in the pons, part of the brainstem, whose fibers form the facial nerve and control facial-expression muscles. Injury can cause weakness of the face and related functions.

name: facial pain
clinical_significance: Pain in the face that may arise from dental or sinus disease, jaw-joint problems, nerve disorders, infection, injury, or other causes. The pattern and associated symptoms guide evaluation.

name: facial paralysis
clinical_significance: Partial or complete loss of facial-muscle movement caused by disease or injury of the facial nerve or its brain pathways. Sudden onset, especially with limb weakness or speech trouble, requires urgent stroke assessment.

name: facial paresis
clinical_significance: Weakness of muscles supplied by the facial nerve, causing reduced facial movement and sometimes poor eye closure, altered taste, or abnormal tearing. The cause may be nerve inflammation, injury, infection, stroke, or a tumor.

name: facial vein
clinical_significance: A vein that drains blood from the superficial face toward the internal jugular vein. Connections with deeper veins mean facial infections can rarely spread toward the eye socket or brain.

name: facilitated diffusion
clinical_significance: Movement of a substance across a cell membrane through a channel or carrier protein, from higher to lower concentration. The process does not directly use cellular energy and helps move substances that cannot cross the membrane unaided.

name: facklamia
clinical_significance: A genus of rare gram-positive bacteria that can be mistaken for streptococci or enterococci in routine laboratory identification. Some species have caused bloodstream, heart-valve, urinary, and other infections; species identification and susceptibility testing are important when a clinical isolate is significant.

name: facklamia hominis
clinical_significance: A rare gram-positive bacterium that has been reported in urinary, bloodstream, wound, joint, and other infections, including occasional endocarditis. It may be difficult to identify with routine methods, and antimicrobial susceptibility can vary, so clinical isolates require careful laboratory assessment.

name: factitious disorder
clinical_significance: A mental-health disorder in which a person deliberately creates, exaggerates, or falsely reports illness to assume the sick role, without a clear external reward.

name: factor v
clinical_significance: A blood-clotting protein that helps generate thrombin and fibrin, the mesh that strengthens a clot. Too little can cause bleeding; an inherited change affecting its regulation can increase venous-clot risk.

name: factor vii
clinical_significance: A liver-made blood-clotting protein that starts clot formation when tissue is injured. Inherited or acquired deficiency can cause easy bruising, nosebleeds, or serious bleeding after injury or procedures.

name: factor viii
clinical_significance: A blood-clotting protein that works with factor IX to form a stable clot. Inherited deficiency causes hemophilia A, with prolonged or spontaneous bleeding, often into joints, muscles, or other tissues.

name: factor xii
clinical_significance: A blood-clotting protein that starts one pathway measured by laboratory clotting tests. Factor XII deficiency can greatly prolong the activated partial-thromboplastin time but usually does not cause abnormal bleeding.

name: factor xiii
clinical_significance: The clot-stabilizing protein that strengthens the fibrin mesh after a clot forms. Factor XIII deficiency can cause delayed bleeding, poor wound healing, or repeated pregnancy loss despite initially normal routine clotting tests.

name: factorial study
clinical_significance: A clinical-study design that tests two or more interventions, often at the same time, to estimate each intervention’s effect and whether their effects interact. Its validity depends on appropriate randomization, prespecified outcomes, and analysis of interactions.

name: faculty
clinical_significance: In clinical education, faculty may teach, supervise trainees, and provide patient care. Their qualifications, supervision, and workload can affect training quality and the safety and continuity of care.

name: faecalibacterium
clinical_significance: A group of oxygen-sensitive bacteria commonly found in the intestine. They can produce butyrate, a substance that supports the colon lining; their presence is studied in relation to gut health and inflammation.

name: faecalibacterium prausnitzii
clinical_significance: A common butyrate-producing gut bacterium associated in research with intestinal barrier function and inflammatory bowel disease. Lower abundance has been reported in some conditions, but stool levels are not a validated stand-alone diagnostic test or treatment target.

name: fair hair
clinical_significance: Fair hair often occurs with lighter skin, which burns more readily and is associated with greater ultraviolet-related skin-cancer risk. Hair color alone does not determine risk; sun exposure, skin response, personal history, and other factors matter.

name: falciform ligament
clinical_significance: A fold of tissue attaching the liver to the front abdominal wall and diaphragm. It marks the division between the liver’s right and left lobes and contains the remnant of a fetal umbilical vein.

name: falimarev
clinical_significance: An investigational poxvirus-based cancer vaccine studied in combinations for selected cancers, including bladder cancer. It is designed to stimulate immune recognition of tumor-associated antigens but is not an approved routine treatment.

name: fall
clinical_significance: An unplanned movement to the ground or another lower level. Falls may result from poor balance, weakness, vision problems, medicines, dizziness, low blood pressure, or environmental hazards and can cause serious injury.

name: fallopian tube
clinical_significance: One of two tubes between the ovaries and uterus. An egg usually travels through a tube, where fertilization may occur, before reaching the uterus; blockage or scarring can affect fertility.

name: false negative
clinical_significance: A test result that says a condition is absent when it is actually present. It can occur because testing was too early, the sample was inadequate, the condition level was low, or the test was not sensitive enough.

name: false positive
clinical_significance: A test result that indicates a condition is present when it is not. It may result from cross-reaction, contamination, technical error, or testing in a group where the condition is uncommon.

name: famciclovir
clinical_significance: An antiviral medicine that changes into penciclovir in the body and limits multiplication of herpes viruses. It can treat selected shingles, cold-sore, or genital-herpes episodes but does not remove the virus permanently.

name: familial dysautonomia
clinical_significance: An inherited nerve disorder affecting sensation and automatic functions such as blood pressure, heart rate, sweating, tears, digestion, and swallowing. Symptoms may include dizziness, temperature problems, repeated lung infections, and poor growth.

name: familial testotoxicosis
clinical_significance: An inherited condition in which boys produce excess testosterone without normal brain stimulation. It causes early sexual development, rapid growth, and advanced bone age but may reduce adult height without treatment.

name: family
clinical_significance: Family relationships and history can affect health through inherited risk, shared exposures, caregiving, and social support. A family history of some diseases may prompt earlier screening or genetic counseling, but family structure itself is not a diagnosis.

name: family medicine
clinical_significance: A medical specialty providing first-contact, continuing, and preventive care across ages and conditions. Family physicians often coordinate referrals and manage multiple health needs over time.

name: family planning
clinical_significance: Personal and healthcare decisions about whether and when to have children. It includes contraception, fertility care, preconception health, pregnancy planning, and support for informed reproductive choices.

name: family study
clinical_significance: A structured review of health information in relatives to understand how a disease or trait occurs in a family. It may include family history, medical records, examination, genetic counseling, or testing.

name: family therapy
clinical_significance: Counseling involving family members or other close relationships to improve communication, manage conflict, and support recovery. It may help with mental illness, addiction, chronic disease, caregiving stress, or family adjustment.

name: famophos
clinical_significance: An organophosphate insecticide that can poison the nervous system by blocking acetylcholinesterase. Exposure may cause sweating, salivation, vomiting, pinpoint pupils, muscle weakness, breathing failure, or death and requires emergency care.

name: famotidine
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks histamine signals to reduce stomach-acid production. It treats reflux, heartburn, and ulcers; dose reduction may be needed in kidney disease, and headache, diarrhea, or confusion can occur.

name: fanconi anemia
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder affecting DNA repair and bone-marrow blood-cell production. It may cause low blood counts, infections, bleeding, short stature, birth differences, organ problems, and a high risk of leukemia or other cancers.

name: Fanconi syndrome
clinical_significance: A kidney-tubule disorder causing excess loss of glucose, phosphate, bicarbonate, amino acids, and other substances in urine. It can lead to dehydration, abnormal blood acidity, weak bones, poor growth, or kidney disease.

name: farad
clinical_significance: The standard unit of electrical capacitance, equal to one coulomb per volt. It is used in medical equipment and electrophysiology to describe how much electrical charge a component can store.

name: farber lipogranulomatosis
clinical_significance: A rare inherited storage disorder caused by deficient acid ceramidase. Fatty material accumulates and may cause painful skin lumps, joint stiffness, hoarseness, bone changes, breathing problems, and neurologic disease.

name: farmer's lung
clinical_significance: Lung inflammation caused by repeatedly inhaling moldy hay, grain, or other farm dust. It can cause fever, cough, chills, and breathlessness hours after exposure and may lead to permanent scarring if exposure continues.

name: fascia
clinical_significance: Sheets or bands of connective tissue that surround, separate, support, and connect muscles, organs, nerves, and blood vessels. Injury or inflammation of fascia can cause pain, stiffness, or restricted movement.

name: fascia adherens
clinical_significance: A strong connection joining neighboring cells, especially heart-muscle cells. It links the internal contractile framework of one cell to the membrane of another so force can pass through the tissue.

name: fasciculation
clinical_significance: A brief, involuntary twitch visible under the skin from contraction of a small group of muscle fibers. It may be harmless, but widespread or persistent twitching with weakness needs neurologic evaluation.

name: fasciitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the connective tissue around muscles and other structures. It may be localized, as in plantar fasciitis, or rapidly destructive, as in necrotizing infection requiring emergency surgery and antibiotics.

name: fasciola
clinical_significance: A genus of parasitic flatworms, or liver flukes, that infect some animals and people. Infection is acquired by swallowing immature parasites on contaminated water plants or water and may affect the liver and bile ducts.

name: fasciola hepatica
clinical_significance: A liver fluke that infects people after contaminated aquatic plants or water are swallowed. Immature worms migrate through the liver, while adult worms live in bile ducts and can cause pain, fever, or obstruction.

name: fascioliasis
clinical_significance: Infection with liver flukes after eating contaminated aquatic plants or drinking contaminated water. It may cause fever, right-upper-abdominal pain, enlarged liver, or high eosinophils and later cause bile-duct pain, infection, or blockage.

name: fasciolopsis buski
clinical_significance: A large intestinal fluke acquired by eating aquatic plants carrying immature parasites. Heavy infection may cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, intestinal inflammation, malnutrition, or swelling.

name: fasting
clinical_significance: Going without food, and sometimes without drinks, for a defined period. It may be required before blood tests, anesthesia, surgery, or certain procedures, or undertaken for personal or religious reasons.

name: fat body
clinical_significance: A specialized tissue in many invertebrates, especially insects, that stores nutrients and contributes to metabolism and immune defense. It is important in research on insect physiology and transmission of some vector-borne infections, not a human body structure.

name: fat measurement
clinical_significance: Estimation of body-fat amount or distribution using methods such as skinfolds, bioimpedance, DEXA, imaging, or laboratory analysis. Results vary by method and should be interpreted with overall health, strength, and metabolic findings.

name: fat necrosis
clinical_significance: Death of fat cells, often after pancreatitis, injury, or breast surgery. It can cause pain, inflammation, or a firm lump that resembles cancer on examination or imaging and may require testing to distinguish the cause.

name: fat pad
clinical_significance: A localized cushion of fatty tissue that protects, supports, insulates, or permits movement around an organ or joint. Inflammation or injury of a fat pad can cause localized pain and swelling.

name: fatigue
clinical_significance: Persistent tiredness or reduced energy that limits physical or mental activity and may not improve fully with rest. Sleep problems, anemia, infection, hormone or organ disease, medicines, mood disorders, and neurologic conditions can cause it.

name: fat-soluble vitamin
clinical_significance: A vitamin that dissolves in fat and can be stored in body tissues. Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble; deficiency or excessive supplementation can cause illness.

name: fatty acid
clinical_significance: An organic molecule with a hydrocarbon chain and a terminal carboxyl group. Fatty acids may circulate freely or be joined to glycerol and other molecules in fats and cell membranes; they can provide energy and serve as starting materials for signaling chemicals. They may be saturated, monounsaturated, or polyunsaturated.

name: fatty degeneration
clinical_significance: Abnormal buildup of fat inside cells, especially liver cells, caused by metabolic problems, alcohol, toxins, poor nutrition, obesity, or other injury. The change may reverse or progress to inflammation and scarring.

name: fatty liver
clinical_significance: Fatty liver disease can progress to inflammation, fibrosis, cirrhosis, and liver cancer; metabolic risk reduction and assessment of fibrosis help guide follow-up.

name: favism
clinical_significance: Rapid destruction of red blood cells after eating fava beans, usually in a person with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. It may cause jaundice, dark urine, weakness, breathlessness, or severe anemia and needs medical care.

name: fazarabine
clinical_significance: An experimental pyrimidine antimetabolite studied as chemotherapy for cancer. It interferes with DNA synthesis but has not become a standard treatment; its clinical relevance is mainly historical oncology research.

name: Fc Receptor
clinical_significance: A protein on an immune cell that binds the tail end of an antibody. This helps the cell recognize, ingest, or destroy the antibody’s target and can also influence inflammation.

name: fear
clinical_significance: An emotional and body response to a perceived threat that prepares a person to protect themselves. Persistent or excessive fear can cause avoidance, panic, sleep problems, and impaired daily functioning.

name: febrile convulsion
clinical_significance: A seizure during fever in a young child without evidence of brain infection or another immediate cause. Most are brief and generalized, but a prolonged, repeated, or one-sided seizure requires emergency assessment.

name: febrile neutropenia
clinical_significance: Fever in a person with a dangerously low neutrophil count, the white cells that fight infection. Infection may be present without obvious symptoms, so urgent examination, cultures, and prompt antibiotics are often needed.

name: febuxostat
clinical_significance: A medicine that lowers uric-acid production for long-term prevention of gout attacks. It does not relieve sudden gout pain immediately and may require monitoring for liver problems and cardiovascular risk.

name: fec protocol
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy regimen combining fluorouracil, epirubicin, and cyclophosphamide for selected cancers. It can cause low blood counts, infection, nausea, hair loss, mouth sores, infertility, and heart or bladder-related toxicity.

name: fecal impaction
clinical_significance: A large, hard mass of stool trapped in the rectum or colon. It may cause pain, abdominal swelling, nausea, urinary symptoms, bowel blockage, or watery leakage around the mass and may require professional removal.

name: fecal incontinence
clinical_significance: Inability to control passage of stool or gas, ranging from soiling to complete loss of bowel control. Causes include diarrhea, constipation, sphincter injury, nerve disease, rectal prolapse, and cognitive impairment.

name: feces
clinical_significance: Solid or semisolid waste passed from the bowel, containing water, undigested material, bacteria, shed cells, and metabolic waste. Changes in stool can provide clues about digestion, bleeding, infection, or inflammation.

name: feeding methods
clinical_significance: Ways of providing food or liquid, including breast or bottle feeding, oral feeding, tube feeding, and intravenous nutrition. The safest method depends on swallowing ability, age, illness, and nutritional needs.

name: feeding poor
clinical_significance: Taking too little food or fluid for age or health needs. In an infant it may signal illness, swallowing difficulty, breathing problems, pain, reflux, or developmental difficulty and requires assessment if persistent.

name: feeding tube
clinical_significance: A flexible tube used to deliver nutrition, fluids, or medicines to the stomach or intestine when eating is inadequate or unsafe. Risks include blockage, leakage, infection, aspiration, and injury.

name: felbamate
clinical_significance: An antiseizure medicine reserved for selected severe or drug-resistant epilepsy. It can rarely cause life-threatening bone-marrow failure or liver failure, so specialist prescribing and regular blood and liver tests are essential.

name: felodipine
clinical_significance: A calcium-channel blocker that relaxes artery walls and lowers blood pressure. It may cause ankle swelling, flushing, headache, fast heartbeat, or gum enlargement and should be taken as prescribed.

name: Felty syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare complication of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis involving a very low neutrophil count and often an enlarged spleen. It increases infection risk and requires specialist treatment of arthritis and neutropenia.

name: female
clinical_significance: Describing the sex category generally associated with ovaries, eggs, and female reproductive anatomy. Biological traits vary among individuals, and sex, gender identity, and gender expression are distinct concepts.

name: female breast
clinical_significance: A mammary gland and its skin, fat, connective tissue, ducts, and lobules on the front of the chest. Its structure changes with age, hormones, pregnancy, breastfeeding, and body composition.

name: female condom
clinical_significance: A soft internal sheath placed in the vagina before sex that forms a barrier against semen and can reduce pregnancy and transmission of some sexually transmitted infections when used correctly.

name: female genitalia
clinical_significance: The external and internal reproductive organs, including the vulva, vagina, cervix, uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. These structures support urination, sexual function, menstruation, fertility, pregnancy, and birth.

name: female infertility
clinical_significance: Difficulty achieving pregnancy because of problems with ovulation, ovarian reserve, fallopian tubes, uterus, hormones, or other factors. Evaluation considers both partners and may be recommended after a defined period of trying or sooner with risk factors.

name: female phenotype
clinical_significance: The observable anatomical, physiologic, and developmental traits associated with female sex. These traits vary with genes, hormones, development, age, and individual biology.

name: feminization
clinical_significance: Development of physical or hormonal traits commonly associated with female puberty, such as breast growth or reduced body hair. It may be normal, part of gender-affirming treatment, or caused by hormones, medicines, or disease.

name: femoral artery
clinical_significance: A major artery carrying blood through the groin and thigh to the leg. Its pulse can be felt in the groin, and it is used for some catheter procedures; injury or blockage can threaten the limb.

name: femoral hernia
clinical_significance: A bulge of abdominal tissue through an opening below the groin ligament and beside the femoral vessels. It has a relatively high risk of trapping or losing blood supply to the contents and often needs surgical assessment.

name: femoral neuropathy
clinical_significance: Damage to the femoral nerve causing weakness in hip flexion or knee extension and numbness or pain in the front thigh or inner leg. Causes include diabetes, injury, bleeding, compression, and pelvic disease.

name: femoral vein
clinical_significance: The major deep vein of the thigh, carrying blood from the leg toward the pelvis and heart. A clot in it can cause deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.

name: femtogram
clinical_significance: A unit of mass equal to one quadrillionth of a gram, or $10^{-15}$ gram. It is used in laboratory measurements of extremely small quantities.

name: femtoliter
clinical_significance: A unit of volume equal to one quadrillionth of a liter, or $10^{-15}$ liter. It is used to describe very small laboratory or cellular volumes.

name: femur
clinical_significance: The thigh bone and the longest, strongest bone in the body. It joins the hip to the knee and includes a head, neck, shaft, and lower end; fractures can threaten mobility and blood supply.

name: femur fracture
clinical_significance: A break in the thigh bone caused by trauma or weakened bone. It may cause severe pain, deformity, blood loss, and inability to bear weight; treatment depends on location, alignment, and overall health.

name: fenamiphos
clinical_significance: An organophosphate pesticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Significant exposure can overstimulate nerves and cause sweating, vomiting, pinpoint pupils, muscle weakness, breathing failure, or death; suspected poisoning requires urgent care.

name: fenclonine
clinical_significance: An experimental inhibitor of tryptophan hydroxylase, the enzyme needed to make serotonin. It has been used mainly as a research tool to study serotonin depletion and has no routine therapeutic role; altering serotonin can cause serious neuropsychiatric effects.

name: fenfluramine
clinical_significance: Fenfluramine is a serotonergic medicine used in some jurisdictions for selected severe epileptic encephalopathies; historical appetite-suppressant use was limited by valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension, so cardiac monitoring is required.

name: fenitrothion
clinical_significance: A poisonous organophosphate insecticide. Exposure can cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, diarrhea, small pupils, muscle twitching, breathing difficulty, seizures, or weakness because it disrupts nerve signals; suspected poisoning needs urgent medical help.

name: fenobucarb
clinical_significance: A carbamate insecticide that can cause nerve poisoning after significant absorption, producing sweating, vomiting, small pupils, muscle weakness, breathing difficulty, or seizures.

name: fenofibrate
clinical_significance: A medicine that lowers blood triglycerides and can modestly change cholesterol levels by increasing the liver's processing of fats. It is used for selected lipid disorders; liver, kidney, muscle, and gallbladder risks require monitoring.

name: fenoldopam
clinical_significance: A short-acting dopamine D1-receptor agonist used intravenously for severe hypertension in selected settings; it can cause hypotension, flushing, headache, and increased intraocular pressure.

name: fenoprofen
clinical_significance: Fenoprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug used for pain and inflammatory arthritis; gastrointestinal bleeding, renal injury, fluid retention, and cardiovascular events are important risks.

name: fenoterol
clinical_significance: A short-acting beta-2 bronchodilator that relaxes airway muscle and relieves bronchospasm. It may cause tremor, nervousness, low potassium, or a fast or irregular heartbeat and is not approved everywhere.

name: fenoxycarb
clinical_significance: An insect-growth regulator that imitates juvenile hormone and disrupts development of immature insects. It is used for pest control, and exposure should be minimized because products can irritate skin, eyes, or airways.

name: fenretinide
clinical_significance: An investigational synthetic retinoid studied for cancer prevention and treatment, including neuroblastoma. It is not a routine approved cancer treatment; research use requires monitoring for retinoid-related toxicity and other adverse effects.

name: fentanyl
clinical_significance: A very potent opioid used in anesthesia and for severe pain, including selected cancer or perioperative pain. It can rapidly suppress breathing and cause sedation, dependence, or fatal overdose, especially with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other sedatives.

name: fentanyl citrate
clinical_significance: The citrate salt of fentanyl, a potent opioid analgesic used for severe pain and anesthesia; respiratory depression, sedation, dependence, and overdose are major risks.

name: fenthion
clinical_significance: A poisonous organophosphate insecticide. Exposure can cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, diarrhea, small pupils, muscle twitching, breathing difficulty, seizures, or weakness because it disrupts nerve signals; suspected poisoning needs urgent medical help.

name: fermentation
clinical_significance: A metabolic process in which microorganisms or cells convert organic substrates without using oxidative respiration, producing products such as acids, alcohols, or gases.

name: ferredoxin
clinical_significance: An iron-sulfur protein that transfers electrons in cellular metabolism, including mitochondrial steroid and iron-sulfur-cluster pathways. Defects in related human ferredoxin systems can cause rare mitochondrial disease with neurologic, visual, or developmental problems.

name: ferritin
clinical_significance: A protein that stores iron inside cells and releases it when needed. Blood ferritin often reflects body iron stores, but inflammation, infection, liver disease, or cancer can raise it even when iron is low.

name: ferroptosis
clinical_significance: A controlled form of cell death caused by iron-dependent damage to cell fats and failure of antioxidant protection. It differs from apoptosis and ordinary tissue necrosis and is being studied in cancer and other diseases.

name: ferrous sulfate
clinical_significance: An oral iron supplement used to prevent or treat iron-deficiency anemia. It may cause nausea, constipation, abdominal discomfort, or dark stools; accidental overdose can be life-threatening, especially in children.

name: fertility
clinical_significance: The biological ability to conceive and produce offspring. It depends on ovulation, sperm production, reproductive anatomy, hormones, age, general health, and other factors affecting either partner.

name: fertility agent
clinical_significance: Medicines that support conception by treating a specific fertility problem or stimulating ovulation. Use requires individualized monitoring because some agents increase the risk of multiple pregnancy or ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

name: fertility domain
clinical_significance: The part of health concerned with reproductive function, ability to conceive, fertility goals, infertility, preservation of fertility, and related medical, emotional, and social care.

name: fertility preservation
clinical_significance: Steps taken to protect the possibility of future pregnancy before treatment or disease may damage reproductive function. Options include freezing eggs, embryos, sperm, or selected reproductive tissue, depending on age, timing, and goals.

name: fertilization
clinical_significance: Fusion of sperm and egg genetic material to form a zygote, usually in a fallopian tube. This begins embryonic development, which may continue after the zygote reaches the uterus and implants.

name: ferumoxytol
clinical_significance: An intravenous iron preparation used for selected adults with iron-deficiency anemia. It can cause allergic reactions, low blood pressure, or iron overload, so monitoring is required during and after infusion.

name: fetal alcohol syndrome
clinical_significance: The most severe recognized form of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, involving characteristic facial features, poor growth, and brain-development problems after prenatal alcohol exposure. No known safe amount of alcohol exists during pregnancy.

name: fetal bradyarrhythmia
clinical_significance: An unusually slow or irregular fetal heart rhythm. Causes include conduction block, extra beats, maternal or fetal disease, or medicines; persistent abnormalities require prompt specialist assessment.

name: fetal death
clinical_significance: Death of a fetus before delivery. Medical and legal definitions vary by gestational age and location; care includes confirming the diagnosis, supporting the family, and discussing delivery and follow-up.

name: fetal disease
clinical_significance: A disease, structural abnormality, or developmental problem affecting a fetus before birth. Causes include genetic changes, infection, medicines, toxins, and poor placental function; ultrasound and prenatal tests may identify it.

name: fetal distress
clinical_significance: A nonspecific term for concerning fetal findings during labor, especially abnormal heart-rate patterns that may indicate low oxygen, cord compression, infection, or placental problems. Clinicians assess the whole pattern and may act urgently.

name: fetal heart
clinical_significance: The developing heart of a fetus, whose rate and rhythm can be assessed by ultrasound or electronic monitoring to evaluate fetal well-being.

name: fetal hemoglobin
clinical_significance: The main oxygen-carrying protein in a fetus’s red blood cells. It binds oxygen more strongly than adult hemoglobin, helping the fetus obtain oxygen from the placenta; its amount normally falls after birth.

name: fetal hypoxia
clinical_significance: Too little oxygen reaching a fetus before or during birth. Placental disease, maternal breathing or circulation problems, cord compression, or prolonged labor can contribute; abnormal heart-rate patterns require prompt obstetric assessment.

name: fetal macrosomia
clinical_significance: A fetus that is larger than expected, often estimated at 4,000–4,500 grams or more at birth depending on the clinical definition. Diabetes and previous large babies increase risk; complications include difficult birth, injury, and cesarean delivery.

name: fetal malpresentation
clinical_significance: A fetal presentation other than the usual vertex presentation, including breech, transverse, or oblique lie, which may affect labor and delivery planning.

name: fetal pyelectasis
clinical_significance: Mild widening of the urine-collecting area of a fetus’s kidney seen on an ultrasound scan. It may go away before birth or be linked to a urinary blockage or another condition, so follow-up depends on its size and other findings.

name: fetal stage
clinical_significance: The fetal stage begins after the embryonic period and continues until birth, characterized mainly by growth and maturation of established organs.

name: fetal tissue
clinical_significance: Fetal tissue is tissue from a developing fetus and may be relevant to pregnancy care, pathology, research, transplantation, or genetic testing under applicable ethical and legal rules.

name: fetal weight
clinical_significance: An estimate of a fetus’s mass, usually calculated from ultrasound measurements. It helps assess growth and identify possible growth restriction or unusually large size, but it is not exact.

name: fetomaternal transfusion
clinical_significance: Movement of fetal blood cells across the placenta into the pregnant person's bloodstream. Small amounts are common, but heavy transfer after trauma, placental problems, or procedures can cause fetal anemia and may require urgent testing and treatment.

name: fetus
clinical_significance: A developing human from the start of the ninth week after fertilization until birth. During this period, established organs grow and mature; medical descriptions may instead use pregnancy weeks counted from the last menstrual period.

name: fever
clinical_significance: A regulated rise in body temperature caused by changes in the body's temperature-control system, commonly in response to infection or inflammation. It may also occur with certain medicines, cancers, autoimmune disorders, or other conditions. Fever differs from hyperthermia, in which body temperature rises without a normal change in the temperature set point.

name: fexofenadine
clinical_significance: An antihistamine used to relieve sneezing, itching, runny nose, and watery eyes from allergies and itching from hives. It usually causes less drowsiness than older antihistamines, but headache or nausea can occur.

name: fiber
clinical_significance: Dietary fiber is plant material that the small intestine cannot digest. It adds bulk to stool, supports regular bowel movements, and some types help lower blood cholesterol and slow rises in blood glucose.

name: fibrin
clinical_significance: An insoluble, threadlike protein that forms a mesh at an injured blood vessel. The mesh traps blood cells and strengthens the clot that helps stop bleeding.

name: fibrinogen
clinical_significance: A blood protein made mainly by the liver that is changed into fibrin during clot formation. Low levels can cause bleeding; levels may rise with inflammation and fall in severe liver disease or widespread clotting.

name: fibrinogen assay
clinical_significance: A laboratory test that measures the amount or clotting activity of fibrinogen in blood. It helps investigate unexplained bleeding, abnormal clotting, liver disease, or suspected widespread clotting disorders.

name: fibrinogen decreased
clinical_significance: A lower-than-normal blood fibrinogen level, which can weaken clot formation and cause bleeding. Causes include inherited deficiency, severe liver disease, major blood loss or transfusion, and widespread activation of clotting.

name: fibrinolysis
clinical_significance: The natural process that dissolves a blood clot after healing begins. An enzyme called plasmin breaks down fibrin; excessive breakdown can cause bleeding, while insufficient breakdown can allow harmful clots to persist.

name: fibrinolytic agent
clinical_significance: A medicine that dissolves a blood clot by helping the body convert plasminogen into plasmin, which breaks down fibrin. It may treat selected emergencies but can cause serious bleeding, including bleeding in the brain.

name: fibrinolytic therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that uses clot-dissolving medicine to restore blood flow in selected emergencies, such as certain strokes, heart attacks, or pulmonary embolisms. The main risk is serious bleeding, so eligibility is assessed urgently.

name: fibroadenoma
clinical_significance: A common noncancerous breast lump made of glandular and connective tissue. It is usually firm, smooth, movable, and painless, especially in adolescents and young adults; imaging helps distinguish it from other breast masses.

name: fibroblast
clinical_significance: A cell that makes collagen and other supporting materials in connective tissue. Fibroblasts help maintain skin, tendons, and organs and become active during wound healing and scar formation.

name: fibrocartilage
clinical_significance: A tough type of cartilage that combines strength with limited flexibility. It helps absorb pressure and resist pulling in the discs between spinal bones, the pubic joint, and the knee menisci.

name: fibrofolliculoma
clinical_significance: A small, usually noncancerous skin growth arising around a hair follicle, often on the face, neck, or upper trunk. Multiple lesions may occur with an inherited disorder that also raises kidney-tumor risk.

name: fibroid tumor
clinical_significance: A noncancerous growth of the uterus made from smooth muscle and connective tissue. It may cause heavy or painful periods, pelvic pressure, frequent urination, infertility, or no symptoms.

name: fibrolipoma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous, slow-growing lump made of mature fat and fibrous tissue. It is often painless and lies beneath the skin, but a new or enlarging lump should be assessed.

name: fibroma
clinical_significance: A usually benign tumor made mainly of fibrous connective tissue. Fibromas can develop in skin, soft tissue, bone, or organs; their effects depend on their location and size, and some site-specific forms may recur or interfere with organ function.

name: fibromatosis
clinical_significance: An overgrowth of connective-tissue cells that does not spread to distant organs but can invade nearby tissue and recur. Desmoid-type disease may cause pain, a firm mass, or impaired organ function.

name: fibromuscular dysplasia
clinical_significance: An abnormal structure of medium-sized artery walls, most often in the kidney or neck arteries. It can cause high blood pressure, headache, or stroke, or produce an artery bulge or tear.

name: fibromyalgia
clinical_significance: A long-term condition that causes widespread body pain and increased sensitivity to pain. It commonly causes fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, stiffness, and difficulty concentrating or remembering. The exact cause is not fully understood, but altered pain processing in the nervous system may contribute. Diagnosis is based mainly on the pattern of symptoms and examination; no single laboratory or imaging test confirms it.

name: fibromyxosarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare cancer of soft tissue containing fibrous and jelly-like material. It may present as a growing lump or pain; diagnosis requires tissue examination, and treatment depends on its site and spread.

name: fibronectin
clinical_significance: A protein found in blood and connective tissue that helps cells attach, move, and organize during tissue repair. It supports wound healing and the structure of tissues around cells.

name: fibrosarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare cancer arising from cells that make fibrous connective tissue. It usually develops in deep soft tissue or bone and may cause a growing mass, pain, or reduced movement.

name: fibrosis
clinical_significance: Excess formation of scar tissue after ongoing injury or inflammation. Fibrosis can make an organ stiff and reduce its function, such as causing breathlessness in the lungs or impaired filtration in the kidneys.

name: fibrous dysplasia
clinical_significance: A noncancerous bone disorder in which normal bone is replaced by weaker abnormal tissue. It may affect one or several bones and cause pain, deformity, fractures, or pressure on nearby nerves.

name: fibula
clinical_significance: The slender bone on the outer side of the lower leg. It provides muscle attachment and forms the outer ankle. The nerve near its upper end can be injured by pressure or fracture.

name: Ficusin
clinical_significance: A naturally occurring furocoumarin found in some plants, including Psoralea species. It has no established therapeutic use; furocoumarin exposure can increase skin sensitivity to ultraviolet light and cause phototoxic reactions.

name: fidaxomicin
clinical_significance: A narrow-spectrum antibiotic used to treat Clostridioides difficile infection of the intestine. It reduces harmful bacteria while having relatively little effect on many other gut bacteria and is an option for lowering recurrence risk; nausea and abdominal symptoms can occur.

name: fiducial markers
clinical_significance: Small visible markers placed on or inside the body to identify a precise location during imaging, radiation treatment, or surgery. They help clinicians align equipment and target the intended tissue accurately.

name: filamentous fungus
clinical_significance: A fungus that grows as branching threads called hyphae, which form a network called mycelium. Some filamentous fungi cause skin, nail, lung, or invasive infections, especially in people with weakened immunity.

name: Filaria bancrofti
clinical_significance: A mosquito-borne parasitic roundworm that causes most cases of lymphatic filariasis worldwide. Adult worms damage lymph vessels and may eventually cause chronic limb swelling, genital swelling, or elephantiasis; many infections remain symptom-free for years.

name: filaria demarquayi
clinical_significance: A historical name for Mansonella ozzardi, a blood-dwelling filarial parasite transmitted by biting midges or blackflies in parts of the Americas. Infection is often asymptomatic or mild, but it can cause itching, fever, joint pain, or other nonspecific symptoms.

name: filarial elephantiases
clinical_significance: Chronic severe swelling and skin thickening caused by damage to lymphatic drainage, often after lymphatic filariasis but also from other lymphatic obstruction. Recurrent skin infections can worsen swelling and disability; care focuses on hygiene, skin treatment, exercise, and managing the underlying cause.

name: filariasis
clinical_significance: Infection with threadlike parasitic worms spread by mosquitoes, flies, or other insects. Depending on the species, worms may affect lymph vessels, skin, or eyes, causing swelling, inflammation, itching, or vision problems.

name: filgrastim
clinical_significance: A granulocyte colony-stimulating factor that raises neutrophil counts and lowers infection risk in selected patients receiving chemotherapy or with certain chronic neutropenias. It is also used to mobilize stem cells for collection; bone pain is common, and rare serious risks include splenic rupture and lung injury.

name: filler excipient
clinical_significance: An inactive ingredient added to a medicine to provide bulk, improve stability, or help form a tablet, capsule, or liquid. It may rarely cause allergy or intolerance.

name: filopodium
clinical_significance: A thin, finger-like projection from a cell surface. It senses nearby surroundings and helps cells attach, move, communicate, or form connections, including connections made by developing nerve cells.

name: filoviridae
clinical_significance: A family of viruses that includes Ebola and Marburg viruses. They can cause severe fever, bleeding, organ failure, and death, and are mainly spread through direct contact with blood or other infected body fluids.

name: fimbriae proteins
clinical_significance: Bacterial surface proteins that form hair-like projections used to attach bacteria to human cells, medical devices, or other surfaces. Attachment can help bacteria form communities and begin infection.

name: finasteride
clinical_significance: A 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor used for male-pattern hair loss and benign prostate enlargement. It can cause sexual adverse effects, lowers prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels and complicates PSA interpretation, and can harm development of a male fetus if absorbed during pregnancy.

name: finegoldia
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria that grow without oxygen and normally live on skin or mucous membranes. They can occasionally cause wound, soft-tissue, bone, joint, or bloodstream infections.

name: finegoldia magna
clinical_significance: A bacterium normally found on skin and mucous membranes that grows without oxygen. It can cause infections after wounds or surgery, including abscesses and deeper soft-tissue infections.

name: finger
clinical_significance: One of the hand’s digits, made of bones, joints, muscles, tendons, nerves, blood vessels, and skin. Fingers support grasping, touch, balance, and precise movements.

name: finger flexors
clinical_significance: Muscles and tendons that bend the fingers at their joints. Injury can cause pain or inability to bend a finger and may require prompt assessment, especially after a cut or forceful injury.

name: finger injury
clinical_significance: Damage to a finger’s bone, joint, tendon, ligament, nerve, blood vessel, nail, or skin, usually from trauma. Assessment checks alignment, movement, sensation, blood flow, and possible hidden fractures.

name: finger joint
clinical_significance: A connection between the bones of a finger that allows bending, straightening, and limited side-to-side movement. Finger joints can be affected by injury, arthritis, inflammation, infection, or dislocation.

name: firefly family
clinical_significance: A family of bioluminescent beetles whose luciferase enzymes are widely used as reporter tools in biomedical research and some laboratory assays. The insects themselves have no established human disease role.

name: firesetting behavior
clinical_significance: Deliberately starting fires. Repeated fire-setting may be linked to an impulse-control disorder, mental illness, substance use, developmental problems, or social stress and requires assessment of safety and risk to others.

name: firmicutes
clinical_significance: A large bacterial group, now formally named Bacillota in current taxonomy and still widely called Firmicutes. It includes common gut bacteria and important pathogens; research abundance patterns are not by themselves a clinical diagnosis.

name: first aid
clinical_significance: Immediate basic care for injury or sudden illness before professional treatment arrives. It includes ensuring safety, calling emergency services, checking breathing, starting resuscitation when needed, and controlling severe bleeding.

name: first-degree burn
clinical_significance: A superficial burn affecting only the outer skin layer. It causes redness, pain, and dryness without blisters, as with mild sunburn, and usually heals within several days without scarring.

name: fish oil
clinical_significance: Oil containing omega-3 fatty acids, usually obtained from oily fish. Supplements may lower triglycerides at prescribed doses, but benefits vary and side effects or medicine interactions should be reviewed with a clinician.

name: fish venom
clinical_significance: Poison produced by certain fish, usually delivered through spines or sharp body parts. It can cause immediate severe pain, swelling, numbness, tissue injury, or rarely whole-body poisoning.

name: fissured tongue
clinical_significance: A usually harmless condition in which grooves develop on the tongue’s surface. Food may collect in the grooves and cause irritation or odor; gentle tongue cleaning and routine oral care can help.

name: fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal passage between two body parts, such as two organs, a blood vessel and another structure, or an organ and the skin. It may result from infection, inflammation, injury, surgery, or cancer. Symptoms and treatment depend on its location; some close with medical treatment, while others need a procedure or surgery.

name: fixative
clinical_significance: A chemical used to preserve cells or tissue for laboratory examination by preventing decay and maintaining structure. Common fixatives can irritate skin, eyes, and airways and must be handled safely.

name: fixed macrophage
clinical_significance: An immune cell that stays within a particular tissue instead of circulating in blood. It removes dead cells and microbes and helps coordinate inflammation and repair.

name: flagellin
clinical_significance: The main protein in a bacterial flagellum, the whip-like structure that helps some bacteria move. Human immune cells can recognize flagellin and respond with inflammation.

name: flagellum
clinical_significance: A long, whip-like structure that helps a cell or microorganism move. Human sperm and some bacteria have flagella, which differ in structure and function.

name: flank pain
clinical_significance: Pain between the lower ribs and hip, often caused by kidney stones, kidney infection, muscle strain, spine problems, or nearby abdominal disease. Fever, vomiting, blood in urine, injury, or severe pain needs prompt evaluation.

name: flare-up
clinical_significance: A sudden or gradual worsening of a long-term disease after a period of relative stability. The cause may be infection, stress, missed treatment, or disease progression and should be assessed if severe or persistent.

name: flat affect
clinical_significance: Very little outward expression of emotion, such as reduced facial movement, gestures, or voice variation. It is a clinical sign, not a diagnosis, and may occur with psychiatric, neurologic, or medication-related conditions.

name: flatfoot
clinical_significance: A foot with a reduced or collapsed inner arch. It may be flexible and painless or rigid and painful; causes include normal development, loose ligaments, tendon problems, injury, arthritis, or bone shape.

name: flatulence
clinical_significance: Passage of gas through the anus, produced by swallowed air and bacterial digestion of food in the intestine. It may increase with diet, constipation, swallowing air, or digestive disorders; persistent troublesome symptoms need assessment.

name: flavin
clinical_significance: A family of yellow pigments and redox cofactors related to riboflavin, including flavin adenine dinucleotide and flavin mononucleotide. These cofactors support many enzyme reactions, and riboflavin deficiency can impair flavin-dependent metabolism.

name: flaviviridae
clinical_significance: A family of single-stranded RNA viruses that includes dengue, yellow fever, Zika, hepatitis C, and West Nile viruses. Different members spread through insects, blood, or other routes and cause different illnesses.

name: flavivirus
clinical_significance: A group of RNA viruses that includes dengue, yellow fever, West Nile, Japanese encephalitis, and Zika viruses. Many spread through mosquitoes or ticks and can cause fever, inflammation, or nervous-system disease.

name: flavobacteriaceae
clinical_significance: A family of mainly gram-negative bacteria found in water, soil, and other environments. Most do not infect people, but some can cause opportunistic infections, especially in hospitalized or immunocompromised patients.

name: flavobacterium
clinical_significance: A group of gram-negative bacteria commonly found in water and soil. A few species can cause opportunistic infections in people or animals, particularly when immunity is weakened.

name: flavodoxin
clinical_significance: A small iron-sulfur protein used by some bacteria and plants to transfer electrons. It is mainly a biochemical research term; bacterial flavodoxin pathways are being studied as possible selective antimicrobial targets.

name: flavonifractor
clinical_significance: A genus of gut anaerobic bacteria that can metabolize flavonoids. Changes in its abundance have been reported in microbiome studies, but detection in stool is not a validated diagnosis or indication for treatment; rare clinical infections require context-specific interpretation.

name: flavonoid
clinical_significance: Plant compounds studied for antioxidant and other biological effects. Eating flavonoid-containing foods can be part of a balanced diet, but concentrated supplements are not proven treatments and may interact with medicines depending on the compound and dose.

name: flavonol
clinical_significance: A subgroup of plant flavonoids found in foods such as onions, tea, and berries. They are studied for vascular and inflammatory effects, but evidence does not support using flavonol supplements to treat or prevent disease.

name: flavopiridol
clinical_significance: An investigational cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor studied as an anticancer medicine. It is not a routine approved cancer treatment; research trials have examined its use alone or in combinations for selected malignancies.

name: flavor enhancer
clinical_significance: A food additive used to strengthen or alter flavor. Health effects depend on the specific ingredient; some people report symptoms with particular additives, but broad self-restriction is usually unnecessary without a reproducible reaction or confirmed allergy.

name: flavoxate
clinical_significance: A medicine used to relieve bladder spasms, urgency, frequency, or painful urination. It treats symptoms rather than infection or blockage and can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, dizziness, or constipation.

name: flaxseed extract
clinical_significance: A preparation made from flaxseed that may contain omega-3 fat, lignans, and soluble fiber. Effects vary by product; it may interact with medicines affecting clotting, blood sugar, or blood pressure.

name: flea
clinical_significance: A small wingless insect that feeds on blood. Flea bites can cause itchy skin reactions, and fleas can transmit infections between animals or, less commonly, to people.

name: flecainide
clinical_significance: A prescription antiarrhythmic medicine that slows electrical signals in the heart to prevent selected abnormal rhythms. It is not suitable for everyone and can worsen dangerous rhythms, especially with structural heart disease.

name: fleshy tab
clinical_significance: A small congenital tag of soft tissue without underlying bone, recorded as a developmental finding in animal studies. Its importance depends on its location and whether other structural abnormalities are present; the label alone does not identify a human disease.

name: flocculation
clinical_significance: The joining of tiny particles suspended in a liquid into larger clumps. Laboratory tests may use this visible reaction to detect antibodies or other substances; it is also used in water treatment and pharmaceutical preparation.

name: flow cytometry
clinical_significance: A laboratory test that examines cells or particles one at a time as they pass through a laser beam. It can count cells and identify their features, helping diagnose blood cancers and immune disorders.

name: flowmeter
clinical_significance: A device that measures the rate at which a gas or liquid moves. In medicine, it may measure oxygen delivery, intravenous fluid flow, or breathing flow such as peak expiratory flow.

name: floxacillin
clinical_significance: An antibacterial medicine used in some countries to treat infections caused by susceptible bacteria, especially staphylococci. It can cause allergic reactions, diarrhea, liver problems, or other antibiotic-related effects.

name: floxuridine
clinical_significance: An anticancer medicine that interferes with DNA production, slowing or killing rapidly dividing cells. It is used only in selected treatment plans and may cause low blood counts, mouth sores, diarrhea, or other toxicity.

name: fluconazole
clinical_significance: An antifungal medicine used for selected yeast and other fungal infections. It can interact with many medicines and may cause nausea, rash, or liver injury; treatment depends on the infection and patient.

name: flucytosine
clinical_significance: An antifungal medicine converted inside susceptible fungi into substances that interfere with genetic-material production. It is used for selected serious infections, usually with another antifungal, and requires blood-count and liver monitoring.

name: fludarabine
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy medicine that interferes with DNA production in abnormal blood cells. It treats selected blood cancers but can severely suppress immunity and blood counts, increasing the risk of serious infections.

name: fludarabine phosphate
clinical_significance: A form of fludarabine used in selected blood-cancer treatment plans. It interferes with DNA production and can cause prolonged low blood counts, immune suppression, infections, and neurologic or other serious effects.

name: fludrocortisone
clinical_significance: A medicine that helps the body retain salt and water and raise blood pressure. It treats some adrenal-hormone deficiencies and selected orthostatic disorders; monitoring is needed for swelling, high blood pressure, and low potassium.

name: fluid management
clinical_significance: Planning and monitoring fluids, salts, and urine output to maintain circulation and organ function. Treatment may involve drinking, intravenous fluids, diuretics, or fluid restriction according to the underlying problem.

name: fluid therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment using fluids, often through a vein, to restore hydration, blood volume, or salt balance. The type and amount depend on the cause; excess fluid can worsen swelling, heart failure, or lung congestion.

name: flumazenil
clinical_significance: An antidote that can reverse sedation and slowed breathing caused by some benzodiazepine medicines. It can trigger seizures or sudden withdrawal and is not suitable for every overdose, especially mixed overdoses.

name: fluocinolone acetonide
clinical_significance: A corticosteroid medicine applied to the skin or scalp to reduce redness, swelling, and itching. Overuse can thin the skin, worsen infections, or rarely affect the body’s hormone system.

name: fluocinonide
clinical_significance: A strong corticosteroid applied to selected inflammatory skin conditions to reduce itching, redness, and swelling. It should be used only as directed because prolonged or extensive use can damage skin or cause systemic effects.

name: fluorescein
clinical_significance: A bright fluorescent dye used in eye examinations and some imaging tests. In the eye, it highlights scratches, ulcers, and abnormal blood-vessel leakage; rare allergic reactions can occur after injection.

name: fluorescein angiography
clinical_significance: An eye test in which fluorescent dye is injected into a vein and photographs track its movement through retinal blood vessels. It can show leakage, blockage, or abnormal vessels in retinal disease.

name: fluorescence
clinical_significance: The emission of visible light by a substance after it absorbs light or other energy. Clinicians and researchers use it to identify cells, chemicals, microbes, or structures in laboratory and imaging tests.

name: fluorescence microscopy
clinical_significance: A microscope method that uses fluorescent labels to make selected cells, molecules, or microbes visible. It helps examine tissue structure, cell proteins, genetic material, and infectious organisms.

name: fluorescence polarization
clinical_significance: A laboratory measurement of how much fluorescent light remains aligned with its original polarization after interacting with a sample. Fluorescence-polarization immunoassays can measure selected medicines or other small molecules in blood and support therapeutic drug monitoring.

name: fluorescent dye
clinical_significance: A substance that absorbs light of one color and emits light of another. It can label cells, tissues, molecules, or microbes so they can be detected during laboratory or imaging examinations.

name: fluoride
clinical_significance: A mineral that strengthens tooth enamel, helps repair early damage, and reduces acid production by cavity-causing bacteria. It is found in some water supplies, toothpaste, mouth rinses, and professional dental treatments.

name: fluoride poisoning
clinical_significance: Illness caused by swallowing too much fluoride. Early symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain; severe poisoning can lower blood calcium and cause muscle spasms, seizures, or dangerous heart rhythms.

name: fluorimetry
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that measures light emitted by a fluorescent substance. It can detect or estimate very small amounts of chemicals, medicines, proteins, or biological material.

name: fluorine
clinical_significance: A highly reactive chemical element found in compounds such as fluoride. Small controlled amounts of fluoride help protect teeth, while excessive exposure can poison the body or damage developing bones and teeth.

name: fluorometholone
clinical_significance: A corticosteroid eye medicine used for selected inflammatory conditions. Prolonged use can raise eye pressure, delay healing, worsen infection, or increase cataract risk, so it requires medical supervision.

name: fluorophotometry
clinical_significance: A method that measures fluorescent light from the eye or another sample. It can help estimate substances or tissue properties, but results must be interpreted with the test method and clinical findings.

name: fluoropyrimidine
clinical_significance: A class of anticancer medicines that resembles substances used to build DNA and RNA. They disrupt genetic-material production in rapidly dividing cells and can cause mouth sores, diarrhea, low blood counts, and hand-foot symptoms.

name: fluoroquinolone
clinical_significance: An antibiotic that kills bacteria by blocking enzymes needed for bacterial DNA copying. It is reserved for selected infections because it can cause tendon injury, nerve symptoms, heart-rhythm changes, blood-sugar changes, or severe diarrhea.

name: fluoroscopy
clinical_significance: An X-ray method that produces moving images inside the body. It helps guide procedures and examine swallowing, blood vessels, joints, and digestive or urinary passages; contrast dye may be used and radiation exposure occurs.

name: fluorouracil
clinical_significance: An anticancer medicine that interferes with DNA production. It is applied to selected precancerous skin lesions or given for some cancers; possible effects include mouth sores, diarrhea, low blood counts, and serious toxicity in susceptible people.

name: fluoxetine
clinical_significance: An antidepressant that increases available serotonin in the brain. It treats depression and several other conditions, but may cause nausea, sleep or sexual problems, agitation, or rarely dangerous serotonin excess or suicidal thoughts.

name: fluoxymesterone
clinical_significance: A synthetic androgen medicine used in selected hormone-related conditions. It can affect the liver, cholesterol, mood, fertility, prostate, and blood count and should be used only with medical supervision.

name: fluphenazine
clinical_significance: An antipsychotic medicine used to treat schizophrenia and related psychotic symptoms. It can cause stiffness, tremor, restlessness, sleepiness, hormonal changes, and rare but serious involuntary movements or fever.

name: fluphenazine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: The hydrochloride salt form of fluphenazine, an antipsychotic medicine for selected psychotic disorders. Monitoring is needed because it can cause movement disorders, sedation, hormonal effects, and other serious adverse reactions.

name: flurandrenolide
clinical_significance: A corticosteroid applied to the skin to reduce inflammation, redness, and itching. Prolonged, extensive, or covered use can thin the skin, worsen infection, or allow steroid effects throughout the body.

name: flurazepam
clinical_significance: A long-acting sedative medicine used for short-term treatment of insomnia in some settings. It can cause next-day drowsiness, falls, memory problems, dependence, and dangerous breathing suppression with alcohol or opioids.

name: flurbiprofen
clinical_significance: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicine used for pain and swelling and, in some forms, eye inflammation. It can cause stomach bleeding, kidney problems, heart risks, or allergic reactions and should be used as directed.

name: flushing
clinical_significance: Temporary redness and warmth of the skin caused by increased blood flow. Triggers include heat, exercise, emotion, alcohol, medicines, fever, or hormone disorders; flushing with wheezing, diarrhea, faintness, or palpitations needs evaluation.

name: flutamide
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks male-hormone effects and is used with other hormone treatment for prostate cancer. It can seriously injure the liver and may cause nausea, breast tenderness, or reduced blood counts.

name: fluticasone
clinical_significance: A corticosteroid available in inhaled, nasal, and topical forms. It treats conditions such as asthma, allergic rhinitis, and inflammatory skin disease; local irritation, nosebleeds, oral thrush, and, with high or prolonged exposure, systemic steroid effects can occur.

name: fluvastatin
clinical_significance: A statin medicine that lowers low-density lipoprotein cholesterol by reducing cholesterol production in the liver. It lowers cardiovascular risk but can cause muscle symptoms, liver abnormalities, or rare muscle breakdown.

name: fluvoxamine
clinical_significance: An antidepressant that increases serotonin signaling and is used mainly for obsessive-compulsive disorder and selected other conditions. It can cause nausea, sleep changes, sexual problems, medicine interactions, or rarely serotonin toxicity.

name: fMRI
clinical_significance: Functional magnetic resonance imaging maps changes in brain blood flow and oxygen use while a person performs tasks or rests. It can help identify language or movement areas and does not use X-ray radiation.

name: foam cell
clinical_significance: A cell containing many fat droplets, giving it a foamy appearance under a microscope. Foam cells, often immune cells that have taken up cholesterol, are common in early artery-wall plaque.

name: focal
clinical_significance: Limited to one specific area rather than spread widely. A focal finding may involve an image, seizure, infection, injury, or neurologic problem and must be interpreted according to its location.

name: focal adhesion
clinical_significance: A specialized attachment site where a cell connects to its surrounding support material. It helps cells stick, sense physical forces, move, and send signals during growth and tissue repair.

name: focal glomerulosclerosis
clinical_significance: Scarring affecting some kidney filters or only parts of affected filters. It can cause protein to leak into urine, swelling, high blood pressure, and gradual loss of kidney function.

name: focal seizure
clinical_significance: A seizure that begins in one area of the brain. It may cause unusual movement, sensation, behavior, emotion, or awareness and can spread to involve both sides of the brain.

name: foetal acidosis
clinical_significance: Excess acidity in fetal blood, usually caused by inadequate oxygen delivery or impaired gas exchange. Fetal heart-rate monitoring and, in selected situations, blood testing help assess its likelihood and severity.

name: folate
