clinical_significance: Vitamin B9, needed for DNA production, cell division, and healthy red blood cells. Adequate folate before and during early pregnancy lowers neural-tube-defect risk; high-dose supplements can hide vitamin B12 deficiency.

name: folate antagonist
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks folate-related processes needed to make DNA. Depending on the drug, it may treat cancer, inflammatory disease, or bacterial infection, but can cause low blood counts, mouth sores, or liver problems.

name: folate deficiency
clinical_significance: Too little vitamin B9, caused by poor intake, increased need, malabsorption, alcohol use, or some medicines. It can cause large abnormal red blood cells, anemia, fatigue, sore tongue, and pregnancy complications.

name: folic acid
clinical_significance: A manufactured form of vitamin B9 needed for DNA production and healthy blood cells. Supplements prevent many fetal neural-tube defects when taken before conception and treat folate deficiency.

name: follicle
clinical_significance: A small sac or organized tissue structure. A hair follicle produces a hair, while an ovarian follicle contains a developing egg; other follicles can occur in glands or lymphatic tissue.

name: follicular fluid
clinical_significance: The liquid inside an ovarian follicle surrounding a developing egg. It contains hormones and other substances that support follicle growth and help coordinate ovulation.

name: follicular hyperkeratosis
clinical_significance: Excess keratin blocking hair follicles and causing small rough bumps. It commonly occurs with keratosis pilaris and, less often, with nutritional deficiency or other skin conditions.

name: follicular lymphoma
clinical_significance: A usually slow-growing cancer of immune cells that often causes painless swelling of lymph nodes. It may involve bone marrow or other organs and can sometimes change into a faster-growing lymphoma.

name: follicular thyroid carcinoma
clinical_significance: A thyroid cancer that begins in follicle-forming cells and can spread through the bloodstream, especially to bone or lungs. Tissue examination is needed to show invasion and distinguish it from a benign growth.

name: folliculitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection around a hair follicle, causing small itchy, red, or tender bumps and sometimes pus. Causes include bacteria, yeast, friction, blocked skin, shaving, and ingrown hairs.

name: follistatin
clinical_significance: A protein that regulates activin and related growth signals involved in muscle, reproductive, and other tissue functions. Follistatin-based gene therapies have been studied for selected muscle diseases, but these approaches remain experimental and are not routine treatment.

name: follow-up
clinical_significance: Ongoing assessment after a diagnosis, treatment, procedure, or test to monitor recovery, response, complications, or recurrence. The timing and type of follow-up depend on the condition, treatment, and individual risks.

name: fomepizole
clinical_significance: An antidote for poisoning with methanol or ethylene glycol. It blocks formation of their toxic breakdown products and may be combined with intensive supportive care and dialysis.

name: fomites
clinical_significance: Objects or surfaces that may carry infectious organisms and transfer them through contact. Examples include shared towels, medical equipment, toys, and other contaminated items; cleaning and hand hygiene reduce risk.

name: fondaparinux
clinical_significance: An injectable anticoagulant that prevents formation or extension of blood clots by blocking activated factor X. It is used for selected clotting disorders and prevention after surgery; bleeding is its main risk.

name: fondaparinux sodium
clinical_significance: The sodium salt form of fondaparinux, an injectable medicine that reduces clotting by blocking activated factor X. It treats or prevents selected blood clots but can cause serious bleeding and requires dose adjustment in kidney disease.

name: fonofos
clinical_significance: A highly poisonous organophosphate insecticide. Exposure can cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, small pupils, muscle twitching, breathing difficulty, seizures, or weakness and requires urgent poison-control or emergency care.

name: fonsecaea
clinical_significance: A group of darkly pigmented fungi that can cause slow-growing skin and soft-tissue infections called chromoblastomycosis. Infection usually follows injury and may produce warty plaques or nodules, especially in tropical regions.

name: food
clinical_significance: Food provides energy and nutrients needed for growth, tissue repair, and normal body function. Food choice and preparation also affect risks from malnutrition, chronic disease, allergy, intolerance, and foodborne infection.

name: food allergy
clinical_significance: An immune reaction to a food protein. It may cause hives, swelling, vomiting, abdominal symptoms, wheezing, or anaphylaxis. Common triggers include milk, egg, peanut, tree nuts, fish, shellfish, soy, and wheat. Severe reactions require an emergency plan.

name: food consumption
clinical_significance: The amount and pattern of food intake, assessed to understand nutrition, growth, metabolic health, or disease risk. Intake records are estimates and should be interpreted with weight trends, health conditions, and nutritional needs.

name: food poisoning
clinical_significance: Illness from eating food contaminated with germs, toxins, or harmful chemicals. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and fever are common.

name: food safety
clinical_significance: Handling, storing, preparing, and labeling food in ways that prevent germs, toxins, harmful chemicals, and allergens from causing illness.

name: foodborne disease
clinical_significance: Illness acquired by eating or drinking material contaminated with germs, toxins, or harmful chemicals. Severity ranges from brief diarrhea to dehydration, organ damage, or life-threatening infection.

name: foot
clinical_significance: The part of the lower limb below the ankle, made of bones, joints, muscles, tendons, ligaments, nerves, and blood vessels. Its shape and arches support standing, balance, shock absorption, and walking.

name: foot pain
clinical_significance: Pain in the foot caused by injury, overuse, arthritis, nerve problems, infection, or poor circulation. Persistent pain, inability to bear weight, numbness, discoloration, fever, or an open wound requires assessment.

name: forceps
clinical_significance: A handheld instrument used to grasp, hold, or move tissue or medical materials. Different designs have smooth or toothed tips and are chosen according to the procedure.

name: forcible intercourse
clinical_significance: Sexual intercourse without freely given consent, involving force, threats, coercion, or inability to consent. It is sexual violence; survivors may need immediate safety support, medical care, emergency contraception, infection prevention, and counseling.

name: forearm
clinical_significance: The part of the arm between the elbow and wrist, containing the radius and ulna bones, muscles, tendons, nerves, and blood vessels.

name: forearm circumference
clinical_significance: The distance around the forearm at a specified point. Measurement can help monitor growth, muscle loss, swelling, nutrition, or changes during treatment and rehabilitation.

name: forehead
clinical_significance: The part of the face above the eyebrows and in front of the frontal skull bone. It contains skin, muscles, nerves, and blood vessels and helps with facial expression and protection.

name: foreign body
clinical_significance: An object that is not normally part of the body and becomes lodged in tissue or a body passage, such as glass, metal, food, or a splinter. It may cause injury, blockage, infection, or inflammation.

name: foreign body reaction
clinical_significance: Inflammation around material that remains in tissue, such as a splinter, stitch, implant, or device. It may cause a lump, redness, pain, drainage, or scar tissue and can resemble infection.

name: forelimb
clinical_significance: The front limb of an animal, corresponding broadly to the human upper limb. In medicine and veterinary care, its structure and function matter when assessing congenital differences, injury, gait, or limb use.

name: forensic medicine
clinical_significance: The use of medical and scientific evidence in legal investigations, such as assessing injury, cause of death, or biological evidence. Forensic clinicians document findings carefully and distinguish medical conclusions from legal determinations.

name: foreskin
clinical_significance: The fold of skin covering and protecting the head of the penis. It normally becomes retractable over time; forceful retraction can cause pain, tearing, or scarring.

name: foretinib
clinical_significance: An investigational oral kinase inhibitor that targets MET and several related growth and blood-vessel signaling receptors. It has been studied in clinical trials for advanced cancers but is not an established standard treatment.

name: formaldehyde
clinical_significance: A strong-smelling chemical used in manufacturing and tissue preservation. It can irritate the eyes, skin, and airways, cause allergic reactions, and increase cancer risk with substantial or long-term exposure.

name: formate
clinical_significance: A salt or ester of formic acid. In medicine, formate is important because it is a toxic breakdown product of methanol and can contribute to severe acidosis and vision loss after poisoning.

name: formetanate
clinical_significance: A carbamate insecticide that can poison the nervous system by disrupting acetylcholine breakdown. Exposure may cause sweating, vomiting, small pupils, muscle weakness, breathing difficulty, or seizures and requires urgent medical advice.

name: formication
clinical_significance: The feeling that insects are crawling on or under the skin when none are present. It may occur with nerve disease, menopause, substance withdrawal, medicines, or psychiatric illness and should be medically evaluated if persistent.

name: formoterol fumarate
clinical_significance: A long-acting inhaled medicine that relaxes airway muscles and helps prevent symptoms of asthma or chronic obstructive lung disease. It is not a rescue medicine for sudden severe breathing difficulty. When used for asthma, it should be combined with an inhaled corticosteroid rather than used alone.

name: formothion
clinical_significance: An organophosphate insecticide that can poison the nervous system. Exposure may cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, muscle twitching, breathing difficulty, seizures, or weakness and requires urgent emergency or poison-control advice.

name: formparanate
clinical_significance: A pesticide-related chemical whose health effects depend on the formulation, dose, and route of exposure. Suspected poisoning should be treated as urgent and assessed through poison-control or emergency services.

name: fosaprepitant dimeglumine
clinical_significance: An intravenous medicine converted to aprepitant that blocks a brain signaling pathway involved in nausea and vomiting. It helps prevent chemotherapy-related sickness and can interact with other medicines.

name: fosbretabulin
clinical_significance: An investigational cancer drug that disrupts tumor blood vessels and has been studied with chemotherapy for selected advanced cancers. Clinical trials have not established it as routine therapy; its use remains research-based.

name: foscarnet
clinical_significance: An antiviral medicine used for selected severe or drug-resistant cytomegalovirus and herpesvirus infections, particularly in immunocompromised patients. It can cause serious kidney injury and electrolyte abnormalities, requiring intravenous hydration and close laboratory monitoring.

name: foscarnet sodium
clinical_significance: An antiviral medicine used for selected serious or resistant cytomegalovirus and herpesvirus infections. It can damage the kidneys and disturb blood salts, so hydration and laboratory monitoring are important.

name: fosfomycin
clinical_significance: An antibiotic that blocks an early step in bacterial cell-wall production. It is used for selected urinary or difficult-to-treat infections; diarrhea, allergic reactions, and resistance can occur.

name: fosinopril
clinical_significance: An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor used for high blood pressure and some forms of heart failure. It relaxes blood vessels and reduces fluid strain; cough, high potassium, kidney problems, or swelling can occur.

name: fotemustine
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy medicine that can cross into the brain and is used in some countries for selected advanced cancers. It can suppress bone marrow, increasing the risk of infection and bleeding.

name: found dead
clinical_significance: A circumstance in which a person is discovered deceased without the death having been observed. Medical or forensic examination may determine identity, timing, cause, and manner of death.

name: fourier analysis
clinical_significance: A mathematical method that separates a complex signal into simpler repeating frequencies. It is used in medical imaging, heart and brain signal analysis, and other measurements to identify patterns.

name: fourth finger
clinical_significance: The ring finger, located between the middle finger and little finger. It contains bones, joints, tendons, nerves, blood vessels, and skin that support movement and grasping.

name: fracture fixation
clinical_significance: Stabilization of a broken bone with a cast, splint, plate, screw, nail, wire, or external frame. The goal is to maintain alignment while the bone heals and, when possible, preserve movement.

name: fractured elbow
clinical_significance: A break involving one of the bones forming the elbow. It can cause pain, swelling, deformity, and limited movement and may injure nearby nerves or blood vessels.

name: fractured ilium
clinical_significance: A break in the broad upper part of the pelvic bone, usually from major trauma or weakened bone. It may cause severe pain and can accompany injury to pelvic organs or blood vessels.

name: fragile X syndrome
clinical_significance: An X-linked inherited condition caused by a CGG-repeat expansion in the \textit{FMR1} gene. It can affect learning, speech, behavior, social development, and physical features and is a common inherited cause of intellectual disability; expression varies because of repeat size, methylation, and sex.

name: frailty
clinical_significance: A state of reduced physical reserve that makes an older or seriously ill person more vulnerable to falls, infection, hospitalization, disability, and other stress. Signs include weakness, slow walking, exhaustion, inactivity, and unintentional weight loss.

name: frameshift mutation
clinical_significance: A genetic change caused by inserting or deleting DNA bases in numbers that are not multiples of three. This shifts how the genetic code is read and often produces a severely altered or nonworking protein.

name: framycetin
clinical_significance: An aminoglycoside antibiotic applied to selected bacterial skin, ear, or eye infections. It can cause local allergy or irritation; prolonged or extensive use may allow absorption and antibiotic-related toxicity.

name: francisella
clinical_significance: A group of small bacteria that includes Francisella tularensis, which causes tularemia. People can acquire infection through ticks, animals, contaminated water, food, or inhaled particles.

name: francisella tularensis
clinical_significance: A bacterium that causes tularemia, usually acquired through ticks, deer flies, infected animals, contaminated water or food, or inhalation. It can cause fever, an ulcer with swollen lymph nodes, pneumonia, or severe systemic illness.

name: francisellaceae
clinical_significance: A family of small bacteria that includes Francisella species. Some cause tularemia or related infections in animals and people; disease type depends on the species and route of exposure.

name: Frasier syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder caused by changes in the WT1 gene. It can cause abnormal sexual development, progressive kidney disease, and increased risk of tumors in the gonads.

name: free radical
clinical_significance: A highly reactive molecule with an unpaired electron. The body makes some during normal metabolism, while excessive amounts can damage cell membranes, proteins, and DNA as part of oxidative stress.

name: freeze drying
clinical_significance: A preservation process that freezes material and removes ice under low pressure. It helps preserve medicines, vaccines, biological samples, and foods while limiting damage from heat and moisture.

name: freeze etching
clinical_significance: A microscopy preparation method in which a frozen specimen is fractured and its exposed surface is replicated for electron microscopy. It is mainly a laboratory research technique and can reveal membrane structure and the distribution of particles within cells.

name: freeze substitution
clinical_significance: A method for preparing frozen biological specimens for microscopy by replacing ice with an organic solvent at low temperature. It helps preserve cellular ultrastructure for electron microscopy and is used chiefly in research and specialized laboratory analysis.

name: freezing
clinical_significance: Exposure to very low temperature that can freeze tissue, cause frostbite, or dangerously lower body temperature. The term also describes preserving food, medicines, or samples by storing them at low temperature.

name: fresh specimen
clinical_significance: A recently collected biological sample tested promptly or preserved correctly before changes affect its cells, organisms, chemistry, or diagnostic accuracy.

name: fresolimumab
clinical_significance: An investigational monoclonal antibody that blocks transforming growth factor beta, a pathway involved in fibrosis, cancer, and immune regulation. It has been studied in clinical trials, including systemic sclerosis, but is not an approved treatment; safety and benefit depend on the condition and remain under study.

name: Freund's adjuvant
clinical_significance: An oil-based immune adjuvant used mainly to produce strong antibody responses in laboratory animals. Complete Freund’s adjuvant contains killed mycobacteria and can cause severe inflammation, ulceration, and tissue injury, so it is not used in human vaccines; animal use requires careful welfare safeguards.

name: Friedreich's ataxia
clinical_significance: An inherited condition that gradually affects balance, coordination, sensation, and strength. Some people also develop heart muscle disease, spinal curvature, or diabetes and need regular neurologic and cardiac care.

name: Friend virus
clinical_significance: A murine retrovirus complex used as an experimental model of virus-induced leukemia and antiviral immunity in mice. It causes disease in susceptible mice and is a research tool, not a human pathogen or human treatment.

name: frontal bone
clinical_significance: The skull bone forming the forehead, roof of the eye sockets, and part of the nasal region. It contains the frontal sinuses and protects the front of the brain.

name: frontal bossing
clinical_significance: An unusually prominent forehead caused by forward bulging of the frontal skull bones. It may be familial or associated with bone disease, excess pressure in the skull, or skeletal disorders.

name: frontal lobe
clinical_significance: The front portion of the brain’s outer layer. It helps control movement, planning, attention, judgment, behavior, personality, and speech production in the language-dominant hemisphere.

name: frontal sinus
clinical_significance: An air-filled cavity within the frontal skull bone above the eye. It connects with the nasal passages and can become inflamed or blocked during sinusitis.

name: frontal sinusitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the air-filled cavities above the eyes, usually from a viral infection or blocked drainage. It can cause forehead pain, congestion, and discharge; severe headache, eye swelling, fever, confusion, or neurologic symptoms require urgent care.

name: frontotemporal dementia
clinical_significance: A group of progressive brain disorders affecting the frontal and temporal lobes. Early changes often involve personality, behavior, judgment, language, or movement rather than memory alone.

name: frostbite
clinical_significance: A freezing injury to the skin and deeper tissues that can cause numbness, pale or waxy skin, swelling, blisters, and tissue death.

name: frozen section
clinical_significance: A rapid tissue examination performed during surgery. A specimen is frozen, cut into thin slices, and examined to provide immediate information about a lesion or surgical margin, although permanent sections are often more accurate.

name: fructose
clinical_significance: A natural sugar found in fruit, honey, some vegetables, and many sweetened foods. It is processed mainly by the liver; poor absorption can cause gas, bloating, cramps, or diarrhea after eating it.

name: frustration
clinical_significance: An emotional response to blocked goals, unmet needs, or difficult circumstances. It may cause irritability, anger, distress, withdrawal, or behavior changes and becomes clinically important when persistent or impairing.

name: Fryns syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited condition present from birth, often involving a hole in the diaphragm, characteristic facial features, and abnormal fingers or toes. Brain, heart, kidney, or genital abnormalities may also occur.

name: Fuchs' dystrophy
clinical_significance: A usually inherited, slowly progressive disease of the inner layer of the cornea. The damaged endothelial cells cannot remove enough fluid, so the cornea becomes swollen and cloudy. It may cause blurred or hazy vision, glare, halos, light sensitivity, and vision that is worse in the morning. In advanced disease, painful blisters and corneal scarring may develop. It usually affects both eyes, although one eye may be worse than the other.

name: fucose
clinical_significance: A sugar found in some cell-surface proteins and fats. It helps cells recognize and attach to one another and participates in immune signaling and other biological processes.

name: fucosidosis
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which cells cannot break down certain sugar-containing substances. Their buildup progressively affects development, movement, bones, growth, sweating, and organ function.

name: fucosyltransferase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that attaches the sugar fucose to proteins or fats. This changes how cells recognize one another, develop, interact with microbes, and display some blood-group markers.

name: full sibling
clinical_significance: A person who shares both biological parents with another person. This relationship is relevant to family medical history, genetic-risk assessment, and some tissue or organ-donor matching.

name: fullerene
clinical_significance: A carbon nanomaterial investigated for possible drug delivery, imaging, and other biomedical uses. Its clinical role is unestablished; safety depends on the specific fullerene formulation, and most therapeutic applications remain preclinical.

name: fulvestrant
clinical_significance: An injectable hormone treatment that blocks and helps destroy estrogen receptors in selected hormone-sensitive breast cancers. It can cause injection-site pain, hot flushes, joint symptoms, fatigue, and liver-test changes.

name: funding
clinical_significance: Financial support for health services, public health programs, or clinical research can affect which care and studies are available. Research funding sources and potential conflicts of interest should be disclosed when interpreting clinical evidence.

name: fundus
clinical_significance: The rounded or farthest part of a hollow organ. Examples include the upper part of the stomach, the top of the uterus, and the inside back surface of the eye.

name: fundus oculi
clinical_significance: The inside back surface of the eye visible through the pupil. It includes the retina, optic nerve, macula, and retinal blood vessels.

name: fundus photography
clinical_significance: Photographing the back of the eye to record the retina, optic nerve, macula, and blood vessels. Images help detect and monitor retinal disease and allow comparison over time.

name: fundus uteri
clinical_significance: The rounded upper part of the uterus above the openings of the fallopian tubes. Its position and size can be assessed during pelvic examination and pregnancy.

name: fungal vaccines
clinical_significance: Vaccines to prevent fungal infections are under investigation, but there are no licensed fungal vaccines for human use. Candidate vaccines may be especially valuable for people at high risk of invasive fungal disease, though protection and safety must be established in clinical studies.

name: fungemia
clinical_significance: The presence of living fungi in the bloodstream, most often Candida in hospitalized patients. It can spread to organs and requires urgent cultures, source evaluation, and appropriate antifungal treatment.

name: fungi
clinical_significance: Organisms including yeasts, molds, and mushrooms. Some live harmlessly in the environment or body, while others cause infections of the skin, mouth, lungs, bloodstream, or other organs.

name: funisitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the umbilical cord, usually associated with infection or inflammation of the membranes around the fetus. It may increase newborn infection risk and requires assessment of the placenta, mother, and baby.

name: furan
clinical_significance: A chemical compound used in manufacturing and found in small amounts in some heated foods. High or repeated exposure may harm the liver and other organs, so occupational exposure should be controlled.

name: furazolidone
clinical_significance: An older antibacterial and antiprotozoal medicine formerly used for selected intestinal infections. It is rarely used in many countries because safer alternatives are available; it can cause serious interactions with tyramine-containing foods and medicines due to monoamine-oxidase inhibition.

name: furocoumarin
clinical_significance: A plant chemical found in some citrus and other plants that can make skin unusually sensitive to ultraviolet light. Contact followed by sunlight may cause redness, blistering, or dark pigmentation.

name: furosemide
clinical_significance: A loop diuretic used to remove excess fluid in conditions such as heart failure, liver disease, and kidney disease. It can also be used for selected cases of hypertension; monitoring may be needed for dehydration, kidney function, and electrolyte loss, especially potassium.

name: fursultiamin
clinical_significance: A fat-soluble form of thiamine, or vitamin B1, used in some countries as a vitamin preparation. Its clinical value and safety depend on the indication, dose, and other medicines.

name: furuncle
clinical_significance: A painful, pus-filled infection of a hair follicle, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus. It forms a red lump and may drain; larger, recurrent, facial, or fever-associated lesions need medical assessment.

name: furunculosis
clinical_significance: Repeated or multiple boils caused by infection of hair follicles, often with Staphylococcus aureus. Risk factors include close contact, skin disease, diabetes, and weakened immunity; treatment may require drainage, antibiotics, and prevention measures.

name: fusarium
clinical_significance: A group of environmental molds that can cause nail, eye, skin, sinus, lung, or widespread infections. Severe disease occurs mainly in people with weakened immunity, especially prolonged neutropenia.

name: fusarium chlamydosporum
clinical_significance: An environmental Fusarium mold that is rarely reported in human clinical specimens. It may cause opportunistic infection, but a culture result must be interpreted with symptoms, specimen quality, and other findings because contamination or colonization is possible.

name: fusarium incarnatum
clinical_significance: An environmental Fusarium mold that can occasionally be recovered from human specimens. Its significance depends on the body site, evidence of tissue infection, and the patient’s immune status; species-level identification may affect antifungal susceptibility assessment.

name: fusarium solani
clinical_significance: An environmental mold that can cause eye, nail, skin, or invasive infections, especially in people with weakened immunity. Its clinical importance depends on the specimen, body site, symptoms, and laboratory confirmation.

name: fused placenta
clinical_significance: A placenta in which areas that normally form separate lobes are joined. It is often an anatomical variation, but careful examination after delivery helps identify any retained placental tissue or abnormal blood vessels.

name: fused teeth
clinical_significance: Dental fusion can alter tooth number, eruption, spacing, and decay risk; dental examination helps plan preventive care or orthodontic treatment.

name: fusidic acid
clinical_significance: An antibiotic that blocks bacterial protein production and is used for selected staphylococcal infections. Resistance can develop, so it is often combined with another antibiotic and used according to local guidance.

name: fusion gene
clinical_significance: A gene formed when parts of two separate genes become joined. It may produce an abnormal protein that drives some cancers and can sometimes be identified by genetic testing.

name: fusion protein
clinical_significance: A protein made when parts of two different proteins become joined, usually because their genes have fused. Some fusion proteins drive cancer; others are deliberately engineered for research or treatment.

name: fusobacterium
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria that grow without oxygen and commonly live in the mouth and intestine. Some species can cause dental, throat, abdominal, wound, bloodstream, or other invasive infections.

name: fusobacterium infection
clinical_significance: Infection caused by Fusobacterium bacteria, which may spread from the mouth or intestine to the throat, lungs, abdomen, skin, joints, or bloodstream. Symptoms and treatment depend on the site and severity.

name: fusobacterium mortiferum
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterium that is only rarely reported in human infections, sometimes in mixed infections or bloodstream cultures. Its clinical importance should be judged from the infection site and specimen rather than from isolation alone.

name: fusobacterium naviforme
clinical_significance: A rarely encountered anaerobic bacterium; its clinical significance in human disease is not well established. When identified in a clinical specimen, results should be interpreted with the site, symptoms, and possibility of mixed infection or contamination.

name: fusobacterium necrogenes
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterium with limited evidence as a human pathogen. A positive culture is uncommon and should be interpreted alongside clinical signs and the specimen source.

name: fusobacterium necrophorum
clinical_significance: A bacterium that can cause severe throat infection and Lemierre syndrome, in which infection spreads to neck veins and may produce infected clots, lung complications, and bloodstream infection.

name: fusobacterium nucleatum
clinical_significance: A common mouth bacterium associated with gum disease. It can occasionally cause bloodstream or other invasive infection and has also been studied for possible links with intestinal and pregnancy-related disease.

name: fusobacterium russii
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterium rarely identified in human clinical samples. Its role in disease is uncertain, so isolation should be assessed in the context of symptoms, specimen quality, and accompanying organisms.

name: fusobacterium varium
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterium that may be found in the intestinal tract and has occasionally been associated with human infection. A positive culture does not by itself establish disease; interpretation depends on the clinical site and evidence of tissue invasion.

name: gaba receptor
clinical_significance: A brain-cell protein that responds to GABA, a chemical messenger that usually reduces nerve activity. GABA receptors help regulate sleep, anxiety, muscle control, and seizures and are targets of several medicines.

name: gabapentin
clinical_significance: A medicine used for certain seizures and nerve-related pain. It can cause sleepiness, dizziness, swelling, or impaired coordination; the dose often needs adjustment in kidney disease and stopping suddenly can cause problems.

name: gadoleic acid
clinical_significance: A monounsaturated fatty acid found in some plant oils and biological lipids. It is mainly of biochemical and nutritional interest; a laboratory measurement is interpreted as part of a broader lipid or metabolic assessment, not as a diagnosis by itself.

name: gadolinium
clinical_significance: A metal used in a chemically bound form to improve some MRI images. Serious reactions are uncommon, but kidney function, pregnancy, prior reactions, and possible tissue retention are considered before use.

name: gadopentetate dimeglumine
clinical_significance: An injectable gadolinium contrast agent used to improve selected MRI images. It can cause allergic reactions and is used cautiously or avoided in severe kidney disease because of rare serious complications.

name: gaffkya homari
clinical_significance: A bacterium historically associated with disease in lobsters and other marine animals. It is not a recognized common human pathogen; an unusual human isolate requires careful laboratory identification and clinical correlation.

name: gag gene
clinical_significance: A retroviral gene that encodes structural proteins forming the virus’s inner support, shell, and core. These proteins help assemble new virus particles inside infected cells.

name: gag protein
clinical_significance: A large retroviral protein that is cut into components forming the virus’s inner support, protective shell, and genetic-material core. These parts are required to assemble new virus particles.

name: gagging
clinical_significance: Retching caused by stimulation of the throat or back of the tongue. It may occur with swallowing difficulty, reflux, infection, examination, aspiration, or distress.

name: gain
clinical_significance: The amount by which a hearing aid or amplifier increases sound intensity, measured in decibels. Correct gain improves hearing while limiting excessive loudness, feedback, discomfort, and further hearing damage.

name: gait
clinical_significance: A person’s pattern of walking, including speed, balance, step length, posture, arm movement, and turning. Gait reflects the combined function of the brain, nerves, muscles, joints, vision, and balance system.

name: gait abnormality
clinical_significance: A change from a person’s usual walking pattern caused by problems with muscles, joints, nerves, balance, vision, heart function, or general health. Assessment examines speed, stability, symmetry, strength, sensation, and pain.

name: gait apraxia
clinical_significance: Difficulty starting or carrying out walking even though basic muscle strength is adequate. It may occur with disease or injury affecting the front of the brain and can cause short steps, freezing, or instability.

name: gait ataxia
clinical_significance: Unsteady, poorly coordinated walking caused by problems in the cerebellum, sensation pathways, balance organs, or other parts of the nervous system.

name: galactans
clinical_significance: A class of complex sugars found in plants and other organisms. Galactans are studied in nutrition, cell biology, and laboratory science; their presence is not ordinarily used alone to diagnose or treat disease.

name: galactolipids
clinical_significance: Lipids containing galactose that occur in cell membranes, including nervous tissue. Changes in specific galactolipids are relevant to myelin biology and some inherited metabolic disorders, while measurements are generally specialized rather than routine clinical tests.

name: galactorrhea
clinical_significance: Milk-like breast discharge outside expected pregnancy or breastfeeding can result from elevated prolactin, medicines, thyroid or kidney disease, or local stimulation. Evaluation may include a pregnancy test, medication review, and prolactin and thyroid testing; spontaneous bloody or clear discharge from one duct needs prompt breast assessment.

name: galactose
clinical_significance: A simple sugar that forms part of lactose in milk. The body normally processes it for energy, but inherited galactosemia can make milk and other galactose-containing foods dangerous for infants.

name: galactosemia
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder in which the body cannot properly process galactose. Classic disease can cause vomiting, jaundice, liver injury, cataracts, serious infection, and developmental problems after milk feeding.

name: galactosialidosis
clinical_significance: A rare inherited storage disorder in which cells accumulate certain sugar-containing substances. It can cause developmental delay, muscle weakness, bone changes, kidney disease, and eye problems, with severity varying widely.

name: galactoside
clinical_significance: A compound in which the sugar galactose is joined to another molecule, such as another sugar, a fat, or a protein. Galactosides occur in cells and in some foods.

name: galactosyltransferase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that attaches galactose to proteins, fats, or other sugars while cells build complex molecules. These molecules support cell structure, recognition, signaling, and nerve insulation.

name: galanin
clinical_significance: A signaling peptide in the nervous system and gut that influences appetite, pain signaling, stress responses, and hormone release. It is relevant to neurobiology research but is not a routine diagnostic marker or established treatment target.

name: galiximab
clinical_significance: An investigational monoclonal antibody against CD80 that has been studied in lymphoma and other cancers. A clinical trial found limited activity in relapsed Hodgkin lymphoma; it is not an established standard cancer treatment.

name: gall bladder disease
clinical_significance: Any disorder of the gallbladder, including stones, inflammation, infection, polyps, abnormal movement, or cancer. Symptoms may include right-upper-abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, or jaundice.

name: gallamine triethiodide
clinical_significance: An older nondepolarizing muscle relaxant formerly used during anesthesia. It can cause marked increases in heart rate and has largely been replaced by newer agents; its use requires anesthesia and respiratory support.

name: gallbladder
clinical_significance: A pear-shaped organ beneath the liver that stores and concentrates bile produced by the liver. When needed for digestion, bile passes through the cystic and common bile ducts into the small intestine.

name: gallbladder carcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer of the gallbladder, most often arising from its lining cells. It may be found incidentally or cause right-upper-abdominal pain, jaundice, weight loss, or bile-duct blockage; treatment depends on its stage and spread.

name: gallbladder infection
clinical_significance: Informal term for inflammation or infection of the gallbladder, often after a stone blocks the cystic duct. Right-upper-quadrant pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, and tenderness may occur; treatment depends on severity and may include antibiotics, drainage, or surgery.

name: gallbladder necrosis
clinical_significance: Death of gallbladder tissue caused by severe inflammation or inadequate blood supply. It can lead to perforation, abdominal infection, and sepsis.

name: gallbladder perforation
clinical_significance: A hole through the gallbladder wall that allows bile or infected contents into the abdomen. It can cause severe inflammation, abscess, peritonitis, or sepsis.

name: gallic acid
clinical_significance: A plant-derived compound with antioxidant and antimicrobial properties studied in laboratory and food research. It has no established role as a stand-alone clinical treatment; concentrated supplements may interact with medicines and should not replace proven care.

name: gallium
clinical_significance: A metallic element used in some radioactive tracers, medical compounds, and technology. Its medical effects depend on the isotope or compound and how it is administered and distributed in the body.

name: gallium nitrate
clinical_significance: A gallium-containing compound formerly used in selected cancer settings to reduce high calcium levels. Its use is limited because it can damage the kidneys and has largely been replaced by other treatments.

name: gametogenesis
clinical_significance: The formation and maturation of sperm or eggs in the testes or ovaries. It includes cell division that reduces chromosome number so gametes can combine during fertilization.

name: gamma globulin
clinical_significance: A group of blood proteins that includes antibodies. The term may refer to antibody-containing plasma fractions or immunoglobulin preparations used to provide temporary immune protection or treatment.

name: gamma rays
clinical_significance: High-energy electromagnetic radiation produced by radioactive decay or nuclear reactions. It can damage cells and is used in controlled amounts for some cancer treatments and medical sterilization.

name: gamma synuclein
clinical_significance: A protein found mainly in the nervous system and other tissues. Changes in its expression have been studied in cancer and neurologic disease, but it is not a routine diagnostic test or established treatment target.

name: gamma-chemokines
clinical_significance: Signaling proteins that attract or activate immune cells through specific receptors. They help coordinate inflammation, immune surveillance, and movement of defensive cells into affected tissue.

name: gammacoronavirus
clinical_significance: A coronavirus subfamily that mainly includes viruses infecting birds and some other animals. Its members are important in veterinary and virology research; human respiratory epidemics such as COVID-19 are caused by betacoronaviruses, not gammacoronaviruses.

name: gammaherpesvirina
clinical_significance: A herpesvirus subfamily that includes Epstein–Barr virus and Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus. These viruses can cause lifelong infection and are linked to some cancers and immune-related disease, especially in people with weakened immunity.

name: gammaretrovirus
clinical_significance: A group of retroviruses that primarily infect animals and is used in virology and cancer research. Some can cause leukemia or other disease in their hosts; the group is not a recognized cause of common human infection.

name: ganciclovir
clinical_significance: An antiviral medicine that interferes with viral DNA production and is used mainly for serious cytomegalovirus infection. It can suppress bone marrow, affect the kidneys, and cause other serious toxicity.

name: ganglia
clinical_significance: Groups of nerve-cell bodies outside the brain and spinal cord. They relay and organize signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body.

name: ganglioglioma
clinical_significance: A usually slow-growing tumor containing nerve cells and supporting brain cells. It often causes seizures and may occur in the brain or spinal cord; treatment commonly involves surgical removal.

name: ganglion cell
clinical_significance: A nerve cell located in a ganglion. Retinal ganglion cells collect visual signals and send them through the optic nerve to the brain.

name: ganglioneuroblastoma
clinical_significance: A tumor made of both mature and immature nerve-related cells, usually in the adrenal or tissue beside the spine. It mainly affects children and may cause a mass, pain, high blood pressure, or other symptoms.

name: ganglioneuroma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous tumor arising from nerve tissue of the autonomic nervous system. It often causes no symptoms but may produce a mass, pain, or hormone-related effects depending on its location.

name: ganglioneuromatosis
clinical_significance: A condition in which nerve-related ganglion tissue grows diffusely or in multiple areas. Effects depend on the organs involved and may include masses, pain, bowel symptoms, or hormone-related changes.

name: ganglionic blocker
clinical_significance: A drug that blocks signaling in autonomic nerve ganglia and was formerly used to lower blood pressure. These agents are largely obsolete because of broad adverse effects such as low blood pressure on standing, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention.

name: ganglioside
clinical_significance: A fat-containing molecule in cell membranes, especially nerve cells. Gangliosides help cells communicate and recognize one another; abnormal accumulation occurs in several inherited storage disorders.

name: gangliosidosis
clinical_significance: A group of inherited disorders in which gangliosides accumulate inside cells because a breakdown enzyme is missing. The buildup often damages the nervous system and may also affect the eyes, bones, organs, and development.

name: gangrene
clinical_significance: Death of body tissue caused by severely reduced blood flow, infection, injury, or a combination of these factors. It may affect skin, muscle, or an internal organ. The area may become discolored, cold, swollen, painful, numb, or foul-smelling; fever, confusion, or feeling very ill may occur with spreading infection.

name: gap junction
clinical_significance: A tiny connection between neighboring cells that allows ions and small molecules to pass directly between them. Gap junctions help coordinate heartbeats, nerve activity, and tissue growth.

name: Gardner syndrome
clinical_significance: An inherited condition caused by an APC gene change, producing many colon polyps and increasing colorectal-cancer risk. It may also cause bone growths, dental abnormalities, skin cysts, and desmoid tumors.

name: gardnerella
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria that may live in the genital tract. Overgrowth of Gardnerella, especially G. vaginalis, can contribute to bacterial vaginosis with discharge, odor, and altered vaginal bacteria.

name: gardnerella vaginalis
clinical_significance: A bacterium associated with bacterial vaginosis, in which normal vaginal bacteria become imbalanced. It may be present without illness; when symptomatic, discharge, odor, irritation, or burning can occur.

name: garlic
clinical_significance: Garlic is used as food and in supplements promoted for cardiovascular health. Evidence for clinically meaningful benefit is limited; supplements can increase bleeding risk and interact with anticoagulants and some other medicines.

name: gartner duct
clinical_significance: A remnant of an embryonic duct in the female reproductive tract. It can persist harmlessly or form a cyst along the side wall of the vagina or broad ligament.

name: gas
clinical_significance: A state of matter without a fixed shape or volume. In medicine, gas may mean air or another gas in the digestive tract, blood, tissues, or a body cavity.

name: gas chromatography
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that separates vaporized chemicals so they can be identified or measured. It is often combined with mass spectrometry to test medicines, poisons, pollutants, or biological samples.

name: gas poisoning
clinical_significance: Illness caused by inhaling a toxic gas, with effects determined by the agent: carbon monoxide and cyanide cause cellular or functional hypoxia, while chlorine, ammonia, and similar irritants injure the airways and lungs. Headache, confusion, cough, bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, seizures, or collapse may occur; identify the gas and provide immediate fresh air, oxygen, and respiratory support.

name: gas scavenger
clinical_significance: A substance or device that removes unwanted gases from a fluid, container, or breathing system. In healthcare it may help prevent toxic exposure or maintain safe gas delivery.

name: gastrectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery removing part or all of the stomach, usually for cancer or severe disease. Food passage is reconstructed, and possible effects include early fullness, weight loss, nutritional deficiencies, reflux, or dumping symptoms.

name: gastric acid
clinical_significance: Strong acid made by the stomach lining that helps break down food, activate digestive enzymes, and kill many swallowed microbes. Excess can contribute to reflux or ulcers; too little can impair digestion and nutrient absorption.

name: gastric balloon
clinical_significance: A temporary balloon placed inside the stomach to create fullness and support weight loss. Nausea, vomiting, reflux, deflation, blockage, bleeding, or perforation can occur.

name: gastric dysplasia
clinical_significance: Abnormal cells in the stomach lining that have some features of cancer but have not invaded deeper tissue. Low- or high-grade changes may increase the risk of stomach cancer.

name: gastric fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal passage between the stomach and another organ or the skin. Stomach contents may leak through it, causing drainage, infection, skin irritation, dehydration, or poor nutrition.

name: gastric fundus
clinical_significance: The upper, rounded part of the stomach, located above the main stomach body and near the diaphragm. It can expand to store food and contains glands that produce digestive secretions.

name: gastric hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from the stomach, commonly caused by an ulcer, a tumor, or blood-vessel damage. It may cause vomiting blood, black stools, dizziness, anemia, or shock. It is one possible source of upper gastrointestinal bleeding, which can also come from the esophagus or duodenum.

name: gastric juice
clinical_significance: Fluid made by the stomach containing acid, digestive enzymes, mucus, water, salts, and intrinsic factor. It helps break down food, protect the stomach lining, and absorb vitamin B12 later in digestion.

name: gastric leiomyosarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare cancer of smooth muscle in the stomach wall. It may cause pain, bleeding, vomiting, or a mass and is evaluated with imaging and biopsy; treatment usually involves surgery when possible.

name: gastric lymphoma
clinical_significance: A lymphoma that starts in the stomach. Some types, especially early-stage mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma, are linked to Helicobacter pylori and may improve after the infection is treated; other types may need cancer treatment.

name: gastric mucosa
clinical_significance: The moist inner lining of the stomach. It contains glands that produce acid, digestive enzymes, mucus, and intrinsic factor and is protected by a mucus barrier; inflammation or injury can cause pain or bleeding.

name: gastric necrosis
clinical_significance: Death of stomach tissue caused by severely reduced blood flow, corrosive injury, extreme stretching, infection, or another serious insult. It can lead to perforation, severe infection, and shock.

name: gastric obstruction
clinical_significance: Partial or complete blockage that prevents food and liquid from leaving the stomach normally. It may cause repeated vomiting, upper-abdominal pain, fullness, swelling, dehydration, and weight loss.

name: gastric stenosis
clinical_significance: Abnormal narrowing of the stomach or its outlet that slows or blocks emptying. It may result from birth defects, ulcer scarring, inflammation, tumors, or thickening of the outlet muscle.

name: gastric ulcer
clinical_significance: An open sore in the stomach lining, commonly caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or anti-inflammatory medicines. It may cause burning upper-abdominal pain, bleeding, anemia, or perforation.

name: gastrinoma
clinical_significance: A tumor that makes too much gastrin, a hormone that causes the stomach to produce acid. It usually starts in the pancreas or duodenum and may cause Zollinger--Ellison syndrome, repeated peptic ulcers, diarrhea, and acid reflux. Some cases are linked to MEN1 and may spread to the liver or nearby lymph nodes.

name: gastritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the stomach lining. It may begin suddenly (acute) or last a long time (chronic), and may cause no symptoms or upper-abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or bleeding. \textit{H. pylori} infection and autoimmune disease are important causes. Some medicines, alcohol, and severe illness can also injure the lining; when injury occurs without prominent inflammation, it is called gastropathy.

name: gastrocnemius muscle
clinical_significance: The large superficial calf muscle that joins the Achilles tendon. It points the foot downward and helps bend the knee and push the body forward during walking, running, and jumping.

name: gastroenteritis
clinical_significance: Infection or inflammation of the stomach and intestines, commonly caused by viruses and sometimes by bacteria, parasites, or toxins. It usually causes diarrhea, vomiting, cramps, and fever and can lead to dehydration.

name: gastroenteritis bacterial
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the stomach or intestines caused by bacteria, usually after contaminated food or water. It can cause diarrhea, cramps, fever, vomiting, and dehydration; blood in stool or severe illness may occur.

name: gastroenterologist
clinical_significance: A physician specializing in disorders of the digestive tract, liver, gallbladder, bile ducts, and pancreas. They diagnose and treat digestive problems using medicines, endoscopy, procedures, lifestyle care, and surgery referrals.

name: gastroepiploic artery
clinical_significance: The gastroepiploic arteries run along the greater curve of the stomach and supply blood to the stomach and nearby omentum.

name: gastroesophageal reflux
clinical_significance: Backward flow of stomach contents into the esophagus. It may cause heartburn, sour fluid in the throat, cough, chest discomfort, or no symptoms. Spitting up is common in healthy infants and usually resolves with age; reflux is called disease when it causes troublesome symptoms or complications.

name: gastrointestinal
clinical_significance: Relating to the stomach and intestines, or to the complete digestive tract from the mouth to the anus. These organs digest food, absorb nutrients and water, move contents forward, and remove waste.

name: gastrointestinal agents
clinical_significance: Medicines or other substances that act on the digestive tract to relieve or treat problems such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, ulcers, reflux, or intestinal spasms. Their effects and risks depend on the specific agent.

name: gastrointestinal disorder
clinical_significance: A disease affecting any part of the digestive tract, from the esophagus to the anus. It may cause pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, bleeding, blockage, or poor nutrient absorption, depending on the affected structure.

name: gastrointestinal gas
clinical_significance: Air or other gas within the stomach or intestines, usually from swallowed air or bacterial digestion of food. Excess gas may cause belching, bloating, cramps, or passing gas and can increase with constipation or food intolerance.

name: gastrointestinal hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from any part of the digestive tract, from the esophagus to the anus. It may cause vomiting blood, black stools, red blood in stool, anemia, dizziness, or shock.

name: gastrointestinal hormone
clinical_significance: A chemical messenger made by cells in the digestive tract that helps regulate stomach acid, intestinal movement, digestion, appetite, gallbladder activity, or blood-glucose control.

name: gastrointestinal neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth arising in the digestive tract. It may be a harmless growth, a precancerous change, or cancer; symptoms and treatment depend on its tissue, location, and behavior.

name: gastrointestinal pain
clinical_significance: Pain arising from the digestive tract or related organs. Causes include infection, ulcers, inflammation, blockage, gallstones, and diseases of the liver or pancreas. It may be severe, persistent, or worsening.

name: gastrointestinal system
clinical_significance: The connected organs that move and digest food, absorb nutrients and water, and remove solid waste. It includes the mouth, esophagus, stomach, intestines, rectum, and anus, with help from the liver, gallbladder, and pancreas.

name: gastroparesis
clinical_significance: A disorder in which the stomach empties too slowly, or sometimes stops emptying, even though there is no physical blockage. The stomach muscles or the nerves that control them do not move food normally. It may cause early fullness, nausea, vomiting, bloating, belching, upper-abdominal pain, heartburn, and poor appetite. Diabetes is the most common known cause; other causes include stomach surgery, nerve or muscle disorders, some autoimmune or viral illnesses, although the cause is often unknown.

name: gastroschisis
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the intestine, and sometimes other organs, protrudes through an opening beside the umbilicus without a protective covering. The exposed bowel may be swollen or damaged.

name: gastroscope
clinical_significance: A thin, flexible instrument with a light and camera used to view the esophagus, stomach, and first part of the small intestine. It can also pass tools for biopsy or treatment.

name: gastroscopy
clinical_significance: Examination of the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum using a flexible camera tube passed through the mouth. It can identify bleeding, ulcers, inflammation, narrowing, or tumors and allows biopsies or selected treatments.

name: gastrostomy
clinical_significance: A surgically created opening through the abdominal wall into the stomach. A tube placed through it can provide food, fluids, or medicines or remove stomach contents when normal feeding is unsafe or impossible.

name: gastrula
clinical_significance: An early embryo stage formed after gastrulation, when cell layers reorganize into ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm that give rise to body tissues.

name: gastrulation
clinical_significance: An early stage of embryo development in which cells move and reorganize into three layers that later form all major tissues and organs.

name: gatifloxacin
clinical_significance: Gatifloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; systemic use is restricted in many settings because of dysglycaemia and other class toxicities, while ophthalmic use remains available in some regions.

name: Gaucher's disease
clinical_significance: Gaucher disease can cause enlarged liver and spleen, low blood counts, bone pain, and fractures; diagnosis may enable enzyme or substrate-reduction therapy and family testing.

name: gauss
clinical_significance: A unit of magnetic flux density equal to $10^{-4}$ tesla, used in physics, imaging, and descriptions of magnetic fields.

name: gefitinib
clinical_significance: An oral epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine-kinase inhibitor used for selected advanced non-small-cell lung cancers with activating EGFR mutations.

name: gel
clinical_significance: A semisolid preparation in which liquid is held in a soft network. Gels may be applied to the skin, eyes, mouth, or other areas to soothe tissue, deliver medicine, or form a protective layer.

name: gel electrophoresis
clinical_significance: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA, RNA, or proteins by moving them through a gel in an electric field, usually according to size and charge.

name: gelatin
clinical_significance: Gelatin is a protein made from collagen and used in foods, medicines, capsules, and some medical materials.

name: geldanamycin analogue
clinical_significance: A geldanamycin-derived heat-shock protein 90 (HSP90) inhibitor studied for possible anticancer effects. Geldanamycin itself is too toxic for clinical use, and its analogues remain investigational rather than established cancer treatments.

name: gelsolin
clinical_significance: A protein that helps control the shape and movement of cells and is present in blood and many tissues. Certain inherited GSN variants can cause gelsolin amyloidosis, which may affect the cornea, nerves, skin, and other organs; routine gelsolin testing is not generally used for screening.

name: gemcitabine
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy medicine that becomes active inside cells and interferes with DNA production, slowing or killing rapidly dividing cancer cells. It is used for several cancers and may cause low blood counts, nausea, rash, or organ toxicity.

name: gemcitabine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: The hydrochloride form of gemcitabine, a chemotherapy medicine that interferes with DNA production in dividing cells. It is used for several cancers; important risks include infection from low blood counts and treatment-related organ injury.

name: gemella
clinical_significance: Gemella is a group of bacteria that normally may inhabit the mouth and upper airway but can rarely cause serious infections, including bloodstream infection.

name: gemella bergeri
clinical_significance: A rare member of the Gemella group, bacteria that normally inhabit the mouth and upper airway but can occasionally cause invasive infection such as endocarditis. Because cases are uncommon, identification and susceptibility testing by a clinical laboratory are important.

name: gemella haemolysans
clinical_significance: A member of the Gemella group that can be part of normal oral flora but has occasionally caused bloodstream infection and endocarditis. Its fastidious growth may delay identification; a positive blood culture should be assessed for true infection and possible heart-valve involvement.

name: gemella morbillorum
clinical_significance: A member of the Gemella group, usually associated with oral flora, that can rarely cause serious infection including endocarditis or bloodstream infection. It may be difficult to identify and should be interpreted with the patient’s symptoms and cultures.

name: gemella sanguinis
clinical_significance: Gemella sanguinis is an oral commensal that can rarely cause bacteremia or infective endocarditis; recovery from blood with compatible illness warrants evaluation of the heart and oral sources.

name: gemfibrozil
clinical_significance: A medicine that lowers very high blood triglycerides and may reduce the risk of pancreatitis. It changes how the liver processes fats but can interact with statins and increase the risk of serious muscle injury.

name: gemifloxacin
clinical_significance: An antibiotic in the fluoroquinolone group used for selected bacterial respiratory infections. It can cause nausea and, rarely, tendon injury, nerve symptoms, abnormal heart rhythm, severe diarrhea, or dangerous allergic reactions.

name: gemtuzumab ozogamicin
clinical_significance: An antibody-linked chemotherapy medicine used for selected acute myeloid leukemia. The antibody attaches to CD33-positive leukemia cells and delivers a toxic drug; liver injury, infusion reactions, and low blood counts are important risks.

name: gender
clinical_significance: A social, cultural, and personal concept involving identity, roles, expression, and expectations. Gender is related to, but distinct from, sex characteristics and sexual orientation.

name: gender identity
clinical_significance: A person’s internal sense of being a woman, man, both, neither, or another gender, which may or may not correspond to sex assigned at birth.

name: gene
clinical_significance: A section of DNA that contains instructions for making a functional product, usually a protein or RNA. Genes are arranged at specific locations on chromosomes and influence inherited traits and cell function.

name: gene amplification
clinical_significance: An increase in the number of copies of a gene or genomic region, which can raise gene expression and drive some inherited conditions or cancers.

name: gene conversion
clinical_significance: A nonreciprocal transfer of sequence information from one DNA region to a homologous region, potentially changing an allele during recombination or repair.

name: gene deletion
clinical_significance: Loss of part or all of a gene from DNA, potentially abolishing its product or altering dosage and causing disease when clinically significant.

name: gene dosage
clinical_significance: The number of functional copies of a gene and the amount of product they produce, influenced by deletions, duplications, chromosome number, and regulation.

name: gene duplication
clinical_significance: An extra copy of a gene created by replication or rearrangement, which may have no effect, alter dosage, or provide material for new gene function.

name: gene expression
clinical_significance: The process by which a cell uses information in a gene to make RNA or protein. Cells control when and how strongly genes are expressed, allowing different tissues to develop and perform specialized functions.

name: gene frequency
clinical_significance: The proportion of all gene copies in a population that carry a particular version, or allele, of that gene. It describes population genetics and does not by itself predict an individual’s disease risk.

name: gene fusion
clinical_significance: A hybrid gene formed when segments of two separate genes join, sometimes producing an abnormal protein that drives cancer or other disease.

name: gene library
clinical_significance: A collection of cloned DNA fragments representing all or selected parts of a genome. Gene libraries support research and the development of genetic tests, but library construction itself is not a patient diagnostic test.

name: gene modification
clinical_significance: An intentional or naturally occurring alteration of DNA sequence or gene regulation that changes cellular function or inherited traits.

name: gene mutation
clinical_significance: A permanent change in the DNA sequence of a gene, which may be harmless, beneficial, or pathogenic depending on its effect and inheritance.

name: gene rearrangement
clinical_significance: Reorganization of DNA segments within or between chromosomes that can alter gene structure, expression, immune-receptor diversity, or cancer biology.

name: gene silencing
clinical_significance: Reduction or stopping of a gene's activity through DNA changes, chromatin control, RNA interference, or other processes that limit protein production.

name: gene targeting
clinical_significance: A molecular method that changes a chosen genomic locus through homologous recombination or engineered editing to study or alter gene function.

name: gene therapy
clinical_significance: A treatment that adds, replaces, silences, or edits genetic material in a patient’s cells. Some gene therapies are approved for specific inherited diseases and cancers; eligibility is highly condition-specific, and immune reactions or other delayed effects may require long-term specialist follow-up.

name: gene transfer
clinical_significance: Movement of genetic material into a cell or organism, naturally or through laboratory vectors, potentially changing gene expression or correcting a defect.

name: gene-environment interaction
clinical_significance: A gene-environment interaction occurs when an environmental exposure changes disease risk differently according to a person's genotype, so inherited susceptibility and exposure jointly influence phenotype.

name: gene-modified
clinical_significance: Describing cells or organisms whose genetic material has been deliberately altered using recombinant DNA or genome-editing methods.

name: general anesthesia
clinical_significance: A controlled, temporary state of unconsciousness produced by medicines so a person does not feel or remember a procedure. Breathing, blood pressure, heart rate, and other body functions are monitored throughout.

name: generalized
clinical_significance: Distributed widely or involving most or all of a body region, system, or population rather than being confined to one focus.

name: generalized lipodystrophy
clinical_significance: A disorder with near-total loss of adipose tissue, severe insulin resistance, diabetes, high triglycerides, fatty liver, and abnormal fat deposition in other tissues.

name: generalized seizure
clinical_significance: A seizure arising from or rapidly involving both cerebral hemispheres, commonly producing impaired awareness, bilateral motor activity, or brief absence episodes.

name: generic drug
clinical_significance: A version of a medicine approved as equivalent to a reference brand product under the relevant national standards. Approved generics are expected to provide the same clinical benefit and risks; the active ingredient, dose, and formulation should be checked when substituting medicines with a narrow therapeutic range.

name: genetic
clinical_significance: Genetic information can help diagnose inherited conditions, estimate disease risk, guide some cancer treatments, and inform family planning. Results may be uncertain and can have implications for relatives, so clinical testing is interpreted with personal and family history and may benefit from genetic counseling.

name: genetic anticipation
clinical_significance: Earlier onset or increasing severity of a hereditary disorder in successive generations, often caused by expansion of unstable repeated DNA sequences.

name: genetic carrier
clinical_significance: A person with one pathogenic variant for a recessive disorder who is usually unaffected but can transmit the variant to children.

name: genetic counseling
clinical_significance: A professional discussion that explains how inherited factors may affect a person or family. It may cover risk, testing choices, results, reproductive options, emotional support, and implications for relatives.

name: genetic disorder
clinical_significance: A disease or disorder caused wholly or partly by a pathogenic change in genetic material. The change may involve one or more genes, chromosome number or structure, mitochondrial DNA, or gene regulation. It may be inherited through germline DNA, arise de novo, or occur only in certain tissues as a somatic change. Some conditions also result from interactions among multiple genetic variants and environmental factors; not every genetic change causes disease.

name: genetic drift
clinical_significance: Random changes in allele frequencies from one generation to the next, especially in small populations, independent of natural selection.

name: genetic engineering
clinical_significance: Deliberate changing, adding, removing, or transferring genetic material using laboratory methods. It supports research, diagnosis, treatment development, agriculture, and biotechnology but requires careful assessment of safety, ethics, and unintended effects.

name: genetic heterogeneity
clinical_significance: The situation in which similar features or the same disease can result from different genetic causes. Different genes or different changes within one gene may produce overlapping effects.

name: genetic linkage
clinical_significance: The tendency of nearby genes or DNA markers on the same chromosome to be inherited together because crossing over is less likely between them.

name: genetic marker
clinical_significance: A detectable DNA variation or feature used to track inheritance, identify a chromosome region, assess disease risk, or distinguish samples.

name: genetic polymorphism
clinical_significance: A common DNA variation with at least two alleles in a population, which may influence traits, drug response, or disease susceptibility.

name: genetic profile
clinical_significance: A set of genetic variants or DNA markers describing an individual, tumor, organism, or sample for diagnosis, risk assessment, identification, or research.

name: genetic recombination
clinical_significance: Exchange or rearrangement of DNA segments that creates new allele combinations during meiosis, repair, immune-cell development, or laboratory manipulation.

name: genetic screening
clinical_significance: Genetic screening estimates the chance of a condition in people who may have no symptoms, including newborn and carrier screening. A positive screen does not establish a diagnosis and may need confirmatory testing; results can guide prevention, monitoring, or reproductive decisions.

name: genetic susceptibility
clinical_significance: Inherited tendency to develop a disease or respond to an exposure, which usually modifies risk rather than determining outcome alone.

name: genetic technique
clinical_significance: A laboratory method used to detect, amplify, sequence, edit, compare, or otherwise analyze DNA, RNA, chromosomes, or gene expression.

name: genetic testing
clinical_significance: Analysis of DNA or chromosomes to assess disease risk, explain symptoms, identify carriers, or guide treatment. Results may also provide information about inherited traits and conditions affecting relatives.

name: genetic transcription
clinical_significance: The first step in using a gene: an enzyme copies information from DNA into RNA. The RNA may then guide protein production or perform another function inside the cell.

name: genetics
clinical_significance: Genetics is the study of genes, heredity, genetic variation, and how DNA and gene regulation influence traits, disease risk, diagnosis, and treatment response.

name: geniculate body
clinical_significance: One of two paired relay structures in the brain. The lateral geniculate body processes visual signals, while the medial geniculate body processes hearing signals before sending them to the cerebral cortex.

name: genistein
clinical_significance: A soy isoflavone with weak estrogen-like activity that is studied for possible effects on menopausal symptoms, bone health, and cancer biology. Evidence for concentrated supplements is limited, and they are not established treatments; people taking medicines or managing hormone-sensitive disease should discuss supplements with a clinician.

name: genital edema
clinical_significance: Swelling of genital tissues from fluid accumulation caused by infection, inflammation, allergy, trauma, venous or lymphatic obstruction, or systemic disease.

name: genital herpes
clinical_significance: An infection of the genital or anal area caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 or type 2 (HSV-1 or HSV-2). It spreads mainly through sexual skin-to-skin contact and can be transmitted even when no sores are present. It may cause painful blisters or ulcers, burning urination, swollen glands, or no symptoms; outbreaks can recur. Infection during pregnancy can threaten the newborn.

name: genital system
clinical_significance: The organs involved in reproduction and sexual function, including the gonads, reproductive ducts, accessory glands, and external genital structures. Anatomy differs between individuals and changes with development and age.

name: genitalia
clinical_significance: Genital anatomy varies naturally and may change with puberty, pregnancy, aging, or treatment. New pain, sores, swelling, bleeding, discharge, or a lump may warrant clinical assessment, with care guided by the person’s symptoms and anatomy.

name: genitourinary neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the urinary or reproductive organs, such as the kidney, bladder, prostate, testis, ovary, or uterus. It may be benign or cancerous; examination, imaging, and sometimes biopsy identify its nature.

name: genome
clinical_significance: The complete genetic material of an organism, including genes and DNA that does not directly code proteins. It contains instructions influencing development, body function, inherited traits, disease risk, and treatment response.

name: genomic imprinting
clinical_significance: A pattern in which a gene’s activity depends on whether its copy came from the mother or father. Abnormal imprinting can cause conditions such as Prader–Willi or Angelman syndrome.

name: genomic instability
clinical_significance: An increased tendency for DNA changes, chromosome damage, and mutations to accumulate, contributing to cancer development, treatment resistance, and disease progression.

name: genomic library
clinical_significance: A collection of an organism’s genomic DNA fragments used in research, gene discovery, and development of molecular tests. A genomic library can support disease-gene studies but is not itself a clinical test or diagnosis.

name: genomic medicine
clinical_significance: Use of a person’s genomic information as part of clinical care, including selected diagnoses, cancer treatment choices, inherited-risk assessment, and medication selection or dosing. A genomic result is interpreted alongside clinical history because many variants have uncertain or limited relevance.

name: genomics
clinical_significance: The study of an organism’s complete genetic material, including its DNA sequence, variation, activity, and interaction with disease and treatment. It supports research, diagnosis, risk assessment, and personalized care.

name: genotype
clinical_significance: A person’s genetic makeup, meaning the versions of one or more genes they carry. The genotype helps influence observable traits and disease risk together with other genes and environmental factors.

name: genotype determination
clinical_significance: Genotype determination is the use of laboratory testing to identify an individual's genetic variants or alleles at one or more locations.

name: gentamicin
clinical_significance: An aminoglycoside antibiotic that interferes with bacterial protein production. It can injure the kidneys or hearing and is used with dose and blood-level monitoring.

name: gentamicin sulfate
clinical_significance: The sulfate salt of gentamicin, an aminoglycoside antibiotic that interferes with bacterial protein production. It can injure the kidneys or hearing and is used with careful dosing and monitoring.

name: gentian violet
clinical_significance: A purple antiseptic and dye with antifungal and antibacterial activity, used in selected topical applications but capable of irritating tissue and staining skin.

name: genu recurvatum
clinical_significance: Hyperextension of the knee beyond the usual straight position, caused by laxity, deformity, muscle imbalance, neurologic disease, or injury.

name: genu varum
clinical_significance: Outward bowing of the legs, commonly called bowlegs. It is often normal in young children and improves with growth, but persistent, worsening, unequal, painful, or severe bowing may result from rickets, growth-plate disease, or another condition.

name: genus dermatophilus
clinical_significance: A bacterial genus that includes Dermatophilus congolensis, a cause of crusting skin disease in animals and occasional zoonotic skin infection in people. Recent reports describe a small cluster of suspected person-to-person spread, so unusual crusted lesions merit clinical and laboratory assessment.

name: genus dickeya
