clinical_significance: A genus of bacteria best known for causing soft-rot disease in plants. It is not a recognized common human pathogen; an unexpected clinical isolate should be confirmed and interpreted by a microbiology laboratory.

name: genus leminorella
clinical_significance: A genus of uncommon gram-negative bacteria that has been isolated from human infections, including urinary, wound, bloodstream, and abdominal infections. Identification can be difficult and antibiotic resistance varies, so treatment should be based on laboratory identification and susceptibility results.

name: genus saimiri
clinical_significance: A genus of squirrel monkeys that is important in biomedical research. Squirrel monkeys can carry herpesvirus saimiri, which is used as a laboratory tool to study lymphocyte biology; the virus is not known to cause natural human infection.

name: geophagia
clinical_significance: Persistent eating of soil or other nonfood substances; it may cause poisoning, infection, intestinal obstruction, or iron-deficiency anemia.

name: geotrichum
clinical_significance: Geotrichum is a genus of fungi that may colonize humans and can rarely cause superficial or invasive infection, especially in people with weakened immunity.

name: geotrichum klebahnii
clinical_significance: A rare species of environmental yeast-like fungus with very limited reports of human infection. In a patient specimen, its significance should be judged by repeat isolation, evidence of tissue disease, and immune status, with expert laboratory identification when needed.

name: geriatric assessment
clinical_significance: A broad review of an older person’s medical conditions, medicines, mobility, memory, mood, daily activities, nutrition, safety, home situation, and goals. It identifies treatable problems and guides an individualized care plan.

name: geriatric nursing
clinical_significance: Nursing care focused on the health, function, medication safety, cognition, mobility, and goals of older adults.

name: geriatrician
clinical_significance: A physician specializing in the health care of older adults, including complex illness, multiple conditions, medications, function, and goals of care.

name: geriatrics
clinical_significance: The medical specialty focused on health, function, independence, and quality of life in older adults. Care considers multiple illnesses, medicines, memory, mobility, nutrition, mood, safety, goals, and support.

name: germ
clinical_significance: Germs can include bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites; identifying the actual cause guides infection treatment and prevents unnecessary antibiotics.

name: germ cell
clinical_significance: A reproductive cell or precursor that gives rise to sperm or eggs and carries genetic material to the next generation.

name: germ layer
clinical_significance: One of the three early layers of an embryo—ectoderm, mesoderm, or endoderm—from which all major tissues and organs develop. Each layer gives rise to characteristic body structures during development.

name: germanium
clinical_significance: A chemical element sometimes included in unproven health supplements. Germanium compounds have no established medical benefit and can cause kidney damage, nerve damage, or other serious toxicity when taken internally.

name: germinoma
clinical_significance: A usually slow-growing germ-cell cancer that most often develops in the pineal or suprasellar area of the brain. Related tumors occur in the testicles or ovaries; treatment commonly uses radiation, chemotherapy, surgery, or combinations.

name: germ-line mutation
clinical_significance: A DNA change present in an egg, sperm, or their precursor cells that can be passed to children and is usually present throughout the body. A pathogenic germ-line variant may explain inherited disease or cancer risk and can have implications for biological relatives; tumor-only changes are not necessarily inherited.

name: gestational age
clinical_significance: The length of a pregnancy measured in weeks from the first day of the last menstrual period. It is usually about two weeks longer than the time since fertilization and helps estimate development, due date, and appropriate care.

name: gestational diabetes mellitus
clinical_significance: Gestational diabetes increases risks of fetal overgrowth, birth complications, and future type 2 diabetes; glucose monitoring and postpartum follow-up improve outcomes.

name: gestational sac
clinical_significance: The first fluid-filled structure usually seen inside the uterus on an early pregnancy ultrasound. Its size and appearance help estimate pregnancy age and assess early development, but an early scan may not yet show an embryo.

name: ghrelin
clinical_significance: A hormone produced mainly in the stomach that increases hunger and helps regulate energy balance. It also stimulates growth-hormone release and changes with eating, fasting, sleep, and body weight.

name: giant cells
clinical_significance: Large cells formed by fusion of macrophages or abnormal cellular growth, seen in granulomatous inflammation, foreign-body reactions, and some tumors.

name: giardia
clinical_significance: A microscopic parasite that infects the small intestine and spreads through contaminated water, food, or hands. It can cause foul-smelling diarrhea, cramps, bloating, nausea, weight loss, or no symptoms.

name: giardia lamblia
clinical_significance: The parasite that causes giardiasis. It is swallowed in contaminated water, food, or material from an infected person and can cause foul-smelling diarrhea, abdominal cramps, gas, bloating, and weight loss.

name: giardiasis
clinical_significance: An intestinal infection caused by the parasite Giardia duodenalis. It spreads when contaminated water, food, surfaces, or material from an infected person is swallowed. It may cause diarrhea, foul-smelling or greasy stools, gas, abdominal cramps, nausea, bloating, weight loss, and poor nutrient absorption.

name: gigabecquerel
clinical_significance: A unit of radioactivity equal to one billion nuclear disintegrations per second. It measures the activity of a radioactive source, not directly the radiation dose absorbed by a person.

name: gigantism
clinical_significance: Excessive growth caused by too much growth hormone during childhood, before the bones finish lengthening. It usually results from a pituitary growth and causes unusual height and enlargement of body tissues.

name: gill
clinical_significance: The breathing organ of a fish and some other aquatic animals. Gill damage or abnormal appearance can impair oxygen exchange and may signal infection, parasites, water-quality problems, or toxic exposure, so it is important in veterinary and aquatic-health assessment.

name: gimatecan
clinical_significance: An investigational camptothecin-derived anticancer drug that inhibits topoisomerase I and has been studied in clinical trials for several cancers. It is not an established or approved cancer treatment; blood-count suppression and other toxicities are relevant in research studies.

name: gingiva
clinical_significance: The firm pink tissue, commonly called the gums, that surrounds and protects the teeth and the bone around their roots. Healthy gingiva usually does not bleed with gentle brushing; redness, swelling, or bleeding may indicate gum disease.

name: gingiva disease
clinical_significance: A disorder of the gums, including plaque-induced gingivitis, periodontitis, infection, immune disease, recession, or tumor.

name: gingival hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from gum tissue, commonly due to inflammation and plaque but also caused by trauma, periodontal disease, medicines, or bleeding disorders.

name: gingival hyperplasia
clinical_significance: An abnormal enlargement or overgrowth of gingival tissue around the teeth that can impair cleaning, cause bleeding, and increase periodontal risk. Causes include plaque-related inflammation and medicines such as phenytoin, cyclosporine, and some calcium-channel blockers; hereditary and systemic conditions can also contribute.

name: gingival infections
clinical_significance: Infections of the gums, usually involving bacteria in dental plaque. They can cause red, swollen, tender, or bleeding gums, bad breath, pus, and sometimes spreading facial swelling; dental assessment helps prevent tissue and bone loss.

name: gingival margin
clinical_significance: The edge of the gum tissue that surrounds and touches a tooth. It normally forms a shallow seal; inflammation or recession can make it bleed or expose the tooth root.

name: gingival neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the gums that may be reactive, benign, precancerous, or cancerous. It may cause persistent swelling, ulceration, bleeding, pain, or a lump; examination and sometimes biopsy identify its nature.

name: gingival overgrowth
clinical_significance: Gingival overgrowth is an abnormal increase in gum tissue, which may be caused by medicines, inflammation, or systemic disease.

name: gingival pocket
clinical_significance: The small space between the gum and tooth surface, measured during a dental examination. A persistently deep pocket usually indicates loss of attachment from periodontal disease and can collect plaque and bacteria.

name: gingival recession
clinical_significance: Pulling back of the gums so that part of a tooth root becomes exposed. Gum disease, forceful brushing, tooth position, thin gum tissue, or treatment can cause it and may lead to sensitivity or root decay.

name: gingivectomy
clinical_significance: Surgical removal of gum tissue to treat overgrowth, reshape the gums, expose decay, or improve access. Possible complications include bleeding, sensitivity, infection, or gum recession.

name: gingivitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the gingiva characterized by redness, swelling, and bleeding with brushing or probing, usually due to dental plaque. It is generally reversible with effective oral hygiene and professional cleaning; it can precede periodontitis, but does not inevitably progress to it.

name: ginkgo biloba
clinical_significance: An herbal product derived from Ginkgo biloba leaves and marketed for cognitive or circulatory benefits; evidence is variable and it may increase bleeding risk or interact with medicines.

name: ginseng preparation
clinical_significance: A product made from ginseng root and sold as a supplement. Products vary in strength and purity; interactions and side effects can occur.

name: Gitelman syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited kidney disorder that causes the body to lose too much salt and magnesium in urine. It may lead to muscle cramps, weakness, tiredness, thirst, or abnormal heart rhythms.

name: gizzard
clinical_significance: A muscular digestive organ in birds and some other animals that grinds food. In poultry and wildlife health, abnormal gizzard contents or lining can reflect nutritional, infectious, toxic, or husbandry problems; it has no direct human clinical role.

name: gland
clinical_significance: An organ or group of cells that produces and releases substances. Endocrine glands release hormones into blood, while exocrine glands release substances through ducts or onto a surface.

name: glanders
clinical_significance: A serious infection caused by the bacterium \textit{Burkholderia mallei}, which mainly affects horses and can rarely infect people exposed to infected animals or tissues. It may cause skin sores, fever, pneumonia, or bloodstream infection.

name: glandular stomach
clinical_significance: The acid- and enzyme-secreting portion of the stomach. In ruminants this refers mainly to the abomasum, where inflammation, ulcers, or displacement can impair digestion and require veterinary care.

name: glans penis
clinical_significance: The expanded, sensitive distal end of the penis containing the external urethral opening and covered by the foreskin when present.

name: glaucoma
clinical_significance: A group of eye diseases in which the optic nerve is damaged, often in association with high pressure inside the eye. Types include open-angle, angle-closure, normal-tension, secondary, and congenital glaucoma. It can cause permanent loss of side or central vision, while early disease may have no symptoms.

name: gleason score
clinical_significance: A grading system estimating prostate cancer aggressiveness by examining tissue patterns under a microscope and combining the two most common patterns.

name: glenoid
clinical_significance: The shallow socket on the shoulder blade that joins the head of the upper-arm bone to form the shoulder joint. Its shape and surrounding labrum help balance mobility with stability.

name: gliclazide
clinical_significance: Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea for type 2 diabetes that stimulates pancreatic beta-cell insulin release; hypoglycaemia, weight gain, and dose accumulation in organ impairment are important considerations.

name: glioblastoma
clinical_significance: A fast-growing cancerous tumor of the central nervous system. It forms from glial tissue, which supports nerve cells, and usually develops in the brain of an adult; it can also occur in the spinal cord. The tumor can grow into nearby healthy tissue. Symptoms depend on its location and may include headache, seizures, weakness, changes in speech, memory, vision, balance, or behaviour. Also called glioblastoma multiforme (GBM).

name: glioblastoma multiforme
clinical_significance: An aggressive cancer arising from supporting cells of the brain or spinal cord. It may cause headache, seizures, personality or memory changes, weakness, or speech problems. Treatment often combines surgery, radiation, and medicines.

name: gliocladium
clinical_significance: A historically used, taxonomically broad name for several groups of environmental molds; some former species have been reassigned to other genera such as Trichoderma or Clonostachys. An isolate from a patient should be identified to species because clinical relevance and infection risk vary.

name: glioma
clinical_significance: A tumor arising from supporting cells of the brain or spinal cord. Some gliomas grow slowly, while others are aggressive; symptoms and treatment depend on the tumor’s type, location, molecular features, and spread.

name: gliosarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare aggressive brain cancer containing both glial and connective-tissue-like tumor features. Symptoms depend on location and may include headache, seizures, weakness, or cognitive changes; tissue examination identifies the tumor type.

name: gliosis
clinical_significance: A reactive increase in glial cells after injury, infection, ischemia, or other damage to the central nervous system.

name: glipizide
clinical_significance: Glipizide is a short-acting sulfonylurea that lowers blood glucose by stimulating insulin secretion from functioning pancreatic beta cells; hypoglycaemia is the principal adverse effect.

name: globicatella
clinical_significance: A rare genus of gram-positive bacteria that may inhabit the mouth or gastrointestinal tract and can occasionally cause bloodstream infection, meningitis, urinary infection, or endocarditis. Growth may be fastidious, so laboratory identification is important when it appears in a clinically significant specimen.

name: globicatella sanguinis
clinical_significance: A rarely isolated Globicatella species reported in bloodstream and other invasive infections. Because it may be difficult to distinguish from related bacteria, accurate identification and susceptibility testing matter, especially in suspected endocarditis or sepsis.

name: globin
clinical_significance: A protein that joins with heme to form hemoglobin and related oxygen-carrying molecules. Different globin chains help determine the type of hemoglobin made at different stages of life.

name: globozoospermia
clinical_significance: A rare sperm disorder in which sperm heads are round and lack a normal acrosome, causing impaired fertilization and male infertility.

name: globule unit
clinical_significance: A count unit used for an individual globule or pellet in some medicine-product records, including homeopathic products. The unit alone does not state how much active ingredient is present; the product’s ingredient, potency, and concentration determine what was actually taken.

name: globulin
clinical_significance: A group of blood proteins that includes antibodies and proteins involved in transport, inflammation, and clotting. Blood tests may divide globulins into several groups; an abnormal level can occur with infection, immune disease, liver disease, kidney disease, or some cancers.

name: globus pallidus
clinical_significance: The globus pallidus is a group of deep brain structures involved in regulating movement as part of the basal ganglia.

name: globus sensation
clinical_significance: A lump-like feeling in the throat that usually occurs without a true blockage. It may accompany reflux, throat irritation, muscle tension, or stress; difficulty or pain with swallowing, weight loss, a neck mass, or persistent hoarseness calls for medical assessment.

name: glomerular filtration
clinical_significance: The first step in urine formation, in which pressure moves water and small dissolved substances from blood through kidney filters into the tubules. Blood cells and most proteins normally remain in the bloodstream.

name: glomerulomegaly
clinical_significance: Abnormal enlargement of kidney glomeruli, seen with diabetes, obesity-related hyperfiltration, congenital syndromes, or other causes of glomerular stress.

name: glomerulonephritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or other immune-related injury of the kidney’s filtering units. It can cause blood or protein in urine, swelling, high blood pressure, and reduced kidney function and may follow an infection or occur with an autoimmune disease.

name: glomerulonephritis acute
clinical_significance: Sudden inflammation of the kidney glomeruli that can cause blood or protein in urine, edema, hypertension, and reduced kidney function.

name: glomerulopathy
clinical_significance: Any disease affecting the kidney’s filtering units. It may cause blood or protein in urine, swelling, high blood pressure, reduced filtration, or kidney failure and may result from diabetes, infection, immune disease, inherited disorders, or other injury.

name: glomerulosclerosis
clinical_significance: Scarring and hardening of the kidney’s filtering units. It can reduce filtration and cause protein in urine, swelling, high blood pressure, or kidney failure; causes include diabetes, inflammation, genetic disease, and other injury.

name: glomus tumor
clinical_significance: A usually harmless growth arising from cells that help control blood flow and temperature, most often beneath a fingernail or in a finger. It typically causes severe pinpoint pain and sensitivity to cold or pressure.

name: glossalgia
clinical_significance: Pain or burning of the tongue, with causes including trauma, infection, nutritional deficiency, neuropathy, medication, or burning-mouth syndrome.

name: glossectomy
clinical_significance: Surgical removal of all or part of the tongue, performed for malignancies, severe trauma, or an unusually large tongue. Procedures range from partial to total removal. Speech and swallowing rehabilitation may follow.

name: glossinidae
clinical_significance: The family of flies belonging to the genus Glossina, commonly known as tsetse flies. These insects are vectors of trypanosomes that cause African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) in humans and nagana in animals.

name: glossitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the tongue, which can cause pain, swelling, and changes in tongue appearance. Causes include nutritional deficiencies (iron, B12, folate), infections (bacterial, viral, fungal), allergic reactions, and autoimmune conditions. Treatment depends on the underlying cause.

name: glossopharyngeal nerve
clinical_significance: The ninth cranial nerve, carrying sensation and taste from the back of the tongue and throat, signals from blood-pressure and blood-chemistry sensors, and motor control for one throat muscle. It also stimulates saliva production.

name: glossoptosis
clinical_significance: Backward displacement of the tongue that can narrow the upper airway, particularly in infants with craniofacial disorders.

name: glottis
clinical_significance: The part of the voice box containing the vocal folds and the opening between them. It opens for breathing, closes to protect the airway during swallowing, and vibrates to produce the voice.

name: glucagon
clinical_significance: A hormone made by pancreatic alpha cells that raises blood glucose when it falls too low. It prompts the liver to release stored glucose and can be given for severe hypoglycemia.

name: glucagonoma
clinical_significance: A rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes excess glucagon, causing diabetes mellitus (mild, new onset), dermatitis (necrolytic migratory erythema, characteristic painful, erythematous, blistering rash on groin, perineum, extremities), diarrhea, and deep vein thrombosis.

name: glucan
clinical_significance: A complex carbohydrate made of many linked glucose molecules. Different glucans occur in plants, fungi, bacteria, and foods and may act as dietary fiber or interact with the immune system.

name: glucarpidase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that rapidly breaks down methotrexate in the bloodstream and is used for toxic methotrexate concentrations when renal clearance is inadequate.

name: glucocorticoid
clinical_significance: A steroid hormone or medicine that reduces inflammation and immune activity and also affects blood sugar, bone, and stress responses. Long-term or high-dose treatment can increase infection risk, weaken bones, and suppress natural adrenal hormone production; stopping prolonged therapy suddenly may be dangerous.

name: gluconates
clinical_significance: Salts or esters of gluconic acid used in some medicines and supplements. Examples include calcium gluconate and ferrous gluconate; their effects, dosing, and risks depend on the specific compound.

name: gluconeogenesis
clinical_significance: A metabolic pathway that generates glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors such as lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids. It occurs mainly in the liver and, to a variable extent, in the kidneys and other tissues.

name: glucose
clinical_significance: A simple sugar that is the main energy source for the body’s cells. It comes from digesting carbohydrates and can also be released from stored energy or made by the liver. Hormones, especially insulin, help keep blood glucose within a healthy range.

name: glucose intolerance
clinical_significance: Glucose levels above normal but below the diagnostic range for diabetes, often called prediabetes. It signals increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease; follow-up and lifestyle support can help delay or prevent progression.

name: glucose transport
clinical_significance: Movement of glucose across cell membranes through specialized transport proteins. Insulin increases glucose entry into muscle and fat cells, while other transporters allow glucose to enter the brain, liver, kidneys, and intestines.

name: glucose transporter
clinical_significance: A membrane protein that moves glucose across a cell membrane; transporter defects or altered regulation can affect glucose metabolism.

name: glucosinolate
clinical_significance: Sulfur-containing compounds found mainly in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cabbage, and kale. Their breakdown products are being studied for possible health effects, but evidence does not support glucosinolate supplements as a proven way to prevent or treat disease.

name: glucosylceramidase
clinical_significance: A lysosomal enzyme that breaks down glucosylceramide, a fat-containing cell substance. Inherited deficiency causes Gaucher disease, allowing fatty material to accumulate in the spleen, liver, bone marrow, bones, or nervous system.

name: glucuronate
clinical_significance: The anion or salt of glucuronic acid, a sugar-acid component of connective-tissue substances and a molecule used in hepatic conjugation reactions.

name: glucuronic acid
clinical_significance: A sugar acid used by the liver to conjugate bilirubin, drugs, hormones, and toxins, increasing their water solubility for excretion.

name: glucuronide
clinical_significance: A compound formed when glucuronic acid is conjugated to a drug, hormone, bilirubin, or other molecule, usually increasing water solubility and facilitating excretion.

name: glutamate
clinical_significance: The main excitatory chemical messenger in the brain and spinal cord. It helps nerve cells communicate, learn, and form memories; excessive glutamate activity can contribute to nerve-cell injury.

name: glutamate decarboxylase
clinical_significance: Glutamate decarboxylase is an enzyme that converts glutamate into the neurotransmitter GABA; antibodies against it are associated with some autoimmune disorders.

name: glutamate receptor
clinical_significance: A neuronal receptor activated by glutamate, the major excitatory neurotransmitter, including NMDA, AMPA, kainate, and metabotropic receptor classes.

name: glutamic acid
clinical_significance: An amino acid that acts as a metabolic intermediate and neurotransmitter precursor; its charged form, glutamate, mediates most fast excitatory signaling in the brain.

name: glutamine
clinical_significance: An amino acid used to build proteins, transport nitrogen, and provide energy for some cells, especially cells in the intestine and immune system. The body usually makes enough, but needs may change during severe illness.

name: glutaral
clinical_significance: Glutaral is a chemical disinfectant and tissue fixative that can irritate the skin, eyes, and airways.

name: glutathione
clinical_significance: A small antioxidant molecule made from glutamate, cysteine, and glycine. Reduced glutathione helps control oxidative stress and helps the liver neutralize reactive chemicals, including NAPQI produced from acetaminophen. N-acetylcysteine can restore glutathione after acetaminophen overdose.

name: glutathione disulfide
clinical_significance: The oxidized form of glutathione, produced after glutathione neutralizes reactive oxygen compounds. Cells normally convert it back to active glutathione to maintain antioxidant protection.

name: glutathione transferase
clinical_significance: A family of enzymes that attaches glutathione to selected medicines, toxins, and products of cell metabolism. This usually makes them less reactive and easier for the body to process or remove.

name: gluteal muscle
clinical_significance: One of the large muscles of the buttock, especially the gluteus maximus, medius, or minimus. These muscles extend, rotate, and move the hip and help stabilize the pelvis during standing and walking.

name: gluten-free diet
clinical_significance: A diet that avoids wheat, barley, rye, and foods contaminated with them. It is essential for celiac disease and may help selected people with non-celiac gluten sensitivity; poorly planned diets can lack fiber or nutrients.

name: glyburide
clinical_significance: An oral sulfonylurea that stimulates pancreatic insulin release for type 2 diabetes; prolonged or severe hypoglycemia is an important risk.

name: glycemic index
clinical_significance: A ranking of carbohydrate-containing foods according to how quickly they raise blood glucose compared with a reference food. It does not account for the amount of carbohydrate eaten in a serving.

name: glycemic load
clinical_significance: A measure that combines a food’s glycemic index with the amount of available carbohydrate in a serving to estimate its effect on blood glucose.

name: glyceraldehyde
clinical_significance: A small sugar with three carbon atoms that appears as the body breaks down glucose and other carbohydrates. It is quickly changed into other substances during the steps that release energy from food.

name: glyceride
clinical_significance: A glyceride is a compound formed when glycerol is linked to one or more fatty acids, including many dietary fats.

name: glycerol
clinical_significance: A colorless, sweet-tasting alcohol that forms part of fats. It is used in medicines, foods, and skin products and can draw water into the bowel when used in some laxatives.

name: glycerol kinase
clinical_significance: Glycerol kinase is an enzyme that adds phosphate to glycerol, allowing it to enter pathways for energy production and fat metabolism.

name: glycerophosphates
clinical_significance: Compounds containing glycerol and phosphate that help build cell membranes and participate in energy metabolism, chemical signaling, and other cellular processes.

name: glycerophospholipids
clinical_significance: The major membrane phospholipids built from glycerol, fatty acids, phosphate, and a polar head group, including phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine.

name: glycerylphosphorylcholine
clinical_significance: A choline-containing substance formed when certain membrane fats are broken down. It occurs in body fluids and cells and participates in membrane metabolism and the supply of choline.

name: glycine
clinical_significance: A small amino acid used to make proteins and heme. It also acts as an inhibitory chemical messenger, especially in the spinal cord and brainstem, helping regulate movement and reflexes.

name: glycine receptor
clinical_significance: A receptor that mediates inhibitory signaling in the spinal cord and brainstem. Inherited receptor defects can cause hyperekplexia, while glycine-receptor antibodies may occur in rare autoimmune neurologic syndromes such as progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus.

name: glycocalyx
clinical_significance: A sugar-rich coating on the outside of many cells, including cells lining blood vessels. It helps protect surfaces, control passage of substances, support cell attachment, and influence inflammation and clotting.

name: glycogen
clinical_significance: The body’s stored form of glucose. It is kept mainly in the liver, which releases it between meals, and in muscles, which use it during activity.

name: glycogenolysis
clinical_significance: The breakdown of stored glycogen. The liver uses it to release glucose into the blood between meals, while muscles use their glycogen locally for energy during exercise.

name: glycolates
clinical_significance: Salts or esters of glycolic acid. Urinary glycolate can be measured in specialist evaluation of inherited oxalate disorders, including primary hyperoxaluria type 1, but an increased result is not diagnostic by itself.

name: glycolipid
clinical_significance: A lipid containing a carbohydrate group that contributes to cell membranes, recognition, signaling, and myelin structure.

name: glycolysis
clinical_significance: A series of reactions in the cytosol that breaks one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules. It produces ATP and other molecules used in further energy production and can proceed when oxygen is limited.

name: glycomics
clinical_significance: The broad study of sugars and sugar chains in cells and organisms. Clinical glycomics is being developed for specialized biomarker and diagnostic testing, including inherited disorders of glycosylation, but most applications remain research or specialist laboratory tools.

name: glycopeptide
clinical_significance: A molecule made of a short protein chain with one or more attached sugar groups. Glycopeptides occur in cell-surface proteins, antibodies, and some medicines, and the attached sugars can affect structure and function.

name: glycophorin
clinical_significance: A sugar-coated protein in the red-blood-cell membrane that helps maintain the cell surface and carries markers used to distinguish blood-cell types.

name: glycoprotein
clinical_significance: A protein with covalently attached carbohydrate chains, important in receptors, antibodies, enzymes, mucus, cell adhesion, and extracellular matrix.

name: glycopyrrolate
clinical_significance: Glycopyrrolate is an anticholinergic medicine used to reduce secretions and, in some inhaled forms, to help control chronic obstructive lung disease; it may cause dry mouth, constipation, or urinary retention.

name: glycosaminoglycans
clinical_significance: Glycosaminoglycans are long chains of sugars found in connective tissue and involved in its structure, hydration, and signaling.

name: glycoside
clinical_significance: A compound in which a sugar is chemically linked to another molecule. Glycosides occur in plants, foods, and medicines; their effects depend on the attached molecule and how the body breaks the bond.

name: glycosphingolipid
clinical_significance: A membrane lipid containing ceramide and one or more sugars, involved in cell recognition, signaling, and nervous-system structure.

name: glycosuria
clinical_significance: The presence of glucose in the urine. It most often occurs when blood glucose is high, but it can also result from pregnancy, certain medicines, or a kidney-tubule problem that prevents normal glucose reabsorption.

name: glycosylation
clinical_significance: Attachment of sugar chains to proteins or fats inside cells. This process helps determine their shape, stability, location, and activity; abnormal glycosylation can contribute to inherited disease, cancer, and immune disorders.

name: glycosylphosphatidylinositol
clinical_significance: A lipid-and-sugar anchor that attaches certain proteins to the outer surface of a cell membrane. Defects in making or attaching this anchor can cause rare blood, nerve, or developmental disorders.

name: glycosyltransferase
clinical_significance: Glycosyltransferase is an enzyme that transfers a sugar to a protein, lipid, or other molecule during glycan synthesis.

name: glycyrrhetinic acid
clinical_significance: An active metabolite of licorice glycosides that inhibits 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase; excess exposure can cause hypertension, low potassium, and fluid retention.

name: glycyrrhizic acid
clinical_significance: The major saponin in licorice root that is converted to glycyrrhetinic acid and can produce mineralocorticoid-like toxicity when consumed excessively.

name: glyoxal
clinical_significance: A reactive dialdehyde used in chemical manufacturing and some laboratory fixatives. Contact or inhalation can irritate the eyes, skin, or airways; exposure assessment depends on concentration, route, and formulation.

name: glyoxysome
clinical_significance: A microbody in plant and some fungal cells that helps convert stored fats into sugars during germination or growth. It has no direct human clinical use but is relevant to plant biology and research.

name: glyphosate
clinical_significance: A widely used herbicide; toxicity after exposure depends on the product formulation, route, and amount. Concentrated products can cause serious illness if swallowed, while spray may irritate skin, eyes, or airways; the surfactants in a formulation can contribute to harm.

name: glyphosine
clinical_significance: A herbicide and plant-growth regulator used mainly in agriculture. It has no medical use; accidental or occupational exposure is assessed as a pesticide exposure, with risk depending on the product formulation and route.

name: gnathostoma
clinical_significance: A group of roundworms that can infect people who eat raw or undercooked freshwater fish, frogs, or other carriers. Larvae may migrate through skin, organs, or the nervous system and cause swelling, pain, or serious neurologic disease.

name: gnathostoma spinigerum
clinical_significance: A roundworm that can cause gnathostomiasis after people eat raw or undercooked freshwater animals. Migrating larvae may produce recurring painful skin swellings and, rarely, eye or brain disease.

name: gnathostomiasis
clinical_significance: A parasitic infection caused by Gnathostoma larvae acquired from undercooked freshwater fish or other hosts, producing migratory skin swellings or deeper neurologic or ocular disease.

name: goblet cell
clinical_significance: A mucus-secreting epithelial cell, abundant in the respiratory and intestinal tracts, that protects surfaces with a mucin-rich layer.

name: goiter
clinical_significance: Enlargement of the thyroid gland, either throughout the gland or as one or more lumps. It may occur with normal, overactive, or underactive thyroid function and can result from iodine deficiency, immune disease, or a tumor.

name: gold
clinical_significance: A metal used in selected dental restorations, implants, laboratory applications, and historical medicinal preparations; exposure can cause contact allergy or toxicity depending on the compound and dose.

name: gold alloys
clinical_significance: Metal mixtures containing gold and other elements, used in selected dental restorations or medical devices; properties and biocompatibility depend on composition.

name: Goldenhar syndrome
clinical_significance: A birth condition, also called oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum, in which one side of the face, ear, eye, or spine develops differently. Features may include facial asymmetry, a small or misshapen ear, hearing loss, eyelid or eye-surface growths, and spinal differences.

name: golgi apparatus
clinical_significance: A structure inside cells that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and fats made by the cell, sending them to other parts of the cell or releasing them outside it.

name: golgi cisternae
clinical_significance: Flattened membrane-bound sacs that form the Golgi apparatus and modify, sort, and package proteins and lipids for transport within or outside the cell.

name: gonad
clinical_significance: A testis or ovary, an organ producing reproductive cells and sex hormones. Gonadal function influences puberty, fertility, menstrual cycles, sexual development, bone health, and other body processes.

name: gonad disorder
clinical_significance: A disease affecting testes or ovaries and causing abnormal reproductive-cell production, hormone secretion, development, fertility, or sexual function.

name: gonadal agenesis
clinical_significance: Congenital absence or severe underdevelopment of a gonad, resulting in impaired sex-hormone production and infertility or differences in sexual development.

name: gonadal dysgenesis
clinical_significance: A developmental condition in which ovaries or testes are absent, streak-like, or incompletely formed, often causing atypical pubertal development, low sex-hormone levels, or infertility. Clinical evaluation considers chromosomes, hormones, anatomy, fertility goals, and—when Y-chromosome material is present—individualized risk of gonadal germ-cell tumors.

name: gonadoblastoma
clinical_significance: A rare tumor that develops in an abnormal or incompletely developed ovary or testicle. It may produce sex hormones and has a risk of becoming a malignant germ-cell tumor, especially when a Y-chromosome change is present.

name: gonadorelin
clinical_significance: Synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone that stimulates pituitary release of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone when given intermittently.

name: gonadotrophs
clinical_significance: Pituitary cells that release luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone after stimulation by GnRH, regulating the ovaries, testes, fertility, and sex-hormone production.

name: gonadotropin
clinical_significance: A hormone, chiefly luteinizing hormone or follicle-stimulating hormone, that acts on the ovaries or testes to regulate gamete production and sex-hormone secretion.

name: gondoic acid
clinical_significance: A 20-carbon monounsaturated fatty acid found in some seed oils and incorporated into dietary and tissue lipids.

name: gonioscopy
clinical_significance: An eye examination using a special contact lens to view the angle where the iris meets the cornea. It helps determine whether glaucoma is open-angle or angle-closure and guides treatment.

name: gonococcal urethritis
clinical_significance: Infection and inflammation of the urethra caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It may cause burning urination or discharge, but some people have no symptoms; untreated infection can spread.

name: gonorrhea
clinical_significance: A sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It may cause discharge, painful urination, pelvic or rectal symptoms, or no symptoms. Untreated infection can lead to infertility, joint infection, or infection in a newborn.

name: gordonia aichiensis
clinical_significance: A rare aerobic actinomycete that has occasionally been recovered from human infections, including device-associated or bloodstream infection. Because it can be confused with related bacteria, a clinically significant isolate should be identified by a capable laboratory and interpreted with symptoms and culture source.

name: gordonia bacterium
clinical_significance: A label for bacteria in the Gordonia group, whose members are environmental organisms and uncommon opportunistic pathogens. They can cause device-related, respiratory, skin, or bloodstream infection, particularly in medically vulnerable patients; species confirmation can be difficult.

name: gordonia bronchialis
clinical_significance: An environmental Gordonia species that has rarely caused human infection, including device-associated or bloodstream infection. It may be mistaken for other actinomycetes, so laboratory identification and susceptibility testing help guide treatment.

name: gordonia rubripertincta
clinical_significance: A rare environmental Gordonia species with occasional reports of human infection. If recovered from a normally sterile site or repeated cultures, it should be assessed as a possible opportunistic pathogen and accurately identified.

name: gordonia sputi
clinical_significance: A Gordonia species that has occasionally caused opportunistic human infection, including bloodstream or device-associated disease. It may grow slowly and be misidentified as related bacteria, so laboratory confirmation matters.

name: gordonia terrae
clinical_significance: An environmental Gordonia species rarely reported in human clinical specimens. Its significance depends on the specimen source, repeated isolation, symptoms, and immune status; unusual isolates may need molecular identification.

name: goserelin
clinical_significance: A gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist that initially stimulates and then suppresses pituitary gonadotropins; it is used in hormone-sensitive prostate or breast cancer and selected gynecologic conditions.

name: gossypol
clinical_significance: A cottonseed-derived compound once studied as a male contraceptive because it suppresses sperm production. It is not an approved contraceptive or established treatment; use was abandoned because of risks including low potassium and sometimes persistent infertility.

name: gout
clinical_significance: A type of inflammatory arthritis caused by a buildup of urate, a substance made when the body breaks down purines. When urate levels stay high, needle-shaped crystals can form in and around joints. These crystals cause sudden attacks, or flares, of severe pain, swelling, warmth, redness, and tenderness, often in the big toe but also in other joints. Repeated flares can damage joints. Long-standing gout may cause firm crystal deposits called tophi and uric acid kidney stones.

name: gout suppressants
clinical_significance: Medicines that lower uric-acid production or increase its excretion to prevent recurrent gout attacks and urate crystal deposition.

name: government
clinical_significance: Government activity can affect health through public-health policy, regulation, surveillance, and delivery or funding of services. Clinical care follows applicable local rules and available programs.

name: government funding
clinical_significance: Public funds support health services, research, prevention, and surveillance programs. Funding priorities affect which services and studies are available, and research support should be disclosed when interpreting evidence.

name: g-quadruplexes
clinical_significance: Four-stranded DNA or RNA structures formed in guanine-rich sequences that can influence gene regulation and genome stability. They are being studied as cancer-drug targets and research tools, but have no established routine diagnostic or treatment role.

name: graafian follicle
clinical_significance: A mature, fluid-filled sac in an ovary that contains an egg ready for release. It enlarges during the menstrual cycle and normally opens at ovulation; after release, the remaining tissue forms the corpus luteum.

name: gracilibacillus
clinical_significance: A genus of salt-tolerant environmental bacteria studied mainly in microbiology and ecology. It is not a recognized common human pathogen; an unexpected clinical isolate should be confirmed before assigning it a role in disease.

name: graft versus host
clinical_significance: Graft-versus-host disease occurs when donor immune cells attack recipient tissues after transplantation; it can damage skin, gut, liver, and lungs and requires early recognition and immunosuppressive care.

name: gram
clinical_significance: A metric unit used to measure mass, equal to one-thousandth of a kilogram. Grams are commonly used for medicines, laboratory samples, food, and body substances; one thousand milligrams make one gram.

name: gramicidin
clinical_significance: Gramicidin is a topical antibiotic that forms channels in bacterial membranes; it is not generally used systemically because it can be toxic.

name: gram-positive cocci
clinical_significance: Round bacteria that appear purple with a Gram stain because they have a thick peptidoglycan cell wall. Important groups include staphylococci, streptococci, and enterococci, which may normally live on the body or cause skin, throat, lung, urinary, heart-valve, or bloodstream infections.

name: gram-positive rods
clinical_significance: Rod-shaped bacteria that retain the purple Gram stain, including important pathogens such as Listeria and Bacillus as well as harmless or contaminating species. Their clinical significance depends on the organism, specimen, and patient; laboratory identification is needed to select treatment.

name: grandchild
clinical_significance: A person’s child’s child. A grandchild’s diagnoses may contribute to a family medical history or help identify an inherited pattern, but genetic risk depends on the specific condition and inheritance pattern.

name: grandparent
clinical_significance: A parent of one’s parent. A grandparent’s health history may inform family risk assessment, especially for conditions that can appear across generations; relatives’ ages and diagnoses should be verified when possible.

name: granisetron
clinical_significance: Granisetron is a selective 5-HT3-receptor antagonist used to prevent chemotherapy-, radiotherapy-, or surgery-related nausea and vomiting; headache, constipation, and QT prolongation can occur.

name: granisetron hydrochloride
clinical_significance: The hydrochloride form of granisetron, a medicine that blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors to prevent nausea and vomiting from chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery. Headache, constipation, and heart-rhythm changes may occur.

name: granulation tissue
clinical_significance: New tissue that grows in a healing wound and contains small blood vessels, connective tissue, and immune cells. Healthy granulation tissue is usually pink or red and moist.

name: granules
clinical_significance: Small solid particles used as an oral medicine form or as an intermediate in making tablets and capsules. Some granules have delayed or extended release; they should not be crushed, chewed, or altered unless the specific product instructions allow it.

name: granulicatella
clinical_significance: Granulicatella is a group of bacteria that may live in the mouth and can rarely cause bloodstream infection or endocarditis.

name: granulicatella adiacens
clinical_significance: A mouth bacterium that can rarely cause serious infection, especially infection of heart valves or the bloodstream. It may be difficult to grow in culture, and treatment depends on susceptibility testing.

name: granulicatella elegans
clinical_significance: A bacterium normally found in the mouth that can rarely cause bloodstream infection or infection of a heart valve. It may grow poorly in routine culture, so repeated positive cultures and compatible symptoms are important when judging its significance.

name: granulocyte
clinical_significance: A type of white blood cell containing visible granules. Neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils are granulocytes that help fight infection, trigger inflammation, and respond to allergic or parasitic disease.

name: granulocyte count
clinical_significance: A granulocyte count measures the number of neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils in the blood and helps assess infection, inflammation, and bone-marrow function.

name: granulocytic sarcoma
clinical_significance: A mass of immature myeloid blood-forming cells outside the bone marrow, also called myeloid sarcoma. It may occur with acute myeloid leukemia or precede it.

name: granuloma
clinical_significance: A small area of organized inflammation formed when immune cells surround material they cannot easily remove, such as certain germs, foreign material, or substances released by the body.

name: granuloma annulare
clinical_significance: A benign, noninfectious inflammatory skin condition that causes raised red, pink, or skin-colored bumps arranged in rings, often with clearer skin in the center. It commonly affects the hands, feet, or elbows and may cause little or no discomfort. Widespread disease may be associated with diabetes or thyroid disease, but the cause is often unknown.

name: granuloma inguinale
clinical_significance: A chronic sexually transmitted infection causing painless, slowly enlarging ulcers in the genital or groin region. It is caused by bacteria and spreads through sexual contact; antibiotics are used in treatment.

name: granulomatosis
clinical_significance: A disease in which long-lasting inflammation forms granulomas, small organized collections of immune cells. Depending on the cause, granulomas may affect the lungs, skin, lymph nodes, intestines, or other organs.

name: granulosa cell
clinical_significance: A granulosa cell is a cell surrounding an ovarian egg that supports its development and produces hormones such as estrogen and inhibin.

name: granulosa cell tumor
clinical_significance: A tumor arising from hormone-producing cells in the ovary. It may release estrogen, causing irregular bleeding or early puberty, and can recur years after treatment even when it initially appears slow-growing.

name: granzyme
clinical_significance: A protease released by cytotoxic T lymphocytes and natural killer cells that enters target cells through perforin-associated pores and promotes programmed cell death.

name: Graves disease
clinical_significance: Graves disease can cause an overactive thyroid, rapid or irregular heartbeat, bone loss, fertility or pregnancy problems, and inflammation around the eyes that may affect vision. Untreated severe hyperthyroidism can rarely become a life-threatening thyroid storm; treatment and monitoring are needed even if eye symptoms are absent.

name: gravidity
clinical_significance: Gravidity is the number of times a person has been pregnant, including the current pregnancy and pregnancies that did not result in a live birth.

name: gravitropism
clinical_significance: Directional growth of a plant or plant organ in response to gravity. It is important in plant biology but has no direct human clinical role.

name: gray matter
clinical_significance: Areas of the brain and spinal cord containing many nerve-cell bodies and connections. Gray matter processes information and helps control movement, sensation, memory, speech, and other functions.

name: greater than
clinical_significance: A comparison operator indicating that one value is larger than another. In clinical records it may show that a laboratory result exceeds a threshold or reference limit; interpretation still depends on units, the test, and the patient’s context.

name: grief
clinical_significance: Grief is a common response to loss and varies across people and cultures. When intense grief after a death remains persistent and disrupts daily life beyond expected cultural or religious norms, assessment for prolonged grief disorder or other treatable distress may help; ordinary grief is not itself an illness.

name: grimontia hollisae
clinical_significance: A salt-loving bacterium from seawater and seafood, formerly called \textit{Vibrio hollisae}. Eating contaminated raw or undercooked seafood can cause watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, and fever; severe infection is uncommon but more likely in people with serious underlying illness.

name: grip strength
clinical_significance: The force generated when the hand closes around an object, commonly measured with a dynamometer to assess hand function, muscle strength, nutrition, or rehabilitation progress.

name: griseofulvin
clinical_significance: Griseofulvin is an oral antifungal that deposits in newly formed keratin and disrupts dermatophyte mitosis, treating infections of skin, hair, and nails; treatment is prolonged and hepatic or drug-interaction risks apply.

name: groin
clinical_significance: The region where the lower abdomen meets the upper thigh, containing the inguinal canal and related muscles, vessels, nerves, and lymph nodes.

name: gross virus
clinical_significance: A term for murine leukemia viruses associated with the experimental work of Ludwik Gross. These viruses cause leukemia in mice and are used in cancer and retrovirus research; they are not human pathogens.

name: ground substance
clinical_significance: The gel-like, noncellular part of connective tissue surrounding cells and fibers. It contains water, proteoglycans, and other molecules that support tissues, allow nutrient movement, and influence inflammation and repair.

name: groundwater
clinical_significance: Water held beneath the ground that may supply wells and public water systems. Germs or chemicals such as arsenic, nitrate, or lead can contaminate drinking sources and cause illness, so well water may need regular testing and treatment.

name: group therapy
clinical_significance: A form of psychotherapy where a small group of individuals with similar issues meet to discuss, interact, and develop coping strategies under the guidance of a trained therapist. Used for depression, anxiety, substance use disorders, grief, and chronic illness. Benefits include peer support and shared experiences.

name: growth
clinical_significance: The process of increasing in physical size and development, including physical, cognitive, and emotional maturation. In medicine, growth is monitored using growth charts and anthropometric measurements to assess health and development in children.

name: growth cone
clinical_significance: A specialized, moving tip at the end of a growing nerve fiber. It senses chemical and physical signals and guides the axon toward its target during nervous-system development or repair.

name: growth disorder
clinical_significance: A condition in which a child or adult grows unusually slowly, quickly, or unevenly because of genetic, hormonal, nutritional, chronic, or other medical causes.

name: growth factor
clinical_significance: A protein that sends signals controlling cell growth, division, specialization, survival, or repair. Different growth factors act on different tissues and are involved in wound healing, blood-vessel formation, immunity, and cancer.

name: growth failure
clinical_significance: Growth that is slower than expected or weight gain that is inadequate for age. It can result from poor nutrition, chronic illness, hormone problems, genetic conditions, or difficulty absorbing nutrients.

name: growth inhibitor
clinical_significance: A substance or medicine that slows or stops cell growth. Growth inhibitors include drugs used in cancer and some immune-mediated diseases; effects and harms depend on the specific agent and its target.

name: growth retardation
clinical_significance: Older wording for growth that is slower than expected for age or developmental stage. Possible causes include inadequate nutrition, chronic illness, hormone or genetic disorders, poor absorption, and normal family variation; growth is assessed over time rather than by one measurement.

name: gtp binding
clinical_significance: GTP binding is the attachment of guanosine triphosphate to a protein, often switching that protein into an active state for cell signaling.

name: guaifenesin
clinical_significance: An expectorant that may loosen chest mucus and make coughing more productive. It can relieve congestion symptoms but does not treat their cause or speed recovery; combination products can lead to accidental overdose if ingredients are duplicated.

name: guanazole
clinical_significance: An experimental antimetabolite that inhibits DNA synthesis and was studied as an anticancer agent. Guanazole is not an established or approved cancer treatment and has no routine clinical role.

name: guanfacine
clinical_significance: Guanfacine is a centrally acting alpha-2A adrenergic agonist used for hypertension and, in extended-release form, ADHD; sedation, hypotension, bradycardia, and rebound hypertension after abrupt withdrawal are important risks.

name: guanine
clinical_significance: Guanine is a purine nitrogenous base in DNA and RNA; it pairs with cytosine and is present in nucleotides such as GMP and GTP that support energy transfer and signaling.

name: guanosine
clinical_significance: A nucleoside made of guanine and ribose that is used to build RNA and other cellular molecules. It is mainly of biochemical and research interest; measurements are not ordinarily used alone to diagnose disease.

name: guanosine diphosphate
clinical_significance: A guanine nucleotide involved in RNA synthesis and cellular energy and signaling pathways. Its level may be studied in specialized biochemical research but is not a routine clinical test.

name: guanosine monophosphate
clinical_significance: A guanine nucleotide used in RNA synthesis and in cellular pathways that make cyclic GMP, an important signaling molecule. GMP is mainly of biochemical interest rather than a stand-alone clinical marker.

name: guanosine triphosphate
clinical_significance: A guanine nucleotide that provides energy and acts as a molecular switch in protein synthesis, cytoskeletal regulation, and G-protein signaling.

name: guanosinetriphosphatase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that hydrolyzes guanosine triphosphate to guanosine diphosphate and phosphate, regulating signaling and other cellular processes.

name: guanylate cyclase
clinical_significance: Guanylate cyclase is an enzyme that converts GTP to cyclic GMP, a second messenger involved in nitric-oxide signaling, smooth-muscle relaxation, phototransduction, and intestinal fluid secretion.

name: guide device
clinical_significance: A tool used to direct, position, or stabilize another instrument during a procedure, such as a guidewire, drill guide, or needle guide. It helps ensure accurate placement and reduces injury to surrounding tissue.

name: guided imagery
clinical_significance: Guided imagery is a relaxation technique that uses imagined sights, sounds, or other sensations to promote calm and sometimes help manage pain or stress.

name: Guillain-Barre syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare disorder in which the immune system attacks peripheral nerves, often after an infection. Weakness and tingling usually begin in the legs and may spread upward; severe cases affect breathing or swallowing.

name: guilt
clinical_significance: Guilt is a common emotion, but persistent, excessive, or inappropriate guilt can occur with depression, trauma-related conditions, or other distress. When it impairs daily life or occurs with thoughts of self-harm, clinical assessment is important.

name: gut epithelium
clinical_significance: The layer of cells lining the intestines. It absorbs nutrients and water, forms a barrier against harmful substances, and interacts with immune cells and gut microorganisms.

name: gynatresia
clinical_significance: Absence of or blockage in an opening of the female reproductive tract, present from birth or acquired later. If menstrual blood cannot leave the body, it may cause absent periods, pelvic pain, or enlargement of the uterus or vagina.

name: gynecological examination
clinical_significance: A gynecological examination may evaluate symptoms such as pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding, discharge, or a lump and may include cervical cancer screening when due. An internal pelvic examination is not needed at every routine visit for an asymptomatic person; its benefits, need, and consent should be discussed.

name: gynecologist
clinical_significance: A gynecologist is a physician who provides care for the female reproductive system, including preventive care, diagnosis, and treatment.

name: gynecology
clinical_significance: Gynecology addresses reproductive and sexual health, including menstrual concerns, contraception, pregnancy-related care, infections, fertility, menopause, and cancers. Preventive screening and examinations are selected according to symptoms, anatomy, age, and individual risk.

name: gynecomastia
clinical_significance: Benign enlargement of glandular breast tissue in males, often related to a shift in the balance between estrogen and androgen effects. It commonly occurs in newborns, during puberty, and with aging; some diseases and medicines can also cause it.

name: gyrate atrophy
clinical_significance: An inherited retinal disorder causing gradually worsening peripheral and night vision loss. It results from abnormal ornithine metabolism and may be managed with dietary treatment, supplements, and regular eye monitoring.

name: habenula
clinical_significance: A small brain structure helping process reward, unpleasant experiences, stress, motivation, and learned behavior. It connects several brain regions and may influence mood, sleep, pain, and responses to negative outcomes.

name: habit
clinical_significance: A repeated behavior or pattern of action that may be ordinary, helpful, or harmful; in clinical assessment, its frequency, control, and effect on functioning determine whether it is a concern.

name: haemophilus aegyptius
clinical_significance: A bacterium associated with eye infections and, rarely, severe bloodstream disease. It can spread through respiratory secretions or direct contact, and laboratory identification helps guide treatment and public-health precautions.

name: haemophilus haemolyticus
clinical_significance: A bacterium that commonly lives harmlessly in the upper airway but can occasionally cause respiratory or invasive infection, especially in people with weakened immunity or serious underlying illness.

name: haemophilus infections
clinical_significance: Infections caused by Haemophilus bacteria, which may affect the ears, sinuses, lungs, bloodstream, joints, or brain coverings. Severity depends on the species, infection site, age, vaccination, and immune health.

name: haemophilus influenzae
clinical_significance: A type of bacteria that can cause ear infections, pneumonia, meningitis, and other infections. Type b, or Hib, can cause severe disease in children, but vaccination greatly reduces this risk.

name: haemophilus paragallinarum
clinical_significance: A bacterium now named Avibacterium paragallinarum that causes infectious coryza in chickens, with nasal discharge, facial swelling, and reduced egg production. It is important in poultry health and is not a recognized human pathogen.

name: haemophilus parainfluenzae
clinical_significance: A small gram-negative bacterium that normally colonizes the upper respiratory tract but can rarely cause respiratory, bloodstream, or other opportunistic infections.

name: haemophilus somnus
clinical_significance: An older name for Histophilus somni, a bacterium that causes respiratory, reproductive, joint, heart, or neurologic disease in cattle. It is a veterinary pathogen rather than a typical human pathogen.

name: haemophilus vaccine
clinical_significance: Vaccines are available against Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) and prevent many severe infections caused by that type, including meningitis and bloodstream disease. Hib vaccine does not protect against nontypeable or other non-b strains of H. influenzae.

name: hafnia
clinical_significance: A genus of gram-negative intestinal bacteria; Hafnia alvei is the species most often identified in human specimens.

name: hafnia alvei
clinical_significance: A Gram-negative bacterium found in the intestine and environment that rarely causes opportunistic infection, usually in people with serious illness or weakened immunity.

name: hair
clinical_significance: Keratinized filaments produced by follicles in the skin. Hair protects the scalp, contributes to temperature regulation and sensation, and grows through anagen, catagen, and telogen phases.

name: hair bulb
clinical_significance: The rounded base of a hair follicle where new hair is produced. It contains growing cells and a small blood-supplied area that provides nutrients and helps determine hair growth and color.

name: hair disease
clinical_significance: A disorder affecting hair growth, the hair shaft, or the scalp; causes include genetics, inflammation, infection, medicines, and nutritional problems.

name: hair follicle
clinical_significance: A small tube in the skin that produces a hair. Each follicle has a growth phase, a brief transition phase, and a resting phase.

name: hair shaft
clinical_significance: The part of a hair that extends above the skin. It is made of dead, hardened cells produced by the follicle and can be affected by cutting, heat, chemicals, friction, or damage to the hair root.

name: hairy cell leukemia
clinical_significance: A rare, usually slow-growing cancer of a type of white blood cell. Abnormal cells build up in the bone marrow, blood, and spleen, causing low blood counts, infections, tiredness, or an enlarged spleen.

name: hairy tongue
clinical_significance: A usually harmless elongation of the tongue’s surface papillae that can look black, brown, or yellow. Dry mouth, smoking, antibiotics, soft diets, or some mouthwashes can contribute; tongue cleaning and addressing the cause often help, while persistent or painful changes should be assessed.

name: halcinonide
clinical_significance: A potent topical corticosteroid used to reduce inflammation and itching in steroid-responsive dermatitis and other inflammatory skin disorders; prolonged or extensive use can cause skin atrophy and systemic effects.

name: half-brother
clinical_significance: A sibling who shares one biological parent. This relationship can matter when recording family history or assessing inherited risk, but the chance of sharing a particular genetic condition depends on which parent and how the condition is inherited.

name: half-life
clinical_significance: The time it takes for the amount of a medicine in the body, or its blood level, to decrease by half. It helps determine how often a medicine should be taken and how long it remains in the body.

name: half-sibling
clinical_significance: A sibling who shares one biological parent with another person. Half-sibling history may help assess familial disease or donor compatibility; genetic risk varies with the condition and the shared side of the family.

name: half-sister
clinical_significance: A female sibling who shares one biological parent. Her health history can inform family risk assessment, with relevance depending on the condition, inheritance pattern, and shared parent.

name: halitosis
clinical_significance: Persistent unpleasant breath odor, most often from bacteria on the tongue, teeth, or gums. Dry mouth, smoking, foods, sinus or throat disease, reflux, and some illnesses or medicines can also contribute.

name: Hallermann's syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare congenital disorder characterized by distinctive craniofacial development, sparse hair, dental abnormalities, and sometimes eye or skeletal findings; it is also called Hallermann--Streiff syndrome.

name: hallucination
clinical_significance: A sensory experience that feels real but occurs without a matching external stimulus. It may involve seeing, hearing, feeling, smelling, or tasting something that is not present.

name: hallucinogen
clinical_significance: A psychoactive substance that can alter perception, thought, and mood and may produce hallucinations; effects and toxicity vary by substance, dose, co-ingestants, and mental state.

name: hallux
clinical_significance: The great toe, or big toe. It has two bones and helps the foot stay stable and push off during walking. Common problems include hallux valgus (a bunion), hallux rigidus (a stiff, arthritic joint), turf toe (a sprain), and gout causing sudden pain and swelling at the joint where the toe meets the foot.

name: hallux rigidus
clinical_significance: Arthritis of the joint where the big toe meets the foot, causing pain, stiffness, swelling, and reduced upward movement. A bony bump may develop and make walking or wearing shoes difficult.

name: hallux valgus
clinical_significance: A bunion: a change in the alignment of the joint at the base of the big toe, with the toe pointing inward and a prominent area on the inner forefoot. It may become painful from pressure or inflammation.

name: hallux varus
clinical_significance: Abnormal medial deviation of the great toe, often following surgery, trauma, neuromuscular imbalance, or congenital deformity; it can cause shoe difficulty and pressure-related pain.

name: halo nevus
clinical_significance: A usually harmless mole surrounded by a ring of lighter skin. The immune system causes the mole and nearby pigment cells to lose color; it often occurs in children or young adults and may slowly fade.

name: halobacillus
clinical_significance: A genus of salt-loving bacteria found in high-salinity environments. It is mainly of microbiologic and environmental interest and is not a recognized common cause of human infection.

name: halobacteriaceae
clinical_significance: A family of salt-loving archaea that inhabit very salty environments such as salt lakes and salted foods. They are primarily relevant to environmental and laboratory microbiology, not human disease.

name: halofenate
clinical_significance: An older lipid-lowering drug investigated for high blood fats and uric acid. It is not a current standard treatment; historical trials reported adverse effects, including low blood sugar in some patients.

name: halofuginone hydrobromide
clinical_significance: An investigational compound with anticoccidial, antifibrotic, and potential anticancer activity. It has been studied in research and clinical trials but is not an established or approved human treatment.

name: halogen
clinical_significance: An element in group 17 of the periodic table, including fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, and astatine; halogens and their compounds have medical, biologic, and toxicologic importance.

name: halogenation
clinical_significance: A chemical reaction that introduces a halogen atom into a molecule. Halogenation is used to make or modify medicines, imaging agents, and disinfectants; the safety and medical effects depend on the resulting compound.

name: haloperidol
clinical_significance: Haloperidol is a first-generation antipsychotic that blocks dopamine D2 receptors and is used for psychosis, agitation, delirium, and tics; extrapyramidal reactions, tardive dyskinesia, hyperprolactinaemia, and QT prolongation are important risks.

name: halothane
clinical_significance: A volatile inhaled anesthetic formerly used to induce or maintain general anesthesia; it can cause hypotension, arrhythmias, and rare severe immune-mediated liver injury.

name: hamartoma
clinical_significance: A usually harmless growth made of an abnormal arrangement of tissue types normally found in that part of the body. It may occur in organs such as the lung, skin, brain, or intestine and may cause problems if it grows or presses on nearby structures.

name: hamartomatous polyposis
clinical_significance: A condition in which multiple hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps develop from disorganized but benign tissue overgrowth, sometimes as part of an inherited cancer-predisposition syndrome.

name: hamate
clinical_significance: A small, wedge-shaped bone on the little-finger side of the wrist. Its hook provides attachment for ligaments and tendons; fractures there may cause wrist pain or pressure on a nearby nerve.

name: hammer toe
clinical_significance: A deformity in which a lesser toe bends downward at its middle joint and may press against the shoe. It can cause pain, stiffness, corns, or calluses and may be flexible at first or become fixed.

name: hand
clinical_significance: The part of the upper limb beyond the wrist, containing the palm, fingers, bones, joints, muscles, nerves, and blood vessels used for grasping and sensation.

name: hand deformity
clinical_significance: An abnormal shape, alignment, or loss of motion of the hand or fingers caused by congenital difference, trauma, arthritis, nerve dysfunction, tendon disease, or other conditions.

name: hannaella luteola
clinical_significance: A species of salt-tolerant yeast usually found in environmental or food settings. It is not a common human pathogen; an isolate from a patient should be assessed cautiously and confirmed if infection is suspected.

name: hanseniaspora
clinical_significance: A genus of yeasts associated with plants, fruit, and fermentation that very rarely appears in human infection reports. A positive culture may represent contamination or colonization, so clinical evidence and reliable species identification are important.

name: hanseniaspora uvarum
clinical_significance: A fermentation yeast found on fruit and in food production that has rarely been reported in human samples or infection. Its significance in a patient depends on repeat isolation, the specimen site, and evidence of tissue disease.

name: hanseniaspora valbyensis
clinical_significance: A yeast associated with fermentation that has extremely limited reports of human infection. When identified in a clinical specimen, it should be interpreted with symptoms and laboratory confirmation rather than assumed to be a cause of disease.

name: hantavirus
clinical_significance: A group of viruses spread mainly by breathing dust contaminated with infected rodent urine, droppings, or nesting material. They can cause severe lung disease or a fever that damages the kidneys.

name: hantavirus infection
clinical_significance: A zoonotic viral infection acquired mainly through inhalation of contaminated rodent excreta. It may cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome or hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, which can progress rapidly to respiratory failure.

name: haploidentical donor
clinical_significance: A donor who shares one human leukocyte antigen haplotype with the recipient, commonly used for selected hematopoietic stem-cell or organ transplantation when a fully matched donor is unavailable.

name: haploidy
clinical_significance: The state of having one complete set of chromosomes, as in human gametes; haploid cells contain 23 chromosomes.

name: haplotype
clinical_significance: A group of nearby gene versions inherited together on one chromosome. Haplotype information can help study inherited disease risk, identify tissue donors, and trace how genetic traits are passed through families.

name: happiness
clinical_significance: Happiness is a subjective sense of well-being that can contribute to quality of life and resilience. It is not a medical diagnosis, and low happiness alone does not establish a mental disorder.

name: hapten
clinical_significance: A hapten is a small molecule that is not immunogenic by itself but can trigger an immune response after binding to a larger carrier protein, as in some drug allergies.

name: haptoglobin
clinical_significance: A blood protein made mainly by the liver that binds free hemoglobin released when red blood cells break down. Low levels can support evaluation of hemolysis, but liver disease and inflammation also affect the result.

name: haptoglobin analyses
clinical_significance: Laboratory tests measuring haptoglobin, a plasma protein that binds free hemoglobin; low values can support evaluation of intravascular hemolysis but are also affected by liver disease and inflammation.

name: haptoglobin decreased
clinical_significance: A low blood haptoglobin result, commonly caused by intravascular red-cell destruction, reduced hepatic production, or severe liver disease; it is interpreted with hemoglobin, bilirubin, reticulocytes, and a blood smear.

name: hard palate
clinical_significance: The bony, mucosa-covered front portion of the roof of the mouth that separates the oral and nasal cavities and provides a surface for chewing and speech.

name: harderian gland
clinical_significance: A gland prominent in many mammals that contributes to eye-surface secretions and other functions. It is largely absent or vestigial in adult humans, so it has little direct clinical relevance in people and is mainly studied in comparative anatomy and laboratory animals.

name: hardness
clinical_significance: A measure of calcium and magnesium in water that affects taste, soap use, and plumbing scale. WHO does not consider typical drinking-water hardness a health concern by itself; specific contaminants in water are a separate safety issue.

name: harringtonines
clinical_significance: Plant-derived alkaloids with cytotoxic activity. Homoharringtonine has a semisynthetic form, omacetaxine mepesuccinate, approved for selected adults with chronic myeloid leukemia after resistance or intolerance to multiple tyrosine-kinase inhibitors; other harringtonines are not interchangeable treatments.

name: Hartnup disease
clinical_significance: A rare inherited problem absorbing and reusing certain amino acids. It may cause a sun-sensitive rash, poor coordination, or mood and thinking changes, although some people have no symptoms.

name: Hashimoto disease
clinical_significance: An autoimmune disorder in which antibodies and lymphocytes progressively damage the thyroid, commonly causing hypothyroidism, goiter, fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, and weight change.

name: hashitoxicosis
clinical_significance: A temporary period of excess thyroid hormone caused by release of stored hormone during Hashimoto thyroiditis.

name: hay fever
clinical_significance: A common name for seasonal allergic rhinitis, an allergic response to airborne outdoor plant pollens and mold spores that causes sneezing, a blocked or runny nose, an itchy palate, and watery, irritated eyes. See also \textit{Seasonal Allergies}.

name: head
clinical_significance: The body region containing the brain, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, skull, and face, connected to the trunk by the neck and supplied by major cranial nerves and vessels.

name: head circumference
clinical_significance: The measurement around the largest part of a baby’s or child’s head, taken above the eyebrows and ears. It is plotted over time to assess brain growth; unusually small, large, or rapidly changing measurements may need evaluation.
