name: head movement
clinical_significance: Motion of the head produced mainly by the cervical spine and neck muscles, including flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending; pain or restricted movement may indicate injury or disease.

name: headache
clinical_significance: Pain or discomfort in the head, scalp, or upper neck. Primary headaches include migraine and tension headache; secondary headaches result from another problem such as infection, injury, bleeding, very high blood pressure, or a brain disorder.

name: health
clinical_significance: Health includes physical, mental, and social well-being and is influenced by biology, behavior, environment, and access to care. In clinical practice it is assessed through a person’s symptoms, function, goals, and lived circumstances, not a single test.

name: health behavior
clinical_significance: An action or pattern of action that affects health, such as eating, physical activity, tobacco use, alcohol use, sexual practices, or taking medicines.

name: health care
clinical_significance: The prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and ongoing support provided to maintain or improve health, delivered by professionals, institutions, public-health systems, and informal caregivers.

name: health care facility
clinical_significance: A place where health services are delivered, such as a clinic, hospital, laboratory, nursing facility, or rehabilitation center; its services and level of care determine appropriate referrals.

name: health care personnel
clinical_significance: Professionals and support workers involved in patient care, including clinicians, nurses, therapists, technicians, aides, and public-health staff.

name: health disparity
clinical_significance: A difference in health outcomes or access to healthcare between population groups. It may be linked to income, housing, education, discrimination, environment, language, disability, geography, or unequal treatment.

name: health education
clinical_significance: The process of giving people understandable information and skills to prevent illness, recognize symptoms, use treatment safely, and make informed health decisions.

name: health insurance
clinical_significance: Health insurance can affect access to clinicians, medicines, tests, and preventive care, as well as out-of-pocket costs. Coverage rules and available services vary by plan and location, so patients may need help understanding benefits and alternatives.

name: health literacy
clinical_significance: The ability to find, understand, judge, and use health information and services to make appropriate decisions. It includes communicating with clinicians, following instructions, reading medicine labels, and recognizing when to seek help; clear communication by healthcare staff also improves health literacy.

name: health service
clinical_significance: Health services include preventive, diagnostic, treatment, rehabilitation, and support care. Availability, quality, affordability, and coordination can affect health outcomes and whether people receive needed care.

name: health services research
clinical_significance: Research on how healthcare is organized, delivered, financed, and experienced, and how it affects quality, access, cost, safety, and outcomes. Findings can guide improvements in clinical practice and health systems.

name: health status
clinical_significance: A summary of a person’s or population’s health based on disease, symptoms, function, well-being, and sometimes self-rated health. It helps monitor change and compare outcomes but depends on how and when it is measured.

name: health survey
clinical_significance: A structured set of questions used to collect information about health, symptoms, behaviors, healthcare use, or population needs.

name: health workforce
clinical_significance: The people and roles needed to deliver health and public-health services, including clinicians, nurses, technicians, support staff, and community workers. Workforce shortages, distribution, and training affect access, continuity, and quality of care.

name: healthy
clinical_significance: In clinical care, “healthy” can describe well-being, function, or the absence of a particular disease, but it does not guarantee that every condition has been excluded. Screening and follow-up depend on symptoms, age, risks, and patient goals.

name: hearing
clinical_significance: The ability to detect and understand sound. Sound vibrations are converted into nerve signals in the inner ear and interpreted by the brain. Hearing loss may result from the outer or middle ear, inner ear, hearing nerve, or brain pathways.

name: hearing aid
clinical_significance: A small electronic device worn in or behind the ear that makes sounds louder or clearer for someone with hearing loss. It contains a microphone, processor, and speaker and is fitted and adjusted according to hearing-test results.

name: hearing disorder
clinical_significance: A condition that reduces or distorts hearing through disease of the outer or middle ear, cochlea, auditory nerve, or central pathways; audiometry and examination help distinguish conductive from sensorineural loss.

name: hearing impairment
clinical_significance: Reduced ability to hear sounds or understand speech, ranging from mild to profound. It can affect communication, learning, safety, and social participation; hearing tests help identify the type and severity and guide treatment or hearing support.

name: hearing test
clinical_significance: An audiologic assessment that measures hearing thresholds and speech perception across frequencies to identify conductive, sensorineural, or mixed hearing loss.

name: heart
clinical_significance: The muscular organ that circulates blood through the lungs and the rest of the body. Problems with its pumping function, blood supply, valves, or rhythm can affect oxygen delivery and cause chest discomfort, breathlessness, fainting, or swelling.

name: heart aneurysm
clinical_significance: A localized bulging or outpouching of a weakened heart wall, often after myocardial infarction or from cardiomyopathy, that can impair contraction or form clots and arrhythmias.

name: heart block
clinical_significance: A delay or interruption in the electrical signal traveling from the heart’s upper chambers to its lower chambers. It may cause a slow or irregular heartbeat, dizziness, fainting, or no symptoms.

name: heart catheterization
clinical_significance: A procedure in which a catheter is passed through a blood vessel into the heart to measure pressures, assess coronary arteries, inject contrast, obtain samples, or perform treatment.

name: heart contraction
clinical_significance: The squeezing of heart muscle that pushes blood from the lower chambers to the lungs and the rest of the body. Electrical signals coordinate the heartbeat, and abnormal contraction can reduce blood flow or cause rhythm problems.

name: heart disease
clinical_significance: A broad term for conditions affecting the heart or blood vessels, including coronary artery disease, heart failure, abnormal rhythms, valve disease, and congenital defects. Symptoms and treatment depend on the part affected and may include chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations, or swelling.

name: heart failure
clinical_significance: Heart failure is a condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs or cannot fill with blood properly. It does not mean that the heart has stopped. The heart may be too weak to pump effectively or too stiff to fill normally. Symptoms may include shortness of breath, tiredness, reduced ability to exercise, and swelling from fluid buildup.

name: heart injury
clinical_significance: Damage to heart muscle or surrounding cardiac structures caused by trauma, ischemia, inflammation, toxins, or procedures; symptoms and tests depend on the injured tissue and severity.

name: heart murmur
clinical_significance: An extra or unusual sound heard when blood flows through the heart or nearby blood vessels. Some murmurs are harmless, while others result from a valve problem, heart defect, or altered blood flow.

name: heart neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the heart or its surrounding tissues. It may be benign or cancerous and can interfere with blood flow, heart rhythm, or pumping; evaluation uses imaging and sometimes biopsy.

name: heart rate
clinical_significance: The number of heartbeats per minute. Resting rates vary with age, fitness, activity, illness, medicines, and emotion; a persistently very fast, slow, or irregular rate may need assessment.

name: heart rhythm
clinical_significance: The rate and pattern of cardiac electrical activation and contraction, normally initiated by the sinoatrial node; abnormal rhythms include bradycardia, tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular arrhythmias.

name: heart septum
clinical_significance: The muscular or membranous wall separating the right and left sides of the heart, including the atrial and ventricular septa; defects can permit abnormal blood flow between chambers.

name: heart sounds
clinical_significance: The sounds made as the heart valves open and close during each heartbeat. The usual two sounds are called “lub-dub”; extra or unusual sounds may suggest a valve problem, heart failure, or another condition.

name: heart surgery
clinical_significance: Operations on the heart or major vessels can treat coronary artery disease, valve disease, congenital defects, aneurysms, or advanced heart failure. Risks and recovery depend on the procedure and the person’s health, and care includes monitoring for bleeding, infection, stroke, rhythm problems, and impaired heart function.

name: heart tamponade
clinical_significance: A life-threatening condition in which fluid or blood builds up around the heart and prevents it from filling normally. It can cause breathlessness, faintness, low blood pressure, and shock and requires emergency treatment.

name: heart transplantation
clinical_significance: Surgical replacement of a failing heart with a donor heart, usually for selected patients with advanced heart failure who meet specialist criteria.

name: heart valve
clinical_significance: One of four structures that keep blood moving in one direction through the heart. Narrowing (stenosis) or leakage (regurgitation) can strain the heart, cause breathlessness or fatigue, and may require monitoring, medicines, or a procedure.

name: heart valve disorder
clinical_significance: Heart valve disease can obstruct or leak blood flow and lead to breathlessness, arrhythmia, or heart failure; examination and echocardiography assess severity and need for intervention.

name: heart ventricle
clinical_significance: One of the two lower heart chambers that pumps blood to the lungs or systemic circulation; the right ventricle pumps to the pulmonary artery and the left to the aorta.

name: heartburn
clinical_significance: A burning sensation behind the breastbone, usually from acid reflux into the esophagus. Frequent symptoms can indicate reflux disease, but new or severe chest pressure, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw may be a heart emergency and should not be assumed to be heartburn.

name: heat shock protein
clinical_significance: A stress-response protein that helps other proteins fold, avoid aggregation, and recover after heat, oxidative, infectious, or other cellular stress; some also influence immunity and cancer biology.

name: Heberden's node
clinical_significance: A hard, bony enlargement of the distal interphalangeal joint caused by osteoarthritis, usually affecting the fingers and sometimes producing pain, stiffness, or reduced dexterity.

name: hedgehog proteins
clinical_significance: Signaling proteins that help guide the growth and organization of tissues before birth and during repair. Abnormal activity in this pathway can contribute to some birth differences and cancers.

name: heel spur
clinical_significance: A bony projection from the heel bone seen on imaging, often alongside plantar fasciopathy. Many heel spurs cause no symptoms, and heel pain is usually related to the surrounding soft tissues rather than the spur itself.

name: height
clinical_significance: The vertical distance from the base of a person to the top of the head, measured for growth assessment, nutritional evaluation, drug dosing, and calculation of body-mass index.

name: Heinz bodies
clinical_significance: Clumps of damaged hemoglobin inside red blood cells, usually formed after oxidative injury. They may occur in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency or after exposure to certain medicines, chemicals, or infections.

name: hela cell
clinical_significance: A continuously growing human cervical-cancer cell line used worldwide in biomedical research, including studies of cancer, infection, and medicines. It is a laboratory model, not a diagnostic test or treatment; its history also raises lasting questions about consent, privacy, and responsible use of human tissue.

name: helcococcus
clinical_significance: A genus of gram-positive cocci that can rarely cause opportunistic skin, wound, bone, or bloodstream infections.

name: helcococcus kunzii
clinical_significance: A Gram-positive round bacterium usually found on skin that rarely causes opportunistic infection. Reported infections may involve wounds, blood, or implanted devices in people with serious illness or weakened defenses.

name: helcococcus pyogenes
clinical_significance: A rarely encountered Gram-positive round bacterium that may cause opportunistic human infection. It has been found in wounds or blood, particularly in people with serious illness, chronic wounds, or weakened immunity.

name: helcococcus sueciensis
clinical_significance: A very rarely reported Helcococcus species isolated from human wounds and blood. It may act as an opportunistic pathogen, but its significance should be judged by the specimen source, symptoms, and repeat culture because clinical experience is limited.

name: helicase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that uses cellular energy to separate the paired strands of DNA or RNA. This allows genetic material to be copied, repaired, or read.

name: helicobacter
clinical_significance: A genus of spiral-shaped bacteria that colonize the stomach or intestine; some species cause ulcers, gastritis, or other disease.

name: helicobacter cinaedi
clinical_significance: A Helicobacter species that can cause bloodstream, skin, bone, joint, or other invasive infections, especially in people with weakened immunity.

name: helicobacter felis
clinical_significance: A gastric bacterium commonly found in cats and dogs and occasionally associated with human gastritis or ulcer disease. Some non-pylori Helicobacter infections may be animal-associated, but the exact transmission risk is uncertain; species-level identification is useful in unusual cases.

name: helicobacter fennelliae
clinical_significance: An intestinal Helicobacter species that rarely causes bloodstream or other opportunistic infection. Disease is more likely in people with weakened defenses, and diagnosis requires specialized laboratory identification.

name: helicobacter mustelae
clinical_significance: A gastric bacterium common in ferrets that can cause chronic gastritis and stomach ulcers in that species. It is used as an animal model for Helicobacter-associated disease and is not a recognized common human pathogen.

name: helicobacter pylori
clinical_significance: A stomach-colonizing bacterium that can cause chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, and gastric cancer, including MALT lymphoma. Testing and eradication treatment are important in selected patients; antibiotic resistance affects regimen choice, and successful eradication can lower later stomach-cancer risk.

name: helicobacter rappini
clinical_significance: An animal-associated, spiral-shaped bacterium reported rarely in human bloodstream and other infections, including in people with weakened immunity. Older isolates called “H. rappini” may represent more than one taxon, so modern identification and clinical context are important.

name: helicobacteraceae
clinical_significance: A family of spiral-shaped bacteria that includes Helicobacter and related genera, many of which inhabit the digestive tract.

name: helium
clinical_significance: A chemically inert gas used in respiratory mixtures, cryogenics, imaging, and laboratory applications; inhalation can displace oxygen and cause hypoxia despite its lack of direct toxicity.

name: heller myotomy
clinical_significance: A surgical procedure that cuts the muscles of the lower esophageal sphincter to relieve obstruction in achalasia, usually performed laparoscopically and often combined with an antireflux procedure.

name: HELLP syndrome
clinical_significance: A pregnancy-associated syndrome named for hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count. It is a form of microangiopathic disease that may occur with preeclampsia and can involve upper-abdominal pain, nausea, headache, or high blood pressure.

name: helminth
clinical_significance: A parasitic worm, including roundworms, tapeworms, and flukes, that may live in or on a host.

name: helminthiasis
clinical_significance: Infection or infestation caused by parasitic worms, including roundworms, tapeworms, and flukes. Symptoms vary by species and may include abdominal problems, anemia, cough, rash, malnutrition, or organ damage.

name: helper virus
clinical_significance: A virus that supplies functions needed for another virus or defective viral genome to replicate.

name: hemagglutination test
clinical_significance: A test in which antibodies or other agents cause red blood cells to clump; the reaction can help detect antibodies, antigens, or selected infectious agents.

name: hemagglutinin
clinical_significance: A surface glycoprotein, especially on influenza viruses, that binds sialic-acid receptors and helps the virus attach to and enter host cells; it is a major target of protective antibodies.

name: hemangioblastoma
clinical_significance: A usually slow-growing tumor made of blood-vessel-forming cells, most often found in the cerebellum or spinal cord. It may cause headache, balance problems, or weakness and can be associated with von Hippel–Lindau disease.

name: hemangioendothelioma
clinical_significance: A rare tumor arising from cells that line blood vessels. Its behavior ranges from slow-growing to cancerous, depending on the subtype and location, so diagnosis requires tissue examination and specialist assessment.

name: hemangioma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous growth made of blood vessels. It may be present at birth or appear during infancy, and can be a small skin mark or a deeper mass. Some become smaller over time; others can cause bleeding, ulceration, or pressure on nearby structures.

name: hemangiopericytoma
clinical_significance: A rare tumor formerly defined by branching “staghorn” vessels and perivascular cells; many lesions classified this way are now recognized as solitary fibrous tumors.

name: Hemangiosarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare, aggressive cancer of blood-vessel lining cells that can arise in the skin or internal organs such as the liver, spleen, or heart. It may grow quickly, bleed, or spread early; diagnosis requires biopsy and treatment is planned by a sarcoma team.

name: hemarthrosis
clinical_significance: Bleeding into a joint, most often the knee, causing rapid swelling, warmth, pain, and limited movement. Injury and bleeding disorders such as hemophilia are common causes; repeated episodes can damage cartilage and lead to long-term joint disease.

name: hematemesis
clinical_significance: Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, usually from bleeding in the esophagus, stomach, or first part of the small intestine. It can be life-threatening.

name: hematochezia
clinical_significance: Passing bright-red or maroon blood from the rectum. It often comes from the large intestine, rectum, or anus, but heavy bleeding higher in the digestive tract can look the same.

name: hematocolpos
clinical_significance: Accumulation of menstrual blood in the vagina, usually because an imperforate hymen or another obstructing anomaly prevents outflow; it may cause cyclic pelvic pain and a bulging vaginal membrane.

name: hematocrit
clinical_significance: The proportion of blood volume occupied by packed red blood cells, expressed as a percentage. One of the most commonly ordered laboratory tests in clinical medicine.

name: hematogenous
clinical_significance: Spread through the bloodstream, as when infection, tumor cells, or embolic material travels from one body site to another.

name: hematologic agents
clinical_significance: Medicines or biologic therapies that act on blood cells, coagulation, marrow, or immune pathways, including agents used for anemia, thrombosis, leukemia, and lymphoma.

name: hematologic response
clinical_significance: A measurable improvement or change in blood counts or marrow findings after treatment, such as recovery of neutrophils, platelets, or hemoglobin or reduction of malignant cells.

name: Hematological Disease
clinical_significance: A disorder of blood cells, bone marrow, lymphatic tissue, or coagulation, including anemia, leukemia, lymphoma, bleeding disorders, and clotting disorders.

name: hematologist
clinical_significance: A physician who diagnoses and treats disorders of blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, clotting, and hematologic cancers.

name: hematology
clinical_significance: The medical specialty focused on disorders of blood cells, bone marrow, lymph nodes, clotting, and bleeding. Hematologists also manage blood cancers and coordinate specialized testing, transfusion, and treatment.

name: hematoma
clinical_significance: A collection of blood outside a blood vessel, usually after injury, surgery, or bleeding caused by illness or medicines. It may cause swelling and pain and can press on nearby nerves or organs.

name: hematopoiesis
clinical_significance: The process of making and maturing blood cells, mainly in the bone marrow. It produces red blood cells for oxygen transport, white blood cells for immune defense, and platelets for stopping bleeding.

name: hematopoietic growth factor
clinical_significance: A cytokine or medicine that stimulates production, maturation, or survival of blood-forming cells in bone marrow, such as erythropoietin or granulocyte colony-stimulating factor.

name: hematopoietic neoplasm
clinical_significance: A cancer arising from blood-forming cells in the bone marrow or immune tissues. Leukemias, lymphomas, and plasma-cell cancers are examples; symptoms and treatment depend on the exact cell type and extent.

name: hematopoietic system
clinical_significance: The bone marrow and related organs and cells that produce, mature, circulate, and remove blood cells, including red cells, white cells, and platelets.

name: hematoporphyrin derivative
clinical_significance: A porphyrin-based photosensitizer that accumulates in some tumors and can be activated by light in photodynamic treatment; it may also cause prolonged photosensitivity.

name: hematosalpinx
clinical_significance: Accumulation of blood within a fallopian tube, often caused by ectopic pregnancy, endometriosis, pelvic surgery, or obstruction, and potentially producing pelvic pain or infertility.

name: hematoxylin
clinical_significance: A dye used in histology, usually with eosin, to stain cell nuclei blue-purple and help show tissue structure.

name: hematuria
clinical_significance: Blood in urine may be visible or detectable only under a microscope and can result from infection, stones, injury, kidney disease, medicines, or urinary-tract tumors. Visible blood or persistent microscopic hematuria needs medical evaluation even if it is painless, because serious causes must be excluded.

name: heme
clinical_significance: Heme is an iron-containing porphyrin group that binds oxygen in haemoglobin and myoglobin and forms the functional centre of several enzymes; abnormal heme metabolism contributes to porphyrias and jaundice.

name: hemerythrin
clinical_significance: An iron-containing oxygen-transport protein found in some marine invertebrates, including certain worms and brachiopods. It is studied in comparative biology and as a possible research basis for artificial oxygen carriers, but has no established clinical use.

name: hemianopsia
clinical_significance: Loss of vision in half of the visual field of one or both eyes, usually from a lesion of the optic tract, radiations, or occipital cortex; sudden onset may indicate stroke.

name: hemidesmosome
clinical_significance: A specialized junction that anchors basal epithelial cells to the underlying basement membrane by linking intracellular keratin filaments with extracellular matrix proteins.

name: hemifacial atrophy
clinical_significance: Progressive wasting of skin, subcutaneous tissue, muscle, and sometimes bone on one side of the face, also called Parry--Romberg syndrome.

name: hemifacial spasm
clinical_significance: Repeated involuntary twitching on one side of the face, usually beginning around the eye and sometimes spreading to the cheek or mouth. Irritation of the facial nerve is a common cause; persistent spasms need evaluation.

name: hemihypertrophy
clinical_significance: Unequal overgrowth of one side or region of the body, producing asymmetry of limbs, trunk, or face; some childhood cases carry increased risk of embryonal tumors.

name: hemilaryngectomy
clinical_significance: Hemilaryngectomy is surgery to remove part of the larynx, usually to treat a selected laryngeal cancer while preserving as much speech and swallowing function as possible.

name: hemimandibulectomy
clinical_significance: Hemimandibulectomy is surgery to remove one side of the lower jaw, usually for a tumor or severe bone disease, sometimes followed by reconstruction.

name: hemimegalencephaly
clinical_significance: A rare developmental brain malformation in which one cerebral hemisphere is abnormally enlarged and dysplastic, often causing infantile seizures, developmental impairment, and contralateral neurologic signs.

name: hemimelia
clinical_significance: A congenital limb-reduction defect in which part or all of a limb segment is absent, such as fibular or radial hemimelia.

name: hemiparesis
clinical_significance: Weakness on one side of the body, affecting the face, arm, leg, or a combination. It is less severe than paralysis and may result from stroke, brain injury, a tumor, multiple sclerosis, or another nervous-system disorder.

name: hemipelvectomy
clinical_significance: Hemipelvectomy is major surgery that removes part or all of one side of the pelvis, with or without removal of the leg, usually for extensive cancer or severe trauma.

name: hemiplegia
clinical_significance: Complete or near-complete paralysis of one side of the body, including the face, arm, or leg. It usually results from injury to movement pathways in the brain, commonly a stroke; sudden onset can occur with a serious brain disorder.

name: hemispherectomy
clinical_significance: Hemispherectomy is surgery that removes or disconnects much of one cerebral hemisphere to treat severe, otherwise uncontrolled epilepsy in selected patients.

name: hemisternebra
clinical_significance: A congenital or developmental partial segment of the sternum, caused by incomplete formation or fusion of sternal elements and sometimes associated with chest-wall anomalies.

name: hemivertebrae
clinical_significance: Congenital vertebrae formed from only part of the normal vertebral body, producing wedge-shaped bone and potentially causing congenital scoliosis or spinal-cord abnormalities.

name: hemochromatosis
clinical_significance: A disorder in which too much iron builds up in the body and can damage the liver, pancreas, heart, joints, skin, and hormone-producing organs. The common HFE-related form is usually autosomal recessive; other inherited forms can have different patterns, and iron overload can also develop from another illness or repeated transfusions.

name: hemocyanin
clinical_significance: A copper-containing oxygen-transport protein in many mollusks and arthropods; unlike human hemoglobin, it circulates dissolved in their hemolymph.

name: hemocytometer
clinical_significance: A ruled counting chamber used with a microscope to determine the concentration of cells or other particles in a measured volume of fluid.

name: hemodialysis
clinical_significance: A treatment for kidney failure in which blood passes through a filter outside the body to remove waste and extra fluid before returning to the person. It usually requires repeated sessions and a blood-vessel access; low blood pressure, infection, clotting, and access problems can occur.

name: hemodialysis clearance
clinical_significance: The volume of plasma from which hemodialysis removes a solute per unit time; it depends on blood and dialysate flow, membrane properties, treatment time, and the substance’s distribution.

name: hemodialysis solution
clinical_significance: The dialysate fluid circulated across a semipermeable membrane during hemodialysis to remove waste and help correct electrolyte, acid--base, and fluid abnormalities.

name: hemodynamics
clinical_significance: The movement of blood through the heart and blood vessels, including pressure, flow, heart output, and resistance. Hemodynamic measurements help assess circulation and guide treatment in conditions such as shock, heart failure, and critical illness.

name: hemofiltration
clinical_significance: A blood-cleaning treatment that removes extra water and dissolved waste through a filter. Replacement fluid is added to maintain the right blood volume; it is used in some forms of temporary or long-term kidney support.

name: hemoglobin
clinical_significance: The iron-containing protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to tissues and helps carry carbon dioxide back to the lungs. Low or abnormal hemoglobin can cause anemia or other blood disorders.

name: hemoglobin A
clinical_significance: The main type of hemoglobin in most adults. It is the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells and is made from two alpha and two beta protein parts.

name: hemoglobin C
clinical_significance: A beta-globin variant caused by a hemoglobin gene mutation; homozygosity can cause mild hemolytic anemia and splenomegaly, while inheritance with hemoglobin S causes a clinically significant sickling disorder.

name: hemoglobin H
clinical_significance: An unusual form of hemoglobin made from four beta protein parts when the body makes too little alpha hemoglobin. It is unstable and can cause ongoing breakdown of red blood cells in alpha-thalassemia.

name: hemoglobin increased
clinical_significance: An increased hemoglobin concentration, which may reflect dehydration, chronic hypoxemia, erythrocytosis, or a myeloproliferative neoplasm and must be interpreted with hematocrit and clinical context.

name: hemoglobin M
clinical_significance: A group of abnormal hemoglobins that stabilize iron in the ferric state and can cause congenital methemoglobinemia and cyanosis.

name: hemoglobin S
clinical_significance: An inherited form of hemoglobin that can make red blood cells become stiff and sickle-shaped when oxygen is low. It can cause anemia, painful blockages, and organ damage in sickle-cell disease.

name: hemoglobin trait
clinical_significance: The inherited presence of a hemoglobin variant in a heterozygous state, usually causing no symptoms but potentially affecting screening results or reproductive risk.

name: hemoglobinopathy
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder affecting the structure or production of hemoglobin. Examples include sickle-cell disease and thalassemia; effects range from no symptoms to anemia, painful blood-vessel blockages, and organ damage.

name: hemoglobinuria
clinical_significance: Haemoglobinuria is free haemoglobin in urine, usually from intravascular haemolysis; urine may be dipstick-positive for blood with few or no red cells, and causes include transfusion reactions, malaria, and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

name: hemolymph
clinical_significance: The circulatory fluid in many invertebrates, including insects and mollusks, that bathes organs and carries nutrients, wastes, immune cells, and sometimes oxygen. It has no direct human clinical role but is important in veterinary, ecological, and laboratory biology.

name: hemolysin
clinical_significance: A toxin or immune substance that damages the outer covering of red blood cells and makes them break open. Some bacteria produce hemolysins, and the resulting destruction of red cells is called hemolysis.

name: hemolysis
clinical_significance: The early destruction of red blood cells, releasing hemoglobin into the blood. It can occur in the bloodstream or in the spleen and liver and may cause anemia, jaundice, dark urine, tiredness, or shortness of breath.

name: hemolytic anemia
clinical_significance: Anemia caused by red blood cells being destroyed faster than the body can replace them. It may result from an inherited cell problem, an immune reaction, infection, medicine, toxin, or another illness and can cause jaundice and dark urine.

name: hemolytic index
clinical_significance: A laboratory-quality indicator estimating hemolysis in a blood specimen; substantial in-vitro hemolysis can interfere with measurement of several analytes.

name: Hemolytic-Uremic syndrome
clinical_significance: A serious illness in which small blood-vessel clots destroy red blood cells, lower the platelet count, and injure the kidneys. It often follows severe diarrhea caused by certain bacteria, but inherited immune problems and other triggers can also cause it.

name: hemopericardium
clinical_significance: Accumulation of blood in the pericardial sac around the heart. If pressure rises and prevents the heart from filling, cardiac tamponade can occur.

name: hemoperitoneum
clinical_significance: Blood collecting inside the abdominal cavity, usually from trauma, a ruptured blood vessel or organ, surgery, or a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. It can cause abdominal pain, distention, dizziness, or shock and may require emergency imaging and surgery or another procedure.

name: hemopexin
clinical_significance: A plasma glycoprotein that binds free heme and transports it to the liver, helping limit oxidative injury during hemolysis.

name: hemophilia
clinical_significance: A bleeding disorder caused by low or ineffective clotting factor VIII (A) or factor IX (B), most often inherited but sometimes acquired from an antibody against a clotting factor. Bleeding into joints and muscles can cause lasting damage; preventive treatment and rapid care for serious bleeds are important. Women and girls may also have low factor levels and symptoms, and family testing can guide care.

name: hemophilia A
clinical_significance: An X-linked recessive deficiency of coagulation factor VIII, causing prolonged bleeding into joints, muscles, and soft tissues. Severity correlates with factor VIII activity levels.

name: hemophilia B
clinical_significance: An X-linked recessive deficiency of coagulation factor IX (Christmas disease), causing prolonged bleeding similar to hemophilia A. Severity correlates with factor IX activity levels.

name: hemophilus
clinical_significance: An older spelling or variant of Haemophilus, a group of small gram-negative bacteria that includes respiratory and genital pathogens.

name: hemophilus ducreyi
clinical_significance: A gram-negative bacterium that causes chancroid, a sexually transmitted infection with painful genital ulcers and tender lymph nodes.

name: hemopoietic tissue
clinical_significance: Tissue that produces blood cells, chiefly bone marrow, containing stem cells and supporting cells that generate erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets.

name: hemoprotein
clinical_significance: A protein containing a heme group with an iron atom, such as hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes, and many oxidoreductive enzymes.

name: hemoptysis
clinical_significance: Coughing up blood or blood-stained mucus from the airways or lungs. Causes include infection, irritated or widened airways, a blood clot, or cancer. Larger amounts may occur with breathlessness or chest pain.

name: hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Abnormal escape of blood from a damaged blood vessel or, less commonly, from the heart. It may be external or internal, acute or chronic, and range from minor bleeding to life-threatening blood loss causing anemia, shock, or organ compression; the cause and site determine management.

name: hemorrhagic disorder
clinical_significance: A condition that causes abnormal bleeding because of platelet number or function, clotting-factor deficiency, excessive fibrinolysis, or blood-vessel fragility.

name: hemorrhagic shock
clinical_significance: Life-threatening loss of circulating blood volume that prevents organs from receiving enough oxygen. It can cause confusion, pale clammy skin, rapid breathing, a weak fast pulse, and collapse; control of bleeding and urgent resuscitation are essential.

name: hemorrhoid
clinical_significance: Hemorrhoids can cause anal itching, discomfort, or bright-red bleeding; persistent bleeding or a change in bowel habits should not be assumed to be hemorrhoids without evaluation.

name: hemorrhoidal hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Rectal bleeding from enlarged or injured hemorrhoidal vessels, usually bright red and associated with defecation; heavy, persistent, painful, or unexplained bleeding requires evaluation for other causes.

name: hemosiderosis
clinical_significance: Excess deposition of hemosiderin, an iron-storage pigment, in tissues. It may follow repeated bleeding or transfusions and can affect organs such as the lungs or liver.

name: hemospermia
clinical_significance: The presence of blood in semen, usually caused by inflammation or infection of the genitourinary tract and often self-limited, but persistent or recurrent cases require evaluation.

name: hemostasis
clinical_significance: The body’s process for stopping bleeding after a blood vessel is injured. Blood vessels narrow, platelets form a plug, and clotting proteins strengthen it; later, the body removes the clot as healing occurs.

name: hemostasis valve
clinical_significance: A valve or sealing device used with an intravascular catheter or sheath to limit blood loss while allowing passage of wires or instruments.

name: hemostatic agent
clinical_significance: A medicine or material used to stop or reduce bleeding. It may form a physical seal, help the blood clot, slow clot breakdown, or replace a missing clotting protein.

name: hemothorax
clinical_significance: Blood collecting in the space between the lung and chest wall, usually after injury or surgery. It can cause chest pain, breathlessness, low blood pressure, and reduced breath sounds and often requires urgent drainage and treatment of the bleeding source.

name: hempa
clinical_significance: Hexamethylphosphoramide (HMPA), an industrial and laboratory solvent. It can irritate the eyes, skin, and airways and is treated as a potential occupational carcinogen based on animal evidence; exposure by inhalation or skin absorption should be minimized.

name: henipavirus
clinical_significance: A genus of paramyxoviruses that includes Nipah and Hendra viruses, which can cause severe encephalitis and respiratory disease.

name: hepadnaviridae
clinical_significance: A family of DNA viruses that includes hepatitis B virus and related animal viruses. Human hepatitis B can become chronic and lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer, but vaccination is highly effective at prevention.

name: heparan sulfate
clinical_significance: A sulfated glycosaminoglycan in cell surfaces and extracellular matrix that binds growth factors, regulates signaling, and contributes to filtration-barrier and connective-tissue structure.

name: heparin
clinical_significance: An anticoagulant medicine that reduces blood clotting by enhancing antithrombin activity. It may be given by injection to prevent or treat blood clots.

name: heparin binding
clinical_significance: The attachment of a protein or other molecule to heparin, a highly charged substance related to blood clotting. Binding can alter the molecule’s activity, movement, or laboratory measurement.

name: heparin lyase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that cleaves heparin and related sugar chains. It is used mainly in laboratory research and biochemical analysis; enzyme preparations are not routine clinical treatments.

name: hepatectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove part or, rarely, nearly all of the liver, usually to treat a tumor or severe localized liver disease. The remaining liver must be large and healthy enough to work. Bleeding, bile leakage, infection, and liver failure are important risks.

name: hepatic
clinical_significance: Relating to the liver. The liver processes nutrients and medicines, makes bile and important blood proteins, stores energy, and helps remove harmful substances; hepatic disease can affect one or several of these functions.

name: hepatic artery
clinical_significance: The main artery supplying oxygen-rich blood to the liver. It divides into branches that deliver blood to the right and left parts of the organ.

name: hepatic fissure
clinical_significance: A natural groove or cleft on the liver's surface. It separates parts of the liver and may contain or provide a route for blood vessels, bile ducts, or supporting ligaments.

name: hepatic lamina
clinical_significance: A sheet of cells in a developing embryo that contributes to the liver and its bile ducts.

name: hepatic necrosis
clinical_significance: Death of liver cells caused by severe ischemia, toxins, viral infection, autoimmune injury, or other insults; extensive necrosis can produce acute liver failure.

name: hepatitis
clinical_significance: Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver caused by viruses, alcohol, medications, toxins, metabolic disease, or autoimmunity and may be acute or chronic.

name: hepatitis A
clinical_significance: A short-term liver infection caused by hepatitis A virus. It spreads when virus from infected stool is swallowed, often through close contact or contaminated food or water. It may cause fever, tiredness, nausea, abdominal discomfort, or jaundice. Most people recover completely; chronic infection is not expected. Vaccination helps prevent it.

name: hepatitis A virus
clinical_significance: The virus that causes hepatitis A. It spreads when virus from infected stool is swallowed, commonly through contaminated food, water, or close contact. It causes a short-term liver infection that may produce fever, nausea, tiredness, dark urine, pale stools, or jaundice; vaccination helps prevent it.

name: hepatitis B
clinical_significance: A liver infection caused by hepatitis B virus (HBV). It spreads when infected blood, semen, or certain other body fluids enter another person's body, including through sex, shared needles or equipment, or from an infected parent to a baby around birth. Infection may be acute or chronic; many people have no symptoms. When symptoms occur, they may include tiredness, fever, loss of appetite, nausea, abdominal or joint pain, dark urine, pale stools, or jaundice. Chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer. Vaccination prevents infection.

name: hepatitis B virus
clinical_significance: The virus that causes hepatitis B. HBV spreads when infected blood, semen, or certain other body fluids enter another person’s body, including through sex, shared needles or equipment, or around childbirth. It can cause acute (short-term) or chronic (long-term) liver infection. Chronic infection can cause liver damage, cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer. Vaccination prevents hepatitis B.

name: hepatitis C
clinical_significance: A liver infection caused by hepatitis C virus (HCV), spread mainly through infected blood, especially by sharing injection equipment. Acute infection often has no symptoms; some people clear the virus without treatment, while many develop chronic infection that can cause cirrhosis or liver cancer. Modern antiviral treatment cures most people. Testing is important because infection can remain silent for years; no vaccine is available.

name: hepatitis c virus
clinical_significance: The virus that causes hepatitis C. HCV spreads mainly when infected blood enters another person's body, especially through shared needles or other injection equipment; it can also spread through some medical exposures, from an infected parent to a baby, or less often through sex. Many people have no symptoms. Infection may be acute or become chronic, which can cause cirrhosis or liver cancer. Modern antiviral medicines cure more than 95% of treated people; no vaccine is available.

name: hepatitis D virus
clinical_significance: A virus that can multiply only when hepatitis B virus is also present. It spreads through infected blood or body fluids and can make hepatitis B more severe, increasing the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer. Hepatitis B vaccination also prevents hepatitis D.

name: hepatitis e virus
clinical_significance: The virus that causes hepatitis E. HEV usually spreads through water or food contaminated with stool and can also spread through undercooked meat from infected animals. It commonly causes short-term liver infection, but it may cause severe illness during pregnancy and can occasionally become chronic in people with weakened immune systems. No vaccine is available in the United States.

name: hepatitis G virus
clinical_significance: A virus also called GB virus C. Despite the historical name, infection has not been established as a cause of hepatitis or other human disease. It may persist in the blood and is mainly of interest in virology and research.

name: hepatitis virus
clinical_significance: A group of viruses that infect the liver and cause hepatitis. The main human hepatitis viruses are A, B, C, D, and E; they differ in transmission, likelihood of chronic infection, and prevention. Vaccines prevent hepatitis A and B, and hepatitis B vaccination also prevents hepatitis D. No vaccine is available for hepatitis C. Chronic hepatitis B or C can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer; hepatitis E can be especially severe during pregnancy.

name: hepatobiliary system
clinical_significance: The liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts. The liver makes and secretes bile, the gallbladder stores and concentrates it, and the bile ducts carry it to the small intestine, where it helps digest fats and carry some waste products out of the liver. The liver also processes nutrients and many medicines and toxins.

name: hepatoblastoma
clinical_significance: A rare cancer that begins in the liver and is the most common type of liver cancer in children, usually diagnosed before age 3. It may cause abdominal swelling or pain, poor appetite, nausea, vomiting, or weight loss, though early tumors may cause no symptoms. Evaluation commonly includes imaging and blood tests such as alpha-fetoprotein (AFP); biopsy may be used when needed to confirm the diagnosis. Prompt assessment by a pediatric liver cancer team is important because treatment often combines chemotherapy and surgery, with transplantation considered for selected tumors.

name: hepatocellular adenoma
clinical_significance: A rare, usually noncancerous tumor made of mature liver cells. It occurs most often in women of reproductive age and is associated with estrogen exposure, although it can also occur with anabolic steroid use, certain inherited metabolic diseases, or without a known cause. It is often found by chance on imaging and may cause no symptoms. Larger tumors can bleed or rupture, and a small number can change into liver cancer, especially certain subtypes.

name: hepatocellular carcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer that begins in liver cells called hepatocytes and is the most common primary liver cancer in adults. It often develops with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B or C, but can occur without a known risk factor. Early disease may cause no symptoms; later signs can include pain or a lump in the upper-right abdomen, abdominal swelling, jaundice, tiredness, poor appetite, or unexplained weight loss. New or worsening symptoms in someone with chronic liver disease need medical assessment; diagnosis and treatment depend on tumor extent and liver function.

name: hepatocyte
clinical_significance: The main working cell of the liver. Hepatocytes process carbohydrates, fats, proteins, medicines, and other substances from the blood. They make bile, albumin, clotting factors, and other blood proteins; store energy as glycogen; change ammonia into urea; and help remove or break down harmful substances. Injury to hepatocytes can reduce these functions and raise liver enzymes in the blood.

name: hepatodiaphragmatic nodule
clinical_significance: A congenital protrusion of part of the liver's median lobe beneath the diaphragm, described mainly in rats and occasionally in mice in toxicologic pathology. The tissue retains normal liver architecture and is generally a sporadic background finding unaffected by treatment; it is recorded in animal pathology studies and is not a recognized human clinical condition.

name: hepatolenticular degeneration
clinical_significance: Another name for Wilson disease, a rare inherited disorder caused by changes in the ATP7B gene. The liver cannot remove excess copper into bile, so copper accumulates and can injure the liver, brain, eyes, kidneys, and other tissues. Manifestations include hepatitis, cirrhosis or liver failure, movement or mood changes, and Kayser–Fleischer rings around the cornea. It is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Early diagnosis and lifelong copper-lowering treatment can prevent or limit organ damage.

name: hepatomegaly
clinical_significance: An enlarged liver, detected on examination or imaging. It is a finding rather than a disease and may result from hepatitis, fatty or alcohol-related liver disease, heart-related congestion, bile-duct obstruction, storage or infiltrative disorders, or cancer. It may cause no symptoms, or abdominal discomfort or fullness. Evaluation is guided by symptoms, examination, blood tests, and imaging to identify the cause; sudden enlargement with severe pain or jaundice needs prompt medical assessment.

name: Hepatorenal syndrome
clinical_significance: Serious kidney dysfunction that occurs mainly in advanced cirrhosis, often with portal hypertension and ascites. Circulatory changes reduce effective blood flow to the kidneys, impairing filtration even when there is no primary structural kidney disease. It may present as rapidly developing acute kidney injury (HRS-AKI) or slower kidney dysfunction. It is a life-threatening complication that requires urgent hospital evaluation, as other causes of kidney injury must be excluded and treatment is time-sensitive.

name: hepatosplenomegaly
clinical_significance: Enlargement of both the liver and spleen, a finding rather than a disease. Causes include infections, chronic liver disease with portal hypertension, blood-cell disorders, blood cancers, and inherited storage or metabolic diseases. It may cause abdominal fullness or no symptoms; other signs depend on the cause. Evaluation commonly includes examination, blood tests, and imaging to identify the underlying condition; treatment is directed at that cause.

name: hepatovirus
clinical_significance: A genus in the Picornaviridae family of small RNA viruses. Its best-known human member is hepatitis A virus (HAV), which causes hepatitis A and usually spreads by the fecal--oral route, when virus from stool reaches the mouth through contaminated food, water, hands, or close contact. Other hepatoviruses infect different animal hosts and are not established causes of human disease.

name: hepcidin
clinical_significance: A peptide hormone made mainly by liver cells and the main regulator of iron balance. When iron stores are high or inflammation is present, hepcidin binds to ferroportin, the protein that exports iron from intestinal cells, macrophages, and liver cells. Ferroportin is then removed, reducing iron absorption from food and the release of recycled or stored iron into the blood. When iron is low or the bone marrow needs more iron to make red blood cells, hepcidin levels usually fall.

name: herbal supplement
clinical_significance: A concentrated plant-derived product marketed for health or symptom relief; composition and evidence vary, and contamination, drug interactions, liver injury, and pregnancy risks must be considered.

name: herbaspirillum
clinical_significance: A genus of gram-negative bacteria found in soil and plants; human infection is rare but can occur opportunistically.

name: herbaspirillum huttiense
clinical_significance: A rare gram-negative bacterium found in water and plant-associated environments. It is an uncommon opportunistic cause of bloodstream or respiratory infection, reported especially in people with serious underlying illness or weakened immunity; accurate laboratory identification can be important because it may be mistaken for other nonfermenting bacteria.

name: herbicide
clinical_significance: A chemical used to kill or control unwanted plants; exposure can irritate skin, eyes, lungs, or the gastrointestinal tract, with toxicity determined by the specific compound and dose.

name: herd immunity
clinical_significance: Protection that occurs when enough people in a community are immune to an infection that it spreads less easily. The proportion needed varies widely by infection, and herd immunity does not protect everyone equally.

name: hereditary
clinical_significance: Transmitted through genetic material from a parent or arising from an inherited variant; a hereditary trait may be dominant, recessive, X-linked, mitochondrial, or multifactorial.

name: hereditary angioedema
clinical_significance: An inherited, usually autosomal dominant and bradykinin-mediated disorder causing repeated episodes of swelling in the skin, hands, feet, stomach or bowel wall, or throat. Types 1 and 2 commonly result from deficiency or dysfunction of C1 inhibitor, often due to variants in the \textit{SERPING1} gene; other forms may have normal C1-inhibitor levels. Attacks may cause severe abdominal pain or swelling that narrows the upper airway and often occur without itchy hives.

name: hereditary coproporphyria
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder of a chemical pathway used to make heme, the oxygen-carrying part of hemoglobin. Attacks may cause severe abdominal pain, vomiting, nerve or mental symptoms, and sometimes blistering skin after sunlight exposure.

name: hereditary elliptocytosis
clinical_significance: An inherited red-cell membrane disorder in which erythrocytes are elliptical on the blood smear; most people are asymptomatic, but hemolytic anemia can occur in severe forms.

name: hereditary hyperbilirubinemia
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder of bilirubin production, conjugation, or excretion that causes persistent or intermittent jaundice, such as Gilbert, Crigler--Najjar, Dubin--Johnson, or Rotor syndrome.

name: hereditary spherocytosis
clinical_significance: Usually an autosomal dominant inherited blood disorder in which red blood cells are round rather than disc-shaped and are broken down too quickly, mainly in the spleen; less often it is autosomal recessive. It may cause anemia, jaundice, gallstones, and an enlarged spleen.

name: Hermanski-Pudlak syndrome
clinical_significance: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome can cause albinism, bleeding due to platelet dysfunction, and sometimes lung or bowel disease; recognition supports bleeding precautions and organ monitoring.

name: hermaphroditism
clinical_significance: An outdated term historically applied to variations in sex development. It is generally avoided in current human clinical care because it is inaccurate and can be stigmatizing. Use the specific diagnosis or a person's preferred term; ovotesticular difference of sex development is the specific diagnosis when both ovarian and testicular tissue are present.

name: hernia
clinical_significance: A bulge formed when an organ or tissue pushes through a weak area in the muscle or connective tissue that normally holds it in place. Hernias commonly occur in the abdominal wall and may become trapped or lose their blood supply, causing severe pain.

name: herniorrhaphy
clinical_significance: An operation to repair a hernia, in which tissue or an organ has pushed through a weak area in the body wall. The surgeon returns the tissue and closes or reinforces the weakness, sometimes with mesh; recurrence, pain, infection, or injury to nearby structures are possible.

name: heroin
clinical_significance: A highly addictive opioid that is converted to morphine in the body. Repeated use can cause opioid dependence, tolerance, and withdrawal; excessive exposure can cause opioid overdose with respiratory depression, coma, and death.

name: heroin dependence
clinical_significance: A pattern of compulsive heroin use despite harm, with tolerance, withdrawal, or both; it is now generally described clinically as opioid use disorder. It increases the risk of fatal overdose, especially after reduced tolerance or when combined with alcohol or sedatives. Effective treatment includes medications such as buprenorphine or methadone with supportive care; naloxone can reverse an opioid overdose.

name: herpes encephalitis
clinical_significance: A life-threatening inflammation of the brain, most often caused by herpes simplex virus. It can cause fever, confusion, seizures, or focal neurologic problems and may lead to brain injury or death without prompt treatment. Suspected cases require emergency hospital evaluation and intravenous antiviral treatment.

name: herpes labialis
clinical_significance: Herpes labialis causes recurrent painful oral blisters and can spread through direct contact; eye involvement, widespread lesions, or immunosuppression increases concern.

name: herpesviridae
clinical_significance: A family of DNA viruses that can remain inactive in the body after infection and reactivate later. Human members include herpes simplex viruses, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein--Barr virus, and human herpesviruses 6, 7, and 8. They can cause skin or mouth lesions, chickenpox, shingles, glandular fever, congenital infection, or disease in people with weakened immunity.

name: herpesviridae infection
clinical_significance: An infection caused by a herpesvirus; symptoms range from localized lesions to serious disease in newborns or people with weakened immunity.

name: herpesvirus saimiri
clinical_significance: A herpesvirus of squirrel monkeys used as a research model because it can transform T cells in experimental settings. It is not known to cause disease in its natural primate host and is not an established cause of human disease.

name: hesperidin
clinical_significance: A flavonoid found in citrus fruits and also sold in supplements. It has been studied for vascular and antioxidant effects, but evidence does not establish it as a treatment for a disease; supplement products may interact with medicines and vary in composition.

name: heterochromatin
clinical_significance: DNA that is tightly packed inside a cell’s nucleus and is usually less active in making proteins. It helps organize chromosomes and control which genes are available for use.

name: heterocyclic amine
clinical_significance: A nitrogen-containing chemical compound formed mainly when meat or fish is cooked at high temperatures; several heterocyclic amines are mutagens and potential dietary carcinogens.

name: heterocyclic compound
clinical_significance: A broad class of compounds whose ring structure contains at least one atom other than carbon, commonly nitrogen, oxygen, or sulfur. Many are important in medicines and natural products; toxic effects depend on the specific compound, so the class name alone does not indicate a health risk.

name: heteroduplex analysis
clinical_significance: A laboratory method for detecting sequence differences by pairing DNA strands from different samples; mismatches can alter how the paired DNA behaves during electrophoresis or chromatography. It has been used to screen for genetic variants, but sensitivity depends on the variant and assay, and a negative result does not exclude all pathogenic changes.

name: heterogeneity
clinical_significance: Variation in composition, structure, or behavior within a tissue, sample, lesion, or population; in tumors, heterogeneity can affect biopsy interpretation and treatment response.

name: heterogeneous echotexture
clinical_significance: An ultrasound appearance in which different parts of a tissue look unlike one another. It is a finding, not a diagnosis, and may result from inflammation, scarring, fat, bleeding, a tumor, or normal variation.

name: heterophile antibody
clinical_significance: A heterophile antibody is an antibody that reacts with antigens from unrelated species and can interfere with some laboratory immunoassays.

name: heterophyes heterophyes
clinical_significance: A small intestinal fluke acquired by eating raw or undercooked fish; it can cause abdominal symptoms and occasionally tissue complications.

name: heterosexuality
clinical_significance: A sexual orientation involving romantic, emotional, or sexual attraction to people of a different sex or gender. It is a normal variation in human sexuality, not a disorder; sexual health care is guided by a person's needs, practices, and preferences rather than orientation alone.

name: Heterotaxy syndrome
clinical_significance: A birth condition in which organs in the chest and abdomen are arranged differently from usual. Heart defects, abnormal spleen function, and problems with the intestines or other organs may occur.

name: heterozygote
clinical_significance: A heterozygote has two different alleles at a genetic locus, one inherited from each parent; phenotype depends on dominance, the variant's effect, and the surrounding genetic and environmental context.

name: hexachlorobenzene
clinical_significance: A persistent organochlorine compound that can cause porphyria, liver injury, neurologic effects, and other toxicity after significant exposure.

name: hexachlorophene
clinical_significance: A topical antiseptic phenolic compound whose excessive or prolonged use can cause neurotoxicity and skin injury; many uses are restricted.

name: hexadecadienoic acid
clinical_significance: A long-chain fatty acid containing 16 carbon atoms and two double bonds, occurring in lipid metabolism and studied as a biochemical or signaling molecule.

name: hexadecatetraenoic acid
clinical_significance: A 16-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid containing four double bonds, present in lipid pathways and investigated for effects on membranes and signaling.

name: hexadecatrienoic acid
clinical_significance: A 16-carbon fatty acid with three double bonds. Different positional isomers occur in plant and animal lipids and have distinct biological roles; the term generally appears in biochemical research and does not by itself indicate a disease or clinical test.

name: hexamethonium compounds
clinical_significance: Compounds that block nicotinic acetylcholine signaling in autonomic ganglia. Hexamethonium was used historically to lower blood pressure but has been replaced by more selective medicines because blocking both sympathetic and parasympathetic signaling causes widespread adverse effects; it is now mainly a research tool.

name: hexanoic acid
clinical_significance: A six-carbon saturated fatty acid, also called caproic acid, found in some fats and odors and used in chemical synthesis; concentrated exposure irritates skin and mucosa.

name: hexestrol
clinical_significance: A synthetic nonsteroidal estrogen with potent estrogen-like effects that was used historically in hormone-related treatment. It is not a routine contemporary therapy; estrogenic activity can cause clinically important effects, so any medical use requires specialist oversight.

name: hexokinase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that begins the use of glucose by adding a phosphate group to it inside cells. This traps glucose in the cell and allows it to enter energy-producing or storage pathways. Most tissues use hexokinase; the liver also uses a related enzyme called glucokinase.

name: hexose
clinical_significance: A six-carbon monosaccharide, such as glucose, fructose, or galactose, that serves as an energy substrate or metabolic intermediate.

name: hexylresorcinol
clinical_significance: A phenolic antiseptic and local anesthetic used in some throat lozenges and topical products; excessive use or allergy can cause adverse effects.

name: hiatus hernia
clinical_significance: Another name for hiatal hernia, in which the upper stomach moves through an opening in the diaphragm into the chest. Many cause no problems, but some are associated with acid reflux, heartburn, or swallowing difficulty; treatment is guided by symptoms and complications.

name: hibernation
clinical_significance: A regulated seasonal state in some animals involving prolonged periods of greatly reduced metabolism, activity, and often body temperature, with intermittent arousal. It is an adaptation, not the same as accidental hypothermia in humans; hibernation physiology is studied for potential relevance to metabolism and organ protection.

name: hibernoma
clinical_significance: A rare benign tumor of brown fat, usually a slow-growing painless soft-tissue mass that may feel warm because of its high metabolic and vascular activity.

name: hiccup
clinical_significance: Hiccups are usually brief, but persistent hiccups can disrupt sleep and eating and may signal medication effects, metabolic illness, or disease affecting the chest or brain.

name: hidradenitis
clinical_significance: A term for inflammation involving sweat glands; it appears in the names of several skin disorders, including hidradenitis suppurativa and neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis.

name: hidradenitis suppurativa
clinical_significance: A chronic, recurrent inflammatory disease of hair follicles, usually affecting skin folds such as the armpits, groin, buttocks, and area beneath the breasts. It causes painful deep lumps and abscesses (pockets of pus); repeated inflammation can form draining tunnels under the skin and scars. It is not contagious and is not caused by poor hygiene.

name: hidrocystoma
clinical_significance: A benign cyst of a sweat gland near the eyelid or skin, appearing as a small translucent or bluish papule that may enlarge with heat or sweating.

name: high arch
clinical_significance: An unusually high curve along the inside of the foot. It may run in families or result from a nerve or muscle disorder and can cause pain, calluses, ankle instability, or difficulty finding comfortable shoes.

name: high-pitched cry
clinical_significance: An unusually shrill infant cry that can occur with pain, neurologic dysfunction, drug withdrawal, or serious illness and warrants assessment when persistent or accompanied by abnormal behavior or feeding.

name: hilar
clinical_significance: Relating to a hilum, the gateway where vessels, nerves, ducts, or bronchi enter or leave an organ, especially the lung or kidney.

name: hind
clinical_significance: A directional term for the rear part of an animal or body structure, often used in veterinary anatomy (for example, hind limb). It describes location rather than a disease or clinical finding.

name: hip
clinical_significance: The joint and surrounding region where the thigh bone meets the pelvis, allowing movement and bearing body weight.

name: hip circumference
clinical_significance: The measurement around the widest part of the hips or buttocks, used in anthropometry and sometimes combined with waist circumference to assess body-fat distribution.

name: hip dislocation
clinical_significance: The ball at the top of the thighbone comes out of the hip socket. It is usually caused by major injury and causes severe pain and inability to move the leg; nearby nerves and the blood supply to the bone may also be injured.

name: hip dysplasia
clinical_significance: A problem present from birth or developing early in life in which the hip socket and upper thighbone do not fit together securely. The hip may be unstable or dislocate. Early examination and ultrasound or X-ray help guide treatment and protect hip development.

name: hip fracture
clinical_significance: A break in the upper thighbone, commonly near the femoral neck or just below it. It often follows a fall in someone with fragile bones and causes hip or groin pain, inability to bear weight, and sometimes a shortened or outward-turned leg.

name: hip injury
clinical_significance: Damage involving the hip joint, surrounding muscles, tendons, ligaments, or bones; causes range from strain and bursitis to fracture and dislocation, with inability to bear weight requiring prompt assessment.

name: hip joint
clinical_significance: The ball-and-socket joint where the top of the thighbone fits into the pelvis. It supports body weight and allows the leg to move in many directions; strong ligaments and a cartilage rim help keep it stable.

name: hip prosthesis
clinical_significance: An artificial hip joint used to replace a damaged hip. It usually has a stem placed in the thighbone, a ball, and a socket; parts may be metal, ceramic, or durable plastic and may be fixed with or without bone cement.

name: hippocampus
clinical_significance: A pair of structures deep in the brain that help form and retrieve new memories and support learning and navigation. Damage to them can cause difficulty forming new memories.

name: hirsutism
clinical_significance: Excess growth of coarse, pigmented hair in androgen-sensitive areas in women or others with a typically female hair pattern. Polycystic ovary syndrome is a common cause, but adrenal or ovarian hormone disorders and medicines can also contribute. Rapid onset or progression, deepening of the voice, increased muscle mass, or other signs of virilization warrant prompt assessment for an androgen-producing condition.

name: hirudin
clinical_significance: A substance first found in medicinal leech saliva that prevents blood from clotting by blocking an important clotting protein. Related medicines have been used or studied for selected clotting conditions.

name: hirudins
clinical_significance: A family of thrombin-inhibiting anticoagulant peptides, including natural and recombinant agents, used or studied to prevent or treat clotting in selected clinical situations.

name: hirudo medicinalis
clinical_significance: The medicinal leech, used in selected medical procedures to relieve venous congestion after reconstructive surgery.

name: histamine
clinical_significance: A chemical messenger released during allergic and inflammatory reactions. It can cause itching, redness, swelling, mucus production, narrowing of the airways, and increased stomach acid.

name: histamine degradation
clinical_significance: The body’s breakdown and removal of histamine after it has acted. This limits effects such as itching, swelling, airway narrowing, and increased stomach acid.

name: histamine receptor
clinical_significance: A protein on or in a cell that responds to histamine. Different receptor types help control allergic symptoms, stomach-acid production, nerve signaling, and immune responses.

name: histamine release
clinical_significance: Discharge of histamine from mast cells or basophils during allergic, immune, or nonimmune activation, causing effects such as itching, vasodilation, swelling, mucus production, and bronchoconstriction.

name: histidine
clinical_significance: Histidine is an amino acid used in protein synthesis and a precursor of histamine; it is essential during growth and can be metabolized to urocanic acid and other products.

name: histidine decarboxylase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that converts the amino acid histidine into histamine. It is found in human cells and some microorganisms; histamine influences allergy, stomach acid, blood-vessel responses, and immunity.

name: histidinemia
clinical_significance: An inherited metabolic disorder caused by reduced histidase activity, leading to elevated histidine in blood and urine; many affected people have few or no clinically important symptoms.

name: histiocytic sarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare aggressive cancer of cells that normally help process immune signals and foreign material. It may arise in lymph nodes, the intestine, skin, or other organs and requires specialist pathology and cancer care.

name: histiocytoma
clinical_significance: A tumor or tumor-like proliferation of histiocytes; the term may refer to a benign fibrous skin lesion or, less commonly, a malignant histiocytic neoplasm depending on classification.

name: histiocytosis
clinical_significance: A group of uncommon disorders in which certain immune cells build up abnormally in the skin, bones, organs, or blood. Effects range from isolated skin or bone problems to serious disease affecting several organs.

name: histocompatibility
clinical_significance: The degree to which donor and recipient tissues are immunologically alike. Matching tissue markers, especially HLA markers, can lower rejection risk, but antibody testing, organ type, and the recipient's health also influence transplant success.

name: histocompatibility testing
clinical_significance: Laboratory typing of HLA and other immune markers to assess donor--recipient compatibility before transplantation and to investigate selected immune or transfusion-related questions.

name: histogenesis
clinical_significance: The developmental process by which unspecialized cells differentiate and organize into mature tissues with characteristic structures and functions.

name: histological techniques
clinical_significance: Laboratory methods for preparing, staining, sectioning, and examining tissue under a microscope to reveal cellular architecture, deposits, organisms, or disease-related changes.

name: histology
clinical_significance: The study of cells and tissues under a microscope. A laboratory prepares a thin tissue section, applies stains that show its structures, and examines it for normal features or changes caused by disease.

name: histology cassette
clinical_significance: A labeled perforated container that holds a tissue specimen during processing, allowing fixation, dehydration, paraffin infiltration, and later embedding for microscopic sectioning.

name: histone
clinical_significance: A protein around which DNA winds so it can fit inside the cell nucleus. Chemical changes to histones help control which genes are turned on or off.

name: histone acetylation
clinical_significance: Addition of acetyl groups to histone proteins that usually loosens DNA packaging and can increase access of transcriptional machinery to genes.

name: histone acetyltransferase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that transfers acetyl groups to histone proteins, generally promoting a more open chromatin state and regulating gene transcription.

name: histone deacetylases
clinical_significance: Enzymes that remove acetyl groups from histones and other proteins, influencing chromatin structure, gene expression, cell differentiation, and disease biology.

name: histone deacetylation
clinical_significance: Removal of acetyl groups from histones, often tightening chromatin and reducing transcription; histone deacetylases are targets of some anticancer drugs.

name: histone modification
clinical_significance: A chemical change to a histone protein that alters how tightly DNA is packed and can change which genes a cell uses. These changes help regulate cell growth, development, and response to disease.

name: histopathologic grade
clinical_significance: A microscopic estimate of how abnormal and aggressive tumor cells appear compared with their tissue of origin; grade contributes to prognosis and treatment planning alongside stage.

name: histopathology
clinical_significance: The diagnosis of disease by examining tissue under a microscope. A pathologist studies a biopsy or surgical specimen for abnormal cells, inflammation, infection, scarring, or cancer.

name: histophilus
clinical_significance: A genus of gram-negative bacteria that includes Histophilus somni, an important cause of respiratory, bloodstream, reproductive, and neurologic disease in cattle. H. somni was formerly called Haemophilus somnus; human infection is not a recognized common clinical concern.

name: histoplasma
clinical_significance: A genus of fungi that includes Histoplasma capsulatum, which can cause histoplasmosis after inhalation of environmental spores.

name: histoplasmosis
clinical_significance: A fungal infection caused by inhaling Histoplasma spores, often from soil enriched with bird or bat droppings. It usually affects the lungs and may cause no symptoms or a flu-like illness; severe or disseminated disease is more likely in people with weakened immunity. Persistent respiratory or systemic illness after exposure may need medical evaluation.

name: hiv antibodies
clinical_significance: Antibodies produced after HIV infection and detected by some screening tests. Modern screening assays may also detect viral antigen; a reactive screen requires the recommended supplemental tests to establish the result. A negative result soon after exposure may fall within the test's window period.

name: hiv infection
clinical_significance: Infection with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which attacks CD4 immune cells and can progress to AIDS if untreated. Antiretroviral therapy is recommended for everyone with HIV and can suppress the virus, protect health, and prevent sexual transmission when suppression is maintained.

name: hiv seropositivity
clinical_significance: A historical term for a positive HIV antibody or other serologic test. A reactive screening result alone does not establish infection; diagnosis requires the recommended confirmatory testing algorithm. Current HIV monitoring also uses viral load and CD4-cell counts.

name: hla antigen
clinical_significance: A marker on the surface of cells that helps immune cells recognize what belongs to the body. HLA markers are important for matching donors and recipients in transplantation and are linked with risk of some immune diseases.

name: hmgb proteins
clinical_significance: Proteins that help organize genetic material inside cells. When released from damaged cells, some can also signal tissue injury and promote inflammation.

name: hmgn proteins
clinical_significance: Proteins that help control how genetic material is arranged and used inside cells. They can influence cell growth, specialization, and repair of genetic material.

name: hoarseness
clinical_significance: A change in the voice that makes it rough, weak, breathy, or strained. Common causes include a viral infection, voice overuse, smoking, reflux, or a growth on the vocal folds. Hoarseness lasting more than a few weeks needs assessment.

name: Hodgkin's disease
clinical_significance: Hodgkin lymphoma is a potentially curable cancer of lymphatic tissue; unexplained lymph-node enlargement, fever, night sweats, or weight loss warrants evaluation.

name: holdemania
