clinical_significance: A genus of anaerobic bacteria originally identified in human intestinal samples. Its members are part of the gut microbial community; their role in human disease is not established, and the name is mainly encountered in microbiology and microbiome research.

name: holdemania filiformis
clinical_significance: An anaerobic bacterial species first described from human fecal samples and classified in the genus Holdemania. It is known mainly from microbiology research; it is not an established cause of a specific human disease.

name: holography
clinical_significance: A method that records or reconstructs three-dimensional images using interference patterns of light. Holographic techniques are used in research, education, and some developing medical visualization applications, but a hologram is not by itself a clinical diagnosis.

name: holoprosencephaly
clinical_significance: A birth difference in which the developing brain does not divide fully into two cerebral hemispheres. Severity varies; it may affect facial development, movement, feeding, seizures, and intellectual development.

name: holorachischisis
clinical_significance: A severe birth defect in which a long section of the spine and spinal cord fails to close during development. It usually causes major weakness, loss of sensation, and other serious nervous-system problems.

name: holter electrocardiography
clinical_significance: Continuous ambulatory ECG recording, usually for 24 hours or longer, used to detect intermittent arrhythmias, correlate symptoms with rhythm, and assess heart-rate patterns.

name: home care
clinical_significance: Support and assistance provided to a person in their home, ranging from help with daily activities to skilled nursing or therapy. The type and intensity of care depend on health needs and may help people recover, manage chronic illness, or remain safely at home.

name: home environment
clinical_significance: The physical and social conditions where a person lives, including housing safety, air quality, sanitation, access to food and medicines, and exposure to hazards. These conditions can affect injury risk, respiratory and infectious disease, treatment adherence, and recovery.

name: home health care
clinical_significance: Health services delivered in a person's home, such as skilled nursing, wound care, or physical and occupational therapy. A clinician typically assesses need and plans care; eligibility and coverage depend on the health system and payer.

name: home hospice
clinical_significance: Hospice services delivered at home for a person with a life-limiting illness, focusing on comfort, symptom relief, and support for the person and family. An interdisciplinary team provides planned visits and on-call help; family or other caregivers usually provide day-to-day presence.

name: homelessness
clinical_significance: Lack of stable, safe housing, which is associated with higher risks of injury, infection, chronic illness, and mental-health problems and can make medication use and follow-up care difficult. Health services may need to address immediate needs and connect people with housing and social support.

name: homeobox gene
clinical_significance: A gene that helps control how an embryo’s body is laid out and how organs and tissues develop. Changes in some homeobox genes can cause birth differences or disease.

name: homeodomain proteins
clinical_significance: Transcription factors containing a homeodomain that bind regulatory DNA sequences and direct developmental patterning and cell differentiation.

name: homeopathy
clinical_significance: An alternative-health system that uses highly diluted preparations selected according to “like cures like”; reliable evidence has not shown homeopathic products to treat serious disease beyond placebo effects.

name: homeostasis
clinical_significance: The body’s ability to keep internal conditions within a safe range despite changes outside it. It regulates temperature, blood sugar, blood pressure, fluid, salts, and acidity through coordinated feedback systems.

name: homicide
clinical_significance: The killing of one person by another, classified legally according to intent and circumstances; medical assessment may address injury patterns, cause of death, toxicology, and safeguarding.

name: Homo sapiens
clinical_significance: The scientific name for modern humans, the living human species with shared biological features, genetic variation, and worldwide populations.

name: homocysteine
clinical_significance: An amino acid formed during methionine metabolism. Persistently elevated blood levels may occur with genetic, nutritional, renal, or other disorders.

name: homocystinuria
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which the body cannot properly process homocysteine, an amino acid. It may cause eye problems, abnormal bones, learning or developmental problems, and an increased risk of blood clots.

name: homologous recombination
clinical_significance: A DNA-repair and genetic-exchange process that uses a matching or nearly matching sequence as a template to repair breaks or reshuffle genetic material.

name: homologous transplantation
clinical_significance: Transplantation of cells, tissue, or an organ between genetically different people of the same species, requiring attention to compatibility, rejection, infection, and immunosuppression.

name: homosexuality
clinical_significance: Sexual or romantic attraction to people of the same sex or gender; it is not a mental disorder or pathology.

name: homovanillic acid
clinical_significance: A breakdown product of dopamine found in cerebrospinal fluid, blood, and urine; levels may reflect dopamine metabolism but are interpreted cautiously because many factors affect them.

name: homozygote
clinical_significance: An individual or cell carrying two identical alleles at a particular gene locus, whether the alleles are normal, pathogenic, or another variant.

name: hoof wall
clinical_significance: The hard outer covering of a hoof, made largely of keratin. Its shape and condition are assessed in veterinary care because cracks, deformity, infection, or poor growth can cause pain and impair an animal's ability to stand or walk.

name: hookworm infection
clinical_significance: An intestinal infection caused by hookworms. Infective larvae commonly enter through skin exposed to contaminated soil, then mature in the intestine and feed on blood; infection can cause abdominal symptoms and iron-deficiency anemia, especially when heavy or prolonged. Children may have impaired growth, and severe anemia requires medical care.

name: hope
clinical_significance: A person's expectation or desire for a positive outcome. In health care, hope can support coping and goal-setting, but it does not replace medical treatment or guarantee recovery.

name: hordeolum
clinical_significance: A hordeolum is a tender eyelid-gland infection that usually resolves with warm compresses; spreading redness, fever, or visual symptoms needs medical review.

name: hormone
clinical_significance: A chemical messenger made by glands or other tissues and carried in the blood to target cells. It binds specific receptors to regulate functions such as growth, metabolism, reproduction, stress responses, and fluid balance.

name: hormone inhibitor
clinical_significance: A medicine or substance that reduces hormone production or blocks a hormone's action. Inhibitors are used for selected endocrine disorders and hormone-sensitive cancers; effects and monitoring depend on the specific target and drug.

name: hormone receptor
clinical_significance: A protein that binds a specific hormone and converts the signal into cellular responses, either at the cell surface or inside the cell nucleus.

name: hormone replacement therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that supplies a hormone the body does not make enough of, such as thyroid, adrenal, sex, or pituitary hormones. Menopausal hormone therapy can relieve hot flushes and vaginal symptoms for selected people, but benefits and risks depend on the hormone, dose, duration, and health history.

name: hormone therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that adds, lowers, blocks, or changes the action of hormones. It may be used for hormone disorders, contraception, or hormone-sensitive cancers; the type and effects depend on the condition and medicine.

name: Horner's syndrome
clinical_significance: A group of findings caused by disruption of sympathetic nerves, including a drooping eyelid, a small pupil, and reduced sweating on one side of the face.

name: horseradish peroxidase
clinical_significance: An enzyme used as a label in laboratory assays, where it produces a detectable color or light signal. It is widely used in immunoassays and research tests; the result depends on assay design and does not itself diagnose a disease.

name: horseshoe kidney
clinical_significance: A birth difference in which the lower parts of the two kidneys join across the middle of the body. Many people have no symptoms, but kidney stones, urine-flow problems, infections, or high blood pressure can occur.

name: hospice
clinical_significance: Care for a person nearing the end of life when the focus is comfort rather than cure. Hospice supports symptoms, emotional and practical needs, and family caregivers at home, in a hospice facility, or in a hospital; eligibility rules vary by location.

name: hospice care
clinical_significance: Team-based care for a person nearing the end of life that prioritizes comfort, symptom control, communication, and family support rather than disease-directed cure.

name: hospital
clinical_significance: A facility that provides inpatient medical and surgical care, diagnostic testing, and emergency treatment. Hospital care is used when a person's condition needs monitoring or treatment that cannot be safely provided in a less intensive setting; risks include hospital-acquired infection, medication harm, and deconditioning.

name: hospital administration
clinical_significance: The planning and coordination of hospital staffing, facilities, finances, safety, and clinical services. Effective administration supports reliable care, infection prevention, emergency readiness, and quality improvement, although it is not itself a clinical diagnosis or treatment.

name: hospitalization
clinical_significance: Admission to a hospital for inpatient evaluation or treatment. It usually indicates a need for care or monitoring beyond outpatient services; risks can include infection, medication complications, delirium, and loss of strength, so discharge planning and follow-up matter.

name: host
clinical_significance: A person, animal, or cell in which an infectious agent lives or replicates. Host species and immune responses influence whether infection occurs, how severe it becomes, and whether the organism can spread to another host.

name: host cell
clinical_significance: A cell in which an infectious agent, parasite, or symbiont lives, replicates, or uses cellular machinery; the host-cell response influences disease and clearance.

name: hostility
clinical_significance: An attitude or behavior marked by antagonism, anger, distrust, or intent to oppose another person; persistent severe hostility may occur with psychiatric, neurologic, substance-related, or situational problems.

name: hot flash
clinical_significance: Hot flashes can disrupt sleep and quality of life during menopause or cancer hormone therapy; new episodes may also reflect medicines or endocrine disease.

name: hounsfield unit
clinical_significance: A number on a CT scan that describes how strongly a tissue absorbs X-rays. Air has a very low value, water is near zero, and bone has a high value; the numbers help distinguish tissues and lesions.

name: hour
clinical_significance: A unit of time equal to 60 minutes, commonly used in medicine to describe symptom duration, dosing intervals, monitoring periods, and treatment timing.

name: household
clinical_significance: People who live together or share a dwelling, often used as a unit in public-health studies. Household members may share exposures, infectious contacts, resources, or caregiving responsibilities, which can affect disease risk and care planning.

name: housing humidity
clinical_significance: Moisture and water vapor conditions inside a home. Persistent dampness can support mold growth and is associated with respiratory symptoms and worsening asthma; very dry air can irritate the eyes, skin, and airways.

name: housing type
clinical_significance: The form and structure of a person's dwelling, such as a detached house, apartment, or shared accommodation. Housing type can shape exposure to hazards, accessibility, crowding, privacy, and access to safe recovery or ongoing care.

name: human calcitonin
clinical_significance: A peptide hormone produced by thyroid parafollicular cells that can lower blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity; synthetic calcitonin is used selectively for bone and calcium disorders.

name: human embryo
clinical_significance: The developing human organism from fertilization through approximately the eighth week, during which the major body plan and organ systems are established.

name: human gastrin
clinical_significance: A peptide hormone produced mainly by gastric G cells that stimulates gastric acid secretion and supports growth of the gastric mucosa after food enters the stomach.

name: human genome
clinical_significance: The complete DNA sequence and genetic content of a human, organized into nuclear chromosomes and mitochondrial DNA; variants influence traits, disease risk, and treatment response.

name: human herpesvirus 6
clinical_significance: A herpesvirus that commonly infects children and can cause roseola; it may reactivate and cause serious disease in people with weakened immunity.

name: human herpesvirus 8
clinical_significance: A herpesvirus associated with Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, and multicentric Castleman disease, especially in people with weakened immunity.

name: human immunodeficiency virus
clinical_significance: A virus that attacks immune cells, especially CD4 cells, and can gradually weaken the body’s defenses. Without effective treatment it may lead to AIDS and serious infections or cancers. HIV-1 is widespread globally and HIV-2 is less common; daily treatment can suppress the virus and protect health.

name: human metapneumovirus
clinical_significance: A respiratory virus that commonly causes cough, fever, runny nose, and wheezing. Infants, older adults, and people with weakened immunity may develop bronchiolitis, pneumonia, or severe breathing difficulty.

name: human nociceptin
clinical_significance: A neuropeptide that binds the nociceptin/orphanin FQ receptor and modulates pain, stress, reward, autonomic function, and other brain and spinal-cord processes.

name: human papillomavirus
clinical_significance: A group of viruses that infect the skin and moist body linings. Some types cause warts; persistent infection with high-risk types can lead to precancerous changes and cancers. HPV vaccination prevents many infections that cause cancer, and recommended screening can detect cervical precancers.

name: humeral epicondyle
clinical_significance: A bony prominence at the distal humerus that provides attachment for forearm muscles and ligaments; the medial and lateral epicondyles are located on opposite sides of the elbow.

name: humeral fracture
clinical_significance: A break in the upper-arm bone, involving the proximal, shaft, or distal humerus; pain, swelling, deformity, and possible nerve or blood-vessel injury guide urgent assessment and treatment.

name: humerus
clinical_significance: The long bone of the upper arm, extending from the shoulder to the elbow. It joins the shoulder blade above and the radius and ulna below; fractures can injure nearby nerves or blood vessels.

name: humidity
clinical_significance: The amount of water vapor in air, influencing heat loss, respiratory comfort, skin hydration, and survival or transmission of some microorganisms.

name: humoral immunity
clinical_significance: The part of the immune system that protects mainly through antibodies made by B cells. Antibodies can block germs and toxins and help other immune cells remove them.

name: hunger
clinical_significance: The physical drive to eat, influenced by stomach fullness, blood glucose, hormones such as ghrelin, emotions, habits, illness, and the availability or appeal of food.

name: Huntington's disease
clinical_significance: An inherited, progressive brain disorder caused by a CAG-repeat expansion in the HTT gene. It can cause involuntary movements, changes in thinking, and psychiatric symptoms, usually beginning in adulthood. Each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the expansion; genetic counseling and testing support informed decisions. Treatment helps manage symptoms, but no cure is available.

name: hurthle cell
clinical_significance: A thyroid follicular cell with abundant granular mitochondria-rich cytoplasm, seen in Hashimoto thyroiditis and Hürthle-cell neoplasms.

name: husband
clinical_significance: A family-relationship term for a married male spouse. Marital or partner relationships may be relevant to caregiving, social support, and family history, but the term itself has no medical diagnosis or treatment significance.

name: hyaline
clinical_significance: A glassy, translucent material or appearance, commonly describing proteinaceous deposits or homogeneous extracellular material seen microscopically in tissues.

name: hyaline cartilage
clinical_significance: The smooth, firm connective tissue that covers the ends of bones in many joints and supports structures such as the nose and windpipe. It reduces friction and distributes load; because it has little blood supply, damaged joint cartilage heals poorly and can contribute to osteoarthritis.

name: hyaloid canal
clinical_significance: A narrow channel through the vitreous body of the eye that marks the former path of the hyaloid artery from the optic disc toward the lens during fetal development.

name: hyaluronic acid
clinical_significance: A naturally occurring carbohydrate polymer that binds water in connective tissue, skin, joints, and the eye.

name: hyaluronoglucosaminidase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that degrades hyaluronan and related glycosaminoglycans; hyaluronidase preparations can increase tissue permeability and assist dispersion of injected fluids or medicines.

name: hybridoma
clinical_significance: A cell line formed by fusing an antibody-producing B lymphocyte with an immortal myeloma cell, allowing continuous production of a monoclonal antibody.

name: hycanthone
clinical_significance: An older antiparasitic drug formerly used against schistosomiasis; its use was abandoned or restricted because of serious toxicity, including liver injury and carcinogenic concern.

name: hydatidiform mole
clinical_significance: A gestational trophoblastic disease in which abnormal placental tissue grows after conception. A complete mole has no embryo; a partial mole may include abnormal embryonic tissue. Vaginal bleeding and unusually high pregnancy hormone (hCG) levels may occur. Prompt obstetric evaluation and follow-up hCG testing are important because persistent trophoblastic disease can rarely develop.

name: hydralazine
clinical_significance: Hydralazine is a direct arteriolar vasodilator used for selected hypertension, including severe hypertension in pregnancy; reflex tachycardia, fluid retention, headache, and drug-induced lupus are recognized adverse effects.

name: hydranencephaly
clinical_significance: A rare brain development disorder in which most of the upper brain is replaced by fluid-filled spaces. It can cause severe developmental and movement problems, seizures, feeding difficulty, and a shortened life expectancy.

name: hydrarthrosis
clinical_significance: Abnormal accumulation of clear synovial fluid within a joint, producing swelling and restricted movement; causes include osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, trauma, and infection.

name: hydration
clinical_significance: The body’s water balance and the process of replacing water and electrolytes lost through urine, stool, sweat, breathing, vomiting, or bleeding.

name: hydrazine
clinical_significance: A highly reactive chemical used in fuels and industry that can cause irritant, neurologic, hepatic, and systemic toxicity after significant exposure.

name: hydrazine sulfate
clinical_significance: A hydrazine-containing chemical once promoted experimentally for cancer-related symptoms; evidence of benefit is inadequate and toxicity can include liver injury, neuropathy, and seizures.

name: hydrazines
clinical_significance: A family of nitrogen-containing chemical compounds used in industry, agriculture, and pharmaceuticals; some are irritants, toxic, mutagenic, or hepatotoxic.

name: hydrazones
clinical_significance: Chemical compounds formed by reaction of hydrazine derivatives with aldehydes or ketones, important in medicinal chemistry, analytical chemistry, and some drug structures.

name: hydroa vacciniforme
clinical_significance: A rare photodermatosis causing recurrent vesicles or papules on sun-exposed skin that heal with varioliform scars; some cases are associated with Epstein-Barr virus.

name: hydrobiology
clinical_significance: The study of aquatic environments and the organisms, chemicals, and physical conditions within them. It supports research on water quality, ecosystem health, and potential exposure to pathogens or pollutants relevant to public health.

name: hydrocarbon
clinical_significance: An organic compound composed only of carbon and hydrogen; ingestion or inhalation of petroleum hydrocarbons can cause chemical pneumonitis and systemic toxicity.

name: hydrocephalus
clinical_significance: Hydrocephalus is an abnormal buildup of cerebrospinal fluid in the brain's ventricles, which can enlarge them and sometimes raise pressure on brain tissue. Causes include blocked flow, poor absorption, bleeding, infection, tumors, or developmental conditions. Symptoms vary by age and may include headache, vomiting, sleepiness, vision problems, poor balance, walking difficulty, memory changes, or an enlarging head in infants. Treatment may require surgery to divert or bypass fluid; new or worsening symptoms need prompt assessment.

name: hydrocephalus acquired
clinical_significance: Acquired hydrocephalus is abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid after birth due to obstruction, impaired absorption, or rarely excess production; raised intracranial pressure may cause headache, vomiting, gait or cognitive change, and visual symptoms.

name: hydrochloric acid
clinical_significance: The strong acid in stomach juice that helps digest proteins and kill many swallowed microorganisms. The stomach’s mucus lining and other protective mechanisms normally prevent this acid from damaging its tissues.

name: hydrochlorothiazide
clinical_significance: Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic that inhibits sodium-chloride reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule and treats hypertension and mild oedema; hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia, and photosensitivity may occur.

name: hydrocodone
clinical_significance: An opioid analgesic used for moderate to severe pain and, in some formulations, cough; it can cause respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, tolerance, dependence, and overdose.

name: hydrocodone bitartrate
clinical_significance: The bitartrate salt of hydrocodone, an opioid analgesic that can cause sedation, constipation, respiratory depression, tolerance, dependence, and overdose.

name: hydrocolpos
clinical_significance: Distension of the vagina with retained fluid, usually because the vaginal outlet is blocked from birth. It may form a pelvic or abdominal mass and can press on the bladder, ureters, or bowel. In a newborn or child it needs prompt specialist evaluation to identify the obstruction and protect nearby organs.

name: hydroflumethiazide
clinical_significance: An older thiazide diuretic that increases urinary salt and water loss to lower blood pressure or reduce swelling. It can disturb sodium, potassium, and glucose levels and may cause dehydration or increased uric acid.

name: hydrogen
clinical_significance: A colorless, odorless gas and the lightest chemical element. In medicine, hydrogen ions are central to pH and acid--base balance; hydrogen gas is also used in breath tests for selected digestive disorders. The gas is highly flammable and can displace oxygen in enclosed spaces.

name: hydrogen cyanide
clinical_significance: A rapidly acting cellular toxin that inhibits cytochrome oxidase and prevents oxidative phosphorylation; significant exposure can cause severe lactic acidosis, seizures, cardiovascular collapse, and death.

name: hydrogen peroxide
clinical_significance: An oxidizing chemical used in some antiseptic and industrial products; ingestion or concentrated exposure can injure tissue and release gas, causing embolic or respiratory complications.

name: hydrogen sulfide
clinical_significance: A toxic, flammable gas with a rotten-egg odor at low concentrations that inhibits cellular respiration and can rapidly cause respiratory failure, neurologic effects, or death.

name: hydrogenase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that catalyzes reactions involving hydrogen gas, found mainly in microorganisms and some plants. Hydrogenases help organisms use or produce hydrogen and are studied in microbial metabolism and bioenergy; they are not routine human clinical markers.

name: hydrogen-ion concentration
clinical_significance: The concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution, expressed through pH and central to acid--base physiology, enzyme activity, and interpretation of blood-gas results.

name: hydrolase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that breaks chemical bonds by adding water. Hydrolases participate in digestion, cellular recycling, and drug metabolism; inherited deficiencies of particular hydrolases can cause metabolic or lysosomal storage disorders.

name: hydrolysis
clinical_significance: A chemical reaction that splits a molecule by adding water. Hydrolysis is important in digestion and in the activation or breakdown of many medicines, so the reaction can affect drug activity and duration.

name: hydrolyzable tannin
clinical_significance: A plant-derived polyphenol that breaks down into smaller phenolic compounds during digestion or processing. Hydrolyzable tannins are studied in food science and pharmacology; high exposure to particular tannins may be harmful, but the term does not identify a specific clinical condition.

name: hydromorphone
clinical_significance: Hydromorphone is a potent opioid analgesic for severe pain; sedation, constipation, respiratory depression, tolerance, and dependence are important risks, especially with alcohol or other sedatives.

name: hydromyelia
clinical_significance: Abnormal widening of the central canal of the spinal cord, which may be congenital or associated with obstruction of cerebrospinal-fluid flow and neurologic symptoms.

name: hydronephrosis
clinical_significance: Swelling of a kidney because urine cannot drain normally. Causes include a stone, narrowing, reflux, a tumor, or prostate enlargement. Prolonged or severe blockage can damage the kidney and may cause pain, infection, or reduced kidney function.

name: hydrops fetalis
clinical_significance: Severe fluid buildup in an unborn baby, affecting at least two areas such as under the skin, around the lungs, around the heart, or in the abdomen. Causes include blood-group incompatibility, anemia, infection, genetic conditions, heart problems, and complications of twin pregnancy.

name: hydrothorax
clinical_significance: An abnormal collection of clear fluid in the pleural space around a lung. It may result from heart, liver, kidney, or other disease and can cause breathlessness, cough, or chest pressure.

name: hydroureter
clinical_significance: Abnormal enlargement of a ureter caused by impaired urine drainage.

name: hydroxamic acid
clinical_significance: An organic functional group containing hydroxylamine attached to a carbonyl, found in chelators and some medicines, including histone-deacetylase inhibitors.

name: hydroxybenzoate
clinical_significance: A salt or ester of hydroxybenzoic acid. Some esters, called parabens, are used as preservatives in medicines, cosmetics, and foods; their safety depends on the specific compound, amount, and route, and a small number of people develop contact allergy.

name: hydroxychloroquine
clinical_significance: Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial and immunomodulatory drug used for malaria prevention or treatment and selected autoimmune diseases; cumulative retinal toxicity requires ophthalmic monitoring.

name: hydroxycholesterols
clinical_significance: Oxidized forms of cholesterol produced in the body or during food processing. They participate in cell signaling and cholesterol regulation and may contribute to inflammation or blood-vessel disease when present in excess.

name: hydroxyl group
clinical_significance: A chemical group made of one oxygen and one hydrogen atom attached to a molecule. It affects a molecule's solubility and reactivity and is common in biologically active compounds and medicines; by itself it has no diagnostic meaning.

name: hydroxyl radical
clinical_significance: A highly reactive oxygen species formed during normal metabolism and inflammation. It can damage DNA, proteins, and cell membranes when antioxidant defenses are exceeded; its role is mainly studied in oxidative injury and disease research, not measured as a routine clinical test.

name: hydroxylamines
clinical_significance: A group of compounds used in chemical synthesis and industry. Some hydroxylamines can oxidize hemoglobin and damage red blood cells, causing methemoglobinemia or hemolytic anemia after significant exposure; toxicity depends on the specific compound and dose.

name: hydroxylation
clinical_significance: An enzymatic or chemical reaction that adds a hydroxyl group to a molecule, often altering the activity, solubility, metabolism, or excretion of a drug or biomolecule.

name: hydroxyproline
clinical_significance: An amino acid formed mainly by post-translational modification of collagen; its measurement has been used as an indicator of collagen turnover but is not a routine diagnostic test.

name: hydroxyprolinemia
clinical_significance: A rare inherited metabolic finding caused by impaired hydroxyproline breakdown, leading to elevated hydroxyproline in blood or urine and usually little clinical illness.

name: hydroxysteroid
clinical_significance: A steroid hormone or steroid-related compound containing a hydroxyl group; hydroxysteroids include intermediates and products of adrenal and gonadal steroid metabolism.

name: hydroxyurea
clinical_significance: A medicine used for some blood cancers and sickle-cell disease. In sickle-cell disease it can reduce painful episodes and other complications by helping red blood cells remain less likely to sickle; blood counts and other safety tests are required.

name: hydroxyzine
clinical_significance: Hydroxyzine is a sedating H1-antihistamine used for itching, anxiety, and preoperative sedation; drowsiness, anticholinergic effects, and QT prolongation can occur.

name: Hydrozoa
clinical_significance: A group of mostly marine animals that includes hydroids and some jellyfish. Contact with certain species can cause painful stings or skin irritation; the medical risk depends on the species and exposure.

name: hygiene
clinical_significance: Practices that reduce exposure to pathogens and support health, including hand hygiene, oral care, skin care, food safety, and appropriate environmental cleanliness.

name: hymenolepiasis
clinical_significance: Intestinal infection with dwarf tapeworms, especially Hymenolepis nana, acquired by ingesting eggs; it may cause abdominal symptoms, diarrhea, or be asymptomatic.

name: hymenolepis diminuta
clinical_significance: A tapeworm that can infect people who accidentally swallow infected insects, usually in contaminated food. Infection may cause abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, or no symptoms and is treated with an antiparasitic medicine.

name: hymenolepis nana
clinical_significance: A small tapeworm that spreads when microscopic eggs are swallowed, often through contaminated hands, food, or water. It can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, poor appetite, or no symptoms and is treatable with antiparasitic medicine.

name: hymenoptera
clinical_significance: An insect order that includes bees, wasps, hornets, and ants; stings or bites can cause pain, allergy, or life-threatening anaphylaxis.

name: hyoid bone
clinical_significance: A small U-shaped bone in the front of the neck that supports the tongue and provides attachment for swallowing and voice-related muscles. It does not directly join another bone; fracture or displacement is uncommon but can threaten the airway and requires urgent assessment.

name: hyoscyamine
clinical_significance: An antimuscarinic medicine that reduces smooth-muscle spasm and secretions; it may be used for selected gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms and can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, or confusion.

name: hyperactivity
clinical_significance: Excessive or developmentally inappropriate motor activity, restlessness, or difficulty remaining still; persistent impairment may occur in ADHD, mania, substance effects, or other conditions.

name: hyperacusis
clinical_significance: Reduced tolerance to ordinary environmental sounds, which may be perceived as excessively loud, painful, or distressing. It can occur with hearing disorders, migraine, head injury, neurologic conditions, or without an identifiable cause.

name: hyperaldosteronism
clinical_significance: Excess production of the adrenal hormone aldosterone. It can cause high blood pressure, low potassium, muscle weakness, cramps, thirst, and frequent urination; an adrenal growth or overactivity of both glands may be responsible.

name: hyperalgesia
clinical_significance: Feeling more pain than expected from something that normally hurts. It can happen with inflammation, nerve injury, changes in nervous-system pain processing, or opioid use; it differs from allodynia, which is pain from a normally painless touch.

name: hyperammonemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high level of ammonia in the blood. It may result from severe liver disease, an inherited metabolic disorder, medicines, or other illness and can cause confusion, sleepiness, vomiting, seizures, coma, or brain swelling.

name: hyperamylasemia
clinical_significance: An elevated blood amylase concentration caused by pancreatic or salivary-gland disease, reduced clearance, macroamylasemia, or other conditions; it is not diagnostic of pancreatitis by itself.

name: hyperargininemia
clinical_significance: An inherited urea-cycle disorder caused by arginase deficiency, leading to high arginine and progressive spasticity, developmental impairment, seizures, or liver-related findings.

name: hyperbaric chamber
clinical_significance: A pressurized chamber in which a person breathes oxygen or another gas at pressure above sea level, used for conditions such as decompression sickness, air embolism, and selected wounds.

name: hyperbilirubinemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high concentration of bilirubin in blood that may cause jaundice; causes include hemolysis, impaired liver processing, hepatocellular injury, and bile-duct obstruction.

name: hypercalcemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high level of calcium in the blood. It may be caused by overactive parathyroid glands, cancer, medicines, or other conditions. Symptoms can include thirst, frequent urination, constipation, nausea, weakness, confusion, kidney stones, or abnormal heart rhythms.

name: hypercalciuria
clinical_significance: Excessive urinary calcium excretion, which can promote calcium kidney stones and, in some settings, bone mineral loss; evaluation considers diet, medications, kidney function, and endocrine causes.

name: hypercapnia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high level of carbon dioxide in the blood, usually because breathing is not removing enough of it. It may cause headache, sleepiness, confusion, flushed skin, tremor, or coma and can occur with severe lung or muscle disease.

name: hypercementosis
clinical_significance: Excessive deposition of cementum around a tooth root, producing a bulbous root contour that can complicate extraction but is often asymptomatic.

name: hypercholesterolemia
clinical_significance: A high level of cholesterol, especially LDL cholesterol, in the blood. It usually causes no symptoms but can gradually narrow arteries and raise the risk of heart attack and stroke; causes may be inherited or related to other diseases, medicines, or diet.

name: hyperemesis gravidarum
clinical_significance: Severe nausea and vomiting during pregnancy that causes dehydration, weight loss, or abnormal body salts and prevents adequate food or fluid intake. It often begins early in pregnancy and may require fluids, nutrition, medicines, and hospital care.

name: hyperemia
clinical_significance: Increased blood flow to a tissue, causing redness and warmth; it may be an active physiologic response to exercise or inflammation or a reactive response after temporary ischemia.

name: hyperemia grade
clinical_significance: A graded clinical or endoscopic estimate of tissue redness and vascular congestion, used to describe the severity of inflammation or mucosal irritation.

name: hyperesthesia
clinical_significance: Abnormally increased sensitivity to touch, temperature, or other sensory input, which may feel unusually intense or uncomfortable. It can occur with nerve injury, neuropathy, migraine, or other neurologic conditions; evaluation focuses on the pattern, cause, and associated neurologic signs.

name: hyperextension
clinical_significance: Movement that extends a joint beyond its usual neutral or anatomical range, potentially stretching or tearing ligaments, capsules, muscles, or nerves.

name: hyperfibrinogenemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high level of fibrinogen, a blood protein needed for clotting. It often rises with inflammation, infection, pregnancy, obesity, or estrogen exposure and may be associated with increased clotting risk.

name: hyperflexion
clinical_significance: Excessive bending of a joint beyond its normal range, which can injure ligaments, discs, muscles, or other supporting structures.

name: hypergammaglobulinemia
clinical_significance: An excess of antibody proteins in the blood. It may result from long-term infection, inflammation, liver disease, or an abnormal immune-cell growth; testing determines whether many antibody types or one type is increased.

name: hyperglycemia
clinical_significance: A higher-than-normal level of glucose in the blood. Severe short-term elevation can cause excessive urination, dehydration, and dangerous changes in body chemistry. Long-term elevation can damage the eyes, kidneys, nerves, heart, and blood vessels.

name: hyperglycinemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high glycine concentration in blood, most notably in nonketotic hyperglycinemia, a disorder of glycine cleavage that can cause neonatal hypotonia, seizures, and developmental impairment.

name: hyperhidrosis
clinical_significance: Sweating that is excessive for the temperature or activity. It may mainly affect the palms, soles, underarms, or face without another illness, or may be caused by medicines, hormone disorders, infection, or cancer.

name: hyperhomocysteinemia
clinical_significance: An elevated blood homocysteine concentration associated with genetic enzyme defects, folate or vitamin B12 deficiency, kidney disease, medicines, and increased vascular or pregnancy-related risk in selected settings.

name: hypericum perforatum
clinical_significance: St. John’s wort, a plant used in some complementary products for depressive symptoms; it can cause drug interactions by inducing hepatic enzymes and transporters and should not be combined casually with medicines.

name: hyperinsulinism
clinical_significance: Excessive insulin secretion or action causing recurrent or persistent hypoglycemia; causes include congenital disorders, tumors, medications, and critical illness.

name: hyperkalemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high serum potassium level, commonly from impaired kidney excretion, medicines, tissue breakdown, adrenal insufficiency, or acidosis; pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis must be excluded. ECG changes may progress from peaked T waves and PR prolongation to QRS widening, sine-wave morphology, ventricular fibrillation, or asystole, making severe or rapidly rising potassium an emergency requiring myocardial stabilization and rapid potassium shifting or removal.

name: hyperkeratosis
clinical_significance: Thickening of the outer keratin layer of skin or mucosa, producing callus, scale, or rough plaques in response to friction, inflammation, infection, inherited disorders, or other causes.

name: hyperkinesia
clinical_significance: Excessive or involuntary movement, such as chorea, dystonia, tics, or tremor, resulting from abnormal activity in motor-control circuits or from drugs and other diseases.

name: hyperlipasaemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high blood lipase concentration, often associated with pancreatic inflammation but also seen with kidney failure, gastrointestinal disease, medications, and other conditions.

name: hyperlipidemia
clinical_significance: Too much cholesterol or triglyceride fat in the blood. It usually causes no symptoms but can build up in artery walls, increasing the risk of heart attack and stroke; inherited disorders and other illnesses, medicines, diet, or alcohol can contribute.

name: hyperlipoproteinemia
clinical_significance: An excess of one or more lipoproteins in blood, producing high cholesterol or triglycerides and increasing risk of atherosclerosis, pancreatitis, or inherited lipid disease.

name: hyperlordosis
clinical_significance: Exaggerated inward curvature of the lumbar spine, often producing a swayback appearance and sometimes associated with pain, muscular imbalance, obesity, pregnancy, or structural spinal disease.

name: hyperlysinemia
clinical_significance: An inherited metabolic abnormality with elevated lysine in blood caused by altered lysine degradation; many people have few symptoms, but some have developmental or neurologic findings.

name: hypernatremia
clinical_significance: A high blood-sodium level, usually because the body has lost too much water or cannot obtain enough. It can cause intense thirst, weakness, confusion, seizures, or coma.

name: hypernatremia result
clinical_significance: A high blood sodium result, usually reflecting too little free water relative to body sodium; severity and rate of onset determine neurologic risk and the urgency and speed of correction.

name: hyperopia
clinical_significance: Hyperopia can cause eyestrain, headaches, or blurred near vision; in children, significant uncorrected farsightedness can contribute to amblyopia or strabismus.

name: hyperornithinemia
clinical_significance: An elevated blood ornithine concentration caused by defects in ornithine metabolism or transport, including disorders that can produce retinal degeneration or neurologic disease.

name: hyperostosis
clinical_significance: Abnormal excessive formation or thickening of bone, which may be localized or widespread and may occur in skeletal dysplasias, inflammation, endocrine disease, or medication effects.

name: hyperoxaluria
clinical_significance: An excess of oxalate in the urine, which can combine with calcium to form kidney stones or calcium deposits. Severe inherited forms can progressively damage the kidneys.

name: hyperoxia
clinical_significance: Exposure to an abnormally high oxygen concentration or tissue oxygen level, which can cause oxygen toxicity, absorption atelectasis, retinal injury in premature infants, or lung injury depending on dose and duration.

name: hyperparakeratosis
clinical_significance: Thickening of the outer skin layer in which cells retain their nuclei instead of fully maturing. It may produce rough scale and can result from irritation, inflammation, infection, or an inherited skin disorder.

name: hyperparathyroidism
clinical_significance: A disorder in which the parathyroid glands release too much parathyroid hormone. Primary hyperparathyroidism usually begins in a gland and often raises blood calcium; secondary hyperparathyroidism is a response to problems such as chronic kidney disease or vitamin D deficiency and may have normal or low calcium. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism can develop after long-standing secondary disease.

name: Hyperphagia
clinical_significance: An unusually strong or excessive appetite. It can occur with diabetes, some genetic or brain disorders, certain medicines, or mental health conditions.

name: hyperphosphatemia
clinical_significance: A high phosphate level in the blood, most often caused by kidney disease. It can disturb calcium balance, weaken bones, and contribute to calcium deposits in blood vessels or soft tissues.

name: hyperpigmentation
clinical_significance: Darkening of an area of skin because the body makes or stores more pigment there. Causes include sun exposure, inflammation, injury, medicines, hormone disorders, and some skin or internal diseases.

name: hyperpituitarism
clinical_significance: Excess production of one or more hormones from the pituitary gland, usually because of a benign pituitary tumor. The effects depend on the hormone involved and may affect growth, menstrual cycles, fertility, metabolism, or stress responses.

name: hyperplasia
clinical_significance: An increase in the number of cells in a tissue or organ, which may make it larger. It can be a normal response or result from disease, hormones, or other stimuli.

name: hyperplastic polyp
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous overgrowth of lining cells, often in the colon or rectum, whose cancer risk depends on size, number, and location.

name: hyperpnea
clinical_significance: Breathing that is deeper, and sometimes faster, than normal, increasing air movement and occurring with exercise, illness, metabolic changes, or anxiety.

name: hyperprolactinemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high level of the hormone prolactin in the blood. Causes include pregnancy, breastfeeding, medicines, an underactive thyroid, kidney disease, or a pituitary tumor. It may disrupt periods, fertility, sexual function, or milk production.

name: hyperproteinemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high total blood-protein concentration, usually from dehydration, chronic inflammation, or a monoclonal immunoglobulin disorder.

name: hyperpyrexia
clinical_significance: An extreme elevation of body temperature, generally above 41.5 °C, that can result from severe infection, heatstroke, malignant hyperthermia, drug toxicity, or other life-threatening conditions.

name: hyperreflexia
clinical_significance: Exaggerated or overactive deep-tendon (stretch) reflexes. It is a neurologic sign, not a diagnosis, and often reflects impaired descending upper-motor-neuron control; it may occur with spasticity, clonus, or an extensor plantar response. Distribution and associated findings help distinguish central nervous-system disease from systemic or toxic causes.

name: hypersensitivity
clinical_significance: An exaggerated immune response to a substance or exposure. Reactions range from mild skin symptoms to severe allergy or anaphylaxis; the pattern and timing help identify the trigger, and severe breathing or circulatory symptoms require emergency treatment.

name: hypersomnia
clinical_significance: Being very sleepy during the day or sleeping much longer than usual even after enough sleep. It can be caused by sleep disorders, medicines, depression, substance use, or other illness; it is different from feeling tired without wanting to sleep.

name: hypersplenism
clinical_significance: A condition in which an enlarged or overactive spleen removes blood cells too quickly. It may lower red cells, white cells, platelets, or all three and can cause anemia, infections, or easy bleeding.

name: hypertelorism
clinical_significance: An unusually wide distance between the eyes because the bony eye sockets are farther apart than usual. It may be present from birth or occur as part of a genetic or developmental condition.

name: hypertension
clinical_significance: Hypertension often has no symptoms but increases risk of stroke, heart disease, kidney failure, and eye damage; accurate repeated measurement guides prevention and treatment.

name: hypertensive retinopathy
clinical_significance: Damage to the retina’s small blood vessels caused by high blood pressure. Findings may include narrowed arteries, changes where arteries cross veins, retinal bleeding, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates; severe cases may cause swelling of the optic disc.

name: hyperthermia
clinical_significance: Hyperthermia is an abnormally high body temperature caused by excessive heat production or impaired heat loss, without a change in the hypothalamic temperature set point. Causes include heat exposure, exertion, medicines, endocrine disorders, infection-related illness, and impaired sweating. Severe hyperthermia can cause confusion, seizures, organ injury, or death and requires urgent treatment.

name: hyperthyroidism
clinical_significance: A condition in which the thyroid makes too much thyroid hormone. It may cause weight loss, sweating, heat intolerance, shaking, anxiety, diarrhea, or a fast or irregular heartbeat. Common causes include Graves disease and overactive thyroid nodules.

name: hyperthyroxinemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high concentration of circulating thyroxine, caused by hyperthyroidism, thyroiditis, medication, binding-protein changes, or assay interference; symptoms and TSH clarify the cause.

name: hypertonia
clinical_significance: Abnormally increased muscle tightness or resistance when a limb is moved. It may cause stiffness, abnormal posture, spasms, or limited movement and can result from brain, spinal-cord, or other nervous-system disorders.

name: hypertrichosis
clinical_significance: Excessive hair growth in any body area, in a localized or generalized pattern, that is not limited to the androgen-dependent male pattern seen in hirsutism. It may be present from birth or develop later because of inherited conditions, medicines, nutritional or metabolic disease, skin disorders, or rarely cancer. New, widespread, or rapidly progressive growth should be assessed.

name: hypertriglyceridemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high level of triglycerides, a type of fat, in the blood. Causes include diabetes, obesity, alcohol, some medicines, and inherited disorders. Very high levels increase the risk of acute pancreatitis and require medical management.

name: hypertrophic gastritis
clinical_significance: Thickening of the gastric mucosal folds caused by glandular overgrowth or inflammation, as in Ménétrier disease; protein loss, pain, nausea, and increased cancer risk may occur.

name: hypertrophic myocardiopathy
clinical_significance: Abnormal thickening of the heart muscle, often inherited. The thickened muscle may become stiff, obstruct blood leaving the heart, cause chest pain or breathlessness, or trigger dangerous abnormal rhythms.

name: hypertrophy
clinical_significance: Enlargement of a tissue or organ because its individual cells become larger. It may develop in response to increased workload, hormones, disease, or other stimulation.

name: hypertropia
clinical_significance: Vertical misalignment of the eyes in which one eye deviates upward relative to the other, causing double vision, eye strain, or abnormal head posture.

name: hyperuricemia
clinical_significance: A high blood uric-acid level. It may remain symptom-free, but in some people urate crystals cause gout or kidney stones. The level alone does not prove gout, and treatment decisions depend on symptoms, stones, kidney health, and overall risk.

name: hyperventilation
clinical_significance: Abnormally rapid, deep, or otherwise excessive breathing that removes more carbon dioxide than the body produces, often causing respiratory alkalosis. It may cause breathlessness, dizziness, tingling, chest tightness, muscle spasms, or fainting. Anxiety or panic can trigger it, but new or severe hyperventilation may reflect heart or lung disease, infection, bleeding, metabolic illness, or another emergency.

name: hypervigilance
clinical_significance: A state of excessive alertness to possible threat, often accompanied by scanning, startle, irritability, and sleep difficulty in anxiety, trauma-related disorders, stimulant use, or medical illness.

name: hypervolemia
clinical_significance: Too much fluid in the bloodstream or body tissues. It may cause rapid weight gain, swelling, breathlessness, raised neck veins, or high blood pressure and can occur with heart, kidney, or liver disease.

name: hypha
clinical_significance: A branching tubular filament that forms the basic structural unit of most molds and many fungi; networks of hyphae form a mycelium and may invade tissue in fungal disease.

name: hyphema
clinical_significance: Blood collecting in the front part of the eye, usually after an injury. It may cause pain, blurred vision, light sensitivity, or increased eye pressure and requires prompt eye assessment to protect vision.

name: hypnic headache
clinical_significance: A rare primary headache that repeatedly awakens a person during sleep, usually in later life and often at a similar time each night.

name: hypnosis
clinical_significance: A state of focused attention and deep relaxation in which a person may respond more readily to guided suggestions. It is not sleep or loss of control and should be used by a trained professional when offered as part of care.

name: hypnotherapy
clinical_significance: Hypnotherapy uses focused attention and guided suggestion as an adjunct to care for selected problems such as pain, anxiety, or unwanted habits.

name: hypoadrenalism
clinical_significance: Insufficient adrenal-cortex hormone production, especially cortisol and sometimes aldosterone; primary disease can cause fatigue, weight loss, low blood pressure, hyperpigmentation, and adrenal crisis.

name: hypoalbuminemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally low blood albumin concentration caused by reduced production, inflammation, kidney or gastrointestinal loss, or severe malnutrition; it can contribute to edema and alter drug binding.

name: hypoalphalipoproteinemias
clinical_significance: Disorders with low HDL-related apolipoprotein levels, which may impair reverse cholesterol transport and increase cardiovascular risk depending on the cause and overall lipid profile.

name: hypoblast
clinical_significance: The inner cell layer of the early embryonic disc that contributes to the yolk-sac lining and helps establish the embryonic body axes during gastrulation.

name: hypocalcemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally low level of calcium in the blood. It may result from parathyroid or vitamin D disorders, kidney disease, low magnesium, or other causes. Symptoms include tingling, cramps, and muscle spasms; severe cases can cause tetany, seizures, or abnormal heart rhythms and need urgent treatment. Interpretation uses albumin-adjusted or ionized calcium as appropriate.

name: hypocapnia
clinical_significance: An abnormally low level of carbon dioxide in the blood, usually because a person is breathing too fast or deeply. Causes include anxiety, pain, low oxygen, lung disease, pregnancy, or excessive ventilator support.

name: hypocholesterolemia
clinical_significance: An unusually low blood cholesterol concentration caused by malnutrition, malabsorption, hyperthyroidism, chronic illness, liver disease, or inherited lipid disorders.

name: hypochondriasis
clinical_significance: An outdated term for persistent fear of having or developing a serious illness. Depending on a person's symptoms and concerns, current diagnostic terms may include illness anxiety disorder or somatic symptom disorder; the term should not be used dismissively, and appropriate care includes assessing physical symptoms as well as distress.

name: hypochromia
clinical_significance: Reduced hemoglobin color in red blood cells, seen as increased central pallor on a blood smear and commonly associated with iron deficiency or thalassemia.

name: hypochromic anemia
clinical_significance: Anemia in which red cells contain too little hemoglobin and appear pale, most often because of iron deficiency, thalassemia, chronic disease, or sideroblastic disorders.

name: hypocitraturia
clinical_significance: Low urinary citrate excretion, which reduces inhibition of calcium-crystal formation and increases risk of calcium kidney stones; potassium citrate may be used when clinically appropriate.

name: hypocupremia
clinical_significance: An abnormally low copper concentration in blood or tissues, caused by inadequate intake, malabsorption, excess zinc, or inherited disorders, and potentially producing anemia, neutropenia, or neurologic disease.

name: hypodermic needle
clinical_significance: A hollow needle designed to inject medicines or withdraw fluid through the skin, with gauge and length selected according to the substance, route, body site, and patient.

name: hypodontia
clinical_significance: A condition present from birth in which one or more permanent teeth fail to develop. It most often affects wisdom teeth, upper side incisors, or second premolars and may affect chewing, appearance, or tooth alignment.

name: hypoesthesia
clinical_significance: Reduced sensitivity to touch, temperature, pain, or other sensations. It may result from nerve compression, injury, neuropathy, or a brain or spinal-cord disorder; sudden or spreading numbness, especially with weakness or speech or vision changes, needs urgent assessment.

name: hypogalactia
clinical_significance: Insufficient breast-milk production for an infant’s needs, caused by ineffective milk removal, hormonal or breast disorders, medications, illness, or other feeding difficulties.

name: hypogammaglobulinemia
clinical_significance: Abnormally low levels of antibodies in the blood, which can lead to repeated infections, especially of the ears, sinuses, lungs, or bloodstream. It may be inherited or develop because of another disease or treatment.

name: hypoglossal nerve
clinical_significance: Cranial nerve XII, which supplies the muscles that move the tongue; a lesion causes tongue weakness, wasting, and deviation toward the affected side on protrusion.

name: hypoglycemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally low blood-glucose level. Early symptoms may include sweating, shaking, hunger, or a fast heartbeat; severe hypoglycemia can cause confusion, seizures, loss of consciousness, or death. Insulin and some diabetes medicines are common causes, especially when food intake, activity, or illness changes.

name: hypoglycemic agent
clinical_significance: Medicines that lower blood glucose, including insulin and several types of diabetes drugs. The risk of hypoglycemia varies by medicine; insulin, sulfonylureas, and meglitinides are important causes, especially with missed meals, illness, or increased activity.

name: hypogonadism
clinical_significance: Reduced function of the testes or ovaries, causing low sex-hormone levels and impaired production of sperm or eggs. It may lead to delayed puberty, absent periods, infertility, low sexual desire, hot flashes, reduced muscle or bone strength, or other symptoms.

name: hypohidrosis
clinical_significance: Reduced or absent sweating. It can make it difficult for the body to cool itself and increase the risk of overheating. Causes include nerve disorders, skin damage, medicines, dehydration, and inherited conditions.

name: hypokalemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally low level of potassium in the blood, often caused by vomiting, diarrhea, diuretics, hormone disorders, or movement of potassium into cells. It may cause weakness, cramps, constipation, or dangerous heart-rhythm changes.

name: hypokinesia
clinical_significance: Reduced or slowed movement. It may cause small steps, less facial expression, reduced arm swing, or small handwriting and commonly occurs in Parkinson disease or other disorders affecting movement control.

name: hypolipidemic agents
clinical_significance: Medicines that lower cholesterol or triglycerides, including statins, ezetimibe, fibrates, bile-acid sequestrants, niacin, and selected injectable therapies.

name: hypolipoproteinemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally low concentration of one or more blood lipoproteins, caused by inherited disorders, malabsorption, malnutrition, liver disease, or other systemic illness.

name: hypomagnesemia
clinical_significance: A low level of magnesium in the blood, often caused by diarrhea, poor nutrition, alcohol use, kidney loss, or some medicines. It may cause tremor, cramps, weakness, seizures, or abnormal heart rhythms.

name: hypomania
clinical_significance: A distinct period of unusually elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy or activity lasting at least four consecutive days. It may involve reduced need for sleep, rapid speech, racing thoughts, inflated self-esteem, or impulsive behavior; the change is observable by others but is not severe enough to cause marked impairment or require hospitalization and has no psychotic features.

name: hypomethylation
clinical_significance: An abnormally low amount of methyl marking on DNA or other molecules. It can change which genes are active and may affect chromosome stability, development, inherited disorders, or cancer cells.

name: hyponatremia
clinical_significance: An abnormally low level of sodium in the blood, often caused by excess water, fluid loss, medicines, heart or liver disease, kidney problems, or hormone disorders. It may cause nausea, headache, confusion, seizures, or coma; severe or rapidly developing cases are emergencies.

name: hypoparathyroidism
clinical_significance: A disorder in which too little parathyroid hormone causes low blood calcium and high phosphate. It most often follows neck surgery but can be inherited or autoimmune. Tingling, muscle cramps, spasms, seizures, or abnormal heart rhythms may occur and need treatment.

name: hypopharyngeal neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the lower part of the throat beside the voice box and esophagus. It may cause persistent sore throat, painful swallowing, difficulty swallowing, ear pain, or a neck lump and may be cancerous.

name: hypopharynx
clinical_significance: The lower part of the pharynx behind and beside the larynx, extending from the oropharynx to the esophagus. It directs food toward the esophagus during swallowing.

name: hypophosphatasia
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder caused by reduced tissue-nonspecific alkaline-phosphatase activity, impairing mineralization of bones and teeth. Severity ranges from early tooth loss to rickets-like skeletal disease, fractures, or respiratory complications. Persistently low alkaline phosphatase can prompt evaluation; treatment depends on age and severity, and specialist care is important.

name: hypophosphatemia
clinical_significance: A low blood phosphate level. Mild cases may cause no symptoms, but severe or rapidly developing deficiency can impair muscle, breathing, heart, and brain function. Causes include malnutrition or refeeding, alcohol use, diabetic ketoacidosis treatment, kidney phosphate loss, and some medicines; management depends on severity and cause.

name: hypophosphatemic ricket
clinical_significance: A group of bone-mineralization disorders caused by low phosphate, often from excessive kidney phosphate loss. In children it can cause bowed legs, bone pain, poor growth, and dental problems; adults may develop osteomalacia, pain, or fractures. Finding the underlying cause guides specialist treatment.

name: hypophysectomy
clinical_significance: Surgical removal of all or part of the pituitary gland, usually performed through the nose and sphenoid sinus (transsphenoidal hypophysectomy) or rarely through an open craniotomy to treat pituitary tumors, relieve optic nerve compression, or control hormone hypersecretion.

name: hypophysitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the pituitary gland that can cause headache, visual symptoms, and deficiency or excess of pituitary hormones; it may be autoimmune, related to pregnancy, or triggered by immune-checkpoint therapy.

name: hypopituitarism
clinical_significance: Reduced production of one or more hormones from the pituitary gland because of disease, injury, surgery, radiation, or a nearby brain disorder. It may affect growth, thyroid or adrenal function, periods, fertility, milk production, or water balance.

name: hypoplasia
clinical_significance: Incomplete development of a tissue, organ, or body structure. The clinical effect depends on what is underdeveloped and may range from no symptoms to impaired organ function or a congenital disorder.

name: hypoploidy
clinical_significance: A chromosome number below the normal diploid complement, caused by loss of one or more chromosomes; in tumor cytogenetics it may have prognostic significance.

name: hypopnea
clinical_significance: A period of unusually shallow or reduced breathing, often during sleep. Repeated episodes can lower blood oxygen, disturb sleep, and contribute to obstructive sleep apnea or other breathing disorders.

name: hypoproteinemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally low amount of protein in the blood, often involving albumin, which can cause swelling and reflect poor nutrition, liver disease, kidney loss, or illness.

name: hypopyon
clinical_significance: A visible white or yellow level of inflammatory material in the front chamber of the eye. It usually indicates severe eye inflammation or infection and may occur with pain, redness, light sensitivity, and reduced vision.

name: hyposmia
clinical_significance: A reduced ability to smell, without complete loss of smell. It can follow a cold or COVID-19, nasal blockage, head injury, medicines, aging, or a neurologic disorder.

name: hypospadias
clinical_significance: A birth condition in which the opening of the urethra is on the underside of the penis rather than at its tip. The penis may curve, and the foreskin may be incomplete; severity depends on the opening’s location and other abnormalities.

name: hypotension
clinical_significance: Abnormally low blood pressure that may reduce blood flow to the brain and other organs. It can result from bleeding, dehydration, heart problems, severe infection, allergy, or medicines and may cause dizziness, fainting, confusion, or shock.

name: hypothalamic hamartoma
clinical_significance: A congenital, noncancerous mass of disorganized hypothalamic tissue that can cause gelastic seizures, precocious puberty, behavioral symptoms, or cognitive decline.

name: hypothalamic hormone
clinical_significance: A releasing or inhibiting hormone produced by the hypothalamus that regulates pituitary secretion, including signals controlling thyroid, adrenal, reproductive, growth, and lactation axes.

name: hypothalamic neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in or near the hypothalamus, a brain region controlling hormones, temperature, appetite, sleep, and water balance. Effects may include vision changes, hormone problems, headaches, seizures, or altered growth.

name: hypothalamus
clinical_significance: A small region at the base of the brain that helps control automatic body functions and hormone release through the pituitary gland. It regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, stress, and parts of emotional behavior.

name: hypothermia
clinical_significance: A dangerously low internal body temperature, usually below 35 degrees Celsius, caused by cold exposure or impaired heat production. It may cause shivering, confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, or an abnormal heart rhythm. Severe cases require urgent medical rewarming.

name: hypothyroidism
clinical_significance: A clinical endocrine syndrome resulting from deficient production or action of thyroid hormones (thyroxine [$T_4$] and triiodothyronine [$T_3$]), causing a generalized slowing of basal metabolism. Primary hypothyroidism (over 95\% of cases, characterized by elevated serum TSH and low free $T_4$) most commonly results from autoimmune destruction (Hashimoto thyroiditis), surgical thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine ablation, or severe iodine deficiency; central hypothyroidism stems from pituitary or

name: hypotonia
clinical_significance: Hypotonia can impair posture, feeding, breathing, and motor development; causes range from prematurity to neuromuscular or central nervous system disease, so persistent or severe cases need evaluation.

name: hypotrichosis
clinical_significance: Abnormally sparse or absent hair caused by inherited follicle disorders, autoimmune disease, endocrine or nutritional problems, medications, or scarring alopecia.

name: hypotropia
clinical_significance: Vertical eye misalignment in which one eye deviates downward relative to the other, potentially causing diplopia, abnormal head posture, or suppression of vision.

name: hypoventilation
clinical_significance: Breathing too slowly or shallowly to remove enough carbon dioxide. It can lower oxygen levels and cause sleepiness, headache, confusion, or respiratory failure; causes include medicines, lung disease, obesity, and muscle or nerve disorders.

name: hypovolemia
clinical_significance: Hypovolemia is reduced effective circulating blood volume, usually from bleeding, fluid loss, or inadequate intake; it can cause tachycardia, hypotension, poor perfusion, kidney injury, and hypovolaemic shock.

name: hypovolemic shock
clinical_significance: Circulatory failure from loss of intravascular volume, reducing venous return, cardiac output, and tissue perfusion. Hemorrhage is the most dangerous cause; other causes include vomiting, diarrhea, burns, third-spacing, and severe dehydration. Tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, cool clammy skin, delayed capillary refill, oliguria, confusion, and elevated lactate may occur.

name: hypoxanthine
clinical_significance: A naturally occurring substance made when the body breaks down certain genetic-material building blocks. It is normally reused or changed into other compounds during purine metabolism.

name: hypoxemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally low oxygen level in the blood. It may result from lung or heart disease, blocked airways, shallow breathing, anemia, poor circulation, or high altitude and can cause breathlessness, confusion, or bluish skin.

name: hypoxia
clinical_significance: Inadequate oxygen availability to body tissues. It can result from low oxygen in the blood, anemia, poor circulation, or impaired oxygen use by cells and may injure the brain, heart, and other organs if severe or prolonged. The cause and urgency depend on the clinical setting.

name: hysterectomy
clinical_significance: Surgical removal of the uterus. The cervix, fallopian tubes, and ovaries may or may not also be removed, depending on the procedure and reason. Hysterectomy permanently ends menstruation and the ability to carry a pregnancy; menopause occurs immediately if both ovaries are removed. Cervical screening may still be needed if the cervix remains. Reasons include cancer, fibroids, severe bleeding, adenomyosis, endometriosis, chronic pelvic pain, or uterine prolapse; risks and recovery depend on the operation and a person's health.

name: hysteria
clinical_significance: An outdated, imprecise term historically applied to varied physical, emotional, or neurologic symptoms, often in a stigmatizing way. It is not an appropriate modern diagnosis; clinicians should describe the person's actual symptoms, assess possible medical causes, and use a specific diagnosis when criteria are met.

name: hysteroscope
clinical_significance: A thin camera-equipped instrument passed through the cervix to inspect the uterine cavity and, when designed for operative use, remove polyps, treat bleeding, or perform other procedures.

name: hysteroscopy
clinical_significance: A procedure that passes a small camera through the cervix to inspect the inside of the uterus and, when needed, obtain tissue or treat conditions such as polyps, fibroids, or intrauterine adhesions.

name: hysterotomy
clinical_significance: A surgical incision into the uterus performed during selected obstetric or gynecologic procedures. It may be used to deliver a baby or reach the uterus, with risks including bleeding and infection.

name: hysterotomy abortion
clinical_significance: A historical operation in which the uterus was opened to end a pregnancy. It is now rarely used because less invasive methods are generally available; as major surgery it carries risks such as bleeding, infection, and injury to nearby organs. Contemporary options depend on gestational age, clinical circumstances, and local law and require qualified medical care.

name: iatrogenic disease
clinical_significance: Illness or injury caused unintentionally by a medical examination, treatment, medicine, procedure, or healthcare device. It may be temporary or permanent and does not by itself imply negligence.

name: ibandronic acid
clinical_significance: A bisphosphonate medicine used in some settings to reduce bone loss and complications from cancer affecting bone. It can rarely damage the jaw or cause unusual thigh fractures.

name: ibogaine
clinical_significance: A psychoactive alkaloid from the iboga plant that has been promoted for substance-use disorders, but has not been established as a safe, effective treatment. It can prolong the heart's QT interval and trigger dangerous arrhythmias, including fatal events; unsupervised use carries serious risk.

name: ibritumomab tiuxetan
clinical_significance: An antibody linked to a radioactive substance and used in selected B-cell lymphomas. The antibody attaches to CD20-positive cells and delivers radiation; low blood counts, infection, and delayed marrow problems are important risks.

name: ibuprofen
clinical_significance: A medicine that reduces pain, fever, and inflammation. It can irritate or bleed the stomach, harm the kidneys, cause fluid retention, or increase heart risks in some people.

name: ichthyosis
clinical_significance: A group of conditions that cause very dry, rough, scaly skin. Some forms are inherited and may be present from birth; others are linked to allergies or another illness.

name: ichthyosis vulgaris
clinical_significance: A common inherited skin condition causing dry, fine scaling, especially on the arms and legs. It often improves with age and can be managed with regular moisturizers and prescribed scale-reducing treatments.

name: icteric index
clinical_significance: The icteric index is a laboratory estimate of serum yellow discoloration related mainly to bilirubin and can signal jaundice or interfere with testing.

name: idarubicin
clinical_significance: Idarubicin is an anthracycline chemotherapy drug that intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II, used mainly in acute myeloid leukaemia; myelosuppression and cumulative cardiotoxicity are important risks.

name: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
clinical_significance: A chronic, progressive scarring disease of the lungs that causes worsening breathlessness and dry cough. Lung function tends to decline over time, although the course varies. There is no cure, but antifibrotic medicines can slow lung-function loss; specialist assessment, pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen when needed, and transplant evaluation may support care.

name: idioventricular rhythm
clinical_significance: A slow heart rhythm that starts in the lower chambers of the heart instead of the normal pacemaker. It may occur when the usual electrical signal is blocked or when the heart is severely ill.

name: idoxuridine
clinical_significance: An older antiviral medicine formerly used as eye drops or ointment for herpes simplex infection of the corneal surface. It can damage or irritate the eye and has largely been replaced by better-tolerated antivirals; suspected herpetic eye disease needs prompt ophthalmic assessment to protect vision.

name: ifosfamide
clinical_significance: Ifosfamide is an alkylating chemotherapy drug that forms DNA cross-links and is used for selected sarcomas and other cancers; haemorrhagic cystitis, encephalopathy, infertility, and myelosuppression require monitoring and mesna protection.

name: IGA nephropathy
clinical_significance: An immune-mediated kidney disease in which IgA-containing deposits inflame the kidney filters. It often causes blood in the urine, sometimes after a respiratory infection, and may also cause proteinuria or high blood pressure. Kidney function and urine protein are monitored because some people progress to chronic kidney disease or kidney failure.

name: igh gene
clinical_significance: The immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene locus, which encodes part of antibodies and undergoes rearrangement as B cells mature. Abnormal rearrangements can occur in B-cell cancers; molecular or cytogenetic testing may help classify a lymphoma or track a known tumor marker, alongside tissue findings and other tests.

name: ikappab kinase
clinical_significance: A kinase complex that regulates NF-kappa-B signaling, a pathway involved in inflammation, immune responses, and cell survival. It is studied in inflammatory disease and cancer biology, but I-kappa-B kinase is not a routine diagnostic test or established direct treatment target in general clinical care.

name: ileal atresia
clinical_significance: A condition present at birth in which part of the ileum, the last section of the small intestine, is closed or missing. It causes bowel blockage in a newborn, with a swollen abdomen, green vomiting, and failure to pass the first stool.

name: ileal fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal connection involving the ileum and another organ, bowel segment, or skin surface, which may cause intestinal contents to leak and lead to infection, malnutrition, or fluid loss.

name: ileal hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from the ileum, the distal portion of the small intestine, caused by ulceration, inflammation, vascular lesions, tumors, trauma, or other disease.

name: ileal neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the ileum, the last part of the small intestine. It may be noncancerous or cancerous and can cause pain, bleeding, blockage, anemia, or no symptoms.

name: ileal obstruction
clinical_significance: Partial or complete blockage of the ileum, the final part of the small intestine. Adhesions, hernias, inflammatory bowel disease, tumors, or twisting may cause cramping pain, vomiting, swelling, and inability to pass stool or gas.

name: ileal stenosis
clinical_significance: Narrowing of the ileum that may impair passage of intestinal contents and result from Crohn disease, inflammation, scarring, ischemia, tumor, or surgery.

name: ileal ulcer
clinical_significance: An ileal ulcer is a break in the lining of the ileum caused by inflammation, infection, medicines, ischemia, trauma, or another intestinal disorder.

name: ileitis
