clinical_significance: Inflammation of the ileum, the last part of the small intestine. Causes include Crohn disease, infection, reduced blood flow, medicines, and other disorders; symptoms may include lower-right abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, or bleeding.

name: ileocecal valve
clinical_significance: A flap-like structure where the last part of the small intestine joins the first part of the large intestine. It helps control passage of intestinal contents and limits backflow from the colon.

name: ileum
clinical_significance: The final and longest part of the small intestine. It absorbs vitamin B12, bile salts, and remaining nutrients before food passes into the large intestine.

name: ileus
clinical_significance: A temporary failure of coordinated intestinal movement without a physical blockage. It can follow abdominal surgery or occur with severe illness, electrolyte disturbances, or medicines such as opioids. Abdominal swelling, nausea, vomiting, and inability to pass gas or stool may occur; evaluation is needed to distinguish ileus from mechanical obstruction and address the cause.

name: iliac artery
clinical_significance: One of the large arteries that carries blood to the pelvis and lower limb. The common iliac arteries divide into internal branches for the pelvic organs and external branches that continue into the legs.

name: iliac crest
clinical_significance: The iliac crest is the curved upper border of the ilium and a landmark and attachment site for abdominal, back, and pelvic muscles.

name: iliac vein
clinical_significance: An iliac vein drains blood from the pelvis and lower limb toward the inferior vena cava; thrombosis can cause swelling and pulmonary embolism.

name: illusion
clinical_significance: A misperception or misinterpretation of a real external stimulus, such as mistaking a shadow for a person. Illusions may occur with visual impairment, delirium, seizures, intoxication, or severe psychiatric illness and differ from hallucinations, which occur without an external stimulus.

name: iloprost
clinical_significance: A prostacyclin analogue that causes vasodilation and inhibits platelet aggregation; inhaled or infused formulations are used for selected forms of pulmonary hypertension and severe peripheral ischemia.

name: image view
clinical_significance: A selected orientation or display of a medical image, such as a particular plane, slice, or projection. Consistent views help clinicians compare anatomy and findings across scans, but interpretation depends on the full study and clinical context.

name: imagination
clinical_significance: The capacity to form mental images, ideas, and possibilities. It can be relevant to memory, creativity, and psychological assessment, but imagination itself is not a medical disorder.

name: imaging
clinical_significance: The production of pictures of internal body structures using methods such as radiography, ultrasound, CT, MRI, or nuclear imaging. Imaging can help diagnose, stage, and monitor disease or guide procedures; the best method depends on the clinical question, accuracy, risks, and patient factors.

name: imaging technique
clinical_significance: An imaging technique is a method for producing pictures of body structures or processes, such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or nuclear imaging.

name: imatinib mesylate
clinical_significance: The mesylate salt of imatinib, a tyrosine-kinase inhibitor used to treat BCR-ABL-positive chronic myeloid leukemia, gastrointestinal stromal tumors with KIT alterations, and other selected cancers.

name: imide
clinical_significance: A nitrogen-containing chemical group found in some organic compounds and medicines. Its properties can affect how a molecule behaves in the body, but the term alone has no clinical or diagnostic significance.

name: imines
clinical_significance: A class of compounds containing a carbon--nitrogen double bond. Imines are intermediates in biochemical and drug-metabolism reactions and are studied in chemistry; effects on health depend on the specific compound.

name: imino acid
clinical_significance: An amino acid-like compound in which the amino group is part of a ring structure, including proline and hydroxyproline. These compounds are important in collagen and other proteins; the category itself is not a disease or routine diagnostic finding.

name: imipenem
clinical_significance: A strong antibiotic, usually given with cilastatin, used for serious bacterial infections. It can cause allergic reactions, stomach problems, seizures, or antibiotic resistance.

name: imipramine
clinical_significance: A medicine used for depression and some bladder problems. It can cause dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, abnormal heart rhythms, and dangerous effects in overdose.

name: imiquimod
clinical_significance: Imiquimod is a topical immune-response modifier that activates Toll-like receptor 7 and induces cytokines; it treats selected actinic keratoses, superficial basal-cell carcinomas, and external genital warts, often causing local inflammation.

name: immature
clinical_significance: A descriptive term for a cell, tissue, organ, or person that has not yet reached full development or maturity. In pathology and medicine it may describe immature cells or developmental stage; significance depends on the tissue and clinical context.

name: immediate hypersensitivity
clinical_significance: A rapid allergic reaction, usually involving IgE antibodies and mast cells. It can cause hives, itching, swelling, wheezing, vomiting, or anaphylaxis within minutes of exposure.

name: immobilization
clinical_significance: Restriction of movement of a body part or the whole patient, using rest, splints, casts, braces, traction, or other methods. It may protect an injury but can cause stiffness, pressure injury, muscle loss, venous thromboembolism, and other complications if prolonged.

name: immune complex
clinical_significance: A cluster formed when an antibody attaches to a foreign or abnormal substance. If these clusters are not cleared, they can collect in tissues and cause inflammation, blood-vessel damage, or kidney disease.

name: immune evasion
clinical_significance: The ability of an infection, tumor, or abnormal cell to avoid being recognized or destroyed by the immune system. It may hide identifying markers, block immune signals, or resist immune-cell attack.

name: immune status
clinical_significance: The current strength and activity of a person’s immune defenses, including protection from previous infection or vaccination and effects of disease, medicines, nutrition, or cancer treatment. It helps estimate infection risk and vaccine response.

name: immune system
clinical_significance: The body's network of cells, tissues, organs, and proteins that recognizes and responds to infections, abnormal cells, and harmful substances. It includes rapid innate defenses and learned adaptive defenses; overactivity can cause allergy or autoimmunity, while weakness increases infection risk.

name: immune tolerance
clinical_significance: The ability of the immune system to avoid attacking the body’s own tissues while still responding to infections. Failure of tolerance can contribute to autoimmune disease; excessive tolerance can allow some cancers or infections to persist.

name: immunity
clinical_significance: The body’s ability to recognize and defend against infections or other foreign substances. Protection may be present from birth, develop after infection or vaccination, or be provided temporarily by transferred antibodies.

name: immunization
clinical_significance: The process of making a person resistant to an infection, usually through vaccination and sometimes through antibodies given after exposure. Recommended vaccines reduce the risk of severe illness and community spread; schedules depend on age, health, prior doses, and exposure risk.

name: immunoblast count
clinical_significance: An immunoblast count measures activated lymphocytes, usually in a tissue or blood sample, and may help evaluate immune responses or lymphoid disease.

name: immunoblotting
clinical_significance: Immunoblotting, or Western blotting, separates proteins by electrophoresis and detects a target with specific antibodies; band pattern and intensity are interpreted with controls and clinical context.

name: immunochemistry
clinical_significance: The study or laboratory measurement of biological molecules using specific antigen-antibody reactions, including immunoassays and immunostaining.

name: immunocompetence
clinical_significance: The ability of the immune system to recognize harmful or foreign substances and produce an effective, appropriately controlled response. Reduced immunocompetence can increase infection risk and weaken responses to vaccines.

name: immunocompromised host
clinical_significance: A person whose immune defenses are weakened by an inherited disorder, infection, cancer, organ failure, malnutrition, or immune-suppressing treatment. Such a person may develop unusual, severe, or repeated infections and may have fewer typical symptoms.

name: immunoconjugate
clinical_significance: A therapeutic or diagnostic molecule in which an antibody or other targeting protein is chemically linked to a drug, toxin, enzyme, or imaging agent.

name: immunocytochemistry
clinical_significance: A laboratory method using labeled antibodies to identify specific proteins or antigens within cells or tissue sections.

name: immunodeficiency
clinical_significance: A condition in which part of the immune system is missing, weakened, or does not work properly. It may be inherited or caused by illness, medicines, cancer treatment, poor nutrition, or infection and can lead to repeated or severe infections.

name: immunoelectrophoresis
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that separates proteins by electrophoresis and identifies them with specific antibodies, often to study immunoglobulins.

name: immunofluorescence technique
clinical_significance: An immunofluorescence technique uses fluorescently labelled antibodies to locate specific proteins, organisms, or immune deposits in a sample.

name: immunogenetics
clinical_significance: The study of how genes influence immune-system development, function, and disease. It includes inherited susceptibility to autoimmune disease, differences in immune responses, and genetic matching for transplantation.

name: immunoglobulin
clinical_significance: A protein made by immune cells that recognizes a particular foreign substance, germ, or abnormal cell. Antibodies can block harmful targets, mark them for removal, or activate other immune defenses.

name: immunoglobulin A
clinical_significance: An antibody found mainly in mucus, saliva, tears, breast milk, and intestinal fluid. It protects surfaces exposed to the outside world and helps prevent germs from attaching and entering tissues.

name: immunoglobulin d
clinical_significance: A type of antibody found in very small amounts in the blood and on the surface of some B cells. Its exact role is not fully understood, but it may help regulate immune responses in the airways and other tissues.

name: immunoglobulin e
clinical_significance: An antibody involved in many immediate allergic reactions and defense against some parasites. It activates mast cells, which release chemicals causing itching, swelling, mucus, wheezing, or other allergy symptoms.

name: immunoglobulin g
clinical_significance: The most common antibody in blood and tissue fluid, helping protect against many infections. It can remain after infection or vaccination, cross the placenta during pregnancy, and sometimes cause harmful immune reactions.

name: immunoglobulin idiotype
clinical_significance: The unique antigenic features in the variable region of an antibody, which distinguish one antibody clone from another. Idiotypes are studied in immune regulation and antibody-based treatments, but they are not routine clinical tests.

name: immunoglobulin isotype
clinical_significance: The class of an antibody, determined by its constant region. The main isotypes are IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, and IgE; each has different roles and locations in immune defense.

name: immunoglobulin m
clinical_significance: A large antibody usually produced early after a new infection or other immune challenge. It helps activate immune defenses and can be measured in blood, but a high result does not by itself prove a recent infection.

name: immunohistochemistry
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that uses specially marked antibodies to find particular proteins in a tissue sample. It helps identify tumor type, infection, or immune disease and can guide treatment choices.

name: immunologic adjuvant
clinical_significance: A substance added to some vaccines to strengthen or guide the immune response. It may improve protection but can also increase temporary pain, swelling, fever, or other vaccine reactions.

name: immunologic factor
clinical_significance: A substance, cell, gene, or process that affects immune-system activity or control. Examples include antibodies, immune cells, signaling proteins, inherited traits, medicines, and conditions that alter defense against disease.

name: immunologic memory
clinical_significance: The capacity of the adaptive immune system to respond more rapidly and strongly after re-exposure to an antigen because of long-lived memory lymphocytes.

name: immunologic skin test
clinical_significance: An immunologic skin test places a small amount of an antigen or allergen in or on the skin to assess immune reactivity, such as allergy or tuberculosis exposure.

name: immunologic surveillance
clinical_significance: The immune system’s ongoing detection and removal of abnormal, infected, or damaged cells. This protection helps control infections and may recognize early cancerous changes, although it is not always successful.

name: immunologic technique
clinical_significance: A laboratory or clinical method that uses antibodies, antigens, or immune reactions to detect or measure a substance.

name: immunologic test
clinical_significance: An immunologic test examines immune cells, antibodies, antigens, or immune-related proteins to help evaluate infection, allergy, autoimmune disease, or immune deficiency.

name: immunological synapse
clinical_significance: The organized contact point where an immune cell meets a target or another immune cell. Signals gathered at this contact help decide whether the immune cell should become active.

name: immunology
clinical_significance: The medical and biological study of the immune system, including its normal defenses and disorders such as allergy, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency, infection, and transplant rejection.

name: immunomodulation
clinical_significance: Modification of immune activity to enhance, suppress, or redirect an immune response. Immunomodulatory medicines are used in cancer, autoimmune disease, transplantation, and infection but may increase susceptibility to infection or other adverse effects.

name: immunophenotyping
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that identifies cells by the proteins on or inside them, usually using flow cytometry or stained tissue. It helps classify leukemias and lymphomas and evaluate some immune disorders.

name: immunoprecipitation
clinical_significance: A laboratory technique that uses an antibody to pull a specific protein or protein complex out of a mixture. It is used to study protein interactions and can support some diagnostic or research assays; results depend on antibody specificity and sample conditions.

name: immunoprotein
clinical_significance: A protein involved in immune defense or immune regulation, such as an antibody, complement protein, cytokine, or antigen-presenting molecule. Immunoproteins identify threats, coordinate immune cells, or help remove damaged or infected material.

name: immunoradiometric assay
clinical_significance: A laboratory test using radioactive labels on antibodies to measure a specific substance, such as a hormone, protein, or other marker.

name: immunoregulation
clinical_significance: Control of the strength, duration, and target of immune responses, including activation, suppression, and tolerance. Abnormal immunoregulation contributes to autoimmunity, allergy, immunodeficiency, and chronic inflammation.

name: immunosenescence
clinical_significance: Age-related changes in immune defenses that can increase susceptibility to some infections, reduce vaccine responses, and alter inflammation. The effects vary with chronic disease, nutrition, medicines, and overall function.

name: immunosuppressive
clinical_significance: Describing a medicine, treatment, or condition that reduces immune-system activity. Immunosuppression can prevent transplant rejection or control autoimmune disease, but it may increase the risk of infection, some cancers, and reduced vaccine responses.

name: immunotherapy
clinical_significance: Cancer treatment that helps the immune system recognize or attack cancer cells, or supplies immune cells or antibodies that do so. Main approaches include checkpoint medicines, engineered immune cells, antibodies, and immune-stimulating treatments. Benefits and side effects depend on the cancer and treatment.

name: immunotoxicity
clinical_significance: Harm to immune-system function caused by chemicals, medicines, infections, or other exposures. It may weaken defenses, trigger excessive sensitivity, cause autoimmunity, or change responses to vaccines and infections.

name: immunotoxin
clinical_significance: A targeted toxin made by linking a toxic protein or drug to an antibody or binding molecule that directs it toward selected cells.

name: immunoturbidimetry
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that measures cloudiness produced when antibodies react with a target antigen, allowing estimation of the target’s concentration.

name: imp dehydrogenase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that helps cells make guanosine nucleotides, building blocks needed for DNA and RNA. Blocking it can slow the growth of immune cells, which is why some immunosuppressive medicines target this pathway.

name: impacted tooth
clinical_significance: A tooth that cannot emerge normally because it is blocked by bone, gum, or another tooth. Wisdom teeth and upper canine teeth are commonly affected and may cause pain, infection, decay, cysts, or damage to neighboring teeth.

name: imperforate anus
clinical_significance: A birth difference in which the anus is absent, closed, or not connected normally to the rectum. A newborn may not pass stool and may develop abdominal swelling; other spine, heart, kidney, limb, or digestive differences can occur.

name: imperforate vagina
clinical_significance: A rare birth condition in which the vagina is absent, closed, or blocked. It can prevent menstrual blood from leaving the body and cause repeated monthly pain, a pelvic swelling, difficulty passing urine, or fertility problems.

name: impetigo
clinical_significance: A contagious bacterial skin infection causing small blisters, sores, or honey-colored crusts. It is common in children but can affect anyone and is usually treated with hygiene measures and, when needed, prescribed antibiotics.

name: implant
clinical_significance: A medical device, tissue, or material placed inside the body to replace, support, monitor, or deliver treatment.

name: implantable defibrillator
clinical_significance: A surgically implanted device that detects dangerous ventricular arrhythmias and delivers pacing or an electrical shock to restore an effective rhythm.

name: implantation procedure
clinical_significance: Placement of a device, tissue, medicine-delivery system, or other material inside the body for treatment or support. Examples include joint, dental, heart, and breast implants; risks include bleeding, infection, movement, failure, or rejection of donor tissue.

name: importance weight
clinical_significance: An importance weight is a statistical weight used to adjust observations so a sample better represents a target population or distribution.

name: impotence
clinical_significance: Erectile dysfunction can signal vascular disease, diabetes, medication effects, or psychological distress; evaluation may identify treatable cardiovascular risk and improve sexual health.

name: impulsive behavior
clinical_significance: Impulsive behavior is action with limited forethought or inhibition despite possible harm and may occur with psychiatric, neurologic, substance-related, or developmental conditions.

name: in situ
clinical_significance: In its original place. In pathology, carcinoma in situ consists of abnormal or cancer-like cells that remain within the surface layer and have not invaded deeper tissue. It has not spread through blood or lymph vessels, but some lesions can become invasive if untreated.

name: in situ hybridization
clinical_significance: A laboratory test that uses marked probes to find a specific DNA or RNA sequence inside cells or tissue. It can detect some gene changes, viruses, or where a gene is active.

name: in vitro
clinical_significance: In vitro means performed outside a living organism, such as in a test tube, culture dish, or laboratory system.

name: in vitro fertilization
clinical_significance: An assisted-reproduction treatment in which eggs are collected, fertilized with sperm in a laboratory, and an embryo is transferred to the uterus. Risks include ovarian hyperstimulation, multiple pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, and procedure-related complications.

name: inalimarev
clinical_significance: An investigational cancer vaccine made with a modified vaccinia virus carrying tumor-associated markers such as CEA and MUC-1. It is designed to stimulate immune recognition of cancer cells and has been studied in clinical trials; it is not an established standard treatment.

name: inamrinone
clinical_significance: Inamrinone is an intravenous medicine that increases heart contraction and widens blood vessels; it was used short term in severe heart failure but can cause low blood pressure and abnormal rhythms.

name: inbreed
clinical_significance: To reproduce between genetically related individuals; inbreeding can increase the chance that recessive inherited disorders will occur.

name: incidence
clinical_significance: The number of new cases of a disease or event in a defined population during a specified period. It describes the chance of developing the condition during that period and differs from prevalence.

name: incidental finding
clinical_significance: An unexpected result discovered during an examination or test performed for another reason. It may be harmless or important; follow-up depends on what was found, its appearance, symptoms, and personal risk factors.

name: incisional biopsy
clinical_significance: Surgical removal of only part of a lesion for diagnosis, generally used when the lesion is too large or located where complete removal would be inappropriate as an initial procedure.

name: incisional hernia
clinical_significance: A hernia through a weak area in a previous surgical incision. It may appear as a bulge or cause discomfort; bowel can rarely become trapped or lose its blood supply. A painful, tender, irreducible bulge, vomiting, or skin color change needs urgent assessment.

name: incisor
clinical_significance: A front tooth shaped mainly for cutting and biting food. Adults usually have eight incisors, and each has a crown above the gum and a root anchored in the jawbone.

name: inclusion body
clinical_significance: A visible collection of material inside a cell. It may consist of viral parts, stored fats or sugars, or abnormal proteins; its appearance can help laboratory specialists identify infection, cell injury, or another disease.

name: inclusion conjunctivitis
clinical_significance: Conjunctivitis caused by \textit{Chlamydia trachomatis}, usually presenting with persistent discharge, follicular inflammation, and sometimes genital infection. In newborns it can be associated with infection elsewhere and complications.

name: incomplete ossification
clinical_significance: Failure of bone or cartilage to mineralize or develop fully. It may be part of normal development or result from genetic, metabolic, nutritional, or skeletal disorders and is interpreted with age, imaging, and laboratory findings.

name: incontinence
clinical_significance: Involuntary loss of control over urination, bowel movements, or both. It may result from weakened muscles, nerve disease, infection, constipation, childbirth, prostate problems, medicines, mobility limits, or other conditions.

name: increased libido
clinical_significance: Increased libido is heightened sexual desire that may be normal or associated with hormones, medicines, mood elevation, neurologic disease, or substance use.

name: increased osteoid
clinical_significance: Increased osteoid is excess unmineralized bone matrix, seen when bone formation outpaces mineralization as in osteomalacia or some metabolic disorders.

name: incretins
clinical_significance: Incretins are gut hormones, mainly GLP-1 and GIP, released after meals that enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion; GLP-1 also suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and reduces appetite.

name: incus
clinical_significance: One of the three small bones in the middle ear, between the malleus and stapes, that transmits sound vibrations toward the inner ear. Damage or fixation of the ossicles can cause conductive hearing loss.

name: incyclinide
clinical_significance: An investigational, chemically modified tetracycline studied for its ability to inhibit matrix metalloproteinases and alter tumor growth or invasion. It has also been studied for inflammatory conditions, but it is not an established routine treatment.

name: indapamide
clinical_significance: Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic used mainly for hypertension; it promotes renal sodium excretion and may cause hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, dehydration, hyperuricaemia, or photosensitivity.

name: indel mutation
clinical_significance: A genetic change in which one or more DNA building blocks are inserted or deleted. If the number is not a multiple of three, it can disrupt the protein reading frame.

name: indeterminate
clinical_significance: Indeterminate means not definitively classified or interpreted because available findings are insufficient, conflicting, or nonspecific.

name: indican
clinical_significance: Indican is a compound formed from tryptophan metabolism and excreted in urine; abnormal levels may occur with intestinal bacterial overgrowth or metabolic disease.

name: indication
clinical_significance: A clinical condition, symptom, or question that provides the reason for performing a test, procedure, or treatment.

name: indigo carmine
clinical_significance: Indigo carmine is a blue dye used in selected medical procedures to visualize urinary or other fluid flow and in laboratory staining.

name: indinavir
clinical_significance: An older HIV protease-inhibitor medicine that is no longer used in routine U.S. HIV care. It can cause kidney stones and other renal problems as well as metabolic adverse effects; contemporary antiretroviral regimens use other medicines.

name: indium
clinical_significance: Indium is a metal used in industry and medical radioisotopes; exposure effects depend on the compound, dose, and route.

name: indocyanine green
clinical_significance: Indocyanine green is a fluorescent dye injected intravenously to assess liver function, blood flow, and retinal or choroidal circulation.

name: indole
clinical_significance: A chemical structure containing a nitrogen atom, found in tryptophan and many natural substances and medicines. Indole-containing compounds can affect the nervous system, blood vessels, digestion, inflammation, or other body processes.

name: indole-3-carbinol
clinical_significance: A compound formed from glucosinolates in cruciferous vegetables and studied for effects on estrogen metabolism and cancer biology.

name: indolent
clinical_significance: Slow to develop, progress, or cause symptoms; it often describes a relatively slow-growing disease or tumor.

name: indoles
clinical_significance: A group of compounds containing an indole ring, including substances involved in biological signaling, metabolism, and medicines.

name: indomethacin
clinical_significance: Indomethacin is a potent NSAID used for inflammatory pain and selected acute conditions such as gout; gastrointestinal ulceration or bleeding, renal injury, cardiovascular events, and headache are important adverse effects.

name: indoximod
clinical_significance: An investigational cancer-treatment compound that modulates the tryptophan-metabolism pathway involving indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase. It has been studied with other therapies to try to restore antitumor immune responses, but it is not an approved standard cancer treatment.

name: induced abortion
clinical_significance: Deliberate termination of a pregnancy using medicines or a procedure. Safe care depends on gestational age, patient preference, accurate information, legal context, trained providers, and assessment for complications such as heavy bleeding or infection.

name: induced hyperthermia
clinical_significance: Induced hyperthermia is deliberate elevation of body or tissue temperature for a therapeutic purpose, with careful monitoring to prevent heat injury.

name: induced labor
clinical_significance: Medical initiation of uterine contractions before labor begins naturally to achieve delivery when continuing pregnancy may pose greater risk.

name: indwelling catheter
clinical_significance: A catheter left in place for ongoing drainage, infusion, monitoring, or access; urinary indwelling catheters require appropriate indications and care because they increase infection and trauma risk.

name: infant
clinical_significance: An infant is a child in the first year of life, a period of rapid growth and changing feeding, immune, neurologic, and developmental needs.

name: infant formula
clinical_significance: Infant formula is manufactured nutrition designed to provide adequate nutrients when breast milk is unavailable, insufficient, or not chosen; preparation and storage must be safe.

name: infant gynecomastia
clinical_significance: Infant gynecomastia is temporary breast enlargement in a newborn or young infant caused by maternal or neonatal hormones and usually resolves spontaneously.

name: infant incubators
clinical_significance: Enclosed devices providing controlled warmth, humidity, oxygen, and monitoring for premature, small, or ill newborns who need extra support after birth.

name: infant leukemia
clinical_significance: Infant leukemia is leukemia diagnosed during infancy, in which abnormal blood-forming cells multiply and interfere with normal blood-cell production.

name: infant mortality
clinical_significance: The death of an infant before the first birthday; the infant mortality rate is usually expressed per 1,000 live births.

name: infant nutrition
clinical_significance: Nutritional support for infants through breast milk, appropriately prepared formula, and developmentally suitable complementary foods. Requirements change with age, growth, illness, prematurity, and feeding ability; unsafe preparation can cause infection or malnutrition.

name: infant reflex
clinical_significance: An infant reflex is an automatic response present during early development, such as rooting, sucking, grasping, or startle, whose timing and symmetry help assess neurologic function.

name: infantile colic
clinical_significance: Repeated periods of intense crying in an otherwise healthy young infant, often beginning in the first weeks and improving by three to four months. The baby may draw up the legs or seem difficult to soothe; persistent vomiting, fever, poor feeding, or poor growth needs assessment.

name: infantile fibrosarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare cancer of connective or soft tissue that usually appears in a baby or young child as a growing lump. It may involve the limbs or trunk; imaging and biopsy guide treatment, which requires specialist care.

name: infantile spasm
clinical_significance: A brief seizure in an infant, often involving sudden bending or stiffening of the body and occurring in clusters. It may affect development.

name: infarct
clinical_significance: An area of tissue that has died because it did not receive enough blood and oxygen. An infarct can occur in the heart, brain, intestine, kidney, spleen, or other organs.

name: infection
clinical_significance: Entry and multiplication of bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, or other microorganisms in the body. Infection may cause tissue damage and illness, although some infections produce no symptoms; the cause and site determine treatment.

name: infection control
clinical_significance: Practices that prevent microorganisms from spreading between people, objects, and healthcare settings. They include hand cleaning, appropriate protective equipment, safe injection and device care, cleaning, sterilization, vaccination, and isolation when needed.

name: infectious arteritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation and damage of an artery caused by infection, which can weaken the vessel, reduce blood flow, or produce aneurysm.

name: infectious arthritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of a joint caused by infection, usually bacterial and sometimes viral or fungal. Acute pain, swelling, warmth, fever, and restricted movement may occur, and joint damage can develop quickly.

name: infectious conjunctivitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by a virus, bacterium, or less commonly another infectious organism, often causing redness and discharge.

name: infectious encephalitis
clinical_significance: Brain inflammation caused by an infectious organism, most often a virus. It may cause fever, headache, confusion, seizures, behavior changes, weakness, or reduced consciousness.

name: infectious encephalomyelitis
clinical_significance: Infection-related inflammation of the brain and spinal cord that may cause fever, headache, confusion, weakness, seizures, or other neurologic signs.

name: infectious enterocolitis
clinical_significance: Infection-related inflammation of the small intestine and colon, commonly causing diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, or vomiting.

name: infectious mediastinitis
clinical_significance: Infection and inflammation of the tissues in the middle of the chest, often after esophageal injury, surgery, or spread from a nearby infection.

name: infectious meningitis
clinical_significance: Infection and inflammation of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Bacterial meningitis may cause headache, fever, neck stiffness, vomiting, confusion, or a new rash.

name: infective cervicitis
clinical_significance: Infective cervicitis is inflammation of the cervix caused by organisms such as chlamydia, gonorrhea, trichomonas, or herpes, producing discharge, bleeding, or pelvic discomfort.

name: infective cystitis
clinical_significance: Infective cystitis is bacterial or other microbial inflammation of the bladder, causing urinary frequency, urgency, burning, and sometimes blood or fever.

name: infective endocarditis
clinical_significance: An infection of the heart’s inner lining, most often involving a native or prosthetic heart valve and usually caused by bacteria; fungi and other organisms can also cause it. It may form infected vegetations, destroy valves, cause fever or a new murmur, and send emboli to other organs. Diagnosis integrates blood cultures, echocardiography or other imaging, and clinical findings.

name: infective phlebitis
clinical_significance: Infective phlebitis is infection and inflammation of a vein, often around an intravenous catheter, causing pain, redness, swelling, and possible bloodstream infection.

name: infective vaginitis
clinical_significance: Infective vaginitis is infection or inflammation of the vagina caused by yeast, bacteria, parasites, or viruses and may cause discharge, itching, odor, or pain.

name: inferior
clinical_significance: Below or nearer the feet compared with another body part. For example, the diaphragm is inferior to the heart, and the inferior vena cava carries blood from the lower part of the body to the heart.

name: inferior colliculus
clinical_significance: The inferior colliculus is a midbrain auditory relay that integrates sound information and helps orient reflexively to auditory stimuli.

name: inferior vena cava
clinical_significance: The body’s largest vein, carrying blood from the legs, pelvis, abdomen, and liver to the right side of the heart. A clot or pressure on it can cause swelling of both legs and increase the risk of serious complications.

name: infertility
clinical_significance: Failure to achieve pregnancy after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse, or sooner when age or medical history warrants evaluation. Causes may involve ovulation, sperm, reproductive organs, age, or unexplained factors.

name: infiltration
clinical_significance: Entry or accumulation of cells, fluid, or another substance within tissue. In clinical care, intravenous infiltration means leakage of nonvesicant fluid into surrounding tissue; extravasation of an irritant or vesicant can cause serious injury.

name: inflammation
clinical_significance: The body’s protective response to injury, infection, or irritation. It may cause redness, warmth, swelling, pain, and reduced function. Short-term inflammation helps healing, while persistent inflammation can damage tissues and contribute to chronic disease.

name: inflammatory bowel disease
clinical_significance: A group of chronic conditions that cause inflammation in the digestive tract, mainly Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Symptoms may come and go and can include abdominal pain, diarrhea, rectal bleeding, and weight loss. The exact cause is unknown, but genes, the immune system, the environment, and gut bacteria may all play a role.

name: inflammatory response
clinical_significance: The body’s organized reaction to infection, injury, or irritation. Blood flow changes and immune cells move into the affected area, causing signs such as redness, warmth, swelling, pain, or reduced function.

name: infliximab
clinical_significance: A biologic medicine that blocks tumor necrosis factor, an inflammatory signal. It treats several inflammatory diseases but can increase the risk of serious infections, tuberculosis reactivation, infusion reactions, and heart-failure worsening.

name: influenza
clinical_significance: A contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza A or B viruses. It often begins suddenly with fever, chills, muscle aches, headache, cough, sore throat, or runny nose. Influenza can cause pneumonia or worsen chronic disease; young children, older adults, pregnant people, and people with certain health conditions are at greater risk of severe illness.

name: influenza a virus
clinical_significance: An influenza virus with segmented RNA that infects people and animals and can cause seasonal epidemics or, after major genetic changes, pandemics.

name: influenza vaccine
clinical_significance: A vaccine that reduces the risk of seasonal influenza and its complications, including hospitalization and death. It is updated as circulating viruses change and is recommended each year for eligible people; age, pregnancy, health conditions, and prior vaccination affect the appropriate product or dose.

name: influenzavirus A
clinical_significance: A group of influenza A viruses that infect people and animals. They are classified into subtypes according to two surface proteins and can cause seasonal outbreaks, severe illness, or pandemics.

name: influenzavirus b
clinical_significance: The virus genus containing influenza B viruses, which mainly infect humans and cause seasonal respiratory illness.

name: informatics
clinical_significance: Informatics applies information science, data, computing, and human factors to organize and improve healthcare, biology, research, or another field.

name: informative
clinical_significance: Providing useful information about a question or outcome. In clinical research, informative data help distinguish among possible explanations; when observations or missing results depend on a participant's health or outcome, estimates can be biased and need appropriate analysis.

name: informed consent
clinical_significance: A patient's voluntary agreement to a proposed intervention after receiving understandable information about its purpose, benefits, risks, alternatives, and the option of declining, with decision-making capacity or appropriate authorization.

name: infrared rays
clinical_significance: Infrared rays are electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible red light; excessive exposure can heat tissue and cause burns.

name: infrared spectrometry
clinical_significance: A method for identifying or measuring substances by examining how they absorb infrared light. Different chemical bonds absorb different wavelengths, creating a pattern that can help analyze medicines, tissues, samples, or pollutants.

name: infrarenal aorta
clinical_significance: The infrarenal aorta is the portion of the abdominal aorta below the renal arteries and above its division into the iliac arteries.

name: infratentorial neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the lower part of the skull, near the cerebellum and brainstem. Its effects depend on size and location and may include headache, vomiting, balance problems, weakness, or changes in coordination.

name: infrequent
clinical_significance: Infrequent means occurring less often than usual or expected, such as infrequent bowel movements, symptoms, or events.

name: infusion pump
clinical_significance: A medical device that delivers a measured amount of fluid or medicine at a controlled rate. Depending on its design, it may deliver material intravenously, subcutaneously, or intrathecally. Common types include volumetric infusion pumps and syringe pumps; alarms may indicate occlusion, air, low battery, or other device conditions.

name: ingestion
clinical_significance: The act of taking a substance into the digestive tract by swallowing. Ingestion of a toxic substance can cause poisoning.

name: ingredient
clinical_significance: An ingredient is a substance included in a medicine, food, cosmetic, or other preparation, whether active or inactive.

name: ingrown nail
clinical_significance: An ingrown nail occurs when the nail edge grows into surrounding skin, causing pain, redness, swelling, and sometimes infection or granulation tissue.

name: inguinal canal
clinical_significance: A short passage through the lower abdominal wall near the groin. It carries the spermatic cord in males and the uterine round ligament in females; weakness here can allow an inguinal hernia.

name: inguinal hernia
clinical_significance: A bulge formed when fat or intestine pushes through a weak area in the groin. It may cause discomfort or a lump that appears with standing or straining; severe pain, vomiting, or a trapped lump may indicate reduced blood flow or bowel blockage.

name: inguinal orchiectomy
clinical_significance: Inguinal orchiectomy is removal of a testicle through an incision in the groin, commonly used when treating suspected testicular cancer.

name: inhalation
clinical_significance: Drawing air, medicine, particles, or vapors into the lungs. Inhalation is a route for respiratory medicines and anesthetics, while accidental inhalation of food, vomit, smoke, or toxic substances can cause airway obstruction or lung injury.

name: inhaler
clinical_significance: A device that delivers medicine into the airways through the mouth. Pressurised inhalers release a measured spray, while dry-powder inhalers release powder during a strong breath in; correct technique is important for the medicine to work.

name: inhibin
clinical_significance: A glycoprotein hormone produced mainly by the gonads that suppresses pituitary follicle-stimulating hormone secretion and contributes to regulation of reproductive function.

name: inhibitory synapse
clinical_significance: A connection between nerve cells that reduces the chance that the receiving cell will generate an electrical signal.

name: iniencephaly
clinical_significance: A rare, severe neural-tube birth defect involving marked backward bending of the head and abnormal development of the skull and cervical spine. It is usually detected by prenatal imaging and is generally incompatible with long-term survival; diagnosis calls for specialist counseling and coordinated pregnancy or newborn care.

name: iniparib
clinical_significance: An investigational anticancer compound once studied with chemotherapy, including for triple-negative breast cancer. Later trials did not establish clinical benefit, and it is not an approved routine treatment.

name: initial insomnia
clinical_significance: Initial insomnia is difficulty falling asleep at the beginning of the sleep period, often related to stress, habits, medicines, mood, or another sleep disorder.

name: injection
clinical_significance: Introduction of a medication, fluid, or other substance into the body with a needle or other injection device.

name: injury site
clinical_significance: The body location where physical harm occurred or where its effects are being examined, documented, treated, and monitored during recovery.

name: innate immunity
clinical_significance: The body’s rapid defense against germs and tissue damage, present from birth. It includes skin, mucus, inflammation, cells that engulf germs, and protective proteins and usually responds within minutes or hours.

name: inoperable
clinical_significance: Not safely treatable by surgery, often because a disease is too extensive, located near vital structures, or the person is too medically fragile. Other treatments may still be possible.

name: inorganic chemical
clinical_significance: A chemical compound that is generally not based on carbon chains, such as water, salts, minerals, or metals. In the body, inorganic substances support fluid balance, nerve signals, bone structure, and many chemical reactions.

name: inosine
clinical_significance: A nucleoside made of hypoxanthine linked to ribose that participates in purine metabolism and cellular energy pathways.

name: inosine monophosphate
clinical_significance: A nucleotide containing inosine and one phosphate group; it is an intermediate in purine metabolism and a precursor of other nucleotides.

name: inosine pranobex
clinical_significance: A medicine combination marketed in some countries as an immunomodulator or antiviral; evidence and approved uses vary by jurisdiction.

name: inositol
clinical_significance: A sugar-like compound involved in cell membranes and signaling; some forms are studied or used for selected metabolic, reproductive, or mental-health conditions.

name: inositol phosphates
clinical_significance: Phosphorylated forms of inositol that act in cell signaling, calcium regulation, and other intracellular processes.

name: inpatient
clinical_significance: An inpatient is a person admitted to a healthcare facility for monitoring, diagnosis, treatment, surgery, or care requiring an overnight or formal stay.

name: inquilinus
clinical_significance: A genus of uncommon nonfermenting gram-negative bacteria found in the environment and occasionally in clinical respiratory samples. Inquilinus species are mainly reported in people with cystic fibrosis or other serious lung disease and can be difficult to identify in the laboratory.

name: inquilinus limosus
clinical_significance: A nonfermenting gram-negative bacterium reported mainly from the airways of people with cystic fibrosis and occasionally from other seriously ill or immunocompromised patients. It may persist in respiratory samples; its contribution to worsening lung disease and optimal treatment can be difficult to determine, so specialist microbiology input may be needed.

name: insect virus
clinical_significance: A virus that infects insects or other arthropods; some are studied for ecology or biological pest control rather than human disease.

name: insecta
clinical_significance: The biological class containing insects. Some insects bite or sting, cause allergic reactions, contaminate food, or spread infections and parasites; medical importance depends on the species and exposure.

name: insemination
clinical_significance: Introduction of sperm into the female reproductive tract, either through intercourse or an assisted-reproduction procedure such as intrauterine insemination. Indications, success rates, infection screening, and risks depend on the method and patient factors.

name: inspiratory capacity
clinical_significance: Inspiratory capacity is the maximum volume inhaled after a normal exhalation and equals tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume.

name: inspiratory time
clinical_significance: The length of time spent breathing in during a natural breath or mechanical-ventilation cycle. Adjusting it can affect airflow, oxygen delivery, comfort, pressure, and the balance between inhaling and exhaling.

name: instinct
clinical_significance: A rapid, unlearned behavioral response to a situation or stimulus. In clinical and behavioral science, instinctive responses are studied in development, neuroscience, and adaptation; the term alone does not identify a disorder.

name: insula
clinical_significance: The insula is a cerebral cortical region involved in sensation, taste, emotion, interoception, pain, and integration of internal and external information.

name: insulin
clinical_significance: A hormone made by the pancreas that helps cells use glucose and lowers blood sugar. It is used to treat diabetes, but too much can cause dangerously low blood sugar with sweating, confusion, seizures, or unconsciousness.

name: insulin antagonist
clinical_significance: A hormone, medicine, or other factor that opposes insulin’s effects and can raise blood glucose.

name: insulin coma
clinical_significance: A state of severe hypoglycemia and unconsciousness caused by excessive insulin; it is a medical emergency and is not a current routine treatment.

name: insulin detemir
clinical_significance: A long-acting insulin analogue used to provide basal insulin replacement in diabetes mellitus; dosing is individualized and hypoglycemia is the principal serious adverse effect.

name: insulin glargine
clinical_significance: A long-acting basal insulin used to control blood glucose in diabetes. Formulations differ in duration and dosing schedule; excess insulin can cause severe hypoglycemia, so dosing is individualized and glucose monitoring is important.

name: insulin isophane
clinical_significance: Intermediate-acting human insulin, also called neutral protamine Hagedorn insulin, used for basal glucose control in diabetes mellitus.

name: insulin lispro
clinical_significance: A rapid-acting insulin analogue used around meals or for correction of high blood glucose in diabetes mellitus.

name: insulin receptor
clinical_significance: A protein on the surface of many cells that binds insulin and sends signals allowing cells to take up and use glucose. It also influences fat, protein, and cell-growth processes.

name: insulin resistance
clinical_significance: A state in which muscle, fat, and liver cells respond poorly to insulin. The pancreas may produce extra insulin at first, but blood glucose can eventually rise, increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome.

name: insulin secretion
clinical_significance: Release of insulin from pancreatic beta cells, mainly in response to rising blood glucose and nutrients after a meal. Too little insulin secretion contributes to diabetes, while inappropriate excess can cause hypoglycemia; secretion can be assessed indirectly with tests such as C-peptide.

name: insulin shock
clinical_significance: An older term for severe hypoglycemia with loss of consciousness caused by too much insulin. It is a medical emergency that can cause seizures, brain injury, or death; the term is now generally replaced by severe insulin-induced hypoglycemia.

name: insulinase
clinical_significance: An enzyme, also called insulin-degrading enzyme, that breaks down insulin and other peptides. The liver and kidneys are important sites of insulin clearance; reduced clearance, especially with kidney dysfunction, can prolong insulin action and increase hypoglycemia risk.

name: insulinoma
clinical_significance: An insulinoma is a usually benign pancreatic beta-cell neuroendocrine tumour that secretes excessive insulin, causing recurrent fasting or exertional hypoglycaemia relieved by glucose.

name: insurance
clinical_significance: A contract or program that helps pay for healthcare services, medicines, or supplies. Coverage, cost sharing, and access rules can affect whether people obtain preventive care, treatment, and follow-up; details vary by plan and location.

name: integrase
clinical_significance: Integrase is an enzyme that inserts viral DNA into a host genome, a process targeted by integrase inhibitors used in HIV treatment.

name: integrin
clinical_significance: A cell-surface receptor that links cells to the extracellular matrix and helps control adhesion, movement, signaling, and immune-cell activity.

name: integrin binding
clinical_significance: The attachment of a molecule or cell to an integrin receptor, which can influence adhesion, migration, signaling, or clot formation.

name: integumentary system
clinical_significance: The body's outer covering system, including skin, hair, nails, and sweat and oil glands. It protects against injury and infection and helps regulate temperature; disorders can affect barrier function, sensation, appearance, and fluid balance.

name: intein
clinical_significance: An intein is a protein segment that excises itself from a precursor protein while joining the surrounding extein sequences.

name: intellectual disability
clinical_significance: A developmental condition involving significant difficulty with learning, reasoning, communication, and everyday independent skills. It begins during childhood and varies widely in severity; support needs depend on the person’s abilities and environment.

name: intelligence
clinical_significance: Intelligence is the capacity to learn, reason, solve problems, understand information, and adapt; tests measure selected abilities rather than a person’s entire worth or potential.

name: intelligence test
clinical_significance: An intelligence test uses standardized tasks to estimate cognitive abilities such as reasoning, memory, language, and problem-solving.

name: intensive care
clinical_significance: Specialized treatment for people who are seriously ill or at risk of organ failure. It provides continuous monitoring, medicines, procedures, and life support such as a ventilator when needed.

name: interatrial septum
clinical_significance: The wall between the heart's right and left upper chambers. It includes the fossa ovalis, a normal remnant of fetal circulation, and contains a thinner area that may be crossed during selected catheter procedures.

name: intercalated disc
clinical_significance: An intercalated disc is a specialized junction connecting cardiac muscle cells and transmitting electrical and mechanical force through the heart.

name: intercalating agent
clinical_significance: An intercalating agent inserts between DNA base pairs and can disrupt replication or transcription; some are laboratory reagents or anticancer drugs.

name: intercostal muscles
clinical_significance: Muscles between the ribs that help expand and compress the chest during breathing and also assist movement of the trunk.

name: intercostal retraction
clinical_significance: Inward pulling of the skin between or below the ribs during breathing, caused by increased effort to draw air into the lungs. It can signal respiratory distress, especially in infants and children, and needs prompt assessment when persistent or accompanied by fast or difficult breathing, bluish color, or poor responsiveness.

name: interferometry
clinical_significance: A measurement method that uses interference between waves to determine distance, motion, thickness, optical properties, or other physical quantities.

name: interferon
clinical_significance: Interferons are cytokines that induce antiviral defenses, alter immune-cell activity, and regulate cell growth; type I, II, and III interferons have different receptors and clinical uses.

name: interferon inducer
clinical_significance: A substance that stimulates cells to produce interferons, proteins involved in antiviral and immune responses.

name: interferon-alpha
clinical_significance: A type I interferon cytokine with antiviral, antiproliferative, and immune-modulating effects; recombinant forms have been used for selected viral infections and cancers.

name: interferon-beta
clinical_significance: A type I interferon cytokine used mainly as an immunomodulatory treatment for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis.

name: interim sacrifice
clinical_significance: An animal-research procedure in which study animals are euthanized at a planned interim time to examine tissues or assess treatment effects. It is used in toxicology and biomedical studies, not as a human clinical procedure, and should follow approved ethical and humane-care protocols.

name: interleukin
clinical_significance: A family of signaling proteins made mainly by immune cells. Interleukins help immune cells grow, communicate, and control inflammation, fever, allergy, infection defense, and tissue repair; different interleukins have different effects.

name: interleukin 1
clinical_significance: A group of proinflammatory cytokines, especially IL-1 alpha and IL-1 beta, that promote fever, leukocyte activation, and inflammatory responses.

name: interleukin 13
clinical_significance: A cytokine produced by type 2 helper T cells and other immune cells that contributes to allergic inflammation, mucus production, and tissue fibrosis.

name: interleukin 2
clinical_significance: Interleukin-2 is a T-cell growth factor that promotes proliferation and survival of activated T cells and natural-killer cells; high-dose therapy can cause capillary-leak syndrome and systemic toxicity.

name: interleukin 7
clinical_significance: A cytokine important for development, survival, and homeostasis of T lymphocytes and some B-cell precursors.

name: interlocutory
clinical_significance: Describing a temporary or intermediate ruling or matter before a final decision, mainly in legal and administrative settings. It has no specific clinical significance by itself.

name: intermediate
clinical_significance: Intermediate means between two stages, positions, or levels, such as an intermediate metabolite, cell, or developmental phase.

name: intermediate filament
clinical_significance: An intermediate filament is a strong cytoskeletal fiber that supports cell shape, mechanical stability, and tissue integrity.

name: intermediate uveitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation mainly affecting the gel inside the eye and nearby tissues at the edge of the retina. It may cause blurred vision, floaters, or little pain and can be linked to autoimmune disease, infection, or no identified cause. Eye examination and imaging guide treatment and monitoring for complications.

name: intermittent claudication
clinical_significance: Cramping, aching, or weakness in a leg muscle that reliably starts with walking or exercise and improves with rest. It usually results from narrowed leg arteries and may indicate peripheral artery disease.

name: intermittent fever
clinical_significance: A fever that rises and falls with periods when temperature returns to normal or near normal.

name: internal
clinical_significance: Internal means located within the body, an organ, a structure, or a system rather than on its outer surface.

name: internal capsule
clinical_significance: A compact bundle of nerve fibers deep inside the brain that carries movement and sensation signals between the brain’s outer layer and lower brain and spinal centers. Damage can cause weakness, numbness, or other neurologic deficits.

name: internal fixator
clinical_significance: An internal fixator is a surgically implanted plate, screw, rod, nail, or frame used to stabilize a fracture or correct skeletal alignment.

name: international cooperation
clinical_significance: Collaboration among countries or organizations to address shared needs such as infectious-disease surveillance, emergency response, research, and health standards. It can improve the exchange of clinical evidence and public-health resources across borders.

name: international unit
clinical_significance: A unit that measures the biological effect of a substance, such as insulin, a vitamin, or a vaccine. The amount represented by one unit differs between substances, so international units cannot be directly converted to milligrams without knowing the substance.

name: interneuron
clinical_significance: An interneuron connects neurons within the central nervous system and helps integrate, inhibit, or coordinate neural signals.

name: internist
clinical_significance: An internist is a physician specializing in adult internal medicine, including diagnosis and management of complex medical conditions.

name: interphase
clinical_significance: Interphase is the portion of the cell cycle between divisions, including growth, DNA replication, and preparation for mitosis or meiosis.

name: interphase cell
clinical_significance: A cell between divisions that grows, performs normal functions, and copies its DNA before possible division.

name: interstitial cystitis
clinical_significance: A chronic bladder pain syndrome involving pressure or pain perceived in the bladder or pelvis with urinary urgency or frequency. Symptoms often worsen as the bladder fills and may fluctuate over time. There is no single diagnostic test; evaluation checks for infection and other causes, and care is tailored to symptoms because no one treatment works for everyone.

name: interstitial fluid
clinical_significance: Interstitial fluid is the fluid surrounding tissue cells, formed from blood plasma and returned to circulation through lymphatic vessels.

name: interstitial lung disease
clinical_significance: A group of lung conditions that affect the tissue around the air sacs. They can cause inflammation, scarring, or both, making it harder for the lungs to expand and oxygen to reach the blood. Symptoms and how the condition changes over time vary by type, but may include shortness of breath, a dry cough, and low oxygen.

name: interstitial nephritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the kidney's interstitium and tubules, which may cause acute kidney injury or, if prolonged, chronic kidney damage. Medicines such as some antibiotics, anti-inflammatory drugs, and acid-suppressing drugs are common triggers, although infection and immune disorders can also cause it. Early recognition and treatment of the cause help limit kidney injury.

name: interval
clinical_significance: An interval is the time, distance, or range between two points or events, such as a dosing or follow-up interval.

name: interventional procedure
clinical_significance: A targeted procedure used to diagnose or treat disease, often through a needle, tube, or small incision and guided by imaging. Examples include biopsy, drainage, vessel treatment, and tumor ablation; risks depend on the body area and technique.

name: intervertebral disk
clinical_significance: A strong, flexible cushion between neighboring spinal bones that absorbs shock and allows movement. A damaged or herniated disk can press on nearby nerves and cause back pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness.

name: intestinal absorption
clinical_significance: Movement of digested nutrients, water, vitamins, and salts through the intestinal lining into the blood or lymph. Damage to the intestine, pancreas, liver, or bile flow can reduce absorption and cause deficiency.

name: intestinal atresia
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which part of the intestine is closed or missing, blocking passage of milk and digestive contents. Newborns may develop swollen abdomen, vomiting, and failure to feed and usually need surgery.

name: intestinal cancer
clinical_significance: A cancer that begins in the small or large intestine. It may cause pain, bleeding, anemia, altered bowel habits, blockage, or weight loss, but early disease may cause no symptoms; diagnosis and treatment depend on its site and stage.

name: intestinal duplication
clinical_significance: A birth difference in which an extra segment or cyst develops beside or within the intestine. It may cause no symptoms or lead to pain, bleeding, infection, blockage, or twisting of the bowel.

name: intestinal fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal passage connecting the intestine with another organ, another bowel segment, or the skin. It may develop after inflammation, infection, surgery, or injury and can cause leakage, infection, dehydration, or poor nutrition.

name: intestinal mucosa
clinical_significance: The inner lining of the intestine, where digestion and nutrient absorption occur. It produces mucus and contains immune defenses that help protect the body from germs and harmful substances in food.

name: intestinal perforation
clinical_significance: A hole through the bowel wall that allows digestive contents and bacteria into the abdomen. It may result from inflammation, infection, blockage, injury, or surgery and can cause severe pain, abdominal rigidity, infection, and shock.

name: intestinal polyp
clinical_significance: A growth that projects from the inner lining of the small or large intestine. Many are harmless, but some can slowly become cancer, so their size, number, type, and location guide follow-up or removal.

name: intestinal polyposis
clinical_significance: The presence of many polyps in the intestine. It may be inherited or acquired and can cause bleeding, anemia, blockage, or increased cancer risk; evaluation often includes colonoscopy and family-history assessment.

name: intestinal pseudo-obstruction
clinical_significance: Bowel swelling and symptoms of blockage caused by poor intestinal movement despite no physical obstruction. It may be temporary after illness or surgery or result from a long-term nerve or muscle disorder.

name: intestinal villi
clinical_significance: Tiny finger-like projections lining the small intestine that greatly increase its surface area. Their blood and lymph vessels absorb digested nutrients; damage to them can cause diarrhea, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies.

name: intestine
clinical_significance: The part of the digestive tract extending from the stomach to the anus, consisting of the small intestine and large intestine.

name: intestine disorder
clinical_significance: Any disease affecting the small or large intestine, including infection, inflammation, poor absorption, blockage, polyps, or cancer. Symptoms may include pain, diarrhea, constipation, bleeding, vomiting, weight loss, or nutritional deficiency.

name: intestine neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the small or large intestine. It may be noncancerous or cancerous and can cause bleeding, anemia, pain, altered bowel movements, blockage, or no symptoms.

name: intestine obstruction
clinical_significance: Intestinal obstruction is partial or complete blockage of the passage of intestinal contents, causing pain, swelling, vomiting, and failure to pass stool or gas.

name: intimal dissection
clinical_significance: A tear in the inner lining of an artery that allows blood to enter and split the vessel wall, creating a false lumen. Aortic or other arterial dissection can compromise blood flow and is a medical emergency.

name: intoplicine
clinical_significance: An investigational anticancer compound studied in early clinical trials. It interferes with topoisomerase I and II, enzymes involved in DNA replication, but it did not become an established treatment and is not used routinely in cancer care.

name: intoxication
clinical_significance: A state of physical or mental impairment caused by recent exposure to a substance, such as alcohol, a medicine, or another drug.

name: intraabdominal hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding inside the abdominal cavity, often after trauma, surgery, rupture of an organ or blood vessel, pregnancy complications, or internal disease. It may cause pain, swelling, dizziness, or shock.

name: intraabdominal infection
clinical_significance: An infection within the abdominal cavity, such as peritonitis or an abscess, often requiring antibiotics and sometimes drainage or surgery.

name: intra-arterial
clinical_significance: Intra-arterial means within an artery, including a catheter, injection, infusion, or measurement performed directly in an arterial vessel.

name: intraarticular
clinical_significance: Intraarticular means within a joint, such as an injection, fracture, loose body, or inflammatory process inside the joint space.

name: intrabronchial
clinical_significance: Intrabronchial means within a bronchus, one of the air passages branching from the trachea into the lungs.

name: intracartilaginous
clinical_significance: Located within cartilage, such as a lesion, injection, or developing structure. The term identifies position and does not by itself indicate whether the finding is normal, injured, inflamed, or cancerous.

name: intracavitary
clinical_significance: Intracavitary means within a body cavity, such as a treatment, device, fluid, or lesion located in the thorax, abdomen, uterus, or another cavity.

name: intracavity radiotherapy
clinical_significance: Intracavity radiotherapy places a radiation source inside a body cavity near a tumor, commonly to treat selected cancers of the cervix, uterus, or vagina.

name: intracellular membrane
clinical_significance: A membrane inside a cell that separates compartments and controls movement of substances between them.

name: intracellular transport
clinical_significance: Movement of proteins and other materials within a cell, often in membrane-bound sacs along the cell's internal framework.

name: intracerebral
clinical_significance: Intracerebral means within the brain tissue, as in an intracerebral hemorrhage, injection, electrode, or lesion.

name: intracisternal
clinical_significance: Intracisternal means within a cistern, especially a cerebrospinal-fluid space at the base of the brain.

name: intracoronal
clinical_significance: Intracoronal means within the crown of a tooth or within a coronary structure, with the exact meaning determined by context.

name: intracoronary
clinical_significance: Intracoronary means within a coronary artery or the coronary circulation, such as a catheter, stent, imaging study, or medicine delivery.

name: intracranial aneurysm
clinical_significance: A weakened, bulging area in a blood vessel inside the skull, usually in an artery supplying the brain. Many cause no symptoms, but a leak or rupture can cause bleeding around the brain and a sudden, severe headache.

name: intracranial hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding inside the skull, either within the brain or around it. It may follow injury, high blood pressure, a ruptured aneurysm, or medicines that prevent clotting and can rapidly cause brain pressure, disability, or death.

name: intracranial pressure
clinical_significance: The pressure inside the skull produced by the brain, blood, and surrounding fluid. Too much pressure can reduce blood flow to the brain and cause headache, vomiting, confusion, unequal pupils, seizures, unconsciousness, or life-threatening brain injury.

name: intraductal papilloma
clinical_significance: A benign growth of cells within a breast milk duct. A solitary papilloma near the nipple may cause spontaneous clear or bloody discharge; multiple papillomas or papillomas with atypical cells have different associations with breast cancer risk.

name: intraduodenal
clinical_significance: Intraduodenal means within the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine beyond the stomach.

name: intraepidermal
clinical_significance: Intraepidermal means within the epidermis, the outermost layer of skin.

name: intraesophageal
clinical_significance: Intraesophageal means within the esophagus, such as a probe, pressure sensor, lesion, or medication delivery.

name: intrahepatic cholestasis
clinical_significance: Reduced bile flow within the liver, causing bile substances to build up in blood and sometimes produce itching, jaundice, dark urine, or pale stools. Causes include liver-cell or small-duct disease, medicines, and pregnancy-related cholestasis. Persistent itching during pregnancy warrants obstetric assessment because bile-acid levels help guide fetal-risk management.

name: intralesional
clinical_significance: Delivered directly into a lesion, such as an injection of corticosteroid into a keloid or a medicine into a skin, joint, or tumor lesion. The drug, dose, sterility, and lesion type determine safety.

name: intralymphatic
clinical_significance: Intralymphatic means within a lymphatic vessel or channel, such as a medicine, tumor spread, infection, or imaging contrast.

name: intramedullary
clinical_significance: Intramedullary means within the medulla of an organ or the central canal of a bone, especially an implant placed inside a long bone.

name: intramural plaque
clinical_significance: An intramural plaque is an atherosclerotic deposit within an artery wall that can narrow the lumen or destabilize and cause thrombosis.

name: intramuscular injection
clinical_significance: Delivery of a medicine into a muscle with a needle. The injection site and needle size depend on the medicine and the person’s age and body size; pain, bleeding, infection, or nerve injury are possible.

name: intramuscular myxoma
clinical_significance: A rare, usually noncancerous tumor made of jelly-like tissue within a skeletal muscle. It often appears as a slow-growing painless lump, but imaging or biopsy may be needed to distinguish it from other masses.

name: intraocular infection
clinical_significance: An infection inside the eye, such as endophthalmitis, that can rapidly threaten vision.

name: intraocular lymphoma
clinical_significance: A lymphoma involving the eye, often the jelly-like vitreous or the retina. It may cause blurred vision, floaters, or inflammation and can occur with lymphoma in the brain or other parts of the body.

name: intrapartum fever
clinical_significance: Fever during labor, which may result from infection, epidural analgesia, dehydration, or other causes and can affect the mother or fetus.

name: intrapartum stillbirth
clinical_significance: Fetal death occurring during labor after a live fetus was documented before labor. It is a devastating obstetric outcome that warrants respectful support for the family and a review of the clinical course and possible causes, both to guide future care and to identify opportunities to improve maternity services.

name: intrapericardial
clinical_significance: Located inside the pericardial sac, the thin membrane surrounding the heart. An intrapericardial mass or fluid collection may affect how the heart fills or beats.

name: intraperitoneal
clinical_significance: Intraperitoneal means within the peritoneal cavity or administered into it, including selected medicines, dialysis fluid, or procedures.

name: intraperitonealroute
clinical_significance: A route of treatment in which fluid or medicine is placed into the abdominal cavity. It is used for peritoneal dialysis and selected treatments and requires sterile technique to prevent infection.

name: intraprostatic
clinical_significance: Located within the prostate gland, describing a lesion, injection, infection, biopsy, procedure, or other finding centered inside prostate tissue.

name: intrapulmonary
clinical_significance: Located within lung tissue or occurring inside the lung’s air spaces, blood vessels, or other structures. Intrapulmonary findings may represent normal anatomy, infection, fluid, bleeding, inflammation, or tumors.

name: intrasynovial
clinical_significance: Intrasynovial means within the synovial lining or fluid-filled space of a joint or tendon sheath.

name: intratendinous
clinical_significance: Located within a tendon, describing a tear, calcium deposit, injection, degenerative change, or other abnormality affecting the tendon's substance.

name: intratesticular
clinical_significance: Located within testicular tissue. An intratesticular mass may be benign or malignant and is usually evaluated with physical examination and scrotal ultrasound, interpreted in the clinical context.

name: intrathoracic
clinical_significance: Intrathoracic means within the chest cavity, including the lungs, heart, mediastinum, vessels, and thoracic lymph nodes.

name: intratracheal
clinical_significance: Intratracheal means within the trachea, such as a tube, medicine, foreign body, lesion, or route of administration.

name: intratympanic
clinical_significance: Intratympanic means delivered through the eardrum into the middle ear, often for selected inner-ear disorders or local treatment.

name: intrauterine
clinical_significance: Located or occurring within the uterus, including a pregnancy, device, medicine, lesion, or procedure. The term describes location and requires additional information to explain the finding’s purpose, cause, or risk.

name: intrauterine device
clinical_significance: A small device placed in the uterus to prevent pregnancy for several years while remaining reversible. Copper devices work without hormones; hormonal devices release a progestogen and often reduce menstrual bleeding. IUDs do not prevent sexually transmitted infections. Rare risks include expulsion or perforation; the small increase in pelvic-infection risk is concentrated in the first few weeks after insertion.

name: intravascular
clinical_significance: Intravascular means within a blood vessel, including a catheter, clot, injection, or process occurring in the circulation.

name: intravenous catheters
clinical_significance: Flexible devices inserted into a vein to deliver fluids, medicines, blood products, nutrition, or contrast, or to obtain blood samples; complications include infection, thrombosis, infiltration, and extravasation.

name: intravenous pyelogram
clinical_significance: An X-ray examination of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder after iodine-containing contrast is injected into a vein and passed into the urine. CT urography or ultrasound often provides this information today.

name: intravital microscopy
clinical_significance: A microscopy method for watching cells and tissues in a living organism, often in animal research. It reveals how cells move and interact in real time and supports studies of infection, inflammation, blood flow, and tumors; routine clinical use remains limited.

name: intrinsic factor
clinical_significance: A protein secreted by stomach parietal cells that is required for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

name: intron
clinical_significance: A noncoding segment within a gene that is transcribed into RNA and then removed during RNA splicing. Variants that alter intron sequence or splicing signals can disrupt a protein and cause inherited disease or contribute to cancer; many intronic variants have no known effect.

name: intrusive thought
