clinical_significance: An unwanted, distressing thought, image, or impulse that enters awareness repeatedly; it does not necessarily reflect intent or desire.

name: intubation
clinical_significance: Placement of a tube into the airway or another body passage to maintain it or deliver treatment.

name: intussusception
clinical_significance: A condition in which one segment of the intestine slides inside an adjacent segment like a folding telescope. It can block the bowel and reduce blood flow, especially in infants and young children, causing cramping pain, vomiting, swelling, or bloody stool. Ultrasound may show a target-like ring, and an air or contrast enema may be used in children.

name: inulin
clinical_significance: Inulin is a plant fructan used as a dietary fiber and in tests of glomerular filtration because it is freely filtered and minimally handled by the kidney.

name: invasive candidiasis
clinical_significance: A serious Candida infection that has spread into the bloodstream or deep organs, such as the heart, eye, bone, or abdomen. It mainly affects people who are already critically ill or immunocompromised, especially with central lines, recent surgery, or chemotherapy. Fever may be the only sign; blood cultures and prompt systemic antifungal care are important.

name: invasive procedure
clinical_significance: A medical examination, test, or treatment that enters the body by piercing the skin or inserting an instrument, tube, needle, or camera into internal tissues or organs. Examples range from needle biopsies and endoscopy to open surgery. Possible risks include bleeding, infection, pain, tissue damage, and anesthesia complications.

name: invertebrata
clinical_significance: A broad grouping of animals without a backbone, including insects, mollusks, and worms. Some species are parasites, venomous, or vectors of human disease, while others are important in food safety, ecology, and biomedical research; significance depends on the organism.

name: invertebrate hormones
clinical_significance: Hormones produced by invertebrate animals, such as insect ecdysteroids and juvenile hormone, that regulate growth, molting, and reproduction. They are relevant to research and pest control and can inform study of parasites and vectors, but they are not human hormones or routine clinical tests.

name: inverted papilloma
clinical_significance: A usually benign but locally destructive tumor arising most often in the nasal cavity or sinuses; it can recur and rarely become cancerous.

name: investigational
clinical_significance: Being studied in clinical research and not yet established as safe and effective for a particular use. Investigational medicines and devices require appropriate oversight, informed consent, and clear communication of uncertainty.

name: involuntary movement
clinical_significance: A movement that occurs without conscious control, such as a tremor, tic, chorea, dystonia, or myoclonus.

name: iodamoeba butschlii
clinical_significance: A usually non-disease-causing intestinal amoeba spread by swallowing cysts in contaminated food or water. Finding it in stool suggests fecal exposure but usually does not require treatment unless another infection is present.

name: iodide
clinical_significance: The negatively charged form of iodine, used by the thyroid to make hormones and present in medicines, supplements, and contrast compounds.

name: iodine
clinical_significance: An essential mineral used to make thyroid hormones, which regulate growth, brain development, and metabolism. Too little iodine can cause thyroid enlargement and hormone deficiency, especially harmful during pregnancy and childhood; too much can also disturb thyroid function. Main sources include iodized salt, seafood, dairy, and some supplements.

name: iodipamide
clinical_significance: An older iodine-containing radiographic contrast agent formerly used to image the gallbladder and bile ducts. It has largely been replaced by newer imaging methods; as with other iodinated contrast agents, allergic-like reactions and other adverse effects were possible.

name: iodoacetamide
clinical_significance: A reactive laboratory reagent that irreversibly alkylates cysteine groups in proteins, commonly used to prepare samples for protein analysis. It is toxic if swallowed and can harm skin or eyes, so it is handled as a hazardous research chemical rather than a medicine.

name: iohexol
clinical_significance: A water-soluble iodine-containing contrast medicine used during CT scans, angiography, and other imaging studies to make vessels and organs easier to see.

name: ion
clinical_significance: An atom or molecule carrying a positive or negative electric charge. Physiologically important ions include sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, and bicarbonate, whose concentrations influence nerves, muscles, fluid balance, and acid-base status.

name: ion transport
clinical_significance: Movement of charged particles across a cell membrane through channels, carriers, or pumps. It maintains membrane potentials, nerve signaling, muscle contraction, fluid balance, and epithelial transport.

name: ionic strength
clinical_significance: A measure of the total concentration of charged particles in a solution. Ionic strength affects protein interactions, cell and membrane behavior, and some laboratory assays; it is a physicochemical property rather than a diagnosis.

name: ionization
clinical_significance: The formation of charged particles by gaining or losing electrons or protons. A medicine's degree of ionization affects its solubility, membrane passage, absorption, distribution, and urinary excretion.

name: ionomycin
clinical_significance: A calcium ionophore used in laboratories to raise calcium levels inside cells and study signaling, secretion, and immune-cell activation. It is a research reagent, not a clinical treatment, and can damage cells at experimental concentrations.

name: ionophore
clinical_significance: A molecule that transports ions across a lipid membrane. Ionophores have research, antimicrobial, and veterinary uses; some can disrupt human cellular ion balance and are toxic.

name: iontophoresis
clinical_significance: Use of a mild electrical current to drive an ionized medicine through the skin or alter sweat-gland activity. It is used in selected dermatologic and rehabilitation settings; skin irritation and burns can occur.

name: iopamidol
clinical_significance: A nonionic iodine-containing contrast medicine used to improve CT, angiography, and other medical images. It can cause warmth, nausea, allergy, kidney problems, or thyroid effects, so risks require assessment beforehand.

name: iothalamate clearance
clinical_significance: A specialized test of kidney filtration that measures how quickly injected iothalamate is removed from the blood, sometimes using timed urine samples. It is used when a more direct estimate of kidney function is needed.

name: iothalamate meglumine
clinical_significance: An ionic, water-soluble iodinated contrast agent used for radiographic imaging of blood vessels and urinary or biliary structures. It is now less commonly used than newer agents; serious allergic-like reactions and kidney or thyroid effects are possible, so administration requires appropriate clinical screening and monitoring.

name: iothalamic acid
clinical_significance: An iodinated aromatic acid used as the active contrast component in older radiographic agents, often supplied as sodium or meglumine salts. These agents made vessels and organs visible on X-rays but have largely been superseded; adverse reactions to iodinated contrast remain clinically relevant.

name: ioxaglic acid
clinical_significance: An older iodinated contrast medium used for radiographic imaging, including selected angiographic and urinary-tract studies. It has largely been superseded by newer agents, but its history is relevant when assessing prior contrast reactions.

name: ipilimumab
clinical_significance: An immunotherapy antibody that blocks CTLA-4, removing a brake on T cells so they can attack cancer. It can cause immune inflammation in the bowel, skin, liver, lungs, hormone glands, or other organs.

name: ipratropium
clinical_significance: Ipratropium is an inhaled short-acting muscarinic antagonist that reduces vagally mediated bronchoconstriction and nasal secretion; it is used in COPD and acute asthma with bronchodilators.

name: ipsilateral
clinical_significance: On or affecting the same side of the body as a stated structure or injury. For example, weakness in the right arm and right leg is ipsilateral to a finding on the right side of the body; the opposite term is contralateral.

name: iratumumab
clinical_significance: An investigational monoclonal antibody, also called MDX-060, that targets CD30 on activated immune cells and some lymphomas. It has been studied as an anticancer treatment but is not an established or routinely approved therapy.

name: irbesartan
clinical_significance: Irbesartan is an angiotensin-II receptor blocker used for hypertension and diabetic kidney disease; it can cause hyperkalaemia, hypotension, and renal-function changes and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

name: iridium
clinical_significance: Iridium is a dense metal whose radioactive isotopes, especially iridium-192, are used in industrial testing and some medical brachytherapy.

name: iridocyclitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of both the iris and ciliary body, the structures at the front of the eye. It is a form of anterior uveitis and may cause pain, redness, light sensitivity, or blurred vision.

name: irinotecan
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy medicine that inhibits topoisomerase I and is used for colorectal and several other cancers.

name: irinotecan hydrochloride
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy medicine that blocks topoisomerase I and damages cancer-cell DNA, used for selected cancers with diarrhea and low blood counts possible.

name: iris
clinical_significance: The colored, muscular ring between the cornea and lens that controls the size of the pupil and therefore the amount of light entering the eye. Its muscles constrict the pupil in bright light and enlarge it in dim light.

name: iris cyst
clinical_significance: An iris cyst is a fluid-filled lesion on or within the iris, usually benign but sometimes affecting vision, pressure, or the appearance of the eye.

name: iris disease
clinical_significance: A disorder of the colored part of the eye, including inflammation, injury, infection, developmental abnormalities, or tumors.

name: iris melanoma
clinical_significance: Iris melanoma is a malignant tumor of pigment cells in the iris and may appear as a growing pigmented lesion, pupil distortion, or glaucoma.

name: iris neoplasm
clinical_significance: An iris neoplasm is an abnormal growth arising in the colored part of the eye; it may be benign or malignant and can affect vision or eye pressure.

name: iritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the iris, the colored part of the eye. It is a form of anterior uveitis and may cause eye pain, redness, light sensitivity, or blurred vision.

name: irofulven
clinical_significance: An investigational anticancer agent derived from a natural fungal toxin. It damages DNA and has been studied in clinical trials for selected cancers, but it is not an established or routinely approved treatment.

name: iron
clinical_significance: A mineral needed to make hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells, and to support muscles and cellular energy. Low iron may result from blood loss, poor intake, increased needs, or poor absorption.

name: iron deficiency
clinical_significance: A shortage of iron needed to make hemoglobin and support normal cell function. It may result from blood loss, low intake, increased needs, or poor absorption and can cause tiredness, pale skin, shortness of breath, brittle nails, or unusual cravings.

name: iron overload
clinical_significance: Excess iron stored in the body, which can damage the liver, heart, pancreas, joints, or endocrine organs.

name: irregular menstruation
clinical_significance: Menstrual bleeding that is unusually early, late, frequent, infrequent, prolonged, heavy, or unpredictable for the person’s age and reproductive context. Causes include pregnancy, ovulatory disorders, endocrine disease, medicines, structural lesions, and perimenopause.

name: irregular respiration
clinical_significance: An abnormal breathing pattern in rate, depth, rhythm, or pauses. It may occur with sleep disorders, metabolic disturbance, lung disease, drug effects, or neurologic injury and may be accompanied by cyanosis or reduced consciousness.

name: irrigation
clinical_significance: Flushing a wound, body cavity, or organ with fluid to remove blood, debris, microorganisms, or unwanted material.

name: irrigation solution
clinical_significance: A sterile or appropriately prepared liquid used to wash a wound, body cavity, organ, or surgical field. The solution must be suitable for the tissue because contamination, pressure injury, electrolyte shifts, or chemical irritation can cause harm.

name: irritable bowel syndrome
clinical_significance: A chronic disorder of gut--brain interaction causing recurrent abdominal pain with diarrhea, constipation, or both. Bloating and changes in stool may occur, but IBS does not cause intestinal inflammation or increase colorectal cancer risk. Evaluation uses symptom patterns and checks for other causes when indicated; rectal bleeding, unexplained weight loss, anemia, fever, or new symptoms later in life warrant assessment.

name: irritable mood
clinical_significance: A mood marked by increased sensitivity, impatience, anger, or a tendency to become upset easily.

name: Isaacs syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare peripheral nerve hyperexcitability disorder, also called acquired neuromyotonia. Continuous nerve activity can cause muscle twitching, cramps, stiffness, delayed relaxation, and excessive sweating. It may be autoimmune or associated with another disorder, including thymoma, so neurologic assessment and evaluation for associated conditions are important.

name: isazophos
clinical_significance: Isazophos is an organophosphate pesticide that can inhibit acetylcholinesterase and cause cholinergic toxicity after exposure.

name: ischemia
clinical_significance: Reduced blood flow causing too little oxygen for a tissue’s needs. It can cause pain, impaired function, permanent injury, or tissue death and may affect the heart, brain, limbs, or bowel.

name: ischemic preconditioning
clinical_significance: An intrinsic cardioprotective phenomenon in which brief, sub-lethal episodes of myocardial ischemia and reperfusion render the myocardium resistant to subsequent prolonged, potentially lethal ischemic insult, significantly reducing ultimate infarct size.

name: ischemic stroke
clinical_significance: A medical emergency caused by blockage of blood flow to part of the brain. Sudden face or limb weakness, speech difficulty, vision loss, imbalance, or confusion needs emergency response even if it improves, because time-sensitive treatment may limit brain injury.

name: ischium
clinical_significance: The lower, back part of each hip bone. Its rounded lower area bears weight when sitting, and nearby parts provide attachment for the hamstring muscles and other pelvic structures.

name: ishak score
clinical_significance: A scoring system used on a liver biopsy to describe inflammation and scarring, especially in chronic hepatitis. Higher scores generally indicate more extensive damage, but the result must be interpreted with other tests and the person’s history.

name: islet cell
clinical_significance: A cell in a pancreatic islet that helps control blood glucose; beta cells make insulin and alpha cells make glucagon.

name: isoantibodies
clinical_significance: Antibodies made against antigens from another individual of the same species, such as antibodies involved in blood-group incompatibility.

name: isoantigen
clinical_significance: An antigen that differs between individuals of the same species and can trigger an immune response after exposure.

name: isocarboxazid
clinical_significance: Isocarboxazid is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor used for depression; it has important interactions with other medicines and tyramine-rich foods.

name: isochromosomes
clinical_significance: Abnormal chromosomes with two identical arms caused by division across the wrong axis of the centromere.

name: isocyanate
clinical_significance: A reactive chemical group found in some industrial products; exposure can irritate the airways and cause occupational asthma or skin reactions.

name: isoelectric point
clinical_significance: The acidity level at which a molecule, especially a protein, has no overall electrical charge. This property affects how the molecule dissolves and moves in laboratory tests.

name: isoetharine
clinical_significance: An older short-acting beta-adrenergic bronchodilator formerly inhaled to relieve wheezing in asthma and other obstructive lung disease. It has largely been replaced by newer medicines; tremor, fast heartbeat, and abnormal heart rhythms are possible adverse effects.

name: isofenphos
clinical_significance: A poisonous organophosphate insecticide. Exposure can cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, diarrhea, small pupils, muscle twitching, breathing difficulty, seizures, or weakness because it disrupts nerve signals.

name: isoflavone
clinical_significance: A group of plant compounds, especially in soy and other legumes, that can interact weakly with estrogen receptors. They are studied for possible effects on menopausal symptoms, bone health, and cancer risk, but supplement benefits and risks are not established for treating disease.

name: isoflurane
clinical_significance: Isoflurane is an inhaled anesthetic used to maintain general anesthesia; it can lower blood pressure and depress breathing.

name: isoflurophate
clinical_significance: An organophosphate compound that irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase. It has been used as a laboratory reagent and studied historically in ophthalmology, but exposure can cause severe cholinergic poisoning with secretions, muscle weakness, seizures, and breathing failure.

name: isogeneic graft
clinical_significance: A transplant between genetically identical individuals, such as identical twins, so immune rejection risk is relatively low.

name: isolate compound
clinical_significance: The laboratory process of separating a specific chemical substance from a mixture so it can be identified, tested, or used in further research. Purity and contamination matter in drug development and analysis; the phrase does not name a clinical test or treatment.

name: isoleucine
clinical_significance: An essential amino acid obtained from food that helps build proteins, support energy production, maintain muscle, and repair body tissues.

name: isomerase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that rearranges atoms within a molecule to form an isomer. Isomerases participate in metabolism, and inherited defects in related pathways can cause metabolic disease.

name: isoniazid
clinical_significance: Isoniazid is a first-line antituberculous drug that inhibits mycolic-acid synthesis in Mycobacterium tuberculosis; hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy are important risks, and pyridoxine is often given.

name: isoprenylation
clinical_significance: A post-translational modification that attaches an isoprenoid lipid group to a protein, helping direct it to cell membranes and signaling partners. Abnormal protein prenylation is studied in cancer and other diseases, but the modification itself is not a routine clinical marker.

name: isoprocarb
clinical_significance: Isoprocarb is a carbamate insecticide that can cause cholinergic poisoning if swallowed or absorbed in a significant amount.

name: isopropyl alcohol
clinical_significance: A volatile alcohol used as a disinfectant and solvent. Ingestion can cause rapid intoxication, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypotension, and coma; management is supportive and differs from treatment of methanol or ethylene-glycol poisoning.

name: isoprostane
clinical_significance: A prostaglandin-like molecule formed when free radicals oxidize fatty acids in cell membranes. Isoprostanes are used mainly in research as indicators of oxidative stress; they are not established routine tests for diagnosing a specific disease.

name: isoproterenol
clinical_significance: Isoproterenol, also called isoprenaline, is a beta-adrenergic medicine that increases heart rate and contractility and is used in selected emergency settings.

name: isoquinolines
clinical_significance: A broad chemical family with a fused benzene and nitrogen-containing ring. Isoquinoline derivatives occur in medicines and natural products, but their effects differ widely; clinical significance depends on the individual compound.

name: isosorbide
clinical_significance: Isosorbide is a nitrate medicine that relaxes blood vessels and is used mainly to prevent or relieve angina; headache and low blood pressure are common adverse effects.

name: isosorbide dinitrate
clinical_significance: A nitrate medicine that widens blood vessels and reduces the heart’s workload. It is used mainly to prevent angina attacks; headache, dizziness, and low blood pressure may occur, and it can interact dangerously with erectile-dysfunction medicines.

name: isospora
clinical_significance: An older name for a group of intestinal coccidian parasites, now generally classified as Cystoisospora. Infection can cause watery diarrhea, especially in people with weakened immunity.

name: isospora belli
clinical_significance: The former name for Cystoisospora belli, a parasite spread by swallowing oocysts in contaminated food or water. It causes watery diarrhea, cramps, nausea, and weight loss and can be severe or prolonged in immunocompromised people.

name: isosporiasis
clinical_significance: Older name for Cystoisosporiasis, an intestinal infection caused by the parasite Cystoisospora belli.

name: iso-sulfan blue
clinical_significance: A blue dye used to map lymphatic drainage or identify sentinel lymph nodes during selected surgical procedures.

name: isothiocyanate
clinical_significance: Isothiocyanate is a sulfur-containing chemical group found in compounds formed when certain plants, especially cruciferous vegetables, are cut or chewed. Some isothiocyanates are studied for effects on cancer-related pathways, but this research does not establish them as cancer treatments or supplements for prevention.

name: isothiocyanates
clinical_significance: Isothiocyanates are sulfur-containing compounds formed from glucosinolates in cruciferous vegetables. They are studied for possible effects on cancer-related pathways, but evidence does not establish concentrated supplements as cancer prevention or treatment.

name: isotonic exercise
clinical_significance: Exercise in which muscles change length while producing force against a relatively constant load, as in lifting or lowering a weight.

name: isotonic solution
clinical_significance: A solution with an effective osmotic concentration close to that of plasma, such as normal saline or balanced crystalloid. Isotonic fluids may expand extracellular volume, but choice and amount must be tailored because excess can cause fluid overload or electrolyte disturbance.

name: isotope
clinical_significance: One of two or more atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

name: isotretinoin
clinical_significance: A vitamin-A-related medicine used for severe acne that has not improved with other treatment. It reduces skin-oil production and clogged pores but can cause birth defects, so pregnancy prevention and regular medical monitoring are essential.

name: isoxsuprine
clinical_significance: Isoxsuprine is a vasodilating medicine that has been used in some countries for circulatory symptoms or to delay preterm labor, although evidence and approval vary. The U.S. FDA found evidence insufficient for its marketed indications and required U.S. products to stop distribution; it can cause low blood pressure, fast heartbeat, or dizziness.

name: isozyme
clinical_significance: One of several molecular forms of an enzyme that catalyze the same reaction but differ in structure, tissue distribution, or regulation.

name: ispaghula husk
clinical_significance: Ispaghula husk, or psyllium, is a soluble fiber that absorbs water and helps regulate stool consistency; adequate fluid is important when using it.

name: ispinesib
clinical_significance: Ispinesib is an investigational anticancer drug that blocks kinesin spindle protein, a motor protein needed for cell division. It has been studied in clinical trials but is not an established standard cancer treatment.

name: isradipine
clinical_significance: Isradipine is a calcium-channel blocker used to lower blood pressure; it may cause flushing, headache, ankle swelling, or dizziness.

name: itraconazole
clinical_significance: Itraconazole is a triazole antifungal that inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis and treats several superficial and systemic mycoses; absorption, extensive drug interactions, liver injury, and negative inotropic effects require attention.

name: ivabradine
clinical_significance: Ivabradine slows the heart rate by acting on the sinus node and is used for selected patients with chronic heart failure or stable angina.

name: ivermectin
clinical_significance: An antiparasitic medicine used for selected worm and mite infections, including strongyloidiasis, onchocerciasis, and scabies, when prescribed appropriately.

name: ixabepilone
clinical_significance: Ixabepilone is a chemotherapy medicine used for some advanced breast cancers; important risks include nerve damage, low blood counts, and allergic reactions.

name: Janus kinase
clinical_significance: One of a family of proteins inside cells that pass signals from hormones and immune chemicals. Janus kinases help control inflammation, blood-cell production, and immune responses.

name: japanese encephalitis
clinical_significance: A viral infection spread by mosquitoes that can inflame the brain. Most infections cause no symptoms, but severe illness can cause fever, confusion, seizures, movement problems, or lasting disability.

name: jaundice
clinical_significance: Yellowish pigmentation of the skin, sclerae, and mucous membranes caused by elevated levels of circulating bilirubin in the blood. Etiologies include pre-hepatic hemolytic processes, intra-hepatic hepatocellular injury (hepatitis, cirrhosis), or post-hepatic biliary obstruction (gallstones, strictures, neoplasms).

name: jaw
clinical_significance: The upper and lower bony structures of the mouth—the maxilla and mandible—which support the teeth and contribute to chewing, speech, facial shape, and the oral airway.

name: jaw fracture
clinical_significance: A break in the lower jawbone or upper jawbone, usually after a blow to the face. Signs may include pain, swelling, loose teeth, numbness, a changed bite, or difficulty opening the mouth. Severe breaks can block the airway, especially when the lower jaw is broken in the front on both sides. Treatment may require realignment, wiring, plates, or surgery.

name: jaw neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the upper or lower jawbone or nearby tissues. It may be a cyst, a benign tumor, or cancer and can cause swelling, pain, loose teeth, numbness, or bone destruction.

name: jeb protocol
clinical_significance: JEB is a chemotherapy combination of carboplatin, etoposide, and bleomycin used for selected malignant germ-cell tumors in children. It can suppress bone marrow and cause infection or bleeding risk; bleomycin can injure the lungs, so treatment requires specialist monitoring.

name: jejunal atresia
clinical_significance: A condition present at birth in which part of the jejunum, a section of the small intestine, is closed or missing. It causes bowel blockage in a newborn, with green vomiting, a swollen abdomen, and failure to pass the first stool.

name: jejunal fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal connection involving the jejunum and another organ, the skin, or a body surface. It may cause intestinal contents to leak, infection, malnutrition, dehydration, or sepsis.

name: jejunal hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from the jejunum, the middle segment of the small intestine, which may cause maroon or black stool, anemia, abdominal pain, or shock depending on its rate and cause.

name: jejunal neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the jejunum, the middle part of the small intestine. It may be benign or cancerous and can cause pain, bleeding, anemia, vomiting, blockage, or weight loss.

name: jejunal stenosis
clinical_significance: Narrowing of the jejunal lumen that can impede intestinal contents and cause cramping, vomiting, distension, malabsorption, or obstruction; causes include Crohn disease, adhesions, tumors, and ischemic injury.

name: jejunal ulcer
clinical_significance: An ulcerated break in the lining of the jejunum, caused by inflammation, infection, ischemia, medicines, tumor, or anastomotic disease and potentially producing pain, bleeding, or perforation.

name: jejunum
clinical_significance: The middle part of the small intestine. It absorbs much of the nutrients from food before the remaining contents pass into the ileum.

name: jeotgalibacillus
clinical_significance: Jeotgalibacillus is a genus of salt-tolerant bacteria described mainly from marine or fermented-food environments. It is not an established cause of human disease; its significance in clinical specimens would need interpretation with the patient’s findings and microbiology results.

name: job satisfaction
clinical_significance: Job satisfaction is a measure of how a person evaluates their work. It is relevant to occupational wellbeing and may be associated with stress, burnout, and mental health, but it is not a medical diagnosis.

name: job syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited immune disorder causing eczema, repeated skin and lung infections, and very high levels of an allergy-related antibody. Dental, bone, and facial differences may also occur.

name: johnsonella
clinical_significance: Johnsonella is a genus of anaerobic bacteria found in the human mouth, especially the gingival crevice. Detection in a clinical sample may relate to oral or periodontal microbial communities, but the organism alone does not establish infection.

name: johnsonella ignava
clinical_significance: Johnsonella ignava is an anaerobic bacterium first described from the human gingival crevice. It is part of oral microbial communities; its presence alone does not establish periodontal disease or another infection.

name: joint
clinical_significance: The place where two or more bones meet. Joints may be fixed, slightly movable, or freely movable, such as the knee, hip, or shoulder.

name: joint capsule
clinical_significance: A tough envelope surrounding a freely movable joint. Its inner lining makes slippery fluid that helps the joint move, while the capsule helps hold the bones together and provides stability.

name: joint contracture
clinical_significance: Permanent or long-lasting limitation of joint movement caused by tightening or scarring of muscles, tendons, ligaments, the joint capsule, skin, or nearby tissues. It may follow immobility, injury, burns, inflammation, or nerve disease.

name: joint prosthesis
clinical_significance: An artificial joint implanted to replace a damaged or painful joint and improve movement. Complications can include infection, loosening, wear, instability, or dislocation; persistent pain, swelling, or reduced function may require assessment.

name: joint stiffness
clinical_significance: Reduced ease or range of joint movement, often worse after rest. Causes include arthritis, injury, inflammation, prolonged immobility, or muscle and tendon disorders. It may occur with swelling, redness, fever, severe pain, or inability to use the joint.

name: judgement impaired
clinical_significance: Impaired judgment is reduced ability to weigh information, consequences, or risk when making decisions. It can occur with intoxication, delirium, dementia, brain injury, or some mental disorders and may affect safety; it is a finding, not a diagnosis by itself.

name: judgment
clinical_significance: Judgment is the ability to weigh information, likely consequences, and risks when making decisions. Changes can occur with brain disorders, mental illness, or substance effects and are interpreted alongside a person’s usual abilities and circumstances.

name: jugular foramen
clinical_significance: An opening at the base of the skull through which a major neck vein and several nerves pass. Disease in this area can cause difficulty swallowing, hoarseness, shoulder weakness, hearing symptoms, or other neurologic problems.

name: jugular vein
clinical_significance: A major vein that carries blood from the head, face, and neck back to the heart. Each side has an internal jugular vein and an external jugular vein.

name: jumping gene
clinical_significance: A jumping gene, or transposable element, is a DNA sequence that can move or copy itself to new positions in a genome. Such elements can alter gene function or regulation and are important in genetic variation and research on some cancers and inherited disorders.

name: junctional nevus
clinical_significance: A usually benign, often flat mole formed by pigment cells at the junction between the outer and deeper layers of skin. It may change in size, shape, color, or symptoms.

name: juvenile arthritis
clinical_significance: A general term for inflammatory joint disease beginning in childhood. It may cause persistent swelling, pain, stiffness, reduced movement, fever, rash, or eye inflammation; the subtype determines monitoring and treatment.

name: juvenile astrocytoma
clinical_significance: A tumor arising from support cells in a child’s or adolescent’s brain or spinal cord. Many grow slowly, but symptoms depend on location and may include headache, seizures, vision changes, weakness, balance problems, or hormone disturbances.

name: juvenile delinquency
clinical_significance: Juvenile delinquency refers to unlawful behavior by a minor and is a legal and social term, not a medical diagnosis. Adversity, trauma, mental illness, substance use, or neurodevelopmental conditions may affect risk for some young people and can warrant supportive assessment.

name: juvenile hormones
clinical_significance: Juvenile hormones are insect hormones that regulate growth, metamorphosis, and reproduction. They are not human hormones; related compounds are used in some pest-control strategies because they disrupt insect development.

name: juvenile osteoporosis
clinical_significance: Low bone strength during childhood or adolescence that increases the risk of fractures. It may occur on its own or result from chronic illness, poor nutrition, hormone disorders, limited mobility, or medicines.

name: juvenile xanthogranuloma
clinical_significance: A rare, usually harmless growth of immune cells in the skin of an infant or young child, appearing as a firm red, yellow, or brown bump. It often fades without treatment, but rarely affects the eye or internal organs.

name: juxtaglomerular apparatus
clinical_significance: A group of specialized kidney cells that senses blood flow and salt levels and releases renin. It helps regulate blood pressure, blood volume, and the body’s salt balance.

name: Kallmann syndrome
clinical_significance: An inherited condition that causes delayed or absent puberty and a reduced or absent sense of smell. It occurs when the brain does not send the hormone signals needed to start puberty.

name: kanamycin
clinical_significance: An antibiotic used for some serious bacterial infections. It can permanently damage hearing and harm the kidneys, especially with prolonged or high-dose use.

name: Kaposi's sarcoma
clinical_significance: A vascular tumor associated with human herpesvirus 8, also called Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus. It may cause purple, red, or brown lesions of the skin or oral mucosa and can involve lymph nodes or internal organs; it is more likely or aggressive when immunity is weakened, such as with HIV infection or after organ transplantation.

name: Kartagener syndrome
clinical_significance: An inherited condition in which tiny hair-like structures that clear mucus do not work properly. It causes repeated sinus and lung infections and may place the internal organs in a reversed position.

name: karyomegaly
clinical_significance: Abnormal enlargement of a cell’s nucleus, the part that contains most of its genetic material. It may occur with injury, infection, toxic exposure, tissue repair, or cancer and is interpreted with other findings.

name: karyometry
clinical_significance: Karyometry is the quantitative measurement of cell-nucleus features, such as size and chromatin pattern, usually in tissue samples. It is used mainly in research and some image-analysis studies of tissue change; it is not by itself a standard standalone diagnosis.

name: karyotype result
clinical_significance: A laboratory report describing the number and visible structure of a person’s chromosomes. It may identify some chromosome differences, such as an extra chromosome, but a normal result does not exclude all genetic disorders.

name: kava
clinical_significance: A plant-derived product traditionally used in the Pacific and marketed for anxiety or relaxation. It can cause sedation, drug interactions, and serious liver injury and should not be treated as risk-free because it is herbal.

name: Kearns-Sayre syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder affecting the mitochondria, the parts of cells that make energy. It usually begins in childhood or young adulthood and can cause drooping or limited eye movement, vision problems, heart-rhythm problems, and muscle weakness.

name: kegel
clinical_significance: A pelvic-floor muscle contraction exercise used to improve pelvic-floor strength and control of selected types of urinary or fecal incontinence.

name: keloid
clinical_significance: A raised, firm scar that grows beyond the edges of the original wound because the body makes too much scar tissue. It may itch or hurt and can develop after surgery, injury, burns, or piercings.

name: keratan sulfate
clinical_significance: A complex sugar found mainly in the clear front of the eye, cartilage, and brain. In some inherited disorders it cannot be broken down properly and builds up, damaging the eyes, bones, or other tissues.

name: keratectomy
clinical_significance: Removal or reshaping of part of the cornea, the clear front surface of the eye. It may be done to correct vision or remove abnormal tissue, and it can affect eyesight.

name: keratin
clinical_significance: A strong structural protein forming much of the skin’s outer layer, hair, nails, and other protective tissues. It helps resist water loss, friction, chemicals, and physical injury.

name: keratinocyte
clinical_significance: The main type of cell in the outer layer of skin. It produces keratin and helps form the skin barrier that limits water loss and protects against injury and infection.

name: keratitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the cornea, the clear front layer of the eye. It may result from infection, injury, contact-lens wear, or other eye conditions and can cause pain, redness, tearing, light sensitivity, blurred vision, or corneal clouding.

name: keratoacanthoma
clinical_significance: A fast-growing, dome-shaped skin growth with a central plug, usually on sun-exposed skin. It may look like a type of skin cancer, so a clinician often removes or samples it. Treatment depends on its appearance, size, site, and the test results.

name: keratoconjunctivitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the cornea and the conjunctiva, the clear surface covering the white of the eye. Infection, allergy, dryness, immune disease, or chemical injury may cause redness, pain, discharge, light sensitivity, and blurred vision.

name: keratoconjunctivitis sicca
clinical_significance: Long-lasting dryness and inflammation of the eye’s front surface, commonly called dry-eye disease. It can cause burning, grittiness, redness, fluctuating vision, or light sensitivity because too few tears are made or tears evaporate too quickly.

name: keratoconus
clinical_significance: A usually bilateral but often asymmetric corneal ectasia in which the central or paracentral cornea progressively thins and steepens, forming a cone-like shape. It can cause irregular astigmatism, blurred or distorted vision, glare, and light sensitivity. Glasses or contact lenses may improve vision; corneal collagen cross-linking can slow progression.

name: keratocyte count
clinical_significance: An estimate of the number of living support cells in the middle layer of the cornea. It can help assess corneal health, injury, disease, or changes after eye surgery, although results are interpreted with the complete eye examination.

name: keratoplasty
clinical_significance: Surgery to replace or reshape part or all of the cornea, the clear front surface of the eye. It can restore vision after corneal damage, but healing problems, infection, and rejection of donor tissue are possible.

name: keratosis
clinical_significance: A thickened, rough, or otherwise abnormal area of skin caused by excess keratin. Some forms are harmless, while others result from infection, inflammation, sun damage, or a change that can precede skin cancer.

name: keratosis follicularis
clinical_significance: Darier disease causes a chronic inherited skin disorder with fragile, crusted papules and sometimes nail or mucosal changes; heat, infection, and friction can trigger flares.

name: keratosis pilaris
clinical_significance: A common, harmless skin condition that causes small, rough bumps around hair follicles, usually on the upper arms, thighs, buttocks, or face.

name: kernicterus
clinical_significance: Permanent brain damage caused by very high levels of bilirubin, a yellow substance that builds up during severe newborn jaundice. It can cause movement problems, hearing loss, problems looking upward, and damage to tooth enamel.

name: kerstersia gyiorum
clinical_significance: Kerstersia gyiorum is a rare Gram-negative bacterium reported in occasional human infections, including respiratory, ear, urinary, wound, and bloodstream infections. It may be difficult to identify with routine methods, so laboratory confirmation and clinical context matter.

name: ketamine
clinical_significance: Ketamine is a dissociative anaesthetic and NMDA-receptor antagonist used for anaesthesia, procedural sedation, and selected treatment-resistant depression; emergence reactions, increased blood pressure, nausea, misuse, and respiratory complications are possible.

name: ketamine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: Ketamine hydrochloride is a dissociative anesthetic used for anesthesia, procedural sedation, and selected pain or depression treatments; it can cause increased blood pressure, hallucinations, and impaired coordination.

name: ketanserin
clinical_significance: Ketanserin is a serotonin 5-HT2 receptor blocker that was studied and used in some settings for high blood pressure. It can prolong the QT interval and has been associated with serious rhythm disturbances, limiting its use.

name: keto acid
clinical_significance: A chemical made when the body breaks down certain amino acids or other nutrients. Keto acids can be used to make energy or new substances, but abnormal amounts may occur in metabolic disease.

name: ketoconazole
clinical_significance: Ketoconazole is an imidazole antifungal that inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis; topical forms treat superficial mycoses, while oral use is restricted because of potentially severe liver injury, adrenal suppression, and drug interactions.

name: ketone
clinical_significance: A type of chemical compound. In medicine, the term often refers to ketone bodies made when the body uses fat for energy; small amounts can be normal, but high levels may cause ketoacidosis.

name: ketone bodies
clinical_significance: Ketone bodies are chemicals made mainly by the liver when the body uses fat for energy, especially during fasting or low carbohydrate availability. Small amounts can be normal, but excessive accumulation can cause ketoacidosis, particularly in diabetes or severe illness.

name: ketonuria
clinical_significance: Ketonuria is the presence of ketone bodies in urine, occurring with fasting, vomiting, low-carbohydrate intake, pregnancy, or uncontrolled diabetes; marked ketonuria with hyperglycaemia may indicate diabetic ketoacidosis.

name: ketoprofen
clinical_significance: A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug that inhibits cyclo-oxygenase and reduces pain, inflammation, and fever; gastrointestinal bleeding, kidney injury, cardiovascular events, and hypersensitivity are important risks.

name: ketorolac
clinical_significance: A potent non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesic used for short-term management of moderate-to-severe acute pain; treatment duration is restricted because gastrointestinal bleeding, kidney injury, and impaired healing can occur.

name: ketorolac tromethamine
clinical_significance: The tromethamine salt of ketorolac, a potent non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesic used short term for moderate-to-severe acute pain; it is contraindicated in several bleeding, renal, pregnancy, and perioperative situations.

name: ketosis
clinical_significance: A state in which the body makes and uses increased amounts of ketones after breaking down fat for energy. It can occur during fasting or a low-carbohydrate diet, but high ketone levels with illness or high blood sugar may signal diabetic ketoacidosis.

name: ketotic hypoglycemia
clinical_significance: Low blood sugar accompanied by ketones, usually after a young child has gone without food or has been ill and unable to eat. Drowsiness, weakness, vomiting, or seizures may occur. Repeated episodes can have other causes.

name: ketotifen
clinical_significance: An antihistamine with mast-cell-stabilizing activity used in some countries for allergic disorders and, in ophthalmic form, allergic conjunctivitis; drowsiness, increased appetite, and irritation may occur.

name: kidney
clinical_significance: One of two bean-shaped organs that filter waste from the blood into urine. The kidneys also help control body water, salts, blood pressure, and the balance of acids in the blood.

name: kidney calculi
clinical_significance: Kidney stones can obstruct urine flow and cause severe colicky pain, bleeding, infection, or kidney injury; fever with obstruction is an emergency.

name: kidney function tests
clinical_significance: Blood and urine tests used to assess how well the kidneys remove waste and control fluid and salts. Common measures include creatinine, estimated filtration rate, urine protein, and urinalysis.

name: kidney neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the kidney that may be noncancerous or cancerous. It may cause blood in the urine, pain, a lump, weight loss, or no symptoms; imaging and sometimes biopsy identify its type and extent.

name: kidney transplantation
clinical_significance: Placement of a donor kidney to replace the filtering work of kidneys that have permanently failed. A living-donor kidney may work sooner, but all recipients need lifelong medicines and monitoring for rejection, infection, blood-vessel problems, and return of kidney disease.

name: Kienbock disease
clinical_significance: Damage and gradual collapse of the lunate, a small bone in the wrist, because its blood supply is reduced. It may cause wrist pain, swelling, stiffness, and weaker grip. Treatment depends on bone damage, wrist alignment, symptoms, and whether arthritis has developed.

name: kilobecquerel
clinical_significance: A unit of radioactive activity equal to 1,000 becquerels, used to describe how many nuclear decays occur per second in a sample or radiopharmaceutical.

name: kilocalorie
clinical_significance: A unit of energy equal to 1,000 small calories; the dietary Calorie, written with a capital C, is one kilocalorie.

name: kilodalton
clinical_significance: A unit of molecular mass equal to 1,000 daltons, commonly used to describe the size of proteins and other large molecules in laboratory research and testing.

name: kilogram
clinical_significance: The SI unit of mass. Body weight is often recorded in kilograms, and some medicine doses are calculated from body mass.

name: kilointernational unit
clinical_significance: A unit equal to 1,000 international units, used for the measured biological activity of some medicines, hormones, and vitamins. The substance and assay must be specified because international units are not a common mass unit.

name: kilojoule
clinical_significance: The SI unit of energy, equal to 1,000 joules; approximately 4.184 kilojoules equal one kilocalorie.

name: kilometer
clinical_significance: A unit of distance equal to 1,000 meters. It may be used to record walking or travel distance in rehabilitation, exercise assessment, and public-health studies.

name: kilovolt peak
clinical_significance: A measure of the peak voltage applied across an X-ray tube, usually expressed in kilovolts peak (kVp). It affects X-ray beam energy and image contrast, while the complete imaging protocol determines patient radiation exposure.

name: Kimura disease
clinical_significance: A rare long-term immune disorder causing painless lumps under the skin, usually in the head or neck, enlarged nearby lymph nodes, and high levels of eosinophils or IgE. It can sometimes affect the kidneys.

name: kinesin
clinical_significance: Kinesins are motor proteins that transport cell material along microtubules and help move chromosomes during cell division. Their functions are studied in neurologic disease and cancer biology.

name: kinesis
clinical_significance: Kinesis is a change in an organism’s movement rate or turning in response to a stimulus, studied mainly in biology. It is not a clinical diagnosis or a measure of human movement by itself.

name: kinesthesis
clinical_significance: Kinesthesis is awareness of body movement and position, largely through sensory input from muscles and joints. It contributes to coordination and balance; impaired proprioceptive sensation can occur with nerve or spinal-cord disorders.

name: kinetochore
clinical_significance: The kinetochore is the chromosome structure that attaches to the spindle during cell division. Errors in attachment or chromosome separation can produce abnormal chromosome numbers and are studied in developmental disorders and cancer.

name: kinetosome
clinical_significance: A kinetosome, or basal body, anchors and organizes a cilium or flagellum. Abnormal basal-body function can disrupt ciliary movement and is relevant to research on ciliary disorders and infertility.

name: kingella
clinical_significance: Kingella is a genus of bacteria that can live in the mouth and can occasionally cause bloodstream, bone, joint, or heart-valve infections.

name: kingella denitrificans
clinical_significance: Kingella denitrificans is a rare bacterium found mainly in the upper airway; it can occasionally cause invasive infection.

name: kingella kingae
clinical_significance: Kingella kingae is a bacterium that can cause bone or joint infection, especially in young children, and can rarely cause endocarditis.

name: kingella oralis
clinical_significance: Kingella oralis is a mouth-associated bacterium that rarely causes invasive infection, including bloodstream infection or endocarditis.

name: kingella potus
clinical_significance: Kingella potus is a rare bacterium that has been associated with occasional human infections; clinical importance depends on the specimen and evidence of true infection.

name: kinin
clinical_significance: A short peptide, such as bradykinin, that widens blood vessels, increases vascular permeability, and contributes to pain and inflammation.

name: kininogenase
clinical_significance: A kininogenase is an enzyme that releases kinins, such as bradykinin, from kininogen proteins. This pathway contributes to blood-vessel dilation, swelling, pain, and inflammation.

name: kinocilium
clinical_significance: A specialized hair-like structure on certain sensory cells, especially in the inner ear. It helps the cell detect the direction of movement and contributes to balance and hearing signals.

name: kit device
clinical_significance: A kit device is a packaged collection of components used for a specific procedure or test. In healthcare, its clinical value and limitations depend on the intended use, instructions, and validation of the particular kit.

name: klatskin tumor
clinical_significance: A cancer arising where the right and left bile ducts join near the liver. It can block bile flow and cause jaundice, itching, pale stools, or weight loss.

name: klebsiella
clinical_significance: A genus of Gram-negative bacteria that can cause pneumonia, urinary-tract infection, bloodstream infection, and other healthcare-associated infections.

name: klebsiella oxytoca
clinical_significance: Klebsiella oxytoca is a bacterium that can cause urinary, bloodstream, wound, and hospital-acquired infections and can sometimes cause antibiotic-associated hemorrhagic colitis.

name: klebsiella pneumoniae
clinical_significance: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a bacterium that can cause pneumonia, urinary infection, bloodstream infection, and liver abscess; some strains are highly antibiotic-resistant.

name: klebsiella rhinoscleromatis
clinical_significance: Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis is a bacterium associated with rhinoscleroma, a rare, chronic granulomatous infection that mainly affects the nose and upper airway and can cause progressive obstruction and scarring.

name: klebsiella singaporensis
clinical_significance: Klebsiella singaporensis is a rare environmental bacterium that has occasionally been recovered from human clinical specimens; its significance depends on the specimen and symptoms.

name: klebsiella variicola
clinical_significance: Klebsiella variicola is a bacterium closely related to K. pneumoniae that can cause human infections, including bloodstream and urinary infections.

name: kleptomania
clinical_significance: A mental-health disorder involving recurrent inability to resist impulses to steal items that are not needed for personal use or monetary value. The acts are typically preceded by rising tension and followed by relief or gratification, and cause distress or impairment.

name: Klinefelter's syndrome
clinical_significance: Klinefelter syndrome can cause infertility, low testosterone, learning or language difficulties, and metabolic or bone risks; earlier diagnosis allows tailored hormone and developmental care.

name: klumpke paralysis
clinical_significance: A nerve injury affecting the lower part of the network that supplies the arm and hand. It can cause severe hand weakness, numbness along the inner forearm and hand, and occasionally drooping of the eyelid and a smaller pupil on one side.

name: kluyvera
clinical_significance: A genus of gram-negative bacteria in the Enterobacterales group; species can rarely cause opportunistic human infections.

name: kluyvera ascorbata
clinical_significance: A gram-negative Kluyvera species found in the environment and occasionally associated with urinary, bloodstream, or other opportunistic infections.

name: kluyvera cryocrescens
clinical_significance: A gram-negative environmental bacterium that rarely causes opportunistic human infection.

name: kluyvera georgiana
clinical_significance: A rarely encountered Gram-negative Kluyvera species that may appear in clinical samples. It can occasionally cause opportunistic infection, especially in people with serious illness, weakened defenses, or invasive medical devices.

name: kluyvera intermedia
clinical_significance: A Gram-negative bacterium occasionally found in human samples and rarely causing opportunistic urinary, wound, bloodstream, or other infections.

name: kluyveromyces
clinical_significance: Kluyveromyces is a genus of yeasts used in food fermentation and biotechnology. Some species have rarely been reported in human infections, so recovery from a clinical specimen is interpreted in context.

name: kluyveromyces lactis
clinical_significance: Kluyveromyces lactis is a yeast used in dairy fermentation and biotechnology, including production of enzymes and proteins. It is not a common human pathogen.

name: kluyveromyces marxianus
clinical_significance: Kluyveromyces marxianus is a yeast found in fermented foods and used in food and industrial biotechnology. Rare human infections have been reported, particularly in people with serious underlying illness.

name: knee
clinical_significance: The synovial joint between the femur, tibia, and patella, stabilized by the cruciate and collateral ligaments and menisci; it permits flexion and extension and bears body weight.

name: knee joint
clinical_significance: The knee joint bears body weight and allows bending and straightening of the leg. Arthritis, ligament or meniscus injury, fractures, and infection can cause pain, swelling, instability, or loss of movement.

name: kniest dysplasia
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder of bone and cartilage growth that causes short stature, enlarged joints, unusual facial features, and progressive joint problems. Some people also develop serious eye, hearing, or breathing complications.

name: knoellia
clinical_significance: Knoellia is a genus of environmental bacteria. It has no established common role in human disease; its significance in a clinical culture depends on the specimen and evidence of infection.

name: knuckle pad
clinical_significance: A firm, usually painless thickening of skin and tissue over a finger joint. It is commonly related to repeated pressure or a fibrous tissue change and is generally harmless.

name: kocuria
clinical_significance: Kocuria is a genus of Gram-positive bacteria commonly found on skin and mucous membranes. It can rarely cause opportunistic infections, including bloodstream or catheter-related infection, especially in medically vulnerable patients; a culture alone may represent contamination.

name: kocuria rosea
clinical_significance: Kocuria rosea is a skin- and environment-associated bacterium that rarely causes opportunistic infection, including bloodstream or catheter-related infection. Its recovery from a sample must be assessed for contamination and supported by clinical findings.

name: kocuria varians
clinical_significance: Kocuria varians is a Gram-positive bacterium found on skin and in the environment. It has rarely been associated with invasive infections, so clinical significance depends on the specimen, repeat cultures, and the patient’s condition.

name: kodamaea ohmeri
clinical_significance: Kodamaea ohmeri is a rare yeast that can cause invasive infection, including bloodstream infection or endocarditis, particularly in hospitalized or immunocompromised people. It may be misidentified as Candida, so accurate laboratory identification can guide care.

name: Krabbe's disease
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which missing enzymes cause myelin loss, progressively damaging nerves and producing weakness, stiffness, vision problems, or developmental decline.

name: KRAS gene
clinical_significance: A gene that helps control cell growth and division. Certain changes can keep its growth signal switched on, contributing to cancers and affecting which targeted treatments are likely to work.

name: Krebs' cycle
clinical_significance: A series of chemical reactions in mitochondria that oxidizes acetyl-CoA and generates energy-rich molecules used for cellular energy production.

name: kringles
clinical_significance: Small folded parts of certain proteins that help them attach to other molecules. They are found in proteins involved in blood clot breakdown and in some growth signals.

name: krukenberg tumor
clinical_significance: An ovarian tumor caused by cancer that has spread from another organ, most often the stomach or digestive tract. It may cause abdominal swelling, pain, menstrual changes, or digestive symptoms.

name: Kupffer's cell
clinical_significance: A Kupffer cell is a resident macrophage lining the liver sinusoids; it removes microbes, damaged blood cells, and particles from portal blood and contributes to hepatic inflammation and iron handling.

name: kurthia
clinical_significance: Kurthia is a genus of bacteria found mainly in soil, food, and other environmental sources. It is not a common human pathogen; recovery from a patient sample needs interpretation for possible contamination or rare opportunistic infection.

name: kuru
clinical_significance: Kuru is a rare fatal prion disease historically associated with ritual cannibalism, causing progressive ataxia, tremor, and neurologic decline.

name: kynurenine
clinical_significance: A substance made when the body breaks down the amino acid tryptophan. It is involved in chemical signaling in the brain and immune system and may change during infection, inflammation, or some diseases.

name: kyphoplasty
clinical_significance: A minimally invasive procedure that uses a balloon to create space in a collapsed vertebral body and then injects bone cement to stabilize a painful compression fracture.

name: kyphosis
clinical_significance: An exaggerated forward curve of the upper spine, sometimes producing a rounded back. Causes include posture, osteoporosis and spinal fractures, growth disorders, arthritis, or inflammation. It may cause pain, weakness, or worsening curvature.

name: kytococcus
clinical_significance: A genus of gram-positive cocci found on skin and in the environment that can rarely cause opportunistic infection.

name: kytococcus sedentarius
clinical_significance: A skin-associated gram-positive coccus that produces enzymes linked to pitted keratolysis and can rarely cause invasive infection.

name: labetalol
clinical_significance: A medicine that lowers blood pressure by slowing the heart and relaxing blood vessels. It is also used for severe high blood pressure during pregnancy and may cause a slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, or breathing problems in people with asthma.

name: labium majus
clinical_significance: One of the paired outer folds of the vulva containing skin, connective tissue, glands, vessels, and nerves and protecting the more internal genital structures.

name: labium minus
clinical_significance: One of the paired inner folds of the vulva bordering the vestibule and helping protect the urethral and vaginal openings.

name: labor complication
clinical_significance: A maternal or fetal problem occurring during labor or delivery, such as abnormal labor progress, hemorrhage, infection, fetal distress, or malpresentation, requiring assessment and management based on the cause.

name: labor pain
clinical_significance: Pain caused by uterine contractions, cervical dilation, and stretching of pelvic tissues during labor; its intensity and management vary with labor stage and individual factors.

name: laboratory
clinical_significance: A facility or department where clinical specimens are examined using microbiologic, hematologic, chemical, molecular, or other diagnostic methods.

name: laboratory procedure
clinical_significance: A method used to collect, prepare, examine, or measure a patient sample such as blood, urine, tissue, or a swab. Results can help diagnose disease or guide treatment and must be interpreted with the clinical findings.

name: labradimil
clinical_significance: Labradimil is an experimental peptide studied for its ability to increase the passage of medicines across the blood–brain barrier. It is not an established treatment, and research has explored its use to deliver anticancer drugs to brain tumors.

name: labyrinth
clinical_significance: The inner-ear system that contains the cochlea for hearing and the balance organs that sense head movement and position. Disease or injury can cause dizziness, unsteadiness, ringing, or hearing loss.

name: labyrinth disorder
clinical_significance: A problem affecting inner-ear hearing or balance structures, potentially causing spinning sensations, nausea, unsteadiness, hearing changes, or abnormal eye movements.

name: labyrinthine membrane
clinical_significance: The delicate, fluid-containing system inside the inner ear that contains the organs for hearing and balance. Injury or abnormal fluid pressure can cause dizziness, hearing loss, or ringing in the ear.

name: lac operon
clinical_significance: The lac operon is a bacterial gene-control system that regulates lactose use in Escherichia coli. It is a foundational model in genetics and laboratory research, with no direct diagnostic significance by itself.

name: Laceration
clinical_significance: A torn wound caused by blunt or irregular force. It may involve only the skin or extend into fat, muscle, tendons, nerves, or blood vessels; deep, gaping, dirty, or heavily bleeding wounds need medical care.

name: lacosamide
clinical_significance: An antiseizure medicine used mainly for focal seizures. It may cause dizziness, double vision, poor coordination, or changes in the heart's electrical rhythm.

name: lacrimal apparatus
clinical_significance: The glands and passages that make, spread, and drain tears. It includes the tear gland, small openings near the inner eyelids, the tear sac, and the duct that drains tears into the nose.

name: lacrimal disease
clinical_significance: A disorder of the tear-producing or tear-draining system, including dry eye, dacryocystitis, obstruction, inflammation, or abnormal tearing.

name: lacrimal duct
clinical_significance: The lacrimal duct drains tears from the tear sac into the nose. Blockage can cause persistent tearing, recurrent discharge, or infection of the tear sac (dacryocystitis).

name: lacrimal gland
clinical_significance: One of two glands above the outer part of the eye that make the watery part of tears. The tears spread across the eye and then drain through passages near the inner corner.

name: lactam
clinical_significance: A ring-shaped chemical structure found in some medicines. Beta-lactam antibiotics use this structure to weaken bacterial cell walls, but allergies and bacterial resistance can limit their use.

name: lactase
clinical_significance: An enzyme in the small intestine that breaks lactose, the natural sugar in milk, into absorbable sugars. Low lactase can cause bloating, cramps, gas, diarrhea, or discomfort after dairy foods.

name: lactate
clinical_significance: A product of cellular metabolism measured in blood. An increased level may occur with strenuous exercise, impaired oxygen delivery, infection, medicines, liver disease, or other conditions and must be interpreted clinically.

name: lactate dehydrogenase
clinical_significance: An enzyme found in many body tissues. Its blood level may rise when cells are damaged, but the test does not identify the cause by itself.

name: lactation
clinical_significance: The production and release of breast milk after childbirth. Early milk, called colostrum, is followed by mature milk; hormones help make and release the milk.

name: lactation disorder
clinical_significance: A problem with making, releasing, or transferring breast milk after childbirth. Examples include low supply, excess milk, painful engorgement, mastitis, or difficulty with the baby’s latch; assessment considers both parent and infant.

name: lactic acid
clinical_significance: An organic acid produced during normal metabolism, especially when pyruvate is converted to lactate. Blood lactate may rise for many reasons, including impaired oxygen delivery, strenuous exercise, or medicines.

name: lactic acidosis
clinical_significance: Metabolic acidosis associated with increased lactate production or reduced lactate clearance. Causes include impaired tissue oxygen delivery, medicines, liver disease, seizures, and other disorders.

name: lactobacillaceae
clinical_significance: Lactobacillaceae is a family of lactic-acid-producing bacteria that includes organisms found in the gut, mouth, and vagina and strains used in fermented foods or probiotics. Rarely, members can cause invasive infection, especially in people with severe illness or impaired immunity.

name: lactobacillus
clinical_significance: A genus of bacteria that produces lactic acid and normally forms part of the healthy vaginal and intestinal microbiota; some species are used as probiotics.

name: lactobacillus acidophilus
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus acidophilus is a lactic-acid-producing bacterium used in some fermented foods and probiotic products. Evidence for benefits depends on the specific strain and condition; rare bloodstream infections have occurred, mainly in medically vulnerable people.

name: lactobacillus brevis
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus brevis, also called Levilactobacillus brevis, is found in fermented foods and some human microbial communities. It is not a routine cause of disease, though rare invasive infections by lactobacilli have been reported.

name: lactobacillus casei
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus casei, now classified as Lacticaseibacillus casei, is used in fermented foods and some probiotic products. Rare bloodstream and heart-valve infections have been reported, particularly in people with underlying illness; probiotic effects are strain-specific.

name: lactobacillus fermentum
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus fermentum, now classified as Limosilactobacillus fermentum, occurs in fermented foods and human microbial communities and has been studied as a probiotic. Benefits are strain- and condition-specific, and rare invasive infections by lactobacilli can occur.

name: lactobacillus gallinarum
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus gallinarum is a lactic-acid-producing bacterium originally described in birds and also found in some food or microbial studies. It has no established routine clinical use or common role in human disease.

name: lactobacillus gasseri
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus gasseri, now classified as Lactobacillus gasseri, is a lactic-acid-producing species found in the human gut and vaginal microbiota and studied in probiotics. Any claimed benefit depends on the strain and condition; rare infections have been reported.

name: lactobacillus jensenii
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus jensenii is a lactic-acid-producing bacterium that commonly contributes to the healthy vaginal microbiota. It is being studied in relation to protection against vaginal infection, but rare invasive infection can occur in medically vulnerable people.

name: lactobacillus johnsonii
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus johnsonii is a bacterium found in the human gut and used in some probiotic research. Its effects depend on the specific strain and condition; it has occasionally been linked to infection in clinical specimens.

name: lactobacillus oris
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus oris is a lactic-acid-producing bacterium associated with the human mouth. It is not a common pathogen, but lactobacilli can rarely cause invasive infection, so recovery from a normally sterile site should be assessed clinically.

name: lactobacillus paracasei
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus paracasei, now classified as Lacticaseibacillus paracasei, occurs in fermented foods and is used in some probiotic products. Effects are strain-specific, and rare bloodstream infections have been reported, mainly in medically vulnerable people.

name: lactobacillus rhamnosus
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus rhamnosus, now classified as Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus, is used in some probiotic products and has been studied for specific gastrointestinal conditions. Benefits depend on the strain; rare bloodstream infections, including probiotic-associated cases, have occurred in medically vulnerable people.

name: lactobacillus salivarius
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus salivarius, now classified as Ligilactobacillus salivarius, is found in the mouth and intestine and has been studied as a probiotic. Evidence is strain-specific, and lactobacilli can rarely cause invasive infection.

name: lactobacillus vaginalis
clinical_significance: Lactobacillus vaginalis is a lactic-acid-producing bacterium found in the vaginal microbiota. Its presence alone does not indicate disease; rare invasive infection by lactobacilli is possible in medically vulnerable people.

name: lactococcus
clinical_significance: Lactococcus is a genus of lactic-acid-producing bacteria used in dairy fermentation. Most species are not associated with human disease, but some, especially L. garvieae, have rarely caused endocarditis or other invasive infections.

name: lactococcus garvieae
clinical_significance: Lactococcus garvieae is a major pathogen of fish and a rare opportunistic cause of human infection, most often endocarditis but also bloodstream, urinary, or bone infection. Accurate identification and clinical context help distinguish infection from contamination.

name: lactococcus lactis
clinical_significance: Lactococcus lactis is widely used in dairy fermentation and has rarely caused human infections, including endocarditis and bloodstream infection. Its isolation from a clinical sample should be interpreted with symptoms and other evidence.

name: lactoferrin
clinical_significance: Lactoferrin is an iron-binding glycoprotein in milk and mucosal secretions that limits microbial iron access and contributes to innate immune defense.

name: lactone
clinical_significance: A lactone is a cyclic ester structure found in many natural compounds and medicines. The ring structure can affect a drug’s activity and how it is absorbed or metabolized; the term alone does not identify a particular treatment.

name: lactose
clinical_significance: The principal sugar in milk, composed of glucose and galactose. Lactase in the small intestine digests it.

name: lactose intolerance
clinical_significance: A condition in which the body cannot fully digest lactose, the sugar in milk and dairy products, because it does not make enough lactase. It may cause bloating, gas, abdominal pain, nausea, or diarrhea after consuming lactose.

name: lactulose
clinical_significance: A medicine that softens stool by drawing water into the bowel. It is also used to lower harmful ammonia levels in some people with severe liver disease. Gas and diarrhea can occur.

name: lacunar stroke
clinical_significance: A small ischemic stroke caused by blockage of a tiny artery deep in the brain, often producing weakness, numbness, clumsiness, or speech problems.

name: laetrile
clinical_significance: A semisynthetic amygdalin-related compound promoted as an alternative cancer treatment; credible evidence has not established anticancer benefit, and cyanide poisoning is a serious risk.

name: Lafora disease
clinical_significance: A rare inherited epilepsy that usually begins during adolescence and progressively worsens. Seizures, brief muscle jerks, visual symptoms, memory problems, and loss of physical or thinking abilities may occur.

name: lamellar body
clinical_significance: A small storage structure inside certain cells that contains layered fats. In lung cells, it stores and releases surfactant, the substance that helps keep the tiny air sacs open.

name: lamellar bone
clinical_significance: Mature bone made of organized layers of mineralized tissue. It forms most adult compact and spongy bone and provides strength while being continually remodeled.

name: lamellipodium
clinical_significance: A lamellipodium is a broad, sheet-like extension of a moving cell. It helps cells migrate and is studied in wound healing, immune-cell movement, and cancer invasion.

name: lamin
clinical_significance: A structural protein forming part of the nuclear lamina, which supports the inner surface of the cell nucleus.

name: lamina propria
clinical_significance: A thin layer of supporting tissue beneath the inner lining of organs such as the intestine, airways, and bladder. It contains small blood vessels, immune cells, glands, and connective tissue.

name: laminectomy
clinical_significance: An operation that removes part of a spinal bone to make more room for the spinal cord or nerves. It may be used for spinal narrowing, a tumor, or selected disk problems.

name: laminin
clinical_significance: A protein in the supporting framework around cells that helps cells attach to underlying tissue. It contributes to tissue structure, development, repair, and the filtering barrier in some organs.

name: lamivudine
clinical_significance: Lamivudine is a nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor used with other antiretrovirals for HIV and as an antiviral for chronic hepatitis B; resistance and rare lactic acidosis or hepatic complications require monitoring.

name: lamotrigine
clinical_significance: Lamotrigine is an antiseizure medicine that inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels and is also used for bipolar-maintenance treatment; rapid dose escalation increases the risk of serious rash including Stevens--Johnson syndrome.

name: landolt ring
clinical_significance: A ring-shaped symbol with a gap used to test visual sharpness. The person identifies which direction the gap faces; smaller symbols indicate better visual acuity.

name: Langerhans' cell
clinical_significance: An immune cell in the skin that captures foreign substances and helps activate T-cell responses.

name: Langerhans-cell histiocytosis
clinical_significance: A rare disorder in which abnormal immune cells collect in one or more organs, especially bone, skin, lungs, lymph nodes, or the pituitary gland. Symptoms depend on the organs involved and may include bone pain, rash, cough, or hormone problems.

name: language development
clinical_significance: The gradual development of understanding, sounds, words, grammar, and communication during childhood. Delays may be related to hearing loss, developmental conditions, neurologic disease, or limited language exposure.

name: language disorder
clinical_significance: A developmental or acquired impairment in understanding, producing, or using spoken, written, or signed language that affects communication and daily function.

name: laniquidar
clinical_significance: Laniquidar is an investigational inhibitor of P-glycoprotein, a cell transporter that can pump some medicines out of cells. It was studied as a way to address chemotherapy resistance but is not an established cancer treatment.

name: lanolin
clinical_significance: Lanolin is a waxy substance derived from sheep wool used as an emollient and in topical products; allergy or irritation can occur.

name: lanosterol
clinical_significance: Lanosterol is an intermediate in the body’s synthesis of cholesterol and other sterols. Its production pathway is relevant to cholesterol-lowering medicines and is studied in eye-lens biology, but lanosterol products are not established cataract treatments.

name: lansoprazole
clinical_significance: A medicine that strongly reduces stomach acid. It is used for heartburn, ulcers, and some H. pylori infections; long-term use may affect mineral or vitamin levels and infection risk.

name: lanthanum
clinical_significance: A chemical element whose carbonate salt can bind dietary phosphate and lower phosphate absorption in people with advanced kidney disease.
