clinical_significance: A medical record documents a person’s health history, findings, tests, diagnoses, medicines, and care. Accurate records support continuity, medication safety, and clinical decision-making while requiring privacy protections.

name: medicare
clinical_significance: Medicare is a U.S. federal health-insurance program, mainly for people aged 65 or older and some younger people with disabilities or specific conditions. Coverage and costs depend on eligibility and plan choices.

name: medication error
clinical_significance: A medication error is a preventable mistake in prescribing, dispensing, preparing, or using a medicine that may cause harm or inappropriate treatment. Medication reconciliation, clear communication, and reporting help reduce repeat errors.

name: medication management
clinical_significance: Medication management is the coordinated selection, use, review, and monitoring of medicines. It helps improve adherence, check effectiveness, identify interactions or side effects, and avoid duplicate or unnecessary treatment.

name: medicine
clinical_significance: A substance or treatment used to prevent, diagnose, relieve, or treat disease. Medicines may be prescription, over-the-counter, biological, or traditional, and all can have benefits, risks, and interactions.

name: meditation
clinical_significance: Meditation is a practice of intentionally directing attention, often toward the breath, a sensation, or an object, while observing thoughts without judgment. It may promote relaxation and stress management but does not replace indicated medical treatment.

name: medroxyprogesterone
clinical_significance: Medroxyprogesterone is a progestogen used for contraception, abnormal uterine bleeding, endometriosis, and hormone therapy; depot injections may cause irregular bleeding, weight change, delayed fertility return, and reduced bone density.

name: medroxyprogesterone acetate
clinical_significance: Medroxyprogesterone acetate is a synthetic progestin used in hormonal contraception, treatment of endometriosis or abnormal uterine bleeding, and hormone therapy. It suppresses ovulation and produces progestational effects; formulation-specific risks and contraindications apply.

name: medulla oblongata
clinical_significance: The lower part of the brainstem, joined to the spinal cord. It helps control breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing, vomiting, and other automatic functions.

name: medullary carcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer whose cells grow in broad groups and are surrounded by many immune cells. The term is used most often for cancers of the breast or thyroid, and its behavior depends on the organ and tumor findings.

name: medullary thyroid carcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer of hormone-producing thyroid cells that make calcitonin. It may occur alone or as part of an inherited syndrome; blood tests, imaging, and a biopsy help confirm it.

name: medulloblastoma
clinical_significance: A fast-growing cancer that usually begins in the cerebellum, the part of the brain involved in balance and coordination. It mainly affects children and may cause headache, vomiting, unsteady walking, or other neurologic problems.

name: medulloepithelioma
clinical_significance: A medulloepithelioma is a rare embryonal tumor arising most often from the nonpigmented ciliary epithelium of the eye in children. It may cause visual symptoms, neovascular glaucoma, or a visible mass and is treated according to its extent and pathology.

name: mefenamic acid
clinical_significance: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicine used for short-term pain, including menstrual pain. It can irritate or bleed from the stomach, affect kidney function, and increase cardiovascular risk, especially with prolonged use or in people with risk factors.

name: mefloquine
clinical_significance: Mefloquine is an antimalarial drug used for prevention and treatment of susceptible malaria. It has a long half-life but can cause neuropsychiatric, vestibular, and cardiac adverse effects, so patient-specific contraindications and warnings are important.

name: megabecquerel
clinical_significance: A megabecquerel (MBq) is a unit of radioactivity equal to one million nuclear disintegrations per second. It is used to state the activity of radiopharmaceuticals and other radioactive materials.

name: megacalycosis
clinical_significance: Megacalycosis is congenital, nonobstructive dilatation of the renal calyces, usually with otherwise preserved renal architecture and function. It is often incidental but must be distinguished from obstructive hydronephrosis.

name: megacolon
clinical_significance: Abnormal enlargement and dilation of the colon, which may be congenital, acquired, toxic, or inflammatory.

name: megakaryocyte
clinical_significance: A very large cell in the bone marrow that makes platelets, the small blood parts that help stop bleeding. It grows long extensions into nearby blood vessels, where pieces break off and enter the bloodstream as platelets.

name: megakaryocytopoiesis
clinical_significance: Megakaryocytopoiesis is the formation and maturation of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, followed by platelet production. It is regulated in large part by thrombopoietin and other hematopoietic signals.

name: megaloblastic anemia
clinical_significance: Anemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis, usually related to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, with abnormally large red blood cells.

name: megamonas
clinical_significance: Megamonas is a genus of anaerobic bacteria found mainly in the gut microbiota. Its clinical significance is still being studied; detection in stool or another specimen does not by itself indicate infection.

name: megamonas funiformis
clinical_significance: Megamonas funiformis is an anaerobic bacterium of the genus Megamonas, commonly associated with the intestinal microbiota. Its detection in a clinical specimen requires interpretation alongside symptoms, specimen quality, and other microbiologic findings.

name: megamonas hypermegale
clinical_significance: Megamonas hypermegale is an anaerobic bacterium in the genus Megamonas, primarily associated with the gastrointestinal microbiota. Its presence in a specimen is interpreted in relation to the site, clinical symptoms, and other microbiologic results.

name: megasphaera
clinical_significance: Megasphaera is a genus of anaerobic bacteria found in the oral cavity and gastrointestinal and genital microbiota. Species identification may be relevant in microbiome studies or when recovered from a clinical specimen.

name: megasphaera elsdenii
clinical_significance: Megasphaera elsdenii is an anaerobic bacterium found mainly in the rumen of cattle and other animals and can also occur in human gut microbiome studies. Its links to human disease remain under study and are not established as a cause of illness.

name: mega-trial
clinical_significance: A mega-trial is a very large clinical trial designed to detect effects that smaller studies may miss. Large sample size can improve precision but does not remove bias or make a poorly designed study reliable.

name: megestrol
clinical_significance: Megestrol is a synthetic progestin used in some settings to treat hormone-responsive cancers and, in certain formulations, anorexia or severe weight loss. It can cause glucocorticoid-like effects, thromboembolic risk, and adrenal suppression.

name: megestrol acetate
clinical_significance: Megestrol acetate is the acetate salt of the progestin megestrol. Depending on formulation and indication, it is used for advanced endometrial or breast cancer and for appetite stimulation in selected patients with severe weight loss.

name: meibomian glands
clinical_significance: Sebaceous glands in the eyelids that produce the oily layer of the tear film and help prevent tear evaporation.

name: Meige syndrome
clinical_significance: A movement disorder causing repeated involuntary eyelid squeezing and muscle spasms around the mouth, jaw, or tongue. Symptoms may worsen with stress, speaking, chewing, or touch.

name: Meigs syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare combination of a usually benign ovarian fibroma, fluid in the abdomen, and fluid around the lungs. The fluid often improves after the ovarian tumor is removed, but cancer and other causes must be excluded.

name: meiosis
clinical_significance: Meiosis is the cell division that produces eggs or sperm with half the usual chromosome number. Errors in meiosis can cause infertility, miscarriage, or chromosome conditions such as trisomy.

name: meiotic recombination
clinical_significance: Meiotic recombination is exchange of DNA between homologous chromosomes during meiosis, usually through crossing over. It creates new combinations of alleles and contributes to genetic variation.

name: melancholia
clinical_significance: An older term for severe depression, often describing pervasive sadness, loss of pleasure, psychomotor change, and biological symptoms.

name: melanin
clinical_significance: Melanin is a pigment produced by melanocytes that gives skin, hair, and eyes their colour and absorbs ultraviolet radiation; its amount and distribution influence pigmentation disorders and melanoma biology.

name: melanocyte
clinical_significance: A melanocyte is a pigment-producing cell derived from the neural crest. It makes melanin in specialized organelles called melanosomes and transfers the pigment to neighboring keratinocytes, helping protect skin from ultraviolet radiation.

name: melanocytic nevus
clinical_significance: A melanocytic nevus is a usually benign, localized proliferation of melanocytes that appears as a macule, papule, or nodule. Changes in size, color, border, or symptoms may require assessment for atypia or melanoma.

name: melanoma
clinical_significance: Melanoma is a malignant tumor of melanocytes, most often arising in skin but also in eye or mucosal sites; early detection matters because it can invade and metastasize.

name: melanophore
clinical_significance: A melanophore is a pigment-containing cell, especially one in lower vertebrates, whose melanin granules can disperse or aggregate to alter visible coloration. In mammals, melanocytes are the principal melanin-producing cells.

name: melanosome
clinical_significance: A melanosome is a specialized organelle in a melanocyte in which melanin is synthesized, stored, and transported. Melanosomes are transferred to keratinocytes and influence skin, hair, and eye pigmentation.

name: MELAS syndrome
clinical_significance: A mitochondrial disorder involving encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes, often beginning before adulthood and caused by pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variants.

name: melatonin
clinical_significance: A hormone produced mainly by the pineal gland that helps coordinate sleep and wake timing. Darkness usually increases its release, while light suppresses it; supplements can cause drowsiness and medicine interactions.

name: melatonin receptor
clinical_significance: A cell-surface receptor activated by the hormone melatonin. The main types, MT1 and MT2, help regulate the body's sleep-wake clock and seasonal rhythms and are targets of some sleep medicines.

name: melena
clinical_significance: Black, sticky, often foul-smelling stool caused by digested blood, usually from bleeding in the stomach or upper intestine. It can signal serious bleeding and requires prompt medical evaluation.

name: melengestrol acetate
clinical_significance: Melengestrol acetate is a synthetic progestin used in veterinary settings, including cattle feed to alter reproduction or promote growth. It is not a human medicine, and food-residue limits are regulated.

name: melioidosis
clinical_significance: Melioidosis is a potentially life-threatening infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, usually acquired from contaminated soil or water in tropical regions. It can cause pneumonia, skin infection, or bloodstream disease and requires prompt diagnosis and prolonged antibiotic treatment.

name: melitten
clinical_significance: Melitten, more commonly spelled melittin, is the principal peptide toxin in honeybee venom. It disrupts cell membranes and contributes to pain, inflammation, hemolysis, and other effects of envenomation.

name: melorheostosis
clinical_significance: Melorheostosis is a rare bone disorder causing dense, irregular bone growth along the outer surface of one or more bones. It may cause pain, stiffness, limb deformity, or restricted movement; severity and affected sites vary.

name: meloxicam
clinical_significance: Meloxicam is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes and reduces prostaglandin synthesis. It is used for pain and inflammation, but can cause gastrointestinal, renal, cardiovascular, and hypersensitivity adverse effects.

name: melphalan
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy medicine that damages cancer cells by interfering with their DNA. It is used for selected blood cancers and other cancers, but can also suppress bone marrow and increase infection or bleeding risk.

name: memantine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: Memantine hydrochloride is an NMDA-receptor antagonist used to help manage moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease. It reduces pathologic glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity; common adverse effects include dizziness, headache, constipation, and confusion.

name: membrane
clinical_significance: A thin sheet of tissue or material that surrounds a cell, organ, or body cavity. Membranes can protect structures, separate spaces, allow selected substances to pass, and produce or absorb fluids.

name: membrane channel
clinical_significance: A membrane channel is a protein-forming pore across a cell membrane that permits selected ions or molecules to pass down an electrochemical or concentration gradient. Many channels are gated by voltage, ligands, or mechanical forces.

name: membrane fusion
clinical_significance: Membrane fusion is merging of two lipid bilayers into one continuous membrane. It is required for processes such as synaptic vesicle release, enveloped-virus entry, fertilization, and intracellular vesicle trafficking.

name: membrane lipids
clinical_significance: Fat-like molecules that form the main structure of cell membranes. They create a flexible barrier, help cells communicate, and provide attachment sites for proteins; abnormal lipid composition can affect signaling and cell function.

name: membrane microdomain
clinical_significance: A membrane microdomain is a small, specialized region of a cell membrane with a distinct composition of lipids and proteins. It can organize receptors, signaling molecules, transporters, and cytoskeletal interactions.

name: membrane part
clinical_significance: A membrane part is a structural or molecular component of a biological membrane, such as a lipid, protein, carbohydrate, channel, or receptor. These components determine membrane integrity, transport, signaling, and cell recognition.

name: membrane potential
clinical_significance: Membrane potential is the electrical voltage difference across a cell membrane, created by ion gradients. It enables nerve signaling, muscle contraction, and heart rhythm; abnormal electrical activity can cause neurologic or cardiac symptoms.

name: membrane protein
clinical_significance: A protein attached to or embedded in a cell membrane. It may transport substances, receive signals, act as an enzyme, join cells, anchor the cytoskeleton, or help the immune system identify cells.

name: membrane raft
clinical_significance: A membrane raft is a cholesterol- and sphingolipid-enriched membrane microdomain that helps cluster selected proteins and signaling molecules. Raft organization is dynamic and may change during receptor signaling or membrane trafficking.

name: memory
clinical_significance: The ability to learn, store, and recall information. Memory depends on several connected areas of the brain and can be affected by sleep problems, stress, medicines, injury, illness, aging, or brain disorders.

name: memory disorder
clinical_significance: Impairment of encoding, storage, retrieval, or recognition of information that exceeds normal variation and may result from neurodegeneration, injury, vascular disease, medication, or other causes.

name: memory impairment
clinical_significance: Memory impairment is reduced ability to learn, store, retrieve, or recognize information. It may be transient or persistent and can result from normal aging, medications, sleep problems, neurologic disease, psychiatric illness, or other medical conditions.

name: memory training
clinical_significance: Memory training uses repeated practice or strategies to improve memory or daily functioning. It may be part of cognitive rehabilitation, but benefit depends on the cause of impairment and does not replace assessment for treatable conditions.

name: menarche
clinical_significance: The first menstrual period, marking the onset of menstruation. Its timing varies with genetics, nutrition, health, and pubertal development; markedly early or delayed menarche may require assessment.

name: Meniere's disease
clinical_significance: An inner-ear disorder causing episodes of vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and a feeling of fullness in one ear. Treatment aims to reduce attacks and protect hearing.

name: meningeal carcinomatosis
clinical_significance: Spread of cancer cells to the thin coverings and fluid around the brain and spinal cord. It may cause headache, nausea, weakness, seizures, vision changes, or problems with movement and needs specialist evaluation.

name: meningeal leukemia
clinical_significance: Meningeal leukemia is leukemia involving the membranes or fluid around the brain and spinal cord, potentially causing headache, weakness, or cranial-nerve problems.

name: meningeal lymphoma
clinical_significance: Meningeal lymphoma is lymphoma affecting the membranes or fluid spaces around the brain and spinal cord.

name: meningeal neoplasm
clinical_significance: A meningeal neoplasm is an abnormal growth arising in or near the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

name: meninges
clinical_significance: Three protective layers surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Fluid between two of the layers cushions the nervous system; bleeding or infection in these layers can be dangerous.

name: meningioma
clinical_significance: A meningioma is a tumor arising from the membranes around the brain or spinal cord. Many grow slowly and are benign, but some grow aggressively; symptoms depend on size and location and may include seizures, headache, vision changes, or weakness.

name: meningism
clinical_significance: Meningism is a syndrome of neck stiffness, headache, and sometimes photophobia or vomiting that resembles meningeal irritation without necessarily indicating meningitis. Serious causes, including infection or subarachnoid hemorrhage, require prompt evaluation.

name: meningitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the meninges around the brain and spinal cord, caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, medicines, or immune disease. Fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, altered mental status, or seizures may occur, but the classic triad is often incomplete. Suspected bacterial meningitis is an emergency requiring blood tests and cerebrospinal-fluid evaluation when safe.

name: meningocele
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the protective coverings around the brain or spinal cord bulge through an opening in the skull or spine, forming a fluid-filled sac. It may cause nerve problems and needs specialist assessment.

name: meningococcal infection
clinical_significance: An infection caused by the bacterium Neisseria meningitidis. It may remain mild or cause life-threatening meningitis or bloodstream infection, with fever, headache, stiff neck, vomiting, confusion, or a purple rash developing quickly.

name: meningococcal vaccine
clinical_significance: Meningococcal vaccines protect against some serogroups of Neisseria meningitidis, a cause of meningitis and bloodstream infection. They are recommended for adolescents and some people at increased risk; vaccine type and schedule depend on age, risk, and local guidance.

name: meningoencephalitis
clinical_significance: Meningoencephalitis is inflammation of the brain and its surrounding membranes, usually caused by infection but sometimes by immune disease. Fever, headache, confusion, seizures, or neurologic deficits may occur; suspected cases require urgent assessment and treatment.

name: meningomyelocele
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the protective coverings and spinal-cord tissue bulge through an opening in the spine. It can cause weakness or paralysis of the legs and bladder or bowel problems.

name: meniscus
clinical_significance: A crescent-shaped fibrocartilage structure in the knee, or a curved fluid surface in a container.

name: Menkes Kinky Hair syndrome
clinical_significance: Menkes disease is a severe inherited copper-transport disorder that causes low copper in the brain and other tissues. It can lead to seizures, developmental decline, weak connective tissue, and characteristic sparse kinky hair; early diagnosis matters because treatment may help before neurologic injury progresses.

name: menogaril
clinical_significance: Menogaril is a semisynthetic anthracycline derivative of nogalamycin. It intercalates into DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II, thereby impairing DNA replication and repair; it was investigated as an antineoplastic agent.

name: menopause
clinical_significance: The permanent end of menstrual periods because of loss of ovarian activity, usually diagnosed after 12 consecutive months without menstruation. Hormonal changes may cause hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal symptoms, sleep problems, or other symptoms.

name: menopause status
clinical_significance: Menopause status describes whether a person is premenopausal, perimenopausal, or postmenopausal. Natural menopause is clinically defined after 12 consecutive months without menstruation when no other cause explains the amenorrhea.

name: menorrhagia
clinical_significance: Heavy menstrual bleeding can cause iron-deficiency anemia and impair daily life; assessment looks for pregnancy, fibroids, bleeding disorders, and other treatable causes.

name: menotropin
clinical_significance: Menotropin is a urinary-derived preparation containing follicle-stimulating and luteinizing hormone activity, used to stimulate follicular development or spermatogenesis; ovarian hyperstimulation and multiple pregnancy are important risks.

name: menses duration
clinical_significance: Menses duration is the number of days of menstrual bleeding in a cycle, counted from the first day of bleeding until bleeding stops. Persistently prolonged, heavy, or irregular bleeding warrants clinical assessment.

name: menstrual cycle
clinical_significance: The menstrual cycle is the recurring hormonal process that prepares the ovaries and uterus for pregnancy. Cycle timing varies; persistent irregularity, unusually heavy bleeding, or severe pain can signal a condition that needs evaluation.

name: menstruation
clinical_significance: The periodic shedding of the endometrial lining as part of the menstrual cycle when pregnancy does not occur.

name: menstruation disturbance
clinical_significance: Menstrual disorders can reflect pregnancy, hormonal imbalance, structural disease, medication effects, or systemic illness; persistent or severe changes merit evaluation.

name: mental disorders
clinical_significance: Health conditions involving a clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotion regulation, or behavior that causes distress, impairment, or both. Examples include mood, anxiety, psychotic, neurodevelopmental, trauma-related, personality, and substance use disorders. A mental-health concern or symptom does not necessarily constitute a mental disorder.

name: mental fatigue
clinical_significance: Mental fatigue is a subjective feeling of reduced mental energy, concentration, or cognitive endurance after sustained effort or illness. Persistent or severe symptoms may accompany sleep disorders, depression, neurologic disease, medication effects, or other medical conditions.

name: mental health
clinical_significance: Mental health encompasses emotional, psychological, and social well-being, affecting how individuals think, feel, behave, and handle stress, relationships, and decision-making.

name: mental process
clinical_significance: A mental process is a cognitive or affective activity of the mind, such as perception, attention, memory, reasoning, language, emotion, or decision-making.

name: mental recall
clinical_significance: Mental recall is retrieval of previously learned or stored information from memory. It may be assessed by asking a person to remember facts, events, words, or experiences after a delay.

name: mental retardation
clinical_significance: Intellectual disability, formerly called by an outdated and stigmatizing term, begins during development and involves significant limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive skills such as communication, self-care, and independent living. Support needs vary among individuals.

name: menthol
clinical_significance: A mint-derived or synthetic compound producing a cooling sensation and used in some topical and respiratory preparations.

name: meperidine
clinical_significance: An opioid analgesic, also called pethidine, whose use is limited by adverse effects and an active neurotoxic metabolite.

name: meperidine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: Meperidine hydrochloride is the hydrochloride salt of the opioid analgesic meperidine. It produces analgesia through opioid-receptor activity and carries risks of sedation, respiratory depression, seizures, dependence, and serotonin toxicity with interacting drugs.

name: mephenytoin
clinical_significance: Mephenytoin is a hydantoin anticonvulsant formerly used to treat seizures. It is metabolized partly to ethotoin and has limited modern use because of potentially serious adverse effects, including hypersensitivity and blood dyscrasias.

name: mepivacaine
clinical_significance: A local anesthetic medicine that temporarily blocks pain signals from nerves. It is injected for numbing skin, dental areas, individual nerves, or larger body regions during procedures.

name: meprobamate
clinical_significance: An older medicine that reduces anxiety and causes sleepiness. It can cause dependence, dangerous breathing and nervous-system depression, and overdose, especially with alcohol or other sedatives, so it is rarely used today.

name: mercaptopurine
clinical_significance: A thiopurine antimetabolite used in selected leukemias and inflammatory disorders, requiring monitoring for marrow and liver toxicity.

name: mercury
clinical_significance: A metal used in some industrial and laboratory products. Its chemical symbol is Hg; mmHg denotes millimeters of mercury, a unit of pressure. Exposure can harm the nervous system, kidneys, lungs, or digestive tract, so it must be handled and disposed of safely.

name: mercury poisoning
clinical_significance: Illness caused by exposure to elemental, inorganic, or organic mercury. Effects depend on the form and dose and may include nerve, kidney, lung, or digestive injury; urgent advice is needed after significant exposure.

name: meridian
clinical_significance: A meridian is a reference line or plane in anatomy or measurement. In acupuncture and traditional Chinese medicine it refers to a proposed pathway for qi, but it is not a discrete anatomical structure identified by modern anatomy.

name: merkel cells
clinical_significance: Specialized touch-sensing cells in the deepest layer of the skin that help detect light touch and sustained pressure.

name: meropenem
clinical_significance: Meropenem is a broad-spectrum carbapenem antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis and treats severe susceptible infections, including meningitis; allergy, gastrointestinal effects, seizures, and resistance are possible.

name: MERRF syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder affecting how cells produce energy. It commonly causes muscle jerks, seizures, balance problems, and muscle weakness, and may also affect hearing, vision, or other organs.

name: mersalyl
clinical_significance: Mersalyl is an obsolete mercury-containing diuretic formerly used to increase urine output. It was abandoned because mercury toxicity could injure the kidneys and other organs.

name: mesalamine
clinical_significance: Mesalamine, or 5-aminosalicylic acid, is an anti-inflammatory drug used to induce and maintain remission in ulcerative colitis and some other inflammatory bowel conditions. It acts mainly topically in the intestinal mucosa and can rarely affect renal function.

name: mesangiolysis
clinical_significance: Mesangiolysis is dissolution or disruption of the mesangial tissue within a renal glomerulus. It may occur in severe endothelial injury and can be associated with microvascular lesions and glomerular capillary aneurysmal changes.

name: mesangium
clinical_significance: The mesangium is the supportive tissue between glomerular capillary loops, composed of mesangial cells and extracellular matrix. Mesangial cells provide structural support, regulate capillary flow, and clear certain substances; abnormal expansion occurs in several glomerular diseases.

name: mesencephalon
clinical_significance: The mesencephalon, or midbrain, is the part of the brainstem between the pons and diencephalon. It contains pathways and nuclei involved in eye movements, motor control, arousal, and auditory and visual reflexes.

name: mesenchymal cell
clinical_significance: A connective-tissue precursor that can develop into bone, cartilage, fat, muscle, or tendon cells.

name: mesenchymal chondrosarcoma
clinical_significance: Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma is a rare aggressive cancer containing cartilage-forming tissue, often arising in bone or soft tissue.

name: mesenchyme
clinical_significance: Embryonic connective tissue that gives rise to much of the skeleton, connective tissue, blood vessels, and smooth muscle.

name: mesenchymoma
clinical_significance: A mesenchymoma is a rare tumor containing more than one type of mesenchymal tissue, sometimes including cartilage, bone, fat, or vascular elements. Behavior depends on the site, age, histology, and presence of malignant components.

name: mesenteric artery
clinical_significance: A mesenteric artery supplies blood to portions of the intestine and associated abdominal organs. The superior and inferior mesenteric arteries are the major vessels; obstruction or embolism can cause acute mesenteric ischemia.

name: mesenteric cyst
clinical_significance: A rare, usually noncancerous, fluid-filled sac in the tissue that supports the intestines. Small cysts may cause no symptoms, while larger ones can cause swelling, pain, infection, twisting, or bowel blockage. Imaging helps locate the cyst, and treatment depends on its size, symptoms, and cause.

name: mesenteric lymphadenitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of lymph nodes in the tissue supporting the intestines, often after a viral or bacterial infection. It can cause right-sided abdominal pain, fever, nausea, and tenderness and may resemble appendicitis.

name: mesenteric veins
clinical_significance: Mesenteric veins drain blood from the small and large intestines and carry it mainly through the superior and inferior mesenteric veins to the portal venous system. Thrombosis or impaired flow can cause intestinal congestion and ischemia.

name: mesentery
clinical_significance: A fold of the abdominal lining that attaches the intestines to the back wall of the abdomen. It carries blood vessels, nerves, and lymph vessels to the bowel and helps hold the intestines in place.

name: mesial surface
clinical_significance: The mesial surface is the surface of a tooth or other structure oriented toward the midline. In dentistry, mesial surfaces contact adjacent teeth and can be involved in caries, periodontal disease, or restoration margins.

name: mesna
clinical_significance: A protective medicine given with certain chemotherapy drugs to reduce irritation and bleeding of the bladder. It binds harmful breakdown products in the urine and does not treat the cancer itself.

name: mesoderm
clinical_significance: The mesoderm is the middle embryonic germ layer, which gives rise to structures including muscle, bone, blood, kidneys, and connective tissue. Abnormal development can cause congenital disorders.

name: mesonephric
clinical_significance: Mesonephric means relating to the mesonephros, a temporary embryonic kidney, or to structures derived from its ducts and tubules. Mesonephric remnants can give rise to uncommon benign or malignant lesions of the genital tract.

name: mesonephric tumor
clinical_significance: A mesonephric tumor is a rare tumor arising from remnants of embryonic mesonephric ducts, usually in the female reproductive tract.

name: mesonephroma
clinical_significance: Mesonephroma is an older, imprecise name that has been used for different tumors, including some ovarian clear-cell and yolk-sac tumors. Modern diagnosis requires the tumor’s site and microscopic type because these conditions behave and are treated differently.

name: mesothelial neoplasm
clinical_significance: A mesothelial neoplasm is a growth arising from the lining of body cavities, such as the pleura, peritoneum, or pericardium.

name: mesothelin
clinical_significance: Mesothelin is a cell-surface glycoprotein expressed mainly by mesothelial cells and overexpressed in several cancers, including mesothelioma and some ovarian and pancreatic cancers. It is being studied as a biomarker and therapeutic target.

name: mesothelioma
clinical_significance: A cancer arising from the thin lining of body cavities, most often the pleura around the lungs. It is strongly associated with asbestos exposure and may cause chest pain, breathlessness, or fluid around the lung.

name: mesothelium
clinical_significance: The mesothelium is a single layer of specialized cells lining serous body cavities and covering their organs, including the pleura, peritoneum, and pericardium. It produces lubricating fluid and participates in inflammation and repair.

name: messenger RNA
clinical_significance: A temporary copy of genetic instructions made from DNA. It carries those instructions to cell structures that build proteins and is then broken down; some vaccines use messenger RNA to teach the immune system to recognize a target.

name: mestranol
clinical_significance: Mestranol is a synthetic estrogen formerly used in early combined oral contraceptives and rarely used in current formulations. Estrogen-containing medicines can increase blood-clot risk, which depends on dose and individual factors.

name: meta analysis
clinical_significance: A meta-analysis statistically combines results from multiple studies to estimate an overall effect. It can inform clinical decisions, but conclusions depend on the quality and comparability of the included studies.

name: metabolic acidosis
clinical_significance: A primary fall in plasma bicarbonate causing acidemia unless respiratory compensation or another process changes the pH. It is classified by anion gap and may result from lactic or ketoacidosis, kidney failure, toxins, or bicarbonate loss from the gastrointestinal tract or kidneys; assessment includes pH, bicarbonate, respiratory compensation, electrolytes, and the cause.

name: metabolic disease
clinical_significance: A disorder that changes how the body processes or uses substances such as sugars, fats, proteins, minerals, or hormones. It may be inherited or acquired and can affect energy, growth, blood chemistry, or organ function.

name: metabolic response
clinical_significance: A metabolic response is a change in energy use, substrate metabolism, or biochemical pathways in response to conditions such as fasting, exercise, infection, trauma, or medication. The response may be adaptive or contribute to illness when excessive or prolonged.

name: metabolic syndrome
clinical_significance: A combination of increased waist size, high blood pressure, high blood sugar, high triglycerides, or low HDL cholesterol. Together these findings increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes.

name: metabolism
clinical_significance: The chemical processes cells use to turn food and medicines into energy and building materials, and to break down substances the body no longer needs.

name: metabolite
clinical_significance: A substance made, changed, or used when the body processes a medicine, nutrient, or naturally occurring molecule. Measuring metabolites in blood or urine can show body function, disease, or drug effects.

name: metabolomics
clinical_significance: Metabolomics is large-scale measurement of small molecules produced or used by cells and tissues. It is used in research and is being studied for disease biomarkers, but most metabolomic findings are not routine standalone clinical tests.

name: metacarpal bone
clinical_significance: A metacarpal bone is one of the five long bones of the hand between the wrist bones and the proximal phalanges. Each has a base, shaft, and head; fractures can affect alignment, grip, and joint function.

name: metadata
clinical_significance: Metadata are information describing a dataset, sample, image, or record, such as collection time, units, or method. In clinical research, accurate metadata support interpretation, reproducibility, and protection of patient privacy.

name: metagenome
clinical_significance: A metagenome is the combined genetic material of microorganisms in a sample, such as gut contents, soil, or water. It can reveal organisms and genes relevant to microbiome research, but results do not automatically identify a treatable infection.

name: metagenomics
clinical_significance: Metagenomics analyzes genetic material from a mixed microbial sample without first growing each organism. It can help investigate complex or difficult-to-culture infections, but contamination, detection of harmless organisms, and uncertain clinical meaning require careful interpretation.

name: metagonimus yokogawai
clinical_significance: Metagonimus yokogawai is a small intestinal fluke acquired by eating raw or inadequately cooked freshwater fish. Infection can cause abdominal symptoms and, rarely, ectopic migration of eggs or adult worms.

name: metal
clinical_significance: A metal is an element such as iron, copper, lead, or mercury. Some metals are essential nutrients, while others can be toxic; exposure testing and treatment depend on the specific metal and dose.

name: metalloendopeptidase
clinical_significance: A metalloendopeptidase is an endopeptidase whose catalytic activity depends on a bound metal ion, commonly zinc. It cleaves peptide bonds within proteins and includes enzymes involved in extracellular matrix remodeling and signaling.

name: metalloporphyrins
clinical_significance: Metalloporphyrins are porphyrin molecules containing a centrally coordinated metal ion. Heme, which contains iron, is a biologically important example and forms the functional group of hemoglobin, myoglobin, and many enzymes.

name: metalloprotease
clinical_significance: A metalloprotease is a proteolytic enzyme that requires a metal ion, commonly zinc, for catalytic activity. Metalloproteases regulate extracellular matrix turnover, cell signaling, inflammation, and tissue remodeling; dysregulation contributes to disease.

name: metalloprotein
clinical_significance: A protein that contains a metal ion or binds one tightly as part of its structure or function. Iron, zinc, copper, and magnesium in metalloproteins support oxygen transport, enzyme activity, electron transfer, or regulation.

name: metallothionein
clinical_significance: Metallothionein is a small, cysteine-rich protein that binds metals such as zinc, copper, and cadmium. It helps regulate essential metals and may protect cells from metal toxicity and oxidative stress.

name: metamorphosis
clinical_significance: Metamorphosis is a major change in body form during the development of some animals. In medicine it is relevant to parasitology and vector biology because life stage can affect how an organism spreads or causes disease.

name: metanephrine
clinical_significance: Metanephrine is a metabolite of epinephrine formed mainly by catechol-O-methyltransferase. Plasma or urinary metanephrine measurements are used in evaluation for catecholamine-secreting tumors such as pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma.

name: metaphase
clinical_significance: The stage of cell division in which chromosomes align at the cell's equatorial plane.

name: metaphase plate
clinical_significance: The metaphase plate is the plane at the center of a dividing cell where chromosomes align during metaphase. It is a geometric arrangement rather than a discrete anatomical structure.

name: metaphyseal widening
clinical_significance: Metaphyseal widening is enlargement of the growth-plate or metaphyseal region of a developing long bone. It may be seen in disorders such as rickets, skeletal dysplasia, infection, or healing injury and must be interpreted with imaging and clinical findings.

name: metaphysis
clinical_significance: The wider part of a growing long bone between its shaft and end. In children it lies next to the growth plate, where new bone forms and the bone lengthens.

name: metaplasia
clinical_significance: A usually reversible change in which one mature cell type is replaced by another that better tolerates ongoing irritation or stress. Some persistent forms may increase the risk of further abnormal changes.

name: metaplastic carcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer whose cells have changed to resemble a different type of tissue. The term is used especially for an uncommon, often aggressive breast cancer; diagnosis requires examination of a tissue sample.

name: metapneumovirus
clinical_significance: A respiratory virus that can cause cough, fever, bronchiolitis, or pneumonia, especially in infants, older adults, and people with chronic disease.

name: metastasectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove one or more cancer deposits that have spread from the original tumor. It may help selected people when the deposits are limited and removable, but benefit depends on the cancer type, location, and other treatment options.

name: metastasis
clinical_significance: The spread of cancer cells from the original tumor to a separate part of the body, where they form new tumors. Spread can occur through the blood, lymphatic system, or body cavities.

name: metastin
clinical_significance: Metastin is an older name for kisspeptin, a peptide derived from the KISS1 gene. It stimulates hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone secretion and helps regulate puberty, reproductive function, and tumor-cell signaling.

name: metatarsal bone
clinical_significance: A metatarsal bone is one of the five long bones of the forefoot between the tarsal bones and proximal phalanges. Metatarsal fractures and alignment abnormalities can affect weight bearing and gait.

name: metatarsal valgus
clinical_significance: Metatarsal valgus is outward deviation of one or more metatarsal bones relative to the foot’s normal axis. It may contribute to forefoot deformity and altered load distribution and is assessed clinically and radiographically.

name: metatarsus varus
clinical_significance: Metatarsus varus is inward deviation of the forefoot caused by medial angulation of the metatarsal bones. It is often recognized in infancy and may be flexible or rigid; management depends on severity and persistence.

name: metencephalon
clinical_significance: The metencephalon is the embryonic brain region that develops into the pons and cerebellum. These structures participate in motor coordination, balance, cranial-nerve functions, and relay of signals between the brain and spinal cord.

name: meter
clinical_significance: A metric unit of length equal to 100 centimeters; medical usage may also refer to a measuring device.

name: metestrus
clinical_significance: The stage of the reproductive cycle after ovulation in many mammals, when the corpus luteum develops and progesterone rises. The exact timing and biological features differ among species.

name: metformin
clinical_significance: A commonly used medicine for type 2 diabetes that lowers the amount of sugar made by the liver and helps the body use insulin better. Nausea or diarrhea are common; serious illness or severe kidney problems increase rare toxicity risk.

name: metformin hydrochloride
clinical_significance: Metformin hydrochloride is the hydrochloride salt of metformin, an oral biguanide used chiefly for type 2 diabetes. It lowers blood glucose without directly stimulating pancreatic insulin release and is available in immediate- and extended-release formulations.

name: methacholine chloride
clinical_significance: Methacholine chloride is a muscarinic cholinergic agonist used in bronchoprovocation testing. In susceptible people it causes airway narrowing, allowing assessment for bronchial hyperresponsiveness under controlled medical supervision.

name: methadone
clinical_significance: A long-acting opioid medicine used in selected pain cases and treatment of opioid-use disorder. It reduces withdrawal and cravings but can cause dangerous breathing suppression, sedation, dependence, or heart-rhythm changes.

name: methadone hydrochloride
clinical_significance: Methadone hydrochloride is the hydrochloride salt of methadone. It provides long-lasting opioid-receptor activity for selected analgesic and opioid-use-disorder indications, with risks of respiratory depression, dependence, overdose, and cardiac arrhythmia.

name: methamidophos
clinical_significance: Methamidophos is a highly toxic organophosphorus insecticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Exposure can cause cholinergic poisoning with sweating, salivation, vomiting, bronchospasm, bradycardia, muscle weakness, and potentially respiratory failure.

name: methamphetamine
clinical_significance: Methamphetamine is a potent central nervous system stimulant that increases synaptic catecholamines. It has limited medical use in some settings but is commonly misused; toxicity and chronic use can cause cardiovascular complications, psychosis, dependence, and neurocognitive harm.

name: methane
clinical_significance: Methane is a colorless, odorless, highly flammable gas produced by anaerobic decomposition and normal intestinal microbial activity. It can displace oxygen in enclosed spaces and cause asphyxiation; it is not itself a direct systemic poison at ordinary exposure levels.

name: methane sulfonate
clinical_significance: Methane sulfonate, or mesylate, is the anion or ester derived from methanesulfonic acid. Mesylate salts are commonly used to improve the formulation of medicines; some methanesulfonate esters are potent alkylating agents and toxic impurities.

name: methanobacteriaceae
clinical_significance: Methanobacteriaceae is a family of methane-producing archaea found in environments and in the human gut. Their role in digestion and conditions such as intestinal methanogen overgrowth is studied, but their presence alone is not a diagnosis.

name: methanol
clinical_significance: A poisonous alcohol whose breakdown products can cause severe acid buildup, blindness, brain injury, or death. Serious poisoning can develop even before symptoms appear.

name: methaqualone
clinical_significance: Methaqualone is a sedative-hypnotic drug formerly prescribed for insomnia and anxiety. It was withdrawn or restricted in many countries because of dependence, misuse, overdose, and dangerous sedation, especially with alcohol or other depressants.

name: methazolamide
clinical_significance: Methazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used mainly to lower intraocular pressure in glaucoma. It reduces aqueous humor production and can cause metabolic acidosis, electrolyte abnormalities, kidney stones, or sulfonamide-related reactions.

name: methemoglobin
clinical_significance: Hemoglobin in which iron has been oxidized so it cannot carry oxygen normally. High levels cause methemoglobinemia, with cyanosis, headache, breathlessness, confusion, or severe tissue oxygen deficiency.

name: methemoglobinemia
clinical_significance: Methemoglobinemia occurs when hemoglobin iron is oxidized and cannot carry oxygen normally, causing cyanosis, headache, breathlessness, or severe tissue hypoxia.

name: methenamine
clinical_significance: Methenamine is a urinary antiseptic that decomposes in acidic urine to release formaldehyde, which inhibits bacterial growth. It is used for prevention of recurrent urinary tract infection in selected patients, not for treatment of active upper-tract infection.

name: methicillin
clinical_significance: Methicillin is an older penicillin-type antibiotic once used against penicillinase-producing staphylococci. It is no longer commonly used to treat patients, but the term remains in MRSA, meaning methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

name: methidathion
clinical_significance: Methidathion is an organophosphorus insecticide and acaricide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Exposure can produce a cholinergic toxidrome with secretions, bronchospasm, bradycardia, gastrointestinal symptoms, weakness, and respiratory failure.

name: methimazole
clinical_significance: A medicine that reduces production of thyroid hormones and is used mainly for hyperthyroidism and Graves disease. It can rarely cause severe low white-cell counts or liver injury; fever or sore throat during treatment needs prompt medical advice.

name: methiocarb
clinical_significance: Methiocarb is a carbamate pesticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase reversibly. Poisoning causes excessive muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic activity and may require urgent supportive care and antidotal treatment.

name: methionine
clinical_significance: An essential amino acid containing sulfur that the body uses to build proteins and make other substances. People must obtain it from food, and it can be converted into homocysteine and related compounds.

name: methionine enkephalin
clinical_significance: Methionine enkephalin is an endogenous opioid pentapeptide that binds opioid receptors and participates in modulation of pain, stress, reward, and neuroendocrine function. It is one of the products of proenkephalin processing.

name: methisazone
clinical_significance: Methisazone is a historical antiviral drug studied for prevention of smallpox and complications of smallpox vaccination. It is no longer used for routine care; vaccination eradicated naturally occurring smallpox.

name: methocarbamol
clinical_significance: Methocarbamol is a centrally acting skeletal-muscle relaxant used with rest and physical measures for acute painful musculoskeletal conditions. It can cause drowsiness, dizziness, impaired coordination, and additive central nervous system depression.

name: methodology
clinical_significance: Methodology is the set of methods used to collect and analyze information. In clinical studies, sound methodology is essential for reliable results and for judging whether findings apply to patient care.

name: methohexital
clinical_significance: Methohexital is an ultra-short-acting barbiturate anesthetic used for induction of general anesthesia and, in selected settings, procedural sedation. It depresses central nervous system activity and may cause respiratory or cardiovascular depression.

name: methomyl
clinical_significance: Methomyl is a carbamate insecticide that reversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Poisoning produces cholinergic symptoms such as salivation, sweating, vomiting, bronchospasm, bradycardia, weakness, and respiratory compromise.

name: methotrexate
clinical_significance: An antimetabolite that inhibits folate-dependent enzymes and is used in cancer and selected autoimmune or inflammatory disorders.

name: methotrimeprazine
clinical_significance: Methotrimeprazine, also called levomepromazine, is a phenothiazine with antipsychotic, sedative, antiemetic, and analgesic properties. It is used in some countries for psychiatric illness and palliative-care symptoms and can cause sedation, hypotension, and anticholinergic effects.

name: methoxamine
clinical_significance: Methoxamine is a predominantly alpha-adrenergic agonist that increases vascular tone and blood pressure. It has been used as a vasopressor for hypotension but is not a routine first-line agent in many current practice settings.

name: methoxsalen
clinical_significance: Methoxsalen is a psoralen that intercalates into DNA and, after exposure to UVA, forms cross-links that suppress abnormal lymphocyte or skin-cell activity. It is used with UVA phototherapy for selected skin diseases; photosensitivity and skin-cancer risk require precautions.

name: methoxyamine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: Methoxyamine hydrochloride, also called TRC102, is an investigational inhibitor of DNA base-excision repair studied with chemotherapy. It is not an established treatment and has been evaluated mainly in early-phase cancer trials.

name: methoxyflurane
clinical_significance: A vapor medicine formerly used to cause general anesthesia and, in some settings, provide short-term pain relief. High or repeated exposure can damage the kidneys, so use requires careful medical supervision.

name: methoxyhydroxyphenylglycol
clinical_significance: Methoxyhydroxyphenylglycol (MHPG) is a breakdown product of norepinephrine. Levels in blood, urine, or cerebrospinal fluid have been used in research on catecholamine turnover, but are not a routine standalone diagnostic test.

name: methyclothiazide
clinical_significance: Methyclothiazide is a thiazide diuretic that inhibits sodium and chloride reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule. It is used for hypertension or edema and may cause hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, and glucose intolerance.

name: methyl bromide
clinical_significance: Methyl bromide, or bromomethane, is a volatile fumigant and alkylating chemical. Inhalation can cause severe neurologic, respiratory, renal, and cardiovascular toxicity, including delayed seizures and pulmonary edema.

name: methyl chloride
clinical_significance: Methyl chloride, or chloromethane, is a volatile industrial gas formerly used in refrigerants and other applications. High-level inhalation exposure can depress the central nervous system and cause headache, ataxia, seizures, or cardiac effects.

name: methyl green
clinical_significance: Methyl green is a laboratory dye used to stain DNA and other cellular material. It supports microscopy and research and is not itself a diagnostic finding.

name: methyl group
clinical_significance: A methyl group is a small chemical unit made of one carbon and three hydrogen atoms. Adding or removing methyl groups can alter how genes are read, how medicines are metabolized, and how other molecules function.

name: methyl isocyanate
clinical_significance: Methyl isocyanate is a highly volatile and reactive industrial chemical. Inhalation or eye and skin exposure can cause severe irritation, pulmonary edema, and delayed respiratory injury; it was the toxic agent in the Bhopal disaster.

name: methyl methanesulfonate
clinical_significance: Methyl methanesulfonate is a laboratory alkylating chemical that damages DNA and can cause mutations. It is used in research and must be handled as a hazardous substance.

name: methyl parathion
clinical_significance: Methyl parathion is an organophosphorus insecticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Exposure can produce severe cholinergic poisoning with secretions, bronchospasm, bradycardia, weakness, seizures, and respiratory failure.

name: methylation
clinical_significance: Attachment of a small chemical group to DNA, proteins, or other molecules. On DNA, this can change how strongly a gene is used and helps regulate normal development, cell function, and some diseases.

name: methylcellulose
clinical_significance: A plant-fiber product used as a bulk-forming laxative and as a thickener in medicines and foods. It absorbs water and adds bulk to stool; it can be unsafe when a bowel blockage is present.

name: methylcholanthrene
clinical_significance: Methylcholanthrene is a potent chemical carcinogen used mainly to induce tumors in experimental research. It is not a medicine and requires strict exposure controls.

name: methyldopa
clinical_significance: A blood-pressure medicine that acts in the brain to reduce nerve signals that tighten blood vessels. It is used in selected cases, including pregnancy, and may cause sleepiness, dizziness, or liver problems.

name: methylene blue
clinical_significance: A medicine used mainly for serious methemoglobinemia, a condition in which blood cannot carry oxygen normally. It may be unsafe in some people with an inherited red-cell enzyme deficiency and can interact with certain antidepressants.

name: methylene chloride
clinical_significance: Methylene chloride, or dichloromethane, is a volatile industrial solvent. Inhalation can cause central nervous system depression and metabolism to carbon monoxide can produce tissue hypoxia; high exposure may be fatal.

name: methylguanidine
clinical_significance: Methylguanidine is a nitrogen-containing compound that can accumulate in kidney failure and has been studied as a uremic toxin. It is not a routine clinical test or treatment target by itself.

name: methylmalonic aciduria
clinical_significance: A disorder in which methylmalonic acid builds up in blood and urine, usually because of an inherited enzyme or vitamin B12-processing problem. It may cause vomiting, poor feeding, acidosis, developmental problems, kidney disease, or neurologic injury.

name: methylmercury compounds
clinical_significance: Methylmercury compounds are organic mercury compounds that can accumulate in aquatic food chains and cross the blood--brain and placental barriers. Exposure primarily injures the nervous system and can impair fetal neurodevelopment.

name: methylmethacrylate
clinical_significance: Methyl methacrylate is a volatile monomer used to make acrylic plastics and dental or orthopedic bone cement. Vapors may irritate the eyes and airways, and liquid exposure can cause dermatitis or sensitization.

name: methylnaltrexone
clinical_significance: Methylnaltrexone is a peripherally acting mu-opioid-receptor antagonist used to treat opioid-induced constipation when laxatives are insufficient. It generally preserves central analgesia but can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, and rarely gastrointestinal perforation.

name: methylnaltrexone bromide
clinical_significance: Methylnaltrexone bromide is the bromide salt of methylnaltrexone, a peripherally restricted opioid antagonist. It reverses opioid effects in the gastrointestinal tract and is used for opioid-induced constipation under indication-specific precautions.

name: methylnitrosourea
clinical_significance: Methylnitrosourea is a mutagenic and carcinogenic chemical used to induce tumors in laboratory studies. It has no therapeutic role and requires stringent exposure controls.

name: methylobacteriaceae
clinical_significance: Methylobacteriaceae is a family of environmental bacteria, many associated with water and plants. Some members can rarely cause healthcare-associated or device-related infection, especially in medically vulnerable people.

name: methylobacterium
clinical_significance: Methylobacterium is a genus of slow-growing environmental bacteria found in water and on plants. It can rarely cause bloodstream or device-related infections, particularly in immunocompromised patients, and may be difficult to identify in routine cultures.

name: methylphenidate
clinical_significance: A stimulant medicine used mainly to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and narcolepsy, a condition causing excessive sleepiness. It affects brain chemicals involved in attention and alertness; reduced appetite, sleep problems, increased blood pressure, and misuse are possible risks.

name: methylprednisolone
clinical_significance: A synthetic glucocorticoid used to suppress inflammation and immune activity.

name: methyltestosterone
clinical_significance: A synthetic androgen related to testosterone. It can affect sexual development and other androgen-sensitive tissues but may cause liver injury, adverse cholesterol changes, infertility, or virilization and is used only in selected medical situations.

name: methylthioinosine
clinical_significance: Methylthioinosine is a sulfur-containing nucleoside involved in purine metabolism and cellular chemistry. It is studied in biochemical research and is not a routine standalone clinical marker.

name: methyltransferase
clinical_significance: A methyltransferase is an enzyme that transfers a methyl group to DNA, RNA, proteins, or other molecules. Methyltransferases influence gene regulation, cell function, and drug metabolism; some are targets of medicines or cancer research.

name: metoclopramide
clinical_significance: A medicine that helps the stomach empty and relieves nausea and vomiting. It is used for selected digestive problems and treatment-related nausea; prolonged or high-dose use can cause involuntary movements and other nervous-system effects.

name: metolazone
clinical_significance: A water-removing medicine used for high blood pressure and swelling. It helps the kidneys remove salt and water and is often combined with another diuretic, but can disturb sodium, potassium, kidney function, or hydration.

name: metolcarb
clinical_significance: Metolcarb is a carbamate insecticide that can inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Exposure may cause cholinergic poisoning with excessive secretions, gastrointestinal symptoms, bronchospasm, bradycardia, weakness, or respiratory compromise.

name: metoprolol
clinical_significance: Metoprolol is a relatively beta-1-selective blocker used for hypertension, angina, heart failure, rate control, and some post-infarction settings; bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue, and bronchospasm can occur.

name: metric system
clinical_significance: The metric system is a decimal system of measurement based on units such as the meter, kilogram, and liter. Modern medicine generally uses the International System of Units, with conventional units retained for some measurements.

name: metronidazole
clinical_significance: An antibiotic and antiparasitic medicine used for certain infections caused by bacteria that grow without oxygen and by some parasites. It can cause nausea or a metallic taste; nerve problems may occur with prolonged use.

name: metronomic chemotherapy
clinical_significance: Cancer treatment given in frequent, usually smaller doses over a long period instead of occasional high doses. The goal is to slow cancer growth and sometimes its blood supply; use depends on the cancer and treatment plan.

name: metrorrhagia
clinical_significance: Uterine bleeding that occurs at unexpected times, including between menstrual periods. Causes include pregnancy, hormonal changes, fibroids, polyps, infection, medicines, and cancer. New, heavy, prolonged, or postmenopausal bleeding can have an underlying medical cause.

name: metschnikowia
clinical_significance: Metschnikowia is a genus of yeasts found in the environment and on plants. Human infections are rare, but occasional opportunistic infections have been reported, so isolation from a sterile site should be evaluated clinically.

name: metyrapone
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks one step in the production of cortisol, a hormone made by the adrenal glands. It is used for selected hormone tests or treatment under specialist supervision because levels can change quickly.

name: mevinphos
clinical_significance: Mevinphos is a highly toxic organophosphorus insecticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Exposure can rapidly cause cholinergic crisis, including bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, muscle weakness, seizures, and respiratory failure.

name: mexacarbate
clinical_significance: Mexacarbate is a carbamate insecticide that interferes with acetylcholinesterase. Toxic exposure may produce muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic symptoms and requires prompt decontamination and medical evaluation.

name: mexiletine
clinical_significance: Mexiletine is an oral class IB antiarrhythmic and sodium-channel blocker used for selected ventricular arrhythmias and sometimes neuropathic pain. It can cause gastrointestinal and neurologic effects and may worsen or provoke arrhythmias in some patients.

name: meyerozyma guilliermondii
clinical_significance: Meyerozyma guilliermondii is a yeast formerly classified as Candida guilliermondii. It is usually an environmental or colonizing organism but can cause opportunistic bloodstream or other infections, particularly in immunocompromised patients.

name: mezlocillin
clinical_significance: Mezlocillin is an extended-spectrum penicillin antibiotic formerly used for serious bacterial infections, including some caused by Pseudomonas. Availability varies and resistance limits its use; allergy and antibiotic-associated diarrhea are possible.

name: micafungin
clinical_significance: Micafungin is an echinocandin antifungal given by intravenous infusion for selected invasive Candida infections and prevention in some transplant patients. It can cause infusion reactions, liver-test abnormalities, or blood-cell changes; choice depends on the fungus and infection site.

name: micelle
clinical_significance: A tiny cluster of molecules that helps carry fats and fat-soluble substances through intestinal fluid for absorption.

name: miconazole
clinical_significance: An antifungal medicine used in creams, gels, or other preparations for infections of the skin, mouth, or vagina. It stops fungi from making an essential part of their outer covering; irritation and medicine interactions are possible, especially with some oral products.

name: microabscess
clinical_significance: A very small pocket of pus containing immune cells, damaged tissue, and sometimes germs. It may occur in the skin or an organ because of infection or inflammation and is usually a finding rather than a diagnosis.

name: microalbuminuria
clinical_significance: A small but abnormal amount of albumin, a blood protein, in the urine. It can be an early sign of kidney damage, especially in diabetes or high blood pressure, but temporary illness or exercise can also raise it and repeat testing may be needed.

name: microaneurysm
clinical_significance: A very small balloon-like bulge in a blood vessel wall. In the retina, microaneurysms are an early sign of diabetic eye disease and may leak fluid, causing swelling and blurred vision. Their number and associated retinal changes help show how diabetes is affecting the eyes.

name: microarray analysis
clinical_significance: Microarray analysis measures the abundance or hybridization of many nucleic-acid sequences simultaneously using an array of immobilized probes. It can assess gene expression, copy-number changes, or selected genetic variants.

name: microbacterium
clinical_significance: A genus of gram-positive bacteria found in soil and water that can rarely cause bloodstream or other opportunistic infections.

name: microbial biofilms
clinical_significance: Microbial biofilms are organized communities of microorganisms attached to a surface and enclosed in a self-produced extracellular matrix. Biofilms can form on tissues and medical devices and often show increased tolerance to antimicrobials and host defenses.

name: microbicide
clinical_significance: A microbicide is a chemical or biological agent that kills microorganisms or inactivates them. The term may refer to disinfectants, topical agents, or investigational products intended to reduce sexual transmission of infection.

name: microbiology
clinical_significance: The study of microorganisms, including bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites, and how they interact with people, animals, plants, and the environment. In medicine, it supports the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of infectious diseases.

name: microbiome
clinical_significance: The community of microorganisms and their genetic material living in a body site, especially the intestine. These organisms can influence digestion, immunity, and health, although the effects differ by person and condition.

name: microbody
clinical_significance: A microbody is a small membrane-bound cell organelle, a term that includes peroxisomes. These structures carry out metabolic reactions, and inherited peroxisomal disorders can damage the brain, liver, eyes, or other organs.

name: microcephaly
clinical_significance: Microcephaly is head size substantially smaller than expected for age and sex, reflecting genetic, developmental, infectious, toxic, or acquired brain causes.

name: microchip site
clinical_significance: A microchip site is the area where a small identification or tracking chip has been implanted, usually in an animal. Swelling, migration, or infection can occur rarely; the site may also be scanned to retrieve identification information.

name: microcirculation
clinical_significance: The movement of blood through the body's smallest blood vessels. In these vessels, oxygen and nutrients pass to tissues and waste products pass into the blood; poor microcirculation can slow healing and damage organs.

name: micrococcaceae
clinical_significance: Micrococcaceae is a family of Gram-positive bacteria commonly found in the environment and on skin. Most isolates are contaminants, but some members can cause opportunistic infection, especially in people with devices or weakened immunity.

name: micrococcus
clinical_significance: Micrococcus is a genus of bacteria commonly found on skin and in the environment. It is often a specimen contaminant but can rarely cause bloodstream or device-associated infection in medically vulnerable people.

name: micrococcus luteus
clinical_significance: Micrococcus luteus is a common skin and environmental bacterium that is usually a contaminant in clinical cultures. It can rarely cause opportunistic bloodstream or device-associated infection, so repeated isolation and symptoms matter.

name: micrococcus lylae
clinical_significance: Micrococcus lylae is a skin- and environment-associated bacterium with no common role in human disease. Its recovery from a patient specimen is usually interpreted in context and may represent contamination.

name: microcolon
clinical_significance: Microcolon is an abnormally small-caliber colon, often identified on contrast imaging. It may result from reduced fetal intestinal use or obstruction and is associated with conditions such as small-left-colon syndrome, meconium ileus, or distal intestinal obstruction.

name: microcornea
clinical_significance: Microcornea is an abnormally small cornea, usually defined in adults by a horizontal diameter below about 10 mm. It may be isolated or associated with microphthalmia, glaucoma, cataract, or genetic syndromes.

name: microcurie
clinical_significance: A microcurie ($\mu$Ci) is a unit of radioactivity equal to one-millionth of a curie, or approximately 37 kilobecquerels. It may be used to express the activity of radioactive tracers or sources.

name: microcytic anemia
clinical_significance: Anemia in which red blood cells are smaller than usual. Common causes include iron deficiency, thalassemia, long-term inflammation, lead exposure, and some bone-marrow disorders. Blood counts and iron tests help find the cause; symptoms may include tiredness, weakness, pale skin, or shortness of breath.

name: microdialysis
clinical_significance: A testing method that uses a very small tube to collect chemicals from the fluid around cells. It can measure local levels of medicines or natural substances, including in the brain or beneath the skin.

name: microdissection
clinical_significance: Microdissection is separation or isolation of very small tissue regions or structures under microscopic or highly magnified visualization. It is used in surgery, pathology, and molecular research to obtain selected cells or tissue.

name: microelectrode
clinical_significance: A microelectrode is a very small electrode used to record or deliver electrical signals in tissue. It supports neurophysiology research and selected procedures such as mapping brain or nerve activity; placement carries site-specific risks.

name: microfibril
clinical_significance: A very small thread-like structure that supports tissues. In connective tissue, microfibrils help organize elastic fibers and provide strength; in plants, they are made mainly of cellulose.

name: microfilament
clinical_significance: A microfilament is a thin cytoskeletal filament composed mainly of actin, about 7 nm in diameter. Microfilaments support cell shape, motility, contraction, cytokinesis, and intracellular transport.

name: microfilament proteins
clinical_significance: Proteins that make, organize, move, or regulate actin microfilaments. They help cells maintain shape, migrate, divide, contract, and transport materials; examples include actin, myosin, and actin-binding proteins.

name: microfluidics
clinical_significance: Microfluidics manipulates tiny volumes of fluid through small channels. It enables compact laboratory tests and research assays, including some rapid diagnostic platforms, but results depend on validation of the specific device.

name: microglandular adenosis
clinical_significance: Microglandular adenosis is an uncommon benign proliferation of small glands in the breast, often associated with hormonal influences such as pregnancy or progestin use. It can mimic invasive carcinoma and is diagnosed histologically.

name: microglia
clinical_significance: Microglia are resident immune cells of the central nervous system. They survey neural tissue, remove debris, and respond to injury or infection; persistent activation can contribute to neuroinflammation.

name: microgliosis
clinical_significance: Microgliosis is proliferation or increased activation of microglia in the central nervous system, usually in response to injury, infection, degeneration, or other inflammation. It is a histopathologic finding rather than a specific disease.

name: micrognathism
clinical_significance: Micrognathism is abnormal smallness of the jaw, usually referring to the mandible. It may be congenital or acquired and can affect feeding, dentition, airway patency, speech, or facial development.

name: microgram
clinical_significance: A microgram (µg) is one-millionth of a gram. It is used for small medicine doses and laboratory measurements; confusing micrograms with milligrams can cause serious dosing errors.

name: microinjection
clinical_significance: Microinjection is delivery of a very small volume of fluid into a cell, tissue, or other microscopic target using a fine needle or micropipette. It is used in assisted reproduction, experimental biology, and some therapeutic procedures.

name: micromole
clinical_significance: A micromole ($\mu$mol) is an amount of substance equal to one-millionth of a mole, or approximately $6.022\times10^{17}$ entities. It is commonly used for small quantities and concentrations of biochemical substances.

name: microneme
clinical_significance: A microneme is a small secretory organelle in many apicomplexan parasites. It releases proteins that support host-cell attachment, motility, and invasion during the parasite life cycle.

name: micronization
clinical_significance: Micronization is a process that reduces particles to micrometer-scale dimensions, often to increase surface area and improve dissolution or absorption of a drug. The resulting particle size and formulation still determine clinical performance.

name: micronutrient
clinical_significance: A micronutrient is a vitamin or mineral required in small amounts for normal growth, metabolism, and physiologic function. Deficiency or excess can cause disease, and requirements vary with age, pregnancy, illness, and other factors.

name: microorganism
clinical_significance: A microscopic living organism, such as a bacterium, fungus, protozoan, or alga; viruses are acellular infectious agents.

name: microorganism genetics
clinical_significance: The study of genetic material, inheritance, variation, and gene activity in microorganisms. It helps explain how microbes grow, cause disease, develop drug resistance, and exchange useful or harmful traits.

name: micropexophagy
clinical_significance: Micropexophagy is a cell-recycling process studied mainly in yeast in which peroxisomes are selectively enclosed and broken down. It has no direct clinical use but informs research on organelle maintenance and autophagy.

name: microphthalmos
clinical_significance: A birth condition in which one or both eyeballs are unusually small. Vision may be reduced, and other eye or genetic problems may occur, so affected children need an eye examination and ongoing specialist care.

name: micropsia
clinical_significance: A change in vision in which objects appear smaller or farther away than they really are. It can occur with migraine, retinal disease, brain disorders, medicines, or other problems and should be assessed if it is new, persistent, or associated with neurological symptoms.

name: microradiography
clinical_significance: Microradiography uses X-rays to make magnified images of very small specimens, such as bone or tissue sections. It is mainly a research or specialized analysis method rather than a routine whole-patient imaging test.

name: microRNA
clinical_significance: A very small, non-coding RNA that helps control which genes are active, mainly by reducing the production of specific proteins. MicroRNAs are being studied as possible disease markers and treatment targets.

name: microsatellite instability
clinical_significance: A tumor pattern in which short repeated DNA sequences gain or lose units because the cell’s DNA repair system is faulty. A high level can occur in inherited or sporadic cancers and may help predict benefit from some immune treatments.

name: microscope
clinical_significance: An instrument that magnifies structures too small to see clearly with unaided eyes. Light, electron, and fluorescence microscopes help examine cells, tissues, blood, microbes, and other samples.

name: microscopic
clinical_significance: Visible only with a microscope or relating to microscopic examination.

name: microscopic polyangiitis
clinical_significance: An autoimmune disease that inflames and damages small blood vessels. It can affect the kidneys, lungs, skin, nerves, or other organs and may cause blood in the urine, breathing problems, rash, weakness, or bleeding.

name: microscopy
clinical_significance: Microscopy is examination of cells, tissues, organisms, or materials with a microscope. Light, fluorescence, electron, and other microscopy methods provide different information about structure and composition.

name: microsome
clinical_significance: A microsome is a small vesicle formed from fragmented cell membranes during laboratory processing. Liver microsomes are used to study drug metabolism and interactions; they are not structures circulating in the body.

name: microspectrophotometry
clinical_significance: Microspectrophotometry measures the absorption or emission spectrum of a microscopic region or individual cell. It can quantify pigments, nucleic acids, proteins, or other chromophores in small biological samples.
