clinical_significance: Proteins whose amino-acid sequence differs because of a genetic mutation. The change may have no effect or may alter folding, stability, location, or function and contribute to inherited disease, cancer, or drug resistance.

name: mutate
clinical_significance: To mutate means to undergo a change in genetic sequence. Mutations arise spontaneously or from replication errors, DNA damage, or mutagen exposure and may be inherited, acquired in somatic cells, harmful, neutral, or beneficial.

name: mutation
clinical_significance: A mutation is a change in DNA sequence that may be inherited or arise in a cell during life. Some mutations cause disease or alter cancer behavior or drug response, while many have little or no known effect; clinical interpretation depends on the gene, variant, and evidence.

name: mutation abnormality
clinical_significance: A mutation abnormality is an atypical change in DNA sequence or chromosome structure identified relative to a reference. Its clinical significance must be classified using evidence, such as pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain significance, likely benign, or benign.

name: mutation rate
clinical_significance: The frequency at which new DNA changes arise in a cell, organism, or generation. The rate differs between genes and species and can be influenced by DNA-copying errors, repair systems, radiation, chemicals, or other factors.

name: mutism
clinical_significance: Absence or refusal of speech despite adequate ability to speak, occurring in conditions such as catatonia, selective mutism, or neurologic disease.

name: myalgia
clinical_significance: Muscle pain or aching. It may affect one area after injury or exercise, or occur throughout the body with infection, inflammation, medicine effects, thyroid disease, or other conditions. Severe pain with weakness or dark urine needs prompt medical assessment because muscle breakdown may be occurring.

name: myasthenia
clinical_significance: Muscle weakness that often becomes more pronounced with activity and lessens after rest. The term may refer generally to this pattern of weakness or to specific disorders such as myasthenia gravis.

name: myasthenia gravis
clinical_significance: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction that causes fluctuating, fatigable weakness, often affecting the eyes, speech, swallowing, limbs, or breathing. Respiratory or severe swallowing weakness can be life-threatening, and treatment and monitoring depend on disease severity and antibody status.

name: mycelium
clinical_significance: The network of fine branching threads that makes up the growing part of a fungus. It spreads through soil, food, or tissue and can produce the structures that form fungal spores.

name: mycetoma
clinical_significance: A chronic localized infection of skin and subcutaneous tissue caused by fungi or filamentous bacteria, producing swelling, sinuses, and grains.

name: mycobacteriaceae
clinical_significance: A family of slow-growing or rapidly growing, acid-fast bacteria that includes Mycobacterium species causing tuberculosis, leprosy, and nontuberculous infections.

name: mycobacterium
clinical_significance: A genus of acid-fast bacteria that includes the causes of tuberculosis and leprosy and several nontuberculous infections.

name: mycobacterium abscessus
clinical_significance: Mycobacterium abscessus is a rapidly growing nontuberculous mycobacterium that can cause chronic lung disease and skin, soft-tissue, or postsurgical infections. It is often resistant to multiple antibiotics, so diagnosis requires specialized cultures and treatment usually needs susceptibility-guided expert care.

name: mycobacterium avium
clinical_significance: A member of the Mycobacterium avium complex that can cause lung disease, lymph-node infection, or disseminated infection, especially in people with weakened immunity.

name: mycobacterium bovis
clinical_significance: A tuberculosis-complex bacterium that mainly infects cattle but can cause tuberculosis in humans through unpasteurized dairy or animal exposure.

name: mycobacterium chelonae
clinical_significance: A rapidly growing nontuberculous mycobacterium that can cause skin, soft-tissue, bone, eye, or disseminated infection.

name: mycobacterium flavescens
clinical_significance: Mycobacterium flavescens is an environmental nontuberculous mycobacterium that only rarely causes human disease. Its detection in a sample may reflect contamination or colonization; clinicians interpret it using the infection site, symptoms, and repeat or confirmatory testing.

name: mycobacterium fortuitum
clinical_significance: A rapidly growing nontuberculous mycobacterium that can cause wound, catheter, bone, lung, or other opportunistic infections.

name: mycobacterium gordonae
clinical_significance: A usually nonpathogenic water-associated nontuberculous mycobacterium that can occasionally cause disease in people with weakened immunity.

name: mycobacterium haemophilum
clinical_significance: A nontuberculous mycobacterium that can cause skin, joint, and bone infections, especially in people with impaired immunity.

name: mycobacterium infection
clinical_significance: Infection caused by a Mycobacterium species, including tuberculosis, leprosy, and nontuberculous mycobacterial disease.

name: mycobacterium kansasii
clinical_significance: A nontuberculous mycobacterium that commonly causes chronic lung disease resembling tuberculosis and can occasionally cause disseminated infection.

name: mycobacterium leprae
clinical_significance: The bacterium that causes leprosy, a long-lasting infection affecting the skin and nerves. It usually spreads only after prolonged close contact, develops slowly, and can cause numbness, weakness, or skin lesions without treatment.

name: mycobacterium marinum
clinical_significance: Mycobacterium marinum is an aquatic nontuberculous mycobacterium that can cause a slowly progressive skin infection after aquarium, fish, or water exposure, sometimes spreading along lymph channels. A history of aquatic contact helps prompt the correct culture and treatment, which differs from routine skin-infection therapy.

name: mycobacterium scrofulaceum
clinical_significance: A nontuberculous mycobacterium associated especially with cervical lymph-node infection in children and occasional other disease.

name: mycobacterium smegmatis
clinical_significance: Mycobacterium smegmatis is a rapidly growing environmental mycobacterium that rarely causes human infection. When recovered from a clinical specimen, its significance depends on the site, symptoms, repeat isolation, and evidence of tissue disease.

name: mycobacterium szulgai
clinical_significance: A rare nontuberculous bacterium that can cause long-lasting lung disease or other infections, especially in people with underlying lung problems or weakened immunity. Diagnosis requires specialist laboratory testing and clinical assessment.

name: mycobacterium terrae
clinical_significance: Mycobacterium terrae is a nontuberculous mycobacterium that can occasionally cause chronic joint, bone, tendon-sheath, or other infection. It is an uncommon cause of disease, so clinicians correlate culture results with symptoms and tissue findings.

name: mycobacterium tuberculosis
clinical_significance: The bacterium that causes tuberculosis. It spreads through the air and most often affects the lungs, but can involve other organs. Latent infection has no symptoms and does not spread; active disease may cause cough, fever, night sweats, or weight loss.

name: mycobacterium ulcerans
clinical_significance: A mycobacterium that causes Buruli ulcer, a chronic destructive skin infection associated with the toxin mycolactone.

name: mycobiome
clinical_significance: The mycobiome is the community of fungi in or on a person and in a body site or environment. Research on it may help explain infection and inflammatory disease, but routine clinical decisions are not yet based on broad mycobiome profiling.

name: mycophenolate mofetil
clinical_significance: Mycophenolate mofetil is a prodrug of mycophenolic acid that inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and lymphocyte proliferation. It is used as an immunosuppressant, especially after organ transplantation, and can cause infection, cytopenias, gastrointestinal effects, and serious fetal harm.

name: mycophenolic acid
clinical_significance: The active immune-suppressing substance formed from mycophenolate medicines. It blocks an enzyme needed by multiplying lymphocytes and helps prevent organ-transplant rejection, but can cause infections, low blood counts, diarrhea, and fetal harm.

name: mycoplasma
clinical_significance: A genus of very small bacteria lacking a cell wall, including organisms that cause respiratory and genitourinary infections.

name: mycoplasma genitalium
clinical_significance: Mycoplasma genitalium is a sexually transmitted bacterium that can cause persistent or recurrent urethritis and cervicitis and is associated with pelvic inflammatory disease. Increasing antibiotic resistance makes accurate testing and guideline-based treatment important; routine screening of people without symptoms is generally not recommended.

name: mycoplasma hominis
clinical_significance: A wall-less bacterium associated with the genital tract that can cause pelvic, postpartum, urinary, wound, or joint infection.

name: mycoplasma orale
clinical_significance: Mycoplasma orale commonly inhabits the mouth and is usually not a cause of disease. Rare invasive infections have been reported, particularly in medically vulnerable people, so a positive result must be interpreted in light of specimen quality and clinical evidence.

name: mycoplasma pneumoniae
clinical_significance: A bacterium without a cell wall that can cause bronchitis, sore throat, or pneumonia, especially in school-age children and young adults. Illness often develops gradually with cough, fever, headache, or tiredness; complications outside the lungs are uncommon but possible.

name: mycoplasmal pneumonia
clinical_significance: Pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma species, most often Mycoplasma pneumoniae, usually producing a gradual cough and fever.

name: mycoplasmataceae
clinical_significance: A family of very small bacteria that lack a cell wall and includes Mycoplasma and related genera.

name: mycosis
clinical_significance: An infection caused by a fungus, including a yeast or mold. Mycoses may be superficial, cutaneous, subcutaneous, or systemic, depending on the tissues involved; the site and organism determine symptoms and treatment.

name: mycosis fungoides lymphoma
clinical_significance: Mycosis fungoides is a type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma that usually begins with persistent patches or plaques on the skin.

name: mycotoxin
clinical_significance: A poisonous substance made by some fungi that can contaminate food, crops, or indoor environments. Exposure may damage the liver, kidneys, nervous system, immune system, or other organs depending on the toxin and dose.

name: mydriasis
clinical_significance: Mydriasis is pupil dilation and may follow prescribed eye drops, medicines, injury, or neurologic disease. Sudden dilation with eye pain, blurred vision, halos, headache, or nausea can indicate acute angle-closure glaucoma and needs emergency assessment.

name: mydriatics
clinical_significance: Mydriatic medicines widen the pupil for eye examination or selected procedures and can temporarily blur near vision and increase light sensitivity. In susceptible people they may precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma, so eye pain or sudden visual symptoms after use require urgent assessment.

name: myelin
clinical_significance: Myelin is an insulating sheath around nerve fibers that speeds electrical conduction; it is produced by oligodendrocytes in the CNS and Schwann cells in the PNS.

name: myelin sheath
clinical_significance: The insulating covering around many nerve fibers that allows electrical signals to travel quickly. It is made by different support cells in the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves and can be damaged in disorders such as multiple sclerosis.

name: myelination
clinical_significance: Myelination is formation of a myelin sheath around an axon by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system or Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system. It increases the speed and efficiency of nerve conduction.

name: myelitis
clinical_significance: Myelitis is inflammation of the spinal cord or, less commonly, other neural tissue described by the term. Transverse myelitis can cause weakness, sensory changes, and bladder or bowel dysfunction and may result from infection, immune disease, reduced blood flow, or pressure on the spinal cord.

name: myeloablative agonist
clinical_significance: A nonstandard expression that most likely means \textit{myeloablative agent}, a drug or treatment that severely or completely destroys blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. Myeloablative therapy may be used before a stem-cell transplant and causes profound, temporary low blood counts; ``agonist'' is not the usual term in this context.

name: myeloablative chemotherapy
clinical_significance: Myeloablative chemotherapy destroys or severely suppresses bone-marrow blood-cell production and is often used before a stem-cell transplant.

name: myeloblast
clinical_significance: An immature precursor of granulocytes in the bone marrow; excess myeloblasts are characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia.

name: myelocyte
clinical_significance: A developing granulocyte precursor in bone marrow that is more mature than a myeloblast and normally absent or rare in peripheral blood.

name: myelodysplastic syndrome
clinical_significance: Myelodysplastic syndromes are clonal bone-marrow disorders that cause cytopenias and can progress to acute myeloid leukemia; blood counts, marrow findings, and genetic risk guide management.

name: myelofibrosis
clinical_significance: A group of bone-marrow disorders in which fibrous tissue disrupts normal blood-cell production. It includes primary myelofibrosis and secondary forms caused by other blood or marrow diseases.

name: myelography
clinical_significance: Myelography uses fluoroscopy and contrast injected into the fluid space around the spinal cord and nerve roots, often followed by CT, to evaluate spinal-canal narrowing, discs, or nerve compression when MRI is unsuitable or insufficient. It involves a spinal needle and radiation; uncommon complications include headache, bleeding, infection, or contrast reaction.

name: myeloid
clinical_significance: Relating to bone marrow or to the non-lymphoid blood-cell lineages derived from hematopoietic stem cells.

name: myeloid cell
clinical_significance: A blood-forming cell from the myeloid lineage, which produces red cells, platelets, and several white blood-cell types.

name: Myeloid Leukemia
clinical_significance: Myeloid leukemia is a blood cancer arising from abnormal myeloid precursor cells in the bone marrow and blood.

name: myeloid sarcoma
clinical_significance: Myeloid sarcoma is a mass of immature myeloid cells occurring outside the bone marrow, often associated with acute myeloid leukemia.

name: myelolipoma
clinical_significance: A usually benign tumor composed of mature adipose tissue and blood-forming tissue, most often arising in the adrenal gland and often found incidentally.

name: myelomonocyte
clinical_significance: A bone-marrow precursor that can develop toward either the monocyte or granulocyte lineages. An immature bone marrow cell that can develop into either monocytes or certain infection-fighting white blood cells.

name: myelopoiesis
clinical_significance: The production and development of myeloid blood cells, including granulocytes, monocytes, and some precursor cells, in the bone marrow.

name: myeloproliferative neoplasm
clinical_significance: A group of clonal blood and bone-marrow disorders in which the marrow makes too many cells of one or more blood-cell types. Examples include polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and myelofibrosis; the specific disorder determines its effects and risks.

name: myelosuppression
clinical_significance: Myelosuppression is reduced bone-marrow production of blood cells, causing anemia, infection risk from low white cells, or bleeding from low platelets. It commonly follows chemotherapy or other medicines; blood-count monitoring and timely management of fever or bleeding are important.

name: myelosuppressive therapy
clinical_significance: Myelosuppressive therapy reduces bone-marrow production of blood cells, sometimes intentionally during cancer treatment but with risk of anemia, infection, and bleeding.

name: myenteric plexus
clinical_significance: A network of enteric nerves between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers of the gastrointestinal tract that coordinates intestinal motility.

name: Myhre syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited connective-tissue disorder caused by variants in SMAD4 and characterized by short stature, stiff joints, distinctive facial features, hearing loss, and cardiovascular abnormalities.

name: myiasis
clinical_significance: Myiasis is infestation by fly larvae in skin, wounds, or body cavities, usually after exposure in endemic or tropical settings. Treatment depends on the site and species and may require removal of larvae, wound care, and assessment for secondary infection or tissue damage.

name: myoblast
clinical_significance: An early muscle cell that develops and joins with others to form skeletal muscle fibers.

name: myoblastoma
clinical_significance: A rare tumor made of cells resembling developing muscle cells. The term has been used for more than one tumor type, so diagnosis requires modern microscopic and molecular classification.

name: myocardial bridging
clinical_significance: Myocardial bridging occurs when a segment of a coronary artery tunnels through heart muscle and may be compressed during contraction.

name: myocardial contusion
clinical_significance: A bruise of the heart muscle caused by blunt chest trauma, which may produce chest pain, arrhythmias, or impaired heart function.

name: myocardial infarction
clinical_significance: Death of part of the heart muscle because its blood supply is suddenly reduced or blocked, usually by a blood clot on an artery plaque. It may cause chest pressure or pain, breathlessness, sweating, nausea, or no clear symptoms. Diagnosis uses symptoms, ECG findings, and heart-damage blood tests. STEMI and NSTEMI describe different ECG patterns and do not simply mean complete versus partial blockage. Emergency treatment aims to restore blood flow and prevent further clots.

name: myocardial reperfusion
clinical_significance: Restoration of blood flow to heart muscle after ischemia, which can limit injury but may also cause reperfusion-related tissue damage.

name: myocarditis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the heart muscle, often after an infection or because of an immune reaction. It can cause chest pain, breathlessness, abnormal heart rhythms, reduced pumping, or sudden severe illness; severity ranges from mild inflammation to heart failure or shock.

name: myocardium
clinical_significance: The thick muscular middle layer of the heart wall that contracts to pump blood throughout the body.

name: myoclonic epilepsy
clinical_significance: An epilepsy syndrome in which seizures include brief, shock-like involuntary muscle jerks; the specific syndrome determines associated seizure types, age of onset, and prognosis.

name: myoclonus
clinical_significance: A sudden, brief, involuntary muscle jerk or group of jerks.

name: myoepithelial cell
clinical_significance: A contractile cell around certain glands that helps push secretions from breast or salivary tissue.

name: myoepithelioma
clinical_significance: A myoepithelioma is a tumor composed of myoepithelial cells and can be benign or malignant, commonly arising in salivary or other glands.

name: myofibril
clinical_significance: A contractile thread-like structure inside a muscle fiber, composed of repeating sarcomeres containing actin and myosin.

name: myofibrillar myopathy
clinical_significance: Myofibrillar myopathy is a group of inherited muscle disorders with abnormal protein aggregates and progressive skeletal-muscle weakness, sometimes involving heart or breathing muscles.

name: myofibroblasts
clinical_significance: Cells that combine features of fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells and help contract wounds and produce scar tissue.

name: myofibromatosis
clinical_significance: Myofibromatosis is a benign proliferation of myofibroblastic tumors, often in infants or children and involving skin, muscle, bone, or internal organs.

name: myofilament
clinical_significance: A contractile protein filament within a muscle fiber; actin and myosin myofilaments interact through cross-bridges to produce muscle contraction.

name: myogenesis
clinical_significance: Myogenesis is the formation and maturation of muscle tissue during development and repair. Defects in this process can contribute to congenital muscle disorders, while understanding myogenesis supports research on muscle regeneration and neuromuscular disease.

name: myogenin
clinical_significance: A muscle-specific transcription factor required for skeletal-muscle differentiation and used as an immunohistochemical marker in diagnosing some soft-tissue tumors.

name: myoglobin
clinical_significance: An oxygen-binding protein stored in skeletal and heart muscle. When muscle is injured, myoglobin can enter the blood and urine; large amounts may contribute to kidney damage and are interpreted with other tests.

name: myoglobinuria
clinical_significance: Myoglobinuria can indicate substantial muscle breakdown, such as rhabdomyolysis, and may accompany muscle pain, weakness, or dark urine. Released myoglobin can injure the kidneys, so prompt evaluation of the cause, kidney function, and hydration status is important.

name: myokymia
clinical_significance: Involuntary, fine, continuous rippling contractions of muscle fibers, often seen around the eye but also associated with nerve hyperexcitability or neurologic disease.

name: myoma
clinical_significance: A usually benign tumor made of muscle tissue. The term often refers to a leiomyoma, especially a uterine fibroid, but myomas can arise from smooth or skeletal muscle in other sites.

name: myometrium
clinical_significance: The thick muscle layer forming most of the uterus. It contracts during menstruation and labor, responds to hormones, and may develop conditions such as fibroids, adenomyosis, or abnormal thickening.

name: myopathy
clinical_significance: A disease that directly affects muscles and causes weakness, fatigue, cramps, or pain. Causes include inherited conditions, inflammation, medicines, hormone disorders, infections, toxins, and problems with muscle energy production.

name: myopericytoma
clinical_significance: A myopericytoma is a usually benign perivascular tumor composed of cells around small blood vessels, often occurring in skin or soft tissue.

name: myopia
clinical_significance: A refractive error in which light focuses in front of the retina, usually because the eyeball is too long or the eye focuses too strongly. Distant objects appear blurred while near objects are usually clearer. It can be corrected with glasses, contact lenses, or selected refractive procedures.

name: myosin atpase
clinical_significance: The activity by which the muscle protein myosin breaks down ATP, the cell’s energy source. This releases energy that lets myosin pull on actin and produce muscle contraction.

name: myositis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of muscle tissue caused by autoimmune disease, infection, medicines, or injury. It may produce weakness, pain, swelling, or fatigue; evaluation often includes examination, blood tests, imaging, and sometimes muscle testing.

name: myositis ossifican
clinical_significance: Myositis ossificans is bone-like tissue that forms within muscle or other soft tissue, often after trauma. It can cause a painful lump and restricted movement; imaging helps distinguish it from other masses, and early lesions can resemble infection or cancer.

name: myotonia congenita
clinical_significance: Myotonia congenita is an inherited muscle-channel disorder that delays relaxation after contraction, causing stiffness that may improve with repeated movement. It is usually not progressive, but severity varies; evaluation helps distinguish it from other myotonic disorders and guide symptom management.

name: myotonic disorder
clinical_significance: A neuromuscular disorder characterized by delayed relaxation after muscle contraction, often with weakness, stiffness, or progressive muscle wasting.

name: myotonic dystrophy
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder causing delayed muscle relaxation, progressive weakness, and wasting. It can also affect the heart, breathing, swallowing, eyes, hormones, or thinking; symptoms and severity vary between types and people.

name: myristic acid
clinical_significance: Myristic acid is a dietary saturated fatty acid found in foods such as dairy and some tropical oils. High intake of saturated fat can adversely affect blood lipids, so it is considered in overall dietary and cardiovascular risk counseling.

name: myroides
clinical_significance: Myroides is a genus of environmental bacteria that can occasionally cause opportunistic wound, bloodstream, or other infections, particularly in medically vulnerable people. Some isolates resist many antibiotics, making accurate identification and susceptibility testing important.

name: myroides odoratus
clinical_significance: Myroides odoratus is an uncommon environmental bacterium that has been implicated in occasional opportunistic infections, including wound and bloodstream infection. A positive culture requires clinical correlation, and susceptibility testing can guide therapy because resistance may be extensive.

name: myxedema
clinical_significance: Severe hypothyroidism causing accumulation of mucin in tissues, with swelling, slowed body functions, and other symptoms.

name: myxococcales
clinical_significance: Myxococcales are environmental bacteria studied for their unusual biology and production of bioactive compounds. They are not established common human pathogens; their significance is mainly in microbiology and drug-discovery research.

name: myxococcus
clinical_significance: Myxococcus is a genus of soil bacteria studied for collective behavior and production of bioactive molecules. It is not a usual human pathogen, and its medical relevance is primarily research into antimicrobial and other natural products.

name: myxofibroma
clinical_significance: A myxofibroma is a benign tumor containing fibrous and gelatinous myxoid tissue, often arising in the jaw or other connective tissue.

name: myxoid cyst
clinical_significance: A myxoid cyst is a gelatinous fluid-filled lesion near a joint or tendon, commonly on a finger near the distal joint and nail.

name: myxoma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous tumor, most often in the upper left chamber of the heart. It may obstruct blood flow or release clots, causing breathlessness, fainting, fever, or stroke-like symptoms; heart ultrasound is commonly used for diagnosis.

name: myxomycete
clinical_significance: Myxomycetes, or slime molds, are environmental organisms that are not true fungi and rarely cause human disease. Their spores can occasionally be confused with fungal material in laboratory specimens, so microscopy findings need expert interpretation.

name: myxopapillary ependymoma
clinical_significance: Myxopapillary ependymoma is a usually slow-growing spinal tumor arising from ependymal cells, commonly in the conus or filum terminale.

name: myxosarcoma
clinical_significance: A rare cancer of soft tissue containing abundant jelly-like material. It can grow into nearby tissue or spread to distant organs; diagnosis requires examination of a tissue sample.

name: nabumetone
clinical_significance: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicine used for pain and inflammation in selected joint or muscle conditions. It can irritate the stomach, affect kidneys, raise cardiovascular risk, or cause allergic reactions, especially with prolonged use.

name: nadolol
clinical_significance: Nadolol is a nonselective beta blocker used for selected cardiovascular conditions, including hypertension and angina. It can slow the heart rate and worsen asthma or some conduction disorders; it should not be stopped abruptly without clinical advice.

name: nadroparin
clinical_significance: Nadroparin is a low-molecular-weight heparin anticoagulant used in some countries to prevent or treat blood clots. Bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia are important risks, and dose selection depends on indication, weight, and kidney function.

name: naegleria
clinical_significance: Naegleria is a genus of free-living amoebae found in water and soil. Naegleria fowleri can rarely cause a rapidly progressive, usually fatal brain infection when contaminated water enters the nose; other species are not known to cause this disease.

name: naegleria fowleri
clinical_significance: Naegleria fowleri can cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis when contaminated warm freshwater enters the nose, usually during swimming or similar water exposure. The infection progresses rapidly and is almost always fatal, so prevention focuses on avoiding nasal exposure; swallowing contaminated water does not cause this infection, and it does not spread person to person.

name: nafcillin
clinical_significance: Nafcillin is a penicillin-class antibiotic used for susceptible staphylococcal infections, including methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. It does not treat MRSA and can cause allergy, kidney or liver effects, and blood-count abnormalities.

name: nafoxidine
clinical_significance: Nafoxidine is an older investigational nonsteroidal antiestrogen studied for hormone-sensitive breast cancer. It is not a routine current treatment; its relevance is historical and pharmacologic.

name: naganishia albida
clinical_significance: Naganishia albida is an environmental yeast that rarely causes opportunistic infection, mainly in people with impaired immunity or implanted devices. A culture result should be assessed against symptoms and specimen source to distinguish infection from contamination.

name: naganishia diffluens
clinical_significance: Naganishia diffluens is an uncommon environmental yeast and only rarely a cause of human infection. Its recovery from a specimen is interpreted with the patient’s immune status, infection site, and other evidence of disease.

name: naganishia randhawae
clinical_significance: Naganishia randhawae is a rare yeast species with limited evidence as a human pathogen. Identification may matter when recovered from a normally sterile site or in an immunocompromised patient, but clinical significance requires correlation with the specimen and symptoms.

name: nail biting
clinical_significance: Repetitive biting of the fingernails or surrounding skin, often associated with stress, habit, or a body-focused repetitive behavior. It can damage the nail, skin, teeth, or jaw and may introduce infection.

name: nail discoloration
clinical_significance: Nail discoloration can result from trauma, fungal infection, psoriasis, medicines, or pigment-producing bacteria. A new dark streak, pigment extending onto surrounding skin, or unexplained change in one nail should be assessed to exclude melanoma or another serious cause.

name: nail disease
clinical_significance: Nail disease can reflect local infection or injury, inflammatory skin disease, medication effects, or systemic illness. Changes in nail color, shape, thickness, or attachment can help guide diagnosis but are not specific on their own.

name: nail infection
clinical_significance: Nail infection may cause discoloration, thickening, pain, nail separation, or swelling around the nail. Fungal and bacterial causes need different treatment, and persistent or severe infection may require sampling and assessment for spread or an underlying condition.

name: nail pits
clinical_significance: Small dents in the surface of a nail. They are common in psoriasis but may also occur with hair-loss disorders, eczema, lichen planus, or other conditions affecting nail growth.

name: nail plate
clinical_significance: The nail plate is the hard keratin structure visible as the nail. Its color, thickness, surface, and attachment can provide clues to fungal infection, trauma, psoriasis, medication effects, or systemic disease.

name: nairovirus
clinical_significance: Nairoviruses are tick-borne viruses; some cause severe human disease, including Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever. Recognition of relevant travel, tick, or animal-blood exposure supports prompt infection-control precautions and public-health assessment when compatible illness occurs.

name: nalbuphine
clinical_significance: Nalbuphine is an opioid agonist-antagonist analgesic used for selected moderate-to-severe pain and in some anesthesia settings. It can cause sedation and respiratory depression, may precipitate withdrawal in people dependent on full opioid agonists, and remains subject to opioid safety precautions.

name: nalidixic acid
clinical_significance: Nalidixic acid is an older quinolone antibiotic formerly used mainly for urinary infections and is now rarely used because of resistance and safer alternatives. Its historical importance is as an early DNA-gyrase inhibitor related to later quinolone antibiotics.

name: nalorphine
clinical_significance: Nalorphine is an older opioid antagonist with mixed agonist-antagonist activity, historically used to reverse opioid effects. It has largely been replaced by naloxone because naloxone is more suitable for acute overdose reversal.

name: naloxone
clinical_significance: A medicine that blocks opioids and can quickly restore breathing during an opioid overdose. It comes as a nasal spray or injection. Emergency help is still needed because its effect may wear off before the opioid does.

name: naltrexone
clinical_significance: Naltrexone hydrochloride is the salt form of naltrexone, an opioid-receptor antagonist used for alcohol use disorder and relapse prevention in opioid use disorder after detoxification. It blocks opioid analgesia and can trigger withdrawal if started before opioids have cleared.

name: naltrexone hydrochloride
clinical_significance: Naltrexone hydrochloride blocks opioid receptors and is used for alcohol or opioid use disorder; it can precipitate withdrawal if opioids remain in the body and blocks opioid analgesia during treatment.

name: nandrolone
clinical_significance: Nandrolone is an anabolic-androgenic steroid used medically only in limited settings and sometimes misused to increase muscle mass or athletic performance. Misuse can suppress natural hormone production, impair fertility, alter lipids, and cause liver, cardiovascular, or psychiatric harms.

name: nanocurie
clinical_significance: A nanocurie is a unit of radioactivity equal to one billionth of a curie. It may appear in radiopharmaceutical or laboratory records; radiation dose to tissue also depends on the isotope, exposure time, and distribution.

name: nanogram
clinical_significance: A nanogram is one billionth of a gram, a mass unit used for small quantities of hormones, drugs, toxins, and laboratory analytes. Units must be checked carefully when interpreting results or calculating doses.

name: nanomedicine
clinical_significance: The use of very small materials or devices in medicine to help diagnose, prevent, monitor, or treat disease. Examples include nanoparticle drug carriers, imaging agents, biosensors, and some vaccine or cancer treatments; their effects and safety depend on the material, size, dose, and how the body handles them.

name: nanometer
clinical_significance: A nanometer is one billionth of a meter and is used to describe wavelengths, molecules, viruses, and engineered particles. In medicine, particle size can affect how a material distributes, enters cells, or is cleared from the body.

name: nanomole
clinical_significance: A nanomole is one billionth of a mole, a unit of amount of substance used in laboratory measurements and medication or biomarker concentrations. The full unit, including volume where applicable, is essential for interpreting a result.

name: nanopore
clinical_significance: Nanopore technology measures changes as DNA, RNA, or other molecules pass through a nanoscale pore. It enables sequencing and molecular analysis, but clinical results depend on validated assays and interpretation.

name: nanosecond
clinical_significance: A nanosecond is one billionth of a second. It is used in biomedical physics and imaging to describe very brief events, including laser pulses and molecular processes, rather than ordinary clinical timing.

name: nanosphere
clinical_significance: A nanosphere is a small spherical particle used in research and some drug-delivery or diagnostic platforms. Its clinical behavior depends on composition, surface properties, size, and clearance; many applications remain under study.

name: nanotechnology
clinical_significance: The design and use of materials, devices, or systems at the nanometre scale. Medical applications include targeted drug delivery, imaging agents, biosensors, tissue engineering, and diagnostic tests; safety depends on the specific material and exposure.

name: nanotube
clinical_significance: Nanotubes are nanoscale hollow structures investigated for sensing, imaging, and drug delivery. Their medical use remains specialized or experimental, and safety depends on the material, dimensions, dose, and persistence in tissues.

name: naphazoline
clinical_significance: A topical alpha-adrenergic agonist used as a nasal decongestant or ocular vasoconstrictor; prolonged use can worsen congestion.

name: naphthalene
clinical_significance: Naphthalene is a toxic chemical found in some moth repellents and industrial products. Ingestion or inhalation can damage red blood cells and cause hemolytic anemia, especially in people with G6PD deficiency; exposure also warrants evaluation for other organ effects.

name: naphthoquinone
clinical_significance: Naphthoquinones are a class of compounds that includes vitamin K-related molecules and some drugs, natural products, and toxins. Their clinical effects vary by compound, including roles in clotting, treatment, or poisoning.

name: naproxen
clinical_significance: Naproxen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug used for pain and inflammation. It can cause stomach bleeding or ulcers, kidney injury, fluid retention, and cardiovascular complications, with greater risk in some patients and with prolonged use.

name: narcissism
clinical_significance: A pattern of excessive self-focus, need for admiration, or sense of superiority. Mild traits are common, while persistent traits that impair relationships or functioning may occur in narcissistic personality disorder.

name: narcolepsy
clinical_significance: A chronic disorder that affects the brain’s control of sleep and wakefulness. It causes overwhelming daytime sleepiness and sudden, irresistible sleep episodes, even after enough nighttime sleep; nighttime sleep may also be broken. The boundary between sleep and wakefulness is less clear, so some features of rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep may occur while awake or when falling asleep or waking. Symptoms may include cataplexy, a brief loss of muscle control triggered by strong emotions; sleep para

name: narcotic
clinical_significance: “Narcotic” is an imprecise term often used for opioid medicines or controlled drugs. In clinical records, the specific substance and formulation should be named because effects, overdose risk, and treatment differ.

name: narcotic antagonist
clinical_significance: A narcotic antagonist blocks opioid receptors and can reverse or reduce opioid effects. Naloxone is used to reverse life-threatening respiratory depression in overdose; emergency care remains necessary because the opioid may outlast the antagonist.

name: narrow
clinical_significance: “Narrow” has no standalone clinical meaning; it describes reduced width or caliber, such as a narrowed airway, blood vessel, spinal canal, or heart valve. The consequences depend on the structure and degree of narrowing.

name: nasal bone
clinical_significance: The nasal bones form the upper bony bridge of the nose and are commonly fractured in facial trauma. Assessment checks alignment, bleeding, septal hematoma, and associated facial injury because a septal hematoma needs urgent treatment.

name: nasal cartilage
clinical_significance: Nasal cartilage supports the shape and airflow of the nose and contributes to the septum and external nose. Injury, inflammation, or surgery can alter nasal structure or breathing; septal hematoma and infection require prompt attention.

name: nasal cavity
clinical_significance: The nasal cavity filters, warms, and humidifies inhaled air and is a common site of infection, allergy, bleeding, and obstruction. Its anatomy also matters for nasal drug delivery and airway management.

name: nasal congestion
clinical_significance: A blocked or stuffy feeling in the nose caused by swelling of the nasal lining, extra mucus, or a structural problem. It occurs with colds, allergies, sinus disease, irritants, and other conditions.

name: nasal decongestant
clinical_significance: Nasal decongestants reduce nasal swelling, but topical sprays used for more than a few days can cause rebound congestion. Oral agents may raise blood pressure or heart rate and need caution in people with cardiovascular disease or certain other conditions.

name: nasal flaring
clinical_significance: Nasal flaring is widening of the nostrils with each breath and signals increased work of breathing, especially in infants and children. When accompanied by retractions, grunting, bluish color, or difficulty feeding or speaking, it needs urgent assessment.

name: nasal lavage
clinical_significance: Nasal lavage rinses the nasal passages with saline to remove mucus, allergens, or crusts and may relieve symptoms in some nasal or sinus conditions. Irrigation water and equipment should be clean to avoid introducing infection.

name: nasal obstruction
clinical_significance: Nasal obstruction can result from swelling, allergy, infection, polyps, a deviated septum, or a mass. Persistent one-sided obstruction, recurrent bleeding, facial swelling, or symptoms in a child may require examination to identify a structural or serious cause.

name: nasal polyps
clinical_significance: Soft, usually noncancerous growths in the lining of the nose or sinuses. They can cause a blocked nose, runny nose, and reduced sense of smell.

name: nasal septum
clinical_significance: The nasal septum divides the nasal cavity and helps support the nose. Deviation can contribute to airflow obstruction, while a septal hematoma after injury requires urgent drainage to prevent cartilage damage and deformity.

name: nasal sinus
clinical_significance: The paranasal sinuses are air-filled spaces around the nasal cavity that can become inflamed or infected. Persistent symptoms, severe pain, eye swelling, visual changes, or neurologic signs may indicate complications requiring prompt evaluation.

name: nasogastric tube
clinical_significance: A tube passed through the nose into the stomach to remove contents or deliver nutrition, fluids, or medicines when clinically indicated.

name: nasolabial sulcus
clinical_significance: The nasolabial sulcus is the crease running from each side of the nose toward the corner of the mouth. Changes in facial movement or symmetry around it can help assess facial-nerve function, swelling, or soft-tissue injury.

name: nasolacrimal duct
clinical_significance: A membranous canal enclosed within a bony canal that conveys tears from the lacrimal sac downward into the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity beneath the inferior nasal concha, guarded by the mucosal valve of Hasner.

name: nasopharyngeal carcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer arising in the upper throat behind the nose. It may cause a blocked or bleeding nose, hearing problems, a neck lump, headache, or swallowing trouble; risk varies with genetics, infections, and geographic background.

name: nasopharyngeal disease
clinical_significance: Nasopharyngeal disease includes infection, inflammation, obstruction, and tumors in the upper throat behind the nose. Symptoms such as persistent nasal blockage, nosebleeds, ear fullness, hearing change, or a neck lump may warrant evaluation.

name: nasopharyngeal neoplasm
clinical_significance: A nasopharyngeal neoplasm may be benign or malignant and can cause nasal obstruction, bleeding, ear symptoms, or a neck mass. Persistent or unilateral symptoms generally require examination and sometimes endoscopy or biopsy.

name: nasopharyngitis
clinical_significance: Nasopharyngitis is inflammation of the nasal passages and upper throat, most often due to a viral upper respiratory infection. Care is usually supportive; breathing difficulty, dehydration, prolonged fever, or worsening symptoms require assessment for complications or another cause.

name: nasopharynx
clinical_significance: The upper part of the throat behind the nose and above the soft palate. It carries air, contains the openings of the tubes that connect to the middle ears, and includes nearby lymph tissue that helps defend against infection.

name: nasoscope
clinical_significance: A nasoscope is an instrument used to examine the nasal passages and nasopharynx, often through endoscopy. It helps evaluate persistent obstruction, bleeding, polyps, or suspected lesions and can support biopsy or other procedures.

name: natal teeth
clinical_significance: Natal teeth are present at birth and are often loose or poorly formed. They can injure the infant’s tongue or interfere with feeding and may pose an aspiration risk if very mobile; dental assessment determines whether monitoring or removal is appropriate.

name: natalizumab
clinical_significance: Natalizumab is a monoclonal antibody used for selected patients with multiple sclerosis and Crohn disease. It reduces immune-cell entry into the brain but increases risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, so patient selection and ongoing safety monitoring are essential.

name: natamycin
clinical_significance: Natamycin is an antifungal medicine used mainly as eye drops for fungal keratitis. Correct diagnosis matters because fungal corneal infection can threaten vision and requires specialist-directed treatment.

name: nateglinide
clinical_significance: Nateglinide is an oral medicine that stimulates insulin release around meals to treat type 2 diabetes. It can cause hypoglycemia, especially if a meal is skipped, and is not used to treat type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis.

name: natural history
clinical_significance: Natural history describes how a disease progresses without treatment or intervention. It provides a comparison for judging prognosis, screening, and the benefits or harms of treatment.

name: natural immunosuppression
clinical_significance: Natural immunosuppression is reduced immune activity arising from physiologic states or disease rather than a prescribed immunosuppressive drug. It can affect infection risk and vaccine responses, but the cause and degree must be specified clinically.

name: natural killer cell
clinical_significance: A type of white blood cell that can recognize and destroy some virus-infected or abnormal cells without previous exposure to that specific target. It helps provide early immune defense and releases signals that guide other immune cells.

name: naturopathy
clinical_significance: Naturopathy is a broad system of complementary practices that may include diet, supplements, and nonpharmacologic therapies. Some approaches can delay effective care or interact with medicines, so clinicians need to know what products and treatments a patient uses.

name: nausea
clinical_significance: An unpleasant feeling that you may vomit. It can occur with stomach or intestinal illness, pregnancy, medicines, migraine, inner-ear problems, metabolic disorders, or serious abdominal or neurologic disease. Persistent vomiting, severe pain, dehydration, blood, or confusion may signal a serious condition.

name: navitoclax
clinical_significance: Navitoclax is an investigational anticancer drug that inhibits BCL-2 family proteins to promote tumor-cell death. It remains under study, and treatment research must account for dose-limiting platelet reduction and bleeding risk.

name: nebivolol
clinical_significance: Nebivolol is a beta blocker used to treat hypertension and selected cardiovascular conditions. It can slow heart rate and lower blood pressure; abrupt discontinuation or use in certain conduction or circulatory disorders may be hazardous.

name: nebulizer
clinical_significance: A device that converts liquid medicine into an aerosol for inhalation through a mouthpiece or mask. Common types include jet nebulizers, ultrasonic nebulizers, and vibrating-mesh nebulizers; they differ in how the aerosol is generated and delivered.

name: necator americanus
clinical_significance: Necator americanus is a human hookworm acquired when larvae in contaminated soil penetrate the skin. Intestinal worms feed on blood and can cause iron-deficiency anemia, fatigue, and impaired growth; diagnosis and antiparasitic treatment are important.

name: necatoriasis
clinical_significance: Necatoriasis is intestinal hookworm infection caused by Necator americanus. Chronic blood loss can lead to iron-deficiency anemia, weakness, and impaired growth, especially in children; stool testing and antiparasitic treatment are used where indicated.

name: neck
clinical_significance: The neck connects the head to the trunk and contains the cervical spine, airway, esophagus, thyroid, vessels, nerves, muscles, and lymph nodes.

name: neck dissection
clinical_significance: Neck dissection removes cervical lymph nodes, sometimes with adjacent structures, to treat or stage cancers of the head and neck. The operation can affect shoulder movement, sensation, voice, swallowing, or lymph drainage, so the extent is balanced against tumor control.

name: neck edema
clinical_significance: Neck edema is swelling in the neck that may result from infection, allergy, trauma, venous or lymphatic obstruction, or a mass. Rapid swelling with breathing or swallowing difficulty is an emergency because the airway can become compromised.

name: neck pain
clinical_significance: Pain or stiffness in the neck, commonly caused by muscle strain, poor posture, injury, arthritis, degenerative disc disease, or nerve compression. It may be localized or spread to the shoulders, arms, or head.

name: neck stiffness
clinical_significance: Reduced ability to move the neck comfortably because of muscle tightness, inflammation, injury, or irritation of tissues around the spine or meninges. Severe stiffness with fever, headache, confusion, rash, or neurologic symptoms requires urgent assessment.

name: necrobiosis lipoidica
clinical_significance: Necrobiosis lipoidica is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder that often causes yellow-brown plaques on the shins, which may ulcerate after minor injury. It is associated with diabetes but can occur without it; persistent ulcers need wound care and assessment for infection.

name: necroptosis
clinical_significance: Necroptosis is a regulated form of cell death involved in inflammation and tissue injury. It is being studied in infection, cancer, and inflammatory disease, but it is not a routine clinical diagnosis or treatment target.

name: necrosis
clinical_significance: Necrosis is death of cells or tissue within a living body caused by ischemia, infection, toxins, trauma, inflammation, or other injury.

name: necrotizing fasciitis
clinical_significance: A life-threatening infection that rapidly destroys tissue beneath the skin. Early skin changes may be mild despite severe pain and deeper damage. Treatment usually includes surgery and antibiotics.

name: needle
clinical_significance: A hollow, sharp tube used to inject medicine or remove blood, fluid, or tissue. Needles come in different lengths and widths; the appropriate size depends on the procedure and body site.

name: negativism
clinical_significance: Negativism is resistance or opposition to instructions or external stimuli and may occur with catatonia, psychosis, neurologic disease, or severe distress. A new marked change in behavior requires assessment for medical and psychiatric causes.

name: neisseria
clinical_significance: Neisseria is a genus that includes common mucosal commensals as well as Neisseria gonorrhoeae and N. meningitidis, which cause serious human infections. Species identification is clinically important because treatment, transmission precautions, and public-health actions differ.

name: neisseria canis
clinical_significance: Neisseria canis is associated mainly with animals and is an uncommon cause of human infection, usually after animal exposure or in people with underlying illness. A culture result is interpreted using the infection site and clinical evidence.

name: neisseria cinerea
clinical_significance: Neisseria cinerea commonly colonizes the upper respiratory tract and rarely causes opportunistic infection. Because it can resemble pathogenic Neisseria in laboratory testing, accurate species identification helps avoid misdiagnosis.

name: neisseria elongata
clinical_significance: Neisseria elongata is an uncommon cause of human infection, including occasional endocarditis or bloodstream infection. Its recovery from a normally sterile site warrants clinical assessment, while findings from nonsterile sites may represent colonization.

name: neisseria flavescens
clinical_significance: Neisseria flavescens is usually an upper-airway commensal but has occasionally been linked to invasive infection. Its significance depends on specimen source, symptoms, and whether it is repeatedly isolated from a normally sterile site.

name: neisseria gonorrhoeae
clinical_significance: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes gonorrhea, which may be asymptomatic or cause urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, or disseminated infection. Antibiotic resistance complicates treatment; diagnosis, partner management, and follow-up follow current public-health guidance.

name: neisseria lactamica
clinical_significance: Neisseria lactamica commonly colonizes the throat, especially in children, and is generally not pathogenic. It can be confused with meningococci in preliminary testing, so species-level identification matters when invasive disease is suspected.

name: neisseria meningitidis
clinical_significance: Neisseria meningitidis can cause rapidly progressive meningitis and bloodstream infection with substantial risk of death or disability. Suspected disease is a medical emergency requiring prompt antibiotics, droplet precautions, and public-health evaluation of close contacts.

name: neisseria mucosa
clinical_significance: Neisseria mucosa is generally a mucosal commensal but has occasionally caused endocarditis or other invasive infection. A positive result is most concerning when recovered from blood or another normally sterile site with compatible illness.

name: neisseria polysaccharea
clinical_significance: Neisseria polysaccharea is usually an oropharyngeal commensal and is rarely associated with human disease. It can resemble meningococci in some laboratory tests, making confirmatory identification important if invasive Neisseria infection is considered.

name: neisseria sicca
clinical_significance: Neisseria sicca commonly inhabits the mouth and upper airway and only rarely causes opportunistic infection, such as endocarditis. The clinical importance of an isolate depends on the specimen and evidence of invasive disease.

name: neisseria subflava
clinical_significance: Neisseria subflava is usually an upper-respiratory commensal and rarely causes invasive infection. It may be relevant when recovered from blood or another sterile site, but nonsterile-site detection alone does not establish disease.

name: neisseria weaveri
clinical_significance: Neisseria weaveri is associated with dogs and has occasionally caused human wound or bloodstream infection after animal exposure. Bite history and specimen source help determine whether an isolate is clinically meaningful.

name: neisseriaceae
clinical_significance: Neisseriaceae is a bacterial family that includes pathogenic and commensal Neisseria species and related genera. Laboratory identification to species level is important because some members cause urgent, transmissible disease while others are normal flora.

name: nelarabine
clinical_significance: Nelarabine is a chemotherapy drug used for selected T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia or lymphoma. It can cause severe neurologic toxicity, including weakness, numbness, seizures, or impaired coordination, and requires careful monitoring.

name: nelfinavir
clinical_significance: Nelfinavir is an HIV protease inhibitor used in combination antiretroviral therapy. It is now infrequently selected because of newer options and may cause diarrhea, metabolic effects, and drug interactions.

name: nelfinavir mesylate
clinical_significance: Nelfinavir mesylate is the salt formulation of nelfinavir, an HIV protease inhibitor. Its clinical use is limited compared with newer antiretroviral regimens; medication interactions and adherence remain relevant when it is prescribed.

name: Nelson syndrome
clinical_significance: Nelson syndrome is growth or progression of an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease. It can cause skin pigmentation, tumor mass effects, or other pituitary hormone problems, so ongoing hormone testing and pituitary imaging are important.

name: nematocyst
clinical_significance: A nematocyst is a stinging capsule used by cnidarians such as jellyfish. Contact can inject venom and cause pain, skin injury, allergic reactions, or rarely systemic toxicity; severe symptoms after a sting need urgent care.

name: nematoda
clinical_significance: Nematodes are roundworms, some of which cause human or animal parasitic disease. Species identification guides testing, treatment, and prevention; many environmental nematodes do not infect humans.

name: neoadjuvant therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment given before the main treatment, such as surgery or radiotherapy, to shrink a tumor or make it easier to treat. It may also show how the tumor responds and help doctors plan the next treatment.

name: neocortex
clinical_significance: The outer part of the cerebral hemispheres involved in conscious perception, language, planning, memory, and voluntary movement.

name: neomycin
clinical_significance: Neomycin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used mainly in topical or selected oral preparations. Systemic absorption can damage the kidneys or hearing, and topical use may cause contact allergy; it is not used systemically in most settings.

name: neonatal death
clinical_significance: Neonatal death is death during the first 28 days after birth and is a key measure of newborn health and care quality. Causes include prematurity, birth complications, infection, and congenital conditions; prevention depends on timely maternal and neonatal care.

name: neonatal deformity
clinical_significance: A neonatal deformity is a structural difference present at or soon after birth. Evaluation may identify an isolated finding or a broader genetic, developmental, or exposure-related condition and guide treatment and family counseling.

name: neonatal disorder
clinical_significance: Neonatal disorders range from transient adaptation problems to serious congenital, infectious, metabolic, or prematurity-related illness. Early recognition matters because newborns can deteriorate quickly and may show nonspecific signs.

name: neonatal hyperbilirubinemia
clinical_significance: An excess of bilirubin in a newborn’s blood, causing yellow skin or eyes. Mild cases are common, but rapidly rising or very high levels can damage the brain; treatment may include frequent feeding, phototherapy, or rarely an exchange transfusion.

name: neonatal jaundice
clinical_significance: Neonatal jaundice reflects elevated bilirubin and is common, but bilirubin levels must be assessed using the infant’s age in hours, gestational age, and risk factors. Severe untreated hyperbilirubinemia can cause permanent brain injury; timely follow-up and threshold-based treatment prevent harm.

name: neonatal nursing
clinical_significance: Neonatal nursing provides specialized monitoring and care for newborns, including feeding support, temperature control, infection prevention, and recognition of respiratory or metabolic problems. Skilled observation is especially important for premature or ill infants.

name: neonatal rickets
clinical_significance: Neonatal rickets is impaired bone mineralization in a newborn, often related to prematurity, low mineral stores, or maternal and infant vitamin D or mineral problems. It can cause bone fragility and biochemical abnormalities and requires evaluation of nutrition and underlying causes.

name: neonatal screening
clinical_significance: Newborn screening detects selected treatable genetic, endocrine, metabolic, or other conditions before symptoms appear. Timely collection, confirmatory testing, and follow-up are essential because early treatment can prevent serious disability or death.

name: neonatal stage
clinical_significance: The neonatal period is the first 28 days after birth, when newborns adapt to breathing, circulation, feeding, and temperature regulation. Premature infants and newborns with illness need close monitoring for rapid changes.

name: neonatology
clinical_significance: Neonatology is the medical specialty focused on newborn health, especially premature or critically ill infants. Neonatal specialists coordinate respiratory, nutritional, developmental, and family-centered care.

name: neoplasm
clinical_significance: A new, abnormal growth of cells that forms a mass or tissue. A neoplasm may be benign and stay localized, or malignant and invade nearby tissues or spread to distant organs.

name: neoplasm micrometastasis
clinical_significance: Neoplasm micrometastasis refers to a very small deposit of tumor cells at a site distant from the primary cancer, sometimes below routine imaging detection. Whether it affects staging or treatment depends on the cancer type and how it was detected.

name: neoplastic cell
clinical_significance: A neoplastic cell is a cell participating in an abnormal clonal growth that may be benign or malignant. Pathologic and molecular assessment distinguishes tumor cells from reactive changes and helps determine diagnosis and treatment.

name: neoplastic process
clinical_significance: A neoplastic process is abnormal cell growth that may form a benign or malignant tumor. Determining its nature requires clinical context and, when appropriate, imaging, pathology, and molecular testing.

name: neoplastic transformation
clinical_significance: Neoplastic transformation is the change by which a normal cell acquires features that support uncontrolled growth and tumor formation. Understanding these changes helps identify cancer mechanisms, biomarkers, and potential treatment targets.

name: neopterin
clinical_significance: Neopterin is a molecule produced by immune cells in response to interferon signaling. Blood or urine levels can rise with immune activation, infection, or some cancers, but the result is nonspecific and is not interpreted alone as a diagnosis.

name: neostigmine
clinical_significance: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used to reverse selected nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade and to treat some disorders of neuromuscular transmission or bowel and bladder motility.

name: neostriatum
clinical_significance: The neostriatum, comprising the caudate nucleus and putamen, is part of the basal ganglia that helps regulate movement and learning. Dysfunction or injury can contribute to movement disorders and changes in behavior or cognition.

name: nephelometry
clinical_significance: Nephelometry measures light scattered by particles in a sample and is used in laboratory tests for proteins such as immunoglobulins and complement. Results depend on assay calibration and can be affected by sample turbidity or interfering substances.

name: nephrectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove part or all of a kidney. It may treat kidney cancer, severe kidney damage, infection, or a kidney that no longer works.

name: nephritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of kidney tissue that can cause blood or protein in the urine, swelling, high blood pressure, reduced urine, or loss of kidney function. Infection, medicines, and immune diseases are possible causes.

name: nephroblastoma
clinical_significance: Another name for Wilms tumor, the most common kidney cancer in children. It may appear as a painless abdominal lump, abdominal pain, blood in the urine, fever, or high blood pressure and needs specialist treatment.

name: nephrocalcinosis
clinical_significance: Buildup of calcium deposits inside kidney tissue. It may result from high calcium levels, hormone or kidney disorders, inherited conditions, dehydration, or medicines and can lead to stones, blood in the urine, or reduced kidney function.

name: nephrogenic rest
clinical_significance: A nephrogenic rest is a remnant of fetal kidney tissue that can persist after birth and may be associated with Wilms tumor, especially when multiple rests are present. It is monitored in context because it can be difficult to distinguish from an early tumor on imaging or pathology.

name: nephrolithiasis
clinical_significance: Formation of stones in the kidneys or urinary tract. Stones can cause severe side or back pain, blood in the urine, nausea, or blockage; dehydration, inherited conditions, medicines, and diet can contribute.

name: nephrologist
clinical_significance: A doctor who specializes in kidney disease. Nephrologists assess reduced kidney function, high blood pressure related to kidney problems, kidney inflammation, and mineral or salt disturbances and may manage dialysis or transplant care.

name: nephron
clinical_significance: The microscopic working unit of a kidney. Each nephron filters blood, returns needed water and substances to the body, and removes waste to make urine; each kidney contains about one million.

name: nephronophthisis
clinical_significance: A rare inherited kidney disease that gradually reduces the kidneys’ ability to concentrate urine. It may cause excessive thirst and urination, anemia, growth problems, and eventually kidney failure.

name: nephropathy
clinical_significance: Disease or damage of the kidneys. It may reduce waste removal, disturb fluid and salt balance, cause protein or blood in the urine, or eventually lead to kidney failure.

name: nephrosclerosis
clinical_significance: Hardening and scarring of kidney tissue, commonly caused by long-standing high blood pressure or blood-vessel disease. Progressive damage can reduce filtering ability, cause protein in urine, and lead to chronic kidney disease.

name: nephrosis
clinical_significance: Nephrosis is an older, nonspecific term for kidney disease, sometimes used for noninflammatory kidney damage or as shorthand for nephrotic syndrome. Current clinical assessment should identify the specific kidney disorder and laboratory findings.

name: nephrostomy
clinical_significance: A procedure that creates a drainage path from the kidney through the skin when urine cannot pass normally to the bladder. A temporary tube usually carries urine into a bag while the blockage is treated.

name: nephrotic syndrome
clinical_significance: A group of findings caused by kidney-filter damage: a large amount of protein in the urine, low albumin in the blood, swelling, and often high blood cholesterol. It may cause frothy urine and swelling around the eyes, legs, or feet, and can increase the risk of blood clots or infection. Causes include diseases of the kidney filters and illnesses such as diabetes or lupus.

name: nephroureterectomy
clinical_significance: Nephroureterectomy removes a kidney and its ureter, commonly to treat upper-tract urothelial cancer or selected severe kidney conditions. Remaining kidney function and cancer staging influence treatment planning and follow-up.

name: nerve
clinical_significance: A bundle of nerve fibers that carries messages between the brain or spinal cord and the rest of the body. Nerves control movement and carry sensations such as touch, pain, and temperature.

name: nerve block
clinical_significance: An injection of numbing medicine near a nerve or group of nerves to temporarily stop pain signals. It may help diagnose the source of pain or provide pain relief during or after a procedure; weakness or other temporary effects can occur.

name: nerve Degeneration
clinical_significance: Nerve degeneration is progressive loss or damage of nerve fibers and may cause sensory loss, pain, weakness, or autonomic symptoms. The pattern helps localize disease and may result from inherited, metabolic, toxic, immune, or compressive causes.

name: nerve ending
clinical_significance: A nerve ending is the terminal part of a nerve fiber that detects stimuli or communicates with another cell. Injury or dysfunction can alter pain, temperature, touch, or autonomic responses.

name: nerve fiber
clinical_significance: The long, thread-like part of a nerve cell that carries signals. Most nerve fibers are axons, sometimes covered by a fatty insulating layer called myelin.

name: nerve graft
clinical_significance: A nerve graft bridges a gap in a damaged nerve when direct repair is not possible. Recovery depends on injury severity, distance to the target, timing, and rehabilitation; function may remain incomplete.

name: nerve injury
clinical_significance: Damage to a nerve that can cause pain, numbness, tingling, weakness, altered reflexes, or changes in sweating, blood pressure, digestion, or bladder function. Recovery depends on the nerve, severity, cause, and treatment.

name: nerve plexus
clinical_significance: A network where nerves join and branch to supply a body region. The brachial plexus, for example, supplies much of the arm.

name: nerve root
clinical_significance: The beginning part of a spinal nerve where it connects with the spinal cord. Sensory and motor roots carry signals into and out of the cord.

name: nerve Tissue
clinical_significance: Nerve tissue consists of neurons and supporting glial cells in the central and peripheral nervous systems. Injury, inflammation, tumors, or degeneration can impair sensation, movement, cognition, or autonomic function.

name: nervonic acid
clinical_significance: Nervonic acid is a long-chain fatty acid found in myelin and some sphingolipids. It is studied in relation to nerve-membrane biology, but its blood or tissue levels are not a standalone diagnostic test for neurologic disease.

name: nervous system
clinical_significance: The brain and spinal cord (central nervous system), peripheral nerves and ganglia (peripheral nervous system), and supporting cells that detect and process information. It coordinates sensation, movement, automatic body functions, cognition, emotion, learning, and behavior.

name: nervous system disorder
clinical_significance: Nervous system disorders affect the brain, spinal cord, peripheral nerves, or neuromuscular pathways and can impair movement, sensation, cognition, behavior, or autonomic function. New focal deficits, seizures, or altered consciousness may require emergency evaluation.

name: nervous system neoplasm
clinical_significance: A nervous system neoplasm is a benign or malignant tumor arising in the brain, spinal cord, or peripheral nerves. Symptoms depend on location and may include seizures, focal deficits, pain, or raised intracranial pressure; imaging and tissue diagnosis guide care.

name: nesidioblastosis
clinical_significance: A rare diffuse or focal hyperfunctional hypertrophy and hyperplasia of pancreatic beta cells budding from the pancreatic ductal epithelium, causing endogenous persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia in neonates (congenital hyperinsulinism) and adults (post-gastric bypass hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia).

name: nesiritide
clinical_significance: Nesiritide is an intravenous recombinant natriuretic peptide formerly used for selected patients with acute decompensated heart failure. It can cause marked hypotension and has limited routine use; treatment decisions prioritize established heart-failure therapies and hemodynamic status.

name: nestin protein
clinical_significance: Nestin is a protein expressed in neural progenitor cells and some other immature or regenerating cells. It is used mainly as a research or tissue marker and is not, by itself, diagnostic of a specific disease.

name: netilmicin
clinical_significance: Netilmicin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used for selected serious bacterial infections, depending on local availability and susceptibility. Kidney injury, hearing or balance damage, and neuromuscular effects are important risks, so dosing and monitoring require care.

name: netropsin
clinical_significance: Netropsin is an experimental DNA-binding antibiotic compound used mainly in biochemical and drug-development research. It is not a routine human treatment.

name: neural crest
clinical_significance: A temporary embryonic multipotent cellular population located along the borders of the closing neural folds that undergoes epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and migrates extensively to form peripheral sensory ganglia, autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, craniofacial bones, and adrenal chromaffin cells.

name: neural inhibition
clinical_significance: Neural inhibition reduces the activity or signaling of neurons and helps shape normal brain and spinal-cord function. Excessive or deficient inhibition can contribute to seizures, movement disorders, or other neurologic symptoms depending on the circuit involved.

name: neural pathway
clinical_significance: A connected route of nerve cells and nerve fibers that carries signals between different parts of the nervous system.

name: neural plate
clinical_significance: The neural plate is an early embryonic structure that folds to form the neural tube, precursor of the brain and spinal cord. Disruption of neural-tube development can cause major congenital abnormalities, making early pregnancy folate prevention important.

name: neural prostheses
clinical_significance: Neural prostheses interface with the nervous system to restore or support functions such as hearing, movement, or communication. Examples include cochlear implants and selected brain or peripheral-nerve stimulators; benefits and risks depend on the device and indication.

name: neural tube
clinical_significance: The neural tube is the embryonic precursor of the brain and spinal cord. Failure of closure can cause neural-tube defects such as spina bifida or anencephaly; adequate folic acid before conception and early in pregnancy lowers risk.

name: neuralgia
clinical_significance: Neuralgia is sharp, burning, or electric pain along the distribution of a nerve, caused by irritation, compression, infection, injury, or other disease.

name: neuraminidase
clinical_significance: Neuraminidase is an enzyme on influenza viruses that helps newly formed virus particles leave infected cells. Neuraminidase inhibitors treat influenza by blocking this step and work best when started early in illness.

name: neurasthenia
clinical_significance: Neurasthenia is a historical diagnostic term for persistent fatigue, weakness, or irritability and is not a specific modern diagnosis in many classification systems. Similar symptoms require assessment for sleep, mood, medical, medication, and social causes.

name: neuregulin
clinical_significance: Neuregulins are signaling proteins involved in nervous-system development and in heart and other tissue biology. Changes in neuregulin pathways are studied in neurologic, psychiatric, and cardiac disease, but testing is not routine for most patients.

name: neurenteric cyst
clinical_significance: A neurenteric cyst is a rare congenital cyst near the spinal cord, often in the thoracic region, that can compress neural structures and cause pain, weakness, or sensory changes. MRI helps define its location, and symptomatic lesions may need neurosurgical treatment.

name: neurilemma
clinical_significance: The outer layer of a Schwann cell that surrounds and supports a nerve fiber outside the brain and spinal cord.

name: neurilemmoma
clinical_significance: Schwannomas are usually benign nerve-sheath tumors, but location can cause pain, weakness, hearing loss, or compression; multiple tumors may suggest an inherited syndrome.

name: neurite
clinical_significance: A neurite is an extension from a developing neuron that may become an axon or dendrite. Neurite growth is studied in neural development, nerve repair, and neurotoxicity research.

name: neuritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or irritation of a nerve, often causing pain, altered sensation, weakness, or other changes in nerve function.

name: neuroanatomy
clinical_significance: The study of the structure and organization of the nervous system, including the brain, spinal cord, peripheral nerves, and their connections.

name: neurobiology
clinical_significance: Neurobiology studies the structure and function of the nervous system, including how disease alters neural circuits. Its findings underpin neurologic diagnosis, drug development, and therapies for brain and nerve disorders.

name: neuroblastoma
clinical_significance: A childhood cancer arising from immature nerve cells, commonly in or near the adrenal glands or spine. It may cause an abdominal mass, pain, weakness, or other symptoms and can range from mild to aggressive.

name: neurochemistry
clinical_significance: Neurochemistry studies chemical signaling and metabolism in the nervous system. Findings help explain neurologic and psychiatric disease and support development of medicines, biomarkers, and diagnostic tests.

name: neurocutaneous syndrome
clinical_significance: A disorder affecting both the nervous system and the skin, often because of an inherited genetic change. Examples include neurofibromatosis and tuberous sclerosis.

name: neurocysticercosis
clinical_significance: Infection of the brain or spinal cord by the larval form of the pork tapeworm. It can cause seizures, headaches, confusion, or movement problems and is acquired by swallowing tapeworm eggs from contaminated food or hands.

name: neurodermatitis
clinical_significance: A chronic itchy skin condition in which repeated scratching or rubbing makes a patch thick, leathery, and irritated. Stress, dry skin, or an initial rash may start the itch–scratch cycle.

name: neurodevelopmental disorders
clinical_significance: A group of conditions that begin during the developmental period and affect cognition, communication, behavior, motor function, learning, or adaptive skills. Examples include attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, communication disorders, specific learning disorder, motor disorders, and tic disorders.

name: neuroectodermal tumor
