clinical_significance: Neuroectodermal tumor is a broad or historical label for tumors arising from embryonic neuroectoderm. Modern pathologic and molecular classification is needed because tumors under older labels can differ greatly in behavior and treatment.

name: neuroeffector junction
clinical_significance: The neuroeffector junction is the site where a nerve signal acts on a muscle, gland, or other target tissue. Medicines that alter signaling at these junctions can affect movement, heart rate, airway tone, secretion, and other autonomic functions.

name: neuroendocrine cell
clinical_significance: Neuroendocrine cells receive neural signals and release hormones or other signaling molecules. Tumors from these cells may arise in several organs and can produce hormones that cause characteristic symptoms.

name: neuroendocrine system
clinical_significance: The neuroendocrine system links the nervous system with hormone-producing organs to regulate stress, growth, reproduction, metabolism, and fluid balance. Disorders may involve multiple organs and require coordinated endocrine and neurologic evaluation.

name: neuroendocrine tumors
clinical_significance: Growths arising from hormone-producing cells that also respond to nerve signals. They can occur in many organs, may release excess hormones, and range from slow-growing tumors to aggressive cancers.

name: neuroendocrinology
clinical_significance: The medical field that studies how the brain and nerves control hormones and how hormones affect the nervous system. It includes conditions involving the pituitary, adrenal glands, thyroid, reproduction, growth, and body-fluid balance.

name: neuroepithelial cell
clinical_significance: Neuroepithelial cells form or support nervous-system tissue during development and may give rise to particular brain or spinal tumors. Their identification and molecular features help pathologists classify tumors and estimate behavior.

name: neuroepithelial neoplasm
clinical_significance: A neuroepithelial neoplasm is a tumor arising from cells of the nervous system or their precursors. Classification by site, histology, and molecular markers guides prognosis and treatment.

name: neurofeedback
clinical_significance: Neurofeedback uses real-time signals such as brain activity to train a person to alter physiologic patterns. Evidence and clinical benefit vary by condition, so it should not replace established treatment without a clear indication.

name: neurofibroma
clinical_significance: A neurofibroma is a usually benign tumor of peripheral nerve-sheath cells that may be solitary or occur with neurofibromatosis type 1. Growth, pain, neurologic deficits, or rapid change warrants evaluation because a small subset can transform into malignant peripheral nerve-sheath tumors.

name: neurofibromatosis
clinical_significance: A group of inherited conditions in which tumors or other changes develop in tissues containing nerves. Type 1 commonly causes café-au-lait spots, soft nerve tumors, bone changes, and learning difficulties; type 2 mainly affects hearing and balance nerves and can cause other nervous-system tumors.

name: neurofibromatosis 1
clinical_significance: An inherited condition that can cause light-brown skin patches, freckles in the armpits or groin, soft growths along nerves, bone changes, vision problems, learning difficulties, or blood-vessel complications. Findings vary widely between people.

name: neurofibromatosis 2
clinical_significance: An inherited condition in which tumors can grow on nerves, especially the nerves for hearing and balance. It may cause hearing loss, ringing in the ears, balance problems, cataracts, or other brain and spinal-cord tumors.

name: neurofibrosarcoma
clinical_significance: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors are aggressive cancers that can arise in major nerves, sometimes in neurofibromatosis type 1; prompt specialist diagnosis and staging are important.

name: neurofilament
clinical_significance: Neurofilaments are structural proteins in neurons that help maintain axons. Their fragments in blood or cerebrospinal fluid can serve as markers of nerve-cell injury in some neurologic diseases, but they are not disease-specific.

name: neurofilament proteins
clinical_significance: Neurofilament proteins form part of the neuronal cytoskeleton and support axon structure. Neurofilament light-chain measurement is used increasingly as a nonspecific marker of neuroaxonal injury and must be interpreted with clinical findings.

name: neurogenesis
clinical_significance: The formation of new nerve cells. It happens mainly before birth but can continue in limited areas of the adult brain.

name: neurogenetics
clinical_significance: Neurogenetics examines how genetic variation affects nervous-system development and disease. Genetic testing can clarify diagnosis, prognosis, family risk, and eligibility for targeted treatment in selected neurologic conditions.

name: neuroglia
clinical_significance: Supporting cells of the nervous system that nourish, protect, insulate, and maintain nerve cells. Different types help control the nerve environment, form protective coverings, remove waste, and respond to injury or infection.

name: neurohormone
clinical_significance: A neurohormone is a hormone released by nerve cells into the blood or surrounding tissue. Neurohormones coordinate brain and body functions such as stress responses, reproduction, appetite, and fluid balance.

name: neuroimaging
clinical_significance: Neuroimaging uses techniques such as MRI, CT, and PET to assess brain, spinal-cord, and nerve structure or function. Imaging can identify stroke, bleeding, tumors, inflammation, or injury, but findings must be matched to symptoms and examination.

name: neuroimmunomodulation
clinical_significance: Neuroimmunomodulation describes interaction between nervous and immune systems and how one can alter the other. This field informs research on inflammation, pain, stress, infection, and neurologic disease.

name: neurokinin a
clinical_significance: Neurokinin A is a tachykinin neuropeptide involved in sensory signaling, smooth-muscle activity, and inflammation. Its pathways are studied in airway and pain disorders, but the peptide itself is not a routine clinical test.

name: neurologic examination
clinical_significance: A neurologic examination assesses mental status, cranial nerves, strength, sensation, reflexes, coordination, and gait. It helps localize nervous-system problems and determines the urgency and choice of imaging or other tests.

name: neurologic manifestation
clinical_significance: A neurologic manifestation is a nervous-system symptom or sign caused by a primary neurologic disease or another condition. The pattern, timing, and examination help distinguish causes such as stroke, infection, medication effects, or metabolic illness.

name: neurologist
clinical_significance: A medical doctor who diagnoses and treats disorders of the brain, spinal cord, nerves, and muscles. Neurologists assess symptoms such as weakness, numbness, seizures, tremor, headaches, memory change, and movement or balance problems.

name: neurology
clinical_significance: Neurologists evaluate disorders of the brain, spinal cord, nerves, and muscles. Sudden weakness, speech or vision changes, seizure, or loss of consciousness can require emergency assessment before routine specialist follow-up.

name: neuroma
clinical_significance: A benign growth or reactive thickening involving nerve tissue, often producing pain or altered sensation.

name: neuromuscular disease
clinical_significance: Neuromuscular diseases affect motor neurons, peripheral nerves, the neuromuscular junction, or muscle and can cause weakness, wasting, cramps, or impaired breathing and swallowing. Identifying the level and cause guides testing, treatment, and safety monitoring.

name: neuromuscular junction
clinical_significance: The small connection where a movement-controlling nerve communicates with a skeletal muscle. The nerve releases a chemical messenger there, causing the muscle to contract.

name: neuromyelitis optica
clinical_significance: An autoimmune disorder that mainly causes inflammation of the optic nerves and spinal cord. It can cause vision loss and weakness or altered sensation and is treated with immune-directed therapy.

name: neuron
clinical_significance: A nerve cell that receives, processes, and sends messages using electrical signals and chemical messengers. It has a cell body, branches that receive information, and usually a long fiber that carries messages to other cells.

name: neuronal plasticity
clinical_significance: Neuronal plasticity is the ability of neural connections and circuits to change with development, learning, injury, or experience. It supports recovery and rehabilitation, although adaptation may also contribute to chronic pain or maladaptive movement.

name: neuronophagia
clinical_significance: Neuronophagia is the engulfment of injured or infected neurons by immune cells, especially microglia. It is a tissue finding that can indicate active neuronal injury and requires interpretation with the suspected disease and other pathology.

name: neuropathologist
clinical_significance: A neuropathologist diagnoses diseases of the brain, spinal cord, nerves, and muscle by examining tissue and sometimes molecular or genetic findings. Specialist review can be crucial for classifying nervous-system tumors and inflammatory disease.

name: neuropathology
clinical_significance: Neuropathology is the study of disease-related changes in nervous-system tissue. Tissue examination can confirm tumors, infection, degeneration, or inflammation and may guide prognosis and treatment.

name: neuropathy
clinical_significance: Disease or damage affecting nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. It may cause burning pain, numbness, tingling, weakness, balance problems, or altered sweating and can result from diabetes, medicines, toxins, poor nutrition, compression, or inherited disease.

name: neuropeptide
clinical_significance: Neuropeptides are signaling molecules released by neurons that can influence pain, appetite, mood, autonomic activity, and hormone release. Altered pathways are studied in neurologic and endocrine disease.

name: neuropeptide receptor
clinical_significance: Neuropeptide receptors are cell-surface or intracellular targets for neuropeptides and can alter neuronal activity, pain, appetite, or hormone signaling. Receptor pathways are potential drug targets in selected conditions.

name: neuropeptide y
clinical_significance: Neuropeptide Y is a signaling peptide involved in appetite, stress responses, vascular tone, and energy balance. It is mainly a research marker and is not used alone to diagnose a clinical disorder.

name: neuropharmacology
clinical_significance: The study of how medicines and other substances affect the brain, spinal cord, and nerves. It examines their actions, benefits, side effects, interactions, and uses in treating neurological or psychiatric conditions.

name: neurophysin
clinical_significance: Neurophysins are carrier proteins that transport oxytocin or vasopressin from the hypothalamus to the posterior pituitary. Abnormalities in these pathways can be relevant to disorders of water balance and hormone release.

name: neuropil
clinical_significance: Neuropil is the dense network of neuronal processes and synapses between cell bodies in the brain and spinal cord. Changes in neuropil can reflect altered connectivity or tissue injury in neurologic disease.

name: neuropilin
clinical_significance: Neuropilins are cell-surface receptors involved in axon guidance and blood-vessel growth. Their signaling is studied in development, cancer angiogenesis, and nerve repair, and may serve as a therapeutic target.

name: neuroprotectant
clinical_significance: A neuroprotectant is a treatment intended to limit injury or death of nerve cells. Many candidate neuroprotectants remain experimental, and benefit depends on the specific disease and timing of treatment.

name: neuroprotection
clinical_significance: Neuroprotection aims to preserve neurons and nervous-system function during injury or disease. Proven strategies vary by condition; rapid treatment of stroke, control of seizures, and prevention of secondary injury are key examples.

name: neuropsychology
clinical_significance: Neuropsychology assesses how brain function relates to thinking, memory, language, emotion, and behavior. Formal testing can help characterize cognitive change, guide rehabilitation, and inform care planning.

name: neurosis
clinical_significance: Neurosis is an outdated term once used for distressing symptoms without loss of reality testing. Modern diagnosis specifies conditions such as anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, trauma-related, or somatic symptom disorders.

name: neurospora
clinical_significance: Neurospora is a genus of mold used extensively in genetics and cell biology research. It is not a common human pathogen; its medical relevance is chiefly as a model organism for studying biological processes.

name: neurosurgeon
clinical_significance: A surgeon trained to diagnose and operate on disorders of the brain, spinal cord, spine, nerves, and nearby supporting structures. Neurosurgeons may treat tumors, injuries, bleeding, pressure, pain, or blood-vessel problems.

name: neurosurgery
clinical_significance: Surgery for disorders of the brain, spinal cord, spine, peripheral nerves, or supporting structures. Procedures may remove tumors, relieve pressure, repair injuries, stop bleeding, treat blood vessels, or improve severe pain.

name: neurosyphilis
clinical_significance: Neurosyphilis is infection of the nervous system by Treponema pallidum and can cause meningitis, stroke, sensory loss, cognitive change, or tabes dorsalis.

name: neurotensin
clinical_significance: Neurotensin is a peptide involved in gut motility, hormone release, pain, and central nervous-system signaling. Its role in disease and cancer is under study, but measurement is not routine in general clinical care.

name: neurothekeoma
clinical_significance: Neurothekeoma is a usually benign skin or soft-tissue tumor, often occurring in children or young adults. Pathology distinguishes it from nerve-sheath and other tumors; complete removal is often curative.

name: neurotoxicity syndromes
clinical_significance: Neurotoxicity syndromes are patterns of nervous-system injury caused by medicines, toxins, immune therapies, infection, or metabolic disturbance. Early recognition matters because stopping or treating the cause may prevent permanent deficits.

name: neurotoxin
clinical_significance: A neurotoxin is a substance that damages or disrupts nervous-system function. Exposure can cause altered sensation, weakness, confusion, seizures, paralysis, or respiratory failure; suspected significant exposure requires prompt toxicology assessment.

name: neurotransmitter
clinical_significance: A chemical messenger released by a nerve cell. It crosses a tiny gap to affect another nerve cell or a muscle or gland cell, either increasing or reducing its activity.

name: neurotransmitter receptor
clinical_significance: Neurotransmitter receptors detect chemical signals between neurons or between nerves and target cells. Many neurologic and psychiatric medicines act on these receptors, so receptor effects help explain both therapeutic benefit and adverse effects.

name: neurotrophic factor
clinical_significance: Neurotrophic factors support neuron survival, growth, and repair. Their signaling is important in development and nerve injury and is studied as a target for neurodegenerative and peripheral-nerve disorders.

name: neurotropism
clinical_significance: Neurotropism is the tendency of a virus or other agent to infect or affect nervous tissue. Neurotropic infections may cause meningitis, encephalitis, paralysis, or latent infection in nerves.

name: neurovascular bundle
clinical_significance: A neurovascular bundle contains nerves and blood vessels traveling together to supply a tissue. Surgeons and radiologists consider its location to avoid injury that could impair movement, sensation, or blood flow.

name: neurulation
clinical_significance: Neurulation is the embryonic process that forms the neural tube, the precursor of the brain and spinal cord. Disruption can cause neural-tube defects; folic-acid intake before conception and early pregnancy reduces risk.

name: neutral red
clinical_significance: Neutral red is a laboratory dye used to stain cells and assess cell viability or lysosomal function. It is mainly a research reagent rather than a routine diagnostic test.

name: neutralization test
clinical_significance: A neutralization test measures whether antibodies block a virus or toxin from infecting cells or producing an effect. It can assess functional immunity or support diagnosis, but requires specialized laboratory methods.

name: neutron
clinical_significance: A neutron is an uncharged particle in an atomic nucleus. Neutrons are used in some radiation therapies and imaging or research applications; exposure and dose must be controlled because ionizing radiation can damage tissue.

name: neutron diffraction
clinical_significance: Neutron diffraction uses neutron scattering to determine atomic or molecular structure. It is mainly a research technique that can inform drug and biomaterial design, rather than a patient diagnostic test.

name: neutropenia
clinical_significance: An abnormally low number of neutrophils, white blood cells that help fight bacterial and fungal infections. The lower the count, the greater the infection risk; fever during severe neutropenia can signal a serious infection.

name: neutrophil
clinical_significance: The most common infection-fighting white blood cell in the bloodstream. It quickly enters injured tissue, surrounds and destroys many bacteria and fungi, and helps start inflammation; unusually low levels increase infection risk.

name: neutrophil activation
clinical_significance: Neutrophil activation is the process by which neutrophils respond to infection or tissue injury by migrating, engulfing microbes, and releasing antimicrobial substances. Excessive activation can also damage tissue in inflammatory disease.

name: never married
clinical_significance: Marital-status data such as “never married” may be collected in health research to study social determinants and population outcomes. It has no diagnostic meaning for an individual and should not be treated as a clinical risk factor by itself.

name: nevirapine
clinical_significance: Nevirapine is a non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor used in some HIV treatment regimens. It can cause severe rash and liver injury, especially early in therapy, so patient selection and monitoring are important.

name: nevus
clinical_significance: A usually harmless, localized change or growth in the skin or mucous membrane, often called a mole. It may contain pigment-producing cells or involve blood vessels or other skin structures; a changing lesion needs assessment.

name: nevus anemicus
clinical_significance: A congenital vascular anomaly presenting as a localized, well-circumscribed, pale, hypopigmented macule or patch that remains pale after rubbing or temperature changes due to localized hypersensitivity of cutaneous alpha-adrenergic receptors producing constant arteriolar vasoconstriction.

name: nevus comedonicus
clinical_significance: Nevus comedonicus is a rare congenital skin lesion with grouped, comedo-like plugs that may become inflamed, infected, or scarred. Extensive or symptomatic lesions may need dermatologic care and can rarely occur with neurologic or skeletal abnormalities.

name: nevus sebaceous
clinical_significance: Nevus sebaceous is a congenital hairless plaque that may thicken or change during puberty. Most lesions remain benign, but new nodules or rapid changes should be assessed by dermatology because secondary tumors can rarely arise.

name: nevus spilus
clinical_significance: Nevus spilus is a pigmented skin patch containing darker spots and is usually benign. A new or changing focal lesion should be examined because melanoma can rarely develop within it.

name: newborn
clinical_significance: A baby during the first 28 days after birth, when special newborn health monitoring and care are important.

name: Newcastle disease
clinical_significance: Newcastle disease is a highly contagious viral disease of birds, especially poultry, and is not an established human disease. People exposed to infected birds may rarely develop mild conjunctivitis, making protective handling and veterinary control important.

name: Newcastle disease virus
clinical_significance: Newcastle disease virus causes severe contagious disease in birds and is important in veterinary and agricultural biosecurity. Human infection is uncommon and generally limited to mild eye disease after close exposure.

name: newton
clinical_significance: A newton is the SI unit of force, used in biomechanics and clinical engineering to quantify loads on tissues, joints, or devices. It is not a diagnostic measure on its own.

name: niacin
clinical_significance: Vitamin B3, needed to help cells release energy and perform many chemical reactions; it forms the coenzymes NAD+ and NADP+ that carry electrons in metabolism. Severe deficiency causes pellagra, with skin changes, digestive problems, confusion, weakness, and potentially life-threatening complications.

name: nicardipine
clinical_significance: A calcium-channel-blocking medicine that relaxes blood vessels and lowers blood pressure. It is used for selected urgent or ongoing blood-pressure problems and may cause headache, flushing, dizziness, fast heartbeat, or swelling.

name: niceritrol
clinical_significance: Niceritrol is an older niacin derivative formerly used to alter blood lipids. It is rarely used now because of limited modern role and adverse effects such as flushing, gastrointestinal symptoms, and liver abnormalities.

name: nickel
clinical_significance: Nickel is a common metal allergen that can cause allergic contact dermatitis after skin exposure. Occupational inhalation can harm the lungs, and certain nickel compounds are carcinogenic; exposure context determines health risk.

name: niclosamide
clinical_significance: An antiparasitic medicine used in some countries to treat selected intestinal tapeworm infections. It acts mainly in the gut and does not reliably treat larval tapeworm infections in tissues, such as neurocysticercosis.

name: nicorandil
clinical_significance: Nicorandil is an antianginal vasodilator used in some countries for chronic angina. It can cause serious persistent ulcers of the mouth, skin, gastrointestinal tract, or other sites, which may heal after the drug is stopped.

name: nicotinamide
clinical_significance: Nicotinamide, also called niacinamide, is a form of vitamin B3 used in cellular metabolism and in selected dermatologic preparations. Unlike nicotinic acid, it usually does not cause flushing at nutritional doses.

name: nicotine
clinical_significance: An addictive stimulant found in tobacco and some vaping products that acts on neuronal nicotinic receptors.

name: nicotine inhaler
clinical_significance: A nicotine inhaler delivers nicotine through the mouth to reduce withdrawal during smoking cessation. Correct use and a planned quit strategy improve its role; combining nicotine with continued smoking can increase nicotine-related adverse effects.

name: nicotine lozenge
clinical_significance: Nicotine lozenges provide short-acting nicotine to reduce cravings during smoking cessation. They can cause mouth irritation, hiccups, or nausea, and dosing should follow product directions to avoid excess nicotine.

name: nicotine patch
clinical_significance: A nicotine patch provides steady nicotine through the skin to reduce withdrawal during smoking cessation. Skin irritation and sleep disturbance can occur; correct dosing and behavioral support improve the chance of quitting.

name: nicotine replacement
clinical_significance: Nicotine replacement therapy supplies nicotine without tobacco smoke to ease withdrawal during smoking cessation. Forms include patches, gum, lozenges, inhalers, and sprays; correct use is safer than continued smoking for most adults.

name: nicotinic agonist
clinical_significance: Nicotinic agonists activate nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and can affect autonomic function, muscle contraction, attention, and reward pathways. Nicotine is one example; excessive exposure can cause nausea, seizures, arrhythmias, or respiratory compromise.

name: nicotinic antagonist
clinical_significance: Nicotinic antagonists block nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Some are used to produce temporary muscle paralysis during anesthesia and require assisted ventilation and monitoring; others act at neuronal receptors for selected indications.

name: nicotinic receptor
clinical_significance: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors mediate signaling in the brain, autonomic nervous system, and neuromuscular junction. They are targets of nicotine, smoking-cessation medicines, and some anesthetic drugs; their blockade or overstimulation can affect alertness, heart rate, and muscle function.

name: nictitating membrane
clinical_significance: The nictitating membrane is a third eyelid in many animals that protects and moistens the eye. It is not normally prominent in humans; visible protrusion can reflect eye disease, dehydration, or neurologic problems in veterinary patients.

name: Niemann-Pick disease
clinical_significance: A group of rare inherited lysosomal storage disorders in which lipids accumulate in cells. The group includes acid sphingomyelinase deficiency, formerly called Niemann-Pick disease types A and B, and Niemann-Pick disease type C, caused by impaired intracellular cholesterol trafficking. Features vary by type and may include enlargement of the liver or spleen, lung disease, difficulty coordinating movement, and progressive neurologic impairment.

name: nifedipine
clinical_significance: A medicine that relaxes blood vessels to lower blood pressure and relieve some types of chest pain. It may cause flushing, headache, dizziness, ankle swelling, or a fast heartbeat; the dose depends on the condition and formulation.

name: nifurtimox
clinical_significance: Nifurtimox is an antiparasitic medicine used to treat Chagas disease caused by Trypanosoma cruzi. It can cause nausea, weight loss, dizziness, or peripheral neuropathy and requires clinician-directed dosing and monitoring.

name: night sweats
clinical_significance: Episodes of excessive sweating during sleep; causes include infection, malignancy, hormonal change, medicines, and environmental heat.

name: nightmare
clinical_significance: Nightmares are distressing dreams that can disrupt sleep and occur with stress, trauma, some medicines, or mental-health conditions. Frequent nightmares that impair daytime function may warrant assessment and treatment of the underlying cause.

name: nigrospora
clinical_significance: Nigrospora is a genus of environmental fungi that rarely causes human infection. A laboratory isolate should be interpreted with specimen source and evidence of disease, especially in immunocompromised patients.

name: nilotinib
clinical_significance: Nilotinib is a tyrosine-kinase inhibitor used for selected Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia. It can prolong the QT interval and cause vascular, metabolic, liver, or pancreatic complications, so ECG and laboratory monitoring are important.

name: nilutamide
clinical_significance: Nilutamide is an androgen-receptor blocker formerly used in prostate cancer, usually with androgen-deprivation therapy. It can cause lung inflammation, liver injury, visual adaptation problems, and alcohol intolerance and is now used infrequently.

name: nimodipine
clinical_significance: Nimodipine is a calcium-channel blocker given after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage to reduce delayed cerebral ischemia and improve neurologic outcomes. It can lower blood pressure and must be given by the prescribed route and schedule.

name: nimorazole
clinical_significance: Nimorazole is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial used in some settings, including as a radiosensitizer in head and neck cancer treatment. It can cause gastrointestinal or neurologic adverse effects and is not widely used in all countries.

name: nimotuzumab
clinical_significance: Nimotuzumab is a monoclonal antibody targeting EGFR, studied or used in selected cancer settings in some countries. Availability and approved indications vary geographically; infusion reactions and skin effects are relevant risks.

name: nimustine
clinical_significance: Nimustine is a nitrosourea chemotherapy drug used in some countries for selected cancers, including brain tumors. It can suppress bone marrow and cause delayed blood-count abnormalities, so treatment requires specialist oversight and monitoring.

name: nintedanib
clinical_significance: Nintedanib is an antifibrotic tyrosine-kinase inhibitor used for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other progressive fibrosing lung diseases, and for selected lung cancers. Diarrhea, liver injury, bleeding, and impaired wound healing are important precautions.

name: nipah virus
clinical_significance: A zoonotic virus in the genus \textit{Henipavirus}, with fruit bats as its natural host. It can spread from infected bats or other animals to people, through contaminated food such as raw date-palm sap, and between people through close contact. Infection ranges from no symptoms to fever, headache, vomiting, and respiratory illness such as cough or difficulty breathing. Severe disease may cause inflammation of the brain (encephalitis), confusion, seizures, coma, or death. There is currently no li

name: nipple deformity
clinical_significance: Nipple deformity may follow congenital variation, infection, trauma, surgery, or an underlying breast lesion. New inversion, distortion, skin change, or a lump should be assessed, particularly if it is one-sided or persistent.

name: nipple discharge
clinical_significance: Fluid leaking from one or both nipples when not pregnant or breastfeeding. Most nipple discharge is harmless, coming from multiple milk ducts in both breasts only when squeezed, and is usually caused by normal hormone changes or medications. Discharge that leaks on its own from a single duct in one breast, especially if clear or bloody, is less common. The most frequent cause is a small, harmless growth inside a milk duct (a papilloma), while breast cancer accounts for about 5\% to 15\% of these

name: nipples
clinical_significance: Nipples contain ducts and sensitive tissue and can be affected by infection, eczema, hormonal changes, trauma, or breast disease. Persistent rash, spontaneous bloody discharge, a new lump, or new nipple inversion warrants clinical evaluation.

name: nippostrongylus
clinical_significance: Nippostrongylus is a parasitic roundworm of rodents used in research on intestinal immunity and allergic inflammation. It is not a common human parasite.

name: nisoldipine
clinical_significance: Nisoldipine is a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker used to treat hypertension in some settings. It can cause dizziness, flushing, ankle swelling, or low blood pressure and may interact with medicines that alter its metabolism.

name: nitracrine
clinical_significance: Nitracrine is an experimental DNA-alkylating anticancer compound studied in laboratory and clinical research. It is not a routine contemporary treatment.

name: nitrates
clinical_significance: Medicines that widen blood vessels by releasing nitric oxide. They can relieve angina and lower the heart's workload but may cause headache, flushing, dizziness, or dangerously low blood pressure with certain medicines.

name: nitrendipine
clinical_significance: Nitrendipine is a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker used for hypertension in some countries. It relaxes blood vessels and may cause headache, flushing, dizziness, or ankle swelling.

name: nitrergic neuron
clinical_significance: Nitrergic neurons release nitric oxide as a signaling molecule and help regulate smooth-muscle relaxation and blood flow in organs such as the gut. Altered nitrergic signaling is studied in gastrointestinal and vascular disorders.

name: nitric acid
clinical_significance: A strong corrosive chemical that can burn skin, eyes, mouth, throat, and digestive organs. Breathing its fumes can injure the lungs, and swallowed or inhaled exposure can cause severe poisoning.

name: nitric oxide
clinical_significance: A short-lived signaling molecule made by many cells. It relaxes blood-vessel muscle, helping regulate blood flow and pressure, and also participates in nerve signaling and immune defense. Too much or too little production may contribute to disease.

name: nitrification
clinical_significance: Nitrification is the microbial conversion of ammonia to nitrite and nitrate in soil and water. It matters to environmental and public health because nitrate contamination of drinking water can pose risks, especially to infants.

name: nitrile
clinical_significance: Nitriles are chemical compounds containing a carbon-nitrogen triple bond; some are used in medicines and manufacturing, while others can be toxic. Health effects depend on the compound and exposure route.

name: nitrilotriacetic acid
clinical_significance: Nitrilotriacetic acid is an industrial chelating agent used to bind metal ions. Occupational or environmental exposure is assessed based on dose and route; high or prolonged exposure has raised toxicologic concerns.

name: nitro compounds
clinical_significance: Nitro compounds contain one or more nitro groups and include medicines, industrial chemicals, and explosives. Toxicity varies widely; some compounds can cause methemoglobinemia, organ injury, or chemical burns.

name: nitroarginine
clinical_significance: Nitroarginine is a research inhibitor of nitric-oxide synthase used to study nitric-oxide signaling. It is not a routine therapeutic medicine, and inhibiting nitric oxide can alter vascular tone and organ blood flow.

name: nitroaspirin
clinical_significance: Nitroaspirin is an experimental nitrate-modified aspirin designed to combine platelet inhibition with nitric-oxide effects. It remains investigational and is not a standard substitute for aspirin or prescribed nitrate therapy.

name: nitrofurantoin
clinical_significance: An antibacterial medicine used mainly for bladder infections caused by susceptible bacteria. It concentrates in urine but is not suitable for many kidney infections; nausea, lung reactions, liver injury, or nerve problems are uncommon but important risks.

name: nitrogen
clinical_significance: An essential element in amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids, and other biological molecules; atmospheric nitrogen is largely inert to humans.

name: nitrogen dioxide
clinical_significance: Nitrogen dioxide is a respiratory irritant produced by combustion and air pollution. Exposure can inflame the lungs, worsen asthma, and cause delayed pulmonary edema after a significant inhalation.

name: nitrogen fixation
clinical_significance: Nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric nitrogen into biologically usable forms and is essential to ecosystems and food production. It is mainly an environmental and agricultural concept, with indirect relevance to nutrition and public health.

name: nitrogen oxide
clinical_significance: Nitrogen oxides are reactive gases from combustion and industrial sources that contribute to air pollution. Inhalation can irritate airways and worsen asthma or other lung disease.

name: nitrogenase
clinical_significance: Nitrogenase is the enzyme complex that enables certain microbes to convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia. It is important in microbial biology and biotechnology rather than routine clinical diagnosis.

name: nitroglycerin
clinical_significance: A nitrate medicine that relaxes vascular smooth muscle and can relieve angina by reducing cardiac workload and improving coronary blood flow.

name: nitroprusside
clinical_significance: Sodium nitroprusside is a potent intravenous vasodilator used under close monitoring for selected hypertensive emergencies or controlled blood-pressure reduction. Prolonged or high-dose infusion can cause cyanide or thiocyanate toxicity and severe hypotension.

name: nitrosamine
clinical_significance: Nitrosamines are compounds that can form in foods, tobacco, and some manufacturing processes; several are carcinogenic in experimental systems. Exposure reduction is relevant to cancer prevention and medication quality control.

name: nitroso compounds
clinical_significance: Nitroso compounds include chemicals that can affect DNA and may be carcinogenic or toxic, depending on their structure. They are relevant to toxicology, occupational exposure, and evaluation of possible food or drug contaminants.

name: nitrosourea compounds
clinical_significance: Nitrosoureas are chemotherapy drugs that cross into the central nervous system and are used for selected brain tumors and other cancers. They can cause delayed bone-marrow suppression, nausea, and organ toxicity, requiring blood-count monitoring.

name: nitrous oxide
clinical_significance: Nitrous oxide is an inhaled anesthetic and analgesic used in selected procedures. Prolonged or repeated exposure can inactivate vitamin B12 and cause neurologic injury; recreational misuse can also cause hypoxia and serious harm.

name: nivolumab
clinical_significance: Nivolumab is an immune-checkpoint inhibitor used for several cancers. By activating immune responses it can cause inflammation of organs such as the lungs, bowel, liver, thyroid, or heart, sometimes after treatment ends; new symptoms need prompt review.

name: nizatidine
clinical_significance: A medicine that reduces stomach-acid production by blocking histamine signals in stomach cells. It may relieve ulcers or reflux symptoms, although availability varies and treatment should consider kidney function and medicine interactions.

name: NMDA receptor
clinical_significance: The NMDA receptor is a glutamate receptor important for learning, memory, and excitatory brain signaling. Overactivation can contribute to neuronal injury, while receptor dysfunction or autoantibodies can cause neurologic or psychiatric symptoms.

name: noble gases
clinical_significance: Noble gases such as helium, argon, and xenon have medical uses in imaging, anesthesia research, and cryogenic systems. They are chemically inert but can displace oxygen and cause suffocation in enclosed spaces.

name: nocardia
clinical_significance: Nocardia are environmental bacteria that can cause lung, skin, or disseminated infection, especially in people with weakened immunity or chronic lung disease. Infection may spread to the brain, and species identification plus susceptibility testing helps guide prolonged therapy.

name: nocardia asteroides
clinical_significance: Nocardia asteroides is an older name associated with organisms in the Nocardia asteroides complex that can cause pulmonary or disseminated nocardiosis. Modern species identification matters because antimicrobial susceptibility varies.

name: nocardia brasiliensis
clinical_significance: Nocardia brasiliensis commonly causes skin and soft-tissue infection, including actinomycetoma, after soil inoculation, and can occasionally spread. Diagnosis requires laboratory identification and treatment is prolonged.

name: nocardia cyriacigeorgica
clinical_significance: Nocardia cyriacigeorgica can cause pulmonary nocardiosis and, particularly in vulnerable patients, disseminated infection or brain abscess. Accurate species identification and susceptibility testing are important for treatment.

name: nocardia dassonvillei
clinical_significance: Nocardia dassonvillei is an uncommon Nocardia species reported in occasional human infection. Its significance depends on symptoms and specimen source, and susceptibility testing is useful because Nocardia species differ in drug response.

name: nocardia farcinica
clinical_significance: Nocardia farcinica can cause serious lung, skin, bloodstream, or brain infection, particularly in immunocompromised people. It may resist multiple antibiotics, so rapid species identification and susceptibility-guided specialist treatment are important.

name: nocardia infection
clinical_significance: An infection caused by Nocardia bacteria, usually affecting the lungs, skin, or brain, especially in people with weakened immunity.

name: nocardia nova
clinical_significance: Nocardia nova can cause pulmonary, skin, bloodstream, or disseminated infection, especially in people with weakened immunity. Treatment depends on species identification and susceptibility testing.

name: nocardia otitidiscaviarum
clinical_significance: Nocardia otitidiscaviarum is an uncommon environmental species that can cause skin, lung, or disseminated infection. A culture requires clinical correlation and susceptibility testing to guide treatment.

name: nocardiaceae
clinical_significance: Nocardiaceae includes Nocardia and related aerobic actinomycetes, some of which cause opportunistic lung, skin, or brain infection. Distinguishing genera and species in the laboratory is important because treatment differs.

name: nociception
clinical_significance: The nervous system's detection and processing of potentially harmful heat, pressure, or chemicals. It can lead to pain, but pain also depends on how the brain interprets these signals.

name: nociceptor
clinical_significance: A sensory nerve ending that detects potentially damaging pressure, heat, cold, or chemicals. It sends warning signals through nerves to the spinal cord and brain, where they can be experienced as pain.

name: nocodazole
clinical_significance: Nocodazole is an experimental drug that disrupts microtubules and cell division and is used mainly in laboratory research. It is not a routine human treatment.

name: nocturia
clinical_significance: Waking during the night one or more times to urinate and then returning to sleep. It may result from evening fluids, medicines, bladder or prostate problems, diabetes, heart disease, or sleep disorders.

name: node of ranvier
clinical_significance: Periodic, unmyelinated gaps or interruptions occurring at regular intervals along the length of a myelinated nerve axon where high concentrations of voltage-gated sodium channels enable rapid saltatory nerve impulse conduction.

name: nodular goiter
clinical_significance: A nodular goiter is an enlarged thyroid with one or more nodules. Thyroid function testing and ultrasound help identify overactivity, compression, or features that require biopsy to exclude cancer.

name: nodular melanoma
clinical_significance: A type of skin cancer that grows downward early and often appears as a rapidly enlarging firm bump. It may be black, brown, pink, or skin-colored, so any quickly changing or bleeding lump needs prompt assessment.

name: nodule
clinical_significance: A small, rounded area of abnormal tissue that may be solid or fluid-filled and may occur in the skin, lung, thyroid, or another organ. Its meaning depends on location, size, appearance, growth, and symptoms; some nodules are harmless, while others need testing or follow-up.

name: nogalamycin
clinical_significance: Nogalamycin is an anthracycline antibiotic with antitumor activity studied as a chemotherapy compound. Its toxicity and limited clinical role mean it is mainly of research or historical relevance.

name: noma
clinical_significance: Noma is a rapidly progressive gangrenous infection of the mouth and face, usually in severely malnourished or immunocompromised children. It destroys oral and facial tissue and is treated with antibiotics, nutritional support, and sometimes surgery.

name: nomograms
clinical_significance: A nomogram combines clinical variables to estimate a probability or guide a decision, such as cancer recurrence risk or medication dosing. It supports but does not replace clinician judgment and should be validated for the population in which it is used.

name: Nonaka myopathy
clinical_significance: Nonaka myopathy, also called GNE myopathy, is an inherited muscle disease causing progressive weakness, often beginning in the lower legs while sparing the quadriceps early. Genetic confirmation and supportive care help guide diagnosis and planning.

name: none
clinical_significance: “None” is a data value indicating absence of a finding or entry, not a medical diagnosis. Its meaning depends on the field and must be distinguished from unknown or not assessed.

name: nonglandular stomach
clinical_significance: The nonglandular stomach is the esophageal portion of the stomach in some animals, especially rodents, and is important in comparative anatomy and toxicology. Humans do not have this distinct nonglandular region.

name: non-Hodgkin's lymphoma
clinical_significance: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma comprises many lymphoid cancers with different behavior and treatment; persistent lymph-node enlargement or systemic symptoms warrants evaluation and tissue diagnosis.

name: non-infectious cystitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the bladder without infection by bacteria or another microorganism. It may cause pain, urgency, and frequent urination after irritants, radiation, medicines, chemical exposure, or other bladder conditions.

name: non-malignant
clinical_significance: Non-malignant means not cancerous, but a benign lesion can still cause symptoms, compression, bleeding, or other problems depending on location. The diagnosis may require imaging or tissue examination.

name: non-narcotic analgesics
clinical_significance: Non-opioid analgesics relieve pain without activating opioid receptors; examples include acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Choice depends on pain type and risks such as liver, kidney, gastrointestinal, or cardiovascular disease.

name: non-protocol
clinical_significance: “Non-protocol” indicates that care or research activity did not follow a specified protocol. In clinical research, deviations can affect safety, data quality, and interpretability and should be documented and assessed.

name: nonsense mutation
clinical_significance: A nonsense mutation introduces a premature stop signal in a gene and can produce a shortened or absent protein. It may cause inherited disease or contribute to cancer, but effect depends on the gene and transcript.

name: non-stop decay
clinical_significance: Nonsense-mediated decay is a cellular quality-control process that degrades messenger RNA containing premature stop signals. It can reduce production of abnormal proteins and influence the severity of some genetic diseases.

name: nontoxic goiter
clinical_significance: A nontoxic goiter is an enlarged thyroid without excess thyroid-hormone production. Nodules or compression may still require ultrasound, thyroid tests, and occasionally biopsy or treatment.

name: nonverbal communication
clinical_significance: Nonverbal communication includes facial expression, posture, gestures, eye contact, and tone. It can help assess pain, distress, cognition, or social interaction, especially when speech is limited, but interpretation depends on culture and context.

name: noonan syndrome
clinical_significance: An inherited condition that may cause distinctive facial features, short stature, heart defects, delayed development, easy bruising, or swelling from lymph problems. Its features vary, and regular heart, growth, hearing, and developmental checks are important.

name: norepinephrine
clinical_significance: A hormone and nerve messenger involved in alertness, stress responses, heart function, and blood-vessel tightening. It can increase blood pressure and is also used in hospitals to support blood pressure during some forms of shock.

name: norethindrone
clinical_significance: Norethindrone is a progestin used in some contraceptives and for menstrual disorders or endometriosis. Bleeding-pattern changes and contraindications such as some thrombotic or hormone-sensitive conditions depend on formulation and patient history.

name: norfloxacin
clinical_significance: Norfloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic formerly used for selected urinary or gastrointestinal infections and is now restricted or uncommon in many places. Tendon, nerve, central nervous system, and other serious class adverse effects limit use.

name: norgestrel
clinical_significance: A synthetic progestogen used in some hormonal contraceptives. It helps prevent pregnancy by suppressing ovulation and changing cervical mucus and the uterine lining.

name: normal
clinical_significance: “Normal” depends on the population, age, context, and method of measurement. A result within a reference interval does not always exclude disease, and an out-of-range result does not establish a diagnosis by itself.

name: normal flora
clinical_significance: The bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms that normally live on the skin and in the mouth, intestine, and urinary or genital tract without causing illness. They can help block harmful germs, support immunity, and contribute to digestion and vitamin production.

name: normal range
clinical_significance: A normal range is the interval of results commonly found in a reference population; a result outside it does not by itself prove disease.

name: normetanephrine
clinical_significance: Normetanephrine is a metabolite of norepinephrine measured in plasma or urine to evaluate for catecholamine-secreting tumors such as pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma. Stress, medicines, posture, and collection conditions can affect results.

name: normocytic anemia
clinical_significance: A form of anemia in which circulating red blood cells are of normal average size (mean corpuscular volume [MCV] between $80$ and $100\,\text{fL}$), but total red blood cell count and hemoglobin concentration are decreased. Diagnostic evaluation relies on the reticulocyte count to differentiate between: (1) hyperproliferative causes with elevated reticulocytes, such as acute blood loss (hemorrhage) or premature red cell destruction (hemolytic anemia), and (2) hypoproliferative causes with low ret

name: norovirus
clinical_significance: A highly contagious virus that causes acute gastroenteritis, or inflammation of the stomach and intestines. Symptoms usually begin 12--48 hours after exposure and include sudden nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, stomach cramps, and sometimes fever, headache, or body aches. It spreads mainly when tiny particles of stool or vomit enter the mouth, through infected people, contaminated food or water, surfaces, or particles released during vomiting. Most illness improves within 1--3 days, but severe

name: Norrie disease
clinical_significance: A rare inherited eye disorder in which the retina develops abnormally, usually causing severe vision loss or blindness from birth or early infancy. Some people also develop hearing loss, developmental differences, or problems in the eye’s blood vessels.

name: northern blotting
clinical_significance: Northern blotting detects specific RNA molecules and can assess gene expression or transcript size. It is mainly a research method, largely replaced in routine diagnostics by newer molecular assays.

name: nortriptyline
clinical_significance: A medicine used to treat depression and sometimes long-lasting nerve pain. It changes the levels of certain chemical messengers in the nervous system and may cause dry mouth, constipation, sleepiness, dizziness, heart-rhythm problems, or overdose toxicity.

name: norwalk virus
clinical_significance: Norwalk virus is an older name for Norovirus, a major cause of acute gastroenteritis and outbreaks. It spreads readily through contaminated food, surfaces, and close contact; hydration and infection-control measures are central.

name: noscapine
clinical_significance: Noscapine is a non-opioid alkaloid with antitussive activity and has also been studied for anticancer effects. Its availability and evidence vary by country and formulation; it can interact with medicines and is not a substitute for evaluating persistent cough.

name: nose
clinical_significance: The external structure and internal passages used for breathing and smell. The nose warms, moistens, and filters air and contains bone, cartilage, skin, mucus, blood vessels, and smell-sensing tissue.

name: nose disease
clinical_significance: Nose diseases include infection, allergy, polyps, bleeding, structural obstruction, and tumors. Persistent one-sided blockage, recurrent nosebleeds, facial swelling, or impaired smell warrants assessment for an underlying cause.

name: nose neoplasm
clinical_significance: A neoplasm of the nose may be benign or malignant and can cause persistent blockage, bleeding, pain, or loss of smell. One-sided or progressive symptoms warrant examination and, when indicated, imaging or biopsy.

name: nosema
clinical_significance: Nosema is a microsporidian parasite that primarily infects insects, especially honey bees, and can weaken colonies. It is not a common human pathogen; its significance is mainly veterinary and agricultural.

name: not applicable
clinical_significance: “Not applicable” means a question or measure does not apply to the subject or situation. In clinical records and research datasets it should be distinguished from missing, unknown, or negative results.

name: notch receptors
clinical_significance: Notch receptors are cell-signaling proteins that regulate cell fate and development. Abnormal Notch signaling contributes to some cancers and developmental disorders and is a target of ongoing research.

name: novobiocin
clinical_significance: Novobiocin is an older antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and is now rarely used clinically. It is also used in laboratory testing to distinguish selected bacteria and has research relevance in antimicrobial development.

name: noxious stimulus
clinical_significance: A noxious stimulus is an event capable of damaging tissue and activating pain pathways. Persistent or intense exposure can cause injury, while reduced response may signal sensory-nerve dysfunction.

name: nuchal cord
clinical_significance: Wrapping of the umbilical cord around the fetal neck, occurring once or more times. It is common and often harmless, but monitoring during labor is needed if fetal heart-rate abnormalities occur.

name: nuchal region
clinical_significance: The nuchal region is the back of the neck and includes muscles, ligaments, cervical spine, and nearby nerves. Pain or stiffness in this area may follow injury or infection; trauma with midline tenderness or neurologic symptoms needs careful assessment.

name: nuclear bodies
clinical_significance: Nuclear bodies are structures inside the cell nucleus that organize gene regulation, RNA processing, and other cellular functions. Their changes are studied in cancer and genetic disease but are not usually interpreted as standalone clinical findings.

name: nuclear division
clinical_significance: Nuclear division is the separation of a cell’s genetic material during mitosis or meiosis. Errors can produce chromosome abnormalities that contribute to infertility, congenital conditions, cancer, or cell death.

name: nuclear envelope
clinical_significance: The nuclear envelope separates DNA from the cytoplasm and regulates molecular movement through nuclear pores. Defects in its proteins can cause rare muscular, cardiac, neurologic, and premature-aging syndromes.

name: nuclear inclusion
clinical_significance: A nuclear inclusion is a visible structure or material within a cell nucleus. In pathology it may be associated with viral infection, storage disease, or tumor change, but its significance depends on morphology and tissue context.

name: nuclear lamin
clinical_significance: Nuclear lamins are proteins that support the nuclear envelope and organize chromatin. Pathogenic variants can cause laminopathies affecting muscle, heart, nerves, or fat tissue.

name: nuclear lamina
clinical_significance: The nuclear lamina is a protein scaffold beneath the nuclear membrane that supports cell structure and gene regulation. Abnormalities can disrupt tissue development and cause inherited multisystem disease.

name: nuclear matrix
clinical_significance: The nuclear matrix refers to an internal framework proposed to organize nuclear contents and gene activity. It is mainly a research concept and has limited direct use in routine clinical testing.

name: nuclear medicine
clinical_significance: A medical specialty that uses small amounts of radioactive substances to diagnose or treat disease. Scans show body function or chemical activity, while treatments deliver radiation to selected tissues.

name: nuclear pore
clinical_significance: Nuclear pores control movement of RNA and proteins between the nucleus and cytoplasm. Disruption can affect cell growth and gene expression and is studied in some cancers and genetic disorders.

name: nuclear proteins
clinical_significance: Nuclear proteins regulate DNA packaging, replication, transcription, repair, and RNA processing. Autoantibodies against some nuclear proteins are used in evaluating autoimmune disease, while tumor mutations can inform diagnosis or therapy.

name: nuclear speckles
clinical_significance: Nuclear speckles are structures involved in RNA processing and gene expression. Their role in disease is under study, especially in cancer and genetic disorders, but they are not routine diagnostic markers.

name: nuclear transport
clinical_significance: Nuclear transport moves proteins and RNA between the nucleus and cytoplasm through nuclear pores. Errors can impair cell function and are implicated in some genetic diseases, infections, and cancers.

name: nucleated cell
clinical_significance: A nucleated cell contains a nucleus and therefore nuclear DNA, unlike mature red blood cells in humans. Nucleated red cells in peripheral blood can indicate severe marrow stress, hypoxia, or serious illness.

name: nucleic acid
clinical_significance: DNA or RNA, the molecules that store, copy, and use genetic instructions. DNA usually stores the long-term information, while RNA helps read those instructions and make proteins or perform other jobs in cells.

name: nucleocapsid
clinical_significance: The nucleocapsid is a virus’s genetic material together with its protective protein coat. Nucleocapsid antigens are targets of some diagnostic tests and can support detection of viral infection.

name: nucleocapsid proteins
clinical_significance: Nucleocapsid proteins package and protect viral genomes and can serve as targets for diagnostic assays or immune responses. Their detection may indicate infection, depending on the pathogen and test timing.

name: nucleocytoplasmic transport
clinical_significance: Nucleocytoplasmic transport regulates movement of proteins and RNA between the nucleus and cytoplasm. It is essential for gene expression and is altered by some viruses, cancers, and neurodegenerative diseases.

name: nucleolus
clinical_significance: Changes in nucleolar size or appearance can occur in rapidly dividing cells and some cancers, but the nucleolus is not diagnostic by itself; pathologists interpret it with the cell and tissue pattern.

name: nucleoplasm
clinical_significance: The nucleoplasm is the fluid environment within a cell nucleus where DNA replication, transcription, and RNA processing occur. Abnormal nuclear contents can be assessed in cytology or pathology in context.

name: nucleoprotein
clinical_significance: A nucleoprotein is a complex of nucleic acid and protein, such as chromatin or a viral nucleocapsid. These complexes are important in genetics, infection, and some diagnostic or vaccine assays.

name: nucleoside
clinical_significance: A small molecule made of a nitrogen-containing base joined to a sugar. Adding one or more phosphate groups makes a nucleotide, the building block used to make DNA or RNA and to carry energy in cells.

name: nucleosome
clinical_significance: Nucleosomes package DNA around histone proteins and help regulate gene accessibility. Their structure and chemical modifications are relevant to gene expression, cancer biology, and epigenetic therapies.

name: nucleotide
clinical_significance: A small molecule made of a sugar, a nitrogen-containing base, and one or more phosphate groups. Nucleotides build DNA and RNA and also carry energy used by cells.

name: nucleotide biosynthesis
clinical_significance: Nucleotide biosynthesis produces the building blocks of DNA and RNA. Inherited enzyme defects can cause immunodeficiency or metabolic disease, while several anticancer and antiviral drugs target nucleotide production.

name: nucleotide metabolism
clinical_significance: Nucleotide metabolism supports DNA and RNA synthesis, energy transfer, and cellular signaling. Enzyme defects can cause inherited disorders, and antimetabolite medicines exploit these pathways to treat cancer or infection.

name: nucleotidyltransferase
clinical_significance: Nucleotidyltransferases transfer nucleotide groups to molecules such as RNA, DNA, or proteins. These enzymes are essential to gene expression and are studied as targets in antiviral, cancer, and genetic research.

name: nucleus accumbens
clinical_significance: A group of nerve cells deep in the brain that helps process reward, motivation, learning, and reinforcement. Its activity is involved in normal behavior and in disorders such as addiction and some psychiatric illnesses.

name: nucleus pulposus
clinical_significance: The soft, gel-like center of a spinal disk, surrounded by a tough outer ring. It helps spread pressure between vertebrae, but a tear may allow it to bulge or press on nerves.

name: numbness
clinical_significance: Numbness is reduced or absent sensation, often from nerve compression, neuropathy, stroke, spinal disease, circulation problems, or anesthetic effects.

name: numerator
clinical_significance: A numerator is the top number in a fraction or rate. In clinical statistics, numerator counts such as cases, adverse events, or deaths must be interpreted with the correct denominator and time period.

name: numerous
clinical_significance: “Numerous” indicates many findings or events but is not a standardized clinical quantity. Reports should specify counts or thresholds when the number affects diagnosis, severity, or treatment.

name: nurse
clinical_significance: Nurses assess health, provide treatment and education, monitor changes, and coordinate care. Their observations often identify early deterioration and support safe transitions between care settings.

name: nurse practitioner
clinical_significance: A nurse practitioner is an advanced-practice nurse who can assess patients, diagnose and treat many conditions, prescribe medicines where authorized, and provide preventive care.

name: nursing
clinical_significance: The professional practice of caring for people, promoting health, preventing illness, and supporting recovery or comfort.

name: nursing diagnoses
clinical_significance: Nursing diagnoses describe patient responses or care needs, such as pain, impaired mobility, or risk of infection, to guide a nursing plan. They complement medical diagnoses and are reassessed as the patient’s condition changes.

name: nursing home
clinical_significance: A nursing home provides long-term residential care, nursing, and help with daily activities for people who cannot safely live independently. Quality of care, medication review, infection prevention, mobility support, and residents’ preferences are key clinical concerns.

name: nursing intervention
clinical_significance: Nursing interventions are actions nurses take to address a patient’s needs, such as monitoring, medication administration, wound care, education, or mobility support. Their effectiveness is evaluated against patient-centered outcomes.

name: nursing process
clinical_significance: The nursing process organizes assessment, care planning, intervention, and evaluation. It supports individualized care and communication, especially for complex or changing health needs.

name: nursing research
clinical_significance: Nursing research evaluates care practices, patient outcomes, safety, and health-service delivery. Evidence from well-designed studies helps improve clinical guidelines and quality of care.

name: nursing therapy
clinical_significance: “Nursing therapy” may refer broadly to nursing care that supports symptom control, recovery, or function; it is not a single standardized treatment. The specific intervention should be stated to assess evidence and safety.

name: nutraceutical
clinical_significance: A nutraceutical is a food-derived product marketed for health effects, but the term does not ensure proven benefit, quality, or safety. Supplements can interact with medicines or vary in strength and purity.

name: nutrient intake activity
clinical_significance: Nutrient intake describes the amount of food energy and nutrients consumed. Assessment helps identify malnutrition, deficiencies, excess intake, or dietary needs during illness, pregnancy, growth, and recovery.

name: nutrigenomics
clinical_significance: The study of how food and nutrients interact with genes and how genetic differences influence responses to diet. It is used in research on metabolism and disease risk; many proposed personalized-nutrition applications remain under study.

name: nutrition
clinical_significance: Nutrition affects growth, immune function, muscle, metabolism, and recovery from illness. Inadequate or excessive intake can contribute to disease, so assessment and support are part of many clinical care plans.

name: nutrition disorder
clinical_significance: Nutrition disorders include undernutrition, nutrient deficiencies, and disorders related to excess intake or abnormal metabolism. They can impair growth, immunity, organ function, and recovery and may require medical and dietary treatment.

name: nutrition therapy
clinical_significance: Nutrition therapy uses individualized food plans, oral supplements, or enteral or parenteral feeding to treat disease or prevent malnutrition. The plan should account for diagnosis, swallowing, metabolism, preferences, and treatment goals.

name: nutritional epidemiology
clinical_significance: Nutritional epidemiology studies relationships between diet and health outcomes in populations. Findings can guide prevention policy but may be affected by measurement error and confounding and do not automatically predict an individual’s response.

name: nutritional requirement
clinical_significance: Nutritional requirements are the amounts of energy and nutrients needed to support health at a particular age and physiologic state. Needs may change with pregnancy, growth, illness, or recovery.

name: nutritional status
clinical_significance: Nutritional status reflects whether a person’s energy and nutrient needs are being met. Assessment can identify malnutrition or obesity and considers intake, weight change, function, examination, and relevant laboratory data.

name: nutritional support
clinical_significance: Nutritional support provides adequate energy, protein, fluids, and micronutrients when ordinary intake is insufficient. It may involve food fortification, oral supplements, tube feeding, or intravenous nutrition, with monitoring for complications.

name: nutritive value
clinical_significance: Nutritive value describes the energy and nutrients supplied by food. In clinical care it helps compare dietary choices and plan meals for conditions such as diabetes, kidney disease, or malnutrition.

name: nyctalopia
clinical_significance: Nyctalopia is difficulty seeing in dim light and may result from vitamin A deficiency, retinal disease, cataracts, or inherited disorders. New or progressive night blindness warrants eye assessment because some causes are treatable.

name: nystagmus
clinical_significance: Involuntary, repetitive eye movements that may be side-to-side, up-and-down, or rotary. It may be present from infancy or develop later and can be associated with inner-ear disease, neurologic disorders, reduced vision, or medicines. New-onset nystagmus, especially with dizziness, weakness, or vision changes, needs medical assessment.

name: nystatin
clinical_significance: Nystatin is an antifungal medicine used for selected Candida infections of the mouth, skin, or gastrointestinal tract. It is not absorbed well from the gut and is not appropriate for invasive fungal infection.

name: obatoclax
clinical_significance: Obatoclax is an investigational drug that inhibits anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins and has been studied in cancer. It is not a routine approved treatment and remains relevant mainly to research.

name: obatoclax mesylate
clinical_significance: Obatoclax mesylate is the investigational salt formulation of obatoclax, a BCL-2 family inhibitor studied in oncology. It has no established routine clinical role.

name: obesity
clinical_significance: A chronic disease involving abnormal or excessive accumulation of body fat that may impair health. It is linked with a higher risk of conditions such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, sleep apnea, osteoarthritis, and some cancers. Many factors can contribute, including genes, metabolism, hormones, medicines, eating patterns, activity, environment, and social conditions; it is not caused by one factor or by lack of willpower alone. Body mass index (BMI) is commonly u

name: obex region
clinical_significance: A small area at the lower end of the brain’s fourth fluid-filled space, where it narrows into the central canal of the spinal cord. It lies near centers controlling breathing, swallowing, and vomiting.

name: oblimersen sodium
clinical_significance: Oblimersen sodium is an investigational antisense drug designed to reduce BCL-2 protein expression in cancer cells. It has not become a standard therapy; its significance is mainly in studies of targeted anticancer treatment.

name: observational study
clinical_significance: An observational study examines health outcomes without assigning an intervention. It can identify associations and describe disease patterns, but confounding means it generally cannot establish causation on its own.

name: obsessive-compulsive disorder
clinical_significance: A mental-health disorder involving unwanted, repeated thoughts, images, or urges and repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed to reduce distress or prevent a feared event. The symptoms are time-consuming or cause clinically significant distress or impairment.

name: obstetric nursing
clinical_significance: Obstetric nursing provides care during pregnancy, labor, birth, and the postpartum period, including monitoring, education, support, and recognition of complications.

name: obstetrical forceps
clinical_significance: A surgical instrument used in selected vaginal births to guide the baby’s head when delivery needs assistance. Safe use requires the correct position, an experienced clinician, and assessment of risks and alternatives.

name: obstetrics
clinical_significance: The branch of medicine concerned with care during pregnancy, labor, birth, and the weeks after birth, including routine care and treatment of complications affecting the pregnant person or baby.

name: obstruction
clinical_significance: A blockage that prevents normal movement through a body passage, such as an airway, intestine, bile duct, blood vessel, or urinary tract. Causes include swelling, stones, scars, tumors, clots, and foreign objects.

name: obstructive hydrocephalus
clinical_significance: Obstructive hydrocephalus is a blockage of cerebrospinal-fluid flow that can raise pressure in the brain. It may cause headache, vomiting, sleepiness, or neurologic changes and can require urgent neurosurgical treatment or cerebrospinal-fluid diversion.

name: obstructive nephropathy
clinical_significance: Kidney damage caused by a blockage that prevents urine from draining normally. Stones, tumors, scarring, an enlarged prostate, or birth-related problems can cause it; untreated blockage may lead to infection, permanent loss of kidney function, or kidney failure.

name: occipital bone
clinical_significance: The bone at the back and base of the skull. It surrounds the opening where the spinal cord joins the brain and connects with the first neck vertebra.

name: occipital diastasis
clinical_significance: Widening or separation of a joint between bones at the back of a newborn’s skull. It may follow difficult birth or abnormal development, and imaging assesses its extent and associated injury.

name: occipital lobe
clinical_significance: The part of the brain at the back of the head that receives and interprets visual signals. Injury or disease may cause missing areas of vision, difficulty recognizing objects, or visual hallucinations.

name: occlusal adjustment
clinical_significance: Selective reshaping of tooth surfaces to improve how the upper and lower teeth meet and reduce abnormal contact or bite interference.

name: occlusal splint
clinical_significance: A removable dental appliance that changes or protects tooth contact and may reduce effects of grinding, jaw-joint strain, or selected bite problems.

name: occlusion
clinical_significance: Complete blockage of a blood vessel or body passage. It may be caused by a blood clot, plaque, pressure, swelling, or an intentional medical procedure; the effects depend on the location and can include loss of blood flow, pain, or organ damage.

name: occupation
clinical_significance: Occupation can affect health through physical demands, exposures, stress, and access to care. Work history helps clinicians assess possible occupational causes of illness and plan accommodations or prevention.

name: occupational disease
clinical_significance: An illness caused or significantly worsened by workplace exposures or conditions. Examples include asthma from dust, hearing loss from noise, skin disease from chemicals, and lung disease from harmful particles.

name: occupational exposure
clinical_significance: Contact with a potentially harmful substance, energy source, or condition during work. Examples include radiation, chemicals, dust, noise, heat, infection, and repetitive strain. Risk depends on the hazard, amount, duration, and protective controls; monitoring and prevention are part of occupational health.

name: occupational health
clinical_significance: The medical field focused on preventing work-related illness, injury, and harmful exposure while supporting workers' health.

name: occupational medicine
clinical_significance: Occupational medicine focuses on preventing, diagnosing, and managing work-related illness and injury. It includes exposure assessment, fitness-for-duty evaluation, rehabilitation, and workplace health protection.

name: occupational therapy
clinical_significance: Rehabilitation that helps a person perform daily activities, work, school, and other meaningful tasks after illness, injury, or disability. It may use exercises, practice, adaptive equipment, changes to the environment, and strategies for movement, thinking, or sensory problems.

name: ochrobactrum
clinical_significance: Ochrobactrum is a genus of environmental bacteria that can cause rare opportunistic infections, particularly in people with devices or weakened immunity. Species-level identification helps distinguish infection from contamination and guide treatment.

name: ochrobactrum anthropi
clinical_significance: Ochrobactrum anthropi is an environmental bacterium that can cause catheter-associated bloodstream and other opportunistic infections. It may resist multiple antibiotics, so clinical correlation and susceptibility testing are important.

name: ochrobactrum intermedium
clinical_significance: Ochrobactrum intermedium is a rare cause of human infection, including occasional bloodstream or device-associated disease. Its significance depends on specimen source and patient findings, with susceptibility testing guiding therapy.

name: ochronosis
clinical_significance: Blue-black or brown discoloration of cartilage, tendons, skin, or the whites of the eyes caused by buildup of a chemical called homogentisic acid. It is most often linked to the inherited disorder alkaptonuria and may cause arthritis.

name: octadecadienoic acid
clinical_significance: Octadecadienoic acid refers to fatty acids with 18 carbon atoms and two double bonds, including linoleic acid. Essential fatty-acid intake supports normal skin and cell function, while dietary balance affects cardiovascular risk.

name: octanoic acid
clinical_significance: Octanoic acid, also called caprylic acid, is a medium-chain fatty acid found in foods and used in some medical nutrition products. It is metabolized differently from long-chain fats and may cause gastrointestinal symptoms at high intake.

name: octopamine
clinical_significance: Octopamine is a biogenic amine used as a signaling molecule in invertebrates and found in some supplements. Human effects and safety data are limited, and products marketed for weight loss or performance may carry cardiovascular or interaction risks.

name: octreotide
clinical_significance: Octreotide is a somatostatin analogue that suppresses growth hormone, several gastrointestinal hormones, and intestinal secretion; it is used for acromegaly, certain neuroendocrine tumors, and selected secretory diarrhoeas.

name: ocular albinism
clinical_significance: Ocular albinism is an inherited disorder with reduced pigment primarily in the eyes, causing decreased visual acuity, nystagmus, photophobia, and abnormal retinal development.

name: ocular fixation
clinical_significance: The ability to hold the eyes steadily on a target; abnormal fixation can impair visual acuity, tracking, or alignment.

name: ocular hypertension
clinical_significance: Higher-than-normal intraocular pressure (pressure inside the eye) without glaucomatous optic neuropathy (damage to the optic nerve) or visual-field loss. It is a risk state for glaucoma, but does not mean glaucoma is already present or certain to develop.

name: ocular melanoma
clinical_significance: Ocular melanoma is a potentially life-threatening cancer, most often arising in the uvea. It may spread to the liver even after treatment of the eye, so specialist care and long-term surveillance are important.

name: ocular orbit
clinical_significance: The bony cavity around the eye. It contains the eyeball, eye-movement muscles, nerves, blood vessels, glands, and protective tissues.

name: ocular pain
clinical_significance: Eye pain may arise from surface irritation, infection, inflammation, trauma, glaucoma, or disease behind the eye. Sudden severe pain with reduced vision, a red eye, light sensitivity, nausea, or headache needs urgent assessment because sight-threatening causes are possible.

name: ocular toxoplasmosis
clinical_significance: A retinal infection or inflammation caused by Toxoplasma gondii, which can produce blurred vision, floaters, pain, and recurrent retinal scars.

name: oculocardiac reflex
clinical_significance: The oculocardiac reflex can cause bradycardia or arrhythmia during eye surgery, orbital pressure, or traction on eye muscles. Anesthesia teams monitor for it and relieve the triggering stimulus if it occurs.

name: oculocerebrorenal syndrome
