clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder, also called Zellweger spectrum disorder, that affects the brain, eyes, kidneys, liver, and other organs. Severe forms begin in newborns and can cause weak muscles, seizures, feeding problems, and major developmental problems.

name: oculomotor nerve
clinical_significance: The third cranial nerve, controlling most eye movements, eyelid lifting, and pupil narrowing. Damage can cause double vision, a drooping eyelid, an outward-turning eye, or an abnormally enlarged pupil.

name: oculomotor nucleus
clinical_significance: A group of nerve cells in the midbrain that controls most eye movements, lifts the upper eyelid, and narrows the pupil through the third cranial nerve.

name: odds ratio
clinical_significance: An odds ratio compares the odds of an outcome between two groups and is commonly reported in clinical studies. It indicates association, not absolute risk or causation; interpretation also depends on study design and confidence intervals.

name: odontoblast
clinical_significance: A cell along the inner part of a tooth that makes dentin, the hard layer beneath enamel. Odontoblasts produce dentin while teeth develop and can make limited repairs after injury.

name: odontodysplasia
clinical_significance: Odontodysplasia is abnormal development of tooth enamel and dentin, producing thin, weak, discolored teeth that may erupt late or be easily damaged.

name: odontogenesis
clinical_significance: The process by which teeth form and develop before and after birth. Problems during development can cause missing teeth, weak enamel, abnormal dentin, or changes in tooth shape and eruption.

name: odontogenic cyst
clinical_significance: A fluid-filled sac arising from tissues involved in tooth development, usually within the jaw. It may be painless or cause swelling, tooth displacement, infection, or bone damage.

name: odontogenic fibroma
clinical_significance: An odontogenic fibroma is a rare benign tumor arising from tooth-forming connective tissue, usually presenting as a jaw lesion.

name: odontogenic neoplasm
clinical_significance: An odontogenic neoplasm is a growth arising from tissues involved in tooth formation, usually in the jaw; it may be benign or malignant.

name: odontoma
clinical_significance: A noncancerous overgrowth of tooth-forming tissue, usually found in the jaw and often discovered when a permanent tooth fails to erupt. It may look like several small teeth or a solid calcified mass and is usually removed if it blocks eruption.

name: odorant
clinical_significance: Odorants are airborne chemicals detected by smell receptors. Loss or distortion of smell can affect food enjoyment and safety and may follow infection, nasal disease, head injury, or neurologic illness.

name: odoribacter splanchnicus
clinical_significance: Odoribacter splanchnicus is an anaerobic bacterium found in the human gut and is generally considered part of the intestinal microbiota. Its presence in a specimen outside the gut may be clinically relevant only with evidence of infection.

name: oerskovia
clinical_significance: Oerskovia is a genus of environmental bacteria that can occasionally cause catheter-related bloodstream or other opportunistic infections. Correct identification and susceptibility testing help distinguish it from contaminants and guide treatment.

name: oerskovia turbata
clinical_significance: Oerskovia turbata is an uncommon environmental bacterium reported in occasional bloodstream and device-associated infections. A positive culture requires assessment of specimen source, symptoms, and susceptibility results.

name: ofatumumab
clinical_significance: A monoclonal antibody against CD20 used for selected blood cancers and relapsing multiple sclerosis; it can increase infection risk and reduce B cells.

name: offspring
clinical_significance: The young or descendants produced by one organism or by a pair. In medicine and genetics, offspring may be studied to understand inherited traits, pregnancy outcomes, developmental conditions, and disease risk.

name: ofloxacin
clinical_significance: A fluoroquinolone antibiotic used for selected susceptible bacterial infections. It can cause serious tendon, nerve, heart-rhythm, and other adverse effects.

name: oidiodendron
clinical_significance: Oidiodendron is an environmental mold that rarely causes opportunistic human infection. Its recovery from tissue or a sterile site may warrant specialist identification, especially in an immunocompromised patient.

name: oil
clinical_significance: A hydrophobic liquid used as a nutrient, solvent, emollient, or medicinal preparation; safety depends on the specific oil.

name: ointment
clinical_significance: A thick, semisolid preparation applied to the skin, inside the nose, or other body surfaces. Its oily base helps protect the area and keep it moist; some ointments also contain medicines that treat infection, inflammation, pain, or other conditions.

name: ointment bases
clinical_significance: Semisolid materials that carry medicines applied to the skin or moist body surfaces. They affect how easily a product spreads, how much moisture it retains, how much medicine enters tissue, and how long it remains stable.

name: okadaic acid
clinical_significance: A toxin made by certain marine organisms that can accumulate in shellfish. Eating contaminated shellfish may cause diarrhoea and vomiting; in laboratories it is used to study enzymes that remove phosphate groups from proteins.

name: Okihiro syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited condition caused by changes in the SALL4 gene. It may combine abnormalities of the thumb or forearm with difficulty moving the eyes, and may also affect hearing, the heart, kidneys, or spine.

name: olanzapine
clinical_significance: Olanzapine is an atypical antipsychotic that blocks dopamine and serotonin receptors and treats schizophrenia and bipolar disorder; weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, sedation, and movement disorders are important risks.

name: olaparib
clinical_significance: Olaparib is a PARP inhibitor used for selected cancers with BRCA or other homologous-recombination repair defects; anaemia, nausea, fatigue, myelosuppression, and rare myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukaemia may occur.

name: olaratumab
clinical_significance: Olaratumab is a monoclonal antibody formerly studied and approved in some settings for soft-tissue sarcoma, but confirmatory trials did not show the expected benefit and its authorization was withdrawn. It is not a routine current cancer treatment.

name: oleandomycin
clinical_significance: Oleandomycin is an older macrolide antibiotic with limited contemporary use because of resistance and safer alternatives. It can cause gastrointestinal effects, liver injury, and drug interactions.

name: oleic acid
clinical_significance: A monounsaturated fat found in olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocados, and many other foods. Replacing some saturated fats with it may support healthier blood cholesterol levels as part of a balanced diet.

name: olfaction
clinical_significance: The sense of smell. Odor molecules stimulate special cells in the upper part of the nose, which send signals to the brain to identify and perceive odors.

name: olfactory bulb
clinical_significance: The olfactory bulb is a forebrain structure that receives signals from nasal smell receptors and begins processing odor information.

name: olfactory cortex
clinical_significance: The olfactory cortex is a group of brain regions that interprets smell signals and links them with memory, emotion, and behavior.

name: olfactory gyrus
clinical_significance: The olfactory gyrus is a cortical region associated with processing olfactory information and includes areas near the medial temporal and frontal lobes.

name: olfactory learning
clinical_significance: Olfactory learning is acquisition or modification of behavior or memory through exposure to odors and their associations.

name: olfactory mucosa
clinical_significance: The olfactory mucosa is specialized nasal lining containing receptor neurons, supporting cells, and glands that detect odor molecules.

name: olfactory nerve
clinical_significance: The first cranial nerve, which carries smell signals from specialized cells high in the nose to the brain. Injury or disease can reduce or eliminate the sense of smell or distort odors.

name: olfactory neuroblastoma
clinical_significance: A rare malignant tumor arising in the upper nasal cavity near the olfactory nerves, often causing nasal blockage, nosebleeds, or reduced smell.

name: olfactory tract
clinical_significance: The olfactory tract is a bundle of nerve fibers carrying smell information from the olfactory bulb to cerebral regions involved in odor perception.

name: olfactory tubercle
clinical_significance: The olfactory tubercle is a ventral forebrain region involved in odor processing, reward, motivation, and integration with limbic circuits.

name: oligella
clinical_significance: Oligella is a genus of bacteria that may colonize the urinary tract and can rarely cause urinary or bloodstream infection. A culture is interpreted with symptoms and specimen quality, and susceptibility testing may be needed.

name: oligella ureolytica
clinical_significance: Oligella ureolytica is an uncommon bacterium that can cause urinary infection, particularly in people with urinary abnormalities or catheters. It may be resistant to multiple antibiotics, so laboratory identification and susceptibility testing are useful.

name: oligella urethralis
clinical_significance: Oligella urethralis is a rare opportunistic bacterium that may be found in urine or other clinical samples. Its importance depends on symptoms, collection quality, and evidence of infection rather than detection alone.

name: oligodendroglia
clinical_significance: Oligodendroglia are glial cells of the central nervous system that produce myelin around axons and support nerve conduction.

name: oligodendroglial neoplasm
clinical_significance: A brain tumor made of cells that resemble oligodendrocytes, the cells that form the insulating coating around nerve fibers. Diagnosis uses tissue examination and genetic testing, and the tumor’s behavior depends on its grade and molecular features.

name: oligodendroglioma
clinical_significance: A brain tumor defined by characteristic changes in the IDH gene and loss of parts of chromosomes 1 and 19. It usually begins in the cerebral hemispheres and may cause seizures, headache, or other neurologic symptoms; grade affects its behavior and treatment.

name: oligogenic inheritance
clinical_significance: A pattern in which changes in a small number of genes work together to influence a disease or characteristic. The combination and strength of the changes can make symptoms differ among affected people.

name: oligohydramnios
clinical_significance: Too little amniotic fluid around the baby during pregnancy. It may result from leaking membranes, placental problems, dehydration, a pregnancy that continues beyond the due date, or problems affecting the baby's kidneys.

name: oligomenorrhea
clinical_significance: Oligomenorrhea is infrequent or widely spaced menstrual bleeding, often from anovulation, polycystic ovary syndrome, endocrine disease, undernutrition, excessive exercise, stress, or perimenopause.

name: oligometastasis
clinical_significance: Cancer that has spread to only a small number of separate sites, often no more than five. In selected people, surgery, focused radiation, or another local treatment may control these deposits for a long time.

name: oligomycin
clinical_significance: Oligomycin is a mitochondrial ATP-synthase inhibitor used primarily as a laboratory tool to study cellular energy production. It is not a therapeutic drug because it disrupts essential energy metabolism.

name: oligonucleotide
clinical_significance: A short piece of DNA or RNA made in the laboratory or found in cells. It can be used to detect genetic material, block or change gene messages, or help read and study genes.

name: oligopeptide
clinical_significance: A short chain of amino acids, usually containing only a few to about 20 building blocks. Oligopeptides can act as hormones, signaling molecules, antimicrobial substances, or parts of larger proteins.

name: oligosaccharide
clinical_significance: A short chain of sugar molecules joined together. Oligosaccharides form parts of cell-surface molecules, affect how cells recognize one another, and occur naturally in foods where some are used by gut bacteria.

name: oligospermia
clinical_significance: A lower-than-expected sperm concentration in semen. It can reduce fertility and may result from hormone problems, infections, medicines, heat, toxins, varicoceles, genetic conditions, or problems with sperm production.

name: oliguria
clinical_significance: Abnormally low urine production. It may result from dehydration, low blood flow, blockage, kidney disease, or medicines and can be an early sign of sudden kidney injury.

name: olivary nucleus
clinical_significance: The olivary nucleus is a brainstem structure that sends timing and motor-learning signals to the cerebellum through climbing fibers.

name: olivomycin
clinical_significance: Olivomycin is an antitumor antibiotic studied in cancer treatment, with limited use because of toxicity and narrow therapeutic margin. Its significance is mainly historical and pharmacologic.

name: olivopontocerebellar atrophy
clinical_significance: Olivopontocerebellar atrophy is a degenerative condition affecting the inferior olives, pons, and cerebellum, causing progressive ataxia and other neurologic dysfunction.

name: olmesartan medoxomil
clinical_significance: Olmesartan medoxomil is converted in the body to olmesartan, an angiotensin-receptor blocker used for hypertension. It can cause low blood pressure, kidney-function changes, or high potassium; rare sprue-like enteropathy can cause persistent diarrhea and weight loss.

name: olopatadine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: Olopatadine hydrochloride is an antihistamine used in eye drops or nasal spray to treat allergic conjunctivitis or rhinitis.

name: olsenella
clinical_significance: Olsenella is a genus of anaerobic bacteria found mainly in the mouth and digestive tract; human infection is uncommon.

name: olsenella uli
clinical_significance: An anaerobic gram-positive bacterium found in the mouth and associated with periodontal disease; invasive infection is rare.

name: oltipraz
clinical_significance: Oltipraz is an investigational drug studied for cancer prevention and treatment and for effects on cellular detoxification pathways. It is not a routine approved therapy.

name: omacetaxine mepesuccinate
clinical_significance: Omacetaxine mepesuccinate is a protein-synthesis inhibitor used for selected chronic myeloid leukemia resistant or intolerant to tyrosine-kinase inhibitors.

name: omalizumab
clinical_significance: Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds circulating IgE and reduces allergic inflammation; it is used for selected allergic asthma, chronic urticaria, nasal polyps, and food allergy, with rare anaphylaxis.

name: omasum
clinical_significance: The omasum is the third compartment of a ruminant stomach, absorbing water and small particles before contents reach the abomasum.

name: omega-n-methylarginine
clinical_significance: Omega-N-methylarginine is a methylated arginine compound that can inhibit nitric-oxide synthase and affect vascular signaling.

name: Omenn syndrome
clinical_significance: A severe inherited immune deficiency that usually begins in infancy. Babies may develop widespread red, peeling skin, swollen lymph nodes, enlarged liver or spleen, diarrhea, poor growth, and repeated serious infections.

name: omentum
clinical_significance: A fold of fatty tissue inside the abdomen that hangs from the stomach and partly covers the intestines. It contains blood vessels and immune cells and can help limit the spread of infection or inflammation.

name: omeprazole
clinical_significance: Omeprazole is a proton-pump inhibitor that irreversibly suppresses gastric H+/K+-ATPase; it treats reflux and peptic-ulcer disease and supports Helicobacter pylori eradication, while prolonged use may affect magnesium, B12, bone, and infection risk.

name: ommaya reservoir
clinical_significance: A surgically implanted reservoir connected to a catheter in a brain ventricle, used to sample cerebrospinal fluid or deliver selected medicines.

name: omphalocele
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which abdominal organs protrude through an opening at the navel into a protective sac. Other chromosome or organ abnormalities may occur, so newborn assessment and imaging are needed.

name: onchocerca volvulus
clinical_significance: A parasitic roundworm spread by repeated bites of infected blackflies that breed near fast-flowing rivers. Adult worms live in lumps under the skin and release young worms that can migrate through the skin and eyes.

name: onchocerciasis
clinical_significance: A parasitic infection caused by Onchocerca volvulus and spread by infected blackflies. It can cause intensely itchy skin, nodules, skin changes, and eye inflammation that may lead to permanent visual impairment or blindness.

name: oncocytic neoplasm
clinical_significance: A growth made of cells containing unusually many energy-producing structures, giving them a granular appearance under a microscope. It may be noncancerous or cancerous, depending on the organ and the tumor’s other features.

name: oncogene
clinical_significance: A gene that can make cells grow or survive without normal control when it is changed, overactive, or present in too many copies. Oncogene changes can contribute to the development and progression of cancer.

name: oncogenic virus
clinical_significance: A virus capable of contributing to cancer by altering cell growth, suppressing tumor defenses, or integrating or maintaining oncogenic genetic material.

name: oncogenicity
clinical_significance: Oncogenicity is the capacity to cause or contribute to cancer and is assessed for chemicals, infections, medicines, and genetic changes. Evidence informs prevention and risk evaluation but does not by itself predict an individual’s outcome.

name: oncologist
clinical_significance: A doctor who specializes in cancer care. Medical oncologists use medicines, radiation oncologists use radiation, and surgical oncologists operate; many people receive care from more than one type of oncologist.

name: oncology
clinical_significance: The medical field concerned with preventing, finding, and treating cancer and supporting people after treatment. Oncologists may use surgery, radiation, medicines, or combinations of treatments and work with other professionals to provide symptom and emotional support.

name: oncology nursing
clinical_significance: Oncology nursing provides cancer-related assessment, treatment support, symptom control, education, coordination, survivorship, and end-of-life care.

name: oncolytic virotherapy
clinical_significance: Oncolytic virotherapy uses modified viruses that preferentially infect and destroy cancer cells and may stimulate an immune response against the tumor.

name: oncolytic viruses
clinical_significance: Viruses selected or engineered to infect and destroy cancer cells while stimulating an immune response against the tumor.

name: oncoprotein
clinical_significance: A protein that promotes abnormal cell growth or survival and can contribute to cancer. It may result from a cancer-causing gene, a mutation, a chromosome change, or infection with certain viruses.

name: oncosis
clinical_significance: A form of cell injury in which cells swell and may die, usually because severe lack of oxygen or another injury disrupts energy production and the movement of salt and water across the cell membrane.

name: oncostatin m
clinical_significance: Oncostatin M is an immune signaling protein in the interleukin-6 cytokine family that can influence inflammation, blood-cell formation, and tissue remodeling. It is studied in inflammatory disease and cancer but is not a routine diagnostic test.

name: ondansetron
clinical_significance: Ondansetron is a selective 5-HT3-receptor antagonist used to prevent nausea and vomiting after chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery, or other triggers; constipation, headache, and QT prolongation can occur.

name: ondansetron hydrochloride
clinical_significance: Ondansetron hydrochloride is a salt formulation of ondansetron used to prevent nausea and vomiting. QT-interval prolongation is a relevant risk, especially with high doses, electrolyte abnormalities, or other QT-prolonging medicines.

name: onycholysis
clinical_significance: Onycholysis is separation of the nail plate from the nail bed, often starting at the tip. Causes include trauma, fungal infection, psoriasis, thyroid disease, and medicines; persistent or unexplained separation should be assessed and kept clean to reduce secondary infection.

name: onychomadesis
clinical_significance: Onychomadesis is proximal separation and shedding of a nail caused by temporary arrest of nail-matrix growth, often after infection, systemic illness, trauma, or medication exposure.

name: onychomycosis
clinical_significance: A fungal infection of a nail, more common in toenails than fingernails. The nail may become thick, yellow or white, brittle, crumbly, or separated from the skin. A sample may be tested before prolonged antifungal treatment because other nail diseases look similar.

name: oocyte
clinical_significance: An immature egg cell in an ovary. It develops before birth, remains paused until a menstrual cycle, and may mature and be released for possible fertilization.

name: oogenesis
clinical_significance: The formation and maturation of egg cells, or ova, in the ovaries. It begins before birth and continues through the reproductive years, with changes during each menstrual cycle.

name: oogonium
clinical_significance: An oogonium is an early female germ cell that proliferates during embryonic development and gives rise to primary oocytes.

name: oophoritis
clinical_significance: Oophoritis is inflammation of an ovary, often occurring with pelvic inflammatory disease or, less commonly, autoimmune disease. Fever, pelvic pain, or an adnexal mass requires evaluation for infection, abscess, and other urgent causes.

name: ooplasm
clinical_significance: Ooplasm is the cytoplasm of an egg cell, containing organelles, nutrients, and molecular factors that support fertilization and early embryo development.

name: open bite
clinical_significance: An open bite is a malocclusion in which upper and lower teeth do not meet in part of the mouth when the jaws are closed.

name: open fractures
clinical_significance: Broken bones associated with a wound that connects the fracture to the outside air. They have a high risk of infection and tissue damage; treatment includes cleaning, antibiotics, and specialist care.

name: open prostatectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery through an abdominal incision to remove the part of an enlarged prostate that blocks urine flow. It can improve severe urinary obstruction but may cause bleeding, infection, urine leakage, or changes in sexual and urinary function.

name: open-angle glaucoma
clinical_significance: A type of glaucoma in which the eye’s drainage angle remains open, but fluid drains too slowly. Pressure may rise and damage the optic nerve, causing gradual, permanent vision loss, often without early symptoms.

name: operant conditioning
clinical_significance: Learning in which the likelihood of a behavior changes because of its consequences, such as reinforcement or punishment.

name: operating room
clinical_significance: An operating room is a controlled sterile or semi-sterile clinical area equipped for surgical procedures, anesthesia, monitoring, and recovery support.

name: operating tables
clinical_significance: Adjustable tables designed to support and position patients during surgery or other procedures while allowing access and maintaining safety.

name: operon
clinical_significance: An operon is a group of genes regulated together, common in bacteria. Operon structure helps explain microbial gene expression, antibiotic resistance, and virulence and is used in molecular diagnostics and research.

name: ophthalmic solution
clinical_significance: A sterile liquid medicine made for application to the eye. It must remain clean and should not be shared or used after contamination because contaminated drops can cause serious eye infections.

name: ophthalmologist
clinical_significance: A medical doctor trained to diagnose and treat eye disease and vision problems. Ophthalmologists can prescribe medicines and glasses, perform eye procedures and surgery, and manage conditions affecting the eye, optic nerve, and visual system.

name: ophthalmoplegia
clinical_significance: Weakness or paralysis of the muscles that move the eyes, causing restricted eye movement, double vision, or abnormal eye alignment. It may result from disorders of the eye muscles, neuromuscular junction, cranial nerves, or brain pathways; causes include myasthenia gravis, thyroid eye disease, stroke, trauma, and mitochondrial disorders.

name: ophthalmoscope
clinical_significance: A lighted instrument used to examine the back and internal structures of the eye, including the retina, macula, optic nerve, and retinal blood vessels. Direct ophthalmoscopes provide a magnified view through the pupil, while indirect ophthalmoscopes use a separate light and lens to provide a wider view. Findings may relate to diabetes, high blood pressure, glaucoma, infection, inflammation, or other eye and nervous-system disorders.

name: ophthalmoscopy
clinical_significance: Examination of the inside of the eye with a lighted instrument. It allows a clinician to inspect the retina, optic nerve, and blood vessels for changes caused by diabetes, high blood pressure, glaucoma, inflammation, or other disease.

name: opiate
clinical_significance: A drug derived directly from chemicals in the opium poppy, such as morphine or codeine, or a closely related semisynthetic form. Opiates can relieve pain but may cause sleepiness, constipation, dependence, and dangerously slow breathing.

name: opiate alkaloid
clinical_significance: An opiate alkaloid is a naturally occurring alkaloid from the opium poppy, such as morphine or codeine, with opioid analgesic and dependence potential.

name: opiate assay
clinical_significance: A laboratory test that detects or measures opiates or their breakdown products in urine, blood, saliva, or another specimen. Results may support clinical care or toxicology testing, but some synthetic opioids require separate tests.

name: opiate overdose
clinical_significance: A life-threatening amount of an opioid medicine or drug that slows brain and breathing activity. Extreme sleepiness, pinpoint pupils, slow or absent breathing, blue lips, or inability to wake may occur. Naloxone can sometimes restore breathing.

name: opioid
clinical_significance: A natural or synthetic substance that acts on opioid receptors to relieve pain and may cause sedation or dependence.

name: opioid receptor
clinical_significance: A cell-surface protein activated or blocked by opioids and naturally produced endorphins. Mu, kappa, and delta receptors influence pain, breathing, mood, bowel movement, and reward; excessive mu-receptor activation can suppress breathing.

name: opisthorchis felineus
clinical_significance: A liver fluke acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish; chronic infection can cause bile-duct inflammation and increase cholangiocarcinoma risk.

name: opportunistic infection
clinical_significance: An infection that causes illness mainly when the immune system is weakened or a normal protective barrier is damaged. Causes may include cancer treatment, HIV, transplantation, severe illness, or prolonged use of immune-suppressing medicines.

name: oprelvekin
clinical_significance: Oprelvekin is a recombinant form of interleukin-11 formerly used to reduce chemotherapy-related low platelet counts in selected patients. It can cause fluid retention, cardiac complications, and other serious effects and is now rarely used.

name: opsoclonus
clinical_significance: Rapid, involuntary, back-and-forth eye movements in many directions without pauses. It may occur with muscle jerks and poor coordination, sometimes because of an immune reaction, infection, medicine, or an underlying tumor, and needs medical evaluation.

name: opsonin
clinical_significance: An immune protein that coats a germ and marks it for destruction. Antibodies and complement proteins can act as opsonins by helping infection-fighting cells recognize and engulf the germ.

name: opsonization
clinical_significance: The coating of a germ or other particle with immune proteins so that infection-fighting cells can recognize, capture, and destroy it more easily. Antibodies and complement proteins commonly perform this function.

name: optic atrophy
clinical_significance: Damage and loss of optic-nerve fibers, causing permanent reduction in vision, color vision, or part of the visual field. Causes include glaucoma, poor blood supply, inflammation, pressure, injury, toxins, and inherited disorders; treatment targets the cause when possible.

name: optic chiasma
clinical_significance: The crossing point beneath the brain where some fibers from the two optic nerves switch sides. Damage there can cause loss of the outer parts of both visual fields.

name: optic disk
clinical_significance: The optic disk is examined for swelling, pallor, and cupping, which can indicate raised intracranial pressure, optic-nerve injury, or glaucoma. Its appearance is interpreted with visual fields and other eye findings.

name: optic glioma
clinical_significance: A usually slow-growing tumor of the optic nerve or the visual pathway leading to the brain, most often in children. It may cause reduced vision, loss of part of the visual field, a bulging eye, or abnormal eye movements and is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1.

name: optic nerve
clinical_significance: The nerve that carries visual signals from each eye to the brain. Damage can cause reduced vision, loss of color or part of the visual field, and sometimes pain with eye movement.

name: optic nerve disorder
clinical_significance: A disease affecting the optic nerve, which carries visual signals from the eye to the brain; it can cause reduced vision, color loss, or visual-field defects.

name: optic neuritis
clinical_significance: Optic neuritis causes inflammation or demyelination of the optic nerve, often with painful eye movement, reduced vision, and impaired color perception. It can be associated with multiple sclerosis or other immune disease and needs prompt evaluation to protect vision and identify the cause.

name: optic tract
clinical_significance: A bundle of nerve fibers carrying visual information from the optic chiasma to brain areas that process sight and control visual reflexes. Damage causes loss of a characteristic part of the visual field.

name: optical illusion
clinical_significance: A visual perception in which an object, image, or movement appears different from its physical properties. Illusions are common, but new or persistent visual distortions may occur with eye, brain, medicine, or migraine-related disorders.

name: optical rotation
clinical_significance: The turning of plane-polarized light as it passes through a substance whose molecules have a particular three-dimensional arrangement. Measuring it can help identify or assess the concentration of some chemicals and medicines.

name: optical trap
clinical_significance: An optical trap uses focused light to hold or move microscopic particles or cells without physical contact. It is a research tool used in cell biology and biophysics, not a routine clinical procedure.

name: optics
clinical_significance: Optics concerns how light behaves and interacts with lenses and tissues. It underlies eyeglass and contact-lens correction, eye imaging, microscopes, and laser procedures.

name: optimism
clinical_significance: Optimism can influence coping, health behavior, and perceived well-being, but it is not a medical diagnosis or a substitute for assessing symptoms and social circumstances.

name: optometrist
clinical_significance: A trained eye-care professional who examines vision and many ocular conditions and prescribes optical correction within local scope of practice.

name: oral
clinical_significance: Relating to the mouth, or taken through the mouth. Oral medicines are swallowed and absorbed through the digestive tract unless otherwise specified.

name: oral administration
clinical_significance: Taking a medicine by mouth so it is absorbed through the digestive tract; absorption can be affected by food, vomiting, interactions, or gastrointestinal disease.

name: oral candidiasis
clinical_significance: A yeast infection of the mouth, usually caused by Candida. It may produce wipeable white patches, soreness, burning, altered taste, or cracks at the mouth corners. Antibiotics, steroid inhalers, dentures, diabetes, dry mouth, and weak immunity increase risk.

name: oral cavity
clinical_significance: The space inside the mouth, extending from the lips to the throat and bounded by the cheeks, palate, tongue, and floor of the mouth. It receives food, begins digestion, and helps with speech, taste, and breathing.

name: oral health
clinical_significance: Oral health is the condition of the teeth, gums, mouth, jaw, and related functions such as eating, speaking, and swallowing.

name: oral hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from the mouth, gums, tongue, throat, or nearby tissues, caused by trauma, dental disease, infection, medicines, or a bleeding disorder.

name: oral leukoplakia
clinical_significance: A persistent white patch in the mouth that cannot be rubbed off and is not explained by another condition. It is often linked to tobacco, alcohol, or betel-nut use and can sometimes develop into mouth cancer, so a persistent patch needs dental or medical assessment.

name: oral mucosa
clinical_significance: The moist lining of the mouth, including the inner lips and cheeks, gums, tongue, and palate. It protects deeper tissues, provides sensation, stays lubricated, and can develop ulcers, infections, inflammation, or tumors.

name: oral spray
clinical_significance: A liquid medicine or preparation sprayed into the mouth or throat for local treatment or absorption through oral tissues.

name: oral ulcer
clinical_significance: An oral ulcer is a break in the mouth lining that may result from trauma, infection, immune disease, nutritional deficiency, or cancer. A persistent ulcer, especially beyond two weeks, or one with a firm edge, bleeding, or a neck lump should be assessed.

name: orantinib
clinical_significance: Orantinib is an investigational tyrosine-kinase inhibitor studied for cancer, including liver and gastrointestinal tumors. It is not a routine approved treatment and remains of research significance.

name: orbital cellulitis
clinical_significance: A serious infection in the tissues around and behind the eye. It can cause eyelid swelling, fever, pain with eye movement, double vision, or reduced vision and can spread to the brain.

name: orbital contusion
clinical_significance: An orbital contusion is bruising around the eye after blunt trauma. Assessment should exclude globe injury, fracture, restricted eye movement, vision loss, and retrobulbar bleeding, which can threaten sight.

name: orbital fractures
clinical_significance: Breaks in the bones surrounding the eye, which may cause swelling, double vision, numbness, restricted eye movement, or injury to the eye itself.

name: orbital myositis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of one or more muscles that move the eye. It can cause pain, eyelid swelling, double vision, and restricted eye movement; treatment depends on the cause and may require urgent specialist assessment.

name: orbital neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the eye socket that may arise from the eye, optic nerve, muscles, glands, bone, or other tissues. It can cause bulging, pain, double vision, or vision loss and may be benign or cancerous.

name: orbivirus
clinical_significance: Orbiviruses are tick- or insect-borne viruses that mainly infect animals, though some can cause human illness. Their medical and veterinary significance depends on the specific virus and geographic exposure.

name: orchiectomy
clinical_significance: Orchiectomy is removal of one or both testes, commonly for testicular cancer or as androgen-deprivation treatment for prostate cancer. It affects fertility and testosterone and requires discussion of sperm preservation, hormone effects, and follow-up when relevant.

name: orchitis
clinical_significance: Orchitis is inflammation of one or both testes, often from infection such as mumps or bacteria, causing pain, swelling, and sometimes impaired fertility.

name: order coleoptera
clinical_significance: The insect order containing beetles, characterized by hardened forewings that protect the flying wings; some species affect health as pests or vectors.

name: order spirochaetales
clinical_significance: A biological order of spiral-shaped bacteria that includes groups causing syphilis, Lyme disease, relapsing fever, and leptospirosis. Identification of the species determines medical significance and treatment.

name: oregovomab
clinical_significance: Oregovomab is an investigational monoclonal antibody targeting the ovarian-cancer-associated antigen CA-125. It has been studied as an immune therapy but is not a routine standard treatment.

name: orexin
clinical_significance: Orexin, or hypocretin, is a hypothalamic neuropeptide that promotes wakefulness, arousal, appetite, and energy regulation; loss of orexin signaling is strongly associated with narcolepsy type 1.

name: organ
clinical_significance: Organ function can be impaired by disease, injury, infection, or treatment, and failure of a vital organ may require urgent support. Clinical assessment evaluates each organ’s function and interactions with other systems.

name: organ culture
clinical_significance: Organ culture keeps tissue outside the body under controlled conditions to study disease, drug effects, or tissue function. It is mainly a research method and does not replace clinical testing in a patient.

name: organ system
clinical_significance: Organ-system problems can affect several functions at once, so clinicians consider interactions among systems when evaluating symptoms and treatment risks.

name: organ transplantation
clinical_significance: Replacement of a failing organ with a healthy organ from a donor. Transplants can restore function but require careful matching, lifelong monitoring, and medicines to prevent rejection; infection, rejection, and medicine-related harm remain possible.

name: organelle
clinical_significance: A specialized part inside a cell that performs a particular job. Examples include the nucleus, which stores genetic instructions, and mitochondria, which release energy; organelles work together to keep the cell alive.

name: organic chemical
clinical_significance: A carbon-containing chemical compound, usually also containing hydrogen and sometimes oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur, or other elements. Organic chemicals include medicines, fats, sugars, proteins, solvents, and many toxins.

name: organic impurity
clinical_significance: An organic impurity is an unintended carbon-containing chemical in a medicine, material, or specimen that may affect safety, quality, or measurement.

name: organic oxide
clinical_significance: Organic oxides include diverse carbon-containing oxygen compounds with widely differing medical and toxicologic effects. The exact chemical identity and exposure route are necessary for clinical risk assessment.

name: organism
clinical_significance: An organism may be a human, animal, plant, bacterium, fungus, or virus. In clinical microbiology, identifying the organism causing infection guides isolation, treatment, and public-health action.

name: organization name
clinical_significance: The formal name of a group, institution, company, or agency; in healthcare records it should identify the responsible organization accurately.

name: organogenesis
clinical_significance: The process during embryonic development in which groups of cells form and organize into organs. Disruption can lead to congenital abnormalities, while the process is also studied in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine.

name: organoid
clinical_significance: Organoids are three-dimensional cell models that reproduce selected features of organs. They support disease research and drug testing and may eventually help personalize therapy, but most are not yet validated for routine clinical decisions.

name: organometallic compound
clinical_significance: Organometallic compounds contain metal-carbon bonds and include medicines, imaging agents, and industrial chemicals. Their toxicity and therapeutic effects depend on the specific compound, metal, dose, and exposure.

name: organosilicon compounds
clinical_significance: Organosilicon compounds contain silicon bonded to carbon and are used in materials, medicines, devices, and industry; biological effects depend on the specific compound.

name: orgasm
clinical_significance: The peak of sexual pleasure, usually accompanied by involuntary muscle and body responses that vary among individuals.

name: orientation
clinical_significance: Awareness of personal identity, place, time, and situation. Clinicians assess orientation as part of mental-status and neurologic examinations.

name: orlistat
clinical_significance: A medicine used with a reduced-calorie diet to help with weight loss or weight control. It stops some dietary fat from being absorbed, so oily stools, gas, and urgent bowel movements can occur; it can also reduce absorption of vitamins and some medicines.

name: ornithine
clinical_significance: Ornithine participates in the urea cycle, which converts ammonia to urea for removal. Abnormal ornithine metabolism can cause inherited hyperammonemia and neurologic injury, so metabolic testing may be needed when symptoms suggest a urea-cycle disorder.

name: ornithine decarboxylase
clinical_significance: Ornithine decarboxylase controls the first step in polyamine synthesis, a pathway important for cell growth. It is a drug target in selected disease and cancer research; excessive pathway activity can support tumor growth.

name: oropharyngeal
clinical_significance: Oropharyngeal means relating to the mouth and the part of the throat behind it, including structures involved in breathing, swallowing, and speech.

name: oropharyngeal carcinoma
clinical_significance: Cancer arising in the part of the throat behind the mouth, including the tonsils, back of the tongue, soft palate, or throat wall. Tobacco, alcohol, and some HPV infections increase risk; assessment usually includes examination, tissue sampling, and scans.

name: oropharyngeal neoplasm
clinical_significance: An oropharyngeal neoplasm is an abnormal growth in the throat behind the mouth, including the tonsils and base of the tongue; it may be benign or malignant.

name: orotic aciduria
clinical_significance: An unusually high amount of orotic acid in urine. It may result from a rare inherited disorder affecting blood-cell and DNA building blocks, causing anemia and poor growth, or from a urea-cycle disorder with high ammonia.

name: orphenadrine
clinical_significance: A centrally acting medicine with anticholinergic properties used in some countries for painful muscle spasm; it can cause drowsiness, dry mouth, and confusion.

name: ortataxel
clinical_significance: Ortataxel is an investigational taxane chemotherapy agent studied for cancers resistant to other treatments. It is not a routine approved therapy and has limited current clinical use.

name: orthobunyavirus
clinical_significance: Orthobunyaviruses include many mosquito- or midge-borne viruses, some of which cause fever, encephalitis, or congenital infection. Travel and vector exposure help guide diagnosis and public-health surveillance.

name: orthodontic appliance
clinical_significance: Orthodontic appliances apply controlled forces to correct tooth alignment or jaw relationships. Poor fit or hygiene can cause pain, sores, or decay, so treatment requires dental monitoring and adherence to care instructions.

name: orthodontic bracket
clinical_significance: Orthodontic brackets anchor braces and transmit force to move teeth. They can irritate oral tissues and trap plaque, increasing the risk of enamel decalcification or gum inflammation without good hygiene and regular dental care.

name: orthodontic retainer
clinical_significance: Retainers help prevent teeth from shifting after orthodontic treatment. Consistent use as prescribed and periodic fit checks reduce relapse and identify breakage or unwanted tooth movement.

name: orthodontic wires
clinical_significance: Metal or other wires used with braces to apply controlled forces that move teeth or help maintain their position.

name: orthodontics
clinical_significance: The dental specialty that corrects teeth or jaws that do not align properly. Braces, clear aligners, or other appliances can improve biting, chewing, appearance, and cleaning; retainers are usually needed afterward because teeth can shift back.

name: orthodontist
clinical_significance: A dentist specially trained to diagnose and treat teeth or jaws that do not align properly. Orthodontists use braces, clear aligners, retainers, and sometimes surgery to improve biting, chewing, appearance, and oral health.

name: orthohepadnavirus
clinical_significance: A group of viruses that includes hepatitis B virus and related viruses infecting mammals. These viruses carry genetic material as DNA and may cause long-lasting liver infection, inflammation, scarring, or cancer.

name: orthokeratosis
clinical_significance: Thickening of the outer skin layer with fully mature skin cells. It can be a normal protective response, such as on the soles, or part of conditions causing thick, scaly, or rough skin.

name: orthomyxoviridae
clinical_significance: A family of viruses that includes influenza A, B, and C. They mainly infect the airways and can cause flu, outbreaks, and sometimes severe pneumonia or other complications.

name: orthopedics
clinical_significance: Orthopedics evaluates and treats musculoskeletal injury and disease, including fractures, arthritis, deformity, and sports injuries. Care may involve rehabilitation, medication, injections, or surgery to preserve movement and function.

name: orthopoxvirus
clinical_significance: A genus of poxviruses that includes variola, mpox, vaccinia, and cowpox viruses. Infection may cause fever and skin lesions; severity and transmission depend on the specific virus.

name: orthoptera
clinical_significance: The insect order containing grasshoppers, crickets, katydids, and locusts; some species cause bites, allergies, or crop-related health effects.

name: orthoreovirus
clinical_significance: A genus of nonenveloped, segmented double-stranded RNA viruses; human infection is often mild or asymptomatic but can occasionally cause disease.

name: orthostatic hypotension
clinical_significance: A fall in blood pressure after standing, often causing dizziness, blurred vision, weakness, or fainting. It may result from dehydration, medicines, autonomic nerve problems, or prolonged bed rest. Repeated symptoms or falls need medical assessment.

name: orthostatic intolerance
clinical_significance: Dizziness, fast heartbeat, weakness, blurred vision, fatigue, or faintness that develops or worsens on standing because the body does not maintain blood flow to the brain adequately. Causes include dehydration, medicines, nerve disorders, and some chronic conditions.

name: orthotic devices
clinical_significance: External supports that hold, align, protect, or assist a body part, such as a brace, splint, shoe insert, or spinal support. They can reduce pain and improve movement, but poor fit may cause pressure, numbness, skin injury, or restricted circulation.

name: os odontoideum
clinical_significance: Os odontoideum is a separate ossicle near the second cervical vertebra’s odontoid process that can cause atlantoaxial instability or spinal-cord risk.

name: oscillometry
clinical_significance: A method that measures pressure-related vibrations, commonly used by automated blood-pressure cuffs and some vascular devices. The result estimates blood pressure or blood-flow characteristics but may be inaccurate with movement or irregular rhythms.

name: oseltamivir
clinical_significance: Oseltamivir is an antiviral medicine used to treat or prevent influenza, with the greatest benefit when started early.

name: oseltamivir phosphate
clinical_significance: Oseltamivir phosphate is the salt form of oseltamivir, an antiviral medicine used for treatment or prevention of influenza.

name: osmium
clinical_significance: A dense metallic element; some osmium compounds are highly toxic and can damage the eyes and respiratory tract.

name: osmium tetroxide
clinical_significance: Osmium tetroxide is a highly toxic, volatile chemical used in microscopy and industry. Exposure can cause severe eye and respiratory injury; suspected contact or inhalation requires immediate poison-control or emergency guidance.

name: osmolality
clinical_significance: A measure of how many dissolved particles are present in a kilogram of fluid. Blood osmolality depends mainly on sodium, glucose, and urea and helps determine how water moves between the bloodstream and cells.

name: osmoregulation
clinical_significance: Control of water and dissolved-solute balance in the body or an organism, maintaining appropriate cell volume and internal concentration.

name: osmosis
clinical_significance: Movement of water through a membrane toward the side with more dissolved particles. This process helps determine how water is distributed between blood, cells, and surrounding tissues.

name: osseointegration
clinical_significance: The firm attachment of living bone to the surface of an implant, such as a dental implant or artificial joint. Good stability, healthy bone, healing, and infection control support this process.

name: osseous metaplasia
clinical_significance: Osseous metaplasia is formation of mature bone in tissue where bone is not normally present, sometimes after injury, inflammation, or within a lesion.

name: ossifying fibroma
clinical_significance: An ossifying fibroma is a usually benign fibro-osseous tumor that replaces normal bone with fibrous tissue and mineralized material, often in the jaw.

name: osteitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of bone caused by infection, injury, inflammatory disease, or another process. It may cause localized pain, swelling, warmth, reduced movement, or fever and sometimes requires imaging, antibiotics, or surgery.

name: osteitis deformans
clinical_significance: Osteitis deformans is Paget disease of bone, in which abnormal remodeling produces enlarged, weakened, or deformed bones.

name: osteoarthritis
clinical_significance: A joint disease in which cartilage and other tissues gradually break down or change. It can cause pain, stiffness, swelling, bone changes, and restricted movement. It usually develops over time but may occur earlier after joint injury, abnormal joint structure, or previous joint disease.

name: osteoblast
clinical_significance: A cell that builds new bone. It makes the soft framework of bone and helps add calcium and phosphate to harden it. Some osteoblasts become osteocytes, which maintain mature bone.

name: osteoblastoma
clinical_significance: A rare benign bone-forming tumor, usually in the spine or long bones, that can cause persistent pain and sometimes neurologic symptoms.

name: osteocalcin
clinical_significance: A protein made mainly by osteoblasts that participates in bone mineralization and serves as a marker of bone formation.

name: osteocalcin assay
clinical_significance: A blood test measuring osteocalcin, a protein made by bone-forming cells. It can provide information about bone formation and turnover, but results are affected by age, kidney function, medicines, and the laboratory method.

name: osteochondritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or injury involving bone and its overlying cartilage, often near a joint. The term includes conditions such as osteochondritis dissecans, in which a fragment may loosen.

name: osteochondritis dissecans
clinical_significance: An area of damaged bone and cartilage beneath a joint surface that may loosen or separate. It most often affects the knee in adolescents and young adults and can cause activity-related pain, swelling, catching, or locking. Treatment depends on lesion stability, age, and symptoms.

name: osteochondroma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous cartilage-covered growth projecting from the surface of a bone, often near a growth plate. It may be single or occur as multiple inherited growths and can cause pain, deformity, or pressure on nearby nerves or vessels.

name: osteochondromatosis
clinical_significance: Osteochondromatosis is formation of multiple cartilage-capped bony outgrowths, usually around growth plates, that can cause deformity, pain, or nerve and vessel compression.

name: osteochondrosis
clinical_significance: A general name for several disorders affecting developing bone and nearby cartilage, often near a growth area or joint. The specific condition depends on the bone and age involved; it may cause pain, swelling, stiffness, or limited movement.

name: osteoclast
clinical_significance: A specialized bone cell that breaks down old bone during normal renewal and repair. Osteoclast activity helps regulate bone strength and blood calcium; excessive activity can contribute to osteoporosis and other diseases causing bone loss.

name: osteocyte
clinical_significance: A mature bone cell embedded in the hard bone it helped form. Osteocytes sense strain and chemical changes and send signals that help control bone strength, repair, and removal of old bone.

name: osteogenesis
clinical_significance: The formation and development of bone. It occurs in the growing skeleton and during fracture repair. Abnormal osteogenesis can contribute to birth disorders, poor healing, or fragile bones.

name: osteogenesis imperfecta
clinical_significance: A group of genetic disorders, also called brittle bone disease, in which bones break easily, sometimes after mild injury or for no clear reason. The disorders are often caused by gene changes that reduce or alter type I collagen, a protein that gives strength to bone and other connective tissues. Osteogenesis imperfecta is present from birth and can range from mild to severe; severe forms may cause fractures before birth. Other features may include short height, loose joints, blue or gray whites

name: osteoid osteoma
clinical_significance: A small noncancerous bone tumor, usually in an adolescent or young adult. It often causes persistent pain that is worse at night and may improve with anti-inflammatory medicine; scans help locate it and guide treatment.

name: osteolysis
clinical_significance: Osteolysis is progressive destruction or resorption of bone caused by tumors, inflammation, prosthesis reactions, infection, metabolic disease, or other processes.

name: osteoma
clinical_significance: A benign, slow-growing tumor made of bone. It often develops in the skull or facial bones and may cause no symptoms unless it blocks a passage or presses on nearby structures.

name: osteoma cutis
clinical_significance: Osteoma cutis is formation of bone within the skin or subcutaneous tissue, occurring as a primary disorder or secondary to acne, trauma, or another condition.

name: osteomalacia
clinical_significance: Osteomalacia is inadequate mineralization of adult bone, commonly from vitamin-D deficiency or phosphate disorders, causing bone pain, weakness, and fractures.

name: osteomyelitis
clinical_significance: Infection and inflammation of bone, usually caused by bacteria and sometimes fungi or other organisms. It can cause pain, fever, swelling, reduced movement, bone damage, or a persistent draining wound.

name: osteon
clinical_significance: A tube-shaped structural unit of hard, compact bone arranged around a small channel containing blood vessels and nerves. Osteons help give bone strength while allowing it to receive nutrients.

name: osteonectin
clinical_significance: An extracellular-matrix protein involved in collagen organization, mineral binding, and tissue remodeling; it is also called SPARC.

name: osteopenia
clinical_significance: Bone density that is below the usual range but does not meet the bone-density threshold for osteoporosis. In some adults, a DXA scan describes osteopenia with a T-score between -1.0 and -2.5; this range is not used to classify everyone. Fracture risk also depends on age, previous fractures, falls, medicines, and other health factors.

name: osteopetrosis
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which old bone is not removed normally. Bones become unusually dense but brittle and may fracture; crowding of the bone marrow and nerves can cause anemia, infections, vision loss, or other problems.

name: osteophyte
clinical_significance: A bony outgrowth forming at the edge of a joint, commonly with osteoarthritis. It may cause stiffness, pain, reduced movement, or pressure on nearby nerves, although some osteophytes cause no symptoms.

name: osteopoikilosis
clinical_significance: Osteopoikilosis is an inherited benign bone condition with multiple small dense spots on imaging, usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally.

name: osteopontin
clinical_significance: A protein involved in bone remodeling, immune responses, inflammation, and attachment between cells and tissues. Its level may change in several diseases, but a measurement is not by itself a specific diagnosis.

name: osteoporosis
clinical_significance: A bone disease in which bone is broken down faster than it is replaced, or its structure and strength change. The bones become less dense and more likely to break, sometimes after a minor fall or other low-impact force. Osteoporosis often causes no symptoms until a fracture occurs. Fractures commonly affect the hip, spine, and wrist; weakened bones in the spine may collapse and cause back pain or loss of height. Osteoporosis can affect anyone, but it is more common in females, especially after m

name: osteoporotic fracture
clinical_significance: A fracture resulting from weakened, porous bone after a low-energy event that would not usually break healthy bone.

name: osteoprotegerin test
clinical_significance: Osteoprotegerin testing may be used in research or specialized evaluation of bone remodeling and inflammatory disease. It is not a standalone routine test for osteoporosis or fracture risk.

name: osteoradionecrosis
clinical_significance: Death of bone within an area treated with radiation, most often the jaw after head-and-neck cancer treatment. The bone may become exposed or fail to heal after injury or dental work and can become infected.

name: osteosarcoma
clinical_significance: An aggressive cancer that begins in bone-forming cells and produces abnormal immature bone. It often develops near the ends of long bones in children and young adults and may cause persistent pain, swelling, or a fracture.

name: osteosclerosis
clinical_significance: Abnormally increased bone density seen on imaging or examination. It may result from inherited disease, altered bone renewal, chronic stress, inflammation, medicines, or cancer; dense bone can still be weak or painful.

name: osteotomy
clinical_significance: Osteotomy cuts and repositions bone to correct deformity, improve joint alignment, or redistribute weight. Recovery requires bone healing and rehabilitation; risks include infection, delayed union, nerve or vessel injury, and persistent pain.

name: ostomy
clinical_significance: A surgically created opening that connects part of the bowel or urinary tract to the skin so stool or urine can leave the body. A colostomy or ileostomy passes stool; a urostomy passes urine. A pouch usually collects the output and protects the surrounding skin.

name: other
clinical_significance: “Other” is a residual category used when a finding does not fit the listed options. In clinical data, a more specific description is preferable when the distinction could affect diagnosis or care.

name: other race
clinical_significance: Other race is a demographic category for a person who does not select or fit the available listed race categories; classification varies by system and should not be treated as a biological diagnosis.

name: otic ointment
clinical_significance: A semisolid medicine formulated for application to the outer ear or ear canal; it should be used only as directed, especially when the eardrum may be perforated.

name: otitis externa
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of the outer ear canal, commonly causing ear pain, itching, tenderness, swelling, or discharge. Keeping water and objects out of the ear can help while it heals.

name: otitis media
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection in the middle ear, often after a cold or other upper-airway infection. It may cause ear pain, fever, reduced hearing, irritability, or fluid behind the eardrum.

name: otocephaly
clinical_significance: Otocephaly is a severe congenital malformation involving absent or markedly underdeveloped lower facial structures and abnormal ear placement. It is usually life-limiting and requires prenatal or neonatal diagnostic and family-support care.

name: otolaryngologist
clinical_significance: An otolaryngologist is a physician specializing in disorders of the ear, nose, throat, head, neck, voice, swallowing, and related surgery.

name: otosclerosis
clinical_significance: An abnormal hardening and fixation of middle-ear bones that can gradually reduce hearing by blocking sound transmission.

name: otoscope
clinical_significance: A lighted instrument used to examine the ear canal and eardrum. It can help identify earwax, infection, a foreign object, fluid, swelling, or a perforated eardrum. Examination findings are interpreted with symptoms and, when needed, hearing tests.

name: ototoxicity
clinical_significance: Damage to the inner ear from a medicine, chemical, or other toxic exposure. It may cause hearing loss, ringing in the ears, dizziness, or imbalance and can be temporary or permanent.

name: ouabain
clinical_significance: Ouabain is a cardiac glycoside that inhibits the sodium-potassium pump and can affect heart contraction and rhythm. It is not a routine human medicine; exposure or misuse can cause dangerous arrhythmias.

name: ounce
clinical_significance: An ounce is a unit of mass or fluid volume whose exact conversion depends on the measurement system; medication instructions should use unambiguous units.

name: outcomes research
clinical_significance: Outcomes research studies how health care affects survival, symptoms, function, quality of life, and use of services. It helps compare treatments and improve care but depends on appropriate measurement and adjustment for differences between patients.

name: outlier
clinical_significance: An outlier is a value far from the rest of a dataset. In clinical testing it may indicate measurement error, a rare but important result, or a true extreme value and should be checked against clinical context before exclusion.

name: outpatient
clinical_significance: A person who receives medical evaluation or treatment without being admitted overnight to a hospital or other inpatient facility.

name: ovalbumin
clinical_significance: Ovalbumin is the main protein in egg white and a common food allergen. It is also used in allergy testing and laboratory research; people with egg allergy may react to ovalbumin-containing products.

name: ovalocyte count
clinical_significance: An ovalocyte count estimates the number or proportion of oval-shaped red blood cells on a blood smear and may help evaluate anemia.

name: ovarian cyst
clinical_significance: Ovarian cysts are common and often resolve, but size, symptoms, and imaging features determine follow-up; sudden severe pain may indicate torsion or rupture.

name: ovarian failure
clinical_significance: Reduced ovarian activity causing irregular or absent periods, difficulty becoming pregnant, and symptoms of low estrogen such as hot flushes or vaginal dryness. When it occurs before age 40, it is usually called primary ovarian insufficiency and needs evaluation.

name: ovarian fibromata
clinical_significance: Usually noncancerous tumors made of fibrous tissue that develop in an ovary. They may cause no symptoms or produce pelvic pressure, pain, menstrual changes, or fluid in the abdomen when large.

name: ovarian follicle
clinical_significance: A small fluid-filled structure in an ovary that contains an immature egg and supporting cells. During each menstrual cycle, one follicle usually matures and releases an egg during ovulation.

name: ovarian gonadoblastoma
clinical_significance: A rare tumor containing cells that normally develop into eggs and cells that support sex-hormone production. It often occurs in an atypically developed gonad, may contain Y-chromosome material, and can produce hormones.

name: ovarian hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding into or around an ovary, often from a ruptured cyst or blood vessel. It may cause sudden pelvic pain, weakness, dizziness, or internal blood loss and can require urgent assessment or surgery.

name: ovarian infection
clinical_significance: Infection involving an ovary, often as part of pelvic inflammatory disease or an abscess, causing pelvic pain, fever, and abnormal discharge.

name: ovarian rupture
clinical_significance: Ovarian rupture is tearing of an ovary or ovarian cyst, which may cause sudden pelvic pain and internal bleeding and sometimes requires urgent treatment.

name: ovarian teratoma
clinical_significance: A tumor of an ovary made from reproductive cells that can form different kinds of tissue, such as skin, hair, or bone. Mature teratomas are usually noncancerous; immature teratomas can be cancerous.

name: ovarian thecoma
clinical_significance: Ovarian thecomas are usually slow-growing ovarian tumors that may produce estrogen and cause abnormal bleeding or endometrial changes; pathology confirms diagnosis.

name: ovarian torsion
clinical_significance: Twisting of an ovary, often together with its fallopian tube, that can cut off blood flow. It causes sudden one-sided pelvic pain, often with nausea or vomiting, and is a gynecologic emergency that is usually treated with surgery.

name: ovariectomy
clinical_significance: Ovariectomy removes one or both ovaries and may be performed for cancer, ovarian disease, or as part of other surgery. Removal of both ovaries before natural menopause causes infertility and abrupt loss of ovarian hormones, affecting bone, cardiovascular, and symptom risks.

name: ovary
clinical_significance: A reproductive organ that releases eggs and produces hormones such as estrogen and progesterone. The ovaries help control menstrual cycles, ovulation, pregnancy preparation, and many body changes during reproductive life.

name: ovary disease
clinical_significance: Any disorder affecting an ovary, including cysts, infection, inflammation, tumors, hormonal dysfunction, torsion, or bleeding.

name: ovary neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in an ovary that may be noncancerous, have uncertain behavior, or be cancerous. Symptoms can include bloating, pelvic pain, pressure, or abnormal bleeding, but some growths are found incidentally on imaging.

name: overbite
clinical_significance: Vertical overlap of the upper front teeth over the lower front teeth; excessive overbite can damage gums, teeth, or jaw function.

name: overdose
clinical_significance: An overdose is exposure to a medicine, drug, or substance in an amount capable of causing toxicity, with effects determined by dose, formulation, route, timing, and patient factors.

name: overgrowth syndrome
clinical_significance: A group of conditions present from birth in which the whole body, one side, or particular tissues grow more than expected. Some forms also cause developmental differences or increase the risk of certain tumors.

name: overlay denture
clinical_significance: A removable denture that fits over remaining teeth, roots, or implants to improve support, chewing, and retention.

name: overriding aorta
clinical_significance: A birth-related heart abnormality in which the main artery leaving the heart sits over a hole between the lower chambers and receives blood from both. It commonly occurs as part of tetralogy of Fallot.

name: oversedate
clinical_significance: To give excessive sedation, causing unusually deep sleep, slowed responses, impaired breathing, or difficulty maintaining the airway.

name: overweight
clinical_significance: Body weight above the usual range for height. In adults, a Body Mass Index of 25 to less than 30 kg/m\(^2\) is commonly classified as overweight, but it does not directly measure body fat.

name: oviposition
clinical_significance: Oviposition is egg laying in animals and is relevant to veterinary reproductive biology, parasite life cycles, and animal breeding. It has no direct human clinical meaning.

name: ovomucin
clinical_significance: A glycoprotein in egg white that contributes to its gel-like viscosity and helps stabilize the egg-white structure.

name: ovotestis
clinical_significance: A gonad containing both ovarian-type and testicular tissue. It is an uncommon difference of sex development and may produce ovarian hormones, testicular hormones, eggs, sperm, or none of these; evaluation is individualized.

name: ovulation
clinical_significance: Ovulation is the release of an egg and defines the fertile window used in conception planning and some fertility treatments. Disorders of ovulation can cause irregular periods or infertility and may reflect endocrine or ovarian disease.

name: ovum
clinical_significance: A mature female gamete; in humans, the cell released at ovulation is usually a secondary oocyte, which completes its final meiotic division when a sperm enters. The resulting genetic material combines with the sperm’s to form a zygote, the first cell of a developing embryo.

name: ownership
clinical_significance: Ownership is not a diagnosis, but ownership of medicines, medical devices, or health data can affect safe use, responsibility, and privacy. Clinical records should distinguish the patient’s property from items managed by a care facility.

name: oxacillin
clinical_significance: A penicillinase-resistant penicillin used mainly to test for methicillin resistance in staphylococci; it is not commonly used as the preferred treatment for most infections.

name: oxalates
clinical_significance: Oxalates are salts or esters of oxalic acid that can bind calcium and form calcium-oxalate kidney stones; excess dietary absorption or inherited hyperoxaluria can cause renal injury.

name: oxaliplatin
clinical_significance: Oxaliplatin is a platinum chemotherapy drug that forms DNA cross-links and is used especially in colorectal cancer regimens; acute cold-triggered neuropathy and cumulative sensory neuropathy are characteristic toxicities.

name: oxaloacetate
clinical_significance: A small molecule used in the cell’s energy-making cycle. It combines with another molecule to begin a step that produces energy and can also help make glucose and the amino acid aspartate.

name: oxandrolone
clinical_significance: An anabolic steroid used in selected conditions involving severe weight loss or catabolic stress; it can affect the liver, lipids, and hormone function.

name: oxaprozin
clinical_significance: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug used to relieve pain and inflammation in conditions such as osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.

name: oxazepam
clinical_significance: A benzodiazepine medicine used short-term for anxiety or alcohol withdrawal, causing sleepiness and possible dependence.

name: oxazole
clinical_significance: Oxazole is a five-membered chemical ring containing oxygen and nitrogen that is used as a building block in medicinal and other chemistry.

name: oxcarbazepine
clinical_significance: Oxcarbazepine is an antiseizure medicine that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and treats focal seizures; dizziness, ataxia, rash, and clinically important hyponatraemia may occur.

name: oxidants
clinical_significance: Substances or reactive molecules that accept electrons or promote oxidation; excessive oxidant activity can damage proteins, lipids, and DNA.

name: oxidation
clinical_significance: Oxidation reactions are central to energy production, drug metabolism, and tissue injury. Excessive oxidative reactions can damage cells, while oxidation also supports normal immune defense and detoxification.

name: oxidation-reduction
clinical_significance: Oxidation-reduction reactions transfer electrons and underpin cellular energy production, antioxidant defenses, and many drug and laboratory reactions. Disturbed redox balance is studied in metabolic, inflammatory, and ischemic disease.

name: oxidative phosphorylation
clinical_significance: A process mainly occurring at the inner mitochondrial membrane in which electron transfer drives a proton gradient that powers ATP synthase to produce ATP. It is linked to, but distinct from, the earlier pathways that generate the electron carriers.

name: oxidative stress
clinical_significance: A harmful imbalance between reactive oxygen-containing molecules and the body’s protective antioxidants. Excessive oxidative stress can injure cell membranes, proteins, and DNA and may contribute to inflammation, aging, or disease, although the term alone does not identify a specific illness.

name: oxide
clinical_significance: Oxides are compounds containing oxygen and another element; some are medicines or materials, while others are corrosive or toxic. Clinical risk depends on the particular oxide and route and amount of exposure.

name: oxidopamine
clinical_significance: Oxidopamine, also called 6-hydroxydopamine, is a neurotoxin used in laboratory models of Parkinson-like nerve-cell injury. It is not a human treatment and illustrates mechanisms of dopaminergic neuron damage.

name: oxidoreductase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that transfers electrons or hydrogen between molecules during a chemical reaction. These enzymes are important in energy production, drug breakdown, and many other cell processes.

name: oxime
clinical_significance: A type of chemical compound. Some oximes, such as pralidoxime, are used as emergency antidotes because they can restore an important nerve enzyme after organophosphate pesticide poisoning.

name: oximetry
clinical_significance: Measurement of oxygen levels in blood or tissue. A pulse oximeter estimates blood oxygen through a skin sensor, while arterial testing measures oxygen more directly; results can be affected by poor circulation or motion.

name: oxonic acid
clinical_significance: Oxonic acid is a uricase inhibitor used in experimental models to raise uric acid and study gout or hyperuricemia. It is not a routine human medicine.

name: oxprenolol
clinical_significance: Oxprenolol is an older nonselective beta blocker used in some countries for hypertension or angina. It can slow heart rate and worsen bronchospasm, and it is not suitable for some conduction or circulatory disorders.

name: oxycodone
clinical_significance: Oxycodone is an opioid analgesic used for moderate-to-severe pain; sedation, constipation, respiratory depression, tolerance, dependence, and overdose risk increase with alcohol or other sedatives.

name: oxycodone hydrochloride
clinical_significance: The hydrochloride salt of oxycodone, an opioid analgesic used for moderate-to-severe pain; it can cause sedation, constipation, dependence, and fatal respiratory depression in overdose.

name: oxygen
clinical_significance: Oxygen is required for cellular energy production, and low blood oxygen can damage vital organs. Supplemental oxygen is prescribed and titrated to measured need because both inadequate and excessive oxygen can be harmful.

name: oxygen consumption
clinical_significance: The amount of oxygen the body uses in a given time. It reflects the body’s energy needs and rises with exercise, fever, or illness; it can be measured during exercise testing to assess heart and lung function.

name: oxygen pulse
clinical_significance: The amount of oxygen used by the body with each heartbeat, estimated during exercise as oxygen uptake divided by heart rate.

name: oxygen therapy
clinical_significance: Giving extra oxygen through a tube, mask, or breathing machine when the blood oxygen level is too low or is expected to fall. The amount is prescribed and monitored because too much oxygen can also be harmful; oxygen must be kept away from flames.

name: oxygen transport
clinical_significance: The movement of oxygen from the lungs to tissues, mainly bound to hemoglobin and partly dissolved in plasma, with delivery affected by blood flow and hemoglobin concentration.

name: oxygenases
clinical_significance: Enzymes that incorporate oxygen from molecular oxygen into a substrate; monooxygenases add one oxygen atom and dioxygenases add both.

name: oxygenator
clinical_significance: A machine that adds oxygen to blood and removes carbon dioxide when the lungs cannot do this adequately. It is used during heart-lung bypass surgery and some forms of extracorporeal life support.

name: oxyhemoglobin
clinical_significance: Oxyhemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying form of hemoglobin in blood. Its level and oxygen saturation help assess oxygen delivery, but interpretation also considers hemoglobin concentration, circulation, and the patient’s clinical state.

name: oxylipins
clinical_significance: Oxylipins are oxygenated fatty-acid derivatives that act as local mediators of inflammation, vascular tone, pain, and other physiologic responses.

name: oxymetazoline
clinical_significance: A topical alpha-adrenergic agonist used as a nasal decongestant or ocular vasoconstrictor; prolonged nasal use can cause rebound congestion.

name: oxymetholone
clinical_significance: Oxymetholone is an anabolic steroid used in selected severe anemias; it can cause liver injury, fluid retention, and hormonal side effects.

name: oxymorphone
clinical_significance: A potent opioid analgesic used for severe pain; it can cause sedation, constipation, dependence, and life-threatening respiratory depression.

name: oxyphil cell
clinical_significance: A cell with many mitochondria, giving it a distinctive granular appearance under a microscope. Oxyphil cells occur in tissues such as the parathyroid and thyroid, where their significance depends on the organ and the surrounding findings.

name: oxyphilic adenoma
clinical_significance: An oxyphilic adenoma is a usually benign glandular tumor composed of cells rich in mitochondria, such as an oncocytic parathyroid or salivary-gland tumor.

name: oxytocic
