clinical_significance: The movement of peptides into, out of, or within cells and tissues through transport proteins, vesicles, or other cellular mechanisms. It helps control peptide signaling, digestion, and removal from the body.

name: peptide yy
clinical_significance: Peptide YY (PYY) is a hormone released mainly by cells in the intestine after eating. It helps reduce appetite and slow movement of food through the digestive tract and is being studied in relation to body weight and metabolism.

name: peptidoglycan
clinical_significance: A strong mesh-like material forming much of the bacterial cell wall. Some antibiotics kill bacteria by preventing them from making or repairing this protective layer.

name: peptococcaceae
clinical_significance: Peptococcaceae are anaerobic bacteria in the normal microbiota that may contribute to abscesses or other polymicrobial infections when barriers are breached. Their significance depends on specimen source and clinical findings.

name: peptococcus
clinical_significance: A genus of anaerobic gram-positive cocci that can contribute to mixed infections, especially in damaged or poorly oxygenated tissue.

name: peptococcus niger
clinical_significance: Peptococcus niger is an anaerobic bacterium that may be part of mixed infections in poorly oxygenated tissue. Isolation from a sterile site can support infection, while findings from nonsterile sites require clinical correlation.

name: peptoniphilus
clinical_significance: A genus of anaerobic gram-positive cocci found on skin and mucosal surfaces that can cause opportunistic infection.

name: peptoniphilus harei
clinical_significance: An anaerobic gram-positive coccus occasionally recovered from wounds, abscesses, or other clinical specimens. An anaerobic Gram-positive bacterium sometimes found in wounds and abscesses, where it may contribute to mixed infections.

name: peptoniphilus indolicus
clinical_significance: An anaerobic gram-positive coccus found in the genital and other microbiota that can occasionally contribute to mixed infection.

name: peptostreptococcus
clinical_significance: A group of anaerobic gram-positive cocci associated with dental, skin, abdominal, pelvic, and other mixed infections.

name: peracetic acid
clinical_significance: A strong oxidizing disinfectant and sterilant used for equipment and surfaces; concentrated exposure irritates or burns skin, eyes, and airways.

name: peracute
clinical_significance: Peracute describes disease or a clinical event that develops extremely rapidly, often over minutes to hours, with little time for adaptation or diagnosis.

name: perception
clinical_significance: The brain’s process of organizing and interpreting sensory information into an experience of objects, events, body sensations, or the environment.

name: perceptual disorder
clinical_significance: A clinically significant disturbance in the way sensory information is interpreted, including altered visual, auditory, tactile, or body perception.

name: perceptual distortion
clinical_significance: An inaccurate or altered interpretation of a real sensory stimulus, which may occur with neurologic disease, psychiatric illness, drugs, migraine, seizures, or sensory impairment.

name: perceptual masking
clinical_significance: Reduction in the ability to detect or identify one sensory stimulus because another stimulus overlaps it in time, space, or processing.

name: percutaneous discectomy
clinical_significance: Percutaneous discectomy removes or decompresses part of a herniated spinal disc through a small needle or incision.

name: perforant pathway
clinical_significance: A group of nerve fibers carrying information from a brain area involved in memory to the hippocampus. It helps the brain form and retrieve memories and can be affected in some dementias and seizure disorders.

name: perforation
clinical_significance: A hole or complete tear through the wall of an organ or tissue. It can release contents into surrounding spaces, cause severe infection or bleeding, and often requires urgent medical treatment.

name: performance
clinical_significance: How effectively a person, organ, treatment, test, or system carries out a defined task. Examples include exercise performance, heart performance, test performance, and response to treatment.

name: performance anxiety
clinical_significance: Performance anxiety can contribute to erectile, orgasmic, or other sexual difficulties and may reinforce a cycle of worry and avoidance. Assessment can identify medical, relationship, medication, and psychological contributors; counseling and treating underlying conditions can help.

name: performed diagnosis
clinical_significance: A performed diagnosis is a diagnosis documented after clinical assessment or testing. Accurate coding and distinction between confirmed, suspected, and ruled-out diagnoses affect care coordination and health records.

name: performed histopathology
clinical_significance: Histopathology performed on a tissue specimen can establish or refine diagnoses such as cancer, infection, or inflammatory disease. Sampling quality and pathologist interpretation affect whether a result is reliable.

name: performed procedure
clinical_significance: A performed procedure is an intervention recorded as completed. Accurate documentation supports continuity, billing, safety review, and monitoring for procedure-related complications.

name: perfusion
clinical_significance: The flow of blood through the small vessels of a tissue or organ. Good perfusion supplies oxygen and nutrients and removes waste; poor perfusion can cause pain, weakness, tissue injury, or organ failure.

name: perfusion culture
clinical_significance: Perfusion culture grows cells or tissue while supplying oxygen and nutrients through flowing medium. It is used in research and some specialized preservation or tissue-engineering settings; sterility and flow control are critical.

name: pergolide
clinical_significance: Pergolide is an ergot-derived dopamine agonist formerly used for Parkinson disease and hyperprolactinemia. It was withdrawn or restricted in many countries because of serious heart-valve fibrosis and other valvular risks.

name: perianal
clinical_significance: Located around the anus; the term describes the skin, glands, pain, inflammation, abscesses, fistulas, and other findings in that region.

name: perianal abscess
clinical_significance: A localized collection of pus near the anus caused by infected anal glands or surrounding tissue, producing severe throbbing pain, swelling, fever, and sometimes a fistula.

name: perianal glands
clinical_significance: Small glands near the anus that contribute secretions to the local tissue; obstruction or infection can contribute to perianal abscesses and fistulas.

name: periarteritis nodosa
clinical_significance: An older name for polyarteritis nodosa, a necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can cause skin, nerve, muscle, kidney, and abdominal ischemic symptoms without typical glomerulonephritis.

name: periarticular
clinical_significance: Periarticular means located around a joint, including nearby tendons, bursae, ligaments, capsule, and soft tissues rather than the joint surface itself.

name: pericardial cavity
clinical_significance: The thin fluid-containing space between the layers of the sac surrounding the heart. A small amount of fluid lets the heart move smoothly; excess fluid or blood can press on the heart and impair its pumping.

name: pericardial effusion
clinical_significance: Abnormal accumulation of fluid in the sac around the heart. Small or slowly developing effusions may cause no symptoms, while rapid or large accumulation can impair heart filling and cause cardiac tamponade; significance depends on the amount, rate of accumulation, and cause.

name: pericardial mesothelioma
clinical_significance: A rare malignant tumor arising from the mesothelial lining around the heart, which can cause effusion, constriction, or impaired cardiac filling.

name: pericardial stripping
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove part or most of the thickened or scarred sac around the heart. It may relieve constrictive pericarditis, in which the stiff sac prevents the heart from filling normally; bleeding, rhythm problems, and other major surgical risks are possible.

name: pericardial wall
clinical_significance: The layered tissue forming the protective sac around the heart. Its inner surfaces produce a small amount of lubricating fluid that lets the heart beat with little friction.

name: pericardiectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove part or most of the sac around the heart when thickening or scarring prevents the heart from filling normally. It is major surgery and may improve constrictive pericarditis but carries bleeding and other serious risks.

name: pericardiocentesis
clinical_significance: A needle or catheter is used to remove fluid or blood from the sac around the heart, usually to relieve dangerous pressure or investigate an effusion. Imaging guidance improves safety, but bleeding, abnormal rhythm, organ injury, or infection can occur.

name: pericardiostomy
clinical_significance: Pericardiostomy creates a surgical drainage opening in the sac around the heart, often for recurrent effusion or infection. It can prevent fluid from compressing the heart but carries surgical and bleeding risks.

name: pericarditis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the sac around the heart. It often causes sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breathing or lying down and improves when sitting up and leaning forward. It may be caused by infections, autoimmune diseases, heart injury, kidney disease, cancer, or some medicines. Severe cases can cause fluid buildup around the heart.

name: pericardium
clinical_significance: A two-layered protective sac surrounding the heart and beginnings of major blood vessels, reducing friction during each heartbeat.

name: pericytes
clinical_significance: Pericytes are contractile support cells wrapped around small blood vessels that help regulate capillary stability, blood flow, repair, and the blood-brain barrier.

name: perifosine
clinical_significance: Perifosine is an investigational Akt-pathway inhibitor studied as an anticancer agent. It has no established routine role in cancer treatment.

name: perillyl alcohol
clinical_significance: Perillyl alcohol is a plant-derived compound investigated for anticancer effects. Evidence remains insufficient for routine treatment, and it may cause gastrointestinal or other adverse effects.

name: perilymph
clinical_significance: Fluid in the bony labyrinth of the inner ear that surrounds the membranous labyrinth and helps transmit sound and balance signals.

name: perimenopausal
clinical_significance: Perimenopausal describes the years of hormonal and menstrual transition before and around menopause, when cycles, bleeding, hot flashes, sleep, and fertility may change.

name: perimenopause
clinical_significance: Perimenopause is the transition before menopause, when ovarian hormone levels fluctuate and periods may become irregular. Hot flashes, sleep changes, and vaginal symptoms may occur; pregnancy remains possible until menopause is established, and unusually heavy or postmenopausal bleeding needs evaluation.

name: perinatal death
clinical_significance: Death of a fetus or newborn during the late pregnancy, birth, or early newborn period; the exact time range varies by definition.

name: perindopril
clinical_significance: Perindopril is an ACE inhibitor used for high blood pressure and cardiovascular risk reduction; it can cause cough, high potassium, or rarely angioedema.

name: perineum
clinical_significance: The area between the external genitalia and the anus. It contains skin, muscles, nerves, and connective tissue and may be affected by injury, infection, childbirth, or surgery.

name: perineural
clinical_significance: Perineural means around a nerve; the term may describe normal connective tissue, inflammation, tumor spread, or imaging findings surrounding a nerve.

name: perineuronal satellitosis
clinical_significance: A microscopic pattern in which supporting brain cells cluster around a nerve cell. It can occur in some brain tumors, inflammation, or reactive changes and has meaning only with the surrounding tissue findings.

name: perinuclear space
clinical_significance: The narrow space between the two membranes surrounding a cell nucleus. It connects with part of the cell’s internal membrane network and helps form the nuclear envelope.

name: periodic acid
clinical_significance: A chemical used to stain tissue samples. In the periodic-acid–Schiff test, it helps highlight sugars, mucus, certain fungi, and supporting membranes so they can be seen under a microscope.

name: periodontal abscess
clinical_significance: A periodontal abscess is a pocket of pus beside a tooth caused by infection in the supporting gum tissues. It can damage bone and spread to the face or neck; dental drainage and treatment of the source are needed, with urgent care for fever or facial swelling.

name: periodontal cyst
clinical_significance: A periodontal cyst is a fluid-filled epithelial-lined lesion near the tooth-supporting tissues, with effects ranging from incidental discovery to local bone destruction.

name: periodontal dressing
clinical_significance: A protective material placed over the gums after selected dental or periodontal procedures. It can protect the surgical area while it heals, reduce irritation, and support comfort; it should be kept clean and reviewed if it becomes loose, painful, foul-smelling, or causes swelling.

name: periodontal pocket
clinical_significance: An abnormally deep space between a tooth and the surrounding gum caused by loss of attachment. Plaque can collect there, leading to bleeding, infection, bone loss, loose teeth, and eventual tooth loss.

name: periodontist
clinical_significance: A periodontist is a dentist specializing in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of gum disease and supporting tissues, including periodontal surgery and implants.

name: periodontitis
clinical_significance: A chronic inflammatory disease caused by dysbiotic dental plaque that destroys the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone supporting the teeth. It can cause bleeding gums, periodontal pockets, tooth mobility, recession, bad breath, and tooth loss; severity and progression vary and require dental evaluation.

name: periodontium
clinical_significance: The tissues that hold and support a tooth, including gums, ligament, root covering, and jawbone. Disease of these tissues can cause bleeding, gum recession, loose teeth, bone loss, and tooth loss.

name: periodontium disease
clinical_significance: Disease of the tissues supporting the teeth, including gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone; periodontitis can cause attachment loss and tooth loss.

name: periorbital edema
clinical_significance: Swelling of the tissues around the eye, caused by allergy, infection, trauma, venous or lymphatic congestion, kidney disease, thyroid eye disease, or other systemic conditions.

name: periorbital infection
clinical_significance: Infection of the tissues around the eye; it can cause swelling and redness and must be distinguished from orbital cellulitis, which threatens vision.

name: periosteum
clinical_significance: A blood-vessel-rich, pain-sensitive tissue layer covering the outer surface of bone, except where joint cartilage covers it. It supplies nutrients, supports repair, and provides attachment for tendons and ligaments.

name: periostitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the periosteum, the pain-sensitive tissue covering the outer surface of bone. It may cause localized bone pain, tenderness, or swelling and can result from repeated stress, infection, injury, or another disease.

name: peripheral blood
clinical_significance: Peripheral blood is blood obtained from a vein or capillary rather than directly from an organ or marrow, used for counts, smears, chemistry, and other testing.

name: peripheral edema
clinical_significance: Peripheral edema is swelling of the arms or legs from fluid accumulation and may reflect venous disease, heart or kidney failure, liver disease, medicines, or lymphatic problems. Sudden one-sided painful swelling or breathlessness may signal a clot or other emergency.

name: peripheral ischemia
clinical_significance: Inadequate arterial blood flow to an arm, leg, digit, or other peripheral tissue, causing pain, pallor, coolness, weak pulses, numbness, ulcers, or tissue loss.

name: peripheral nerve
clinical_significance: A nerve outside the brain and spinal cord that carries motor, sensory, and autonomic signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body.

name: peripheral nervous system
clinical_significance: All nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. It carries messages between the central nervous system and the skin, muscles, organs, and glands, controlling movement, sensation, and automatic functions such as heartbeat and digestion.

name: peripheral neuropathy
clinical_significance: Damage or dysfunction of nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. It may cause burning pain, tingling, numbness, weakness, or problems with sweating and other automatic body functions, often beginning in the feet or hands.

name: periplasm
clinical_significance: The periplasm is the space between the inner and outer membranes of Gram-negative bacteria, containing enzymes, transport proteins, and structural components.

name: perirenal hematoma
clinical_significance: A collection of blood around the kidney, usually caused by trauma, a bleeding lesion, a procedure, or anticoagulation.

name: peristalsis
clinical_significance: Peristalsis is coordinated, wave-like contraction of smooth muscle that propels food, fluid, or other contents through the gastrointestinal tract and some ducts.

name: peritoneal
clinical_significance: Peritoneal means relating to the peritoneum, the thin membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering many abdominal organs.

name: peritoneal cavity
clinical_significance: The narrow space inside the abdominal lining around the abdominal and pelvic organs. A small amount of fluid normally lubricates it; blood, pus, excess fluid, or cancer cells can collect there during disease.

name: peritoneal dialysis
clinical_significance: A treatment for kidney failure that uses the lining of the abdomen to remove waste and extra water. Clean dialysis fluid enters through a permanent tube and is later drained; it can be done at home but may cause infection, fluid imbalance, or catheter problems.

name: peritoneal diseases
clinical_significance: Disorders affecting the thin lining of the abdomen, including infection, inflammation, cancer, bleeding, scar tissue, or abnormal fluid buildup. Symptoms depend on the cause and may include abdominal pain, swelling, fever, or vomiting.

name: peritoneal fluid
clinical_significance: The small amount of slippery fluid normally present inside the abdominal cavity. Excess fluid, blood, pus, or cancer cells can collect there and may cause swelling, pain, infection, or other signs of abdominal disease.

name: peritoneal infection
clinical_significance: Peritoneal infection can cause diffuse abdominal pain, fever, tenderness, and sepsis. Causes include bowel perforation, infected ascites, or contamination during dialysis; suspected peritonitis needs urgent investigation and antimicrobial treatment.

name: peritoneal lavage
clinical_significance: Washing or sampling the abdominal cavity with sterile fluid. It was once used more often to detect internal bleeding or intestinal contents after injury; imaging and other tests now commonly provide this information.

name: peritoneal necrosis
clinical_significance: Death of peritoneal tissue caused by ischemia, severe infection, inflammation, trauma, or tumor, potentially leading to peritonitis, adhesions, sepsis, or organ failure.

name: peritoneal sac
clinical_significance: The space formed by the abdominal lining around the abdominal and pelvic organs. It normally contains only a small amount of lubricating fluid, but blood, pus, excess fluid, or cancer can collect there.

name: peritoneum
clinical_significance: A thin, slippery lining that covers the inside of the abdomen and many abdominal organs. It allows organs to move smoothly; inflammation, infection, bleeding, fluid, or cancer in this lining can cause severe abdominal symptoms.

name: peritoneum neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the lining of the abdominal cavity. It may begin there or spread from cancer in another organ and can cause abdominal pain, swelling, fluid buildup, or bowel blockage.

name: peritonitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of the peritoneum, the lining inside the abdomen. It may result from a hole in the stomach or bowel, appendicitis, abdominal injury, surgery, or infected abdominal fluid. It can cause severe abdominal pain, tenderness, a swollen or hard abdomen, fever, nausea, vomiting, or inability to pass stool or gas. It is a medical emergency because it can cause sepsis or shock.

name: peritonsillar abscess
clinical_significance: A collection of pus beside a tonsil, usually after a throat infection. It can cause severe one-sided throat pain, fever, muffled speech, drooling, difficulty opening the mouth, or trouble breathing and requires urgent treatment and drainage.

name: periventricular leukomalacia
clinical_significance: Injury to the brain’s developing nerve fibers near its fluid-filled spaces, most often in premature infants. It may later affect movement, muscle tone, vision, learning, or development and is associated with cerebral palsy.

name: perivitelline space
clinical_significance: The perivitelline space is the narrow region between an egg’s plasma membrane and surrounding vitelline or zona material, important in fertilization and early development.

name: permease
clinical_significance: A permease is a membrane transport protein that facilitates movement of a specific molecule or ion across a cell membrane.

name: permethrin
clinical_significance: A skin-applied medicine that kills scabies mites and head lice. It is usually applied as directed and washed off later; itching may continue briefly after treatment even when parasites are gone.

name: permissiveness
clinical_significance: Permissiveness describes whether a cell or organism allows a virus, microbe, or biological process to proceed. It is used in infection research and laboratory diagnostics, not as a patient diagnosis.

name: pernicious anemia
clinical_significance: Anemia caused by vitamin B12 deficiency when the immune system damages stomach cells that make a substance needed for B12 absorption. It may cause tiredness, sore tongue, numbness, balance problems, or permanent nerve damage if untreated.

name: peroneal nerve
clinical_significance: The common fibular nerve, a branch of the sciatic nerve that winds around the fibular neck and supplies sensation and muscles responsible for ankle dorsiflexion and eversion.

name: peroxidase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that uses hydrogen peroxide or another peroxide to oxidize a substrate; thyroid peroxidase is essential for thyroid-hormone synthesis.

name: peroxisomal disorder
clinical_significance: An inherited condition in which small cell structures that process certain fats do not form or work properly. It may affect the brain, nerves, liver, eyes, hearing, bones, or development.

name: peroxisome
clinical_significance: A small structure inside a cell that breaks down certain fats and harmful substances. It also helps control hydrogen peroxide and makes substances needed for cell membranes and nerve function.

name: peroxisome proliferation
clinical_significance: An increase in the number or size of peroxisomes, small cell structures that process certain fats and harmful chemicals. It can be triggered by some medicines, chemicals, hormones, or metabolic conditions and may alter cell function.

name: perphenazine
clinical_significance: A first-generation (typical) phenothiazine antipsychotic used for schizophrenia and, in some settings, severe nausea or vomiting. Adverse effects can include sedation, orthostatic hypotension, extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

name: perseveration
clinical_significance: Involuntary repetition of a word, idea, movement, or response after the appropriate stimulus has changed, associated with frontal or basal-ganglia disease, aphasia, delirium, or psychiatric illness.

name: persistent cloaca
clinical_significance: Persistent cloaca is a congenital malformation in which the rectum, vagina, and urinary tract join into one channel, requiring specialist evaluation and reconstructive care.

name: person
clinical_significance: “Person” is a demographic or record category, not a diagnosis. Clinical care should reflect the individual’s symptoms, preferences, capacity, and social context.

name: person name
clinical_significance: A person’s name identifies them in clinical records and is essential for safe matching of tests, medicines, and procedures. Identity checks should use approved identifiers rather than name alone.

name: person with disability
clinical_significance: A person with disability has a long-term physical, sensory, intellectual, or mental-health impairment that may interact with barriers to limit participation; care should be accessible and person-centered.

name: personality
clinical_significance: Personality is the relatively enduring pattern of thoughts, emotions, motivations, and behaviors through which a person experiences and responds to the world.

name: personality change
clinical_significance: Personality change is a new or marked alteration in behavior, emotional responses, judgment, or interpersonal style, which may reflect neurologic disease, psychiatric illness, substances, or medical conditions.

name: personality disorder
clinical_significance: Personality disorders involve enduring patterns that cause distress or impaired relationships and function; individualized psychotherapy and assessment for coexisting conditions can help.

name: personality test
clinical_significance: A psychological assessment using structured questions or stimuli to describe enduring traits, patterns, or possible personality pathology; results require validated instruments and clinical interpretation.

name: persuasive communication
clinical_significance: Persuasive communication can support health education and informed behavior change when it is accurate, respectful, and transparent. It should not replace shared decision-making or pressure patients into choices.

name: pertussis
clinical_significance: Pertussis causes prolonged coughing and can be life-threatening in infants; vaccination, early diagnosis, and prompt treatment or prophylaxis for close contacts reduce spread.

name: pertussis toxin
clinical_significance: A toxin produced by Bordetella pertussis that disrupts cell signaling and contributes to the cough and systemic effects of whooping cough.

name: pertussis vaccine
clinical_significance: Pertussis vaccines reduce whooping-cough illness and severe outcomes, especially in infants. Tdap during every pregnancy transfers protective antibodies to newborns before their first routine doses; routine childhood and booster schedules also matter.

name: pertuzumab
clinical_significance: A monoclonal antibody targeting the HER2 receptor and blocking its dimerization, used with other medicines for selected HER2-positive cancers.

name: pessary
clinical_significance: A device placed inside the vagina to support pelvic organs, treat prolapse, or sometimes prevent leakage of urine.

name: pessimism
clinical_significance: A tendency to expect negative outcomes or interpret situations unfavorably.

name: pestalotiopsis
clinical_significance: Pestalotiopsis is a genus of environmental fungi that can occasionally cause skin, eye, or other opportunistic infections. A laboratory identification should be interpreted with tissue findings and immune status.

name: pesticide
clinical_significance: A substance used to control insects, weeds, fungi, or other pests; exposure can cause poisoning.

name: petechia
clinical_significance: Petechiae can indicate low platelets, infection, vasculitis, or other bleeding disorders; sudden widespread spots with fever or illness require urgent evaluation.

name: petri dish
clinical_significance: A Petri dish is a laboratory container used to culture cells or microorganisms. Proper labeling, sterile technique, and containment help prevent contamination and laboratory exposure.

name: petrolatum
clinical_significance: A semisolid purified mixture of hydrocarbons used on skin as a protective ointment and moisture barrier. It reduces water loss, shields minor irritation, and supports healing of dry, cracked, or chafed skin.

name: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
clinical_significance: An inherited condition causing dark spots on the lips, mouth, fingers, or skin and multiple growths in the digestive tract. These growths can bleed or block the bowel and increase the risk of several cancers.

name: pexophagy
clinical_significance: A cell-cleaning process that removes damaged or unneeded peroxisomes, the small structures that process certain fats and harmful chemicals. The cell breaks them down and reuses some of their materials.

name: peyronie disease
clinical_significance: Scar tissue forming inside the penis, causing a new bend or indentation that may make erections painful or intercourse difficult. Symptoms may stabilize or worsen; treatment ranges from observation and injections to surgery in selected severe cases.

name: Pfeiffer syndrome
clinical_significance: Pfeiffer syndrome causes premature skull-suture fusion and can affect skull shape, midface development, breathing, hearing, and vision. Severity varies by genetic cause; early craniofacial and airway assessment helps plan staged care.

name: P-glycoprotein
clinical_significance: A transport protein in cell membranes that pumps many medicines and other substances out of cells. It affects how medicines are absorbed and removed and can cause interactions when its activity is blocked or increased.

name: pH meter
clinical_significance: An instrument that measures acidity or alkalinity as pH in a solution or specimen; clinical applications include gastric, urinary, laboratory, and environmental measurements.

name: phacoemulsification
clinical_significance: The standard modern microsurgical technique for cataract extraction in which an ultrasonic handpiece vibrating at high frequencies (28--40~kHz) emulsifies (fragments and liquefies) the cataractous crystalline lens nucleus and cortex, which are simultaneously aspirated while balanced salt solution irrigates the anterior chamber to maintain intraocular pressure and cool the tip. Performed through a micro-incision (typically 1.8--2.8~mm) via a continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (CCC), it preserve

name: phagocyte
clinical_significance: An immune cell that surrounds, swallows, and breaks down germs, dead cells, or foreign particles. Phagocytes help prevent infection, remove damaged material, and alert other immune cells to danger.

name: phagocytic vesicle
clinical_significance: A small membrane-bound compartment formed inside a cell after it surrounds and swallows a germ, dead cell, or particle. It later joins a digestive compartment so the material can be broken down.

name: phagocytosis
clinical_significance: The process by which a cell surrounds, takes in, and breaks down a particle or microorganism. Immune cells use it to remove germs, dead cells, and harmful debris from tissues.

name: phagolysosome
clinical_significance: A compartment formed when an immune cell’s swallowed-particle compartment joins a digestive compartment. Enzymes and other chemicals inside it destroy germs and break down cellular debris.

name: phagophores
clinical_significance: Phagophores are early membrane structures that initiate autophagy, a cellular process that recycles damaged components. Autophagy is studied in cancer, infection, and neurodegeneration, but phagophore measurements are not routine clinical tests.

name: phalanx unspecified
clinical_significance: A phalanx is one of the bones of a finger or toe; “unspecified” indicates that the particular digit or proximal, middle, or distal segment is not identified.

name: phantom limb
clinical_significance: The feeling that an amputated body part is still present. Sensations may include position, movement, itching, pressure, or pain and often change over time after amputation.

name: phantom pain
clinical_significance: Pain perceived in a body part that has been amputated, caused by changes in peripheral nerves and central pain-processing pathways.

name: phantosmia
clinical_significance: Phantosmia is smelling an odor that is not present and can follow sinus disease, viral infection, head injury, migraine, seizures, or neurologic disease. Persistent or new symptoms warrant evaluation, especially with other neurologic changes.

name: pharmaceutical adjuvant
clinical_significance: A pharmaceutical adjuvant is an inactive or auxiliary ingredient added to improve a medicine’s stability, absorption, preservation, delivery, or therapeutic effect.

name: pharmaceutical excipient
clinical_significance: A pharmaceutical excipient is a non-active ingredient in a dosage form, such as a filler, binder, coating, solvent, preservative, or disintegrant.

name: pharmaceutical solutions
clinical_significance: Liquid preparations in which one or more active pharmaceutical ingredients are dissolved in a suitable vehicle for administration, with concentration, sterility, stability, and route determining safe use.

name: pharmacist
clinical_significance: A medicine expert who prepares and dispenses drugs, checks safety, and explains correct use and possible side effects.

name: pharmacodynamics
clinical_significance: The study of the biochemical and physiological effects of drugs on the body and their mechanisms of action, describing what the drug does to the body.

name: pharmacogenetics
clinical_significance: Pharmacogenetics studies how inherited genetic variation alters a person's response to medicines, including efficacy, metabolism, and adverse-effect risk, to support individualized prescribing.

name: pharmacogenomic testing
clinical_significance: Testing that examines genetic variants affecting drug metabolism, transport, targets, or adverse reactions to help select or dose certain medicines.

name: pharmacogenomics
clinical_significance: Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic differences affect drug response, including benefit, dose, and adverse-effect risk. Validated testing can guide selected prescriptions, but results must be interpreted for the specific medicine and clinical situation.

name: pharmacokinetics
clinical_significance: The study of what the body does to a medicine, including its absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination. It helps explain drug concentrations over time and supports dose selection.

name: pharmacologic substance
clinical_significance: A pharmacologic substance is a chemical that produces a biological effect by interacting with cells, receptors, enzymes, transporters, or other targets.

name: pharmacology
clinical_significance: The study of medicines and other drugs, including how they work, how the body handles them, their uses, side effects, and interactions. This knowledge helps guide safe choice, dosing, testing, and monitoring of treatment.

name: pharmacotherapy
clinical_significance: Pharmacotherapy uses medicines to prevent or treat disease and relieve symptoms. Safe prescribing considers indication, dose, interactions, allergies, kidney and liver function, monitoring, and the patient’s goals.

name: pharmacovigilance
clinical_significance: Pharmacovigilance detects, assesses, and prevents adverse effects and other medicine-related problems after drugs are used in practice. Reporting suspected reactions helps identify rare or delayed harms and improve medication safety.

name: pharmacy facility
clinical_significance: A pharmacy facility is an authorized location where medicines may be stored, prepared, dispensed, monitored, and supplied under applicable professional and safety standards.

name: pharyngeal carcinoma
clinical_significance: Pharyngeal carcinoma is cancer arising in the throat and may cause persistent sore throat, swallowing difficulty, hoarseness, or a neck mass.

name: pharyngeal disease
clinical_significance: A disorder affecting the throat, including infection, inflammation, blockage, injury, muscle or nerve problems, or a tumor. Symptoms may include sore throat, swallowing difficulty, choking, voice changes, or breathing problems.

name: pharyngeal hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from the pharynx caused by trauma, surgery, infection, vascular lesions, tumor, or severe mucosal disease and potentially threatening the airway.

name: pharyngeal mucositis
clinical_significance: Inflammation and ulceration of the throat lining, commonly caused by radiation, chemotherapy, infection, trauma, or medications and producing pain, difficulty swallowing, and reduced intake.

name: pharyngeal stenosis
clinical_significance: Narrowing of the pharyngeal passage caused by scarring, congenital abnormality, tumor, inflammation, or surgery, which may impair swallowing or breathing.

name: pharyngectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove part or all of the throat, usually to treat cancer. Depending on the extent, reconstruction or a temporary feeding tube may be needed, and treatment can affect swallowing, speech, breathing, or appearance.

name: pharyngitis
clinical_significance: Acute inflammation of the mucous membranes of the pharynx, commonly producing sore throat, odynophagia, pharyngeal erythema, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Caused primarily by respiratory viruses or Group A \textit{Streptococcus}.

name: pharyngolaryngeal pain
clinical_significance: Pain involving the pharynx and larynx, commonly associated with infection, inflammation, irritation, trauma, reflux, or malignancy.

name: pharynx
clinical_significance: The muscular passage behind the nose and mouth that carries air toward the voice box and food toward the esophagus. It helps with breathing, swallowing, and speech.

name: pharynx necrosis
clinical_significance: Death of tissue in the throat caused by severe infection, ischemia, radiation, caustic injury, or tumor, with risk of deep infection, bleeding, airway compromise, and sepsis.

name: pharynx neoplasm
clinical_significance: A pharyngeal neoplasm may be benign or cancerous and can cause persistent sore throat, swallowing difficulty, voice changes, ear pain, or a neck lump. Persistent or progressive symptoms warrant examination and possible imaging or biopsy.

name: phase-contrast microscopy
clinical_significance: A microscope technique that makes transparent cells and other specimens easier to see by converting small differences in light passing through them into visible contrast. It is useful for examining living, unstained cells.

name: phenacetin
clinical_significance: Phenacetin is a former analgesic and fever-reducing drug withdrawn or restricted because long-term use can cause kidney damage and increase cancer risk.

name: phenazopyridine
clinical_significance: Phenazopyridine is a urinary analgesic that temporarily relieves dysuria without treating its cause; it can turn urine orange and prolonged or excessive use may cause haemolysis or methemoglobinaemia.

name: phencyclidine
clinical_significance: A dissociative drug that can cause altered perception, agitation, hallucinations, impaired coordination, or dangerous behavior.

name: phenelzine
clinical_significance: An antidepressant that blocks monoamine oxidase, an enzyme breaking down several brain chemicals. It has important interactions with medicines and tyramine-rich foods and can cause dangerous high blood pressure if precautions are ignored.

name: phenethyl isothiocyanate
clinical_significance: Phenethyl isothiocyanate is a plant-derived compound found in some cruciferous vegetables and studied for effects on carcinogen metabolism. Laboratory findings do not establish that supplements prevent or treat cancer.

name: phenethylamines
clinical_significance: Phenethylamines are a chemical family including neurotransmitters, medicines, and psychoactive substances that can affect adrenergic, dopaminergic, or serotonergic signaling.

name: phenformin
clinical_significance: Phenformin is a former biguanide diabetes medicine withdrawn because it can cause life-threatening lactic acidosis.

name: phenobarbital
clinical_significance: Phenobarbital is a long-acting barbiturate antiseizure medicine that enhances GABA-A receptor inhibition; sedation, respiratory depression, cognitive effects, dependence, and enzyme-inducing drug interactions are important risks.

name: phenocopy
clinical_significance: A phenocopy is a condition resembling an inherited disorder but caused by environmental or other non-genetic factors. Recognizing phenocopies can prevent incorrect genetic counseling and help identify a treatable exposure or acquired disease.

name: phenol
clinical_significance: Phenol is corrosive and can be absorbed through skin or inhaled, causing burns and systemic toxicity that may affect the nervous system, heart, liver, and kidneys. Exposure requires prompt decontamination and poison-control guidance.

name: phenolphthalein
clinical_significance: Phenolphthalein was formerly used as a laxative and remains a laboratory pH indicator. It is no longer used in many medicines because of safety concerns; product exposure should be assessed by amount and route.

name: phenols
clinical_significance: A group of aromatic chemicals that can burn skin and mucous membranes and cause systemic poisoning if absorbed or swallowed.

name: phenothiazine
clinical_significance: Phenothiazine is a chemical class that includes several antipsychotic and antiemetic medicines, with possible sedation, movement, and cardiac adverse effects.

name: phenothiazines
clinical_significance: A class of medicines that includes antipsychotics and antiemetics. They can cause sedation, low blood pressure, movement disorders, heart-rhythm changes, and other adverse effects.

name: phenotype
clinical_significance: The observable features of a person, such as appearance, growth, body functions, and behavior. These features result from the interaction between inherited genetic information and the environment.

name: phenoxodiol
clinical_significance: Phenoxodiol is an investigational anticancer compound studied for effects on tumor-cell survival and chemotherapy resistance. It has no established routine clinical role.

name: phenoxybenzamine
clinical_significance: A long-acting alpha-blocker used mainly before surgery for a catecholamine-secreting tumor such as pheochromocytoma. It can cause dizziness, low blood pressure, rapid heartbeat, and nasal congestion.

name: phenprocoumon
clinical_significance: Phenprocoumon is a long-acting vitamin-K antagonist anticoagulant that reduces clotting-factor production and requires coagulation monitoring.

name: phentermine
clinical_significance: A stimulant medicine that reduces appetite and may be used short term with diet and activity changes for weight management. It can raise heart rate and blood pressure and may cause insomnia, anxiety, dependence, or dangerous interactions with some medicines.

name: phenthoate
clinical_significance: Phenthoate is an organophosphate insecticide that can inhibit acetylcholinesterase and cause cholinergic poisoning after exposure.

name: phentolamine
clinical_significance: Phentolamine is a short-acting alpha-adrenergic blocker used for catecholamine-related hypertension and to limit tissue injury after certain vasoconstrictor leaks.

name: phenylacetate
clinical_significance: A salt or ester of phenylacetic acid used in some metabolic and experimental medical applications; it can bind nitrogen-containing metabolites.

name: phenylalanine
clinical_significance: An essential amino acid incorporated into proteins and converted to tyrosine; impaired metabolism causes phenylketonuria and requires dietary or medical management.

name: phenylbutyrate
clinical_significance: A nitrogen-scavenging medicine converted to phenylacetate, which combines with glutamine and facilitates nitrogen excretion in selected urea-cycle disorders.

name: phenylephrine
clinical_significance: A medicine that narrows blood vessels. It may reduce a blocked nose, raise dangerously low blood pressure in hospital care, or widen the pupil in an eye examination; it can worsen high blood pressure, heart problems, or urinary difficulty in some people.

name: phenylketonuria
clinical_significance: An autosomal recessive metabolic disorder, usually caused by disease-causing variants in the \textit{PAH} gene that reduce phenylalanine hydroxylase activity. Phenylalanine accumulates in the blood and tissues, while tyrosine availability may decrease. Untreated or poorly controlled disease can affect brain development and may be associated with intellectual disability, seizures, eczema, behavioral or psychiatric symptoms, and a musty odor. Severity ranges from classic to milder forms, and the d

name: phenylpropanolamine
clinical_significance: A sympathomimetic decongestant formerly used in some products; it can raise blood pressure and has been restricted because of safety concerns.

name: phenytoin
clinical_significance: A medicine used to prevent or control some seizures. It reduces repeated electrical activity in brain cells; levels in the blood may need monitoring because interactions and side effects can include dizziness, poor coordination, gum overgrowth, skin reactions, or serious toxicity.

name: phenytoin sodium
clinical_significance: The sodium salt of phenytoin, an anticonvulsant used for selected focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures; toxicity can cause nystagmus, ataxia, arrhythmia, or severe skin reactions.

name: pheochromocytoma
clinical_significance: A rare tumor, usually in an adrenal gland, that may release excess adrenaline-like hormones. It can cause episodes of high blood pressure, headache, sweating, a pounding heartbeat, shakiness, or paleness.

name: pheromone
clinical_significance: A pheromone is a chemical signal released by an organism that alters behavior or physiology in another member of the same species.

name: phialemonium atrogriseum
clinical_significance: Phialemonium atrogriseum is an environmental mold that can rarely cause opportunistic infection, including bloodstream or deep-tissue disease. Identification and antifungal susceptibility are important in immunocompromised patients.

name: phialophora
clinical_significance: A genus of darkly pigmented fungi that can cause chromoblastomycosis or other subcutaneous and opportunistic infections.

name: phialophora verrucosa
clinical_significance: A dark-pigmented fungus that commonly causes chromoblastomycosis, a long-lasting infection of skin and tissue beneath it. Infection usually follows implantation through injured skin and produces slowly enlarging warty or raised lesions.

name: philadelphia chromosome
clinical_significance: A rearrangement of genetic material between chromosomes 9 and 22 that creates the BCR::ABL1 gene. It is found in most cases of chronic myeloid leukemia and some acute leukemias and helps guide treatment.

name: phimosis
clinical_significance: Tightness of the foreskin that prevents it from being pulled back over the head of the penis. It can be normal in young children, but pain, repeated infection, scarring, or difficulty passing urine may indicate a problem.

name: phlebitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of a vein causing pain, warmth, redness, or tenderness along its course. It may follow irritation from an intravenous line or occur with a clot in a surface vein; sudden limb swelling or breathlessness may indicate a more serious clot.

name: phlebotomy
clinical_significance: Taking blood from a vein, usually with a needle, for testing, donation, or treatment. The procedure may cause brief pain, bruising, bleeding, fainting, or rarely infection; trained staff use safe collection and labeling practices.

name: phlebovirus
clinical_significance: A genus of segmented RNA viruses, many transmitted by sandflies or mosquitoes; some cause fever, encephalitis, or hemorrhagic disease.

name: phlegm
clinical_significance: Thick mucus brought up by coughing from the lower airways. Its amount and appearance can change with infection, asthma, smoking, chronic lung disease, or other conditions.

name: phobia
clinical_significance: An excessive, persistent fear of a specific object or situation that leads to avoidance or distress.

name: phocomelia
clinical_significance: A rare congenital limb-development defect in which hands or feet are attached close to the trunk because of absent or severely shortened long bones.

name: phonation
clinical_significance: Production of voiced sound when exhaled air makes the vocal folds vibrate in the larynx; disorders cause hoarseness, weak voice, or loss of voice.

name: phonophobia
clinical_significance: Unusual sensitivity to sound or distress caused by ordinary sounds. It often occurs with migraine but may also accompany concussion, infection, anxiety, or other conditions; new severe sound sensitivity with headache or neurological symptoms needs assessment.

name: phorate
clinical_significance: Phorate is a highly toxic organophosphate pesticide whose exposure can produce excessive cholinergic activity and medical emergency.

name: phorbol ester
clinical_significance: Phorbol esters activate protein kinase C and can cause inflammation and promote tumor formation in experimental systems. They are used as laboratory tools and are not therapeutic agents.

name: phorbols
clinical_significance: Phorbols are diterpene compounds related to phorbol esters that can activate cellular protein kinase C signaling.

name: phosgene
clinical_significance: A highly toxic industrial gas that reacts with moist respiratory tissues and can cause delayed pulmonary edema, cough, chest tightness, and respiratory failure after exposure.

name: phosgene oxime
clinical_significance: A highly corrosive chemical warfare agent that causes immediate severe pain, skin and eye injury, airway damage, and tissue necrosis on contact.

name: phosmet
clinical_significance: Phosmet is an organophosphate insecticide that can inhibit acetylcholinesterase and cause cholinergic toxicity after substantial exposure.

name: phosphamidon
clinical_significance: A poisonous organophosphate insecticide. Exposure can cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, diarrhea, small pupils, muscle twitching, breathing difficulty, seizures, or weakness because it disrupts nerve signals; suspected poisoning needs urgent medical help.

name: phosphatidic acid
clinical_significance: A membrane phospholipid and signaling intermediate that serves as a precursor for other glycerolipids and influences membrane curvature, trafficking, and cell growth.

name: phosphatidylcholine
clinical_significance: A major membrane phospholipid and component of pulmonary surfactant, lipoproteins, and bile; it also participates in cell signaling.

name: phosphatidylethanolamines
clinical_significance: Membrane phospholipids containing ethanolamine that help determine membrane structure, fusion, and cell signaling. A group of cell-membrane fats that help maintain membrane shape, join membranes, and support cell signaling.

name: phosphatidylinositol
clinical_significance: A membrane phospholipid that serves as a precursor for signaling molecules and helps anchor proteins to cell membranes.

name: phosphatidylserine
clinical_significance: A membrane phospholipid normally concentrated on the inner cell surface that becomes exposed during apoptosis and helps signal cell removal.

name: phosphatidylserines
clinical_significance: Molecules of phosphatidylserine, a membrane phospholipid involved in apoptosis, coagulation, membrane structure, and cell signaling.

name: phosphine
clinical_significance: A highly toxic gas used in some industrial or pest-control settings that can cause severe lung, heart, liver, kidney, and neurologic injury.

name: phosphocreatine
clinical_significance: Phosphocreatine stores and rapidly transfers high-energy phosphate in muscle and brain, helping regenerate ATP during brief intense activity. Abnormal levels are studied in metabolic and neuromuscular disease.

name: phosphodiesterase inhibitor
clinical_significance: Phosphodiesterase inhibitors raise cyclic nucleotide signaling and are used for conditions such as erectile dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, or selected heart failure, depending on the drug. Hypotension and interactions with nitrates are important class concerns.

name: phosphoenolpyruvate
clinical_significance: Phosphoenolpyruvate is a high-energy intermediate in glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. Its metabolism is relevant to cellular energy production and laboratory research, but it is not a routine clinical measurement.

name: phosphofructokinase
clinical_significance: Phosphofructokinase regulates a key step in glycolysis. Inherited muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency can cause exercise intolerance, cramps, and episodes of muscle breakdown.

name: phosphoglucomutase
clinical_significance: Phosphoglucomutase converts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate in carbohydrate metabolism. Inherited enzyme defects can cause rare glycogen-storage or metabolic disorders.

name: phosphoglycerate kinase
clinical_significance: Phosphoglycerate kinase is an enzyme in glycolysis; inherited deficiency can cause hemolytic anemia, muscle weakness, or neurologic problems. Genetic and biochemical testing may establish the diagnosis.

name: phosphoglycerate mutase
clinical_significance: Phosphoglycerate mutase participates in glycolysis. Rare inherited muscle enzyme deficiency can cause exercise intolerance, cramps, and myoglobinuria after exertion.

name: phospholipase
clinical_significance: Phospholipases break down membrane phospholipids and participate in digestion, inflammation, and cell signaling. Some bacterial and venom phospholipases damage tissues, while human enzymes are studied as disease targets.

name: phospholipid
clinical_significance: A type of lipid with a water-attracting phosphate-containing head and water-repelling fatty-acid tails. Phospholipids form the basic double-layered structure of cell membranes and also help with cell signaling and transport.

name: phospholipid binding
clinical_significance: Phospholipid-binding tests detect antibodies or proteins that attach to membrane phospholipids. Antiphospholipid antibody testing can help evaluate clotting or pregnancy complications but requires clinical criteria and confirmatory results.

name: phospholipid metabolism
clinical_significance: Phospholipid metabolism maintains cell membranes and produces signaling molecules. Inherited or acquired disturbances can affect liver, brain, lung, and lipid function and are relevant to drug and biomarker research.

name: phosphonoacetic acid
clinical_significance: Phosphonoacetic acid inhibits viral DNA polymerase and has been used as a laboratory reagent to study viral replication. It is not a routine human antiviral medicine.

name: phosphoprotein phosphatase
clinical_significance: Phosphoprotein phosphatases remove phosphate groups from proteins and regulate signaling, metabolism, and cell division. Abnormal activity is studied in cancer, diabetes, and other diseases.

name: phosphoproteins
clinical_significance: Phosphoproteins are proteins modified by phosphorylation, a common way cells regulate activity and signaling. Their patterns are studied in cancer and other disease research and can inform selected laboratory assays.

name: phosphoric acid
clinical_significance: Phosphoric acid is used in foods, medicines, and industrial products; concentrated material can cause corrosive burns. In the body, phosphate balance is clinically important for bone, energy, and kidney function.

name: phosphoric ester
clinical_significance: Phosphoric esters include important cellular molecules such as nucleotides, phospholipids, and phosphorylated sugars. Their formation and breakdown regulate energy transfer and cell signaling.

name: phosphorus
clinical_significance: Phosphorus is required for bone, cell membranes, DNA, and energy metabolism. Blood phosphate abnormalities can affect muscles, bones, nerves, and heart function, particularly in kidney disease.

name: phosphorylation
clinical_significance: Protein phosphorylation rapidly switches many enzymes and signaling proteins on or off. Abnormal kinase or phosphatase signaling can drive cancer and other disease and is targeted by several medicines.

name: phosphorylcholine
clinical_significance: Phosphorylcholine is a component of phosphatidylcholine in cell membranes and lipoproteins. Antibodies to phosphorylcholine are studied in inflammation and cardiovascular disease but are not a standard standalone diagnostic test.

name: phosphoserine
clinical_significance: Phosphoserine is serine carrying a phosphate group, commonly created during protein signaling. Its measurement is mainly used in biochemical research and specialized assays.

name: phosphotransferases
clinical_significance: Phosphotransferases transfer phosphate groups between molecules and include enzymes central to metabolism and signaling. Defects or dysregulation can contribute to inherited metabolic disease or cancer.

name: photobacterium
clinical_significance: Photobacterium are marine bacteria; some species can cause wound or foodborne infection after seafood or seawater exposure. Species identification and exposure history help interpret an isolate.

name: photobiology
clinical_significance: Photobiology studies how light affects living organisms and tissues. It informs phototherapy, laser medicine, sun-damage prevention, and treatment risks such as burns or ultraviolet-associated skin cancer.

name: photochemistry
clinical_significance: Photochemistry examines chemical changes triggered by light. In medicine it underlies photodynamic therapy, light-activated drugs, and some diagnostic methods; unintended phototoxic reactions can also occur.

name: photochemotherapy
clinical_significance: Photochemotherapy combines a light-activated treatment with controlled exposure to light, as in PUVA for selected skin diseases. It can help severe conditions but increases photosensitivity and cumulative skin-cancer risk, requiring specialist dosing and surveillance.

name: photolysis
clinical_significance: Photolysis is chemical breakdown caused by light and can alter medicines, biological molecules, or environmental chemicals. It is relevant to drug storage, phototoxicity, and light-based treatment.

name: photometer
clinical_significance: A photometer measures light intensity or transmission and is used in clinical laboratories to quantify analytes in colorimetric assays. Calibration and sample quality affect result accuracy.

name: photometry
clinical_significance: Photometry measures light intensity or absorption and underlies many laboratory tests, including colorimetric measurements of blood, urine, and other analytes.

name: photomicrography
clinical_significance: Photomicrography records images seen through a microscope and is used to document pathology, microbiology, and research findings. Image quality and preparation affect interpretation.

name: photon
clinical_significance: Photons are packets of light energy used in medical imaging, radiation therapy, and laser procedures. Their energy and dose determine tissue effects, including both diagnostic benefit and radiation injury.

name: photopheresis
clinical_significance: A treatment in which some blood cells are removed, mixed with a light-sensitive medicine, exposed to ultraviolet light, and returned to the body. It is used for selected immune, blood, and skin disorders under specialist care.

name: photophobia
clinical_significance: Unusual discomfort or pain caused by light, sometimes leading a person to avoid bright surroundings. It may occur with migraine, corneal injury, eye inflammation, infection, concussion, or meningitis. Severe eye pain, vision loss, fever, stiff neck, or a sudden severe headache needs urgent care.

name: photoprotection
clinical_significance: Photoprotection reduces ultraviolet and visible-light injury through shade, clothing, sunscreen, and selected medicines. It helps prevent sunburn, photoaging, and skin cancer and is especially important with photosensitizing drugs or photosensitive disease.

name: photopsia
clinical_significance: Photopsia is seeing flashes, sparks, or flickering lights without an external source. New flashes, especially with floaters, a curtain-like shadow, or sudden vision loss, can signal retinal tear or detachment and need urgent eye examination.

name: photoreceptor cells
clinical_significance: Photoreceptor cells in the retina detect light and convert it into neural signals. Their dysfunction can cause night blindness, color or central-vision loss, or inherited retinal degeneration.

name: photorefractive keratectomy
clinical_significance: Laser surgery that removes a very thin surface layer of the cornea and reshapes the layer beneath it. It can reduce short-sightedness, long-sightedness, or astigmatism, but recovery is slower than some procedures and pain, haze, infection, or imperfect vision can occur.

name: photorhabdus
clinical_significance: Photorhabdus are bacteria that live symbiotically with nematodes and infect insects. They are studied for insect control and antimicrobial compounds and are not common human pathogens.

name: photorhabdus luminescens
clinical_significance: Photorhabdus luminescens is an insect-pathogenic bacterium carried by nematodes and studied for antimicrobial products. Human infection is rare and may cause wound or soft-tissue disease.

name: photosensitizing agent
clinical_significance: A photosensitizing agent makes tissue more responsive to light and is used in photodynamic therapy or may cause adverse phototoxic reactions. Patients may need to avoid bright light for a period determined by the specific drug.

name: photosynthesis
clinical_significance: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy in plants and some microbes. It supplies much of the oxygen humans breathe and is relevant to nutrition and environmental health.

name: photosystem
clinical_significance: Photosystems are protein-pigment complexes that capture light energy during photosynthesis. They are important in plant biology and research on bioenergy and are not a direct clinical test.

name: phototaxis
clinical_significance: Phototaxis is directed movement toward or away from light in organisms or cells. It is studied in microbiology and cell biology, including how pathogens or cells respond to environmental cues.

name: phototherapy
clinical_significance: Treatment using carefully controlled light for conditions such as newborn jaundice, psoriasis, eczema, or seasonal depression. The wavelength, dose, duration, and eye or skin protection depend on the condition treated.

name: phototoxicity
clinical_significance: Skin injury occurring when a chemical makes skin unusually sensitive to ultraviolet light. It resembles severe sunburn and may cause redness, pain, blistering, or later darkening after medicine or chemical exposure.

name: phototropism
clinical_significance: Phototropism is directional growth in response to light, most often studied in plants. Its medical relevance is indirect through biology, agriculture, and environmental research.

name: phoxim
clinical_significance: Phoxim is an organophosphate insecticide that can inhibit acetylcholinesterase and cause cholinergic poisoning after substantial exposure. Symptoms may include secretions, vomiting, weakness, breathing difficulty, or seizures and require urgent toxicology care.

name: phrenic nerve
clinical_significance: The phrenic nerve drives diaphragm contraction and is essential for breathing. Injury can cause one-sided or bilateral diaphragm weakness, breathlessness, or ventilatory failure.

name: phycobilins
clinical_significance: Phycobilins are light-capturing pigments in algae and cyanobacteria. Related fluorescent pigments are used as labels in laboratory immunology and cell analysis.

name: phycobilisome
clinical_significance: Phycobilisomes are light-harvesting complexes in cyanobacteria and red algae. Their fluorescent components are widely used as labels in flow cytometry and biomedical research.

name: phyllodes tumor
clinical_significance: A rare fibroepithelial tumor that arises from connective tissue in the breast. It may be benign, borderline, or malignant and often grows quickly.

name: phylum fusobacteria
clinical_significance: Fusobacteria are anaerobic bacteria that include organisms from the mouth and gut; some can cause periodontal, abdominal, or bloodstream infection. Species and specimen source guide clinical interpretation.

name: physiatrist
clinical_significance: A doctor who specializes in rehabilitation and in improving movement, function, independence, and quality of life after illness, injury, or disability.

name: physical dependence
clinical_significance: A state in which the body adapts to a substance or medication and develops withdrawal symptoms when it is reduced or stopped.

name: physical examination
clinical_significance: A systematic assessment of the body using inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation, and other examination methods.

name: physical fitness
clinical_significance: Physical fitness supports mobility, cardiometabolic health, balance, and recovery from illness. Assessment helps tailor safe activity, rehabilitation, and exercise prescriptions to a person’s capacity.

name: physical therapy
clinical_significance: Physical therapy, also called physiotherapy, uses movement, exercise, and manual or physical techniques to improve function, reduce pain, and support recovery after illness or injury.

name: physician
clinical_significance: Physicians diagnose and treat illness, prescribe care, and coordinate with other health professionals. Scope and specialty vary, but informed consent, communication, and continuity are central to safe care.

name: physics
clinical_significance: Physics underpins medical technologies such as imaging, radiation therapy, ultrasound, lasers, and medical devices. Understanding energy and measurement helps optimize treatment while limiting tissue exposure.

name: physiologic pseudocyesis
clinical_significance: Physiologic pseudocyesis is pregnancy-like symptoms without an actual pregnancy, sometimes arising from hormonal, neurologic, or psychological factors. Evaluation must first exclude pregnancy and identify medical causes while providing respectful support.

name: physiological
clinical_significance: “Physiological” describes normal body function or a response within expected biologic limits. In a clinical report, the population, age, and context determine what is considered physiologic.

name: physiology
clinical_significance: The study of how healthy body parts, organs, and living organisms normally work together. It examines processes such as breathing, circulation, digestion, movement, hormone action, nerve signaling, and maintaining internal balance.

name: physostigmine
clinical_significance: A reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that may reverse severe central anticholinergic delirium in carefully selected patients after assessment for contraindications and cardiac conduction abnormalities.

name: phytic acid
clinical_significance: Phytic acid is a plant seed compound that binds minerals such as iron, zinc, and calcium and can reduce their absorption from some foods. Its effect depends on diet and food preparation; it is not inherently harmful in a balanced diet.

name: phytochemical
clinical_significance: Phytochemicals are plant-derived compounds studied for effects on health. They are not necessarily nutrients or proven treatments, and concentrated supplements may differ from eating whole foods.

name: phytoestrogen
clinical_significance: Phytoestrogens are plant compounds with weak estrogen-like activity. Their effects vary by compound and dose; patients with hormone-sensitive conditions should discuss concentrated supplements with clinicians.

name: phytohemagglutinin
clinical_significance: Phytohemagglutinin is a lectin in raw or undercooked beans that can cause severe nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Thorough cooking inactivates it; raw kidney beans are a notable exposure source.

name: phytol
clinical_significance: Phytol is a plant-derived diterpene alcohol used in research and some products. Safety depends on formulation and exposure; it is not an established therapeutic agent.

name: phytosterol
clinical_significance: Phytosterols are plant compounds that can modestly reduce intestinal cholesterol absorption when consumed in foods or fortified products. They may affect absorption of fat-soluble nutrients and are not a replacement for indicated lipid-lowering therapy.

name: phytotherapy
clinical_significance: A treatment approach using medicinal plants or plant-derived preparations. Safety and effectiveness vary by product and condition; interactions, contamination, incorrect dosing, and delayed effective care are possible.

name: pia mater
clinical_significance: The thin, delicate inner covering that closely follows the surface of the brain and spinal cord. Together with the other coverings and fluid around the nervous system, it helps protect these organs.

name: pibrozelesin
clinical_significance: Pibrozelesin is an investigational anticancer compound studied for DNA damage and tumor-cell effects. It is not a routine approved treatment.

name: pica
clinical_significance: Repeated eating of things that have no useful nutritional value, such as soil, paper, ice, or hair, when this is not expected for a person's age or culture. It may cause poisoning, infection, blockage, or poor nutrition and can be linked with iron deficiency or mental-health conditions.

name: pichia
clinical_significance: Pichia is a genus of yeasts used in biotechnology and food fermentation; some species can cause opportunistic infection. Species identification is important when recovered from blood or another sterile site.

name: pichia anomala
clinical_significance: Pichia anomala, now often called Wickerhamomyces anomalus, is a yeast used in fermentation and has occasionally caused bloodstream infection in vulnerable patients. A sterile-site isolate should be assessed for true infection.

name: pichia fermentans
clinical_significance: Pichia fermentans is a yeast associated with fermentation and rare opportunistic human infection. Its significance depends on culture source, symptoms, and immune status.

name: pichia kluyveri
clinical_significance: Pichia kluyveri is mainly used in food fermentation and biotechnology and is not a common human pathogen. A clinical isolate should be correlated with evidence of infection.

name: pichia kudriavzevii
clinical_significance: Pichia kudriavzevii, also known as Candida krusei, can cause invasive candidiasis and is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole. Accurate identification is important for selecting antifungal therapy.

name: pichia norvegensis
clinical_significance: Pichia norvegensis is an uncommon yeast that can cause opportunistic infection, particularly in immunocompromised patients. Species identification and antifungal susceptibility may guide treatment.

name: picibanil
clinical_significance: Picibanil (OK-432) is a streptococcal-derived immunostimulant used in some countries for selected cancers or cystic lesions. It can cause fever and inflammation, and indications vary by region.

name: picogram
clinical_significance: A picogram is one trillionth of a gram and is used for very small amounts of hormones, drugs, or laboratory analytes. Units and assay sensitivity matter when interpreting results.

name: picolines
clinical_significance: Picolines are methylated pyridine chemicals used in industry and synthesis. Exposure may irritate skin, eyes, or airways; clinical risk depends on the specific isomer and dose.

name: picometer
clinical_significance: A picometer is one trillionth of a meter, used to describe atomic-scale distances. It is relevant to molecular structures and medical-material research rather than direct bedside measurement.

name: picoplatin
clinical_significance: Picoplatin is an investigational platinum-based chemotherapy drug designed to overcome some forms of platinum resistance. It is not a routine approved treatment.

name: picornaviridae
clinical_significance: Picornaviridae includes enteroviruses, rhinoviruses, and hepatitis A virus, which can cause respiratory, gastrointestinal, neurologic, or liver disease. Transmission and prevention depend on the specific virus.

name: picosecond
clinical_significance: A picosecond is one trillionth of a second and is used to describe ultrafast events in lasers, imaging, and molecular processes. It is relevant to biomedical technology rather than routine clinical timing.

name: picrotoxin
clinical_significance: Picrotoxin is a toxic convulsant that blocks inhibitory GABA signaling and can cause severe seizures. It is primarily a laboratory reagent and has no routine therapeutic role.

name: piebaldism
clinical_significance: A rare condition present from birth in which some areas of skin and hair lack pigment. It usually causes stable, sharply outlined white patches and often a white section of hair at the front; it is commonly inherited through a change in the KIT gene.

name: piedraia
clinical_significance: Piedraia is a genus of fungi that includes the cause of black piedra, a superficial hair-shaft infection. It is generally localized and treated with antifungal care or hair management.

name: piedraia hortae
clinical_significance: Piedraia hortae causes black piedra, a superficial fungal infection that forms hard dark nodules on hair shafts, especially on the scalp. It is not usually invasive but can be persistent or cosmetically troublesome.

name: pierre-robin sequence
clinical_significance: A condition present at birth in which a small lower jaw allows the tongue to fall backward and may block breathing. Many affected infants also have a U-shaped opening in the roof of the mouth and feeding difficulty.

name: Pierson syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited condition causing severe kidney protein loss from birth and unusually small pupils. It can lead to swelling, kidney failure, poor vision, and developmental problems.

name: pigmentation
clinical_significance: Coloration of skin, hair, eyes, or other tissue produced mainly by melanin, carotenoids, blood, or exogenous material; abnormal changes may reflect inflammation, endocrine disease, drugs, or tumors.

name: pigmentation disorder
clinical_significance: A condition causing abnormal increase, decrease, or uneven distribution of pigment in the skin, mucosa, hair, or eye.

name: pill
clinical_significance: A solid medicine designed to be taken by mouth. It may contain one or more active ingredients and may be made to release them immediately or slowly; pills should be taken as directed and not crushed unless the instructions allow it.

name: pilocarpine
clinical_significance: A medicine that activates muscarinic receptors, causing pupil constriction and increased secretions. It may lower eye pressure in glaucoma or relieve dry mouth, but can cause sweating, blurred vision, headache, or breathing problems.

name: pilocytic astrocytoma
clinical_significance: A usually slow-growing brain tumor arising from support cells, most often in children. It commonly affects the cerebellum or visual pathway and may cause headache, vomiting, seizures, balance problems, or vision changes.

name: piloerection
clinical_significance: Elevation of hair shafts producing gooseflesh, caused by contraction of arrector pili muscles under sympathetic stimulation from cold, fear, pain, fever, or certain drugs.

name: pilomatrixoma
clinical_significance: Pilomatrixoma is a usually benign skin tumor derived from hair-matrix cells, presenting as a firm subcutaneous nodule, often on the head or neck.

name: pilonidal fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal tunnel from a pilonidal sinus to the skin, usually in the natal cleft, that can drain pus or recur after abscess formation.

name: pilot project
clinical_significance: A pilot project is a small preliminary implementation used to assess feasibility, acceptability, and logistics before a larger clinical program or study. It can identify problems but is not usually powered to establish treatment effectiveness.

name: pilus
clinical_significance: A tiny hair-like structure on some bacteria. It may help bacteria attach to human cells, move, or transfer genetic material to other bacteria, which can contribute to infection or antibiotic resistance.

name: pimozide
clinical_significance: An antipsychotic medicine used for selected disorders involving severe tics or abnormal thoughts. It can cause movement problems, sleepiness, and dangerous heart-rhythm changes, so dosing and heart monitoring require careful medical supervision.

name: pinch strength
clinical_significance: Pinch strength is the force produced when the thumb presses against one or more fingers and can help assess hand, nerve, muscle, and functional impairment.

name: pindolol
clinical_significance: Pindolol is a beta-blocker used for selected cardiovascular conditions; it can slow the heart rate and worsen asthma in susceptible people.

name: pineal cyst
clinical_significance: A fluid-filled sac in the small gland deep in the brain that helps regulate sleep-related signals. Most are found incidentally and cause no harm, but a large cyst can rarely cause headache, eye problems, or fluid buildup.

name: pineal germinoma
clinical_significance: A pineal germinoma is a malignant germ-cell tumor in the pineal region, often causing headache, eye-movement abnormalities, or hydrocephalus and usually responsive to radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

name: pineal gland
clinical_significance: A small hormone-producing gland deep in the brain that releases melatonin. Melatonin helps coordinate the body's day-night clock and influences sleep timing, seasonal rhythms, and related biological functions.

name: pineoblastoma
clinical_significance: An aggressive cancer in the pineal region of the brain, occurring mainly in children. It may block brain-fluid flow and cause headache, vomiting, sleepiness, or eye-movement problems and requires specialist treatment.

name: pineocytoma
clinical_significance: Pineocytoma is a usually slow-growing tumor of pineal cells that may obstruct cerebrospinal-fluid flow and cause raised intracranial pressure.

name: pinguecula
clinical_significance: A benign yellowish, raised deposit on the conjunctiva near the edge of the cornea. It does not grow onto the cornea and is associated with long-term exposure to ultraviolet light, wind, and dust; it may cause irritation.

name: pinhole meatus
clinical_significance: An unusually tiny external opening, most often the opening of the urethra. It can make urine flow weak or spraying, cause discomfort, or make catheter placement difficult.

name: pinocytosis
