clinical_significance: A process in which a cell takes in small drops of surrounding fluid and dissolved substances. The cell membrane folds inward to form tiny bubbles that carry the material inside for use, transport, or breakdown.

name: pint
clinical_significance: A pint is a unit of volume; its exact amount varies by measurement system, so the local standard must be specified when measuring fluids or medicines.

name: pinta
clinical_significance: A long-lasting skin infection caused by Treponema carateum bacteria. It spreads through close skin contact and produces changing stages of discolored, scaly, or thickened patches, usually without damage to internal organs.

name: pioglitazone
clinical_significance: A medicine for type 2 diabetes that helps muscle and fat cells respond better to insulin, lowering blood sugar. It can cause weight gain and swelling and may worsen heart failure, so it is unsuitable for some people.

name: pipemidic acid
clinical_significance: Pipemidic acid is an older quinolone antibiotic formerly used for urinary infections and is now rarely used because of resistance and safety concerns. Its use depends on local availability and susceptibility.

name: pipendoxifene
clinical_significance: Pipendoxifene is an investigational selective estrogen-receptor modulator studied for hormone-sensitive disease. It is not a routine approved treatment.

name: piperacillin
clinical_significance: Piperacillin is an extended-spectrum penicillin antibiotic often combined with tazobactam to treat serious infections including Pseudomonas; allergy, diarrhoea, cytopenias, electrolyte effects, and renal dosing are important.

name: piperazine
clinical_significance: An older antiparasitic medicine that paralyzes certain intestinal worms, especially roundworms and pinworms. Its use depends on local guidance and the particular infection.

name: piperonyl butoxide
clinical_significance: A pesticide synergist that inhibits insect detoxification enzymes and increases the activity of certain insecticides; it can irritate skin, eyes, or airways.

name: pipette
clinical_significance: A pipette measures or transfers small liquid volumes in laboratories and clinical testing. Calibration, technique, and contamination control affect assay accuracy.

name: pipobroman
clinical_significance: Pipobroman is an alkylating chemotherapy drug used in some countries for selected chronic myeloproliferative disorders. It can cause prolonged bone-marrow suppression and increases concern for secondary cancers, requiring specialist monitoring.

name: pirfenidone
clinical_significance: Pirfenidone is an antifibrotic medicine used to slow decline in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; nausea, photosensitivity, fatigue, and liver-enzyme elevation may occur and require monitoring.

name: pirimicarb
clinical_significance: Pirimicarb is a selective carbamate insecticide targeting aphids; exposure can inhibit acetylcholinesterase and cause cholinergic symptoms.

name: pirinitramide
clinical_significance: Pirinitramide is a synthetic opioid analgesic used in limited settings in some countries. It can cause sedation, respiratory depression, tolerance, and dependence and requires opioid safety precautions.

name: piritrexim
clinical_significance: Piritrexim is an investigational antifolate drug studied for cancer and opportunistic infections. It is not a routine current treatment and remains of research significance.

name: piromidic acid
clinical_significance: An older quinolone-like antibacterial investigated or used for urinary and gastrointestinal infections; current use depends on local availability, susceptibility, and safety guidance.

name: piroxicam
clinical_significance: A long-acting nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug used for pain and inflammation; gastrointestinal bleeding, kidney injury, cardiovascular events, and hypersensitivity are important risks.

name: pisiform bone
clinical_significance: A small pea-shaped carpal bone embedded in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris on the ulnar side of the wrist; fracture or arthritis can cause localized wrist pain.

name: pithomyces
clinical_significance: Pithomyces is an environmental mold that rarely causes opportunistic human infection, usually involving the skin, eye, or respiratory tract. Identification matters when isolated from a sterile site or in an immunocompromised patient.

name: pituicytoma
clinical_significance: A rare, usually slow-growing tumor near the pituitary gland. It may cause headache, vision problems, or hormone disturbances by pressing on nearby structures and is usually assessed with brain imaging and tissue examination.

name: pituitary
clinical_significance: The pituitary is an endocrine gland at the base of the brain that releases hormones controlling growth, thyroid and adrenal function, reproduction, lactation, and water balance.

name: pituitary adenoma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous growth arising from the front part of the pituitary gland. It may release too much of a hormone or press on nearby tissue, causing headache, vision changes, or hormone problems.

name: pituitary apoplexy
clinical_significance: Sudden bleeding or loss of blood supply inside a pituitary growth, causing severe headache, vision changes, vomiting, eye-movement problems, or confusion. It is an emergency because hormone failure can cause life-threatening low blood pressure.

name: pituitary carcinoma
clinical_significance: Pituitary carcinoma is a rare malignant pituitary tumor defined by spread to distant or separate sites, often producing excess hormones.

name: pituitary disease
clinical_significance: A disorder of the pituitary gland that alters hormone secretion or causes mass effects, including adenomas, inflammation, hemorrhage, genetic disease, or hypopituitarism.

name: pituitary dwarfism
clinical_significance: Pituitary dwarfism is severe short stature caused by deficient growth hormone or broader pituitary dysfunction, with evaluation focused on endocrine and genetic causes.

name: pituitary hormone
clinical_significance: A hormone secreted by the anterior or posterior pituitary that regulates growth, thyroid and adrenal function, reproduction, lactation, water balance, or other endocrine organs.

name: pituitary neoplasm
clinical_significance: A pituitary neoplasm is an abnormal growth in or near the pituitary gland and may affect hormones, vision, or nearby brain structures.

name: pityriasis lichenoides
clinical_significance: An uncommon inflammatory skin disorder producing recurrent small scaly papules, with forms ranging from mild chronic lesions to an acute ulceronecrotic eruption.

name: pityriasis rosea
clinical_significance: Pityriasis rosea is a usually self-limited rash that often begins with one larger patch followed by smaller oval lesions on the trunk. It may itch and can resemble other rashes; atypical or prolonged cases may need evaluation for infection or another skin disease.

name: pivampicillin
clinical_significance: An orally absorbed prodrug of ampicillin used for selected bacterial infections; its use is limited in some settings by adverse effects and availability.

name: pixantrone
clinical_significance: Pixantrone is an anthracenedione antineoplastic drug developed for selected aggressive lymphomas, with potential marrow, infection, and cardiac risks.

name: place
clinical_significance: “Place” may refer to a location recorded in clinical or research data. Geography can matter for exposure, access to care, and disease risk, but location alone is not a diagnosis.

name: placebo
clinical_significance: An inactive substance, treatment, or procedure designed to resemble an active treatment. In a clinical trial, it is given to a control group so researchers can compare outcomes and estimate the specific effect of the treatment being studied.

name: placebo control
clinical_significance: A placebo control is an inactive treatment designed to resemble the intervention in a clinical trial, helping separate treatment effects from expectation and natural change.

name: placebo effect
clinical_significance: A real change in symptoms or wellbeing that can occur after a person receives an inactive treatment, partly because of expectations, attention, and the treatment setting. It does not prove that the inactive treatment changed the disease itself.

name: placenta
clinical_significance: The placenta supplies oxygen and nutrients, removes fetal waste, and produces hormones during pregnancy. Placental dysfunction or abnormal attachment can threaten maternal or fetal health and may affect timing and method of delivery.

name: placenta accreta
clinical_significance: Placenta accreta spectrum occurs when placental tissue abnormally attaches to or invades the uterine wall, creating major risk of hemorrhage during attempted delivery or removal.

name: placenta disorder
clinical_significance: A disorder of placental implantation, structure, perfusion, or separation, including previa, accreta spectrum, abruption, infarction, or placental insufficiency.

name: placenta increta
clinical_significance: Placenta increta is a placenta accreta-spectrum disorder in which placental villi invade the uterine muscle. Attempted placental removal can cause catastrophic bleeding; planned multidisciplinary delivery and blood-bank support reduce risk.

name: placenta percreta
clinical_significance: Placenta percreta is the most invasive form of placenta accreta spectrum, with villi growing through the uterine wall and sometimes into nearby organs such as the bladder.

name: placenta previa
clinical_significance: Implantation of the placenta over or near the internal cervical opening, which can cause painless bleeding during the second half of pregnancy.

name: placental hormone
clinical_significance: A hormone produced by placental tissue, such as hCG, progesterone, estrogens, or human placental lactogen, that supports pregnancy, fetal growth, and maternal metabolic adaptation.

name: placental infarction
clinical_significance: A region of placental tissue damaged by inadequate maternal blood flow and coagulation, which may be incidental or, when extensive, associated with fetal growth restriction or pregnancy complications.

name: placental lactogen
clinical_significance: Placental lactogen is a hormone made by the placenta that alters maternal metabolism and supports breast development and fetal nutrient availability during pregnancy.

name: placentation
clinical_significance: The developmental process by which the placenta forms and attaches to the uterus, establishes maternal--fetal circulation, and develops the exchange and endocrine functions needed for pregnancy.

name: plagiocephaly
clinical_significance: Asymmetric flattening of an infant’s skull. The common positional form develops from repeated pressure on one area; rare skull-shape changes from early fusion of a cranial suture are called synostotic plagiocephaly and need medical assessment.

name: plague
clinical_significance: A serious infection caused by Yersinia pestis, transmitted mainly by infected fleas or respiratory droplets in pneumonic disease.

name: planococcaceae
clinical_significance: Planococcaceae is a family of environmental bacteria rarely associated with human infection. A clinical isolate should be interpreted with specimen source, symptoms, and laboratory identification.

name: planococcus bacteria
clinical_significance: Planococcus bacteria are commonly found in soil, water, and other environments and are not usual human pathogens. Their recovery from clinical specimens may represent contamination unless supported by evidence of infection.

name: plant development
clinical_significance: Plant development affects food supply and the availability of medicinal compounds and toxins. It has indirect clinical importance through nutrition, allergen exposure, and plant-derived medicines.

name: plant extract
clinical_significance: Plant extracts contain mixtures of biologically active compounds and may be used in supplements or medicines. Composition and dose can vary; interactions, contamination, allergy, and unproven treatment claims are safety concerns.

name: plant oils
clinical_significance: Plant oils may be used as foods, emollients, or medicinal products, but composition and effects differ widely. Some oils can trigger allergy, irritation, poisoning, or interactions depending on route and concentration.

name: plant part
clinical_significance: Plant parts such as leaves, seeds, roots, and bark may contain nutrients, medicines, allergens, or toxins. Correct identification is important when evaluating ingestion or exposure.

name: plant poisoning
clinical_significance: Illness caused by eating, touching, or inhaling a toxic plant or plant product; effects range from local irritation to organ failure.

name: plant proteins
clinical_significance: Plant proteins provide dietary amino acids and can support nutrition, but some are food allergens. Protein quality and adequacy matter in restrictive diets and clinical nutrition planning.

name: plant tumor
clinical_significance: A plant tumor is an abnormal growth in plant tissue and is not a human cancer. Some plant galls or tumors can affect food safety or agriculture but do not directly represent human neoplasia.

name: plant virus
clinical_significance: Plant viruses infect crops and can affect food supply but generally do not infect humans. Their indirect health relevance is through nutrition, agriculture, and research on viral biology.

name: plantar nerve
clinical_significance: A nerve supplying sensation to the sole of the foot and motor branches to intrinsic foot muscles; compression can cause burning pain, numbness, or altered toe movement.

name: plantar wart
clinical_significance: A wart on the sole of the foot caused by human papillomavirus. Pressure from standing and walking can push it inward and make it painful; small black dots may represent tiny clotted blood vessels.

name: plantaris muscle
clinical_significance: A small posterior-leg muscle with a long tendon that assists weakly with knee flexion and plantar flexion; it can be strained during sudden athletic movement.

name: plasma
clinical_significance: The liquid part of blood carrying cells, proteins, nutrients, hormones, wastes, and other dissolved substances through the body.

name: plasma cell
clinical_significance: An immune cell that develops from a B cell and produces antibodies. Antibodies help recognize and control germs and other foreign substances.

name: plasma cell neoplasm
clinical_significance: A clonal disorder of antibody-producing plasma cells, ranging from localized plasmacytoma to multiple myeloma with marrow, bone, kidney, calcium, or blood abnormalities.

name: plasma kallikrein
clinical_significance: A blood enzyme that helps produce bradykinin, a substance that widens blood vessels and increases leakage from them. It contributes to inflammation and swelling and is involved in some inherited swelling disorders.

name: plasma membrane
clinical_significance: The selectively permeable lipid bilayer surrounding a cell, containing proteins that control transport, signaling, adhesion, recognition, and communication with the extracellular environment.

name: plasma substitutes
clinical_significance: Intravenous fluids intended to expand plasma volume, including crystalloids and colloid solutions; choice depends on the clinical indication and risks.

name: plasmablastic lymphoma
clinical_significance: Plasmablastic lymphoma is an aggressive B-cell lymphoma often associated with immune deficiency, HIV infection, or immunosuppression.

name: plasmacytoma
clinical_significance: A solitary mass of neoplastic plasma cells, which may occur in bone (solitary plasmacytoma of bone) or soft tissue (extramedullary plasmacytoma). It can progress to multiple myeloma.

name: plasmalogen
clinical_significance: A special type of fat found in cell membranes, especially in the brain, nerves, and heart. The body makes it partly in structures called peroxisomes; very low levels occur in some inherited metabolic disorders.

name: plasmapheresis
clinical_significance: A specialized medical procedure that filters and separates the pale yellow liquid portion of blood (the plasma) from blood cells. In therapeutic plasma exchange, whole blood is drawn through an intravenous catheter into a machine that spins or filters it, separating out the patient's plasma---which often carries disease-causing autoantibodies, abnormal proteins, or inflammatory toxins---and discarding it. The patient's red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets are then mixed with replace

name: plasmid
clinical_significance: A plasmid is a small usually circular DNA molecule separate from a bacterial chromosome that can replicate independently and sometimes carries antibiotic-resistance genes.

name: plasmin
clinical_significance: An enzyme that breaks down fibrin, the protein mesh holding a blood clot together. It is formed from plasminogen and helps remove clots after a damaged blood vessel has been repaired.

name: plasminogen
clinical_significance: An inactive blood protein that can be changed into plasmin, an enzyme that breaks down the protein framework of blood clots. The body activates it when a clot needs to be removed.

name: plasminogen activator
clinical_significance: An enzyme or medicine that changes plasminogen into plasmin, which breaks down the protein mesh of blood clots. These medicines can dissolve dangerous clots but may cause serious bleeding.

name: plasminogen inactivators
clinical_significance: Substances or medicines that reduce the conversion of plasminogen into plasmin, thereby slowing breakdown of blood clots. They may be used or studied when limiting bleeding is important.

name: plasmodesma
clinical_significance: Plasmodesmata are channels connecting plant cells and allowing movement of molecules between them. They are relevant to plant biology and crop science rather than human clinical diagnosis.

name: plasmodium
clinical_significance: A group of parasites spread through bites from infected Anopheles mosquitoes and responsible for malaria. The parasites first infect the liver, then red blood cells, causing fever and potentially severe organ complications.

name: plasmodium berghei
clinical_significance: Plasmodium berghei is a malaria parasite of rodents used in research on malaria biology and drug or vaccine development. It is not a usual cause of human malaria.

name: plasmodium falciparum
clinical_significance: Plasmodium falciparum causes the most severe form of human malaria and can progress rapidly to coma, severe anemia, kidney injury, respiratory failure, or death. Fever after travel to an endemic area requires urgent testing and prompt treatment.

name: plasmodium knowlesi
clinical_significance: Plasmodium knowlesi is a zoonotic malaria parasite transmitted from macaques by mosquitoes in Southeast Asia. It can multiply rapidly in humans and cause severe disease, so rapid diagnosis and treatment are important.

name: plasmodium malariae
clinical_significance: Plasmodium malariae causes a human malaria that can persist at low levels for years and occasionally lead to kidney complications. Accurate species identification guides treatment and follow-up.

name: plasmodium ovale
clinical_significance: Plasmodium ovale causes malaria and can relapse months or years later because dormant liver forms reactivate. Treatment must address both blood-stage infection and relapse risk, with safety testing before certain anti-relapse medicines.

name: plasmodium vivax
clinical_significance: A parasite spread by infected Anopheles mosquitoes that causes malaria. It infects red blood cells and can remain dormant in the liver, allowing illness to return months or years after the first infection.

name: plastic
clinical_significance: Plastic materials are used in medical devices, packaging, and prostheses. Biocompatibility, leaching chemicals, degradation, and infection risk depend on the material and intended use.

name: plastic surgeon
clinical_significance: Plastic surgeons repair or reconstruct tissue after injury, cancer, congenital differences, or disease and may also perform elective procedures. Treatment planning considers function, appearance, healing, and procedural risks.

name: plastic surgery
clinical_significance: Plastic surgery can restore function after trauma, cancer, burns, or congenital conditions and can also alter appearance. Risks include infection, bleeding, scarring, anesthesia complications, and the possibility that outcomes differ from expectations.

name: plasticizer
clinical_significance: Plasticizers make materials flexible and may be present in medical tubing, devices, and packaging. Exposure risk depends on the chemical, route, amount, and duration; device standards limit harmful leaching.

name: plastid
clinical_significance: Plastids are plant-cell organelles, including chloroplasts, that support photosynthesis and biosynthesis. They have no direct role in human cells but matter to nutrition and plant-derived medicines.

name: plastocyanin
clinical_significance: Plastocyanin is a copper-containing protein that transfers electrons during photosynthesis. It is primarily relevant to plant biochemistry and research.

name: platelet
clinical_significance: A small piece of a blood cell that helps stop bleeding. Platelets have no nucleus, gather at damaged blood vessels, and stick together to form an early blood clot. They are made in the bone marrow from larger cells called megakaryocytes.

name: platelet activation
clinical_significance: Platelet activation changes platelets so they adhere, release signaling molecules, and support clot formation. Excess activation contributes to arterial thrombosis, while inadequate function increases bleeding risk.

name: platelet aggregation
clinical_significance: Platelet aggregation is necessary to form a clot after vessel injury, but excessive aggregation can cause heart attack or ischemic stroke. Antiplatelet medicines reduce this risk while increasing bleeding risk.

name: platelet count
clinical_significance: A platelet count helps assess bleeding risk, bone-marrow function, infection, and clotting disorders. Very low counts raise bleeding risk, while marked elevation or platelet dysfunction can contribute to thrombosis.

name: platelet transfusion
clinical_significance: Platelet transfusion treats or prevents bleeding in selected patients with low or dysfunctional platelets. Risks include transfusion reactions, infection, alloimmunization, and circulatory overload; thresholds depend on clinical context.

name: platinum
clinical_significance: Platinum is used in chemotherapy drugs such as cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin, which damage tumor DNA. These medicines can also cause kidney injury, hearing loss, neuropathy, nausea, or bone-marrow suppression.

name: platybasia
clinical_significance: An unusually flattened base of the skull. It may cause no symptoms, but in some people it narrows the space around the lower brain or spinal cord and contributes to headache, imbalance, weakness, or other nerve problems.

name: platyhelminthes
clinical_significance: Platyhelminthes are flatworms, including tapeworms and flukes that can cause human parasitic disease. Species and exposure determine diagnosis, organ complications, and treatment.

name: play therapy
clinical_significance: Play therapy uses structured play to help children express feelings, develop coping skills, and address behavioral or emotional problems. It may support treatment but is tailored to the child’s developmental and family context.

name: pleasure
clinical_significance: Pleasure and reward are shaped by brain, body, and social processes and can be affected by depression, medication, trauma, or neurologic disease. Reduced pleasure, or anhedonia, can be an important symptom in mood disorders.

name: pleistophora
clinical_significance: Pleistophora is a genus of microsporidian parasites that can infect fish and rarely cause human disease. Clinical relevance is mainly in immunocompromised patients and specialized infectious-disease diagnosis.

name: pleocytosis
clinical_significance: Pleocytosis is an increased number of white blood cells in cerebrospinal fluid and suggests inflammation or infection of the central nervous system. Causes include meningitis, encephalitis, autoimmune disease, and malignancy; interpretation uses cell type and other CSF findings.

name: plerixafor
clinical_significance: Plerixafor mobilizes hematopoietic stem cells from bone marrow into blood for collection before autologous transplantation, often with a growth factor. It can cause gastrointestinal symptoms, injection reactions, and increased circulating cells and requires specialist administration.

name: plesiomonas
clinical_significance: Plesiomonas is a water-associated bacterium that can cause diarrhea after contaminated water or seafood and rarely causes extraintestinal infection. Exposure history and culture results support diagnosis.

name: plesiomonas shigelloides
clinical_significance: Plesiomonas shigelloides can cause acute watery or bloody diarrhea after exposure to contaminated freshwater or seafood and, rarely, bloodstream infection. Hydration is central; antibiotics are reserved for selected severe or invasive cases.

name: plethysmography
clinical_significance: A test that measures changes in the size of a body part or the amount of blood or air it contains. It can assess circulation in the limbs, lung volume, or changes in blood flow during breathing or exercise.

name: pleura
clinical_significance: A thin, two-layered lining surrounding each lung and covering the inside of the chest wall. A small amount of fluid between its layers allows the lungs to move smoothly during breathing.

name: pleural cavity
clinical_significance: The narrow space between the two slippery layers surrounding each lung. A small amount of fluid normally allows smooth breathing, while extra air, blood, pus, or fluid can restrict lung expansion.

name: pleural disease
clinical_significance: Pleural disease affects the lining around the lungs and includes effusion, infection, inflammation, pneumothorax, and tumors. It can cause pleuritic pain or breathlessness and may restrict lung expansion.

name: pleural empyema
clinical_significance: Pleural empyema is pus in the space around a lung, usually following pneumonia or chest surgery. It can cause fever, chest pain, and breathlessness and usually requires antibiotics plus drainage.

name: pleural fluid
clinical_significance: Pleural fluid normally lubricates the lung surface, but excess fluid can compress the lung and cause breathlessness. Fluid analysis may identify infection, cancer, heart failure, or another cause.

name: pleural infection
clinical_significance: Pleural infection can progress from infected fluid to empyema and sepsis. Prompt antibiotics and drainage are often needed, guided by imaging and fluid findings.

name: pleural neoplasm
clinical_significance: A pleural neoplasm may be primary, such as mesothelioma, or metastatic from another cancer. It can cause persistent chest pain, breathlessness, or recurrent fluid and requires imaging and tissue diagnosis.

name: pleural sac
clinical_significance: The potential space and enclosing pleural membranes around a lung, normally containing a small amount of lubricating fluid.

name: pleural tuberculosis
clinical_significance: Tuberculous infection or inflammation of the pleura, often producing a lymphocyte-rich pleural effusion, chest pain, fever, and breathlessness and requiring microbiologic or tissue evaluation.

name: pleurectomy
clinical_significance: Pleurectomy removes part or all of the pleura to treat selected pleural tumors, recurrent pneumothorax, or other disease. It is major chest surgery with risks of bleeding, infection, prolonged air leak, and impaired breathing.

name: pleurisy
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the thin layers around the lungs, often causing sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breathing or coughing. Causes include viral infection, pneumonia, a blood clot, autoimmune disease, or injury; associated features vary with the underlying cause.

name: pleuritic pain
clinical_significance: Sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing, often caused by inflammation of the pleura or nearby tissues.

name: pleurodesis
clinical_significance: A procedure that makes the two layers around a lung stick together so air or fluid cannot collect repeatedly. It may use a chemical or surgery and can cause pain, fever, infection, or breathing complications.

name: pleuropulmonary blastoma
clinical_significance: A rare aggressive childhood cancer arising in the lung or pleura, usually associated with DICER1-related tumor predisposition.

name: plexiform neurofibroma
clinical_significance: A plexiform neurofibroma is a diffuse nerve-sheath tumor, strongly associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, that can grow along multiple nerve branches and sometimes become malignant.

name: pliability
clinical_significance: Pliability is the ability of a material or tissue to bend, stretch, or deform without breaking; it is relevant to skin, vessels, lungs, and medical devices.

name: plitidepsin
clinical_significance: Plitidepsin is an antineoplastic compound that targets eukaryotic elongation factor 1A and has been studied for selected cancers and viral infections.

name: Ploidies
clinical_significance: Ploidy describes the number of complete chromosome sets in a cell, such as haploid, diploid, or polyploid; abnormal ploidy can characterize tumors or developmental disorders.

name: plozalizumab
clinical_significance: Plozalizumab is an investigational antibody studied for inflammatory and immune-mediated conditions. It is not a routine approved therapy.

name: Plummer-Vinson syndrome
clinical_significance: A condition involving iron-deficiency anemia, difficulty swallowing, and thin webs in the upper swallowing tube. Treating the iron deficiency and stretching the web can improve swallowing and may reduce complications.

name: pluralibacter gergoviae
clinical_significance: A gram-negative environmental bacterium that can contaminate medicines or cosmetics and rarely cause opportunistic infection.

name: pluripotent stem cell
clinical_significance: Pluripotent stem cells can give rise to nearly any body cell type and are studied for modeling disease, drug testing, and regenerative medicine. Transplantation requires control of immune rejection and tumor risk; most uses remain experimental.

name: plutonium
clinical_significance: Plutonium emits radiation and is toxic if inhaled or ingested because particles can remain in the body and irradiate tissues. Suspected exposure requires radiation-safety and emergency-toxicology assessment.

name: pneumocephalus
clinical_significance: Air or another gas inside the skull, usually after a head injury, brain surgery, or a skull fracture near the sinuses. A large or trapped collection can press on the brain and cause headache, vomiting, confusion, or reduced alertness.

name: pneumococcal infection
clinical_significance: Infection caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, ranging from ear or sinus infection to pneumonia, meningitis, or bloodstream infection.

name: pneumococcal vaccine
clinical_significance: Pneumococcal vaccines prevent invasive disease, pneumonia, and some ear infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. Vaccination is especially important for young children, older adults, and people with certain chronic conditions or immune risks.

name: pneumoconiosis
clinical_significance: A group of work-related lung diseases caused by breathing mineral or industrial dust over time. Dust can scar lung tissue and cause cough, breathlessness, reduced oxygen, and progressive breathing disability.

name: pneumocystis
clinical_significance: A genus of fungi that includes Pneumocystis jirovecii, which can cause pneumonia in people with weakened cellular immunity.

name: pneumocystis carinii
clinical_significance: Pneumocystis carinii is the species that infects rats; it was historically used as a name for the organism causing human Pneumocystis pneumonia, now called P. jirovecii. Correct species terminology matters in laboratory and clinical records.

name: pneumocystis infection
clinical_significance: Infection by Pneumocystis jirovecii, most often causing pneumonia with dry cough, fever, and progressive shortness of breath in immunocompromised people.

name: pneumocystis jiroveci
clinical_significance: Pneumocystis jirovecii causes Pneumocystis pneumonia, especially in people with impaired T-cell immunity, including some with HIV, cancer, or transplant immunosuppression. Early diagnosis and treatment are important because hypoxemia and respiratory failure can develop.

name: pneumocystis pneumonia
clinical_significance: Pneumocystis pneumonia is an opportunistic lung infection that typically causes progressive dry cough, fever, and breathlessness in people with weakened cellular immunity. Diagnosis, antimicrobial treatment, and prophylaxis for high-risk patients can be lifesaving.

name: pneumonectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove an entire lung. It is usually performed for selected lung cancers or severe one-sided lung disease when removing only part of the lung is not suitable.

name: pneumonia
clinical_significance: An infection of one or both lungs that inflames the air sacs. The air sacs may fill with fluid or pus, making breathing harder. Pneumonia is commonly caused by bacteria or viruses and less often by fungi or parasites. Symptoms may include cough, fever or chills, chest pain, and shortness of breath.

name: pneumonitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of lung tissue, often caused by a medicine, radiation, an immune reaction, inhaled irritants, or material entering the lungs rather than by infection. It may cause dry cough and breathlessness.

name: pneumopericardium
clinical_significance: Air around the heart, usually after a chest injury, surgery, a medical procedure, or a tear in the esophagus. A large or trapped collection can prevent the heart from filling and pumping properly and requires urgent assessment.

name: pneumoperitoneum
clinical_significance: Air or gas inside the abdominal cavity around the organs. It may be expected after abdominal surgery, but unexpected gas can indicate a torn intestine and requires urgent assessment, especially with pain or illness.

name: pneumothorax
clinical_significance: Air in the space between the lung and chest wall (pleural space), which can partly or completely collapse the lung. It may happen spontaneously, after an injury, or after a medical procedure and can cause sudden chest pain or breathlessness; severe symptoms need emergency care.

name: pneumovirinae
clinical_significance: Pneumovirinae is a subfamily of viruses that includes respiratory pathogens such as respiratory syncytial virus and human metapneumovirus.

name: pneumovirus
clinical_significance: A group or genus of respiratory viruses; human pneumovirus terminology often refers to human metapneumovirus or related paramyxoviruses.

name: pocket erosion
clinical_significance: Loss of tissue at the margin or base of a periodontal or surgical pocket, potentially exposing deeper structures and promoting infection, bleeding, or impaired healing.

name: podiatrist
clinical_significance: A healthcare professional specializing in diseases and injuries of the feet, ankles, and related lower limbs. Care may include examination, wound treatment, medicines, footwear advice, procedures, and prevention of complications.

name: podocyte
clinical_significance: A specialized cell covering the tiny blood vessels that filter blood in the kidney. Its delicate extensions help keep proteins in the bloodstream; damage can cause protein to leak into urine.

name: podofilox
clinical_significance: Podofilox is a topical antimitotic medicine used to treat selected external anogenital warts caused by human papillomavirus; irritation and correct application are important.

name: podophyllin
clinical_significance: Podophyllin is a plant-derived resin with antimitotic activity formerly used topically for warts; it can be severely toxic if absorbed and is generally replaced by safer products.

name: podosome
clinical_significance: A temporary attachment structure on the surface of some cells, including immune cells and bone-removing cells. It helps the cell grip tissue and break down nearby material while moving or carrying out its function.

name: POEMS syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare disorder linked to abnormal plasma cells that affects several body systems. It may cause nerve damage, enlarged organs, hormone problems, skin changes, fluid buildup, eye swelling, and unusual bone changes.

name: poikilocytosis
clinical_significance: The presence of red blood cells with unusually varied shapes on a blood smear. It may occur with anemia, inherited blood disorders, or damage to red blood cells.

name: poikiloderma
clinical_significance: A skin pattern combining mottled pigmentation, visible small vessels, and epidermal thinning, seen in connective-tissue disease, chronic sun damage, inflammation, and some cutaneous lymphomas.

name: point mutation
clinical_significance: A change affecting one DNA building block. Depending on its location, it may have no effect, change the protein made by a gene, stop protein production early, or contribute to an inherited condition or cancer.

name: poisoning
clinical_significance: Harmful effects caused by swallowing, inhaling, injecting, or absorbing a toxic substance. The effects depend on the substance, amount, route, timing, and person’s health; inducing vomiting can worsen some poisonings.

name: pokeweed mitogen
clinical_significance: Pokeweed mitogen is a plant-derived laboratory reagent that stimulates lymphocyte proliferation. It is used in immune-function research and is not a clinical treatment; pokeweed itself can be toxic if ingested.

name: pol gene
clinical_significance: The HIV gene encoding enzymes required for viral replication, including protease, reverse transcriptase, and integrase; antiretroviral drugs target these products.

name: Poland syndrome
clinical_significance: Poland syndrome involves absent or underdeveloped chest-wall muscle on one side and may include hand or breast differences. Severity varies; evaluation addresses function, associated anomalies, and reconstructive options.

name: polarity
clinical_significance: The arrangement or direction of positive and negative electrical, chemical, or biological properties. Cell polarity helps organize tissue structure and directs processes such as movement, division, absorption, and secretion.

name: polarography
clinical_significance: Polarography is an electrochemical analytical method that measures current while voltage changes at an electrode to identify or quantify reducible substances.

name: policy
clinical_significance: A health policy sets rules or priorities that shape care access, safety, and resource use. Its clinical effects depend on how it is implemented and whether it supports evidence-based, equitable care.

name: polidocanol
clinical_significance: Polidocanol is a detergent sclerosant injected to close selected varicose veins or vascular lesions by damaging the vessel lining and promoting fibrosis.

name: poliomyelitis
clinical_significance: Poliomyelitis can cause meningitis or irreversible flaccid paralysis; vaccination prevents disease and suspected cases require urgent public-health investigation.

name: poliosis
clinical_significance: A localized patch of white or depigmented hair caused by reduced melanin in follicles, occurring in vitiligo, alopecia areata, inflammatory disease, genetic syndromes, or after injury.

name: poliovirus
clinical_significance: An enterovirus that causes poliomyelitis. It is transmitted mainly by the fecal-oral route; most infections are asymptomatic, but a small proportion cause meningitis or acute flaccid paralysis by damaging motor neurons in the spinal cord. Diagnosis uses molecular testing, usually reverse-transcription PCR of stool or other appropriate specimens.

name: poliovirus vaccine
clinical_significance: Poliovirus vaccines prevent poliomyelitis and reduce transmission. Inactivated and oral vaccine formulations are used differently across national programs; maintaining high coverage prevents outbreaks and paralysis.

name: pollakisuria
clinical_significance: Pollakisuria is unusually frequent urination, often in small amounts, caused by irritation, infection, stones, bladder disorders, anxiety, or other urinary conditions.

name: pollen
clinical_significance: Tiny plant grains released for reproduction that can trigger allergies, asthma symptoms, or eye inflammation.

name: pollen tube
clinical_significance: A pollen tube grows from a pollen grain to deliver sperm cells to a plant ovule during fertilization. It is relevant to plant reproduction and crop science, not human fertility.

name: pollination
clinical_significance: Pollination transfers pollen between flowers and is essential to plant reproduction and food production. Pollens can also trigger allergic rhinitis, conjunctivitis, or asthma in susceptible people.

name: poly A
clinical_significance: A sequence of adenine nucleotides added to the end of many messenger RNA molecules, helping regulate stability, transport, and translation.

name: poly I-C
clinical_significance: Polyinosinic-polycytidylic acid (poly I:C) is a synthetic double-stranded RNA that stimulates innate antiviral signaling. It is used mainly in immune research and as a vaccine-adjuvant candidate.

name: poly ICLC
clinical_significance: Poly ICLC is a stabilized synthetic double-stranded RNA that activates innate immune pathways and has been studied as a vaccine adjuvant and immunotherapy. It remains investigational and can cause inflammatory or flu-like reactions.

name: polyadenylation
clinical_significance: Addition of a polyadenosine tail to the 3$^{\prime}$ end of many eukaryotic messenger RNAs, promoting stability, nuclear export, and efficient translation.

name: polyamine
clinical_significance: A small positively charged molecule, such as putrescine, spermidine, or spermine, required for cell growth and nucleic-acid function.

name: polyamine catabolism
clinical_significance: The enzyme-controlled breakdown of polyamines, natural substances involved in cell growth and function. This process produces chemicals that can affect cell signals, oxidative stress, inflammation, development, and cancer biology.

name: polyarthritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation involving multiple joints, commonly defined as five or more. It is a clinical pattern rather than a single diagnosis and may result from autoimmune, infectious, crystal-related, or other inflammatory disorders.

name: polybrominated biphenyl
clinical_significance: A group of brominated industrial chemicals that can persist in the environment and cause toxic effects after exposure.

name: polychlorinated biphenyl
clinical_significance: A group of persistent industrial chemicals that can accumulate in body fat and are associated with cancer, endocrine, immune, and neurologic effects.

name: polychromasia
clinical_significance: The presence of unusually bluish, immature red blood cells on a blood smear. It usually means bone marrow is releasing cells quickly, often because of blood loss, red-cell destruction, or treatment response.

name: polycystic ovary syndrome
clinical_significance: A common hormonal and metabolic condition that affects ovulation and the levels or effects of certain hormones. It may cause irregular or absent periods, reduced or absent ovulation, acne, extra facial or body hair, scalp hair thinning, or difficulty becoming pregnant. It may also cause higher levels or effects of androgens, hormones found in everyone but usually present at higher levels in males. Some people have many small follicles in the ovaries, but this finding is not required for the cond

name: polycythemia
clinical_significance: An abnormally high red-cell concentration or total red-cell amount. It may result from a bone-marrow disorder, low oxygen, dehydration, smoking, medicines, or another illness and can increase the risk of blood clots.

name: polycythemia vera
clinical_significance: A long-term bone-marrow cancer that produces too many red blood cells and sometimes too many white cells and platelets. The thicker blood can cause headaches, itching, clots, bleeding, or an enlarged spleen.

name: polydactyly
clinical_significance: A birth condition in which a person has one or more extra fingers or toes. The extra digit may be on the thumb or big-toe side, the little-finger or little-toe side, or between the usual digits. It may occur alone or as part of a genetic syndrome. Treatment depends on its size and function and may involve reconstructive surgery.

name: polydipsia
clinical_significance: Excessive thirst that leads to drinking unusually large amounts of fluid. Common causes include uncontrolled diabetes, water-balance disorders, medicines, and some mental health conditions.

name: polyene
clinical_significance: A molecule containing multiple carbon-carbon double bonds; polyene medicines such as amphotericin B act against fungal cell membranes.

name: polyethylene
clinical_significance: A plastic polymer used in packaging and medical devices; implanted polyethylene components may wear over time and produce foreign-body reactions.

name: polyethylene glycol
clinical_significance: Polyethylene glycol (PEG) is used in laxatives, medicines, and drug formulations. Rare immediate allergy can occur, and some patients develop antibodies that affect PEG-containing therapeutics; medication and formulation history may matter.

name: polygenic inheritance
clinical_significance: Inheritance in which many genes, each with a small effect, together influence a trait or disease risk. Height, skin color, blood pressure, diabetes risk, and heart-disease risk are examples; environment also contributes.

name: polygenic obesity
clinical_significance: Obesity influenced by many small genetic differences together with eating patterns, activity, sleep, medicines, and the surrounding environment.

name: polyglutamate camptothecin
clinical_significance: Polyglutamate camptothecin is an investigational polymer-linked formulation of the anticancer drug camptothecin designed to alter delivery. It is not a routine approved treatment.

name: polygraphy
clinical_significance: Polygraphy is the simultaneous recording of several physiologic signals, such as breathing, heart rate, oxygen level, and movement, often during sleep testing.

name: polyhydramnios
clinical_significance: An unusually large amount of amniotic fluid during pregnancy. It may cause abdominal discomfort, breathlessness, or swelling and can increase the risks of early birth, abnormal fetal position, cord problems, or heavy bleeding after delivery.

name: polyketide synthase
clinical_significance: An enzyme system that builds complex natural products from repeated carbon units, producing many antibiotics, toxins, and other biologically active molecules.

name: polylysine
clinical_significance: Polylysine is a polymer of the amino acid lysine used in research, cell-culture surfaces, and some delivery systems. Medical effects depend on formulation and exposure; it is not a standard therapeutic drug.

name: polymer
clinical_significance: A large molecule made of repeating smaller units called monomers; polymers are widely used in biology, medicines, and medical materials.

name: polymerase chain reaction
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that makes millions of copies of a selected piece of DNA so it can be detected and studied. It is used to identify infections, inherited conditions, cancer-related gene changes, and other genetic material. The test must be chosen and interpreted for the specific question.

name: polymerization
clinical_significance: Chemical joining of many small monomers into a larger polymer, a process important in biomolecules, plastics, dental materials, drug delivery, and laboratory techniques.

name: polymicrogyria
clinical_significance: A brain-development abnormality in which the outer brain surface has too many small, unusually formed folds. It may cause seizures, developmental delay, movement problems, or learning difficulties, depending on the areas involved.

name: polymyalgia rheumatica
clinical_significance: Polymyalgia rheumatica causes new bilateral shoulder and hip-girdle pain and morning stiffness in adults over 50 and often responds rapidly to low-dose glucocorticoids. It is associated with giant-cell arteritis, so new headache, jaw pain, or visual symptoms need urgent evaluation.

name: polymyositis
clinical_significance: An uncommon immune-related disease causing gradual, usually symmetrical weakness in muscles close to the body, especially the shoulders, hips, and thighs. It can make climbing stairs, lifting, or swallowing difficult and may raise muscle-enzyme levels.

name: polymyxin b
clinical_significance: An antibiotic active against selected gram-negative bacteria; kidney and nerve toxicity limit its use to difficult infections.

name: polyneuritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or injury affecting multiple peripheral nerves, causing symmetric pain, numbness, weakness, or autonomic dysfunction; causes include immune disease, infection, toxins, and deficiency.

name: polyneuropathy
clinical_significance: A generalized disorder affecting multiple peripheral nerves, often causing symmetric numbness, tingling, burning pain, weakness, or impaired reflexes in the limbs.

name: polynucleotide
clinical_significance: A chain of linked nucleotides forming DNA, RNA, or a related laboratory molecule. Its sequence stores or carries genetic information and determines how cells make proteins or regulate biological processes.

name: polyoma virus
clinical_significance: A polyomavirus; some human polyomaviruses are widespread and cause serious disease mainly in immunocompromised people.

name: polyomavirus hominis 2
clinical_significance: A human polyomavirus designation associated with a virus found in people; clinically important disease is uncommon and mainly associated with immune suppression.

name: polyp
clinical_significance: Polyps can bleed, obstruct, or cause symptoms, and some types can become cancerous over time. Risk and follow-up depend on the organ, number, size, histology, and family history.

name: polyphenol
clinical_significance: Polyphenols are plant compounds studied for antioxidant and other biological effects. Evidence for concentrated supplements varies, and high-dose products can interact with medicines; they are not substitutes for established treatment.

name: polyploid
clinical_significance: Polyploidy is the presence of extra complete chromosome sets in a cell. It is normal in some tissues but can indicate chromosome abnormality, miscarriage risk, or tumor-cell changes in other contexts.

name: polyposis
clinical_significance: A condition in which many polyps develop, especially in the bowel or other digestive organs. Polyposis may be inherited or acquired, and some types increase the risk of colorectal or other cancers.

name: polypropylene
clinical_significance: A synthetic plastic polymer used in medical supplies, sutures, meshes, and containers; implanted materials may rarely cause infection or foreign-body reactions.

name: polyradiculopathy
clinical_significance: Disease affecting multiple spinal nerve roots, producing pain, weakness, sensory loss, or reflex changes in a distribution determined by the involved roots.

name: polysaccharide
clinical_significance: A carbohydrate made of many linked simple sugar units. Examples include starch, glycogen, cellulose, and some bacterial capsules.

name: polysome
clinical_significance: A group of ribosomes attached to one messenger RNA molecule at the same time. Together they make many copies of the protein instructions, helping cells produce proteins efficiently.

name: polysomnography
clinical_significance: An overnight sleep study that records brain activity, eye movements, muscle activity, heart rhythm, airflow, breathing effort, and blood oxygen. It helps identify sleep-related breathing problems, unusual movements, seizures, and other sleep disorders.

name: polysplenia
clinical_significance: A congenital condition with multiple small spleens and variable abnormalities of organ arrangement, heart, blood vessels, or intestinal rotation.

name: polystyrene
clinical_significance: Polystyrene is used in medical packaging and laboratory supplies. Burning or overheating it can release hazardous fumes; devices and packaging should meet material-safety requirements for their intended use.

name: polytene chromosome
clinical_significance: An enlarged chromosome formed by repeated DNA replication without cell division, displaying visible bands and commonly used to study gene activity in insect tissues.

name: polythiazide
clinical_significance: A thiazide diuretic formerly used to treat high blood pressure and fluid retention by increasing renal salt and water excretion.

name: polyurethane
clinical_significance: A family of synthetic polymers used in medical tubing, implants, dressings, and other products; tissue response depends on formulation and site.

name: polyuria
clinical_significance: Producing unusually large amounts of urine, commonly more than about three liters daily in an adult. Causes include diabetes, excess fluids, medicines, kidney problems, hormone disorders, and some inherited conditions.

name: polyvinyl
clinical_significance: A family of polymers used in plastics and medical materials; properties vary according to attached chemical groups.

name: pomalidomide
clinical_significance: An immunomodulatory medicine used with other treatments for selected multiple myeloma and related blood cancers; it can cause severe birth defects and blood abnormalities.

name: pons
clinical_significance: The middle part of the brainstem, containing pathways and nuclei involved in movement, sensation, breathing, and cranial-nerve function.

name: Pontiac fever
clinical_significance: A mild, self-limited flu-like illness caused by Legionella bacteria without the pneumonia typical of Legionnaires’ disease.

name: popliteal cyst
clinical_significance: A fluid-filled swelling behind the knee, also called a Baker cyst, caused by communication between the joint and a bursa and often associated with arthritis, meniscal injury, or inflammation.

name: population density
clinical_significance: Population density can affect infectious-disease transmission, service demand, and access to care. It is an epidemiologic context measure, not an individual patient diagnosis.

name: population genetics
clinical_significance: The study of how gene frequencies and genetic variation change within and between populations through inheritance, mutation, selection, migration, and genetic drift.

name: population group
clinical_significance: A defined set of people sharing a characteristic such as age, location, exposure, ancestry, occupation, or health condition for epidemiologic or clinical analysis.

name: population health
clinical_significance: Population health focuses on health outcomes and their distribution across groups, including prevention, access, and social conditions. It helps guide public-health interventions and measure inequities.

name: pore
clinical_significance: A pore is a small opening or channel in a surface, membrane, tissue, or material that permits passage of fluid, gas, particles, or cellular contents.

name: porencephaly
clinical_significance: A fluid-filled cavity within the brain caused by abnormal development or damage before or after birth. Effects vary with its size and location and may include seizures, weakness, movement problems, or developmental delay.

name: porfimer sodium
clinical_significance: A photosensitizing medicine used with light therapy to destroy selected abnormal tissues, including some tumors; it causes prolonged light sensitivity.

name: porfiromycin
clinical_significance: Porfiromycin is an antitumor antibiotic related to mitomycin and studied as chemotherapy. It is not a routine contemporary treatment and can cause bone-marrow suppression and other toxicities.

name: porifera
clinical_significance: Porifera are sponges, aquatic animals that produce compounds studied for antimicrobial and anticancer drug discovery. They are not human parasites or pathogens.

name: porin
clinical_significance: A porin is a channel-forming protein in an outer membrane, especially of Gram-negative bacteria, allowing passage of selected small molecules.

name: porokeratosis
clinical_significance: A group of skin conditions that cause one or more ring-shaped, scaly patches with a raised border. Some forms can rarely develop into skin cancer, so changing, bleeding, or persistent lesions need dermatology assessment.

name: poroma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous tumor arising from a sweat gland. It often appears as a flesh-colored, pink, or red lump on the palms, soles, or other skin and may be removed if painful, bleeding, or uncertain in diagnosis.

name: porphyria
clinical_significance: A group of mostly inherited disorders of heme biosynthesis in which reduced activity of a pathway enzyme causes porphyrins or their precursors to accumulate. Acute hepatic porphyrias can cause episodic abdominal, neurologic, or psychiatric symptoms, while cutaneous porphyrias can cause photosensitivity and skin injury; some forms have both patterns. Porphyria cutanea tarda is usually acquired rather than inherited.

name: porphyrin
clinical_significance: A ring-shaped compound involved in heme and other biological molecules; abnormal accumulation occurs in porphyrias.

name: porphyromonas
clinical_significance: A genus of anaerobic gram-negative bacteria found especially in the mouth and associated with periodontal and other infections.

name: porphyromonas bennonis
clinical_significance: Porphyromonas bennonis is an anaerobic oral bacterium rarely isolated from clinical specimens. Its significance depends on whether it is recovered from a normally sterile site or a mixed infection with compatible findings.

name: porphyromonas catoniae
clinical_significance: An anaerobic gram-negative bacterium found in the mouth and occasionally associated with periodontal or mixed infection.

name: porphyromonas endodontalis
clinical_significance: A mouth bacterium that grows without oxygen and is associated with infected tooth pulp and root canals. It may contribute to dental infection, but diagnosis depends on symptoms, examination, imaging, and laboratory findings.

name: porphyromonas levii
clinical_significance: A Porphyromonas species found mainly in animals and rarely associated with human infection. An animal-associated bacterium rarely linked to human infection, usually in wounds or other opportunistic settings.

name: porphyromonas somerae
clinical_significance: A bacterium that grows without oxygen and is occasionally found in human wounds, abscesses, or other samples. When it causes infection, treatment depends on laboratory identification, infection location, and antibiotic susceptibility.

name: portal hypertension
clinical_significance: Abnormally high pressure in the veins carrying blood from the digestive organs to the liver, most often because of cirrhosis. It can enlarge veins in the esophagus or stomach, cause abdominal fluid buildup, enlarge the spleen, or lead to bleeding.

name: portal vein
clinical_significance: The large vein that carries blood from the digestive organs, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder to the liver. A clot or increased pressure in this vein can cause enlarged abdominal veins, bleeding, or fluid buildup.

name: portion of cytosol
clinical_significance: A region of the cell’s aqueous internal fluid outside membrane-bound organelles, containing ions, metabolites, proteins, and enzymes that support cellular reactions.

name: port-wine stain
clinical_significance: A port-wine stain is a congenital capillary malformation that persists and may darken or thicken over time. Facial lesions near the eye or forehead can be associated with glaucoma or Sturge-Weber syndrome and may need specialist assessment.

name: positive
clinical_significance: Positive means that a test, finding, result, or response is present or above a defined threshold; interpretation depends on the test and clinical setting.

name: positive finding
clinical_significance: A positive finding is an observed symptom, examination sign, image, laboratory result, or test response that supports the presence of a specified condition or feature.

name: positron camera
clinical_significance: A positron camera detects paired gamma rays from positron annihilation and is used in positron-emission tomography to map tracer distribution.

name: positron-emission tomography
clinical_significance: An imaging test that uses a small amount of radioactive tracer to show tissue activity, such as glucose use, blood flow, or specific proteins. It is often combined with CT or MRI to locate abnormal areas more precisely.

name: postal service
clinical_significance: Postal services can affect delivery of medicines, specimens, and medical supplies. Temperature control, packaging, identity protection, and timing are important for safe transport.

name: posterior rhinorrhea
clinical_significance: Posterior rhinorrhea is mucus draining from the nose into the throat, commonly causing throat clearing or cough from allergy, infection, irritation, or sinus disease.

name: posterior uveitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation at the back of the eye involving the retina, the layer beneath it, or both. It may cause floaters, blurred or missing vision, or eye pain and can result from infection, immune disease, or another inflammatory condition.

name: postganglionic fiber
clinical_significance: An autonomic nerve fiber extending from a ganglion to its target organ after the synapse, carrying sympathetic or parasympathetic signals to smooth muscle, glands, or the heart.

name: postherpetic neuralgia
clinical_significance: Postherpetic neuralgia is persistent neuropathic pain after shingles, often with burning, touch sensitivity, or itching. It is more common with older age and severe acute rash; treatment can reduce symptoms, and shingles vaccination lowers risk.

name: postmenopause
clinical_significance: The stage of life after menopause, when menstrual periods have permanently stopped because the ovaries no longer release eggs regularly and produce much less estrogen.

name: postnatal care
clinical_significance: Health care for the parent and baby after birth. It includes checking bleeding, blood pressure, wounds, pain, feeding, mood, newborn growth, and warning signs, while providing guidance about recovery, contraception, vaccination, and follow-up.

name: postoperative hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding after surgery that may occur at the operative site or internally and can cause shock, anemia, or the need for urgent intervention.

name: postoperative infection
clinical_significance: An infection developing after surgery, involving the incision, an organ space, implanted material, or the bloodstream.

name: postoperative period
clinical_significance: The postoperative period is the time after an operation when recovery, pain control, wound care, mobility, nutrition, complications, and follow-up are monitored.

name: postpartum
clinical_significance: Relating to the period after childbirth. Recovery includes changes in bleeding, pain, breasts, hormones, sleep, mood, and body function; important complications include heavy bleeding, infection, high blood pressure, blood clots, depression, and psychosis.

name: postpartum depression
clinical_significance: Depression that begins during pregnancy or after childbirth and lasts beyond ordinary short-term mood changes. It may cause persistent sadness, loss of interest, guilt, anxiety, sleep or appetite changes, difficulty bonding, or thoughts of self-harm and needs treatment.

name: post-partum hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Postpartum hemorrhage is severe bleeding after childbirth and can rapidly cause shock, organ injury, or death. It requires immediate obstetric treatment, blood-loss assessment, and often medicines, procedures, or transfusion.

name: postpartum thyroiditis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the thyroid during the first year after childbirth, caused by an immune reaction. It may first cause anxiety, sweating, and a fast heartbeat, followed by tiredness, cold intolerance, or low thyroid function; recovery varies.

name: postprandial period
clinical_significance: The postprandial period is the interval after eating when digestion and nutrient absorption occur and glucose, insulin, and other metabolic responses change.

name: postsynaptic membrane
clinical_significance: The receiving surface of a nerve or muscle cell where a neighboring nerve releases a chemical signal. Receptors in this surface detect the signal and help start or change an electrical response.

name: posttraumatic stress disorder
clinical_significance: Posttraumatic stress disorder can develop after trauma and cause intrusive memories, avoidance, negative mood or beliefs, and heightened arousal that impair daily life. Evidence-based trauma-focused psychotherapy and medicines can help; self-harm risk requires urgent support.

name: potassium
clinical_significance: The chemical symbol for potassium, a major intracellular electrolyte needed for nerve signaling, muscle contraction, and cardiac electrical activity.

name: potassium acetate
clinical_significance: A potassium salt used to replace potassium or provide acetate in selected medical and laboratory applications; dosing requires monitoring of kidney function and serum potassium.

name: potassium channel
clinical_significance: A membrane protein that allows potassium ions to cross cells and helps control electrical excitability, heart rhythm, and hormone release.

name: potassium chloride
clinical_significance: A salt used to prevent or treat low blood potassium. It may be taken by mouth or given into a vein; too much can cause dangerous heart-rhythm problems, especially when kidney function is reduced.

name: potassium citrate
clinical_significance: A medicine that makes urine less acidic and increases urinary citrate, helping prevent some kidney stones. It can dangerously raise blood potassium in people with kidney disease or those taking certain medicines.

name: potassium cyanide
clinical_significance: A highly poisonous chemical that prevents cells from using oxygen. Swallowing or inhaling it can rapidly cause headache, confusion, seizures, collapse, heart failure, and death and requires emergency treatment.

name: potassium deficiency
clinical_significance: An abnormally low blood potassium level, which can cause weakness, cramps, constipation, abnormal heart rhythms, or paralysis.

name: potassium dichromate
clinical_significance: A toxic, corrosive chemical that can burn the skin, eyes, mouth, and digestive tract. Swallowing or inhaling it may damage the kidneys, liver, blood, or lungs and requires urgent poison-control or emergency care.

name: potassium iodide
clinical_significance: Potassium iodide supplies iodide and is used in selected thyroid conditions, radiation emergencies, and some expectorant preparations; excess can disturb thyroid function.

name: potassium ion
clinical_significance: The positively charged form of potassium, the principal intracellular cation that helps establish resting membrane potential, nerve transmission, muscle contraction, and cardiac rhythm.

name: potential
clinical_significance: Potential describes a capacity, possibility, or stored energy that may become clinically relevant depending on circumstances and additional findings.

name: potentiometry
clinical_significance: Potentiometry measures voltage differences to determine ion concentration or chemical activity. Clinical applications include blood-gas, electrolyte, and pH testing, where calibration and sample handling affect accuracy.

name: poultice
clinical_significance: A poultice is a moist topical preparation applied to skin. It may irritate or burn tissue, introduce infection, or delay effective treatment; its benefit depends on the ingredients and condition.

name: pound
clinical_significance: A unit measuring weight or force, with meaning determined by context. In healthcare, pounds may describe body weight, pressure, equipment loads, or medicine instructions and should be distinguished from metric units.

name: povidone
clinical_significance: Povidone is a water-soluble polymer used in medicines, eye products, and other preparations; it is also part of povidone-iodine antiseptic.

name: povidone-iodine
clinical_significance: Povidone-iodine is an iodine-containing antiseptic used on skin or tissue before selected procedures; it can irritate skin and affect the thyroid with extensive use.

name: powder diffraction
clinical_significance: An analytical method that identifies crystalline substances by measuring how an X-ray or other beam is diffracted by powdered material.

name: poxviridae
clinical_significance: A family of large DNA viruses that includes orthopoxviruses, molluscipoxvirus, and parapoxviruses; some cause significant human disease.

name: poxviridae infection
clinical_significance: An infection caused by a poxvirus, ranging from localized skin lesions to severe systemic disease depending on the virus and host.

name: ppar alpha
clinical_significance: A protein inside cells that helps control how the body uses fats. Fibrate medicines activate it to lower some blood fats, especially triglycerides.

name: ppar delta
clinical_significance: A protein inside cells that helps regulate fat use, energy balance, inflammation, and the development of some tissues. It is mainly studied in laboratory and drug research.

name: pracinostat
clinical_significance: Pracinostat is an investigational histone-deacetylase inhibitor studied for myeloid cancers and other tumors. It is not a routine approved treatment and can cause blood-count and gastrointestinal toxicities in trials.

name: practitioner
clinical_significance: Healthcare practitioners assess, advise, or treat patients within their training and legal scope. Credentials and scope matter when selecting care and ensuring accountability.

name: Prader-Willi syndrome
clinical_significance: A genetic disorder that often causes weak muscle tone and feeding difficulty in infancy, followed later by unusually strong hunger, obesity, short stature, learning difficulties, hormone problems, and behavioral changes.

name: pragmatic trial
clinical_significance: A pragmatic trial evaluates an intervention under usual real-world care conditions to estimate how well it works in routine practice.

name: pralatrexate
clinical_significance: A folate-blocking chemotherapy medicine used for some relapsed or treatment-resistant peripheral T-cell lymphomas. It can cause mouth sores, low blood counts, infection, fatigue, nausea, and other serious treatment-related effects.

name: pravastatin
clinical_significance: Pravastatin lowers LDL cholesterol and reduces cardiovascular risk in appropriate patients. Muscle symptoms, liver-enzyme changes, and rare severe muscle injury are important to monitor; pregnancy and interacting medicines may affect treatment decisions.

name: pravastatin sodium
clinical_significance: A statin medicine that lowers harmful LDL cholesterol by reducing cholesterol production in the liver. It helps reduce heart attack and stroke risk alongside diet, exercise, and other risk-factor treatment.

name: praziquantel
clinical_significance: A medicine used to treat several infections caused by parasitic worms, including schistosomiasis, tapeworms, and flukes. It damages the worms so the body can remove them; dizziness, sleepiness, nausea, or abdominal discomfort may occur.

name: prazosin
clinical_significance: Prazosin is an alpha-1 blocker used for hypertension and urinary symptoms from enlarged prostate and sometimes for trauma-related nightmares. It can cause dizziness or fainting from low blood pressure, especially after the first dose or dose increases.

name: prealbumin
clinical_significance: Another name for transthyretin, a protein made mainly by the liver that carries thyroid hormone and vitamin A in the blood. Its blood level changes with inflammation, illness, kidney disease, and nutrition, so it is not a nutrition measure by itself.

name: precancerous condition
clinical_significance: Precancerous changes are not cancer, but some can progress if untreated. Risk and management depend on the organ, grade, size, and test findings; appropriate surveillance or removal can prevent invasive cancer.

name: precancerous polyp
clinical_significance: A precancerous polyp is a growth with cellular changes that can become cancerous over time if not removed or monitored appropriately.

name: precipitating factor
clinical_significance: A precipitating factor is an event or exposure that triggers the onset or worsening of symptoms or disease in a susceptible person.

name: precision medicine
clinical_significance: An approach that matches prevention or treatment to biological differences between people, often using genetic, molecular, or clinical information. It is related to but not identical to personalized medicine.

name: preclinical study
clinical_significance: Preclinical studies assess a potential medicine or device in laboratory systems and animals before human trials. They help identify biological effects and toxicity but do not establish safety or effectiveness in people.

name: precocious puberty
clinical_significance: Development of puberty-related body changes earlier than expected. It may result from early brain signals, hormone-producing disorders, medicines, or other conditions and requires evaluation to protect growth and emotional wellbeing.

name: preconception care
clinical_significance: Health care before pregnancy to improve the chance of a healthy pregnancy. It reviews medical conditions, medicines, vaccinations, genetic risks, nutrition, folic acid, substance exposure, and lifestyle, and helps plan changes before conception.

name: precursor
clinical_significance: A substance that the body can change into another substance with a useful biological effect. For example, some vitamins, hormones, and medicines begin as precursors and are changed by enzymes in particular tissues.

name: prediabetes syndrome
clinical_significance: Blood glucose levels above normal but below the diabetes threshold, associated with increased future risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

name: prednimustine
clinical_significance: Prednimustine is a former antineoplastic drug combining a corticosteroid-related group with an alkylating component and causing immunosuppression and marrow toxicity.

name: prednisolone
clinical_significance: Prednisolone is a corticosteroid used to reduce inflammation and immune activity; prolonged or high-dose use can cause infection, bone loss, and other effects.

name: prednisone
clinical_significance: Prednisone is a corticosteroid used for inflammatory, allergic, and autoimmune conditions; it should often be tapered after prolonged use.

name: pre-eclampsia
clinical_significance: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy complication marked by new hypertension after 20 weeks, often with proteinuria or organ involvement. It can progress to seizures, stroke, placental problems, or maternal and fetal harm, so prompt obstetric monitoring and treatment are essential.

name: preexcitation syndrome
clinical_significance: A heart-rhythm condition in which an extra electrical pathway activates the lower heart chambers too early. It can cause episodes of a very fast heartbeat, dizziness, or fainting and may require specialist assessment.

name: prefix
clinical_significance: A prefix is a word element placed before a term and can change its clinical meaning, such as hypo- or hyper-. Accurate prefixes matter because they may distinguish opposite conditions or medication effects.

name: prefrontal cortex
clinical_significance: The prefrontal cortex is the front part of the frontal lobe involved in planning, judgment, working memory, impulse control, and social behavior.

name: pregabalin
clinical_significance: Pregabalin is used for certain nerve pain and seizures and may cause dizziness, sleepiness, swelling, or dependence.

name: preganglionic fiber
clinical_significance: A nerve fiber that carries automatic body signals from the brain or spinal cord to a relay station before they reach an organ. These signals help control the heart, blood vessels, glands, digestion, and bladder.

name: pregnancy
clinical_significance: The period during which an embryo or fetus develops in the uterus, usually lasting about 40 weeks from the first day of the last menstrual period until birth.

name: pregnancy complication
clinical_significance: A maternal, fetal, placental, or labor-related problem that disrupts an otherwise expected pregnancy, such as preeclampsia, hemorrhage, diabetes, growth restriction, or preterm labor.

name: pregnancy outcome
clinical_significance: Pregnancy outcome describes what happens to a pregnancy, such as live birth, miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, or other maternal or fetal result.

name: pregnancy status
clinical_significance: Pregnancy status indicates whether a person is pregnant, not pregnant, or of unknown status and can affect medication, imaging, and treatment decisions.

name: pregnancy test
clinical_significance: A urine or blood test that detects human chorionic gonadotropin, a hormone made soon after an embryo attaches to the uterus. Testing too early can be falsely negative; an unexpected result may need repeat testing or medical assessment.

name: pregnancy trimester
clinical_significance: One of three approximate stages of pregnancy: first through 13 weeks, second from 14 through 27 weeks, and third from 28 weeks until birth. The stages help organize fetal development, screening, and care.

name: pregnane
clinical_significance: Pregnane is a 21-carbon steroid hydrocarbon that forms the structural backbone of progesterone and several corticosteroid and progestin compounds.

name: pregnanolone
clinical_significance: Pregnanolone is a neuroactive steroid metabolite that can modulate GABA-A receptors and influence neuronal excitability, mood, and sedation.

name: pregnenolone
clinical_significance: Pregnenolone is a steroid hormone precursor made from cholesterol that can be converted into progesterone, corticosteroids, and sex hormones.

name: prehypertension
clinical_significance: “Prehypertension” is an older term for blood pressure above optimal but below the former hypertension threshold. Current guidance uses blood-pressure categories and cardiovascular risk to guide confirmation, lifestyle changes, and treatment.

name: premalignant
clinical_significance: Describing cells or tissue changes that have a higher chance of becoming cancer but have not grown into nearby tissues. Not every premalignant change becomes cancer; follow-up or removal depends on its type, location, size, and risk.

name: premature adrenarche
