clinical_significance: A pattern in which a person feels a strong emotional or mental need for a substance or behavior, often with craving, preoccupation, or distress when it is unavailable.

name: psychological transfer
clinical_significance: The process in which feelings, expectations, or relationship patterns from earlier experiences become directed toward someone in the present, especially a therapist. Recognizing this pattern can help understand distress and relationships during therapy.

name: psychology
clinical_significance: The scientific study of behavior, emotion, learning, and mental processes. Psychological care may include assessment, counseling, and behavioral therapies.

name: psychometrics
clinical_significance: The design and use of tests that measure mental abilities, feelings, behavior, or personality. It also examines whether a test gives consistent results and truly measures the quality it claims to measure.

name: psychomotor agitation
clinical_significance: Restless, excessive, or purposeless movement associated with inner tension, anxiety, mania, delirium, depression, substance effects, or medication reactions.

name: psychomotor disorder
clinical_significance: A condition affecting the speed, starting, coordination, or expression of movement and mental activity. A person may move unusually slowly or quickly, seem restless, or have difficulty organizing purposeful actions.

name: psychomotor performance
clinical_significance: The ability to coordinate mental processing with physical movement, assessed through tasks involving speed, precision, reaction time, balance, or sequencing.

name: psychoneuroimmunology
clinical_significance: The study of how thoughts, emotions, the brain, hormones, and the immune system influence one another in health and illness. It examines links involving stress, inflammation, infection, and recovery.

name: psychopathology
clinical_significance: The study and description of abnormal mental processes, symptoms, behaviors, and mechanisms underlying psychiatric disorders. The study or description of abnormal mental states and behavior.

name: psychopharmacology
clinical_significance: The study of how medicines affect mood, behavior, thinking, sleep, and other mental functions in people.

name: psychophysics
clinical_significance: The study of how physical stimuli, such as light, sound, pressure, or heat, are experienced by a person. It measures detection thresholds, ability to distinguish stimuli, and perceived strength.

name: psychophysiology
clinical_significance: The study of links between psychological processes and measurable bodily functions such as heart rate, skin conductance, muscle activity, and brain signals.

name: psychosexual development
clinical_significance: Development of sexual identity, interest, relationships, and behavior across the lifespan as influenced by biology, cognition, attachment, culture, and experience.

name: psychosocial rehabilitation
clinical_significance: Support that helps a person with mental illness build skills, relationships, confidence, and independence. It may include daily-living training, education, work support, peer support, therapy, and help taking part in family and community life.

name: psychosurgery
clinical_significance: Surgery intended to alter brain circuits for severe, treatment-resistant psychiatric illness; it is rarely used and highly specialized.

name: psychotherapy
clinical_significance: Structured treatment using therapeutic communication and psychological techniques to reduce distress, change unhelpful patterns, and improve coping or relationships. Common approaches include cognitive behavioral and interpersonal therapies.

name: Psychotic Disorder
clinical_significance: Psychotic disorders involve impaired reality testing, such as delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized thought. Causes include primary psychiatric illness, substances, medicines, and medical or neurologic disease, so a new episode needs assessment.

name: psychotropic drug
clinical_significance: Psychotropic drugs affect mood, thought, perception, or behavior and include antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, and sedatives. Benefit, adverse effects, interactions, and withdrawal risks depend on the specific medicine.

name: psychrobacter
clinical_significance: Psychrobacter are cold-adapted bacteria found in marine and other environments; some species can occasionally cause human infection. A clinical isolate is interpreted with the specimen and evidence of disease.

name: psychrobacter immobilis
clinical_significance: Psychrobacter immobilis is an uncommon environmental bacterium reported in rare bloodstream, wound, or other opportunistic infections. Confirmatory identification and susceptibility testing help guide treatment.

name: pteridine
clinical_significance: A nitrogen-containing chemical structure found in folate vitamins, natural pigments, and other active body compounds. Pteridine-containing molecules participate in cell growth, chemical reactions, color production, and inherited metabolic disorders.

name: pterygium
clinical_significance: A raised, often triangular growth of tissue with blood vessels that begins on the conjunctiva and extends onto the cornea. Long-term exposure to ultraviolet light, wind, or dust may contribute; it can cause irritation and redness, and growth over the cornea may blur vision or induce astigmatism.

name: ptosis
clinical_significance: Drooping of an eyelid or another body structure. Eyelid ptosis may result from muscle, nerve, tendon, aging, injury, or a neurologic disorder.

name: pubertal failure
clinical_significance: Puberty that does not begin or stops progressing as expected. Causes may involve the brain’s hormone centers, pituitary gland, testes or ovaries, chromosomes, chronic illness, inadequate nutrition, excessive exercise, or other factors.

name: puberty
clinical_significance: The stage when hormone changes cause the body to mature sexually and become capable of reproduction. It includes growth, development of breasts or testes and genitals, body hair, voice changes, and menstrual periods or sperm production.

name: public assistance
clinical_significance: Government or community support providing eligible people with food, housing, income, healthcare, disability, or other essential services.

name: public policy
clinical_significance: Public policy can shape vaccination, screening, access to care, environmental health, and disease prevention. Its health effects are assessed across populations and should account for equity and unintended consequences.

name: publication
clinical_significance: Publication of clinical or research findings supports evidence sharing and scrutiny. Publication alone does not establish that a result is reliable; study design, peer review, conflicts, and replication matter.

name: puerperal disorder
clinical_significance: A physical or mental health disorder occurring during the postpartum period, including infection, bleeding, hypertension, depression, or psychosis.

name: puerperal infection
clinical_significance: An infection after childbirth, commonly involving the uterus, surgical wound, urinary tract, breast, or bloodstream, often causing fever, pain, or foul discharge.

name: pulmonary artery
clinical_significance: The large blood vessel carrying oxygen-poor blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs. There, blood releases carbon dioxide, receives oxygen, and returns through pulmonary veins.

name: pulmonary blastoma
clinical_significance: A rare malignant lung tumor composed of primitive epithelial and mesenchymal tissue, usually treated with specialist oncology care.

name: pulmonary circulation
clinical_significance: The blood-flow circuit from the right ventricle through the pulmonary arteries and lung capillaries to the left atrium, where blood releases carbon dioxide and gains oxygen.

name: pulmonary compliance
clinical_significance: How easily the lungs expand when pressure changes during breathing. Low compliance means the lungs are stiff and harder to inflate; high compliance can mean they expand easily but may not recoil effectively.

name: pulmonary edema
clinical_significance: Pulmonary edema is fluid accumulation in the lungs that impairs oxygen exchange and can cause severe breathlessness, low oxygen, or frothy sputum. Sudden onset is an emergency, often related to heart failure or another acute illness.

name: pulmonary embolism
clinical_significance: A blockage of a pulmonary artery, usually caused by a blood clot that traveled from a deep vein. It may cause sudden breathlessness, chest pain that worsens with breathing, rapid heartbeat, coughing blood, dizziness, or fainting. A large embolism can severely strain the heart or cause cardiac arrest and requires emergency assessment.

name: pulmonary emphysema
clinical_significance: Pulmonary emphysema is a form of COPD involving destruction of air sacs and loss of elastic recoil, causing air trapping and breathlessness. Smoking and other inhaled exposures are major risks; stopping exposure and treatment can slow decline.

name: pulmonary fibrosis
clinical_significance: Scarring and stiffening of lung tissue, often as part of an interstitial lung disease. The scarring can make it harder for the lungs to expand and for oxygen to pass into the blood. It may cause worsening shortness of breath, a dry cough, and tiredness. Causes include some autoimmune diseases, medicines, radiation, and inhaled dusts or chemicals; sometimes no cause is found. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a specific type with no known cause.

name: pulmonary fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal passage between the lung or an airway and another structure, such as the space around the lung, skin, or swallowing tube. It can allow air or infected fluid to travel where it should not.

name: pulmonary hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding into the airways or lung tissue, which may cause coughing blood, low oxygen, anemia, or respiratory failure.

name: pulmonary hypertension
clinical_significance: Abnormally high blood pressure in the blood vessels that carry blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs. Narrowed, blocked, or damaged vessels make the right side of the heart work harder to pump blood and may eventually weaken it. Pulmonary hypertension may occur on its own or result from left-sided heart disease, lung disease or low oxygen, long-term blood clots, or other conditions affecting the blood vessels. Symptoms may include breathlessness, tiredness, chest discomfort, dizzin

name: pulmonary infarction
clinical_significance: Death of a small area of lung tissue after its blood supply is blocked, usually by a pulmonary embolism. It may cause sharp pain with breathing, coughing up blood, breathlessness, or a shadow on imaging.

name: pulmonary infection
clinical_significance: Pulmonary infection can cause cough, fever, chest pain, and impaired oxygenation, with severity ranging from mild bronchitis to life-threatening pneumonia. The likely organism and host risk guide testing, isolation, and treatment.

name: pulmonary mass
clinical_significance: A space-occupying lesion in or near the lung, which may represent infection, inflammation, benign growth, or cancer and requires appropriate imaging assessment.

name: pulmonary nodule
clinical_significance: A rounded opacity in the lung, usually smaller than 3 cm, caused by scar, infection, inflammation, or tumor and assessed according to size and risk factors.

name: pulmonary reactance
clinical_significance: A measure of how the stretch and movement of the lungs and chest wall affect airflow during breathing. It is obtained during specialized tests and can help describe stiffness or altered movement of the respiratory system.

name: pulmonary stenosis
clinical_significance: Narrowing that obstructs blood leaving the right ventricle on its way to the lungs, usually at the pulmonary valve. It is often congenital and increases right-ventricular pressure; severe disease may cause a murmur, fatigue, breathlessness, fainting, or right-heart failure.

name: pulmonary surfactant
clinical_significance: A slippery mixture made by cells lining the lung’s air sacs that reduces surface tension and helps keep the sacs open. Too little in premature babies can cause serious breathing difficulty.

name: pulmonary trunk
clinical_significance: The pulmonary trunk carries blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs. Enlargement or obstruction can reflect pulmonary hypertension or congenital heart disease and may strain the right heart.

name: pulmonary valve
clinical_significance: A one-way valve between the right lower heart chamber and the artery leading to the lungs. It opens to let blood leave the heart and closes to prevent backward flow; narrowing or leakage can strain the right side of the heart.

name: pulmonary valve insufficiency
clinical_significance: Leakage of blood backward through the pulmonary valve into the right lower heart chamber while the heart relaxes. Mild leakage may cause no symptoms, but severe disease can enlarge the heart and reduce exercise ability.

name: pulmonary vein
clinical_significance: Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Congenital abnormal drainage, obstruction, or pressure changes can impair oxygenation and heart function.

name: pulmonary ventilation
clinical_significance: The movement of air into and out of the lungs. It brings oxygen into the air sacs and removes carbon dioxide; inadequate ventilation can cause low oxygen or a buildup of carbon dioxide.

name: pulmonologist
clinical_significance: A pulmonologist is a physician specializing in diseases of the lungs and breathing system, including asthma, COPD, infections, and sleep-related breathing disorders.

name: pulp canal
clinical_significance: The pulp canal is the passage within a tooth root containing dental pulp, nerves, and blood vessels; infection may require root-canal treatment.

name: pulp disease
clinical_significance: A problem affecting the living tissue inside a tooth, including inflammation, infection, loss of blood supply, or tissue death. It may cause toothache or sensitivity and can follow decay, a crack, a filling, or injury.

name: pulpectomy
clinical_significance: Complete removal of infected or damaged pulp from inside a tooth, usually a primary tooth. The space is cleaned and filled with a material that can safely resorb as the adult tooth develops.

name: pulpitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the dental pulp, usually caused by caries, trauma, cracks, or restorative treatment. Reversible pulpitis causes brief pain provoked by cold or sweet stimuli; irreversible pulpitis causes spontaneous or lingering pain and may progress to pulp necrosis, requiring endodontic treatment or extraction.

name: pulpotomy
clinical_significance: Removal of inflamed soft tissue from the crown of a baby tooth while keeping the root tissue alive. It treats suitable decay or injury and preserves the tooth until it naturally falls out.

name: pulse irregular
clinical_significance: An irregular pulse has uneven timing or varying beats and may reflect premature beats, atrial fibrillation, other arrhythmias, or measurement variation.

name: pulse pressure
clinical_significance: The systolic blood pressure minus the diastolic blood pressure. A widened or narrowed value may provide clues about circulation but must be interpreted with the full blood-pressure reading and clinical context.

name: pulse radiolysis
clinical_significance: Pulse radiolysis uses a brief radiation pulse to create and study short-lived chemical species. It is a research method used in radiation chemistry and biomolecular studies, not a routine clinical test.

name: pulse rate
clinical_significance: Pulse rate is the number of palpable arterial beats per minute and usually approximates heart rate, although some arrhythmias produce a pulse deficit.

name: pulvinar
clinical_significance: A region at the back of the thalamus, a deep brain structure. It helps direct visual attention, combine sensory information, and communicate with areas of the cerebral cortex.

name: puncture biopsy
clinical_significance: Needle biopsy samples cells or tissue to diagnose a lesion; image guidance and adequate sampling improve accuracy while limiting injury and unnecessary surgery.

name: punicic acid
clinical_significance: A conjugated polyunsaturated fatty acid found mainly in pomegranate seed oil and studied for lipid and inflammatory effects; clinical supplement benefits remain uncertain.

name: punishment
clinical_significance: Punishment is a consequence intended to reduce a behavior; in healthcare, coercive or harmful punishment is inappropriate and behavior support should prioritize safety and dignity.

name: pupil
clinical_significance: The central opening in the colored iris through which light enters the eye. Muscles change its size to control incoming light, and unequal or poorly reactive pupils may indicate eye or nerve disease.

name: purine
clinical_significance: A nitrogen-containing building block of DNA, RNA, and energy-carrying molecules. The body breaks down purines into uric acid, which can accumulate and contribute to gout or kidney stones.

name: purine nucleosides
clinical_significance: Molecules made from a purine base, such as adenine or guanine, joined to a sugar. Examples include adenosine and guanosine, which help form genetic material and participate in cell energy and signaling.

name: purine nucleotides
clinical_significance: Molecules containing adenine or guanine joined to a sugar and phosphate groups. They build DNA and RNA and include ATP and GTP, which store energy and help transmit signals inside cells.

name: purinoceptor
clinical_significance: A protein on a cell’s surface that detects substances such as ATP, ADP, or adenosine outside the cell. It helps regulate cell communication, inflammation, blood-vessel activity, and other body responses.

name: purkinje cell
clinical_significance: A major nerve cell in the cerebellum, the brain region that coordinates movement and balance. It sends signals that help fine-tune posture, coordination, and learned movements.

name: puromycin
clinical_significance: Puromycin is an antibiotic that blocks protein synthesis and is used mainly as a research reagent or cell-culture selection marker. It is not a routine human treatment and can be toxic to mammalian cells.

name: purpura
clinical_significance: Non-blanching red, purple, or violaceous macules, papules, or patches produced by the extravasation of erythrocytes into the dermis or submucosa. It is classified by lesion size into petechiae (less than three millimetres), purpura (three to ten millimetres), and ecchymoses (greater than one centimetre), and divided clinically into palpable purpura (indicating small-vessel vasculitis) and non-palpable purpura (caused by thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, vascular fragility, or coagulation d

name: purulent discharge
clinical_significance: Purulent discharge is pus draining from a wound, body cavity, or organ and often indicates infection, though sterile inflammation can look similar. The site, odor, fever, pain, and culture findings guide evaluation and treatment.

name: pus
clinical_significance: A thick fluid made of dead cells, germs, immune cells, and damaged tissue. It commonly collects during infection and may appear in wounds, abscesses, infected organs, or other inflamed body spaces.

name: pustule
clinical_significance: A small raised skin lesion filled with pus. Pustules can occur with acne, follicle infection, impetigo, psoriasis, or a medicine reaction; their cause is determined from their location, appearance, symptoms, and timing.

name: putamen
clinical_significance: A deep brain structure that helps select and smooth purposeful movements and supports learning of repeated movement habits. Damage to it can cause abnormal movements, weakness, or changes in behavior.

name: putrescine
clinical_significance: A chemical with a strong unpleasant smell made when proteins break down. It is found in decaying material and is also produced in small amounts during normal cell processes; its presence alone does not diagnose disease.

name: p-value
clinical_significance: A p-value estimates how compatible study data are with a specified null hypothesis under statistical assumptions. It does not measure effect size, clinical importance, or the probability that a hypothesis is true.

name: pycnodysostosis
clinical_significance: A rare inherited bone disorder in which bones are unusually dense but fragile. It can cause short stature, frequent fractures, short fingers, delayed closure of skull bones, crowded teeth, and problems with the jaw.

name: pyelitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the renal pelvis, the funnel-shaped part of the kidney that drains urine. It is often associated with urinary infection and may cause flank pain, fever, or painful urination.

name: pyelonephritis
clinical_significance: Infection and inflammation of the kidney and its urine-collecting area, usually caused by bacteria traveling upward from the bladder. Symptoms may include fever, chills, side pain, nausea, and painful urination.

name: pyloric antrum
clinical_significance: The pyloric antrum is the lower stomach region that grinds food and regulates its passage toward the pyloric canal and duodenum.

name: pyloric sphincter
clinical_significance: A ring of muscle at the outlet of the stomach. It opens in a controlled way to let partly digested food enter the first part of the small intestine and helps prevent the intestine's contents from flowing backward.

name: pyloric stenosis
clinical_significance: Narrowing of the outlet between the stomach and small intestine. In infants, the usual form is thickening of the outlet muscle, causing progressively forceful, non-green vomiting. In adults, narrowing is usually acquired, for example from ulcer scarring or a tumor. It can prevent food from leaving the stomach and cause dehydration.

name: pylorus
clinical_significance: The pylorus regulates emptying of the stomach into the small intestine. Scarring, tumors, or muscle thickening can obstruct it, causing vomiting, dehydration, and inability to tolerate food.

name: pyoderma
clinical_significance: A bacterial infection of the skin that can produce pus-filled spots, crusts, open sores, or deeper inflammation. Staphylococcus and Streptococcus are common causes; the infection may spread and require medical treatment, especially with fever, pain, or rapidly worsening redness.

name: pyoderma gangrenosum
clinical_significance: A rare inflammatory skin disease that causes very painful ulcers, often with a dark purple edge. It may occur with bowel inflammation, arthritis, or blood disorders; injury can make it worse, so treatment differs from ordinary wound infection.

name: pyogenic granuloma
clinical_significance: A common benign vascular proliferation (lobular capillary hemangioma) of the skin or mucous membranes that arises rapidly following minor trauma or during pregnancy ('pregnancy tumor' / granuloma gravidarum), presenting as an erythematous, smooth or lobulated, pedunculated or sessile vascular papule prone to profuse bleeding.

name: pyometra
clinical_significance: A collection of pus inside the uterus, usually caused by infection combined with blockage of drainage through the cervix. It may cause lower abdominal pain, fever, tenderness, or foul-smelling discharge; in older adults it can be linked to cervical narrowing or a tumor and needs prompt evaluation.

name: pyonephrosis
clinical_significance: Pus trapped in the kidney's urine-collecting system, usually because infection occurs behind a blockage. It is a medical emergency requiring urgent drainage, antibiotics, and treatment of the obstruction.

name: pyramidal cell
clinical_significance: A triangular-shaped excitatory neuron with a prominent apical dendrite, found especially in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus and involved in long-range brain signaling.

name: pyramidal tract
clinical_significance: The pyramidal tract is a major motor pathway from the cerebral cortex to the brainstem and spinal cord that controls voluntary movement.

name: pyrazinamide
clinical_significance: An antibiotic used with other medicines during the initial treatment of tuberculosis. It helps shorten treatment but can injure the liver or raise uric acid, so monitoring and prescribed dosing are important.

name: pyrazines
clinical_significance: A family of chemical compounds found naturally in some foods and used in flavors, medicines, and industry. Their effects on health depend on the specific compound, amount, and route of exposure.

name: pyrazole
clinical_significance: A small five-membered chemical structure used to build medicines, pesticides, and other compounds. The word names a chemical family and does not identify one particular treatment or effect.

name: pyrazoles
clinical_significance: Pyrazoles are a chemical scaffold found in some medicines and pesticides. The health effects and therapeutic role depend on the individual compound rather than the shared ring structure.

name: pyrene
clinical_significance: Pyrene is a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon produced by combustion and present in some smoke and environmental pollution. It is used as a marker of combustion exposure, while health risk depends on dose and co-exposures.

name: pyrenochaeta
clinical_significance: A group of fungi found mainly in soil and plants that rarely infect people. When infection occurs, it usually affects tissue beneath injured skin or people with weakened immunity.

name: pyridine
clinical_significance: A nitrogen-containing ring-shaped chemical structure found in many medicines, vitamins, and biologically active substances. Pyridine groups can change how compounds dissolve, react, travel through the body, and produce medical effects.

name: pyridostigmine bromide
clinical_significance: Pyridostigmine bromide increases communication between nerves and muscles and is used mainly for myasthenia gravis; it may cause abdominal cramps, diarrhea, or excess secretions.

name: pyridoxal phosphate
clinical_significance: The active form of vitamin B6 used by many enzymes. It helps the body process amino acids, make certain brain chemicals and red blood cells, and maintain normal nerve function.

name: pyridoxine
clinical_significance: One form of vitamin B6, converted in the body to pyridoxal phosphate, a coenzyme for amino-acid metabolism. It is needed for processing food, making red blood cells, and supporting nerves and the immune system; deficiency can cause anemia or nerve problems, while excessive supplements can damage nerves.

name: pyrimethamine
clinical_significance: A parasite-fighting medicine that blocks folate use in certain protozoa. It is used for selected infections, often with another medicine, and can suppress bone marrow or cause serious skin reactions.

name: pyrimidine analog
clinical_significance: A medicine or chemical resembling a pyrimidine nucleotide that can interfere with DNA or RNA synthesis, often for cancer or antiviral treatment.

name: pyrimidine dimer
clinical_significance: A DNA lesion formed when adjacent pyrimidine bases bond abnormally after ultraviolet exposure, potentially causing mutations if unrepaired.

name: pyrimidine nucleosides
clinical_significance: Nucleosides containing cytosine, thymine, or uracil bases linked to a sugar, serving as components or precursors of DNA and RNA.

name: pyrimidine nucleotides
clinical_significance: Genetic and energy-related building blocks containing pyrimidine bases, including cytidine, uridine, and thymidine. Cells use them to make DNA, RNA, cell membranes, and other substances needed for growth and repair.

name: pyrimidines
clinical_significance: Pyrimidines include cytosine, thymine, and uracil, which are essential components of DNA and RNA. Medicines that resemble pyrimidines can disrupt nucleic-acid synthesis and are used in some cancers and viral infections.

name: pyrogen
clinical_significance: A pyrogen is a substance that induces fever, commonly through immune signaling; bacterial endotoxin is an important example in contaminated medicines or fluids.

name: pyroglyphidae
clinical_significance: Pyroglyphidae is a mite family that includes house-dust mites whose allergens can trigger allergic rhinitis, asthma, or atopic dermatitis.

name: pyronine
clinical_significance: Pyronine is a laboratory dye used to stain RNA-rich structures and cells. It supports microscopy and research but is not a standalone clinical diagnostic test.

name: pyrophosphatase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that hydrolyzes inorganic pyrophosphate and helps drive many biosynthetic reactions forward. An enzyme that breaks down pyrophosphate, helping many chemical reactions needed to build cellular materials.

name: pyropoikilocytosis
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder that makes red blood cells unusually small, irregular, and fragile. The cells break down easily, causing hemolytic anemia with tiredness, jaundice, pale skin, or an enlarged spleen, often beginning in infancy or childhood.

name: pyroptosis
clinical_significance: A form of controlled cell death that causes inflammation. The cell swells, breaks open, and releases signals that alert the immune system, often in response to infection or severe cell stress.

name: pyrosequencing
clinical_significance: A laboratory method for reading selected DNA sequences by detecting light produced as DNA building blocks are added. It can identify some genetic changes or microbes but is not suitable for every sequencing need.

name: pyroxamide
clinical_significance: Pyroxamide is an investigational histone-deacetylase inhibitor studied for anticancer activity. It is not a routine approved therapy.

name: pyrroles
clinical_significance: A group of five-membered nitrogen-containing ring compounds found in heme, bile pigments, medicines, and other biologically active molecules.

name: pyrrolidonecarboxylic acid
clinical_significance: A cyclic amino-acid derivative, also called pyroglutamic acid, found in proteins and metabolic pathways; abnormal accumulation may occur in selected metabolic or medication-related conditions.

name: pyrrolnitrin
clinical_significance: Pyrrolnitrin is an antimicrobial compound produced by some bacteria and studied for antifungal activity and biological control.

name: pyruvate decarboxylase
clinical_significance: Pyruvate decarboxylase is an enzyme that converts pyruvate to acetaldehyde and carbon dioxide during fermentation in some organisms.

name: pyruvate kinase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that helps red blood cells make energy from glucose. If it is inheritedly deficient, red cells may break down too early, causing chronic hemolytic anemia, jaundice, gallstones, tiredness, or an enlarged spleen.

name: pyuria
clinical_significance: Pyuria is white blood cells in urine and may indicate urinary infection or inflammation, but can also occur without bacterial infection. Urine culture and symptoms help determine whether antibiotics are appropriate.

name: q fever
clinical_significance: An infection caused by the bacterium Coxiella burnetii, usually caught by breathing dust contaminated by infected cattle, sheep, goats, or their birth products. It often causes sudden fever, severe headache, tiredness, and muscle aches; some people develop pneumonia, hepatitis, or long-term heart-valve infection.

name: qigong
clinical_significance: Qigong combines gentle movement, posture, breathing, and attention and may support balance, stress reduction, or well-being. Evidence varies by condition and it should complement, not replace, necessary medical treatment.

name: quadrantectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove one section of an organ, most often part of the breast containing a tumor plus a margin of healthy tissue. The need for lymph-node surgery or further treatment depends on the tumor and test results.

name: quadriceps femoris
clinical_significance: The group of four muscles at the front of the thigh. It straightens the knee for standing, walking, climbing, and kicking; one part also helps bend the hip.

name: quadriplegia
clinical_significance: Paralysis affecting both arms and both legs, usually with weakness of the trunk, because of damage to the neck portion of the spinal cord or another major nervous-system injury. It can impair breathing and bladder or bowel control.

name: quadruplet pregnancy
clinical_significance: A pregnancy involving four fetuses. It has increased risks of preterm birth, restricted fetal growth, high blood pressure, metabolic problems, and illness in the pregnant person.

name: quality
clinical_significance: Quality in health care includes safety, effectiveness, timeliness, patient-centeredness, equity, and efficient use of resources. Quality measures help identify gaps and guide improvement.

name: quality control
clinical_significance: Quality control checks whether laboratory or manufacturing processes produce reliable results and products. In health care, it helps detect errors before they affect diagnosis, treatment, or patient safety.

name: quality of life
clinical_significance: A person’s experience of physical health, emotional well-being, relationships, independence, and ability to do meaningful activities. Illness and treatment may affect these areas differently for each person.

name: quantum dot
clinical_significance: Quantum dots are semiconductor nanoparticles that emit light and are studied for imaging, diagnostics, and drug delivery. Clinical use is limited; composition and long-term toxicity, including heavy-metal exposure, require assessment.

name: quarantine
clinical_significance: Temporary separation or movement restrictions for people exposed to an infectious disease while monitoring whether they become ill. It differs from isolation, which separates people who are already infected.

name: quassins
clinical_significance: Quassins are intensely bitter plant compounds from quassia and related species. They have been used in traditional preparations and as insecticidal agents, but concentrated products can cause adverse effects and lack established broad therapeutic benefit.

name: quercetin
clinical_significance: Quercetin is a plant flavonoid sold as a supplement and studied for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. Evidence for treating disease is limited, product doses vary, and interactions with medicines are possible.

name: questionnaire
clinical_significance: A questionnaire gathers standardized information about symptoms, function, exposures, or quality of life. Clinical use depends on validated wording, scoring, language, and interpretation; it does not replace examination when needed.

name: quetiapine fumarate
clinical_significance: A form of quetiapine, a medicine used for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and selected depression treatment. It can cause sleepiness, dizziness on standing, weight or blood-sugar changes, and movement problems.

name: quinalphos
clinical_significance: A poisonous insecticide that disrupts nerve-signal control. Significant exposure can cause sweating, excess saliva, vomiting, muscle twitching, weakness, seizures, breathing failure, or death.

name: quinapril
clinical_significance: Quinapril is an angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitor used for hypertension and heart failure; cough, hyperkalaemia, renal-function changes, angioedema, and fetal toxicity are important risks.

name: quinazoline
clinical_significance: Quinazoline is a chemical scaffold found in medicines, including some anticancer and cardiovascular drugs. The specific compound determines its action, benefit, and toxicity.

name: quinidine
clinical_significance: A heart-rhythm medicine that changes electrical conduction in the heart. It is used selectively because it can cause dangerous abnormal rhythms, low blood pressure, low platelets, diarrhea, or other serious side effects.

name: quinine
clinical_significance: A medicine derived from cinchona bark that can treat selected malaria infections. It is used less often because safer options are available and it can cause low blood sugar, ringing in the ears, blood-cell problems, or abnormal heart rhythms.

name: quinolinic acid
clinical_significance: Quinolinic acid is a tryptophan-metabolism product and NMDA-receptor agonist that can contribute to neuroinflammation and neuronal injury at elevated levels. Measurement is mainly used in research or specialized evaluation.

name: quinone metabolism
clinical_significance: Quinone metabolism includes cellular reactions that activate, detoxify, or generate reactive quinones. These pathways affect drug metabolism, oxidative stress, and toxicity from some medicines and environmental chemicals.

name: quinones
clinical_significance: Quinones are reactive compounds found in biology, medicines, and pollutants. Some participate in electron transfer, while others can damage proteins or DNA; risk depends on the specific compound and exposure.

name: quinuclidines
clinical_significance: Quinuclidines are a chemical class that includes medicines acting on acetylcholine receptors and other targets. Their clinical effects vary by drug and may include changes in cognition, movement, or autonomic function.

name: quipazine
clinical_significance: Quipazine is a serotonergic research compound used to study serotonin receptors and behavior. It is not an approved routine treatment and can cause serotonergic adverse effects.

name: quorum sensing
clinical_significance: A density-dependent bacterial intercellular communication mechanism mediated by the release and detection of small diffusible autoinducer signaling molecules, coordinating group behaviors such as biofilm formation, bioluminescence, and virulence factor expression once a threshold bacterial population density is achieved.

name: rabeprazole
clinical_significance: A medicine that greatly reduces acid made by the stomach. It treats reflux and ulcers and may be combined with antibiotics for Helicobacter pylori infection; possible effects include headache, diarrhea, and rarely low magnesium or bowel infection.

name: rabies
clinical_significance: A viral infection of the brain and nervous system caused by rabies virus, a virus that infects mammals. It spreads mainly when saliva from an infected animal enters a bite, scratch, broken skin, or the eyes, mouth, or another mucous membrane. After a variable symptom-free period, early symptoms may include fever, weakness, headache, or pain, itching, or unusual sensations near the exposure site. Later symptoms may include confusion, agitation, hallucinations, fear of water, difficulty swallowing

name: rabies vaccine
clinical_significance: Rabies vaccine is used before or after exposure to prevent rabies, a nearly always fatal infection once symptoms begin. After a possible exposure, immediate wound washing and urgent public-health or medical assessment determine whether vaccine and immune globulin are needed.

name: rabies virus
clinical_significance: The virus that causes rabies, a usually fatal viral infection of the central nervous system transmitted most often through the saliva of an infected animal.

name: raclopride
clinical_significance: Raclopride is a dopamine D2/D3 receptor antagonist and radiotracer used in brain imaging research, including PET studies of dopamine signaling. It is not a routine therapeutic medicine.

name: radial nerve
clinical_significance: A major nerve of the arm that helps straighten the elbow, wrist, and fingers and carries feeling from part of the back of the hand. Injury can cause wrist drop, finger weakness, or numbness.

name: radiation dosage
clinical_significance: The amount of radiation given during an imaging test or radiation treatment. The dose is planned to obtain the needed benefit while limiting unnecessary exposure.

name: radiation enteritis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or injury of the small or large intestine after radiation treatment. Early symptoms may include diarrhea, cramps, nausea, or urgency; months or years later, scarring can cause narrowing, poor absorption, bleeding, or blockage.

name: radiation exposure
clinical_significance: Contact with ionizing or non-ionizing radiation from medical imaging, treatment, sunlight, workplaces, or other sources. The possible harm depends mainly on the type, dose, body area, and duration of exposure.

name: radiation fibrosis
clinical_significance: Long-term thickening and stiffening of tissue caused by radiation injury, sometimes appearing months or years after treatment. It can affect skin, lungs, bowel, or other organs and may cause pain, reduced movement, or shortness of breath.

name: radiation field
clinical_significance: The area and distribution of radiation delivered during imaging or radiation treatment. In therapy, its size, shape, direction, and dose are planned to cover the target while limiting exposure to nearby healthy tissue.

name: radiation leukemia
clinical_significance: Radiation leukemia is leukemia that develops after significant exposure to ionizing radiation; it is a late treatment- or exposure-related complication.

name: radiation necrosis
clinical_significance: Permanent death of tissue caused by radiation injury, often developing months or years after treatment. In the brain it may cause headache, seizures, swelling, weakness, or speech and vision problems and can resemble returning cancer on scans.

name: radiation oncologists
clinical_significance: Radiation oncologists use ionizing radiation to treat cancer and selected benign conditions. They plan target coverage, protect nearby tissues, monitor side effects, and coordinate treatment with surgery or medicines.

name: radiation pneumonitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of lung tissue occurring weeks or months after radiation to the chest. It may cause dry cough, fever, breathlessness, or low oxygen and can later leave permanent scarring; new breathing symptoms need medical assessment.

name: radiation protection
clinical_significance: Radiation protection minimizes unnecessary exposure while preserving diagnostic or treatment benefit. It includes justification, dose optimization, shielding, and monitoring for patients, staff, and the public.

name: radiation therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that uses carefully aimed ionizing radiation to damage cancer cells so they stop dividing or die. It may be given from outside the body or from a source placed near or inside a tumor. Side effects depend on the body area and dose and may include tiredness or skin changes.

name: radiation tolerance
clinical_significance: The amount of radiation that a tissue or organ can receive before injury becomes likely. It varies with the tissue, dose, treatment schedule, and previous radiation.

name: radiation-recall dermatitis
clinical_significance: Radiation-recall dermatitis is inflammation in previously irradiated skin triggered later by a medicine or other exposure. It may resemble a burn or infection; identifying the trigger guides treatment and decisions about continuing it.

name: radical cystoprostatectomy
clinical_significance: Radical cystoprostatectomy removes the urinary bladder, prostate, and nearby structures, usually to treat invasive bladder cancer in men.

name: radical hysterectomy
clinical_significance: An operation that removes the uterus and cervix together with surrounding parametrial tissues and the upper vagina, usually with pelvic lymph-node assessment or removal. It is used mainly for selected invasive cervical cancers and is more extensive than a simple or total hysterectomy.

name: radical lymphadenectomy
clinical_significance: Extensive surgery to remove lymph nodes and nearby tissue to look for or treat cancer spread. It may provide important staging information but can cause pain, nerve or vessel injury, and long-term swelling from lymph-fluid blockage.

name: radical mastectomy
clinical_significance: Radical mastectomy removes the breast, chest muscles, and many underarm lymph nodes; it is now rarely used because less extensive cancer surgery is often effective.

name: radical nephrectomy
clinical_significance: Radical nephrectomy removes an entire kidney, often for localized kidney cancer. Kidney function, tumor stage, and the health of the remaining kidney affect operative planning and long-term monitoring.

name: radical prostatectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove the whole prostate gland and usually the nearby seminal vesicles, most often to treat prostate cancer that has not spread widely. The urinary passage is rejoined to the bladder; possible effects include urine leakage, erection problems, bleeding, and infection.

name: radicular cyst
clinical_significance: An inflammatory odontogenic cyst arising at the apex of a nonvital tooth, usually from chronic pulpal infection and apical periodontitis.

name: radiculitis
clinical_significance: Irritation or inflammation of a nerve root where it leaves the spine. It can cause pain spreading along an arm or leg, tingling, numbness, weakness, or changed reflexes because of a disk problem, narrowing, infection, or other disease.

name: radiculopathy
clinical_significance: Radiculopathy occurs when a spinal nerve root is compressed or injured, causing radiating pain, numbness, weakness, or reflex changes. Progressive weakness, saddle numbness, or bladder or bowel dysfunction requires urgent evaluation.

name: radioactive iodine
clinical_significance: A radioactive form of iodine taken up by thyroid cells. It is used to image the thyroid or destroy overactive thyroid tissue and selected thyroid cancer cells; radiation-safety precautions are needed after some treatments.

name: radioactivity
clinical_significance: Energy released when unstable atoms change into more stable forms. The energy may be particles or rays and can be used in medical imaging or treatment, but enough exposure can damage living tissue.

name: radioallergosorbent test
clinical_significance: An in vitro radioimmunoassay that detects and quantifies allergen-specific IgE antibodies in a patient's blood serum, used to identify allergic sensitization to environmental aeroallergens, foods, medications, or venoms without risking in vivo anaphylaxis.

name: radiobiology
clinical_significance: The study of how radiation affects living cells and tissues, including DNA damage, cell death, repair, mutations, treatment effects, and the development of cancer.

name: radiochemistry
clinical_significance: The chemistry of radioactive substances and compounds. In medicine it includes making and labeling radiopharmaceuticals, studying radioactive decay, separating products, and checking radiochemical purity and safety.

name: radiodermatitis
clinical_significance: Skin injury caused by ionizing radiation, such as radiation treatment. It may cause redness, dryness, itching, hair loss, peeling, sores, or long-term skin changes; severity depends on the dose, treatment area, and repeated exposure.

name: radioembolisation
clinical_significance: Radioembolization delivers radioactive microspheres through an artery to liver tumors. It can control selected primary or metastatic liver cancers while limiting exposure to other tissue, but requires careful assessment of liver function and vascular anatomy.

name: radiofrequency ablation
clinical_significance: A procedure that uses high-frequency electrical energy to heat and destroy selected tissue, often under imaging guidance.

name: radioimmunoassay
clinical_significance: A laboratory test that uses an antibody and a small radioactive label to measure a hormone, medicine, or protein in a sample. It can be very sensitive but is often replaced by newer nonradioactive tests.

name: radioimmunodetection
clinical_significance: Radioimmunodetection uses a radioactive tracer linked to an antibody to locate cells carrying a target marker, often tumor tissue. It is a specialized imaging and research approach with limited routine use.

name: radioimmunoguided surgery
clinical_significance: Surgery in which a radioactive tracer attached to an antibody helps the surgeon locate tissue carrying a particular marker, often tumor tissue. Special equipment detects the tracer during the operation.

name: radioimmunotherapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that attaches a radioactive substance to an antibody so the antibody carries radiation toward cells with a particular marker, often cancer cells. Radiation can still affect nearby normal tissue and cause side effects.

name: radioisotope
clinical_significance: An unstable isotope that emits radiation as it decays; radioisotopes are used in medical imaging, diagnosis, and selected treatments.

name: radiologic health
clinical_significance: The safe use of medical imaging and radiation-based treatment to protect patients, workers, and the public from unnecessary ionizing radiation while preserving clinical benefit. Safety measures include appropriate justification, shielding, and dose optimization.

name: radiologic response
clinical_significance: The change seen on medical scans after treatment, such as shrinkage, disappearance, stability, growth, or new lesions. Standard measurement rules help classify the response, but scans do not always show the full biological effect.

name: radiologist
clinical_significance: A doctor trained to interpret medical images and sometimes perform image-guided procedures. Radiologists evaluate X-rays, ultrasound, CT, MRI, and other scans to diagnose disease, guide treatment, or obtain tissue samples.

name: radiology
clinical_significance: The medical field that uses images to find and monitor disease and guide procedures. Radiologists interpret X-rays, ultrasound, CT, MRI, and other scans and may perform image-guided biopsies, drainages, injections, or treatments.

name: radiometry
clinical_significance: Radiometry measures electromagnetic radiation, including intensity and energy. It is relevant to dosimetry, phototherapy, imaging, and laboratory instrument calibration.

name: radionuclide angiography
clinical_significance: An imaging test in which a small amount of radioactive tracer is used to follow blood flow through the heart or blood vessels. A camera detects the tracer and produces information about circulation or heart pumping.

name: radionuclide generator
clinical_significance: A device that produces a short-lived radioactive substance from a longer-lasting radioactive substance. It supplies certain tracers for nuclear scans or treatment when needed and must be operated under strict safety and quality controls.

name: radionuclide imaging
clinical_significance: A scan that uses a small amount of radioactive tracer to show the structure or activity of an organ. A camera detects the tracer, helping evaluate blood flow, bone, thyroid, kidney, heart, or cancer-related changes.

name: radionuclide therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that delivers radiation from inside the body using a radioactive substance directed toward selected tissue. It can treat some thyroid diseases, cancers, or painful bone lesions. The medicine, dose, precautions, and side effects depend on the target and the person’s kidney, blood, and overall health.

name: radiopharmaceutical
clinical_significance: A medicine containing a small amount of radioactive material. It can show how an organ or tissue works on a scan or deliver radiation to selected diseased cells; its distribution determines the information or treatment it provides.

name: radioprotective agent
clinical_significance: A medicine or substance intended to reduce injury to healthy tissue from ionizing radiation. It may limit chemical damage or support cell repair, but its benefit and risks depend on the type, dose, and treatment setting.

name: radiosurgery
clinical_significance: Radiosurgery delivers highly focused radiation to a small target, usually in the brain or body, without making a conventional surgical incision.

name: radiotherapy bolus
clinical_significance: A layer of material placed on the skin during selected radiation treatments so more radiation reaches the skin surface. It is positioned carefully to deliver the planned dose to the target area.

name: radiotherapy dosage
clinical_significance: Radiotherapy dosage is the amount of ionizing radiation prescribed for a treatment target, usually divided into carefully planned fractions.

name: radium
clinical_significance: A naturally radioactive chemical element that releases penetrating radiation as it breaks down. Internal exposure can damage bone and other tissues and increase cancer risk, so handling requires strict safety controls.

name: radius
clinical_significance: The forearm bone on the thumb side. It joins the elbow and wrist and rotates around the ulna, allowing the palm to turn up or down.

name: radius fracture
clinical_significance: A break in the radius, one of the two bones of the forearm, often occurring near the wrist after a fall onto an outstretched hand.

name: radon
clinical_significance: A naturally occurring radioactive gas that can accumulate indoors and increase lung-cancer risk when inhaled over time.

name: raffinose
clinical_significance: Raffinose is a plant trisaccharide found in beans and some vegetables. Human digestive enzymes do not break it down fully, so gut bacteria ferment it and may cause gas or bloating.

name: rahnella
clinical_significance: Rahnella are environmental bacteria found in water, soil, and plants that rarely cause human infection. Clinical isolates need interpretation in context and species confirmation.

name: rahnella aquatilis
clinical_significance: Rahnella aquatilis is an environmental bacterium that can rarely cause opportunistic bloodstream, urinary, or wound infection. The specimen source and susceptibility profile help distinguish disease from contamination.

name: rale
clinical_significance: A rale, or crackle, is an abnormal discontinuous breath sound produced by fluid, collapsed airways, or opening of small airways during breathing.

name: raloxifene
clinical_significance: A medicine that acts like estrogen in bones but blocks some estrogen effects elsewhere. It may reduce spine fractures and selected breast-cancer risk after menopause, but can increase blood-clot risk.

name: raloxifene hydrochloride
clinical_significance: Raloxifene hydrochloride is a selective estrogen-receptor modulator used to prevent or treat osteoporosis and reduce breast-cancer risk in selected postmenopausal women.

name: ralstonia
clinical_significance: Ralstonia are water-associated bacteria that can contaminate medical solutions or devices and occasionally cause bloodstream or respiratory infection. Outbreak investigation and source control may be needed when multiple cases occur.

name: ralstonia mannitolilytica
clinical_significance: Ralstonia mannitolilytica is a water-associated bacterium implicated in occasional device- or fluid-associated infections and healthcare outbreaks. Accurate identification and susceptibility testing support treatment and infection control.

name: ralstonia pickettii
clinical_significance: Ralstonia pickettii can contaminate water, saline, or medical products and cause occasional bloodstream or respiratory infection, particularly in vulnerable patients. Repeated cases may indicate a contaminated source.

name: raltegravir potassium
clinical_significance: Raltegravir potassium is an HIV integrase inhibitor used with other antiretroviral medicines to suppress HIV replication.

name: raltitrexed
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy medicine used for some colorectal cancers. It blocks a cell process needed to make DNA, slowing the growth of cancer cells; possible effects include diarrhea, mouth sores, low blood counts, tiredness, and liver problems.

name: ramipril
clinical_significance: Ramipril is an angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitor used for hypertension, heart failure, and cardiovascular risk reduction; cough, hyperkalaemia, renal-function changes, angioedema, and fetal toxicity are important risks.

name: ramucirumab
clinical_significance: A monoclonal antibody that blocks vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 and is used in selected advanced cancers, including gastric, colorectal, lung, and liver cancers.

name: random allocation
clinical_significance: Assignment of participants to study groups by chance to reduce selection bias and balance known and unknown factors.

name: randomization
clinical_significance: Randomization assigns study participants to groups by chance, reducing selection bias and balancing confounding factors. It supports credible comparison of treatment effects but does not guarantee that a trial is unbiased in every other way.

name: randomization validation
clinical_significance: Checking that a clinical trial's assignment process truly places participants into study groups by chance and is implemented as planned. This helps reduce selection bias and protects the reliability of comparisons between treatments.

name: ranibizumab
clinical_significance: An intravitreal monoclonal antibody fragment that inhibits vascular endothelial growth factor and treats neovascular macular degeneration, diabetic macular edema, retinal vein occlusion, and related retinal disease.

name: ranitidine
clinical_significance: Ranitidine is an H2-receptor blocker formerly used for reflux and ulcers. It was withdrawn or restricted in many markets because of contamination concerns; current availability and alternatives vary by jurisdiction.

name: ranolazine
clinical_significance: Ranolazine is an antianginal drug that inhibits the late sodium current in cardiac cells and reduces chronic angina without substantially lowering heart rate or blood pressure; QT prolongation and drug interactions require caution.

name: ranpirnase
clinical_significance: Ranpirnase is an investigational ribonuclease studied as an anticancer agent. It has no established routine role in current cancer treatment.

name: raoultella
clinical_significance: Raoultella is a genus of gram-negative bacteria that can cause opportunistic urinary, respiratory, wound, or bloodstream infections.

name: raoultella planticola
clinical_significance: Raoultella planticola is an environmental bacterium that can cause rare urinary, respiratory, wound, or bloodstream infection. Accurate identification and susceptibility testing help guide therapy.

name: raoultella terrigena
clinical_significance: Raoultella terrigena is an uncommon environmental bacterium that may rarely cause opportunistic infection. A clinical isolate is interpreted with specimen source, symptoms, and susceptibility testing.

name: raphe nuclei
clinical_significance: The raphe nuclei are brainstem groups of neurons that produce serotonin and influence mood, pain, sleep, arousal, and autonomic functions.

name: rare diseases
clinical_significance: Rare diseases can be difficult to recognize because symptoms are uncommon and specialized testing may be needed. Early diagnosis can connect patients to appropriate treatment, surveillance, and genetic counseling.

name: ras peptide
clinical_significance: A small protein fragment related to Ras proteins, which help control cell growth and division. Changes in Ras signaling can contribute to cancer.

name: rasburicase
clinical_significance: Rasburicase rapidly lowers uric acid and is used to prevent or treat tumor-lysis syndrome in selected patients receiving cancer therapy. It can cause severe allergy or hemolysis, especially in G6PD deficiency, so screening and monitoring are important.

name: rat-bite fever
clinical_significance: Rat-bite fever is a bacterial infection transmitted by bites, scratches, or contact with rodents or their secretions. It can cause fever, rash, and migratory joint pain and may progress to endocarditis or systemic infection without treatment.

name: ratio
clinical_significance: A ratio compares two quantities by division, such as a measurement of risk, concentration, or body proportions.

name: rationalization
clinical_significance: A psychological defense in which a person creates plausible explanations for behavior or feelings while avoiding the underlying motive or conflict.

name: rauscher virus
clinical_significance: Rauscher virus is a murine leukemia virus used in animal research on retroviruses and cancer. It does not cause ordinary human infection.

name: rauwolfia alkaloid
clinical_significance: Rauwolfia alkaloids are plant-derived compounds that alter monoamine signaling and historically were used for hypertension or psychiatric symptoms. They can cause depression, sedation, low blood pressure, and drug interactions and are now rarely used.

name: ravuconazole
clinical_significance: Ravuconazole is a triazole antifungal medicine studied and used in some settings for invasive fungal infections.

name: raynaud phenomenon
clinical_significance: Episodes in which small blood vessels in the fingers or toes suddenly narrow after cold or stress. The digits may turn white, blue, then red and become numb or painful; severe or new symptoms may indicate another disease.

name: Raynaud's disease
clinical_significance: The primary form of Raynaud phenomenon, in which small blood vessels in the fingers or toes narrow episodically without an associated underlying disease. Cold or emotional stress may trigger attacks that cause numbness, tingling, or pain and a characteristic change in color from white to blue and then red as blood flow returns.

name: razoxane
clinical_significance: Razoxane is an older anticancer agent related to dexrazoxane and studied for tumor treatment. Its clinical role is limited; dexrazoxane is used in selected settings to reduce anthracycline-related cardiac injury or tissue damage.

name: reaction
clinical_significance: A response of the body or mind to a stimulus, illness, medicine, treatment, or event. Examples include an allergic reaction, an immune reaction, a treatment response, and a psychological reaction; the cause and severity determine its importance.

name: reaction time
clinical_significance: Reaction time is the interval between a stimulus and a response. Changes can reflect medication effects, fatigue, intoxication, neurologic disease, or cognitive impairment and may affect driving or other safety-sensitive activities.

name: reactive arthritis
clinical_significance: Painful inflammation of joints that develops during or after certain intestinal or genital infections. It may also cause eye inflammation, skin changes, or urinary symptoms, and the triggering infection may already have cleared.

name: reactive hypoglycemia
clinical_significance: A fall in blood sugar occurring within a few hours after eating. It may cause shakiness, sweating, hunger, weakness, dizziness, or confusion; repeated episodes need assessment to confirm low sugar and identify the cause.

name: reagent
clinical_significance: A reagent is a substance used to cause or measure a chemical reaction in a laboratory test. Reagent quality, storage, and calibration affect diagnostic accuracy.

name: reality testing
clinical_significance: The ability to recognize whether perceptions, thoughts, and beliefs match shared reality. Clinicians assess it during a mental-status examination; impaired reality testing can occur with psychosis, severe mood episodes, delirium, or some brain disorders.

name: rebeccamycin
clinical_significance: Rebeccamycin is an antibiotic natural product that inhibits DNA processes and has been studied as an anticancer lead compound. It is not a routine clinical medicine.

name: receive
clinical_significance: “Receive” may document that a patient was given a treatment, medicine, transfusion, or service. Accurate records should specify what was received, when, and whether it was completed or tolerated.

name: receptor
clinical_significance: A protein on or inside a cell that recognizes a specific signal, such as a hormone, nerve chemical, or medicine, and starts or changes a cell response.

name: receptor binding
clinical_significance: The attachment of a signaling molecule, medicine, or other ligand to a receptor on or inside a cell. Binding can activate, block, or change the receptor and its downstream cellular response.

name: recombinant
clinical_significance: Recombinant technology enables production of medicines such as insulin, clotting factors, hormones, and antibodies and supports some vaccines and gene therapies. Manufacturing quality and immune reactions are important clinical considerations.

name: recombinant DNA
clinical_significance: DNA made by joining genetic material from different sources. It is used in biotechnology to produce medicines such as insulin and growth hormone, develop some vaccines, and create vehicles for gene therapy.

name: recombinant protein
clinical_significance: A protein produced by putting its gene into a laboratory cell and growing the cell so it makes the protein. This method supplies some hormones, vaccines, antibodies, enzymes, and research materials.

name: recombinase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that cuts, joins, or rearranges DNA segments. It helps cells exchange genetic material, repair some DNA damage, and assemble the gene parts needed to make a varied immune response.

name: recombinational repair
clinical_significance: A way cells repair a serious DNA break by using a matching, undamaged DNA copy as a guide. It restores genetic information accurately; inherited problems with this repair can increase cancer risk and treatment sensitivity.

name: record
clinical_significance: A health record is a documented account of a person’s history, findings, tests, diagnoses, treatments, decisions, and outcomes.

name: recreation therapy
clinical_significance: Recreation therapy uses adapted games, arts, exercise, and leisure activities to support physical, emotional, cognitive, or social functioning.

name: rectal
clinical_significance: Rectal means relating to the rectum, the final section of the large intestine before the anal canal.

name: rectal carcinoma
clinical_significance: Rectal carcinoma is cancer arising in the rectum and may cause bleeding, altered bowel habits, pain, or anemia.

name: rectal disease
clinical_significance: A disorder affecting the rectum, including inflammation, infection, bleeding, obstruction, prolapse, functional disease, or neoplasm.

name: rectal fistula
clinical_significance: A rectal fistula is an abnormal tract connecting the rectum with skin or another organ, often causing drainage, infection, or passage of stool through an abnormal route.

name: rectal hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding from the rectum, which may result from hemorrhoids, fissure, inflammation, ischemia, polyps, cancer, trauma, or other gastrointestinal disease.

name: rectal mucositis
clinical_significance: Rectal mucositis is inflammation and injury of the rectal lining, often after radiation, chemotherapy, infection, inflammatory disease, or trauma.

name: rectal necrosis
clinical_significance: Rectal necrosis is death of rectal tissue from inadequate blood flow, severe inflammation, infection, pressure, or another destructive process.

name: rectal neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the rectum that may be noncancerous, precancerous, or cancerous. It can cause bleeding, altered bowel habits, pain, anemia, or no symptoms and may require examination and biopsy.

name: rectal obstruction
clinical_significance: Impaired passage through the rectum caused by fecal impaction, stricture, tumor, foreign body, inflammation, or functional outlet disorder.

name: rectal perforation
clinical_significance: A tear or hole through the rectal wall that can release bowel contents and cause peritonitis, sepsis, or severe bleeding.

name: rectal polyposis
clinical_significance: Rectal polyposis is the presence of multiple polyps in the rectum, which may be sporadic or part of an inherited syndrome and can increase cancer risk.

name: rectal prolapse
clinical_significance: The rectum slipping downward and partly or completely coming through the anus. It may cause a visible bulge, bleeding, mucus, discomfort, or difficulty controlling or passing stool and can result from weakened pelvic support, straining, or nerve problems.

name: rectal route
clinical_significance: The rectal route administers a medicine or fluid through the anus into the rectum, where it may act locally or be absorbed systemically.

name: rectal stenosis
clinical_significance: Abnormal narrowing of the rectal lumen caused by inflammation, scarring, surgery, radiation, ischemia, trauma, or neoplasm.

name: rectal tenesmus
clinical_significance: Rectal tenesmus is a persistent or urgent feeling of needing to pass stool despite an empty or nearly empty rectum, caused by inflammation, infection, mass, or motility disorder.

name: rectocele
clinical_significance: Bulging of the rectum into the back wall of the vagina because supporting tissues have weakened. It may cause pelvic pressure, difficulty emptying the bowel, or a vaginal bulge.

name: rectosigmoid neoplasm
clinical_significance: A rectosigmoid neoplasm is an abnormal growth where the sigmoid colon joins the rectum and may be benign or malignant.

name: rectovaginal fistula
clinical_significance: Abnormal connection between the rectum and vagina causing passage of stool or gas

name: rectum
clinical_significance: The final straight section of the large intestine, approximately 12-15 cm long,

name: rectus abdominis
clinical_significance: The rectus abdominis is a paired abdominal muscle that flexes the trunk, stabilizes the pelvis, and helps compress abdominal contents.

name: recurrent disease
clinical_significance: Return of a disease after a period of improvement, remission, or apparent absence, either at the original site or elsewhere.

name: recurrent fractures
clinical_significance: Repeated bone fractures, suggesting persistent trauma, osteoporosis, bone fragility, metabolic disease, tumor, or an inherited skeletal disorder.

name: red nucleus
clinical_significance: A group of nerve cells in the midbrain that helps coordinate movement through connections with the cerebellum and spinal cord. Damage to nearby pathways can cause weakness, tremor, or abnormal movement.

name: reducing agents
clinical_significance: Reducing agents are used in laboratory assays and some treatments because they donate electrons; exposure to strong agents can damage tissue, and compatibility matters in compounding and specimen handling.

name: reducing diet
clinical_significance: A reducing diet is a dietary pattern intended to reduce body weight. Clinically, sustainable calorie reduction and nutritional adequacy matter, especially when weight loss is used to improve obesity-related conditions.

name: reductase deficiency
clinical_significance: A disorder or laboratory finding caused by inadequate activity of a reductase enzyme, impairing a specific metabolic or hormone pathway.

name: reduviidae
clinical_significance: A family of insects including assassin bugs; some species transmit pathogens such as the parasite causing Chagas disease.

name: referral
clinical_significance: A request for assessment or treatment by another healthcare professional or service. Referrals help patients access specialized expertise, tests, procedures, rehabilitation, or coordinated care for a particular concern.

name: reflex
clinical_significance: A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus, such as pulling the hand away from heat. Reflex testing helps assess pathways involving the nerves, spinal cord, and brain.

name: reflex epilepsy
clinical_significance: Reflex epilepsy is epilepsy in which specific stimuli such as flashing light, sound, reading, or touch reliably trigger seizures.

name: reflux nephropathy
clinical_significance: Renal scarring and chronic kidney damage caused by vesicoureteral reflux, recurrent

name: refractive error
clinical_significance: A refractive error occurs when the eye does not focus light correctly on the retina, causing nearsightedness, farsightedness, astigmatism, or presbyopia.

name: refractometer
clinical_significance: A refractometer measures how much light bends through a substance and is used for fluid concentration, optical properties, or eye refraction.

name: refractometry
clinical_significance: Measurement of the eye’s refractive power to determine the optical correction needed for myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, or presbyopia.

name: refractory
clinical_significance: Resistant to a treatment or not responding adequately to it. The term may refer to cancer or other diseases.

name: refractory anemia
clinical_significance: An older term for anemia that does not improve with usual treatment. It may refer to a myelodysplastic syndrome or another cause, so evaluation looks for blood-cell disorders, bleeding, nutritional problems, kidney disease, and other conditions.

name: refractory cancer
clinical_significance: Refractory cancer is cancer that does not respond adequately to a treatment or begins progressing during treatment.

name: refractory disease
clinical_significance: Disease that does not improve adequately with appropriate standard treatment or that continues to worsen despite therapy. The term does not mean that every possible treatment has failed.

name: refsum disease
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which a fatty substance builds up in the body. It may cause night blindness, loss of smell, nerve damage, poor coordination, hearing loss, and scaly skin.

name: regeneration
clinical_significance: Growth or replacement of damaged or lost cells and tissues, helping restore structure or function after injury.

name: regional
clinical_significance: Relating to a particular body area, geographic area, or localized distribution rather than the whole body.

name: regional chemotherapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that delivers anticancer medicine directly to a body region or organ to produce a high local concentration while reducing, but not eliminating, exposure elsewhere. It is suitable only for selected cancers and carries procedure-related and medicine-related risks.

name: regulatory assessment
clinical_significance: Regulatory assessment evaluates evidence on a medicine, device, or biologic product to determine whether its quality, safety, and effectiveness support authorization and appropriate use.

name: regulatory authority
clinical_significance: A regulatory authority is a government or official body that sets and enforces standards for medicines, devices, facilities, professionals, or public health.

name: regulatory gene
clinical_significance: A gene that controls when, where, or how strongly another gene is used. Changes in regulatory genes or their control regions can alter development, cell growth, metabolism, or disease risk.

name: regulatory report
clinical_significance: A regulatory report documents safety, quality, or compliance information for health products or services; accurate reporting can prompt investigation, labeling changes, recalls, or other protective action.

name: regurgitation
clinical_significance: Backward flow of blood through a heart valve that does not close fully. Mild leakage may cause no symptoms; more severe leakage can enlarge or weaken the heart and cause breathlessness, tiredness, or swelling.

name: rehabilitation
clinical_significance: A coordinated process that helps a person restore or adapt physical, cognitive, psychological, and social

name: reifenstein syndrome
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder of androgen action, usually involving partial androgen insensitivity in an individual with a 46,XY chromosome pattern.

name: reiki
clinical_significance: Reiki is a complementary practice involving light touch or hands near the body. Evidence that it treats disease is limited.

name: reinfection
clinical_significance: A new episode of infection by the same or a related pathogen after the original

name: Reiter's syndrome
clinical_significance: Reiter’s syndrome is an outdated name for reactive arthritis, an inflammatory joint condition that can follow gastrointestinal or genital infection; current terminology emphasizes the postinfectious association and evaluation of the trigger.

name: relaxation
clinical_significance: A reduction in muscle tension, physiologic arousal, or psychological stress; techniques may include breathing, biofeedback, or progressive muscle relaxation.

name: relaxation therapy
clinical_significance: Techniques such as breathing, muscle relaxation, or imagery used to reduce stress, arousal, or symptom burden.

name: relaxin
clinical_significance: Relaxin is a reproductive hormone that helps remodel connective tissue and may contribute to cervical, pelvic, and vascular changes during pregnancy.

name: religion
clinical_significance: A system of spiritual beliefs and practices that may influence health decisions, coping, diet, treatment preferences, and end-of-life care.

name: REM sleep
clinical_significance: A sleep stage with rapid eye movements, active brain activity, and temporary relaxation of most skeletal muscles. Vivid dreams are common, and REM sleep supports memory, learning, emotional processing, and healthy development.

name: remission
clinical_significance: A period when the signs and symptoms of a disease decrease or disappear. Complete remission means no evidence of the disease can be found with available tests; partial remission means it has improved but remains detectable.

name: removal technique
clinical_significance: The method used to take away a foreign object, diseased tissue, stone, clot, or other material from the body. The appropriate method depends on its location, size, cause, and risk of bleeding, infection, or injury to nearby structures.

name: renal adenoma
clinical_significance: A renal adenoma is a usually benign kidney tumor, often discovered incidentally; its size, imaging features, and growth determine whether follow-up is needed.

name: renal artery
clinical_significance: One of the two main arteries carrying blood from the abdominal aorta to the kidneys. Each divides into smaller branches inside the kidney so blood reaches the filtering tissue.

name: renal carcinoma
clinical_significance: Renal carcinoma is cancer arising from kidney tissue, most commonly renal cell carcinoma. Cancer arising from kidney tissue, most often from cells lining the kidney's small filtering tubes.

name: renal cell carcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer beginning in the kidney’s small filtering tubes, most often the clear-cell type. It may cause blood in urine, pain, weight loss, fever, or no symptoms until found on imaging.

name: renal circulation
clinical_significance: Blood flow through the kidneys, which supports filtration, oxygen delivery, hormone production, and regulation of fluid and electrolytes.

name: renal colic
clinical_significance: Severe, wave-like pain caused when a kidney stone or other blockage stretches the urine tube. Pain usually starts in the side and may move toward the groin, with nausea, vomiting, or blood in urine; fever with blockage is an emergency.

name: renal cortex
clinical_significance: The outer layer of the kidney. It contains many of the structures that filter blood and process the first fluid that will become urine, while extensions of the cortex separate the inner kidney pyramids.

name: renal cyst
