clinical_significance: Kidney cysts are often benign incidental findings, but complex features, growth, pain, blood in urine, or impaired kidney function may require imaging follow-up.

name: renal dialysis
clinical_significance: Alternate term for dialysis: kidney replacement therapy using hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis to remove excess fluid and dissolved waste products when kidney function is inadequate.

name: renal failure
clinical_significance: Severe loss of kidney function, causing waste, extra fluid, and abnormal body salts to build up. It may develop suddenly and sometimes improve, or progress gradually as chronic kidney disease; dialysis or transplant may be needed.

name: renal function
clinical_significance: The kidneys’ ability to filter blood, remove waste, regulate fluids and electrolytes, maintain acid-base balance, and produce or activate hormones.

name: renal glomerulus
clinical_significance: A tiny ball of blood vessels inside each kidney filtering unit. Water and small dissolved substances pass from the blood through its walls to begin urine formation, while blood cells and most proteins remain in the bloodstream.

name: renal hamartoma
clinical_significance: A renal hamartoma is a benign disorganized overgrowth of mature tissues in the kidney, sometimes used to describe an angiomyolipoma-like lesion.

name: renal hypertension
clinical_significance: High blood pressure caused by kidney disease or narrowing of the renal arteries. High blood pressure caused by kidney disease or narrowed renal arteries, often requiring treatment of both causes.

name: renal hypertrophy
clinical_significance: Renal hypertrophy is enlargement of kidney tissue, often compensating for loss or reduced function of the other kidney but sometimes caused by disease.

name: renal insufficiency
clinical_significance: Renal insufficiency is reduced kidney function that impairs waste removal, fluid and electrolyte balance, acid handling, or hormone production.

name: renal medulla
clinical_significance: The inner part of the kidney containing tubes and blood vessels that help concentrate urine. It receives the fluid processed by the outer kidney and directs the finished urine toward the kidney’s central collecting area.

name: renal necrosis
clinical_significance: Renal necrosis is death of kidney tissue caused by severe ischemia, toxins, infection, obstruction, or other injury and can cause acute kidney failure.

name: renal oncocytoma
clinical_significance: A renal oncocytoma is a usually benign kidney tumor arising from oncocytic cells; imaging may not always distinguish it reliably from renal cancer.

name: renal parenchyma
clinical_significance: The working tissue of the kidney, containing the tiny filtering units and supporting structures that remove waste from blood, balance body fluids, and produce urine.

name: renal pelvis
clinical_significance: The funnel-shaped expansion of the ureter within the kidney, formed by the union of

name: renal reabsorption
clinical_significance: The return of water and useful substances, such as salt, sugar, and bicarbonate, from kidney tubes into the blood. This prevents their unnecessary loss and helps control body fluids and chemistry.

name: renal sarcoma
clinical_significance: Renal sarcoma is a rare malignant tumor arising from connective or supporting tissues of the kidney.

name: renal tubule
clinical_significance: A tiny nephron tube that reabsorbs needed water and substances and removes others into urine.

name: renal tubule acidosis
clinical_significance: A group of disorders in which the kidney tubules do not remove enough acid or conserve enough bicarbonate. The blood becomes too acidic, and complications may include low potassium, kidney stones, bone disease, weakness, or poor growth.

name: renal vein
clinical_significance: One of two large veins that carry blood away from the kidneys to the body’s main abdominal vein. A clot in a renal vein can impair drainage and damage kidney function.

name: renaut body
clinical_significance: A Renaut body is a specialized cluster of cells in the peripheral nerve endoneurium, associated with pressure sensitivity and sometimes nerve pathology.

name: renin
clinical_significance: An enzyme from kidney cells that starts a hormone chain controlling blood pressure, salt balance, and fluid levels.

name: renovascular hypertension
clinical_significance: High blood pressure caused by reduced blood flow through one or both kidney arteries, usually from narrowing. It may be suspected when hypertension begins suddenly or is difficult to control; treatment addresses blood pressure and, in selected cases, the narrowed artery.

name: renshaw cell
clinical_significance: A nerve cell in the spinal cord that helps limit and regulate the activity of motor neurons.

name: reoviridae
clinical_significance: Reoviridae is a family of segmented double-stranded RNA viruses. Human infections are often mild or unrecognized, but some reoviruses can cause respiratory or neurologic illness, particularly in vulnerable patients.

name: reoviridae infection
clinical_significance: An infection caused by a reovirus; illness varies by virus and host and is often mild or asymptomatic in humans.

name: repeat surgery
clinical_significance: Repeat surgery is a second or subsequent operation on the same or related area to treat persistent disease, recurrence, complications, or failure of prior treatment.

name: reperfusion therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that restores blood flow to tissue deprived of oxygen, such as clot-dissolving medicine, angioplasty, stenting, or surgery. Benefit depends on the tissue, duration of blockage, and risk of bleeding.

name: replication initiation
clinical_significance: The time and process when copying of DNA or another genetic molecule begins. Specific proteins recognize a starting region, separate the strands, and recruit enzymes that build matching new genetic material.

name: replicon
clinical_significance: A unit of genetic material that can replicate from one origin, such as a chromosome segment, plasmid, or viral genome.

name: reporter gene
clinical_significance: Reporter genes help researchers measure gene activity and validate laboratory systems; they are research tools rather than routine clinical tests, though the same principle informs some diagnostic assays.

name: repression
clinical_significance: The reduction or stopping of gene activity, cell activity, behavior, or a body process. In genetics, regulatory proteins can silence genes; in psychology, the term may describe unconsciously keeping distressing thoughts outside awareness.

name: reproduction
clinical_significance: The biological process by which living organisms produce new offspring, either sexually or without combining reproductive cells. In humans, it involves reproductive organs, hormones, eggs, sperm, pregnancy, and childbirth.

name: reproduction spores
clinical_significance: Some organisms reproduce by forming spores, which can persist in the environment and contribute to transmission; identifying the organism and its spore-forming capacity can guide infection control.

name: reproductive behavior
clinical_significance: Reproductive behavior can affect fertility, pregnancy risk, and exposure to sexually transmitted infections; sensitive, nonjudgmental assessment can inform counseling and preventive care.

name: reproductive history
clinical_significance: Reproductive history records pregnancies, births, miscarriages, abortions, menstrual function, fertility, contraception, and related conditions relevant to health assessment.

name: reproductive process
clinical_significance: Reproductive processes affect fertility, pregnancy, and sexual development; disturbances may signal endocrine, genetic, or reproductive-tract conditions requiring evaluation.

name: reproductive system
clinical_significance: The organs and tissues that produce gametes and reproductive hormones and support sexual development and reproduction. Depending on the anatomy present, it may enable sperm or egg production, fertilization, pregnancy, childbirth, and lactation.

name: reproductive technique
clinical_significance: A reproductive technique is a medical or laboratory method used to assist conception, preserve fertility, diagnose reproductive disease, or manage pregnancy.

name: reprogram
clinical_significance: To reprogram a cell means to alter its gene-expression state so it acquires a different developmental potential or function.

name: reptiles
clinical_significance: Reptiles can carry pathogens such as Salmonella without appearing ill, making hand hygiene and exposure history relevant when evaluating gastrointestinal infection, especially in young children or immunocompromised people.

name: research activity
clinical_significance: Research activity generates evidence that informs prevention, diagnosis, and treatment; ethical oversight and reliable methods are necessary before findings can guide patient care.

name: research design
clinical_significance: Research design determines how a study addresses its question and limits bias; clinicians use design and risk of bias to judge how much confidence to place in reported benefits and harms.

name: research personnel
clinical_significance: Research personnel conduct or oversee study procedures and data handling; training and role clarity support participant safety, informed consent, and data integrity.

name: research study
clinical_significance: A research study can provide evidence about health interventions or disease patterns; its design, size, limitations, and conflicts of interest affect how findings should be applied to patients.

name: resectable
clinical_significance: Describing a tumor or lesion that can be removed completely by surgery with acceptable risk and an appropriate margin, based on its extent and relationship to vital structures.

name: resectoscope
clinical_significance: An endoscopic surgical instrument with a viewing system and working loop used to remove or cauterize tissue, especially during prostate or bladder procedures.

name: reserpine
clinical_significance: Reserpine is an older blood-pressure medicine that depletes catecholamines. It can cause low blood pressure, slow heart rate, nasal congestion, and mood or movement-related adverse effects, so use requires careful selection and monitoring.

name: residential mobility
clinical_significance: Residential mobility is movement between homes or communities and can affect continuity of care, social support, exposure, and health access.

name: residual neoplasm
clinical_significance: A residual neoplasm is tumor tissue that remains after treatment intended to remove or destroy the original tumor.

name: residual risk
clinical_significance: Residual risk is the chance of harm that remains after preventive measures, treatment, screening, or controls have been applied.

name: residual tumor
clinical_significance: A residual tumor is cancer or other tumor tissue that remains after surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, or another treatment.

name: residual volume
clinical_significance: The amount of air remaining in the lungs after breathing out as forcefully as possible. It keeps small airways open and cannot be measured accurately by ordinary spirometry alone.

name: resin
clinical_significance: Resins are used in some medical devices, dental materials, and drug formulations; allergy or irritation to a specific resin may matter when selecting materials or investigating contact dermatitis.

name: resiquimod
clinical_significance: Resiquimod is an investigational immune-response modifier that activates Toll-like receptors 7 and 8. It has been studied topically for skin lesions and cancer, but it is not established routine therapy.

name: resistance training
clinical_significance: Exercise in which muscles work against weights, bands, body weight, or other resistance. Regular training can improve strength, endurance, balance, bone health, function, and independence when progressed safely.

name: resistant starch
clinical_significance: Starch that resists digestion in the small intestine and is fermented by gut bacteria in the colon.

name: resorption
clinical_significance: The body's breakdown and removal of tissue or material, especially old bone. The released components may be absorbed, reused, or removed from the body.

name: respiration
clinical_significance: The processes of breathing, gas exchange, and cellular energy production involving oxygen and carbon dioxide.

name: respiratory acidosis
clinical_significance: A condition in which breathing does not remove enough carbon dioxide, making the blood too acidic. It can result from lung disease, blocked airways, weak breathing muscles, brain disorders, or medicines that slow breathing.

name: respiratory alkalosis
clinical_significance: A condition in which breathing removes too much carbon dioxide, making the blood less acidic. It can occur with anxiety, pain, fever, low oxygen, pregnancy, severe infection, or other conditions that cause rapid breathing.

name: respiratory arrest
clinical_significance: Stopping of effective breathing. It is an immediate emergency that may require airway support, rescue breathing or ventilation, and treatment of the cause.

name: respiratory burst
clinical_significance: A rapid release of chemically reactive oxygen molecules by certain immune cells after they engulf germs. This helps kill the germs inside the cell, although excessive activity can also damage nearby tissue.

name: respiratory disorder
clinical_significance: A disease affecting the airways, lungs, pleura, respiratory muscles, or control of breathing and causing impaired ventilation, oxygenation, or gas exchange.

name: respiratory distress
clinical_significance: Difficult or labored breathing caused by problems such as asthma, infection, a blood clot, a collapsed lung, an allergic reaction, or heart failure. Fast breathing, struggling to speak, blue lips, or severe exhaustion may occur.

name: respiratory infection
clinical_significance: An infection of the upper or lower respiratory tract caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi, or other organisms.

name: respiratory muscle
clinical_significance: A muscle used for breathing, especially the diaphragm and muscles between the ribs. These muscles expand and contract the chest to move air into and out of the lungs.

name: respiratory neoplasm
clinical_significance: A respiratory neoplasm is an abnormal growth in the airways or lungs and may be benign or malignant.

name: respiratory paralysis
clinical_significance: Respiratory paralysis is failure of the muscles needed for breathing because of nerve, muscle, brainstem, toxin, or spinal-cord dysfunction and is an emergency.

name: respiratory rate
clinical_significance: The number of breaths taken per minute. The expected rate varies with age, activity, temperature, illness, and other factors.

name: respiratory system
clinical_significance: The nose, mouth, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, lungs, pleura, and breathing muscles, including the diaphragm and chest-wall muscles. It moves air into and out of the lungs and exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide between the alveoli and blood.

name: respiratory therapy
clinical_significance: Respiratory therapy includes treatments and breathing support that improve ventilation, oxygenation, airway clearance, or lung function.

name: respiratory transport
clinical_significance: Respiratory transport is movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide between lungs, blood, and tissues, largely through hemoglobin and dissolved gas.

name: respirovirus
clinical_significance: A genus of paramyxoviruses that includes human parainfluenza viruses, which can cause croup and other respiratory infections.

name: respite care
clinical_significance: Temporary care for a person who needs support so that a usual family or unpaid caregiver can rest, attend appointments, or manage other responsibilities. It may be provided at home, in a facility, or through short-term services.

name: response element
clinical_significance: A response element is a DNA sequence that regulates gene activity. Changes in these elements can alter protein expression and contribute to disease, while their study helps identify mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets.

name: restenosis
clinical_significance: Re-narrowing of a blood vessel after it has been opened by angioplasty or another procedure.

name: restless legs syndrome
clinical_significance: A neurological and sleep-related condition causing an irresistible urge to move the legs, often with crawling, pulling, aching, or tingling sensations. Symptoms begin or worsen during rest, improve temporarily with movement, and are worse in the evening or at night; they may disrupt sleep and daytime function. Iron deficiency, kidney disease, pregnancy, some medicines, and genetic factors may contribute.

name: restlessness
clinical_significance: Restlessness is an uncomfortable need to move or inability to remain still, caused by anxiety, akathisia, restless-legs syndrome, pain, stimulants, withdrawal, or medical illness.

name: restriction mapping
clinical_significance: Restriction mapping uses enzyme-cut DNA patterns to analyze genetic material; it has historical and research value, while modern clinical genetic testing generally uses sequencing or other validated methods.

name: restrictive cardiomyopathy
clinical_significance: A disease in which stiff heart muscle cannot relax and fill normally. It may cause breathlessness, tiredness, swelling, or abnormal rhythms and can result from conditions such as amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, iron overload, or scarring.

name: resuscitation
clinical_significance: Emergency measures used to restore or support breathing and circulation, including opening the airway, rescue breathing, chest compressions, defibrillation, medicines, and treatment of the cause.

name: resveratrol
clinical_significance: Resveratrol is a plant-derived compound marketed as a supplement. Evidence for preventing or treating disease is insufficient, and supplement quality or interactions may complicate its use with medicines.

name: retainer
clinical_significance: A dental appliance worn after orthodontic treatment to help keep teeth in their corrected positions.

name: retching
clinical_significance: Repeated involuntary effort to vomit without necessarily producing stomach contents.

name: reticular dermis
clinical_significance: The deeper layer of the dermis containing dense connective tissue, collagen, elastin, blood vessels, nerves, glands, and hair follicles.

name: reticular formation
clinical_significance: A network of nerve cells in the brainstem that helps control alertness, sleep, attention, muscle tone, posture, breathing, heart function, and responses to pain.

name: reticulin
clinical_significance: A network-forming type of collagen that supports bone marrow, liver, lymph nodes, and other organs.

name: reticulocyte
clinical_significance: A young red blood cell recently released from bone marrow. The number of reticulocytes shows how actively the marrow is replacing red cells and helps distinguish reduced production from blood loss or red-cell breakdown.

name: reticulocyte count
clinical_significance: The number or percentage of immature red blood cells in blood. It reflects recent bone-

name: reticulocytopenia
clinical_significance: An abnormally low reticulocyte count indicating reduced effective red-cell production, which may occur with marrow failure, nutrient deficiency, inflammation, or kidney disease.

name: reticulocytosis
clinical_significance: Reticulocytosis is an increased number of immature red blood cells in blood, usually indicating stimulated marrow production after blood loss or hemolysis.

name: reticuloendothelial system
clinical_significance: A diffuse anatomical network of specialized phagocytic cells (primarily monocytes and tissue macrophages) situated in reticular connective tissue frameworks of the spleen, liver (Kupffer cells), lymph nodes, and bone marrow, responsible for filtering particulate foreign matter, microbial pathogens, and senescent erythrocytes.

name: reticulophagy
clinical_significance: A cell-cleaning process that removes worn or damaged parts of the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's internal membrane network. The material is broken down and recycled, helping cells control quality and respond to stress.

name: reticulosarcoma
clinical_significance: Reticulosarcoma is an older, imprecise name for certain malignant tumors of reticular tissue; current classification and pathology are needed to identify the specific lymphoma or other cancer and guide treatment.

name: reticulum
clinical_significance: A network-like structure; in anatomy or cell biology it may refer to a tissue network, endoplasmic reticulum, or ruminant stomach compartment.

name: retina
clinical_significance: The light-sensitive neural tissue lining the back of the eye that converts light into nerve signals.

name: retina disorder
clinical_significance: A disease affecting the retina, including vascular, degenerative, inflammatory, infectious, traumatic, inherited, or neoplastic conditions that can impair vision.

name: retina hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding within or beneath the retina caused by vascular disease, diabetes, hypertension, trauma, retinal vein occlusion, inflammation, or other disorders.

name: retinal cone
clinical_significance: A light-sensing cell in the retina that provides color vision and sharp detail, especially in daylight. Damage to cone cells can reduce color perception and central vision.

name: retinal damage
clinical_significance: Injury or disease affecting the retina, potentially causing blurred vision, field loss, flashes, floaters, or permanent visual impairment.

name: retinal degeneration
clinical_significance: Progressive damage or loss of light-sensitive cells in the retina at the back of the eye. It may cause blurred or reduced central vision, night blindness, or loss of side vision and can result from inherited disease, aging, or other injury.

name: retinal detachment
clinical_significance: Separation of the light-sensitive retina from the supporting retinal pigment epithelium beneath it. A rhegmatogenous detachment follows a retinal break, a tractional detachment results from scar tissue pulling on the retina, and an exudative detachment results from fluid collecting beneath it. It can cause flashes, floaters, a curtain-like shadow, or reduced vision.

name: retinal dysplasia
clinical_significance: Abnormal development and arrangement of the retina, the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye. It may impair vision and can occur with conditions present from birth, genetic disorders, or problems affecting development before birth.

name: retinal dystrophy
clinical_significance: Gradual loss or damage of retinal cells, often caused by an inherited condition. It may begin with night blindness, difficulty seeing in dim light, or loss of side vision and can progress to serious sight impairment.

name: retinal fold
clinical_significance: A retinal fold is a crease or ridge in the retina caused by traction, developmental abnormality, detachment, swelling, or another ocular process.

name: retinal ganglion
clinical_significance: A nerve cell in the retina that collects signals from other retinal cells and sends them through the optic nerve to the brain. It is essential for carrying visual information out of the eye.

name: retinal macula
clinical_significance: The macula is the central region of the retina responsible for detailed straight-ahead vision, reading, and color discrimination.

name: retinal neoplasm
clinical_significance: A retinal neoplasm is an abnormal growth arising in or near the retina, such as retinoblastoma or a metastatic tumor.

name: retinal perforation
clinical_significance: A full-thickness hole or tear in the retina. Fluid can pass through the opening and separate the retina from the tissue beneath it, causing flashes, floaters, or loss of vision.

name: retinal pigment
clinical_significance: Retinal pigment refers to melanin-containing pigment in the retinal pigment epithelium, which supports photoreceptors and absorbs excess light.

name: retinal vasculitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of blood vessels in the retina. Leaking or blocked vessels can cause blurred vision, bleeding, swelling, or permanent sight loss; it may be linked to infection, autoimmune disease, or inflammation elsewhere in the body.

name: retinaldehyde
clinical_significance: A form of vitamin A used in the eye’s light-sensing cycle. Light changes it inside photoreceptor cells, helping start the nerve signals that allow vision.

name: retinitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. It may cause blurred vision, floaters, flashes, or loss of sight and needs prompt eye assessment.

name: retinitis pigmentosa
clinical_significance: A group of inherited retinal disorders in which light-sensing cells gradually degenerate, usually first affecting rod cells. It commonly causes night blindness and progressive loss of peripheral vision; central vision may decline later.

name: retinoblastoma
clinical_significance: The most common eye cancer in infants and young children, starting in the retina at the back of the eye. It is caused by changes in the \textit{RB1} gene. It can be inherited (often affecting both eyes) or occur by chance (usually affecting only one eye). The most common early signs are leukocoria (an abnormal white glow in the pupil, often noticed in flash photographs instead of the normal red reflex) and strabismus (crossed or misaligned eyes). Diagnosis is made through a specialized dilated e

name: retinoblastoma protein
clinical_significance: A protein made from the RB1 gene that helps prevent cells from dividing when they should not. Loss of its protective function can contribute to retinoblastoma and other cancers.

name: retinoid
clinical_significance: A vitamin-A-related substance used in selected skin treatments and other medical care. Retinoids can improve acne or abnormal cell growth but may irritate skin, interact with medicines, and harm an unborn baby.

name: retinopathy of prematurity
clinical_significance: Abnormal development of retinal blood vessels in premature infants. Mild disease may resolve, while severe abnormal vessel growth and scar tissue can pull on the retina, causing retinal detachment and vision loss.

name: retinoschisis
clinical_significance: Splitting between layers of the retina. It may result from aging or an inherited condition and can cause reduced sharpness or loss of part of the visual field; it differs from retinal detachment but may look similar on examination.

name: retinoscope
clinical_significance: An instrument that shines light into the eye to help determine refractive error. A lighted instrument used to estimate focusing error by observing how light reflects from the retina.

name: retirement
clinical_significance: Retirement is withdrawal from regular employment or a career; changes in income, activity, social contact, and health coverage can affect wellbeing.

name: retortamonas intestinalis
clinical_significance: Retortamonas intestinalis is an intestinal protozoan generally regarded as nonpathogenic; finding it in stool usually does not establish the cause of symptoms and should be interpreted with other test results.

name: retractile testis
clinical_significance: A testis that moves between the scrotum and groin because of a strong reflex but can be gently brought into the scrotum. It should be monitored because it may later become undescended.

name: retractor
clinical_significance: A surgical instrument used to hold tissue or an organ aside so the area can be seen and reached during an examination or operation. Some retractors are held by hand; others stay in place by themselves.

name: retreatment
clinical_significance: Retreatment is additional therapy after an initial course fails, disease returns, or the response is incomplete; the choice depends on prior treatment, current disease status, expected benefit, and cumulative toxicity.

name: retrobulbar hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding behind the eyeball within the orbit, often after trauma or surgery, that can rapidly increase orbital pressure and threaten vision.

name: retroesophageal
clinical_significance: Retroesophageal means located behind the esophagus, such as a mass, lymph node, vessel, or collection in the posterior mediastinum.

name: retrognathia
clinical_significance: Retrognathia is backward positioning of the lower jaw relative to the upper jaw and may affect facial structure, bite, airway, or sleep breathing.

name: retrograde amnesia
clinical_significance: Loss of memory for events that occurred before an injury, illness, or other triggering event, with variable preservation of more remote memories.

name: retrograde degeneration
clinical_significance: Breakdown of a nerve fiber that spreads back toward the nerve cell body after the fiber is injured. It can reduce movement, sensation, or organ function depending on which nerve is affected and how severe the injury is.

name: retrograde ejaculation
clinical_significance: A condition in which semen enters the bladder instead of leaving through the penis during orgasm. It may cause little or no semen to appear and can result from diabetes, surgery, nerve problems, or medicines. It may affect fertility.

name: retroperitoneal fibrosis
clinical_significance: Formation of abnormal scar-like tissue in the space behind the abdominal organs. It often surrounds the tubes draining urine from the kidneys, causing back or abdominal pain, urine blockage, and reduced kidney function; medicines, immune disease, or cancer can cause it.

name: retroperitoneal neoplasm
clinical_significance: A retroperitoneal neoplasm is an abnormal growth in the tissue space behind the abdominal lining and may be benign or malignant.

name: retroperitoneal space
clinical_significance: The retroperitoneal space is the area behind the peritoneal lining containing the kidneys, adrenal glands, pancreas, parts of the bowel, vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.

name: retropharyngeal abscess
clinical_significance: A collection of pus in the tissues behind the throat, usually after infection or injury. Fever, severe throat or neck pain, difficulty swallowing, drooling, noisy breathing, or a stiff neck can occur. The abscess can threaten the airway.

name: retrospective studies
clinical_significance: Retrospective studies examine existing records or past exposures and outcomes; they are efficient but vulnerable to missing data, bias, and confounding.

name: retrotracheal
clinical_significance: Retrotracheal means located behind the trachea, such as a mass, lymph node, vessel, or collection in the posterior mediastinum.

name: retrotransposition
clinical_significance: The copying and insertion of a genetic sequence into a new place in the genome using an RNA copy as an intermediate. New insertions can be harmless or disrupt a gene and cause disease.

name: retroviral vector
clinical_significance: Retroviral vectors are modified viruses used to deliver genes into cells, including in some gene and cell therapies. Their integrating behavior can enable durable expression but carries risks such as insertional effects and requires specialized safety monitoring.

name: retroviridae
clinical_significance: A family of RNA viruses that make a DNA copy of their genetic material and insert it into infected cells. HIV is a member; these viruses can cause persistent infection, immune disease, or cancer.

name: retroviridae infection
clinical_significance: An infection caused by a retrovirus, which may persist through genomic integration and cause immune, neurologic, or malignant disease.

name: rett syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare genetic disorder that affects brain development and occurs almost exclusively in girls. Development may appear typical for the first 6 to 18 months, followed by loss of previously learned language, purposeful hand use, coordination, or movement. Repeated hand movements such as hand-wringing or clapping are common. Slowed head growth, seizures, breathing changes, feeding problems, sleep problems, and curvature of the spine (scoliosis) may occur. Most cases are caused by a new change in the

name: revascularization surgery
clinical_significance: Revascularization surgery restores blood flow around a blocked or narrowed vessel, such as in coronary artery bypass or limb bypass surgery.

name: reversal learning
clinical_significance: Reversal learning is the ability to change a learned response when the previously rewarded or correct choice is no longer so.

name: reverse transcription
clinical_significance: The production of DNA using RNA as a template, carried out by reverse transcriptase. Some viruses use this process to copy their genetic material, and laboratories use it to study RNA.

name: Reye's syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare, potentially fatal illness causing acute brain dysfunction and liver injury, associated particularly with viral illness and aspirin exposure in children.

name: R-factor
clinical_significance: A laboratory measure comparing the amount of an antibiotic needed to stop a bacterium with the expected effective amount. A higher value suggests reduced susceptibility and may help guide antibiotic choice.

name: rgs proteins
clinical_significance: Regulators of G-protein signaling are proteins that speed the switch-off of signals from G-protein-coupled receptors. They help control responses to hormones, neurotransmitters, and other signals and may influence disease when altered.

name: rh isoimmunization
clinical_significance: Maternal alloantibody production against fetal Rh D-positive red blood cells in an Rh

name: rhabdoid tumor
clinical_significance: A rare, fast-growing cancer that usually affects infants and young children. It may begin in the kidney, brain, or other tissues; changes in genes that control cell growth, especially SMARCB1, are common.

name: rhabdomyolysis
clinical_significance: Rhabdomyolysis is rapid breakdown of skeletal muscle that releases muscle proteins and salts into the bloodstream. Causes include crush injury, extreme exertion, seizures, heat illness, medicines, and metabolic disease. It may cause muscle pain, weakness, dark urine, kidney injury, abnormal heart rhythms, or dangerous pressure in a limb. A high creatine kinase level supports the diagnosis.

name: rhabdomyoma
clinical_significance: A usually noncancerous tumor made of heart-muscle cells, seen mainly in infants and children. It is strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis and may shrink on its own, but large or multiple tumors can block blood flow or disturb the heart rhythm.

name: rhabdomyosarcoma
clinical_significance: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a malignant tumor showing skeletal-muscle differentiation, occurring most often in children but also in adults.

name: rhabdoviridae
clinical_significance: Rhabdoviridae includes viruses such as rabies virus. Suspected rabies exposure is a medical emergency because prompt wound care and post-exposure prophylaxis can prevent an otherwise almost invariably fatal infection.

name: rhamnose
clinical_significance: Rhamnose is a sugar used in microbiology and biochemical research; its detection can help characterize organisms or molecules but is not generally a standalone clinical diagnostic marker.

name: rhesus incompatibility
clinical_significance: Rhesus incompatibility occurs when an RhD-negative pregnant person forms antibodies against RhD-positive fetal red cells, risking haemolytic disease in a later or affected pregnancy; anti-D immunoglobulin prevents sensitization.

name: rheumatic chorea
clinical_significance: Involuntary, irregular, fidgety movements caused by an immune reaction after group A streptococcal infection. It is a feature of acute rheumatic fever and may affect the face, arms, legs, speech, or handwriting.

name: rheumatic fever
clinical_significance: An immune-mediated inflammatory illness that can develop after a group A streptococcal infection, usually strep throat. It may affect the heart, joints, skin, or brain. Heart inflammation can cause lasting valve damage (rheumatic heart disease). Diagnosis uses clinical criteria and evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection.

name: rheumatic heart disease
clinical_significance: Permanent damage to heart valves after rheumatic fever, an immune reaction following group A streptococcal throat infection. It most often affects the mitral valve and can cause breathlessness, tiredness, swelling, abnormal rhythms, or heart failure.

name: rheumatism
clinical_significance: Pain, stiffness, or discomfort in joints and surrounding soft tissues.

name: rheumatoid arthritis
clinical_significance: A long-term autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of the joints. This causes inflammation, pain, swelling, warmth, and stiffness, often worse after waking or resting. It commonly affects the same joints on both sides of the body, especially the hands, wrists, and feet. Over time, the inflammation can damage cartilage and bone and reduce joint function. It may also cause tiredness, low-grade fever, or loss of appetite and can affect the eyes, lungs, heart, bl

name: rheumatoid factor
clinical_significance: An antibody that mistakenly recognizes part of another antibody. A blood test may support the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, but it can also be positive in other diseases or in healthy people.

name: rheumatoid nodule
clinical_significance: A rheumatoid nodule is a firm inflammatory lump under the skin or near a joint in rheumatoid arthritis, often over pressure points.

name: rheumatologist
clinical_significance: A medical doctor who diagnoses and treats diseases affecting joints, muscles, bones, and connective tissues, especially autoimmune and inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, gout, and vasculitis.

name: rhinitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or irritation of the lining of the nose. It can cause a blocked or runny nose, sneezing, itching, and reduced smell and may result from allergy, infection, smoke, strong smells, medicines, or other triggers.

name: rhinocephaly
clinical_significance: A very rare birth defect involving severe abnormal development of the face and forebrain, with a nose-like structure that may lie unusually high or between the eyes. It is usually associated with major neurologic and developmental abnormalities.

name: rhinophyma
clinical_significance: Progressive thickening and enlargement of the nose caused by long-standing changes often associated with rosacea. It may produce a rough, irregular appearance and can sometimes interfere with breathing or require surgical treatment.

name: rhinoplasty
clinical_significance: Surgery to reshape, repair, or reconstruct the nose for breathing, injury, birth differences, or appearance. Recovery includes swelling and bruising, and results depend on anatomy, technique, healing, and patient goals.

name: rhinorrhea
clinical_significance: Excessive watery or mucoid discharge from the nose, commonly caused by infection, allergy, irritants, or changes in temperature.

name: rhinoscopy
clinical_significance: Examination of the nasal cavity and nasopharynx using an instrument or endoscope to assess the mucosa, septum, turbinates, masses, bleeding, or obstruction.

name: rhinovirus
clinical_significance: A genus of non-enveloped, positive-sense RNA viruses in the Picornaviridae family. Rhinoviruses

name: rhinovirus A
clinical_significance: A species group of rhinoviruses that commonly causes the common cold and can worsen asthma or trigger wheezing.

name: rhinovirus C
clinical_significance: A rhinovirus group associated with common-cold symptoms and, in some children, more severe wheezing or lower-respiratory illness.

name: rhizobiaceae
clinical_significance: Rhizobiaceae bacteria are primarily known for plant associations and nitrogen fixation; they are not usual human pathogens, though unusual infections may occur in people with impaired immunity.

name: rhizobium
clinical_significance: Rhizobium species are mainly environmental and plant-associated bacteria. They rarely cause human disease, but recovery from a clinical specimen should be assessed for contamination versus true infection.

name: rhizomucor
clinical_significance: A genus of molds that can cause mucormycosis, especially in people with diabetes, neutropenia, or severe immune suppression.

name: rhizomucor pusillus
clinical_significance: A mold that can cause invasive mucormycosis involving the lungs, sinuses, skin, or other organs in severely immunocompromised people.

name: rhizopus
clinical_significance: A genus of molds that includes important causes of mucormycosis, a rapidly invasive infection of sinuses, lungs, skin, or other tissues.

name: rhizopus oryzae
clinical_significance: A mold, also called Rhizopus arrhizus, that is a common cause of invasive mucormycosis.

name: rhizoxin
clinical_significance: Rhizoxin is a compound studied for antitumor activity and as a natural toxin; it is not an established routine cancer treatment, and toxic exposure can damage cells.

name: rhodium
clinical_significance: A chemical element used in industrial and dental materials; its compounds can irritate tissues and may cause allergic reactions.

name: rhodobacteraceae
clinical_significance: Rhodobacteraceae are environmental bacteria with no common role in human disease; their significance depends on the species and whether they are recovered from a normally sterile clinical site.

name: rhodococcus
clinical_significance: A genus of gram-positive bacteria that includes Rhodococcus equi, an opportunistic pathogen causing pneumonia mainly in immunocompromised people.

name: rhodococcus equi
clinical_significance: A gram-positive bacterium that can cause cavitary pneumonia and disseminated infection, especially in people with advanced immune suppression.

name: rhodopseudomonas
clinical_significance: Rhodopseudomonas are environmental photosynthetic bacteria and are not common human pathogens; an isolate from a patient requires clinical correlation to distinguish contamination from rare opportunistic infection.

name: rhodopsin
clinical_significance: A light-sensitive protein in rod cells of the retina that enables vision in dim light.

name: rhodospirillaceae
clinical_significance: A family of metabolically diverse bacteria found in soil and water; some species carry out photosynthesis or nitrogen fixation.

name: rhodospirillales
clinical_significance: Rhodospirillales is an order of environmental bacteria, not a usual cause of human infection; clinical relevance depends on species identification and the source of the specimen.

name: rhodospirillum
clinical_significance: A genus of spiral-shaped aquatic bacteria capable of photosynthesis or nitrogen fixation; human infection is rare.

name: rhodotorula glutinis
clinical_significance: Rhodotorula glutinis is an environmental yeast that can rarely cause opportunistic infection, particularly in immunocompromised patients or those with intravascular devices; species identification and susceptibility may guide treatment.

name: rhombencephalon
clinical_significance: The hindbrain region of an early embryo. It develops into the pons, medulla, cerebellum, and related structures that help control breathing, balance, movement, swallowing, and other essential functions.

name: rhonchi
clinical_significance: Low-pitched breathing sounds caused by air moving through narrowed or mucus-filled larger airways, often changing after coughing.

name: rib
clinical_significance: One of 12 paired, curved bones forming the thoracic cage, protecting the heart, lungs,

name: rib fracture
clinical_significance: A break in one or more ribs, usually causing localized chest pain worsened by breathing, coughing, or movement and sometimes associated with injury to underlying organs.

name: ribavirin
clinical_significance: An antiviral medicine used in selected viral infections, usually in combination and under specialist supervision.

name: riboflavin
clinical_significance: A water-soluble vitamin that forms the coenzymes FAD and FMN. These cofactors

name: riboflavin assay
clinical_significance: A riboflavin assay measures vitamin B2 status or concentration in a sample. Testing may help investigate suspected deficiency or research metabolism, but results must be interpreted with diet, symptoms, and other findings.

name: riboflavin deficiency
clinical_significance: Deficiency of vitamin B2, which can cause inflammation or fissuring of the mouth and lips, sore throat, dermatitis, anemia, and other mucosal or systemic findings.

name: ribonuclease
clinical_significance: An enzyme that cuts RNA, a molecule involved in reading genetic instructions, into smaller pieces. Ribonucleases help control how long RNA lasts, recycle cell material, and protect cells from some unwanted genetic material.

name: ribonuclease h
clinical_significance: An enzyme that removes the RNA strand when RNA and DNA are joined together. Cells use it during DNA copying, and some viruses depend on related activity when making DNA from their RNA.

name: ribonuclease iii
clinical_significance: An enzyme that cuts double-stranded RNA into smaller pieces. The products can help control gene activity, make proteins, or process genetic material in cells and some microorganisms.

name: ribonucleic acid
clinical_significance: RNA is a nucleic acid that carries genetic instructions, helps make proteins, and regulates cell activity; some viruses use RNA as their genetic material.

name: ribonucleoprotein
clinical_significance: A structure made of RNA joined to one or more proteins. It helps make, process, transport, or control RNA; antibodies against certain ribonucleoproteins can occur in autoimmune diseases.

name: ribonucleoside
clinical_significance: A molecule made of a ribose sugar joined to one of the bases used in RNA. Examples include adenosine, guanosine, cytidine, and uridine; adding phosphate groups produces RNA building blocks.

name: ribonucleotide reductase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that changes RNA building blocks into the related building blocks needed to make DNA. Cells require it to copy and repair DNA, so it is important for growth and is a target of some cancer medicines.

name: ribonucleotides
clinical_significance: Nucleotides containing ribose sugar and RNA bases, serving as RNA building blocks and cellular energy or signaling molecules.

name: ribophagy
clinical_significance: A cell-cleaning process that breaks down some ribosomes, the structures that make proteins, so their parts can be recycled. It helps cells adjust protein production when nutrients or growth conditions change.

name: ribose
clinical_significance: A five-carbon sugar used to build RNA, ATP, and other molecules involved in storing genetic information and transferring energy. Cells make ribose from other nutrients and use it in many normal chemical processes.

name: ribosomal protein
clinical_significance: A protein that combines with ribosomal RNA to form a ribosome, the cell structure that builds proteins. Inherited changes in some ribosomal proteins can cause bone-marrow failure or developmental syndromes.

name: ribosomal RNA
clinical_significance: RNA that forms the main structural and working part of ribosomes, the cell structures that make proteins. It helps position messenger RNA and joins amino acids together; its genes are also used in some laboratory studies to identify organisms.

name: ribosome
clinical_significance: A cellular structure made of RNA and proteins that reads messenger RNA and links amino acids together to make proteins.

name: ribosome subunit
clinical_significance: One of the two RNA-and-protein parts of a ribosome. The small and large parts join around messenger RNA and work together to assemble amino acids into a protein.

name: ribostamycin
clinical_significance: Ribostamycin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used in some settings against susceptible bacteria. As with this drug class, kidney injury and hearing or balance toxicity are important considerations, and susceptibility guides use.

name: ribozyme
clinical_significance: Ribozymes are RNA molecules with catalytic activity; they are studied in gene regulation and therapeutic development, but are not routine clinical tests or treatments.

name: Richter's syndrome
clinical_significance: Transformation of chronic lymphocytic leukemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma into an aggressive lymphoma, most often diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

name: ricin
clinical_significance: Ricin is a highly toxic plant protein that blocks protein synthesis; ingestion, inhalation, or injection can cause severe organ injury and death.

name: rickets
clinical_significance: A condition in children whose growing bones do not harden normally, usually because of too little vitamin D, calcium, or phosphate. It can cause weak or bowed bones, bone pain, and problems with growth.

name: rickettsia
clinical_significance: A group of small intracellular bacteria transmitted mainly by arthropods and causing diseases such as typhus and spotted fevers.

name: rickettsia felis
clinical_significance: A flea-associated bacterium that can cause a spotted-fever-like illness in people. Infection may produce fever, headache, rash, fatigue, or muscle aches and is assessed with exposure history and laboratory testing.

name: rickettsia infections
clinical_significance: Rickettsial infections are illnesses caused by intracellular bacteria spread mainly by ticks, fleas, lice, or mites and often causing fever and rash.

name: rickettsia japonica
clinical_significance: A bacterium spread by ticks and associated with Japanese spotted fever. Infection may cause fever, headache, rash, and a dark mark where the tick bit; treatment uses suitable antibiotics.

name: rickettsia prowazekii
clinical_significance: A bacterium that causes epidemic typhus and is mainly spread through infected body-lice feces. Disease can cause high fever, headache, rash, confusion, and serious organ complications without prompt antibiotic treatment.

name: rickettsia rickettsii
clinical_significance: A bacterium spread by infected ticks that causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Fever, severe headache, rash, muscle aches, or confusion may develop; prompt antibiotic treatment is important because the illness can rapidly become life-threatening.

name: rickettsia typhi
clinical_significance: A bacterium spread mainly by infected fleas and responsible for murine typhus. The illness commonly causes fever, headache, chills, and sometimes a rash; prompt antibiotic treatment usually works, but untreated infection can become severe.

name: rickettsiaceae
clinical_significance: A family of bacteria that live inside cells and includes several organisms spread by ticks, fleas, lice, or mites. They can cause fever, rash, blood-vessel inflammation, and serious organ complications.

name: ridaforolimus
clinical_significance: Ridaforolimus is an investigational mTOR inhibitor studied for cancer treatment. Its immune-suppressing and metabolic effects, including infection risk and abnormal glucose or lipids, are relevant to clinical trials.

name: ridged nail
clinical_significance: A ridged nail has longitudinal or transverse grooves in its surface, which may result from aging, trauma, inflammation, nutritional problems, or systemic disease.

name: Riedel's thyroiditis
clinical_significance: A rare form of thyroid inflammation in which tough scar-like tissue makes the thyroid hard and may spread into nearby structures. It can cause a neck lump, difficulty swallowing or breathing, or reduced thyroid function.

name: Rieger syndrome
clinical_significance: A genetic condition affecting development of the front of the eye and often the teeth. It may cause glaucoma, unusual teeth, or changes around the navel and can result from changes in genes such as PITX2 or FOXC1.

name: rifabutin
clinical_significance: A rifamycin antibiotic used mainly for selected mycobacterial infections and tuberculosis regimens; it has important drug interactions and can discolor body fluids.

name: rifampin
clinical_significance: Rifampin is a rifamycin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and is a key component of tuberculosis treatment; it causes orange body fluids and has many drug interactions and hepatotoxicity risk.

name: rifamycin
clinical_significance: Rifamycin is an antibiotic that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase; related rifamycin medicines are used for tuberculosis and other infections.

name: rifaximin
clinical_significance: Rifaximin is a minimally absorbed rifamycin antibiotic used for selected intestinal infections, prevention of recurrent hepatic encephalopathy, and some diarrhoeal syndromes; indication and resistance patterns guide use.

name: right atrium
clinical_significance: The upper-right chamber of the heart. It receives oxygen-poor blood from the body and passes it through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which sends it to the lungs.

name: right eye
clinical_significance: Right-eye findings must be documented separately from left-eye findings because visual acuity, fields, pupils, and retinal disease can differ between eyes and affect diagnosis and treatment.

name: right kidney
clinical_significance: Right-kidney imaging or examination findings should be distinguished from the left kidney; laterality guides procedures and helps interpret obstruction, stones, masses, and changes in function.

name: right lung
clinical_significance: Right-lung findings should be localized by lobe and side because pneumonia, collapse, nodules, and pleural disease may be unilateral and guide imaging, sampling, or treatment.

name: right ventricle
clinical_significance: The lower-right chamber of the heart. It receives oxygen-poor blood from the right atrium and pumps it through the pulmonary valve into the lung arteries to receive oxygen.

name: righting reflex
clinical_significance: The righting reflex is an automatic response that restores head and body orientation when balance or position changes.

name: rigosertib sodium
clinical_significance: Rigosertib is an investigational anticancer agent studied mainly in myelodysplastic syndromes and other cancers; it is not routine therapy, and use should be confined to appropriate clinical trials.

name: rilotumumab
clinical_significance: Rilotumumab is an investigational antibody targeting hepatocyte growth factor. It has been studied in cancer, but it is not an established treatment; trial results and toxicity determine any research use.

name: rilpivirine
clinical_significance: An HIV medicine that blocks an enzyme the virus needs to copy itself. It is taken with other antiretroviral medicines, and missed doses or drug interactions can allow resistance to develop.

name: riluzole
clinical_significance: A medicine used to modestly slow disease progression in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and to treat selected forms of spinal muscular atrophy.

name: rimantadine
clinical_significance: Rimantadine is an older influenza A antiviral to which circulating viruses are widely resistant; it is generally not recommended for current seasonal influenza treatment or prevention.

name: ring chromosome
clinical_significance: A chromosome whose two ends have joined to form a ring, often with loss or disruption of genetic material. It may cause developmental or other health problems, depending on the chromosome and changes involved.

name: risedronate sodium
clinical_significance: The sodium salt of risedronate, a bisphosphonate used to prevent or treat osteoporosis and other disorders of excessive bone resorption.

name: risk
clinical_significance: Risk is the probability of an unwanted event or outcome, considered together with its severity and the circumstances that influence it.

name: risk adjustment
clinical_significance: Risk adjustment accounts for differences in baseline patient characteristics so outcomes or payments can be compared more fairly across groups.

name: risk factors
clinical_significance: Risk factors are characteristics or exposures associated with a greater chance of disease; identifying modifiable factors can guide prevention, screening, and shared decisions without determining an individual outcome.

name: risk management
clinical_significance: Finding possible sources of harm, judging how likely and serious they are, and taking steps to reduce them. In healthcare, it includes safe systems, reporting problems, learning from errors, and checking whether safety measures work.

name: risk-taking
clinical_significance: Risk-taking is behavior involving deliberate or inadvertent exposure to possible harm, influenced by perception, reward, development, mental health, and circumstances.

name: risperidone
clinical_significance: Risperidone is an atypical antipsychotic that blocks dopamine and serotonin receptors and treats schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and selected severe behavioral symptoms; hyperprolactinaemia, metabolic effects, movement disorders, and sedation may occur.

name: ristocetin
clinical_significance: Ristocetin is used in laboratory testing of platelet-von Willebrand factor interaction; ristocetin-based assays help investigate von Willebrand disease and related platelet-function disorders.

name: ritodrine
clinical_significance: Ritodrine is a beta-adrenergic medicine formerly used to delay preterm labor. Maternal cardiovascular and metabolic adverse effects limit its use, and it is not a routine long-term preventive treatment.

name: ritonavir
clinical_significance: Ritonavir is an HIV protease inhibitor mainly used at low doses to boost levels of other antiviral medicines by slowing their breakdown.

name: ritual
clinical_significance: A ritual is a repeated, structured behavior or ceremony; repetitive rituals may also occur as compulsions in obsessive-compulsive disorder.

name: rituximab
clinical_significance: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody against CD20 that depletes B cells and is used for B-cell malignancies and selected autoimmune diseases; infusion reactions, infections, hepatitis-B reactivation, and rare PML are important risks.

name: rivaroxaban
clinical_significance: Rivaroxaban is an oral direct factor Xa inhibitor used to prevent or treat venous thromboembolism and reduce stroke risk in selected atrial fibrillation; bleeding and renal-function-dependent dosing are important considerations.

name: RNA binding
clinical_significance: The attachment of a protein or other molecule to RNA, affecting RNA stability, transport, folding, processing, or translation.

name: RNA biosynthesis
clinical_significance: The cellular production of RNA from a DNA template or, for some viruses, from an RNA template.

name: RNA degradation
clinical_significance: The enzyme-controlled breakdown of RNA molecules. It controls how long genetic messages last, removes damaged or unnecessary messages, recycles their building blocks, and helps regulate protein production and cell behavior.

name: RNA folding
clinical_significance: The process by which an RNA strand forms secondary and three-dimensional structures that influence its function.

name: RNA helicase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that uses energy to separate, reshape, or move RNA structures and RNA-protein complexes. It helps cells copy, process, transport, and destroy RNA and is important for some viruses.

name: RNA interference
clinical_significance: A gene-silencing process in which small RNAs guide proteins to degrade or block specific messenger RNA molecules.

name: RNA splicing
clinical_significance: Removal of introns and joining of exons from a precursor RNA to produce mature messenger RNA or other functional RNA.

name: RNA transport
clinical_significance: Movement of RNA within a cell or between cells, often mediated by transport proteins and required for translation or signaling.

name: RNA virus
clinical_significance: A virus whose genetic material is RNA; its replication often involves an RNA-dependent polymerase and may have a high mutation rate.

name: RNase P
clinical_significance: An RNA-protein enzyme complex that processes precursor transfer RNA by removing its extra 5-prime sequence.

name: Robinow syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited skeletal-development disorder with distinctive facial features, short stature, vertebral or rib abnormalities, and genital differences.

name: rod photoreceptor
clinical_significance: A light-sensitive cell in the retina that supports vision in dim light and the peripheral field. Rods do not provide color vision; their loss can cause night blindness and narrowing of the visual field.

name: roentgen
clinical_significance: The roentgen is an obsolete unit of radiation exposure in air. Modern radiation protection and imaging use SI units such as coulombs per kilogram, gray, or sievert, so older values require careful conversion and context.

name: rofecoxib
clinical_significance: Rofecoxib is a selective COX-2 anti-inflammatory drug withdrawn in many countries because of increased cardiovascular risk.

name: romidepsin
clinical_significance: A histone deacetylase inhibitor used for selected T-cell lymphomas; it can cause cytopenias, infection risk, and ECG-related effects.

name: romiplostim
clinical_significance: A thrombopoietin-receptor agonist that stimulates platelet production and is used mainly for chronic immune thrombocytopenia.

name: ronnel
clinical_significance: Ronnel is an organophosphate insecticide that can inhibit acetylcholinesterase and cause cholinergic toxicity after exposure.

name: rooting reflex
clinical_significance: A primitive reflex present from birth to 3-4 months, triggered by stroking the infant's

name: ropivacaine
clinical_significance: A long-acting local anesthetic used for regional nerve blocks and epidural anesthesia; excessive blood levels can cause neurologic or cardiac toxicity.

name: ropivacaine hydrochloride
clinical_significance: The hydrochloride salt of ropivacaine, a long-acting local anesthetic used for regional and epidural anesthesia.

name: rosacea
clinical_significance: A chronic inflammatory skin disorder that most often affects the central face. It may cause recurrent flushing, persistent redness, visible small blood vessels, burning or stinging, and acne-like bumps or pustules without being acne. Eye involvement may cause irritation or inflammation, and long-standing disease may produce thickening of the skin, especially of the nose (rhinophyma). Rosacea is not contagious, and its severity and features vary over time.

name: rose bengal
clinical_significance: Rose bengal is a dye used in eye-surface testing and laboratory or diagnostic procedures; it highlights damaged or poorly protected conjunctival cells.

name: roseolovirus
clinical_significance: A genus of herpesviruses that includes human herpesvirus 6 and 7, commonly associated with roseola and sometimes serious disease after reactivation.

name: roseomonas
clinical_significance: Roseomonas species are uncommon environmental bacteria that can cause opportunistic infection, often bloodstream infection associated with intravascular catheters in immunocompromised patients; culture findings need clinical correlation.

name: roseomonas gilardii
clinical_significance: Roseomonas gilardii is a rare opportunistic pathogen associated especially with catheter-related bloodstream infection in immunocompromised people; species identification and susceptibility testing can guide management.

name: roseomonas mucosa
clinical_significance: Roseomonas mucosa is an uncommon environmental bacterium that can rarely cause bloodstream or other invasive infection, particularly in patients with impaired immunity or indwelling devices.

name: rosiglitazone
clinical_significance: A medicine for type 2 diabetes that helps the body respond better to insulin and lower blood sugar. It can cause weight gain, swelling, fractures, or worsening heart failure and is used selectively.

name: rosiglitazone maleate
clinical_significance: The maleate salt of rosiglitazone, a thiazolidinedione that improves insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes but may cause weight gain, edema, fractures, and heart-failure worsening.

name: ross river virus
clinical_significance: A mosquito-borne alphavirus that causes Ross River fever, with fever, rash, and often prolonged joint pain or swelling.

name: rostaporfin
clinical_significance: Rostaporfin is an investigational photosensitizing drug studied for photodynamic treatment of selected tumors; it is not standard cancer care, and photosensitivity and trial-specific procedures are relevant.

name: rostral
clinical_significance: Positioned toward the nose or front of the head. In descriptions of the brain, it usually means toward the forehead or front rather than toward the back of the head.

name: rosuvastatin calcium
clinical_significance: Rosuvastatin calcium is a statin medicine that lowers LDL cholesterol and reduces the risk of cardiovascular events.

name: rotation
clinical_significance: Movement around an axis; in anatomy it describes turning a body part inward, outward, or around its longitudinal axis.

name: rotator cuff
clinical_significance: The group of four shoulder muscles and tendons that stabilize the glenohumeral joint and rotate the arm.

name: rotavirus
clinical_significance: A very contagious virus that commonly causes vomiting and watery diarrhea in infants and young children. It can cause dangerous dehydration; vaccination greatly reduces severe illness, and testing is not always needed.

name: rotavirus infection
clinical_significance: A highly contagious viral gastroenteritis causing vomiting and watery diarrhea, especially in infants and young children; vaccination prevents most severe disease.

name: rotavirus vaccine
clinical_significance: A live-attenuated oral viral vaccine administered to young infants in a 2- or 3-dose series to prevent severe dehydrating gastroenteritis and diarrhea caused by rotavirus infection, carrying a slight, transient risk of intussusception.

name: rotenone
clinical_significance: Rotenone is a naturally occurring pesticide that inhibits mitochondrial complex I and can be toxic to people and animals after exposure.

name: rothia dentocariosa
clinical_significance: Rothia dentocariosa is part of normal oral flora but can rarely cause bacteremia or endocarditis, sometimes associated with dental disease. A blood-culture isolate should be assessed for true infection, with susceptibility-guided treatment.

name: rothia mucilaginosa
clinical_significance: Rothia mucilaginosa is an oral and respiratory commensal that can cause opportunistic bacteremia, pneumonia, or other invasive infection, especially in immunocompromised patients; interpretation depends on specimen and clinical context.

name: Rothmund-Thomson syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited condition that causes a mottled, red, and thin skin rash beginning in infancy, short stature, sparse hair, skeletal or dental problems, and sometimes cataracts. It also increases the risk of certain cancers.

name: rotifera
clinical_significance: Rotifers are microscopic aquatic organisms with no established role as human pathogens; their presence is generally environmental rather than evidence of human infection.

name: round ligament
clinical_significance: A round ligament is a cord-like supporting structure, including the uterine ligaments that pass toward the groin and help maintain uterine position.

name: roxithromycin
clinical_significance: A macrolide antibiotic used in some countries for selected bacterial infections. It stops bacteria making proteins, but resistance, medicine interactions, stomach upset, liver problems, and heart-rhythm changes can occur.

name: rubber
clinical_significance: Rubber is an elastic material used in gloves, devices, and equipment; natural-rubber latex can cause irritant or allergic reactions.

name: rubber dams
clinical_significance: Sheets used in dentistry to isolate teeth from saliva and the rest of the mouth during procedures.

name: rubella
clinical_significance: A contagious viral infection causing mild fever, swollen lymph nodes, and a fine rash. Infection during pregnancy can cause miscarriage, fetal growth problems, hearing loss, eye disease, congenital heart disease, or other congenital rubella syndrome; vaccination prevents most cases.

name: rubella virus
clinical_significance: The virus that causes rubella, a contagious illness with fever, swollen glands, and rash. Infection during pregnancy can seriously harm the developing baby, causing hearing loss, eye disease, heart problems, or other birth defects.

name: rubeosis iridis
clinical_significance: Growth of abnormal new blood vessels on the colored part of the eye. It usually results from poor blood flow in the retina, often caused by diabetes or a blocked retinal vein, and can lead to painful glaucoma and vision loss.

name: rubidium
clinical_significance: A chemical element whose radioactive isotopes can be used in medical imaging; nonmedical rubidium compounds can affect potassium-related physiology.

name: rubitecan
clinical_significance: Rubitecan is an investigational topoisomerase I inhibitor studied as an anticancer drug; it is not an established routine therapy, and clinical-trial evidence and marrow or gastrointestinal toxicity are relevant.

name: rubivirus
clinical_significance: A genus of viruses that includes rubella virus, which causes rubella and congenital rubella syndrome.

name: rubredoxins
clinical_significance: Small proteins containing iron that help move electrons in some bacteria and other organisms. They take part in chemical reactions that release energy and protect cells from harmful oxygen-related chemicals.

name: rubricyte count
clinical_significance: A measurement of rubricytes, an older name for immature red blood cells, in blood or bone marrow. It may help assess how actively the marrow is making red cells, but modern tests usually report reticulocytes or other marrow findings.

name: rubulavirus
clinical_significance: Rubulavirus is a historical virus genus that includes mumps virus and related paramyxoviruses; infection can cause parotitis and complications such as orchitis, meningitis, or hearing loss, and vaccination prevents mumps.

name: rumen
clinical_significance: The rumen is the first major chamber of the ruminant stomach and is relevant to veterinary medicine and food safety; it is not a human organ.

name: rumination
clinical_significance: Repeated regurgitation and rechewing of food after eating, without the usual vomiting process. It is a behavior or symptom that may occur in rumination disorder or with other gastrointestinal, developmental, or behavioral conditions.

name: rumination disorder
clinical_significance: A feeding or eating disorder involving repeated, usually effortless return of recently eaten food to the mouth, followed by rechewing, reswallowing, or spitting. It differs from ordinary vomiting and causes clinically significant distress, impairment, or nutritional or medical consequences.

name: ruminococcus
clinical_significance: Ruminococcus is a genus of gut bacteria involved in digestion and fermentation; changes in abundance are studied in relation to health, but detection alone is not a validated diagnosis or treatment target.

name: ruminococcus gnavus
clinical_significance: An intestinal bacterium involved in mucin and carbohydrate metabolism and studied in relation to gut inflammation.

name: rupture
clinical_significance: A tear or complete break in an organ, vessel, muscle, or other tissue, often causing bleeding or loss of function.

name: rural health
clinical_significance: Rural health concerns access and outcomes in rural communities, where distance, workforce shortages, and limited services can delay preventive, emergency, and specialty care.

name: Russell-Siver syndrome
clinical_significance: Russell-Silver syndrome is a growth disorder associated with prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, feeding difficulty, and sometimes low blood sugar. Early recognition supports nutrition, glucose monitoring, and growth care.

name: ruthenium
clinical_significance: Ruthenium compounds have specialized uses in medical research and some devices or anticancer agents; toxicity depends on the compound and exposure, so the element name alone does not establish clinical risk.

name: rutin
clinical_significance: Rutin is a plant flavonoid sold in supplements, but evidence that it prevents or treats disease is limited; potential medicine interactions and variable supplement quality should be considered.

name: ryanodine
clinical_significance: Ryanodine is a plant-derived compound used mainly in research on calcium-release channels; it is not a clinical treatment, and exposure can disrupt muscle and cardiac calcium handling.

name: s phase
clinical_significance: The stage of the cell cycle when a cell copies all of its DNA before dividing. This duplication allows each new cell to receive a complete set of genetic instructions.

name: sabarubicin
clinical_significance: Sabarubicin is an investigational anthracycline anticancer drug studied for hematologic malignancies; it is not routine therapy, and marrow suppression and cardiac toxicity are key class-related concerns.

name: saccade
clinical_significance: A quick, coordinated eye movement that shifts the eyes from one target to another. Abnormal saccades can occur with disorders affecting the eye muscles, balance system, or brain and nerves.

name: saccharomyces
clinical_significance: Saccharomyces yeasts are used in food and biotechnology and can rarely cause invasive infection, especially in critically ill or immunocompromised patients and those receiving probiotic preparations; isolate significance depends on clinical context.

name: saccharomyces cerevisiae
clinical_significance: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is used in research, food production, and some probiotics. It can rarely cause bloodstream or device-associated infection in critically ill or immunocompromised patients, particularly after probiotic exposure; culture results need clinical correlation.

name: saccular aneurysm
clinical_significance: A rounded pouch bulging from one side of an artery because that part of the vessel wall is weak. It may enlarge, form clots, or burst; risk depends on its location, size, shape, and growth.

name: sacral dimple
clinical_significance: A small indentation in the skin over the lower spine that is present at birth. Most are harmless, but a deep, large, high, hairy, discolored, or draining dimple may need imaging for an underlying spinal abnormality.

name: sacral fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal channel near the lower spine that connects the skin with deeper tissue or another body space. It may cause persistent drainage, pain, repeated infection, or a skin opening and can result from birth differences, injury, or pilonidal disease.

name: sacral region
clinical_significance: The lower back and posterior pelvic region overlying the sacrum, a fused triangular bone that connects the lumbar spine with the pelvis.

name: sacral vertebra
clinical_significance: One of the fused vertebrae forming the sacrum, which supports the spine, joins the pelvic bones, and transmits trunk weight to the lower limbs.

name: sacrococcygeal teratoma
clinical_significance: A tumor present from birth at the base of the spine and made of several tissue types. It may grow outside or inside the pelvis; a large fetal tumor can strain the heart and increase amniotic fluid.

name: sacroiliac joint
clinical_significance: The joint connecting the triangular sacrum at the base of the spine to each hip bone. It transfers weight between the spine and legs and may become painful or inflamed after injury, pregnancy, arthritis, or infection.

name: sacroiliitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of one or both joints connecting the lower spine to the pelvis. It can cause pain in the lower back, buttock, or back of the thigh and may result from inflammatory arthritis, infection, injury, or wear.

name: sacrum
clinical_significance: A large triangular bone at the back of the pelvis formed by five fused spinal bones. It connects the spine to the hip bones, transfers body weight to the legs, and contains openings for nerves supplying the pelvis and lower limbs.

name: sad mood
clinical_significance: Sad mood is a feeling of unhappiness or low mood that may be a normal response or a symptom of depression, grief, illness, or another condition.

name: s-adenosylmethionine
clinical_significance: A substance made naturally in the body that helps chemical reactions involving cell membranes, genetic material, and brain chemicals. It is also sold as a supplement, but its benefits and interactions vary by condition.

name: safety
clinical_significance: Safety in healthcare includes reducing preventable harm from medicines, procedures, equipment, and care processes; reporting and learning from errors support system-level prevention.

name: safety study
clinical_significance: A safety study evaluates whether a medicine, device, procedure, or treatment causes harmful effects and identifies risks before or during clinical use.

name: safflower oil
clinical_significance: Safflower oil is a dietary oil rich in unsaturated fats. It contributes calories and may be used in nutrition plans, but evidence for treating disease with supplements is limited.

name: safingol
clinical_significance: Safingol is an investigational sphingolipid-signaling inhibitor studied in cancer research; it is not an established treatment and should be used only in research settings.

name: safrole
clinical_significance: Safrole is a natural aromatic compound found in some plants and oils; high or prolonged exposure is toxic and has carcinogenic concern.

name: sagopilone
clinical_significance: Sagopilone is an investigational epothilone anticancer drug studied in clinical trials; it is not routine therapy, and expected benefit and neurotoxicity are considered in trial monitoring.

name: salicylic acid
clinical_significance: A medicine applied to the skin to soften and remove excess surface skin. It is used for acne, psoriasis, warts, corns, and similar thickened or blocked skin; irritation is common and large exposures can be toxic.

name: saline
clinical_significance: A sterile solution of sodium chloride in water. Different concentrations are used for intravenous fluids, wound or eye irrigation, inhalation, laboratory work, or dilution of medicines.

name: saliva
clinical_significance: Fluid made by the salivary glands that moistens food, begins digestion, protects the mouth and teeth, and helps swallowing and taste. Too little saliva can cause dry mouth, mouth soreness, and tooth decay.

name: salivary gland
clinical_significance: A gland that makes saliva and releases it into the mouth. The three major paired glands are the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands; many smaller glands lie in the mouth lining.

name: salivary gland neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in a salivary gland that may be noncancerous or cancerous. It can cause a lump, pain, facial weakness, dry mouth, or swallowing problems and may require imaging and biopsy.

name: salmonella
