clinical_significance: A genus of Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacteria in the Enterobacteriaceae family.

name: salmonella arizonae
clinical_significance: Salmonella enterica serovar Arizonae is associated particularly with reptiles and poultry and can cause human gastroenteritis or invasive infection, especially in young children or immunocompromised people.

name: salmonella choleraesuis
clinical_significance: A Salmonella serotype adapted to pigs that can cause severe, invasive infection in humans, including bloodstream infection and pneumonia.

name: salmonella enterica
clinical_significance: A major Salmonella species causing human disease. It can produce diarrhea and fever, enteric fever, or bloodstream infection after contaminated food, water, animals, or infected people spread the bacteria.

name: salmonella gallinarum
clinical_significance: Salmonella Gallinarum primarily causes disease in poultry and is not a common human pathogen; its importance is mainly veterinary and food-safety surveillance.

name: salmonella infection
clinical_significance: An infection caused by Salmonella bacteria, usually acquired through contaminated food, water, animals, or hands. It commonly causes diarrhea, fever, cramps, and vomiting but can spread into blood or other organs.

name: salmonella pullorum
clinical_significance: Salmonella Pullorum primarily causes disease in poultry and is not a usual cause of human illness; detection is relevant to veterinary diagnosis and food-safety control.

name: salmonella typhi
clinical_significance: The bacterium that causes typhoid fever, usually acquired through contaminated food or water and capable of spreading through the bloodstream.

name: salmonella typhimurium
clinical_significance: A common Salmonella serotype that usually causes foodborne gastroenteritis but can cause invasive disease in vulnerable people.

name: salmonella typhisuis
clinical_significance: A Salmonella serotype mainly associated with swine; human infection is uncommon but may cause enteric or invasive disease.

name: salmonella vaccines
clinical_significance: Vaccines used mainly to prevent typhoid fever, including typhoid conjugate, Vi polysaccharide, and oral live-attenuated vaccines; routine vaccination does not prevent all Salmonella gastroenteritis.

name: salpingectomy
clinical_significance: Surgical removal of a fallopian tube. It may be used to treat a tubal ectopic pregnancy,

name: salpingitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of one or both fallopian tubes, usually as part of pelvic inflammatory disease spreading upward from the vagina or cervix. It may cause lower-abdominal pain, fever, unusual discharge, infertility, or pregnancy outside the uterus.

name: salpingo-oophorectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove one or both fallopian tubes and ovaries. It may treat cancer, an ovarian or tubal problem, or reduce cancer risk in people with certain inherited gene changes. Removing both ovaries causes permanent loss of ovarian hormone production.

name: salt
clinical_significance: An ionic chemical compound; dietary sodium chloride is essential in small amounts but excess intake can increase blood pressure.

name: salt gland
clinical_significance: Salt glands in some animals excrete excess salts and are relevant to comparative physiology and veterinary biology; the term does not refer to a human gland.

name: salvage therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment used when a disease, especially cancer, has not improved with earlier treatment or has returned. The choice depends on the disease, previous treatments, overall health, and treatment goals.

name: sample fixation
clinical_significance: Preserving a tissue or cell sample soon after collection so it does not decay or change shape. The preserved sample can then be processed, stained, and examined under a microscope for diagnosis.

name: sample size
clinical_significance: Sample size affects how precisely a study estimates effects and whether it can detect meaningful differences; an underpowered study may miss benefit or harm, while large studies can detect trivial effects.

name: Sandhoff disease
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which fatty substances build up in nerve cells. It usually begins in infancy or childhood with loss of skills, weakness, seizures, movement problems, and sometimes an enlarged liver or spleen.

name: sanitation
clinical_significance: Public-health measures that safely manage human waste, water, food, hygiene, and environmental contamination to prevent infection and disease transmission.

name: saphenous vein
clinical_significance: A superficial vein of the lower limb that drains the foot and leg. The great and small saphenous

name: sapovirus
clinical_significance: A virus that can cause vomiting and watery diarrhea, especially in children. It spreads through contaminated food, water, surfaces, or close contact.

name: sapporo virus
clinical_significance: Sapporo virus is the former name for sapovirus, a cause of acute viral gastroenteritis. It spreads by the fecal-oral route and can cause outbreaks, especially in children and institutional settings.

name: sapropterin
clinical_significance: A synthetic form of tetrahydrobiopterin used for some people with phenylketonuria and certain tetrahydrobiopterin deficiencies; response and diet requirements vary.

name: saquinavir
clinical_significance: An HIV protease inhibitor used with other antiretroviral medicines; drug interactions, gastrointestinal effects, and cardiovascular concerns limit its use.

name: saquinavir mesylate
clinical_significance: The mesylate salt form of saquinavir, an HIV medicine that blocks viral protein processing. It is used with other antiretroviral drugs, but interactions, liver problems, and dangerous heart-rhythm changes require careful monitoring.

name: saracatinib
clinical_significance: Saracatinib is an investigational Src-family kinase inhibitor studied in cancer and other conditions; it is not an approved routine therapy, and clinical trial evidence guides its evaluation.

name: saralasin
clinical_significance: Saralasin is an older experimental angiotensin II receptor blocker used in physiologic testing of renin-mediated hypertension; it is not routine treatment and has been superseded by established therapies.

name: sarcocystis
clinical_significance: Sarcocystis parasites can infect humans through undercooked meat or contaminated food and water; intestinal or muscular disease may follow, so food exposure and species matter in diagnosis.

name: sarcocystis hominis
clinical_significance: A protozoan parasite acquired by eating undercooked beef; people may develop intestinal symptoms, while cattle serve as an intermediate host.

name: sarcocystis suihominis
clinical_significance: A protozoan parasite acquired by eating undercooked pork that can cause intestinal sarcocystosis; pigs serve as an intermediate host.

name: sarcocystosis
clinical_significance: Parasitic infection by Sarcocystis species, acquired from undercooked meat or contaminated food and sometimes causing muscle pain, fever, diarrhea, or no symptoms.

name: sarcoglycan complex
clinical_significance: A group of proteins that helps strengthen the outer covering of muscle cells during movement. Inherited problems with these proteins can cause progressive muscle weakness and sometimes heart-muscle disease.

name: sarcoidosis
clinical_significance: An inflammatory condition in which small clumps of immune cells, called granulomas, form in organs. The cause is unknown. It most often affects the lungs and lymph nodes in the chest but can also affect the skin, eyes, heart, nervous system, or other organs. Some people have no symptoms; others have symptoms that depend on which organs are affected.

name: sarcolemma
clinical_significance: The thin outer covering of a muscle cell. It carries electrical signals that start contraction and helps maintain the cell’s structure and internal chemical balance.

name: sarcoma
clinical_significance: A malignant tumor arising from connective or supporting tissues, including bone, cartilage, fat,

name: sarcomere
clinical_significance: The smallest working unit that makes skeletal and heart muscle contract. It contains protein threads that slide past one another, shortening the muscle and producing force.

name: sarcopenia
clinical_significance: Loss of muscle strength and muscle mass that reduces physical function, often with aging but also with inactivity, poor nutrition, or chronic disease. It can cause weakness, slower walking, falls, and difficulty with daily activities.

name: sarcoplasm
clinical_significance: The material inside a muscle cell surrounding its specialized structures. It contains energy-producing parts, stored fuel, oxygen-holding myoglobin, and the protein machinery that produces contraction.

name: sarcoplasmic reticulum
clinical_significance: A network inside muscle cells that stores calcium. It releases calcium to start contraction and takes calcium back up so the muscle can relax.

name: sarcosine
clinical_significance: Sarcosine is an amino-acid derivative involved in one-carbon metabolism and studied as a biomarker in some disorders; blood or urine levels require clinical context and are not diagnostic alone.

name: sarcosinemia
clinical_significance: Sarcosinemia is a rare inherited metabolic condition causing elevated sarcosine, usually without symptoms but sometimes associated with developmental or neurologic findings; biochemical or genetic evaluation clarifies significance.

name: sardomozide
clinical_significance: Sardomozide is an investigational enzyme inhibitor studied for anticancer activity; it is not standard treatment, and any use belongs in a monitored clinical trial.

name: sargramostim
clinical_significance: A recombinant granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor used to promote white-cell recovery after selected cancer treatments or transplantation; bone pain and fever may occur.

name: SARS virus
clinical_significance: The coronavirus that causes severe acute respiratory syndrome, a serious respiratory infection that can spread through respiratory droplets and close contact.

name: satellite DNA
clinical_significance: Repeated stretches of DNA found mainly in tightly packed parts of chromosomes. They help organize chromosome structure and can vary between people, usually without providing instructions for making proteins.

name: satellite virus
clinical_significance: A small virus-like infectious agent that can multiply only when a separate helper virus is present. It uses the helper’s machinery and may change how severe or persistent the combined infection becomes.

name: satiation
clinical_significance: The feeling of fullness that terminates a meal, produced by gastrointestinal stretch, nutrients, hormones, and brain signals regulating food intake.

name: satisfaction
clinical_significance: Patient satisfaction reflects a person’s experience of care, including communication, access, and respect; it can identify service problems but should be considered alongside clinical outcomes and safety measures.

name: satraplatin
clinical_significance: Satraplatin is an investigational oral platinum-based anticancer drug that has been studied in advanced cancers; it is not an established routine treatment, and trial evidence and toxicity determine its role.

name: saturated fat
clinical_significance: A dietary fat whose fatty-acid chains contain no carbon-carbon double bonds. It is found in foods such as fatty meat, butter, full-fat dairy, coconut oil, and palm oil; replacing some saturated fat with unsaturated fat can help lower LDL cholesterol and cardiovascular risk.

name: saturated phytosterol
clinical_significance: Saturated phytosterols are plant-derived compounds used in some foods and supplements; their effect on cholesterol and interactions with lipid disorders or medicines should be considered in clinical context.

name: saxitoxin
clinical_significance: A powerful poison made by some marine algae that can build up in shellfish. Eating contaminated seafood may cause tingling, weakness, trouble breathing, or paralysis.

name: scab
clinical_significance: A crust of dried blood, serum, pus, or tissue fluid over a healing skin injury.

name: scabies
clinical_significance: An infestation caused by tiny mites that burrow into the skin, causing intense itching that is often worse at night and a rash or thin burrows. It spreads mainly through prolonged close skin-to-skin contact.

name: scaffold seeding
clinical_significance: Placing living cells onto or inside a three-dimensional framework so they can attach, multiply, and begin forming tissue in laboratory or regenerative-medicine research.

name: scalp
clinical_significance: The skin and underlying tissues covering the skull. It contains hair follicles, glands, blood vessels, nerves, and connective tissue and can be affected by injury, infection, or skin disease.

name: scalpel
clinical_significance: A sharp surgical knife used to make precise incisions or cuts in tissue. It may be a reusable handle with a detachable blade or a disposable single-piece instrument. Blade designs and numbers differ in size and shape; for example, a No. 10 blade is commonly used for larger incisions, a No. 11 for puncture or stab incisions, and a No. 15 for shorter precise cuts.

name: scan gallium
clinical_significance: A nuclear-medicine scan using radiolabeled gallium to identify areas of inflammation, infection, or some tumors; uptake is interpreted with anatomy and clinical context.

name: scanning
clinical_significance: Systematic examination of a body region or specimen using imaging, microscopy, or another detection method to locate, characterize, or monitor abnormalities.

name: scanning electron microscopy
clinical_significance: A method that scans a specimen’s surface with an electron beam to produce a highly magnified, three-dimensional-looking image of its shape and surface details.

name: scaphoid abdomen
clinical_significance: A scaphoid abdomen is an unusually hollowed abdominal contour, classically seen with severe diaphragmatic hernia in a newborn but also possible with marked wasting.

name: scaphoid bone
clinical_significance: The largest proximal-row carpal bone on the thumb side of the wrist; its waist is vulnerable to fracture and avascular necrosis because of its blood supply.

name: scaphycephaly
clinical_significance: A long, narrow head shape caused when the major seam running from front to back of the skull closes too early. It is a form of craniosynostosis and may require specialist assessment to protect brain and skull development.

name: scapula
clinical_significance: The shoulder blade, a flat triangular bone at the back of the chest. It connects the upper arm to the collarbone and provides attachment for muscles that move and stabilize the shoulder.

name: scar
clinical_significance: Fibrous tissue formed during healing after injury, inflammation, or surgery.

name: scarlet fever
clinical_significance: An illness caused by toxin-producing group A Streptococcus. It usually causes sore throat, fever, and a widespread fine, rough-textured rash; a red tongue and pale skin around the mouth may also occur.

name: scavenger receptor
clinical_significance: A protein on or inside a cell that recognizes and helps remove altered fats, germs, cell debris, or dying cells. It supports early immune defense but can also help fatty material build up in artery walls.

name: scedosporium
clinical_significance: A genus of environmental molds that can cause difficult-to-treat lung, sinus, skin, bone, or disseminated infections, especially in immunocompromised people.

name: scedosporium apiospermum
clinical_significance: A mold that can cause localized or disseminated infection, including mycetoma, pneumonia, sinusitis, and brain abscesses; treatment often requires specialist antifungal care.

name: scedosporium prolifican
clinical_significance: An environmental mold, now commonly classified as Lomentospora prolificans, that causes severe disseminated infection and is often resistant to antifungal drugs.

name: schaalia radingae
clinical_significance: A normally slow-growing anaerobic bacterium of the human mouth and skin that can rarely cause abscesses or other invasive infections.

name: schaalia turicensis
clinical_significance: A filamentous anaerobic bacterium that may be part of normal flora but can cause actinomycosis-like abscesses and other opportunistic infections.

name: scheduled notification
clinical_significance: A scheduled notification is a planned alert or reminder in a health system; reminders can support appointments, medication adherence, and follow-up, but require accurate timing and privacy safeguards.

name: Scheuermann's disease
clinical_significance: A growth disorder beginning in adolescence that causes several spinal bones to become wedge-shaped. This can produce a lasting rounded upper back, stiffness, pain, and sometimes breathing or activity limitations.

name: schiff base
clinical_significance: A chemical compound formed when a primary amine reacts with an aldehyde or ketone; Schiff bases occur in biochemistry and drug chemistry.

name: Schiller test
clinical_significance: An examination of the cervix in which iodine solution is applied to highlight areas of abnormal tissue. Areas that do not stain may need further examination or biopsy; the test alone cannot diagnose cancer.

name: schistocyte count
clinical_significance: Measurement of fragmented red blood cells on a blood smear, supporting evaluation of microangiopathic hemolysis, mechanical valve damage, disseminated intravascular coagulation, or severe burns.

name: schistosoma
clinical_significance: A group of parasitic worms that live in blood vessels. Their young forms can enter through skin exposed to contaminated fresh water and later cause intestinal, urinary, liver, or other disease.

name: schistosoma haematobium
clinical_significance: A parasitic blood fluke that can cause urinary schistosomiasis, including hematuria and chronic

name: schistosoma intercalatum
clinical_significance: A parasitic blood fluke that causes intestinal schistosomiasis, mainly in parts of Central and West Africa, after freshwater exposure.

name: schistosoma japonicum
clinical_significance: Schistosoma japonicum causes intestinal schistosomiasis after exposure to contaminated freshwater in endemic regions. Chronic infection can damage the intestine or liver and may rarely involve the nervous system; exposure history and testing guide diagnosis.

name: schistosoma mansoni
clinical_significance: Schistosoma mansoni causes intestinal and hepatosplenic schistosomiasis. Egg-driven inflammation can lead to chronic bowel disease, liver fibrosis, and portal hypertension after freshwater exposure in endemic regions.

name: schistosoma mekongi
clinical_significance: Schistosoma mekongi is a cause of intestinal schistosomiasis in parts of the Mekong basin. Chronic infection can injure the bowel and liver, so travel and freshwater exposure history are important for diagnosis.

name: schistosomiasis
clinical_significance: An infection caused by parasitic worms called \textit{Schistosoma}. The worms live in freshwater snails, and their larvae can penetrate the skin when a person swims, wades, or works in contaminated freshwater. The infection may cause an itchy rash, fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea, blood in the stool or urine, and painful urination. Long-term infection can damage the intestine, liver, urinary tract, or other organs.

name: schistosomiasis japonica
clinical_significance: Schistosomiasis japonica is intestinal infection by Schistosoma japonicum; chronic egg-related inflammation can cause bowel and liver disease, including fibrosis and portal hypertension.

name: schistosomiasis mansoni
clinical_significance: Schistosomiasis mansoni is intestinal infection by Schistosoma mansoni; untreated chronic disease can cause bowel injury, liver fibrosis, and portal hypertension.

name: schizencephaly
clinical_significance: A rare condition present from birth in which a fluid-filled cleft extends through part of the brain. It results from abnormal early brain development and may cause seizures, weakness, movement problems, or delayed development, depending on the cleft’s size and location.

name: schizoid personality
clinical_significance: Schizoid personality describes a persistent pattern of social detachment and limited emotional expression; assessment should distinguish it from autism, depression, psychosis, and culturally shaped preferences, and address distress or functional impairment.

name: schizophrenia
clinical_significance: A serious, long-term mental disorder that can affect a person’s thoughts, perceptions, emotions, behavior, and ability to function. Symptoms are often grouped as psychotic, negative, and cognitive. Psychotic symptoms include hallucinations, such as hearing or seeing things that others do not, delusions, which are firmly held beliefs not supported by shared evidence, and disorganized thought or speech. Negative symptoms may include reduced emotional expression, motivation, pleasure, or social int

name: schizophyllum
clinical_significance: Schizophyllum is a genus of environmental fungi that can rarely cause opportunistic infection, particularly in people with impaired immunity; identification and susceptibility testing matter when recovered from a clinical specimen.

name: school
clinical_significance: School settings influence child health through access to meals, learning support, vaccination, mental-health services, and identification of illness; school-based services can reduce barriers to care.

name: school nursing
clinical_significance: School nursing supports student health, medication administration, chronic-disease plans, immunization, and response to urgent illness or injury, while helping connect families with healthcare services.

name: schwann cell
clinical_significance: A supporting cell of the peripheral nervous system. It wraps around many nerve fibers to form their insulating myelin covering and helps maintain or repair peripheral nerves.

name: schwannomatosis
clinical_significance: A condition in which multiple schwannomas, usually slow-growing tumors of the covering of nerves, develop. The main problem is often long-lasting pain, although numbness, weakness, or other nerve symptoms can occur depending on tumor location.

name: sciatic nerve
clinical_significance: The body's largest nerve, running from the lower spine through the buttock and down the back of the leg. It supplies movement and sensation to much of the leg and foot.

name: sciatica
clinical_significance: Pain, tingling, numbness, or weakness that travels from the lower back or buttock down the leg, usually because a nerve root is irritated by a disk problem or narrowing of the spine. Progressive weakness, numbness around the inner thighs or genitals, or new loss of bladder or bowel control may indicate severe nerve compression.

name: science
clinical_significance: Scientific evidence underpins clinical decisions, screening, and public-health policy; study quality and reproducibility affect whether findings can be applied safely to patients.

name: Scimitar syndrome
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which some veins from the right lung drain to the wrong large vein instead of directly to the heart. The right lung may be smaller, and the condition can cause repeated chest infections, breathing problems, high pressure in the lung arteries, or heart failure.

name: scintillation camera
clinical_significance: A scintillation camera detects gamma rays emitted by radiotracers to create nuclear-medicine images; image quality and tracer distribution help assess organ function or disease.

name: scintillation counter
clinical_significance: A scintillation counter measures ionizing radiation in samples or instruments; clinical laboratories use radiation measurements for quality control, tracer studies, and radiation safety.

name: scirrhous adenocarcinoma
clinical_significance: Scirrhous adenocarcinoma is a densely fibrotic pattern of gland-forming cancer, often associated with infiltrative growth; the primary site and pathology determine staging and treatment.

name: sclera
clinical_significance: The sclera is the tough white outer coat of the eye that protects the globe and provides attachment for eye muscles.

name: scleral buckling
clinical_significance: A retinal-detachment repair procedure in which a silicone band or buckle is placed around the outside of the eye to support the retinal break and reduce traction.

name: scleral diseases
clinical_significance: Scleral diseases can threaten eye integrity or vision. Pain, redness, tenderness, or visual change may indicate inflammation such as scleritis and warrants prompt ophthalmic assessment.

name: scleredema
clinical_significance: A sclerosing skin disorder causing thick, hard, often waxy skin, classically on the neck, upper back, and shoulders. It may follow infection, occur with diabetes or a monoclonal gammopathy, or rarely be associated with other systemic disease.

name: sclerema neonatorum
clinical_significance: Sclerema neonatorum is a rare, severe hardening of skin and subcutaneous tissue in critically ill newborns, associated with serious systemic illness and high mortality; urgent neonatal intensive care is required.

name: scleritis
clinical_significance: A severe inflammation of the sclera, the tough white outer wall of the eye. It typically causes deep, boring eye pain, marked redness that may have a bluish or violaceous hue, tenderness, photophobia, and sometimes reduced vision. Unlike episcleritis, scleritis affects the deeper protective coat of the eye and is often associated with systemic autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, or vasculitis; infection, trauma, surgery, and medicines can also contribute. It may be anterior,

name: scleroderma
clinical_significance: A group of autoimmune diseases that cause inflammation and too much collagen to build up, making skin and sometimes deeper tissues hard, thick, and tight. Localized scleroderma, also called morphea or linear scleroderma, mainly affects the skin and tissues just beneath it. Systemic scleroderma, also called systemic sclerosis, can affect the skin, small blood vessels, and internal organs such as the esophagus, lungs, kidneys, and heart. The cause is not fully known, and symptoms vary with the typ

name: scleromyxedema
clinical_significance: A rare long-term skin disorder in which many small, firm, waxy bumps and thickened skin develop, especially on the face, neck, and hands. It may also affect muscles, joints, swallowing, lungs, or other organs.

name: scleroproteins
clinical_significance: Scleroproteins are structural proteins such as collagen and keratin; defects or abnormal deposition can contribute to connective-tissue, skin, or organ disease.

name: sclerosing peritonitis
clinical_significance: Thickening and scarring of the lining inside the abdomen, sometimes after long-term peritoneal dialysis. The scar tissue can restrict the intestines and cause pain, vomiting, poor nutrition, or bowel blockage.

name: sclerosis
clinical_significance: Abnormal hardening or scarring of tissue, often from excess connective tissue, chronic inflammation, degeneration, or neurologic plaques; the affected organ determines the specific disease.

name: sclerosteosis
clinical_significance: A rare inherited condition in which bones, especially the skull, become abnormally thick. It may cause a broad or tall build, joined fingers, headaches, hearing loss, facial weakness, or pressure on nerves inside the skull.

name: sclerotherapy
clinical_significance: A treatment in which an irritating or closing agent is injected into a blood vessel or body cavity to make it scar and seal, commonly used for varicose veins and selected vascular lesions.

name: scolecobasidium terreum
clinical_significance: Scolecobasidium terreum is an environmental mold rarely implicated in human infection; a culture result requires confirmation and correlation with symptoms, specimen source, and immune status.

name: scoliosis
clinical_significance: An abnormal sideways curve of the spine that may look like the letter “C” or “S.” The bones of the spine may also rotate, changing the shape of the back or rib cage. In many children and teenagers, the cause is unknown; this is called idiopathic scoliosis. Other causes include differences present at birth, nerve or muscle conditions, spinal injury, or age-related changes. Mild scoliosis may cause no symptoms, while larger curves may cause uneven shoulders or hips, a prominent shoulder blade, bac

name: scopolamine
clinical_significance: Scopolamine is a muscarinic antagonist used mainly to prevent motion sickness and postoperative nausea; dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, confusion, and other anticholinergic effects may occur.

name: scopolamine hydrobromide
clinical_significance: The hydrobromide salt of scopolamine, an anticholinergic medicine used mainly to prevent motion sickness and postoperative nausea.

name: scopoletin
clinical_significance: Scopoletin is a plant-derived coumarin studied for biological effects; it has no established role as a clinical treatment, and supplement safety and interactions are uncertain.

name: scopulariopsis
clinical_significance: Scopulariopsis is a mold genus that rarely causes opportunistic infection, especially in people with immune suppression or implanted devices.

name: scotoma
clinical_significance: A blind or blurred spot within an otherwise usable field of vision. It may result from retinal disease, optic-nerve damage, migraine, stroke, or another eye or brain disorder.

name: scrapie
clinical_significance: Scrapie is a fatal prion disease of sheep and goats. It is an animal-health and food-chain surveillance concern; it is not known to cause human disease.

name: screening procedure
clinical_significance: A test or examination offered to people without symptoms to detect disease or risk early enough for effective prevention or treatment; eligibility and intervals depend on evidence and risk.

name: screening study
clinical_significance: A planned investigation of an asymptomatic population to identify early disease, precursor lesions, or risk factors using a validated test and follow-up pathway.

name: scrotal infection
clinical_significance: Infection of the scrotal skin or underlying structures, which may cause redness, swelling, warmth, pain,

name: scrotal pain
clinical_significance: Pain in the scrotum caused by infection, trauma, hernia, fluid collections, varicocele, testicular torsion, or other conditions affecting the testes and surrounding structures.

name: scrotum
clinical_significance: The scrotum is the external skin-and-muscle sac containing the testes and epididymides; its muscles help regulate testicular temperature, and swelling or pain may indicate infection, torsion, hernia, or tumor.

name: scurvy
clinical_significance: A disease caused by severe vitamin C deficiency. It can cause bleeding or swollen gums, easy bruising,

name: sea-blue histiocyte
clinical_significance: An immune cell that appears blue-green under a microscope because it contains stored fats or cell-waste pigment. It may be seen in some storage, blood, or metabolic disorders, but the finding alone does not identify a disease.

name: sebaceous adenoma
clinical_significance: A sebaceous adenoma is a usually benign tumor of sebaceous glands that can appear as a yellowish skin nodule and may be associated with Muir-Torre syndrome.

name: sebaceous gland
clinical_significance: A small gland in the skin that secretes sebum (oil) into hair follicles to lubricate and

name: sebaceous gland carcinoma
clinical_significance: Sebaceous gland carcinoma is an uncommon skin cancer arising from oil glands, often appearing as a firm yellowish eyelid or skin lump.

name: seborrheic dermatitis
clinical_significance: A common long-term inflammation of oily skin, especially the scalp, eyebrows, sides of the nose, chest, and skin folds. It causes red or pink patches with greasy white or yellow scale; dandruff is a mild scalp form.

name: seborrheic keratosis
clinical_significance: A benign epidermal tumor appearing as stuck-on, waxy, hyperpigmented plaques with a

name: sebum
clinical_significance: An oily substance made by skin glands that lubricates and protects the skin and hair. Excess production can contribute to oily skin, acne, and dandruff, while changes may accompany some skin disorders.

name: Seckel syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited condition causing severe growth restriction before and after birth, a very small head, characteristic facial features, and often developmental or intellectual disability. Bone, blood, and other birth differences may also occur.

name: secondary amenorrhea
clinical_significance: Absence of menstruation for at least three months in someone with previously regular cycles or six months with previously irregular cycles, caused by pregnancy, endocrine, ovarian, uterine, or systemic factors.

name: secondary hyperparathyroidism
clinical_significance: Overactivity of the parathyroid glands in response to low calcium, abnormal phosphate, vitamin-D deficiency, or kidney disease. It can weaken bones, cause bone pain, and contribute to calcium deposits in blood vessels.

name: secondary hypertension
clinical_significance: High blood pressure caused by an identifiable medical condition, medicine, or substance, rather than primary (essential) hypertension. Causes include kidney disease or narrowed kidney arteries, hormone disorders, sleep apnea, pregnancy-related conditions such as preeclampsia, and certain medicines or drugs, including steroids, stimulants, decongestants, and some pain relievers. Treating the cause may improve blood pressure.

name: secondary hypothyroidism
clinical_significance: Low thyroid-hormone production because the pituitary or nearby brain area does not provide enough thyroid-stimulating signal. It may cause tiredness, feeling cold, constipation, dry skin, slow heart rate, or menstrual changes.

name: secondary metabolism
clinical_significance: Secondary metabolism produces compounds not directly required for basic growth, including microbial toxins, pigments, and antibiotics; these products can affect infection, drug discovery, and toxicology.

name: secondary prevention
clinical_significance: Finding and treating a disease early to stop it worsening or causing complications. Examples include screening for some cancers, checking blood pressure, testing for early diabetes, and treating an abnormality before it produces serious symptoms.

name: second-degree burn
clinical_significance: A burn that damages the outer skin and part of the layer beneath it. The area is usually painful, red, moist, and blistered; deeper burns may look pale and heal slowly. Large, deep, or sensitive-area burns need medical assessment.

name: second-look surgery
clinical_significance: Second-look surgery is a planned or follow-up operation performed to inspect healing, remove remaining disease, assess treatment response, or manage complications.

name: secretin
clinical_significance: A hormone released by the first part of the small intestine when acidic stomach contents enter it. Secretin prompts the pancreas and bile ducts to release alkaline fluid, helping neutralize acid and support digestion.

name: secretion
clinical_significance: The release of a substance from cells or glands into the blood, a body passage, or outside the body. Examples include saliva, hormones, digestive juices, mucus, and substances removed into urine or bile.

name: secretory granule
clinical_significance: Secretory granules store hormones, enzymes, or other cell products for regulated release; abnormal formation or secretion can impair endocrine, immune, or digestive function.

name: secretory vesicle
clinical_significance: Secretory vesicles transport cellular products to the cell surface or other compartments; disrupted trafficking can contribute to endocrine, neurologic, and immune disorders.

name: sectioning technique
clinical_significance: Sectioning techniques prepare thin tissue or material slices for microscopy; artifact-free preparation is essential for accurate histopathology and diagnostic interpretation.

name: sedentary lifestyle
clinical_significance: A sedentary lifestyle is associated with cardiometabolic disease, some cancers, and loss of physical function; reducing prolonged sitting and increasing activity can improve health even when structured exercise is limited.

name: segmental
clinical_significance: Segmental findings affect a defined part of an organ, nerve, or body region; specifying the segment helps localize disease and plan imaging, surgery, or treatment.

name: segmental mandibulectomy
clinical_significance: Segmental mandibulectomy removes a full-thickness portion of the lower jaw, usually for cancer or severe bone disease; reconstruction and dental, speech, and swallowing rehabilitation may be needed.

name: segmental mastectomy
clinical_significance: Segmental mastectomy removes the portion of breast containing a lesion with a margin of surrounding tissue; selection depends on tumor extent and may be followed by radiation and systemic treatment.

name: segmentectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery removing one or more defined sections of a lung rather than an entire lobe. It may treat a small, localized lung cancer or another focal problem while preserving more lung tissue; bleeding, air leakage, infection, and reduced breathing capacity are possible.

name: seizure
clinical_significance: A temporary episode caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain. It may cause shaking, stiffening, unusual sensations, staring, confusion, or loss of awareness and can be triggered by fever, illness, injury, medicines, or epilepsy.

name: selectin
clinical_significance: Selectins are adhesion molecules that help white blood cells and platelets interact with blood-vessel walls; their activity contributes to inflammation, thrombosis, and immune-cell trafficking.

name: selection bias
clinical_significance: Selection bias occurs when study participation or inclusion differs systematically between groups, distorting estimated associations or treatment effects and limiting how results apply to patients.

name: selenium
clinical_significance: A mineral needed for antioxidant enzymes, thyroid function, reproduction, and immune activity. Deficiency is uncommon in many regions, while excessive supplements can cause hair or nail changes, stomach upset, nerve problems, or toxicity.

name: selenocysteine
clinical_significance: Selenocysteine is an amino acid incorporated into enzymes involved in antioxidant defense and thyroid-hormone metabolism; selenium availability affects production of these proteins.

name: selenomethionine
clinical_significance: Selenomethionine is a dietary form of selenium used in supplements; excessive selenium can be toxic, and supplementation is not a substitute for evaluating the cause of symptoms or deficiency risk.

name: selenomonas
clinical_significance: Selenomonas species are anaerobic bacteria found in the mouth and gut; their presence in clinical samples may reflect normal flora, but infection is possible in mixed oral or dental infections.

name: selenomonas noxia
clinical_significance: Selenomonas noxia is an oral bacterium studied in relation to periodontal disease and obesity; detection alone does not diagnose either condition or establish a treatment need.

name: selenomonas sputigena
clinical_significance: Selenomonas sputigena is an oral anaerobe associated with dental plaque and periodontal infections; it may contribute to polymicrobial disease and should be interpreted with the clinical findings.

name: self
clinical_significance: The self is a person’s sense of identity and continuity; changes in self-experience may be relevant when assessing mental health, cognition, trauma, or recovery from illness.

name: self concept
clinical_significance: Self-concept can influence coping, mental health, adherence, and adjustment to chronic illness or disability; assessment may help identify support needs.

name: self efficacy
clinical_significance: A person's confidence in their ability to manage a health condition, follow a treatment plan, and handle symptoms. It can influence participation in care and health outcomes.

name: self medication
clinical_significance: Self-medication is use of medicines without direct clinician supervision; risks include wrong dosing, interactions, delayed diagnosis, and adverse effects, especially with prescription or high-risk drugs.

name: self stimulation
clinical_significance: Self-stimulation may refer to repetitive sensory behavior or sexual stimulation; clinical relevance depends on context, consent, distress, injury, and interference with daily life.

name: self-examination
clinical_significance: Self-examination can help people notice changes such as a new breast, skin, or testicular finding, but it does not replace recommended screening or prompt evaluation of concerning symptoms.

name: self-harm
clinical_significance: Deliberate injury or poisoning of oneself. It may be related to overwhelming emotions, mental illness, trauma, or suicidal thoughts, and can include cutting, burning, hitting, or taking too much medicine. Every episode deserves compassionate safety assessment.

name: self-help devices
clinical_significance: Self-help devices support daily activities for people with disability or limited mobility; appropriate selection and training can improve independence and reduce falls or caregiver burden.

name: self-neglect
clinical_significance: Self-neglect is inability or unwillingness to meet essential needs such as food, hygiene, medication, or safe housing; it may signal cognitive, psychiatric, medical, or social problems and requires careful assessment.

name: self-report
clinical_significance: Self-report provides information about symptoms, behavior, or quality of life that may not be observable clinically; recall, literacy, language, and social desirability can affect accuracy.

name: selumetinib
clinical_significance: Selumetinib is a MEK inhibitor approved for adults and children aged 1 year and older with neurofibromatosis type 1 and symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas. Monitoring is needed for cardiac, ocular, gastrointestinal, skin, and muscle-related adverse effects.

name: semantic dementia
clinical_significance: Semantic dementia is a form of frontotemporal degeneration with progressive loss of word meaning and knowledge about objects or people; assessment helps distinguish it from Alzheimer disease and plan communication support and caregiver care.

name: semantic differential
clinical_significance: A semantic differential records ratings of a person’s perceptions or concepts; in healthcare research it can help measure attitudes or quality of life, but results depend on validated questions and context.

name: semaxinib
clinical_significance: Semaxinib is an investigational kinase inhibitor studied as an anticancer drug; it is not established routine treatment, and its role depends on clinical-trial evidence.

name: semen
clinical_significance: The fluid released during ejaculation, containing sperm from the testes mixed with fluids from the seminal vesicles, prostate, and other glands. It carries and supports sperm; changes in amount, color, blood, or pain may need assessment.

name: semicircular duct
clinical_significance: The semicircular ducts of the inner ear detect rotational head movement and support balance; dysfunction can contribute to vertigo, nausea, and abnormal eye movements.

name: semiconductor
clinical_significance: Semiconductors are used in medical sensors, imaging systems, implants, and diagnostic devices; material reliability and electrical safety affect device performance.

name: semilunar bone
clinical_significance: The semilunar (lunate) bone is a wrist bone; fracture or dislocation can compromise blood supply and lead to chronic pain, stiffness, or bone collapse if missed.

name: seminal fluid
clinical_significance: Seminal fluid carries sperm and supports their survival and movement; semen analysis can help evaluate male fertility, while blood or pain in ejaculate may need assessment.

name: seminal vesicle
clinical_significance: One of a paired set of male accessory reproductive glands behind the urinary bladder.

name: seminoma
clinical_significance: A cancerous tumor arising from sperm-forming cells in the testis. It often grows slowly and is highly treatable with surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, or careful monitoring depending on its stage.

name: semustine
clinical_significance: Semustine is an older alkylating chemotherapy drug associated with delayed leukemia risk and is no longer a routine cancer treatment; prior exposure may matter in a patient’s history.

name: senile dementia
clinical_significance: Senile dementia is an outdated, nonspecific term for cognitive decline in older adults; current assessment should identify the specific cause, function, and potentially reversible contributors without treating age as the diagnosis.

name: senile plaque
clinical_significance: Senile plaques are amyloid-beta deposits found in the brain in Alzheimer disease and some other conditions; they support disease research but do not alone establish a clinical diagnosis.

name: senna extract
clinical_significance: Senna extract is a stimulant laxative used for short-term constipation relief; prolonged or excessive use can cause cramps, diarrhea, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances.

name: sense organ
clinical_significance: Sense organs provide information needed for vision, hearing, balance, smell, taste, and touch; impairment can affect safety, communication, nutrition, and independence.

name: sensorineural hearing loss
clinical_significance: Hearing loss caused by damage to the inner ear or the nerve carrying sound to the brain. It may cause difficulty understanding speech, especially in noise, and can result from aging, loud noise, infection, inherited conditions, or medicines.

name: sensory deprivation
clinical_significance: A major reduction in normal input from sight, sound, touch, movement, or other senses. Prolonged deprivation can affect mood, thinking, sleep, orientation, and perception, especially in isolated or vulnerable people.

name: sensory disorder
clinical_significance: Sensory disorders alter one or more senses and may result from nerve, brain, eye, or ear disease; targeted assessment can identify treatable causes and reduce injury risk.

name: sensory feedback
clinical_significance: Sensory feedback helps the nervous system adjust movement and posture; impaired feedback can affect balance, coordination, and safe performance of daily tasks.

name: sensory ganglia
clinical_significance: Sensory ganglia contain nerve-cell bodies carrying sensation from the body to the spinal cord or brain; injury or infection can cause pain, numbness, or sensory loss.

name: sensory nerve
clinical_significance: Sensory nerves carry information such as pain, temperature, and touch to the central nervous system; testing their function helps localize neuropathy or nerve injury.

name: sensory neuropathy
clinical_significance: Sensory neuropathy damages nerves that carry sensation, causing numbness, burning, pain, or loss of protective feeling; foot checks and cause-directed evaluation can prevent ulcers and falls.

name: sensory process
clinical_significance: Sensory processing affects how the brain interprets sound, touch, movement, and other input; differences may influence function and should be evaluated in context rather than assumed to indicate a single disorder.

name: sensory threshold
clinical_significance: A sensory threshold is the minimum stimulus a person can detect; altered thresholds can help characterize hearing, vision, pain, or nerve dysfunction when measured with validated methods.

name: seocalcitol
clinical_significance: Seocalcitol is a vitamin D analog investigated for antiproliferative effects, including in cancer; it is not routine treatment, and calcium-related effects require attention in research use.

name: sepsis
clinical_significance: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Findings may include altered mental status, hypotension, fast breathing or heart rate, low urine output, elevated lactate, low oxygenation, or other organ injury; the infection source and organ dysfunction must be assessed urgently.

name: septal nuclei
clinical_significance: The septal nuclei are brain regions involved in memory, emotion, and autonomic functions; lesions or research findings may help explain neurologic symptoms but are not assessed as a standalone clinical diagnosis.

name: septate
clinical_significance: Septate structures contain internal partitions; in medicine the term often describes fungal hyphae, which can help laboratories characterize a mold but must be interpreted with culture and clinical findings.

name: septic shock
clinical_significance: A life-threatening complication of sepsis in which infection causes dangerously low blood pressure and poor blood flow to organs, even after initial fluids. Treatment may include antibiotics, fluids, and medicines to support circulation.

name: septicemia
clinical_significance: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection; bacteremia means bacteria are present in blood, but sepsis can occur without a positive blood culture.

name: septo-optic dysplasia
clinical_significance: A condition present from birth involving underdevelopment of one or both optic nerves, parts of the brain’s midline, and sometimes the pituitary gland. It may cause poor vision, involuntary eye movements, seizures, developmental differences, or hormone deficiencies.

name: septum pellucidum
clinical_significance: The septum pellucidum is a thin membrane between the brain’s lateral ventricles; its absence or abnormality may accompany developmental brain conditions and warrants interpretation with imaging and clinical findings.

name: sequence analysis
clinical_significance: Sequence analysis reads the order of DNA or RNA bases and can identify disease-associated variants; results require appropriate interpretation, counseling, and consideration of uncertain findings.

name: sequential
clinical_significance: Sequential treatment or testing follows a defined order; the sequence can affect diagnostic yield, treatment safety, and interpretation of response.

name: serine
clinical_significance: Serine is a nonessential amino acid used in protein synthesis, one-carbon metabolism, membrane formation, and signaling.

name: serine protease
clinical_significance: Serine proteases participate in digestion, clotting, inflammation, and tissue remodeling; abnormal activity or inhibition is relevant to disorders such as bleeding, thrombosis, and inflammatory disease.

name: serious breach
clinical_significance: A serious breach in healthcare privacy or safety may expose patients to harm; prompt containment, reporting, and corrective action support patient protection and trust.

name: seroma
clinical_significance: A pocket of clear body fluid that forms near a surgical incision or injured tissue. It may cause swelling, pressure, or discomfort and often resolves, though large or painful collections may need drainage.

name: serositis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the smooth lining around the lungs, heart, or abdominal organs. It can cause sharp pain that worsens with breathing or movement and may cause fluid to collect around the affected organ.

name: serotonin
clinical_significance: A chemical messenger used by nerve cells and other tissues. It helps regulate mood, sleep, appetite, bowel function, and pain; too much activity from medicines can cause serotonin syndrome.

name: serotonin agonist
clinical_significance: Serotonin agonists activate serotonin receptors and include medicines for migraine and other conditions; effects and risks vary by receptor target and drug, including possible interactions with other serotonergic agents.

name: serotonin antagonist
clinical_significance: Serotonin antagonists block one or more serotonin receptors and are used for conditions such as nausea, migraine, or psychiatric illness; indication-specific benefits and adverse effects differ by drug.

name: serotonin degradation
clinical_significance: Serotonin degradation regulates neurotransmitter availability; altered metabolism can affect research measures and drug response, but is not usually diagnosed from a single serotonin level.

name: serotonin receptor
clinical_significance: Serotonin receptors mediate effects on mood, sleep, gut movement, blood vessels, and nausea; receptor subtype helps explain the actions and adverse effects of serotonergic medicines.

name: serotonin transporter
clinical_significance: The serotonin transporter recycles serotonin at nerve endings and is a target of many antidepressants; genetic or drug-related changes may affect response, interactions, and adverse effects.

name: serotyping
clinical_significance: Serotyping distinguishes microorganisms by surface antigens; it helps track outbreaks, identify clinically important strains, and inform infection-control or vaccine decisions.

name: serous
clinical_significance: Thin, watery, and usually clear, resembling blood serum. Serous fluid can occur normally or collect in a wound, body cavity, or blister.

name: serous membrane
clinical_significance: A thin tissue lining a closed body cavity and covering the organs within it. The pleura, pericardium, and peritoneum are serous membranes; their surfaces produce a small amount of fluid that reduces friction.

name: serous sac
clinical_significance: A serous sac surrounds or supports an organ and may contain a small amount of lubricating fluid; inflammation or excess fluid can impair organ movement or function.

name: serpin
clinical_significance: Serpins regulate proteases involved in clotting, inflammation, and tissue repair; inherited or acquired deficiencies can contribute to bleeding, thrombosis, or lung and liver disease.

name: serratia
clinical_significance: Serratia species are environmental and healthcare-associated bacteria that can cause urinary, respiratory, wound, or bloodstream infections, especially in hospitalized or immunocompromised patients; resistance testing guides treatment.

name: serratia ficaria
clinical_significance: Serratia ficaria is an uncommon environmental bacterium and rare human pathogen; isolation from a patient should be interpreted according to specimen quality, symptoms, and immune status.

name: serratia fonticola
clinical_significance: Serratia fonticola is an uncommon environmental bacterium that rarely causes human infection; clinical significance depends on a compatible illness and recovery from a meaningful specimen.

name: serratia liquefaciens
clinical_significance: Serratia liquefaciens can cause opportunistic infections, including bloodstream or device-associated disease; its identification and antimicrobial susceptibility are important because resistance can occur.

name: serratia marcescens
clinical_significance: Serratia marcescens is an opportunistic healthcare-associated pathogen that can cause urinary, respiratory, wound, and bloodstream infections; antimicrobial resistance and outbreak control are clinically important.

name: serratia odorifera
clinical_significance: Serratia odorifera is an uncommon opportunistic pathogen reported in healthcare-associated infection; culture results require clinical correlation and susceptibility-guided management.

name: serratia plymuthica
clinical_significance: Serratia plymuthica is mainly environmental but can rarely cause opportunistic infection; interpretation of a positive culture depends on specimen source and the patient’s clinical state.

name: serratia rubidaea
clinical_significance: Serratia rubidaea is a rare cause of human infection, including bloodstream infection in vulnerable patients; accurate identification and susceptibility testing help distinguish infection from contamination and guide care.

name: Sertoli cell
clinical_significance: A support cell inside the seminiferous tubules that helps sperm develop and forms part of the blood-testis barrier.

name: sertraline
clinical_significance: Sertraline is an SSRI used for depression, anxiety, and related conditions; common effects include nausea and sexual dysfunction, while serious concerns include serotonin toxicity, bleeding interactions, and suicidal thoughts in some young people.

name: serum
clinical_significance: The clear liquid left after blood has clotted. It contains water, salts, hormones, antibodies, nutrients, and waste products but lacks fibrinogen and most clotting proteins, making it useful for laboratory tests.

name: serum albumin
clinical_significance: Serum albumin helps maintain blood fluid balance and transports substances; low levels may reflect inflammation, liver disease, kidney loss, or malnutrition and are not a specific nutrition marker by themselves.

name: serum globulin
clinical_significance: Serum globulins include antibodies and other proteins; abnormal levels can prompt evaluation for infection, immune disorders, liver disease, or monoclonal protein disorders.

name: serum sickness
clinical_significance: A delayed immune reaction, usually one to three weeks after exposure to certain medicines, injected proteins, or antiserum. It can cause fever, rash or hives, painful swollen joints, enlarged lymph nodes, and sometimes organ problems.

name: sesame oil
clinical_significance: Sesame oil is used in foods, medicines, and topical products; sesame allergy can cause severe reactions, and patients with known allergy should check ingredient and excipient sources.

name: sesamoid bone
clinical_significance: Sesamoid bones sit within tendons, commonly beneath the big-toe joint; fracture or inflammation can cause focal pain and affect weight-bearing.

name: sesquiterpene
clinical_significance: Sesquiterpenes are plant-derived compounds found in fragrances and medicines; some can cause allergic contact dermatitis or other toxicity depending on the compound and exposure.

name: sestamibi scan
clinical_significance: A sestamibi scan uses a radiotracer to assess blood flow or locate abnormal parathyroid tissue; interpretation supports evaluation of selected cardiac or endocrine conditions.

name: setosphaeria rostrata
clinical_significance: Setosphaeria rostrata is an environmental mold with rare reports of human disease; suspected infection requires specialist identification and clinical correlation because evidence and treatment options are limited.

name: sevelamer
clinical_significance: Sevelamer is a nonabsorbed phosphate binder used to control high blood phosphate in chronic kidney disease; gastrointestinal effects and proper timing with meals and other medicines matter.

name: severe
clinical_significance: Severe describes high intensity or substantial impact, but clinical decisions depend on specific findings, organ dysfunction, and validated severity criteria rather than the word alone.

name: severe dengue
clinical_significance: The modern World Health Organization (WHO) classification term for the critical, life-threatening form of dengue virus infection, typically developing around the time of fever defervescence (days 3 to 7). It is characterized by one or more of three major clinical manifestations: severe plasma leakage resulting in hypovolemic shock (dengue shock syndrome) or respiratory distress from fluid accumulation, severe bleeding (such as massive gastrointestinal hemorrhage), or severe organ impairment incl

name: severe myelosuppression
clinical_significance: Severe myelosuppression is marked suppression of blood-cell production, increasing risks of infection, anemia, and bleeding; it may require urgent monitoring, treatment interruption, or supportive care.

name: severe preeclampsia
clinical_significance: Severe preeclampsia can rapidly threaten the pregnant patient and fetus through seizures, stroke, organ injury, placental complications, or fetal compromise; urgent obstetric management and delivery planning are needed.

name: severe sepsis
clinical_significance: Severe sepsis is an older term for sepsis with organ dysfunction; current care treats sepsis as a medical emergency requiring prompt recognition, infection treatment, and organ support.

name: severity
clinical_significance: Severity describes the intensity or impact of disease and helps guide triage and treatment; standardized measures improve communication but do not replace clinical judgment.

name: sevoflurane
clinical_significance: An inhaled anesthetic gas used to start and maintain general anesthesia. It acts in the brain to produce unconsciousness and reduces awareness of pain; it can lower breathing and blood pressure and may trigger malignant hyperthermia in susceptible people.

name: sex
clinical_significance: Sex may refer to biological attributes relevant to anatomy, hormones, reproduction, or disease risk; clinicians should document the specific attribute needed for care rather than assume it from identity.

name: sex behavior
clinical_significance: Sexual behavior can affect reproductive health and risk of sexually transmitted infections; respectful, confidential history-taking supports tailored prevention, testing, and counseling.

name: sex characteristic
clinical_significance: Sex characteristics include anatomy, hormones, chromosomes, and reproductive traits; accurate, respectful documentation supports appropriate screening and care for each patient.

name: sex chromatin
clinical_significance: Sex chromatin reflects condensed X-chromosome material in cells and has historical uses in sex-chromosome evaluation; modern genetic testing is more definitive when clinically indicated.

name: sex chromosome
clinical_significance: Sex chromosomes influence some genetic and reproductive conditions; chromosome analysis can clarify specific diagnoses, but chromosome patterns do not alone determine a person’s gender identity.

name: sex counseling
clinical_significance: Sex counseling provides information and support about sexual health, relationships, function, and risk reduction; it should be confidential, nonjudgmental, and responsive to the patient’s needs.

name: sex determination
clinical_significance: Sex determination is the biological developmental process that establishes reproductive traits; variations may warrant individualized evaluation and counseling when associated with health concerns.

name: sex differentiation
clinical_significance: Sex differentiation shapes development of reproductive anatomy and secondary sex traits; variations can arise from genetic, hormonal, or developmental factors and may require specialized assessment.

name: sex distribution
clinical_significance: Sex distribution in a population can reveal differences in disease burden or treatment outcomes; interpretation should account for age, access to care, and other confounders.

name: sex education
clinical_significance: Sex education can improve knowledge about consent, relationships, contraception, pregnancy, and infection prevention; accurate, age-appropriate information supports health and safety.

name: sex offense
clinical_significance: Sexual offenses can cause physical injury, sexually transmitted infections, pregnancy, and psychological trauma; trauma-informed medical care should address immediate safety, consent, evidence options, and follow-up.

name: sexual abstinence
clinical_significance: Sexual abstinence prevents pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections when practiced consistently; counseling should provide accurate information and respect individual choice.

name: sexual dysfunction
clinical_significance: A group of conditions involving persistent or recurrent difficulty with sexual desire, arousal, erection, ejaculation, orgasm, or pain that causes clinically significant distress. Causes may be physical, psychological, medication-related, hormonal, or related to life circumstances.

name: sexual maturation
clinical_significance: Sexual maturation includes pubertal development and reproductive capacity; unusually early, delayed, or arrested changes may signal endocrine, genetic, or systemic disease and merit evaluation.

name: sexual sterilization
clinical_significance: Sexual sterilization permanently prevents reproduction and requires informed, voluntary consent; counseling should cover alternatives, permanence, risks, and applicable safeguards.

name: sexuality
clinical_significance: Sexuality is part of health and well-being and may be affected by illness, disability, medicines, relationships, and culture; clinicians should make space for relevant concerns without assumptions.

name: sexually transmitted disease
clinical_significance: A sexually transmitted disease is an infection spread mainly through sexual contact. The term sexually transmitted infection is also used because some infections cause no symptoms.

name: Sezary syndrome
clinical_significance: An uncommon form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma involving widespread red skin and abnormal lymphocytes in the blood.

name: sham intervention
clinical_significance: A sham intervention mimics treatment without its active component and can help separate specific treatment effects from expectation or procedure effects in research; ethical design requires informed consent and risk minimization.

name: shame
clinical_significance: Shame can contribute to distress, concealment of symptoms, and avoidance of care; sensitive, nonjudgmental communication may help patients discuss stigmatized conditions and seek support.

name: shampoo
clinical_significance: Shampoo cleans the scalp and hair; certain medicated shampoos treat conditions such as dandruff or fungal disease, while fragrances or preservatives can trigger irritation or allergy.

name: shave biopsy
clinical_significance: Removal of a raised or superficial skin lesion by shaving off a thin layer with a sterile blade. The tissue is examined under a microscope; bleeding, infection, scarring, or an inadequate sample can occur.

name: Sheehan syndrome
clinical_significance: Permanent injury to the pituitary gland caused by severe bleeding or very low blood pressure during or after childbirth. Because the gland makes several hormones, symptoms may include inability to breastfeed, low blood pressure, fatigue, and menstrual or fertility problems.

name: shellfish allergy
clinical_significance: An immune reaction to proteins in crustaceans or mollusks that can cause hives, digestive or respiratory symptoms, or anaphylaxis.

name: shelterin
clinical_significance: Shelterin is a protein complex that protects chromosome ends; defects can cause telomere dysfunction, bone-marrow failure, and pulmonary or liver disease, while telomere testing may support evaluation of telomere biology disorders.

name: shewanella
clinical_significance: Shewanella are environmental bacteria, often associated with water, that can rarely cause wound, ear, biliary, or bloodstream infection, especially in people with chronic illness or water exposure; culture and susceptibility results guide interpretation and care.

name: shewanella algae
clinical_significance: Shewanella algae is a water-associated bacterium that can cause wound, ear, or invasive infection, sometimes after seawater exposure; accurate identification matters because serious disease and antimicrobial resistance can occur.

name: shewanella putrefaciens
clinical_significance: Shewanella putrefaciens is an uncommon water-associated pathogen linked to skin, soft-tissue, and intra-abdominal infection; clinical significance depends on the specimen and symptoms, and susceptibility testing guides treatment.

name: shield
clinical_significance: A shield may refer to protective equipment or a medical barrier; correct fit and use can reduce exposure to infectious agents, radiation, or other hazards.

name: shiga toxin
clinical_significance: Shiga toxin is a bacterial toxin that can damage blood vessels and cause bloody diarrhea, kidney injury, and hemolytic uremic syndrome; identifying toxin-producing infection affects monitoring, infection control, and treatment choices.

name: shigella
clinical_significance: A genus of bacteria causing shigellosis, an acute diarrheal illness that may include fever and bloody stools.

name: shigella boydii
clinical_significance: Shigella boydii causes shigellosis, a highly contagious diarrheal illness that may include fever, cramps, and bloody stool; hydration and hygiene are important, and antibiotic use depends on severity and susceptibility.

name: shigella dysenteriae
clinical_significance: Shigella dysenteriae can cause severe dysentery and, in some strains, Shiga toxin-associated hemolytic uremic syndrome; prompt assessment, hydration, hygiene, and susceptibility-informed treatment are important.

name: shigella flexneri
clinical_significance: Shigella flexneri causes shigellosis, which spreads readily by fecal-oral and sexual contact; antimicrobial resistance can complicate treatment and make culture or susceptibility testing important.

name: shigella sonnei
clinical_significance: Shigella sonnei is a common cause of shigellosis, a contagious diarrheal infection; most cases improve with fluids and supportive care, while severe disease and resistant strains may require targeted treatment.

name: shigella vaccines
clinical_significance: Shigella vaccines are under development because shigellosis causes substantial diarrheal illness and antimicrobial resistance is increasing; no routinely available vaccine currently prevents the infection.

name: shingles
clinical_significance: Herpes zoster, reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in sensory nerves causing a painful one-sided blistering rash. Pain, burning, or tingling may begin before the rash. Eye or ear involvement can threaten vision or hearing, and persistent nerve pain after the rash heals is called postherpetic neuralgia; prompt assessment is important for facial or eye-area rashes.

name: shivering
clinical_significance: Repeated, involuntary muscle contractions that generate heat, usually in response to cold or fever. Severe or unexplained shivering may occur with infection, medicine reactions, or other illness and should be assessed with the other symptoms.

name: shock
clinical_significance: A life-threatening failure of circulation in which organs do not receive enough blood and oxygen. It can result from severe blood or fluid loss, heart failure, overwhelming infection, a severe allergic reaction, or an obstruction to blood flow. Signs may include confusion, faintness, cold or mottled skin, rapid breathing, little urine, or very low blood pressure and require emergency treatment.

name: shone complex
clinical_significance: A group of congenital left-sided obstructive heart lesions, classically including

name: shope papilloma
clinical_significance: Shope papillomavirus causes papillomas in rabbits and is an animal research model for studying papillomavirus-related tumors; it is not a human pathogen.

name: short stature
clinical_significance: Height substantially below the expected range for age and sex, requiring assessment of growth pattern and cause.

name: short tandem repeat
clinical_significance: Short tandem repeats are repeated DNA sequences used in forensic identification, kinship testing, and some genetic analyses; clinical interpretation depends on validated methods and informed consent.

name: short-term memory
clinical_significance: The ability to hold and use a small amount of information for seconds or minutes. It helps with following instructions, doing mental tasks, and remembering a recent conversation before information is stored more permanently or forgotten.

name: shoulder
clinical_significance: The area where the upper limb joins the body, including the shoulder blade, collarbone, and upper-arm bone. Its main joint allows a wide range of arm movement but is less stable and can be injured or dislocated.

name: shoulder dislocation
clinical_significance: Complete displacement of the upper arm bone from the shoulder socket, usually caused by a fall, collision,

name: shoulder dystocia
clinical_significance: A childbirth emergency in which the baby’s head is born but a shoulder becomes stuck behind the mother’s pelvic bone. It requires immediate maneuvers because delay can cause lack of oxygen, fractures, or nerve injury in the baby and heavy bleeding in the mother.

name: shoulder fracture
clinical_significance: A shoulder fracture can involve the collarbone, scapula, or upper arm bone and may impair arm function; displacement, nerve or vessel injury, and bone healing determine treatment and rehabilitation.

name: shoulder joint
clinical_significance: The shoulder joint provides a wide range of arm motion but is prone to instability, rotator-cuff injury, and arthritis; pain or loss of motion may warrant examination and imaging.

name: shoulder pain
clinical_significance: Pain in or around the shoulder caused by injury, tendon or bursa disorders, arthritis, nerve disease, or

name: shunt
clinical_significance: A passage that diverts blood, cerebrospinal fluid, urine, or another fluid from one channel to another.

name: shunt thrombosis
clinical_significance: Shunt thrombosis is clot formation that blocks a surgically created or implanted shunt, potentially interrupting dialysis access or blood or fluid flow; sudden loss of function requires prompt evaluation.

name: Shwachman syndrome
clinical_significance: An inherited multisystem disorder usually involving exocrine pancreatic insufficiency,

name: shwartzman phenomenon
clinical_significance: The Shwartzman phenomenon describes tissue injury from an exaggerated response to bacterial endotoxin, historically used in research; it is not a routine clinical diagnosis but illustrates mechanisms of severe inflammation and coagulation.

name: sialadenitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of a salivary gland, causing painful swelling near the cheek or under the jaw, often worse during meals. Causes include bacteria, viruses, dehydration, or a blocked duct; persistent fever or pus needs medical care.

name: sialorrhea
clinical_significance: Excess saliva or difficulty controlling and swallowing it, causing drooling. It commonly occurs with neurologic disease, swallowing difficulty, dental problems, or some medicines; treatment addresses the cause and may include swallowing therapy or selected medicines.

name: sialuria
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which cells make and release too much sialic acid, a sugar used on cell surfaces. It may cause developmental delay, enlarged liver and spleen, distinctive facial features, and variable learning difficulties.

name: sibling
clinical_significance: A person's brother or sister; family history from siblings can inform genetic and disease risk assessment.

name: sicca syndrome
clinical_significance: Persistent dryness of the eyes and mouth caused by reduced tears and saliva. It may result from Sjögren syndrome, medicines, dehydration, radiation, or other illnesses and can lead to eye irritation, mouth sores, tooth decay, or difficulty swallowing.

name: sickle cell anemia
clinical_significance: An inherited blood disorder in which abnormal haemoglobin makes red blood cells stiff, sticky, and crescent-shaped. These cells break down easily and can block small blood vessels, causing anaemia, severe pain, stroke, lung problems, jaundice, and serious infections.

name: Sickle Cell Dactylitis
clinical_significance: Painful swelling of the hands or feet caused by blockage of small blood vessels during a sickle-cell

name: side
clinical_significance: Side may indicate laterality in clinical documentation; correct right-left labeling is essential for imaging, procedures, medication delivery, and avoiding wrong-site errors.

name: side effect
clinical_significance: An unintended effect that occurs while a medicine is used at a normal dose. It may be mild, such as nausea or drowsiness, or serious, such as bleeding, severe allergy, organ injury, or an abnormal heart rhythm.

name: sideroblastic anemia
clinical_significance: Anemia caused by faulty hemoglobin production. Iron builds up inside developing red blood cells instead of being used properly; causes include inherited disorders, alcohol, some medicines or toxins, vitamin B6 deficiency, and bone-marrow disease.

name: siderophore
clinical_significance: Siderophores are microbial molecules that bind and acquire iron; they support pathogen growth and are studied as targets for antimicrobial strategies and as tools for drug delivery.

name: sievert
clinical_significance: A unit used to estimate how much biological harm ionizing radiation could cause. It accounts for the type of radiation and the sensitivity of different tissues and is used when discussing radiation risk.

name: sigmoid colon
clinical_significance: The curved, S-shaped section of the large intestine between the descending colon and rectum. It stores stool before bowel movements and is a common site for diverticular disease, twisting, and colorectal cancer.

name: sigmoidoscope
clinical_significance: A sigmoidoscope is the instrument used to examine the rectum and lower colon; findings can identify bleeding, inflammation, polyps, or cancer and may guide biopsy or treatment.

name: sigmoidoscopy
clinical_significance: Endoscopic examination of the rectum and lower colon using a flexible or rigid sigmoidoscope. It can identify inflammation, bleeding, polyps, or tumors and may allow biopsy or treatment.

name: sign language
clinical_significance: Sign language is a complete visual language using hand shape, movement, position, facial expression, and body movement rather than spoken sound.

name: signal peptide
clinical_significance: A short part of a newly made protein that acts like an address label, directing the protein to the cell membrane, outside the cell, or a particular internal compartment. It is often removed after delivery.

name: signal transduction
clinical_significance: The chain of events by which a hormone, nerve chemical, or medicine attaches to a cell and produces a response inside it. The response can change cell activity, movement, growth, survival, or gene use.

name: sildenafil citrate
clinical_significance: The citrate salt of sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor used for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

name: silent mutation
clinical_significance: A DNA change that usually does not alter the amino acid in the protein made from the gene. It may still affect how the gene is copied, how long its RNA lasts, or how much protein is produced.

name: silicate
clinical_significance: A salt or ester containing silicon and oxygen, found in minerals and industrial materials; inhalation of some silicate dusts can irritate the lungs or contribute to pneumoconiosis.

name: silicon dioxide
clinical_significance: A mineral found in soil, rock, dust, and industrial materials. Breathing crystalline forms over time can scar the lungs, cause silicosis, and increase the risk of lung cancer.

name: silicone
