clinical_significance: A family of synthetic silicon-containing polymers used in medical devices, implants, sealants, and consumer products; medical risks depend on the product and exposure.

name: silicone elastomer
clinical_significance: A flexible, rubber-like silicone material used in implants, tubing, dressings, and other devices; complications may include infection, leakage, allergy, or device failure.

name: silicosis
clinical_significance: A permanent lung-scarring disease caused by breathing crystalline silica dust. It can cause cough, breathlessness, reduced lung function, tuberculosis risk, and progressive respiratory disability after workplace or environmental exposure.

name: silk
clinical_significance: Silk is a protein fiber used in textiles and some medical sutures or biomaterials; reactions and tissue response depend on the product and processing.

name: siltuximab
clinical_significance: A monoclonal antibody that binds interleukin-6 and is used to treat adults with multicentric Castleman disease who are negative for HIV and human herpesvirus 8.

name: silver
clinical_significance: A metal used in some dressings, creams, and medical devices for antimicrobial activity; excessive exposure can cause permanent blue-gray skin discoloration called argyria.

name: silver nitrate
clinical_significance: A caustic antiseptic used topically to cauterize tissue, control minor bleeding, or treat some wounds; it can burn healthy skin and permanently stain tissue.

name: silver sulfadiazine
clinical_significance: A topical antimicrobial cream formerly used widely for burns; it may delay healing in some wounds and is not appropriate for everyone, including some newborns and people with sulfonamide allergy.

name: silymarin
clinical_significance: A mixture of flavonolignans from milk thistle marketed as a dietary supplement; evidence for treating liver disease is limited and product quality varies.

name: simeprevir
clinical_significance: An older hepatitis C virus NS3/4A protease inhibitor formerly used with other antivirals; it is no longer a usual first-line treatment because better direct-acting regimens are available.

name: simethicone
clinical_significance: Simethicone is a non-absorbed antifoaming agent that coalesces gas bubbles in the gastrointestinal tract and is used for symptomatic relief of bloating; it does not treat the underlying cause of pain.

name: simian virus 40
clinical_significance: Simian virus 40 is a monkey polyomavirus used extensively in laboratory research; historical concerns about contaminated vaccines have not established that it causes human cancer, and it is not a recognized human disease diagnosis.

name: simple mastectomy
clinical_significance: Simple mastectomy removes the breast tissue and nipple while leaving most chest muscles and usually the underarm lymph nodes.

name: simplexvirus
clinical_significance: A genus of herpesviruses that includes herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, which cause cold sores, genital herpes, and other infections.

name: simuliidae
clinical_significance: The family of black flies; bites can cause itchy skin reactions, and some species transmit Onchocerca volvulus, the parasite that causes river blindness.

name: simultanagnosia
clinical_significance: An inability to see more than one object, or the whole visual scene, at the same time even though basic eyesight may be adequate. It usually results from damage to brain areas that combine visual information.

name: simvastatin
clinical_significance: A statin medicine that lowers LDL, often called bad cholesterol, by reducing cholesterol production in the liver. It helps lower the risk of heart attack and stroke; muscle pain, liver problems, and medicine interactions are possible.

name: sincalide
clinical_significance: A synthetic form of cholecystokinin used during gallbladder imaging to stimulate contraction and measure bile flow; it may cause abdominal pain, nausea, or flushing.

name: sindbis virus
clinical_significance: A mosquito-borne virus that can cause fever, rash, and joint pain. It occurs mainly in parts of Africa, Europe, Asia, and Australia.

name: sinecatechins
clinical_significance: A topical green-tea catechin ointment used for external genital and perianal warts caused by human papillomavirus; it can cause local irritation and should not be used internally.

name: singlet oxygen
clinical_significance: A highly reactive form of oxygen involved in oxidative reactions, immune defenses, photodynamic therapy, and tissue injury from oxidative stress.

name: sinuatrial node
clinical_significance: The sinoatrial node, a group of specialized cells in the right atrium that normally initiates the heartbeat and sets the cardiac rhythm.

name: sinus
clinical_significance: A sinus is a cavity, channel, or tract; in anatomy it may mean a paranasal air space, venous channel, or abnormal passage from a diseased area to the surface.

name: sinus arrhythmia
clinical_significance: Sinus arrhythmia is normal variation in sinus-heart rate, commonly speeding during inhalation and slowing during exhalation, especially in young people.

name: sinus bradycardia
clinical_significance: Sinus bradycardia is a sinus rhythm slower than the expected rate; it can be normal during sleep or athletic conditioning but may also reflect drugs or disease.

name: sinus histiocytosis
clinical_significance: An increase in cleanup immune cells within the open spaces of a lymph node. It is often a response to nearby inflammation, infection, a tumor, or tissue breakdown and is interpreted with the rest of the biopsy.

name: sinus pain
clinical_significance: Pressure or pain around the forehead, cheeks, nose, or eyes caused by sinus inflammation, infection, migraine,

name: sinus rhythm
clinical_significance: A heart rhythm started by electrical impulses from the sinoatrial node, the natural pacemaker. It is usually regular, although sinus rhythm can be too fast, too slow, or affected by illness.

name: sinus tachycardia
clinical_significance: A heart rhythm originating in the sinoatrial node with a rate faster than normal, commonly occurring as a physiologic response to exercise, fever, pain, dehydration, or stress.

name: sinusitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the lining of one or more paranasal sinuses. It may follow a viral respiratory infection or be associated with allergy, nasal inflammation, or other causes. Common features include nasal obstruction, discharge, facial pressure or pain, headache, and reduced smell. Acute and chronic forms differ in duration and pattern.

name: sinusoid
clinical_significance: A small, wide blood vessel with unusually open walls, found especially in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Its structure allows blood to exchange cells, proteins, nutrients, and waste with nearby tissue.

name: siplizumab
clinical_significance: Siplizumab is an investigational antibody targeting CD2 studied for immune-mediated disease and transplantation; it is not routine therapy, and infection and immune-suppression risks require trial monitoring.

name: sipuleucel-T
clinical_significance: A personalized cancer immunotherapy made from a patient’s immune cells and used for selected advanced prostate cancers. The cells are trained to recognize a prostate-cancer target before being returned to the patient.

name: sirenomelia
clinical_significance: A rare congenital malformation in which the lower limbs are partially or completely

name: sirolimus
clinical_significance: Sirolimus is an mTOR inhibitor used for immunosuppression after transplantation and selected vascular or lymphatic disorders; mouth ulcers, hyperlipidaemia, cytopenias, infection, impaired wound healing, and pneumonitis can occur.

name: sisomicin
clinical_significance: An aminoglycoside antibiotic related to gentamicin that has activity against some aerobic gram-negative bacteria; use is limited by kidney and hearing toxicity.

name: sitagliptin phosphate
clinical_significance: Sitagliptin phosphate is a DPP-4 inhibitor that prolongs incretin activity and improves glucose-dependent insulin secretion in type 2 diabetes; dose adjustment in kidney disease and rare pancreatitis or severe joint pain are important considerations.

name: site-directed mutagenesis
clinical_significance: Site-directed mutagenesis deliberately changes selected DNA bases to study gene function or engineer proteins; it is a research method rather than a routine patient test.

name: sitosterolemia
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which the body absorbs and stores too much plant sterol, a substance found in plant foods. The buildup can cause early artery disease, skin lumps, anemia, easy bleeding, or low platelets.

name: sitosterols
clinical_significance: Sitosterols are plant sterols that can lower intestinal cholesterol absorption; in sitosterolemia they accumulate abnormally and can cause early atherosclerosis, so dietary intake and specialist treatment matter.

name: sitting position
clinical_significance: An upright or semiupright position in which the patient's torso is elevated and the hips and knees are flexed; it is used for selected shoulder and neurosurgical procedures.

name: situs ambiguus
clinical_significance: A birth difference in which internal organs are arranged irregularly rather than in the usual left-right pattern. It is often associated with congenital heart defects and an absent, small, or abnormally functioning spleen.

name: Situs Inversus
clinical_significance: A congenital condition in which the thoracic and abdominal organs are reversed or

name: size perception
clinical_significance: The brain’s judgment of how large or small an object or body part is. Vision, touch, distance, and context all contribute; eye or brain disorders can make objects appear unusually large or small.

name: sizofiran
clinical_significance: Sizofiran is an investigational fungal-derived immune modulator studied as an anticancer adjunct; it is not standard treatment, and evidence from clinical trials determines any potential role.

name: Sjogren's syndrome
clinical_significance: Older name for Sjögren disease, an autoimmune disease that commonly causes dry eyes and dry mouth.

name: skeletal development
clinical_significance: Skeletal development is formation, growth, remodeling, and maturation of bones and cartilage from embryonic life through adulthood.

name: skeletal dysplasia
clinical_significance: An inherited disorder of bone or cartilage development that may cause short or uneven growth, unusually shaped limbs, spine problems, or other differences in the skeleton. Effects vary widely between conditions.

name: skeletal muscle tissue
clinical_significance: Voluntary striated muscle attached to bones or other structures, composed of contractile fibers that generate movement, posture, heat, and joint stability.

name: skeletal myocytes
clinical_significance: Skeletal myocytes are striated muscle cells responsible for voluntary movement, posture, heat production, and stabilization of joints.

name: skeletal system
clinical_significance: The skeletal system consists of bones, cartilage, joints, and supporting ligaments that provide structure, protect organs, enable movement, and store minerals.

name: skeleton
clinical_significance: The body’s framework of bones and cartilage that supports movement and protects organs. It also stores minerals, contains marrow that makes blood cells, and provides attachment points for muscles and ligaments.

name: skin
clinical_significance: The body's outer covering, consisting mainly of the epidermis and dermis with appendages such as hair, nails, and glands. It protects against injury, infection, ultraviolet light, and water loss; detects touch, pressure, pain, and temperature; helps regulate body temperature; and contributes to immune defense and vitamin D production.

name: skin absorption
clinical_significance: Movement of a substance through the skin into underlying tissues or the bloodstream. Absorption depends

name: skin aging
clinical_significance: Natural aging and long-term sun exposure gradually thin and dry the skin, reduce elasticity, slow healing, and cause wrinkles or dark spots. Limiting ultraviolet exposure, using protective clothing, and applying broad-spectrum sunscreen can reduce further damage.

name: skin carcinoma
clinical_significance: Cancer arising from skin cells, most commonly basal-cell or squamous-cell carcinoma. It may appear as a changing sore, lump, scaly patch, or wound that does not heal and needs examination.

name: skin care
clinical_significance: Measures that protect and maintain the skin, including gentle cleansing, moisturization, sun protection, wound care, avoidance of irritants, and treatment of identified disease.

name: skin erosion
clinical_significance: A shallow loss of the epidermis that leaves a moist or crusted surface but does not extend deeply into the dermis, often caused by friction, scratching, blister rupture, or inflammation.

name: skin examination
clinical_significance: Systematic inspection and palpation of the skin, hair, nails, and mucous membranes to assess color, lesions, texture, distribution, vascular signs, infection, and cancer warning features.

name: skin induration
clinical_significance: Unusual hardness or firmness of the skin or tissue beneath it. Causes include scar formation, inflammation, swelling, infection, an infiltrating disease, or a growth; examination determines the cause.

name: skin mastocytoma
clinical_significance: A localized collection of mast cells in the skin, usually a yellow-brown or reddish plaque or nodule in a child that may swell, itch, or redden when rubbed.

name: skin necrosis
clinical_significance: Death of skin tissue from ischemia, infection, pressure, toxins, trauma, vasculitis, or severe inflammation, producing discoloration, blisters, ulcers, or black eschar.

name: skin neoplasm
clinical_significance: A skin neoplasm is an abnormal growth in the skin that may be benign, precancerous, or malignant.

name: skin nodule
clinical_significance: A new or changing skin nodule may be benign, infectious, inflammatory, or cancerous; examination and, when indicated, biopsy help identify lesions needing treatment.

name: skin papilloma
clinical_significance: A skin papilloma is usually a benign growth, but appearance, site, symptoms, and change over time determine whether examination or biopsy is needed.

name: skin pigmentation
clinical_significance: Skin color is produced mainly by melanin made by pigment-producing cells. Sun exposure, hormones, inflammation, medicines, and illness can make areas darker or lighter; new or changing discoloration may need examination.

name: skin tag
clinical_significance: A small, harmless (benign) growth of soft skin that hangs from a narrow stalk (peduncle). Commonly appearing in body folds and friction areas—such as the neck, armpits, groin, eyelids, and under the breasts—they consist of loose collagen fibers and small blood vessels. While medically harmless, they are frequently associated with skin friction, aging, pregnancy, obesity, or insulin resistance, and can be easily removed if irritated or for appearance.

name: skin transplantation
clinical_significance: Skin transplantation replaces damaged or missing skin after burns, trauma, or surgery; graft take, infection prevention, scarring, and rehabilitation affect recovery.

name: skin ulcer
clinical_significance: A skin ulcer is an open wound that may result from pressure, poor circulation, diabetes, infection, or inflammation; identifying the cause and protecting the wound are essential to healing and preventing complications.

name: skin vesicle
clinical_significance: A skin vesicle is a small fluid-filled blister that may occur with infection, allergy, burns, or autoimmune disease; distribution and associated symptoms help determine the cause.

name: skin wrinkling
clinical_significance: Skin wrinkling is commonly age-related or due to sun exposure, but sudden skin changes can accompany dehydration or connective-tissue disease; sun protection helps limit photoaging.

name: skull
clinical_significance: The bony framework of the head that protects the brain and supports the face, eyes, ears, and jaw.

name: skull fracture
clinical_significance: A break in one or more skull bones caused by trauma. It may occur with bleeding inside the skull, brain injury, or leakage of clear fluid from the nose or ear and requires medical assessment.

name: skull neoplasm
clinical_significance: A skull neoplasm may be benign or malignant and can cause pain, swelling, cranial-nerve symptoms, or neurologic complications; imaging and pathology guide treatment.

name: slackia exigua
clinical_significance: Slackia exigua is an oral anaerobic bacterium associated with dental and periodontal infections and rarely invasive disease; its significance depends on specimen source and clinical findings.

name: sleep
clinical_significance: A naturally recurring state in which awareness and responses to the surroundings decrease while the brain and body follow organized patterns. Sleep supports learning, memory, emotional health, physical recovery, immune function, and metabolism.

name: sleep apnea
clinical_significance: Repeated pauses or reductions in breathing during sleep. It can result from the airway closing, the brain failing to signal breathing, or both, and may cause loud snoring, gasping, poor sleep, daytime sleepiness, and low oxygen.

name: sleep deprivation
clinical_significance: Sleep deprivation impairs attention, mood, reaction time, and immune and metabolic health; persistent insufficient sleep raises risks of accidents and chronic disease.

name: sleep disorder
clinical_significance: Sleep disorders can impair daytime function, safety, mood, and cardiometabolic health; evaluation is guided by the pattern of symptoms, sleep schedule, medicines, and possible breathing or movement problems.

name: sleep disorders
clinical_significance: A group of conditions affecting sleep quality, timing, duration, breathing, movement, or behavior. Major groups include insomnia, sleep-related breathing disorders, central disorders of hypersomnolence, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders, parasomnias, and sleep-related movement disorders. Examples include sleep apnea, narcolepsy, restless legs syndrome, and sleep paralysis.

name: sleep paralysis
clinical_significance: Temporary inability to move or speak when falling asleep or waking, while awareness is partly or fully preserved.

name: sleep stage
clinical_significance: Sleep stages reflect changing brain activity and body function across the night; disruption or abnormal stage patterns may help characterize sleep disorders but require clinical context.

name: sleep terror
clinical_significance: Sleep terrors are episodes of intense fear and autonomic arousal, usually during deep sleep in children; frequent, injurious, or atypical episodes may warrant assessment for other sleep or neurologic conditions.

name: sleeplessness
clinical_significance: Insomnia involves persistent difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or returning to sleep despite adequate opportunity, with daytime impairment; chronic symptoms can benefit from structured behavioral treatment and evaluation of contributing conditions.

name: slow respiration
clinical_significance: Slow respiration can result from sedatives, neurologic disease, metabolic problems, or sleep-related breathing disorders; significant slowing with reduced alertness can indicate respiratory failure and needs urgent assessment.

name: slow-wave sleep
clinical_significance: The deepest stage of non-REM sleep, marked by slow brain waves and reduced response to sounds or touch. It supports physical recovery, memory, and hormone release and is often reduced by ageing, illness, alcohol, or sleep disruption.

name: small
clinical_significance: Small is a size descriptor whose clinical meaning depends on the structure, age, and measurement method; growth or organ size should be interpreted against appropriate reference ranges.

name: small intestine
clinical_significance: The long, coiled part of the digestive tract between the stomach and large intestine. It receives bile and pancreatic juices, completes digestion, and absorbs most nutrients and much of the body's water.

name: small molecule
clinical_significance: Small molecules include many medicines and signaling compounds; size influences absorption, distribution, metabolism, and drug-target interactions.

name: smallpox
clinical_significance: A severe contagious disease caused by variola virus, producing fever and rash; global eradication was certified in 1980.

name: smallpox vaccine
clinical_significance: Smallpox vaccines were used to eradicate smallpox and may be used for selected high-risk exposures or preparedness; replication-competent vaccines can cause serious adverse effects in some people.

name: smallpox virus
clinical_significance: Variola virus causes smallpox, an eradicated but highly contagious and severe disease; any suspected release or case requires immediate public-health and infection-control response.

name: smegma
clinical_significance: A collection of shed cells, oils, and moisture around the genital folds, which may promote irritation if hygiene is poor.

name: Smith-Magenis syndrome
clinical_significance: A genetic neurodevelopmental disorder, usually involving deletion of 17p11.2 or an RAI1

name: smokeless tobacco
clinical_significance: Smokeless tobacco delivers nicotine and causes dependence, oral lesions, gum recession, tooth loss, cardiovascular risk, and cancers of the mouth, throat, and pancreas. Quitting reduces harm, and counseling plus approved medicines improve cessation success.

name: smoking
clinical_significance: Inhalation of smoke from burning tobacco or other substances, associated with addiction, cancer, cardiovascular disease, and lung disease.

name: smoking behavior
clinical_significance: Smoking behavior includes patterns of tobacco use and dependence; understanding triggers and frequency helps tailor cessation support and reduce cardiovascular, respiratory, and cancer risks.

name: smoking cessation
clinical_significance: The process of stopping tobacco or nicotine use. It may involve counseling, behavioral support, medicines, or nicotine

name: smooth muscle
clinical_significance: Muscle that works automatically in the walls of hollow organs, blood vessels, and airways. It controls processes such as bowel movement, bladder emptying, blood-vessel width, airway narrowing, and childbirth contractions.

name: smooth muscle cell
clinical_significance: Smooth muscle cells control involuntary contraction in blood vessels and hollow organs; abnormal growth or function contributes to conditions such as asthma, hypertension, and gastrointestinal motility disorders.

name: smooth pursuit
clinical_significance: Smooth pursuit is the eye movement that tracks a moving target; impairment can indicate neurologic or ocular dysfunction and is assessed during examination of eye movements.

name: smrt protein
clinical_significance: SMRT is a corepressor protein that regulates gene transcription and hormone-receptor signaling; altered function is studied in cancer and endocrine disease but is not a routine diagnostic marker.

name: Sneddon syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare disorder in which small arteries become blocked, causing a net-like purplish skin pattern and repeated strokes or stroke-like events. Headache, high blood pressure, memory problems, or heart-valve changes may also occur.

name: sneeze
clinical_significance: Sneezing is a protective reflex that clears nasal irritants; persistent or frequent sneezing commonly reflects allergy or infection and may respond to cause-directed care.

name: snoring
clinical_significance: Noisy breathing during sleep caused by vibration of relaxed or narrowed tissues in the throat. It can be harmless, but loud frequent snoring with pauses in breathing, choking, morning headaches, or daytime sleepiness may indicate sleep apnoea.

name: soblidotin
clinical_significance: Soblidotin is an investigational anticancer agent that disrupts microtubules; it is not an established treatment, and its potential benefit and toxicity have been evaluated in clinical trials.

name: social behavior
clinical_significance: Social behavior affects relationships, support, and daily functioning; changes may be relevant to mental-health, neurologic, or developmental assessment.

name: social disinhibition
clinical_significance: Social disinhibition is reduced restraint in social situations and can occur with brain injury, dementia, some psychiatric conditions, or substance use; new onset warrants evaluation for underlying causes and safety concerns.

name: social group
clinical_significance: Social groups can influence health behaviors, belonging, and access to support; group context may matter in public-health interventions and care planning.

name: social media
clinical_significance: Social media can affect health information, social support, body image, and mental well-being; clinicians may ask about online exposure when relevant to symptoms or behavior.

name: social perception
clinical_significance: Social perception is the interpretation of others’ emotions and intentions; difficulties may affect relationships and can occur in autism, brain injury, or psychiatric and neurologic disorders.

name: social problem
clinical_significance: Social problems such as isolation, housing insecurity, or interpersonal conflict can worsen health and make treatment plans harder to follow; identifying needs can connect patients with support.

name: social psychology
clinical_significance: Social psychology examines how social contexts shape behavior and health; its findings inform communication, adherence, stigma reduction, and public-health interventions.

name: social role
clinical_significance: A social role can change with illness, disability, caregiving, or treatment; understanding role demands helps clinicians address functional impact and support needs.

name: social support
clinical_significance: Social support can improve coping, treatment adherence, and recovery, while isolation is associated with poorer health outcomes; care plans can include family, peers, or community resources when desired.

name: social work
clinical_significance: Social work helps address practical and psychosocial barriers such as housing, finances, safety, and access to services; it can support care coordination and discharge planning.

name: socialization
clinical_significance: Socialization shapes communication, relationships, and health behavior across development; disruptions may affect mental health and participation in care.

name: sociobiology
clinical_significance: Sociobiology studies biological influences on social behavior; it is mainly a research framework and should not be used to infer an individual’s health or behavior without evidence.

name: socioeconomics
clinical_significance: Socioeconomic conditions influence exposure to health risks, access to care, and health outcomes; assessing these factors can guide appropriate support and equitable treatment.

name: sociometric technique
clinical_significance: Sociometric techniques measure relationships and patterns within groups; in health research they can help assess social networks and support, with privacy and interpretation safeguards.

name: sodium
clinical_significance: A mineral and body salt helping control fluid balance, nerves, muscles, and blood pressure; abnormal levels can be harmful.

name: sodium acetate
clinical_significance: Sodium acetate is used in some intravenous fluids, dialysis solutions, and laboratory preparations; its sodium and alkalinizing effects matter in patients with fluid, electrolyte, or acid-base disorders.

name: sodium bicarbonate
clinical_significance: Sodium bicarbonate is used in selected cases of metabolic acidosis, poisoning, or urinary alkalinization; inappropriate use can cause sodium overload, alkalosis, or low potassium.

name: sodium borocaptate
clinical_significance: Sodium borocaptate is a boron carrier studied for boron neutron capture therapy, including brain tumors; its clinical role depends on specialized treatment protocols and tumor boron uptake.

name: sodium cation
clinical_significance: Sodium is the main extracellular cation and a key blood electrolyte; abnormal levels can cause neurologic symptoms, and rapid correction of severe abnormalities can itself be dangerous.

name: sodium channel
clinical_significance: Sodium channels generate electrical signals in nerves, muscles, and the heart; channel disorders or channel-blocking drugs can affect pain, seizures, rhythm, and muscle function.

name: sodium chloride
clinical_significance: The salt sodium chloride; sterile solutions are used for fluid replacement, irrigation, and drug dilution.

name: sodium citrate
clinical_significance: Sodium citrate is used as an anticoagulant in blood collection and dialysis and as a urinary alkalinizer; excess citrate can alter calcium levels or acid-base balance.

name: sodium cyanide
clinical_significance: Sodium cyanide is a rapidly acting, potentially fatal poison that blocks cellular oxygen use; suspected exposure is an emergency requiring immediate specialist response and antidotal care.

name: sodium fluoride
clinical_significance: Sodium fluoride is used topically to prevent dental caries; excessive ingestion, especially by children, can cause gastrointestinal symptoms and, at high doses, serious toxicity.

name: sodium hypochlorite
clinical_significance: The active chemical in many bleach and disinfectant products. It kills many germs when used correctly, but concentrated liquid can burn skin, eyes, and the digestive tract; mixing it with acids or ammonia can release dangerous gas.

name: sodium lactate
clinical_significance: Sodium lactate is used in some intravenous solutions and as a laboratory reagent; its effect on sodium balance and acid-base status depends on the formulation and the patient’s metabolism.

name: sodium salicylate
clinical_significance: Sodium salicylate is an older salicylate medicine with analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects; toxicity can cause ringing in the ears, rapid breathing, acid-base disturbances, and neurologic symptoms.

name: sodium selenite
clinical_significance: Sodium selenite is a selenium compound used in nutrition and research; selenium is essential in small amounts but excess exposure can cause gastrointestinal, neurologic, and hair or nail effects.

name: sodium stibogluconate
clinical_significance: Sodium stibogluconate is an antimonial drug used for selected leishmaniasis infections; toxicity can affect the heart, pancreas, liver, and blood counts, so specialist monitoring is required.

name: sodium sulfite
clinical_significance: Sodium sulfite is used as a preservative and in some medicines; it can trigger bronchospasm or allergic-like reactions in sensitive people, particularly some people with asthma.

name: sodium thiosulfate
clinical_significance: Sodium thiosulfate is used for cyanide poisoning and selected other indications; it is also studied to reduce cisplatin-related hearing damage, with use guided by the specific protocol and risks.

name: sofosbuvir
clinical_significance: Sofosbuvir is a direct-acting antiviral used in combination regimens to cure hepatitis C; regimen choice depends on genotype, prior therapy, liver status, and drug interactions.

name: soft palate
clinical_significance: The soft palate separates the mouth from the nasal passage during swallowing and speech; weakness or structural defects can cause nasal regurgitation, speech changes, or aspiration.

name: soft tissue
clinical_significance: Soft tissue includes structures such as muscle, fat, tendons, and connective tissue; masses, infection, or injury may need imaging or biopsy to establish the cause.

name: soleus muscle
clinical_significance: A deep calf muscle that joins the Achilles tendon and helps point the foot downward. It is important for standing, walking, and running; injury or overuse can cause calf pain and weakness.

name: solid neoplasm
clinical_significance: A solid neoplasm is a tissue mass rather than a blood or marrow cancer; imaging and biopsy determine whether it is benign or malignant and guide staging and treatment.

name: solid organ
clinical_significance: Solid organs such as the liver, kidneys, and spleen can sustain injury, infection, or tumors; organ-specific function and imaging guide assessment and treatment.

name: solobacterium moorei
clinical_significance: Solobacterium moorei is an oral anaerobic bacterium associated with halitosis and occasionally invasive infection; its detection should be interpreted in relation to oral disease and the specimen source.

name: solubility
clinical_significance: Solubility affects how a medicine dissolves and becomes available for absorption; it is important in formulation, dosing, and interpretation of drug delivery.

name: solution
clinical_significance: A homogeneous mixture in which one or more substances are dissolved in a solvent; medical solutions include saline and antiseptics.

name: solvent
clinical_significance: Solvents can cause irritation, poisoning, or organ injury depending on the chemical and exposure route; occupational and household exposure history can guide toxicology assessment.

name: somatic mutation
clinical_significance: A genetic change acquired by a body cell during life rather than inherited from a parent. It is passed to descendants of that cell and may contribute to cancer, but it usually is not passed to children.

name: somatization
clinical_significance: The experience or expression of psychological distress through physical symptoms such as pain, fatigue, or stomach problems. The symptoms are real and not intentional; assessment should consider both physical and psychological causes.

name: somatoform disorder
clinical_significance: Somatoform disorder is an older term for conditions involving distressing physical symptoms not fully explained by medical findings; current assessment validates symptoms while evaluating medical causes and psychological or functional factors.

name: somatomedins
clinical_significance: Somatomedins, especially insulin-like growth factor 1, mediate many growth-hormone effects; measurement can help investigate abnormal growth or pituitary function.

name: somatosensory cortex
clinical_significance: The somatosensory cortex processes touch, pain, temperature, and body position; injury can cause numbness, altered sensation, or difficulty recognizing objects by touch.

name: somatostatin
clinical_significance: A hormone made in the brain, pancreas, and digestive tract that slows growth hormone, insulin, glucagon, and digestive-hormone release. It also reduces movement and secretion within parts of the digestive system.

name: somatostatin receptor
clinical_significance: Somatostatin receptors are targets for diagnostic imaging and treatment of some neuroendocrine tumors; receptor expression can guide use of receptor-targeted scans or medicines.

name: somatostatinoma
clinical_significance: A rare hormone-producing tumor usually arising in the pancreas or small intestine. It may cause diabetes, diarrhea or greasy stools, gallstones, weight loss, or no symptoms; treatment depends on whether it has spread and may include surgery or cancer medicines.

name: somatotrophs
clinical_significance: Somatotrophs are pituitary cells that produce growth hormone; excess or deficient activity can cause disorders of growth, metabolism, and bone health.

name: somatotropin
clinical_significance: Growth hormone, produced by the pituitary gland. It supports childhood growth and influences protein, fat, and carbohydrate metabolism; excess or deficiency can cause characteristic growth and metabolic disorders.

name: somite
clinical_significance: Somites are embryonic structures that form vertebrae, skeletal muscle, and parts of the skin; abnormal development can contribute to congenital skeletal or muscular disorders.

name: somnambulism
clinical_significance: Sleepwalking or performing other activities while only partly awake, usually during deep sleep. Episodes are more common in children and may be triggered by lack of sleep, stress, illness, or medicines; safety measures are important, especially if wandering or injury occurs.

name: somnolence
clinical_significance: Unusual sleepiness or a tendency to fall asleep when a person should be awake. It may result from too little sleep, medicines, alcohol or drugs, sleep disorders, metabolic illness, or neurologic disease.

name: somnolence syndrome
clinical_significance: Somnolence syndrome is a term for excessive sleepiness, sometimes used for treatment-related drowsiness in oncology; persistent sleepiness can impair function and may reflect medication effects or another sleep or medical disorder.

name: sonication
clinical_significance: Sonication uses sound waves to disrupt cells or remove material in laboratory and clinical procedures; controlled energy can assist specimen preparation, stone treatment, or targeted tissue therapy.

name: soot
clinical_significance: Soot inhalation can irritate or injure the airways and may accompany toxic smoke exposure; respiratory symptoms after a fire warrant assessment for inhalation injury and carbon monoxide or cyanide exposure.

name: sorafenib
clinical_significance: Sorafenib is a multikinase inhibitor used for selected cancers; it can cause hypertension, hand-foot skin reaction, diarrhea, bleeding, and liver injury, so indication-specific monitoring is needed.

name: sorafenib tosylate
clinical_significance: Sorafenib tosylate is the salt form of sorafenib used in cancer treatment; monitoring for hypertension, skin toxicity, bleeding, diarrhea, and liver effects is important during therapy.

name: sorbitol
clinical_significance: A sugar alcohol used as a sweetener and in some medicines. Larger amounts draw water into the bowel and act as a laxative, but may cause gas, cramps, diarrhea, or dehydration.

name: sore throat
clinical_significance: Pain, scratchiness, or irritation in the throat. Common causes include viral infections, bacterial infections, allergies, dry air, smoke, voice strain, and acid reflux; persistent or severe symptoms, drooling, inability to swallow, a muffled voice, neck swelling, or breathing difficulty need prompt medical assessment.

name: sorivudine
clinical_significance: Sorivudine is an antiviral formerly used for shingles in some countries; it can cause fatal toxicity when combined with fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy, so the interaction is a critical medication-safety concern.

name: sotalol
clinical_significance: A medicine with beta-blocking and class III antiarrhythmic effects, used for selected cardiac rhythm disorders.

name: Sotos' syndrome
clinical_significance: A genetic disorder that causes unusually rapid growth in childhood, a large head, distinctive facial features, and delayed development or learning difficulties. Coordination, behavior, seizures, heart problems, or kidney problems may also occur. Growth usually slows with age. A change in the \textit{NSD1} gene causes most cases.

name: southern blotting
clinical_significance: Southern blotting detects specific DNA sequences and has historical diagnostic and research uses; most clinical laboratories now use faster molecular methods, but the technique established principles of genetic testing.

name: soybean oil
clinical_significance: Soybean oil is used in nutrition, parenteral nutrition, and as an ingredient in medicines; soy allergy and the specific formulation should be considered when selecting products.

name: space perception
clinical_significance: Space perception helps a person judge distance and location; impairment can affect mobility and safety and may occur with visual, vestibular, or neurologic disease.

name: sparfosic acid
clinical_significance: Sparfosic acid is an investigational antimetabolite studied for cancer treatment; it is not routine therapy, and clinical-trial evidence and toxicity determine its potential role.

name: sparganosis
clinical_significance: Sparganosis is a parasitic infection acquired from contaminated water or undercooked amphibians or reptiles; larvae can migrate into tissues, including the eye or brain, and may require surgical removal and antiparasitic care.

name: spasm
clinical_significance: An involuntary, often painful tightening of one muscle or a group of muscles. Spasms may result from fatigue, dehydration, nerve disease, injury, medicines, inflammation, or problems affecting the brain or spinal cord.

name: spastic quadriplegia
clinical_significance: Spastic quadriplegia causes increased muscle tone and motor impairment in all four limbs, often from cerebral palsy or spinal or brain injury; it can affect mobility, swallowing, communication, and care needs.

name: spasticity
clinical_significance: Velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone caused by an upper motor-neuron lesion, producing stiffness, spasms, abnormal reflexes, and restricted movement.

name: special education
clinical_significance: Special education provides individualized instruction and support for students with disabilities or learning needs; coordination with healthcare can support medication, accessibility, and participation at school.

name: specimen
clinical_significance: A specimen is a patient sample collected for examination or testing; correct identification, timing, and handling are essential for reliable results and safe clinical decisions.

name: specimen collection
clinical_significance: Specimen collection must match the test and use appropriate technique, labeling, and transport; poor collection can cause contamination, false results, or repeat procedures.

name: specimen treatment
clinical_significance: Specimen treatment includes preparation or preservation before analysis; correct processing maintains sample integrity and prevents misleading laboratory or pathology results.

name: spectinomycin
clinical_significance: Spectinomycin is an antibiotic used in limited settings, including as an alternative for gonorrhea where available; resistance and local guidance affect whether it is appropriate.

name: spectral karyotyping
clinical_significance: Spectral karyotyping uses fluorescent probes to distinguish chromosomes and detect complex rearrangements; it can help characterize cancers or congenital chromosomal abnormalities.

name: spectrin
clinical_significance: Spectrin supports the membrane skeleton of red blood cells and other cells; inherited defects can cause hemolytic anemia, including hereditary spherocytosis or elliptocytosis.

name: spectrometry
clinical_significance: Spectrometry measures properties of atoms or molecules and supports clinical chemistry, toxicology, and drug testing; method validation and sample quality determine reliability.

name: spectrophotometer
clinical_significance: A spectrophotometer measures how much light a sample absorbs or transmits; clinical laboratories use it to quantify analytes in validated diagnostic assays.

name: spectrophotometry
clinical_significance: Spectrophotometry quantifies substances by measuring light absorption; it is widely used in laboratory tests, though results depend on calibration and assay specificity.

name: spectrum analysis
clinical_significance: Spectrum analysis separates a signal into its component frequencies or wavelengths; medical uses include electrocardiography, imaging, and laboratory identification of compounds.

name: speculum
clinical_significance: An instrument used to gently separate or hold open the walls of a body passage so that the area can be visualized, examined, sampled, or treated. Common types include vaginal, nasal, ear, and rectal specula; design and size depend on the body site and intended procedure.

name: speech
clinical_significance: The production of spoken language using breathing, voice, and movements of the tongue, lips, palate, and other structures. Hearing, brain function, teeth, illness, and dental appliances can affect speech.

name: speech disorder
clinical_significance: A speech disorder affects production, fluency, voice, or intelligibility and may follow neurologic injury, developmental conditions, or structural problems; assessment guides therapy and communication support.

name: speech therapy
clinical_significance: Assessment and treatment to help with speaking, understanding language, voice, communication, or swallowing. A speech and language therapist may use exercises, practice, communication aids, and advice for the person and family.

name: sperm bank
clinical_significance: A sperm bank stores screened and cryopreserved sperm for future fertility treatment; infectious-disease testing, consent, and donor or patient screening protect recipients and offspring.

name: sperm capacitation
clinical_significance: Sperm capacitation is a set of changes that enables sperm to fertilize an egg; abnormalities can contribute to infertility and are relevant to assisted reproduction research.

name: sperm cell
clinical_significance: Sperm cells are assessed for count, movement, shape, and viability during fertility evaluation; abnormal results may prompt repeat testing and evaluation of reproductive or general health.

name: sperm granuloma
clinical_significance: A sperm granuloma is an inflammatory lump caused by sperm leaking from the reproductive tract, often after vasectomy or injury; it may cause tenderness and can mimic other scrotal masses.

name: sperm head
clinical_significance: The sperm head contains genetic material and structures needed to penetrate the egg; abnormal head shape can be associated with impaired fertilization and male infertility.

name: sperm midpiece
clinical_significance: The sperm midpiece supplies energy for movement; abnormalities may contribute to poor motility and can be assessed in selected infertility investigations.

name: sperm motility
clinical_significance: Sperm motility is the ability of sperm to move effectively; reduced motility can lower the chance of natural conception and informs fertility evaluation and treatment planning.

name: sperm retrieval
clinical_significance: A procedure that obtains sperm from semen, the epididymis, or testicular tissue for fertility treatment or laboratory testing. The method depends on whether sperm are present in the semen and on the cause of infertility.

name: sperm tail
clinical_significance: The sperm tail propels sperm; structural or functional defects can reduce motility and contribute to male infertility.

name: spermatic cord
clinical_significance: A cord-like structure carrying the vas deferens, testicular blood vessels, nerves, lymph vessels, and supporting tissue. It extends through the groin to the testis and may be affected by hernia, twisting, or infection.

name: spermatic stasis
clinical_significance: Spermatic stasis refers to impaired movement or drainage of sperm within the reproductive tract; it may be considered in evaluation of obstruction or infertility.

name: spermatid
clinical_significance: Spermatids are immature cells that develop into sperm; impaired maturation can disrupt sperm production and contribute to infertility.

name: spermatocele
clinical_significance: A usually harmless, fluid-filled cyst beside or within the epididymis, the coiled tube behind the testicle. It often causes no symptoms but may feel like a lump and should be checked if newly noticed or painful.

name: spermatocyte
clinical_significance: Spermatocytes are developing germ cells in the testis; their maturation is required for sperm production, and abnormalities can affect fertility.

name: spermatogenesis
clinical_significance: The production and maturation of sperm in the seminiferous tubules of the testes. It depends on germ cells, Sertoli cells, hormones, and suitable testicular temperature.

name: spermatogonium
clinical_significance: An early male reproductive cell in the testis that divides and develops into primary spermatocytes, beginning sperm production.

name: spermicide
clinical_significance: A contraceptive substance that kills or immobilizes sperm, often used with condoms or other barrier methods.

name: spermidine
clinical_significance: Spermidine is a polyamine involved in cell growth and metabolism; abnormal levels are studied in disease research but do not alone establish a clinical diagnosis.

name: spermine
clinical_significance: Spermine is a polyamine present in cells and seminal fluid; it participates in cellular growth and sperm function, but testing is not a routine standalone fertility assessment.

name: spermiogenesis
clinical_significance: Spermiogenesis is the final maturation of developing germ cells into sperm; disruption can produce abnormal sperm morphology and impaired fertility.

name: S-phase fraction
clinical_significance: S-phase fraction estimates the proportion of tumor cells synthesizing DNA; it can help characterize tumor growth but is interpreted with histology and other prognostic markers.

name: sphenoid bone
clinical_significance: A central bone at the base of the skull that helps form the eye sockets and skull base. It contains the sphenoid sinuses and a hollow that holds the pituitary gland.

name: sphenoid sinusitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of the sphenoid sinus, which lies deep behind the nasal cavity. It may cause

name: sphenoidal sinus
clinical_significance: A paired air-filled sinus within the sphenoid bone at the base of the skull. It lies near important nerves and blood

name: spherocyte count
clinical_significance: A spherocyte count estimates round, dense red blood cells on a smear; increased spherocytes can support evaluation for hereditary spherocytosis or immune hemolysis.

name: spherocytes
clinical_significance: Red blood cells that are unusually round and dense instead of having their normal flattened shape. They may occur when the cell membrane is damaged or removed, especially in hereditary spherocytosis or immune red-cell destruction.

name: spherocytosis
clinical_significance: Spherocytosis is a condition in which red blood cells become spherical and fragile, causing hemolytic anemia and sometimes jaundice or gallstones; cause and severity guide monitoring and treatment.

name: spheroplast
clinical_significance: A spheroplast is a bacterial cell with a weakened or removed cell wall; this laboratory form helps study antibiotics and bacterial physiology but is not itself a clinical diagnosis.

name: spherosomes
clinical_significance: Spherosomes are lipid-storage structures in plant cells and are mainly relevant to biology and laboratory research, not routine human diagnosis.

name: sphincter
clinical_significance: A ring-shaped muscle that opens and closes a body passage. Sphincters help control urine, stool, food, bile, and other fluids; examples include the muscles around the anus, bladder outlet, and stomach outlet.

name: sphingobacterium
clinical_significance: Sphingobacterium species are environmental bacteria that rarely cause opportunistic infection; a positive culture requires correlation with symptoms, specimen source, and immune status.

name: sphingobacterium mizutaii
clinical_significance: Sphingobacterium mizutaii is an uncommon environmental bacterium with rare reports of human infection; clinical significance depends on reliable identification and recovery from a relevant specimen.

name: sphingolipid
clinical_significance: Sphingolipids are membrane fats involved in cell signaling and nerve structure; abnormal metabolism can cause inherited storage diseases and neurologic injury.

name: sphingolipidosis
clinical_significance: Sphingolipidoses are inherited disorders of sphingolipid breakdown that cause progressive storage in tissues, often affecting nerves and organs; early diagnosis may guide enzyme, substrate-reduction, or supportive treatment.

name: sphingomonadaceae
clinical_significance: Sphingomonadaceae are environmental bacteria that can rarely act as opportunistic pathogens; species identification and clinical context help distinguish infection from contamination.

name: sphingomonas
clinical_significance: Sphingomonas are environmental bacteria that can rarely cause bloodstream or other infections, especially in healthcare settings; isolate significance depends on specimen source and patient status.

name: sphingomonas paucimobilis
clinical_significance: Sphingomonas paucimobilis is an uncommon opportunistic pathogen associated with occasional bloodstream, respiratory, or device-related infection; susceptibility testing and assessment for contamination are important.

name: sphingomyelinase
clinical_significance: Sphingomyelinase breaks down sphingomyelin; deficiency of acid sphingomyelinase causes Niemann-Pick disease types A and B, and enzyme or genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis.

name: sphingomyelins
clinical_significance: Sphingomyelins are membrane lipids abundant in nerve tissue; abnormal accumulation from enzyme deficiency can cause inherited neurovisceral storage disease.

name: sphingosine
clinical_significance: Sphingosine is a component of sphingolipids and a signaling molecule; its metabolic pathways are studied in cancer, inflammation, and inherited lipid disorders.

name: sphygmomanometer
clinical_significance: A device used to measure arterial blood pressure with an inflatable cuff and pressure-measuring system. Manual versions commonly use an aneroid or mercury manometer with a stethoscope, while electronic versions use sensors to analyze pressure oscillations and display the reading.

name: spider bite
clinical_significance: An injury caused by a spider, usually producing a small painful or itchy area. Some species can cause worsening tissue damage, severe muscle cramps, sweating, vomiting, breathing problems, or other serious effects; rapidly worsening symptoms need emergency care.

name: spider venom
clinical_significance: Spider venom can cause local tissue injury or systemic neurotoxic effects depending on species; suspected serious envenomation requires identification when possible and urgent poison-control or medical assessment.

name: spina bifida
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the neural tube and the bones protecting the spinal cord do not close completely during early development. It can range from mild to severe and may cause weakness, loss of feeling, or problems controlling the bladder or bowel.

name: spinal artery
clinical_significance: An artery supplying the spinal cord and its coverings, including the anterior spinal artery and paired posterior spinal arteries; blockage can cause characteristic neurologic deficits.

name: spinal block
clinical_significance: A spinal block is injection of local anesthetic into cerebrospinal fluid in the lower back, producing temporary numbness and weakness for surgery or pain control.

name: spinal canal
clinical_significance: The spinal canal is the bony passage through the vertebral column containing the spinal cord, its coverings, nerve roots, and blood vessels.

name: spinal cord
clinical_significance: The cylindrical nervous tissue within the vertebral canal that carries signals between brain and body and mediates reflexes.

name: spinal cord disease
clinical_significance: Spinal cord disease can impair movement, sensation, and bladder or bowel control; new weakness, numbness, or sphincter dysfunction may indicate urgent compression or inflammation.

name: spinal cord injury
clinical_significance: Spinal cord injury can cause permanent motor, sensory, and autonomic deficits; immediate stabilization and rehabilitation reduce secondary injury and support function.

name: spinal cord neoplasms
clinical_significance: Spinal cord tumors can compress neural tissue and cause pain, weakness, sensory loss, or sphincter symptoms; MRI and pathology guide urgent treatment and neurologic preservation.

name: spinal disease
clinical_significance: Spinal disease can cause pain, nerve compression, deformity, or impaired mobility; red-flag symptoms such as progressive weakness or bladder dysfunction require prompt assessment.

name: spinal fracture
clinical_significance: A fracture of one or more vertebrae caused by trauma, osteoporosis, tumor, or other bone-weakening disease.

name: spinal ganglion
clinical_significance: A small group of nerve-cell bodies beside the spinal cord. It contains sensory nerve cells that carry information about touch, pain, temperature, and body position from the skin, muscles, and joints.

name: spinal muscular atrophy
clinical_significance: Spinal muscular atrophy causes progressive weakness from loss of motor neurons; disease-modifying treatments are available, and early genetic diagnosis enables timely therapy and respiratory and nutritional support.

name: spinal neoplasms
clinical_significance: Tumors arising in the spinal cord, its coverings, vertebrae, or nearby tissues. They may be noncancerous or cancerous and can cause back pain, weakness, numbness, walking difficulty, or bladder and bowel changes when they press on nerves.

name: spinal nerve
clinical_significance: One of 31 pairs of nerves leaving the spinal cord through openings between the spinal bones. Each carries messages for sensation, movement, and automatic functions between the body and spinal cord.

name: spinal stenosis
clinical_significance: Narrowing of the passage containing the spinal cord or nerve roots. It may cause back pain, numbness, weakness, or leg pain with walking that improves when sitting or leaning forward.

name: spindle pole
clinical_significance: One end of the temporary structure formed during cell division. Fibers extending from each pole attach to duplicated chromosomes and pull the copies into the two new cells.

name: spindle pole body
clinical_significance: A structure in fungal cells that organizes the fibers used to separate duplicated chromosomes during cell division. It performs a role similar to the centrosome in animal cells.

name: spine injury
clinical_significance: Damage to the bones, discs, ligaments, nerves, or spinal cord. It may cause back pain, weakness, numbness, loss of movement, or bladder and bowel problems and can require emergency care.

name: spinocerebellar ataxia
clinical_significance: Spinocerebellar ataxias are inherited disorders that progressively impair balance, coordination, speech, and sometimes swallowing; genetic testing and rehabilitation help clarify diagnosis and support safety and function.

name: spiral colon
clinical_significance: Spiral colon is an anatomic term used mainly in veterinary descriptions of the large intestine; it has no standard diagnostic role in human medicine.

name: spiramycin
clinical_significance: A macrolide antibiotic used for selected bacterial infections and sometimes during pregnancy for toxoplasmosis. Choice depends on the infection, local guidance, pregnancy stage, allergies, resistance, and other treatment needs.

name: spirillum
clinical_significance: Spirillum is a genus of spiral-shaped bacteria; clinical significance depends on the species, exposure, and specimen, since some related organisms can cause zoonotic infection.

name: spirillum minus
clinical_significance: Spirillum minus is a spiral Gram-negative bacterium that causes rat-bite fever, characterized by fever, rash, and migratory joint pain after rodent exposure; culture is difficult and diagnosis may be clinical or molecular.

name: spiritual support
clinical_significance: Spiritual support can help patients cope with illness, grief, and difficult treatment decisions when it reflects their own beliefs and preferences; it should be offered without imposing a belief system.

name: spirochaetaceae
clinical_significance: A family of spiral-shaped bacteria that includes medically important spirochetes such as Borrelia, Treponema, and Leptospira.

name: spirochaetales infection
clinical_significance: Infection caused by spiral-shaped bacteria in the order Spirochaetales, including syphilis, Lyme disease, relapsing fever, and leptospirosis.

name: spirometry
clinical_significance: A breathing test that measures how much air a person can blow out and how quickly. It helps identify narrowing of the airways, as in asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and can monitor treatment. The person must follow instructions and blow forcefully several times; results are interpreted with age, height, and symptoms.

name: spironolactone
clinical_significance: An aldosterone antagonist and potassium-sparing diuretic used for heart failure, hypertension, hyperaldosteronism, and other indications.

name: spitting
clinical_significance: Forceful expulsion of saliva or other material from the mouth. New or excessive spitting may occur with oral disease, reflux, nausea, difficulty swallowing, medication effects, or habit.

name: splanchnic nerve
clinical_significance: A nerve carrying automatic signals between the spinal cord and internal organs, especially organs in the chest and abdomen. It helps regulate digestion, blood-vessel tone, and other functions that do not require conscious control.

name: spleen
clinical_significance: A lymphoid organ in the upper-left abdomen. Its red pulp filters blood and removes aged or abnormal blood cells; its white pulp supports immune responses. It also stores platelets and helps clear blood-borne microorganisms.

name: spleen development
clinical_significance: The formation and maturation of the spleen before and after birth. The spleen gradually develops its blood-filtering and immune functions, including removal of aged blood cells and responses to germs in the bloodstream.

name: spleen disorder
clinical_significance: A disease affecting the spleen, such as enlargement, infection, infarction, rupture, inflammation, cyst, or tumor, with possible effects on blood cells and immunity.

name: spleen hemangioma
clinical_significance: A spleen hemangioma is a usually benign blood-vessel tumor of the spleen, often incidental but occasionally associated with enlargement, anemia, or rupture risk.

name: splenectomy
clinical_significance: Surgical removal of the spleen, performed for selected traumatic, hematologic, malignant, vascular, or other disorders. It increases the risk of severe infection with encapsulated bacteria and requires preventive planning.

name: splenic abscess
clinical_significance: A localized collection of pus in the spleen, usually from bloodstream infection, trauma, infarction, or spread from nearby disease and potentially causing fever, left-upper-quadrant pain, and sepsis.

name: splenic infection
clinical_significance: Infection of the spleen, often an abscess caused by bacteria spreading through the bloodstream or from nearby tissue. It may cause fever, chills, left-upper-abdominal pain, and severe illness and usually needs urgent medical treatment.

name: splenic neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the spleen. It may be noncancerous, cancerous, or cancer that has spread from another organ; symptoms and treatment depend on its type, size, and effect on nearby tissues or blood cells.

name: splenic rupture
clinical_significance: A tear of the spleen, usually after blunt abdominal trauma but sometimes spontaneous in an enlarged or diseased spleen. It can cause life-threatening internal bleeding; diagnosis and treatment depend on hemodynamic stability and imaging, with urgent surgery or embolization sometimes required.

name: splenomegaly
clinical_significance: Abnormal enlargement of the spleen. It may result from infection, liver disease, blood disorders, cancer, or other conditions and may cause no symptoms. Some people feel fullness or pain in the upper-left abdomen. An enlarged spleen can trap blood cells and is more easily injured or ruptured.

name: spliceosome
clinical_significance: The spliceosome is a nuclear RNA-protein complex that removes introns from pre-messenger RNA and joins exons to form mature RNA.

name: split brain
clinical_significance: A state after surgical or pathological disruption of the corpus callosum in which information transfer between cerebral hemispheres is reduced, producing characteristic disconnection findings.

name: spondylarthritis
clinical_significance: A family of inflammatory rheumatic diseases affecting the spine, sacroiliac joints, entheses, peripheral joints, skin, eyes, or bowel, including ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis.

name: spondylitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of one or more vertebrae or parts of the spine. Causes include infection, autoimmune disease, and inflammatory arthritis; pain, stiffness, fever, or neurologic symptoms may occur.

name: spondylolisthesis
clinical_significance: Slipping of one spinal bone forward or backward compared with the bone below it. It may cause back pain, stiffness, leg pain, numbness, or weakness, although some people have no symptoms.

name: spondylolysis
clinical_significance: A small stress crack or defect in part of a spinal bone, usually in the lower back. It may cause back pain in adolescents or athletes and can sometimes allow one spinal bone to slip on another.

name: spondylosis
clinical_significance: Wear-related changes in the bones, discs, and small joints of the spine. It becomes more common with age and may cause stiffness or pain, but many people have no symptoms; nerve pressure can cause numbness or weakness.

name: sponge
clinical_significance: A sponge is a porous material used to absorb fluid, clean or dress wounds, or deliver a product; retained surgical sponges are a preventable complication.

name: spontaneous abortion
clinical_significance: Unintentional loss of a pregnancy before fetal viability. Causes include chromosomal abnormalities, uterine or cervical problems, infection, and maternal medical conditions.

name: spontaneous perforation
clinical_significance: Unexpected rupture of a hollow organ without a clear external injury, allowing contents to escape and potentially causing peritonitis, mediastinitis, sepsis, or hemorrhage.

name: sporothrix
clinical_significance: A genus of environmental fungi that can cause sporotrichosis, usually after inoculation through the skin and sometimes through inhalation or dissemination.

name: sporothrix schenckii
clinical_significance: A group of fungi that causes sporotrichosis, a typically nodular skin and lymphatic infection acquired from plants, soil, or animal scratches.

name: sports medicine
clinical_significance: Medical care focused on preventing, diagnosing, and treating exercise- and sports-related injuries and conditions. It also supports safe training, rehabilitation, performance, and return to activity.

name: spousal abuse
clinical_significance: Spousal abuse is physical, sexual, emotional, financial, or coercive harm by an intimate partner; immediate safety planning and confidential support may be needed.

name: spouse
clinical_significance: A spouse is a person’s legally or socially recognized partner; involving a spouse in healthcare requires the patient’s consent unless law provides otherwise.

name: sprain
clinical_significance: An injury in which a ligament that supports a joint is stretched or torn. It can cause pain, swelling, bruising, and looseness; severity ranges from minor stretching to a complete tear and joint instability.

name: spray drying
clinical_significance: Spray drying converts a liquid mixture into a dry powder by atomizing it into a heated gas stream, often used in pharmaceutical and food manufacturing.

name: spumavirus
clinical_significance: Spumaviruses, also called foamy viruses, are retroviruses found in several animal species; human infection has been reported after animal exposure but is not known to cause a typical human disease.

name: sputum
clinical_significance: Mucus or other material brought up by coughing from the airways or lungs. Its amount, color, smell, and blood content may provide clues, but sputum alone cannot identify the cause; laboratory testing may be needed.

name: squalamine lactate
clinical_significance: Squalamine lactate is an investigational compound studied for antimicrobial and anticancer effects; it is not established routine therapy, and clinical-trial evidence determines any role.

name: squalene
clinical_significance: Squalene is a lipid found in the body and used in some vaccine adjuvants and cosmetic products; reactions depend on the formulation, and supplement claims for disease prevention are not established.

name: squamous cell carcinoma
clinical_significance: A cancer of flat cells that line the skin or certain body passages. On the skin it may appear as a rough, scaly, crusted, wart-like, or nonhealing sore and can invade nearby tissue or spread if untreated.

name: square foot
clinical_significance: A square foot is a unit of area equal to a square measuring one foot on each side, used to describe surfaces, rooms, wounds, or treatment areas.

name: square inch
clinical_significance: A square inch is a unit of area equal to a square measuring one inch on each side, used for small surfaces or wound measurements.

name: square metres
clinical_significance: Square metres are a unit of area used to calculate body-surface area, which helps determine some medication doses and assess burns; accurate height and weight measurements are important.

name: sscp analysis
clinical_significance: Single-strand conformation polymorphism analysis screens DNA for sequence variants by detecting changes in strand shape; it is mainly a research method and does not replace validated clinical genetic testing.

name: stable angina
clinical_significance: Repeated, predictable chest pressure or discomfort brought on by activity or stress because the heart muscle receives too little blood. It usually improves with rest or prescribed medicine; new, severe, prolonged, or rest pain may be a heart attack and needs emergency care.

name: Staghorn calculi
clinical_significance: Large branching kidney stones that fill part or all of the kidney's urine-collecting system. They are often linked with infection, can damage kidney tissue, and usually require specialist treatment to remove them.

name: staining
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that uses colored dyes to make cells, tissue structures, or microorganisms easier to see under a microscope. Different stains highlight different features and can help guide diagnosis, although results may need culture or other tests for confirmation.

name: standing position
clinical_significance: Standing position can affect blood pressure, balance, and symptoms such as dizziness; orthostatic measurements help assess volume depletion, autonomic dysfunction, or medication effects.

name: stanozolol
clinical_significance: A synthetic anabolic androgenic steroid with limited medical use and potential liver, lipid, and cardiovascular toxicity.

name: stapes
clinical_significance: The smallest middle-ear bone, passing sound vibrations from the incus to the inner ear for hearing.

name: staphage lysate
clinical_significance: Staphage lysate is an older immune-modulating preparation derived from staphylococcal phages and bacterial material; it is not a standard substitute for evidence-based treatment of staphylococcal infection.

name: staphylococcaceae
clinical_significance: Staphylococcaceae is a family of bacteria that includes Staphylococcus species, common colonizers and potential pathogens; laboratory identification helps distinguish contamination from infection.

name: staphylococcal infections
clinical_significance: Staphylococcal infections range from minor skin disease to bacteremia and endocarditis; source control, species identification, and antimicrobial susceptibility are central to management.

name: staphylococcus
clinical_significance: A genus of gram-positive cocci that includes S. aureus and common skin colonizers and pathogens.

name: staphylococcus arlettae
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus arlettae is mainly an animal-associated coagulase-negative staphylococcus and a rare human isolate; a positive culture should be interpreted for contamination versus opportunistic infection.

name: staphylococcus aureus
clinical_significance: A bacterium that commonly lives on the skin or in the nose but can cause infections of the skin, blood, lungs, bones, joints, or heart valves. Some strains are resistant to several antibiotics.

name: staphylococcus capitis
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus capitis is a coagulase-negative skin commensal that can cause bloodstream or device-associated infection, especially in premature infants and people with implanted devices.

name: staphylococcus caprae
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus caprae is an animal-associated coagulase-negative staphylococcus that can rarely cause bone, joint, or bloodstream infection; reliable species identification and susceptibility testing help guide care.

name: staphylococcus carnosus
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus carnosus is used in food fermentation and is not a usual human pathogen; recovery from a clinical specimen generally requires assessment for contamination or rare opportunistic infection.

name: staphylococcus cohnii
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus cohnii is a coagulase-negative skin-associated bacterium that can rarely cause opportunistic infection, including device-related disease; interpret cultures in clinical context.

name: staphylococcus epidermidis
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a common skin commensal and an important cause of infections involving catheters, prosthetic joints, and other implanted devices; repeated positive cultures and symptoms support true infection.

name: staphylococcus equorum
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus equorum is primarily associated with animals and fermented foods and is not a common human pathogen; its significance in a culture depends on specimen quality and patient risk.

name: staphylococcus felis
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus felis is associated mainly with cats and is an uncommon human isolate; consider zoonotic exposure and clinical correlation if recovered from a suspected infection.

name: staphylococcus gallinarum
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus gallinarum is primarily associated with birds and is rarely implicated in human disease; identification from a clinical sample should be correlated with symptoms and specimen source.

name: staphylococcus haemolyticus
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus haemolyticus is a coagulase-negative skin commensal and healthcare-associated opportunistic pathogen that may infect blood or devices; antimicrobial resistance is common, so susceptibility testing matters.

name: staphylococcus hominis
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus hominis is a common skin commensal that can cause bloodstream or device-associated infection in vulnerable patients; culture pattern and clinical findings help distinguish infection from contamination.

name: staphylococcus hyicus
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus hyicus is primarily an animal pathogen, especially in pigs, and rarely causes human infection; occupational or animal exposure may be relevant when it is isolated.

name: staphylococcus intermedius
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus intermedius is associated mainly with animals and may cause human wound infection after bites or scratches; accurate identification can distinguish it from related species and guide susceptibility-based treatment.

name: staphylococcus kloosii
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus kloosii is an uncommon coagulase-negative staphylococcus found in animals and the environment; human infection is rare, so clinical significance depends on repeated recovery from a relevant site.

name: staphylococcus lentus
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus lentus is associated with animals and the environment and is a rare human opportunistic pathogen; specimen source, immune status, and susceptibility results guide interpretation.

name: staphylococcus lugdunensis
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus lugdunensis is a coagulase-negative species that can cause aggressive skin infection, bacteremia, and endocarditis resembling Staphylococcus aureus disease; clinically significant isolates warrant careful evaluation.

name: staphylococcus pasteuri
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus pasteuri is an uncommon coagulase-negative staphylococcus that may contaminate specimens or rarely cause opportunistic infection; repeated isolation and clinical context help establish significance.

name: staphylococcus saprophyticus
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of urinary tract infection, especially in young adults; urine culture and symptoms help distinguish infection from colonization.

name: staphylococcus schleiferi
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus schleiferi can cause skin, wound, ear, or bloodstream infection and is associated with animals as well as humans; species identification and antimicrobial susceptibility can affect treatment.

name: staphylococcus sciuri
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus sciuri is primarily an animal-associated coagulase-negative species that can rarely cause human opportunistic infection; identification and resistance testing are relevant for invasive isolates.

name: staphylococcus simulans
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus simulans is a coagulase-negative species that can occasionally cause bone, joint, or device-associated infection; it should not automatically be dismissed when recovered from a sterile site.

name: staphylococcus succinus
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus succinus is mainly associated with food and the environment and is rarely a human pathogen; a clinical isolate requires correlation with specimen quality and patient findings.

name: staphylococcus warneri
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus warneri is a coagulase-negative skin commensal that can rarely cause bacteremia, endocarditis, or device infection; repeated positive cultures and compatible illness support pathogenic significance.

name: staphylococcus xylosus
clinical_significance: Staphylococcus xylosus is common in animals and fermented foods and is an uncommon human pathogen; its recovery from clinical material should be interpreted in light of exposure and specimen source.

name: starch
clinical_significance: Starch is a major dietary carbohydrate and is used in some medicines as an excipient; digestion affects blood glucose, and formulation ingredients may matter for allergy or dietary restrictions.

name: startle reflex
clinical_significance: The startle reflex is an automatic response to sudden stimuli; unusually exaggerated, reduced, or persistent responses can occur with neurologic disorders, medication effects, or anxiety.

name: starvation
clinical_significance: Severe lack of food or usable energy over time, causing weight and muscle loss, weakness, changes in body chemistry, reduced immunity, and eventually organ failure. Restarting nutrition after prolonged starvation must be done carefully because dangerous shifts can occur.

name: statistical cluster
clinical_significance: Statistical clustering groups observations with similar characteristics; in clinical research it can identify patterns but does not by itself prove disease subtypes or causal relationships.

name: statistical distribution
clinical_significance: A statistical distribution describes how measured values vary in a population; it informs reference ranges, risk estimates, and the choice of appropriate analyses.
