clinical_significance: Tinnitus is perception of sound without an external source, often related to hearing loss, noise exposure, ear disease, medications, vascular causes, or neurologic factors.

name: tinzaparin
clinical_significance: A low-molecular-weight heparin anticoagulant used for prevention or treatment of venous thromboembolism; bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia are important risks.

name: tinzaparin sodium
clinical_significance: The sodium salt of tinzaparin, a low-molecular-weight heparin used to prevent or treat venous blood clots; bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia are important risks.

name: tiopronin
clinical_significance: A thiol-containing medicine used in selected cases of cystinuria to increase urinary cystine solubility; rash, proteinuria, and blood abnormalities may occur.

name: tiotropium bromide
clinical_significance: A long-acting inhaled medicine that relaxes airway muscles and keeps the airways open. It is used regularly to control COPD and sometimes asthma; it does not provide immediate relief during a sudden attack.

name: tipifarnib
clinical_significance: Tipifarnib is an investigational farnesyltransferase inhibitor studied for selected cancers and genetic disorders; use remains dependent on trial evidence and indication-specific risks.

name: tirapazamine
clinical_significance: Tirapazamine is an investigational anticancer drug designed to act in low-oxygen tumor regions; it is not standard therapy and clinical trials did not establish routine benefit.

name: tirbanibulin
clinical_significance: A topical medicine used in short courses to treat actinic keratoses on the face or scalp; local redness, scaling, or irritation may occur.

name: tirofiban
clinical_significance: An intravenous medicine that temporarily prevents platelets from sticking together. It is used in selected urgent heart conditions or coronary procedures to reduce clotting, but can cause serious bleeding and requires close monitoring.

name: tissierella
clinical_significance: Tissierella are anaerobic bacteria found in the environment and sometimes human flora; rare infections have been reported, so culture results need clinical correlation.

name: tissierella praeacuta
clinical_significance: Tissierella praeacuta is a rare anaerobic bacterial isolate that may be associated with wound or bloodstream infection; significance depends on specimen source, symptoms, and identification quality.

name: tissue
clinical_significance: A group of cells and the supporting material around them that work together for a particular function. Examples include muscle, nerve, bone, connective, and lining tissues.

name: tissue adhesions
clinical_significance: Bands of fibrous scar tissue that abnormally connect surfaces or organs, often after surgery, inflammation, infection, or bleeding and potentially causing pain, infertility, or obstruction.

name: tissue banks
clinical_significance: Facilities that recover, screen, process, preserve, store, and distribute donated human tissue for transplantation, research, or reconstructive treatment under safety and traceability standards.

name: tissue congestion
clinical_significance: Accumulation of blood or fluid within tissue because of impaired venous drainage, inflammation, obstruction, or increased vascular flow, producing swelling, redness, or impaired function.

name: tissue culture
clinical_significance: Tissue culture grows cells or microorganisms under controlled conditions; it supports infection diagnosis, pathology, vaccine production, and research, but contamination or poor sampling can mislead results.

name: tissue elastance
clinical_significance: How strongly a tissue or organ resists being stretched. In the lungs and chest wall, high elastance means more pressure is needed to expand them, which can make breathing harder.

name: tissue engineering
clinical_significance: The use of cells, supportive materials called scaffolds, and biologically active substances to create or repair tissues that restore, maintain, or improve body function.

name: tissue kallikrein
clinical_significance: An enzyme made in several tissues that releases chemical messengers affecting local blood flow, blood-vessel leakiness, pain, and inflammation.

name: tissue membrane
clinical_significance: A thin layer of tissue that covers a surface, surrounds an organ, or separates spaces in the body. Its structure and function depend on the type of tissue forming it.

name: tissue processor
clinical_significance: A tissue processor preserves and embeds biopsy samples for microscopic examination; reliable processing is essential for accurate pathology diagnosis.

name: tissue scaffold
clinical_significance: A tissue scaffold provides a framework for cells in regenerative medicine and wound repair; compatibility, infection risk, and mechanical strength affect clinical performance.

name: titanium
clinical_significance: A strong, lightweight, corrosion-resistant metal used in implants, prostheses, dental devices, and surgical instruments. Bone can form a stable connection with some titanium implant surfaces.

name: t-lymphocyte
clinical_significance: A white blood cell that matures in the thymus and directs cell-based immune responses. Different T cells kill infected cells, coordinate immunity, remember previous threats, or reduce excessive immune activity.

name: tmax
clinical_significance: The time after a dose when a medicine reaches its highest measured concentration in blood or plasma.

name: TNM staging
clinical_significance: TNM staging describes the extent of cancer by primary tumor, lymph-node involvement, and distant spread; it informs prognosis and treatment planning.

name: tobacco
clinical_significance: A plant product containing nicotine and many toxic combustion or processing chemicals. Its use causes dependence and increases the risk of cancer, cardiovascular disease, and lung disease.

name: tobacco use
clinical_significance: Tobacco use exposes the body to nicotine and toxic combustion or aerosol chemicals, causing addiction and increased risks of cancer, vascular disease, and lung disease.

name: tobramycin
clinical_significance: An aminoglycoside antibiotic used for selected serious bacterial infections, including some Gram-negative infections. It can damage the kidneys or hearing and is used with dosing and laboratory monitoring when appropriate.

name: tocolytic agents
clinical_significance: Tocolytic agents suppress uterine contractions temporarily to delay preterm birth, often allowing time for corticosteroids or transfer to specialist care.

name: tocopherol
clinical_significance: A form of vitamin E, a fat-soluble vitamin that helps protect cell membranes. Deficiency is uncommon but may cause nerve problems, muscle weakness, or abnormal red blood cells; excessive supplements can also be harmful.

name: tocotrienols
clinical_significance: Tocotrienols are forms of vitamin E studied for antioxidant and lipid effects; evidence for supplements in disease prevention or treatment remains limited.

name: toe
clinical_significance: Toe injuries or deformities can impair walking and balance; diabetes, poor circulation, or neuropathy increases the risk of unnoticed wounds and infection.

name: toe joint
clinical_significance: Any joint connecting the bones of a toe. Toe joints include the metatarsophalangeal and interphalangeal joints; they permit toe movement and may be affected by arthritis, gout, injury, or deformity.

name: togaviridae
clinical_significance: A family of viruses that includes some mosquito-borne viruses, such as chikungunya and eastern equine encephalitis virus, which can cause fever, rash, joint pain, or brain inflammation.

name: togaviridae infections
clinical_significance: Infections caused by viruses in the Togaviridae family. Symptoms vary by virus and may include fever, rash, joint pain, or encephalitis.

name: toilet training
clinical_significance: Toilet training is a developmental process that can be delayed by constipation, urinary problems, or developmental differences; pressure or punishment can worsen avoidance and distress.

name: tolazamide
clinical_significance: An older sulfonylurea diabetes medicine that increases insulin release; hypoglycemia and weight gain can occur, especially in older adults or people with kidney disease.

name: tolbutamide
clinical_significance: Tolbutamide is an older sulfonylurea diabetes medicine that can cause prolonged hypoglycemia, especially in older adults or people with kidney or liver impairment; safer alternatives are commonly used.

name: tolcapone
clinical_significance: A medicine used with levodopa for selected people with Parkinson disease to prolong levodopa’s effect. It can cause diarrhea, involuntary movements, confusion, and potentially fatal liver injury, so liver monitoring is required.

name: tolerance
clinical_significance: A decreased response to a drug after repeated administration, requiring dose escalation to achieve the same effect. Unlike tachyphylaxis, tolerance develops over weeks to months of chronic use.

name: tolmetin
clinical_significance: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug used for pain and arthritis; gastrointestinal bleeding, kidney injury, and cardiovascular events are important risks.

name: tolnaftate
clinical_significance: A topical antifungal medicine used for some dermatophyte infections such as athlete's foot and ringworm; it is not effective for every type of fungal infection.

name: tolonium chloride
clinical_significance: Tolonium chloride is a dye used in selected diagnostic or surgical settings to highlight tissue; local irritation and staining can occur, and its use depends on the procedure.

name: tolterodine tartrate
clinical_significance: Tolterodine tartrate is an antimuscarinic medicine used for overactive bladder and urinary urgency; dry mouth, constipation, and urinary retention can occur.

name: toluene
clinical_significance: Toluene is a volatile solvent that can irritate tissues and, with substantial inhalation or ingestion, injure the nervous system, liver, kidneys, or heart.

name: tolvaptan
clinical_significance: A vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist used in selected patients with hyponatremia or autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease; thirst, rapid sodium correction, and liver injury require attention.

name: tomography
clinical_significance: Imaging that produces cross-sectional views, or slices, through the body. Computed tomography uses X-rays, while other forms use ultrasound, magnetic fields, or radioactive tracers.

name: tomotherapy
clinical_significance: Tomotherapy combines CT imaging with rotating, precisely shaped radiation beams to deliver radiation treatment while adjusting for the target and nearby tissues.

name: tongue
clinical_significance: A muscular organ in the mouth that helps move food, form speech sounds, swallow, and detect taste. Swelling, sores, weakness, numbness, or restricted movement may result from injury, infection, inflammation, nerve disease, or cancer.

name: tongue carcinoma
clinical_significance: Tongue carcinoma is cancer of the tongue, usually squamous-cell cancer, and may cause a persistent sore, lump, pain, or difficulty speaking or swallowing.

name: tongue disease
clinical_significance: Any disorder affecting the tongue, such as infection, inflammation, injury, nerve disease, nutritional deficiency, or cancer. Symptoms may include pain, sores, swelling, altered taste, or difficulty speaking or swallowing.

name: tongue neoplasm
clinical_significance: An abnormal growth in the tongue that may be noncancerous, precancerous, or cancerous. A persistent lump, ulcer, pain, bleeding, numbness, or difficulty speaking or swallowing needs examination and may require biopsy.

name: tonic pupil
clinical_significance: A pupil that reacts poorly to light but constricts slowly when focusing on something nearby. It often results from injury to nerves controlling the pupil and should be assessed with other eye and neurologic findings.

name: tonic seizures
clinical_significance: Seizures causing sustained stiffening of muscles, usually for seconds to minutes. They may affect one area or the whole body, cause falls or breathing difficulty, and require individualized seizure evaluation.

name: tonometer
clinical_significance: An instrument that measures pressure inside the eye. Eye-pressure readings help detect glaucoma or monitor treatment, but they must be interpreted with the optic nerve, visual field, cornea, and other findings.

name: tonometry
clinical_significance: Measurement of pressure inside the eye, usually to assess for glaucoma or monitor its treatment. Methods include applanation, noncontact air-puff, rebound, and electronic devices; results must be interpreted with corneal thickness and the clinical context.

name: tonsil
clinical_significance: A small mass of immune tissue at the back of the throat. Tonsils help detect germs entering through the mouth and nose but can become enlarged or infected, causing sore throat, difficulty swallowing, or breathing problems.

name: tonsillar neoplasm
clinical_significance: A tonsillar neoplasm is an abnormal growth in a tonsil that may be benign or malignant and can cause a persistent sore throat, swallowing difficulty, or neck swelling.

name: tonsillectomy
clinical_significance: Surgery to remove the tonsils, performed for selected repeated infections, obstructive sleep apnea, or other tonsil disease after the expected benefits and risks are assessed.

name: tonsillitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of the tonsils, usually caused by a virus and sometimes by group A streptococcal bacteria. It can cause sore throat, fever, swollen neck glands, painful swallowing, and white patches.

name: tooth
clinical_significance: A hard mineralized structure anchored in the jaw, used for biting, tearing, chewing, and grinding food.

name: tooth abrasion
clinical_significance: Loss of tooth substance caused by external mechanical friction, such as aggressive brushing, abrasive products, or habits, producing grooves, notches, or sensitivity.

name: tooth ankylosis
clinical_significance: Fusion of a tooth root to alveolar bone through loss of the periodontal ligament, preventing normal eruption and making the tooth appear infraoccluded as neighboring teeth grow.

name: tooth attrition
clinical_significance: Toothbrushing removes plaque and helps prevent tooth decay and gum disease; gentle technique and fluoride toothpaste support oral health.

name: tooth calcification
clinical_significance: Deposition of mineral that forms and hardens enamel, dentin, cementum, and other tooth structures during development; abnormal timing or amount can affect tooth strength and appearance.

name: tooth component
clinical_significance: Tooth components include enamel, dentin, cementum, pulp, and supporting tissues, each contributing to tooth strength, sensation, nutrition, and attachment.

name: tooth crowding
clinical_significance: Tooth crowding occurs when teeth lack enough space to align normally, often from tooth size, jaw size, eruption pattern, or retained primary teeth.

name: tooth crown
clinical_significance: The tooth crown is the visible portion above the gum, covered mainly by hard enamel and containing underlying dentin and pulp.

name: tooth discoloration
clinical_significance: Abnormal tooth color can result from plaque, decay, trauma, fluorosis, medicines, enamel defects, or staining, and the cause determines treatment.

name: tooth disease
clinical_significance: Any disorder affecting a tooth, including decay, infection, cracks, developmental defects, or wear. It may cause pain, sensitivity, discoloration, swelling, or difficulty chewing and should be assessed by a dental professional.

name: tooth enamel
clinical_significance: Tooth enamel is the highly mineralized outer covering of the crown that protects dentin and pulp from wear, acid, and bacteria.

name: tooth eruption
clinical_significance: The process by which a developing tooth moves through the gum into the mouth. Baby teeth usually appear from about 6 months to 3 years, and permanent teeth from about 6 years onward; timing varies and delays may need assessment.

name: tooth extraction
clinical_significance: Removal of a tooth from its socket because of severe decay, infection, periodontal disease, fracture, impaction, orthodontic planning, or another clinical indication.

name: tooth fracture
clinical_significance: A crack or break in a tooth caused by injury, biting hard material, decay, grinding, or weakened enamel. It may expose the inner nerve, causing pain, sensitivity, infection, or loss of the tooth.

name: tooth infection
clinical_significance: Infection of the tooth, its pulp, or surrounding tissues, commonly caused by untreated decay, cracks, or gum disease.

name: tooth loss
clinical_significance: Tooth loss is absence of a tooth due to decay, gum disease, trauma, developmental absence, or extraction and can affect chewing, speech, and oral health.

name: tooth resorption
clinical_significance: Breakdown of part of a tooth, usually starting inside the tooth or on its root. It may follow injury, infection, orthodontic treatment, or occur without a known cause and can weaken or destroy the tooth.

name: tooth root
clinical_significance: The tooth root anchors a tooth in its socket and contains dentin, cementum, pulp, nerves, and blood vessels beneath the gum.

name: toothache
clinical_significance: Pain arising from a tooth or nearby gum, ligament, bone, or other supporting tissue. Common causes include decay, infection, cracks, trauma, and gum disease.

name: toothbrushing
clinical_significance: Toothbrushing with fluoride toothpaste removes plaque and reduces tooth decay and gum disease; gentle twice-daily brushing supports oral health.

name: toothpaste
clinical_significance: Toothpaste delivers fluoride and other agents that help prevent decay and sensitivity; swallowing large amounts can cause fluoride toxicity, particularly in children.

name: topical
clinical_significance: Applied directly to skin or a moist lining, usually to act at the treatment site with limited whole-body exposure.

name: topiramate
clinical_significance: An antiseizure medicine also used to prevent migraine. It may cause tingling, slowed thinking, weight loss, kidney stones, or acid imbalance and can harm a developing fetus; pregnancy planning and medicine changes require medical advice.

name: topoisomerase ii
clinical_significance: An enzyme that cuts both DNA strands, passes another DNA segment through the break, and rejoins the strands; it is targeted by some anticancer drugs.

name: topoisomerase inhibitors
clinical_significance: Drugs that interfere with DNA topoisomerases; some are antibiotics and others are anticancer medicines, with toxicity depending on the drug and target enzyme.

name: topotecan
clinical_significance: A topoisomerase-I inhibitor used for selected ovarian, small-cell lung, and cervical cancers; bone-marrow suppression is a major toxicity.

name: topotecan hydrochloride
clinical_significance: A salt form of topotecan, a chemotherapy medicine that interferes with DNA copying. It treats selected cancers but can cause dangerously low blood counts, infection, bleeding, diarrhea, nausea, or fatigue.

name: toremifene
clinical_significance: A selective estrogen-receptor modulator used for metastatic breast cancer in postmenopausal women; hot flashes and, rarely, dangerous QT prolongation may occur.

name: torsade de pointes
clinical_significance: A dangerous, fast heart rhythm in which the lower chambers beat in a twisting pattern. It is often linked with a prolonged electrical recovery time, abnormal body salts, certain medicines, or inherited heart conditions and can cause collapse or cardiac arrest.

name: torsemide
clinical_significance: A water tablet that helps the kidneys remove salt and water. It treats swelling caused by heart, kidney, or liver disease but can cause dehydration, low blood pressure, or abnormal body-salt levels.

name: torsion dystonia
clinical_significance: A movement disorder in which repeated or sustained muscle contractions twist part of the body into abnormal postures. It may affect one area or many areas and can be inherited or develop after illness, injury, or medicine exposure.

name: torticollis
clinical_significance: A condition in which the neck muscles pull the head into a tilted or rotated position. It may be present from birth or result from pain, injury, muscle spasm, nerve disease, or another condition.

name: torulaspora
clinical_significance: A genus of yeasts used in food and fermentation; human infection is rare and usually opportunistic.

name: torulaspora delbrueckii
clinical_significance: Torulaspora delbrueckii is a yeast used in food fermentation that rarely causes human infection; isolation from a clinical specimen should be assessed for contamination versus opportunistic disease.

name: tositumomab
clinical_significance: Tositumomab is a radiolabeled antibody formerly used for selected B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas; it is no longer routinely available, and radiation exposure, marrow suppression, and secondary malignancy were important risks.

name: total laryngectomy
clinical_significance: Total laryngectomy removes the entire voice box and creates a permanent opening in the neck for breathing, usually to treat advanced laryngeal cancer.

name: total pancreatectomy
clinical_significance: Total pancreatectomy removes the entire pancreas and causes permanent loss of insulin and digestive-enzyme production, requiring lifelong replacement treatment.

name: total tissue
clinical_significance: Total tissue refers to the aggregate tissue amount or sample submitted; adequacy and representativeness affect pathology interpretation and treatment decisions.

name: touch
clinical_significance: The sensory perception of contact, pressure, texture, vibration, or movement across the skin. Signals travel through sensory nerves to the spinal cord and brain.

name: touch perception
clinical_significance: Touch perception allows detection of pressure, texture, vibration, and movement; impaired sensation can indicate nerve or brain disease and increase injury risk.

name: Tourette's syndrome
clinical_significance: A neurodevelopmental disorder involving multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic persisting for more than one year.

name: tourniquet
clinical_significance: A band or pneumatic device placed around a limb to temporarily occlude or greatly reduce arterial blood flow. Emergency tourniquets are designed for control of severe limb bleeding, while pneumatic surgical tourniquets create a relatively bloodless operative field. Prolonged inflation can cause nerve, muscle, or skin injury.

name: Townes syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited birth disorder that commonly causes blockage or absence of the anal opening and unusual thumbs. Kidney, heart, hearing, foot, or genital abnormalities may also occur. The specific problems vary, so treatment is planned around each child’s findings.

name: toxaphene
clinical_significance: A persistent organochlorine insecticide mixture that can accumulate in soil, water, and body fat. Significant exposure may overstimulate the nervous system and cause tremors, seizures, liver injury, or other toxic effects.

name: toxic
clinical_significance: Poisonous or capable of harming living cells, tissues, organs, or the whole body. Toxicity depends on the substance, dose, route, duration, and individual susceptibility.

name: toxic effect
clinical_significance: Harmful change caused by a chemical, medicine, poison, radiation, or other exposure. The effect may involve one or more organs and depends on the dose, route, duration, metabolism, and individual susceptibility.

name: toxic shock syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare, life-threatening illness caused by toxins made by certain bacteria. It can cause sudden fever, a widespread rash, low blood pressure, vomiting or diarrhea, and failure of organs such as the kidneys or heart.

name: toxicity grade
clinical_significance: A standardized rating of how severe a harmful effect is, often used for adverse effects of medicines or cancer treatment. Grades generally range from mild to life-threatening and help guide monitoring and management.

name: toxicity test
clinical_significance: A toxicity test evaluates harmful effects of a substance in cells, animals, or people; results inform safety, but test design and species differences limit how directly they predict human risk.

name: toxicogenomics
clinical_significance: Toxicogenomics studies how genes respond to harmful exposures; it can help identify susceptibility and mechanisms but is not a standalone clinical diagnosis.

name: toxicokinetic description
clinical_significance: An account of how a harmful substance enters the body, is absorbed, distributed, changed by metabolism, and eliminated. These processes determine the concentration and duration of exposure at target organs.

name: toxicokinetics
clinical_significance: Toxicokinetics describes how a toxic substance is absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and eliminated; it helps estimate exposure severity and guide monitoring or treatment.

name: toxicology
clinical_significance: The study of poisons and harmful effects of chemicals, medicines, and other substances. It includes how exposure happens, how the body is affected, how poisoning is recognized, how it can be prevented, and how it is treated.

name: toxin
clinical_significance: A poisonous substance made by a living organism, such as a bacterium, plant, animal, or fungus. Toxins can damage specific tissues or disrupt nerve, muscle, or cellular functions.

name: toxocara
clinical_significance: A genus of parasitic roundworms that commonly infect dogs and cats. People acquire infection by swallowing eggs from contaminated soil or food; migrating larvae can cause fever, enlarged organs, or eye or nervous-system disease.

name: toxocara canis
clinical_significance: A dog roundworm whose eggs can infect people. Larvae migrate through tissues and may cause toxocariasis, with fever, cough, enlarged liver, eye inflammation, or rarely nervous-system involvement.

name: toxocara cati
clinical_significance: A cat roundworm whose eggs can infect people. The larvae may migrate through organs and cause toxocariasis, including fever, cough, enlarged liver, eye inflammation, or rarely neurologic disease.

name: toxocariasis
clinical_significance: Infection caused by dog or cat roundworm larvae after a person swallows eggs from contaminated soil, food, or hands. The larvae can migrate through the body and cause fever, cough, enlarged liver, eye inflammation, or rarely brain disease.

name: toxoid
clinical_significance: A bacterial toxin that has been chemically or otherwise inactivated so it cannot cause its usual harm but can still stimulate protective immunity. Toxoids are used in vaccines against diseases such as tetanus and diphtheria.

name: toxoplasma
clinical_significance: A genus of intracellular parasites; Toxoplasma gondii is the species that infects people. Infection is often mild, but it can seriously affect a fetus or people with weakened immunity, especially the brain and eyes.

name: toxoplasma gondii
clinical_significance: A parasite that causes toxoplasmosis. Cats are its main host and can spread infective forms in their stool; people may also acquire it from undercooked meat, contaminated soil, or contaminated food and water.

name: toxoplasmosis
clinical_significance: An infection caused by the single-celled parasite \textit{Toxoplasma gondii}. People may acquire it by eating undercooked contaminated meat or shellfish, swallowing the parasite from cat feces or contaminated soil, or consuming contaminated food or water. Most people with a healthy immune system have no symptoms; others may have swollen lymph nodes, fever, tiredness, or muscle aches. Infection can cause serious disease of the eyes or brain in people with weakened immunity, may reactivate after i

name: tra gene
clinical_significance: A gene involved in sex determination and sexual differentiation in some organisms, especially insects; its function and sequence vary by species.

name: trabectedin
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy medicine that attaches to DNA and disrupts cancer-cell growth and repair. It is used for selected advanced soft-tissue sarcomas and ovarian cancers and can cause low blood counts, liver injury, nausea, or muscle damage.

name: trabecular meshwork
clinical_significance: A sieve-like tissue near the front of the eye through which the clear fluid called aqueous humor drains. If the drainage pathway becomes blocked, pressure inside the eye may rise and damage the optic nerve in glaucoma.

name: trabeculectomy
clinical_significance: An operation for glaucoma that creates a new drainage path for fluid inside the eye. Lowering eye pressure can protect the optic nerve, but bleeding, infection, scarring, or pressure that becomes too low can occur.

name: trabulsiella
clinical_significance: Trabulsiella species are rare environmental or animal-associated bacteria; human infections are uncommon, and a positive culture should be interpreted with specimen source and clinical findings.

name: trabulsiella guamensis
clinical_significance: Trabulsiella guamensis is an uncommon bacterial isolate with limited clinical reports; significance depends on reliable identification and evidence of infection rather than colonization or contamination.

name: trace element
clinical_significance: Trace elements are minerals needed in small amounts for enzyme and hormone function; both deficiency and excess can cause disease, so supplementation should be based on clinical need.

name: tracer
clinical_significance: A detectable substance used to follow a biological, chemical, or physical process. Medical tracers can show blood flow, organ function, metabolism, or disease location through imaging or laboratory testing.

name: trachea
clinical_significance: The windpipe connecting the larynx to the right and left main bronchi. Cartilage rings help keep it open so air can move to and from the lungs.

name: trachea neoplasm
clinical_significance: A tracheal neoplasm can narrow or obstruct the airway and cause cough, wheezing, hoarseness, or breathlessness; imaging and bronchoscopy with biopsy establish diagnosis.

name: tracheal atresia
clinical_significance: Tracheal atresia is a rare congenital absence or closure of the windpipe and causes severe neonatal respiratory distress; immediate airway and surgical management are required.

name: tracheal calcification
clinical_significance: Tracheal calcification may be an incidental age-related imaging finding but can also occur with cartilage disorders or chronic disease; symptoms and airway narrowing determine significance.

name: tracheal disease
clinical_significance: Tracheal disease can obstruct or inflame the airway and impair breathing; stridor, worsening breathlessness, or inability to clear secretions requires prompt evaluation.

name: tracheal extubation
clinical_significance: Tracheal extubation removes a breathing tube when a patient can maintain airway and ventilation; readiness assessment and post-removal monitoring reduce risk of respiratory failure.

name: tracheal fistula
clinical_significance: A tracheal fistula is an abnormal connection between the windpipe and another structure, potentially causing aspiration, infection, or air leak; it often requires specialized airway and surgical care.

name: tracheal hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Tracheal hemorrhage can obstruct the airway and cause rapid blood loss; bleeding after tracheostomy or airway surgery is an emergency.

name: tracheal mucositis
clinical_significance: Tracheal mucositis is inflammation and injury of the windpipe lining, often after radiation, infection, or instrumentation; swelling and secretions can compromise the airway.

name: tracheal stenosis
clinical_significance: Narrowing of the windpipe, often after prolonged breathing-tube use, tracheostomy, injury, or inflammation. It may cause worsening breathlessness, noisy breathing, or wheezing and can require airway procedures or surgery.

name: tracheal syrinx
clinical_significance: A tracheal syrinx is a fluid-filled cavity within or adjacent to the trachea and is rare; airway symptoms and imaging determine whether intervention is needed.

name: tracheitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of the windpipe. Mild cases may occur with a viral illness, but bacterial infection can rapidly block a child's airway and cause high fever, a harsh cough, noisy breathing, and severe illness. It requires emergency airway and antibiotic treatment.

name: trachelectomy
clinical_significance: Trachelectomy is surgical removal of the cervix, sometimes with nearby tissue, used in selected cervical cancers or other conditions.

name: tracheobronchial tree
clinical_significance: The tracheobronchial tree conducts air from the trachea into the lungs; obstruction, infection, or structural disease can impair ventilation and gas exchange.

name: tracheobronchomalacia
clinical_significance: Weakness of the windpipe or larger airways that allows them to collapse during breathing. It may cause noisy breathing, chronic cough, repeated infections, or difficulty clearing mucus and may be present from birth or develop later.

name: tracheobronchomegaly
clinical_significance: Unusual widening of the windpipe and the main airways, usually because their supporting tissue is weak. It can cause a weak cough, breathlessness, repeated chest infections, and difficulty clearing mucus.

name: tracheoesophageal fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal opening between the windpipe and food pipe, usually present from birth. It can let milk enter the lungs, causing coughing, choking, blue coloring, repeated chest infections, or poor growth, and usually needs surgery.

name: tracheomalacia
clinical_significance: Weakness of the windpipe wall that allows it to narrow or collapse during breathing out. It may cause noisy breathing, cough, breathlessness, repeated infections, or difficulty clearing mucus and may be present from birth or develop later.

name: tracheostomy
clinical_significance: A surgically created artificial opening (stoma) on the front of the neck leading directly into the trachea (windpipe), through which a curved plastic or metal breathing tube (a tracheostomy tube) is placed. It allows air to enter the lungs directly, bypassing severe upper airway obstructions (such as from throat swelling, facial trauma, vocal cord paralysis, or tumors), facilitates the suctioning of deep mucus, and provides a secure route for long-term mechanical ventilation when patients cannot

name: tracheostomy tube
clinical_significance: A tube inserted through a tracheostomy opening to maintain access to the airway and permit breathing,

name: trachoma
clinical_significance: A chronic eye infection caused by certain types of \textit{Chlamydia trachomatis}. It spreads through contact with infected eye or nose discharge, contaminated items, or, in some areas, flies. Repeated infections can scar the inside of the eyelid, turn the eyelid inward, and cause the eyelashes to rub against the eye. This can scar the cornea and lead to permanent visual impairment or blindness.

name: traction
clinical_significance: A controlled pulling force used to align or immobilize a fracture, reduce a dislocation, or relieve pressure on tissues. It may be applied manually, with weights, or through a medical device.

name: training
clinical_significance: Training in healthcare procedures improves competence and patient safety; supervision and regular assessment help ensure skills remain current.

name: training level
clinical_significance: Training level describes a clinician’s stage of education or experience; appropriate supervision and role clarity support safe care and informed patient communication.

name: tramadol
clinical_significance: Tramadol is an opioid analgesic used for selected moderate-to-severe pain; it can cause sedation, respiratory depression, dependence, seizures, serotonin toxicity, and dangerous interactions.

name: tramadol hydrochloride
clinical_significance: Tramadol hydrochloride is the salt form of tramadol used for pain; opioid-related respiratory depression, dependence, seizures, and interactions with serotonergic medicines are important risks.

name: tranexamic acid
clinical_significance: A medicine that helps control bleeding by preventing the body from breaking down blood clots too quickly. It is used for selected heavy bleeding, including some surgical, injury-related, menstrual, and postpartum bleeding.

name: tranquilizing agents
clinical_significance: Tranquilizing agents can reduce agitation or anxiety but may cause sedation, impaired coordination, dependence, or respiratory suppression; the specific drug and cause of symptoms guide safe use.

name: transabdominal ultrasound
clinical_significance: Transabdominal ultrasound images pelvic or abdominal organs through the abdominal wall; it is used in pregnancy and other evaluations, but image quality depends on technique and patient factors.

name: transaminase
clinical_significance: Transaminases ALT and AST are blood enzymes used to assess liver-cell injury; elevations can also arise from muscle or other disease and must be interpreted with the clinical picture.

name: transcobalamin
clinical_significance: Transcobalamin carries vitamin B12 in blood to cells; inherited deficiency can cause functional B12 deficiency with anemia, developmental delay, or neurologic injury despite normal serum B12.

name: transcortin
clinical_significance: Transcortin, or corticosteroid-binding globulin, transports cortisol in blood; abnormal levels can alter total cortisol measurements and complicate endocrine testing.

name: transcription factor
clinical_significance: A protein that attaches to DNA and increases or decreases the copying of selected genes into RNA. Transcription factors help control cell growth, development, specialization, and responses to hormones or injury.

name: transcytosis
clinical_significance: Transcytosis moves substances across a cell by vesicles; it helps transport antibodies and nutrients across barriers and is studied in drug delivery and disease mechanisms.

name: transdermal
clinical_significance: Delivering a medicine through the skin, usually with a patch or gel, so it enters the bloodstream gradually. The medicine, dose, skin condition, heat, and application site affect how much is absorbed.

name: transdermal system
clinical_significance: A transdermal system delivers medicine through the skin at a controlled rate; correct placement, heat exposure, and disposal affect absorption and safety.

name: transducin
clinical_significance: Transducin is a G protein in retinal photoreceptors that relays light signals; inherited defects can cause night blindness or retinal degeneration.

name: transfection
clinical_significance: Transfection introduces genetic material into cells for research or therapy development; delivery efficiency and immune response affect experimental or clinical gene-based approaches.

name: transfer factor
clinical_significance: Transfer factor refers to immune-cell-derived preparations claimed to transfer immune responses; evidence and product standardization are limited, and it is not a substitute for vaccination or established treatment.

name: transfer RNA
clinical_significance: Transfer RNA brings amino acids to ribosomes during protein synthesis; defects in tRNA processing or function can cause mitochondrial, neurologic, or metabolic disease.

name: transferase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that moves a chemical group from one molecule to another. Transferases help cells make and break down substances, and some transferase levels in blood help identify tissue injury or disease.

name: transferrin
clinical_significance: A blood protein made mainly by the liver that carries iron to tissues. Its level and the amount of iron it carries help assess iron deficiency, inflammation, and iron overload when interpreted with other blood tests.

name: transferrin receptor
clinical_significance: Transferrin receptors regulate cellular iron uptake; elevated soluble receptor levels can help distinguish iron deficiency from inflammation-related anemia in selected evaluations.

name: transformer
clinical_significance: A transformer alters electrical voltage and isolation in medical equipment; reliable electrical isolation helps reduce shock and device malfunction risks.

name: transgene
clinical_significance: A transgene is inserted genetic material in a cell or organism; transgenes enable some gene and cell therapies but require assessment of insertion effects, expression, and immune response.

name: transglutaminase
clinical_significance: Transglutaminases cross-link proteins in tissue repair and blood clotting; tissue transglutaminase antibodies are also used in evaluating celiac disease.

name: trans-golgi network
clinical_significance: The trans-Golgi network sorts proteins and lipids for delivery within or outside the cell; trafficking defects can disrupt endocrine, immune, and neurologic function.

name: transient ischemic attack
clinical_significance: A temporary episode of stroke-like symptoms caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, eye, or spinal cord without lasting tissue damage. It can be an early warning of a possible stroke even when symptoms resolve.

name: transition rule
clinical_significance: A transition rule defines how a system moves between states; in clinical pathways it can standardize escalation or follow-up, but rules must allow for individual clinical judgment.

name: transitional cell carcinoma
clinical_significance: Transitional cell carcinoma, now generally called urothelial carcinoma, arises in the lining of the urinary tract; blood in urine is a common warning sign and staging guides treatment.

name: transitional epithelium
clinical_significance: A stretchable protective lining in the kidneys’ drainage areas, ureters, bladder, and part of the urethra. It allows these organs to expand as urine collects without allowing urine to leak into surrounding tissue.

name: transitory
clinical_significance: Transitory describes a temporary finding or symptom; persistence, recurrence, or progression may signal a condition requiring further evaluation.

name: translation initiation
clinical_significance: The first stage of protein synthesis, when a ribosome recognizes messenger RNA, selects the start codon, and assembles the initiator transfer RNA and ribosomal subunits.

name: translucent
clinical_significance: Translucent tissue allows some light to pass through; abnormal changes in translucency can help identify edema, opacity, or surface injury during examination or imaging.

name: transmembrane transport
clinical_significance: Movement of salts, nutrients, medicines, or other substances across a cell’s outer membrane. Channels and carrier proteins may allow passage directly, while pumps use energy to move substances against a concentration difference.

name: transmission
clinical_significance: Passage of an infection, signal, genetic trait, force, or substance from one source to another; in infectious disease, route, dose, and host susceptibility determine risk.

name: transplacental
clinical_significance: Passing from the pregnant person's blood across the placenta to the fetus, or in the opposite direction. Antibodies, medicines, chemicals, and some infections can cross the placenta, with effects that depend on the substance and timing.

name: transplant
clinical_significance: Transfer of cells, tissue, or an organ from one site or person to another to replace damaged tissue or restore function. Donor matching, rejection prevention, infection risk, and long-term follow-up depend on the type of transplant.

name: transplant rejection
clinical_significance: An immune reaction in which the body attacks a donated organ or tissue. It may occur soon after transplantation or later and can reduce organ function; regular monitoring and medicines help prevent or treat it.

name: transplantation
clinical_significance: Transfer of an organ, tissue, or cells from a donor to a recipient to replace or restore failing function. Care includes donor matching, surgery, prevention of rejection, infection monitoring, and long-term follow-up.

name: transplantation conditioning
clinical_significance: Treatment given before some stem-cell transplants to suppress the recipient's bone marrow and immune system and make room for donated cells. It may use chemotherapy, radiation, or both and can cause infection, bleeding, infertility, or organ injury.

name: transplantation immunology
clinical_significance: Transplantation immunology addresses matching, rejection, and immune suppression in organ or cell transplantation; it guides donor selection, monitoring, and treatment of rejection.

name: transport protein
clinical_significance: A protein that carries a substance through body fluids or across a cell boundary. It helps control how nutrients, medicines, salts, and waste products are absorbed, distributed, and used.

name: transport vesicle
clinical_significance: A transport vesicle is a membrane-bound carrier that moves proteins, lipids, or other cargo between cellular compartments.

name: transtracheal
clinical_significance: Transtracheal means passing through or relating to the trachea, such as a catheter, oxygen delivery route, or diagnostic procedure.

name: transtympanic
clinical_significance: Transtympanic means passing through the tympanic membrane, such as medicine delivered into the middle ear or a procedure crossing the eardrum.

name: transverse colon
clinical_significance: The section of the large intestine that crosses the upper abdomen from the right side to the left. It absorbs water and moves partly digested food toward the descending colon.

name: transvestism
clinical_significance: Transvestism is an outdated term for wearing clothing associated with another gender; clothing expression alone is not a disorder, and respectful care focuses on distress or health needs.

name: trapezoid bone
clinical_significance: A small distal-row carpal bone between the trapezium and capitate that articulates mainly with the index metacarpal and helps stabilize the radial side of the hand.

name: trastuzumab
clinical_significance: Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody targeting HER2 used for HER2-positive breast, gastric, and other cancers; infusion reactions and potentially reversible cardiomyopathy require cardiac monitoring.

name: traumatic injury
clinical_significance: Damage to the body caused by an external force, such as a fall, collision, blow, cut, burn, or penetrating object. Injury may affect skin, bones, organs, blood vessels, nerves, or the brain.

name: traumatic shock
clinical_significance: A life-threatening failure of blood flow after serious injury, often because of major bleeding, but sometimes because of heart damage or another cause. It can cause pale clammy skin, confusion, rapid breathing, and collapse and requires immediate treatment.

name: Traumeel S
clinical_significance: Traumeel S is a multi-ingredient complementary product marketed for pain and inflammation; evidence, formulation, and safety depend on the product and it should not replace needed care.

name: travoprost
clinical_significance: Travoprost is a prostaglandin analogue eye drop that increases uveoscleral outflow and lowers intraocular pressure in glaucoma or ocular hypertension; iris pigmentation and eyelash changes may occur.

name: trazodone
clinical_significance: A prescription medicine used mainly for depression and sometimes for sleep problems. It can cause drowsiness, dizziness, low blood pressure, falls, and rare prolonged painful erection; dangerous reactions are more likely with certain medicines or substances.

name: trb gene
clinical_significance: A gene involved in biological processes that vary by species; its precise identity and function must be interpreted from the organism and gene nomenclature used.

name: trd gene
clinical_significance: The gene encoding the delta chain of the T-cell receptor in humans, contributing to gamma-delta T-cell antigen recognition.

name: treatment epoch
clinical_significance: A treatment epoch is a defined time period in a clinical study or care plan; clear timing helps relate interventions to outcomes and adverse events.

name: trematoda
clinical_significance: A class of parasitic flatworms called flukes; human infections include schistosomiasis and liver or lung fluke disease.

name: trematosphaeria grisea
clinical_significance: Trematosphaeria grisea is an environmental fungus that can cause eumycetoma, a chronic tissue infection with swelling, draining sinuses, and grains; prolonged specialist treatment is often needed.

name: tremelimumab
clinical_significance: A monoclonal antibody that blocks CTLA-4 and enhances T-cell activity; it is used with durvalumab for selected unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma and other cancers, with immune-related adverse effects possible.

name: tremor
clinical_significance: An involuntary, rhythmic shaking of a body part. It may occur at rest, while holding a position, or during movement and can result from medicines, caffeine, anxiety, essential tremor, Parkinson disease, or other neurologic or metabolic conditions.

name: trendelenburg
clinical_significance: Trendelenburg position places the body supine with the feet higher than the head; its use is procedure-specific and may affect breathing, pressure, and circulation.

name: treosulfan
clinical_significance: An alkylating chemotherapy drug used in conditioning before allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation; infection, mucositis, infertility, and organ toxicities may occur.

name: trephine
clinical_significance: A circular cutting instrument used to remove a disk of tissue or bone, such as during a bone-marrow biopsy or corneal procedure.

name: treponema
clinical_significance: A group of spiral-shaped bacteria, including Treponema pallidum, which causes syphilis. Different species can live in people or the environment, and identifying the species helps determine whether disease and treatment are present.

name: treponema pallidum
clinical_significance: The spiral-shaped bacterium that causes syphilis. It spreads mainly through contact with an infectious sore during sex and can cross the placenta to an unborn baby. Untreated infection can later affect the skin, nerves, eyes, heart, or brain.

name: treponemal infections
clinical_significance: Infections caused by spiral-shaped Treponema bacteria. They include syphilis and related diseases and may affect the skin, nerves, heart, eyes, or other organs; diagnosis usually combines clinical findings with blood or lesion tests.

name: tretinoin
clinical_significance: A vitamin-A-related medicine applied to the skin for acne and sun-related skin changes, or taken by mouth for a type of acute leukemia. Skin irritation is common; oral treatment can cause serious fluid buildup, fever, and breathing problems.

name: TRG gene
clinical_significance: A gene encoding the gamma chain of the T-cell receptor, contributing to gamma-delta T-cell development and antigen recognition.

name: trial compliance
clinical_significance: Trial compliance means following the study protocol, including visits, dosing, and reporting; deviations can affect participant safety and whether results are interpretable.

name: trial indication
clinical_significance: A trial indication is the disease or clinical circumstance being studied; eligibility criteria determine whether trial evidence applies to a particular patient.

name: trial phase
clinical_significance: Trial phase describes a stage of clinical testing that generally progresses from initial safety and dose evaluation toward larger efficacy and comparative studies; phase affects what is known about benefits and risks.

name: trial screening
clinical_significance: Trial screening checks whether a person meets eligibility and safety criteria before enrollment; it should include informed consent and explain that screening does not guarantee enrollment or benefit.

name: triamcinolone
clinical_significance: A corticosteroid medicine used on skin, by injection, or in other forms to reduce inflammation and itching.

name: triamcinolone acetonide
clinical_significance: A synthetic corticosteroid used topically, by injection, or in other preparations to reduce inflammation; prolonged or extensive use can cause local and systemic steroid effects.

name: triamterene
clinical_significance: A water tablet that helps the kidneys remove salt and water while conserving potassium. It is used for high blood pressure or swelling, but can cause dangerously high potassium, kidney problems, or kidney stones.

name: triazenes
clinical_significance: A group of chemical compounds that includes some chemotherapy medicines. Their effects and risks depend on the specific drug; possible problems include nausea, low blood counts, infection, and damage to other organs.

name: triazine
clinical_significance: Triazines are a chemical family that includes some medicines and pesticides; toxic effects and therapeutic use depend on the specific compound and exposure.

name: triaziquone
clinical_significance: An older alkylating anticancer drug that cross-links DNA; its clinical use is limited by toxicity and availability.

name: triazolam
clinical_significance: Triazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine hypnotic for short-term insomnia; amnesia, falls, dependence, respiratory depression, and dangerous interactions with opioids or other sedatives can occur.

name: triazole
clinical_significance: A five-membered nitrogen-containing chemical ring found in several antifungal medicines and other drugs; clinical effects depend on the specific compound.

name: triazophos
clinical_significance: An organophosphate insecticide that blocks acetylcholinesterase, allowing nerve signals to remain active. Significant exposure can cause sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, small pupils, breathing difficulty, weakness, seizures, or life-threatening poisoning.

name: tributyrin
clinical_significance: Tributyrin is a dietary triglyceride and butyrate precursor studied for intestinal and metabolic effects; evidence for treating disease with supplements is limited.

name: trichiasis
clinical_significance: Inward misdirection of eyelashes so they rub against the eye.

name: trichilemmoma
clinical_significance: A usually harmless tumor arising from a hair follicle, most often appearing as a small skin-colored bump on the face. Multiple growths can be associated with an inherited condition called Cowden syndrome.

name: trichinella
clinical_significance: Trichinella is a genus of parasitic worms acquired from raw or undercooked meat; infection may cause fever, muscle pain, facial swelling, and, in severe cases, heart or neurologic complications.

name: trichinella spiralis
clinical_significance: Trichinella spiralis is a parasite transmitted in undercooked pork or wild game; early diagnosis and antiparasitic treatment can limit progression to muscle disease.

name: trichinellosis
clinical_significance: Trichinellosis is an infection caused by Trichinella worms, usually after eating undercooked infected meat. It may cause diarrhea followed by fever, muscle pain, and swelling around the eyes.

name: trichlorfon
clinical_significance: Trichlorfon is an organophosphate pesticide and antiparasitic agent that inhibits acetylcholinesterase; excessive exposure can cause life-threatening cholinergic poisoning.

name: trichlormethiazide
clinical_significance: Trichlormethiazide is a thiazide diuretic used for hypertension or edema in some settings; electrolyte abnormalities, gout, dehydration, and kidney effects require monitoring.

name: trichloroethylene
clinical_significance: Trichloroethylene is an industrial solvent associated with neurologic, kidney, liver, and cancer risks after substantial exposure; occupational history and exposure reduction are important.

name: trichocephalus trichiura
clinical_significance: Trichuris trichiura, formerly called Trichocephalus trichiura, is the whipworm that causes intestinal infection; heavy burden can lead to anemia, abdominal symptoms, or rectal prolapse.

name: trichoderma
clinical_significance: Trichoderma is an environmental mold that rarely causes invasive infection, mainly in immunocompromised patients; identification and susceptibility testing are important for clinically significant isolates.

name: trichodiscoma
clinical_significance: A trichodiscoma is a usually benign skin tumor or hamartoma that may occur with Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome; multiple lesions can prompt assessment for associated kidney tumors and lung cysts.

name: trichoepithelioma
clinical_significance: A rare benign follicular adnexal tumor that usually presents as a skin-coloured papule or nodule on the face or scalp; it can resemble basal-cell carcinoma and may require histopathologic confirmation.

name: trichofolliculoma
clinical_significance: A trichofolliculoma is a rare benign hair-follicle tumor, usually a small facial papule; examination distinguishes it from other skin lesions when diagnosis is uncertain.

name: trichomonas
clinical_significance: A flagellated protozoan, Trichomonas vaginalis, that infects the urogenital tract and causes trichomoniasis.

name: trichomonas infection
clinical_significance: Trichomonas infection is a sexually transmitted urogenital infection that can cause discharge, irritation, or no symptoms; partner treatment and retesting reduce reinfection.

name: trichomonas vaginalis
clinical_significance: A flagellated protozoan that causes trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection.

name: trichomonas vaginitis
clinical_significance: Trichomonas vaginitis is vaginal inflammation caused by Trichomonas vaginalis; testing confirms the diagnosis, oral treatment is effective, and current sex partners should also be treated.

name: trichomonascus ciferrii
clinical_significance: Trichomonascus ciferrii is a yeast associated with rare invasive infection, often in people with weakened immunity; reliable identification and antifungal susceptibility testing may be needed.

name: trichophyton equinum
clinical_significance: Trichophyton equinum is a dermatophyte fungus primarily associated with horses; it can cause ringworm in people after animal contact, with diagnosis confirmed by fungal testing when needed.

name: trichophyton rubrum
clinical_significance: Trichophyton rubrum is a common cause of athlete’s foot, nail fungus, and ringworm; nail infection often requires prolonged treatment and confirmation before oral antifungal therapy.

name: trichophyton soudanense
clinical_significance: Trichophyton soudanense causes scalp ringworm, particularly in parts of Africa and in people with relevant travel or family exposure; scalp disease often needs oral antifungal treatment.

name: trichophyton tonsurans
clinical_significance: Trichophyton tonsurans commonly causes scalp ringworm and can spread among children through close contact or shared items; untreated infection can cause hair loss and outbreaks.

name: trichophyton verrucosum
clinical_significance: Trichophyton verrucosum is associated with cattle and can cause inflammatory ringworm in people after animal exposure; source control and antifungal treatment help limit spread and scarring.

name: trichophyton violaceum
clinical_significance: Trichophyton violaceum causes scalp and skin ringworm, especially in some geographic regions; species identification can help manage persistent infection and household transmission.

name: trichophyton yaoundei
clinical_significance: Trichophyton yaoundei is a dermatophyte associated with scalp ringworm; diagnosis is particularly relevant with exposure or travel to endemic regions and may require systemic treatment.

name: trichosporon
clinical_significance: Trichosporon yeasts can colonize skin or cause superficial and, rarely, invasive infection in immunocompromised patients; they may be resistant to common antifungals, so species identification matters.

name: trichosporon asahii
clinical_significance: Trichosporon asahii can cause severe bloodstream or disseminated infection in immunocompromised patients, especially those with cancer or neutropenia; prompt identification and specialist-directed therapy are important.

name: trichosporon beigelii
clinical_significance: Trichosporon beigelii is an older name for yeasts now classified among several Trichosporon species; accurate identification matters because invasive species can be difficult to treat.

name: trichostrongylus
clinical_significance: Trichostrongylus is a genus of intestinal roundworms acquired from contaminated food or soil; infection may cause abdominal symptoms, diarrhea, and eosinophilia.

name: trichostrongylus axei
clinical_significance: Trichostrongylus axei is a zoonotic intestinal worm acquired from contaminated vegetation or animal environments; infection is uncommon but may cause gastrointestinal symptoms and eosinophilia.

name: trichostrongylus vitrinus
clinical_significance: Trichostrongylus vitrinus is a parasitic roundworm of livestock that can occasionally infect people; exposure history and stool testing help interpret gastrointestinal illness.

name: trichothiodystrophy syndrome
clinical_significance: A group of inherited disorders characterized by brittle sulfur-deficient hair with a

name: trichotillomania
clinical_significance: Recurrent pulling out of one’s hair, causing hair loss, distress, or impairment, together with repeated attempts to reduce or stop the behavior.

name: triclosan
clinical_significance: Triclosan is an antimicrobial chemical in some consumer products; routine antibacterial use offers limited added benefit over soap and water, and exposure can contribute to allergic or environmental concerns.

name: tricuspid atresia
clinical_significance: A congenital absence or complete closure of the tricuspid valve, blocking normal flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle. Survival depends on an atrial communication and usually a ventricular septal defect or patent ductus to allow blood to reach the lungs; newborns typically have cyanosis and need urgent specialist care and staged treatment.

name: tricuspid regurgitation
clinical_significance: Backward flow through the tricuspid valve from the right ventricle to the right atrium during systole. It may result from primary valve disease or annular enlargement caused by right-ventricular or right-atrial dilation, pulmonary hypertension, or left-sided heart disease; severe regurgitation can cause fatigue, edema, ascites, liver congestion, or right-sided heart failure.

name: tricuspid stenosis
clinical_significance: Narrowing of the tricuspid valve opening, making it harder for blood to move from the right upper chamber to the right lower chamber. It can cause fatigue, swelling, enlarged liver, or neck-vein fullness.

name: tricuspid valve
clinical_significance: The heart valve between the right upper and right lower chambers. It opens to let blood move forward and closes to prevent backflow; leakage or narrowing can strain the heart.

name: tricyclic antidepressant
clinical_significance: Tricyclic antidepressants treat depression and some chronic pain conditions but can cause anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, cardiac conduction abnormalities, and fatal toxicity in overdose.

name: triethylenemelamine
clinical_significance: Triethylenemelamine is an obsolete alkylating chemotherapy agent with substantial toxicity and carcinogenic potential; it has no routine modern therapeutic role.

name: trifluoperazine
clinical_significance: A phenothiazine antipsychotic used for selected psychotic disorders. It can cause drowsiness, movement disorders, and other serious effects, so treatment requires medical supervision.

name: trifluridine
clinical_significance: Trifluridine is an antiviral used topically for herpes eye infection and in combination with tipiracil for selected cancers; blood-count and ocular effects depend on formulation and route.

name: trigeminal ganglion
clinical_significance: The trigeminal ganglion contains sensory nerve-cell bodies for the face; irritation or damage can cause severe facial pain, numbness, or corneal sensory loss.

name: trigeminal nerve
clinical_significance: The fifth cranial nerve, carrying sensation from the face and controlling muscles used for chewing.

name: trigeminal neuralgia
clinical_significance: A chronic pain disorder causing sudden, repeated bursts of severe electric-shock-like, stabbing, or burning pain on one side of the face along one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve, the fifth cranial nerve. Attacks usually last from a fraction of a second to about two minutes and may occur in clusters, with pain-free periods between them. Light touch, brushing the teeth, eating, drinking, speaking, or a breeze may trigger an attack. The usual cause is pressure on the nerve near the brains

name: trigeminal nuclei
clinical_significance: Trigeminal nuclei process facial sensation and motor signals; lesions can cause facial numbness, pain, or weakness and help localize brainstem disease.

name: trigger point
clinical_significance: A trigger point is a tender, irritable area in muscle that may reproduce local or referred pain; assessment helps guide physical therapy or other treatment while excluding structural causes.

name: triggered by
clinical_significance: A trigger is an event or exposure that provokes symptoms, such as an allergen, medication, seizure stimulus, or migraine factor; recognizing triggers can support prevention and diagnosis.

name: triglyceride
clinical_significance: A lipid composed of glycerol and three fatty acids, transported in blood and stored in adipose tissue.

name: triglyceride metabolism
clinical_significance: Triglyceride metabolism governs transport and storage of fats; abnormalities can cause severe hypertriglyceridemia, pancreatitis, or cardiovascular risk and may signal genetic or metabolic disease.

name: trigonocephaly
clinical_significance: Trigonocephaly is a triangular forehead shape caused by premature closure of the metopic skull suture; assessment determines whether surgery or evaluation for associated developmental conditions is needed.

name: triiodothyronine
clinical_significance: The thyroid hormone T3, which contains three iodine atoms and has stronger biological activity than T4. It helps regulate metabolism, heart rate, temperature, and growth.

name: trimetazidine
clinical_significance: Trimetazidine is a metabolic antianginal medicine used in some countries; it can cause or worsen movement disorders and is not appropriate for people with Parkinsonian symptoms.

name: trimethacarb
clinical_significance: Trimethacarb is a carbamate insecticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase; exposure can cause cholinergic symptoms and requires prompt toxicology assessment.

name: trimethadione
clinical_significance: Trimethadione is an obsolete antiseizure medicine associated with serious fetal, blood, kidney, and eye toxicity; it is rarely used when safer treatments are available.

name: trimethoprim
clinical_significance: An antibiotic that blocks bacterial folate production and is often combined with sulfamethoxazole. It treats selected infections but can cause rash, blood-cell changes, high potassium, kidney effects, or medicine interactions.

name: trimethylaminuria
clinical_significance: A metabolic disorder in which impaired oxidation of trimethylamine causes a

name: trimetrexate
clinical_significance: Trimetrexate is an antifolate chemotherapy used with leucovorin in selected Pneumocystis infections and studied in cancer; marrow suppression and mucositis require monitoring.

name: trimetrexate glucuronate
clinical_significance: Trimetrexate glucuronate is the salt form of trimetrexate, an antifolate used in limited settings; leucovorin rescue and close monitoring are needed to reduce toxicity.

name: trinucleotide repeat
clinical_significance: A short DNA sequence of three building blocks repeated many times. Extra copies can interfere with genes and cause inherited disorders such as Huntington disease, fragile X syndrome, myotonic dystrophy, or Friedreich ataxia.

name: triose
clinical_significance: Trioses are three-carbon sugars involved in energy metabolism; abnormal levels may help characterize rare metabolic disorders but are not usually measured alone in routine care.

name: triploidy syndrome
clinical_significance: A chromosome condition in which cells have three complete sets of chromosomes instead of two. It usually causes severe growth restriction and multiple birth defects and often prevents long-term survival; rare mosaic forms may be less severe.

name: triptans
clinical_significance: A group of medicines used to stop a migraine attack. They act on serotonin receptors and pain pathways; they are not suitable for some people with heart or blood-vessel disease and can cause chest or pressure sensations.

name: triptorelin
clinical_significance: Triptorelin is a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist used for hormone-sensitive cancers and selected reproductive conditions; initial hormone flare and later effects on bone and sexual function matter.

name: triptorelin pamoate
clinical_significance: Triptorelin pamoate is a depot formulation that suppresses sex-hormone production after an initial flare; use in cancer or reproductive care requires monitoring for bone, metabolic, and mood effects.

name: trismus
clinical_significance: Difficulty opening the mouth because the jaw muscles are tight or painful. Causes include dental infection, injury, medicines, muscle disorders, and tetanus; severe or rapidly worsening restriction can interfere with eating or breathing and needs urgent assessment.

name: trisomy
clinical_significance: A chromosome condition in which cells have an extra copy of a whole chromosome or chromosome segment, giving three copies instead of the usual two. It may affect all cells or only some cells (mosaicism); effects depend on the chromosome or segment involved and may include developmental differences, birth defects, or pregnancy loss.

name: tristetraprolin
clinical_significance: Tristetraprolin regulates inflammatory messenger RNA breakdown; altered expression is studied in immune disease and cancer but is not a routine clinical test.

name: triterpene
clinical_significance: Triterpenes are plant or fungal compounds studied for pharmacologic activity; supplement claims are not established treatments, and concentrated products may interact with medicines.

name: tritirachium
clinical_significance: Tritirachium is an environmental fungus rarely associated with human infection; its significance depends on reliable identification, specimen source, and immune status.

name: tritium
clinical_significance: Tritium is radioactive hydrogen used in research and industry; internal contamination can expose tissues to low-energy radiation, so occupational controls and dose assessment are important.

name: tRNA methyltransferases
clinical_significance: tRNA methyltransferases modify transfer RNA and support accurate protein synthesis; inherited defects can cause mitochondrial, neurologic, or developmental disorders.

name: trocar
clinical_significance: A pointed instrument placed inside a hollow tube to enter a body cavity or tissue. It is used in minimally invasive procedures to create an opening for cameras, instruments, or drainage tubes.

name: trochlear nerve
clinical_significance: Cranial nerve IV, which supplies the superior oblique eye muscle. Injury can cause vertical or tilted double vision, often worse when looking down or inward.

name: troglitazone
clinical_significance: Troglitazone was a diabetes medicine withdrawn because it caused severe, sometimes fatal liver injury; prior exposure is relevant when evaluating historical treatment or drug-induced liver disease.

name: tromethamine
clinical_significance: Tromethamine is an alkalinizing buffer used in selected severe acid-base disorders and pharmaceutical formulations; administration can cause electrolyte shifts and requires monitoring.

name: tropane
clinical_significance: Tropane alkaloids include anticholinergic medicines such as atropine and scopolamine; overdose can cause delirium, blurred vision, urinary retention, rapid heart rate, and hyperthermia.

name: tropheryma
clinical_significance: Tropheryma whipplei causes Whipple disease, a rare chronic infection that can affect the intestine, joints, heart, and brain; diagnosis may require tissue testing and prolonged antibiotics.

name: tropheryma whipplei
clinical_significance: Tropheryma whipplei causes Whipple disease, a rare infection that may begin with joint pain and progress to diarrhea, weight loss, heart, or neurologic disease; tissue or molecular testing is often needed.

name: trophoblast
clinical_significance: The outer cell layer of an early embryo that attaches to the uterus and helps form the placenta. It supports implantation, exchanges nutrients, and produces hormones needed to maintain early pregnancy.

name: trophoblastic neoplasm
clinical_significance: Trophoblastic neoplasms arise from placental-type cells and include gestational trophoblastic disease and choriocarcinoma; persistent hCG after pregnancy or molar pregnancy requires follow-up.

name: tropical medicine
clinical_significance: The medical specialty concerned with diseases common in tropical and subtropical regions and illnesses related to travel. It includes infections, parasites, insect-borne diseases, environmental hazards, prevention, diagnosis, and treatment.

name: tropicamide
clinical_significance: Tropicamide dilates the pupil for eye examination; temporary blurred near vision and light sensitivity occur, and rarely it can trigger acute angle-closure glaucoma in susceptible eyes.

name: tropisetron
clinical_significance: Tropisetron blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors to prevent nausea and vomiting, especially with chemotherapy or surgery; constipation, headache, and QT-related risk may matter.

name: tropism
clinical_significance: Tropism describes a pathogen’s or cell’s preference for particular tissues; it helps explain disease patterns and guides targeted testing or treatment.

name: tropomyosin
clinical_significance: Tropomyosin is a muscle and cell structural protein; antibodies against it are studied in some autoimmune diseases, while genetic variants can affect muscle function.

name: troponin
clinical_significance: A protein released into the blood when heart muscle is injured. A raised level can support a heart-attack diagnosis, but it may also result from other heart, lung, kidney, or severe systemic illnesses.

name: troponin i
clinical_significance: An inhibitory subunit of the troponin regulatory complex of cardiac striated muscle; cardiac troponin I (cTnI) possesses an amino acid sequence unique to myocardium, serving as an exquisitely sensitive and specific clinical blood biomarker for acute myocardial injury and infarction.

name: troponin t
clinical_significance: Cardiac troponin T is released when heart muscle is injured; a rise or fall supports evaluation for myocardial infarction but must be interpreted with symptoms and ECG findings.

name: troxacitabine
clinical_significance: Troxacitabine is an investigational nucleoside anticancer drug; it is not standard treatment, and clinical-trial evidence and marrow toxicity determine its potential role.

name: truncus arteriosus
clinical_significance: A birth defect in which one large blood vessel leaves the heart instead of separate vessels for the body and lungs. A large hole between the lower chambers usually allows oxygen-poor and oxygen-rich blood to mix, causing blue skin and heart failure. Early surgery is usually required.

name: trunk
clinical_significance: The central part of the body excluding the head and limbs, or a major nerve or vessel trunk.

name: trusses
clinical_significance: Trusses are external supports historically used for hernias; they may not prevent complications and should not delay evaluation of a painful, irreducible hernia.

name: trypan blue
clinical_significance: Trypan blue is a dye used in eye surgery and laboratory viability testing; it helps visualize tissue or distinguish dead cells, with rare local reactions possible.

name: trypanosoma
clinical_significance: A genus of protozoan parasites causing African and American trypanosomiasis.

name: trypanosoma cruzi
clinical_significance: Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease, which can lead years later to cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, heart failure, or digestive nerve damage; exposure history and testing guide care.

name: trypanosomatina
clinical_significance: Trypanosomatina is a group of parasitic protozoa that includes organisms causing Chagas disease and leishmaniasis; species identification determines the infection and treatment.

name: trypanosomiasis
clinical_significance: Disease caused by Trypanosoma parasites, including African sleeping sickness and Chagas disease. Infected insects spread them, and illness may affect blood, lymph nodes, the nervous system, heart, or digestive organs.

name: trypsin
clinical_significance: A digestive enzyme made by the pancreas and activated in the small intestine. It breaks proteins in food into smaller parts and activates other pancreatic digestive enzymes.

name: trypsin inhibitor
clinical_significance: Trypsin inhibitors reduce protein digestion and are found in some foods and research compounds; adequate cooking inactivates many dietary inhibitors, while therapeutic relevance depends on the specific inhibitor.

name: trypsinogen
clinical_significance: Trypsinogen is an inactive pancreatic enzyme precursor; abnormal activation within the pancreas can contribute to acute pancreatitis, and blood trypsinogen may help assess selected pancreatic disorders.

name: tryptase
clinical_significance: Tryptase is released by mast cells and can support diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis or anaphylaxis when measured at appropriate times; a normal result does not exclude anaphylaxis.

name: tryptophan
clinical_significance: An amino acid the body cannot make and must obtain from food. It is used to make proteins and can be changed into serotonin, melatonin, and niacin, which help regulate mood, sleep, and other body functions.

name: tryptophanase
clinical_significance: Tryptophanase is a bacterial enzyme that converts tryptophan into indole; its detection helps identify bacteria in laboratory microbiology.

name: tsukamurella
clinical_significance: Tsukamurella are environmental bacteria that can cause opportunistic catheter, lung, or bloodstream infections, especially in immunocompromised patients; identification and susceptibility testing guide care.

name: t-Test
clinical_significance: A t-test compares the means of two groups; assumptions and study design affect validity, and statistical significance does not by itself show clinical importance.

name: tubal ligation
clinical_significance: A permanent birth-control procedure that closes, cuts, or removes the fallopian tubes so sperm and egg cannot normally meet. It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections, and pregnancy after the procedure, though uncommon, can be ectopic.

name: tubal pregnancy
