name: vero cell
clinical_significance: Vero cells are a laboratory cell line used to grow viruses and produce some biological products; quality controls prevent contamination and ensure product safety.

name: verruciform xanthoma
clinical_significance: A rare, noncancerous growth usually found in the mouth or genital area. It may look like a wart, so examination and sometimes a tissue sample are needed to distinguish it from cancer.

name: verrucous carcinoma
clinical_significance: A low-grade, well-differentiated variant of squamous cell carcinoma with a warty,

name: versican
clinical_significance: Versican is a connective-tissue proteoglycan involved in cell adhesion and tissue repair; altered expression is studied in fibrosis and cancer but is not a routine diagnostic marker.

name: vertebra
clinical_significance: One of the bones forming the spinal column. Each vertebra helps support the body, allows movement, provides attachment for muscles, and surrounds and protects the spinal cord.

name: vertebral column
clinical_significance: The chain of bones running from the neck to the pelvis. It supports the head and trunk, protects the spinal cord, allows bending and twisting, and provides attachment for muscles and ribs.

name: vertebrate
clinical_significance: Vertebrates have a backbone and include humans and many animals; the term is relevant to comparative biology and animal-borne infection research.

name: vertebroplasty
clinical_significance: A procedure in which medical cement is injected into a collapsed spinal bone to help stabilize it and sometimes reduce pain. It is used selectively because cement leakage, infection, nerve injury, or other complications can occur.

name: verteporfin
clinical_significance: Verteporfin is a photosensitizing medicine used with laser therapy for selected eye and vascular conditions; patients must avoid intense light exposure temporarily after treatment.

name: vertical talus
clinical_significance: A stiff flatfoot present from birth in which one of the ankle bones points downward and the middle of the foot is bent upward. It may occur alone or with other conditions and usually needs early orthopedic treatment.

name: vertical transmission
clinical_significance: Passage of an infection or genetic condition from parent to child during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding.

name: verticillium hypocreales
clinical_significance: Verticillium species are plant-associated fungi and rare human pathogens; recovery from a clinical specimen requires confirmation and correlation with illness.

name: vertigo
clinical_significance: A false feeling that you or your surroundings are moving, spinning, tilting, or shifting when they are not. It is a symptom rather than a disease and often comes from the inner ear, but brain and other conditions can also cause it.

name: vesicle
clinical_significance: A small, circumscribed, raised skin lesion containing clear, serous, or sometimes bloody fluid, usually less than 1 cm in diameter. A vesicle is a small blister; causes include viral infection, contact irritation, eczema, burns, friction, and immune-mediated skin disease.

name: vesico-ureteral reflux
clinical_significance: Vesicoureteral reflux allows urine to flow backward from the bladder toward the kidneys; recurrent infection or kidney scarring can result, especially in children.

name: vesicovaginal fistula
clinical_significance: An abnormal connection between the bladder and vagina that causes continuous or frequent leakage of urine through the vagina. It may follow childbirth injury, pelvic surgery, radiation, or advanced infection and usually requires specialist repair.

name: vesiculovirus
clinical_significance: Vesiculovirus is a genus of viruses that includes vesicular stomatitis virus; human infection is usually uncommon and may cause a flu-like illness or oral lesions after animal or laboratory exposure.

name: vestibular labyrinth
clinical_significance: The vestibular labyrinth detects head movement and position to support balance and gaze stabilization; dysfunction can cause vertigo, nausea, and imbalance.

name: vestibular nerve
clinical_significance: The vestibular nerve carries balance signals from the inner ear to the brain; inflammation or injury can cause acute vertigo and imbalance.

name: vestibular nuclei
clinical_significance: Vestibular nuclei integrate balance and eye-movement signals in the brainstem; lesions can cause vertigo, nystagmus, and gait instability.

name: veterinarian
clinical_significance: Veterinarians diagnose and treat animal disease and help prevent zoonotic transmission; animal health also supports food safety and public health.

name: veterinary medicine
clinical_significance: Veterinary medicine protects animal health and can reduce human exposure to zoonoses, foodborne pathogens, and antimicrobial-resistant organisms.

name: vial device
clinical_significance: A vial device helps access or administer medicines from a vial; correct needle, stopper, and aseptic technique reduce contamination and medication errors.

name: vibration problem
clinical_significance: Symptoms or injury caused by repeated exposure to vibrating tools or equipment, which may affect nerves, blood vessels, muscles, and joints in the hands or arms.

name: vibrator
clinical_significance: A device that produces mechanical vibration and may be used for sexual stimulation, therapeutic massage, or selected rehabilitation purposes.

name: vibrio
clinical_significance: A genus of curved, Gram-negative bacteria; species include \textit{V. cholerae}, which causes cholera, and \textit{V. vulnificus}, which can cause severe wound or bloodstream infection.

name: vibrio alginolyticus
clinical_significance: Vibrio alginolyticus is a marine bacterium that can cause ear, wound, or gastrointestinal infection after seawater or seafood exposure; open wounds exposed to coastal water deserve prompt assessment.

name: vibrio cholerae
clinical_significance: A bacterium that causes cholera, a severe diarrheal illness spread mainly through contaminated water or food. It can cause sudden, large-volume watery diarrhea, dehydration, shock, and death without rapid fluid replacement.

name: vibrio fluvialis
clinical_significance: Vibrio fluvialis can cause watery or bloody diarrhea after contaminated seafood or water exposure and rarely causes invasive infection; culture and exposure history help guide evaluation.

name: vibrio furnissii
clinical_significance: Vibrio furnissii is an uncommon marine bacterium associated with occasional gastroenteritis; a positive stool or wound culture should be interpreted with symptoms and seafood or water exposure.

name: vibrio infection
clinical_significance: Infection caused by Vibrio bacteria, acquired through contaminated seafood or exposure of wounds to warm seawater. It may cause watery diarrhea, wound infection, or rapidly worsening bloodstream infection, especially in people with liver disease or weakened immunity. Severe wound pain, blistering, fever, or shock can occur.

name: vibrio metschnikovii
clinical_significance: Vibrio metschnikovii is a rare cause of human wound, ear, or bloodstream infection, often after water or seafood exposure; accurate identification and susceptibility testing are important.

name: vibrio mimicus
clinical_significance: Vibrio mimicus can cause cholera-like watery diarrhea or wound infection after seafood or water exposure; stool culture and hydration assessment guide care.

name: vibrio parahaemolyticus
clinical_significance: Vibrio parahaemolyticus commonly causes seafood-associated gastroenteritis and can infect wounds exposed to coastal water; severe illness warrants prompt assessment, especially in medically vulnerable people.

name: vibrio vulnificus
clinical_significance: Vibrio vulnificus can cause rapidly progressive wound infection or sepsis after seawater, seafood, or raw oyster exposure, with greatest risk in liver disease or immunocompromise; urgent treatment is critical.

name: vibrionaceae
clinical_significance: Vibrionaceae are marine and aquatic bacteria that include Vibrio species causing foodborne diarrhea and severe wound infections; seafood and coastal-water exposure history is clinically important.

name: vibrissae
clinical_significance: Vibrissae are specialized hairs, such as nasal hairs, that help filter particles and provide sensory input; loss or irritation may affect local protection but is rarely a major diagnosis.

name: vidarabine
clinical_significance: Vidarabine is an older antiviral with limited current use; topical formulations were used for herpes eye infection, while systemic use is limited by toxicity and safer alternatives.

name: vidarabine phosphate
clinical_significance: Vidarabine phosphate is a phosphorylated form of an older antiviral; its clinical use is limited and depends on formulation, indication, and availability.

name: video microscopy
clinical_significance: Video microscopy records microscopic movement or cell behavior over time; it supports laboratory diagnosis and research but requires validated interpretation for clinical use.

name: vildagliptin
clinical_significance: An oral dipeptidyl-peptidase-4 inhibitor used in some countries for type 2 diabetes, alone or with other medicines. It improves glucose-dependent insulin secretion; liver function and pancreatitis symptoms may require attention.

name: villous adenoma
clinical_significance: A high-risk subtype of neoplastic colonic adenomatous polyp characterized histologically by long, finger-like, frond-like epithelial projections covering more than 75% of the polyp mass, associated with a high potential for malignant transformation and excessive secretory mucus/electrolyte loss (secretory diarrhea with hypokalemia).

name: villus
clinical_significance: A small finger-like projection, especially one of the intestinal mucosa that increases absorptive surface area; chorionic villi mediate exchange between placenta and fetus.

name: vimentin
clinical_significance: Vimentin is a structural protein expressed by mesenchymal cells; immunostaining helps classify tumors but is not specific enough to diagnose a cancer alone.

name: vinblastine
clinical_significance: Vinblastine is a chemotherapy drug that disrupts cell division and is used for selected lymphomas and solid tumors; low blood counts, infection risk, and nerve effects require monitoring.

name: vinblastine sulfate
clinical_significance: Vinblastine sulfate is the injectable salt form of vinblastine; dosing must be carefully controlled because severe marrow suppression and tissue injury can occur.

name: vinca alkaloid
clinical_significance: Vinca alkaloids block microtubule formation and are used in cancer chemotherapy; neuropathy, constipation, and marrow suppression vary by agent.

name: vincristine
clinical_significance: Vincristine is a chemotherapy drug used for leukemias, lymphomas, and other cancers; peripheral and autonomic neuropathy are dose-limiting risks, while severe marrow suppression is less common.

name: vincristine sulfate
clinical_significance: Vincristine sulfate is the injectable salt form of vincristine; it is for intravenous use only because accidental intrathecal administration is usually fatal.

name: vinculin
clinical_significance: Vinculin anchors the cell’s internal skeleton to adhesion sites; altered expression is studied in cardiomyopathy and cancer but is not a routine clinical marker.

name: vindesine
clinical_significance: Vindesine is a vinca alkaloid chemotherapy used in limited settings; neuropathy and bone-marrow suppression require monitoring, and availability varies.

name: vinflunine
clinical_significance: Vinflunine is a vinca alkaloid used for selected advanced cancers in some regions; marrow suppression, infection, constipation, and neuropathy are important treatment risks.

name: vinorelbine
clinical_significance: A chemotherapy medicine that interferes with cell division. It is used for selected lung and breast cancers and can cause low blood counts, infection, constipation, nerve symptoms, nausea, or irritation if it leaks outside a vein.

name: vinorelbine tartrate
clinical_significance: Vinorelbine tartrate is the salt form of vinorelbine, a chemotherapy used for selected lung and breast cancers; blood counts and neuropathy require monitoring.

name: vinyl chloride
clinical_significance: Vinyl chloride is a carcinogenic industrial gas associated with liver angiosarcoma and other disease after occupational exposure; exposure history and workplace controls are important.

name: violence
clinical_significance: Violence can cause injury, trauma, chronic illness, and mental-health effects; private, trauma-informed assessment can help identify immediate safety needs and connect patients with support.

name: viomycin
clinical_significance: An older aminoglycoside antibiotic related to capreomycin that was used against tuberculosis and other mycobacterial infections; kidney and hearing toxicity limit its use.

name: vipoma
clinical_significance: A rare functioning neuroendocrine tumor arising from the non-beta islet cells of the pancreas (or occasionally extra-pancreatic sympathetic ganglia in children) that hypersecretes vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), causing refractory secretory diarrhea and hypokalemia.

name: viral
clinical_significance: Caused by or relating to a virus. Viruses enter living cells to multiply and can cause illnesses ranging from mild colds to serious brain, lung, liver, or bleeding diseases; testing and treatment depend on the specific virus.

name: viral antibody
clinical_significance: A protective protein made by the immune system after infection or vaccination that recognizes a virus. Blood tests for these antibodies may show past exposure, immune response, or selected current infections, depending on timing and test design.

name: viral carcinogenesis
clinical_significance: Cancer development caused or promoted by a viral infection. Some viruses alter cell growth directly, weaken immune protection, or cause long-lasting inflammation; examples include human papillomavirus, hepatitis B and C viruses, and Epstein-Barr virus.

name: viral conjunctivitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by a virus, often producing red, watery, irritated eyes and sometimes discharge. It is usually contagious and can spread through contact with infected secretions or contaminated hands and surfaces.

name: viral encephalitis
clinical_significance: Inflammation of the brain caused by a virus. It may cause fever, headache, confusion, behavior change, seizures, weakness, or reduced consciousness. Severe cases can be life-threatening.

name: viral envelope
clinical_significance: A viral envelope is a lipid membrane surrounding some viruses and helps them enter host cells; envelope proteins are targets for antibodies, vaccines, and antiviral drugs.

name: viral gastroenteritis
clinical_significance: Viral gastroenteritis causes vomiting and diarrhea, often with dehydration; fluids and hygiene are central to care, and blood in stool or severe dehydration warrants evaluation.

name: viral genome
clinical_significance: A viral genome is the DNA or RNA carrying a virus’s genetic instructions; sequencing can identify variants, track outbreaks, and guide selected diagnostic or treatment decisions.

name: viral hepatitis
clinical_significance: Liver inflammation caused by hepatitis viruses A, B, C, D, or E. Hepatitis A and E usually spread through contaminated food or water; B, C, and D can spread through blood or body fluids and may become long-term infections that damage the liver.

name: viral meningitis
clinical_significance: Infection and inflammation of the coverings of the brain and spinal cord caused by a virus. It may cause fever, headache, neck stiffness, vomiting, light sensitivity, or confusion. Bacterial meningitis can cause similar symptoms and is more dangerous.

name: viral pneumonia
clinical_significance: Infection and inflammation of lung tissue caused by a virus, producing cough, fever, chills, breathlessness, chest discomfort, fatigue, and variable impairment of oxygenation. Severe disease can cause respiratory failure or secondary bacterial infection.

name: viral vaccine
clinical_significance: Viral vaccines expose the immune system to a weakened, inactivated, or selected viral component to prevent infection; vaccine type determines eligibility, dosing, and safety considerations.

name: viremia
clinical_significance: The presence of a virus in the bloodstream. It may be brief or persistent and can allow infection to spread to other organs. Laboratory tests may detect the virus itself or its genetic material.

name: virginiamycin
clinical_significance: Virginiamycin is a streptogramin antibiotic used mainly in veterinary and agricultural settings; it is not a routine human medicine, and antimicrobial resistance is a public-health concern.

name: viridans streptococci
clinical_significance: Viridans streptococci are a group of bacteria commonly found in the mouth that can cause dental infections and, after entering the blood, infect heart valves.

name: virilism foetal
clinical_significance: Prenatal or neonatal masculinization of a genetically female fetus or infant due to

name: virion
clinical_significance: A virion is a complete infectious virus particle; measuring or identifying virions can support virology research, vaccine production, and diagnostic testing.

name: virogenic stroma
clinical_significance: Virogenic stroma refers to tissue or cell conditions that support virus production; it is mainly a virology research concept rather than a clinical diagnosis.

name: viroid
clinical_significance: Viroids are small infectious RNA molecules that cause plant disease but are not known to infect humans; they matter mainly to agriculture and plant pathology.

name: virosome
clinical_significance: A virosome is a virus-derived membrane structure used in some vaccine or drug-delivery approaches; its clinical relevance depends on the product and safety evidence.

name: virulence
clinical_significance: How severely a microorganism can cause disease or tissue damage. It depends on the organism’s harmful properties and on the person’s immune defenses and other health factors.

name: virulent
clinical_significance: Capable of causing severe disease or extensive harm. Virulence describes the harmfulness of a microorganism and is different from infectivity, which describes how easily it spreads or establishes infection.

name: virulizin
clinical_significance: Virulizin is an investigational immune-modulating product studied as an anticancer treatment; it is not established routine therapy and should not replace proven cancer care.

name: virus
clinical_significance: An infectious agent made of genetic material inside a protective protein coat, sometimes with an outer membrane. It can reproduce only inside living cells and may cause illness by damaging cells or triggering inflammation.

name: virus activation
clinical_significance: Virus activation is the switch from a dormant or inactive viral state to production of new viral components and particles.

name: virus assembly
clinical_significance: Virus assembly is the stage of the viral life cycle when viral genetic material and proteins are packaged into new virus particles.

name: virus diseases
clinical_significance: Illnesses caused by viruses. They range from mild infections of one area, such as a cold, to severe diseases affecting the lungs, liver, brain, blood, or several organs; prevention and treatment depend on the virus.

name: virus integration
clinical_significance: Virus integration is insertion of viral genetic material into the DNA of a host cell, a process used by some viruses and important in certain cancers.

name: virus protein
clinical_significance: A virus protein is a protein made from viral genetic instructions that helps form the virus, enter cells, replicate, or evade immunity.

name: virus receptor
clinical_significance: A virus receptor is a molecule on a host cell that a virus binds to in order to attach to and enter the cell.

name: virus replication
clinical_significance: Virus replication is the process by which a virus copies its genetic material and makes proteins and new virus particles inside a host cell.

name: virus uncoating
clinical_significance: Virus uncoating is removal of the virus's protective outer layer after entry into a host cell, releasing its genetic material for replication.

name: viscera
clinical_significance: The internal organs of the body, particularly those within the thoracic and abdominal

name: visceral
clinical_significance: Relating to the internal organs, especially those within the thorax or abdomen, rather than the body wall or limbs.

name: visceral pleura
clinical_significance: The visceral pleura is the membrane covering the lung surface; inflammation, tumor involvement, or injury can cause pain, fluid, or impaired lung expansion.

name: viscosity
clinical_significance: Viscosity describes a fluid’s resistance to flow; high blood viscosity can impair circulation and may occur with excess blood cells or proteins, while fluid viscosity matters in laboratory and medication delivery.

name: visilizumab
clinical_significance: Visilizumab is an investigational antibody targeting activated T cells studied for immune-mediated disease; it is not routine therapy and can cause serious immune and infection-related adverse effects.

name: vision
clinical_significance: The sense that detects light and enables the brain to form and interpret images, including shape, color, movement, and spatial relationships. It depends on the eyes, optic nerves, and visual pathways in the brain.

name: vision disorder
clinical_significance: Vision disorders can limit reading, mobility, driving, and independence; early assessment can detect refractive error, eye disease, or neurologic causes and prevent avoidable loss.

name: vision screening
clinical_significance: Brief checks used to find possible eye or vision problems before symptoms are obvious. Newborn checks may detect cataracts or other serious disorders; screening in young children looks for poor vision, misaligned eyes, or risks for reduced vision and leads to a full eye examination when needed.

name: vision test
clinical_significance: An examination that measures visual acuity, fields, color, alignment, or eye structures to detect refractive error, retinal disease, optic-nerve dysfunction, glaucoma, or other causes of visual impairment.

name: vismodegib
clinical_significance: Vismodegib blocks Hedgehog signaling and is used for selected advanced basal-cell cancers; muscle spasms, taste changes, hair loss, and severe fetal harm require counseling and monitoring.

name: visual accommodation
clinical_significance: Visual accommodation changes lens focus between near and distant objects; impaired accommodation can cause eyestrain or blurred near vision and may follow aging, medication, or neurologic disease.

name: visual acuity
clinical_significance: How clearly a person can see fine details, usually measured by reading letters or symbols at a set distance. It can be reduced by focusing problems, eye disease, or disorders affecting the visual nerves or brain.

name: visual agnosia
clinical_significance: Inability to recognize familiar objects, faces, or symbols by sight even though the eyes may see adequately. It usually results from damage to brain areas that interpret vision, such as after a stroke or head injury.

name: visual cortex
clinical_significance: The visual cortex processes visual information in the occipital brain; injury can cause field loss or visual recognition problems even when the eyes are structurally normal.

name: visual field
clinical_significance: The entire area that can be seen while the eyes remain fixed in one position. Visual-field loss may result from retinal, optic-nerve, or brain lesions and is assessed by perimetry.

name: visual impairment
clinical_significance: Reduced vision that cannot be fully corrected by ordinary glasses or contact lenses. Causes include refractive error, cataract, glaucoma, retinal disease, optic-nerve injury, and disorders of the brain or nervous system.

name: visual learning
clinical_significance: Visual learning uses sight to acquire and recall information; difficulties may occur with visual impairment, neurologic injury, or learning disorders and affect education and daily function.

name: visual pathway
clinical_significance: The visual pathway carries signals from the retina through the optic nerves and brain to the visual cortex; lesions produce characteristic patterns of vision loss that help localize disease.

name: visual perception
clinical_significance: Visual perception is the brain’s interpretation of visual input; deficits can affect object recognition, spatial judgment, and safety despite adequate visual acuity.

name: vital sign
clinical_significance: Vital signs such as temperature, pulse, breathing rate, blood pressure, and oxygen level help detect acute illness and track response to treatment; trends can be more informative than a single reading.

name: vital statistics
clinical_significance: Vital statistics on births, deaths, and disease inform public-health planning and health-system evaluation; completeness and accurate classification affect population estimates.

name: vitamin
clinical_significance: Vitamins are essential micronutrients needed for normal metabolism and tissue function; deficiency and excess can both cause disease, so supplementation should match clinical need.

name: vitamin A
clinical_significance: A fat-soluble vitamin needed for vision, immune function, skin and mucosal health, and growth; deficiency causes night blindness, while excess can injure the liver and developing fetus.

name: vitamin B complex
clinical_significance: A group of eight water-soluble vitamins that act mainly as coenzymes or their precursors in cell metabolism. The group includes thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), pantothenic acid (B5), pyridoxine (B6), biotin (B7), folate (B9), and cobalamin (B12), which together support energy metabolism, red-blood-cell formation, and nervous-system function. These vitamins occur together in whole grains, meat, eggs, and legumes; individual deficiencies cause distinct disorders, and combined suppleme

name: vitamin B12
clinical_significance: A vitamin needed for red-cell formation, DNA production, and normal nerve function. Deficiency can cause anemia, numbness, balance problems, or cognitive changes.

name: vitamin B6
clinical_significance: A group of related vitamins needed for amino-acid metabolism, red-cell production, and nerve function. Excess supplements can cause sensory nerve damage.

name: vitamin D
clinical_significance: Vitamin D supports calcium and phosphate balance, bone mineralization, muscle function, and immune processes; deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia or bone loss in adults.

name: vitamin d deficiency
clinical_significance: Too little vitamin D for the body’s needs. It can result from low intake or sunlight, poor absorption, or liver or kidney disease and may weaken bones, cause muscle weakness, or lead to rickets in children.

name: vitamin deficiency
clinical_significance: Vitamin deficiency can cause organ-specific symptoms, anemia, impaired growth, or neurologic injury; diet, absorption, medicines, and laboratory findings help identify the cause and guide replacement.

name: vitamin E
clinical_significance: Vitamin E is a group of fat-soluble compounds with antioxidant activity. It is found in foods such as nuts, seeds, and vegetable oils; high-dose supplements can increase bleeding risk and interact with medicines.

name: vitamin K
clinical_significance: A fat-soluble vitamin required to activate several blood-clotting proteins and support bone metabolism; the main dietary form is phylloquinone, found especially in leafy green vegetables and some vegetable oils. Deficiency can cause bleeding and is treated or prevented with replacement.

name: vitamin k deficiency
clinical_significance: Too little vitamin K for normal production of clotting factors, causing an increased bleeding tendency. It can result from poor intake, malabsorption, liver disease, or certain medicines; newborns receive vitamin K prophylaxis.

name: vitellin
clinical_significance: Vitellin is a yolk protein in egg-laying animals and has no routine human clinical role; it may be used in laboratory or food science research.

name: vitelline membrane
clinical_significance: The vitelline membrane surrounds the yolk in an egg and is relevant to embryology and food science rather than human clinical diagnosis.

name: vitellogenesis
clinical_significance: Vitellogenesis is yolk production in egg-laying animals and is primarily a reproductive biology concept with no routine human clinical application.

name: vitellogenin
clinical_significance: Vitellogenin is a yolk precursor protein in egg-laying animals and is used in environmental research as a biomarker of estrogenic exposure; it has no routine human diagnostic role.

name: vitespen
clinical_significance: Vitespen is an autologous tumor-derived heat-shock protein vaccine studied for cancer; it is not an established routine treatment, and clinical-trial results determine any potential role.

name: vitiligo
clinical_significance: Vitiligo is a condition in which areas of skin lose pigment because melanocytes are destroyed or stop functioning. It is not contagious, and treatment may include camouflage, topical medicines, or light therapy.

name: vitrectomy
clinical_significance: Eye surgery that removes some or all of the vitreous, the clear gel that fills the middle of the eye. Small instruments are inserted through the wall of the eye to remove cloudy gel, blood, scar tissue, or a foreign object and to repair problems of the retina. It may be used for retinal detachment, diabetic eye disease, macular hole, macular pucker, severe eye injury, or serious eye infection. The removed gel may be replaced with a salt solution, air or gas, or silicone oil.

name: vitreous body
clinical_significance: The transparent gel filling the large space between the lens and retina. It helps maintain the shape of the eye and transmits light; age-related liquefaction can cause floaters or contribute to retinal traction.

name: vitreous detachment
clinical_significance: Separation of the vitreous gel from the retina, usually related to aging and often causing new floaters or flashes. Sudden symptoms can occur with a retinal tear or detachment.

name: vitreous floaters
clinical_significance: Vitreous floaters are moving spots or threads in vision, often from age-related vitreous change; sudden new floaters, flashes, or a curtain-like shadow may signal retinal tear or detachment and need urgent eye assessment.

name: vitreous hemorrhage
clinical_significance: Bleeding into the vitreous cavity that causes sudden painless floaters, cobwebs, haze,

name: vitreous humor
clinical_significance: The clear gel that fills the space between the lens and retina. It helps maintain the shape of the eye and transmits light to

name: vitritis
clinical_significance: Vitritis is inflammation within the vitreous gel, often from infection, autoimmune disease, or lymphoma; blurred vision and floaters warrant ophthalmic evaluation to protect sight.

name: vitronectin
clinical_significance: Vitronectin is a blood and tissue protein involved in clotting, cell adhesion, and repair; it is studied in thrombosis and cancer but is not a routine diagnostic test.

name: vivax malaria
clinical_significance: Vivax malaria can relapse months or years after the initial illness because dormant liver forms persist; preventing relapse requires species-specific treatment and quantitative G6PD testing before certain medicines to avoid hemolysis.

name: vocabulary
clinical_significance: Vocabulary reflects language comprehension and expression; loss or delay can indicate neurologic, developmental, or hearing problems and may guide speech-language assessment.

name: vocal cord
clinical_significance: The vocal cords, or vocal folds, produce voice and help protect the airway during swallowing; persistent hoarseness, breathing difficulty, or aspiration warrants evaluation.

name: vocal cord paralysis
clinical_significance: Inability of one or both vocal folds to move normally, often because of nerve damage. It may cause hoarseness, weak cough, choking, or difficulty protecting the airway; sudden breathing trouble is an emergency.

name: vocational guidance
clinical_significance: Vocational guidance helps people choose or adapt work based on abilities, health, and interests; it can support safe employment and participation after illness or injury.

name: vocational rehabilitation
clinical_significance: Vocational rehabilitation helps people with illness or disability prepare for, return to, or remain in work through therapy, accommodations, and job support.

name: voice
clinical_significance: Sound produced by vibration of the vocal folds as air passes through the larynx, then shaped by the throat, mouth, and nose for speech.

name: voice disorder
clinical_significance: Voice disorders affect pitch, loudness, quality, or endurance and may result from vocal strain, infection, nerve injury, or laryngeal disease; persistent hoarseness needs assessment.

name: volatile oil
clinical_significance: Volatile oils can irritate skin, eyes, or airways and may be toxic if ingested or inhaled in concentrated form; exposure depends on the specific product and dose.

name: volition
clinical_significance: Volition is the ability to initiate and direct purposeful actions; impaired volition may occur with depression, brain injury, dementia, or medication effects and can affect daily function.

name: volkmann contracture
clinical_significance: A permanent, severe ischemic contracture of the forearm flexor musculature leading to a claw-like hand deformity, resulting from untreated acute compartment syndrome of the forearm following supracondylar humeral fractures, crush injuries, or tight casting.

name: Volkmann's canal
clinical_significance: Volkmann canals carry blood vessels and nerves through compact bone; disruption from fracture or surgery can impair bone healing and tissue perfusion.

name: volociximab
clinical_significance: Volociximab is an investigational antibody targeting tumor-cell adhesion and angiogenesis; it is not standard therapy and remains dependent on clinical-trial evidence.

name: volt
clinical_significance: A volt measures electrical potential; in medical devices, correct voltage and insulation help prevent shock, burns, and equipment failure.

name: volume fraction
clinical_significance: Volume fraction is the proportion of a mixture occupied by a component; in medicine it can describe hematocrit, gas mixtures, or concentration and affects clinical interpretation.

name: volvulus
clinical_significance: Twisting of a loop of intestine that blocks passage through the bowel and may cut off its blood supply. It can cause severe pain, vomiting, swelling, and tissue death and can be life-threatening.

name: vomer bone
clinical_significance: The vomer is a thin bone forming part of the nasal septum; fracture or deviation can contribute to obstruction or bleeding, while anatomic variation is common.

name: vomiting
clinical_significance: Forceful emptying of stomach contents through the mouth. It may result from infection, digestive disease, medicines, pregnancy, migraine, brain disorders, or poisoning. Repeated vomiting can cause dehydration, disturbed body salts, or inhalation of vomit.

name: vomitus
clinical_significance: Material expelled from the stomach or upper gastrointestinal tract during vomiting. Its color and contents can provide clues but do not by themselves establish a diagnosis.

name: voriconazole
clinical_significance: An antifungal medicine used for selected serious fungal infections. It stops fungi making an essential part of their outer structure; vision changes, liver problems, medicine interactions, and skin sensitivity require monitoring.

name: vorinostat
clinical_significance: Vorinostat is an HDAC inhibitor used for cutaneous manifestations of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma after prior systemic therapy; blood counts, glucose, electrolytes, and thromboembolic risks may require monitoring.

name: voyeurism
clinical_significance: A recurrent sexual interest in observing an unsuspecting person who is naked, disrobing, or engaging in sexual activity. The interest alone is not a mental disorder; voyeuristic disorder is the diagnostic term when required criteria are met.

name: vulva
clinical_significance: The external female genital structures, including the mons pubis, labia, clitoris, and vestibule. It protects the openings of the urinary and reproductive tracts and contains specialized sensory and glandular tissue.

name: vulva neoplasm
clinical_significance: A vulvar neoplasm may be benign, precancerous, or malignant; persistent itching, a lump, ulcer, or skin-color change should be examined and sometimes biopsied.

name: vulval infection
clinical_significance: Vulvar infection can cause itching, pain, redness, sores, or discharge; causes include yeast, bacteria, viruses, and sexually transmitted pathogens, so testing guides treatment.

name: vulvar adenocarcinoma
clinical_significance: Vulvar adenocarcinoma is a rare gland-forming cancer of the vulva; diagnosis requires biopsy and specialist staging, and symptoms may include a persistent mass, ulcer, or bleeding.

name: vulvar disease
clinical_significance: Vulvar disease includes inflammatory, infectious, dermatologic, pain, and neoplastic conditions; examination and targeted testing help avoid delayed diagnosis or inappropriate treatment.

name: vulvar melanoma
clinical_significance: A rare cancer of the pigment-producing cells in the vulva. It may appear as a dark or skin-colored lump, patch, sore, or bleeding area; diagnosis requires a biopsy, and treatment depends on size and spread.

name: vulvar vestibulitis
clinical_significance: Vulvar vestibulitis is an older term for localized provoked vulvar pain, now often classified as vulvodynia; evaluation excludes infection or skin disease and guides pelvic-floor and pain care.

name: vulvodynia
clinical_significance: Persistent or recurring pain in the vulva without an identifiable cause or specific disorder. The pain may be localized or widespread, triggered by touch or pressure, or occur without touch; it is often described as burning, rawness, or soreness.

name: vulvovaginal candidiasis
clinical_significance: A yeast infection of the vulva and vagina, usually caused by Candida. It commonly causes intense itching, burning, soreness, redness, and thick discharge; recurrent, severe, unusual, or treatment-resistant symptoms need testing to confirm the cause.

name: vulvovaginitis
clinical_significance: Simultaneous inflammation or infection of the vulva and vagina, commonly presenting with pruritus, burning, dysuria, dyspareunia, and abnormal vaginal discharge, resulting from infectious etiologies (such as Candida albicans, Bacterial vaginosis, Trichomonas vaginalis) or non-infectious causes (atrophic vaginitis, contact irritants).

name: Waardenburg syndrome
clinical_significance: A group of inherited conditions that may cause hearing loss and unusual coloring of the eyes, hair, or skin. Some forms also affect the arms or the nerves controlling the bowel; findings vary by type.

name: wafer
clinical_significance: A wafer is a thin solid dose form that dissolves in the mouth or on a mucosal surface; correct placement and storage support reliable medication delivery.

name: WAGR syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare genetic condition that may cause an increased risk of Wilms kidney tumor, missing or poorly formed irises, urinary or reproductive differences, and developmental delay. Children need regular specialist monitoring, especially for kidney tumors.

name: waist circumference
clinical_significance: The distance around the abdomen, measured at a standard level. A larger measurement can indicate more abdominal fat and a higher risk of diabetes and heart disease, but it must be interpreted with other health information.

name: waist-hip ratio
clinical_significance: A measurement comparing waist size with hip size. It provides an estimate of where body fat is stored and may add information about diabetes and cardiovascular risk, but it does not diagnose disease by itself.

name: wakefulness
clinical_significance: The state of being conscious and able to respond to the surroundings. Sleep, medicines, illness, brain injury, and metabolic problems can change the level of wakefulness.

name: walker
clinical_significance: A walker provides stability and reduces fall risk for people with impaired balance or strength; correct height, fit, and training improve safe mobility.

name: wallerian degeneration
clinical_significance: Breakdown of the part of a nerve beyond a severe injury after it loses contact with the nerve cell. The nerve may regrow slowly if the surrounding pathway remains intact, but recovery depends on the injury.

name: wandering spleen
clinical_significance: A spleen that can move unusually because its supporting bands are loose or missing. It may cause no symptoms or lead to abdominal pain, enlargement, twisting, loss of blood supply, or sudden severe illness.

name: Ward's triangle
clinical_significance: Ward’s triangle is a region of the hip measured in bone-density studies; its bone-mineral-density value is less reliable for diagnosis than standard hip sites.

name: warfarin
clinical_significance: A blood-thinning medicine that reduces production of vitamin-K-dependent clotting proteins. It prevents and treats clots but requires regular blood tests because food, illnesses, and many medicines alter its effect.

name: Warfarin syndrome
clinical_significance: A pattern of fetal abnormalities caused by warfarin exposure during pregnancy, including nasal and skeletal abnormalities, eye or neurologic defects, and fetal or neonatal bleeding.

name: warm ischemia
clinical_significance: Lack of blood and oxygen reaching tissue while it remains at body temperature. It can quickly cause cell damage and is important during some injuries, operations, and organ transplantation.

name: wart
clinical_significance: A usually harmless rough skin growth caused by human papillomavirus. Warts may spread by contact and often disappear over time. Common types include common, plantar, and flat warts; appearance and symptoms vary by site.

name: warty dyskeratoma
clinical_significance: A usually harmless skin growth, often on the head or neck, with a small central dip filled with keratin. It may look like skin cancer, so examination and sometimes a biopsy are needed.

name: washout period
clinical_significance: A washout period is time allowed for a medicine or treatment effect to diminish before a new test or therapy; it reduces carryover but must be balanced against disease risk.

name: water
clinical_significance: Water is essential for circulation, temperature control, digestion, and kidney function; needs vary with illness, activity, climate, and heart or kidney disease.

name: water channel
clinical_significance: A protein pore in a cell membrane that lets water cross quickly. These pores help the kidneys and other tissues move water and maintain the body’s fluid balance.

name: water consumption
clinical_significance: Intake of water and other fluids to replace normal losses and maintain hydration. Requirements vary with body size, diet, activity, climate, pregnancy, illness, and kidney or heart function; thirst and urine concentration can help guide intake, while excessive intake can cause dangerous hyponatremia.

name: water pollution
clinical_significance: Water pollution can expose communities to pathogens and toxic chemicals, causing gastrointestinal, neurologic, or developmental harm; surveillance and safe-water controls prevent disease.

name: water supply
clinical_significance: A reliable safe water supply supports hydration, hygiene, infection control, and medication preparation; disruption can increase disease risk in communities and healthcare facilities.

name: water-soluble vitamin
clinical_significance: A vitamin that dissolves in water and is stored only in limited amounts. The group includes vitamin C and the B vitamins, so regular intake is generally needed.

name: watery eyes
clinical_significance: Excessive tearing caused by irritation, allergy, infection, dry-eye reflex tearing, or

name: watt
clinical_significance: A watt measures power; it is used to specify the output of medical equipment such as lasers, heaters, and imaging devices, where correct settings affect safety.

name: weakness
clinical_significance: Reduced ability to generate force, which may be generalized or limited to one body region. Causes include disorders of muscle, nerve, neuromuscular junction, brain, or spinal cord, as well as metabolic illness, infection, medication effects, and deconditioning; sudden one-sided weakness or weakness with breathing, swallowing, or speech difficulty requires emergency assessment.

name: weaning
clinical_significance: Gradual reduction and eventual discontinuation of breastfeeding, bottle-feeding, or a medicine or other treatment, according to the relevant clinical context.

name: Weaver syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare genetic condition causing rapid growth before and after birth, a large head, distinctive facial features, low muscle tone, and delayed development or learning. Bone age may be advanced. Most cases involve a change in the \textit{EZH2} gene; care is tailored to the child’s needs.

name: webbed neck
clinical_significance: Extra folds of skin extending from the sides of the neck toward the shoulders. They may be present from birth and can occur with conditions such as Turner syndrome or Noonan syndrome.

name: weber
clinical_significance: A name used in hearing assessment, especially the Weber test, in which a vibrating tuning fork is placed on the forehead or skull. It helps compare hearing between the two ears but is not a unit of measurement.

name: wedge excision
clinical_significance: Surgical removal of a triangular or wedge-shaped portion of tissue; commonly performed for breast biopsies, cervical lesions, and skin tumors.

name: weeksella
clinical_significance: Weeksella is a genus of environmental bacteria that rarely causes human infection; clinical isolates should be identified accurately and interpreted with specimen source and symptoms.

name: weeksella virosa
clinical_significance: Weeksella virosa is an uncommon gram-negative bacterium occasionally isolated from clinical specimens; true infection is rare, so culture findings need clinical correlation.

name: wegener's granulomatosis
clinical_significance: Wegener’s granulomatosis is the former name for granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a small-vessel vasculitis that can damage the lungs, kidneys, sinuses, and other organs; early treatment can prevent organ failure.

name: weight gain
clinical_significance: Increase in body weight; may be intentional (muscle building, pregnancy) or unintentional (fluid retention, endocrine disorders, medication effects).

name: Werner's syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited condition that causes signs of aging earlier than usual, often after puberty. It may cause early cataracts, short stature, thin skin, gray hair, diabetes, weak bones, and increased cancer risk.

name: wernicke area
clinical_significance: A brain region, usually in the left temporal lobe, that helps a person understand spoken and written language. Damage can cause fluent speech that lacks meaning and poor understanding of language.

name: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
clinical_significance: A brain disorder caused by severe vitamin B1 deficiency. It may begin with confusion and poor coordination and leave lasting memory problems, difficulty learning, and inaccurate made-up explanations; alcohol misuse, poor nutrition, and prolonged vomiting are common causes.

name: West Nile virus
clinical_significance: A mosquito-borne flavivirus that can cause asymptomatic infection, a febrile illness, or neuroinvasive

name: West syndrome
clinical_significance: A serious seizure disorder beginning in infancy, with repeated sudden spasms and an abnormal brain-wave pattern. Development may slow or regress; causes include brain injury, genetic conditions, and metabolic disease, and urgent treatment is needed.

name: western blotting
clinical_significance: Western blotting detects specific proteins or antibodies and has been used in infectious-disease and molecular testing; many clinical uses have been replaced by more accurate assays.

name: wheeled stretcher
clinical_significance: Mobile patient transport device with wheels; used in hospitals and emergency services for moving patients who cannot walk.

name: wheezing
clinical_significance: A musical or whistling sound caused by narrowed lower airways, usually louder when breathing out. It may result from asthma, infection, chronic lung disease, allergy, airway swelling, mucus, or an inhaled object.

name: whiplash injury
clinical_significance: Whiplash can cause neck pain, stiffness, headache, and dizziness after rapid acceleration-deceleration injury; neurologic deficits or severe trauma require evaluation for structural injury.

name: Whipple disease
clinical_significance: A rare bacterial infection that can damage the small intestine, joints, brain, heart, or other organs. It may cause years of joint pain followed by weight loss, persistent diarrhea, abdominal pain, and poor nutrient absorption.

name: whirlpool bath
clinical_significance: Hydrotherapy device providing agitated water for therapeutic bathing; used in wound care, physical therapy, and rehabilitation.

name: white matter
clinical_significance: Tissue in the brain and spinal cord made mainly of nerve fibers covered by a protective substance called myelin. It carries signals between different brain areas and between the brain and spinal cord.

name: whole-body irradiation
clinical_significance: Radiation treatment directed at the entire body, most often given before a stem-cell transplant to suppress the immune system and make room for donated cells. It can affect the bone marrow, fertility, and other organs.

name: wickerhamiella pararugosa
clinical_significance: Wickerhamiella pararugosa is an uncommon yeast that can rarely cause bloodstream or other opportunistic infection; identification and antifungal susceptibility are relevant in vulnerable patients.

name: widow
clinical_significance: Widowhood can affect mental health, social support, finances, and access to care; screening for grief-related distress and practical needs can guide support.

name: Williams syndrome
clinical_significance: A genetic condition caused by loss of a small section of chromosome 7, including a gene important for elastic tissues. It may cause characteristic facial features, heart-vessel narrowing, high blood calcium, developmental differences, learning difficulties, and connective-tissue problems. Regular heart, calcium, hearing, and developmental checks are important.

name: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited immune disorder that mainly affects boys and causes eczema, repeated infections, and a low number of unusually small platelets. It can also cause bleeding and autoimmune problems and requires specialist care.

name: Wolfram syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder that commonly causes diabetes requiring insulin and progressive loss of vision from optic-nerve damage. It may also cause excessive thirst and urination, hearing loss, bladder problems, balance difficulty, or other nerve-system problems. Treatment monitors and supports each affected function.

name: wolinella
clinical_significance: Genus of anaerobic, Gram-negative bacteria found in the oral cavity and gastrointestinal tract; associated with periodontal disease.

name: wolinella succinogenes
clinical_significance: Wolinella succinogenes is an anaerobic bacterium associated with the oral and gastrointestinal tract; it can rarely be implicated in infection, and significance depends on specimen and symptoms.

name: Wolman's disease
clinical_significance: A severe lysosomal acid-lipase deficiency presenting in infancy with hepatosplenomegaly,

name: women's health
clinical_significance: Medical specialty focusing on conditions unique to or more prevalent in females, including reproductive health, pregnancy, menopause, and gender-specific disease patterns.

name: worker compensation
clinical_significance: Workers’ compensation covers evaluation and benefits for work-related injury or illness; accurate documentation of exposure, function, and restrictions supports appropriate care and return to work.

name: world health organization
clinical_significance: The World Health Organization coordinates international public-health guidance, surveillance, and response; its recommendations inform but do not replace local clinical and public-health policies.

name: wortmannin
clinical_significance: Wortmannin is a potent inhibitor of phosphoinositide 3-kinases used in laboratory research; it is not a clinical treatment and can disrupt essential cellular signaling.

name: wound care
clinical_significance: Assessment and treatment of a wound through cleansing, bleeding control, removal of dead or contaminated tissue when indicated, appropriate closure or dressing, pain control, and follow-up. Care also includes tetanus prevention, pressure relief, and treatment of infection or underlying conditions; antibiotics are reserved for selected contaminated wounds, bites, or infections.

name: wound complication
clinical_significance: A problem that develops during healing, such as infection, separation of wound edges, bleeding, fluid

name: wound dehiscence
clinical_significance: Partial or complete reopening of a surgical wound after it has been closed. It may follow infection, poor blood supply, diabetes, increased pressure, or strain on the wound. New separation, drainage, fever, severe pain, or visible deeper tissue needs prompt medical assessment.

name: wound healing
clinical_significance: The body’s process of stopping bleeding, controlling inflammation, replacing damaged tissue, covering the surface, and strengthening the repair. Blood supply, infection, nutrition, diabetes, medicines, smoking, wound depth, and movement can affect healing.

name: wound infection
clinical_significance: Infection of a wound by microorganisms, causing findings such as increasing pain, redness, warmth,

name: wrist
clinical_significance: The joint connecting the hand to the forearm. It contains eight small wrist bones, ligaments, tendons, nerves, and blood vessels and allows the hand to bend, turn, and move from side to side.

name: wrist injury
clinical_significance: Damage to the bones, ligaments, tendons, nerves, or vessels of the wrist from a fall, twist, impact, or overuse; fracture, instability, severe swelling, or neurovascular symptoms require assessment.

name: wrist joint
clinical_significance: The joint where the forearm bones meet the small bones of the hand. It allows bending, straightening, side-to-side movement, and limited rotation while ligaments and cartilage provide stability.

name: written documentation
clinical_significance: Formal recording of patient information, clinical decisions, and treatment plans; essential for continuity of care and medicolegal purposes.

name: wuchereria
clinical_significance: A genus of filarial nematodes that includes Wuchereria bancrofti, a major cause of

name: X chromosome
clinical_significance: One of the two types of human sex chromosomes. It carries genes involved in sex development as well as many other body functions. Most people have one or two X chromosomes.

name: xanthelasma
clinical_significance: A harmless yellowish patch or bump caused by fat deposits in the skin of the eyelids, usually near the inner corners of the eyes. It can occur with high blood fats but may also occur when blood-fat levels are normal.

name: xanthine
clinical_significance: A natural breakdown product of substances found in cells and foods. It normally changes into uric acid, but can build up when a rare enzyme disorder blocks this pathway and may then contribute to kidney or urinary stones.

name: xanthine dehydrogenase
clinical_significance: Xanthine dehydrogenase converts purine breakdown products toward uric acid; deficiency can cause xanthinuria, kidney stones, and muscle symptoms, while enzyme activity is studied in purine metabolism.

name: xanthine oxidase
clinical_significance: An enzyme that helps convert cell and food breakdown products into uric acid. Medicines used for gout can block this enzyme, lowering uric-acid production and helping prevent urate crystal deposits.

name: xanthoma
clinical_significance: A yellow-orange spot, bump, or patch formed by fat deposits in the skin, tissue beneath the skin, or tendons. It may occur with high blood fats, diabetes, some liver diseases, or an inherited lipid disorder.

name: xanthomatosis
clinical_significance: A disorder in which fatty deposits called xanthomas develop in the skin, tendons, or organs. It may be linked to inherited or acquired problems with blood fats.

name: xanthomonadaceae
clinical_significance: Xanthomonadaceae is a family of environmental bacteria that includes plant pathogens and occasional human opportunists; clinical significance depends on species and specimen source.

name: xanthomonas
clinical_significance: Xanthomonas species primarily cause plant disease but can rarely cause opportunistic human infection, especially in vulnerable patients; accurate species identification is needed for clinical isolates.

name: xenobiotic metabolism
clinical_significance: The body’s processing of foreign chemicals, including medicines, pollutants, and toxins. Enzymes, especially in the liver, change them so they can be removed; the changed substances may remain active or become harmful.

name: xenograft
clinical_significance: Tissue, cells, or a biological material transplanted between different species, such as animal tissue used in a human. Rejection and infection are important risks, although some materials are used temporarily as tissue coverings or substitutes.

name: xenograft procedure
clinical_significance: A xenograft procedure transplants cells or tissue between species, including animal-to-human research or engineered grafts; immune rejection and zoonotic transmission are key safety considerations.

name: xenon
clinical_significance: Xenon is an inert gas used in specialized anesthesia and lung-function imaging; it can cause sedation and respiratory or cardiovascular effects and requires controlled medical administration.

name: xenophagy
clinical_significance: Xenophagy is selective autophagy that targets intracellular pathogens for destruction; defects can weaken host defense, and the process is studied in infection and inflammatory disease.

name: xenophobia
clinical_significance: Xenophobia can contribute to discrimination, chronic stress, and barriers to healthcare; culturally safe care and attention to social determinants support patient well-being.

name: xeroderma pigmentosum
clinical_significance: A rare usually autosomal-recessive disorder of nucleotide-excision DNA repair, with a variant form affecting translesion synthesis. Minimal ultraviolet exposure can cause severe sunburn or persistent redness, early freckle-like pigmentation, and rapid photoaging; skin and ocular-surface cancers occur at a young age, and some people develop progressive neurologic disease. Strict ultraviolet protection, regular skin and eye examinations, and early treatment of suspicious lesions are essential.

name: xerophthalmia
clinical_significance: Dryness and damage of the eye caused by severe vitamin A deficiency. It may begin with poor night vision and dry eyes and can progress to corneal damage and permanent sight loss.

name: xeroradiograph
clinical_significance: Xeroradiography is an older X-ray imaging technique used historically for breast imaging; it has been replaced by modern mammography and other imaging methods.

name: xerostomia
clinical_significance: Xerostomia is dry mouth from reduced saliva, often caused by medicines, radiation, dehydration, or salivary-gland disease; it increases risk of tooth decay, oral infection, and difficulty swallowing.

name: xipamide
clinical_significance: Xipamide is a thiazide-like diuretic used for hypertension or edema in some countries; dehydration, low sodium or potassium, gout, and kidney effects require monitoring.

name: X-ray
clinical_significance: An imaging test that uses a small amount of radiation to create a picture of structures inside the body. It is especially useful for bones, lungs, teeth, and some other tissues.

name: X-ray crystallography
clinical_significance: A laboratory method that uses X-rays to work out the three-dimensional structure of molecules such as proteins. The molecule is made into a crystal, and the pattern produced by the X-rays is analyzed.

name: X-ray therapy
clinical_significance: Treatment that uses carefully aimed X-ray radiation to damage abnormal cells or relieve symptoms. It is used mainly for cancer and may be given from a machine outside the body or near the target.

name: xylose
clinical_significance: A simple sugar found in some plants. A form called D-xylose has been used in tests of how well the small intestine absorbs nutrients and is also used in laboratory studies.

name: Y chromosome
clinical_significance: One of the two human sex chromosomes. It usually carries genes involved in testis development and is passed by a biological father to a child who inherits it; chromosome patterns and body development can vary.

name: yarrowia
clinical_significance: Yarrowia is a genus of yeast used in biotechnology and rarely associated with human infection; a positive clinical culture should be interpreted with symptoms and immune status.

name: yarrowia lipolytica
clinical_significance: Yarrowia lipolytica is a yeast used in industrial biotechnology and food production that can rarely cause opportunistic infection; species identification and clinical context determine significance.

name: yawn
clinical_significance: An involuntary behavior consisting of a deep inhalation followed by a slower exhalation, often with stretching of the jaw and facial muscles. Yawning is common with fatigue but excessive or unusual yawning can occur with some medications or neurologic conditions.

name: yaws
clinical_significance: Yaws is a chronic infection caused by Treponema pallidum subsp. pertenue and spread mainly through close skin contact. It can cause an initial papilloma or ulcer and later destructive lesions of skin, bone, and cartilage; antibiotics can cure the infection.

name: yeast
clinical_significance: A type of fungus made of single cells. Some yeasts normally live on or in the body, while others can cause infections of the mouth, skin, vagina, lungs, blood, or other organs.

name: yeast present
clinical_significance: A laboratory report showing yeast in a specimen. This may mean harmless colonization, contamination, or infection; the meaning depends on the symptoms, specimen, and type of yeast.

name: yellow fever
clinical_significance: Yellow fever is an acute mosquito-borne infection caused by yellow fever virus. Fever, headache, muscle aches, nausea, and vomiting may be followed by jaundice, bleeding, shock, and organ failure; vaccination is the main preventive measure.

name: yellow fever virus
clinical_significance: A flavivirus transmitted mainly by infected mosquitoes that can cause yellow fever, ranging from a mild febrile illness to jaundice, bleeding, shock, and organ failure.

name: yersinia
clinical_significance: A group of bacteria that can cause intestinal illness, swollen lymph nodes in the abdomen, or plague. Different species spread through contaminated food or water, infected animals, or fleas.

name: yersinia aldovae
clinical_significance: Yersinia aldovae is an uncommon environmental Yersinia species not known as a common human pathogen; clinical isolates require confirmation and correlation with illness.

name: yersinia bercovieri
clinical_significance: Yersinia bercovieri is a rare Yersinia species occasionally found in human or environmental samples; its clinical importance depends on reliable identification and compatible symptoms.

name: yersinia enterocolitica
clinical_significance: A bacterium that can cause diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain, sometimes mimicking appendicitis. People usually acquire it from contaminated food, water, or contact with infected animals.

name: yersinia frederiksenii
clinical_significance: Yersinia frederiksenii is an environmental and food-associated species that can rarely cause gastrointestinal illness; exposure history and culture findings guide interpretation.

name: yersinia infection
clinical_significance: Infection caused by Yersinia bacteria, usually producing diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, or vomiting. Some cases resemble appendicitis; bloody diarrhea, dehydration, or severe or persistent illness can occur.

name: yersinia intermedia
clinical_significance: Yersinia intermedia is found in water, animals, and foods and is an uncommon cause of human gastroenteritis; specimen quality and symptoms determine clinical relevance.

name: yersinia kristensenii
clinical_significance: Yersinia kristensenii is a rare human isolate and occasional opportunistic pathogen; it should be interpreted in light of the specimen source and the patient’s illness.

name: yersinia mollaretii
clinical_significance: Yersinia mollaretii is an uncommon Yersinia species with limited evidence of human pathogenicity; isolate significance requires clinical correlation.

name: yersinia pestis
clinical_significance: The bacterium that causes plague, a severe infection usually spread by infected fleas or animals. It may cause painful swollen lymph nodes, bloodstream infection, or lung disease and can be life-threatening.

name: yersinia pseudotuberculosis
clinical_significance: A bacterium usually acquired from contaminated food or water. It can cause fever, diarrhea, and pain from swollen lymph nodes in the abdomen, sometimes resembling appendicitis.

name: yersinia rohdei
clinical_significance: Yersinia rohdei is a rare Yersinia species found in environmental or clinical samples; accurate identification is needed to assess whether it represents infection.

name: yersinia ruckeri
clinical_significance: Yersinia ruckeri primarily causes disease in fish and is not a usual human pathogen; its main significance is veterinary and aquaculture health.

name: yoga
clinical_significance: Yoga combines movement, breathing, and attention practices and may support flexibility, balance, and stress management; adaptations are needed for injury, pregnancy, or medical limitations.

name: yohimbine
clinical_significance: Yohimbine is an alkaloid marketed for sexual function and weight loss; it can cause anxiety, high blood pressure, rapid heart rate, and dangerous interactions, and supplement content may vary.

name: yokenella
clinical_significance: Yokenella is a rare environmental and gastrointestinal bacterium that can cause opportunistic human infection; culture findings should be interpreted with symptoms and susceptibility results.

name: yokenella regensburgei
clinical_significance: Yokenella regensburgei is an uncommon gram-negative bacterium reported in rare bloodstream, wound, or urinary infections; accurate identification and clinical correlation are important.

name: yolk sac
clinical_significance: A temporary structure that supports an early embryo before the placenta is fully working. It helps form the first blood cells and part of the early intestine and can be seen on early pregnancy ultrasound.

name: ytterbium
clinical_significance: Ytterbium is a rare-earth element used in some research and specialized medical devices; radioactive isotopes require radiation-safety controls, and toxicity depends on compound and exposure.

name: yttrium
clinical_significance: Yttrium is a metal used in medical imaging, radiotherapy, and some implants; radioactive yttrium isotopes require controlled dosing and radiation protection.

name: zafirlukast
clinical_significance: A leukotriene-receptor antagonist used for long-term control and prevention of asthma symptoms. It is taken orally and is not a rescue treatment for an acute asthma attack; liver injury and drug interactions are important safety considerations.

name: zalcitabine
clinical_significance: Zalcitabine is an older HIV nucleoside drug withdrawn or discontinued in many settings because of severe peripheral neuropathy and pancreatitis; it is not a routine current treatment.

name: zanamivir
clinical_significance: An inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor used to treat or prevent influenza A and B when started appropriately. It may cause bronchospasm and is used cautiously in people with underlying airway disease.

name: zebrafish
clinical_significance: Zebrafish are widely used in biomedical research to study development, genetics, and disease; findings can generate hypotheses but do not directly establish human diagnosis or treatment benefit.

name: Zellweger syndrome
clinical_significance: A severe inherited disorder in which cells cannot make peroxisomes, structures that help process fats and other substances. It begins in infancy and may cause weak muscle tone, feeding problems, seizures, liver disease, and impaired brain development.

name: Zenker diverticulum
clinical_significance: A pouch that forms in the upper swallowing tube near the throat, usually because the nearby muscle does not relax normally. It may cause difficulty swallowing, return of undigested food, bad breath, a neck lump, cough, or repeated lung infections.

name: zibotentan
clinical_significance: Zibotentan is an investigational endothelin-receptor antagonist studied for cancer and other conditions; it is not established routine therapy, and trial evidence determines its clinical role.

name: ziconotide
clinical_significance: A strong pain medicine delivered continuously into the fluid around the spinal cord for selected severe chronic pain. It can cause dizziness, confusion, hallucinations, and other serious nervous-system or mental-health effects.

name: zidovudine
clinical_significance: An HIV medicine that interferes with the virus’s ability to copy itself. It may be used in selected treatment plans and to reduce transmission around childbirth; important risks include anemia, low white-cell counts, muscle problems, and other toxicity.

name: Zika virus
clinical_significance: A virus spread mainly by infected \textit{Aedes} mosquitoes and also through sexual contact and, less commonly, blood or pregnancy-related transmission. Infection is often mild or symptom-free but can injure a developing fetus.

name: zileuton
clinical_significance: A medicine used for long-term prevention and control of asthma. It does not relieve a sudden asthma attack and can cause liver problems or interact with other medicines.

name: zimmermannella
clinical_significance: Zimmermannella is a genus of uncommon environmental bacteria with rare human isolates; clinical importance depends on species confirmation and recovery from a meaningful specimen.

name: zinc
clinical_significance: An essential mineral needed for many body reactions, normal growth, immunity, reproduction, and wound healing. Too little can cause deficiency; excessive supplements can cause stomach symptoms and copper deficiency.

name: zinc acetate
clinical_significance: A zinc salt used to treat zinc deficiency and, in some forms, to reduce copper absorption in Wilson disease. It may cause nausea or stomach irritation.

name: zinc oxide
clinical_significance: An insoluble zinc compound used topically as a skin protectant and barrier, including in preparations for diaper dermatitis and minor irritation. It can reduce contact with moisture and irritants but does not treat every cause of a rash.

name: zinc sulfate
clinical_significance: An oral or parenteral zinc salt used to prevent or treat zinc deficiency when clinically indicated. Gastrointestinal upset is common with oral therapy, and prolonged excessive use can cause copper deficiency.

name: zingiber officinale
clinical_significance: Zingiber officinale, or ginger, is used as food and in supplements; it may ease some nausea but can cause gastrointestinal effects and interact with anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicines.

name: zinostatin
clinical_significance: Zinostatin is an antitumor antibiotic used in selected regional or intralesional cancer treatments in some countries; tissue injury and systemic toxicity require specialist administration.

name: zirconium
clinical_significance: Zirconium is used in medical materials and industrial products; most exposure is low, but dust can irritate lungs and toxicity depends on the compound and route.

name: zoledronic acid
clinical_significance: A potent intravenous bisphosphonate used for osteoporosis and certain cancer-related conditions, including hypercalcemia of malignancy and skeletal complications of bone metastases. Renal injury, hypocalcemia, acute-phase reactions, and rare osteonecrosis of the jaw are important risks.

name: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
clinical_significance: A rare condition in which a hormone-producing tumor makes too much gastrin, causing the stomach to produce excess acid. It can lead to repeated ulcers, severe reflux, abdominal pain, and diarrhea.

name: zolpidem
clinical_significance: A nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic used for short-term treatment of insomnia. It can cause next-day impairment, complex sleep behaviors, dependence, and respiratory or central-nervous-system depression, especially with other sedatives.

name: zolpidem tartrate
clinical_significance: Zolpidem tartrate is the salt form of zolpidem used for insomnia; next-day impairment, falls, dependence, and rare complex sleep behaviors are important safety concerns.

name: zona pellucida
clinical_significance: A protective layer of proteins surrounding an egg cell. It helps sperm attach to the egg and changes after fertilization to prevent more than one sperm from entering.

name: zonisamide
clinical_significance: An antiseizure medicine used mainly for focal seizures. It can cause sleepiness, thinking problems, kidney stones, reduced sweating with overheating, acid imbalance, severe rash, or other serious reactions.

name: zonula adherens
clinical_significance: A belt-like connection between neighboring cells that helps hold them together. It is especially important in sheets of lining cells.

name: zoology
clinical_significance: Zoology studies animal biology and can inform comparative medicine, zoonotic disease, and drug research; animal findings do not automatically predict human outcomes.

name: zoonosis
clinical_significance: An infection that naturally spreads between animals with backbones and people. Examples include rabies, brucellosis, leptospirosis, toxoplasmosis, and some influenza infections; spread may involve bites, food, water, droplets, or direct contact.

name: zoophobia
clinical_significance: Zoophobia is an intense fear of animals that can cause distress or avoidance; when it impairs daily life, assessment for a specific phobia and evidence-based therapy may help.

name: zygomatic bone
clinical_significance: A paired facial bone that forms the prominence of the cheek and part of the lateral orbital wall and floor. It articulates with the frontal, sphenoid, temporal, and maxillary bones.

name: zygomatic gland
clinical_significance: A zygomatic gland is a salivary gland described in some animal species; it has no standard human clinical role.

name: zygomycosis
clinical_significance: A serious infection caused by molds called Mucorales. It mainly affects people with weakened immunity or poorly controlled diabetes and can rapidly damage the nose, brain, lungs, skin, or other tissues.

name: zygote
clinical_significance: The first cell formed when a sperm joins an egg. It contains genetic material from both parents, divides repeatedly, and develops into an embryo.
